In 902 the three sons of Countess Adelindis were killed while trying to abduct their sister, the abbess, to marry her. The countess entered the abbey to atone and is still honoured as a benefactress. A mint and market are mentioned in 1014 or 1022, and in 1417 the abbey became a secular convent that accepted daughters of the Swabian nobility.

A Jewish community is recorded in the city from 1577 under its protection, with a cemetery built in 1650 and synagogues erected in 1730 and 1837. In 1802 and 1803 both abbey and city lost their independence and passed to the Prince of Thurn and Taxis, and in 1806 Buchau became a township of the Kingdom of Württemberg. The community gained its civil liberties in 1828. Hermann Einstein, father of Albert Einstein, was born there in 1847. In 1938 the synagogue was burned and its stone later sold for road building. The Jewish people of Buchau, who had made up a substantial part of the population, were deported from 1941, and only four returned after the Second World War.

The town, with about 4,000 inhabitants, is in Baden-Württemberg, and its people speak the Swabian dialect in daily life. It was given the title Bad, meaning spa, in 1963, after the civic spa opened in 1949. Excavations in the moor beginning around the early 20th century uncovered the Wasserburg Buchau, a settlement of the late Bronze Age, about 1100 to 800 BCE. The Federsee Museum opened in 1968 with exhibits from the Stone and Bronze Ages. The prehistoric settlement at Siedlung Forschner is part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
bad-durkheim: Bad Dürkheim lies at the edge of the Palatinate Forest on the German Wine Route, some 30 km east of Kaiserslautern and just under 20 km west of Ludwigshafen and Mannheim. The river Isenach flows through the town from west to east. It is the seat of the Bad Dürkheim district in Rhineland-Palatinate. Its quarters are Grethen, Hardenburg, Hausen, Leistadt, Seebach and Ungstein with Pfeffingen. The mild climate allows fig, olive and stone pine to grow in gardens and public spaces.

Celts settled the eastern end of the Isenach valley between 1200 and 500 BCE and built the Heidenmauer, a ring wall about 2.5 km long. Roman remains include a villa and a quarry used in the 4th century. The town's name first appears in the Lorsch codex of 1 June 778 as Turnesheim. Building of Limburg Abbey began about 1025. Town rights were granted on 1 January 1360 but withdrawn in 1471, after Elector Friedrich the Victorious of the Palatinate conquered and badly damaged the town. In 1554 it passed to the Counts of Leiningen.

In 1689 French troops carrying out a scorched earth campaign in the Nine Years' War almost completely destroyed it, but rebuilding was swifter and Count Johann Friedrich of Leiningen restored town rights in 1700. In 1725 it became the main seat of the Counts, later Princes, of Leiningen, who lived in Schloss Dürkheim. After the French Revolution it belonged to the Department of Mont-Tonnerre, and after the Napoleonic Wars to the Kingdom of Bavaria. In 1860 Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff discovered the element caesium in the mineral water of the springs. Because of its seven springs the town was called a brine bath, and in 1904 it was allowed to become Bad Dürkheim.
The number of Jews in the town fell from 184 in 1933 to 40 in 1938, and the 19 who remained were deported to Gurs in October 1940. An Allied air raid on 18 March 1945 killed more than 300 people.

Winegrowing is the main industry, with 855 ha of vineyards, alongside tourism and spa clinics. The Dürkheimer Wurstmarkt, a wine festival whose name means sausage market, draws more than 600,000 visitors a year. Beside its grounds stands the Dürkheimer Riesenfass, a giant barrel that houses a restaurant. The ruins of Limburg Abbey and of the Hardenburg castle, seat of the Counts of Leiningen from the 13th century, lie on the town's edge. The Rhein-Haardtbahn tramway, opened in 1913, links the town with Ludwigshafen and Mannheim.
bad-ems: Bad Ems lies on both banks of the River Lahn, the natural border between the Taunus and the Westerwald, two parts of the Rhenish Slate Mountains, within the Nassau Nature Reserve. It is the administrative seat of the Rhein-Lahn district and stands on a cluster of mineral hot springs. The waters are high in sodium bicarbonate and range in temperature from 27 to 57 °C. Natural Ems salt is produced from them and is sold for drinking and inhalation.

In Roman times a castrum was built at Bad Ems as part of the Upper Germanic Limes, and distinct traces of the border remain in the woods around the town. Bad Ems was first mentioned in official documents in 880 and received its town charter in 1324. The Counts of Nassau and Katzenelnbogen rebuilt the bath. In the 17th and 18th centuries it was considered one of Germany's best-known bathing resorts, and in the 19th century it welcomed visitors from all over the world and became the summer residence of European monarchs and artists, among them Kaiser Wilhelm I, Tsars Nicholas I and Alexander II of Russia, Richard Wagner and Fyodor Dostoevsky.

Metal ores, mainly lead, silver, zinc and copper, were mined here from Roman times, with underground mining first mentioned in 1158 and continuing, with long interruptions, until 1945. In 1870 the town, then part of Prussian Hesse-Nassau, became known as the place where the Ems Dispatch originated, instigating the Franco-Prussian War. In 1876 Alexander II signed the Ems Edict, banning the use of the Ukrainian language, in the Haus Vier Türme.

Bad Ems has around 9,000 inhabitants. In 2021 it became part of the transnational UNESCO World Heritage Site Great Spa Towns of Europe, because of its hot springs and its 18th to 20th century architecture. Its former mine, known as Mercur, has been a museum since 1996.
bad-gandersheim: Bad Gandersheim lies in southern Lower Saxony, in the district of Northeim, between the Leine Uplands, the Weser Uplands and the Harz Foreland. It stands in the valley of the Gande River, into which its tributary the Eterna flows within the town's territory. The Harz Mountains begin about 10 kilometres to the east.

The town dates back to 852, when Gandersheim Abbey, a house of secular canonesses, was created at nearby Brunshausen by Liudolf and his wife Oda. The first abbey church in the town itself was begun in 856. In 990 the abbey received market and tax rights, and during the 10th century Gandersheim was one of the most important towns of Saxony. The first German poet, Hrosvit, lived and worked there until 973. It was first mentioned as a town in 1159.

A mineral spring discovered in 1240 led Pope Gregory IX to initiate the building of the Holy Spirit hospital. Around 1330 the Dukes of Brunswick built a castle as a secular counterbalance to the abbey church. In the late 19th century the town became known for the curative powers of its springs, and in 1932 it received the right to call itself a spa town, hence Bad Gandersheim.

A Roswitha Memorial Celebration in 1926 was the first time the medieval author served as a symbolic figure for the town, and similar celebrations in 1930 and 1933 had clear National Socialist themes. From October 1944 to April 1945 the town was the site of a subcamp of the Buchenwald Concentration Camp that produced aircraft parts.

The Gandersheimer Domfestspiele have been held yearly on the plaza in front of the abbey church since 1959. It has become Lower Saxony's largest professional summer theatre festival, and in 2006 its four major productions drew about 55,000 visitors.

The castle built around 1330 now serves as the magistrates' court and a youth correctional facility. The town is twinned with Rotselaar in Belgium and Skegness in the United Kingdom. It had 9,492 inhabitants in December 2020. Its notable natives include the field marshal Wilhelm Keitel, executed for war crimes, the aircraft engineer Wolfgang Liebe, who invented the wing fence, and the bass-baritone Wolfgang Schöne.
bad-homburg-vor-der-hohe: Bad Homburg lies on the southern slope of the Taunus mountains and is the district town of the Hochtaunuskreis in Hesse. It belongs to the Frankfurt Rhein-Main urban area. Its official name, Bad Homburg v.d.Höhe, distinguishes it from other places called Homburg; the name derives from the Hohenberg Castle, and the suffix vor der Höhe was probably first recorded in a document of 1399. The prefix Bad, meaning bath, was conferred in 1912.

Local tradition places the first documented mention in 782, as the Villa Tidenheim of the Lorsch codex. The local historian Rüdiger Kurth questioned this, and University of Frankfurt excavations begun in 2002 found no settlement between the start of the Christian era and the 13th century. The first solid evidence is the Eberbach chronicles, which name Wortwin von Hohenberch as founder about 1180. Homburg acquired market rights about 1330. In 1622 it became the capital of the Landgraviate of Hesse-Homburg, whose first landgrave was Friedrich I; the landgraviate passed to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1866 after the Austro-Prussian War.

The spa industry began with the discovery of the Elisabethenbrunnen in 1834. The brothers François and Louis Blanc built the first spa building and casino in 1841–1842, and the town was linked to Frankfurt by railway in 1860. Russian nobility favoured it, and Edward VII of the United Kingdom took fasting cures there 32 times. In 1888 Kaiser Wilhelm II made the castle his imperial summer residence. A Jewish community, permanent from the early 16th century, had a Judengasse from 1703 and a Hebrew printing house in the early 18th century; of the 74 Jews who remained on 17 May 1939, 42 were deported in 1942 and 1943 and did not return.

After the two world wars the spa trade declined, and the town became the seat of financial and administrative bodies: in 1947 the Bizone Economic Council placed its Special Money and Credit Centre there, managed by Ludwig Erhard, and several federal debt and equalization offices stayed after the founding of West Germany. The Bad Homburger Golf Club is Germany's oldest golf club, and the Russian Chapel, laid down in 1896, and a garden pavilion sent by King Chulalongkorn of Siam in thanks for a cure, erected in 1914, recall the town's international guests. Among those born there are the physician Paul Ehrlich and the writer Shmuel Yosef Agnon.
bad-kreuznach: Bad Kreuznach lies between the Hunsrück, Rhenish Hesse and the North Palatine Uplands, at the mouth of the Ellerbach where it empties into the lower Nahe, about 14 kilometres south-southwest of Bingen am Rhein. It stands in the Nahe wine region, known for Riesling, Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau wines. The town is the seat of its district and acts as the administrative, cultural and economic centre of a region with more than 150,000 inhabitants. Its best-known landmark is the Alte Nahebrücke, a medieval bridge from around 1300 that carries houses built between 1582 and 1612.

There is evidence of a Celtic settlement here as early as the 5th century BCE. About 58 BCE the area became part of the Roman Empire and a Roman vicus arose on the road between Mainz and Trier, named according to legend after a Celt called Cruciniac. About 250 CE a very large luxurious villa-style palace was built, and in 370 Emperor Valentinian I had an auxiliary castrum built to help defend the frontier against Alemannic raids. After Rome's fall, Kreuznach became a royal estate in the Frankish realm around the year 500, and Louis the Pious stayed at its royal palace in 819 and 839.

In the 11th century the settlement passed to the High Foundation of Speyer and shortly after 1105 to the Counts of Sponheim. They built the castle Kauzenburg between 1206 and 1230, and a New Town grew up on the Nahe's north bank. Kreuznach received town rights, market rights and tolling rights in 1235 and 1270, and withstood a siege by Archbishop-Elector Baldwin of Trier in 1320. In 1375 the townsfolk rose against the town council, and Count Walram I of Sponheim had four leaders beheaded. The Reformation was introduced in 1557. Karl Marx married Jenny von Westphalen in the Pauluskirche on 19 June 1843.

Bad Kreuznach is a spa town, advertised as the world's oldest radon-brine spa, and a centre for the care of rheumatic illness. Its baths contain the noble gas radon, and graduation towers stand in the Salinental. Winegrowing is also important: its 777 hectares of vineyard make it the largest winegrowing centre in the Nahe region. Its economy rests mainly on small and medium businesses, with chemical, optical and machine-building industries.
bad-lobenstein: Bad Lobenstein lies in the Thuringian Highlands between the Thuringian Forest and the Franconian Forest. It is a spa town in the Saale-Orla district with about 6,000 inhabitants and until 2005 was called Lobenstein. The name may come from the phrase Lobe den Stein, praise the stone. A legend ties it to the emperor Ludwig the Bavarian, who is said to have lost and found his favourite dog in the area and rewarded the knight who carried the animal back with the land as a fief.

The high medieval castle stands above the centre of the town on the right bank of the Lemnitz, where it was used to watch traffic on the route from Leipzig to Bamberg. Lobenstein is first mentioned in 1250 as the seat of a knight, Otto von Lobenstein, and was probably a foundation of the Lords of Lobdeburg. It was called a city by 1278. The castle was so decayed by 1600 that the Reuss moved to a palace, and in 1632, in the Thirty Years' War, imperial troops stormed it. The town belonged to the junior line of the House of Reuss from 1597 to 1918.

On 8 October 1806 Napoleon's army marched through, and around 190,000 men passed through the town, with looting, so that the population suffered greatly despite its neutrality. In 1848 Lobenstein, with Schleiz and Hirschberg, was a centre of the bourgeois movement. A fire in 1862 destroyed almost all its historic buildings.

From 1868 healing earth from a nearby high moor and an iron mineral spring led to the development of a spa, and railways reached the town in 1896, 1901 and 1907. Since 21 March 2005 it has officially been called Bad Lobenstein, the twelfth spa town in Thuringia.

The ruins of the castle, with the 35-metre keep, a baroque New Palace built between 1714 and 1718, and the church of St. Michaelis, rebuilt after the fire of 1862, survive. A figure in the town hall tower, the Lommesteener Fäßlesächer, is the town's mascot.
bad-mergentheim: Mergentheim is mentioned in chronicles as early as 1058, as the residence of the family of the counts of Hohenlohe. In 1219 the brothers Andreas, Heinrich and Friedrich von Hohenlohe joined the Teutonic Order and gave it their two castles near Mergentheim. One was abandoned and the other became the seat of the Order's local commander. Mergentheim received town privileges in 1340 and rapidly became the most important of the Order's eleven commanderies.

Around the time the Deutschmeister moved there, Grand Master Albrecht von Zollern-Brandenburg resigned, left the Order, introduced the Reformation and, supported by the King of Poland, turned the Order's eastern territories into a secular duchy. The Order's rulers in Germany, now styling themselves Hoch- und Deutschmeister, made Mergentheim the new headquarters and expanded the castle into a palatial residence.

For the next centuries the town served as the centre of the Order's southern German lands, much like the residence of a ruling prince. Maximilian Franz, a son of Maria Theresa, loved the place, and for the general chapter of 1791 he brought the orchestra of the Archbishopric of Cologne, in which Ludwig van Beethoven played viola. Napoleon dissolved the Order in the states of the Rheinbund in 1809.

Mergentheim's fortunes declined after 1809, but they revived in 1826, when a shepherd, Franz Gehring, discovered rich mineral springs nearby. The water proved to be the strongest sodium-sulfate water in Europe and was reported to help in treating digestive disorders. The town became an officially recognised spa in 1926 and took the name Bad Mergentheim. Its best-known building is the Mergentheim Palace, the Teutonic Order's former home, a complex built over eight hundred years, which now houses the museum of the Order. The inventor of the Linotype, Ottmar Mergenthaler, was born in the village of Hachtel, now part of the town.
bad-pyrmont: Bad Pyrmont stands on the river Emmer, about 10 km west of the Weser, in the district of Hamelin-Pyrmont in Lower Saxony, Germany. It has a population close to 19,000. It gained its reputation as a fashionable place for princely holidays in the 17th and 18th centuries, and it is the centre of the Religious Society of Friends, the Quakers, in Germany. Its economy is geared largely to tourism, and Bad Pyrmonter mineral water is bottled in the town.

The town was formerly called simply Pyrmont and was the seat of a small county for much of the Middle Ages. The county gained its independence from the County of Schwalenberg in 1194 and kept it until the comital line died out in 1494. It then passed by inheritance to Spiegelberg, in 1557 to Lippe and in 1583 to the County of Gleichen.

In 1625 it became part of the much larger County of Waldeck, also by inheritance. In 1668 the Imperial Chamber Court rejected the claim of the Bishopric of Paderborn that Pyrmont had been pledged as security for a loan, and confirmed the rights of the Count of Waldeck, who gave the Amt of Lügde, until then the county's capital, to the bishopric in compensation. In January 1712 Emperor Charles VI raised the Count of Waldeck and Pyrmont, who had combined the two titles the previous year, to hereditary prince.

From 1805 to 1812 Pyrmont was again a separate principality, after the death of the previous prince. The two parts were reunited in 1812, and Waldeck-Pyrmont kept its status after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and joined the German Confederation. The people of Pyrmont protested in 1813 at their lack of autonomy, and until a formal union in 1849 the two territories remained constitutionally separate.

From 1868 Prussia administered the principality, under a ten-year contract that was repeatedly renewed, and in 1871 it became a state of the German Empire. The prince abdicated during the German Revolution at the end of World War I, and after a local plebiscite the town and district of Pyrmont were detached and incorporated into the Prussian Province of Hanover.

The spa has a large Kurpark with an outdoor palm garden. The Baroque castle, built in 1706–10, is part of a substantial complex of fortifications dating from the 16th century and now houses the Museum of Municipal and Spa History. The physicist Max Born, a Nobel Prize winner, spent his last years in the town.
bad-reichenhall: Bad Reichenhall is the administrative centre of the Berchtesgadener Land district in Upper Bavaria, Germany. It lies near Salzburg in a basin ringed by the Chiemgau Alps, among them Mount Staufen (1,771 m) and Mount Zwiesel (1,781 m). It is a traditional centre of salt production, in which water saturated with salt from brine ponds is evaporated.

The earliest known inhabitants belonged to the Glockenbecher culture, a Bronze Age culture, from about 2000 BCE. In the La Tène period, about 450 BCE, organised salt production began using the local brine pools, and a Celtic place of worship stood at the Langacker. From 15 BCE to 480 CE the area was part of the Roman province of Noricum. A monastery of St Zeno was founded in 1136.

Between 1617 and 1619 a wooden pipeline 31 km long, with a fall of more than 200 m, was built to carry brine to Traunstein. In 1834 a major fire destroyed two thirds of the town's buildings. Tourism began in the early 19th century, and Reichenhall became a health resort; from 1890 it was called Bad Reichenhall. The Predigtstuhl Cable Car, an aerial tramway up the Predigtstuhl mountain, opened in 1928.

Allied bombing on 25 April 1945 killed 200 people and nearly destroyed the town centre, with its hospitals and railway station, while the barracks were undamaged. The area was under American military governance from 1945 to 1948, and the Americans set up a displaced persons camp where Holocaust survivors lived for several years before emigrating. David Ben-Gurion visited it in 1947 and saw the artworks of Samuel Bak, one of the survivors there.

The town was named Alpine Town of the Year in 2001 and later joined the Alpine Pearls. It remains a spa town and a traditional centre of salt production, and the nearest airport is Salzburg Airport, 12 km to the north-east.
bad-schussenried: Bad Schussenried lies on the river Schussen in Upper Swabia, between Ulm and Lake Constance, in the district of Biberach in Baden-Württemberg. The 48th parallel north runs through the town, which stands on the Upper Swabian Baroque Route and the Swabian Spa Route.

Archaeological finds show prehistoric settlement in the region. A Paleolithic campsite of hunters and gatherers discovered in 1866 yielded the first Paleolithic finds in Central Europe. At Aichbühl, about 1.5 kilometres north of the source of the Schussen, excavations at the end of the 19th century in the bog of the Federsee uncovered Neolithic pile-dwelling settlements, which are part of the Prehistoric Pile dwellings around the Alps UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The place was first mentioned in 1153, as Shuozenried. Its history is closely tied to Schussenried Abbey, a Premonstratensian monastery founded in 1183 by the local lords Konrad and Beringer. The abbey gained many privileges, among them in 1521 the high jurisdiction, the right of blood court, which allowed it to show the sword beside the crozier in its coat of arms. Until secularisation the canons governed the monastic community. Peat extraction was an important industry in the town until the middle of the 20th century.

Bad Schussenried is a spa town. Schussenried Abbey, with its church and Baroque library and their ceiling frescoes, is its chief monument. The town has a monastery museum, a museum of beer steins and the Upper Swabian open-air museum at Kürnbach, a village with 31 buildings and furnishings from six centuries. In the district of Steinhausen the Sanctuary Church of Our Lady was built in 1728–1731.
bad-urach: Bad Urach lies in the district of Reutlingen in Baden-Württemberg, 14 km east of Reutlingen, at the foot of the Swabian Jura. The area was settled in the early Stone Age, and several caves in the region show signs of use as shelter. The Runder Berg, a former volcano, is of archaeological interest and shows an old Alemanni castle. Several million years ago the area was volcanically active, and an anomaly in the subsurface gives the town a thermal spring with water at 61 °C, which was developed for spa baths.

Hohenurach Castle was built around 1025 on a hill above the Erms valley. In the late Middle Ages it became a state prison, and the poet Philipp Nikodemus Frischlin died there in 1590 while trying to escape over its walls. In the 18th century the townspeople razed the fortress. Around 1260 Urach became part of Württemberg. When Württemberg was divided, the southern part was governed from Urach, the so-called secret capital, and from 1442 to 1482 it was the residence of the Counts and Dukes of Württemberg.

Count Eberhard the Bearded was born there in 1445 and returned often throughout his life. Over the following centuries the town prospered as a centre of weaving, and it escaped serious damage in wars, which is why its historical centre remains in excellent condition. In 1867 a cousin of the king of Württemberg was created Duke of Urach, though he lived 21 km away at Lichtenstein Castle.

The town has a late medieval marketplace with a town hall and half-timbered houses of the 15th and 16th centuries. The Residenzschloss, the home of the Counts of Württemberg-Urach and the birthplace of Eberhard the Bearded, has rooms from the Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque periods, including the Renaissance Goldener Saal. The Church of Saint Amandus dates from 1477 and was built in the Gothic style for Eberhard; his praying desk dates from 1472 and the pulpit is considered an important piece of German stonemasonry. It is a recognised spa town, with a thermal spring developed for mineral baths.
bad-waldsee: Bad Waldsee lies in Upper Swabia, 20 km south of Biberach an der Riß and 20 km north-east of Ravensburg. The old city stands on an isthmus between two lakes: the Stadtsee to the east and the smaller Schlosssee to the west, which empties into the Stadtsee. The town's colours are black and silver. Its arms include a fish for the fishing in the lakes, a star for devotion to the Virgin Mary, venerated at the mountain chapel of Our Dear Lady of the Mountain, and an oar that may stand for fishing or farming.

Waldsee is first documented in 926 in the Weissenburger Codex, which records that a royal estate was destroyed by the Hungarians during their invasion of southern Germany. The town received city rights in 1298. Authority was held by the Lords of Waldsee, a title that was soon sold to the Habsburg Duke of Austria. In 1386 the House of Habsburg pledged the city to the steward Johann von Waldburg. The pledge was renewed in 1406, when Waldsee and four other towns were sold off by the House of Habsburg; together they are known as the five Danube towns. The House of Waldburg kept control until 1806, when Napoleon's reordering of Europe made Waldsee part of the Kingdom of Württemberg.

In 1807 it became a township. In 1918 nickel and copper coins had grown scarce because of the First World War, and the council decided to issue its own coins of 5, 10 and 50 Pfennig. In 1923, at the height of inflation, the town printed its own banknotes, with values from 500,000 marks to ten trillion, some showing the Iron Man, the Steward of Waldburg. Waldsee lost its township status in 1938, when the Nazi government dissolved townships. In 1942 Erich Bachem founded Bachem-Werke in the town, which built and tested the Bachem Ba 349 rocket plane.

During the economic restructuring after the war the town opened its first mud bath, in 1950. As more spas were built it received the designation Moorheilbad, and in 1974 it became a Kneippkurort. The Waldsee-Therme, opened in 1994, is fed by a spring of nearly 65 °C. The camper manufacturer Hymer has its base in the town. Among people connected with it are the mystic Elizabeth of Reute, known as Good Beth, born in 1386 and beatified in 1755, and Georg, Truchsess von Waldburg, a commander of the Swabian League in the German Peasants' War.
bad-wimpfen: Bad Wimpfen lies on the west bank of the Neckar, about 15 kilometres north of Heilbronn. It has two parts: the older Wimpfen im Tal, on the river, and Wimpfen am Berg, on the hill, which holds the town centre. An old trade road running from France forks here towards Nuremberg and Öhringen and links to the Danube, and finds show the route has existed since prehistoric times.

The first traces of settlement date from the Neolithic and the Bronze Age. The Romans built a castellum at Wimpfen im Tal, opposite the mouth of the Jagst, around 98 CE. After the frontier moved forward under Antoninus Pius, in 138–161 CE, it lost its military role but grew as a civilian town, the centre of the Civitas Alisinensium. At about 19 hectares and with a city wall, it was one of the biggest Roman towns in what is now Baden-Württemberg. The Alamanni governed the Neckar area from 260 CE, and around 500 Wimpfen became part of Franconia. It is first documented as Wimpina in 829.

King Otto I granted market rights in 965, and the Talmarkt, the valley market, has run for more than a thousand years. The Staufer built a Kaiserpfalz on the hill; most of it stood by around 1200, including the Blue Tower, and it is the largest Stauferpfalz preserved north of the Alps. Henry VI stayed there at least three times and Frederick II eight times. Wimpfen became an imperial city as Staufer power declined. Erhard Schnepf preached the Reformation there from 1523 to 1526, and by 1588 only 30 Catholic inhabitants were left. During the Thirty Years' War the Battle of Wimpfen was fought nearby in 1622, and by 1648 the population had fallen to a tenth of its pre-war size.

Salt-water boreholes were first drilled in 1752 and a permanent saltworks was set up in 1817. The first therapeutic hotel opened in 1835, and after the railway from Heilbronn to Heidelberg was built in the 1860s the spa business grew greatly. The town received the prefix Bad on 26 April 1930. Wimpfen was a Hessian exclave until after the Second World War. In a plebiscite on 29 April 1951 a majority of 57 per cent chose the district of Heilbronn, and the change took effect on 1 May 1952. The old town is protected, and the Catholic parish still belongs as an exclave to the Diocese of Mainz.
badagry: Badagry is a coastal city and local government area in Lagos State, Nigeria, on the north bank of Porto Novo Creek, an inland waterway linking Lagos with Porto-Novo in Benin. It lies 43 miles (69 km) south-west of Lagos and 14 miles (23 km) east of Seme on the border with Benin, with the lagoon about a mile from the ocean. The preliminary 2006 census gave the municipality a population of 241,093. The name is explained as a European corruption of a Gbe phrase meaning inside the blacksmith's walls: the first settler, a blacksmith called Gbede or Agbede, is said to have built a low mud wall round his okra farm.

A traditional Yoruba account says the first settlers were an Awori group from Ile-Ife. The historian Robin Law traces the town to a resettlement of displaced peoples, mostly Ogu, Ewe and Oyo Yoruba. A European trader known locally as Yovo Huntɔkonu, often identified as a Dutch trader called Hendrik Hertogh, was given farmland, and from his trading post of 1736 Badagry became a slave port, mainly an outlet for Oyo. The peak of the trade was between 1736 and 1789, and it continued into the early nineteenth century with Portuguese and Brazilian traders taking over from the Dutch. Ouidah, Oyo and Lagos sacked the town in 1784. In 1821 the exiled Oba Adele made it politically independent.

Methodist missionaries led by Thomas Birch Freeman and Charles DeGraft preached under an Agia tree and later built a bamboo church; Freeman and Henry Townsend are said to have held the first Christmas in Nigeria there on 25 December 1842. A Church Missionary Society party including Townsend, Samuel Ajayi Crowther and Gollmer arrived in 1845 and built a two-storey mission house. A civil war from 1851 to 1854 and the founding of the colony of Lagos reduced Badagry's standing, and in 1863 colonial Lagos signed a treaty of cession with the Badagry chiefs.

Badagry's economy rests on fishing, trade and tourism. Its remains of the slave trade include barracoons built by Brazilian merchants under Chief Sunbu Mobee, of which about forty once stood, the Seriki Williams Abass museum and the Point of No Return on Gberefu Island. The Ogu, or Egun, people keep the Zangbeto masquerade, a custom of night watch and dispute settlement.
badajoz: Badajoz is the capital of the province of Badajoz in the autonomous community of Extremadura, Spain. It stands on the left bank of the river Guadiana, close to the Portuguese border, 61 kilometres from Mérida and 227 kilometres east of Lisbon. Its municipal territory of 1,470 square kilometres, one of the largest in Spain, includes the main city and about 26 secondary settlements. Archaeological finds in the area date to the Bronze Age, megalithic tombs to as far back as 4000 BCE, and excavations have revealed remnants from the Lower Paleolithic. Artifacts also come from the Roman town of Colonia Civitas Pacensis in the area.

The Muladi nobleman Ibn Marwan founded Badajoz, known to its Muslim rulers as Batalyaws, around 875, after he had been expelled from Mérida, and it was the seat of an autonomous rebel state until the 10th century. In 1021, or possibly 1031, it became the capital of the small Taifa of Badajoz, with some 25,000 inhabitants, noted for high cultural production under the Aftasids despite military and political instability. Alfonso VI of León invaded it in 1086, the Almoravids in 1092 and the Almohads in 1147. The Kingdom of León conquered it in 1230, and it became a royal demesne and the seat of an opulent diocese.

The city endured spells of calamity from civil wars and conflicts with Portugal; the Portuguese attacked in 1660, and the Peace Treaty of Badajoz between Spain and Portugal was signed on 6 June 1801. In 1812 Arthur Wellesley, Earl of Wellington, besieged the French garrison of about 5,000 men from 16 March. The assault of 6 April on the breaches cost some 5,000 of 15,000 British soldiers and failed, but an attack on the castle and an undamaged wall took the town. The victorious troops then sacked it, killing and raping civilians; some 200 to 300 civilians were probably killed or injured, and it took three days to restore order. Wellington wrote that he hoped never again to put his troops to such a test.

In the Spanish Civil War the Nationalists took Badajoz. After the battle several thousand inhabitants were taken to the bullring, and on 14 August 1936 hundreds of Republicans were shot there. It is estimated that over 4,000 people were murdered by the Nationalists afterwards. Their commander, Juan Yagüe, later became Minister of Aviation and was popularly known as the Butcher of Badajoz.

Badajoz is the most populated city of Extremadura, with 150,376 inhabitants in 2010, and a major commercial centre in southwestern Spain and a bridge for trade and cultural relations with Portugal. A heavy flood on 6 November 1997 devastated several neighbourhoods and killed 21 people. The Badajoz-Elvas-Campo Maior eurocity initiative seeks closer cross-border cooperation with Elvas and Campo Maior.
badami: Badami, formerly Vātāpi, is a town and taluk headquarters in the Bagalkot district of Karnataka. It lies in a ravine at the foot of a rugged red sandstone outcrop that surrounds the Agastya lake, at an average elevation of 586 metres. The man-made lake, once called the Vatapi lake, was completed in the 7th century as a likely source of water for the capital, and many Hindu temples were built around it. The cliffs protect the town on three sides, which probably explains why Pulakeshin I chose the site.

Pulakeshin I is generally regarded as the founder of the Badami Chalukya dynasty, and an inscription of his on a boulder records the fortification of the hill above Vatapi in the 540s. His son Kirtivarman I and his brother Mangalesha built the cave temples. When Kirtivarman died his sons were minors, and Mangalesha ruled, as the Mahakuta Pillar inscription mentions. Pulakeshin II came to power in 610 and ruled until 642. The Chalukyas ruled much of Karnataka, Maharashtra and parts of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh between the 6th and 8th centuries, and Badami became a regional centre of art in the Malprabha valley, with Dravida and Nagara styles of temple side by side.

In 642 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman defeated Pulakeshin II and his army descended on the city. The palace was ransacked, men were killed, women were taken captive and temples were stripped of their treasures; survivors fled and did not return for many years. Narasimhavarman took the victory pillar Pulakeshin II had raised after defeating Harsha and Vengi to Kanchi, and a Pallava inscription still at Badami describes the attack as retaliation for earlier conquests. Later the Rashtrakutas and Later Chalukyas added temples, including the Northern Bhutanatha group and the Yellamma Temple, completed in the early 13th century. Badami was afterwards fought over by Vijayanagara and the Deccan sultans, and Vijayanagara rulers had its fort walls expanded.

Badami is known for its rock-cut cave temples and for structural temples such as the Bhutanatha groups, the Badami Shivalaya and the Jambulingesvara Temple, mostly built between the 6th and 8th centuries. The caves were probably painted inside by the late 6th century. Most of the paintings are lost, but fragments remain in Cave 3, a Vaishnava cave, and Cave 4, a Jain one; those of Shiva and Parvati in Cave 3 are among the earliest datable paintings of Hindu legends in India.

The town has eighteen inscriptions. Among them are a Sanskrit inscription in old Kannada script from 543 CE, a cave inscription of Mangalesha of 578 in Kannada, and the Kappe Arabhatta record, the earliest available Kannada poetry in the tripadi metre. The main language is Kannada. The 2011 census counted 30,943 people.
baden-wurttemberg: Baden-Württemberg is a landlocked state east of the Rhine, which forms the southern part of Germany's western border with France. It also borders Switzerland, Rhineland-Palatinate, Hesse and Bavaria. Baden runs along the flat right bank of the Rhine from the north-west to Lake Constance, while Württemberg and Hohenzollern lie further inland among hillier country such as the Swabian Jura. The Black Forest formed part of the border between Baden and Württemberg, and most of the major cities stand along the Neckar, which flows past Tübingen, Stuttgart, Heilbronn, Heidelberg and Mannheim.

Around 100 CE the Roman Empire occupied Württemberg and built a limes along its northern border. In the third century the Alemanni forced the Romans back beyond the Rhine and Danube, and in 496 the Alemanni were defeated by a Frankish invasion led by Clovis I. The region later formed part of the Holy Roman Empire and stayed largely Catholic after the Reformation, though northern and central Württemberg has been Protestant since 1534, with its centre at the Tübinger Stift.

At the start of the 20th century the area consisted of the Grand Duchy of Baden, the Kingdom of Württemberg and the Prussian province of Hohenzollern, all part of the German Empire since 1871. In the revolution of 1918 their monarchs were deposed, and after 1933 their democratic institutions were abolished. After the Second World War the Allies created South Baden, Württemberg-Baden and Württemberg-Hohenzollern, and in April 1952 these merged to form Baden-Württemberg as a state of West Germany.

Baden-Württemberg has more than 11 million inhabitants. Stuttgart is the capital and largest city, followed by Mannheim and Karlsruhe, where Germany's supreme constitutional court sits. The state is divided into four administrative districts: Freiburg, Karlsruhe, Stuttgart and Tübingen. Heidelberg, founded in 1386, is the oldest university within the territory of modern Germany, and Freiburg and Tübingen followed in 1457 and 1477. Alemannic and Franconian dialects are spoken, and the Black Forest and Lake Constance are popular destinations.
badia-fiorentina: The abbey was founded as a Benedictine house in 978 by Willa, Countess of Tuscany, in memory of her husband Hubert, and became one of the chief buildings of medieval Florence. A hospital was founded there in 1071, and the church bell marked the main divisions of the Florentine day. Between 1284 and 1310 Arnolfo di Cambio rebuilt the Romanesque church in Gothic style, though in 1307 part of it was demolished to punish the monks for not paying taxes. The campanile, completed between 1310 and 1330 under the oversight of the chronicler Giovanni Villani, is Romanesque at its base and Gothic above.

The church was remodelled in Baroque style between 1627 and 1631, and Giovanni Domenico Ferretti painted the murals in the apse in 1734. Its works of art include Filippino Lippi's Apparition of the Virgin to St. Bernard of about 1486 and the tomb of the lawyer and diplomat Bernardo Giugni by Mino da Fiesole. The Chiostro degli Aranci, the Cloister of the Oranges, holds a fresco cycle of about 1435 to 1439 on the life of St Benedict, from the time of the reforming abbot Dom Gomes Eanes; it is most likely the work of Zanobi di Benedetto Strozzi under the guidance of Fra Angelico, and the young Bronzino repainted its fourth scene. The abbey is now home to the Monastic Communities of Jerusalem.

Dante supposedly grew up across the street, in what is now called the Casa di Dante, and by legend first saw Beatrice in this church. In 1373 Boccaccio gave his lectures on the Divine Comedy in the chapel of Santo Stefano beside its north entrance. Giotto's Badia Polyptych, now in the Uffizi Gallery, once stood here. In 1958 Ugo Procacci had a later wall removed and found frescoes beneath: an Annunciation, a Presentation of Jesus at the Temple and Joachim Among the Shepherds, of which only one head survived.
badis-ibn-al-mansur: Known fully as Abū Manād Bādīs Nāṣir al-Dawla, he was the third ruler of the Zirids and succeeded his father al-Mansur ibn Buluggin as viceroy of Ifriqiya on 8 April 996. At the start of his reign the Zenata Berbers rose in revolt and threatened the Zirid lands from Tiaret to Tripoli, and to deal with them he left the eastern parts of the emirate to a deputy. Throughout his reign he also had to fend off Fatimid forays into Tripolitania.

He kept close to his Fatimid overlords in Egypt because his right to rule was challenged within the family by his great-uncle Zawi ibn Ziri, who was finally driven into Andalusia and founded the Zirid dynasty of Granada. By 1001 Badis had won a convincing victory over the Zenata, their allies the Maghrawa, and Zawi. Much of the credit belonged to Hammad ibn Buluggin, who beat off another Zenata attack in 1004/5 and in 1007/8 built the castle of Qal'a. When Hammad rebelled, Badis marched against him in May 1015 and defeated him at Chelif on 17 October, but could not take Qal'a and had to besiege it.

Badis died on 10 May 1016 with the siege still under way. His death made the separation of the Hammadid state from the Zirids inevitable. The anti-Shi'a riots that broke out in Tunis during his last year foreshadowed the break between the Zirids and the Fatimids under his son and successor al-Mu'izz, who came to the throne as a minor with Badis's sister Saïda bint Mansour as regent.
badr-al-din-lulu: His name, meaning The Pearl, marks his servile origins: he was a freed slave, of either Armenian or Kurdish origin, in the household of the Zengid ruler Nur al-Din Arslan Shah I. Valued as an administrator, he rose to the rank of atabeg and after 1211 served the child rulers Nur al-Din Arslan Shah II and Nasir al-Din Mahmud. Their grandfather Gökböri, Emir of Erbil, was his enemy, and in 1226 Gökböri and al-Muazzam of Damascus attacked Mosul and forced his submission. Nasir al-Din Mahmud, the last Zengid of Mosul, was killed by Lu'lu', by strangulation or starvation.

In 1234 he struck coins in his own name, and the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir gave him the title al-Malik al-Rahim, The Merciful King. He kept al-Jazira by submitting in turn to Ayyubid, Rûmi Seljuq and Mongol overlords, and his lands reached their maximum in 1251, from Kurdistan and Sinjar to Qarqisiya on the Euphrates. In 1254 he had the Yezidi leader Hasan ibn Adi and 200 of his followers executed. He strengthened Mosul's walls, built the shrines of Imam Yahya and Awn al-Din, and his workshops produced some of the finest inlaid metalwork of the age, including the Blacas ewer, which is generally attributed to him. He also seems to have kept a balance between Sunnis and Shiites and tolerated Mosul's large Christian community.

After the Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243 he recognised Mongol authority, sending envoys to Karakorum, and in 1258 he supplied Baiju's army with provisions and weapons and built a bridge of boats over the Tigris for the Siege of Baghdad.

About 80 years old, he went in person to Meraga to renew his submission to Hulagu, and he sent his son Al-Salih to lead the siege of Amid. He died in 1259, and his sons Isma'il, Ishaq and 'Alī took Mosul, Jazirat ibn 'Umar and Sinjar. After the Mongol defeat at Ain Jalut in 1260 Isma'il sided with the Mamluks, and Hulagu besieged Mosul for nine months before destroying it.
badr-al-jamali: Badr was born sometime between 1005 and 1008, most likely into a Christian family, and later converted to Islam. He was bought as a military slave by Jamal al-Dawla ibn Ammar, ruler of Tripoli, from whom he took the name al-Jamali. His career is documented from April 1063, when he became governor of Damascus. Clashes with the townspeople and the urban militia ended that post in 1064, and his second governorship from 1066 was no calmer: he persecuted the Banu Abi'l-Jinn, had the Alid notable Abu Tahir strangled, and in 1068 retreated to the coast, holding Acre, Ascalon, Sidon and Caesarea.

With Egypt in anarchy, Caliph al-Mustansir secretly summoned him. Badr sailed with his Armenian troops in winter, landed at Damietta in December 1073 and came to Cairo alone on 27 January 1074. Once some 900 of his men had gathered, he invited the rival Turkish commanders to a banquet and had them killed. The caliph then gave him plenary powers as commander of the armies, chief justice and head of the Isma'ili mission, a vizierate of the sword and the pen.

He purged officials and executed former viziers and qadis, crushed the Luwata Berbers in the Nile Delta and the Bedouin of Upper Egypt, and by 1076 had restored central rule as far as Aswan. Isma'ilism remained official, but Sunnis and other Shi'a could worship freely, and he sponsored both mosques and churches. He replaced the old small districts of Egypt with 23 provinces and encouraged Armenian immigration; by the end of the century the community numbered almost 100,000. His army heavily defeated the Turkoman chieftain Atsiz north of Cairo in February 1077, but Damascus and most of Syria fell to the Seljuks.

Badr died on 21 June 1094, aged over 80. Most of his officers backed his son al-Afdal as vizier against the caliph's attempt to recover power. His rule saved the regime but set a pattern: until 1171 the vizierate was held mostly by military strongmen, many of them Armenian, who sidelined the caliphs. He also built the Juyushi Mosque on the Muqattam Hill in memory of his son al-Awhad, and commissioned the minbar for the shrine of Husayn's head at Ascalon, now in the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron.
badra-iraq: Badra lies on the Mandali-Badra-Tib alluvial fans, which spread along the foot of the mountains on the frontier between Iraq and Iran. The fans are made of gravelly and sandy sediments laid down by braided rivers, mostly limestone pebbles with varying amounts of clay, and near Badra they reach a thickness of 65 m. Two extensive clay layers have been identified there; one of them separates the upper and lower parts of the fan, so that the area has an unconfined upper aquifer and a confined lower one.

The town's name goes back to the ancient Sumerian city of Der, at nearby Tell 'Aqar. In the time of Tiglath-pileser III the place was called Bīt-Derāya, a form later Syriac sources also use. It became Badarāya, the medieval Arabic name of the city, and finally Badrah in modern times.

An Ottoman treaty of 1639 named Jassan, Badra and Zurbatiyah as part of the Ottoman Empire, an arrangement that divided the Arab tribes of the area. Badra was long inhabited by an Arab majority and a Turkmen minority, most of them Sunni Shafi'i with a Shia minority, speaking a Turkish mixed with Arabic, Kurdish and Persian. Feyli Kurds settled in the 19th century; Hursid Pasha explained that before the rule of Davud Mamluk Pasha, Baghdad's governors had oppressed the Arab inhabitants and forced them to sell land to the Kurds. In 1847 the Ottomans acquired Badra by a treaty with Persia.

Badra is a town of Wasit Governorate, near the Iranian border. Its people are Arabs and Turkmen, joined more recently by Kurds who migrated from western Iran. In 2014 Iraq made its first crude oil delivery from the newly developed Badra oilfield in Wasit Governorate. Its initial capacity was 15,000 barrels a day, and it was run under a profit-sharing agreement between Gazprom of Russia and companies of Iraq, Korea, Malaysia and Turkey, with a 165-km pipeline to the export terminals of Al Basrah Governorate.
badrinath: Badrinath stands at an average elevation of 3,100 metres in the Garhwal Himalayas, on the banks of the Alaknanda River, between the Nar and Narayana mountain ranges. The name comes from the Sanskrit Badarīnātha, formed from badarī, the jujube tree, and nātha, lord, an epithet of Vishnu. The area is also called Badarikashrama in Hindu scriptures. It is a gateway for mountaineering expeditions, among them those to the peak of Nilkantha.

According to tradition, Adi Shankaracharya found a black stone image of Badrinarayan, made of shaligram stone, in the Alaknanda and first enshrined it in a cave near the Tapt Kund hot springs. In the sixteenth century the King of Garhwal moved the image to the present temple. The temple is about 15 metres tall, with a small cupola under a gilt roof, and a stone facade with arched windows that resembles a Buddhist vihara. Earthquakes and avalanches have repeatedly destroyed it.

In earlier times pilgrims walked hundreds of miles to reach it. As late as the First World War the settlement consisted only of some twenty huts for the temple's staff, though the site drew thousands of visitors each year and up to 50,000 at the festivals held every twelve years.

The Bhagavata Purana says that Vishnu, in his form as the sages Nara and Narayana, has practised austerity at Badrikashram since time immemorial. Another story holds that the area was full of badari, a wild berry, and that Lakshmi took the form of a badari tree to shade Vishnu as he meditated. The Pandavas are said to have passed through Badrinath and Mana, 4 kilometres to the north, on their way to heaven, and a cave at Mana is where Vyasa is said to have written the Mahabharata.

Jains also hold the place sacred, holding that many Jain monks attained liberation by austerity there. The Ganges is said to have been divided into two channels when it came to earth, with the Alaknanda as one of them.
baekje-historic-areas: The Baekje Historic Areas relate to the last period of the Koreanic kingdom of Baekje, which lasted from 18 BCE to 660 CE. Baekje was founded on the banks of the Han River, in present-day Seoul, by migrants from Goguryeo. After Goguryeo occupied its capital, the court moved to Ungjin, where the Gongsanseong fortress was built in 475. The move brought Chinese ideas of city planning and architecture and a commitment to Buddhism. In 538 King Seong shifted the capital to Sabi, in Buyeo, partly for reasons of trade, and Iksan became a second capital for administration. In 660 Baekje fell to Silla, which was allied with the Tang dynasty of China.

Buddhism reached Baekje from China in the late 4th century, and in the 6th century the monk Gyeomik travelled to India to bring back scriptures. Many large temples and pagodas were built, and Baekje took part in exchanges with China and Japan, including the building of temples in both countries between the 5th and 7th centuries.

Gongsanseong, on Gongsan mountain, has a rampart 2,666 metres long, 1,925 metres of it stone, and served as both fortress and palace. The Songsan-ri tombs include that of King Muryeong, the 25th king, found intact in 1971 with more than 4,600 objects; the king's tomb and tomb no. 6 are of brick with vaulted ceilings. Busosanseong, an earth fort with a perimeter of 2,495 metres, was the palace's back garden and an escape route; a legend tells of 3,000 royal ladies leaping from Nakhwaam Rock. The Jeongnimsa temple site has a five-storey pagoda about 8 metres high. Mireuksa is considered the largest temple site in East Asia. Neungsan-ri has seven tombs, and the 6.3-kilometre Naseong wall guarded Sabi.

UNESCO inscribed the Baekje Historic Areas as a World Heritage Site on 8 July 2015, under criteria II and III, for the architecture, Buddhism and exchange with China and Japan they show. The sites lie in three cities of South Korea, Gongju, Buyeo and Iksan, and a conservation foundation of central, provincial and local bodies manages them under a plan for 2015 to 2019.
bagalkot-district: Bagalkot district lies in northern Karnataka on the North Karnataka Plateau, part of the Deccan Plateau, and covers about 6,593 km². The Ghataprabha, Malaprabha and Krishna rivers flow through it. Kudalasangama, at the confluence of the Krishna and the Malaprabha, is known as the samadhi of Basavanna. Stone inscriptions give Bagadige as the ancient name of Bagalkot, and a legend says that Rāvana gave the area to his musicians. Badami, formerly Vatapi, was named after an asura king who according to the Mahābhārata ruled the area with his brother Ilvala; Aihole was formerly Ayyavole and Aryapura, and Pattadakal Raktapura.

More than 191 Middle Palaeolithic localities have been found in the Kaladgi basin, and a pre-Chalukyan brick temple and evidence of megalithic habitation lie at the foot of Bachinagudda at Pattadakal. The first documented evidence is Ptolemy's mention of Badami, Indi and Kalkeri in the 2nd century CE. In the 6th century the Chalukyas ruled much of South India, and the district kept its prominence until the Rashtrakutas sacked the Chalukyan empire in 753. Pulakeshin II fought the Kadambas, Gangas, Gurjaras and Emperor Harshavardhana, whom he defeated on the banks of the Narmada, and accounts of the wars are inscribed at Aihole. The Chinese traveller Hieun-Tsang visited Badami and described its people as tall, proud and brave.

The Kalyani Chalukyas, descendants of the Badami Chalukyas, conquered the area before the 10th century, and Akkadevi ruled there for more than 40 years from 1024. The Yadavas of Deogiri annexed Bagalkot in 1190, and Ala ud din Khalji's invasion of 1294 ended their rule. In the late 15th century the Adil Shahi dynasty founded by Yusuf Adil Shah set up an independent state with Bijapur as its capital, and from then Bagalkot's history is that of Bijapur. In 1818 the Maratha Peshwas of Satara became underlords, and the district later passed to the British and the Bombay Presidency. After 1956 Bijapur, with Bagalkot, belonged to Mysore State, renamed Karnataka in 1971. A separate Bagalkot district was carved out of Bijapur in 1997.

The district has ten taluks and its headquarters in the town of Bagalkot. Its population was 1,889,752 at the 2011 census, and Kannada is spoken by about 86% of the people, with Urdu second. Agriculture employs more than 65% of the working population; the black soil suits cotton, and jowar is a main crop. The Yadahalli Wildlife Sanctuary protects the chinkara, or Indian gazelle.
baganda: The Baganda share a culture, history, language and clan system and are primarily native to Buganda, a kingdom within Uganda. They are sometimes called the King's Men because of the importance of the king, the Kabaka, in their society, and number about 16 million in Uganda, with organised communities abroad. According to the most widely accepted account, Buganda was founded by Kato Kintu, a historical figure who took the name Kintu from the legend of the first man to establish his legitimacy, and who united scattered clans into a strong kingdom. In the creation myth Kintu married Nnambi, the daughter of the god Ggulu, and the Baganda are called the children of Nnambi.

By the 18th century Buganda was eclipsing the formerly dominant kingdom of Bunyoro. Behind a centralised kingship the Baganda turned from defence to expansion, and by the middle of the 19th century Buganda had doubled and redoubled its territory, conquering much of Bunyoro. Conquered lands were put under chiefs nominated by the king, armies travelled on specially built roads, and a royal navy of outrigger canoes under an admiral called Gabunga could carry commandos to any shore of Lake Victoria.

The explorer John Speke visited Buganda in the 1860s, and Henry Morton Stanley in 1875 found a well-ordered capital of about 80,000 people around the king's palace. In 1876 Christian missionaries began to enter the kingdom, and between 1881 and 1890 the Baganda began to convert to both Islam and Christianity.

Every Muganda belongs to a clan, normally the father's; the Kabaka alone takes his mother's, so that every clan can produce a future king. The Baganda traditionally had 52 clans, of which 46 have been officially recognised since a 1993 survey. Each clan has a plant or animal totem that its members may not eat or harm, and members of one clan do not marry each other. Surnames depend on the clan and show whether the bearer is male or female.

Ekitiibwa, meaning honour or dignity, is the chief ideal. Unlike comparable notions in more stratified societies such as Rwanda, it was not conferred by birth, and all people openly competed for it. According to the 2002 census, 42.7 per cent of Baganda are Roman Catholic, 27.4 per cent Anglican and 23 per cent Muslim, while some also follow the old Kiganda religion. They speak Luganda.
baggara-arabs: The Baggara are a nomadic confederation of people of mixed Arab and Arabized indigenous African ancestry, living in a part of the Sahel mainly between Lake Chad and the Nile near south Kordofan. They number over six million. Their name comes from the Arabic for heifer herder. They are known as Baggara and Abbala in Sudan and as Shuwa Arabs in Chad, Cameroon and Nigeria. Baggara tribes claim descent from the Juhaynah Arab tribe.

The first documented evidence of Arab settlement in the region is a letter of 1391 in which the King of Bornu, Abu 'Amr Uthman b. Idris, complained to the Mamluk sultan Barquq that the Judham and other Arabs were raiding his territory and enslaving his subjects. Braukämper dates the formation of Baggara culture to the 17th century in Wadai, where camel-herding Arabs met cattle-rearing Fula people migrating east.

The Baggara of Darfur and Kordofan were the backbone of the Mahdist revolt against Turko-Egyptian rule in Sudan in the 1880s. The Mahdi's second-in-command, the Khalifa Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, was a Baggara of the Ta'aisha tribe. During the Mahdist period, from 1883 to 1898, tens of thousands of Baggara moved to Omdurman and central Sudan and supplied many of the Mahdist troops. After the defeat at the Battle of Karari in 1898 the survivors went home. Under British indirect rule each major tribe was ruled by its own paramount chief, or nazir. The Fur sultans gave the main Baggara tribes of Darfur land grants, called hawakir, in the 1750s.

From 1985 the Government of Sudan armed local tribes, among them the Rizeigat of south Darfur and the Messiria and Hawazma of Kordofan, as militia in a proxy war against the Sudan People's Liberation Army. Some formed mounted raiders, the Muraheleen, who attacked southern villages to loot valuables and take slaves. During the Second Sudanese Civil War thousands of Dinka women and children were abducted and enslaved by members of the Missiriya and Rezeigat. By the mid-1990s the Baggara groups had mostly negotiated local truces with the SPLA.

The Baggara mostly speak a distinct dialect known as Chadian Arabic. Their common mode of subsistence is nomadic cattle herding, although many now live settled lives. Those who remain nomads move seasonally between grazing lands in the wet season and river areas in the dry season. The tribes in Sudan include the Rizeigat, Ta'isha, Beni Halba, Habbaniya, Salamat and Messiria in Darfur, and the Hawazma and Awlad Himayd in Kordofan. They have camel-owning relatives, the Abbala, who live mainly in North and West Darfur.
baghaberd: The fortress stands west of Kapan, on the road to Kajaran, on a spur of the Barkushat range about 200 metres above the confluence of the Voghjaget and its tributary the Giratagh. Sheer cliffs make its western side impregnable, so the walls were built mainly on the east. It was also known as Baghats Fortress, Baghberd and Paghabert, and is now in the territory of Andokavan village.

Three tiers of walls climb the slope. The highest line, on the east, has five semicircular buttress-towers of 7 to 12 metres, the largest guarding the only entrance. Inside the gate an attacker faced a rock face and a corridor wide enough for one or two rows of men, covered by a guard-tower and an embrasure.

According to a tradition reported by the historian Stepanos Orbelian, Patriarch Baghak, a descendant of Sisak, inherited the province of Dzork, or Kapan, built the fortress and named it Baghaberd. It was known as a stronghold from the 4th or 5th century and often sheltered the people of the area in times of danger. It is mentioned by Shapuh Bagratuni, Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi, Vardan Areveltsi and Mkhitar Ayrivanetsi as well as Orbelian.

Its importance grew under the Kingdom of Syunik, whose capital moved to Kapan after King Gagik I took the province of Vayots Dzor. Baghaberd was the main link in a ring of strongholds about 10 kilometres around the city, and the riches and many thousands of manuscripts of the Tatev Monastery and other monasteries were gathered there. Local legend holds that Queen Pharandzem spent her youth at the fortress, and mothers bathed their children in water from a spring named after her.

Earthquakes have damaged the site over the centuries, most recently in 1968, but hundreds of metres of wall and five or six towers survive. Excavations in the citadel began in the spring of 2024 and by August 2025 had uncovered a probable kitchen of the 12th to 13th centuries and a building of the 11th to 12th centuries thought to be the palace of the princes of Syunik.
baghdad: Baghdad stands on a vast, almost entirely flat and low-lying plain bisected by the Tigris, formed by the periodic flooding of the river. The river divides the city into an eastern half, Risafa, and a western half, Karkh. The Diyala river, a tributary of the Tigris, flows south-east of the city and borders its eastern suburbs.

After the fall of the Umayyads the victorious Abbasids sought a new capital. On 30 July 762 the Caliph al-Mansur commissioned the construction of Baghdad, guided by the Iranian Barmakids, believing the site ideal for ruling the Islamic Empire. He hired two designers, Naubakht, a Zoroastrian, and Mashallah, a Jew from Khorasan, who chose an auspicious founding date under the sign of Leo. The historian al-Tabari recorded a prophecy of Christian monks about a leader named Miklas who would build a great city there, and al-Mansur, once called Miklas, saw it as a good omen.

Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and an intellectual and cultural centre, with institutions such as the House of Wisdom and a multi-ethnic, multi-religious population. For much of the Abbasid era, the Islamic Golden Age, it was one of the largest cities in the world, and its population peaked at more than a million. The Round City, its original core, ceased to exist as a result of the Mongol siege. The Mongol Empire largely destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and a long decline followed, marked by frequent plagues and shifts of power between successive empires.

Later Baghdad was the administrative centre of Ottoman Iraq, with authority over the provinces of Basra, Mosul and Shahrizor. During the First World War it was made the capital of Mandatory Iraq. After Iraq was recognised as an independent monarchy in 1932 the city gradually regained some of its prominence as a centre of Arab culture. It suffered severe damage in the Iraq War, which began with the invasion of 2003, and lost much cultural heritage and many historical artifacts.

Baghdad is the capital and largest city of Iraq and its seat of government, on the banks of the Tigris. Its estimated population is 8 million. Historic mosques, churches, mandis and synagogues reflect its diversity, and the Masjid al-Kadhimayn, the Buratha Mosque, the Shrine of Abdul-Qadir Gilani and the Abu Hanifa Mosque are visited by millions each year. The University of Baghdad is the largest university in Iraq, and the city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Literature in December 2015.
baghdad-pact: The Central Treaty Organization, also called the Baghdad Pact and at first the Middle East Treaty Organization, was a Cold War military alliance formed on 24 February 1955 by Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey and the United Kingdom. It was modelled on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and committed its members to mutual cooperation and protection and to non-intervention in each other's affairs. Its aim was to contain the Soviet Union by a line of strong states along its south-western frontier, which gave it the name Northern Tier. American pressure and promises of aid were key in the negotiations, but the United States could not at first take part.

Unlike NATO, the pact had no unified military command, and few American or British bases were established in member countries. The United States did have communications and intelligence facilities in Iran and flew U-2 flights over the Soviet Union from bases in Pakistan. The headquarters were in Baghdad from 1955 to 1958 and then in Ankara until 1979. In 1958 the United States joined the military committee.

Turkey had signed a Pact of Mutual Cooperation with Pakistan in February 1954. A secretary general served renewable three-year terms. The organisation also sponsored research and cultural bodies such as the CENTO Institute of Nuclear Science, which moved from Baghdad to Tehran in 1958, and a railway from Lake Van in Turkey to Sharafkhaneh in Iran, funded largely by the United Kingdom.

On 14 July 1958 the Iraqi monarchy was overthrown in a military coup, and the new government under Abd al-Karim Qasim withdrew Iraq from the pact, which formally ended on 24 March 1959, and adopted a non-aligned stance. The organisation then took the name CENTO. In the 1960s it declined to become involved in the Arab-Israeli conflict or the Indo-Pakistani wars: Pakistan's requests for help in 1965 and 1971 were rejected on the ground that the alliance aimed to contain the Soviet Union, not India.

After the Turkish invasion of Cyprus in 1974 the United Kingdom withdrew the forces earmarked for the alliance, and the United States Congress halted military aid to Turkey. Iran withdrew on 11 March 1979 and Pakistan the next day, and on 16 March 1979 the organisation was formally dissolved. Later defence agreements between the United States or the United Kingdom and regional states were made bilaterally.
baghdadi-jews: Jewish traders from the Middle East had crossed the Indian Ocean since the time of ancient Rome, when the caravan route from India ended at Aleppo and the spice trade tied Basra, Yemen and Cairo to the Malabar Coast. Persian-speaking Jewish merchants, trading allies of the Jews of Baghdad, Basra and Aleppo, were the first to reach the Indian heartland. Mughal sources first mention Jewish merchants from Baghdad trading with India in the 17th century, and some became courtiers: Shalom Cohen, who later founded the Calcutta community, was court jeweller to the Nawab of Awadh and to Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire.

With the rise of British power, settlement shifted from Surat to Bombay and then principally to Calcutta, the capital of British India. Leading families fleeing the persecution of Dawud Pasha in Baghdad strengthened the community there: a Jewish cemetery opened in 1812, a first synagogue in 1823, a second in 1856 and in 1884 a third, which was to be the largest in Asia. By the end of the 19th century more than 1,800 Baghdadi Jews lived in Calcutta. Their merchants dominated the export of Indian opium to China, and the Sassoon family eventually controlled 70 percent of that trade.

The Second World War began the end of this world. Refugees from the Japanese occupation of Burma swelled the Jewish population of Calcutta to over 5,000, while much of the community in Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore and Indonesia was interned by the Japanese army. Fearing the violence of Partition and the policies of independent India and Burma, their trade cut by the Communist victory in China and by later nationalisations, the Baghdadi Jews left for Israel, Britain and Australia, almost all of them by the 1970s.

The communities were bound by religion, language and above all marriage: brides, and occasionally grooms, were sent from one community to another, and business alliances followed family ties. Most members were of Iraqi Jewish origin, but families from Syria, Yemen, Egypt, Afghanistan and Iran, and a few Sephardic Jews from Italy and Turkey, joined and assimilated. Sir Manasseh Meyer, born in Baghdad in 1846, schooled in Calcutta and Singapore and later a trader in Rangoon and Singapore, moved across Asia while staying inside this Judeo-Arabic speaking network. Their cuisine mixed Arab, Turkish, Persian and Indian influences.
bagler: The Bagler faction was founded in Skåne, then part of Denmark, by Bishop Nicholas Arnesson of Oslo and Archbishop Erik Ivarsson of Nidaros, around the pretender Inge Magnusson, nicknamed the Baglar-King. Its forerunners had supported King Inge I of Norway and later King Magnus V and his father and regent, Earl Erling Skakke. The Birkebeiner, essentially a peasant faction, had been formed in 1174 to depose Magnus and Erling, and under King Sverre Sigurdsson they took control of much of the country. Sverre's claim to descend from King Sigurd II was doubted in his own time, and historians generally regard him as a pretender.

The Bagler drew principally on the aristocracy, the clergy and the merchants, above all the wealthier classes of Viken, where social distinctions were growing deeper. They favoured the church and its privileges and possessions. Historians read them as conservatives opposed to developments such as the growth of landless border men, the markamenn, who settled along the Swedish border, lived by raiding the old settlements and formed the chief support of the Birkebeiner. Like their rivals, the Bagler rallied around a royal son set up to contest the rule of the other party's king.

The Bagler remained powerful in Hedmark and Østerdal even when Sverre held most of Norway, and their strength grew after his death in 1202. His successor, King Haakon III, died in 1204 and left a posthumous son, Haakon Haakonsson, in Hamar, then under Bagler control; in 1206 a group of Birkebeiner carried the two-year-old boy through mountains and forests to Trondheim.

The Bagler pretenders were Inge Magnusson until 1202, Erling Steinvegg from 1204 to 1207 and Philip Simonsson from 1207 to 1217. Under the pact of 1208 Philip ruled Oppland and Viken without the title of king, while Inge Bårdsson was recognised as King Inge II. Both died in 1217, and Haakon IV came to the throne under the regency of Duke Skule Baardsson; in 1240 he ended the civil wars.
bagoas: Bagoas rose to be vizier, or chief minister, of Artaxerxes III. He allied himself with the Rhodian mercenary general Mentor, and with his help Egypt was made a province of the Achaemenids once more, probably from 342 BCE. Mentor took command of the maritime provinces while Bagoas ran the satrapies, and towards the end of the reign he was almost the real master of the empire. According to Diodorus Siculus he grew rich by confiscating the sacred writings of the Egyptian temples and returning them to the priests for large bribes. Josephus tells that after the high priest Johannes murdered his brother Jesus in the Jerusalem temple, Bagoas, who had backed Jesus, put a new tax on the Jews.

Diodorus writes that when Bagoas fell out of favour he poisoned Artaxerxes III and most of his family with the help of a physician, but a cuneiform tablet in the British Museum, BM 71537, suggests that the king died of natural causes. Bagoas then placed the king's youngest son Arses on the throne as Artaxerxes IV, expecting him to be easy to control. Arses ruled for two years as little more than a puppet, and when he began to plan Bagoas's murder, perhaps urged by nobles who held the vizier in contempt, Bagoas poisoned him first and raised his cousin as Darius III. When Darius tried to free himself, Bagoas prepared poison for him as well, but Darius was warned and made him drink it.

Alexander the Great later gave Bagoas's house at Susa, with its treasures, to Parmenion, and Theophrastus mentions his gardens at Babylon. A later story by Aelian, that Bagoas was an Egyptian who killed Artaxerxes for slaying the living Apis bull, has no historical basis. Plutarch reports an angry letter from Alexander to Darius that named Bagoas among those who organised the murder of Alexander's father, Philip II of Macedon.
bagram: Bagram lies about 60 kilometres north of Kabul in Parwan Province, at the junction of the Ghorband and Panjshir valleys, near Charikar. The location made it a key passage from ancient India along the Silk Road. One route led west through the mountains towards Bamiyan, and another north over the Kushan Pass to the Baghlan Valley, the Kushan site of Surkh Kotal and the commercial centre of Balkh.

The ancient city of Kapisi is identified with the site. Ancient Buddhist and Hindu sculptures suggest that it was first ruled by Indic people who migrated to or mixed with Iranian populations, among them Kambojas from Bactria. In 305 BCE Seleucus I, after a brief conflict with the Mauryan founder Chandragupta Maurya, ceded Gandhara, Arachosia and lands south of Bagram to the Mauryans. During about 120 years of Mauryan rule in southern Afghanistan Buddhism was introduced and became a major religion beside Zoroastrianism and local beliefs. Mauryan punch-marked coins found at Begram point to early trade or administrative presence.

In the first century CE Bagram was the capital of the Kushan Empire. The Bagram treasure indicates intense commercial exchange between the cultural centres of the classical world, with the Kushan Empire at the junction of land and sea trade between east and west. The Begram ivories and other pieces are purely Hellenistic, Roman, Chinese or Indian, with little of the mixing seen in Greco-Buddhist art.

The Islamic conquest of the region began in the seventh century, but conversion was not complete until Ghaznavid rule. The modern town is believed to have been founded by Babur on the ancient site. In the Baburnama he describes a visit in 1519, dwelling on the colony of Hindu ascetics at Gurh Kattri that fascinated him.
A runway was built at Bagram in 1976, and from 1979 to 1989 it was a Soviet air base. It later served as a major base for US forces in Afghanistan, which left it in July 2021.
bagrat-iii-of-georgia: Bagrat was the only known son of King Gurgen of Iberia and Gurandukht, daughter of King George II of Abkhazia. As a child he was adopted and named heir by his father's cousin David III Kuropalates, ruler of Upper Tao, who raised and educated him. In 976 David defeated Kvirike II of Kakheti and expelled the Kakhetians from Iberia, and installed Bagrat as ruler under his father's regency. Two years later, nobles allied with the new prince of Kakheti seized the fortress of Uplistsikhe and took Bagrat and his parents hostage, until David III negotiated their release.

Meanwhile Abkhazia, under the blind King Theodosius III, a maternal uncle of Bagrat, was weakened by conflict with its nobles. The eristavi Ioane Marushisdze, who had installed Bagrat in Iberia, helped to raise him to the Abkhazian crown, generally dated to 978, though some sources give two years later.

Bagrat then had to put down a revolt in Kartli, where his mother Gurandukht, the regent, had tried to assert independence. He defeated the rebels at Moghri, took Uplistsikhe from her and put her under supervision. A later quarrel with the duke Rati, son of Liparit, ended in the king besieging Kldekari. Rati was pardoned and made duke of Argveti.

When David III died on 31 March 1000, possibly murdered, Emperor Basil II claimed Tao, which David had been compelled to bequeath to Byzantium, and took it within months. He gave Bagrat's father Gurgen the title of magistros and Bagrat that of Kouropalates. In 1008 Bagrat inherited the title King of the Georgians from his father, along with the duchy of Lower Tao and Javakheti. He invaded Kakheti and Hereti and had completed the conquest of Kakheti by 1010.

He took the title King of the Abkhazians, Kartvelians, Rans and Kakhs. In 1012 he allied with the Armenian king Gagik I and marched on Ganja, took Shamkor, and made the emir Fadl his vassal, bound to pay tribute. He also defeated the Klarjeti princes Sumbat and Gurgen.

Bagrat spent the winter of 1013–1014 at Panaskerti in Tao and died there on 7 May 1014 after a reign of thirty-six years. He was buried that year in Bedia Cathedral, which he had completed in 999. He founded the office of Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia and began the Bagrati Cathedral at Kutaisi, completed in 1003. His wife Martha bore him George I, who succeeded him.

Most historians regard him as the first monarch of a unified Kingdom of Georgia, excluding the early Iberian ruler Pharnavaz I. Ten later Georgian monarchs took his name. The Georgian Orthodox Church canonised him on 22 December 2016.
bagrat-vi-of-georgia: Bagrat was born around 1435, the son of Prince George, youngest son of Constantine I of Georgia. Around 1455 King George VIII made him Eristavi (duke) of Samokalako, the lands of Kutaisi and western Imereti. In the early 1460s Bagrat supported the rebel Qvarqvare II Jaqeli, atabeg of Samtskhe, and the king deprived him of his duchy. In 1463 he led the coalition of western Georgian nobles that defeated George VIII at the Battle of Chikhori, then captured Kutaisi and was crowned king of Imereti.

In return for their help Bagrat had to create a principality for each of his four allies. From then on the Gelovani ruled Svaneti, the Shervashidze Abkhazia, the Dadiani Odishi (Mingrelia) and the Vardanidze Guria as semi-independent princes. When George VIII was defeated and imprisoned by Qvarqvare of Samtskhe in 1465, Bagrat crossed into Inner Kartli and proclaimed himself King of all Georgia, though in fact he held only western Georgia and Inner Kartli and stayed mostly in the west.

In his western lands he set up a separate church, the Catholicosate of Abkhazia, independent of the Patriarchate of Mtskheta. To justify it he asked Michael IV, Patriarch of Antioch and Jerusalem, to compose a Law of Faith stating that western and eastern Georgia had been converted separately. Once freed, George VIII held only Kakheti, while his nephew Constantine established himself in Lower Kartli, so that Georgia was divided among three rulers.

During these years Uzun Hasan of the Ak Koyunlu attacked Georgia at least twice, and Bagrat had to make peace by abandoning Tbilisi, which the Georgians recovered only after Uzun Hasan's death. In 1477 Vameq II Dadiani, eristav of Odishi, raised the Abkhazians and Gurians and raided Imereti, but Bagrat defeated and subdued him.

Bagrat died in 1478 and was buried at the Gelati Monastery near Kutaisi. His wife Helen outlived him until 3 November 1510. Of their three sons, Alexander II succeeded him and, after a brief failed attempt on the throne, ruled as King of Imereti from 1484 to 1510.
bagrati-cathedral: The Cathedral of the Dormition, known as the Kutaisi Cathedral and more often as Bagrati Cathedral, stands on Ukimerioni Hill in the centre of Kutaisi, in the Imereti region of Georgia. It was built in the early years of the eleventh century during the reign of King Bagrat III, from whom it takes its name, meaning Bagrat's cathedral. An inscription on the north wall states that the floor was laid in the year 223 of the chronicon, that is, 1003.
