The cathedral is dedicated to the Dormition of the Mother of God, and its main feast day is Mariamoba. It is described as a masterpiece of medieval Georgian architecture, and William Lethaby called it the finest of Georgian monuments. King George I of Georgia is buried there.

In 1692 the cathedral was devastated during the Ottoman invasion of the Kingdom of Imereti. The cupola and the ceiling collapsed, and it suffered heavy damage over the following centuries. Conservation, restoration and archaeological work began in the 1950s under the Georgian architect Vakhtang Tsintsadze. His restoration was carried out in six stages and continued through 1994. In that year the cathedral was included in UNESCO's World Heritage list together with the Gelati Monastery as a single entity. In 2001 ownership passed from the Georgian state to the Georgian Orthodox Church, and it is the cathedral seat of the Metropolitan of Kutaisi, with a monastery on the grounds and regular services.

Further works to reconstruct the building ended in 2012 and were controversial. In 2010 UNESCO placed the cathedral on its list of World Heritage in Danger, fearing for the structural integrity and authenticity of the site, and in 2017 it removed Bagrati Cathedral from the World Heritage list, while Gelati Monastery kept its status. The cathedral remains a symbol of the city of Kutaisi and one of its main tourist attractions.
bagrationi-dynasty: The origins of the Bagrationi are disputed. Georgian scholars argue they were of Georgian origin, while Armenian and Western scholars see them as a branch of the Armenian Bagratuni dynasty. A tradition first recorded by the 11th-century chronicler Sumbat Davitis-Dze held that the family descended from the biblical King David and came from Israel around 530. Modern scholarship has discounted this. Cyril Toumanoff concluded that the Georgian line began with Adarnase, who passed to Kartli after a failed rising against Arab rule in 775, and whose son Ashot I acquired the principality of Iberia in 813. The legend of Davidic descent later helped maintain the dynasty's legitimacy.

The sons and grandsons of Ashot I founded three branches, Kartli, Tao and Klarjeti, which fought each other and their neighbours. The Kartli line prevailed, and in 888 Adarnase I restored the Iberian royal authority that had lain dormant since 580. Bagrat III consolidated his inheritance in Tao-Klarjeti and Abkhazia with the help of his foster-father David III of Tao. The united monarchy flourished under David IV the Builder (1089–1125), who finished the unification by retaking Tbilisi in 1122, and under his great-granddaughter Tamar the Great (1184–1213). When the male line ended with George III, the dynasty continued through Tamar's marriage to David Soslan, an Alan prince of reputed Bagratid descent.

The Khwarezmians in 1225 and the Mongols in 1236 ended the golden age. Timur's eight invasions between 1386 and 1403 dealt a heavy blow, and by 1490/91 the kingdom had split into three: Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti, each under a branch of the family. For three centuries they lived under Ottoman and Persian overlordship, and many converted to Islam to be invested by their suzerains.

After the death of Erekle II in 1798 and of his son George XII, Emperor Paul I of Russia declared Kartli-Kakheti annexed on 18 December 1800, and Alexander I formally deposed the dynasty on 12 September 1801. Solomon II of Imereti was dethroned by Russian forces on 20 February 1810 and died in exile in Trabzon in 1815. Most Bagrationi princes who resisted were arrested and deported.

In the Russian Empire the family became prominent aristocrats, among them Prince Pyotr Bagration, a general and hero of the war of 1812. The dynasty remained a Russian noble family until the February Revolution of 1917. After Soviet rule was established in 1921 some members lost property, others moved to Western Europe, and some returned after Georgia regained independence in 1991.
bagratuni-dynasty: The name comes from the Parthian form of the Iranian name Bagadata, God-bearer. The family's origin was long debated. The History of Movses Khorenatsi derives the Bagratuni from a Jew named Shambat; Leo and Grigor Khalatyants thought this an attempt to give the dynasty an older origin, and Nikoghayos Mar linked the claim to a Christian preference for descent from King David. Josef Markwart, Nikoghayos Adontz and Leo saw their ancestor in Bagadat, a general of Tigranes the Great. Kirill Tumanov proposed a relationship with the Yervanduni, and Grigor Kapantsyan and Rafael Matevosyan sought roots in the Urartian and Manai periods. Modern Armenian historiography is largely unanimous that the origin was Armenian.

According to Tumanov, the Bagratids first appear as members of the hereditary nobility of Armenia in the early 4th century. The Arshakuni dynasty, which ruled Armenia from 52 to 428, granted the family hereditary rights, among them the titles aspet, head of cavalry, which appears to have been ceremonial, and taagakir, the privilege of crowning the Arshakuni kings. Their holdings included the Speri region in the valley of the Chorokhi, known for gold and silver, and Tayk. After the Arab invasions of the 7th century, members of the house often bore the title of prince of Armenia but were subordinate to the Muslim ruler appointed by the caliphs.

The chronicler Stepannos Orbelian reports that Armenian princes, among them the rulers of Syunik, asked the Arab governor to make Ashot Bagratuni king. The kingdom lasted from about 885 until 1045. Bagaran was the capital under Ashot I, Kars from 928 to 961, and later Ani. From the middle of the 10th century large feudal houses grew stronger and more independent, and new kingdoms arose, in addition to Vaspurakan, in Syunik; Soviet Armenian historiography calls this a period of fragmentation.

In 1042 Constantine Monomakh took the Byzantine throne and, as heir to the will of Hovhannes-Smbat, demanded his inheritance from King Gagik II. Gagik tried diplomacy and then resisted; two Byzantine campaigns in 1044 failed. Monomakh then invited Gagik to Constantinople, where after a month he agreed to hand Ani over in exchange for Kalon Pelat and Pisa in Cappadocia and a palace in Constantinople. At home, Vahram Sparapet, who held out for resistance, was isolated, and at the beginning of 1045 Ani, and with it the kingdom, surrendered to Byzantium. Many historians, among them Toumanoff, Adontz and Suny, regard the Bagratuni as the progenitors of the Georgian royal Bagrationi dynasty.
bagyidaw: He was born Maung Sein on 23 July 1784, the son of Crown Prince Thado Minsaw, Prince of Shwedaung, and his half-sister Min Kye, Princess of Taungdwin. His grandfather King Bodawpaya granted the infant Sagaing as his fief, and he was commonly known in his day as the Prince of Sagaing. Not yet nine, he was made a general of the Northern and Southern Corps of Royal Cavalry in 1793. In 1803 he married Princess Hsinbyume, and he was fond of theatre, elephant catching and boat racing.

After his father's death Bodawpaya raised him to crown prince, which brought his servants Maung Yit, later General Maha Bandula, and Maung Sa, later Lord of Myawaddy, to prominence. When Hsinbyume died in childbirth in 1812 he built the Myatheindan Pagoda at Mingun in her memory. His chief queen, Nanmadaw Me Nu, built the brick Maha Aungmye Bonzan Monastery in 1818.

Crowned at Amarapura on 7 June 1819, he soon faced the vassal Raja Marjit Singh of Manipur, who failed to attend the coronation. In October 1819 a force of 25,000 soldiers and 3,000 cavalry under Maha Bandula reconquered Manipur, and by July 1822 Bandula had defeated the Assamese king Chandrakanta Singha. Burmese accounts say Assam was made a province under a military governor-general; Assamese accounts say a new Ahom king, Jogeswar Singha, was installed. Bagyidaw moved the capital from Amarapura back to Ava in 1823.

Raids from British protectorates continued, and a war party of Bandula, Queen Me Nu and her brother urged a decisive blow. War broke out on 5 March 1824. A British naval force under Archibald Campbell took Yangon on 11 May, Bandula's attempt to retake it failed in December, and Bandula was killed in the Irrawaddy delta. Of some 40,000 British and Indian troops involved, 15,000 were killed.

The British used Tenasserim as bait for the indemnity, returned the Kabaw Valley in 1830, and kept the other territories after the last payment in November 1832. The king grew reclusive and suffered bouts of depression, and power passed to Me Nu and her brother Maung O. His brother Tharrawaddy rebelled in February 1837, Bagyidaw abdicated on 30 April, and the new king executed Me Nu and her brother. Bagyidaw lived under house arrest until his death on 15 October 1846. His reign is seen as the beginning of the Konbaung dynasty's decline.
baha-al-dawla: Baha al-Dawla, born Abu Nasr Firuz Kharshadh, was the third son of Adud al-Dawla; his laqab means Splendour of the State. In 986 the Dailamite officer Asfar ibn Kurdawayh rebelled against Samsam al-Dawla, the ruler of Iraq, and declared for Firuz, who was soon given his epithet. Samsam al-Dawla, aided by Fuladh ibn Manadhar, put down the revolt and imprisoned him, releasing him when he made peace with Sharaf al-Dawla. Sharaf al-Dawla then betrayed Samsam al-Dawla, conquered Iraq and had him imprisoned in a fortress.

On succeeding Sharaf al-Dawla he took the further title Diya al-Milla, but Samsam al-Dawla escaped and seized Fars, Kerman and Khuzestan. Threatened by their granduncle Fakhr al-Dawla of Jibal, who invaded Khuzestan, the brothers allied: Baha al-Dawla kept Iraq and Khuzestan, Samsam al-Dawla Arrajan, Fars and Kerman, and both took the title of king (malik). In 991 Baha al-Dawla claimed the old Persian title of Shahanshah and invaded his brother's lands, but his forces were defeated and Khuzestan was lost.

After the death of Fakhr al-Dawla in 997 he prepared a new expedition with the support of the Hasanwayhid ruler Badr ibn Hasanwayh. It began in December 998; Samsam al-Dawla was killed almost at once by rebel sons of Izz al-Dawla, and Baha al-Dawla took Shiraz, defeated the rebels and was joined by the Dailamites of Fars. He stayed in Fars for the rest of his life, making Ibn Ustadh-Hurmuz governor of Ahvaz in 1001 and of Iraq a year later, and in 1007 made Ali ibn Mazyad his vassal. By 1009 or 1010 Majd al-Dawla and Shams al-Dawla, the sons of Fakhr al-Dawla, recognised him as senior amir.

His reign marks the beginning of the Buyids' decline. The Kurdish chief Badh laid the foundations of the Marwanid amirate in Diyarbakr, the Uqaylids of Mosul expanded into Iraq, the Ziyarids of Gorgan and Tabaristan broke free, the Ghaznavids pressed on the Khurasan border and the Kakuyids began a state in Isfahan. He did little to defend the borders, and when he died in Arrajan in December 1012 Baghdad and Wasit were the only major Iraqi cities he directly held. Shortly before, he had named his son Sultan al-Dawla his successor.
baha-al-din-al-amili: Baha al-Din Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Amili came of an Arab family from Jabal Amil, which had moved from a village near Jezzine. After the execution in 1558 of al-Shahid al-Tani, his father's teacher, the family went to the Safavid Empire, first to Isfahan and then to Qazvin, the royal capital, where Tahmasp I appointed his father Husayn ibn Abd al-Samad shaykh al-Islam in several cities, Herat among them. Baha al-Din completed his studies in Isfahan. Setting out for Mecca in 1570, he spent four years travelling in Iraq, Syria and Egypt before returning to Iran.

Shah Abbas I admired his learning and made him Sheikh ul-Islam of Isfahan. In the Twelver tradition he is regarded as a mujaddid of the seventeenth century, and he wrote on tafsir, hadith, grammar and fiqh. He had a distinct Sufi leaning, for which Mohammad Baqer Majlesi criticised him: he dressed as a dervish on his travels and appears in the chains of the Nurbakhshi and Ni'matullahi orders, yet he held strict observance of the Sharia to be the condition for the mystical path. Much of the planning of Safavid Isfahan is credited to him, as are the canal network of the Zayanderud and a public bath heated by a single candle, but none of the designs attributed to him can be substantiated from sources.

He probably wrote 17 works on astronomy. In Tashrih al-Aflak, a summary of theoretical astronomy, he argued that the rotation of the Earth was possible, independent of Western influence, and another treatise addressed problems of the Moon and Mercury in the Ptolemaic system. His Arabic arithmetic Khulasat al-Hisab was used from Egypt to India into the 19th century and was translated into German by G. H. F. Nesselmann in 1843. In Persian he wrote Jame-e Abbasi and the masnavis Shir u Shakar and Nan u Halwa, and his Kashkul gathers stories, proverbs and scientific topics. He died in Isfahan and was buried in Mashhad, as his will asked.
bahadur-shah-ii: Bahadur Shah Zafar, born on 24 October 1775, was the second son of Akbar II and succeeded him in 1837. By then the Mughal Empire had been reduced to the city of Delhi and the territory around it as far as Palam. The East India Company was the dominant power in India, provided the emperor with a pension, and collected taxes in Delhi and maintained a military force there. Zafar had no interest in statecraft or imperial ambition.

He was a noted Urdu poet and wrote many ghazals. His court was home to Mirza Ghalib, Daagh Dehlvi, Momin Khan Momin and Mohammad Ibrahim Zauq, who was also his mentor. He was a devout Sufi, and in one of his verses he stated that Hinduism and Islam share the same essence.

When sepoys of the rebellion reached Delhi in May 1857, Zafar asked why they had come, since he had no means to maintain them. He yielded to their demands when told that they could not defeat the Company without him. On 16 May sepoys and palace servants killed fifty-two Europeans held prisoner in the palace, despite his protests. It was later believed that he was not directly responsible but might have prevented the killings.

As the siege of Delhi turned against the rebels, Zafar took refuge at Humayun's Tomb. Company forces under Major William Hodson captured him on 20 September 1857. The next day Hodson shot his sons Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan and his grandson Mirza Abu Bakht.

Zafar's trial in the Red Fort in 1858 lasted 21 days. He was charged with aiding the mutinies, encouraging war against the British Government, assuming the sovereignty of Hindostan, and being accessory to the murder of Christians. In his defence he stated that he was helpless before the will of the sepoys. Because of Hodson's guarantee on his surrender, he was exiled to Rangoon rather than sentenced to death.

He died on 7 November 1862 at the age of 87 and was buried that afternoon near the Shwedagon Pagoda. His exile ended the nearly 500-year Timurid line, and he is seen as a hero of the rebellion of 1857.
bahadur-shah-of-gujarat: Born Bahadur Khan into the Muzaffarid dynasty, he was the son of Prince Khalil Khan, who became sultan in 1511 as Muzaffar Shah II, and of Rani Lakshmi Bai, daughter of a Gohel Rajput. His grandfather, Sultan Mahmud Begada, kept him at court. When his elder brother Sikandar Shah was named heir, Bahadur Khan feared for his life and fled, first to Chittor and then to Ibrahim Lodi; he was present at the Battle of Panipat without taking part in the fighting.

Muzaffar Shah II died in 1526. Sikandar Shah was murdered after a few weeks on the instructions of his slave Imad-ul-Mulk Khush Kadam, who put an infant brother on the throne as Mahmud Shah II. Bahadur Khan returned, the nobles joined him, and he marched on Champaner, executed Imad-ul-Mulk and had the child poisoned.

Bahadur Shah campaigned in the Deccan in 1528 and 1529, taking the fort of Ahmednagar and forcing the rulers of Ahmadnagar and Berar to sign a humiliating treaty. The fortress of Mandu fell on 28 March 1531, when Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Malwa and his seven sons were captured; they were later put to death by their guards during a rescue attempt. In 1532 he raised a siege of Chittor in return for an enormous ransom. Until his defeat by Humayun the power of Gujarat was at its height, with the rulers of Ahmednagar and Burhanpur acknowledging him as overlord.

The quarrel with Humayun began because Bahadur Shah had sheltered the Mughal prince Muhammad Zaman Mirza. The rout near Mandasur is usually explained by the treachery of Rumi Khan, the Turkish head of the Gujarat artillery. Bahadur Shah fled to Mandu, Champaner and finally Diu. When Humayun left to face the revolt of Sher Shah Suri, the country rose, and Bahadur Shah defeated the Mughals at Kanij and expelled them from Gujarat.

The Treaty of Bassein was signed on 23 December 1534 aboard the galleon St. Mattheus. Having recovered his kingdom, Bahadur Shah regretted the alliance. In February 1537 he visited the Portuguese viceroy's ship off Diu and was attacked and killed on his way back, on 13 February; his body was thrown into the sea. According to the Mirat-i-Sikandari, the viceroy had intercepted his message inviting the Deccan sultans to ally against the Portuguese. He left no son, and after his chosen heir, his nephew Miran Muhammad Shah of Khandesh, died on the way to Gujarat, the nobles chose Mahmud Shah III, son of his brother Latif Khan.
bahia: Bahia lies in the Northeast Region of Brazil, bordered on the east by the Atlantic Ocean, which gives it the longest coastline of any Brazilian state, 1,103 km. Salvador stands on a spit of land that separates the Bay of All Saints, the largest bay on the Brazilian coast, from the Atlantic. The state has three main regions: the Atlantic Forest and the maritime Recôncavo around the bay, a centre of sugar and tobacco cultivation; the Chapada Diamantina, a mountainous plateau; and the dry sertão of the far interior. Under the Brazilian Empire its borders were the Rio Real in the north and the Jequitinhonha in the south, but some neighbouring states were later formed from it.

Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted Monte Pascoal and landed at what is now Porto Seguro on the southern coast in 1500, claiming the territory for Portugal. In 1549 Portugal established the city of Salvador on a hill facing the Bay of All Saints. The city and its captaincy served as an administrative capital of Portugal's American colonies until 1763 and remained the religious capital of the Brazilian Catholic hierarchy, its archbishop serving as national primate until 1907. Bahia's captaincy was the first to fail, its lands reverting to the Portuguese crown in 1549. While Portugal was united with Spain the Dutch West India companies tried to conquer Bahia without success, and Dutch Brazil was restricted to the area from Pernambuco northward.

Bahia was once a stronghold of supporters of direct rule of Brazil by the Portuguese monarchy and was dominated by agricultural, slaving and ranching interests. It was the chief centre of the early Brazilian slave trade. A slave rebellion known as the Revolt of the Tailors took place in 1798. Salvador holds the country's oldest cathedral and its first medical college, founded in 1810. In the 19th century the Bahian abolitionist poet Castro Alves, from Cachoeira, wrote the poem Navio negreiro about slavery, regarded as a central anti-slavery text.

Because of its place in the slave trade, Bahia is considered to have the most distinctive African imprint in Brazil. This includes the Yoruba-derived religion of Candomblé, capoeira, African-derived music such as samba-de-roda, and a cuisine with strong links to West Africa, mainly in Salvador. In the interior the vaqueiro culture of cattle farmers dates from the 1550s. Bahia is the fourth most populous Brazilian state, with a population of over 14 million, and Salvador, its capital, includes a World Heritage Site in the Pelourinho. Once a year the capital moves to Cachoeira, in recognition of that city's part in the struggle for Brazilian independence.
bahla: Bahla is a town in the Ad Dakhiliyah Governorate of Oman, about 40 km from Nizwa and about 200 km from Muscat, the capital of Oman. It lies at the foot of Djebel Akhdar, where the fortresses of Rustaq to the north and Izki, Nizwa and Bahla to the south have each been a capital at some time and so played an important part in Omani history. Most of its buildings are of traditional mud brick, many of them hundreds of years old. The town and its fort are enclosed by the remains of a fortified wall 12 km long.

Bahla's history is said to reach back to 3000 BCE, and its pottery to as early as 2500 BCE. The clay comes from the wadi, where men trample it to make it pliable; the finished object is then fired in a kiln. Oman was a hub of the frankincense trade, and from the 16th to the 19th century its sultans ruled a trading empire stretching from the coast of East Africa to the tip of the Indian subcontinent. In the mountains below Djebel Akhdar, Kharijite communities resisted all attempts at normalisation by the Caliph Harun al-Rashid and put into practice religious concepts that were at once radically puritanical and democratic.

The oasis owed its prosperity to the Banu Nabhan, who from the mid-12th to the end of the 15th century imposed their rule on the other tribes. The adobe walls and towers of the great fort stand on a stone base. They probably include some elements from before Islam, but most of the construction dates from the time of the Banu Nabhan, and the latest reconstruction was at the beginning of the 16th century. At the foot of the fort, to the south-west, stands the Friday Mosque, whose sculpted mihrab probably dates from the 14th century.

Bahla Fort is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the largest forts in Oman. The old souq stands across the main road that leads to it, and its shops sell mostly pottery, silver and other traditional handcrafted items. Bahla was long known for its Qur'anic schools and mosques and as a centre for scholars and imams, among them Abu 'Ubaidah Abdullah bin al-Qasim in the 8th century and Sheikh Mohammed ibn Barakah in the 10th, whose school attracted students from the Maghreb. Jabrin Castle, with painted ceilings and carved interiors, lies 5 km to the south-west.
bahlul-lodi: Bahlul Lodi was the chief of the Pashtun Lodi tribe. His grandfather Malik Bahram Lodi, a tribal chief from Dera Ismail, took service under the governor of Multan. Bahram's eldest son, Malik Sultan Shah Lodi, served the Sayyid dynasty under Khizr, killed Khizr's worst enemy Mallu Iqbal Khan in battle, and in 1419 was appointed governor of Sirhind with the title Islam Khan.

Bahlul was the son of Malik Kala Lodi, Sultan Shah's younger brother, and married Sultan Shah's daughter. In his youth he traded horses and sold finely bred animals to the Sayyid sultan Muhammad Shah, who paid him with a pargana and raised him to amir. After Sultan Shah's death he became governor of Sirhind and was allowed to add Lahore.

When Mahmud Khalji of Malwa invaded, Muhammad Shah asked for help and Bahlul joined the imperial army with 20,000 horsemen. By his cleverness he presented himself as the victor over the Malwa army, and the sultan gave him the title Bahlul and accepted his occupation of a large part of the Punjab.

He attacked Delhi without success in 1443 and again in 1447, under the last Sayyid ruler Alam Shah. In 1448 Alam Shah retired to Badaun, and his minister Mohamad Hamid invited Bahlul to take the throne. After Alam Shah's voluntary abdication, Bahlul ascended the throne of Delhi on 19 April 1451 as Bahlul Shah Ghazi, founder of the Lodi dynasty. Alam Shah lived on at Badaun until July 1478.

Bahlul decided to dispose of Hamid, who was imprisoned by his cousin and brother-in-law Malik Mahmud, governor of Samana. In 1479 he defeated and annexed the Jaunpur Sultanate, fortified Jaunpur and made it a kasbah with several mosques and madrasas. He worked to stop rebellions, extended his holdings over Jaunpur and upper Uttar Pradesh, and kept Delhi as his capital. In 1486 he appointed his son Babrak Shah viceroy of Jaunpur.

Bahlul died on 12 July 1489. His second son Nizamudin, later Sikandar Lodi, had been named successor, and a power struggle followed his death. The site of his grave is disputed. The Archeological Survey of India has long designated a building near the shrine of the Sufi saint Nasiruddin Chirag-e-Delhi as his tomb, while other historians identify the Sheesh Gumbad in the Lodi Gardens as it. He married twice: Shams Khatun, his first cousin and the daughter of Malik Sultan Shah Lodi, and Bibi Ambha, the daughter of a Hindu goldsmith.
bahnar-people: The Bahnar, or Ba-Na, are an indigenous people of the Central Highland provinces of Gia Lai and Kon Tum and also live in the coastal provinces of Bình Định and Phú Yên. Their language, Bahnar, belongs to the Bahnaric group of the Mon-Khmer, or Austroasiatic, family. The name is similar to the Khmer word phnom, meaning mountain, and they are known by many other names, among them Bonom, Jolong, Rongao, Tolo, Kriem and Roh.

They include several sub-groups, such as the Bahnar Jơlơng, Rơngao, Gơlar, Kriem, Tơlô and Roh. The Haroi, now counted as a sub-group of the Cham people, are said to have been Bahnar who lived in the Champa city-states and were slowly assimilated into the Cham, adopting their language and culture.

Most Bahnar follow traditional religions, animism and polytheism, and like other peoples of the Central Highlands, the Montagnards, they include a large Christian population. Their epics, called H'amon, such as Dam Noi, carry the aspirations of the people over centuries. They play many traditional instruments, including ensembles of pitched gongs and string instruments made of bamboo, sometimes in concert on special occasions with ceremonial drinking of rice wine, rượu cần, and group dancing.

The festival of Koh Kpo, or Groong Kpo Tonơi, gives thanks to Yang, the god, and its main rite is the stabbing of a water buffalo. A possible Chamic reconstruction of the name means Dedication to the God of the Corn, and Bahnar today shorten it further to Gong Kpo.

Bahnar figures of the past include Dinh Nup, a hero who led villagers in a war of resistance against the French colonial regime and became the main character of the novel Đất nước đứng lên (A Rising Nation) by Nguyên Ngọc, and Ya Do, a heroine who was the wife of Nguyễn Nhạc.
bahrain: Bahrain is a generally flat and arid archipelago in the Persian Gulf, lying between Qatar and the northeastern coast of Saudi Arabia. A low desert plain rises gently to a low central escarpment, whose highest point is the 134 metre Mountain of Smoke (Jabal ad Dukhan). About 92 per cent of the country is desert, with periodic droughts and dust storms. Land reclamation has enlarged the area from 665 to 780 square kilometres, and by August 2008 the number of islands and island groups had risen from 33 to 84.

The name Bahrain is the dual form of the Arabic word bahr, 'sea', so al-Bahrayn originally means 'the two seas'. Which two seas is disputed: the bay east and west of the island, the seas north and south of it, and the salt and fresh water above and below the ground have all been proposed. The term appears five times in the Quran but does not refer to the modern island, which the Arabs originally called Awal. Until the late Middle Ages 'Bahrain' meant a region of Eastern Arabia stretching from Basra in Iraq to the Strait of Hormuz.

Bahrain was home to Dilmun, a Bronze Age trade centre linking Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, and was later ruled by the Sumerians and Babylonians. From the 6th to the 3rd century BCE it was part of the Achaemenid Empire. By about 250 BCE Parthia had brought the Persian Gulf under its control, and it established garrisons along the southern coast of the Gulf to control trade routes.

The ancient Greeks called the island Tylos and knew it as a centre of pearl trading. The admiral Nearchus, serving under Alexander the Great, is believed to have been the first of Alexander's commanders to visit it. He recorded large plantations of cotton trees on Tylos, from which cloth called sindones was made. Bahrain became part of the Hellenised world: the language of the upper classes was Greek, with Aramaic in everyday use, and local coinage shows a seated Zeus, who may have been worshipped there as a form of the Arabian sun-god Shams.

Bahrain is a kingdom, a semi-constitutional monarchy since 2002, with a bicameral National Assembly. Its capital and largest city is Manama. The King Fahd Causeway, completed in December 1986, links it with the Saudi Arabian mainland. It has been ruled by the Al Khalifa family since 1783 and became independent from the United Kingdom in 1971.
bahrain-island: Bahrain Island, also called Awal Island and formerly Bahrein, forms the bulk of the land area of the Bahrain archipelago and holds most of its people. It lies mostly in a shallow inlet of the Persian Gulf known as the Gulf of Bahrain. The seabed beside it is rocky and, mainly off the northern part of the island, covered by extensive coral reefs. Most of the island is low-lying, barren desert. Outcrops of limestone form low rolling hills, stubby cliffs and shallow ravines, and the limestone is covered by saline sand that supports only hardy desert vegetation, chiefly thorn trees and scrub.

A fertile strip about 5 km wide runs along the northern coast, where date, almond, fig and pomegranate trees grow. In the interior an escarpment rises to 134 m, the highest point on the island. It is called the Mountain of Smoke because mists often wreathe its summit, and most of the country's oil wells stand near it. The climate is arid, with an average annual temperature of 28 °C, about 38 °C in August and 18 °C in January, and average annual rainfall of 144 millimetres, most of it in November.

Manama, the capital of the Kingdom of Bahrain, stands on the north-eastern tip of the island. The main port, Mina Salman, and the major oil refining facilities and commercial centres are also on the island, which is divided among three of the country's governorates. Causeways and bridges link it to neighbouring islands and to the mainland of Saudi Arabia.

The oldest causeway, built in 1929, joins it to Muharraq Island, the third largest, which three further crossings connect with Manama. Sitra, on its eastern shore and linked by a bridge, is the site of the main oil export terminal. On the west a causeway leads to Umm an Nasan and continues through the King Fahd Causeway to the Saudi town of Al Khobar.
bahram-chobin: Bahram was a member of the House of Mihran, one of the seven Great Houses of Iran, a family of Parthian origin centred on Ray. His father, Bahram Gushnasp, fought the Byzantines and campaigned in Yemen under Khosrow I, and his grandfather Gurgin Milad was marzban of Armenia from 572 to 574. His nickname Chobin, 'wooden shaft' or 'javelin-like', referred to his tall, slender build; his epithet Mihrbandak means servant of Mithra. Parvaneh Pourshariati argues that he was probably a worshipper of Mithra, since both Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and Sebeos record him as one.

Bahram began as marzban of Ray, took part in the capture of the Byzantine stronghold of Dara, and became army chief (spahbed) of the north. In 588 the Turkic khagan Bagha Qaghan and his Hephthalite subjects invaded the Sasanian lands south of the Oxus and took Balkh, Talaqan, Badghis and Herat. Bahram, given the governorship of Khorasan and a reported 12,000 hand-picked horsemen, ambushed them at Hyrcanian rock in April 588 and again in 589, retook Balkh, crossed the Oxus and personally killed Bagha Qaghan with an arrow. His victory reached as far as Baykand, near Bukhara.

The shah Hormizd IV, already distrustful, removed him from office and humiliated him; sources differ on the reason, and the Sasanian court was suspicious of his rising fame. Bahram rebelled, the first time a Parthian dynast had challenged the Sasanian family's legitimacy. Before he reached Ctesiphon, Hormizd was blinded and killed in a palace coup that put his son Khosrow II on the throne. Bahram defeated Khosrow's men at the Nahrawan Canal and took Ctesiphon, and in the summer of 590 declared himself king of kings, claiming to restore the Arsacids.

Many hailed Bahram as the promised saviour of Zoroastrian apocalyptic belief, but nobles and priests largely sided with Khosrow II, who gained Byzantine help from the emperor Maurice. In 591 Khosrow and the Byzantine armies invaded Mesopotamia, and Bahram was defeated at the Battle of Blarathon. He fled east with 4,000 men to the Turkic khagan, probably Birmudha, whom he had once captured, and served him until Khosrow had him assassinated through bribes to the Turkic royal family.

His son Noshrad was the ancestor of the Samanids, who stressed their descent from him. Bahram's life is told in the Pahlavi romance Bahrām Chōbīn Nāma, and the Shahnameh chapters on Hormizd IV and Khosrow II are almost as much about him. Among Iranian nationalists he remained popular after the Arab conquest.
bahram-v: Bahram was born around 400, the son of the Sasanian shah Yazdegerd I. As a boy he was sent to the Lakhmid court at al-Hira, where the king al-Nu'man I provided teachers from the Sasanian court to instruct him in law, archery and horsemanship. When Yazdegerd I was murdered in 420, the nobles and priests elected Khosrow, a son of Bahram IV, as shah.

Bahram refused this and asked for help from the Lakhmid king al-Mundhir I, who gave him an army. According to a long-standing legend in the Shahnameh, he proposed that the royal crown and robes be placed between two lions and that whoever retrieved them should be shah. Khosrow withdrew and Bahram won the throne. Distrusting the nobles, he turned to the Zoroastrian priesthood and was the first Sasanian shah crowned by a chief priest.

He began his reign with a persecution of the Christians. Refugees fled to Roman territory, and when the Sasanians asked for their return Theodosius II declared war instead. In 421 the Roman general Ardaburius entered Armenia and defeated the Iranian general Narses, then besieged Nisibis but withdrew when Bahram advanced. The peace of 422 restored the earlier position, with both sides agreeing to guarantee freedom of religion in their territories.

While Bahram was occupied in the west, the Kidarites crossed the Oxus, took the rich city of Marw and reached as far as Ray. After the peace with Rome Bahram marched to Merv, where his forces routed the Kidarites and killed their king. The war ended in 427. He set up a pillar at the Oxus to mark it as his eastern frontier, and the Sogdian city of Bukhara later struck coins with his image. Armenia became a frontier province governed by a marzban.

Bahram died in 438 and his manner of death is unclear. Ferdowsi says he died in his sleep, while Nizami and Amir Khusrau say he vanished in a cave while chasing an onager. His son Yazdegerd II succeeded him. He is remembered for cancelling taxes and debts at celebrations, for encouraging musicians, and for his love of hunting, which gave him the epithet Gur, 'onager'. Nizami's romance Haft Peykar, of 1197, tells of the seven princesses who became his wives.
bai-bureh: Bai Bureh was born in Kasseh, a village near Port Loko in the north-west of Sierra Leone. His father was a Muslim cleric and an important Loko chief, and his mother a Temne trader from Makeni. As a young man he was sent to the village of Gbendembu to be trained as a warrior, where he earned the nickname Kebalai, translated as one who does not tire of war. On his return he was crowned ruler of Kasseh.

In the 1860s and 1870s he became the leading warrior of Port Loko and the whole north, fighting villages and chiefs who opposed his plan to establish correct Islamic and indigenous practices. In 1882 his fighters drove Susu invaders from French Guinea out of Kambia and returned the land to its people. In 1886 he was crowned chief of Northern Sierra Leone. He would not cooperate with the colonial government in Freetown and refused to recognise a peace treaty the British had made with the Limba without him.

The hut tax introduced on 1 January 1893 could be paid in money, grain, stock or labour. Bai Bureh argued that his people should not pay tribute to foreign rulers and that chiefs should settle their own affairs. When Governor Frederic Cardew offered one hundred pounds for his capture, he offered five hundred pounds for the governor's. In 1898 he declared war.

His fighters were mostly Temne and Loko, joined by men from Limba, Kissi and Kuranko villages; they also killed dozens of Creoles they believed supported the government, among them the trader John Taylor. By 19 February 1898 they had cut the road and river links between Freetown and Port Loko. The war cost hundreds of casualties on both sides.

On 11 November 1898 a patrol of the newly organised West African Regiment tracked him down in swampy country near Port Loko. Crowds gathered in Freetown to see him. He was exiled to the Gold Coast with the Sherbro chief Kpana Lewis and the Mende chief Nyagua, both of whom died there; Bai Bureh returned to be reinstated as chief of Kasseh and died in 1908.

Some historians attribute his escape from execution to British admiration for him as an adversary. A large statue of him stands in central Freetown, and his portrait appears on the one-leone banknote issued in 2022. The only known photograph of him was found for sale on eBay in August 2012 and put on display in the Sierra Leone National Museum in 2013.
bai-qi: Bai Qi, also known as Bo Qi and Gongsun Qi, was born around 332 BCE in Mei, in present-day Mei County, Shaanxi. Later writers gave him different ancestries: the New Book of Tang traced him to Baiyi Bing, a general of Duke Mu of Qin, while the Tang poet Bai Juyi claimed descent from Baigong Sheng, a grandson of King Ping of Chu. He commanded the Qin army for more than 30 years under King Zhaoxiang of Qin, who promoted him to the rank of Da Liang Zao in 292 BCE.

His campaigns were marked by mass killing. At Yique in 293 BCE his army reportedly slaughtered around 240,000 enemy soldiers, and at the capture of Ying in 278 BCE he reportedly drowned 100,000 people in a flood attack, earning the title Lord Wu'an. In 273 BCE he defeated Zhao and Wei at Huayang and massacred about 150,000 soldiers who had submitted. In 264 BCE he took five Han fortresses and beheaded 50,000 men.

At Changping in 260 BCE he replaced Wang He as Qin commander after Zhao had put the inexperienced Zhao Kuo in place of Lian Po. He split the Zhao army and cut its supply lines and retreat; after Zhao Kuo was shot dead, more than 400,000 Zhao soldiers who had surrendered were buried alive on his orders. According to the Shiji he seized more than 73 cities, and no record shows him losing a battle.

Bai Qi wished to finish Zhao, but the prime minister Fan Ju, fearing his power, persuaded the king to halt and negotiate. When Qin besieged Handan in 257 BCE, Bai Qi pleaded illness, argued that Qin lacked the resources for a long war and refused command several times while the siege failed under Wang Ling and Wang He. The angry king stripped his titles, expelled him from Xianyang and, persuaded by Fan Ju that he might serve another state, forced him to kill himself at Duyou.

Before dying Bai Qi said he deserved his end for killing so many. Known as Ren Tu, the human butcher, he is remembered in China more as a symbol of brutality than of military talent, and human remains are still found at Changping.
baia-romania: Baia is a commune in Suceava County, in the historical region of Western Moldavia in north-eastern Romania, on the Moldova River. It consists of two villages, Baia and Bogata. The Romanian word baia and the Hungarian bánya both mean mine. The town was also called Târgul Moldovei, the market of Moldavia, and its Hungarian name was Moldvabánya. A Latin name, Civitas Moldaviae, appears on an early seal of the town, and German names included Baja, Stadt Molde and Moldenmarkt.

A settlement has existed at Baia since the 13th century, and the first written evidence is from the following century. A document from Poland of 1335 may mention it, and in 1345 Baia appears on a list of towns of the Franciscan missionaries. The army of King Louis I of Hungary passed through it when conquering the region around 1345 to 1347. Early Moldavian chronicles place the first capital of Moldavia in Baia, but it was only an interim capital, and the court soon moved to Siret.

After the Hungarian conquest, colonists from Transylvania settled in the town, which gained a special status. According to the chronicler Grigore Ureche, the market at Baia was founded by German potters. The colonists built a wooden church and a central marketplace. By 1400 the houses were heated by cocklestoves, the streets were paved with river gravel and a wooden palisade defended the town. Documents of the 15th century speak of the Saxons in Baia, and the local council and the mayors were at first elected among the Germans.

In 1467 Matthias Corvinus began an expedition against Ștefan the Great, who had conquered the stronghold of Chilia, previously held by Hungary. His armies set fire to the Moldavian towns of Trotuș, Bacău, Roman and Neamț, but he spared Baia and settled in a fortified stone house in its centre. Ștefan the Great attacked and burnt the town on the night of 15 December 1467, in the prelude to the Battle of Baia.

The town declined after the Protestant Reformation and the persecutions of Catholics in the 16th century, when the Catholics of Baia turned to Protestantism. The last bishop of Baia is recorded in 1523. Suceava took over its importance in trade, and Baia reverted to being a simple village. At the 2021 census the commune had 7,261 inhabitants, 93.49 per cent of them Romanians.
baikonur-cosmodrome: The cosmodrome lies on the Kazakh Steppe about 90 metres above sea level, 200 kilometres east of the Aral Sea and 33 kilometres north of the Syr Darya, close to Töretam, a station on the Trans-Aral Railway. It is the largest operational space launch facility in terms of area. The site was chosen by a commission led by General Vasily Voznyuk, influenced by Sergey Korolyov, chief designer of the R-7 missile. It had to be surrounded by plains, because the rocket's radio control system needed uninterrupted signals from ground stations hundreds of kilometres away, and the trajectory had to lie away from populated areas. A site nearer the equator is also an advantage. The commission chose Tyuratam, a village in the heart of the steppe.

The Soviet government issued the decree for Scientific Research Test Range No. 5 on 12 February 1955, and the range was founded on 2 June 1955 as a test centre for the R-7 Semyorka, the first intercontinental ballistic missile. It was soon expanded with launch facilities for space flights. The cost of the launch facilities and of several hundred kilometres of new road and railway made it one of the most costly infrastructure projects of the Soviet Union. A supporting town was built for the workers and became the city of Leninsk in 1966.

An American U-2 reconnaissance plane first photographed the range on 5 August 1957. Until 1991 its primary purpose was to test liquid-fuelled ballistic missiles, and it remained under the control of the Ministry of Defense until the second half of the 1990s.

Many historic flights began here: Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957, Luna 1, the first spacecraft to pass close to the Moon, on 2 January 1959, Yuri Gagarin's flight on 12 April 1961 and Valentina Tereshkova's in 1963. In 1960 a prototype R-16 missile exploded before launch and killed over 100 people.

Most sources say the name Baikonur was chosen about 1961 to mislead the Western Bloc towards a mining town some 320 kilometres to the northeast; NASA's history says it was the name of the Tyuratam region. Leninsk was renamed Baikonur on 20 December 1995.

Russia has retained control of the facility since the Soviet Union ended, first through the Commonwealth of Independent States, and in 2005 ratified an agreement with Kazakhstan to lease it until 2050. All Russian crewed spaceflights are launched from Baikonur, which has supported the Soyuz, Proton, Tsyklon, Dnepr, Zenit and Buran rockets. Its internal railway, of 1,520 mm gauge, is the largest industrial railway in the world. A museum beside the cottages once used by Korolyov and Gagarin holds space artefacts, and a test article of the Buran programme stands at its entrance.
baiyue: The Baiyue, Hundred Yue, or simply Yue, were various ethnic groups of southern China and northern Vietnam, known for their short hair, body tattoos, fine swords and naval prowess. The term Baiyue first appears in the Lüshi Chunqiu, compiled around 239 BCE, and was later used as a collective term for many non-Huaxia, non-Han populations of the south. According to Chunming Wu, their prehistoric ancestors were active seafarers who communicated with proto-Austronesians in Southeast Asia and the Pacific. The Baiyue were mostly Austronesian and Kra-Dai in ethnicity, though some were perhaps related to Hmong-Mien or Austroasiatic groups, and they were not necessarily related to one another.

From the 9th century BCE two Yue tribes, the Gouwu and the Yuyue, came under the cultural influence of their northern Chinese neighbours. Traditional accounts attribute the exchange to Taibo, a Zhou prince who had gone into exile in the south. In the Spring and Autumn period the Gouwu founded the state of Wu and the Yuyue the state of Yue. After Qin Shi Huang unified China, those states were absorbed, and Qin armies advanced south along the Xiang River into modern Guangdong. He allegedly sent half a million troops in five armies against the Yue, who defeated the first attack and killed the Qin commander.

Zhao Tuo, a Qin general born around 240 BCE in the state of Zhao, served as magistrate of Nanhai. After the Qin fell in 206 BCE he had also conquered Guilin and Xiang, and he declared himself King Wu of Nanyue, with his capital at Panyu, modern Guangzhou. Unlike Qin Shi Huang, he respected Yue customs, let local chieftains keep their traditions and encouraged settlers to intermarry with the Yue. In 111 BCE the Han conquered Nanyue and divided it into nine commanderies and two outpost commands, seeking its maritime trade routes and luxury goods such as pearls, ivory and incense.

Periods of war in the north sent waves of Han Chinese southward, and intermarriage with the indigenous peoples quickened sinicisation. By the Tang dynasty Yue had become largely a regional name. Features of southern Chinese vocabulary, phonology and syntax are attributed to Yue substrate languages, and Cantonese kept some features of the extinct Nanyue language. The name Vietnam derives from Nam Viet, the Vietnamese form of Nanyue. Vietnamese tradition tells of Van Lang, a state of the Lac Viet founded c. 2879 BCE and ruled by the Hung kings, though the history of the Lac Viet begins only in the 7th century BCE.
baja-california: The Baja California peninsula is divided between two Mexican states, and the northern one, Baja California, takes in the half of the peninsula north of the 28th parallel and the oceanic Guadalupe Island. It has an area of 70,113 square kilometres. Its backbone is the Sierra de Baja California, where Picacho del Diablo, the highest point of the peninsula, stands. The mountains divide the weather: the north-west is semi-dry and Mediterranean, the Valle de Guadalupe produces wine, and to the east the Sonoran Desert dominates, while the south gives way to the Vizcaíno Desert.

The first people reached the peninsula at least 11,000 years ago. Cochimí hunter-gatherers lived in the centre, and groups of the Yuman language family, among them the Kiliwa, Paipai, Kumeyaay, Cocopa and Quechan, lived in the north; the Cocopa and Quechan farmed the floodplain of the lower Colorado River. Francisco de Ulloa reached the coast in 1539.

After the Jesuits founded the mission at Loreto in 1697, they extended their missions northward, until their expulsion in 1768. Franciscan administration followed briefly, and in 1773 the Dominicans took over, founding a chain of missions from El Rosario in 1774 to Descanso in 1817. In 1804 the Spanish crown divided California into Alta and Baja California along the line between the Franciscan and Dominican missions. Mexico mandated the secularisation of the missions in 1833.

After the Mexican–American War ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Alta California passed to the United States, while the area of Tijuana, Mexicali and Tecate stayed Mexican. In 1853 the mercenary William Walker captured La Paz and declared himself president of the Republic of Baja California; the Mexican government forced his retreat after several months.

In 1905 the Magonista revolution, an anarchist movement based on the writings of Ricardo Flores Magón and Enrique Flores Magón, began, and in 1911 the Mexican Liberal Party captured Mexicali and Tijuana before surrendering to federal forces. The peninsula was divided into northern and southern territories in 1931. The northern territory became the 29th Mexican state in 1952, and the southern became Baja California Sur in 1974.

The state has an estimated 3,769,020 inhabitants, more than three quarters of it in Mexicali, the capital, Ensenada and Tijuana, the largest city. It borders the United States to the north and Sonora across the northern Gulf of California.
bajaur: Bajaur is a district in the Malakand Division of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, in Pakistan, with its headquarters at Khar. It covers 498 square kilometres, about 72 kilometres long and 32 wide, in a small mountain basin, and shares a 52-kilometre border with Afghanistan's Kunar Province. Its streams drain eastwards from the ridge above the Kunar valley to the Panjkora River. Until 2018 it was Bajaur Agency, the northernmost and smallest of the seven tribal agencies of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, and it has seven tehsils.

The area was the site of the ancient Gandhara kingdom of Apraca from the 1st century BCE to the 1st century CE, and of the Aspasioi, who resisted Alexander the Great. Near the town of Nysa, Alexander met people who placed their dead in cedar coffins in trees and made wine; they claimed descent from settlers of the god Dionysus, and Alexander left them free after demanding 300 cavalry. The Bajaur casket, a schist reliquary dated to about 5 to 6 CE, shows the Scythian kings of Apraca, notably Indravarman, as patrons of Buddhism. The region came under Kushan control after the conquests of Kujula Kadphises.

In 1518 Babur took the fortress of Bajaur from Sultan Mir Haider Ali Gabari and ordered a general massacre of the Pashtun defenders, with women and children taken captive; he wrote that more than 3,000 men died. In 1585 and 1586 a Mughal army under Zain Khan Koka, sent by Akbar against the Yusufzai, was beaten at the Battle of the Malandari Pass. Bajaur later became a princely state under the Nawab of Khar, the last of whom, Abdul Subhan Khan, ruled until 1990. In the 1980s it was a staging ground for Afghan mujahideen, and in August 2008 the Pakistani military launched an offensive against the Tehrik-e-Taliban there, during which an estimated 300,000 people fled.

The 2023 census counted 1,287,960 people in the district, all living in rural areas. About 99.85 per cent speak Pashto as their first language, and the population is nearly entirely Muslim. Its mountains include Koh-i-Mor, identified with the Meros of Arrian, and marble and nephrite are quarried.
baji-rao-i: Baji Rao, born Visaji on 18 August 1700, belonged to the Bhat family of Sinnar, near Nashik. His father, Balaji Vishwanath, was Peshwa to Shahu I. He learned reading, writing and Sanskrit, but showed a passion for soldiering early and often accompanied his father on campaign, including the expedition to Delhi in 1719. He came away convinced that the Mughal Empire was disintegrating and could not resist Maratha expansion northward. When Balaji Vishwanath died in 1720, Shahu appointed the 20-year-old Baji Rao Peshwa despite the opposition of other chieftains.

Baji Rao persuaded Shahu that the Marathas must go on the offensive, and reportedly said that if the withering tree were struck at the trunk its branches would fall of themselves. He promoted young commanders who were not from hereditary Deccan families, among them Malhar Rao Holkar, Ranoji Shinde and the Pawar brothers. His main rival in the Deccan was Asaf Jah I, the Nizam of Hyderabad, who contested the Maratha right to collect chauth. In the Palkhed campaign of 1727–28 Baji Rao outmanoeuvred the Nizam with a purely mounted army that carried no artillery or baggage and lived off the country. Bernard Montgomery called it a masterpiece of strategic mobility.

In March 1729 he marched into Bundelkhand with 25,000 horsemen to relieve the rebel Chhatrasal, besieged by a Mughal force under Muhammad Khan Bangash. Chhatrasal granted him a large jagir, gave him his daughter Mastani, and before he died in December 1731 ceded a third of his territory to the Marathas. In Gujarat, Baji Rao's brother Chimaji Appa won the right to collect chauth in 1730, which provoked Trimbak Rao Dabhade into rebellion. He was defeated at Dabhoi in 1731. In Konkan, Baji Rao fought the Siddis of Janjira, and he campaigned against the Portuguese.

In 1737 he marched on Delhi, and later that year he faced a large Mughal army reinforced with artillery near Bhopal, where the Nizam sheltered. By the agreement at Doraha on 7 January 1738, Malwa was ceded to the Marathas and the Mughals promised reparations.

Exhausted by constant campaigning, Baji Rao fell ill on 23 April 1740 and died on 28 April, the night of a Sunday. He was cremated the same day on the bank of the Narmada, where a memorial stands. His eldest son by his first wife Kashibai, Balaji Bajirao, known as Nanasaheb, succeeded him as Peshwa. His son by Mastani was Shamsher Bahadur, whom Kashibai raised after both parents died in 1740. Shamsher died of wounds after the Third Battle of Panipat. By Baji Rao's death the Maratha Empire had reached its largest extent to that time.
baji-rao-ii: Baji Rao II was born on 10 January 1775 to Raghunathrao, a former Peshwa, and his wife Anandibai. His father's alliance with the British East India Company had led to the First Anglo-Maratha War, and when Baji Rao was born both his parents were held in confinement by the ruling Peshwa's council. He and his brothers spent their early years in captivity, with little access to education.

When Peshwa Madhavrao II died without an heir, the general Daulat Rao Scindia and the minister Nana Fadnavis installed Baji Rao as a puppet Peshwa. His accession was controversial, because some believed his parents had been involved in the murder of Peshwa Narayanrao in 1773, and parts of the Maratha elite distrusted him.

After Nana Fadnavis died in 1800, Scindia took control of the Peshwa's administration, and Baji Rao, fearing for his safety, turned to the British Resident at Poona, Colonel William Palmer. In 1802 Yashwant Rao Holkar, whose brother Vithoji Rao Holkar the Peshwa had ordered executed, marched on Poona and defeated the forces of Scindia and the Peshwa at the Battle of Hadapsar on 25 October. Baji Rao fled by way of Sinhagad and the Konkan coast to Bassein, while Holkar set up a government under Amrut Rao as nominal Peshwa.

The treaty signed in December 1802 restored him in return for a British subsidiary force of 6,000 infantry, paid for by the Peshwa, and a permanent Resident at Poona. In 1817 the Company's intervention in his revenue dispute with the Gaekwads of Baroda forced him to sign the Treaty of Poona on 13 June, ceding territory. On 5 November 1817 his forces under his legal adviser Mor Dixit attacked the British Residency and were beaten at the Battle of Khadki, and late in December they were repelled at the Battle of Koregaon.

Pursued by five British columns, he surrendered to John Malcolm in 1818. He kept his personal fortune and received an annual pension of £80,000–£100,000, but had to live where the British chose and give up the title of Peshwa, though he could call himself Maharaja. He spent 33 years at Bithur, near Kanpur on the Ganges, building temples and bathing ghats, and died there in 1851. Contemporary accounts call him an able administrator but an indecisive leader. In the Indian Rebellion of 1857 Bithur was sacked and his residence destroyed.
baji-rout: Baji Rout was born on 5 October 1926 in the village of Nilakanthapur, in what was then the state of Dhenkanal. He was the youngest son of Hari Rout, a boatman on the Brahmani river, and Rania Devi. His father died while he was still a child, and Baji himself came to work as a boatman. His mother earned a living by grinding and husking paddy at a quern for neighbours and could spend nothing on his schooling, and his two elder brothers earned too little to do more than help support the family.

As a boy he joined the Banar Sena of the Prajamandal, the party of the people, and volunteered to keep watch by the river at night. On the night of 11 October 1938, at Nilakanthapur Ghat near Bhuban, the police ordered him to take them across the river in his boat. He refused, and they shot and killed him.

A large procession was held for him in Cuttack. His body was first taken to 9 Pithapur, then the headquarters of Bhagawati Charan Panigrahi, and he was cremated at Satichaura in Cuttack. He is remembered for his part in the Indian independence movement.

His memory has been kept in sport and film. On 3 November 2022 Dharmendra Pradhan, the Union Education Minister, opened a national football tournament named in his honour, the Baji Rout Cup, which Rajasthan United won. A Hindi short film, Baji Rout: India's Freedom Fighter, a documentary drama made by students and directed by Riyyan Farooq and Diksha Nayak, follows his life up to his encounter with the police.
bak-hyeokgeose: According to the Samguk sagi and the Samguk yusa, refugees of Gojoseon lived in the valleys of what is now Gyeongsang Province, in six villages: Yangsan, Goheo, Jinji, Daesu, Gari and Goya. At a well called Najeong at Yangsan a strange light shone from the sky and a white horse descended. Chief Sobeolgong of Goheo found a large egg there, and a boy came out of it. When the boy was bathed, his body radiated light and birds and beasts danced. The egg was gourd-shaped, which has been proposed as the origin of the name Bak, close to the Korean word for gourd.

Sobeolgong raised the boy and the six chieftains revered him. They made him king when he was 13 years old, and the state was named Seorabeol. He married Lady Aryeong, who is said to have been born from the ribs of a dragon. Modern scholars see in the legend the city-state stage, with the six chieftains standing for a loose group of Gojoseon refugees. The story implies the ascendancy of the Bak clan over the native peoples and may point to horse and sun worship.

His title, Geoseo-khan or Geoseul-han, means ruler or king in the language of the Jinhan confederacy. According to the Samguk sagi, the king and his queen travelled the realm in 41 BCE and helped the people improve their harvests, and the people praised them as the Two Saints. In 37 BCE he built Geumseong in the capital, in present-day Gyeongju, and in 32 BCE a royal palace inside it. In 20 BCE the king of the Mahan confederacy demanded tribute, and Silla sent its minister Hogong, who criticised the Mahan king's lack of courtesy and was allowed to return.

The Samguk sagi gives him a reign of about 60 years and says he died at 73, and was buried at Sareung. According to the Samguk yusa, in the 61st year he went up to the sky and eight days later his body was scattered on the ground. A large snake disturbed the burial, so the head and limbs were buried separately in five tombs. His eldest son Namhae succeeded him and in 6 CE founded an ancestral shrine where Hyeokgeose was worshipped.

The Samguk sagi was written in the 13th century from the viewpoint of Silla and claims Silla's antiquity over Goguryeo and Baekje, so the founding date is widely questioned. Archaeological evidence suggests that Goguryeo is the oldest of the three kingdoms. All the Bak clans of Korea trace their ancestry to him.
bakelite: The reaction between phenol and an aldehyde was first reported in 1872 by Adolf von Baeyer, but its commercial use was not considered then. Leo Baekeland was already wealthy after selling the rights to his Velox photographic paper to Eastman Kodak in 1899, when he began to study phenol and formaldehyde in his home laboratory. His first aim was to find a substitute for shellac, a material in limited supply because it is made from the secretion of lac insects. He produced a soluble phenol-formaldehyde shellac called Novolak, which was not a market success. By controlling pressure and temperature he then produced a hard, mouldable material that he named Bakelite, after himself and the heat curing it needed.

Bakelite is a thermosetting phenol formaldehyde resin, formed by a condensation reaction of phenol with formaldehyde. At ordinary pressure the mixture foams violently and the cooled material is porous and breakable. Baekeland's innovation was to heat the product under pressure at about 150 degrees in an egg-shaped vessel he called a Bakelizer, which suppressed the foaming and gave a substance that is extremely hard and both infusible and insoluble. Moulded Bakelite used wood flour or asbestos fibre as a filler. Millions of parts could be made quickly and cheaply, and objects needed little finishing.

Baekeland's patent was filed on 13 July 1907 and granted on 7 December 1909, and he announced the invention to the American Chemical Society on 5 February 1909. In the summer of 1909 he licensed the continental European rights to Rütger AG, whose subsidiary Bakelite AG was the first to make it on an industrial scale. In 1922, after patent litigation that favoured Baekeland, the Bakelite Corporation was formed by a merger of three companies, and it marketed the material as the material of a thousand uses.

When Baekeland's heat and pressure patents expired in 1927, competitors appeared. Because moulded Bakelite incorporated fillers, it was usually made in dark colours, while the Catalin company made jewellery in fifteen new colours using another process. Old Bakelite objects are now collected.
bakenranef: Bakenranef, known to the Greeks as Bocchoris, was briefly a king of the 24th Dynasty of Egypt. Based at Sais in the western Delta, he ruled Lower Egypt. The historian Manetho of the Ptolemaic period treats him as the sole member of the dynasty, but modern scholars include his father Tefnakht in it. Sextus Julius Africanus quotes Manetho as giving Bocchoris six years, and some modern scholars assign a shorter reign.

Few contemporary records survive. The chief inscription of his reign concerns the death and burial of an Apis bull in his fifth and sixth years, and a few stelae were recovered by Auguste Mariette at the Serapeum of Saqqara. An inscribed vase with his names was found in a tomb at Tarquinia in Italy.

Greek and Roman writers remembered him more than the records warrant. Diodorus Siculus, writing about three centuries after Manetho, calls him contemptible in appearance but wiser than all earlier kings of Egypt. The Egyptians credited him with a law on contracts that provided a way to discharge debts where no bond was signed, and it was observed down to Diodorus' time.

Diodorus counts him one of the six most important lawgivers of ancient Egypt, and also credits him with abolishing debt slavery, a claim that rests on a lost work of Hecateus of Abdera, who may have invented it to support a Greek debate on debt slavery. Land reform has also been attributed to him, though the brevity of his reign, the small area he ruled and the indirect evidence cast doubt on it.

Other writers judged him differently. Plutarch calls him a man of very cruel nature, and Aelian says he gained a false reputation for justice. Tacitus reports that many Greek and Roman writers thought Bocchoris had a part in the origin of the Jewish nation, when he consulted the oracle of Ammon during a disease and was told to expel a people the gods detested. Manetho also tells of a lamb that prophesied that the Assyrians would conquer Egypt.

According to Manetho, a Kushite king of the 25th Dynasty captured Bakenranef and had him burned alive, which ended the short-lived 24th Dynasty as a rival to the Nubian rulers. The Manethonic and classical traditions hold that this invasion brought Egypt under Kushite rule, which had been split since the 21st Dynasty. There is no direct evidence that Bakenranef was killed in this way, and although earlier scholarship generally accepted the tradition, it has recently been treated more sceptically. Diodorus's inclusion of a briefly ruling kinglet of the Delta among Egypt's great lawgivers has struck modern writers as surprising.
bakhchysarai: Bakhchysarai lies in a narrow valley of the Çürük Suv river, about 30 kilometres south-west of Simferopol. The name comes from the Persian bāghche-sarāy, "Garden Palace"; in Crimean Tatar bağça means garden and saray palace. The earliest known man-made objects in the valley date from the Mesolithic period, and settlements have existed there since Late Antiquity. The fortress of Qırq Yer, now Çufut Qale, Salaçıq and Eski Yurt were built before the town itself and have since been absorbed into its urban area.

Bakhchysarai first appears in documents in 1502. In 1532 Sahib I Giray, Khan of Crimea from 1532 to 1551, established his residence there, and from then it was the capital of the Crimean Khanate and the centre of the political and cultural life of the Crimean Tatars. Cossacks sacked the town in 1675 during Ivan Sirko's Crimean campaign, and it was burned in 1736 during the Russo-Turkish War of 1735 to 1739. After the Russian Empire annexed the Khanate in 1783 it became an ordinary town without administrative importance, but it stayed a cultural centre of the Crimean Tatars for several decades, helped by Ismail Gaspirali, who founded the newspaper Terciman there in 1883.

During the Crimean War the town served as a hospital for wounded Russian soldiers. The Battle of the Alma was fought not far away in 1854, but Turkish and allied forces never took the town, since their main objective was Sevastopol. In 1930 it had 10,450 inhabitants, 7,420 of them Crimean Tatars. On 18 May 1944 the Sürgün, the deportation of the Crimean Tatars, prompted by accusations of collaboration with the Axis occupiers, emptied the city of them. They could not return until 1989, when Soviet policies relaxed.

The main landmark is the Hansaray, or Khan's Palace, the only surviving palace of the Crimean khans, which is open as a museum. Other sites in or near the town include the Zincirli Madrasa, the Orta Cami and Tahtali-Jami mosques, the Cave Monastery, Chufut-Kale and Tepe-Kermen. Russian readers know the town from Alexander Pushkin's poem The Fountain of Bakhchysarai (1822), and Adam Mickiewicz devoted some of the best of his Crimean Sonnets (1825) to its landmarks.
bakhchysarai-palace: The Khan's Palace, in Crimean Tatar Hansaray, is in the town of Bakhchysarai in Crimea. The Crimean Khan dynasty commissioned both the town and the palace and moved their capital there from Salaçıq in the first half of the 16th century. The palace's complex design and its minarets were constructed in that century by Ottoman, Persian and Italian architects. It became the home of a succession of Crimean khans. Some buildings now in the palace were added later, while some of the original ones did not survive past the 18th century.

The walled enclosure contains a mosque, a harem, a cemetery, living quarters and gardens. Its interior has been decorated to look lived in and reflects the traditional 16th-century Crimean Tatar style. The Big Khan Mosque, built in 1532 by Sahib I Giray, is one of the largest mosques in Crimea. It has a three-aisle square prayer hall and two octagonal minarets twenty-eight metres high. A fire damaged it in 1736 during the Russo-Turkish War, and it was restored under Khan Selâmet II Giray.

The Small Khan Mosque, in the main building, was designed for the Khan's family and important dignitaries. Its mihrab has an upper part cut with seven ornamented belts, symbolising the seven levels of heaven, and above it a stained glass window shows the seal of Suleiman.

A small fountain in one courtyard moved the Russian writer Alexander Pushkin so much that he wrote the long narrative poem The Fountain of Bakhchisaray. By the story told of it, one of the last Crimean khans, Qırım Giray, fell in love with a Polish girl named Maria in his harem, and after her early death he is said to have wept and commissioned a marble fountain so that the rock would weep like him forever. It was moved to the Ambassadors' courtyard after Catherine II ordered the annexation of Crimea. Pushkin's verses are credited in part with ensuring the palace's survival. It was added to UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage Sites in 2003.
bakhtiyar-khalji: Ikhtiyar al-Din Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji was born and raised in Garmsir, Helmand, in what is now southern Afghanistan. He belonged to the Khalaj tribe, originally of Turkic origin, which had settled in south-eastern Afghanistan for over 200 years and contributed to the making of the Pashtun Ghilji tribe; he is therefore seen as Turko-Afghan. He went in search of employment to Ghazni and Delhi, where he was rejected because of his appearance, and then to Badaun, where he found his first post. His background was not obscure: his uncle Muhammad bin Mahmud had fought in the Second Battle of Tarain and held the iqta of Kashamandi, which passed to Bakhtiyar.

The commander of Benaras, Husamudin Aghul Bek, gave Bakhtiyar the iqtas of Bhagwat and Bhilui. From there he displaced minor Gahadavala chiefs and raided Maner and Bihar, where he took a large amount of booty, and many Khaljis joined him. He led the Ghurid forces of Muhammad of Ghor in Bihar, where his invasions destroyed the monasteries of Odantapuri and Vikramashila. Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani's Tabaqat-i Nasiri records the sack of a Buddhist monastery. Satish Chandra and Mohammad Habib held him responsible for the destruction of the mahaviharas, while D. N. Jha and Namit Arora argued that Nalanda may not have been destroyed by him.

He then conquered Bengal. The Sena king Lakshmana Sena, said to be in his eighties, could offer little resistance. By tradition Bakhtiyar advanced so fast on Nabadwip that only 18 horsemen kept up with him; they entered the city unchallenged and took the king by surprise, and he fled to eastern Bengal. Bakhtiyar went on to take Gauda, or Lakhnauti, and made it his seat. Minhaj al-Siraj, who visited Bengal about 40 years later, wrote that he had the khutbah read and coins struck, and that mosques, colleges and monasteries for dervishes were founded.

In 1206 Bakhtiyar left Devkot to attack Tibet. His force was defeated by Tibetan guerrillas in the Chumbi Valley, and he returned to Devkot with only about a hundred surviving soldiers. While he lay ill there he was assassinated in August 1206 by Ali Mardan Khalji. The Khalji nobles chose Muhammad Shiran Khalji as successor, and Bakhtiyar's dynasty ruled Bengal from 1203 to 1227. Muhammad Yusuf Siddiq attributes the quick conquest to the Sena rulers' failure to win the support of the common people. Locals honour Bakhtiyar as Pir Sahib, and Muslims and Hindus alike pray at his shrine in Gangarampur during a yearly festival.
bakircay: The Bakırçay rises in the Gölcük Dağları mountains. The ancient Caicus appears to have been formed by two streams that met between 50 and 65 km above its mouth, and it drained an extensive and fertile country. Strabo placed its sources in a plain separated by the Temnos range from the plain of Apia, and wrote that the Mysius joined it below its source. The river reached the sea about 12 km from Pitane and 3 km from Elaea, the port of Pergamon, which lay on the Caicus about 25 km inland.

Because the river's course has changed since antiquity, it is not clear how the ancient names apply to the modern streams. Leake inferred from the direction of L. Scipio's march from Troy to the Hyrcanian plain that the Caicus was the north-eastern branch of the river of Pergamon, the one flowing by Menduria and Balıkesir.

The Kaikos is mentioned by Hesiod. Plutarch claimed that it was first called Astraeus and was renamed after Caicus, a son of Hermes, threw himself into it after sleeping with his sister Alcippe. Near Pergamon the river gave its name to the Battle of the Caecus River. The river is also one of two candidates for the Seha River Land, the Hittite place name known from texts such as the Manapa-Tarhunta letter; the Gediz River is the other.
baku-tbilisi-ceyhan-pipeline: The Caspian Sea lies above one of the largest collections of oil and gas fields, but being landlocked it makes the export of oil to Western markets difficult. In Soviet times every transport route from the region ran through Russia. After the Soviet collapse, producers sought new routes. Russia first insisted that a new pipeline cross its territory and then declined to take part.

In the spring of 1992 the Turkish prime minister Süleyman Demirel proposed a route through Turkey, and Azerbaijan and Turkey signed the first document on the project on 9 March 1993. A route through Armenia was politically impossible because of the unresolved war over Nagorno-Karabakh, which left the longer and costlier route through Georgia. The Ankara Declaration of 29 October 1998 gave the project momentum, and Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey signed an intergovernmental agreement on 18 November 1999 in Istanbul.

The pipeline is 1,768 km long and runs from the Sangachal Terminal near Baku to the Ceyhan Marine Terminal on the south-eastern Mediterranean coast of Turkey. Of its length, 443 km lie in Azerbaijan, 249 km in Georgia and 1,076 km in Turkey. It crosses mountain ranges at up to 2,830 m and passes under or over 3,000 roads, railways and utility lines and 1,500 watercourses. It is buried at least a metre deep and measures 1,070 mm in diameter for most of its length, narrowing to 865 mm near Ceyhan. Eight pump stations push the oil at about two metres a second, and at normal capacity it carries one million barrels a day.

It takes oil chiefly from the Azeri-Chirag-Guneshli field in the Caspian Sea. Kazakh oil has also reached it by tanker across the Caspian. The line cost US$3.9 billion, of which 70 per cent came from third parties including the International Finance Corporation and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

BTC Co. was established in London on 1 August 2002, with BP managing the consortium. Construction began in April 2003. The pipeline was inaugurated at the Sangachal Terminal on 25 May 2005, and the first oil reached Ceyhan on 28 May 2006. Archaeological surveys sponsored by BP began in 2000, and construction uncovered cultural artefacts, leading to coordinated research at sites in Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey.

The pipeline drew criticism for its environmental risks, notably its route through the watershed of the Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park in Georgia, and for the bypassing of Armenia. Its supporters in Georgia saw it as a guarantee of the country's independence and security. It removed about 350 tanker cargoes a year from the Bosphorus and Dardanelles.
bal-gangadhar-tilak: Tilak was born Keshav Gangadhar Tilak on 23 July 1856 in a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family in Ratnagiri; the family moved to Poona in 1867. His father, a schoolteacher and Sanskrit scholar, died when Tilak was sixteen. Tilak took a degree in mathematics at the Deccan College in 1877 and a law degree in 1879. In 1880 he co-founded the New English school, and in 1884 the Deccan Education Society, which set up Fergusson College in 1885, where he taught mathematics. He left the society in 1890 for more openly political work. He had started the weeklies Kesari, in Marathi, and Mahratta, in English, in 1880 to 1881.

Tilak joined the Indian National Congress in 1890 and opposed its moderate approach to self-rule. Measures against the plague in Pune in 1897 caused widespread resentment, and Tilak published inflammatory articles in Kesari and Mahratta. After two British officers were shot by the Chapekar brothers he was charged and sentenced to 18 months in prison. He took up the slogan Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it. After the Partition of Bengal he promoted the Swadeshi and boycott movements. At the Surat session of 1907 Congress split into a radical faction led by Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai, and a moderate one.

In 1908 he was convicted of sedition over articles in Kesari and sentenced to six years in Mandalay, where he was held until 16 June 1914. He rejoined Congress at the Lucknow pact of 1916 and helped found the All India Home Rule League, whose membership grew from 1400 in April 1916 to about 32,000 in 1917. He also turned the household worship of Ganesha into a public festival in 1894 and began celebrations of Shivaji's birthday in 1895, though these celebrations also contributed to religious tensions. He died on 1 August 1920.

In prison at Mandalay he wrote the Gita Rahasya, interpreting the Bhagavad Gita as justifying activism, which he called karma-yoga, against the dominant renunciate readings. Tilak supported self-rule without a complete break with the British Empire. He opposed the age of consent bill and the first girls' high school in Pune, and he refused to sign a petition against untouchability in 1918. He also wrote The Arctic Home in the Vedas, arguing that the Vedas were composed in the Arctic.
balaji-baji-rao: Balaji Rao was born on 8 December 1720 into the Bhat family, the son of Peshwa Baji Rao I and Kashibai. When Baji Rao I died in April 1740, the Chhatrapati Shahu I appointed the 19-year-old Balaji Rao as Peshwa in August, despite opposition from several Maratha chiefs including Raghoji I Bhonsle. He had married Gopikabai of the Raste family on 11 January 1730, and they had three sons: Vishwasrao, who was killed at Panipat; Madhavrao I, who succeeded him; and Narayan Rao.

Under Balaji Baji Rao the Chhatrapati was largely a titular head, and the Maratha Empire became a confederation in which the Holkars, the Scindias and the Bhonsles of Nagpur held semi-autonomous power. Assisted by his cousin Sadashivrao Bhau he introduced fiscal and administrative reforms and sponsored canals, bridges and temples, especially in Pune. When Tarabai imprisoned the Chhatrapati Rajaram II in November 1750, the Peshwa defeated her ally Damaji Gaekwad at the Venna River on 15 March 1751, and in September 1752 Tarabai swore peace at Jejuri. Rajaram II stayed on as a powerless figurehead.

In 1752 the Marathas and the Mughals agreed that the Marathas would defend the empire, and Balaji Baji Rao was named Governor of Ajmer and Agra. The Maratha invasions of Bengal in these years devastated its economy; the Dutch factory chief Jan Kersseboom estimated that about 400,000 civilians died in western Bengal and Bihar. A treaty of 1751 made the Nawab pay chauth of ₹1.2 million a year. In 1758 his brother Raghunathrao captured Lahore and Peshawar, and Maratha influence then reached from north of the Sindhu River to northern Kerala.
