Mughal loyalists appealed to Ahmad Shah Durrani, who reached Lahore by the end of 1759 with Rohilla and Awadh allies. Balaji Baji Rao sent a large army under Sadashivrao Bhau, but reinforcements never passed the Narmada, and on 14 January 1761 the Durranis defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat. The historian Suresh K. Sharma blames the Peshwa's love of pleasure for the delay. He heard of the defeat on 24 January at Bhilsa, where his son Vishwasrao and cousin Sadashivrao Bhau were among the dead. He died on 23 June 1761 at Parvati Hill near Pune, and Madhavrao I succeeded him.
balaji-vishwanath: Balaji Vishwanath Bhat was born on 1 January 1662 into a Konkanastha Chitpavan Brahmin family that held the hereditary office of Deshmukh of Shrivardhan under the Siddi of Janjira. According to the Purandare daftar he came up to the Desh before 1692, serving Ambajipant Purandare of Saswad and later Ramchandrapant Amatya and Shankrajipant Sachiv. He was Sarsubhedar of Pune from 1699 to 1702 and of Daulatabad from 1703 to 1707, joined Senapati Dhanaji Jadhav at the siege of Sinhagad in 1703, and in 1708 was named Senakarte, the maker of armies.

After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the Mughals released Shahu, the son of Sambhaji, and a civil war followed with Tarabai, the widow of Rajaram. Balaji sided with Shahu against the Senapati Chandrasen Jadhav, and in 1712 helped bring about Tarabai's fall at Kolhapur, where Rajaram's other widow Rajasbai installed her son Sambhaji II. Sent against the admiral Kanhoji Angre, who had defeated and imprisoned the Peshwa Bahiroji Pingale, Balaji negotiated instead at Lonavala and won him over to Shahu. Shahu then dismissed Pingale and made Balaji Peshwa on 16 November 1713.

In July 1718 Balaji agreed a treaty with Sayyid Hussain Ali Khan, the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan: the Marathas were to have chauth and sardeshmukhi of the Deccan provinces, Gujarat and Malwa, in return for nominal Mughal overlordship and 15,000 horsemen. When Emperor Farrukhsiyar refused to ratify it, Balaji marched to Delhi with Hussain Ali Khan and Maratha cavalry under Parsoji Bhosale; Farrukhsiyar was deposed, and his successor Rafi-ul-Darjat ratified the treaty in 1719. Balaji also brought back Shahu's mother Yesubai from captivity. That year he defeated and killed Yashwantrao Thorat at the Battle of Panhala. He retired to Saswad in October 1719 and died on 12 April 1720; his son Baji Rao I succeeded him as Peshwa.
balaklava: Balaklava is a settlement on the Crimean Peninsula, now part of the city of Sevastopol and the administrative centre of Balaklavsky District. It lies at the entrance to the Balaklava Inlet, above which stand the ruins of a Genoese fortress on a clifftop. It is known in Ukrainian and Russian as Балаклава, in Crimean Tatar as Balıqlava and in Greek as Σύμβολον.

Ancient Greeks founded a settlement on the site under the name Symbolon, and it was an important commercial city for them. In the Middle Ages it was controlled by the Byzantine Empire, who called it Yamboli, and then by the Genoese, who conquered it in 1365 and named it Cembalo. The Genoese built a large trading empire across the Mediterranean and Black Sea, buying slaves in Eastern Europe and shipping them to Egypt through Crimea, a lucrative market contested by the Venetians. The fortress is the subject of Mickiewicz's penultimate poem in his 1826 cycle of Crimean Sonnets.

In 1475 the Turks conquered Cembalo and renamed it Balyk-Yuva, meaning Fish's Nest, from which the name Balaklava came. Russian troops invaded Crimea in 1771, during the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774, and Crimea was annexed by the Russian Empire thirteen years later. Afterwards the Crimean Tatar and Turkish population was forcibly replaced by Greek Orthodox settlers from the Archipelago.

The town became known for the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War and the Charge of the Light Brigade, in which a British cavalry brigade, because of a misunderstanding, was sent up a valley held on three sides by the Russians. About 250 men were killed or wounded and over 400 horses lost, reducing the mounted brigade by two thirds. Alfred, Lord Tennyson commemorated it in verse. The balaclava, a knitted garment covering the head and neck, takes its name from the place, where soldiers first wore it, and several towns in English-speaking countries were named Balaklava later in the 19th century.

In 1954 Crimea was transferred from the Russian Soviet republic to the Ukrainian Soviet republic, and in 1957 Balaklava was incorporated into Sevastopol by the Soviet government and lost its city status. An underground submarine base, built to survive a nuclear strike, was operational until 1993, when it began to be decommissioned; the last Russian submarine left in 1996. Balaklava was one of the most secret residential areas in the Soviet Union, and the base is now a naval museum complex. Monuments in the town commemorate the Crimean War, the Russian Civil War and the Great Patriotic War.
balambangan-island: Balambangan Island lies in the Kudat Division of Sabah, off the northern tip of Borneo, about 3 kilometres west of Banggi Island. It is now part of the Tun Mustapha Marine Park. Its history as a trading station began with Alexander Dalrymple, an officer of the East India Company, who on 12 September 1762 concluded an agreement with Sultan Bantilan Muizzud-Din by which the Sultanate of Sulu ceded the island to the company. Dalrymple took possession of it on 22 January 1763.

A committee of the company's directors approved a factory on the island in 1768 and offered its management to Dalrymple, but he quarrelled with the directors over his demand for absolute control and was dismissed in March 1771. His replacement, John Herbert, brought soldiers and supplies from India in the Britannia. The settlement traded opium, munitions and fabrics with the Tausugs and Maguindanaons, but Herbert's mismanagement and poor relations with the Tausugs ended in its destruction on 26 February 1775. Herbert and the other survivors escaped to Brunei. The Dutch of Batavia also tried to settle the island's western coast but withdrew by 1797.

In 1803, after the Treaty of Amiens restored the Moluccas to the Dutch, Lord Wellesley, Governor-General of India, ordered the island resettled under R. J. Farquhar, the British Resident at Amboina. Farquhar re-established the settlement by the end of September 1803, although the Anstruther and Thornhill were wrecked off Banggi Island on the way and the General Baird burned in the harbour on 29 October. Placed under Penang, the post was to be fortified, but the renewed war with France led the directors to veto the plan, and the island was abandoned in 1805.
balangir: Balangir, also written Bolangir, is a town and municipality and the headquarters of Balangir district in the state of Odisha, India. The municipality is divided into 21 wards and spreads over an area of 12,200 acres, or 4,900 hectares. Its average elevation is 383 metres above sea level.

Between Balangir and Bargarh districts rise the Gandhamardan Hills, a hill of 3,296 feet known for its medicinal plants. The Botanical Survey of India has reported 220 plant species of medicinal value there, while local people claim more than 500. Tradition holds that the god Hanuman resides on the hill.

On the slopes of the Gandhamardan Hills stands the Harishankar temple, connected with the two Hindu gods Vishnu and Shiva. Its deity was discovered in the 14th century by a Chauhan king of the Patna kingdom of Odisha and has been worshipped since. A dancing Ganesha image found there can be traced to the early 12th century. The temple was built by order of Durlabha Devi, queen of Maharaja Vaijjal Dev Chauhan.

On the opposite side of the hills stands the temple of Nrusinghanath. The plateau between the two temples holds ancient Buddhist ruins, which are considered remains of the ancient Parimalgiri University. Another historical site, Ranipur Jharial, lies near Kantabanji and has an ancient circular temple in rocky terrain.

Balangir Junction railway station lies on the Jharsuguda-Sambalpur-Titlagarh line of East Coast Railways. The town is joined by road to the state capital, Bhubaneswar, 327 km to the east. The nearest airport is at Jharsuguda.

Two festivals mark the town's year. Nuakhai, a harvest festival mostly observed in western Odisha, falls on the day after Ganesh Puja in the month of Bhadraba. The first of the new grain is offered to the local deity, and people wear new clothes and prepare special food. The Ratha Yatra, or chariot festival, carries the deities in chariots from the Jagannath Temple to the Gundicha Temple, where they stay nine days before returning.
balasagun: Balasagun, called Balasagyn in Kyrgyz, was an ancient city in modern Kyrgyzstan, in the Chüy Valley between Bishkek and Lake Issyk-Kul. It stood on the Silk Road. Its ruins were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014 as part of the Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor. It should not be confused with Karabalghasun, now Ordu-Baliq in Mongolia, which was the capital of the Uyghur Khaganate.

Balasagun was founded in the ninth century by the Kara-Khanid Khanate and soon supplanted Suyab as the main political and economic centre of the Chüy Valley. It was the capital of the Kara-Khanid Khanate from the 10th century until the Qara Khitai, the Western Liao dynasty, took it in 1134. The Mongols captured it in 1218 and called it Gobalik, meaning Pretty City. Its prosperity declined after the Mongol conquest. The city had a sizable Nestorian Christian population, and one graveyard was still in use in the 14th century. The poet Yūsuf Balasaguni, who wrote the Kutadgu Bilig, is thought to have been born there in the 11th century.

Since the 14th century Balasagun has been a village, with many ruins, 12 kilometres (7.5 miles) southeast of Tokmok. The Burana zone, at the edge of Tokmok and 6 kilometres (3.7 miles) from the present village, was the west end of the ancient city. It includes the Burana Tower and a field of stone petroglyphs, the Kurgan stelae. The tower is a minaret built in the 11th century on the ruins of the city. It is 24 metres (79 feet) high, though it once topped 46 metres (151 feet). Earthquakes damaged it over the centuries, and the present building is largely the result of a renovation in the 1970s.
balash: Balash, in Middle Persian Wardakhsh or Walakhsh, was the brother of the Sasanian king Peroz I, who reigned from 459 to 484. In 484 Peroz was defeated and killed by a Hephthalite army near Balkh. His army was completely destroyed, his body was never found, and four of his sons and brothers also died. The eastern cities of Khorasan, Nishapur, Herat and Marw, now came under Hephthalite rule. Sukhra, a member of the Parthian House of Karen, one of the Seven Great Houses of Iran, quickly raised a new force and stopped the Hephthalites from gaining more ground. The Iranian magnates, most notably Sukhra and the Mihranid general Shapur Mihran, elected Peroz's brother Balash as shah.

Immediately after taking the throne Balash sought peace with the Hephthalites, which cost the Sasanians a heavy tribute. Little is known about him. Eastern sources see him as a mild and tolerant ruler, and his tolerance of Christianity gave him a good reputation among Christian authors, who describe him as mild and generous. He appears, however, to have been only a nominee of the powerful nobleman Sukhra, the de facto ruler.

When news of Peroz's death arrived, the Iranian nobles of Sasanian Armenia, including Shapur Mihran, wished to go to the capital Ctesiphon to elect a new sovereign, and this let the Armenians under Vahan Mamikonian proclaim independence. Given the weakness in Iran, Balash did not send an army and made peace on terms that provided: existing fire-altars in Armenia were to be destroyed and no new ones built, Christians were to have freedom of worship, conversions to Zoroastrianism were to stop and no land was to be given to converts. In 485 he appointed Vahan Mamikonian marzban of Armenia.

A few months later a son of Peroz named Zarer rebelled, and Balash, with Armenian help, put the rising down and had him killed. In 488 Balash, an unpopular figure among the nobility and clergy, was deposed after a reign of four years. Sukhra played the main part in this and made Peroz's son Kavad the new shah.
balasore: Balasore, officially Baleshwar, lies in eastern India about 215 km from the state capital Bhubaneswar and 240 km from Kolkata. It is the administrative headquarters of Balasore district. Excavations at villages near the city have shown three phases of settlement: a Chalcolithic phase (2000 to 1000 BCE), an Iron Age phase (1000 to 400 BCE) and an early historic phase (400 to 200 BCE). The area was part of the ancient kingdom of Kalinga, which later became a territory of Utkal, until the death of Mukunda Deva.

The Mughal Empire annexed the region in 1568 and held it under its suzerainty until the 1700s. The English East India Company established a factory at Balasore in 1633, and merchants of the Trieste Company set up a trading post there in 1719. Company forces bombarded the city during the Anglo-Mughal War in 1686 but were repulsed by the Mughal forces. As Calcutta grew in importance, Balasore became a centre for river pilots guiding vessels up the Hooghly River, and it gave its name to a type of cotton muslin.

The Marathas, under the Bhonsle rajas of Nagpur, later held this part of Odisha, and ceded it to the British through the Treaty of Deogaon in 1803. It belonged to the Bengal Presidency until 1912. Balasore became a separate district in October 1828, and on 7 November 1845 all of Danish India was sold to the British. Mahatma Gandhi visited in 1921, and the independence fighter Jatindranath Mukherjee, known as Bagha Jatin, was wounded and died fighting the British here. Odisha became a separate state on 1 April 1936, with Balasore as part of it. The princely state of Nilagiri merged with Odisha in January 1948 and joined the district; in 1993 Bhadrak became a district of its own.

Odia is the official and most widely spoken language, followed by Urdu, Bengali, Santali and Hindi. The census of 2011 counted 144,373 people in the municipality and its outgrowth. Chandipur is a seaside resort known for its long beach, and the Kshirachora Gopinatha Temple at Remuna was built by King Langula Narasimha Deva, who also built the temple at Konarka. Fakir Mohan University is named after the Odia novelist Fakir Mohan Senapati, who came from the town.
balban: Balban, whose original name was Baha-ud-Din, was an Ilbari Turk born in 1216. As a child he was captured by the Mongols and sold to the Sufi Khwaja Jamal ud-din of Basra, who brought him to Delhi in 1232, where Sultan Iltutmish bought him. He became one of the forty Turkic nobles known as the Chalissa, rising from water carrier to the sultan's personal attendant, and under Razia Sultan he was lord of the hunt.

He helped to overthrow Ala ud-din Masud and installed Nasiruddin Mahmud as sultan, serving as his vizier from 1246 to 1265. Rivals persuaded the sultan that Balban was a usurper, but he was reinstated in 1254. As vizier he raised a Mongol siege of Uch in 1246 and campaigned against the Mewatis, who raided the neighbourhood of Delhi. According to the chronicler Barani, the western gates of the city were shut at afternoon prayer. Balban destroyed their strongholds and villages and cleared jungles.

Nasiruddin left no male heir, and in 1266, at the age of fifty, Balban took the throne as Ghiyas-ud-din Balban. Barani wrote that his aim was to instil fear of the governing power, the basis of good government. Balban held that the sultan was the shadow of God and introduced strict court discipline, including prostration before the king and kissing his feet. He broke up the Chahalgani, the group of forty leading nobles, and set up spies who answered only to the sultan. He reorganised the army against the Mongols and repelled their incursions. He recaptured Gwalior from the Rajputs but failed to take Ranthambore.

When the governor of Bengal, Tughral Tughan Khan, rejected Delhi's authority in 1275, two armies failed against him, and Balban joined a third, which killed Tughral and his followers. He made his son Bughra Khan governor there. He also patronised Persian poetry and introduced the Persian festival of Nowruz.

Balban's heir, his elder son Muhammad Khan, died fighting the Mongols on 9 March 1285. Balban died on 13 January 1287, and the nobles nominated his grandson Qaiqubad as sultan. Bughra Khan declared himself independent in Bengal, and Qaiqubad's weak rule undid much of Balban's work. The Slave dynasty ended in 1290. Although his military achievements were few, his civil and military reforms gave a stable government, and he is counted with Iltutmish and Alauddin Khalji among the most powerful rulers of the Delhi Sultanate. His tomb stands in the Mehrauli Archaeological Park in Delhi.
baldwin-i-latin-emperor: Baldwin was the son of Count Baldwin V of Hainaut and Countess Margaret I of Flanders. In 1186 he married Marie, daughter of Count Henry I of Champagne, who was a niece of Richard I of England and Philip II of France. Through her he had ties to the defenders of the Holy Land, and his uncle Count Philip I of Flanders had died on crusade at the siege of Acre in 1191. Baldwin became Count of Flanders in 1194 and Count of Hainaut in 1195.

His eight years in Flanders were taken up with recovering lands, including Artois, that had gone to the French crown as dowry. The Treaty of Péronne, signed in January 1200, made him a vassal of Philip II and returned parts of Artois to him. On 23 February 1200, at Bruges, Baldwin took the cross, and he left for the Fourth Crusade on 14 April 1202.

The crusade's leaders, short of money, were persuaded by the Venetians to divert to Constantinople, and the city fell in April 1204. The crown was first offered to Enrico Dandolo, Doge of Venice, who refused it. The choice then lay between Baldwin and Boniface of Montferrat, the nominal leader of the crusade. With Venetian support Baldwin was elected on 9 May 1204 and crowned on 16 May in the Hagia Sophia, in a ceremony that closely followed Byzantine practice.

The Latin Empire was organised on feudal lines. His own share included Constantinople and nearby regions in Europe and Asia, with the islands of Lemnos, Lesbos, Chios and Tenos. He quarrelled with Boniface, who received Thessalonica, before Dandolo and Count Louis I of Blois arranged a settlement. In February 1205 the Greeks of Thrace rose, relying on Kaloyan, tsar of Bulgaria, whose offer of alliance Baldwin had rejected.

At Adrianople on 14 April 1205 the Frankish knights were defeated, the count of Blois was killed and Baldwin was taken. His fate was uncertain for more than a year; reliable word of his death reached Constantinople only in July 1206, and his brother Henry of Flanders was crowned emperor in August. Accounts of his end differ. A tower at Veliko Tarnovo is still called Baldwin's Tower.

In 1225 a man appeared in Flanders claiming to be Baldwin and drew followers among the peasantry. He was unmasked as a Burgundian serf, Bertrand of Ray, and executed in 1226. Baldwin's daughters Joan and Margaret II both later ruled as countesses of Flanders.
baldwin-i-of-flanders: Baldwin I, also called Baldwin Iron Arm or Baldwin the Good, was probably born in the 830s. His ancestry and early life are unknown. The Annales Blandiniensis, a later source from the monks of Saint-Peter at Ghent, name his father as Audacer, who appears with the title of count and lay abbot in an entry of the year 856, and give Baldwin for the first time the nickname the Iron, in Latin ferreus.

He first appears in the record when he eloped with Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, king of West Francia. Judith had been married to the kings of Wessex Æthelwulf and then Æthelbald, and returned to France after Æthelbald's death in 860.

Around Christmas, at Baldwin's instigation and with the consent of her brother Louis, Judith escaped the custody in which she had been placed at Senlis. Charles had not consented to a marriage and had his bishop Hincmar excommunicate the couple. They sought support from Pope Nicholas, and by 23 November 862 their plea had succeeded. In June 863 the pope sent Rodoald, Bishop of Porto, and John, Bishop of Cervia, to press Charles. Charles reconciled with his daughter in October 863 at Verberie, and the couple married at Auxerre in December 863 in his presence. Hincmar, who opposed the marriage in his Annales Bertiniani, was told to lift the excommunication.

Charles sent Baldwin to the northern regions of his kingdom, where Vikings made repeated incursions, and appointed him margrave of Flanders. The Annales Bertiniani report that the Vikings were driven from the Scheldt estuary in 864 and sailed north to the Rhine. In 866 Pope Nicholas again urged Charles to grant more honours to his son-in-law. By 870 Baldwin was lay abbot of Saint Peter's Abbey in Ghent, and he is assumed to have gained the county of Waasland. In 871 he mediated between Charles and his rebellious son Carloman.

Baldwin died in 879 and was buried at the Abbey of St-Bertin near Saint-Omer. The monks there did not allow women in, even for burial, so his daughter-in-law Ælfthryth buried her husband Baldwin II at Saint-Peter's in Ghent, which became the necropolis of the next four counts of Flanders. The monks of Saint-Peter later claimed in the eleventh century that Baldwin lay there too, which caused confusion, though the Annales Vedastini record his burial at Saint-Bertin.

He and Judith had at least two sons. Baldwin II, born around 866, succeeded as margrave of Flanders. Rudolf, born around 869, became count of Cambrai around 888 and with his brother attacked Vermandois, but was killed in 896 when Herbert I of Vermandois retook the towns. Accounts of a third son, Charles, and of daughters rest on unreliable sources.
baldwin-i-of-jerusalem: Baldwin was born some time after 1060, the youngest son of Count Eustace II of Boulogne and Ida of Lorraine. Because he was the youngest he was intended for a church career, held prebends in cathedrals, but for unknown reasons abandoned that path and became a knight. He married a Norman noblewoman, Godehilde of Tosny. His brother Godfrey of Bouillon named him in most of his charters, which suggests that he regarded him as his heir. When the First Crusade was proclaimed in 1095, Godfrey sold or mortgaged his domains, and Baldwin received the County of Verdun in 1096. He left with Godfrey's army on 15 August 1096, taking his wife and children, which suggests that he did not plan to return.

In 1097 Baldwin and the Norman Tancred led a separate expedition into Cilicia. Their quarrel over Tarsus began an enduring conflict. Baldwin seized fortresses west of the Euphrates with the help of local Armenians. In early 1098 Thoros, the Armenian lord of Edessa, asked for his help against the Seljuks. Baldwin reached Edessa on 20 February, and after a riot against Thoros he took the town and established the first Crusader state on 10 March 1098. Having been widowed, he married the daughter of an Armenian lord to strengthen his rule. He supplied the crusader army with food during the siege of Antioch, and he held Edessa for three weeks against Kerbogha of Mosul, delaying him until the crusaders took Antioch.

When Godfrey of Bouillon died, Baldwin left Edessa on 2 October 1100 and reached Jerusalem around 9 November. The patriarch crowned him king at Bethlehem on 25 December. With Genoese and Venetian fleets he took Arsuf and Caesarea in 1101, Acre in 1104, Beirut in 1110 and Sidon in 1111, though his attempts on Ascalon and Tyre failed. After his victory at the third battle of Ramla in 1105 the Egyptians launched no further major campaigns against the kingdom. Soldiers pillaged Caesarea and massacred most of its adult population.

Baldwin was the only crowned monarch in the Latin East and claimed suzerainty over the other crusader rulers. He died on 2 April 1118 at Al-Arish, during an expedition against Egypt, and was buried beside Godfrey in the Calvary Chapel of the Holy Sepulchre. Fulcher of Chartres called him his subjects' 'shield, strength and support', and Christopher Tyerman credits him with a stable kingdom with defensible borders.
baldwin-ii-margrave-of-flanders: Baldwin II was born around 865 to Margrave Baldwin I of Flanders and Judith, daughter of Emperor Charles the Bald. He was nicknamed the Bald after his maternal grandfather. He ruled Flanders from 879 to 918, and the early years of his rule were marked by a series of devastating Viking raids.

By 883 Baldwin was forced to move north to the Pagus Flandransis, which became the territory most closely associated with the Counts of Flanders. He built a series of wooden fortifications at Saint-Omer, Bruges, Ghent and Kortrijk, and seized lands abandoned by royal and ecclesiastical officials. Many of these citadels later formed castellanies housing government, militia and local courts.

In 888 the Western Frankish king Charles the Fat was deposed, and several candidates sought the crown. As a grandson of Charles the Bald, Baldwin could have competed, but he and others tried instead to persuade the East Frankish king Arnulf to take the West Frankish crown, which Arnulf declined. Odo, Count of Paris, of the Robertine family, was made king. Relations between Odo and Baldwin worsened when Odo failed to support Baldwin's attempt to control the Abbey of Saint Bertin.

Odo attacked Baldwin at Bruges but could not prevail, and Baldwin went on to gain Artois, including the Abbey of St. Vaast. When that abbey came under Archbishop Fulk of Reims in 900, Baldwin had the archbishop assassinated and was excommunicated by Pope Benedict IV. When Herbert I, Count of Vermandois, opposed his advance into the upper Somme valley, Baldwin had him assassinated too.

Between 893 and 899 Baldwin married Ælfthryth, daughter of King Alfred the Great of Wessex. The aim of the Anglo-Flemish alliance was to help him control the lower Canche valley. Baldwin died on 10 September 918. Some of his warriors wished to bury him beside his father at the Abbey of Saint Bertin, but that abbey did not admit women even after death and Ælfthryth wanted to lie beside him, so he was buried at Saint Peter's Abbey in Ghent. This began a tradition lasting five generations that made Ghent the burial place of the early counts of Flanders. His eldest son Arnulf I of Flanders succeeded him, and his younger son Adalulf became the first Count of Boulogne.
baldwin-ii-of-jerusalem: Baldwin's birth year is unknown. He was the son of Count Hugh I of Rethel and Melisende of Montlhéry, probably a younger child, and was a kinsman of the brothers Godfrey of Bouillon and Baldwin of Boulogne. His family spoke the Champenois dialect of Old French, and he was probably illiterate. As lord of Bourcq he joined Godfrey's army at the beginning of the First Crusade. William of Tyre describes him as very religious, with callouses on his hands and knees from frequent prayer.

Baldwin of Boulogne granted him the County of Edessa when he left for Jerusalem on 2 October 1100. Baldwin married Morphia, the daughter of the Armenian lord Gabriel of Melitene, which strengthened his position among his largely Armenian subjects. At the Battle of Harran on 7 May 1104 Sökmen and Jikirmish drew the crusaders into an ambush, and he was captured; Tancred governed Edessa as regent. Joscelin of Courtenay ransomed him in 1108, and Tancred gave back the county only after the prelates arbitrated in Baldwin's favour. He returned to Edessa on 18 September 1108.

Mawdud besieged Edessa in April 1110, and Baldwin I of Jerusalem came to relieve it. The childless Baldwin I died on 2 April 1118, and Baldwin of Bourcq was elected king by the nobles. After the army of Antioch was almost destroyed in June 1119 he became regent for Bohemond II of Antioch, and his time in the north caused discontent in Jerusalem.

Belek captured the king on 18 April 1123 while he prepared to hunt with falcons, and held him at Kharput, later at Harran and Aleppo. Jerusalem's regents captured Tyre on 7 or 8 July 1124. Baldwin was released in August 1124, but al-Bursuqi forced him to lift the siege of Aleppo in January 1125. In 1126 Bohemond II married his daughter Alice, and in 1129 his eldest daughter Melisende married Count Fulk V of Anjou. He took monastic vows and died on 21 August 1131; Melisende and Fulk were crowned on 14 September. William of Tyre called him devout and experienced in war, but others criticised his love of money.
baldwin-iii-of-jerusalem: Baldwin was born in the first half of 1130, the eldest son of Queen Melisende and King Fulk. His mother was the eldest daughter and designated heir of King Baldwin II, who conferred the kingdom on the young Baldwin and his parents in 1131. Fulk had been count of Anjou before he left France to marry Melisende. Fulk died in a hunting accident on 10 November 1143, and Baldwin was crowned with Melisende on Christmas Day. Because he was only 13, his mother became his guardian and the true ruler; William of Tyre presented her rule as grounded in hereditary right, and the historian Bernard Hamilton argues she should be considered a queen regnant.

In 1144 Baldwin put down a rebellion at Wadi Musa by cutting down the inhabitants' olive trees and offering pardons, his first military success. When Zengid forces besieged Edessa that year, Melisende sent an army without involving him, and the city fell. Baldwin joined the Second Crusade's failed attempt to capture Damascus in 1148. In 1150 he arranged the sale of the last Edessan fortresses to the Byzantine Empire. His relations with his mother worsened as he sought a larger role, and in April 1152 he deposed her in a swift military action.

In January 1153 the Franks began the siege of Ascalon, which Baldwin conquered that year. After he nearly lost his life in a battle against Nur ad-Din in 1157, he allied with Emperor Manuel I Komnenos and married the emperor's niece Theodora in 1158. He spent ten days with Manuel at Antioch in 1159 and received a subsidy of 22,000 hyperpyra and 3,000 marks of silver. In 1161 he took up rule in Antioch again after Turkic forces captured Raynald of Châtillon. William of Tyre describes him as affable and quick-witted, and says he respected the rights of the Church.

In late 1162 Baldwin took pills from a Syrian physician and contracted dysentery. He was carried to Beirut and died there on 10 February 1163, aged 33. William of Tyre reports a widespread suspicion of poisoning, which the historians Peter W. Edbury and John G. Rowe dismiss. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre on 18 February. William says that Nur ad-Din refused to attack while the Franks mourned. Baldwin had no children with Theodora and was succeeded by his brother Amalric. He was the longest-reigning of the 12th-century kings of Jerusalem and widened the kingdom's borders.
baldwin-iv-of-jerusalem: Baldwin was born in mid-1161, probably at Ascalon, the son of Amalric, then count of Jaffa and Ascalon, and Agnes of Courtenay. His parents separated when he was two, after the High Court forced Amalric to annul the marriage on grounds of consanguinity as the price of being accepted as king in 1163. At nine he was sent to be educated by William of Tyre, who noticed early signs of leprosy, though the disease was diagnosed only after Baldwin became king.

After Amalric's death the High Court chose Baldwin unanimously, expecting that a husband would be found for his sister Sibylla to succeed him if he proved to be ill. He was crowned on 15 July 1174. Miles of Plancy and then Count Raymond III of Tripoli ruled as regent until Baldwin came of age at 15 in 1176. His planned attack on Egypt failed for lack of cooperation from his vassals.

In November 1177 Saladin invaded the kingdom while the Frankish army was in northern Syria. Baldwin and Raynald of Châtillon repelled him at Montgisard. Baldwin could not marry, and the question of succession dominated his reign. In 1180 Baldwin had Sibylla marry Guy of Lusignan, to forestall a coup by Raymond III and Bohemond III of Antioch, but Guy was opposed by much of the nobility. In 1182 Baldwin won the Battle of Le Forbelet.

From 1183 he could neither walk unsupported nor use his hands, and he went blind. He entrusted the government to Guy, but Guy's failure to lead and his insubordination led Baldwin to disinherit him, and to have Sibylla's young son crowned as Baldwin V. He was carried in a litter to lift Saladin's siege of Kerak, but failed to have Sibylla's marriage annulled.

In his last months Baldwin named Raymond regent for his nephew and died of a fever in 1185, no later than 16 May. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, near his father. Baldwin V died the next year, Sibylla made Guy king, and Saladin destroyed the kingdom at the Battle of Hattin in 1187.

Historians have traced the instability to his reign, yet the kingdom lost no territory while he ruled. His chief contribution, in the view of historians, was his refusal to abdicate before finding a suitable successor, since only he could keep the nobles united. Pope Alexander III called his leprosy a just judgement of God.
baldwin-of-ibelin: Baldwin was the second son of Barisan of Ibelin, younger brother of Hugh of Ibelin and older brother of Balian of Ibelin. He first appears in the record as a witness to charters in 1148. In 1156 he may have planned to kill the Hanbali preacher Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Qudama of Jamma'in, who was warned and fled to Damascus with his followers. When Hugh died in 1169, Baldwin kept Ramla and Mirabel and passed the castle of Ibelin to Balian.

In 1174 Baldwin brought the Lusignan family to court in the person of Aimery of Lusignan, who had married his daughter Eschiva. That year he and Balian backed Count Raymond III of Tripoli against Miles of Plancy as regent for King Baldwin IV. After his second wife died in 1177 he was probably Raymond's choice of husband for the king's widowed sister Sibylla. The Chronicle of Ernoul claims the two were in love, but historians doubt it.

Captured at the Battle of Marj Uyun in 1179, he was ransomed by the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Comnenus and visited Constantinople in 1180; the story goes that the emperor covered him to the head in the gold coins of his ransom. Raymond seems to have planned to marry Sibylla to Baldwin, but the king needed a husband from the West to win support for a new crusade, and she married Guy of Lusignan, Aimery's younger brother.

In 1183 Baldwin supported Raymond against Guy, then regent, and was among the barons who advised the crowning of Sibylla's son as Baldwin V to keep Guy from the throne. When the boy died in 1186 and Sibylla was crowned with Guy as consort, Baldwin and Raymond alone of the barons refused homage. Baldwin called Guy a madman and a fool and would not pay homage because his father had not paid homage to Guy's father. He placed his young son Thomas in Balian's care, went to Antioch, where he was welcomed, refused to return to help Guy against Saladin and probably died there in 1187. His daughter Eschiva was the mother of Hugh I of Cyprus.
baldwin-v-count-of-hainaut: Baldwin was the son of Count Baldwin IV of Hainaut and of Alice of Namur. His mother's inheritance gave him a claim to Namur, which came to him through her. In 1169 he acquired Flanders by marrying his widowed third cousin once removed, Margaret I of Flanders. A description of him from his own time called him the count with eyes of blue.

In the winter of 1182 or 1183 the count of Namur-Luxembourg, Baldwin's uncle, lay seriously ill and completely blind. Baldwin went at once to Luxembourg, where his uncle reconfirmed him as heir and let him receive the homage of several vassals. Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa confirmed the succession on 22 May 1184 at the Diet of Pentecost in Mainz, where Baldwin served as imperial sword bearer. He ruled Namur as margrave, with the name Baldwin I, from 1189 until 1195, and Flanders as Baldwin VIII from 1191 until the same year.

Baldwin died on 17 December 1195 and was buried at the monastery of Saint Waudru, before the altar of Blessed James the apostle. He and Margaret had many children. Isabelle of Hainaut, born in Valenciennes in April 1170, married King Philip II of France and died in Paris on 15 March 1190. Baldwin VI of Hainaut, born in 1171, was also count of Flanders and Latin Emperor, and his brother Henry of Flanders, born in 1176, became Latin Emperor too.

Yolanda of Flanders married Peter II of Courtenay, another Latin Emperor. Philip I of Namur lived from 1175 to 1212. Sybille of Hainaut married Guichard IV, Sire de Beaujeu, around 1197. Eustace of Flanders, who died in 1219, served as regent of the Kingdom of Thessalonica and married a daughter of Michael I Komnenos Doukas, ruler of Epirus.
baldwin-vi-count-of-flanders: Baldwin was the eldest son of Baldwin V of Flanders and Adela of France. A serious illness in childhood left him in weak health. His father planned to expand Flanders eastwards into the Holy Roman Empire, and at Easter 1051 Baldwin married Richilde, widow of Herman of Mons and heir of Hainaut. Emperor Henry III, who had not been consulted, was enraged. At his instigation the bishop of Cambrai banned the marriage as a breach of the rules of consanguinity, but Richilde had the ban lifted through her uncle Pope Leo IX.

When the prince-bishop of Liège, another vassal of Henry, reinstated the ban, the Baldwins invaded his land in 1053 and destroyed the cities of Thuin and Huy. In 1054 Henry invaded Flanders and laid waste the regions of Cambrai, Valenciennes and Douai, but failed to take Lille or Tournai. The next year the Baldwins allied with Godfrey the Bearded and besieged Antwerp, the father commanding the Flemish fleet on the Scheldt and the son the land troops. The campaign failed, and Baldwin VI was severely wounded and never fully recovered.

Henry died in October 1056. His successor accepted Baldwin VI as vassal for Hainaut, while Baldwin V remained a vassal for Imperial Flanders, the lands west of the Scheldt. Baldwin V had made his younger son Robert swear never to claim Flanders. On his father's death in 1067 Baldwin VI became count of both Flanders and Hainaut, uniting the two counties in a personal union. In his short reign he founded the town of Geraardsbergen to reinforce the border with the Empire.

In 1070, fearing he might die soon, Baldwin summoned Robert to Bruges and had him repeat his oath in St. Donatian's Church before the nobles of Flanders. He died in Bruges on 17 July 1070 and was buried at Hasnon Abbey, where he had built the church of St. Peter's. His young son Arnulf III succeeded under the regency of Richilde and was killed at the Battle of Cassel in 1071. Baldwin's younger son, Baldwin II of Hainaut, could not claim Flanders from Robert I.
balearic-islands: The archipelago lies in the western Mediterranean off the eastern coast of the Iberian Peninsula. It has two groups: the western Pityusic Islands, comprising Ibiza, Formentera and smaller islets, and the eastern Gymnesian Islands, principally Mallorca and Menorca. The Greeks called the islands Gymnesiai, and the Carthaginians and Romans used the name Baleares. Most ancient writers derived the name of the people from the Greek word for "to launch", from their skill as slingers. The earliest known habitation dates to about 2500 to 2300 BCE, by people associated with the Bell Beaker culture.

In ancient times the islanders of the Gymnesian Islands built talayots and were known for the sling. They served as mercenaries first under the Carthaginians and later under the Romans, each man carrying three slings of different lengths for stones of different sizes. Greek and Roman writers also told stories about their customs that the Romans found peculiar. The Phoenicians took possession of the islands early, and a trace survives in the town of Mago, now Mahón. Quintus Caecilius Metellus conquered the islands in 123 BCE, was given the surname Balearicus, settled 3,000 Roman and Hispanic colonists and founded Palma and Pollentia.

The Vandals under Genseric took them between 461 and 468, and Belisarius's troops restored Roman control in late 533 or early 534. In 707 the islands submitted to an Umayyad fleet, and in 903 Muslim forces captured them for the Emirate of Córdoba.

A crusade led by Pisa, with 420 ships, sacked Palma in 1115 and withdrew, and within a year the Berber Almoravids conquered the islands. King James I of Aragon captured Palma on the last day of 1229 after a three-month siege, took Menorca in 1232 and Ibiza in 1235. His will of 1276 created a Kingdom of Mallorca for his son James II, as a vassal of Aragon.

The kingdom ended when James III was killed at the Battle of Llucmajor in 1349 and the islands passed directly to the Crown of Aragon. Ottoman privateers raided them in the early 16th century, and in 1558 the corsair Turgut Reis ravaged them and 4,000 people were enslaved. Menorca was British for most of the 18th century after the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713, and returned to Spain by the Treaty of Amiens.

The islands form an autonomous community and province of Spain, with Palma as capital and largest city. They achieved self-government under a Statute of Autonomy in 1983, and Catalan and Spanish are co-official languages. They have 1,249,844 inhabitants and an area of 4,991.70 square kilometres. The four principal islands are major international tourist destinations.
balfour-declaration: Early British support for a larger Jewish presence in Palestine began in the early 1840s under Lord Palmerston and rested on geopolitical calculation, backed by evangelical sympathy for the restoration of the Jews, notably in Lord Shaftesbury. Zionism arose in the late nineteenth century in reaction to antisemitic and exclusionary nationalism in Europe. Around 1916 Jews were about 3 per cent of Palestine's population, which was mostly Muslim, with Christians second.

The British Cabinet first discussed Palestine on 9 November 1914. Within two months Herbert Samuel circulated a memorandum proposing support for Zionist ambitions to win Jewish support in the war. The first negotiations with the Zionists took place on 7 February 1917, and on 19 June Arthur Balfour asked Lord Rothschild and Chaim Weizmann to draft a public declaration. The War Cabinet decided to release it on 31 October 1917, after discussion that referred to the propaganda benefit among Jews worldwide. Palestine's Arab majority was not represented.

The text was a single sentence of 67 words, sent on 2 November 1917 from Balfour to Walter Rothschild for transmission to the Zionist Federation of Great Britain and Ireland. Two clauses promise support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, and two safeguard clauses cover the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities there and the rights and political status of Jews in other countries. The term national home had no precedent in international law and was intentionally vague about whether a Jewish state was contemplated. Lord Milner's amendment replaced the draft's reconstituted with in Palestine. The text was published in the press on 9 November.

The declaration was the first public support for Zionism by a major political power and greatly raised support for it among Jewish communities. Christians and Muslims, almost 90 per cent of Palestine's population, strongly opposed it, and in the wider Arab world it was seen as a betrayal of the McMahon-Hussein correspondence with the Sharif of Mecca. Jerusalem surrendered to the British on 9 December 1917.

The declaration became a core part of the British Mandate for Palestine. The British government acknowledged in 1939 that the wishes and interests of the local population should have been taken into account, and in 2018 that the declaration should have called for protection of the Palestinian Arabs' political rights. It is considered a principal cause of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and indirectly led to the emergence of Israel.
balfour-declaration-of-1926: The Imperial War Conference of 1917 passed a resolution drafted by the Canadian prime minister Robert Borden, which described the Dominions as autonomous nations within an Imperial Commonwealth with a right to an adequate voice in foreign policy and foreign relations. It also called for a constitutional conference after the war to readjust relations between the parts of the Empire. At the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 the Dominions sent separate representatives who were treated, for negotiation purposes, as part of one British Empire delegation. They signed the Treaty of Versailles under that designation but were admitted as separate members of the League of Nations. The confusion over their status prompted calls for a formal statement.

The Inter-Imperial Relations Committee, chaired by Arthur Balfour, who was Lord President of the Council, drew up the text, and the imperial prime ministers approved it unanimously on 15 November 1926. It was first proposed by the South African prime minister J. B. M. Hertzog and the Canadian prime minister William Lyon Mackenzie King. Balfour drafted the wording after two weeks of discussion with prime ministers and heads of delegations, with Hertzog, the Colonial Secretary Leo Amery and the Secretary of State for India Lord Birkenhead playing key roles.

It stands in the conference proceedings under the heading "Status of Great Britain and the Dominions" and describes the Dominions as in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown.

The declaration accepted the growing political and diplomatic independence of the Dominions since the First World War. It recommended that the governors-general, the King's representatives in each Dominion, should no longer also act automatically as the representative of the British government in diplomatic relations. High commissioners were gradually appointed, and their duties were soon recognised to be virtually those of an ambassador; the first British high commissioner was appointed to Canada in 1928. The conference's conclusions were restated at the 1930 conference and incorporated in the Statute of Westminster of December 1931, in which the British Parliament undertook not to make a law apply to a Dominion unless the law stated that the Dominion had requested and consented to it.
bali: Bali is the westernmost of the Lesser Sunda Islands, 3.2 km east of Java across the Bali Strait and about 8 degrees south of the equator. It spans roughly 153 km from east to west and 112 km from north to south. Its fauna is Asian in character, since it lies just west of the Wallace Line. The name appears in ancient inscriptions in the compound Vāli-dvīpa, "island"; one of the earliest attestations is the Belanjong pillar inscription of King Sri Kesari Warmadewa, dated about 914 CE. The meaning of Vāli is uncertain, and one proposal derives it from Sanskrit bali, "offering".

Austronesian peoples, who migrated from Taiwan through maritime Southeast Asia, inhabited Bali around 2000 BCE, and stone tools of that time have been found near Cekik in the west. Ancient Bali had nine Hindu sects, each revering a particular deity. The first known European contact came in 1512, when a Portuguese expedition led by António Abreu and Francisco Serrão sighted the northern shores. Cornelis de Houtman, a Dutch merchant-explorer, arrived in 1597.

Dutch political and economic control began in the 1840s on the north coast, where the Dutch set competing Balinese realms against each other, and was extended in the late 1890s by exploiting struggles between the kingdoms of the south. British forces took the Japanese surrender in 1945 and handed the island to the Dutch in 1946, who made it one of the 13 districts of the State of East Indonesia. Bali became part of the Republic of the United States of Indonesia when the Netherlands recognised independence on 29 December 1949, and a province in 1958.

Bali is an Indonesian province whose capital, Denpasar, is the most populous city of the Lesser Sunda Islands; the upland town of Ubud is regarded as its cultural centre. About 86 per cent of its people follow Balinese Hinduism, which combines local beliefs with Hindu ones, and Balinese and Indonesian are the most widely spoken languages. Pre-modern society had four castes. Temples and homes are oriented between the mountain Gunung Agung (kaja) and the sea (kelod). The Subak irrigation system of the rice fields was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012. Gamelan orchestras and dances such as legong, barong and kecak are central to its arts, and Nyepi, the Hindu New Year, is marked by a day of silence.
bali-aga: The Bali Aga are an Austronesian people, living mostly in eastern Bali, in Bangli and especially the Kintamani mountains, East Buleleng and East Karangasem, with others in the north-west and centre of the island. Many regard the name Bali Aga, or Bali Pegunungan (Mountain Balinese), as an insult carrying the sense of foolish mountain people, and prefer Bali Mula, Original Balinese.

Tradition traces the first inhabitants to the village of Bedulu, long before the Hindu-Javanese migration, and tells of Sri Aji Asura Bumibanten, last king of Pejeng, whose head was replaced by a pig's, so that he became known as Dalem Bedulu. In 1344 Bali Aga people under Ki Kayuselem revolted against the Majapahit Empire. B. Hauser-Schäublin points out that the 20 copperplate inscriptions of Sembiran show rapid change in Sembiran and Julah between the 10th and 12th centuries, so that these villages cannot be said to have lasted unchanged since pre-Hindu times.

A survey of 1988-1989 recorded about 38 traditional villages, while research published in 2015 found 62 across seven regencies, 25 of them in Bangli Regency. Their relative isolation preserved older Austronesian elements, visible in their architecture. They hold to a folk Hinduism that differs slightly from that of other Balinese. In Trunyan the dead are not cremated but laid on the ground by a Taru Menyan tree until only bones remain. Tenganan holds the three-day Udaba Sambah festival in June or July and forbids divorce and polygamy.

Most speak a Bali Aga dialect of Balinese that varies from village to village, as well as Indonesian, and use Kawi and Sanskrit in ritual. Tenganan is the only village that still weaves geringsing, a double ikat in which both warp and weft are dyed before weaving. The cloths, red, neutral and black, are held to be sacred and to assist in healing. Indigo is considered impure in Tenganan Pegringsingan, so its first dyeing stage is done in neighbouring Bugbug. Tourism and modernisation are changing this culture quickly.
bali-strait: The Bali Strait is one of the bodies of water around the island of Bali, with the Lombok Strait to the east, the Badung Strait to the southeast, the Bali Sea to the north and the Indian Ocean to the southwest. At its narrowest it is 2.4 kilometres wide. Geologically Bali and Java were joined until the end of the last ice age, when the rising sea cut the land bridge between them. Both islands share part of the Sunda shelf.

The water temperature varies with the monsoons. It averages about 28 to 29 degrees in the northwest monsoon, from January to March, and about 26 degrees in the southeast monsoon, from July to September. Currents are complex and depend on the monsoon; they reach up to 13 kilometres an hour in the northern, narrowest part. Tidal currents have a semi-diurnal amplitude.

In the Bali Strait incident of 28 January 1797, a French Navy squadron of six frigates met six British East Indiaman in the strait. The British ships disguised themselves as ships of the line and so intimidated the French into withdrawing.

There is no fixed link across the strait. The only crossing is a ferry between Ketapang in Java and Gilimanuk in Jembrana Regency, Bali. The Indonesian government has considered a bridge, but the project has been obstructed by economic hardship and by objections from some people in Bali. Early in the twenty-first century, pollution of the water by industrial waste, fertilizers and chemicals used in gold mining on the Javanese shore was recorded.
balian-of-ibelin: Balian was the youngest son of Barisan of Ibelin, a knight in the County of Jaffa who had been rewarded with the lordship of Ibelin after the revolt of Hugh II of Jaffa, and of Helvis of Ramla. He was baptised Barisan and adopted the Old French form Balian around 1175–76; Arabic sources call him Balian ibn Barzan. He first appears in charters in 1158. After the death of his eldest brother Hugh, the next brother, Baldwin, preferred to remain lord of Ramla and gave Ibelin to Balian, who held it as his vassal.

Balian supported Raymond III of Tripoli as regent in 1174 and led the vanguard at the Battle of Montgisard in 1177. That year he married Maria Komnene, widow of King Amalric I, and received the lordship of Nablus, her dower. In 1186 he and Maria put forward Amalric's daughter Isabella for the throne, but her husband Humphrey IV of Toron swore fealty to Guy of Lusignan, and Balian reluctantly paid homage to Guy.

Balian escaped from the defeat at Hattin on 4 July 1187 and reached Tyre. Saladin allowed him to go to Jerusalem to bring out his wife and children, on condition that he swear never to bear arms against him; the patriarch Eraclius absolved him of the oath. Finding the city almost without knights, Balian made 60 burgesses knights and prepared for a siege, which began on 20 September 1187. When the walls could not hold, he negotiated terms: Saladin would free seven thousand men for 30,000 bezants, and Balian handed over the Tower of David on 2 October.

After the fall of Jerusalem he and Maria backed Conrad of Montferrat, whom Isabella married after her first marriage was annulled. This brought them the hatred of Richard I of England's supporters. In 1192 Balian commanded the rearguard at the Battle of Jaffa and helped negotiate the Treaty of Jaffa between Richard and Saladin.

Balian died in 1193, in his early fifties. He and Maria had four children, among them John of Ibelin, Lord of Beirut, and Philip of Ibelin, regent of Cyprus. His squire Ernoul wrote parts of the Old French continuation of William of Tyre's chronicle, with a strong bias in favour of the Ibelin family. The name Balian remained common in the family through the 13th century.
balikesir: Close to modern Balıkesir stood the Roman town of Hadrianutherae, which, as its name recalls, was founded by the emperor Hadrian. He came to the region in 124 CE and, after a successful bear hunt, established a city bearing his name. In the Byzantine period the neglected small town was known as Palaiokastron, Old Castle.

When the Turkomans came from Middle Asia into Mysia, they called the place Balukiser after the castle remains. Balıkesir, formerly called Karasi, was founded by Karasi Bey in the 13th century on the remains of the small town, and 1297 is taken as the date of its establishment, one of few cities founded by Turks in Anatolia. The Ottomans annexed it in 1345. An earthquake in 1898 destroyed much of it, leaving only 51 buildings undamaged. The Greek army occupied the city on 30 June 1919 and the Turkish army retook it on 6 September 1922.

Balıkesir lies in the Marmara region and is the seat of Balıkesir Province. The urban part had a population of 314,958 in 2022. A fire on 3 August 1950 destroyed the centre of the city, burning 498 shops, and it was rebuilt; it was the second biggest disaster in the city after the 1898 earthquake. The Yildirim Mosque, built in 1388, is the oldest surviving Ottoman work in the city, and of the Zaganos Pasha Mosque, built in 1461 and named after the grand vizier of Mehmet the Conqueror, only the mosque and baths remain.
balikh-river: The Balikh is a perennial river that rises in the karstic spring of Ain al-Arous, just south of the Syria–Turkey border, and flows due south to join the Euphrates at Raqqa. It is the second largest tributary of the Euphrates in Syria, after the Khabur River.

Besides the spring it receives water from periodic streams and wadis draining the Harran Plain to the north and the plains on either side of its valley, among them the Jullab, the Wadi Qaramogh and the Wadi al-Kheder. These wadis can carry large amounts of water after heavy rain. Numerous dried-up wells in the old city of Harran suggest that the water table was once much higher.

The river forms the heart of a rich cultural region. Settlement mounds on both banks go back in some cases to the Late Neolithic, in the 6th millennium BCE. In the Bronze Age, in the 3rd millennium BCE, ancient Tuttul, near Raqqa at the mouth of the Balikh, and Tell Chuera to the north were important cities. Over the millennia nomadic tribes and settled populations interacted, and sometimes one gained the upper hand over the other.

In classical antiquity the region was called Osrhoene, with its capital at Edessa. Edessa, known in Arabic as ar-Ruha', and Harran, the Roman Carrhae, appear in Muslim and Jewish traditions respectively in the stories of Abraham and the other Hebrew patriarchs. After the Islamic conquest in the 7th century CE the region took the name of an Arab tribe, Diyar Mudar, the land of the Mudar. In 762 the caliph al-Mansur built the garrison city of ar-Rafiqa where the Balikh meets the Euphrates, and it merged with the Hellenistic city of Kallinikos into the urban agglomeration of Raqqa.

Nineteenth-century European travellers noted remains in the valley, but the first investigations came in 1938, when Sir Max Mallowan spent six weeks at five sites dating from the seventh to the second millennium BCE. In 1969 a French team under Jacques Cauvin exposed eight Neolithic occupation levels at one site.

Excavations at Tell Hammam al-Turkman began under Maurits N. van Loon in 1981 and continued under Diederik J. W. Meijer from 1988 to 2001, providing a well-stratified sequence for the valley's settlement history. Tell Sabi Abyad, one of the oldest sites, has been excavated under Peter Akkermans. The Turkish site of Göbekli Tepe stands on a hill directly north of the Harran Plains that feed the Balikh system.
balilla: The name Balilla is thought to mean little boy, and it is one of only two clues to the boy's age; the other is an Austrian report that mentions a little boy throwing stones at officials. The revolt took place while Habsburg forces occupied Genoa during the War of the Austrian Succession.

According to the legend, Austrian soldiers were dragging an artillery piece along a muddy road in the Portoria neighbourhood when it stuck in a ditch, and they forced onlookers to free it, cursing and lashing them. The boy picked up a stone, threw it at the patrol and asked his fellow citizens in Genoese, "Che l'inçe?" ("Shall I start?"). The uproar that followed ended with the Austrian garrison driven from the city, and the phrase became proverbial in Italian.

For his supposed youth and his revolt, Balilla became a symbol of the Italian struggle for independence and unification. The national anthem, Il Canto degli Italiani, composed in 1847, sings that the children of Italy are all called Balilla. Accounts of the sack of Genoa by Piedmontese troops in 1849 record soldiers shouting that the Genoese were all Balilla and deserved no mercy.

The Fascist government named its youth organisation, the Opera Nazionale Balilla, after him, and its anthem began "Fischia il sasso" ("The stone whistles"). The name was also given to the Ansaldo A.1 fighter of 1917, to several versions of the Fiat 508 car of the 1930s, and to two Italian navy submarines: the former German U42, sunk in 1916, and the name ship of the Balilla class, laid up in 1941 and scrapped after World War II.
balingen: Balingen is a town in Baden-Württemberg, capital of the district of Zollernalbkreis, near the Swabian Jura. It lies about 35 kilometres south of Tübingen and 70 kilometres south-southwest of Stuttgart. After Albstadt it is the second largest town in the district, and in 1973 it became the seat of the newly formed district of Zollernalb, which continued the old tradition of an official town. It is nicknamed Waagenstadt, the city of scales, and it is the home of the scale maker Bizerba.

Balingen is first mentioned in 863, and the earliest traces of settlement in the area are Alemannic terraced graves. According to historical records the town itself was established in 1255 by Count Friedrich von Zollern, and it was fortified before 1377. In 1403 the town, its castle and the Schalksburg estate were sold to the County of Württemberg, which made it the seat of an administrative district, Amt Balingen.

Fire repeatedly devastated the town. Chroniclers say it burned in 1286 during a feud between the Zollern and Hohenberg families, and further fires followed in 1546, 1607, 1672, 1724 and 1809. The last left only 55 of 445 buildings standing, and the rebuilding gave the town its classicist character. A civic foundation established a hospital in 1489 to care for the poor and the elderly. Balingen became part of the unified Germany in 1870. From 1939 to 1945 the town was the site of a subcamp of the Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp, which after the war became a French internment camp for former Nazi war criminals.

The castle, reconstructed in 1935, stands beside the old tanners' quarter, known as Little Venice. The Protestant church, finished in 1541, escaped the fire of 1809 and has a characteristic sundial in its apse. A publicly accessible sulphur spring, whose water has the smell of rotten eggs, is said to have healing powers. Among Balingen's natives are the Carthusian monk and humanist Gregor Reisch, who produced an encyclopedia of general knowledge.
balj-ibn-bishr: Balj ibn Bishr belonged to the Banu Qushayr, a branch of the Hawazin tribe, and was a nephew of Kulthum ibn Iyad al-Qasi, whom the Umayyad caliph Hisham appointed governor of Ifriqiya. In 741 he served as cavalry lieutenant in his uncle's army of 30,000 Arab troops, drawn from the regiments (junds) of Damascus, Jordan, Qinnasrin, Homs, Palestine and Egypt and sent against the Berber Revolt. He led the vanguard, which reached Kairouan in the summer of 741.

Billeting and supplies soon set the Syrians against their hosts, the Ifriqiyan Arabs under Habib ibn Abi Obeida al-Fihri, and old rivalries between the Qaysid tribes of the Syrian junds and the largely Yemenite Arabs of Ifriqiya and al-Andalus sharpened the quarrel. Balj, himself a Qaysid, inflamed it near Tlemcen until his uncle arrived. The divisions probably contributed to the defeat by the Berbers at the Battle of Bagdoura near Fes, where Kulthum was killed and 20,000 Syrians were killed or captured. Balj fled with the remaining 10,000 to Ceuta and barricaded himself there.

The governor of al-Andalus, Abd al-Malik ibn Qatn al-Fihri, at first refused the besieged Syrians passage and supplies, and is reported to have had an Arab merchant tortured and executed for sending them two boats of grain. A Berber rising in his own lands made him relent: Balj signed a treaty, secured by hostages, to help put down the Berbers and to return to North Africa within a year. The Syrians then helped defeat the three main Berber armies at Medina-Sidonia, Córdoba and Toledo.

When Ibn Qatn pressed for their departure, Balj claimed the governorship as his uncle's designated successor and had the elderly governor publicly tortured to death. Ibn Qatn's sons Qattan and Umayya raised the Andalusian Arabs, but the Syrian junds defeated them at the Battle of Aqua Portora outside Córdoba on 6 August 742. Balj was wounded there and died two days later; his lieutenant Thalaba ibn Salama al-Amili succeeded him. The chronicler Ibn al-Khatam names his killer as Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib al-Fihri, probably confusing him with Abd al-Rahman ibn Alqama al-Lakhmi, governor of Narbonne, who is reported to have struck Balj with his spear.
balkan-league: After the Crimean War, Russia pursued indirect expansion in the Balkans by creating friendly states under its patronage, on the basis of the Panslavic movement. It helped establish an autonomous Bulgaria after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 and expanded Serbia. After its humiliation in the Bosnian Crisis, Russia pressed the two to compromise and ally against Austria-Hungary and the Ottomans. The Italo-Turkish War, which began in September 1911, exposed Ottoman weakness, and the Albanian Uprising of 1911 raised Serbian fears of an Albanian state closing its last direction of expansion. Serbia and Bulgaria signed an alliance on 13 March 1912; a secret chapter redirected it against the Ottoman Empire, and Serbia then allied with Montenegro and Bulgaria with Greece.

Their agreement stipulated that Bulgaria would receive all of Macedonia south of the Kriva Palanka–Ohrid line, while Serbia would expand to the north of it, including Kosovo, and westward to the Adriatic coast. Bulgaria refused to agree on any division of gains with Greece, as it expected its own army to occupy most of Macedonia and Thessaloniki first. Greece, led by Eleftherios Venizelos, was nevertheless essential, since alone of the four it had a major fleet that could prevent Ottoman reinforcements from crossing from Asia by sea. Montenegro, a small country and a close ally of Serbia, was regarded as a second-class partner with limited aims around Shkodër.

The Great Powers officially agreed on the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire and warned the Balkan states, but their private signals differed, and the warning had no effect. Russia was the prime mover of the League, and France refused to support Russia in any conflict with Austria-Hungary caused by it. Montenegro declared war on 8 October 1912, and the other three states did so on 17 October, after an ultimatum on 13 October. The allied armies destroyed Ottoman power in Europe in a series of victories.

The old rivalries returned after victory, above all over the partition of Macedonia. The Great Powers insisted on an Albanian state and denied Serbia its gains on the Adriatic, so the Serbian share in Macedonia became more important. On 16 June 1913 Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece in the Second Balkan War. They repulsed it and invaded Bulgaria, and the Ottoman Empire and Romania also moved in. The peace left Bulgaria with some gains but cost it Eastern Thrace and most of Macedonia, and Bulgaria later entered the First World War on the side of the Central Powers. The Balkan Wars permanently broke the Russo-Bulgarian alliance and left Serbia and Montenegro as Russia's only allies in the region.
balkan-mountains: The range is conventionally taken to begin at the peak of Vrashka Chuka on the border between Bulgaria and Serbia. It runs more than 500 kilometres, first south-east along the border and then eastward across Bulgaria as a natural barrier between the northern and southern halves of the country, before reaching the Black Sea at Cape Emine. Botev Peak, at 2,376 metres, is the highest point. In the central and eastern sections the summit forms the watershed between the Black Sea and the Aegean. Bulgaria's longest river, the Iskar, cuts through the Iskar Gorge a few miles north of Sofia. The karst relief has produced many caves, among them Magura, with the most important European post-Palaeolithic cave paintings.

In antiquity and the Middle Ages the mountains were called Haemus, from a Thracian word for "mountain ridge". Greek myth explained the name either from haima, "blood", spilled when Zeus deflected the mountains Typhon hurled at him, or from King Haemus, who with his wife Rhodope was turned into a mountain for calling himself Zeus. The name Balkan is widely believed to have been brought by the Ottoman Turks and may derive from a Persian word for "high house". The Slavic name Stara Planina, "old mountain", is first attested at the beginning of the 16th century.

The range has had a special place in Bulgarian history since the founding of the state in 681, serving for centuries as a natural fortress and a barrier to Moesia, where most medieval capitals stood. Battles with the Byzantines took place at the Rishki Pass in 759, the Varbitsa Pass in 811, Tryavna in 1190 and Devina in 1279. At the Varbitsa Pass Khan Krum defeated a very large Byzantine army and killed Emperor Nikephoros I. Under Ottoman rule many haiduks found refuge there, and the poet Hristo Botev died in the western range near Vratsa in 1876. The Shipka Pass saw four battles in the Russo-Turkish War.

Twenty passes and two gorges cross the range. Central Balkan National Park protects ancient beech forests, listed in 2017 as part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Raysko Praskalo, the highest waterfall in the Balkans. Brown bears, wolves, chamois and deer live in the mountains, and edelweiss grows near Kozyata stena. The Belogradchik Rocks are the best-known rock formation. The range gave its name to the Balkans.
balkan-pact: The Balkan Pact, also called the Balkan Entente, was a treaty signed in Athens on 9 February 1934 by Greece, Romania, Turkey and Yugoslavia. Its aim was to maintain the geopolitical status quo in the region after World War I. Regional irredentist tensions had risen, and to present a united front against Bulgarian designs on their territories, the signatories agreed to suspend all disputed territorial claims against one another and against their immediate neighbours.

Other states in the region that had taken part in related diplomacy refused to sign the document, among them Italy, Albania, Bulgaria, Hungary and the Soviet Union. The pact took effect on the day it was signed and was registered in the League of Nations Treaty Series on 1 October 1934. Its signatories thus bound themselves to press no territorial claims in the region against one another, while Bulgaria, against whose designs the pact was directed, stayed outside it.

The pact helped to ensure peace between its signatories but did not end regional intrigues. Although it was directed against Bulgaria, its members signed the Salonika Agreement with Bulgaria on 31 July 1938. That agreement repealed the clauses of the Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine and the Treaty of Lausanne that had required demilitarised zones on Bulgaria's borders with Greece and Turkey, and it allowed Bulgaria to rearm.

The pact then broke down. Romania, under pressure from Nazi Germany, signed the Treaty of Craiova in 1940, and after the Axis invasions of Yugoslavia and Greece in 1941 the pact effectively ceased to exist. Turkey remained the only signatory that avoided any conflict during World War II, even after it joined the Allies in 1945.
balkan-wars: The wars grew out of the incomplete emergence of nation-states on the European territory of the Ottoman Empire in the second half of the 19th century. Serbia gained territory in 1877 to 1878, Greece acquired Thessaly in 1881, and Bulgaria incorporated Eastern Rumelia in 1885. All three, with Montenegro, sought more land in Rumelia, which comprised Eastern Rumelia, Albania, Macedonia and Thrace. After the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 hopes of reform rose among the Balkan peoples, but after the failed counter-coup of 1909 the nationalist element dominated. Italy's victory in the Italo-Turkish War and revolts in Albania showed the empire's weakness, and in 1912 Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro formed the Balkan League.

The First Balkan War began on 8 October 1912, when the League attacked the Ottoman Empire. The Bulgarian army, the best trained, was expected to carry the main burden in Thrace and the Serbian army to act in Macedonia, while Greece was needed above all for its navy, which could cut Ottoman forces off from reinforcement by sea. The war ended with the Treaty of London on 30 May 1913.

The allies then quarrelled over Macedonia. Serbia and Greece revealed that they meant to keep the territory their forces held, although Serbia had promised Bulgaria most of Macedonia in the League's original agreement. Bulgaria attacked its former allies on 16 June 1913. Serbian and Greek forces repelled the offensive and invaded Bulgaria. Romania, whose armies were intact, invaded from the north, and the Ottoman Empire advanced in Thrace and regained Adrianople.

The Treaty of Bucharest, of 10 August 1913, partitioned Macedonia. Serbia gained north-east Macedonia and the eastern half of the Sanjak of Novi Pazar, doubling its size, while Montenegro took the western half. Greece more than doubled in size, gaining southern Epirus, most of southern Macedonia and the port of Kavala. Romania took the southern part of Dobruja, and Bulgaria kept western Thrace with the port of Alexandroupolis. The Great Powers had also secured an independent Albania.

The wars ended Ottoman rule over most of the Balkan Peninsula. They were marked by ethnic cleansing, and all parties were responsible for grave atrocities against civilians. In Turkey they are remembered as a major disaster. The enlargement of Serbia and the relative weakening of Austria-Hungary set the stage for the July crisis of 1914.
balkans: The Balkans take their name from the Balkan Mountains, which stretch across the whole of Bulgaria. The Balkan Peninsula is bordered by the Adriatic Sea in the northwest, the Ionian Sea in the southwest, the Aegean Sea in the south, the Turkish Straits in the east and the Black Sea in the northeast, and has an area of about 470,000 square kilometres.

Its northern border is variously defined, often as the Danube, Sava and Kupa rivers. Most of the area is covered by mountain ranges running from the northwest to the southeast, among them the Balkan Mountains, the Rila-Rhodope massif, the Dinaric Alps and the Pindus range. The highest point is Musala, at 2,925 metres, in the Rila range in Bulgaria.

The concept of the Balkan Peninsula was created by the German geographer August Zeune in 1808, who mistakenly considered the Balkan Mountains the dominant mountain system of south-eastern Europe. Geographers such as Carl Ritter objected, and in the 19th century the term was a synonym for Rumelia, the European provinces of the Ottoman Empire. Its definition is geopolitical rather than geographical, and the term has acquired a stigmatised, pejorative meaning related to Balkanization; the region may instead be called Southeast Europe.

The Balkans have been inhabited since the Paleolithic and were the route by which farming spread from the Middle East to Europe in the Neolithic, in the 7th millennium BCE. The first known Neolithic culture of Old Europe, the Kakanj culture, appeared in central Bosnia and covers the period from 6795 to 4900 BCE. The region of the Old Europe or Danube civilisation peaked between 5000 and 3500 BCE.

In the Early Middle Ages the Byzantine Empire was the dominant state in the region, militarily and culturally. In the second half of the 9th century the Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius spread the Byzantine variety of Christianity to the majority of the previously pagan inhabitants; it was adopted first by the Bulgarians and Serbs, with the Romanians joining a little later. In 1912 and 1913 Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro allied against the Ottoman Empire in the First Balkan War and partitioned almost all its remaining European territories, and events led to the creation of an independent Albanian state.

Bulgaria began the Second Balkan War by attacking its former allies, and collapsed when the Greek army invaded and Romania intervened; the Ottoman Empire used the chance to recapture Eastern Thrace, fixing its western borders that still stand today as part of modern Turkey.
balkars: The Balkars are a Turkic people of the North Caucasus and one of the titular populations of Kabardino-Balkaria. They call themselves Malqarlıla, Alanla or Tawlula, meaning mountaineers. They share their language with the Karachays, and the two peoples are sometimes treated as a single ethnicity. Their ethnogenesis has been described as one of the most difficult problems in Caucasian studies. Proposed contributions include ancient Caucasian peoples, the Bulgars and Khazars, the Iranian Alans and Kipchaks with their Cuman allies; one account points to the war between Timur and Tokhtamysh in 1395, which drove Kipchak soldiers into the mountains.
Most Balkars adopted Islam in the eighteenth century through contact with the Kumyks, Circassians, Nogais and Crimean Tatars, and the Sufi Qadiriya order has a strong presence in the region.

During the Caucasian War the Balkars and Karachays helped the Kabardians in their rebellions against Russia. In the battle on the Chegem river on 9 May 1804, Lieutenant General Glazenap reported that Kabardians, Balkars, Karachays and Ossetians fought from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. In 1828 General Emmanuel led an expedition of more than 3,000 men into Karachay, and the Karachays then gave hostages and accepted Russian terms. After the Caucasian War and the Circassian Genocide, about 10,000 to 15,756 Karachays and Balkars emigrated to the Ottoman Empire.

In 1944 the Soviet government forcibly deported almost the entire Balkar population to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Omsk Oblast in Siberia. Starting on 8 March 1944 and finishing the next day, the NKVD loaded 37,713 Balkars onto 14 train echelons. By October 1946 deaths from malnutrition and disease had reduced their number to 32,817. The special settlement restrictions ended on 28 April 1956, but the Balkars could return to their mountain homeland only in 1957; during 1957 and 1958, 34,749 returned.

The Karachay-Balkar language belongs to the Kipchak group of Turkic languages. In the past Arabic was the written language for religious services and Turkish for business matters. From 1920 Balkar became the language of instruction in primary schools, with later instruction in Russian. Arabic letters were used to write Balkar until 1928, and Cyrillic after 1937. Ninety-six percent of the Balkars are bilingual in Balkar and Russian. The Balkars are considered deeply religious. The poet Kaisyn Kuliev wrote of his love for the Balkar land and its traditions.
balkh: Balkh lies about 24 km north-west of Mazar-i-Sharif and about 74 km south of the Amu Darya, at an elevation of about 365 m. French archaeologists found remains of a first settlement in the citadel, Bala Hissar, dating to the Early Iron Age, about 1500 to 1000 BCE. An earlier name, or the name of part of the city, was Zariaspa, which may come from the Zoroastrian fire temple Azar-i-Asp. The city's nickname is the mother of all cities.

The first historical reference is in the Mahabharata, which calls the place Valhika and says an important trade route passed through it. Balkh is the home town of Trapusa and Bahalika, the two merchants who, according to Buddhist scripture, became the Buddha's first disciples. Balkh was a refuge for Yazdegerd III when the Arabs conquered Persia in the 7th century; they attacked it in 645, compelled it to pay tribute in 653, and the Umayyad caliph Muawiya reconquered it in 663.

In 1220 Genghis Khan sacked Balkh, massacred its inhabitants and levelled the buildings that could be defended. Marco Polo, probably referring to its past, described it as a noble city and a great seat of learning, while Ibn Battuta, visiting about 1333, found it dilapidated and uninhabited.
