Vegetation on the coastal dunes is rare, though tamarisk bushes and dwarf acacias grow at the foot of ridges. The climate is humid but temperate, shaped by trade winds from the Canary Islands, and rainfall is minimal.

Geologically the northern bank is a flat-topped platform of carbonate deposits built up in water less than 10 m deep, made largely of barnacle and mollusc remains. Offshore, mud wedges have grown continuously over the past 9,000 years, since the sea flooded the shelf early in the Holocene. The surrounding waters are among the richest fishing waters of western Africa.

Because of its rich fishery and strategic position the territory was coveted by the European powers Portugal, France, England, Prussia and Holland. The Portuguese established a trading fort at Arguin in 1455, the first Portuguese installation south of Cape Bojador. Having little success in finding gold, they quickly turned to dealing in slaves, and in the mid-15th century as many as 1,000 slaves a year were exported from Arguin to Europe and to the sugar plantations of São Tomé. After the union of the Portuguese and Spanish crowns in 1580 the Spaniards became dominant, and in 1638 the Dutch replaced them and began exploiting the gum arabic trade. By 1678 the French had driven out the Dutch.

On 2 July 1816 the French frigate La Méduse ran aground at high tide off the bank. The account of the survivors Alexandre Corréard and Jean-Baptiste-Henri Savigny inspired Théodore Géricault's painting The Raft of the Medusa, completed in 1819 and now in the Louvre.

The park was established in 1976 as a nature reserve to protect its natural resources and fisheries. Its mudflats host more than two million migrant waders from northern Europe, Siberia and Greenland, and between 25,000 and 40,000 pairs of 15 nesting species form the largest colonies of water birds in West Africa. At least 108 bird species have been recorded, and marine mammals include Mediterranean monk seals and dolphins. About 500 Imraguen live in seven villages inside the park and fish by traditional methods, and no motor boats are allowed. It is a World Heritage Site and an Important Bird Area.
banca-monte-dei-paschi-di-siena: The bank traces its history to a mount of piety (monte di pietà) founded by order of the Magistrature of the Republic of Siena on 4 March 1472, when its statute was approved. Its basis was the Statuto dei Paschi, written in 1419, a law regulating agriculture and pastoralism in the Maremma. Its present form dates from 1624, when Siena had been incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Tuscany and Grand Duke Ferdinando II granted depositors, as their warranty, the income of the state-owned pastures of the Maremma, the Paschi that gave the bank its name. It consolidated and increased its banking activity during the 17th and 18th centuries.

After the unification of Italy the bank expanded across the peninsula and began new activities, among them mortgage loans, the first experience of them in Italy. It was still state-owned in the late 19th century. A decree of 8 August 1995 created two bodies, the joint-stock Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena and the non-profit Fondazione Monte dei Paschi di Siena, devoted to charity in education, science, health and art. The bank was listed on the Borsa Italiana on 25 June 1999.

After listing, the bank expanded, acquiring Banca Agricola Mantovana and Banca del Salento, and in November 2007 announced an agreement with Banco Santander to buy Banca Antonveneta for €9 billion. To finance this expansion it entered into hidden derivatives, the Santorini operation in 2002 and the Alexandria operation in 2006. Its top management, including the president Giuseppe Mussari, later contracted derivatives with Deutsche Bank and Nomura to hide the losses. The new board discovered the contracts at the end of November 2012, and the scandal became public on 23 January 2013. On 26 January 2013 the Bank of Italy approved a bailout of €3.9 billion.

In November 2019 thirteen former executives and bankers of Deutsche Bank and Nomura were sentenced to prison; a Milan appeals court overturned the convictions in May 2022, and Italy's Supreme Court of Cassation confirmed the acquittals in October 2023. After a failed recapitalisation the bank asked the Italian government for aid on 23 December 2016, and its industrial plan was approved in July 2017. In November 2023 the Italian government sold a 25% stake in the bank, partly privatising it, and it sold further stakes in 2024. In January 2025 the bank launched a takeover bid for Mediobanca, which succeeded in September 2025.

The bank's headquarters, the Palazzo Salimbeni in Siena, houses an art collection and historical documents. Until the euro crisis, the bank's profits financed the Palio di Siena, the renovation of Siena's historic buildings and biotech programmes.
band-e-kaisar: The Band-e Kaisar, also called Caesar's dam, the Pol-e Kaisar or Bridge of Valerian, was an arch bridge combined with a dam at Shushtar in Khuzestan, the first in Iran to join the two. According to Persian tradition it is named after the Roman emperor Valerian, who was captured with his army by Shapur I after his defeat at the Battle of Edessa in 260. The captives, a labour force that may have numbered up to 70,000 and included the Roman engineering corps, were put to work on irrigation at Shushtar, an important farming centre.

The Muslim historians Tabari and Masudi tell the story in the 9th and 10th centuries; their narrative cannot be trusted blindly, but local names such as Roumischgan and a tribe called Rumian point to a Roman presence.

The scheme had three steps. The Karun was first redirected into the Ab-i Gargar, a channel that rejoins the river some 50 kilometres to the south and encloses the orchard island of Mianab. The Band-e Kaisar was then built across the dried riverbed, about 500 metres long and 9 to 10 metres thick, with foundations following sandstone strata. Water flowed over its top, so it functioned as a weir, probably raising the level by 3 to 4 metres.

A roadway carried on at least forty arches ran along it, on the road between Pasargadae and the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon. Facing was of cut sandstone joined by iron clamps, filled with Roman concrete. A smaller barrage, the Band-e Mizan, controlled flow into the canal and may be later than the Roman works.

The system watered some 150,000 hectares and gave Shushtar its agricultural productivity. The dam bridge was repaired repeatedly in Islamic times, which accounts for the pointed arches seen today, and it stayed in use until the late 19th century. Combining a bridge with a dam became standard in Iranian hydraulic engineering until about 1000, ending with the Band-e Amir at Shiraz. Two further dam bridges on the same road, the Pa-i-Pol across the Karkheh and one at Dezful, are also assumed to be work of Roman prisoners. UNESCO designated the Shushtar system a World Heritage Site in 2009, Iran's tenth.
banda-aceh: Banda Aceh lies on the northwestern tip of Sumatra, at the mouth of the Aceh River, at an elevation of 35 metres. It is a semi-enclave within Aceh Besar Regency, bordering the Andaman Sea to the northwest. The first part of its name comes from the Persian bandar, meaning port or haven. It has been called the porch of Mecca, Serambi Mekkah, from the days when pilgrims travelling by sea from Indonesia stopped there before continuing to Mecca.

Banda Aceh has long been a strategic transport and trading hub in the eastern Indian Ocean. Marco Polo visited in 1292 and called it Lambri, from the Lamuri Kingdom that existed there, noting it as the logical first port of call for travellers from Arabia and India. By the mid-14th century it was under the trading kingdom of Samudera Pasai, which collapsed under declining economic conditions and pressure from the Portuguese, who occupied Malacca in the early 16th century. Sultan Ali Mughayat Syah of the newly founded Sultanate of Aceh expanded aggressively in the 1520s, built the sultanate on the remains of Pasai and other extinct kingdoms, and made the city its capital.

The Dutch declared war on Aceh on 26 March 1873 and bombarded the capital. With British support the city had been modernised and fortified, and the Dutch underestimated its defences. Their commander, General Johan Köhler, was killed in a skirmish near the city and the first expedition failed. A second expedition within months overwhelmed it, and the Dutch entered the capital in January 1874 believing the Acehnese had surrendered, but the conflict moved into the countryside. The city's name was changed back to Banda Aceh on 9 May 1963.

Banda Aceh is the capital and largest city of the Indonesian province of Aceh. On 26 December 2004 a tsunami caused by a 9.2-magnitude earthquake in the Indian Ocean struck the city, which was the closest major city to the epicentre. It destroyed more than 60 per cent of the city's buildings, and figures for the dead run from 60,000 to 167,000 inhabitants. Memorials include mass graves at Ulee Lheue, the Tsunami Museum and PLTD Apung 1, a floating diesel power ship carried inland. The Baiturrahman Grand Mosque, built in the reign of Iskandar Muda (1607 to 1636), was rebuilt in 1875 after burning in the Aceh war.
banda-islands: The Banda Islands are a volcanic group of ten small islands in the Banda Sea, about 140 km south of Seram and some 2,000 km east of Java, with a land area of about 172 square kilometres. The main group lies in the drowned caldera of a former volcano, with Banda Neira and the active volcano Gunung Api at its centre and Banda Besar, the largest island, forming part of the rim. Further west lie Ai and Run, which the English held in the early 17th century. Fort Belgica and Fort Nassau still stand on Banda Neira.

A rock shelter on Ai was in use at least 8,000 years ago, and Chinese records mention the islands as early as 200 BCE. Before the Dutch came, Banda was governed by an oligarchy of leading citizens, the orang kaya, each the head of a district, and the Bandanese traded actively across the archipelago. Nutmeg and mace, valued in Europe as flavourings, medicines and preservatives, came only from here, and Arab traders sold them to the Venetians without revealing their source. The Portuguese first arrived in early 1512 but never built a permanent post.

The Dutch were resented from the outset, and spices bought in Banda sold for about 300 times the price in Europe. They formed the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in 1602. Some orang kaya signed a treaty giving the Dutch a monopoly, the Eternal Compact, though not all leaders agreed to it. In May 1609 the orang kaya ambushed Admiral Pieter Willemsz Verhoeff and killed him and 46 others. The Dutch fought the English on Ai in 1615 and again a year later.

In 1621 Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen landed soldiers, forced the orang kaya at gunpoint to sign an impossible treaty and then punished alleged violations with a massacre. Forty orang kaya were beheaded by Japanese mercenaries hired by the Dutch. Before the conquest the population is estimated at 13,000 to 15,000; perhaps a thousand remained as forced labourers, and many fled to other islands.

Coen divided the land, with about half a million nutmeg trees, into sixty-eight plots held by Dutch planters called perkeniers and worked by slaves, convicts and indentured labourers brought in from elsewhere. The VOC held a monopoly on nutmeg production and export for almost two hundred years. The conquest marked the start of the first overt colonial rule in Indonesia, under the VOC. In 1667 the Treaty of Breda ended the English claim to Run.
banda-singh-bahadur: He was born Lachman Dev on 27 October 1670 at Rajouri, in the poor Hindu family of a farmer, Ram Dev. Sources from his lifetime, such as the Akhbar-i-Darbar-i-Mualla and the Sri Gur Sobha, do not name his caste; much later tradition calls him a Dogra Rajput or a Sodhi Khatri. A tale holds that at 15 he was so moved by a doe he killed while hunting that he became an ascetic. The ascetic Janaki Prasad named him Madho Das, and as a bairagi of the Vaishnavite tradition he founded a monastery at Nanded on the Godavari.

After Guru Gobind Singh's visit in 1708 he took Amrit and joined the Khalsa. In September 1708 the Guru gave him the title Bahadur, a war drum, the Nishan Sahib, five arrows and letters calling on all Sikhs to join him. He won support in Haryana by suppressing bandits and wrote to the Sikh communities of Majha, Doaba and Malwa. His first major action was the sack of the Mughal provincial capital of Samana in November 1709.

Against Wazir Khan, Governor of Sirhind, whose army of more than 20,000 had artillery and elephants, his forces had only spears, arrows and swords. He made the village of Mukhlisgarh his capital, renamed it Lohgarh, and struck coins there, while Sikh forces took Saharanpur and Muzaffarnagar. Emperor Bahadur Shah I marched on Punjab, and on 29 August 1710 ordered all Hindus to shave their beards so that no Sikh agents could enter his camps. A Mughal army under Munim Khan retook Sirhind and besieged Lohgarh with 60,000 troops.

In 1714 Emperor Farrukh Siyar had Guru Gobind Singh's widow Mata Sundari urge Banda to submit. He refused, she excommunicated him, and the Sikhs split into the Tat Khalsa and his own Bandais, divided over his red robes, his insistence on vegetarianism and his slogan Fateh Darshan. About fifteen thousand followers left him. In March 1715 Abd al-Samad Khan, Governor of Lahore, besieged him at Gurdas Nangal, and on 7 December 1715 the Mughals broke into the starving garrison.

He was taken to Delhi with 780 prisoners, who were executed at about 100 a day. His four-year-old son Ajai Singh was killed before him, and on 9 June 1716 he was tortured and beheaded. A British East India Company diplomat's letter on the executions is one of the earliest Western accounts of the Sikhs. The 328-foot Fateh Burj at the site of the Battle of Chappar Chiri is dedicated to him.
bandar-abbas: Bandar Abbas stands on flat ground about 9 metres above sea level on the southern coast of Iran, at the narrow Strait of Hormuz, just across from Oman's Musandam. The island of Qeshm lies to the south, and the nearest hills are Mount Geno, 17 kilometres to the north. Because it has always been a port, its names have reflected that function. The commonest was Gamrūn, which Henry Yule derives either from gümrük, "customhouse", or, which he found more convincing, from Persian kamrūn, "shrimp". The present name means "Port of Abbas", after Abbas the Great, who reigned from 1588 to 1629.

The earliest record of the place is from the reign of Darius the Great, between 522 and 486 BCE, when his commander Scylax embarked from here for India and the Red Sea. The Portuguese conquered it in 1514 and made it an important base for protecting their commerce in the Persian Gulf and India, calling it Comorão for the lobsters and crabs on its shores. Shah Abbas took it from them in 1614, and in 1622 he defeated Portuguese troops in the region with the help of the English Navy and the Persian commander Imam Quli Khan. The city was renamed Bandar-e Abbas, and with English naval backing he developed it into a major port.

In 1625 a combined Anglo-Dutch fleet attacked the Portuguese and took the trade posts. The Dutch East India Company soon outcompeted the English, and from 1654 it controlled the local spice and silk trade completely until 1765. From 1794 to 1868 the city was held by the Sultanate of Oman and Zanzibar under a lease from Persia, whose Arabic and Persian versions apparently differed. Persia tried to oust the Omanis in 1823 and recovered the city in 1854. Under British pressure after the Anglo-Persian War of 1856 the lease was renewed, and in 1868 it was renewed once more and cancelled two months later by the Persian government.

An earthquake in July 1902 damaged parts of the city. Under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi the government invested heavily in the port: in 1955 it was a small fishing port of about 17,000 people, and in 1977 the bulk of the Iranian Navy was moved from Khorramshahr to a new headquarters and naval base here. The city is the capital of Hormozgan Province and has been the southern terminus of Iran's main north-south railway since 1993. Its original inhabitants speak Bandari, a variety of Persian. Its pottery was once exported to England as goombroon ware.
bandar-e-anzali: Bandar-e Anzali lies on the Caspian Sea in Gilan province and consists of an island called Mianposhteh and the surrounding lands. The Anzali Lagoon divides the port in two parts, and the city is connected by two bridges to Beheshti Island. The humid subtropical climate, with heavy autumn and early winter rain and water draining from the Elburz Mountains, allows crops such as rice and tea that need much moisture. Anzali Gulf was a safe harbour for trade ships and fishing boats, and the city was home to the first and biggest port on the southern shores of the Caspian Sea.

The city is described as an old settlement first inhabited by the Cadusii. Its name is given in Middle Persian as Anzalag. It was renamed Pahlavi in 1935. In 1919, after the collapse of General Anton Denikin's White Russian army, eighteen of his ships sought refuge there.

On 18 May 1920 a Soviet flotilla of thirteen ships made a surprise attack on Anzali and captured the British garrison and the eighteen White Russian ships. This allowed the establishment of the short-lived Persian Socialist Republic and the Persian Communist Party. Soviet authorities denied responsibility for the attack and blamed the local Russian naval commander for acting on his own authority.

The people of Anzali speak Gilaki, Azerbaijani and Persian, and the city is the biggest after Rasht where Gilaki is spoken. Most are adherents of Shia Islam, with a sizeable Armenian Christian minority. The 2016 census counted 118,564 people. Historically the townspeople were mostly involved in the fish trade, and the city is a centre of caviar production. Its sights include a clock tower called Manareh, the harbour promenade, the lagoon, and buildings such as the Mian Poshte Palace and the Motamedi Edifice.
bandar-lengeh: Bandar Lengeh is a port on the Persian Gulf, 280 km from Lar, 192 km from Bandar Abbas and 420 km from Bushehr. It is the capital of Bandar Lengeh County in Hormozgan province, and its climate is hot and humid. Its population was 25,303 at the census of 2006 and 30,435 in 2016. The French traveller Abbé Carré made the first written mention of it in 1674, under the name Talanga, describing a large Arab village with houses made only of canes and leaves.

In 1773 the English traveller Edward Ives still found a small village. A Dutch document of 1764 describes inhabitants called Mersousies, with 50 vessels and 700 men, living from the sale of firewood and charcoal. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747, factions on both sides of the Gulf contested the coast. The Qavasem tribe backed Mohammad Naser Khan Lari, the governor of Lar, who besieged Bandar Lengeh without success in 1760.

After Qavasem attacks on Qeshm Island, Sheikh Mohammad Khan Bastaki, governor of Bandar Abbas, allowed them to settle at Bandar Lengeh and placed them under the governor of Bastak. Their leader there held the title of sheikh and collected revenue. In the 1790s the Qavasem of Lengeh joined the Wahhabi movement, and the British, who saw the town as a stronghold of piracy, destroyed twenty Qavasem vessels there in 1809.

In 1856 the Iranian government ended the town's status as a free-trade zone, and governors were soon appointed by the governor of Fars. The government arrested the Qavasem ruler Sheikh Qazib ibn Rashed on 11 September 1887; he died in Tehran in 1897 without children, and no later Arab governed the town. Sheikh Mohammad ibn Khalifa seized it on 4 July 1898, and a force of 700 soldiers retook it on 2 March 1899. In March 1903 a Belgian, Lambert Molitor, became customs director at the port. The Pahlavi dynasty set up its first police department in Bandar Lengeh in March 1926.

The town is still a port of the Iranian coast, and its port handles agricultural exports, mostly bound for the UAE. In 2026 the United States Navy struck two Iranian corvettes anchored off the coast on 6 March, during the 2026 Iran war, and strikes hit the town and nearby Kong on 5 and 6 April, killing at least six people and wounding seventeen.
bandung: Bandung lies in a river basin on the western highland of Java, about 145 kilometres south-east of Jakarta, ringed by volcanic mountains rising to 2,400 metres. These mountains were the main reason the Dutch East Indies government planned to move its capital from Batavia, now Jakarta, to the city. The basin's main river is the Citarum, and its branch the Cikapundung divides the city from north to south. The altitude gives it one of the coolest climates among Indonesia's provincial capitals.

The earliest reference to the area dates to 1488. In the 17th and 18th centuries the Dutch East Indies Company established plantations in the area, and in 1786 a supply road linked Batavia, Bogor, Cianjur, Bandung, Sumedang and Cirebon. In 1809 Napoleon ordered Governor Herman Willem Daendels to improve Java's defences against a possible British invasion. Daendels had a road of about 1,000 km built across the island; laid in Bandung in 1810 as De Groote Postweg, the Great Post Road, it follows the present Jalan Asia-Afrika.

On his orders the regency's chief administrator, R. A. Wiranatakusumah II, moved his office to a site near a pair of holy wells, now the city square, where he built a palace, a grand mosque and a pendopo in the classical Sundanese orientation. In 1856 the town became capital of the Preanger Regencies Residency, which it remained until 1925.

In the early 20th century the Dutch residents demanded a municipal government, which was granted in 1906, and the city developed into an exclusive resort for Europeans with hotels, cafés and shops. Braga Street, lined with boutiques selling Paris fashions, gave the city the nickname Parijs van Java, the Paris of Java. In 1920 the architect Henri Maclaine Pont planned the first technical university in the Dutch East Indies, the Technische Hogeschool te Bandung, now the Bandung Institute of Technology. After Indonesia declared independence in 1945 it grew from a quiet town into a dense metropolis. In 1955 President Sukarno hosted the first Asian-African Conference there.

Bandung is the capital of West Java province. Most of its people are Sundanese, and Sundanese is widely spoken alongside standard Indonesian. The population was 2.444 million at the May 2020 census. It is known for its music, including the angklung, and for its universities and creative industries, and it belongs to the UNESCO Creative Cities Network.
bandung-conference: The conference took place on 18 to 24 April 1955 in Bandung, West Java. Its twenty-nine participating countries represented a total population of 1.5 billion people, 54 per cent of the world's population. It was organised by Indonesia, Burma, India, Ceylon and Pakistan. Sukarno and Jawaharlal Nehru were key organisers in an effort to build a nonaligned movement. Nehru's idea went back to the Asian Relations Conference of March 1947. Indonesia proposed a global conference at the Colombo Powers meeting in April 1954, and a planning group met at Bogor in December 1954.

The aims were to promote goodwill and cooperation among the new nations and to take up racism and colonialism. The organisers resented what they saw as the Western powers' reluctance to consult them in a setting of Cold War tension. Sukarno also wanted support for Indonesia's claim to West New Guinea against the Netherlands. Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai also backed the meeting, with China hoping to lead anti-colonial forces.

A main debate was whether Soviet policies in Eastern Europe and Central Asia should be condemned along with Western colonialism. The delegates agreed to condemn colonialism in all of its manifestations, which implicitly censured the Soviet Union as well as the West. Zhou Enlai, who survived an assassination attempt on the way to the conference, was moderate and conciliatory, endorsed the right of every nation to choose its own system, and calmed the fears of some anticommunist delegates. Nehru advocated non-alignment and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and warned against military alliances with either side in the Cold War, but was disappointed by the generally cool reception.

The conference unanimously adopted a ten-point declaration on the promotion of world peace and cooperation, known as the Dasasila Bandung, which drew on the principles of the Charter of the United Nations and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. It called for respect for human rights, sovereignty and territorial integrity, equality of all races and nations, non-intervention and the peaceful settlement of disputes. The final communiqué urged developing countries to loosen their dependence on the industrialised nations through technical assistance to one another. The declaration became a foundational framework for the Non-Aligned Movement, though the two initiatives ran in parallel in the 1960s.
banffshire: Banffshire had a 30-mile stretch of coast on the Moray Firth from Spey Bay to Cullykhan Bay, with its hinterland and a long, tapering tail running some 55 miles inland along the Spey into the Grampian Mountains. It bordered Moray and Inverness-shire to the west and Aberdeenshire to the east and south. The county town was Banff, while the largest settlement was Buckie. The area holds evidence of prehistoric settlement near the coast, such as the cairns at Longman Hill and Cairn Lee, as well as ruined medieval castles and the 12th-century kirk of Gamrie.

The origins of the shire, the area run by a sheriff, are obscure: there is some evidence that it existed under David I, who reigned from 1124 to 1153, but the first documented Sheriff of Banff dates from the 13th century. The sheriff's jurisdiction covered small provincial lordships lying between the larger provinces of Moray and Buchan, among them Boyne and Enzie on the coast and Strathisla, Glenlivet, Strathavon and Glenfiddich inland. In 1242 Alexander II granted five properties of the king's forest of Banff to Waleran de Normanville.

Commissioners of Supply governed the shire from 1667, and after the Acts of Union of 1707 the English word county came to be used beside shire. An elected county council first met on 22 May 1890 at Banff Sheriff Court. Boundary changes that took effect on 15 May 1891 removed four detached parts surrounded by Aberdeenshire, the largest being the parish of St Fergus. In 1975 the county was placed in the Grampian region and divided between the districts of Banff and Buchan and Moray.

Since 1996 the area has been shared between the Moray and Aberdeenshire council areas. The pre-1975 boundaries are still used as a registration county for land registration and as a lieutenancy area. Its towns include Banff, Buckie, Keith, Cullen, Dufftown, Macduff, Portsoy and Tomintoul, and the Aberdeen–Inverness railway runs through Keith.
bangkok: Bangkok lies in the Chao Phraya River delta in Thailand's central plain. The river flows southwards through the city and empties into the Gulf of Thailand about 25 kilometres south of the centre. The area is flat and low-lying, with an average elevation of 1.5 metres above sea level. Most of it was originally swampland, gradually drained and irrigated by canals (khlong) dug between the 16th and 19th centuries. The origin of the name is unclear. Bang is a Thai word for a village on a stream, and the name may derive from Bang Ko, 'island', or from Bang Makok, after a plant bearing olive-like fruit.

The history of Bangkok goes back at least to the early 15th century, when it was a village on the west bank of the Chao Phraya under Ayutthaya. It served as a customs outpost with forts on both sides of the river, and was the site of a siege in 1688 in which the French were expelled from Siam. After Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767, King Taksin made the town his capital. The City Pillar was erected on 21 April 1782, regarded as the date of the city's foundation as the capital, and foreign visitors continued to call it Bangkok.

The city was at the heart of the modernisation of Siam in the late 19th century. Charoen Krung Road, the first built by Western techniques, was completed in 1864, and rail transport was introduced in 1893. Through the 20th century the city was at the centre of political struggles, as Siam abolished absolute monarchy and adopted constitutional rule. It became a special administrative area under the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration in 1972.

Bangkok is governed by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration and is a special administrative area at provincial level, divided into fifty districts. Its landmarks include the Grand Palace and the Buddhist temples Wat Arun and Wat Pho. Thailand's five oldest universities, Chulalongkorn, Thammasat, Kasetsart, Mahidol and Silpakorn, founded between 1917 and 1943, are in the city.
bangladesh-liberation-war: Pakistan came into being in August 1947 in two geographically and culturally separate parts, with India between them. In 1948 Governor-General Muhammad Ali Jinnah declared that Urdu alone would be the federal language, although Bengali speakers made up over 56% of the population. East Pakistan had the larger population but West Pakistan dominated politically and received more from the common budget. The 1970 Bhola cyclone struck the East Pakistan coast on 12 November and killed an estimated 300,000 people, and eleven East Pakistani leaders charged the government with gross neglect.

On the night of 25 March 1971 the Pakistan Army began Operation Searchlight, a planned pacification meant to take the major cities and eliminate all opposition within a month. Foreign journalists were deported beforehand, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was arrested. Major Ziaur Rahman broadcast the declaration of independence from the radio station at Chittagong on 26 March. Resistance grew as Bengali soldiers defected and merged into the Mukti Bahini, supplied from India, while Pakistan raised the Razakar, Al-Badr and Al-Shams militias.

India joined the war on 3 December after Pakistani air strikes on northern India. Indian aircraft achieved near-total air supremacy within a week, and the East Pakistan ports were blockaded. On 16 December 1971 the Pakistani commander in East Pakistan signed the Instrument of Surrender in Dhaka, and over 93,000 Pakistani troops surrendered, the largest surrender since the Second World War.

The Pakistani military and supporting militias carried out widespread killings, deportation and rape. Estimates range from 300,000 to 3,000,000 killed and from 200,000 to 400,000 women raped. On 14 December 1971 the army and the Razakars seized at least 100 physicians, professors, writers and engineers in Dacca and murdered them. An estimated 10 million refugees fled to India and 30 million were internally displaced.

Bhutan was the first state to recognise Bangladesh, on 6 December 1971. The Simla Agreement of 1972 between India and Pakistan secured Pakistani recognition of Bangladesh in exchange for the return of prisoners of war. In West Pakistan the defeat discredited Yahya Khan's rule. The war changed the geopolitical landscape of South Asia and became an episode of Cold War tension involving the United States, the Soviet Union and China.
bangor-on-dee: The anglicised name refers to the River Dee, while the older Welsh name, Bangor-is-y-Coed, means a settlement with a wattle enclosure below the wood. That form was first recorded in 1699, and another name for the parish, Bangor Monachorum, or Bangor of the monks, in 1677. Until 1974 the village lay in the Maelor Saesneg, an exclave of Flintshire, and from 1974 to 1996 in the county of Clwyd.

The monastery was founded in about 560 by Saint Dunod, or Dunawd. It was destroyed by Æthelfrith of Northumbria after he defeated the Welsh at the Battle of Chester, which probably took place near the village. Before the battle the monks had fasted for three days and climbed a hill to pray for a Welsh victory; Æthelfrith had them massacred, and Bede wrote that only 50 escaped. Other accounts give very different numbers, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 200 priests. Some monks went to Bardsey Island and appear in lists of saints. No trace of the monastery remains and even its site is uncertain, perhaps because it was built of wattle and daub.

The settlement probably continued and drew pilgrims, though it is not in the Domesday Book. A village certainly existed by 1300, when the present church of Saint Dunawd is believed to have been built. In the late 1690s the historian Edward Lhuyd counted only 26 houses, but by the end of the 19th century it had a free school, a coaching inn, a shop and a brewery. Walter Scott told the massacre in his poem The Monks of Bangor's March, which Ludwig van Beethoven set to music.

The village is a community with a population of 1,110 at the 2011 census. Its five-arched stone bridge over the Dee was rebuilt in 1658, it is believed to the designs of Inigo Jones, in place of a medieval bridge. A railway line from Wrexham to Ellesmere served the village from 1895 until passenger services ended in 1962, and a National Hunt racecourse lies to the south-west.
bangsamoro: Bangsamoro lies in the southwestern part of the island of Mindanao and includes the Sulu archipelago. The name derives from the Old Malay word bangsa, meaning race or nation, and Moro, the collective term for the various predominantly Muslim ethnic groups of the Philippines. The Maranao and Iranun form a large part of the population, and the Tausūg, Yakan and Sama are the main groups of the Sulu archipelago.

Two other groups live among the Moros: the Lumad, of whom the Teduray are the largest group, and settler communities, mainly Christian, including Tagalog, Ilocano and Visayan peoples. Cebuano and Tagalog serve as lingua francas.

The westernmost and west-central parts of Mindanao have been the traditional homeland of Muslim Filipinos since the 15th century, before the Spanish began to colonize most of the Philippines in 1565. Most of Mindanao was the homeland of indigenous Lumad groups who were neither Christian nor Muslim. Spanish rule did not fully conquer the archipelago because of Moro resistance, and modern Moro leaders see centuries of resistance to the Spanish, Americans and Japanese as one national liberation movement.

The American colonial government began promoting migration to Mindanao in 1903, and later presidents continued it. The share of indigenous peoples fell from a majority in 1913 to a minority by 1976, and the best lands went to settlers and corporate agriculture. The Tripoli Agreement of 23 December 1976 between the government and the MNLF promised an autonomous region, but its implementation collapsed and hostilities resumed. Salamat Hashim then led a splinter faction that became the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

The MILF rejected the validity of the earlier autonomous region and called for one with more powers. In 2014 the government and the MILF negotiated the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, and the Bangsamoro Organic Law was signed on 26 July 2018. A two-part plebiscite on 21 January and 6 February 2019 approved the new region, which replaced the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. Cotabato City voted to join, and 63 barangays of Cotabato province were added.

The organic law provides for a parliamentary system headed by a chief minister, and states that the region remains an integral part of the national territory. Kulintang gong music is central to the culture of Muslims, Lumads and Christians alike, and the region includes Lake Lanao and the Liguasan Marsh.
bani-utbah: The members of the confederation are called the Utub, singular Utbi; English sources wrote it Attoobee or Uttoobee until the late 19th century. Most of its clans and families, among them the Al Sabah and Al Khalifa, trace their descent to the Anizah tribe, while some, such as the Al Bin Ali, trace theirs to the Banu Sulaym. The Al Bin Ali and the present ruling families of Bahrain and Kuwait led the confederation.

Their homeland was Najd in central Arabia. During a long drought in the 17th century the clans left it, travelling through Al Aflaj, Qatif and Al Ahsa to Freiha in north-western Qatar, which they made a fortified coastal base close to trade routes and pearling waters. After clashes with the dominant Al Musallam tribe they left for the area near Basra in 1716, but the Ottomans soon expelled them from Umm Qasr for raiding caravans and ships on the Shatt al-Arab.

The Utub were already sea-going before their settlement. Some served as mariners in the Persian navy and, revolting against their treatment, sailed off with several ships. In 1717 they helped the Imam of Oman, Sultan bin Saif II, take Bahrain, Qishm and other islands from the Safavids.

After their expulsion from Iraq the clans moved to Kuwait and set up a government under the Al Sabah. Around the 1760s the Al Jalahma and Al Khalifa moved on to Zubarah, leaving Kuwait to the Al Sabah. The two clans opened a free-trade port there, but the Al Khalifa would not share its profits, and the Al Jalahma moved to Al Ruwais while the Al Khalifa took control of the pearl banks around Qatar.

Persian attacks on Zubarah led the Al Bin Ali, Al Jalahma and Al Khalifa to set aside their quarrels and, with other Arab clans, to drive the Persians out of Bahrain. A Utub fleet from Kuwait set Manama ablaze, and the Persian garrisons were overrun. The army of Nasr Al-Madhkur was defeated, his sword falling to Salama bin Saif Al Bin Ali, and the House of Khalifa has ruled Bahrain ever since. In 1811 the confederation defeated Rahmah ibn Jabir al-Jalhami, who was preparing to invade Bahrain from Al Khuwayr in the service of the Emirate of Diriyah.
bani-yas: The Bani Yas came from the Najd region of Central Arabia and, with the Awamir, trace their descent from Yas ibn Amer ibn Sa'sa'a. Around 1700 the Al Bu Falah, then the most powerful house of the confederation, settled with the Bani Yas clans in the Liwa oasis. The tribe later also settled around Al Ain and Buraimi when the Al Bu Falah acquired land in the Buraimi Oasis, and it kept close relations with the Dhawahir tribe, rivals of the Na'im and the Bani Ka'ab there.

After fresh water was found on the island of Abu Dhabi, the Al Bu Falah moved there in 1793 and settled in 1795, founding the town that grew in trade and became the seat of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, with Qasr al-Hosn built as its fort. The Al Maktoum, a branch of the Al Bu Falasah, established their own Emirate of Dubai, and in 1835 members of the tribe settled Khor Al Adaid in south-eastern Qatar. Within the United Arab Emirates the ruler of Abu Dhabi is customarily elected president and the ruler of Dubai vice president and prime minister.

J. C. Lorimer's Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf estimated the Bani Yas, the largest single tribe of the coast, at about 12,000 early in the 20th century, of whom some 2,000 were nomads; half the settled members lived in the Liwa Oasis, 2,800 in Abu Dhabi town and about 2,000 in Dubai. Their numbers fell to about 8,000 by the early 1950s as families left for work in Qatar, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, returning only after Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan came to power.

Observers have counted the sections differently: Lorimer named 15 in 1907, J. B. Kelly 14 major and 6 minor ones, and leading members today name more than 20, as allied tribes at times sought full integration under the Ruler of Abu Dhabi and at other times asserted their autonomy.
banias: Banias lies at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Golan Heights, beside the spring that feeds the Banias River, one of the main tributaries of the Jordan. The spring once gushed from a large cave in a cliff, until an earthquake moved it to the foot of the terrace below. Before Greek influence its god was called Ba'al-gad or Ba'al Hermon; the Ptolemaic kings built a cult centre there in the 3rd century BCE, and the cave was dedicated to Pan. The name Paneas, which became Baniyas in Arabic, comes from Pan.

Antiochus III defeated the Ptolemaic army near the place at the Battle of Panium around 200–198 BCE. After 20 BCE the district passed to Herod the Great. Agrippa II renamed the city Neronias in 61 CE, a name dropped in 68 CE, and Vespasian visited it in 67 CE. Excavations show severe decline in the early Byzantine period, which scholars link to heavy taxation after Diocletian's reforms. In 635 the city surrendered on favourable terms to Khalid ibn al-Walid, and it remained the chief town of the district of al-Djawlan.

The Crusaders, who called it Belinas, held it in 1129–1132 and 1140–1164, when it was the centre of the fief of Humphrey II of Toron. Nur ad-Din besieged it in 1157 and captured it on 18 November 1164. Al-Mu'azzam Isa had its fortress destroyed in March 1219. In the Mamluk period it was the seat of a subdistrict under Damascus. A traveller counted about 500 inhabitants in 1825.

In 1923 the border between French Syria and British Palestine was set 750 metres south of the spring. The Golani Brigade captured the village on 10 June 1967, the last day of the Six-Day War; its residents fled to Majdal Shams, and Israeli bulldozers destroyed the village, leaving the mosque, church and shrines. The site, in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, has been the Hermon Stream (Banias) Nature Reserve since 1977, and Christians come on pilgrimage to the place the Gospels name Caesarea Philippi.
banjarmasin: Banjarmasin lies on a delta island near the confluence of the Barito and Martapura rivers, and the Martapura bisects it. The land is flat and low-lying, and several smaller rivers affected by the tides form its drainage. The city sits in a swampy region, generally below water level, and is prone to flooding by tidal bores. Its climate is tropical monsoon, with heavy rain from November to June.

The name is thought to be a corruption of Bandar Masih, Port Masih, after Patih Masih, who ruled the port and surrounding villages. Dayaks from the interior visited the port to trade, and some settled there.Europeans first met the Banjar through trade, mostly at Banten from 1596. Dutch traders came to the port only after Banten's rulers banned them. On 17 July 1607 the Sultan took revenge on a Dutch ship at Banjarmasin by hijacking it and massacring the crew. A trade agreement gave the Dutch East India Company a monopoly of trade in the port, but the sultan expelled the company in 1638 after waging war and burning much of its property around the port.

The Imperial Japanese Army occupied the city in the Second World War, and control then passed to the Imperial Japanese Navy, whose rule locals described as harsher. Australian forces liberated the city in September 1945. The people opposed the return of Dutch rule, which led to the four-year Kalimantan Physical Revolution between Indonesian nationalists and the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army, ending with Dutch recognition of Indonesia in 1949. The city was granted city status in 1959 and became the capital of the new province of South Kalimantan.

Banjarmasin is the largest city in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, and the centre of Banjarese culture. The provincial capital was legally moved to Banjarbaru on 15 February 2022. The culture of the Banjar people is described as a river culture, influenced by Dayak, Javanese, Malay, Arab and even Persian peoples, and keeps elements of a Hindu-Buddhist past despite a Muslim majority.
banjul: Banjul stands on St Mary's Island, also called Banjul Island, in the Gambia River where it enters the Atlantic Ocean. Bridges connect the island to the mainland, and ferries cross the river. There are several explanations of the name. One tradition says that Bandjougou, son of Barafin, came to the island fleeing the attacks of Soumaoro Kante on the Manding region, and that his name became Bandjoulou. Another derives it from Bang julo, the Mandinka word for the rope fibre gathered on the island.

In 1651 the island was leased from the King of Kombo by the Duke of Courland and Semigallia, as part of the Curonian colonization. On 23 April 1816 Tumani Bojang, the King of Kombo, ceded it to Alexander Grant, the British commandant, in exchange for an annual fee of 103 iron bars. Grant's expedition of 75 men had been ordered by Charles MacCarthy to establish a military garrison. Grant founded a trading post and base to control the entrance to the Gambia estuary and suppress the slave trade.

The British renamed the island St Mary's and called the town Bathurst, after the 3rd Earl Bathurst, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies. The streets were laid out in a modified grid and named after Allied generals at the Battle of Waterloo.

Within a few years the town drew migrants: Africans of various origins, Levantines and Europeans. Most of its people were Muslim, with a significant Christian minority including the Aku. The Wolof, mainly from Gorée and Saint-Louis, were the largest African group, rising from 829 in 1881 to 10,130 in 1944. Islamic schools called dara were founded early, and the first Muslim court in 1905. Bathurst was declared capital of the Protectorate of the Gambia in 1889, and became a centre of British activity in the colony. It was an important Allied naval and air hub in the Second World War, when its population rose from 14,370 in 1931 to 21,154 in 1944. After independence the town was renamed Banjul on 24 April 1973.

Banjul is the capital of the Gambia and its economic and administrative centre, with the Central Bank of the Gambia and a port that ships groundnut products, beeswax, palm oil and hides. The city proper had 26,461 people at the 2024 census, and the Greater Banjul Area, which includes the Kanifing municipality, 405,809. Arch 22, 35 metres tall, was built as an entrance portal to commemorate the bloodless coup of 22 July 1994 and houses a textile museum. The Gambian National Museum, the Albert Market and the State House are in the city.
bank-of-amsterdam: Established on 31 January 1609, the bank answered a practical problem: some 500 different coins, legal and illegal, circulated in Amsterdam, with no good system for setting their rates of exchange. Its main aim was a stable silver bank currency for the Dutch Republic's growing trade, safe from the depreciations that followed independence from Spain. After 1618 it fixed the rijksdaalder of 25.4 g of fine silver at 50 stuivers, so that each bank gulden stood for 10.16 g of fine silver.

When the provinces later raised the value of coins from the Spanish Netherlands, the bank held to its original gulden banco, so that bank money came to carry a premium, or agio, over the circulating guilder. Unlike the Bank of England, founded almost a century later, it neither managed a national currency nor lent money, except to the government in emergencies. David Hume praised its policy of keeping deposits fully backed by coin.

The city of Amsterdam owned the bank, guaranteed its deposits and drew a considerable revenue from it through fees for opening accounts and making transfers. Account holders grew from 708 in 1611 to 1,202 in 1620 and reached 2,918 in 1721, the highest number in two centuries.

A system of receipts became permanent after 1683. A depositor of gold or silver bullion was credited about 5% below its mint price and given a receipt that let him reclaim the metal within six months by returning the bank money and paying a small keeping fee. Receipts and bank money were freely bought and sold, and the agio floated between 4 and 5%.

In the crisis of August 1763, set off by the failure of Leendert Pieter de Neufville, the bank opened a new lending window that accepted unminted silver bullion. Its decline began with the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, when the Dutch East India Company defaulted on large unsecured advances from the bank.

After 1783 the agio fell slowly to almost nothing. The bank's loans, kept confidential, were public knowledge by July 1790, and that year it declared itself insolvent. The City of Amsterdam took direct control in 1791, and on 23 January 1795, during the Batavian Revolution, its doors were locked and its treasure sealed. The Nederlandsche Bank, founded in 1814, took over the issue of money for the new Kingdom of the Netherlands.
bank-of-brazil: Banco do Brasil was founded on 12 October 1808 by the prince regent John, later King John VI of Portugal, to finance the kingdom's public debt when he moved from Europe to Brazil. As a mixed institution under state control, it served as a commercial bank, as the government's fiscal agent and as Brazil's first bank of issue. It is the oldest bank in Brazil and among the oldest banks in continuous operation in the world.

The bank went bankrupt twice. The first time was in 1821, at independence, when John VI returned to Portugal taking some of the bank's assets with him; the second was in 1898. From 1821 to 1964 it occasionally performed tasks beyond those of a commercial bank: issuing currency, holding the monopoly of currency exchange transactions and acting as National Treasury holder for the government. These tasks passed gradually to other government institutions, mainly with the creation of the Central Bank of Brazil in 1964 and the separation from the National Treasury in 1987.

From 1992 the bank was restructured as a commercial bank, using its wide geographic distribution and credit assets, and tens of thousands of workers were laid off. After decades of losses from financing some of the federal government's public policies, it became very profitable. The government has also used it to steady the market, for example during the global crisis of 2008 and 2009.

Banco do Brasil is controlled by the Brazilian government and listed on the B3 stock exchange in São Paulo, with its headquarters in Brasília. Traditionally the chief executive is appointed by the president, usually from a list of career directors. The bank holds the monopoly of a number of government funding programmes, such as Pronaf for subsistence farming, and is the bank of choice for most municipal and state governments. Employees are recruited by a public selection process, the concurso público, held separately for each region. It also keeps branches and offices abroad, among them Lisbon, London, Tokyo and Washington.

The current logo has been in use since the 1960s, when the standard colours changed from brown and yellow to blue-grey and yellow, echoing the colours of the Brazilian flag. Since the early 1980s the bank has sponsored sports competitions, and it supports cultural events through the Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil and amateur sport through the Associação Atlética Banco do Brasil.
bank-of-england: After the Revolution of 1688 brought William III and Mary II to the throne, a national bank became possible. During the Nine Years' War the Royal Navy was defeated by the French at the Battle of Beachy Head in 1690, and the government decided to rebuild it, but low public funds and poor credit made it impossible to borrow the £1.5 million it wanted. The idea of a public bank was two decades old. John Locke was an early supporter and, once it was set up, an early investor, and in 1691 the Scottish trader William Paterson proposed a national bank to bolster public finances. It was chartered in 1694.

The Ways and Means Act of 1715 authorised the bank to take subscriptions for a government issue of 5% annuities meant to raise £910,000; this began its role in managing government stocks, which it kept until 1998. The bank has been on Threadneedle Street since 1734, and a satirical cartoon by James Gillray in 1797 gave it the nickname the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street. Its first branches opened in 1826, and by 1829 there were eleven; the last five closed in 1997.

Britain was on the gold standard until 1931, when the Great Depression forced the bank to take it off. Banknotes were issued from 1694, hand-written at first and fully printed from 1855. After the First World War the bank withdrew increasingly from private and commercial accounts to concentrate on central banking. It was privately owned by stockholders until its nationalisation in 1946 by the Attlee ministry.

The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and the model on which most modern central banks have been based. It is the world's second oldest central bank, after Sweden's of 1668. In 1998 it became an independent public body, and the Debt Management Office took over government debt. The bank is custodian of the official gold reserves of the United Kingdom and holds a monopoly on issuing banknotes in England and Wales.
bank-of-indochina: After the first phases of the French conquest of Vietnam, the Comptoir d'escompte de Paris (CEP) opened offices in French Cochinchina in 1864, and in the early 1870s it and its rival, the Crédit Industriel et Commercial (CIC), each planned a bank that would hold the privilege of issuing money in French Indochina. In October 1874 they agreed to found it jointly, with the CEP as the dominant partner and its chairman Édouard Hentsch as the first chairman. A presidential decree established the bank on 21 January 1875, with the right to issue notes backed by its bullion, at first in francs and from 1885 in piastres.

The first notes, printed in Paris by the Bank of France, reached Saigon on 8 January 1876 and were quickly taken up by ethnic-Chinese traders. In 1888 the issuing privilege was extended to Annam, Tonkin and New Caledonia, and the Société Générale and later the Crédit Lyonnais joined the capital, making the bank a joint vehicle of the Paris banking community in the Indo-Pacific. Offices followed in Hanoi, Phnom Penh, Hong Kong, Bangkok, Shanghai, Beijing, Singapore, Papeete and Djibouti, often at the French government's request, and the Shanghai office handled French interests in the Boxer indemnity.

A law of 31 March 1931 extended the privilege by 25 years in return for a 20 percent state stake and government seats on the board. During the Second World War the bank was chaired by Paul Baudoin, Vichy France's first foreign minister, while its chief executive Jean Laurent was involved in the Resistance, and in August 1944 its Paris headquarters hosted the talks between Raoul Nordling and Dietrich von Choltitz. The privilege was revoked in principle in 1948 and ended in practice in Indochina in December 1951 and in the Pacific territories in March 1967.

Without its issuing role the bank became an investment bank in France and a commercial bank abroad, with branches in Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia and subsidiaries in San Francisco and Johannesburg. The Compagnie Financière de Suez took a controlling interest in 1972 and in 1975 merged it with its own banking subsidiary to form Banque Indosuez, part of the Crédit Agricole group since 1996. Several of its buildings survive, among them the Saigon seat inaugurated in 1931, the Hanoi office, head office of Vietnam's central bank since 1954, and the Shanghai building on the Bund.
bank-of-saint-george: The bank was founded on 23 April 1407 to consolidate the public debt of the Republic of Genoa, which had grown with the war against Venice for dominance in trade and finance. Its main task was to manage the San Giorgio shares, the luoghi held by the state's creditors. Its formal name was the Casa delle compere e dei banchi di San Giorgio, and it was also called the Ufficio di San Giorgio or simply the Banco. Its seat was the Palazzo San Giorgio, built in the 13th century on the orders of Guglielmo Boccanegra, uncle of Simone Boccanegra, the first Doge of Genoa.

The bank needed frequent injections of money to support the war against Venice and the republic's weak finances. By 1445 it had suspended its business with the public to serve the Genoese state alone, and it reopened to the public only in 1530. In 1453 the republic handed the government of Corsica, Gazaria and other possessions to its officials, though over the rest of the century the republic took many of them back.

In the 15th and 16th centuries the bank lent large sums to rulers across Europe. Ferdinand and Isabella held accounts there, as did Christopher Columbus, who wrote to its governors from Seville on 2 April 1502, before his fourth voyage. Charles V was heavily in its debt for much of his reign. In the 17th century it became heavily involved in maritime trade and for a time competed with the Dutch East India Company and the English East India Company. After Napoleon invaded Italy he suppressed independent banks, and the bank closed in 1805.

Writers on government long cited the bank. Niccolò Machiavelli, in his Florentine Histories of 1532, saw in it liberty and tyranny, integrity and corruption within one community. Joseph Addison, travelling in Italy in 1701, noted that its managers had been called a second kind of senate but judged it a check on the aristocracy. Montesquieu in The Spirit of Law (1748) wrote that its administration gave the people a certain influence in the government, and David Hume held that while Genoa was full of sedition the bank was conducted for several ages with the utmost integrity and wisdom.

Thomas Babington Macaulay, in The History of England (1848), recalled it with the Bank of Amsterdam as one of the two public banks held up as models when the Bank of England was established in 1694. On 11 June 1857 the old lock of its vault was presented to the Philadelphia historical society.
banska-stiavnica: Banská Štiavnica stands in the middle of an immense caldera created by the collapse of an ancient volcano, known for its size as the Štiavnica Mountains. Its fate has been closely linked to the exploitation of abundant silver ore. Excavations show that the site was settled in the Neolithic period. The Slavic population named the settlement in the valley Štiavnica, meaning acidic stream, and the settlement on the hill above came to be called Bánya, the mine.

The first mining settlement was founded by Celts in the 3rd century BCE, probably by the Cotini tribe. The site was called terra banensium, the land of miners, as early as 1156. Skilled German settlers began arriving in the 13th century and adapted the local name to Schemnitz. Banská Štiavnica gained the status of a royal town in 1238, one of the first in the Kingdom of Hungary, and in the High and Late Middle Ages it was the main producer of silver and gold in the kingdom.

During the Ottoman Wars the town built powerful fortifications, including two castles, in the 16th century. It was also a centre of mining innovation: in 1627 gunpowder was used in a mine there, one of the first uses in the world. In the 18th century local scientists, among them Jozef Karol Hell, Maximilian Hell and Samuel Mikovíny, designed a system of reservoirs and channels called tajchy to drain flooded mines.

Samuel Mikovíny founded a Mining Academy in 1735, the first mining school in the Kingdom of Hungary. From 1763 it became the Academy of Mining with the support of Queen Maria Theresa, and in 1848 the Academy of Mining and Forestry, described as the first technical university in the world. In 1782 the town was the third biggest in the kingdom, but mining declined progressively from the second half of the 19th century.

Banská Štiavnica is a town in central Slovakia with a population of less than 10,000. The surviving urban centre was formed during the 16th century, and the town and its surroundings were proclaimed a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 11 December 1993. Sixty reservoirs were built between the 15th and 18th centuries, connected by more than 100 kilometres of channels, and they are now used mainly for recreation. The old and new castles have become museums.
banteay-kdei: Banteay Kdei stands in the Angkor Archaeological Park, 3 kilometres east of Angkor Thom and reached from the east gate of Ta Prohm by a path of 600 metres. The sanctuary is packed into a space of 65 by 50 metres within three enclosures and a laterite outer wall of 700 by 300 metres, on a single level.

Its structures consist of two concentric galleries from which towers rise, preceded to the east by a cloister. The east gate is cruciform and carries images of Lokesvara, and the carvings include apsaras in the Bayon style and, in the inner enclosure, traces of an earlier style. To the east lies Srah Srang, a pool dug under Rajendravarman in the 10th century and given laterite steps by Jayavarman VII.

The name goes back to an earlier name, Kuti, found in the Sdok Kak Thom stele, which records an estate and village of that name granted to the family of the royal chaplain Sivakaivalya. Jayavarman VII came to power at the age of 55 after defeating the Chams, who had invaded and devastated Angkor, and built many temples and rest houses for pilgrims.

Banteay Kdei is reported to be his first temple, of 1181. Small inscriptions name him and the royal architect Kavindrarimathana as its builders. In the 13th century most of his temples were vandalised, though some Mahayana frontons and lintels survive. Later the temple lay neglected under vegetation until it was cleared in 1920 to 1922 under Henri Marchal, using anastylosis.

Monks occupied the temple at intervals until the 1960s. Its sandstone was poor and its construction faulty, and vaults have collapsed in places, so parts are cordoned off and tied together with cables during renovation. A Sophia University mission found a cache of fragments of 274 Buddhist sandstone statues in 2001, and from 2004 the University of California, Sophia University and the nonprofit CyArk made laser scans of the temple.
banten: Banten lies at the western tip of Java. It is bordered by the Java Sea on the north, the Sunda Strait on the west and the Indian Ocean on the south, and by West Java and Jakarta on the east. The Sunda Strait carries sea lanes linking Australia and New Zealand with Southeast Asia, and Banten forms a link between Java and Sumatra. The province covers 9,355.76 square kilometres and ranges from sea level to 2,000 metres, with lowlands in the north and south and hills in the centre.

In the fourth and fifth centuries the area belonged to the kingdom of Tarumanagara. A Sanskrit inscription found in 1947 in Munjul describes life under Purnawarman. After Tarumanagara fell to an attack by Srivijaya, western Java became part of the Sunda Kingdom. Islam began to spread in the 15th century and by the late 16th century had replaced Hinduism and Buddhism as the main religion, with the establishment of the Banten Sultanate. According to the Babad Banten, Sunan Gunung Jati and Maulana Hasanuddin spread Islam widely.

The Portuguese were established in Banten before the Dutch, and the English, French and Danish also traded there. The Portuguese left in 1601 after the Dutch destroyed their fleet off the coast. The Dutch East India Company gradually weakened the sultanate, and on 22 November 1808 Governor-General Herman Willem Daendels declared it absorbed into the Dutch East Indies. Japan occupied the region from March 1942 and built the Saketi-Bayah railway to carry brown coal, using about 1,000 forced labourers, rōmusha, drawn mainly from Banten; casualties are estimated at 20,000 to 60,000, not counting mine workers. Banten became a separate province on 17 October 2000.

The capital of the province is Serang and its largest city is Tangerang. Most residents are Muslims, and the Bantenese, at 47 per cent, are the largest ethnic group. The Baduy people of Kanekes practise Sunda Wiwitan and keep their ancestral customs. The Great Mosque of Banten and Ujung Kulon National Park, a sanctuary of the Javan rhinoceros, are among its notable sites.
bantry-bay: The bay runs about 35 km from north-east to south-west, three to four kilometres wide at its head and 10 km at its entrance, and is about 40 metres deep in the middle. It is a ria, a river valley drowned by a relative rise in sea level. The Beara Peninsula borders it on the north, dividing it from Kenmare Bay, and the Sheep's Head Peninsula on the south, dividing it from Dunmanus Bay. Its main islands are Bere Island, near the entrance, with Berehaven Harbour on its north side, and Whiddy Island at the head of the bay near the south shore.

The Battle of Bantry Bay was fought here in 1689, during the Nine Years' War. In December 1796 a French fleet of 43 ships carrying 15,000 troops, which had split up in mid-Atlantic to avoid the Royal Navy, was to gather again in the bay. Most of it arrived, but the flagship Fraternité, with General Hoche aboard, was delayed. Bad weather, the lack of leadership and fear of being trapped led to the decision to return to France. Wolfe Tone wrote in his diary that they were close enough to toss a biscuit ashore.

A longboat from a French scouting party that landed on Bere Island lay in Berehaven Harbour for 102 years and is now in the National Museum of Ireland. The French frigate La Surveillante, scuttled in a storm north of Whiddy Island on 2 January 1797, was found in 1981. On 8 January 1979 the French tanker Betelgeuse caught fire and exploded while unloading at Whiddy Island, killing 50 people.

Whiddy Island is the main petroleum terminus for Ireland, its harbour suited to large tankers. Bantry, Glengarriff and Castletownbere stand on the shores of the bay, and the O'Sullivan Beara castle of Dunboy faces Bere Island across Berehaven Harbour. The square in Bantry is named after Wolfe Tone.
bantu-peoples: The Bantu peoples are a grouping of about 400 distinct Indigenous African ethnic groups who speak Bantu languages, of which there are between 440 and 680 depending on how language and dialect are defined. They are not a single ethnic group. The term Bantu is an artificial one, introduced into modern scholarship by Wilhelm Bleek in 1857 or 1858, based on a reconstructed Proto-Bantu word for people. Proto-Bantu is estimated to have been spoken 4,000 to 3,000 years ago in the area of modern Cameroon. The spread of Bantu speakers across Central, East and Southern Africa, the Bantu expansion, took roughly two millennia, during the 1st millennium BCE and the 1st millennium CE.

In the course of the expansion Bantu-speaking peoples absorbed or displaced many earlier inhabitants. Central African Pygmy groups, the Hadza of northern Tanzania and various Khoisan populations of southern Africa remained. Genetic analysis shows admixture with earlier local populations, and interaction with Cushitic, Nilotic and Central Sudanic speakers. Pioneering groups had reached parts of KwaZulu-Natal before the 3rd century CE and the Northern Cape by 500 CE.

Between the 9th and 15th centuries Bantu-speaking states began to emerge in the Great Lakes region and in the savanna south of the Central African rainforest, and from the 12th century state formation became more frequent. Examples include the Kingdom of Kongo, the Luba Empire, the Lunda Empire, Buganda, Rwanda and the Zulu Kingdom. The Monomotapa kings built the Great Zimbabwe complex, ancestral to the Shona. On the East African coast contact with Arab and Persian traders produced Swahili culture, whose language holds many Arabic loanwords.

Speakers of Bantu languages number in the hundreds of millions, roughly 350 million in the mid-2010s, about 30 per cent of Africa's population. About 90 million are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo alone.

In South Africa the term Bantu came into use in the 1920s in preference to Native. After World War II the National Party governments adopted it officially, and it became identified with apartheid, which named its eleven rural reserves Bantustans. It is now used there only in its linguistic sense.
bantustan: From 1913 successive white-minority South African governments set up reserves to segregate the black population, as the Natives Land Act of 1913 limited black people to seven percent of the land. When the National Party came to power in 1948, Hendrik Verwoerd, Minister for Native Affairs and later Prime Minister, built on this with measures such as the Group Areas Acts and the Natives Resettlement Act of 1954. The creation of homelands was central to the strategy, since the long-term goal was to make them independent, so that black people would lose their South African citizenship and voting rights and whites would remain in control.

The word, first used in the late 1940s, was coined by supporters of the policy to echo Pakistan and Hindustan, and it quickly became a pejorative; the National Party preferred homelands. Nelson Mandela wrote in 1959 that the word was a complete misnomer that helped the Nationalists perpetrate a fraud, since Africans would have no rights outside the reserves.

The Bantu Authorities Act of 1951 established homelands for the black ethnic groups, amounting to 13% of the country's land. The Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set out a plan called Separate Development, in four steps: a single Territorial Authority, a legislative assembly with limited powers, self-governing status, and nominal independence. Cooperative chiefs ran the homelands, and uncooperative ones were forcibly deposed. The Black Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 designated all black South Africans citizens of the homelands, even if they lived in white South Africa, and cancelled their South African citizenship.

By 1984 all ten homelands in South Africa were self-governing, and four, Transkei, Bophuthatswana, Venda and Ciskei, had been declared independent between 1976 and 1981. Only South Africa recognised them. An estimated 3.5 million people were forced from their homes from the 1960s to the 1980s, many resettled in the homelands, yet only about 39% of black South Africans lived in them in 1986. Following the Odendaal commission, ten homelands were also set up in South West Africa from 1968.

The homelands were generally poor, with few local jobs. Bophuthatswana, with deposits of platinum, was the wealthiest, and the casino resort of Sun City was built there, taking advantage of laws that differed from those of South Africa. Homeland leaders were widely seen as collaborators with the apartheid system, though some gained a following. All the Bantustans were dismantled and reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994, when the Interim Constitution came into force; in Ciskei South African security forces intervened in March 1994 to defuse a crisis. The term is now used more generally, in a disapproving sense, for any area where people are forced to live without full civil and political rights.
banu-amir: The Banu Amir were an independent branch of the Hawazin confederation, whose first homeland lay on the border between Najd and the Hejaz, around Khurmah and Ranyah. After the rise of Islam they dominated Najd for centuries. Before Islam they fought a long war with the Quraysh, seen above all in the Fijar War, and they gave their allegiance to Muhammad and his first successors only late.

The tribe produced several poets. The best known was Labid ibn Rabi'ah, author of one of the Seven Hanged Poems; others were the chief Amir ibn al-Tufayl, al-Ra'i al-Numayri, an opponent of Jarir, and the woman poet Layla al-Akhyaliyyah. Qays and Layla, the lovers of the saga of Layla and Majnun, were also said to belong to the tribe.

Four months after the Battle of Uhud a delegation of the Banu Amir brought Muhammad a gift. According to the historian al-Tabari he refused it because it came from a polytheist and invited their leader Abu Bara to accept Islam. Abu Bara did not convert, but asked Muhammad to send missionaries to Najd and guaranteed their safety. Ibn Ishaq's biography says forty men were sent under Al-Mundhir ibn Amr, while Sahih al-Bukhari gives seventy. In June 629 Muhammad ordered the Expedition of Shuja ibn Wahb al-Asadi to raid the Banu Amir for camels.

Later the branches moved apart. The Banu Kilab, who had led the confederation before Islam, were allied with the Qarmatian movement of eastern Arabia, dominated central Arabia after its end and then went north to Syria. The Banu Numayr left al-Yamamah for the Euphrates after an Abbasid campaign against them in the 9th century. The Banu Uqayl, largest of the Ka'b section, went to northern Iraq; some of its sections later returned to the Province of Bahrain and gave rise to the Usfurid and Jabrid dynasties. The Banu Hilal, enlisted by the Fatimid rulers of Egypt in the 11th century, went on to invade North Africa.

Many later tribes trace their descent to the Banu Amir. Iraqi groups such as the Khafajah, Ubadah and al-Muntafiq come from the Uqayl, and the Bani Kaab live mostly in the Ahwaz region of Iran, in Iraq and in the United Arab Emirates. The Bani Yas confederation of the Emirates, led by the Al Nahyan and Al Maktoum families, claims descent from Yas bin Amer bin Sa'sa'ah, and the Subay', the Suhool of Najd and sections of the Bani Khalid also trace their lineage to the tribe.
banu-hashim: Banu Hashim was a clan of the Quraysh, to which the Prophet Muhammad belonged, named after his great-grandfather Hashim ibn Abd Manaf. According to tradition Hashim was married to Salma bint Amr of the Banu Najjar, an Azdi clan. Among the pre-Islamic Arabs people classified themselves by tribe, then clan, then house. Banu Hashim is counted an Adnanite clan, descended from Adnan, the traditional ancestor of the Arabs of northern, central and western Arabia. Together with the clans of Banu Abd-Shams, Banu al-Muttalib and Banu Nawfal it forms the Banu Abd al-Manaf section of the Quraysh.

Members of the clan and their descendants are called Hashimites and often carry the surname al-Hashimi. Descendants who trace their lineage to Muhammad through his daughter Fatima hold the traditional title of Sharif, often used as a synonym of Sayyid. From the 8th century onwards Hashimid descent was regarded as a mark of nobility, and many dynasties based their right to rule on it.

Among the most prominent were the Abbasids, who ruled from Baghdad from 750 to 945 and then held the caliphate without temporal power, in Baghdad until 1258 and in Cairo from 1261 to 1517. The Fatimids, who ruled from Cairo and claimed the caliphate from 909 to 1171, also claimed descent. So did the Alawi dynasty, rulers of Morocco from 1631, and the Hashemites, rulers of Jordan from 1921.

The claim to Hashimid descent spread widely across the Islamic world. Dynasties of Arabia, Africa, Indo-Persia and Southeast Asia claimed it, among them the Idrisid dynasty of Morocco, the Senussi of Libya, the Rassid dynasty of Yemen, the Walashma dynasty of Ifat and Adal, and the Sultans of Brunei and Siak. The Hummudid dynasty did the same. Many of these lines traced their descent through a particular ancestor, such as Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib for the Abbasids or Idris ibn Abdullah for the Idrisid dynasty.
banu-hassan: The Beni Hassan were one of the four sub-tribes of the Banu Maqil, who came to the Maghreb in the 11th century alongside the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym, Bedouin tribes sent by the Fatimids to punish the Zirids for turning to the Abbasid Caliphate. The Maqil probably came from South Arabia; they claimed descent from Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, a claim Ibn Khaldun rejected. The tradition of the Beni Hassan traces them to Hasan ibn Ali, though they were Sunni Muslims.

Under the protection of the Banu Hilal the Maqil wandered between the Moulouya River and the Tafilalt oases, and in the 13th century they held southern Algeria and the oases of Tuat and Gourara. Around 1250, as the Almohad Caliphate ended, the Beni Hassan defeated the Sanhaja Berber confederation and took tribute from it.

By the mid-15th century they controlled much of the oases and the western Sahara. Taking advantage of the weakening Marinid Sultanate around 1460 they crossed the Atlas, and by the early 16th century they dominated the Haouz of Marrakesh, where the Rahamna served the Saadian Sultanate. Other groups went north to Fez or settled south of Rabat, while part of the tribe moved into Mauritania.

The Char Bouba War was fought against the Berber marabouts, who followed the doctrine of Nasr al-Din. In 1673 Nasr al-Din invaded Futa Tooro and the Wolof states beyond the Senegal River, gaining the gum-trade ports along it. A scholar of Shinqit issued a fatwa denying that he was a caliph with the right to levy zakat. In 1674 the Beni Hassan defeated the marabouts and founded the emirates of Trarza, Brakna, Tagant, Adrar and Hodh, which fought each other repeatedly and raided the Wolof of Senegal through the 18th century.

After 1674 the defeated Berber tribes had to give up their arms and pay the horma tribute to the Arab warrior tribes. They became either religious tribes, the marabouts or zawiya, or the lower znaga, semi-sedentary farmers and fishermen. This order held until French colonisation broke the power of the Hassane, though the tribes' traditional roles remain socially important, and the hierarchy has led to oppression, discrimination and enslavement of other groups in Mauritania. In the 19th century the emirates led the cultural and linguistic Arabization of Mauritania, and the Sahrawi nation counts the Beni Hassan among its founding peoples.
banu-hilal: The Banu Hilal were an Arab tribe from the Najd region of the central Arabian Peninsula, sometimes travelling towards Iraq in search of pastures and oases. According to Arab genealogists they were a sub-tribe of the Mudar confederation, specifically of the Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, and their progenitor was Hilal. They were very numerous, effectively a nation divided into sub-tribes, of which the most notable were the Athbaj, Riyah, Jusham, Zughba, Adi and Qurra.

They probably did not accept Islam until after Muhammad's victory at the Battle of Hunayn in 630, and like other tribes of their group they did not join the Ridda Wars. In the early 8th century some of them moved to Egypt, and in the 9th century they migrated from Najd to Iraq and later to the Levant.

In the 970s the Hilal and the Banu Sulaym joined the Qarmatians in their attacks on the Fatimid Caliphate. After his victory in 978 the Fatimid caliph al-Aziz forcibly relocated the two tribes to Upper Egypt, where they were forbidden to cross the Nile. They plundered the region as far as the port of Aydhab. According to al-Tijani, they refused to cross the Nile until each warrior received a dinar and a fur garment, after which around 3,000 Bedouin departed for Ifriqiya.

The migration to the Maghreb began after the Zirid dynasty of Ifriqiya declared independence from the Fatimids. As a punishment, the Fatimids sent the Banu Hilal and the Banu Sulaym west, giving each man a camel and money, and a severe drought in Egypt added to the pressure to leave. Estimates of the number of nomads who moved in the 11th century run from 50,000 to 250,000, and some scholars propose much higher figures. They defeated the Zirids after the battle of Haydaran, and the Zirids abandoned Kairouan for the coast. In the second half of the 12th century the Hilal reached the Moulouya valley and the Atlantic coast.

Their arrival was a major factor in the linguistic, cultural and ethnic Arabization of the Maghreb and spread nomadism in areas where agriculture had prevailed. Ibn Khaldun wrote that lands ravaged by the invaders had become desert. Originally Isma'ili Shia, most of the tribe adopted the Maliki school of Sunni Islam in the Maghreb.
