In the 17th century the Moroccan sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif built a guich army from Hilal and Banu Maqil warriors.

Their journey is told in the Taghribat Bani Hilal, an Arab epic gathered by the folk poet Abdul Rahman al-Abnudi from the bards of Upper Egypt. It was performed from Morocco to Iraq until the early 20th century.
banu-ifran: According to Ibn Khaldun, the tribe took its name from an ancestor, Ifri, a Berber word meaning cavern. The oldest mentions place most of the Banu Ifran in the west of Mauretania Caesariensis, and they were one of the four major tribes of the Zenata confederation in the Aurès Mountains. Ibn Khaldun says they resisted the Romans, Vandals and Byzantines, and Corippus records them challenging the Byzantine armies of John Troglita between 547 and 550. In the 7th century they sided with the Kahina against the Umayyad invaders.

At the time of the Arab conquests the Banu Ifran lived around Yafran in Tripolitania. The conquests probably pushed them to the Aurès, and an Abbasid invasion of Ifriqiya in 761 further west. Their chief Abu Qurra founded Tlemcen in 765 over the site of the Roman city of Pomaria. In the 10th century they fought the Fatimids; led by Abu Yazid they attacked Kairouan in 945, and Ya'la ibn Mohammed took Oran and built a capital at Ifgan near Mascara until the Fatimid general Jawhar killed him in 954 and destroyed it.

Some Ifranids then settled in al-Andalus, where the house of Corra ruled Ronda, and others held Tadla and built a capital at Salé. Ya'la's son Yaddū took Fes in January 993, and his grandson Tamīm took it again in 1033; Tamīm began a persecution of the Jews and is said to have killed 6,000 of their men, though Ibn Khaldun speaks of persecution without killing. The emirate fell in 1058, and in 1066 the Almoravids under Ibn Tashfin took Tlemcen and ended the Banu Ifran's power.

The Banu Ifran were known as expert cavalrymen. Before Islam animism was their main belief, and Ifri was also the name of a Berber deity, a sun and cave goddess and protector of the home whose rites were held in caves for the protection of merchants. After conversion they joined the Kharijite movement, opposing the Sunni Arab armies, and in the 8th century they rose around the Sufri doctrine against the Umayyads and Abbasids.
banu-kalb: In Arab genealogical tradition the tribe descended from a man named Kalb, meaning dog, whose mother was called mother of wild animals because all her children bore animals' names. The Kalb were Bedouin camel herders. Before Islam their earliest known home was the al-Jawf depression with the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal, from which they moved seasonally into the Samawa, the desert between Syria and Mesopotamia that was named after them. By the 6th century most had become Christian and came under the Ghassanids, the leaders of the Byzantines' Arab allies.

A few companions of Muhammad were Kalbites, among them Zayd ibn Haritha and Dihya, but most of the tribe stayed Christian until after the Battle of Yarmouk and remained neutral in the Muslim conquest of Syria. From 639 Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Damascus and Jordan, built close ties with them. Caliph Uthman married the Kalbite noblewoman Na'ila bint al-Furafisa, and Maysun was the daughter of Bahdal ibn Unayf, the tribe's leading chief. The Kalb became the military foundation of the Umayyad Caliphate and in 684 routed their rivals the Qays at the Battle of Marj Rahit, which began a long blood feud.

They lost influence under Marwan II and the Abbasids. From the Ghouta and Palmyra they rose in 750 to 751 behind the Umayyad prince Abu Muhammad al-Sufyani, backed another claimant, Abu al-Umaytir al-Sufyani, who took Damascus in 811, and later fought as troops of the Qarmatians, whose suppression left them isolated. In 955 the Hamdanid emir Sayf al-Dawla crushed a tribal uprising and forced the Kalb out of Homs.

When the Fatimid general Ja'far ibn Falah invaded Syria in 970, Ibn Ulayyan, emir of the Palmyra-based Banu Adi clan, handed him the fleeing chief of the Damascus militia for a large bounty. This began a century of mostly close cooperation, and the Fatimids employed the Kalb more often than any other Syrian tribe. In 1024 and 1025 the Kalb joined the Tayy and Kilab in a rebellion to divide Syria among themselves but failed to take Damascus. In 1084 they joined the coalition of Muslim ibn Quraysh of Aleppo against the Seljuks.

Over the 10th century the Kalb were weakened by settling down, by holding no towns from which to draw tribute and by their loose structure, and they lost ground to the more numerous and nomadic Tayy and Kilab. Their centre shifted to the farmlands between Damascus, the Hauran and the Anti-Lebanon Mountains. In 1131 Kalbites of the Hauran captured the Mazyadid emir Dubays ibn Sadaqa. After the 12th century the tribe no longer appears in the record.
banu-kanz: Arab tribes, the largest of them the Mudhar, Rabi'ah, Juhaynah and Qays 'Aylan, moved to the Egyptian frontier with Nubia in the 9th century after gold and emerald mines were found there. In 855 Abdullah ibn Abd al-Hamid al-Umari, a native of Medina, came to Aswan to profit from the gold mines and built a virtually independent principality on them, twice defeating the army of Ahmad ibn Tulun, governor of Egypt, before he was assassinated by Mudhar tribesmen.

The Rabi'ah then became the strongest of the frontier tribes, running a principality of their own by the 10th century in alliance with the Hadariba, a Muslim tribe of the Beja, with whom they shared the mining business. Abu Yazid ibn Ishaq made Aswan its capital and was recognised by the Fatimid Caliphate as protector of Aswan. In 1006 his son Abu al-Makarim Hibatallah received the title Kanz al-Dawla, Treasure of the State, from Caliph al-Hakim for capturing the rebel Abu Rakwa.

The principality took in the countryside of Aswan, the frontier with Nubia and most of the Eastern Desert to the Red Sea, with the mines of Wadi Allaqi and the routes to the port of Aydhab. The Kanz al-Dawla answered to the Fatimid governor of Qus and handled relations and trade with Nubia, frontier taxes and the protection of caravans.

After Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate, the Banu Kanz first helped the Ayyubids drive a Nubian invasion out of Upper Egypt in 1171-1172, but when their fiefs were given to an Ayyubid emir they killed him. In 1174 the Kanz al-Dawla Ibn al-Mutawwaj rose to restore the Fatimids; he was defeated at Aswan, captured and executed, and the Banu Kanz moved south to Maris, where they took up Nubian culture and language while remaining Muslim.

In 1317 the Mamluk sultan an-Nasir Muhammad arrested the Kanz al-Dawla, a nephew of King Karanbas of Makuria, but he was soon released and seized the throne, holding it against two Mamluk expeditions, the last in 1324. Later in the century the Banu Kanz attacked Aswan in 1366 and burned it in 1370. Sultan Barquq sent the Hawwara tribesmen against them, and the Hawwara gradually replaced them. Their descendants, the Kunuz, live in Upper Egypt.
banu-kinana: In the Arab genealogical tradition the tribe's eponymous ancestor was Kinana, a son of Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah, and its line went back to Ishmael, who according to Islamic tradition married a woman of the Yemenite Jurhum tribe and settled near Mecca. Its traditional territory ran from the Tihama coast near Mecca north-eastward to the lands of the related Banu Asad. Before Islam the Kinana were polytheists whose worship centred on the goddess al-Uzza.

Tradition names six principal branches: the Nadr, Malik, Milkan, Amir, Amr and Abd Manat. The Nadr were the parent tribe of the Quraysh, who were counted apart from the Kinana. Within the Abd Manat the strong Bakr ibn Abd Manat divided into the Mudlij, Du'il, Layth and Damra, and the Harith ibn Abd Manat formed the core of the Ahabish, a collection of small clans that were most likely unrelated. Fihr ibn Malik, ancestor of the Quraysh, led the Kinana to victory over a branch of the Himyarites, and the tribe backed his descendant Qusayy ibn Kilab in taking Mecca, though the Bakr generally opposed him.

Islamic historians did not record the Kinana acting as one tribe in Muhammad's time. Before Badr in 624 the Quraysh sought assurances from the Kinana, and the Mudlij promised not to attack their rear. An attack by the Bakr on the Khuza'a, Muhammad's allies, prompted his conquest of Mecca in 630, in which the Ghifar, Layth and Damra backed him. After the conquest of Palestine in the 630s the Kinana were one of the main components of the garrison of Jund Filastin, and Caliph Umar appointed two of its men, Alqama ibn Mujazziz and Alqama ibn Hakim, as joint governors around 638/639.

When the Crusaders took Ascalon in 1153, the Kinana emirs of southern Palestine left for Fatimid Egypt, and the vizier Ṭalāʾīʿ ibn Ruzzīk resettled them in and around Damietta, where they were known as the Kinaniyya. Under the Ayyubids they were paid half the rate of Kurdish, Turkish and Turkmen troops and fought at the Battle of Montgisard. When the fleet of Louis IX landed at Damietta in June 1249, the Kinani garrison fled, and Sultan as-Salih Ayyub executed its commanders.
banu-makhzum: The Banu Makhzum are regarded as one of the three most powerful clans of Mecca before Islam, beside the Banu Hashim and the Banu Umayya. Arab genealogical tradition counts some twenty branches descended from their progenitor, Umar ibn Makhzum, of which the line of al-Mughira ibn Abd Allah became the principal family. According to the traditional sources they belonged to the Ahlaf, or allies, faction of the Quraysh with the clans of Abd al-Dar, Banu Sahm, Banu Jumah and Banu Adi, rivals of the Banu Hashim and Banu Abd Shams. The historian Martin Hinds held that the extent of their power in the 6th century cannot be established with certainty.

Toward the end of that century Hisham ibn al-Mughira grew so prominent that the Quraysh dated events from his death. He, his brothers al-Walid, Hashim and Abu Umayya and several of their sons dominated Meccan trade with Yemen and Ethiopia.

The clan was among Muhammad's foremost opponents in Mecca. Its chieftain Abu Jahl organised a boycott of the Banu Hashim in about 616–618. At the Battle of Badr the clan lost seven or eight nobles of the al-Mughira line and about as many from its cadet lines, and the Banu Abd Shams under Abu Sufyan overtook it in prominence. At least three members of the clan fought for Muhammad at Badr, and by his conquest of Mecca in January 630 others had joined him, among them Khalid ibn al-Walid, a grandson of al-Mughira.

Abu Jahl's son Ikrima, the clan's principal leader, fled to Yemen, while al-Harith ibn Hisham and Sa'id ibn Yarbu reconciled with Muhammad. Ikrima was later pardoned, fought with Khalid in the Ridda wars and died fighting the Byzantines, possibly at the Battle of Ajnadayn. Al-Muhajir ibn Abi Umayya and Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a governed parts of Yemen under the caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar. Khalid won victories against Musaylima in the Yamama and in the Muslim conquest of Syria, and his son Abd al-Rahman governed Homs and the Jazira. The forty or so male descendants of Khalid died in a plague in Syria toward the end of Umayyad rule.
banu-qasi: According to the 10th-century historian Ibn al-Qūṭiyya, Count Cassius converted to Islam in 714 as a client of the Umayyads and travelled to Damascus to swear allegiance to the Caliph Al-Walid I. The family's lands on the upper Ebro, around Tudela and present-day southern Navarre and Logroño, formed a semi-autonomous principality threatened by Frankish ambitions in the western Pyrenees, the expanding Kingdom of Asturias and Córdoba. The family intermarried with Muslim and Christian nobles alike and used Arabic, Latin and Basque names, such as Musa, Lubb and Garshiya.

The family reached its height under Musa ibn Musa al-Qasawi, maternal half-brother and son-in-law of Íñigo Arista of Pamplona. After revolts against Abd ar-Rahman II in the 840s, he was named governor of the Upper March by Muhammad I of Córdoba and came to hold Zaragoza, Tudela, Huesca and Toledo; the Chronicle of Alfonso III says his followers called him the third king of Spaniae. In 859 Ordoño I of Asturias and García Íñiguez of Pamplona crushed him at Albelda, remembered in Christian legend as the Battle of Clavijo, and he died in 862.

His sons recovered their father's lands from 870, but the emir crucified Mutarrif and three of his sons in Córdoba. Muhammad ibn Lubb al-Qasawi then dominated the family, fought off campaigns from Córdoba and began a 17-year siege of Zaragoza, held by the rival Banu Tujib, before he was killed while reconnoitring the city. His son Lubb ibn Muhammad was routed and killed fighting Sancho Garcés of Pamplona at Liédena on 30 September 907, a defeat that began the family's final decline.

After 907 Sancho, the Tujibids and the Banu al-Tawil of Huesca took the family's lands piece by piece, and Abd ar-Rahman III removed the Banu Qasi from Tudela to Córdoba after 923, putting the Tujibids in their place. The last leader, Muhammad ibn Lubb, grandson of the earlier man of that name, was ambushed and killed in 929, ending the dynasty in the Ebro valley. The Tujibids followed their model and later founded the Taifa of Zaragoza. Later rulers at Alpuente and Mértola bore similar names, but no family link to them is proven.
banu-sulaym: According to Arab genealogical tradition the Banu Sulaym descended from Sulaym ibn Mansur, which made them part of the wider grouping of Qays Aylan. They formed three main divisions, Imru' al-Qays, Harith and Tha'laba, founded by sons or grandsons of Sulaym. Their homeland was the northern Hejaz, with the Harrah volcanic field, once named Harrat Bani Sulaym after them, at its heart: a region enemy horsemen could not manage, where the tribe kept protected pastures and the Bahz branch owned gold mines.

The Sulaym kept close ties with the Quraysh of Mecca and sold horses, camels, sheep and clarified butter in the markets of Medina, where they mediated between clans of the Banu Aws. They worshipped Khamis, an idol shared with the Banu Khazraj.

Allied with the Quraysh, the Sulaym were at first hostile to Muhammad. Several of their clans joined the attack on Muslim missionaries at Bi'r Ma'una in 625, and they fought beside the Quraysh at the Battle of the Trench in 627, but by the conquest of Mecca in January 630 most had converted and joined him, and they fought for him at the Battle of Hunayn. Most defected from Islam after his death in 632, yet after the Ridda Wars they took part in the conquests of Syria and Iraq.

Most of the tribe backed Mu'awiya in the First Muslim Civil War. As members of the Qays they recognised Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr as caliph, lost about 600 men at the Battle of Marj Rahit in 684, and in 686, under Umayr ibn al-Hubab, deserted the Umayyads at the Battle of Khazir. A war with the Taghlib along the Khabur River followed, in which Umayr was killed in 689.

From the late 9th century the Harb tribe from Yemen absorbed much of the Sulaym of Arabia. Those in Syria allied with the Qarmatians against the Fatimids, and the caliph al-Aziz expelled them with the Banu Hilal to Upper Egypt. By the mid-12th century the Sulaym in North Africa had driven the Hilal from Ifriqiya, and in the late 12th century those of Cyrenaica joined Sharaf al-Din Qaraqush and Ali ibn Ishaq ibn Ghaniya against the Almohad Caliphate.

Descendants of the Sulaym, known as the Sa'ada, are dominant in Cyrenaica today, and many of the region's Arab tribes trace their descent to them. The Sa'ada are divided into two groups: the Harabi, among them the Ubaydat and Bara'asa, and the Jabarina, among them the 'Awaqir and Magharba.
banu-taghlib: The Taghlib were originally a Bedouin tribe of the Najd, named after their ancestor Taghlib ibn Wa'il, also called Dithar ibn Wa'il, and they traced their descent through the Rabi'a confederation to the Nizar branch of the Adnanites. Their brother and rival tribe was the Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il. In the late 5th century the murder of the Taghlibi chieftain Kulaib ibn Rabiah by his brother-in-law Jassas ibn Murra al-Shaybani of the Bakr began the long Basus War, and after a decisive defeat at Yawm al-Tahaluq most of the tribe left the Najd for the Lower Euphrates.

The war ended in the mid-6th century with a peace treaty signed at the Dhu al-Majaz market near Mecca. The tribe moved further north into the Jazira after its chieftain Amr ibn Kulthum assassinated the Lakhmid king Amr ibn Hind in 568, and Taghlibi tribesmen still praised Amr as a poet and warrior in the 8th century. At the Battle of Dhi Qar in 605 the Taghlib fought for the Sasanians against the Bakr.

Much of what is known of the tribe's branches goes back to the pre-Islamic Taghlibi genealogist al-Akhzar ibn Suhayma. Genealogists dealt mainly with the descendants of Ghanm ibn Taghlib, among whom the al-Araqim, six divisions descended from the sons of Bakr ibn Hubayb, were the most important. The two largest of these, the Jusham and the Malik, were together called al-Rawkān, the two horns. The Hamdanid dynasty traced its descent to the Malik division.

In the Ridda Wars of 632–633 the Taghlib fought on the side of the apostate tribes, and sections of the tribe fought the Muslim armies in Iraq and Upper Mesopotamia, but during the conquests they changed sides while keeping their Christian faith. They refused to pay the jizya like other Christian subjects, arguing that as Arabs they should be treated like Muslims, and Caliph Umar instead levied on them the zakat or sadaqah, taxes normally imposed on Muslims.

In the Second Muslim Civil War the tribe backed the Umayyads and fought the Qaysi tribes, with the court poet al-Akhtal as its champion against the Qaysi poet Jarir, and won a decisive victory at Yawm al-Hashshak near the Tigris. Under the Abbasids Taghlibi Muslims became governors, and the mass conversion of the tribe to Islam apparently came in the reign of al-Mu'tasim (833–842). In 935 the Banu Habib, a rival Taghlibi clan of 12,000 horsemen and their families, defected to Byzantium.
bao-dai: Bảo Đại was born Nguyễn Phúc Vĩnh Thụy on 22 October 1913, the only child of Emperor Khải Định. The Nguyễn dynasty had ruled Vietnam since 1802, but after the French conquest of 1883 the country was divided into the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin and the colony of Cochinchina, and the dynasty kept only nominal rule of Annam and Tonkin. In 1922 the boy was adopted by a former French Resident-Superior of Annam and sent to France to study. He was the first Vietnamese monarch to receive a full Western education.

Khải Định died in 1925, and on 8 January 1926 Vĩnh Thụy was enthroned at the age of twelve, taking the era name Bảo Đại, meaning keeper of greatness. A regent governed for him while he returned to France to study. He came back to Vietnam in 1932 and began to reform the court, abolishing the kowtow and the rule against looking directly at the emperor.

In March 1945 the Japanese, who had occupied French Indochina since 1940, ousted the French administration and kept Bảo Đại as emperor. On 11 March he signed a declaration of independence, prepared by the Japanese, that cancelled the treaty of 1884 with France and proclaimed the Empire of Vietnam, in practice a client state of Japan. After Japan surrendered, the Viet Minh forced the imperial government to hand over power, and he abdicated, saying that he would prefer to be a citizen of an independent country than emperor of an enslaved one.

Hồ Chí Minh invited him to Hanoi as supreme adviser to the new Democratic Republic of Vietnam, a post he held for nearly a year. In 1946 he left a delegation to China and settled in Hong Kong. From 1949 to 1955 he was chief of state of the French-associated State of Vietnam. He was criticised for being too closely tied to France and for spending much of his time outside Vietnam, and in 1955 Prime Minister Ngô Đình Diệm removed him in a referendum.

Bảo Đại lived in exile in France. He died in Paris on 31 July 1997, aged 83, and was buried in the Passy Cemetery. The Communist Party of Vietnam regarded him as a traitor, and many overseas Vietnamese opposed to communism also judged him weak, though recent studies have questioned both views.
bao-si: Legend gave Bao Si a supernatural origin. In the last years of the Xia dynasty two dragons were said to have entered the king's palace, and their saliva was kept in a wooden box. When King Li of Zhou opened it against a taboo, the saliva spilled and became a black lizard, which crawled before a seven-year-old slave girl. Eight years later the girl, still a virgin, bore a daughter and abandoned her. A couple took the baby to the State of Bao and raised her, and the ruler of Bao later presented her to King You of Zhou.

She entered the palace in 779 BCE, won the king's favour and bore him a son, Bofu, and King You set aside Queen Shen and Crown Prince Yijiu in favour of Bao Si and Bofu. Because she was melancholic, the king offered a thousand ounces of gold to anyone who could make her laugh, which led to the story of the beacons on Mount Li. From the few references available she is presumed to have been born in 792 BCE, three years after the king.

When the Marquis of Shen and the Quanrong attacked, King You and Bofu were killed, and Bao Si was captured at Xi and taken to the Quanrong leader. The marquis later obtained her for himself; she accepted a bribe from him and left the capital, and during a later Quanrong attack, unable to escape, she hanged herself. The date of her death is unknown, though it is presumed to be 771 BCE on the assumption that she died soon after the attack.

The story became a cautionary tale of how one beauty could topple a state, but it is contested. The Tsinghua Bamboo Slips record that King You attacked the Marquis of Shen, who then allied with the Quanrong, and warning beacons are not attested before the Han dynasty; Liu Guozhong of Tsinghua University believes the story fabricated. Poems of the Classic of Poetry already blame her: Zheng Yue accuses her of destroying Zhou, and Shi Yue zhi Jiao lists her among corrupt ministers. She also has a prominent place in Feng Menglong's late Ming novel Chronicles of the Eastern Zhou Kingdoms.
baoji: Baoji is a prefecture-level city that covers 18,159 square kilometres and had a population of 3,321,853 at the 2020 census. It is surrounded on three sides by hills and lies in a valley opening out to the east. Its location is strategic, because it controls a pass on the Qin Mountains between the Wei River valley and the Jialing River. Since the early 1990s it has been the second largest city in Shaanxi.

South of the city lies the beginning of a plank road into the Qin Mountains, and the Jialing Jiang Fountainhead has small waterfalls and forests. To the north is Bei Puo, a giant hill of loess with a view over the city and the surrounding farming villages.

The area has roots reaching back to about 2000 BCE, and a number of Longshan archaeological sites have been found north of the Wei River near the Northern Silk Road. The city thrived early in the Tang dynasty. The Northern Silk Road, the northernmost of the routes, ran for about 2,600 kilometres through Baoji. It connected the ancient capital Chang'an to the West over the Wushaoling Mountain to Wuwei and on to Kashgar, where it linked to ancient Parthia.

Mount Taibai still has traces of roadways from the Three Kingdoms period (220 to 280 CE), built as wooden plank bridges along the mountainside. They are generally unusable through decay but remain a popular attraction. Zhuge Liang's Memorial Temple stands about 20 kilometres from the city, and visitors interested in the Three Kingdoms go there.

The Baoji area was home to Yandi, traditionally regarded as a forefather of the Han Chinese. His tomb lies in the southern part of the city and his temple in the north. Famen Temple in Fufeng County holds one of the Buddha's finger bones. Railways first reached Baoji in 1937 and have been key to its modern growth.

Baoji is a large industrial centre and is regarded as the gateway between western and eastern China, since most trains from Beijing, Shanghai and Xi'an pass through it on their way to Gansu, Sichuan, Xinjiang and Tibet. The Baoji Bronze Museum holds more than 120,000 cultural relics, primarily of the Zhou dynasty. Baoji University of Arts and Sciences is based in the city.
baol: Baol, or Bawol, lay in what is now central Senegal, on a strip of land running east from the ocean that included the towns of Touba, Diourbel and Mbacke, between the Kingdom of Cayor to the north and the Kingdom of Sine to the south. It was founded in the 11th century. There are no written sources for its early history and few oral traditions. The earliest recorded ruler, Kayamangha Diatta, belonged to the Soninke Wagadu matrilineage, a sign of influence from the Ghana Empire.

Serer people fleeing Islamization in the Senegal River valley moved into the region in the 11th or 12th century, and Wolof groups came later. The Wagadu dynasty drew them into the government. At some point Baol was integrated into the Jolof Empire; the legend that its ruler submitted to Ndiadiane Ndiaye of his own will is probably a later invention.

The Portuguese began trading on its coast in the 15th century, bringing mainly horses and iron. After the Battle of Danki, Amary Ngoné Sobel Fall, Damel of Cayor, ruled both kingdoms in a personal union as the first Damel-Teigne, founding the Fall dynasty. Such unions returned from time to time, alongside frequent wars between the two states. In 1697 Teigne Lat Sukaabe Fall conquered Cayor and built a centralised state with an army armed with firearms, but he left each kingdom to a different son.

In the 18th century Damel Maïsa Teindde Ouédji of Cayor annexed Baol, which regained its independence in 1756. The French conquest began in 1859 under Governor Louis Faidherbe; most of Baol was taken by 1874, and full control came in 1895, when it was divided into two provinces. Under colonial rule Mouridism, whose founder Amadou Bamba came from Baol, spread widely in the region.

The ruler bore the title Teigne and reigned from Lambaye. As in Cayor, great electors chose him, a bureaucracy of crown slaves served under him, and the dependent communities of herders, fishermen, clergy, castes and women had representatives. The heir, the Thialao, governed the province of Salao. Baol was known for its fast, robust horses. Through its ports of Saly Portudal and Mbour the nobles bought luxuries and firearms with slaves raided from outlying villages or taken in war.
bappa-rawal: The story of Bappa's youth comes from the 15th-century Ekalinga Mahatmya, also called the Ekalinga Purana, and other bardic chronicles. They make him the ninth descendant of Guhadatta, founder of the Guhila dynasty, and say that his father Nagaditya and all the other men of his family were killed fighting the Bhils of Idar. Bappa survived in disguise with two loyal Bhil attendants and was raised by a Brahmin woman of Nagda, who set him to herd cows.

According to the same tradition he met the sage Harit Rashi, who initiated him into the Shaivite order and told him to build the Eklingji temple at Nagda. After completing his spiritual training Bappa defeated his father's killers and founded the Mewar Kingdom, which the Ekalinga Mahatmya dates to 728 CE. In this account the Guhila rulers governed not as absolute sovereigns but as Diwans, custodians ruling on behalf of the family deity, Lord Eklingnath ji.

Some records say that Bappa captured Chittor Fort, the ancient Chitrakuta, from the mlechchhas. R. C. Majumdar held that the Moris ruled Chittor when Arab forces invaded north-western India around 725 CE, that the Arabs defeated them, and that a confederacy including Bappa then defeated the Arabs; his fame in this war, Majumdar thought, led to his being wrongly remembered as the dynasty's founder. R. V. Somani placed him in the anti-Arab confederacy of the Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Nagabhata I, while Shyam Manohar Mishra suggested he began as a vassal of the Mori ruler Manuraja and later replaced him.

Because Bappa means father and Rawal is a royal title, scholars such as C. V. Vaidya, D. R. Bhandarkar, G. H. Ojha and Kaviraj Shyamaldas regard the name as an epithet rather than a proper name. He appears in some genealogical inscriptions, such as the Unawas inscription of 959 CE, but not in others, such as the Atpur inscription of 977 CE. Ojha and others identified him with Kalabhoja; Dasharatha Sharma and D. C. Sircar with Shiladitya; Bhandarkar with Kalabhoja's son Khumana.

Gold coins bearing the legend Shri Voppa or Shri Vopparaja, with a trident, a linga and a bull, have been attributed to him by Ojha and others, though a 1960 journal of the Numismatic Society of India assigned them instead to King Vappuka of the Surasena dynasty. A temple to Bappa Rawal stands at Mathatha, near the Eklingji temple, 24 kilometres north of Udaipur, and the 1925 silent film Mewadpati Bappa Rawal told his life.
baptist-war: Many of the rebels had been educated by missionaries and had followed the progress of the abolitionist movement in London, and their first aim was a peaceful general strike. Baptist slaves proved readier to act than Presbyterian, Wesleyan or Moravian converts, perhaps because white Baptist missionaries were often absent and Black deacons, left largely to themselves, reinterpreted Baptist teaching in the light of their own experience. When the missionary Thomas Burchell returned to Montego Bay late in 1831, rumours spread that he carried documents signed by William IV granting full emancipation, and the governor's denial deepened the discontent.

Samuel Sharpe, called Daddy by his followers, and his officers, literate slaves like himself, among them Robert Gardner, Thomas Dove, John Tharp and the deacon George Taylor, bound the workers by oath to stay away from work until they were paid half the going wage. Violence broke out on 27 December, when slaves burned the Kensington estate in the hills above Montego Bay. Colonel William Grignon, a lawyer, landowner and militia commander, led the militia against them but was forced back by rebels armed with stockpiled guns, leaving Sharpe's forces in control of the rural Parish of St James.

Martial law was declared on 31 December. Sir Willoughby Cotton of the British Army enlisted the Maroons of Accompong Town, who after an early retreat at Catadupa defeated the rebels, killing Sharpe's deputy Campbell, and relieved Cotton's regulars when they were besieged at Maroon Town. When the Windward Maroons of Charles Town and Moore Town also pledged to fight, the rising collapsed, and the last rebels under Gardner surrendered. Fourteen white people were killed, and the rebels set fire to more than 100 properties, destroying over 40 sugar works.

The reprisals were far more brutal than anything the rebels had done. An estimated 310 to 340 enslaved Jamaicans, Sharpe and Gardner among them, were put to death by various forms of judicial execution, some for offences as small as the theft of a pig. White mobs destroyed churches built for Black congregations, and the missionaries William Knibb and Henry Bleby were arrested and tarred and feathered before being released. Historians argue that this brutality hastened emancipation: the accounts Burchell and Knibb gave before the House of Commons outraged its members, and Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act 1833, followed by partial emancipation in 1834 and full emancipation in 1838.
baqt: The name derives either from a Coptic term for barter or from the Byzantine Greek paktos, pact. Little is known about the treaty, and almost all information comes from Muslim sources. Later Islamic historians held that Nubia was not worth conquering and that the expedition of Abd Allah ibn Sa'd was meant only to subordinate it to Egypt, but earlier sources suggest the Arab armies suffered a rare defeat at the second battle of Dongola and accepted terms when they saw that conquest would be difficult. The Makurian king who negotiated is recorded only in Arabic, as Qalidurut.

No copy survives; the earliest versions date from centuries later and differ widely, and the agreement may have been oral. Its clearer provisions were that neither side would attack the other, that their people could trade and travel freely under safe passage, that settlement in the other's land was forbidden, that fugitives and escaped slaves would be returned, and that the Nubians would maintain a mosque for Muslim visitors. Muslims had no duty to defend Nubia against third parties.

The chief provision was that 360 slaves a year, men and women but neither children nor the elderly, would be sent to Egypt, in some reports with forty more for Egyptian notables. Ibn Abd al-Hakam gives two versions, one with Nubia alone sending slaves north and one with goods sent south in return. The second is held more reliable, since it agrees with the Nubian version.

The treaty was unprecedented among the early Muslim conquests and resembled arrangements the Byzantine Empire made with its neighbours, and Islamic theologians disagreed over whether it breached the duty to expand the dar al-Islam. In the 830s, during the Fourth Fitna, King Zacharias III of Makuria stopped payment; his son Georgios travelled to Baghdad in 835, had the arrears cancelled and won payment every three years. Relations were closest under the Fatimids, whose army relied on Nubian slaves, and worsened under the Ayyubid dynasty and the Mamluk Sultanate until war broke out. The Baqt ended in the mid-fourteenth century with the collapse of organised government in the region.
bar-le-duc: Bar-le-Duc, formerly known as Bar, is the capital of the Meuse département in the Grand Est region of north-eastern France. The lower town, the more modern and busier part, extends along a narrow valley shut in by wooded or vine-clad hills, and the Ornain runs through it. The upper town, the Ville Haute, lies on the left bank of a small arm of the river, the Canal des Usines.

Bar-le-Duc was the seat of a county and, from 1354, of the Duchy of Bar. The town is probably of ancient origin but was unimportant until the 10th century, when Frederick I of Upper Lorraine fortified it. Bar was an independent duchy from 1354 to 1480, when the Duchy of Lorraine acquired it.

In 1916, during the Battle of Verdun, Bar-le-Duc was the assembly point for the supplies sent to the besieged city of Verdun. Thousands of trucks carrying men, equipment and food travelled north around the clock on the road linking the two towns, which the writer and politician Maurice Barres named the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way, in April 1916.

The Ville Haute is crossed by a long, quiet street lined with houses of the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries, and holds 16th-century remains of the château of the dukes of Bar, dismantled in 1670. The church of Saint-Étienne contains the Cadaver Tomb of René of Châlon, who died in 1544, a carved white stone effigy of a half-decayed corpse by the 16th-century artist Ligier Richier. Among the natives of Bar-le-Duc are Mary of Guise, mother of Mary, Queen of Scots, and the mathematician Henri Poincaré. Bar-le-Duc jelly, made from currants and first mentioned in 1344, is known as Bar caviar.
bar-montenegro: Bar lies on the Adriatic shore in the coastal region of Montenegro, about 53 kilometres from Podgorica, with Lake Skadar, the largest lake in southern Europe, to the east. Its name is thought to be a shortened Slavic form of Antivari, from the Latin Antibarum or Antibari, meaning opposite Bari, for its position across the Adriatic from that Italian city. It is called Tivari in Albanian. Finds from the Neolithic show that people lived there in prehistoric times, and the name Antibarium is first quoted in the 10th century.

In the Middle Ages Bar was linked to the Slavic state of Duklja. Stefan Vojislav, ruler from 1018 to 1043, defeated the Byzantines in a battle on a hill near Bar and made it his seat. His son Mihailo I established the Archdiocese of Antivari, founded in 1089. Byzantium held the town from 1166 to 1183, until Stefan Nemanja conquered and destroyed it. The Nemanjić dynasty ruled it until 1360, then the Balšić family. The Venetians controlled Bar from 1405 to 1412, when it grew most and became a city-state, with its own Statute of Communes and coinage. They ruled again from 1443 to 1571, until the Ottomans captured Antivari and held it until 1878.

The Ottomans ceded Antivari to Montenegro at the Treaty of Berlin in 1878, and the town was made militarily neutral. In the late 1850s it had 4,000 inhabitants, 62.5 per cent of them Muslims; more than half left or were expelled after 1878. On 30 August 1904 Guglielmo Marconi made a radio link between Antivari and Bari, and in 1908 the first railway in this part of the Balkans opened there. In 1914 and 1915 Austro-Hungarian ships bombarded the port, and on 16 August 1914 a French fleet sank the cruiser SMS Zenta off the town in the Battle of Antivari. Bar joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918.

The old town of Stari Bar and the newer settlement by the sea are distinct: the district of Pristan was demolished in 1976 to enlarge the port, and its people moved mostly to Topolica. The Port of Bar and the Belgrade–Bar railway, opened in 1976, are the basis of its economy. King Nikola's castle at Topolica, built in 1885, houses the Bar Homeland Museum. Bar is the birthplace of Saint Jovan Vladimir, and has Orthodox and Catholic churches and mosques built by the Ottomans.
bar-sur-aube: The town is old. Remains of an Iron Age oppidum survive, and a coin bearing a horse and the name of Togirix, a chief of the Lingones, was found on the hill of Sainte Germaine. In Roman times it appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana as Segessera, and villas of the 1st to 4th centuries have been found in and around it. Tradition tells that the city was devastated by Attila, and Sainte Germaine is said to have been beheaded on his order in 451. After the division of the kingdom of Clovis it became part of Austrasia, and under Charles the Bald coins were struck with its name on the reverse. The name Bar comes from a Gallic word meaning summit.

Under the counts of Champagne the town was of great importance because of the Champagne fairs, where merchants from Flanders and Italy traded oriental spices and silk for the textiles and raw materials of northern Europe. The town was later joined to the crown of France. In 1318 Philip V the Tall sold it to Jacques de Croÿ; the residents then bought it themselves, so that the king could no longer sell or alienate their lands. A long plague in 1636 ended the fair.

The fortifications were demolished in 1862 and replaced by a boulevard. The French Revolution was well received there, and from 1790 to 1800 the town was the chief town of its district. On 27 February 1814, near the end of the Napoleonic era, the Battle of Bar-sur-Aube was fought in the town and its surroundings.

Bar-sur-Aube is a commune and sub-prefecture in the Aube department of the Grand Est region, about 30 kilometres west-north-west of Chaumont. It lies on the Aube among hills and Champagne vineyards. Its heritage includes the 12th-century church of Saint Maclou, the 16th-century church of Saint Peter, which holds most of the commune's more than 200 registered historical objects, and the chapel of Saint John, held in turn by the Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller.
bara-imambara: Asaf-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Awadh, began the building in a year of devastating famine, and one of his aims was to give employment to the people of the region while the famine lasted. A story holds that ordinary people built the walls by day while nobles and other members of the elite worked at night to pull down what had been raised, so that the work would go on. The cost is estimated at between half a million and a million rupees, and after completion the Nawab spent four to five hundred thousand rupees a year on its decoration.

The design was chosen by competition, won by the Delhi architect Kifayatullah, who is buried in the main hall beside his patron, Asaf-ud-Daula. The style reflects mature ornamented Mughal design, with the Badshahi Mosque as a model, and it is one of the last major projects to use no European elements or iron. The vaulted central chamber measures 50 by 16 metres and rises over 15 metres with no beams supporting the ceiling, one of the largest such arched constructions in the world.

Around it stand eight chambers of different roof heights. The space above them forms a three-dimensional labyrinth, the Bhul-bhulaiya, whose passages connect through 489 identical doorways; it arose unintentionally from the need to carry the weight of a building set on marshy land, and is possibly the only existing maze in India. The complex also holds the large Asfi mosque and the Bowli, a steep well with running water, and two gateways lead to the main hall.

Outside the complex Asaf-ud-Daula also built the 18-metre Roomi Darwaza, the richly decorated portal that served as the west-facing entrance. The Bara Imambara is counted among the grandest buildings of Lucknow and is said to be the second largest imambara in the world, after the Nizamat Imambara. It is a Monument of National Importance administered by the Archaeological Survey of India, and its labyrinth draws local visitors and tourists alike.
baracoa: Baracoa, whose full original name is Nuestra Señora de la Asunción de Baracoa, lies near the eastern tip of Cuba on the Bay of Honey, which is Bahía de Miel. A wide mountain range, including the Sierra del Purial, surrounds it and kept it isolated: until the 1960s the only access was by sea, when a 120-kilometre mountain road called La Farola was built from Guantánamo. The name is thought to come from a Taíno word meaning the presence of the sea. The nearby table mountain of El Yunque shelters several species of ferns and palms found nowhere else.

The original inhabitants of the island included the Guanahatabey, Ciboney and Taíno, who were almost wiped out by European diseases. Hatuey, who fled the Spanish on Hispaniola and raised an army against them in Cuba, is remembered as a local hero. According to the story, he was betrayed and sentenced to burn at the stake, and when a priest offered him salvation he asked whether the Spanish dead went to heaven, and said that he would rather go to hell.

Christopher Columbus landed in Cuba on 27 November 1492 at a place he named Porto Santo, generally taken from his description to be Baracoa, though Gibara has also been claimed. Tradition says he set up a cross, the Cruz de la Parra, on the sand. About 15 August 1511, the official foundation day, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, first governor of Cuba, built a town here, making it the island's first capital. In 1518 it received the title of city and the first Cuban bishop was appointed there. Spanish fortifications, El Castillo, Matachín and La Punta, and a cemetery remain.

In the 17th and 18th centuries its isolation made Baracoa a haven for illegal trade with French and British merchants. In 1744, during the War of Jenkins' Ear, the officer Luis de Unzaga, as chief commander, used a network of Irish merchants and French military personnel to be warned of British attacks, which kept the town at peace and let trade between Saint-Domingue and Cuba prosper. Early in the 19th century refugees from the Haitian Revolution settled and began growing coffee and cocoa. From the middle of that century, expeditions of independence fighters, among them Antonio Maceo and José Martí, landed here.

Baracoa is Cuba's main chocolate-manufacturing area, with cacao grown under royal palms by the rivers Miel, Toa and Yumuri, as well as bananas and coconuts. The Catedral Nuestra Señora de la Asunción holds the Cruz de la Parra. Carbon dating places it at about the period of Columbus, but it is made of a local wood, so part of the tradition cannot be right.
barakah-nuclear-power-plant: The station stands on the coast between the Persian Gulf and the E11 highway, about 53 km west-southwest of Al Dhannah City. It consists of four APR-1400 reactors with a total nameplate capacity of 5,600 MW, and it is the first nuclear power station in the United Arab Emirates and the first commercial nuclear power station in the Arab world. It is intended to supply up to 25% of the country's electricity needs.

In December 2009 the Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation (ENEC) awarded a $20 billion contract to a coalition led by the Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO), with the first reactor due to supply electricity in 2017. Later estimates of the cost ranged from $24.4 billion to $32 billion. South Korean President Lee Myung-bak attended the ground-breaking on 14 March 2011, and construction of Unit 1 began on 18 July 2012 despite talk of delays after the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster. Work on the other units followed between 2013 and 2015, when more than 18,000 staff were employed on the site.

The project ran late. In December 2018 voids were reported in the concrete containment buildings of Units 2 and 3, and the Federal Authority for Nuclear Regulation raised 400 adverse findings that had to be rectified. Fuel loading in Unit 1 was completed in March 2020, about two and a half years after the planned date. The units entered commercial service in April 2021, March 2022, February 2023 and September 2024.

In March 2019 Qatar complained to the IAEA about the plant's safety, the lack of co-operation with neighbouring states and its threat to regional stability and the environment; the UAE denied any safety problem. In December 2017 the Houthis claimed to have fired a cruise missile towards Barakah, which Emirati authorities said never reached the country. On 17 May 2026 a drone from Iraq started a fire at an electrical generator outside the inner perimeter, and emergency diesel generators powered Unit 3. No one was injured and no radioactive material was released. The Emirati presidential adviser Anwar Gargash blamed Iran or its regional proxies.
barakzai-dynasty: The Barakzai belong to the Durrani Pashtuns, alongside the Popalzai and Alakozai. Their name means children of Barak, a son of Sulaiman, also called Zirak Khan, who is regarded as the forefather of the Durrani. The family traditionally claimed descent from the children of Israel through Saul, and through a figure named Qais, who is said to have met the prophet Muhammad and embraced Islam. The ruling sub-clan is known as the Muhammadzai.

After the Durrani Empire of Ahmad Shah Durrani lost power, its territories broke up into small units as the sons of Timur Shah struggled for supremacy. Dost Mohammad Khan rose to preeminence alongside his brother Sultan Mohammad Khan, and Barakzai rulers governed Kabul from March 1823. In that year the Afghans lost the Peshawar Valley to the Sikh Khalsa Army of Ranjit Singh at the Battle of Nowshera. Kandahar was held separately by the Dil brothers from 1818, until Dost Mohammad Khan joined it to Kabul in 1855.

Dost Mohammad's descendants ruled in direct succession until 1929, when King Amanullah Khan and his brother Inayatullah Khan abdicated and Habibullah Kalakani briefly held power. Their cousin Mohammed Nadir Shah defeated Kalakani and took the throne. During the Barakzai era Afghanistan lost territory to the British in the south and east, to Persia in the west and to Russia in the north, and it fought three Anglo-Afghan wars and a civil war in 1928 and 1929. The monarchy ended in 1973 when Mohammad Daoud Khan took power as first president, and the dynasty's rule is dated to 1978.

The royal Barakzai divided into cadet branches. The Seraj descend from Dost Mohammad Khan and were mainly the emirs of the first Emirate of Afghanistan. The Telai descend from Sultan Mohammad Khan and produced Nadir Shah and Zahir Shah. The Shaghasi descend from the brothers of these two emirs and held many posts at court and in the provinces under Amanullah Khan. All descendants of Emir Payindah Mohammed hold the hereditary title Sardar.

The principal language of the Barakzai is Pashto, while Persian was formerly used for records and correspondence. They follow the Sunni Sufi branch of Islam, mostly of the Hanafi school. The emirs and kings acted as custodians of the shrine at Mazar Sharif, which Afghans hold to be the tomb of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Dost Mohammad Khan, Wazir Akbar Khan and Sher Ali Khan are buried there.
baraq-hajib: Buraq Hajib was a Khitan, thought to be a member of the Qara Khitai dynasty and a son of the Khitan noble Kulduz. In 1210 he and his brother Hamid Pur Tayangu were detained or captured by Muhammad of Khwarezm and given important posts. He served the Khwarazm prince Ghiyas-ad-Din Purshah and was made commander of Isfahan. He first came to Kerman at the head of Purshah's army, fighting the Salghurid atabeg Sa'd I.

After a quarrel with Purshah's vizier, and hearing that a Mongol army under Tolun Cherbi was approaching, he set out for India. On the way he was attacked by the governor of Kerman, Shuja ad-Din Abul-Qasim, whom he defeated when Turks went over to his side, and he then laid siege to the city. He submitted to Sultan Jalal ad-Din of Khwarazm, offering him his daughter in marriage, and with his help took Kerman. In 1225 he backed the Nasrid emir Ali b. Harb in a struggle for the throne.

In 1228 Ghiyas-ad-Din Purshah fled to Kerman after angering his brother Jalal ad-Din. Buraq forced him to give him his mother in marriage, and after a conspiracy involving Purshah and two Khitan nobles came to light he had the prince and his mother killed. He later converted to Islam and asked the Abbasid Caliph for investiture, receiving the title Qutlugh Sultan, and allied himself by marriage with the atabegs of Yazd. He then submitted to the Mongol Empire, and he and his successors ruled as Mongol vassals with the title Qutlugh Khan.

His daughters married into the ruling houses around him: Sevinch Khatun married Chagatai, and Yaqut Turkan married Mahmud Shah, atabeg of Yazd. Shortly before his death he sent his only son, Rukn al-Din Mubarak Khwaja, to the court of Ögedei, but he was succeeded by his nephew Qutb al-Din Mohammad. The dynasty was still known as Qara Khitai throughout its rule and had nine rulers in all, two of them women.
baraqish: The town stands on a high hill in Wādī Farda in al-Jawf Governorate, about 120 miles east of Sanaa. The wadi was a favoured caravan route because it had water. The Greeks and Romans knew the town as Athlula or Athrula, from the Sabaean name yθl, probably pronounced Yathill. It was inhabited as early as the Bronze Age, each generation building its houses on the ruins of the one before.

In the 6th century BCE the city was under Saba, and a document of the Sabaean ruler Yitha'amar Bayyin II mentions a rebellion there. Inscriptions record that the Sabaeans rebuilt its wall in 450 BCE. The Minaean kingdom established itself in the 5th century BCE, and the city is named in a document dated to 343 BCE. Under the Minaean kingdom it was an important stop on the incense route and a religious centre. Saba retook it in the 2nd century BCE.

The Romans under Aelius Gallus, the general of Augustus, took the city but soon left because of disease and poor water; the tomb of a Roman cavalryman, P. Cornelius, has been found there. Hadhramaut took the city in 242. People lived in the town until the 1960s, after which it was abandoned. In 2015, while it was held by Houthi forces, the site was reported badly damaged by bombing by the Saudi Arabian military.

The wall, 14 metres high with 57 towers and two gates, is still largely visible. In the south of the city stand the ruins of a temple of 16 columns in the Minaean style, which archaeologists think was dedicated to the god Athtar, with a necropolis of grave stelae beside it. Another temple in the centre keeps four standing columns. Italian archaeologists, in two campaigns begun in 1989 and 2003, excavated a temple with its roof intact, holding stone tables or altars with bulls' heads at each end, believed to belong to a sanctuary of a god of healing.
barasoain-church: The name comes from Barásoain in Navarre, Spain, birthplace of José Julián de Aranguren, Archbishop of Manila from 1847 to 1861. The place was first known as Bangkál, a village of Malolos, and its people worshipped in a hermitage of nipa and bamboo and later in chapels that were repeatedly lost to fire. In 1859 Barásoain was separated from Malolos as a town and parish of its own under Our Lady of Mount Carmel, with Francisco Arriola as its first parish priest.

Francisco Royo built a hewn stone church between 1871 and 1878, which fire soon destroyed, and the earthquakes of 1880 ruined the cemetery chapel used after it. In 1885 his successor Juan Girón hired the contractor Miguel Magpayo and began the present church of masonry and brick. Martín Arconada started the belfry in 1889, and three bells were hung in 1897.

As tension grew between the Filipino revolutionaries and the Americans after the Spanish–American War, the revolutionary government of Emilio Aguinaldo moved its capital from Cavite to Malolos. The Malolos Congress first met in the church on 15 September 1898 to draft a constitution, which was ratified on 21 January 1899, two days before the republic was inaugurated.

The Philippine–American War broke out on 4 February 1899, the congress held its last session late that month as the government withdrew to Nueva Ecija, and American forces captured Malolos and Barásoain on 31 March 1899. In 1903 the town of Barásoain was dissolved and joined again to Malolos.

President Ferdinand Marcos proclaimed the church a national shrine by Presidential Decree No. 260 on 1 August 1973, and a museum run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines opened in its old convent. Joseph Estrada was inaugurated as president there on 30 June 1998. The church appeared on the one-peso and ten-peso notes until 2001 and, from 2010, on the 200-peso note, which later showed its interior with the opening of the Malolos Congress.
barattarna: Barattarna, also written Parattarna, Paršatar or Parshatatar, is the first known king of Mitanni. Very few records from Mitanni itself survive, so what is known of its early kings comes mostly from the records of other states, and their dates are worked out by comparing Mitanni's chronology with that of other kingdoms, above all Egypt. On the middle chronology, the historian H. Klengel places his reign between about 1510 and 1490 BCE, and he is said to have ruled when Mitanni was at its peak and widest extent.

The main source for his reign is the biography of Idrimi of Alalakh. Barattarna conquered that area and made Idrimi his vassal, and by a treaty Idrimi became king of Aleppo, while Pilliya, king of Kizzuwatna, also became a vassal of Mitanni; Pilliya is known to have made peace with Zidanta II of Hatti as well. In his time Mitanni probably reached as far as Arrapha in the east, Terqa in the south and Kizzuwatna in the west. He may have been the Mitannian king whom Pharaoh Thutmosis I met at the Euphrates on a campaign early in his reign, around 1493 BCE.

Scholars do not agree on the order of the early Mitannian kings. Eva von Dassow argued in 2022 that Barattarna or Parattarna and Paršatar or Parshatatar were two different kings, and that there were two kings named Parattarna. Her sequence runs Parattarna I, Parsatatar, Saustatar, Saitarna and Parattarna II, with the beginning of Parattarna I's rule linked to Idrimi of Alalakh and that of Saustatar to Idrimi's son Niqmepa. A record from Nuzi is dated by the death of a king Barattarna.
barbados-labour-party: The party was founded on 31 March 1938 at the home of James Martineau and was called the Barbados Progressive League until 1944. At its first meeting Chrissie Brathwaite was elected chairman and Grantley Adams vice-chairman. Adams had entered the House of Assembly in 1934 partly by taking apart the labour efforts of Charles Duncan O'Neal's Democratic League, but the new party set out to organise the movement born of the unrest of 1937, which he had earlier opposed. Its aims took up many of the league's goals: adult suffrage, free education, and better housing and health care.

The party first contested general elections in 1940. It governed from 1954 to 1961 and from 1976 to 1986, and its leaders have included Hugh Gordon Cummins, Harold Bernard St. John and Henry Forde as well as Grantley and Tom Adams. Under Owen Arthur it governed again from 1994 to 2008. It won 23 of the 30 seats in 2003 and gained a 24th in 2006, when the leader of the opposition left his own party after an internal battle and joined it.

In the 2008 election the party won 10 seats to the Democratic Labour Party's 20, and Arthur was replaced as leader by Mia Mottley, a former deputy prime minister. The party returned to power on 25 May 2018, when Mottley became the first woman prime minister of Barbados, winning every seat; Joseph Atherley soon left to sit as an independent and lead the opposition. In January 2022, in the first general election since Barbados became a republic in 2021, the party again won all 30 seats, and it did so once more on 11 February 2026.

Like the Democratic Labour Party, the party has been broadly described as centre-left and social democratic, in a politics largely driven by personalities and the state of the economy. It traces its roots to Asquithian Liberal policies, putting trade as a means of growth ahead of the creation of social services. It was formerly an observer member of the Socialist International. Its women's branch is the Women's League and its youth branch the League of Young Socialists.
barbar-temple: The site in the village of Barbar holds three temples built one on top of another, the third added between 2100 and 2000 BCE. They are thought to have been built for the worship of Enki, god of wisdom and freshwater, and his wife Ninhursag. The temples were built of limestone blocks believed to have been cut on Jidda Island and carried over by boat, although the earliest used local Bahraini stone.

Temple I stood on a rectangular platform about 25 metres long and 16 to 18 metres wide, laid on clean sand bound with blue clay. Offerings were buried in its foundations: dozens of clay goblets in groups of seven beakers, broken before burial, and copper objects. Steps in its south-western corner led down to a square well, and a trapezoid shrine stood on its central terrace, preserved to its full height of 2 metres.

In Temple II a double circular altar and an offering table stood in the shrine, with three cult stones shaped like the anchors of merchant ships to the south. Square holes lined with bitumen and copper on the plinths beside the stairs may have held poles bearing the emblems of gods, as shown on stamp seals, or wooden statues.

A ceremonial stairway led down to an underground shrine around a pool fed by a natural spring, which probably explains the choice of site; channels carried its water to the fields and gardens around. The shrine is interpreted as a symbolic abzu, the freshwater abyss on which the world was believed to rest and the home of Enki. Ashes and the bones of cattle and sheep covered the floor of an oval sacrificial court to the east.

Temple III, larger than its predecessors, was in use until the early centuries of the 2nd millennium BCE. Two circular offering tables with a low altar between them still stand in its courtyard, beside three pierced stone blocks thought to have been tethering points for sacrificial animals.

P. V. Glob discovered the site in 1954, and a Danish team led by Hellmuth Andersen and Peder Mortensen excavated it from that year until 1962; work resumed in 2004. Tools, weapons, pottery and small pieces of gold found there are shown in the Bahrain National Museum, the best known being a copper bull's head. The site is on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites.
barbary-coast: The Barbary Coast, also called Barbary, Berbery or the Berber Coast, covered the coastal areas of central and western North Africa, more precisely the Maghreb and the Ottoman borderlands. It was never a single political entity. From the sixteenth century it was divided into four states, from west to east: the Alawi Sultanate of Morocco and the Regencies of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli. Their main rulers were the sultan of Morocco, the dey of Algiers, the bey of Tunis and the pasha of Tripoli. The name comes from an exonym for the Berbers, now called Amazigh.

The slave trade was an economic lifeline of the Barbary states. Most captives came from piracy at sea and from raids on coasts around the Mediterranean, although there were also Atlantic raids as far as Iceland. In 1625 the pirate fleet of Algiers, by far the largest, numbered 100 ships carrying 8,000 to 10,000 men, and the corsair industry accounted for a quarter of the city's workforce. The corsairs were Arabs and Berbers but also Turks, Greeks, Albanians, Syrians and renegade Italians, especially Corsicans.

Spain fought back after the fall of Granada completed the Reconquista. Ferdinand II launched campaigns to curb Barbary piracy and took North African cities including Melilla. In the seventeenth century pirates, now including expelled Moriscos, adopted European naval tactics. The Moriscos of the Republic of Salé used their knowledge of Spanish shores to raid the Spanish Levante, and from 1617 raids struck Galicia, which led Spain to form a fleet around 1621, with limited success.

The United States fought the Barbary Wars from 1801 to 1805 against some of the states, leading to the Battle of Derna, the second overseas military land action of the United States. The Second Barbary War ended with an agreement that American ships had free passage without paying tribute. Slaving came to an end in the early 1830s after the French conquest of Algeria.
barbastro: Barbastro is a city in the Somontano county of the province of Huesca, at the junction of the rivers Cinca and Vero. It was known originally as Barbastra or Bergiduna. An ancient Celtiberian city called Bergidum or Bergiduna stood there; in Roman times, as Barbastro, it lay within Hispania Citerior and later Hispania Tarraconensis, and after the fall of the Western Roman Empire it belonged to the Visigoth kingdom.

Musa bin Nusair overtook Barbastro and the surrounding Barbitaniya in 717, as part of the Umayyad push into the northern territories of the Marca Hispanica, and the town was called Madyar. It was later settled by the Banu Jalaf, who made it the capital of an emirate of Barbineta and Huesca until 862, and it was known as the Emirate of Brabstra until 882.

In 1064 Sancho Ramírez, King of Aragón, and Frankish Christian forces led by William VIII of Aquitaine and a Norman commander called Le Bon Normand invaded the city, which then belonged to the emirate of Zaragoza. The attack is known as the Siege of Barbastro. Contemporary sources state that 50,000 people were killed or captured, but modern historians regard this as an exaggeration, since the whole population of the town probably did not exceed 8,000. Muslim forces reconquered the city in 1065.

A Sephardic Jewish community flourished in Barbastro in the Middle Ages and suffered little compared with others in Spain; the first written record of it dates from 1144. After the Disputation of Tortosa its members all became conversos, and the old synagogue became a centre of converso life. In June 1837, during the First Carlist War, the French Foreign Legion, attached to the liberal government's army, fought the Carlist foreign legion there, and its commander, Colonel Joseph Conrad, was killed.

In the Spanish Civil War 51 Catholic Claretians, mostly young seminarians, were executed in Barbastro by anarchist militia of the Popular Front, and the diocese suffered the highest proportion of clergy killed in the war. The city's economy flourished until the early 20th century, declined, and recovered from the 1960s with the growth of agricultural production.
barbed-wire: Fencing of flat, thin wire with bristling points was first proposed in France by Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans in 1860. In April 1865 Louis François Janin proposed a double wire with diamond-shaped metal barbs. In 1867 alone six patents were issued, only two of them for livestock, one to Lucien B. Smith of Ohio, regarded as the American inventor. After the Civil War the plains were extensively settled, and ranchers, railroads and farmers all needed to fence large open spaces where wood and stone were costly and hedges unreliable.

In 1873 Joseph Glidden, a farmer, saw at a fair in DeKalb, Illinois a display by Henry B. Rose of a wooden strip with metallic points. With the hardware dealer Isaac L. Ellwood and the lumber merchant Jacob Haish he began experimenting, twisting two wires round the barbs with a grindstone and shaping barbs with a coffee mill. Glidden applied for a patent in October 1873; Haish, who held patents of his own, accused him of interference, and approval of Glidden's wire, nicknamed The Winner, was deferred until 24 November 1874.

In 1876 John Warne Gates demonstrated the wire in Military Plaza, San Antonio, showing cattle held by it, and sales rose sharply. Between 1873 and 1899 as many as 150 companies made barbed wire, then consolidated, notably into the American Steel and Wire Company, later part of U.S. Steel. A US District Court upheld the Glidden patent in 1880 and the Supreme Court affirmed it in 1892. Wire cut the cost of enclosing land and set farmers against open-range ranchers in the range wars. Heavy penalties were set for cutting fences, and some historians date the end of the Old West to the wire's spread.

Portuguese troops used barbed wire in the Battle of Magul in 1895, and it was used extensively in the Boer War, where it held the captured Boer population in concentration camps. In the First World War all combatants placed entanglements before their trenches to halt charges or funnel soldiers into machine-gun fire. The tank defeated it, as the Allied breakthrough at Amiens on 8 August 1918 showed.

Barbed wire is still the standard fencing for enclosing cattle in most regions of the United States. Fences are built between heavy braced posts and kept under great tension, often up to half a ton. The wire is galvanized, and high-tensile wire is thinner but resists stretching better. Razor wire, which replaces the barbs with near-continuous cutting surfaces, is used where humans must be kept out.
barbuda: Barbuda lies north of Antigua and covers about 160 square kilometres. Coral limestone makes up most of the island, which has very little variety in its landscape. Hills in the Barbuda Highlands on the eastern side reach about 38 metres, while the northwest corner holds many lagoons, and Codrington Lagoon dominates the western part. Salty ponds and scrubland are spread across the interior. The climate is tropical marine. Codrington, which grew up as the main residential area by 1666, is still the only town and the main settlement.

The first settlers arrived by canoe, as hunter-gatherers, around 2,900 to 3,000 BCE. Sources disagree on whether they came from South America, the Greater Antilles or the Yucatán region. They made cutting blades, hoes and picks from the shells of conch, trumpet and whelk. They were followed by Arawak people, present on Barbuda and Antigua from at least 1,000 BCE, whose numbers on Barbuda peaked between 1,500 and 800 years ago. They probably came from present-day Venezuela and Guyana, grew sweet potatoes, corn, cotton and tobacco, and made pottery in the Saladoid style, with white-on-red designs.

English colonisation was attempted from St. Kitts under a patent of 1625 granted to the Earl of Carlisle, and the island appears there as Barbado. In 1668 about 240 Kalinago attacked the 20 English inhabitants, and eight settlers died. Strong Kalinago resistance and drought caused this attempt to fail. In 1685 the crown granted the island to the brothers John and Christopher Codrington. The colonisers intended Barbuda to be a colony for the forced reproduction of enslaved people, but this never went through. Slavery was abolished there in 1834. Because a single land grant had covered the whole island, Barbudans went on farming communal property on their own account.

Barbuda forms part of the twin-island state of Antigua and Barbuda as an autonomous entity. It gained autonomy in 1976 through the Barbuda Local Government Act, which created the Barbuda Council, and gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1981 as part of Antigua and Barbuda. The Council has eleven members and sits in Codrington. Under the Barbuda Land Acts, land is held communally. The 2011 census counted 1,634 people. Fishing, especially for lobster, supplies most exports, and tourist attractions include the Frigate Bird Sanctuary in Codrington Lagoon, a 19th-century Martello Tower and the ruins of Highland House, the Codrington family home.
barcelona: Barcelona lies on the north-east coast of the Iberian Peninsula, facing the Mediterranean Sea, on a plain about 5 km wide limited by the Collserola mountain range, the Llobregat river to the south-west and the Besòs river to the north. It lies 120 km south of the Pyrenees. The escarpment of Montjuïc overlooks the harbour and is topped by Montjuïc Castle, a fortress built in the 17th and 18th centuries to control the city.

According to tradition Barcelona was founded by Phoenician or Carthaginian settlers, and some historians credit the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca with naming it Barcino in the 3rd century BCE, though this theory has been questioned. Coins of the 3rd century BCE found at the foot of Montjuïc carry the name Barkeno in Iberian script.

In the Middle Ages Barcelona became the capital of the County of Barcelona. After the union with Aragon it remained capital of the Principality of Catalonia and the most important city of the Crown of Aragon, until Valencia overtook it shortly before 1516. Its industrial rise began in 1833, when Catalonia's textile industry began to use steam power. It became capital of autonomous Catalonia in 1931 and was taken by the fascists in 1939.

Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia and the second most populous municipality of Spain. Its old centre, the Barri Gòtic, has buildings from medieval times and some from the Roman settlement. Works of Antoni Gaudí and Lluís Domènech i Montaner are World Heritage Sites, and the city hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics.
barcelona-may-days: After the military rising of July 1936 failed in Barcelona, the city and the rest of Catalonia came under the control of workers' militias, chiefly those of the anarchist union CNT-FAI and the socialist UGT, and industries were collectivised. The Communist Party of Spain and its Catalan counterpart, the Unified Socialist Party of Catalonia (PSUC), held that the war had to be won before any revolution, while the POUM and the anarchists wanted to carry out the revolution during the war. Through the spring of 1937 tension rose: on 26 March Josep Tarradellas ordered political organisations to hand over their weapons, and on 25 April Carabineros took the customs house at Puigcerdà from CNT patrols in a clash that killed its mayor, Antonio Martin.

On 3 May about 200 police under Eusebio Rodríguez Salas, Catalan minister of public order, tried to take the Telefónica exchange, which an anarcho-syndicalist committee held under a decree of the Generalitat itself. Shooting broke out, and within hours several hundred barricades rose across the city: the PSUC and the government held the districts east of the Ramblas, the anarchists the west and the suburbs.

On 4 May the anarchist ministers Joan García Oliver and Federica Montseny appealed on the radio for their followers to lay down their arms. On 5 May the anarchist writers Camillo Berneri and Francesco Barbieri were arrested and murdered, and fighting spread to Tarragona, Tortosa and other towns. A force of about 5,000, most of them Assault Guards, arrived from Madrid and Valencia on 7 May and disarmed and arrested many members of the CNT, FAI, Libertarian Youth and POUM. By 8 May the streets were calm. The officially given toll was 400 dead and 1,000 wounded; detailed later studies counted 218 dead in Barcelona.

The days showed that the anarchists no longer spoke with one voice: their ministers, intent on winning the war, had lost touch with their youth, who put the revolution first. The Republican government outlawed the POUM on 16 June and arrested its leaders, among them Julián Gorkin and Andreu Nin. Largo Caballero's government fell and the four anarchist ministers left it, a clear gain in power for the Communists. George Orwell, who served with the POUM, described the fighting in Homage to Catalonia.
barcid-family: In the 3rd century BCE the Barcids were one of the leading families in the ruling oligarchy of Carthage. Barcid is a form coined by historians, like Ramesside or Abbasid; the family's own byname was the Northwest Semitic Barca or Barcas, meaning lightning, a word related to barq in Arabic, berqa in Maltese and mebrek in Amharic. The patriarch was Hamilcar Barca, who lived from 275 to 228 BCE. He and his wife, whose name is unknown, had three sons, who all became military leaders, and three daughters, who married allies of the family.

Hamilcar served as a general in the First Punic War, from 264 to 241 BCE, and in the Mercenary War that followed. He is said to have made Hannibal swear on an altar never to be a friend of Rome. He then extended Carthage's holdings in Hispania, where he drowned crossing a river. His son-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair succeeded to the command, extended the new province by diplomacy, founded Qart Hadast, later Carthago Nova and now Cartagena, as its capital and fixed the Ebro as the boundary with Rome by treaty, before he was killed by a Celtic assassin.

Hannibal won the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE and lost at Zama in 202 BCE, and crossed the Alps with 60,000 soldiers and 38 elephants. His brother Hasdrubal defended the cities of Hispania after Hannibal left for Italy in 218 BCE, and was defeated and killed at the Battle of the Metaurus in 207 BCE while bringing reinforcements. The youngest, Mago, fought in most of Hannibal's battles and often led the decisive push.

The Barcids founded several Carthaginian cities in the Iberian Peninsula, some of which still exist, among them Mahón and Cartagena, and their name is often given as the origin of the name of Barcelona. One of Hamilcar's daughters married the Numidian chieftain Naravas; the name Salammbo sometimes given to her comes from the title of a novel by Gustave Flaubert.
bard: The word goes back to the Proto-Celtic noun *bardos, a poet-singer, itself derived from a Proto-Indo-European compound meaning praise-maker. It is attested in Gaulish as bardus in Latin and bárdoi in Greek, and survives in Middle Welsh bardd, Middle Irish bard and Middle Breton barz. The fullest early accounts descend from the lost history of Posidonius, who travelled in southern Gaul in the early 1st century BCE, and reach us through Diodorus Siculus, Strabo and Athenaeus. Because these writers share one source they count as a single tradition. Caesar, who wrote at length about the druids, does not mention the bards at all.

The sources agree on what the bard did: praise poetry and satire, sung to a stringed instrument that Diodorus compares to a lyre. The power to raise or lower a patron's standing gave successful bards a privileged and well-paid position. Athenaeus, citing Posidonius, tells of the Arvernian Louernios, to whom a poet arrived late after a feast and sang of the king's greatness; Louernios threw him a bag of gold, and the poet answered with a second song. Appian describes a singer in the train of an embassy sent by the Arvernian king Bituitus, who praised the king, his people and the envoy. Diodorus adds that bards, together with druids, could step between two armies and halt them.

In medieval Wales the court poet held an office set out in the Laws of Hywel Dda, with the pencerdd, or chief of song, at its head. The Gogynfeirdd of the 12th and 13th centuries composed praise and elegy for the princes of independent Wales, and the order broke up in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. In Ireland the professional poet was the file, and the baird were held to rely on talent rather than formal learning. Irish bardic poetry lasted into the 17th century, and in Gaelic Scotland the MacMhuirich family kept the classical tradition into the early 18th century.

A Welsh tradition holds that Edward I had the Welsh bards put to death after the conquest of 1282, but no medieval source records it, and the historian Prys Morgan treats it as a fable. Thomas Gray's ode The Bard, published in 1757, fixed the legend in the public mind. James Macpherson's Works of Ossian, published in the 1760s as the verse of an ancient Highland bard, was read across Europe. In Wales, Edward Williams, writing as Iolo Morganwg, founded the Gorsedd Beirdd Ynys Prydein in 1792, supporting his claims with forgeries exposed only after his death. The image of an aged, visionary bard that grew from these works remains familiar in popular culture.
bardas-phokas-the-younger: Bardas Phokas belonged to the Phokas family, the most prominent Byzantine aristocratic clan of the 10th century. His father, Leo Phokas the Younger, held the rank of curopalates and was the brother of Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas. The historian Michael Psellos wrote that Bardas resembled his uncle, always gloomy and watchful, thoroughly versed in siege warfare, ambush and pitched battle, and so strong that a blow from his hand killed a man outright. His revolt of 969 was directed against the new emperor John I Tzimiskes, who was his own cousin.

In 978 the eunuch Basil Lekapenos, uncle and de facto regent of Basil II, released him and sent him in disguise to his native Cappadocia to rouse the local aristocracy against Bardas Skleros, whose revolt had reached the Hellespont. After several setbacks, and with a Georgian army led by John Tornikios, Phokas suppressed the revolt. As Domestic of the Scholae he then led the Byzantine armies to reconquer Aleppo, and according to Psellos he was granted a triumph and counted among the emperor's personal friends.

Basil II's growing resolve to rule and command the army himself alarmed both Basil Lekapenos and Phokas. In 987 they negotiated in secret with Skleros, agreeing to partition the empire if the revolt succeeded. Phokas proclaimed himself emperor, put on the imperial robes and crown, and overran most of Asia Minor. He then imprisoned Skleros and laid siege to Abydos, threatening to blockade the Dardanelles.

Basil II received Varangian mercenaries from his brother-in-law Vladimir, prince of Kiev, and marched to Abydos. As the armies faced each other, Phokas rode out to seek single combat with the emperor, but suffered a seizure, fell from his horse and was found dead on 13 April 989. His head was cut off and brought to Basil, and the rebellion ended. By his wife Adralestina, a cousin, he left two sons, Leo and Nikephoros. His grandson Bardas Phokas was blinded by the imperial authorities in 1025, and the Cretan family of the Phokades is believed to descend from him.
