bardas-skleros: Bardas Skleros was the son of Niketas Skleros, of the great Skleroi family, which held enormous estates on the eastern edge of Asia Minor; his mother Gregoria descended from Bardas, brother of Basil I. His chief early success was the defence of Constantinople against Svyatoslav I of Kiev in 970: at the Battle of Arcadiopolis he reportedly inflicted as many as 20,000 casualties on the Rus for the loss of only 25 Byzantine soldiers. He became a trusted adviser to John I Tzimiskes, his brother-in-law and a fellow Armenian.

When John died, Skleros hoped to succeed him, but the eunuch Basil Lekapenos, who led the government, removed him from his post as general in the East in 976. Skleros won the backing of Armenian, Georgian and Muslim rulers and quickly made himself master of Caesarea, Antioch and most of Asia Minor. His fleet under Michael Kourtikios was beaten by the imperial fleet under Theodoros Karantenos, and he turned to besiege Nicaea, defended by Manuel Erotikos Komnenos.

Basil recalled Bardas Phokas the Younger, to whom David III Kuropalates of Tao pledged 12,000 Georgian horsemen under John Tornikios. Skleros beat Phokas twice but lost a third battle, and on 24 March 979 the two men met in single combat. Skleros was gravely wounded in the head, the rumour of his death put his army to flight, and he took refuge with his Muslim allies before retreating with his family to Baghdad in 980, where he lived for six years in honourable captivity.

In 987 Phokas recalled him to join a new revolt, then imprisoned him. After Phokas died at Abydos in 989, Skleros led the rebellion himself; the date and circumstances of his surrender are disputed. In 991 Basil II, on his way to Bulgaria, visited him in Thrace, blinded and broken, and Skleros accepted the title of curopalates, dying a few days later, presumably on 6 March. His line continued through his son Romanos Skleros; his grandson Basil Skleros married a sister of Emperor Romanos III, and Basil's niece Pulcheria Skleraina married the future emperor Constantine Monomachos.
bardi-family: The family's nobility is documented from 1164, when Emperor Friedrich Barbarossa granted the county of Vernio, a castle and nine communes near the Mugello, to Count Alberto with the right to confer noble titles. Countess Margherita, the last of Alberto's line, sold Vernio to her son-in-law Piero de' Bardi. In 1215 the Bardi took the side of the Buondelmonti, and so of the Guelph faction, in Florence's feuds; Geri di Ricco de' Bardi was exiled after the Guelph defeat at Montaperti in 1260, and his nephew Cino fought beside Dante Alighieri at Campaldino in 1289.

The Bardi and the Peruzzi opened branches in England in the 1290s and were the main European bankers by the 1320s. They eased trade with bills of exchange, by which money paid in one town could be paid out to a creditor in another. The Bardi had thirteen branches, in Barcelona, Seville, Mallorca, Paris, Avignon, Marseille, London, Bruges, Constantinople, Rhodes, Cyprus, Jerusalem and Nice. Edward III of England borrowed 900,000 florins from them and 600,000 from the Peruzzi for his war with France, and his default in the 1340s ruined both houses.

The family kept its noble standing and its trade. Contessina de' Bardi's marriage to Cosimo de' Medici around 1415 helped establish the Medici in Florence, and Cosimo restored the family's political rights in 1434 and freed them from certain taxes in 1444. In the 15th century the Bardi helped finance some of the early voyages to the Americas, including those of Christopher Columbus and John Cabot.

The Bardi were patrons of the friars. Ridolfo de' Bardi founded the family chapel of St. Francis around 1310, the year he inherited the company, and the family built a larger chapel dedicated to Louis of Toulouse, the Franciscan bishop canonised in 1317. Sandro Botticelli's Bardi Altarpiece, now in Berlin, and the Palazzo Busini Bardi in Florence also bear the family's name.
bardiya: The prince's name appears in several forms. In Darius the Great's Behistun inscription he is Bardiya or Bardia, called Pirtiya in the Elamite version and Barziya in the Akkadian. Herodotus calls him Smerdis, the usual Greek form, and Ctesias calls him Tanyoxarces. English histories traditionally followed Herodotus and used Smerdis, but recent ones tend to prefer Bardiya.

He was the younger son of Cyrus the Great and a full or half-brother of Cambyses II. According to Ctesias, Cyrus on his deathbed named Cambyses king and appointed Bardiya satrap of Bactria, Chorasmia, Parthia and Carmania. Darius's inscription says instead that Cambyses killed Bardiya in secret, after becoming king and before leaving for Egypt.

The sources agree that in the spring of 522 BCE a man claiming to be Bardiya was proclaimed king, but they differ on who he was. According to Darius, he was a Median magus named Gaumata. In Herodotus the usurper is a magus whose brother, the palace steward Patizeithes, had put him forward after Bardiya's secret murder; Ctesias names him Sphendadates, who was said to resemble Tanyoxarces and took his place after Cambyses had the prince killed.

In these accounts the new king was widely accepted, helped by granting tax relief for three years, and ruled for about seven months, moving the seat of government to Media. Herodotus has Cambyses die of a wound to his thigh while marching against him. In Herodotus the nobleman Otanes grew suspicious and had his daughter Phaedymia, who was in the king's harem, check whether the king had ears, since the impostor's had been cut off. Seven nobles then plotted against him.

In September 522 BCE the seven nobles, among them Darius, surprised the ruler in a castle at Nisa and killed him. Darius was proclaimed king, and Herodotus and Ctesias say he won the throne by a trick in a horse-neighing contest. Another man claiming to be Bardiya, Vahyazdāta, rose in eastern Persia the next year, had great success and was finally captured and executed. Persia is said to have marked the death of the false Bardiya each year in a feast called the killing of the magian.

Most modern historians do not find Darius's version convincing. They assume that the man who ruled was the real Bardiya and that Darius invented the impostor to justify seizing the throne, though others call this hypothetical. Contracts of his reign survive from Babylonia. Darius claimed that Bardiya had destroyed some temples and seized herds and houses. Bardiya's only daughter, Parmys, married Darius.
bardylis: Bardylis was born around 448 BCE and became king despite humble roots. He is said to have been a charcoal-burner and coal miner who gained power by force and won the sympathy of Illyrian warriors by dividing the spoils of war fairly. He founded the first attested Illyrian dynasty and brought various Illyrian tribes together. Most scholars place his kingdom along Lake Ohrid and east to the Prespa Lakes, later called Dassaretis, on the border between Macedon and Epirus.

Unlike earlier Illyrian kings, Bardylis developed both the military and the economy of his state. His subjects, the Damastini, issued fine silver coins from about 395 BCE at Damastion, and further coins followed from about 365 BCE at Daparria, a mining city in what is now Kosovo. The spread of the coins suggests trade across the central Balkans and north to the Danube.

He fought Macedon repeatedly. According to the account, he defeated Amyntas III, expelled him and ruled Macedon through a puppet king, and he later forced Macedon to pay him an annual tribute. In 385 BCE the Illyrians under his rule allied with Dionysius of Syracuse, who sent 2,000 men and 5,000 weapons, to restore the Molossian Alcetas. Bardylis invaded Epirus and killed 15,000 Molossians, but the Spartans under Agesilaus intervened and expelled the Illyrians. Further raids on Epirus in 360 BCE were defeated by the Molossian king Arymbas.

In 359 BCE Perdiccas III of Macedon marched north to end the tribute. The Macedonians lost the battle and the king was among about 4,000 dead. The Illyrians then extended their control south to Lake Ohrid and west into Upper Macedonia, bringing Macedon close to collapse.

Philip II, the youngest brother of Perdiccas, first reaffirmed the treaty imposed by the Illyrians and sealed it by marrying Audata, a descendant of Bardylis. By spring 358 BCE he was ready to act. Bardylis offered a treaty that would leave each side the cities it held, but Philip demanded full withdrawal from north-western Macedon.

The armies met in the Erigon Valley near Bitola, with about 10,000 infantry each. Philip's cavalry turned the Illyrian flank, and his hypaspists broke into the Illyrian formation, which was then routed by the phalanx. Diodorus Siculus reports more than 7,000 Illyrians killed. Bardylis, who is said to have been about 90, probably died in the battle. The Illyrians gave up the Macedonian cities, and Philip annexed territory as far as Lake Ohrid. Bardylis' son Cleitus later revolted against Alexander the Great at Pelium in 335 BCE.
barebones-parliament: After the execution of King Charles I, the Rump Parliament was the last remaining part of the English government, with little claim to represent the country, and it made slow progress on the reforms many expected. Its forced dissolution on 20 April 1653 left no plan for what should follow. On 29 April Cromwell set up a Council of State of thirteen members, while the Council of Officers debated the new form of government.

John Lambert wanted power given to ten or twelve men; Thomas Harrison, a Fifth Monarchist, wanted it in the hands of godly men to hasten the kingdom of Christ; and John Rogers proposed an assembly of 70 modelled on the Jewish Sanhedrin. The officers settled on 140, chosen from names put forward by their own members: 129 for England, five for Scotland and six for Ireland, the last two groups English soldiers serving there.

The assembly first met on 4 July in the council chamber at Whitehall, where Cromwell opened it with a speech of about two hours. It chose Francis Rous as chairman, later Speaker, and on 12 July declared itself the parliament of the Commonwealth of England. Opponents mocked its members as tradesmen of low birth, although most came from the richest five per cent of the population; one analysis counts 76 religious moderates and 47 radicals.

Debates on tithes, the trial of John Lilburne and reform of the law divided the members, and bills to abolish the Court of Chancery stalled. Cromwell complained that he was "more troubled now with the fool than before now with the knave", and attendance fell from over a hundred in July to about 70 by October.

On 6 December a committee's report on tithes was defeated by 56 votes to 54. Two days later moderates demanded that the assembly give up its powers, and Rous and about 40 members went to Cromwell at Whitehall with a document signed by nearly 80 members; troops then cleared those who remained. The collapse of the radical consensus led the Grandees to pass the Instrument of Government, which opened the way to the Protectorate.
bareilly: Bareilly lies in the Indo-Gangetic Plains on the bank of the Ramganga River, about 252 kilometres north-west of Lucknow and 265 kilometres east of New Delhi. The plain is level and well watered, with fertile alluvial soil, although the lower plain is flood-prone. According to the Mahabharata, the region, called Panchala, was the birthplace of Draupadi, and folklore says that Gautama Buddha visited the ancient fortress city of Ahichchhatra.

The earliest settlement was founded in 1537 by the Rajput chieftain Jagat Singh Katehriya, who named it after his two sons Bansaldev and Baraldev. The town came under Mughal rule in 1569, and in 1657 the Mughal governor Mukrand Rai laid the foundation of the modern city. As Mughal power weakened, the Kingdom of Rohilkhand rose, with Bareilly as a major centre. Under Hafiz Rahmat Khan Barech, Rohilkhand blocked Maratha expansion into northern India at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

In 1774 the combined forces of Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the East India Company defeated Hafiz Rahmat Khan, who was killed in battle, ending Rohilla rule. The Nawab of Awadh surrendered Rohilkhand to the Company in a treaty of 10 November 1801. A military station was established south of the city in 1811, and a fort was built in 1816. Bareilly was freed by rebels during the Indian Rebellion of 1857 and remained independent under Khan Bahadur Khan until the British re-annexed it in 1858.

Bareilly is a city in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh and the centre of the historical region of Rohilkhand. It is the place of origin of the Barelvi movement, a Sunni Islamic movement formed by the scholar Ahmad Raza Khan to counter the growing influence of the Deobandi movement; his shrine at the Bareilly Dargah is visited by millions of followers each year. The city has been known as Nath Nagri because of its ancient Shiva temples, and is a centre of furniture manufacturing and of trade in cotton, cereal and sugar.
bargal: Bargal, also written Bargaal, lies on the eastern coast of the Bari region, facing the Guardafui Channel of the Indian Ocean. It is 35 nautical miles south of Cape Guardafui and 30 nautical miles south of Tohen, while Ras Binnah lies 11 nautical miles and Gumbah 26 nautical miles to its south. The town is the centre of Bargal District, which has around 6,798 inhabitants.

Bargal may have been founded in the early modern period, when it served as a seasonal headquarters of the Majeerteen Sultanate. The monograph Migiurtinia ed il Territorio del Nugál, written early in 1925 before the military occupation of the sultanate, describes it as the usual residence of Boqor Osman Mahmud. Its people were mainly Majeerteen, among them 800 of the Adan Abdirahman clan and 150 of the Osman Mahmud clan.

The same work counts four forts, the king's house, about 120 brick buildings and some 200 huts. Drinking water, slightly brackish, was available on the spot. The village was divided into two parts, Old Bargal and Eirod, and the sultan lived in the latter. On 28 and 29 October 1925 Bargal was bombed and destroyed.

In June 2007 the town was the scene of the Battle of Bargal. In 2012 the Puntland Highway Authority announced a project to link Bargal and other towns of Puntland to the main regional highway, a road of 750 km that joins Bosaso, Galkayo and Garowe with towns further south.

Bargal is a town of Puntland State in north-eastern Somalia. According to the Puntland Ministry of Education its district has three primary schools and one secondary school; the town's schools include Wadikhayr, Taageer, Qorraxad, Abdehan and Bargaal Primary.
barghash-bin-said: Sayyid Barghash bin Said al-Busaidi was born to the Omani sultan Said bin Sultan and an Ethiopian concubine. In 1859 a dispute broke out between him and his half-brother Majid, then Sultan of Zanzibar. Their sister Sayyida Salme bint Said, later known as Emily Ruete, acted at the age of fifteen as secretary of Barghash's party. With the help of an English gunboat the rising was soon put down, and Barghash was sent into exile in Bombay for two years, held under virtual house arrest in the compound of the British political resident.

After Majid's death Barghash became sultan. Emily Ruete wrote in 1886 that as soon as he took the throne he imprisoned their younger brother Khalifah, next in the succession, in heavy fetters for three years, freeing him only when a sister about to go on pilgrimage to Mecca refused to pardon him otherwise. Barghash is credited with building much of the infrastructure of Stone Town, including public baths, a police force, roads, parks, hospitals and large administrative buildings. He dealt with diplomats from Britain, America, Germany, France and Portugal and was often able to play one country off against another.

He had a treaty with the British against the slave trade but was suspected of taking money from slave traders to let it go on. In June 1873 John Kirk, the acting British Consul, received two instructions from London, one to threaten a blockade unless the trade was stopped, the other not to enforce it. Kirk showed Barghash only the first, and within two weeks the sultan signed a further treaty prohibiting the slave trade and closed the great slave market.

Late in his reign the empire he had inherited broke apart. In 1884 the German Carl Peters had chiefs on the Tanganyika mainland sign documents placing their lands under German protection, ratified by an imperial letter in February 1885, and in April 1885 the Sultan of Witu came under German protection too. When Barghash sent troops against Witu, a German fleet forced him to give way. The British-German agreement of 29 October 1886 left him a 10-mile strip along the coast. He died on 26 March 1888, before the agreement of that year handed the coast of later Tanganyika to the Germans.
bari: Bari stands on the Adriatic coast of southern Italy, the largest urban area on that sea. Its old town is closely built on a peninsula between two modern harbours and holds the Basilica of Saint Nicholas, the Cathedral of San Sabino, built between 1035 and 1171, and the Norman-Swabian Castle. To the south lies the Murat quarter, laid out on a rectangular grid after Joachim Murat, King of Naples, began a new urbanisation in 1813. The port has long linked the city to Greece, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean.

In antiquity Bari was Barium, a harbour of the Iapygian Peuceti, with strong Greek influence. It became part of the Roman Republic in the 3rd century BCE and gained importance as the junction of the coast road and the Via Traiana and as a port for eastern trade. After 476 it was occupied by the Ostrogoths, taken by the Byzantines in the Gothic wars and then disputed for two centuries with the Lombards of Benevento. Through the Middle Ages it was one of the major slave depots of the Mediterranean, in particular for Slavic slaves bound for Byzantine and Muslim lands.

Its first emir, Kalfun, took Bari in 847. The Frankish emperor Louis II conquered the city and ended the emirate in 871 after a five-year campaign, helped by a Byzantine fleet. In 885 it became the residence of the Byzantine catapan. Robert Guiscard captured Bari in 1071 after a three-year siege. The former praetorium became the Basilica of Saint Nicholas, where the relics were installed in 1087 and which Pope Urban II consecrated in 1089. Peter the Hermit preached the First Crusade there in 1095.

Bona Sforza, widow of King Sigismund I of Poland, settled in Bari in 1556, fortified the castle and died in the city in 1557, after which the kings of Naples ruled it directly. On 2 December 1943 a German air raid destroyed the American ship SS John Harvey, which carried a secret cargo of mustard gas bombs, and the gas killed and injured sailors and civilians; the number of deaths is disputed.
barings-bank: Barings Bank began as the John and Francis Baring Company, founded by Sir Francis Baring with his older brother John as a mostly silent partner. They were sons of a wool trader of Exeter born in Bremen. The firm started in offices off Cheapside and moved to Mincing Lane, diversifying from wool into other commodities, including the slave trade, which enriched the family considerably. Its success owed much to a network of corresponding houses, above all Hope and Company of Amsterdam. In 1774 it began business in North America.

In 1802 Barings and Hope and Company facilitated the Louisiana Purchase. After a down payment of 3 million dollars in gold, the remainder was paid in United States bonds, which Napoleon sold to Barings through Hope at 87.50 per 100 of face value, with Alexander Baring making the arrangements in Paris. Barings also helped finance the United States government in the War of 1812, and by 1818 it was called the sixth great European power. In the 1820s and 1830s it grew entangled in the slave-powered economy through mortgages on enslaved people and Caribbean cotton plantations. It was appointed in 1845 to supply maize to Ireland for famine relief.

Overexposure to Argentine and Uruguayan debt led to the Panic of 1890. William Lidderdale, governor of the Bank of England, arranged a consortium to bail the bank out, and a limited liability company took over its viable business. Barings never regained its dominant position.

The bank was brought down by Nick Leeson, its derivatives trader in Singapore. He hid his losses in an error account numbered 88888, and his positions were hit by the Kobe earthquake. The losses reached 827 million pounds, twice the bank's available trading capital. Barings was declared insolvent on 26 February 1995. The Dutch bank ING bought it for one pound and took over its liabilities. Leeson was captured in Frankfurt on 2 March and sentenced in Singapore to six years and six months in prison. The Barings name survives in an asset management business owned by MassMutual.
baripada: Baripada lies on the east bank of the Budhabalanga river, the only perennial river flowing through the city, at an average elevation of 36 metres. It is the cultural centre of north Odisha and the headquarters of Mayurbhanj district, the largest district of Odisha by area. The name is an Odia word meaning land of water, from bari, water, and refers to the many ponds, water bodies and the river. In another version it was probably derived from the Bauri or Bathudi tribe. The nearby villages have a large tribal population, including Santhals and Hos.

Baripada became the headquarters of the state, now the district, at the end of the 18th century during Sumitra Devi's rule, succeeding Haripur. Haripur, earlier Hariharpur, had been founded by Maharaja Harihar Bhanj in 1400 and was the capital of the Bhanja dynasty. Major James Rennell had already recorded Baripada as Burpuddah in his 1779 atlas. The old mud fort in the centre of the city has disappeared, and a temple of Ambika Devi is its sole survivor. The chief shrine is a Jagannath temple dating from 1575, the oldest structure in the area, and a statue of the Buddhist deity Lokeshvara in one of its rooms is older still.

Baripada developed into a town only under Maharaja Jadunatha Bhanja, who died in 1863, and his successors, especially Maharaja Sriram Chandra Bhanj Deo, added public works. The Maharaja Krushna Chandra Bhanjdeo linked it to the Howrah-Chennai railway corridor by the narrow-gauge Mayurbhanj State Railway. The city continued to grow after the merger of Mayurbhanj State with the Union of India in 1949.

Baripada is known for the Chhau dance, and its Ratha Yatra is the second place after Puri where the car festival of Lord Jagannath began, so the city is called Dwitiya Srikhetra, the second Puri. Only women pull the chariot of Goddess Subhadra. The practice began in 1975, International Women's Year, after a woman was seriously hurt in the mid-1950s trying to touch the chariot ropes.

Maa Ambika Temple is one of its chief temples and Jagadhatri Mela at Bhanjpur is a large annual fair. Baripada is the seat of MSCB Public University, and its Government Sanskrit College, established in 1894, is the oldest Sanskrit college in Odisha. Similipal National Park, a reserve for elephants and tigers, lies 30 kilometres away. The population in the 2011 census was 110,058.
barisan-nasional: Barisan Nasional, or National Front, is the direct successor to the Alliance, a three-party coalition of the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the Malaysian Chinese Association and the Malaysian Indian Congress. It arose from the 1969 general election. The Alliance won a majority of seats but less than half the popular vote, losing ground to the newly formed Democratic Action Party and Gerakan and to the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party. Tension between communities led to the riots of 13 May 1969 and a state of emergency.

After Parliament reconvened in 1971, negotiations began to widen the coalition. Gerakan and the People's Progressive Party joined the Alliance in 1972, followed by the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party in 1973. The new coalition included regional parties from Sabah and Sarawak and began with nine parties. It contested the 1974 general election under the prime minister Tun Abdul Razak and won with considerable success.

The coalition kept the Alliance's inter-communal model on a larger scale and grew to include as many as 14 communal parties at its peak. In 1977 the Islamic Party was expelled after a revolt in the Kelantan state legislature. The coalition still won the 1978 election convincingly. It never took more than 67% of the popular vote between 1974 and 2008, but held a two-thirds majority of seats until 2008, helped by the first-past-the-post voting system.

In 2008 it lost more than one third of the seats to Pakatan Rakyat. In 2013 it won 47% of the popular vote but about 60% of the 222 seats. The 1MDB scandal, which broke in 2015, damaged its reputation. In 2018 it won only 79 seats and lost power to Pakatan Harapan, ending 61 years of rule counting its predecessor. Many component parties then left, and four remained: UMNO, MCA, MIC and PBRS.

After the Pakatan Harapan government collapsed in 2020, the coalition joined a Perikatan Nasional government. In the 2022 election it won 30 of 222 seats, behind Pakatan Harapan with 82 and Perikatan Nasional with 74. The result was a hung parliament, and the coalition supported Pakatan Harapan in a national unity government.

Each component party claims to represent one community and limits its membership accordingly, UMNO for the Malays and MCA for the Chinese. Membership of the coalition is mostly indirect, through its parties, though direct membership is allowed. It defines itself as a confederation of political parties. At elections all candidates stand under its symbol and there is a common manifesto, but each party also issues its own, and the parties compete among themselves for seats before nomination day.
barisone-ii-of-arborea: Barisone was born early in the 12th century, the son of Comita II and Elena de Orrubu, and may have been associated with his father in the government of the Judicate before succeeding him at his death. In his early years he was on good terms with Pisa and at peace with the church. With most of the Arborean clergy and Villano, Archbishop of Pisa, his overlord, he attended the consecration of Santa Maria di Bonarcado, and he gave the church land from his own demesne.

In 1157 he repudiated his first wife, Pellegrina de Lacon, of an old island family, and married Agalbursa de Cervera, daughter of Ponce and Almodis and a close kinswoman of Raymond Berengar IV, Count of Barcelona. The marriage brought an alliance with Barcelona, the first Catalan influence in Sardinia: Barisone fought the Balearic Almoravids on the count's behalf, and the count backed his attempts to unite the judicates under his rule. Claiming Cagliari as a direct descendant of Constantine II of Cagliari, he invaded it and drove out its ruler Peter.

In the spring of 1164 the Judicates of Torres and Cagliari, joined by the Pisans of the island, retook Cagliari and invaded Arborea, and Barisone took refuge in the castle of Cabras. Through the Republic of Genoa he won the support of the emperor. In return for the royal title he promised annual payments of four thousand silver marks and recognised imperial sovereignty over the island. In September he made a treaty with Genoa, granting market rights and pledging the port of Oristano and the castles of Arculentu and Marmilla as surety for a large sum.

Unable to raise that sum, he was kept in Genoa from early 1165, and on 12 April the emperor withdrew the grant and named the archdiocese of Pisa lord of the whole island. Barisone returned to Arborea in 1168 with the Genoese diplomat Nuvolone Alberici, while his wife and his brother-in-law Ponç de Bas went to Genoa as hostages until the debt was paid in 1171.

In 1180 Barisone attacked Cagliari again and was captured after early successes. In his last years he gave the church of San Nicolas di Gurgo to the Abbey of Montecassino in 1182 and founded a hospital and a monastery in Oristano. He died in 1186 and was succeeded by Peter I, his eldest son by his first wife.
barkur: Barkur, also spelt Barcoor, lies in the Brahmavara taluk and is made up of three villages, Hosala, Hanehalli and Kachoor. It stands on the bank of the Seetha River, which flows through it to the Arabian Sea, 16 km from Udupi and 3 km from Brahmavara. Because of its many shrines it is also called a temple town.

Known in early times as Barakanyapura and later as Barakkanur, Barkur was a capital of the Alupa kingdom, whose rulers spoke Tulu; many of the inscriptions found there are in that language and are an essential source for the history of Tulunadu. For a time it was also a subsidiary capital of the Hoysala kings, and it was a flourishing port in the 15th and 16th centuries. Archaeological finds suggest that it was a province of the Vijayanagara Empire in the 14th century, governed by Pandarideva under Harihara II. Remains of forts built by the Alupas and by the Vijayanagara governors survive.

Kerala Muslim tradition counts Barkur among the places with the oldest mosques of the Indian subcontinent. The Qissat Shakarwati Farmad lists its mosque with those of Kodungallur, Kollam, Madayi, Mangalore, Kasaragod and other coastal towns as built in the era of Malik Dinar.

The temples of Barkur have sloping terracotta-tiled roofs like those of Kerala but lack the gopurams of temples in the Dravidian style. The Panchalingeshwara Temple, dedicated to Shiva, is the largest and one of the oldest, with a double-storeyed gateway and carved pillars round its circumambulatory path. The Kathale Basadi, a ruined Jain complex that archaeologists date to between the 8th and 12th centuries, has a 20-feet monolithic pillar at its entrance and twenty-four hollows that once held images of the Jain thirthankaras. The Barkur fort, attributed to Harihara I, founder of the Vijayanagara Empire, covers 20 acres; part of it has been excavated and is now visited.
barmakids: The family is traceable to the hereditary administrators of the Buddhist monastery of Nava Vihara (Nawbahar), west of Balkh in northern Afghanistan, which the Chinese Buddhist Xuanzang described in the seventh century. The name Barmak has been derived from the Sanskrit pramukha, meaning leader or chief, though the exact role of the office is uncertain.

Some Islamic sources and later historians took the family for Zoroastrian priests, a view the evidence does not support, and Roxann Prazniak has suggested a possible Kashmiri descent. The family became Muslim after the Arab invasion of the Sasanian Empire, and the Buddhist ancestry of the Barmakids seems to have stimulated interest in Indian sciences in the eighth century.

Khalid al-Barmaki served the first Abbasid caliphs, al-Saffah and al-Mansur, as vizier and as head of the department of finance, the diwan al-Kharaj, which handled taxation and land tenure. Genuine budgets began to be drawn up under it for the first time. In 765 he received the governorship of Tabaristan, where he crushed an uprising, and he later brought Upper Mesopotamia to order and curbed the Kurds. He was also in charge of the building of Baghdad, which al-Mansur completed on 30 July 763.
His son Yahya ibn Khalid was entrusted by the caliph al-Mahdi with the education of the future Harun al-Rashid, and Yahya's sons al-Fadl and Jafar both held high office under Harun.

In 803 the family lost the caliph's favour and many of its members were imprisoned, a decision that surprised many. Jafar was beheaded. A popular story linked this to a secret marriage of Jafar and Harun's sister Abbasa, but the story is regarded as legend without basis. Al-Tabari and Ibn Khaldun instead give reasons that made the decline gradual: the family's extravagance, which overshadowed the caliph; the hostility of the official al-Fadl ibn al-Rabi; al-Fadl ibn Yahya's connivance in the escape of the rebel Yahya ibn Abdullah al-Talibi; and an army of 50,000 men controlled by al-Fadl ibn Yahya.

The Barmakids patronised scholars and physicians and had Sanskrit works on astronomy, medicine and mathematics translated into Arabic. They are credited with founding the first paper mill in Baghdad, and the first extant Arabic report on India was prepared under Yahya's direction. Jafar became known for eloquence and calligraphy, and Arab historians regard the family as founders of the class of people of the pen (ahl al-qalam). Canals, mosques and other public works owe their existence to them.

The vizier Jafar appears in stories of the One Thousand and One Nights, one of which gave rise to the expression Barmecide feast. The fall of the family did not end the prominent position of Persians at the Abbasid court. Baramkeh, a district of Damascus, is named after them.
barnim-i-duke-of-pomerania: Barnim was the son of Duke Bogislaw II and Miroslava of Pomerelia, of the Samborides dynasty. He succeeded to the Duchy of Pomerania-Stettin when his father died in 1220, but had to share the rule of Pomerania with his cousin Wartislaw III, who resided at Demmin. As he was a minor, his mother governed his lands as regent until about 1226. Pomerania was then still a Danish fief, and it fell back to the Holy Roman Empire after the victory of several North German princes at the Battle of Bornhöved in 1227.

In 1231 Emperor Frederick II placed the duchy under the suzerainty of the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg, disregarding the Griffin dynasty's tenure and opening a long conflict between Brandenburg and Pomerania. Wartislaw III accepted Brandenburg's overlordship by the Treaty of Kremmen in 1236. In the Treaty of Landin of 1250 Barnim declared himself a Brandenburg vassal and gave up the Uckermark, but won the agreement that his cousin's fief would stay with the Griffin dynasty when Wartislaw died, which allowed him to unite the whole duchy in 1264.

He promoted the Ostsiedlung, bringing German settlers and customs into the duchy, and founded many towns, among them Prenzlau, Szczecin, Gartz, Anklam, Stargard, Gryfino, Police, Pyrzyce, Ueckermünde and Goleniów. He made generous church foundations and supported the extension of the secular rule of the bishops of Cammin in the Kołobrzeg area.

Barnim married three times. His first wife, Marianna, whose origins modern historians consider unknown, bore him a daughter, Anastasia, who married Henry I the Pilgrim, Lord of Mecklenburg. His second wife, Margareta, probably a daughter of Nicholas I, Lord of Werle, was the mother of Bogislaw IV. His third wife, Matilda, a daughter of Otto III, Margrave of Brandenburg, bore him five children, among them Barnim II and Otto I, born after his father's death.

Barnim died on 13 November 1278 at the town of Dąbie, in German Altdamm, today part of Szczecin. Bogislaw IV, his co-ruler since 1276, then ruled as sole duke, sharing power with his younger half-brothers. The Minnesinger Meister Rumelant wrote a dirge in his honour.
barometer: On 27 July 1630 Giovanni Battista Baliani wrote to Galileo Galilei about a siphon led over a hill about 21 m high that failed to work: the water in the limb sank to about 10 m above the reservoir. Galileo answered that the power of a vacuum held the water up until its weight grew too great, a restatement of the old doctrine that nature abhors a vacuum. After his Discorsi reached Rome in December 1638, Gasparo Berti and Raffaello Magiotti sought a better way to produce a vacuum. W. E. Knowles Middleton places their experiment between 1639 and 1643, with Athanasius Kircher and Niccolò Zucchi present.

Torricelli, who had been Galileo's amanuensis in the last three months of his life, read the results differently. In a letter to Michelangelo Ricci in 1644 he argued that the weight of the atmosphere explained the resistance, and that it was foolish to attribute to a vacuum what followed from another evident cause.

Marin Mersenne was shown the experiment by Torricelli toward the end of 1644, and in 1646 Blaise Pascal and Pierre Petit repeated and perfected it. Pascal tested the Aristotelian claim that vapours from the liquid filled the space above it by comparing water with wine, thought more spiritous. He did so in public, inviting the Aristotelians to predict the result. They expected the wine to stand lower, and it did not.

Mercury barometers broke at sea, and in 1668 Robert Hooke's marine barometer, made by Henry Hunt, was presented to the Royal Society. The compact sympiesometer was widely used on ships in the early 19th century. Leibniz proposed an aneroid barometer around 1700, and Lucien Vidi invented a working one in 1844.

Pressure readings and the pressure tendency, the change over time, have been used in weather forecasting since the late 19th century. Combined with wind observations they allow reasonably accurate short-term forecasts, and readings from a network of stations produced maps of air pressure, the first form of the modern weather map. A rapid fall suggests an approaching low-pressure system and more chance of rain, while a rapid rise follows a cold front and goes with clearing skies. Readings are corrected for temperature, since the density of mercury changes, and reduced to sea level.
baroque: The word comes into English from French, and its roots are disputed. One line of explanation traces it to the Portuguese barroco, a flawed pearl; another to baroco, a term of medieval scholastic logic that by the 16th century had come to describe anything absurdly complex. The French philosopher Michel de Montaigne helped give it the sense of bizarre and uselessly complicated.

The style itself was shaped by the Catholic Church. The Council of Trent, meeting in 1545–1563, decided that the arts should reach a wide public and communicate religious themes with direct and emotional involvement, in response to the Protestant Reformation. The first Baroque façade in Rome was that of the Church of the Gesù in 1584, plain by later standards but a break with Renaissance façades. Lutheran Baroque art also developed, as a marker of confessional identity.

Baroque painters used intense, warm colours and strong contrasts of light and dark to direct attention to the central action. They chose moments of most intense movement and drama, and their figures show clear emotion. Allegory was essential: a picture carried a message in symbols that an educated viewer was expected to read. The dominant sculptor was Gian Lorenzo Bernini, who worked under Pope Urban VIII and made the Chair of St. Peter beneath the dome of St. Peter's Basilica.

Architecture varied by country. In Central Europe many ornate cathedrals, abbeys and pilgrimage churches were built between 1680 and 1750, and the princes of the German states chose Baroque for their palaces. French Baroque, associated with Louis XIV, is more restrained and has no broken pediments or curved façades. Louis XIV invited Bernini to design the east wing of the Louvre but chose a more classical design by Claude Perrault and Louis Le Vau. In Russia, Peter the Great's visit to western Europe in 1697–1698 preceded the Petrine Baroque of Saint Petersburg.

Beyond Europe, the style travelled with Spanish and Portuguese rule. In the Americas, European artists and missionaries were joined by Criollo and indigenous craftsmen, who gave it local features; the Cusco School of painting and the Quito School are examples. In Portuguese Goa, Baroque forms mixed with Hindu elements, and its churches and convents were declared a World Heritage Site in 1986.

By the 1730s the style had turned into the Rococo, which began in France as a reaction against the grandeur of Versailles. The Baroque itself was condemned by Johann Joachim Winckelmann, who praised classical art, and in the 19th century the British critic John Ruskin called its sculpture morally corrupt. Interest returned through Romanticism and later through Postmodernism, which promoted the inclusion of elements of historic styles in new designs.
barquq: Barquq was born around 1336 in Circassia to a Christian father. He was acquired as a slave, presumably after a battle, and sold to a bathhouse in Crimea. According to one account he tried to escape towards Constantinople and was attacked by Bulgarian bandits and sold to Egypt, while according to another he was brought directly from Crimea to Egypt. About 1363–64 he became a mamluk in the household of Yalbugha al-Umari.

In March 1381, when he held considerable influence under the sultan al-Mansur Ali, he brought his father to Egypt. The father converted to Islam, took the name Anas and was raised to emir of one hundred, the highest Mamluk military rank. He died ten months after arriving.

Since 1341 the Mamluk state had been ruled by descendants of al-Nasir Muhammad, none strong enough to rule effectively, and many of them minors who served as puppets of rival factions. After the sultan al-Ashraf Sha'ban was overthrown and killed in 1377, the rebels set his seven-year-old son on the throne, and then his younger brother al-Salih Hajji. Barquq belonged to the faction behind the throne, and in November 1382 he deposed al-Salih Hajji and took the sultanate, with the reign name al-Zahir.

In his first reign Barquq placed many family members in positions of power at the expense of other Mamluks. He built the Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Barquq in the centre of Cairo, completed in 1386 as both a khanqah and a madrasa, one of three dominant monuments on the street Bayn al-Qasrayn. He ended the public holiday for the Coptic New Year.

In 1389 two governors, Mintash of Malatya and Yalbogha al-Nasiri of Aleppo, rebelled, captured Barquq and sent him to the castle of al-Karak. They restored Hajji as al-Mansur, but fighting broke out among the factions in Cairo and Barquq's supporters prevailed. He returned to Cairo in February 1390.

In his second reign he replaced almost all governors and senior officials with members of his own household. After Timur invaded Baghdad in 1393 and intended to invade Syria, Barquq became his enemy and allied with the Ottoman Empire.

Barquq died in June 1399 and was succeeded by his son Nasir-ad-Din Faraj, who built a mausoleum for him in Cairo's Northern Cemetery. Despite its common name, the Mausoleum of Barquq at Bayn al-Qasrayn holds only his daughter's burial.
barsbay: Al-Ashraf Sayf ad-Din Barsbay was a Circassian by birth and a former slave of Barquq, the first Burji sultan. He was made governor of Tripoli on 2 May 1418 and later became tutor to Muhammad, the son of Sultan Tatar, who came to the throne at the age of ten. In the struggle among the emirs that followed, Barsbay became regent and the emir Taribay commander-in-chief. When the two fell out, Barsbay prevailed and imprisoned Taribay in Alexandria. With the support of the viceroy of Damascus, he deposed the young sultan on 1 April 1422.

Barsbay was the ninth Burji sultan, and his 16-year reign was long by Mamluk standards and saw few wars or revolts. He secured for Egypt exclusive rights over the Red Sea trade between Yemen and Europe, diverting the Indian Ocean routes through Jeddah, and introduced state monopolies on sugar and pepper; he also destroyed the declining port of Aydhab in 1426. To attract merchants he lowered customs duties, which angered some European powers and earned him the title of Merchant Sultan. Egypt suffered severe famine and plague in 1430. Contemporaries remembered him as greedy and bad-tempered but generous to the poor and to Sufis.

He kept good ties with Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah, the Sultan of Bengal, whom he sent investiture and a robe of honour. When the Bengali embassy's ship sank off Jeddah and only part of its gifts were recovered in 1436, Barsbay had its members arrested and banned them from Cairo.

The revenues of his conquests and trade policies may have paid for his buildings, of which three survive: a madrasa-mosque complex on al-Muizz street in Cairo of 1424, a mausoleum complex with a madrasa and khanqah in the Northern Cemetery of 1432, and a mosque at al-Khanqa, north of Cairo, of 1437. His wives included Khawand Jolban, his favourite, and Khawand Shahzada, a great-granddaughter of the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I, who after his death married Sultan Jaqmaq.
bartatua: The Akkadian name Partatua or Bartatua and the Greek Protothues come from a Scythian name meaning either with far-reaching strength or mighty in battle. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE the Scythians, pushed west by the Massagetae or the Issedones, drove the Cimmerians from the Caspian Steppe and moved south along the Caspian into the region of present-day Azerbaijan, which became their base in Western Asia until the early 6th century BCE, while their kings kept their headquarters in the steppes north of the Caucasus.

Bartatua succeeded Išpakaia, perhaps his father, after Išpakaia died in battle against Esarhaddon around 676 BCE. In the later mid-670s his Scythians, allied with Cimmerians on the Iranian plateau, threatened the Assyrian provinces of Parsumaš and Bīt Ḫamban and Assyria's links with its vassal Ḫubuškia. The Assyrians had opened talks with him at once, and in 672 BCE his request for a daughter of Esarhaddon was put to the oracle of the sun god Šamaš.

The texts do not record whether the marriage took place, but the close alliance that followed suggests it did. It would have been the first marriage of an Assyrian king's daughter to a nomadic lord, and it made Bartatua a vassal holding his lands as a fief of the Assyrian king. In 660 to 659 BCE, after the Mannaean king Aḫsēri was overthrown and killed, his son Ualli asked Assyria for help, which came through the Scythian king, and the Scythians then extended their hegemony over Mannai.

The alliance with the Assyrian dynasty and the nearness of Mannai and Urartu brought the Scythians under strong Assyrian cultural influence. Bartatua was succeeded by his son Madyes, under whom Scythian power in Western Asia reached its peak. Greek and Roman writers merged Bartatua, his predecessors and his successors into one king who drove out the Cimmerians, defeated the Medes and the Egyptian king Sesostris, a figure of legend, and ruled Asia for many years, later calling him Idanthyrsos or Tanausis. One theory identifies him with Paroyr Skayordi, an Armenian king of legend named in the history of Movses Khorenatsi.
barthelemy-boganda: Boganda was born around 1910 to a family of farmers in Bobangui, a large M'Baka village in the Lobaye basin, at the edge of the equatorial forest some 80 kilometres south-west of Bangui. His father, Swalakpé, was a village head and the wealthy owner of several palm plantations who had taken numerous wives; his mother, Siribé, was the third. French companies exploited the region through forced labour, and coercive labour practices, violence and disease had badly disrupted traditional society. After the death of his parents Boganda was adopted and educated by Roman Catholic missionaries, and in 1938 he was ordained a priest.

After the Second World War the Bishop of Bangui urged Boganda to enter politics. On 10 November 1946 he was elected deputy for Oubangui-Chari to the National Assembly of France, winning 10,846 votes, almost half of those cast, and became the first Oubanguian member. In Paris he spoke against racism and colonial abuses but found little support for his proposals. Returning to the territory, he launched a co-operative in 1948 and in 1949 founded the Movement for the Social Evolution of Black Africa (MESAN), which became popular among villagers and peasants. He was later laicized after marrying Michelle Jourdain, a parliamentary secretary.

He became the first Mayor of Bangui on 18 November 1956, and MESAN won every seat in the Territorial Assembly on 31 March 1957. Worried that a single small state would be weak, Boganda promoted a wider union of central African territories. On 1 December 1958 he declared the Central African Republic for Oubangui-Chari alone, and on 6 December he became president of its Council of Government. He designed its flag and wrote the words of its anthem, La Renaissance.

On 29 March 1959 Boganda boarded a Nord Noratlas plane at Berbérati for a flight to Bangui. The plane went missing and its wreckage was found the next day in the district of Boda; all nine people aboard had died. Experts found a trace of explosives in the wreckage, but a full report was never published and the possibility of an assassination remains unresolved. His funeral on 3 April was attended by thousands.
The Legislative Assembly declared him Father of the Nation in June 1959, and Boganda Day is observed each year on 29 March. His phrase zo kwe zo was placed in the state's coat of arms.
bartholomaus-ziegenbalg: Ziegenbalg was born in Pulsnitz, Saxony, into a devout family; his father was a grain merchant. He studied at the University of Halle under August Hermann Francke, then the centre of Pietist Lutheranism. Under Francke's influence King Frederick IV of Denmark chose Ziegenbalg and his fellow student Heinrich Plütschau for a mission to the Danish colony of Tranquebar, where they landed on 9 July 1706. The plan was for Ziegenbalg to learn Portuguese and Plütschau Tamil, but the roles changed, and Ziegenbalg set out to master Tamil without a grammar to help him.

Together the two founded the Danish-Halle Mission and baptised their first Indian converts on 12 May 1707. Their work met opposition from local Hindus and from the Danish authorities. After Ziegenbalg intervened for the widow of a Tamil barber in a debt case, the commander of the Danish fort, Hassius, had him arrested, and he spent a little more than four months in prison. His strained relations with Hassius were one reason for his return to Europe in 1714–1716, during which he married.

Ziegenbalg began translating the New Testament in 1708 and finished in 1711; his revisions and the need for a Tamil typeface delayed printing. In 1712 the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London sent the mission a press with type, paper, ink and a printer, making his work one of the first ecumenical ventures of Protestant missions. He went on to the Old Testament and had reached the Book of Ruth at his death. He listed the 161 Tamil books he had read in his Bibliothece Malabarke of 1708, and his press produced perhaps the first almanac printed in India.

Ill all his life, Ziegenbalg died at Tranquebar on 23 February 1719, aged thirty-six, and was buried in the New Jerusalem Church he had helped to found there in 1718. His writings on Hinduism and Tamil ethics were printed in Europe and Madras only 150 to 250 years later; Francke had told him the missionaries' duty was "to extirpate heathenism, and not to spread heathenish nonsense in Europe". Johann Phillip Fabricius later revised his Tamil New Testament, which soon fell out of use. The historian Stephen Neill judged him too ready to call on the civil power in Denmark.
bartle-frere: Frere was born on 29 March 1815 at Clydach House in Clydach, Monmouthshire, the son of Edward Frere, manager of Clydach Ironworks, and Mary Ann Green; John Hookham Frere was his uncle. Educated at the East India Company College, he joined the Bombay Presidency civil service as a writer in 1834. In 1842 he became private secretary to Sir George Arthur, Governor of Bombay, whose daughter Catherine Arthur he married on 10 October 1844.

As political resident at the court of Raja Shahaji of Satara, he administered the province after the raja's death in 1848, before and after its annexation in 1849. Made chief commissioner of Sindh in 1850, he reformed its postal system on the British model in 1851 and decreed that Sindhi replace Persian in government. In 1857, during the Indian Mutiny, he sent detachments to Multan and the Punjab, for which he received the thanks of Parliament and the KCB. As Governor of Bombay from 1862 he founded the Deccan College at Pune and had the ramparts of the old Bombay Fort pulled down so that the city could grow.

In 1877 Lord Carnarvon, the Secretary of State for the Colonies, made him High Commissioner for Southern Africa and governor of the Cape Colony to impose a confederation that the region's peoples and governments opposed. When a conflict broke out on the Cape frontier in 1877, Frere declared war on Gcalekaland, and in 1878, with the Colonial Office's authority, he dismissed the Cape's elected government of John Charles Molteno and asked John Gordon Sprigg to form a ministry.

To make confederation succeed he sought the annexation of Zululand, timing his letters around the slow mail to circumvent London's opposition, and in December 1878 sent King Cetshwayo an ultimatum he could not meet. After the disaster at Isandlwana he was censured but kept in office. His order disarming people of African descent led to the Basotho Gun War of 1880. Gladstone's government recalled him on 1 August 1880.

Frere was preparing a fuller defence of his conduct when he died at Wimbledon on 29 May 1884, and he was buried in St Paul's Cathedral. Frere Hall in Karachi was built in his honour, the Prince of Wales unveiled his statue on the Thames embankment in 1888, and Mount Bartle Frere in Queensland is named after him.
bartolome-de-las-casas: Bartolomé de las Casas was born in Seville on 11 November 1484. For centuries his birth was dated to 1474, until archival work in the 1970s uncovered records of a contemporary lawsuit showing that he was born a decade later. His father, Pedro de las Casas, was a merchant. He arrived in Hispaniola as one of the first Spanish settlers and took part in the colonial economy built on forced Indigenous labour. In 1513, as a chaplain, he joined the conquest of Cuba, where he witnessed many atrocities against the Ciboney and Guanahatabey. He later wrote that he saw cruelty on a scale no living being has ever seen.

In 1515 he gave up his Indigenous laborers and his encomienda and met King Ferdinand to argue against the encomienda system. He was given the title Protector of the Indians. In his early writings he advocated African slaves to replace Indigenous labour, a position he later retracted, writing that black slavery was as unjust as Indian slavery. His attempt at peaceful settlement in Venezuela failed, and in 1522 he entered the Dominican monastery of Santa Cruz in Santo Domingo, taking vows in 1523.

He worked as a missionary among the Maya of Guatemala and lobbied for the abolition of the encomienda, winning an important victory in the New Laws of 1542. He was consecrated Bishop of Chiapas on 30 March 1544. Conflicts with the encomenderos and colonists forced him back to Spain. In 1550 he took part in the Valladolid debate, in which Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that the Indians were less than human. De Las Casas maintained that they were fully human and that forcible subjugation was unjustifiable.

De Las Casas resigned his bishopric and spent the rest of his life at the imperial court, where he had great influence on matters concerning the Indies. He died on 18 July 1566. A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written in 1542 and published at Seville in 1552, was one of the first attempts by a colonial-era Spanish writer to describe the mistreatment of Indigenous peoples. His efforts improved the legal status of Indigenous people and sharpened the ethical debate over colonialism, though he did not change Spanish policy as a whole. After his death he was widely venerated, and a cause for beatification was opened.
bartolome-esteban-murillo: Murillo was probably born in December 1617 to Gaspar Esteban, a barber surgeon, and María Pérez Murillo, and was baptised in the parish of Santa María Magdalena in Seville on 1 January 1618. After his parents died in 1627 and 1628 he became the ward of his older sister Ana and her husband Juan Agustín Lagares, and he stayed in their house until his marriage in 1645.

He studied in Seville in the workshop of Juan del Castillo, his uncle and godfather. His first works were also influenced by Francisco de Zurbarán, Jusepe de Ribera and Alonso Cano. According to the painter and art historian Antonio Palomino he travelled to Madrid in 1642, but there is little evidence for this, and Palomino denied claims by Joachim von Sandrart that he went to Italy.

In 1645 Murillo married Beatriz Cabrera y Villalobos, with whom he had ten children. The year of his marriage he received his first major commission, eleven canvases for the convent of San Francisco in Seville, on which he worked until 1648. They show a range from the tenebrism of the Ecstasy of St Francis to the softly luminous style, seen in the Death of St Clare, that became typical of his mature work. Also about 1645 he painted The Young Beggar, now in the Louvre, the first of his many paintings of children, in which the influence of Velázquez is apparent.

After a pair of pictures for Seville Cathedral he specialised in the Virgin and Child and the Immaculate Conception. He was again in Madrid from 1658 to 1660. On returning to Seville he was one of the founders of the Academia de Bellas Artes, sharing its direction in 1660 with the architect Francisco Herrera the Younger. This was his period of most activity, and the paintings for Santa María la Blanca were completed in 1665.

Murillo died in Seville on 3 April 1682, a few months after he fell from a scaffold while working on a fresco at the church of the Capuchines in Cádiz. He had many pupils and followers, and the imitation of his paintings ensured his reputation in Spain and his fame throughout Europe. Before the 19th century his work was more widely known than that of any other Spanish artist, and Gainsborough and Greuze were among those influenced by his style. His paintings of flower girls, street urchins and beggars form an extensive record of the everyday life of his times.
bartolome-mitre: Bartolomé Mitre was born on 26 June 1821 in Buenos Aires. His father was of Greek descent, and the family name was originally Mitropoulos. In 1831 the family settled in Uruguay, and in 1839 he graduated from the Military School of Montevideo as a second lieutenant of artillery. He wrote for newspapers in support of Fructuoso Rivera and joined the Colorado Party against the Blancos, which led him to side with the unitario opponents of the Rosas regime. He then went to Bolivia and Chile, where he wrote for newspapers and met fellow exiles Juan Bautista Alberdi and Domingo Faustino Sarmiento.

Mitre returned to Argentina after Juan Manuel de Rosas was defeated at the Battle of Caseros in 1852. He helped lead the revolt of Buenos Aires Province against Justo José de Urquiza's federal system on 11 September 1852. His victory at the Battle of Pavón in 1861 won concessions, notably an amendment providing for indirect elections through an electoral college. The college elected him president, with Marcos Paz as vice president, and he took office on 12 October 1862.

He later founded the newspaper La Nación, in 1870. In 1874 he ran again for president against Nicolás Avellaneda, took up arms when the electoral college awarded him only three provinces, was defeated and was spared only by Avellaneda's commutation. After the Revolution of the Park in 1890 he co-founded the Civic Union with Leandro Alem; it split in 1891, Mitre founding the National Civic Union and Alem the Radical Civic Union.

The Supreme Court began to operate on 15 January 1863, and federal courts were organised in the provinces. National colleges were founded in the provinces and railways began with British capital. In the Paraguayan War Mitre was first named head of the allied forces. His government also fought the federal rebels of La Rioja, and Mitre wrote that he wanted a police war there, declaring the montoneros thieves so that prisoners could be executed. The caudillo Chacho Peñaloza surrendered on 12 November 1863 and was murdered by Pablo Irrazábal. Mitre also wrote poetry, plays and histories and translated Dante into Spanish. He died on 19 January 1906.
bartolomeo-colleoni: Bartolomeo Colleoni was born at Solza near Bergamo, then part of the Duchy of Milan. The Colleoni were a noble family who had been exiled with the rest of the Guelphs by the Visconti of Milan. His father Paolo Colleoni seized the castle of Trezzo but was assassinated by his cousins, probably on the orders of Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan. The young Colleoni trained as a soldier in the retinue of Filippo d'Arcello, the new master of Piacenza, and then served several condottieri, beginning with Braccio da Montone, who was fighting in Apulia. He took the side of Alfonso of Aragon and later that of Carmagnola.

After Carmagnola was put to death in Venice in 1432, Colleoni entered the direct service of the Republic of Venice, the major phase of his career. Gianfrancesco I Gonzaga, Marquess of Mantua, was nominally commander-in-chief, but Colleoni was the real leader of the army and recaptured many towns from the Milanese. When Gonzaga went over to the enemy Colleoni stayed with Venice under Gattamelata and Francesco I Sforza, winning battles at Brescia, Verona and on Lake Garda.

When Milan and Venice made peace in 1441 he joined Milan with Sforza in 1443, but the Visconti came to suspect him and imprisoned him at Monza until the duke died in 1447. He then served Sforza under the Golden Ambrosian Republic and defeated the French at the Battle of Bosco Marengo. He returned to Venice in 1448, left it in 1452 when he was not elected captain-general, and was lured back in 1453 with greater pay. In 1455 he was appointed captain-general of the republic for life. He was regarded as a foremost tactician and disciplinarian, and although he often changed sides no act of treachery is imputed to him.

Colleoni lived at the castle of Malpaga, which he bought in 1465 and restored, and devoted himself to agricultural improvements on the estates Venice had granted him and to charitable works. He died there in 1475, leaving a large sum to the republic for the Turkish war with a request that an equestrian statue of him be raised in the Piazza San Marco. Andrea del Verrocchio modelled it and Alessandro Leopardi cast it in bronze after his death. Since no monument was permitted in the piazza, it was set near the Scuola Grande of St Mark outside the Church of SS Giovanni e Paolo. In Bergamo he built himself the Cappella Colleoni, a mortuary chapel.
bartolomeu-dias: Dias came from a family with a maritime background. One of his ancestors, Dinis Dias e Fernandes, explored the African coast in the 1440s. Tracing his own biography is complicated by the existence of several Portuguese seafarers of the same name. In 1481 he accompanied an expedition led by Diogo de Azambuja to build the fortress and trading post of São Jorge da Mina in the Gulf of Guinea, and indirect evidence suggests he may have joined Diogo Cão's first expedition to the Congo River. On 10 October 1486 King John II of Portugal granted him an annuity of 6,000 reis for services to come.

Probably in July or August 1487 Dias left Lisbon with three ships, to continue the exploration advanced by Cão and to look for Prester John, a Christian ruler believed to reign somewhere beyond Europe. He carried stone pillars, padrões, to mark landfalls, and six Africans kidnapped by Cão and taught Portuguese, whom he meant to leave along the coast. On 8 December 1487 he reached modern Walvis Bay. The ships then turned southwest, away from land; historians debate whether a storm drove them or they sought better winds. After 30 days at sea, on 4 February 1488, they reached the southern cape of Africa at what became Mossel Bay.

They continued east until 12 March 1488, when they anchored at Kwaaihoek. The crew were restless and the ships battered, and the officers unanimously urged a return, which Dias accepted. In May 1488 he first saw the Cape of Good Hope; tradition says he named it the Cape of Storms and King John II renamed it. He reached Lisbon in December 1488 after 16 months. Almost all maritime records were destroyed in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, and much comes from João de Barros, writing about sixty years later. His reception at court was muted.

Dias contributed to the design and construction of the São Gabriel and São Rafael used by Vasco da Gama, and accompanied da Gama's fleet to the Cape Verde Islands in 1497. In 1500 he was a captain on Pedro Álvares Cabral's expedition, which reached Brazil on 22 April 1500. He died on 29 May 1500 when four ships, his among them, were lost in a storm off the Cape of Good Hope. His grandson Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Luanda in 1576.
bartoszyce: Bartoszyce lies on the left shore of the Łyna River in a valley, about 90 kilometres east of Elbląg and 55 kilometres south of Kaliningrad, at an altitude of 3 metres. It is the capital of Bartoszyce County and has 20,767 inhabitants. The Teutonic Knights built their castle on the border between the Old Prussian regions of Natangia and Bartia, and it belonged to the district of Balga.

The Old Prussians besieged the castle for four years during an uprising that began in 1260, and it was destroyed in 1264. The Order rebuilt it, and after the uprisings ended it was rebuilt in stone in 1274–80. A settlement developed across the river, first documented in 1326 as Rosenthal; it received town privileges from the Grand Master Luther von Braunschweig in 1332 and was renamed Bartenstein. Poles settled there in sizeable numbers from the 14th to the 17th century and used the names Bartoszyce and Barsztyn. In 1440 the town joined the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation, and by the Peace of Toruń of 1466 it became part of Poland as a fief held by the State of the Teutonic Order.

The town became Protestant in 1525, when the Order's Prussian lands were secularised as the Duchy of Prussia, and in 1701 it passed to the Kingdom of Prussia. Prussia and the Russian Empire signed the Treaty of Bartenstein there on 26 April 1807. A railway reached it in 1868 and brought an iron foundry, a machine factory and a train-car factory. It became the district capital in 1902, and the district was renamed Landkreis Bartenstein in 1927. About half the town was destroyed in fighting between German and Soviet forces in 1945, and on 15 June 1945 the Soviets handed it to Polish authorities. The remaining German residents were evacuated or expelled and the town was repopulated with Poles.

Bartoszyce belongs to the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship, which it joined in 1999 after lying in Olsztyn Voivodeship from 1946. It is a member of Cittaslow. The future priest Jerzy Popiełuszko did his military service in a special unit there in 1966–1968, and a memorial to him stands in the town. A scene of Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace is set there.
baruch-spinoza: Spinoza was born in Amsterdam on 24 November 1632 to a marrano family that had fled Portugal for the more tolerant Dutch Republic. His ancestors, adherents of crypto-Judaism, had faced persecution during the Portuguese Inquisition. His father, Michael, was a prominent merchant whose business had a wide reach and who was elected an administrative officer of the congregation Talmud Torah in 1649. Spinoza attended the congregation's school, where pupils were taught in Spanish to read the prayerbook and the Torah in Hebrew. His name does not appear on the school's registry after the age of fourteen, and he was needed in his father's business after his brother died in 1649.

Between 1654 and 1657 he began studying Latin with Franciscus van den Enden, a former Jesuit and political radical, who likely introduced him to scholastic and modern philosophy, including Descartes. Many of his friends were freethinkers or belonged to dissenting Christian groups such as the Collegiants. In 1654, when his father died, Spinoza became public and defiant in a series of financial and legal clashes with the synagogue, and the community, anxious for its reputation, expelled him permanently in 1656. He then supported himself by grinding lenses.

Around 1660 to 1661 Spinoza moved to Rijnsburg, near Leiden, where he wrote a Short Treatise on God, Man, and His Well-Being, which he never published, and began his Ethics. His Descartes' Principles of Philosophy, a geometric exposition in the manner of Euclid, appeared in 1663. He published sparingly in his lifetime to avoid persecution.

The Tractatus Theologico-Politicus, published in 1670, questioned the divine origin of the Hebrew Bible and argued that ecclesiastical authority should have no role in a secular, democratic state; it caused an uproar across Europe. The Ethics, which he regarded as his chief work, is written in a mathematical form modelled on Euclid. It equates God with nature, a view that scholars interpret as pantheist, panentheist or atheist. Spinoza denied that God has personality, intelligence or will, which is why he was often called an atheist. His unfinished Tractatus Politicus treats forms of government.

Spinoza's health failed in 1676, and he died at The Hague on 21 February 1677, aged 44, of a lung ailment, probably tuberculosis, perhaps worsened by glass dust. His friends published his works after his death. In 1785 Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi condemned his pantheism after Gotthold Ephraim Lessing was thought to have confessed to being a Spinozist, which then meant much the same as atheist, and Moses Mendelssohn disagreed with him. Later he came to be seen as a cultural hero and the first secular Jew. According to his biographer Jonathan I. Israel, thinkers from Lessing and Goethe to Kant, Hegel and Nietzsche remained preoccupied with him throughout their lives.
barwick-in-elmet: Barwick-in-Elmet lies 7 miles (11 km) east of Leeds city centre, in the civil parish of Barwick in Elmet and Scholes. Its name comes from the Old English bere, barley, and wīc, a settlement or specialised farm, so a barley farm or a grange producing barley for the lord. It is first recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Bereuuith; the form Berewyke in Elmet appears in 1329. Scholes-in-Elmet and Sherburn-in-Elmet keep the same suffix, which medieval records also give to Clifford, Micklefield and Saxton.

The earthworks of the Iron Age fort are centred on Wendel Hill near the village; the site later held a Norman motte-and-bailey castle and, much later, a Second World War observation post. Some scholars believe the capital of the kingdom of Elmet lay at or near Barwick. A taxation survey of 1379 counted 197 adults in about 100 households, and by 1821 the parish had 1,481 inhabitants.

The manor of Barwick and Scholes was for a time owned by the Gascoigne family of Parlington and Lotherton. The first known school opened in 1720, and Morwick Hall was built in the 18th century for Edward Gray, Lord Mayor of Leeds in 1749 and 1768. From the late 17th century to the early 20th, many villagers worked in the mines of Garforth, Cross Gates and Whitkirk, and the Cross Gates to Wetherby railway served nearby Scholes from 1874 until 1965.

The parish church, a grade II* listed building, keeps Anglo-Saxon and Norman stonework and a 14th-century chancel. A wooden maypole 86 feet (26 m) high, the tallest in the UK, stands at the junction of Main Street and the Cross and is lowered and raised again at a festival every three years. Arthur Wood named his 1924 maypole dance Barwick Green, later the theme tune of The Archers.
bas-rhin: Bas-Rhin, meaning Lower Rhine, is a department of Alsace in the Grand Est region of France. The name refers to its lower altitude, since it lies downstream of Haut-Rhin. The Rhine forms its eastern border, and the area includes foothills of the Vosges Mountains. To the north lies the Palatinate Forest in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate, and to the east the state of Baden-Württemberg. Strasbourg is its prefecture and most populous commune. With Haut-Rhin it formed the traditional region of Alsace, which until 1871 also included the area now called the Territoire de Belfort. It is the last French department to keep the term Bas in its name.

Bas-Rhin is one of the original 83 departments, created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution. On 14 January 1790 the National Constituent Assembly decreed that Alsace be divided into two departments with Strasbourg and Colmar as their capitals. Its borders then changed many times. In 1793 it absorbed newly annexed territories such as the County of Sarrewerden and the County of Drulingen. In 1808 some territories east of the Rhine, including the city of Kehl, were annexed, and in 1814 and 1815 the treaties of Paris first gave France the lands north of the Lauter, including Landau, and then took them away. Troops from Baden and Saxony occupied the department from June 1815 to November 1818.

In 1871 the Treaty of Frankfurt annexed it to Germany, and it became the Bezirk Unterelsass in the Reichsland Elsaß-Lothringen. It became French again in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles and kept the cantons of Schirmeck and Saales that Germany had taken from the Vosges. The Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp operated there between 1941 and 1944. Kehl was attached to Bas-Rhin in 1944 and reassigned to West Germany in 1953. In 1982 the department joined the newly created Alsace region.

Strasbourg is the official seat of the European Parliament and of the Council of Europe. The department had 1,163,810 inhabitants in 2023 and is densely populated, with more than twice the French average density. The Rhine has always been of great historical and economic importance to the area. On 1 January 2021 the departmental councils of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin merged into the European Collectivity of Alsace. Its inhabitants are known as Bas-Rhinois.
basarab-i: Many details of Basarab's life are uncertain. A charter of Charles I of Hungary of 1332 names his father as Thocomerius, whose social position cannot be determined. According to two popular theories Basarab either came to power between 1304 and 1324 by dethroning or peacefully succeeding Radu Negru, the traditional founder of Wallachia, or in 1310 by succeeding his father. His name is of Turkic origin and suggests Cuman or Pecheneg ancestry, though this has not been proven. Historians dispute whether he was Catholic or Eastern Orthodox: Neagu Djuvara argued from a papal letter of 1327 that he was Catholic, while Matei Cazacu and Dan Mureșan point to sources such as the Illuminated Chronicle, which called him a perfidious schismatic.

A royal charter of 26 July 1324 is the first document to mention him, describing him as voivode of Wallachia under Charles I of Hungary. A charter of 18 June 1325 calls him disloyal to the Holy Crown of Hungary. He seems to have controlled the Banate of Severin between 1324 and 1330. In 1330 he supported Michael Shishman of Bulgaria against Serbia, and their armies were routed at the Battle of Velbazhd on 28 July. Charles then invaded Wallachia and took Severin. According to the Illuminated Chronicle, Basarab offered 7,000 marks of silver and a yearly tribute, which Charles refused.

Hunger overtook the royal army on its march to Curtea de Argeș, and Charles agreed an armistice. On 9 November 1330, as the army withdrew, the Wallachians ambushed it in a narrow pass of the Southern Carpathians, shooting arrows and throwing rocks from the cliffs. The battle at Posada lasted until 12 November, the royal army was decimated, and Charles narrowly escaped. Basarab then moved his seat to Câmpulung and supported his son-in-law Ivan Alexander in seizing the Bulgarian crown in 1331. According to a charter of his grandson Vladislav I Vlaicu he died in 1351 or 1352.

Tudor Sălăgean writes that the victory at Posada sanctioned Wallachia's independence from the Hungarian crown, and Vlad Georgescu calls Wallachia the first independent Romanian principality. Basarab's descendants ruled it for at least two centuries and included Mircea the Old and Vlad Dracula. From the middle of the 14th century chroniclers used the name Basarab for Wallachia, and the southern part of the land between the Dniester and Prut came to be called Basarabia, later Bessarabia.
basava: Basava was born in the town of Basavana Bagewadi in the north of Karnataka, to Maadhavarasa and Madalambike, a Kannada Brahmin family devoted to Shiva. His name is the Kannada form of the Sanskrit Vrishabha, given in honour of Nandi, the bull who carries Shiva. He grew up at Kudalasangama, near the Krishna River and its tributary the Malaprabha, and spent twelve years studying at the temple of Sangameshwara, a Shaivite school of learning that was probably of the Lakulisha-Pashupata tradition. He married Nilambike, whose father was the provincial prime minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala, and began work as an accountant at the king's court.

As chief minister of the kingdom Basava used the state treasury to begin social reforms and a religious movement that aimed to revive Shaivism and to recognise and empower the ascetics called Jangamas. In the 12th century he founded the Anubhava Mantapa, a public assembly open to men and women from many walks of life, where spiritual, economic and social questions were discussed openly. He composed poetry in the local language and so spread his message to ordinary people. His verses, such as Kāyakavé Kailāsa ("Work is the path to Kailasa", that is, work is worship), became popular.

Basava taught that every person can reach salvation regardless of caste and that all manual labour is equally important. He rejected temple worship and rituals led by Brahmins in favour of personal devotion to Shiva, and he gave each follower an Ishtalinga, a necklace with a small linga, as a constant reminder of that devotion. His poems often contrast the static, represented by temples and ancient books, with the moving, represented by work and discussion. In one vachana, translated by A. K. Ramanujan, he says that "things standing shall fall, but the moving ever shall stay". He urged the use of Kannada in spiritual discussion so that no elite interpreter was needed.

Traditional legends and hagiographic texts name him the founder of the Lingayats. Modern scholarship, relying on evidence such as the Kalachuri inscriptions, holds instead that he revived and refined an existing tradition. The earliest account of his life is the Basavarajadevara Ragale by the Kannada poet Harihara, written around 1180. Palkuriki Somanatha's Telugu Basava Purana of the 13th century tells his life in full. Scholars note that the poems and legends were written down long after his death, and the vachana collections as they now exist are probably much later than the 15th century.
basavakalyan: Before 1956 the town was called Kalyani. After the states of India were reorganised on linguistic lines in that year, it was renamed Basavakalyan in memory of Basava, the social reformer. Over the centuries it was ruled by the Western Chalukyas, the Kalachuris of Kalyani, the Yadavas of Devagiri, the Kakatiyas, the Delhi Sultanate, the Bahamani, Bidar and Bijapur sultanates, the Mughals and the Nizams of Hyderabad.

Someshvara I moved the Western Chalukya capital to Kalyani from Manyakheta, now Malkhed in Kalaburagi district. The Kalyani Chalukyas, so named to distinguish them from the Chalukyas of Badami, ruled from the town until 1195. Their king Vikramaditya VI had scholars at his court, among them Bilhana, the poet from Kashmir, and Vigyaneshwara, a legal expert. The Kalyani style of temple architecture reached its maturity in the twelfth century, and nearly a hundred monuments of the period are scattered across the Deccan.
