The province has 29 municipalities and 5 cities, with its capital at Batangas City, and the 2024 census counted 2,994,795 people. Tagalogs are the predominant people, and the Batangas dialect of Tagalog resembles the Old Tagalog spoken before the Spanish arrived. Musicologists identify Batangas as the origin of the kumintang, an ancient war song that later evolved into the kundiman, the signature of Filipino love songs. The town of Taal keeps ancestral houses, churches and other buildings from the 19th century, and the province is known for the balisong, or butterfly knife.
batavian-republic: After the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, the Patriot party revolted against Stadtholder William V but was struck down in September 1787 when Frederick William II of Prussia intervened. Most Patriots went into exile in France, and the Dutch Republic became in effect an Anglo-Prussian protectorate, formalised by the Act of Guarantee in 1788. The French Revolution embraced many Patriot ideas, and the Patriots hoped to be treated as a sister republic rather than conquered territory. In the severe winter of 1794 and 1795 a French army under General Charles Pichegru, with a Dutch contingent under General Herman Willem Daendels, crossed the frozen rivers. Many cities rose before the French arrived, and William fled to England on 18 January 1795.

The republic was proclaimed on 19 January 1795. The harsh Treaty of The Hague of 16 May 1795 imposed territorial concessions, a large indemnity and a French army of occupation of 25,000 men, and it made the state a French client, the first of the sister republics. Even so, the programme of reform was driven mostly by Dutch needs. A National Assembly met at The Hague on 1 March 1796, divided between unitary democrats such as Pieter Vreede and federalists such as Rutger Jan Schimmelpenninck.

The constitution of 1798 was the first in Dutch history of a democratic character. France supported coups in turn: Daendels seized the Assembly on 12 June 1798 and arrested its members, and a coup in 1801 brought a new regime and a revised constitution.

From October 1801 the state was called the Batavian Commonwealth. Napoleon disliked the Dutch government, partly because Amsterdam bankers had refused him a large loan in 1800. After a clash over French customs men in November 1804 he settled on a new constitution, and Schimmelpenninck became Grand Pensionary. This regime also failed to satisfy him. The republic ended on 5 June 1806 with the accession of his brother, Louis Bonaparte, as king of Holland.

The Kingdom of Holland lasted four years: Louis refused to follow French dictates, abdicated on 2 July 1810 and the territory was incorporated into the French Empire. After the French defeat the independent Netherlands re-emerged in 1813, and William VI of Orange landed at Scheveningen on 30 November. The republic's reforms outlasted it. The confederal structure of the old Dutch Republic was replaced for good by a unitary state, a type of ministerial government appeared for the first time, and many present government departments date their history to this period. Its influence also eased the move to the more democratic constitutional revision of 1848 by Johan Rudolph Thorbecke.
bathsheba: Bathsheba is called the daughter of Eliam in 2 Samuel 11:3 and the daughter of Ammiel in 1 Chronicles 3:5, where she is named Bathshua. Because a man named Eliam is listed in 2 Samuel 23:34 as a son of Ahithophel, a counsellor of David, Jewish tradition and several scholars take her to be Ahithophel's granddaughter, though some doubt that Ahithophel was old enough. According to the Hebrew Bible she had five children with David, among them Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon.

The account in 2 Samuel 11 says David saw her bathing from the roof of his palace, learned that she was Uriah's wife, and slept with her. When Uriah, away on campaign, would not go home to his wife, David ordered his general Joab to place him on the front lines, and Uriah was killed during the siege of Rabbah. Bathsheba mourned him, and David then took her into his house.

David's act displeased God, who sent the prophet Nathan to reprove him with a parable of a rich man who took a poor man's lamb. David confessed, but the first child born to Bathsheba fell ill and died after seven days. She later bore Solomon. In David's old age she secured Solomon's succession to the throne in place of David's older surviving sons, on the strength of promises David had made to her. Nathan's prophecy was held to be fulfilled when Absalom rebelled and took ten of his father's concubines in public.

Scholars disagree on how to read her part. Some, among them David J. Zucker, see her as a victim of what he calls power rape, and Michael D. Coogan notes that the text faults David from its first verse; Kenneth E. Bailey argues instead that she displayed herself deliberately. The story affected how David's later decline was understood. In Christianity she appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:6 and in medieval typology is linked with the Virgin Mary, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church venerates her as a saint. Islam does not mention her in the Quran, and some tradition rejects the story as incompatible with the infallibility of prophets. Artists often showed her at her bath, as in Rembrandt's painting in the Louvre.
bato-the-daesitiate: Bato was probably born between 35 and 30 BCE in the lands around the upper Bosna river, the homeland of the Daesitiates. From 33 BCE his people lived under Roman rule as a semi-independent peregrine civitas within the province of Illyricum, whose capital was Salona on the Adriatic coast. He probably came from a distinguished native family and, as an adult, probably held political and military office among the Daesitiates. He is said to have wished to emulate the Illyrian king Bardylis.

In 6 CE Augustus planned a campaign against the Marcomanni in Magna Germania and ordered the mobilisation of Illyrian auxiliary forces. That spring the Illyrian forces in Bosnia rebelled under Bato, while in Pannonia the Breuci rose under another Bato. The two centres of resistance joined in the autumn of 6 CE, and the two leaders commanded an allied rebel army in the conflict the Romans called Bellum Batonianum, Bato's War.

Rome sent 10 legions and as many auxiliaries, allies and mercenaries under the future emperor Tiberius. Bato failed to take Salona and, defeated by Marcus Valerius Messalla Messallinus, governor of Illyricum, withdrew north to join the leader of the Breuci. In the summer of 8 CE Bato of the Breuci surrendered to Tiberius on the river Bathinus, probably the Bosna; soon afterwards Bato of the Daesitiates captured him, and his assembly had him put to death.

In 9 CE Tiberius and his nephew Germanicus moved against the Daesitiates. After hard fighting, Bato and his people surrendered in September, a few days before the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest. Asked why they had rebelled, Bato is reported to have answered that the Romans were to blame, for they sent as guardians of their flocks not dogs or shepherds but wolves. He spent the rest of his life at Ravenna.
baton-rouge: Baton Rouge stands on the eastern bank of the Mississippi River, in the Florida Parishes region of south-eastern Louisiana. Its historical importance rests on the Istrouma Bluff, the first natural bluff upriver from the Mississippi River Delta at the Gulf of Mexico. The bluff allowed a business quarter to develop safe from seasonal flooding, and a levee system was later built from it southward to protect the riverfront and the low-lying farmland.

Human habitation in the area has been dated to between 12000 and 6500 BCE, from evidence found along the Mississippi, Comite and Amite rivers. Hunter-gatherer societies built earthwork mounds from roughly the fourth millennium BCE. In 1698 the French explorer Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville led a party up the Mississippi and saw a red pole marking the boundary between the hunting grounds of the Houma and the Bayagoula. The French name le bâton rouge, 'the red stick', translates a native term rendered as Istrouma, possibly a corruption of the Choctaw iti humma, 'red pole'.

Baton Rouge was incorporated in 1817, and the Pentagon Barracks were completed in 1822. The site had been used by Spanish, French and British authorities, was part of the short-lived Republic of West Florida, and was later occupied by both the Confederate States Army and the United States Army. The city has therefore been ruled by six different nations: the French, Spanish and British in the colonial era, the Republic of West Florida, the United States, the Confederate States of America, and the United States again after the American Civil War. The state of Louisiana took ownership of the barracks in 1951, and the complex was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1976.

Baton Rouge is the capital of Louisiana and the seat of East Baton Rouge Parish, with which its government has been consolidated since 1947. It had 227,470 inhabitants at the 2020 census, and its metropolitan area had 870,569. It is the home of Louisiana State University, the state's largest university, and of Southern University, the flagship of the only historically black university system in the United States. Its port is the farthest upstream on the Mississippi that can handle Panamax ships, and the city is a centre of the petrochemical industry.
battambang: Battambang lies on the Sangkae River, which winds through the province of the same name. The province is considered the rice bowl of Cambodia, and the city has many mills that process rice for national and international markets; its jasmine rice is well known. The river long served as the main link to Phnom Penh and Saigon, and the city is also joined to Phnom Penh and Bangkok by National Highway 5.

Battambang began as a fishing village on the Sangkae River in the 11th century, founded under the Khmer Empire. In 1795 Siam annexed much of north-western Cambodia as the province of Inner Cambodia and ruled Battambang as a provincial capital through the Abhaiwongse family. By 1880 it was an important trading city of about 2,500 residents. The Siamese built one road, a fort for the governor, a market, several pagodas and a Catholic hospital.

In 1907 the province was ceded to France and rejoined Cambodia within French Indochina. The French laid out a grid of streets, canals and bridges in what is now the Heritage Conservation Area, linked both riverbanks by two bridges in 1917 and in 1926 began a second phase of building, with a railway to Phnom Penh, villas, the central market and state buildings.

In 1953 Prince Norodom Sihanouk chose Battambang as the centre of Cambodia's independence movement. It was Cambodia's second largest city in the 20th century, with garment factories, an airport, schools and a university. Under Democratic Kampuchea its population was forcibly evacuated into labour camps and land tenure was abolished; the Battambang Provincial Museum became a prison, and the Phnom Sampeau killing caves, a Khmer Rouge execution site, lie about six kilometres from the city. A Vietnamese invasion toppled the Khmer Rouge in 1980, but the province remained a Khmer Rouge stronghold into the 1990s. Guerrillas besieged the city in 1990 without taking it, and conflict around it continued until 1997.

Battambang is the capital of its province and one of Cambodia's larger cities. The municipality established a Heritage Protection Area in 2009 to safeguard around 800 historic buildings, among them French colonial architecture and the Art Deco central market, Psar Nath, built in 1936. Wat Damrei Sar, built in the 19th century, is the oldest pagoda in the city. UNESCO named it a City of Gastronomy in 2023, the first Cambodian city in its Creative Cities Network.
battenberg-family: The House of Battenberg was a non-dynastic cadet branch of the House of Hesse-Darmstadt, which ruled the Grand Duchy of Hesse until 1918. Its first member was Countess Julia von Hauke, the orphaned daughter of Count Moritz von Hauke, a Polish nobleman who had served as a general in the Imperial Russian Army. She married Prince Alexander of Hesse, the third son of Grand Duke Louis II, in a morganatic marriage. Her rank was too low for their children to qualify for the succession, so Grand Duke Louis III created the title of Countess of Battenberg for her and her descendants in 1851.

The name refers to the town of Battenberg in Hesse, and a previous family of counts of that name had become extinct in the 14th century. In 1858 the title was raised to princely status, with the style of Serene Highness. There was never a principality of Battenberg, and the family had no right of succession to the Grand Duchy.

The couple's eldest son, Prince Louis of Battenberg, became First Sea Lord of the Royal Navy. Prince Alexander of Battenberg was elected ruling Prince of Bulgaria in 1879 and was forced to abdicate in 1886. Prince Henry of Battenberg married Princess Beatrice, the youngest daughter of Queen Victoria, and their daughter Victoria Eugenie became queen consort of Spain after Edward VII raised her style to Royal Highness. Prince Francis Joseph married Princess Anna of Montenegro in 1897.

Louis's daughter Alice married Prince Andrew of Greece and Denmark, and their son, Prince Philip, took the surname Mountbatten and married the future Elizabeth II. Louis's daughter Louise married the future Gustaf VI Adolf of Sweden in 1923.

In 1917, with anti-German feeling rising in Britain during the First World War, most of the family, then living in the British Empire, renounced their Hessian titles and changed the name to Mountbatten, an anglicised version of Battenberg. Prince Louis became the first Marquess of Milford Haven and Prince Alexander, Henry's eldest son, Marquess of Carisbrooke, both peerages granted by their cousin George V. Louis's younger son, Louis Mountbatten, became Earl Mountbatten of Burma and the last Viceroy of India. Juan, Count of Barcelona, son of Victoria Eugenie, bore the surname Borbón y Battenberg until his death in 1993, and Prince Francis Joseph, who died childless in 1924, was the last born member to keep the name.
battering-ram: A battering ram is a siege engine designed to break open the masonry walls of fortifications or to splinter their wooden gates. In its simplest form it is a large, heavy log carried by several people and driven against an obstacle. Later rams enclosed the log in an arrow-proof, fire-resistant canopy mounted on wheels, with the log swung inside from chains or ropes. Many canopies had curved or slanted wooden roofs covered in fresh wet hides, which reduced the risk of fire and protected the crew from arrows and javelins.

Rams worked because stone and brick were weak in tension and cracked under force. With repeated blows the cracks grew until a breach opened. A capped ram had an iron or steel head, sometimes shaped like the head and horns of a sheep, which did more damage but weighed more to carry.

The earliest depiction of a possible ram is in the tomb of Khety, a noble of the 11th Dynasty of Egypt, where two soldiers advance on a fortress under a mobile roofed shelter, carrying a long pole. In the Iron Age in the ancient Middle East and the Mediterranean the log was slung from a wheeled frame. An Assyrian image of the 9th century BCE shows defenders trying to burn a ram with torches and to trap it with a chain, while the wet hides on the canopy protect it from the flames.

The first confirmed use in the Occident was in 503 to 502 BCE, when the Roman consul Opiter Verginius attacked Pometia, according to Livy. The Spartans used rams at the siege of Plataea in 427 BCE, and rams with siege towers appeared in Sicily at the siege of Selinus in 409 BCE.

Defenders answered rams by dropping obstacles such as a sack of sawdust in front of the head, by catching the log with grappling hooks, by setting the ram on fire, or by making a sudden sally. Some rams ran on rollers instead of hanging, so that they gained more speed, and Vitruvius describes one used by Alexander the Great.

Rams influenced the design of defensive walls, and they were used in sieges of major cities, among them the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, the Crusades, the Sack of Rome in 410 and the sieges of Constantinople. The siege cannons of the later Middle Ages ended their use. A story that the rhyme about Humpty Dumpty concerns a ram at the siege of Gloucester in 1643 is almost certainly untrue, and began in a spoof essay of 1956.
battiad-dynasty: Battus I, the founder of Cyrene, reigned until about 600 BCE and was followed by his son Arcesilaus I, who ruled until about 583 BCE. The next king, Battus II, known as the Blessed, reigned until about 560 BCE. The later kings were Arcesilaus II the Cruel, Battus III the Lame, Arcesilaus III, who ruled from about 530 to 515 BCE, Battus IV, whose reign of about 515 to 465 BCE was the longest, and Arcesilaus IV, the last of the line, from about 465 to 440 BCE.

The reign of Arcesilaus II, about 560 to 550 BCE, was marked by quarrels within the family. Four of his younger brothers, Perseus, Zacynthius, Aristomedon and Lycus, rebelled against him and left Cyrene to found Barke in about 560 BCE. A fifth, Learchus, stayed behind, murdered the king and ruled as regent, until he was killed in turn by the king's widow Eryxo with the help of her brother Polyarchus. Eryxo and Polyarchus were the children of Critola, a sister of Battus II. Plutarch, however, describes Learchus only as a friend of Arcesilaus II.

The kingship passed from father to son at first: Arcesilaus I was the son of Battus I, Battus II of Arcesilaus I and Arcesilaus II of Battus II. Under Battus III, about 550 to 530 BCE, the reformer Demonax of Mantinea transferred most of the royal prerogatives to the citizens. Battus III's wife Pheretima was the mother of Arcesilaus III and of Ladice, who married Amasis II. The poet Callimachus was counted among the descendants of Battus, and his style was a chief inspiration for the Latin poets known as the Neoteroi.
batticaloa: Batticaloa lies on the flat coastal plain of eastern Sri Lanka, 111 kilometres south of Trincomalee, at an average elevation of about 5 metres. Its old town stands on the island of Puliyanthivu in the Batticaloa Lagoon, the largest of the district's three lagoons, which is 56 kilometres long and covers 162 square kilometres. Bridges link the island with the mainland, the largest being the Lady Manning bridge at Kallady. The climate is tropical monsoon, with heavy rains from November to February and an average annual rainfall of about 1,650 millimetres. The lagoon is known as the land of the singing fish, after musical sounds heard there. The name is a Portuguese form of the Tamil Matakkalappu, interpreted as Muddy Swamp or Flat Lagoon.

The Tamil chronicle Mattakallappu Manmiyam tells that the Mukkuvas, a coastal community with roots in the Tamil country, were the first to migrate to the area and built seven villages. Mukkuvas also served Sinhalese kings as a mercenary force. Hindu temples to Kannaki Amman across the Eastern Province are traditionally linked to the king Gajabahu I, who is said to have brought settlers and her worship from the Chera kingdom.

Portuguese power reached the coast in the early 17th century. The Dutch admiral Joris van Spilbergen anchored at Batticaloa on 31 May 1602, and found the local chief willing to trade in pepper and cinnamon. He was then taken to the court of King Rajasinghe at Kandy, who welcomed the chance to be rid of the Portuguese. The Portuguese fortified Batticaloa in the 1620s, the fort being built in 1628, and the Dutch captured it on 18 May 1638, the first of the Portuguese forts to fall to them. It stands on Puliyanthivu and is regarded as one of the most picturesque of the small Dutch forts of Sri Lanka. The first Catholic church in Batticaloa was established in 1624.

In 1814 the Wesleyan Methodist William Ault founded Methodist Central College, the town's first educational institution. In 1942 the aircraft carrier HMS Hermes and the destroyer HMAS Vampire were sunk by Japanese aircraft off Batticaloa. The tsunami of 26 December 2004 hit the town severely, with water rising 4.7 metres within 90 minutes.

Batticaloa is the administrative capital of the Batticaloa District and a commercial centre of the Eastern Province. Its people are mainly Sri Lankan Tamils, with Moors, Sinhalese, Burghers and the indigenous Vedda. The town has long been a centre of Portuguese Burgher culture, and Hinduism is its major religion, with Muslim and Christian communities beside it.
battle-cry-of-freedom: The song opens with the call to rally round the flag, and each verse ends with the line that gives it its title. Its chorus begins "The Union forever, hurrah! boys, hurrah!" and goes on to "Down with the traitors, up with the stars". One verse promises that "although he may be poor, he shall never be a slave". A longer Union version printed in Hoge's The Boys in Blue of 1867 adds verses about marching to the field and meeting the Rebel host.

The historian Christian L. McWhirter argued that the song succeeded because its definition of the Northern cause was open-ended: those who wanted anti-slavery sentiment could find it, yet it was not pronounced enough to offend those who were solely unionists. Freedom, he noted, had many meanings in the war, but in the light of Root's own beliefs the word suggested some degree of abolitionism.

The song spread quickly through the Union camps. Henry Stone, a veteran writing in 1887, recalled a glee club from Chicago bringing it to his camp, where "it ran through the camp like wildfire" and "put as much spirit and cheer into the army as a victory". It was so popular that the composer H. L. Schreiner and the lyricist W. H. Barnes adapted it for the Confederacy, with the chorus "Our Dixie forever!" and the line "Down with the eagle and up with the cross". A modified Union version served as the campaign song of the Lincoln-Johnson ticket in the presidential election of 1864, and the song was used again in later elections, among them Garfield's in 1880.

Louis Moreau Gottschalk wrote in his diary that he thought "it should be our national anthem", and in 1863 he based his concert paraphrase for solo piano, Le Cri de délivrance, opus 55, on it, dedicating the work to Root, a personal friend. Charles Ives quoted it in several compositions, among them his song They Are There. It is performed in Ken Burns' documentary The Civil War and in John Williams's score for the 2012 film Lincoln, and Billy Bragg set new words to it in There Is Power in a Union.
battle-hymn-of-the-republic: The song is an American patriotic hymn by the abolitionist writer Julia Ward Howe, adapted from the soldiers' song John Brown's Body. That song was played at a flag-raising at Fort Warren, near Boston, on 12 May 1861, a month after the Civil War began. George Kimball later wrote that the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the Massachusetts militia worked out its words together, partly in jest at a Scottish soldier in the battalion named John Brown. Howe heard the song at a public review of troops at Munson's Hill, Virginia, near Washington, and her companion, the Reverend James Freeman Clarke, suggested she write new words for it. She wrote the verses at the Willard Hotel in Washington.

Howe's own account says she woke in the grey light of morning, found a stub of pencil and scrawled the verses almost without looking at the paper. She sold them for 4 dollars to The Atlantic Monthly, which printed them on its front page in February 1862.

Unlike the soldiers' song, her version links the Union cause with God's vengeance at the Day of Judgment, through allusions to Isaiah 63:1-6 and to Revelation 14 and 19. The published text ends with the lines in which Christ, who died to make men holy, is the model for dying to make men free. Her sixth verse, less often sung, was not published at the time. Her husband, Samuel Gridley Howe, was a member of the Secret Six, who funded John Brown's work.

The hymn became a frequent American patriotic song. Marian Anderson sang it before a television audience of 60 million in 1953, and the Mormon Tabernacle Choir's recording won a Grammy Award in 1960. Martin Luther King Jr. drew on its words in his speech of 25 March 1965 at the Alabama State Capitol and ended his last sermon, on 3 April 1968, with its first line. John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath took its title from the first verse, as did several other books.

The tune has been reused widely. The Marching Song of the First Arkansas, a Civil War song, kept its structure, and the University of Georgia's rally song of 1909 is set to it. Football supporters adopted the Glory, glory, hallelujah refrain, beginning with Tottenham Hotspur supporters in September 1961, and later Hibernian, Leeds United and Manchester United.
battle-of-abydos: After the Athenian victory at Cynossema, the Athenian fleet set up a base at Sestos, from which it could answer any move by the Spartan fleet at Abydos. The Spartan navarch Mindarus, hoping to end the war with a decisive victory, summoned the Rhodian commander Dorieus with his 14 ships. Spotted by Athenian lookouts before he reached Abydos, Dorieus was driven ashore: at Rhoeteum according to Xenophon, at Dardanus according to Diodorus Siculus, while Donald Kagan suggests he was trapped at both in turn.

Mindarus hurried from Troy, where he had been sacrificing to Athena, and led his ships out to rescue Dorieus, while the Persian Pharnabazus brought his army up to support Dorieus from the land. Seeing the Spartan ships put out from Abydos, the Athenians set out from Sestos to challenge them.

With Dorieus's ships, Mindarus had 97 ships against 74 Athenian. The Spartans formed up with the Asian shore of the Hellespont at their backs, Mindarus on the right and the Syracusans on the left; opposite them Thrasybulus led the Athenian right and Thrasyllus the left. Trumpeters relayed the signal to begin, and an evenly matched fight followed, pilots trying to ram and disable enemy triremes while marines fought whenever ships came within range.

Neither side gained the advantage until, as the day wore on, Alcibiades appeared with 18 triremes from Samos. Both fleets at first thought the ships might be theirs, until Alcibiades ran up a red flag, the agreed signal to the Athenians. The Spartan fleet fled towards Abydos and suffered heavy losses as the Athenians attacked its strung-out ships. In all the Athenians captured 30 Spartan ships and recovered the 15 of their own lost at Cynossema.

Mindarus returned to Abydos to repair his fleet and sent to Sparta for reinforcements, planning new campaigns with Pharnabazus. The Athenians could not press their advantage: with their treasury low and Euboea in revolt, they sent 30 ships under Theramenes, who failed to stop the rebels building a causeway to Boeotia but raised much money by plunder. Soon afterwards the satrap Tissaphernes arrested Alcibiades, who had sailed to meet him with gifts, and imprisoned him at Sardis; he escaped within a month, but his claims of influence with the satrap were destroyed.
battle-of-actium: The Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus was renewed in 37 BCE but broke down. Antony left his wife Octavia Minor, Octavian's sister, and settled in Egypt with Cleopatra VII. In 34 BCE he and Cleopatra raised her son Caesarion, said to be Julius Caesar's, to power as King of Kings, which was seen as a threat to Roman republican tradition. Octavian, whom Caesar had adopted, began a propaganda war, claiming that Antony meant to set up a monarchy and move the capital to Alexandria.

In 32 BCE both consuls and a third of the Senate sided with Antony and left Rome. Antony divorced Octavia and went to Ephesus with Cleopatra, where a vast fleet gathered. The publication of Antony's will provoked an outburst of feeling in Rome, and Antony was deprived of the consulship. The Senate declared war on Cleopatra, which was understood to mean Antony, and left him without legal authority.

Antony's fleet lay in the Ambracian Gulf and his army camped near Actium. In 31 BCE Octavian's general Marcus Agrippa raided the Greek coasts and cut Antony's communications with Egypt. Disease and desertion afflicted Antony's camp, and malaria left many ships short of rowers. One of his generals, Quintus Dellius, defected with his battle plans. His heavy ships were hard to board but less manoeuvrable than Octavian's smaller Liburnian vessels.

On 2 September the fleets met outside the gulf. Octavian refused to be drawn out, and the battle raged through the afternoon without result. Cleopatra's squadron then retreated without fighting, and Antony, believing all was lost, followed her in a smaller vessel. The ships left behind fought on until after nightfall, and were captured or sunk. J. M. Carter gives a different account, in which Antony deliberately broke through a gap in Octavian's line.

Some 19 legions and 12,000 cavalry left Antony in the night, and his camp was occupied the next day. Antony was defeated at Alexandria in 30 BCE and stabbed himself on false news that Cleopatra was dead; she killed herself on 12 August. Octavian had Caesarion killed, and Egypt became a Roman province, ending the Ptolemaic Kingdom. He took the title Princeps, and in 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus. Historians generally regard this as the end of the Roman Republic. He founded the city of Nicopolis, meaning City of Victory, opposite Actium.
battle-of-ad-decimum: The Vandal Kingdom under King Hilderic kept close ties with Emperor Justinian I. Hilderic ceased the persecutions and allowed a new Chalcedonian bishop to take office at Carthage, rejecting the Arian Christianity that most Vandals followed, to the alarm of the Vandal nobility. In 531 his cousin Gelimer, a military commander who had campaigned against the Moors, overthrew him. Justinian refused Gelimer's gifts and rejected his legitimacy. Revolts in Tripolitania and Sardinia, both of which appealed to Justinian, weakened the kingdom further, and Gelimer sent his brother Tzazon with 5,000 Vandals on 150 ships to Sardinia.

In June 533 Justinian sent Belisarius with 5,000 cavalry, 10,000 infantry, 600 Huns and 400 Heruls, carried on 500 transports escorted by ninety-two dromons. The army landed at Caputvada and marched toward Carthage. On 13 September Gelimer planned an ambush at the narrows of Ad Decimum. His brother Ammatas was to block the path, his nephew Gibamundus was sent with 2,000 men to reinforce him, and Gelimer would attack the Byzantines from the rear.

The plan unravelled. Ammatas arrived about half a day early with a few men, met the scouts of John the Armenian and was killed after killing twelve Byzantines, and his death set off a Vandal rout. In a second encounter Hun mercenaries routed Vandals at the Salt Marsh. Gelimer later drove back the Byzantine foederati cavalry, but found the body of Ammatas and stopped to mourn instead of pressing his advantage. Belisarius rallied his cavalry and counter-attacked, found the Vandals in disorder and pursued them until nightfall.

The army reached Carthage the next evening, and Belisarius camped outside, fearing an ambush and wishing to prevent looting. The following day he entered the city in battle formation, found no resistance and occupied the palace. His soldiers kept discipline, though sailors under Calonymus looted merchants' property. He repaired the neglected walls and restored Orthodox control of churches held by Arian clergy. The loss of Carthage deprived the Vandals of their main harbour and most of their fleet. In December 533 Belisarius defeated them again at Tricamarum, which ended the Vandal Kingdom.
battle-of-adrianople: In 376 the Goths, led by Alavivus and Fritigern, asked to settle in the Eastern Roman Empire after the Huns displaced them. The emperor Valens admitted them as allies, hoping for farmers and soldiers, but the dishonesty of the Roman commanders Lupicinus and Maximus led them to revolt. In 378 Valens took command himself and moved to Adrianople. A letter from the western emperor Gratian and his own officers advised him to wait for reinforcements, but he decided to fight. On 8 August Fritigern offered peace and an alliance in return for Roman territory, and Valens rejected it, having failed to count a part of the Gothic cavalry that was away foraging.

On 9 August 378 Valens left Adrianople and reached the Gothic camp around noon after marching eight miles over difficult terrain, with tired and dehydrated troops. The Goths held a wagon circle on a hill and delayed the Romans with talks about hostages until their cavalry returned. Some Roman units attacked without orders and were pushed back. Then the Gothic cavalry under Alatheus and Saphrax arrived and surrounded the Romans, who broke. The killing went on until nightfall. Valens was abandoned by his guards and his body was never found. One story says he died when Goths set fire to a cottage where he hid.

A third of the Roman army escaped. Many officers, including Sebastianus, were killed in the worst Roman defeat since the Battle of Edessa, and the eastern army's core was destroyed. Valens' successor Theodosius I accepted the Goths again as allies, and they were never expelled or assimilated but remained a distinct entity within the frontiers. The battle is often considered the start of the events that led to the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century. Charles Oman held in 1885 that it showed cavalry triumphing over infantry, which T. S. Burns later disputed.
battle-of-adwa: In 1889 Italy signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Menelik of Shewa, after occupying Eritrea. The treaty recognised Italy's claim to the coastal colony and promised financial help and military supplies. A dispute arose over its two versions. In the Italian text, Article 17 obliged the Emperor of Ethiopia to conduct all foreign affairs through Italian authorities, making Ethiopia a protectorate. The Amharic text said only that he could use Italy's good offices if he wished. Italian diplomats claimed that Menelik had knowingly signed a modified copy. Italy tried to force its reading on Ethiopia, and Menelik mobilised a large army, estimated at between 73,000 and over 100,000 men, mostly with modern rifles imported from France and Russia.

The Italian army under General Oreste Baratieri, of between 14,519 and 17,770 men by modern estimates, was unfamiliar with the terrain and had poor reconnaissance. Under pressure from Rome to act decisively, Baratieri ordered a surprise attack on the Ethiopian camp near Adwa. At about 9 p.m. the night before the battle, his brigades under Generals Matteo Albertone, Giuseppe Arimondi and Vittorio Dabormida marched towards the Ethiopian positions in three columns, with Giuseppe Ellena's brigade following in reserve. The fighting took place on 1 March 1896.

Albertone's vanguard was charged around 6 a.m. by Ethiopian units, and his brigade was routed, with two mountain batteries captured. Dabormida, trying to help, moved into the valley of Mariam Shewito, away from the rest of the army, and a gap of about two miles opened. Ras Makonnen pushed into it and cut Dabormida off. The Ethiopians then attacked Arimondi's centre, and a column of 25,000 men outflanked its right. The columns were isolated from one another, and the Italian positions were overwhelmed by sustained, numerically superior assaults.

Estimates of Italian dead run from about 5,900 to 6,133, and between 3,800 and 4,000 men were taken prisoner. Ethiopian losses are put at between 3,886 and 7,000 killed and 6,000 to 10,000 wounded. The Italians abandoned all their artillery and 11,000 rifles. Menelik did not pursue them into Eritrea. His army was short of rations, the rains were near, and he feared that Italy would send a larger force. He asked little beyond the abrogation of the Treaty of Wuchale, since his crucial aim was to preserve independence.

Italy recognised Ethiopian sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa, and the government of Francesco Crispi fell. Adwa became a rallying point for later African nationalists and the Pan-African movement, and it left Ethiopia with a unique position in Africa. Some historians trace part of the roots of Italian Fascism to the wish to avenge the defeat, and in May 1936, when Italian troops occupied Addis Ababa, Mussolini declared Adua è vendicata, Adwa has been avenged.
battle-of-aegospotami: In 405 BCE, after the Spartan defeat at the Battle of Arginusae, Lysander, who had won the first Spartan naval successes, was reinstated in command. Because Spartan law barred a commander from being navarch twice, he was appointed vice-admiral. His close relationship with the Persian prince Cyrus let him raise money to rebuild the fleet, and Cyrus gave him the revenues of his cities in Asia Minor. Lysander seized Athenian-held cities, drew the Athenian fleet away by raiding Aegina and Salamis and landing in Attica, then sailed to the Hellespont, set up a base at Abydos and took Lampsacus. Control of the strait would let him cut the trade routes that brought Athens most of its grain.

An Athenian fleet of 180 ships followed him and based itself at Sestos, but camped on a beach much nearer Lampsacus that had no harbour. Each day it sailed out in battle formation and waited outside the harbour, and returned when Lysander would not come out. The exiled Alcibiades advised the generals to move to Sestos and offered them an army from Thracian kings in return for a share of the command, but they refused.

Two accounts of the battle survive. In Diodorus Siculus, the general Philocles sailed out with thirty ships and the rest were caught unprepared on the beach. In Xenophon, the whole fleet came out as usual, and when the sailors scattered to find food after returning, Lysander's fleet crossed from Abydos and captured most of the ships on the beach without fighting at sea. Only nine ships escaped, led by the general Conon, and Lysander took nearly all the rest with some three or four thousand sailors. Some historians suspect treachery, but this remains speculation.

Citing an earlier Athenian atrocity, Lysander and his allies killed Philocles and 3,000 Athenian prisoners. His fleet then moved towards Athens, capturing cities on the way. Without a fleet to import grain from the Black Sea, and with the Spartans holding Deceleia and cutting off land transport, Athens began to starve and surrendered in March 404 BCE. Its walls were demolished and a pro-Spartan oligarchy, the Thirty Tyrants, was established. The victory ended 27 years of war and left Sparta dominant in the Greek world. At Delphi the Spartans dedicated statues of the trierarchs who had fought.
battle-of-agincourt: Henry V of England claimed the title of King of France through his great-grandfather Edward III, although English kings had in practice been prepared to renounce the claim if the French acknowledged English rights in Aquitaine and other lands. After a Great Council in the spring of 1414 the lords insisted that Henry negotiate further.

He offered to give up the claim if the French paid the 1.6 million crowns outstanding from the ransom of John II and conceded Anjou, Brittany, Flanders, Normandy, Touraine and Aquitaine, with a marriage to Charles VI's daughter Catherine and a dowry of 2 million crowns. When negotiations failed, the English resumed the war in 1415. Disease killed many soldiers during the Siege of Harfleur, and the weakened army tried to withdraw to Calais, where its path was blocked by a considerably larger French army.

On 25 October 1415 Henry drew up his army, about 1,500 men-at-arms and 7,000 longbowmen by one reckoning, across a narrow strip of open land between woods. The archers drove pointed stakes into the ground to turn aside cavalry. The French, under Constable Charles I d'Albret, had about 10,000 men-at-arms and several thousand other troops, since King Charles VI, who suffered from mental illness, did not command. For three hours after sunrise neither side attacked, the French expecting reinforcements.

The French cavalry then charged, but could not outflank the archers because of the woods or break through the stakes. Wounded horses panicked and trampled their own infantry, and the charge churned up recently ploughed ground. The men-at-arms who followed walked several hundred yards through thick mud in armour weighing 50 to 60 pounds, with visors lowered, and were so closely packed that those in the third rank could scarcely use their swords.  The French also attacked the English baggage train, and the sources disagree on whether this came at the start or the end. Fearing that the French were regrouping, Henry had French prisoners killed.

Around 6,000 French fighting men were killed, among them the constable, three dukes (Alençon, Bar and Brabant), nine counts and the Archbishop of Sens. Entire noble families were wiped out in the male line. The victory boosted English morale and began a period of English dominance in the war that lasted until the Siege of Orléans in 1429.

Historians disagree about the numbers. Most contemporary accounts have the English outnumbered several times over, while Anne Curry argued from administrative records for about 12,000 French and 9,000 English. Juliet Barker, Jonathan Sumption and Clifford J. Rogers criticised her reliance on those records. The exact location of the field is also debated. The battle is the setting of Act IV of William Shakespeare's Henry V, written in 1599.
battle-of-agnadello: On 15 April 1509 a French army under King Louis XII left Milan and invaded Venetian territory. Venice had gathered a mercenary army near Bergamo under the joint command of the Orsini cousins Bartolomeo d'Alviano and Niccolò di Pitigliano, with orders to avoid a direct confrontation, and for several weeks the two sides only skirmished. By 9 May Louis had crossed the Adda at Cassano d'Adda. The two commanders, camped around Treviglio, disagreed: Alviano wanted to attack in defiance of his orders. In the end they decided to move south towards the Po in search of better positions.

On 14 May, as the Venetian army marched south, Alviano's rearguard under Piero del Monte and Saccoccio da Spoleto was attacked near the village of Agnadello by a French detachment under Charles II d'Amboise. Alviano hurried back from Pandino and placed his force of around eight thousand men on a ridge above some vineyards. French cavalry and Swiss pikemen could not break the line, having to climb a slope cut by irrigation ditches filled with mud from the pouring rain.

Pitigliano, several miles ahead, answered Alviano's call for help with a note advising against a pitched battle and marched on. Louis then arrived with the rest of the army, and the French, now 30,000 strong, surrounded Alviano on three sides. Over three hours they destroyed his force. A Venetian cavalry charge against the French centre was outnumbered and surrounded, and when Alviano was wounded and captured his formation collapsed. More than four thousand Venetians were killed, among them Spoleto and del Monte, and 30 guns were taken.

News of the defeat reached Pitigliano that evening, and by morning most of his troops had deserted. He fell back towards Treviso and Venice while Louis occupied the rest of Lombardy. Niccolò Machiavelli wrote in The Prince that in one day the Venetians "lost what it had taken them eight hundred years' exertion to conquer". The economic historian Niall Ferguson links the defeat to the fall of Venice's monte nuovo bonds from 102 to 40 percent of their face value.
battle-of-ain-jalut: Möngke Khan, Great Khan from 1251, set out to carry out Genghis Khan's plan for a world empire and chose his brother Hulegu to subdue the west. The invasions began in 1256. Hulegu's forces sacked Baghdad in 1258, destroying the Abbasid Caliphate, and the Ayyubid dynasty in Damascus fell as well.

In 1260 Hulegu sent envoys to Qutuz in Cairo demanding surrender. Qutuz killed them and displayed their heads on the gate of Bab Zuweila. Möngke Khan had died fighting the Southern Song, and Hulegu withdrew with most of his army, leaving about one tumen, nominally 10,000 men, under the Naiman Nestorian Christian general Kitbuqa.

Qutuz left Cairo on 26 July 1260, and Baybars, at the head of the vanguard, took Gaza. The Franks of Acre stayed neutral, let the army pass and supplied it. Kitbuqa, with perhaps 10,000 to 12,000 men including Georgian and Armenian contingents, took a stand at the spring of Ain Jalut at the foot of Mount Gilboa in the Jezreel Valley.

On 3 September 1260 Qutuz hid most of his force in the highlands while Baybars harried the Mongols with hit-and-run attacks. Baybars then feigned a retreat, and Kitbuqa followed him into an ambush. Timothy May suggests that the defection of the Mongols' Syrian allies was a key moment. When the Mamluk left wing nearly broke, Qutuz threw off his helmet and rallied his men. The Mongols fled, rallied, and were driven back, and Kitbuqa died.

The Mamluks took Damascus five days later and Aleppo within a month. On the way back to Cairo, Qutuz was assassinated in a conspiracy led by Baybars, who became sultan. Berke Khan of the Golden Horde, a Muslim, was hostile to Hulegu, and Hulegu suffered a severe defeat north of the Caucasus in 1263, the first open war among the Mongols. Baybars and his successors captured the last Crusader states by 1291. The battle is often described as the first time the Mongols were permanently halted.
battle-of-al-qadisiyyah: The Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 left the Sasanian Empire exhausted. Khosrow II was overthrown and executed by his son Kavadh II, who died of plague within months, and a civil war followed in which several rulers briefly held the throne. Yazdegerd III eventually came to power. Meanwhile, after Muhammad's death Abu Bakr launched campaigns against Syria and Palestine, and Khalid ibn al-Walid won a series of victories in Iraq in 633. When Khalid left for Syria, Iraq remained unstable and was held by Persians and Muslims in turn. Yazdegerd then sought an alliance with the Byzantine emperor Heraclius in 635 and ordered a concentration of armies to reclaim Iraq.

Caliph Umar raised a new army and appointed Sa'd ibn Abī Waqqās to command it. Sa'd camped at al-Qadisiyyah, where talks with the Persians went on for three months and an embassy to Yazdegerd III failed. Modern estimates put each side at about 30,000 men, though most scholars think the Sasanians and their allies outnumbered the Muslims considerably. Fighting began on 16 November with duels between champions, and the Sasanian commander Rustam Farrokhzad then attacked with arrows and elephants. On the second day reinforcements from Syria arrived, and Al-Qaqa ibn Amr al-Tamimi sent them in small groups to suggest a larger force.

On the third day the elephants again led the Persian attack and the Muslims fell back. On the last day Qa'qa and his men pushed towards the Sasanian headquarters, and Rustam was found dead in a sandstorm; accounts of his death differ. The Persians, demoralised, gave way.

The victors took large spoils, including the jewelled royal standard, the Darafsh-i Kāwiyān, which was cut up and sold in Medina. The Arab fighters became known as Ahl al-Qādisiyyah and held the highest prestige among later Arab settlers in Iraq and in Kufa. Umar ordered Sa'd to push on, and Ctesiphon fell in March 637 after a siege of two months. The Muslims then took Persian provinces as far as Khuzistan, and the Sasanian Empire was annexed by 651. In 2024 researchers from Durham University and the University of al-Qadisiyyah identified the likely site of the battle as an open field about 19 kilometres south of Kufa.
battle-of-alarcos: In 1190 the Almohad caliph al-Mansur crossed from North Africa to al-Andalus to invade Portugal, which had captured Silves the year before. After a campaign of about 15 months he recaptured the city in July 1191 and returned to his capital. An armistice followed between the Almohads and the Christian kings of Castile and Leon. When it expired in 1194, Alfonso VIII of Castile invaded the south of al-Andalus, having learned that al-Mansur was gravely ill and that his brother Abu Yahya, the governor of al-Andalus, had gone to Marrakesh to claim the throne. Al-Mansur recovered, reasserted control and landed at Tarifa on 1 June 1195.

Al-Mansur reached Cordoba on 30 June, reinforced by local troops and by a Christian cavalry contingent under Pedro Fernandez de Castro, who had a personal feud with Alfonso. His army destroyed a Christian cavalry detachment on the way north. Alfonso gathered his forces at Toledo and marched to Alarcos, near the Guadiana, where a fortress was being built, without waiting for reinforcements from Alfonso IX of Leon and Sancho VII of Navarre. On 18 July the Almohad army formed up around the hill called La Cabeza, with the vizier Abu Yahya ibn Abi Hafs commanding the vanguard and al-Mansur the rearguard.

Alfonso ordered a charge by about 8,000 heavy cavalry under Diego Lopez de Haro. The knights at first drove back the Almohad front lines and killed the vizier, but after three hours of fighting the Arab left under Yarmun ibn Riyah enveloped their flank and rear, and al-Mansur's rearguard surrounded them. Alfonso fought hand to hand until his bodyguard removed him almost by force and led him to Toledo. Lopez de Haro took refuge in the unfinished fortress and later negotiated a surrender, leaving 12 knights as hostages for a ransom. Three bishops and the masters of the Order of Santiago and of the Portuguese Order of St Benedict were among the dead.

The defeat shook Castile for several years: Malagon, Benavente, Calatrava, Caracuel and Torre de Guadalferza surrendered or were abandoned, leaving the way to Toledo open. Al-Mansur took the title al-Mansur Billah, and for two years his forces devastated Extremadura, the Tagus valley and La Mancha, though without territorial gains. He won an alliance with Alfonso IX of Leon and the neutrality of Navarre, both temporary. He returned to Africa in 1198 and died in February 1199. In 1212 his successor Muhammad al-Nasir was defeated at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, a turning point toward the end of Moorish rule in the peninsula.
battle-of-albulena: Skanderbeg had fought the Ottoman Empire since 1444, and after more than a decade of war his resources were worn out. His siege of Berat in 1455 ended in catastrophe when an Ottoman counterattack fell on the Albanians during his temporary absence. Afterwards some of his most trusted officers deserted. Moisi Golemi returned in May 1456 at the head of an Ottoman force, was defeated at the Battle of Oranik and was taken back without punishment.

A graver loss was his nephew Hamza Kastrioti, one of his most important officers, who had grown dissatisfied with Skanderbeg's increasing power and was promised control of much of Albania once it was conquered. Relations with Venice were at their lowest point. Alfonso V of Aragon and Pope Calixtus III, his allies, could not provide for him fully, and a fleet the pope promised in 1457 did not arrive.

By the end of May 1457 an Ottoman army of between 50,000 and 80,000 men approached, against which Skanderbeg had between 8,000 and 10,000. He stalled the akıncı vanguard marching through Dibër, then withdrew before the main force. Since both Ottoman commanders knew his usual ambushes, he split his army into several groups and ordered them to march through the forests and mountains in different directions, supplied by the local people and by depots, and not to assemble or attack without his word.

The Ottomans pillaged the Mat valley and camped at Albulena, north of Mount Tumenishta and south of modern Laç. Through July and August Skanderbeg stayed out of sight, and rumours spread that he had fled. On 2 September his reassembled army attacked the camp in three groups with a great noise of clashing metal. The Ottomans, believing the attackers more numerous than they were, panicked. Their dead may have been as many as 30,000, though it is unlikely that more than 15,000 were killed; 15,000 were taken prisoner and twenty-four standards were captured.

Hamza Kastrioti was captured and sent as a prisoner to Naples. An Ottoman envoy came to ransom the standard bearers and forty distinguished prisoners and proposed a truce, which Skanderbeg would accept only if Svetigrad and Berat were restored to him. In 1460 Sultan Mehmed II and Skanderbeg signed an armistice that lasted three years, giving Skanderbeg the opportunity to cross to Italy and help Ferdinand I of Naples. The historian Franz Babinger called the battle Skanderbeg's most brilliant victory. Desertions from his army became rare afterwards, but the war continued until the fall of Krujë in 1478.
battle-of-alcacer-quibir: Sebastian became king of Portugal at the age of three, on the death of his grandfather John III in 1557. The Portuguese Cortes asked him several times to act against the Ottoman military presence in Morocco, which threatened Portuguese coasts and trade. In 1574 he led a successful raid beyond Tangier. That year the Saadi sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib died, and two years later his son Muhammad II al-Mutawakkil was overthrown by his uncle Abd al-Malik, backed by Ottoman troops. Al-Mutawakkil went to Portugal and asked Sebastian to help him recover his throne.

Against the advice of his mother and of his uncle Philip II of Spain, Sebastian gathered a fleet and an army of about 23,000 men, including Castilian volunteers, mercenaries from Flanders and Germany and Italians. He sailed from Lagos on 24 June 1578 and landed at Arzila, where al-Mutawakkil joined him with about 6,000 troops. Abd al-Malik, gravely ill, called on his countrymen to wage jihad, and the armies camped on opposite sides of the Loukkos River near Ksar-el-Kebir.

On 4 August 1578 the Moroccans advanced on a broad front, with 10,000 cavalry on the wings, to encircle the Christians. Thomas Stukley, commanding the Portuguese centre, was killed early by a cannonball. After nearly four hours the Portuguese and their allies were defeated: about 8,000 died and 15,000 were captured and sold into slavery. Sebastian charged into the enemy and was cut off, and his body was never found. Abd al-Malik died during the battle, of unknown causes by one account and poisoned by another, and al-Mutawakkil drowned while fleeing.

Three rulers died, so in Morocco the battle is called the Battle of the Three Kings. Abd al-Malik was succeeded by his brother Ahmad al-Mansur, who later conquered Timbuktu, Gao and Jenne. In Portugal the ransom of the captured nobles nearly bankrupted the kingdom. Sebastian, aged 24, left no heir, and his elderly uncle Cardinal Henry reigned from 1578 to 1580, mostly raising the ransoms. Philip II of Spain then invaded and defeated Anthony, Prior of Crato, at the Battle of Alcântara. Portugal stayed a separate realm under the Spanish Habsburgs until 1640. The trauma gave rise to Sebastianism, a belief that the lost king would return to save his nation.
battle-of-alcoraz: In 1094 Sancho Ramírez, King of Aragon and Pamplona, laid siege to the strategic Muslim city of Huesca, directing it from camps at the Castle of Montearagón and at Pueyo de Sancho, a temporary fortress on San Jorge hill 3 km west of the city. In June 1094 he was struck and killed by an arrow while inspecting the ramparts around Huesca, and his son and heir Peter I took command and kept up the siege for nearly two and a half years.

In November 1096 a relief army under Al-Musta'in II, ruler of the Taifa of Zaragoza, marched on Huesca to break the siege. It was supported by Castilian forces under Counts García Ordóñez de Nájera and Gonzalo Núñez de Lara, who represented King Alfonso VI. On 15 November 1096 the two armies met on the fields of Alcoraz, between the walls of Huesca and the Castle of Montearagón, and Peter I's army defeated the relief force. Less than two weeks later Huesca surrendered.

Later legends held that Saint George appeared above the Aragonese crown during the battle to inspire a Christian army heavily outnumbered. The story parallels that of the Battle of Clavijo, more than two hundred years earlier, at which Saint James was said to have appeared before the forces of the Kingdom of Asturias. The heraldic shield known as the Cross of Alcoraz, made to commemorate the victory, was later adopted as the personal arms of King Peter III of Aragon and then placed in the flag of the Kingdom of Aragon, where it remains.
battle-of-alesia: In 58 BCE Julius Caesar, after his consulship of 59 BCE, was appointed proconsul of Cisalpine Gaul, Illyricum and Gallia Narbonensis for an unprecedented five years, with four legions. In the Gallic Wars of 58 to 50 BCE he conquered Gaul beyond Narbonensis. In 53 BCE he announced that Gaul would be treated as a Roman province under Roman law and religion. The Gauls feared for the holy land watched over by the Carnutes, and the threat finally united them. Over the winter Vercingetorix, king of the Arverni, assembled an unprecedented coalition.

Vercingetorix avoided open battle and raided Roman foragers, hoping to starve the legions. Caesar took Avaricum by assault, but at Gergovia, the capital of the Arverni, the Romans suffered a clear defeat. After Caesar defeated Vercingetorix's cavalry at the Battle of the Vingeanne, Vercingetorix withdrew towards Alesia.

Alesia was a fortified settlement of the Mandubii on a lofty hill with two rivers on different sides. After Gergovia a direct assault was no longer attractive, so Caesar chose to starve the defenders. Vercingetorix sent out his cavalry to call a relief army. Within about a month the Romans built roughly 25 miles of works in two lines, one facing the town and one facing outward, with trenches, a moat, towers and hidden pits. Excavation suggests the lines were not continuous, as Caesar claims, but made use of the terrain.

The Gauls expelled their old, sick, women and children, but Caesar refused to admit them and they were left between the lines. The relief force arrived and attacked the outer works while the besieged attacked the inner ones, without success. Then 60,000 men under Vercassivellaunus struck a weak point on a hill the Romans could not enclose. Caesar sent reinforcements under Labienus and joined the fight himself, while cavalry took the Gauls in the rear. The relief army fled. The next day Vercingetorix proposed to the council that he be killed or surrendered, and he was handed over.

Alesia ended organised Gallic resistance, though southwest Gaul was not yet pacified, and the Gallic territories north of Gallia Narbonensis did not become a Roman province until 27 BCE. The Senate granted Caesar 20 days of thanksgiving but, for political reasons, refused him a triumph. Two years later, in 49 BCE, he crossed the Rubicon. Vercingetorix was held in Rome for five years, paraded in Caesar's triumph and ritually garrotted in 46 BCE.

The size of the armies is uncertain, since the only records are Roman. Caesar speaks of a relief force of a quarter of a million, probably an exaggeration, and modern historians usually think between fifty and a hundred thousand more credible. The site is most probably Mont Auxois above Alise-Sainte-Reine; Napoleon III funded excavations there in the 1860s.
battle-of-aliwal: The war began six years after the death of Ranjit Singh, founder of the Sikh Empire, when the Sikh Khalsa Army crossed the Sutlej into British territory. After the costly Battle of Ferozeshah on 21 and 22 December 1845 both sides paused. The Sikhs then held a bridgehead at Sobraon, while Ranjodh Singh Majithia crossed higher up the river with 7,000 men and 20 guns to besiege Ludhiana and threaten the supply lines of Sir Hugh Gough and Sir Henry Hardinge, who sent a division under Smith against him.

On 16 January 1846 Smith recovered the outposts of Fategarh and Dharmkot. Marching to reach Ludhiana before the Sikh main body, he left Buddowal on 21 January under constant attack from the Sikh irregular cavalry, who took most of his baggage animals and cut down stragglers. He reached Ludhiana with his men exhausted and was reinforced by a brigade from Delhi that included two Gurkha battalions.

The Sikhs had fallen back to a ridge 4 miles long between the villages of Aliwal and Bhundri, with the Sutlej close behind them along the whole line. Smith had about 10,000 men and 28 guns. Judging Aliwal the weak point, he sent two of his four infantry brigades to take the village, from which they could fire along the Sikh centre and threaten the fords.

As the Sikhs swung back their left, a cavalry brigade led by the 16th Lancers dispersed Sikh horsemen and then broke a square of infantry trained in the European manner by the Neapolitan mercenary Paolo Di Avitabile, with heavy losses on both sides. The Sikh centre was driven from a dry stream bed and cut down by the Bengal Horse Artillery. Unusually for the Anglo-Sikh Wars, the retreat became a rout across the fords.

The Sikhs lost 2,000 men and 67 guns, abandoning nearly all their artillery with their baggage, tents and supplies. British casualties numbered 589, of whom 151 were killed; the 16th Lancers alone lost 144 of about 300 men. Smith called it one of the most glorious battles ever fought in India, and many commentators named it the battle without a mistake. The victory is sometimes regarded as the turning point of the First Anglo-Sikh War.
battle-of-aljubarrota: King Ferdinand I of Portugal died in October 1383 with no son. His daughter Beatrice was to marry Juan I of Castile under the Treaty of Salvaterra de Magos, which left the Portuguese nobility and the merchants of Lisbon discontented. Portugal had no king from 1383 to 1385, in a period known as the 1383–85 Crisis. John, Grand Master of the Military Order of Aviz, was named defender of the realm, and the Cortes acclaimed him king at Coimbra on 6 April 1385.

In April 1384 Nuno Álvares Pereira had defeated a Castilian force at Atoleiros with a defensive infantry square. In May 1385 Juan I invaded with 31,000 men. English mercenaries, about 200 longbowmen and some 500 men-at-arms, had arrived from Gascony at Easter.

Álvares Pereira chose a small hill at São Jorge between creeks, and the Portuguese took position there on 14 August 1385. When the Castilians moved to attack the gentler southern slope, the Portuguese turned their line round and dug ditches, pits and caltrops. The army stood with dismounted men-at-arms in the centre and archers on the flanks, among them the young nobles of the Lovers' Flank.

French heavy cavalry in Castilian service charged first, uphill under arrows and bolts, and was destroyed. Froissart reports that the Portuguese council then decided to kill their prisoners. The main Castilian body was crowded between the creeks and shot at from behind the Portuguese line. About sunset the Castilian standard-bearer fell, and Juan's army fled.

As many as 5,000 more Castilians were killed by local people during the night and next day. Tradition tells of Brites de Almeida, the baker of Aljubarrota, who killed seven soldiers hiding in her bakery, though the story is clouded in legend. John of Portugal offered the survivors amnesty and free passage home. Castile decreed mourning until Christmas 1387. Álvares Pereira beat another Castilian army at Valverde in October 1385, and border skirmishes lasted until the death of Juan I of Castile in 1390.
battle-of-almansa: The Battle of Almansa was fought between an army loyal to Philip V of Spain, the Bourbon claimant, and one supporting his Habsburg rival, Archduke Charles of Austria. Campaigning in Spain was limited by logistics: armies relied on local forage in arid country, and control of the sea let the Allies mount short offensives on the coast but, lacking popular support, they could not hold territory. Britain captured Gibraltar in 1704, and the Pact of Genoa of 1705 between English and Catalan representatives opened a second front. Allied forces took Barcelona and Valencia, and in 1706 briefly Madrid, but could not be resupplied and withdrew. By November 1706 Philip held Castile, Murcia and parts of Valencia.

For 1707 James FitzJames, Duke of Berwick, an illegitimate son of James II of England, commanded the Bourbon forces in the north-east, about 33,000 men split equally between French and Spanish troops with exiled Irish regiments. The Allied army was led by Henri de Massue, Earl of Galway, an exiled French Huguenot, so that it was said to be probably the only battle in which a Frenchman commanded the English forces and an Englishman the French. Berwick detached 8,000 men to besiege Xativa. The Earl of Peterborough kept his forces in Catalonia, leaving Galway and the Marquess of Minas with 16,500 men, outnumbered.

On 25 April the Allies reached Almansa after a long march. Berwick had formed two lines before the town, infantry in the centre and cavalry on the wings. Galway attacked in mid-afternoon and drove back the Bourbon centre, but a gap opened between his infantry and the Portuguese on the right. The Franco-Spanish cavalry charged and the Portuguese fled. Thirteen Allied battalions lost contact with the army, retreated some 12 km and surrendered the next morning. Estimates of the losses vary widely: Henry Kamen gives 4,000 Allied killed or wounded and 3,000 captured, and around 5,000 Franco-Spanish casualties, while Joaquim Albareda gives about 1,500 Bourbon losses and 7,000 Allied.

Almansa has been described as the single most important battle fought in Spain during the war. It confirmed Philip's control of the north-east and Valencia, and by the end of 1707 the Allies were again confined to Catalonia and the Balearic Islands. Xativa surrendered in June, much of it was destroyed and its name was changed to San Felipe; a portrait of the monarch still hangs upside down in the local museum. The defeat gave rise to two proverbs, De ponent, ni vent ni gent (From the west, neither wind nor people) and Quan el mal ve d'Almansa, a tots alcanca (Bad news from Almansa reaches everybody). Frederick the Great later called it the most impressive battle of the century.
battle-of-anegawa: The battle grew out of Oda Nobunaga's moves against the castles of Odani and Yokoyama. As the Oda and Tokugawa allies marched on Odani, Azai Nagamasa called for help from Echizen, and Asakura Yoshikage sent an army. The combined Azai and Asakura force came out to meet Nobunaga in the field, and he screened the Azai fort he had been reducing from Yokoyama and advanced to the southern bank of the Anegawa. The Oda and Azai later called the fight the Battle of Nomura, the Asakura the Battle of Mitamura. It was the first battle fought by the alliance of Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

On the morning of 30 July 1570 the Oda met the Azai on the right while the Tokugawa faced the Asakura on the left, and the fighting became a melee in the shallow river. Nobunaga gave Hashiba Hideyoshi his first command in open battle. Accounts tell that Honda Tadakatsu charged the advancing Asakura alone, drawing Ieyasu forward to save him, and that Tokugawa troops under Tadakatsu and Sakakibara Yasumasa turned the Asakura's left flank.

Once the Asakura gave way, the Tokugawa units wheeled to strike the Azai's right flank, while the reserve of the Mino Triumvirate under Inaba Ittetsu hit their left. The Azai and Asakura lines broke. Nobunaga is often said to have used 500 arquebusiers in the battle.

No reliable source allows the battle to be reconstructed. The only valuable one, the Shinchōkō-ki, describes it briefly and counts 1,100 Asakura samurai killed, while much in the books of the later Edo period is fiction. A study of 1901 put the losses at about 1,700 on the Azai and Asakura side and 800 on the Oda and Tokugawa side. In October 1570 Asakura Kagetake struck back at the Battle of Shimosakamoto, killing over 750 Oda soldiers, among them Mori Yoshinari and Nobunaga's brother Oda Nobuharu. A memorial marker stands in Nomura-cho, Nagahama.
battle-of-angamos: After Peru lost the armoured frigate Independencia at Punta Gruesa in May 1879, Rear Admiral Miguel Grau Seminario avoided the larger Chilean fleet and turned to raiding. Aboard the monitor Huáscar he sank or captured 14 transports, one of them carrying a whole cavalry regiment. The losses provoked protests in Chile, and the fleet commander Juan Williams Rebolledo resigned on 5 August. His successor, Commodore Galvarino Riveros Cárdenas, could not sail until September, and the government then ordered the fleet to hunt down the Huáscar at all costs.

Learning on 7 October that Grau had been sighted off Coquimbo, Riveros split his fleet. His own division, with the armoured frigate Blanco Encalada, waited off Antofagasta, while Commander Juan José Latorre's faster ships, led by the Almirante Cochrane, formed a barrier out to sea. At dawn on 8 October the Peruvians were caught between them; the corvette Unión escaped, but the Huáscar had to fight off Punta Angamos, about 80 kilometres north of Antofagasta.

Grau opened fire at 09:25. The Cochrane's armour-piercing Palliser rounds pierced the monitor's turret and cut her steering, and at 10:00 a shot struck the bridge, killing Grau and his adjutant Diego Ferre. Captain Elías Aguirre took command and was killed in the turret soon after the Blanco Encalada joined the fight. Lieutenant Pedro Garezon ordered the ship scuttled, but at 11:08 Chilean boarding parties seized her, closed the leaks and put out the fires.

With the Huáscar taken and Grau dead, the Chilean navy held uncontested control of the Peruvian coast, ending the naval campaign. The allies could no longer supply or concentrate their armies in southern Peru by sea, and the invasion of the Tarapacá department followed in early November. It was the first combat use of such anti-armour shells. The Huáscar served under the Chilean flag and is now a floating museum at Talcahuano, and Peru marks the battle with an annual public holiday.
battle-of-ankara: Timur, a Turco-Mongol from Transoxiana, had built an empire in Central Asia and sought to rebuild the Mongol Empire. In the 1380s and 1390s he conquered parts of Persia, ravaged southern Russia and Ukraine in 1395–96 and sacked Delhi in 1398. Relations with the Ottomans were tense but no cause of war existed until Bayezid demanded tribute from an emir loyal to Timur, which Timur took as a personal affront. In 1400–01 he took Sivas from the Ottomans and parts of Syria from the Mamluks, and then turned towards Anatolia. In 1402 Bayezid broke off his blockade of Constantinople and marched to Ankara.

The armies are reliably estimated at 140,000 for Timur, mostly cavalry, with 32 war elephants, and no more than 85,000 for Bayezid. Contemporary figures of 800,000 and 1.6 million are exaggerations. The Ottoman force included Janissaries, Anatolian Muslim vassals and Balkan Christian vassals, among them Serbian vassals under Stefan Lazarević. Bayezid's tired army marched through the midsummer heat, and his generals advised him to take up defensive positions. Instead he marched east, while Timur's army secretly marched round to the Ottoman rear and occupied the camps and water sources they had left.

The battle was fought on 28 July 1402 on the Çubuk plain near Ankara. Timur's horse archers met the Ottoman attack with swarms of arrows. Stefan Lazarević and his knights, in heavy black plate armour, cut through the Timurid ranks three times, and Timur said of them that they fight like lions. Timur diverted Çubuk creek, the main water supply of both armies, leaving the Ottomans without water. The Black Tatars and the sipahis of the Anatolian beyliks deserted to Timur. Bayezid escaped to the mountains with a few hundred horsemen but was surrounded and captured, and died in captivity three months later.

Timur moved through western Anatolia to the Aegean coast and took Smyrna, a stronghold of the Christian Knights Hospitalers. The battle was catastrophic for the Ottoman state, bringing near collapse and a civil war among Bayezid's sons that continued until 1413. It is also remembered as the only occasion on which an Ottoman sultan was captured in person.
battle-of-appomattox-court-house: The Union Army of the Potomac crossed the James River in June 1864 and laid siege to Petersburg, south of Richmond. On 1 April 1865 Philip Sheridan's cavalry turned Robert E. Lee's flank at the Battle of Five Forks, and the next day Ulysses S. Grant's army broke through. Lee's men left their trenches on the night of 2-3 April, hoping to join Joseph E. Johnston's Army of Tennessee in North Carolina. They found no provisions at Amelia Courthouse, and on 6 April nearly a quarter of the army was cut off at Sailor's Creek, where about 7,700 Confederates were captured, among them Lieutenant General Richard S. Ewell. On 8 April George Armstrong Custer captured and burned three supply trains at Appomattox Station.

Grant had written to Lee on 7 April suggesting surrender, and Lee had asked what terms he had in mind. On the morning of 9 April, hoping to break through what he took to be cavalry alone, the Confederate Second Corps under John B. Gordon attacked Sheridan's line and took the ridge, only to find the Union XXIV Corps and V Corps in line of battle. Gordon sent word that he had fought his corps to a frazzle. Lee said there was nothing left but to see General Grant, and he chose the house of Wilmer McLean at Appomattox Court House for the meeting.

Lee came in his ceremonial uniform; Grant arrived in a mud-spattered one. The terms Grant offered were generous: officers and men were to be paroled, arms and artillery stacked, officers kept their sidearms and horses, and Grant let the men take home their horses and mules for spring planting and provided rations for the hungry army. The document was written out by his adjutant Ely S. Parker, a Seneca, and finished around 4 p.m. Grant stopped his soldiers' cheering, saying the Confederates were now countrymen.

On 12 April about 28,000 Confederates passed by and stacked their arms in a ceremony led on the Union side by Joshua Chamberlain. Chamberlain recalled a salute of arms to the Confederates, and Gordon remembered it too, but the historian William Marvel doubts the account because Chamberlain did not mention it in his letters of the time. Roughly 175,000 Confederates were still in the field. Johnston surrendered to William T. Sherman at Bennett Place on 26 April, Richard Taylor at Citronelle on 4 May, and Edmund Kirby Smith on 2 June; Stand Watie surrendered the last sizeable organised force on 23 June. Jefferson Davis was captured on 10 May.
battle-of-arginusae: In 406 BCE Callicratidas replaced Lysander as navarch of the Spartan fleet. A traditionalist, he distrusted Persian influence and would not ask the Persian prince Cyrus for help, so he raised a fleet of about 140 triremes from Sparta's Greek allies. After storming Methymna on Lesbos he swelled his force to 170 ships and attacked the Athenian commander Conon, who fled to Mytilene and was blockaded there after losing 30 ships. Conon slipped a messenger ship to Athens.

The assembly approved extreme measures: the golden statues of Nike were melted down to pay for ships, and slaves and metics were enlisted as crews. Contributions from allies raised the fleet to 150 triremes, commanded by eight generals acting together.

The Athenians camped at the Arginusae islands, opposite Cape Malea on Lesbos. Callicratidas saw their signal fires but a thunderstorm kept him from attacking at night. At dawn he came out with 140 ships and left 50 to watch Conon. For the first time in the war the Spartan crews were more experienced than the Athenian, whose best crews were with Conon.

The Athenians therefore divided into eight autonomous divisions and formed a double line to prevent the diekplous, in which a trireme drove through a gap to strike another in the side. They extended their left flank out to sea.

Callicratidas's helmsman advised retreat but he pressed on, dividing his force in two. He was killed when his ship rammed an enemy ship, and the Spartan right collapsed; the left soon followed. The Spartans lost some 70 ships and the Athenians 25.

The generals planned to send most of the fleet against the Spartans at Mytilene while Thrasybulus and Theramenes rescued the survivors of the 25 lost ships. A storm thwarted both, and many sailors drowned. When anger rose at Athens, the generals blamed the two trierarchs, but these cleared themselves and the public turned on the generals. Two fled; the other six came back.

Socrates, epistates of the assembly that day, refused to put the motion to a vote, saying he would do nothing contrary to the law, but the motion to try them together carried and all six were executed, Pericles the Younger among them. The Athenians soon regretted it. Athens rejected a Spartan offer of peace, and Lysander won at Aegospotami less than a year later.
battle-of-arsuf: After the capture of Acre, Richard I of England chose to take the port of Jaffa as a source of provisions and reinforcements before attempting Jerusalem. He began marching south along the coast in August 1191, and Saladin, whose main aim was to prevent the recapture of Jerusalem, moved to stop him. Mindful of the disaster at Hattin, Richard knew that water and heat exhaustion were the main dangers. He marched only in the mornings, rested beside water, and kept the fleet sailing alongside. His column kept tight order, with infantry on the landward flank and crossbowmen on the outside, while Saladin's mounted archers harassed it without breaking its formation.

On 7 September 1191 the Crusaders marched across a narrow plain north of Arsuf, between wooded hills and the sea. The Knights Templar under Robert de Sablé led, and the Knights Hospitaller under Garnier de Nablus formed the rearguard. Saladin's army burst from the woods with drums, cymbals and gongs and pressed hardest on the Hospitallers. Richard meant to hold his knights back until the enemy tired, and was waiting for a signal of six trumpet blasts. According to the traditional account, the Hospitallers charged in disobedience of his orders. Others propose that Richard had given trusted subordinates freedom to seize a good moment.

The marshal of the Hospitallers and Baldwin le Carron charged first, and Richard ordered a general charge. The right wing of Saladin's army, close to the Crusaders, suffered heavily. Richard halted the first charge after about 1.5 kilometres to avoid a rash pursuit, and James d'Avesnes was among the knights cut down when some outran the rest. A second charge and a third followed, and the Ayyubid cavalry scattered into the woods. Christian chroniclers claim that Saladin lost 32 emirs and 7,000 men, though the true number may be lower, and Richard's dead are said to have numbered no more than 700.

The Ayyubid army was not destroyed, but its rout was thought shameful by Muslims and raised Crusader morale. Saladin would not risk another full-scale attack, and he evacuated and demolished most fortresses of southern Palestine, including Ascalon, Gaza, Lydda and Ramleh. Richard held Jaffa and rebuilt its fortifications. The Third Crusade did not retake Jerusalem, but a three-year truce, the Treaty of Jaffa, allowed Christian pilgrims to visit the city and left the Crusaders the coast as far south as Jaffa.
