battle-of-artemisium: The Persian invasion of 480 BCE was a delayed response to the defeat at Marathon. The Athenians, guided by Themistocles, had decided in 482 BCE to build a large fleet of triremes, and a congress of city states at Corinth formed an alliance. After a first plan to hold the Vale of Tempe was abandoned, Themistocles proposed that the allies block the Persian army at the pass of Thermopylae and the Persian navy at the Straits of Artemisium. The Allied fleet sailed to Cape Artemisium and waited. It was led by the Spartan Eurybiades, since the Athenians, who had asked for command, yielded it to preserve unity.

Approaching the strait, the Persian navy was caught in a gale off Magnesia that wrecked about a third of its ships. The Persians then sent 200 ships round Euboea to trap the Greeks, and a second storm wrecked them. On the first day the Persians attacked late, and about 30 of their ships were captured or sunk. On the second day the Allies destroyed a patrol of Cilician ships.

On the third day the Persians formed a semicircle to enclose the Greek fleet, and the fleets fought until nightfall with roughly equal losses. The smaller Allied fleet could scarcely afford them, and half the Athenian ships were damaged or lost. News then came from Thermopylae that the Allied rearguard had been destroyed. Since holding Artemisium no longer served a purpose, the Allies evacuated at once.

The Persians sailed on to Histiaea and sacked the surrounding region, while the Allied fleet withdrew to Salamis to help evacuate the remaining Athenians. The Persian army took the evacuated Athens, and the Persians were later defeated at Salamis. Xerxes withdrew to Asia, leaving Mardonius, and the Greek victory at Plataea in August 479 BCE ended the invasion.

Taken by itself the battle was indecisive: the Allies did not defeat the Persian navy, and the Persians did not destroy the Greek fleet. In the wider war it mattered because the Allies showed themselves they could stand up to the Persians, the crews gained experience and the admirals learned how the Persian fleet fought. The pre-battle events had also reduced the Persian fleet, so that the odds at Salamis were not overwhelming. Pindar called Artemisium the place where the sons of the Athenians laid the shining foundation-stone of freedom.
battle-of-ascalon: In 1097 the Fatimids of Egypt sought an agreement with the Crusaders against the Seljuk Empire in Syria, and in 1098 they captured Jerusalem from the Seljuks. The Crusaders had negotiated with the Fatimids on the march, but no compromise was reached: the Fatimids would give up Syria but not Palestine, which the Crusaders, whose goal was the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, could not accept. Jerusalem fell to the Crusaders on 15 July 1099, and they at once learned that a Fatimid army was coming.

Godfrey of Bouillon was named Defender of the Holy Sepulchre on 22 July, and Arnulf of Chocques became patriarch of Jerusalem on 1 August. On 10 August Godfrey led the army out of Jerusalem towards Ascalon, carrying the relic of the True Cross. Raymond IV of Toulouse and Robert of Normandy stayed behind at first and marched out the next day, once the Egyptian presence was confirmed.

The Fatimid army was led by the vizier al-Afdal Shahanshah and numbered perhaps as many as 20,000. It included Seljuk Turks, Arabs, Persians, Armenians, Kurds and Ethiopians. The Crusader numbers are unknown; Raymond of Aguilers gave 1,200 knights and 9,000 infantry. Al-Afdal camped on the plain of al-Majdal outside Ascalon, apparently unaware that the Crusaders were coming to meet him.

At dawn on 12 August the Crusaders attacked the camp. According to most accounts, Crusader and Muslim, the Fatimids were caught unprepared and the battle was short, although Albert of Aix says it went on for some time. The Fatimids fled to the walls of Ascalon, were chased into the sea or were killed; the vizier fled by ship to Egypt and left his camp and treasures to the Crusaders. The Fatimids lost 10,000 infantry and 2,700 residents of Ascalon; Crusader losses are unknown.

The first Muslim attempt to retake Jerusalem ended in complete defeat. Godfrey and Raymond both claimed Ascalon, and when its garrison learned of the dispute it refused to surrender. Almost all the remaining Crusaders then went home, their pilgrimage vows fulfilled, leaving perhaps only a few hundred knights in Jerusalem by the end of the year. Ascalon stayed in Fatimid hands and became a base for yearly attacks on the Kingdom of Jerusalem until the Crusaders took it in 1153.
battle-of-ashdown: By 870 the Vikings had conquered two of the four Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, Northumbria and East Anglia. At the end of that year they marched from East Anglia to Reading to attempt the conquest of Wessex. A large foraging party was defeated at the Battle of Englefield by local levies under Æthelwulf, Ealdorman of Berkshire, but four days later the main West Saxon army under Æthelred and Alfred was beaten at the Battle of Reading. The two armies met again at Ashdown four days after that. The battle is described in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and in Asser's Life of King Alfred.

The Vikings arrived first and deployed along the top of the ridge in two divisions, one under their kings, Bagsecg and Halfdan, the other under their earls. The West Saxons copied the formation, with Æthelred facing the kings and Alfred the earls. Æthelred withdrew to his tent to hear Mass and would not cut short his devotions, and Alfred, in danger of being outflanked, led his men in an uphill charge. The fighting raged around a small thorn tree until the West Saxons won and pursued the Vikings until nightfall.

Both the Chronicle and Asser stress Alfred's part, but in the view of the historian Richard Abels it was Æthelred's attack when he joined the battle that was decisive, and he may have meant all along to take the Vikings unaware. The five earls who fell were Sidroc the Old, Sidroc the Younger, Osbern, Fræna and Harold.

The victory was short-lived: the West Saxons were defeated at Basing and at Meretun, and soon after Easter, which fell on 15 April that year, Æthelred died and Alfred succeeded him. The date of Ashdown is worked out backwards from the death of Bishop Heahmund of Sherborne at Meretun on 22 March 871. The Chronicle places Basing two months before Meretun and Ashdown fourteen days before Basing; because the two-month interval is probably not exact, the earlier dates are approximate. Kingstanding Hill in Berkshire and a spot near Starveall, north of Aldworth, have both been suggested as the site.
battle-of-aspern-essling: On 10 April 1809 Austrian troops under Archduke Charles crossed into Bavaria, a French client state, beginning hostilities without a declaration of war. The French defeated the Austrians at Abensberg, Eckmühl and Ratisbon, and by 13 May Napoleon had entered Vienna. Charles then gathered 115,000 men on the Marchfeld, while Napoleon could muster only 82,000 on the spot. Napoleon wanted an early battle. He feared unrest in his rear, the approach of Archduke John and Prussian intervention, and believed the main Austrian army was retreating into Moravia.

After a first crossing attempt failed, the French bridged the channels to the island of Lobau on the night of 19–20 May. By daybreak on 21 May three infantry and two cavalry divisions stood on the Marchfeld, with their left in the village of Aspern and their right in Essling. That afternoon the Austrians, hidden by a ridge and a dust storm, drove French outposts into Aspern. The French held it through repeated attacks, and it changed hands six times. Boudet's division beat off three attacks on Essling.

On 22 May Masséna retook Aspern, and Napoleon ordered an attack from the centre under Lannes, but Charles's grenadiers halted it. The bridge broke down again, so Davout's corps could not cross, and Napoleon ordered a withdrawal. Aspern fell to the Austrians after 1:00 p.m., and Lannes was fatally wounded by a cannonball. Charles did not pursue, and the last French troops left the north bank by 23 May.

French casualties were estimated at 20,000 to 23,000 killed and wounded and 3,000 captured; the Austrians lost about 19,000 killed and wounded. Napoleon's own bulletin admitted 4,100 killed and wounded. The death of Marshal Jean Lannes, one of the few marshals capable of independent command, was a severe blow to him. Emperor Francis wrote to his brother that Charles had been the first to interrupt his proud enemy's fifteen years of good fortune. The battle damaged Napoleon's reputation for invincibility, but it brought the Fifth Coalition no lasting gain, since he defeated the Austrians decisively at Wagram six weeks later.
battle-of-assaye: In October 1802 Yashwantrao Holkar defeated Daulat Rao Scindia and the Peshwa Baji Rao II at the Battle of Poona. Baji Rao fled to the East India Company and, by the Treaty of Bassein of December 1802, accepted its control of his foreign affairs in return for being restored. The other Maratha leaders saw the subsidiary alliance as interference in their affairs, and Scindia joined Raghoji II Bhonsle, the Raja of Berar, against the British. In August 1803 Arthur Wellesley declared war on both.

Wellesley took Ahmednagar by escalade and, with a second force under Colonel James Stevenson, pursued the Maratha army through the Deccan. The two commanders planned to converge on its camp on 24 September. On 23 September Wellesley found the whole army much closer than he had been told, with about 4,500 troops, 5,000 allied Mysore and Maratha horse and 17 cannon against a force of around 50,000 and over 100 guns, commanded in the absence of the chiefs by the Hanoverian officer Anthony Pohlmann.

Judging a frontal assault across the only known ford suicidal, Wellesley guessed that a second ford lay between the villages of Peepulgaon and Waroor and crossed the Kaitna there to strike the Maratha left. Pohlmann swung his line to face him between the river and Assaye. The Maratha guns cut deep into the British ranks, and Wellesley abandoned his own artillery and sent his infantry forward with the bayonet. The 78th Highlanders and the Madras battalions overran the guns and the Maratha right gave way.

On the right, Lieutenant Colonel William Orrock mistook his orders and led the pickets and the 74th Highlanders towards Assaye, where they were nearly destroyed until Colonel Patrick Maxwell's cavalry charged to their relief. Gunners who had feigned death turned their cannon on the British rear and had to be driven off a second time. Maxwell was killed in a final charge, and Pohlmann's infantry withdrew across the Juah.

British losses were 1,584 killed, wounded and missing, over a third of the force engaged. British despatches put the Maratha dead at 1,200; some modern historians estimate 6,000 dead and wounded. The Marathas lost 98 cannon, and many of their European officers surrendered or deserted. Victories at Argaon and Gawilghur followed, and with Gerard Lake's campaign in the north they brought the two chiefs to sue for peace. Wellesley later called Assaye the bloodiest battle for the numbers he ever saw.
battle-of-assietta: The battle belonged to the Italian campaign of the War of the Austrian Succession, in which Habsburgs and Bourbons contested Northern Italy. The Kingdom of Sardinia had joined Maria Theresa's side in 1742 and, after several defeats in the field, had turned to a defensive strategy. Late in the war France resolved to destroy the Sardinian army. Marshal Charles Louis Auguste, duke of Belle-Isle, favoured threatening Turin across the Alps; held up by the defence of the southern passes, he sent his brother, the Chevalier de Belle-Isle, with fifty infantry battalions, fifteen cavalry squadrons and many guns towards the northern passes.

Charles Emmanuel III had to guard every pass, while the French needed to force only one. They chose the Assietta, a bare plateau at about 2,500 metres, which the Sardinians under Giovanni di Bricherasio had fortified with obstacles, redoubts and an eighteen-foot palisade, held by thirteen battalions, nine Sardinian and the rest Austrian and Swiss.

Thirty-two French battalions attacked at about 16:30. The centre pressed the assault up the slope, dismantling the obstacles under musket fire from concealed positions, while the flanking columns made only half-hearted attacks. The French were driven back four times and returned each time, climbing over their dead at the palisades as the defenders fired and threw rocks down on them. The Chevalier de Belle-Isle was killed while raising the French flag near the top of the slope. After five hours the French withdrew in better order than they had attacked. They lost 6,400 killed and wounded, among them 400 officers, of whom 3,700 were dead, against 299 Sardinian casualties.

It was the last major battle of the Italian campaign, and the French withdrew entirely from Italy afterwards. Belle-Isle's body was buried with full military honours in Embrun Cathedral. Frederick II of Prussia is said to have declared that with such troops he could easily become King of Italy. Strategically the battle settled nothing in Italy, but tactically it exposed the failure of massed bayonet assaults in column without covering fire. By the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle the following year Sardinia gained the territories around Lake Maggiore and Ticino.
battle-of-aughrim: After their defeat at the Boyne and James II's departure for France, the Jacobites held Connacht behind the line of the Shannon, and William III's siege of Limerick failed in August 1690. Their command was split between the peace party of the viceroy Tyrconnell and the war party of Patrick Sarsfield. Louis XIV sent Charles Chalmot de Saint-Ruhe to take command; he reached Limerick on 9 May 1691 with arms and food but neither troops nor money.

Godert de Ginkel took Athlone on 30 June after a bloody siege and advanced cautiously towards Limerick and Galway. Saint-Ruhe, hoping to redeem the loss of Athlone, chose to fight, and on the morning of 12 July Ginkel found the road blocked at Aughrim by about 20,000 men, roughly as many as his own.

The Jacobite infantry held the crest of Kilcommadan Hill behind hedged enclosures and a large bog, with cavalry guarding a causeway on the left. Serious fighting began between five and six in the afternoon. Assaults under Hugh Mackay on the centre were thrown back through waist-deep water by Irish foot fighting with clubbed muskets, and most observers, even those sympathetic to William, judged that the Irish infantry fought exceptionally well.

Williamite cavalry then forced the causeway on the left, where the Jacobite cavalry and dragoons under Luttrell had pulled back. Riding to meet them, Saint-Ruhe paused to direct a battery and was decapitated by a cannonball. Without him the left collapsed, and at around nine o'clock the infantry on the hill broke; most of the Jacobite dead fell in the pursuit that followed.

Some 7,000 men are generally agreed to have died. Many Jacobite officers were killed or taken, and prisoners of the rank and file held on Lambay Island died of disease and hunger. Irish tradition remembered the battle in Séamas Dall Mac Cuarta's words as Aughrim of the slaughter, with the dead left unburied, while Loyalist and Orange Order commemorations marked it on 12 July until the Boyne replaced it in the early 19th century. A battlefield interpretative centre opened in Aughrim village in 1991.
battle-of-auray: The battle was the decisive confrontation of the Breton War of Succession, a part of the Hundred Years' War. Early in 1364, after the failure of the negotiations of Evran, John de Montfort, helped by John Chandos, attacked Auray, which Franco-Bretons had held since 1342. He entered the town and besieged the castle, which was blockaded from the sea by the ships of Nicolas Bouchart. Without food, the defenders agreed to surrender if no help came before Michaelmas, 29 September. Two days before, Charles of Blois reached a position east of the abbey of Lanvaux, with Bertrand du Guesclin commanding the vanguard at nearby Brandivy.

On 28 September du Guesclin took up position before the castle, and Montfort left Auray to avoid being caught between the castle and the French army, drawing up on the slope of the right bank of the river. The next day Charles of Blois led his army across and lined up facing south on a marshy plain north of the town, a poor position in the view of some of his commanders. Montfort faced north on higher ground. Rejecting the advice of du Guesclin, Charles ordered the attack. Each division had roughly 1,000 men. On the Anglo-Breton side Olivier de Clisson commanded the right, Robert Knolles the left and Montfort and Chandos the centre, with a significant reserve under Hugh Calveley.

The fight opened with a short skirmish between French crossbowmen and English longbowmen. Orders were given on both sides to give no quarter, and the combat was bloody. The Anglo-Breton reserves restored each division as it was attacked head on, then drove back the Franco-Breton right, which folded toward the centre and then the left. The Count of Auxerre was captured and the army broke. Charles of Blois was struck by a lance and finished off by an English soldier. Du Guesclin, having broken all his weapons, surrendered to Chandos.

Du Guesclin was ransomed by Charles V for 100,000 francs. The victory ended the war of succession. In 1365, under the first Treaty of Guerande, the king of France recognised John IV, son of John de Montfort, as Duke of Brittany. The new duke then paid homage to Charles V of France rather than to his patron Edward III of England, so that the Anglo-Breton military victory appeared to bring a diplomatic gain to the French king.
battle-of-austerlitz: Britain declared war on France in May 1803, after the Treaty of Amiens broke down over Malta and the return of captured colonies. In December 1804 an Anglo-Swedish agreement created the Third Coalition. Britain and Russia signed an alliance by April 1805, and Austria, twice defeated by France and eager for revenge, joined a few months later. In August 1805 Napoleon turned his army from the English Channel to the Rhine, and 23,000 Austrians surrendered at Ulm on 20 October. Vienna fell in November.

Napoleon retreated from the dominant Pratzen Heights near Austerlitz and gave every sign that his army was in poor state. He deliberately weakened his right flank to tempt the Allies to attack it, and hid his main force in dead ground. The Allies adopted the plan of the Austrian chief of staff Franz von Weyrother, a main drive against the French right. Napoleon began with some 72,000 men against about 85,000, since the corps of Marshal Davout was still far to the south.

The battle began about 8 am on 2 December 1805 with Allied attacks on the village of Telnitz, where Davout's first men arrived in time to hold the French right. At about 8:45 am Napoleon saw the weakness of the Allied centre, which had been stripped to extend against his right, and ordered Marshal Soult's corps to storm the Pratzen Heights, saying that one sharp blow would end the war.

The Allies lost about 36,000 men, 186 guns and 45 standards; the French lost around 9,000. France and Austria agreed an armistice at once, and the Treaty of Pressburg of 26 December took Austria out of the war. It confirmed Austria's loss of lands in Italy and Bavaria to France and in Germany to Napoleon's German allies, and imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs. The victory also allowed the creation of the Confederation of the Rhine.

The battle is often cited by military historians as one of Napoleon's tactical masterpieces, in the company of Hannibal's Cannae and Alexander the Great's Gaugamela. It did not establish a lasting peace, since neither Russia nor Britain was driven to settle. The battlefield has been protected by law as a landscape monument zone since 1992.
battle-of-avarayr: The Kingdom of Armenia under the Arsacid dynasty was the first nation to convert officially to Christianity, in 301 under Tiridates III. In 428 Armenian nobles petitioned Bahram V to depose Artaxias IV, and the country became a Sasanian dependency with a Sasanian governor. The nobles at first welcomed Persian rule, provided they could practise Christianity. Yazdegerd II, however, was concerned that the Armenian Church depended on the Latin- and Greek-speaking church aligned with Rome and Constantinople, rather than on the Persian-backed Church of the East, and tried to make it abandon Rome and Byzantium or convert to Zoroastrianism.

Yazdegerd faced the Kidarites in the east and an uneasy relationship with his aristocracy. His policy of bringing Christian nobles into the bureaucracy led to a major rebellion in Armenia, caused by an attempt by his minister Mihr-Narseh to impose the Zurvanite variant of Zoroastrianism. Many Armenian nobles, though not all, rallied under Vardan Mamikonian, the sparapet, or supreme commander, of Armenia. They appealed to the Romans for help without success. Another faction, led by the marzban Vasak Siwni, allied itself with the Sasanians.

The battle was fought on 26 May 451 on the Avarayr Plain in Vaspurakan. The Armenian army, put at 66,000 men, took Holy Communion beforehand. It was a popular uprising rather than a professional force, but the nobles who led it and their retinues included many veterans of Sasanian wars against Rome and the nomads of Central Asia.

The Persian army, said to be three times larger, included war elephants and the Savārān, or New Immortal, cavalry. Several Armenian nobles with weaker Christian sympathies, led by Vasak Siuni, went over to the Persians and fought on their side. Vardan won early successes but was slain with eight of his top officers.

Nine generals, Vardan among them, and many Armenian nobles and soldiers died. The Sasanians also suffered heavy losses from the rebels' resistance. Yazdegerd II dismissed Vasak Siwni and allowed religious freedom in Armenia, so the Persian victory on the field is called pyrrhic. Tensions continued until 510, when Vard Mamikonian, a kinsman of Vardan, was appointed marzban by Kavad I, Yazdegerd's grandson. The battle is seen as one of the most significant events in Armenian history and as one of the first fought in defence of the Christian faith. Vardan Mamikonian is regarded as a national hero and has been canonised by the Armenian Apostolic Church.
battle-of-ayacucho: A revolt in Spain in January 1820, encouraged by General Rafael Riego, forced King Ferdinand VII to restore the liberal Constitution of 1812 and ended the reinforcements meant for America. In Peru this left the royalists to face the patriots alone. In 1821 General José de la Serna overthrew Viceroy Joaquín de la Pezuela in a coup at Aznapuquio. In 1823 Ferdinand recovered absolute power, and at the beginning of 1824 the royalist army of Upper Peru under Pedro Antonio Olañeta rose against the liberal viceroy, so that by August 1824 the royalist forces were divided and decimated in fighting in Upper Peru.

By the end of 1824 the royalists still held most of southern Peru and the Real Felipe Fortress at Callao. On 3 December they struck at Corpahuaico, costing Sucre more than 500 casualties and much of his ammunition and artillery against about 30 of their own, but Sucre kept his United Army in good order. The armies met on 9 December at the Pampa de Ayacucho near Quinua. The numbers are disputed; perhaps 5,780 patriots faced 6,906 royalists.

The royalist plan was to flank Sucre while the rest of the army came down from the Condorcunca hill. Sucre saw the danger, and the division of José María Córdova, supported by William Miller's cavalry, fired on the royalists as they came down in disorder. Colonel Joaquín Rubín de Celis was killed. Viceroy de la Serna was wounded, and José de Canterac negotiated the capitulation with Sucre.

The royalist army agreed to end hostilities, and the remaining soldiers were to stay in the Callao fortresses. Peru regards the battle as the end of the Spanish American wars of independence, although Sucre's campaign in Upper Peru continued through 1825 and Callao and Chiloé held out until 1826. A Spanish historian, Juan Carlos Losada, argues that the outcome had been agreed in advance by liberal-minded royalist officers.

Sucre entered Upper Peru on 25 February 1825. A constituent assembly he reconvened in Chuquisaca declared independence on 6 August 1825, and the new republic was named after Bolívar. Bolívar declined its presidency, and Sucre became the first president of Bolivia.
battle-of-baekgang: In 660 the allied armies of Silla and Tang China conquered Paekche. The Buddhist monk Dochim and the former Paekche general Buyeo Boksin rose to restore the kingdom and brought the Paekche prince Buyeo Pung back from Japan to reign, with their headquarters at Juryu. After early successes, by 662 they held little more than the fortress and its surroundings, and Buyeo Pung had Boksin killed for fear of insurrection.

Paekche and Yamato Japan were long-standing allies whose royal houses were related, and the fall of Paekche shocked the Yamato court. Crown Prince Naka no Ōe, later Emperor Tenji, and Empress Kōgyoku sent an expeditionary force under Abe no Hirafu, drawn largely from local strongmen of western Honshū, Shikoku and above all Kyūshū. Around August 661 some 5,000 soldiers and 170 ships arrived, followed in 662 by further reinforcements, among them 27,000 men under Kamitsukeno no Kimi Wakako.

In 663 the Yamato fleet was to carry troops up the Geum River to relieve Juryu, besieged by Silla. Tang sent 7,000 soldiers and 170 ships to block the way. On 4 October 663 (27 August in the lunar calendar) the Japanese advance guard tried to force a passage, but the Tang ships held their formation.

The next day Japanese reinforcements made their fleet several times larger, yet the river was narrow enough for the Tang line to cover its front and flanks. The Japanese attacked at least three times. When they tired and lost cohesion, the Tang counterattacked, broke both flanks and hemmed the Japanese ships in so that they could neither move nor retreat. Many ships were burned and sunk, and the Yamato general Echi no Takutsu was killed.

Japanese, Korean and Chinese sources all report heavy Japanese losses; the Nihon Shoki puts them at 400 ships. Yamato withdrew completely from Korean affairs. Historians have asked why Japan threw itself into the war: some point to the close ties between its court and Paekche, others to Yamato's wish to keep its last ally on the peninsula after Kaya fell to Silla in 562.
battle-of-baideng: After the fall of the Qin dynasty, the Han emperor Liu Bang was still securing his realm against rivals. Judging the fief of Xin of Han too close to the central plain, he moved Xin north to guard the border against the Xiongnu. Defeated by the Xiongnu leader Modu Chanyu, Xin defected and joined him in taking Jinyang, part of present-day Taiyuan. Liu Bang's army recaptured Taiyuan and the places around it, and the enemy withdrew.

Han envoys reported that the Xiongnu soldiers were weak, and an army of 320,000, mostly infantry, prepared to follow them. The adviser Lou Jing warned that a show of weakness could be a ruse; the emperor, angered, had him detained. When Liu Bang and his vanguard reached Pingcheng, Xiongnu cavalry surrounded them on Mount Baideng and cut them off from the rest of the Han army. The Book of Han puts the Xiongnu at over 300,000, while Lev Gumilev argues for 20,000 to 40,000, given the nomads' numbers and the limited pasture.

The two sides were locked in a stalemate for seven days, and the emperor could not resupply his food. The adviser Chen Ping sent an envoy to Modu Chanyu's wife; what was said is unknown, but she told Modu that taking Han territory did not mean he could live there. Modu was also waiting for two of Xin's generals who failed to arrive, and fearing they had gone over to the Han, he opened a corner of the encirclement and let the emperor's force escape.

Once free, Liu Bang executed the envoys who had misjudged the Xiongnu and released and promoted Lou Jing. As the raids went on, he took Lou Jing's advice to give a daughter in marriage to Modu Chanyu, later replaced by another woman of the royal clan, which began the heqin policy. Government horse pastures were also set up in the northern provinces to build a stronger Han cavalry.
battle-of-ballon: After the death of Louis the Pious, Nominoë at first backed Charles the Bald in the struggle among Louis's sons. When Count Ricuin of Nantes was killed at the Battle of Fontenoy, Charles refused the county to Lambert II, whose father had fought against him, and gave it to his supporter Renaud, Count of Herbauge. Renaud attacked Breton territory and was killed by Bretons under Erispoe, Nominoë's son, allied with Lambert, who then occupied Nantes with Nominoë's support.

While Charles was campaigning in Aquitaine, Nominoë raided Maine. In 845 Charles made peace with Pepin II of Aquitaine and was reconciled with Lambert. In November, instead of attending a religious festival at Tours, he moved against Nominoë, having heard that discontented Bretons would come over to him.

Charles gathered an army of about 3,000 men in haste; Nominoë's force was probably much smaller, made up mostly of mobile light cavalry. Nominoë drew the king into marshland where the Oust meets the Aff, between Redon and Bains-sur-Oust, near Ballon Abbey, and the Bretons used their knowledge of the wetland. Details are sketchy: the Annals of Saint-Bertin say Charles had attacked recklessly with limited forces, and the First Annals of Fontenelle that the difficult ground helped the Bretons prevail.

Rumours that Charles had been killed forced him to show himself in Maine. He rebuilt his army and late in 846 concluded a treaty with Nominoë whose exact terms are unknown; Breton raids went on that Christmas, but the agreement held until 849. The battle is often confused with the more decisive Battle of Jengland, won by Erispoe in 851, a confusion that goes back to Arthur de la Borderie's history of 1894. Some date the birth of a unified Brittany under a single ruler to Ballon, and Breton nationalists raised a statue of Nominoë by Raffig Tullou at Bains-sur-Oust in 1952.
battle-of-bannockburn: The Wars of Scottish Independence began in 1296, and by 1304 Scotland had been conquered, but in 1306 Robert the Bruce seized the throne and reopened the war. Edward I died in 1307, and his son Edward II proved unable to give the same determined leadership.

In 1313 Bruce demanded that remaining supporters of the ousted John Balliol acknowledge him or lose their lands, and he demanded the surrender of the English garrison at Stirling Castle. His brother Edward Bruce besieged it in 1314, and the English agreed that it would surrender if not relieved by midsummer. Edward II summoned troops from England, Wales and Ireland and raised the largest army ever to invade Scotland.

The battle lasted two days. Bruce drew up his army at New Park in four divisions of schiltrons, dense squares of men with pikes. On 23 June 1314 Henry de Bohun, a nephew of the Earl of Hereford, charged Bruce, who killed him with an axe. Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, then routed a second English force. That night the Scottish knight Alexander Seton, serving in Edward's army, deserted and told Bruce that English morale was low.

On 24 June the Scots advanced from the wood and knelt briefly in prayer. The Earl of Gloucester, accused of cowardice by the king, led a charge and was surrounded and killed. The schiltrons pushed the English back against the Bannock Burn, where their cavalry could not manoeuvre, and Scottish horse under Sir Robert Keith dispersed the longbowmen. Edward fled, was refused entry to Stirling Castle and escaped by ship from Dunbar to Berwick.

Stirling Castle surrendered and Bruce razed it. The Earl of Hereford was among the nobles taken, and Edward exchanged them for Bruce's wife Elizabeth de Burgh, his sisters, his daughter Marjorie and Bishop Robert Wishart, held in England for eight years. By 1315 only Berwick remained outside Bruce's control. The defeat opened northern England to Scottish raids. The exact site is debated, and the National Trust for Scotland accepts the Carse of Balquhiderock as the most likely site of the second day.
battle-of-bapheus: Osman I had become leader of his clan around 1281 and over the next two decades launched ever deeper raids into the Byzantine borderlands of Bithynia. His Turkish warrior bands roamed the countryside, prevented the harvest from being gathered and threatened the port city of Nicomedia with famine. They also besieged Nicaea, the former imperial capital, and pillaged the outskirts of Prusa.

In the spring of 1300 the co-emperor Michael IX launched a campaign that reached south to Magnesia. The Turks avoided battle at first and resumed their raids once his generals dissuaded him from confronting them. His army dissolved, as local troops went home to defend their families and the Alan mercenaries left to rejoin theirs in Thrace, and Michael withdrew by sea.

To relieve Nicomedia, Michael's father, the emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos, sent a force of some 2,000 men, half of them recently hired Alan mercenaries, under the megas hetaireiarches George Mouzalon. It crossed the Bosporus and met a Turkish army of some 5,000 light cavalry on the plain of Bapheus, a site that has not been identified but lay perhaps east of Nicomedia within sight of the city.

Osman commanded in person. His army combined his own troops with allies from the Turkish tribes of Paphlagonia and the Maeander River area. The Turkish cavalry charged, and the Alan contingent did not take part. The Turks broke the Byzantine line and Mouzalon withdrew into Nicomedia under the cover of the Alans.

The Byzantines effectively lost control of the countryside of Bithynia and withdrew to their forts, which, isolated, fell one by one. Osman took the castle of Koyunhisar and the coastal town of Gemlik, and the defeat drove much of the Christian population of the area to the European parts of the empire. According to Halil İnalcık, the battle allowed the Ottomans to acquire the character of a state. Thousands of Turkish gazi warriors came from inland Anatolia to raid, and the Byzantine historian George Pachymeres wrote that the fame of Osman Gazi had reached Paphlagonia. The conquest of Bithynia was gradual: Nicomedia, the last Byzantine outpost there, fell only in 1337.

The year of the battle is disputed. Edward Gibbon placed it on 27 July 1299, following the chronology of Pachymeres, while Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall proposed a later year, accepted by many scholars. A study of 2017 argued again for the earlier date.
battle-of-basiani: At the end of the 12th century the Sultanate of Rum was weakened by Turkmen raids, the Crusades and a struggle for power among the sons of Kilij Arslan II. In 1197 his fifth son, Suleiman II of Rum, seized Konya and drove his brother Kaykhusraw I into exile in Constantinople. Suleiman then challenged Byzantium, the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia and Georgia, which under Queen Tamar had defeated a Muslim coalition at the Battle of Shamkor in 1195.

The two powers competed along the southern coast of the Black Sea. With his brother Tughril, the Mengujekid ruler Bahram Shah of Erzincan and Turkmen warriors, Suleiman captured Erzurum and deposed Saltuk, Georgia's vassal there. His envoys brought letters to Tamar demanding her capitulation, and according to the Georgian account Zakaria II Mkhargrdzeli struck the messenger who delivered the sultan's oral insult to the queen.

The Georgian army, put at approximately 65,000 to 90,000 troops, was readied within ten days. Its commanders included David Soslan, Zakaria and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli, and Shalva and Ivane Akhaltsikheli. The Life of Queen Tamar says the army gathered at Vardzia, where the queen addressed it from the balcony of a church. Muslim sources give the sultan's army as 400,000 men; estimates range from 150,000 upwards.

The Georgians opened with a night attack by their advance troops that threw the Seljuk camp into confusion. Suleiman rallied his men and pressed the Georgians so hard that many cavalrymen fought on foot, until the main divisions under David Soslan struck from the flanks and encircled the Turks. Ibn Bibi blamed the collapse on the sultan's standard-bearer, whose fall started rumours of Suleiman's death; Aqsarayi spoke of a Georgian ambush.

Both sides suffered heavy casualties. Suleiman retreated to Erzurum, and the Georgians took many banners and prisoners, among them the Emir of Erzincan, Fahrettin Behramşah, whom Tamar ordered sold for the price of a single iron horseshoe, though she kept him in Tbilisi as a guest. Tamar went on to annex Arran and Dvin and to extend her authority over Kars, the Shah-Armens, Erzurum and Erzincan, and in 1206 the Georgians occupied Erzurum and Kars.
battle-of-bataan: Under War Plan Orange 3, the American plan of April 1941, the Philippine garrison was to withdraw to the Bataan Peninsula, the key to Manila Bay, if the enemy landed in strength, and hold it to the "last extremity". MacArthur rejected the plan as defeatist and won approval to defend the whole archipelago at the beaches, with supplies spread behind them. When the main force of Masaharu Homma's Fourteenth Army landed at Lingayen Gulf on 22 December 1941 and the beaches could not be held, the old plan was revived. By the end of the year Bataan held 15,000 Americans, 65,000 Filipinos and 26,000 refugees, but food for only about two months instead of the six the plans required.

General Jonathan Wainwright's North Luzon Force fell back through five defensive lines to keep the road to Bataan open. From 9 January 1942 the Japanese attacked the main line at Abucay in the east and Mauban in the west. A roadblock behind Wainwright's flank led MacArthur to order a withdrawal to the Pilar-Bagac Road on 22 January. Japanese landings behind the lines on the west coast were destroyed in the Battle of the Points, and two battalions that broke through the new line were wiped out in the Battle of the Pockets. By 8 February Homma had only three effective infantry battalions and halted his attacks.

The defenders were by then on a starvation diet. MacArthur was ordered out and left Corregidor on the night of 12 March; Edward P. King took command of the Luzon Force. On 3 April a bombardment by 196 guns opened Homma's final offensive along Mount Samat, the 41st Division gave way, and the line collapsed before the surrender of 9 April.

The fall of Bataan hastened that of Corregidor a month later. The stand cheered the Allied peoples after the loss of Singapore and the Indies. MacArthur's intelligence officer, Willoughby, later claimed it upset the Japanese timetable decisively, while the historian Gavin Long held that the Japanese had let resistance on Luzon run on in order to speed their conquest of the Indies. In the Philippines, 9 April is a national holiday, the Day of Valor, and the Shrine of Valor stands on Mount Samat.
battle-of-benevento: The Papacy had long been in conflict with the Hohenstaufen over their rule in Italy. The Hohenstaufen ruler of the Kingdom of Sicily, which included Sicily and southern Italy, was Manfred, an illegitimate son of the Emperor Frederick II. The rightful heir was Frederick's legitimate grandson Conradin, aged 14. Manfred had been regent since 1254 and took the throne in 1258, using a false rumour of Conradin's death. Pope Urban IV resolved to take the kingdom from him and in 1263 made a secret treaty promising the Sicilian throne to Charles of Anjou. After Urban's death, Pope Clement IV continued the support.

Charles reached Rome in May 1265 but was held up by the need to raise money. Manfred spent his time hunting, trusting his German knights and Saracen horsemen. He took the field only in January 1266, after Charles's main army had crossed the Alps. Alarmed by the surrender of towns and castles and by desertions, Manfred sought a swift battle.

Charles tried to turn Manfred's position at Capua by crossing the Apennines, which wrecked his supply line. Manfred, informed of the move, waited across the River Calore, which could be crossed only by one bridge. Charles had about 12,000 men, nearly all vassals of the French and Provençal crowns. Manfred's army was more mixed: Saracen archers in front, then 1,200 German mercenary knights and men-at-arms, then Italian mercenary cavalry and Saracen light horse, and finally the barons of the kingdom under his own command, whom he distrusted.

On the morning of 26 February 1266 Manfred sent his Saracens forward and Provençal sergeants overwhelmed them. His German knights then crossed the bridge to attack and at first pushed the Provençals back. Charles committed his second battle and 400 Italians. According to the chronicle of Andrew of Hungary, a French knight noticed that the new plate armour left the armpits exposed when the arm was raised, and the shorter, sharper French blades did great damage in close fighting. The German corps was practically annihilated.

Manfred's second battle arrived late, after the long crossing of the bridge, and fell to Charles's third battle. Most of the nobles in his third corps deserted. Manfred, who had exchanged his royal surcoat with his friend Tebaldo Annibaldi, rode into the enemy and was killed. Many fugitives drowned in the flooded Calore, and only 600 of his 3,600 heavy cavalry escaped death or capture.

The destruction of Manfred's army ended Hohenstaufen rule in Italy. The rest of the Kingdom of Sicily was conquered almost without resistance. Charles then awaited Conradin, the last hope of the Hohenstaufen, and met him at the Battle of Tagliacozzo in 1268.
battle-of-beneventum-275-bc: Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, had sailed to southern Italy ostensibly to aid the Greek city of Tarentum in a dispute with Rome, though ancient historians agreed that his real motive was conquest. The Samnites, Lucani and Bruttii fought beside him. He won the Battle of Heraclea and the Battle of Asculum, but at such heavy cost that he could not sustain further battles against Rome's far larger pool of manpower. When Greek cities of Sicily asked for help against the Carthaginians, he went there and seized all their holdings except Lilybaeum. His despotic treatment of the Greek cities, which he levied to man and equip a fleet, turned many against him, and he returned to Italy.

Plutarch gives the fullest account. The Samnites had lost much territory to the Romans during Pyrrhus's three years in Sicily, and most did not join him. The consuls of 275 BCE, Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Caudinus and Manius Curius Dentatus, were in Lucania and Samnium. Pyrrhus divided his army, sent one part against Lentulus and marched by night with the other against Curius, who was camped near Beneventum. His men lost their way in the woods and he came into view of the enemy at dawn, advancing from the heights.

Curius attacked the advance guard and captured some elephants, then fought on the plain. An elephant charge drove him back to his camp, but the guards on the rampart threw javelins at the elephants and turned them into Pyrrhus's own ranks. Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Cassius Dio add that a wounded young elephant caused confusion; the Romans killed two elephants and took eight. No numbers of troops or casualties are known.

Some modern historians argue that the battle was a draw rather than a Roman victory. Whichever it was, Pyrrhus, whose money was running short, was forced onto the defensive and lost control of southern Italy. He returned to Tarentum, left a garrison there under his son Helenus and Milon, and sailed to Epirus with some 8,000 infantry and 500 cavalry, in autumn 275 or early 274 BCE. In 272 BCE, on news of his death, the Tarentines surrendered to Rome. The city of the battle was then called Maleventum, a name Romans took as ill-omened; after founding a colony there in 268 BCE they renamed it Beneventum.
battle-of-berestechko: The armies met on a hilly plain south of the Styr River near the town of Berestechko, in the Volhynian Voivodeship, between marshes on one side and a forest on the other. Their lines stretched over seven to eight kilometres. Numbers are uncertain on both sides. Duke Bogusław Radziwiłł put the Crown Army at 80,000, half of them nobles of the levée en masse, while modern historians such as Zbigniew Wójcik reduce it to 60,000–63,000. Estimates of the Cossack and Crimean Tatar forces range from 90,000 to 130,000, with the Tatars put at 25,000–30,000.

On 28 June Polish cavalry under Stefan Czarniecki and others repulsed the Tatars without a decisive result. On 29 June the Poles threw all their cavalry at the Tatars and were driven back to their camp, losing 300 szlachta. On 30 June Prince Jeremi Wiśniowiecki led 18 cavalry companies into the Cossack right wing, and German mercenaries under Colonel Houwaldt drove the Tatars off the field. Polish artillery fired on the khan's standard, mortally wounding his brother Amurat, and the Tatar forces fled, taking Khmelnytsky and Ivan Vyhovsky hostage as they tried to bring the khan back.

The Cossacks then fortified a camp by the Pliashivka River and held out for ten days under Colonel Fylon Dzhalaliy and later Ivan Bohun. When Bohun crossed the river on 10 July to attack Stanisław Lanckoroński, the peasants in the camp thought themselves abandoned and fled, and the Poles stormed the camp. A rearguard of 200 to 300 Cossacks died defending the crossing. Participants reported 3,000 killed in the retreat.

John II Casimir did not press the pursuit, hampered by rain, hunger, disease and the levée's unwillingness to march into Ukraine. Khmelnytsky, released by the khan, raised a new army, and the Treaty of Bila Tserkva of 28 September 1651 cut the registered Cossacks from 40,000 to 20,000. The historian Natalia Yakovenko sees the battle as the point where the uprising turned from a civil war into a Polish-Ukrainian war. A memorial church of Saint George was built nearby in 1912–1914.
battle-of-beth-horon-66: The First Jewish–Roman War began in the spring of 66 CE. A land dispute in the mixed city of Caesarea, in which the Roman authorities sided with the Greek community, was followed by the procurator Gessius Florus seizing 17 talents from the Temple treasury and crushing the protests with killings and crucifixions. Herod Agrippa II failed to calm Jerusalem and fled to Antioch to inform Cestius Gallus. Eleazar ben Hanania halted the daily sacrifices for the emperor, the Sicarii seized Masada, and in mid-September the last Roman garrisons in Jerusalem surrendered and were killed.

Gallus assembled an army of between 29,000 and 36,000 men around Legio XII Fulminata, with detachments of the other three Syrian legions, auxiliary cohorts and cavalry, and troops of client kings such as Antiochus IV of Commagene and Sohaemus of Emesa. He marched by way of Akko-Ptolemais, burned Chabulon and Jaffa, razed Lydda, reached Jerusalem and burned parts of it, then lifted the siege for reasons that remain unclear.

From his camp on Mount Scopus Gallus began to retreat. Jewish forces harried the column from the rear and both flanks, killing senior officers such as Priscus, commander of the Sixth Legion, and forcing it to abandon most of its baggage. After two days' rest at Gabaon, near modern Al-Jib, Gallus ordered the pack animals killed, keeping only those needed for weapons and siege engines, and marched on towards the coastal plain.

In the narrow pass of Beth Horon, where the Maccabees had defeated a Seleucid army two centuries earlier, rebels on the cliffs above met the column with arrows and missiles. Rebel commanders included Simon Bar Giora and Eleazar ben Simon. The survivors escaped to the foot of the pass under cover of darkness, leaving 5,300 infantry and 480 cavalry dead. Fergus Millar called the defeat a rare case of Roman regulars beaten decisively in a province by its own population.

The rebels pursued the Romans to Antipatris and seized their artillery and battering rams. Gallus died soon afterwards, possibly by his own hand, and Mucianus succeeded him. Many more volunteers and towns joined the revolt; Eleazar ben Simon, Joshua ben Zafia and Niger the Perean became regional governors of the new Judean government, while Simon Bar Giora was driven from Jerusalem and raised his own army in the south. Nero and the senate then sent Vespasian with four legions to crush the rebellion.
battle-of-bi: Jin and Chu were among the most powerful states of their time, but while Jin was held to be a legitimate Zhou state by culture and lineage, Chu, whose lands in the middle Yangtze took in many non-Chinese peoples, was regarded as half-civilised at best. Jin had decisively defeated Chu at the Battle of Chengpu some three and a half decades earlier, making Duke Wen of Jin hegemon.

After Duke Wen's death Chu campaigned in the north again, but avoided direct conflict while Zhao Dun led the Jin government. Zhao Dun died in 601 BCE, Duke Cheng of Jin the following year, and Zhao's successor Xi Que in 598 BCE. King Zhuang of Chu used the resulting instability to lead a campaign north in person.

King Zhuang forced Zheng, an ally of Jin, to change sides. The new Jin commander, Xun Linfu, learned of Zheng's surrender while camped on the northern bank of the Yellow River and favoured retreat, but his adjutant Xian Hu, holding that the hegemonic state could not avoid battle, crossed the river with his own troops without orders, and the rest of the army had to follow. Chu pulled back 30 li and waited.

King Zhuang and his commander Sunshu Ao were at first inclined to withdraw, until the commander Wu Can pointed to Xun Linfu's inexperience, Xian Hu's rashness and the quarrels among the Jin leaders. While truce talks went on, two Jin generals impatient with Xun Linfu provoked the Chu forces, and the king pursued them himself. Dust raised by a Jin force sent to bring them back was taken for a general advance, and Sunshu Ao, fearing the king would be cut off, ordered the whole Chu army forward. The unexpected attack broke the Jin army, which was routed.

After the victory King Zhuang led his generals to water their horses in the Yellow River. He refused a request to pursue and destroy the remnants of the Jin army, on the grounds that the humiliation of Chengpu had been avenged and further slaughter was unnecessary. The battle confirmed his position as a hegemon among the vassal states of the Zhou dynasty.
battle-of-bir-hakeim: Bir Hakeim was a fortress built by the Ottomans at the crossing of two Bedouin paths. It stood at the southern end of the Gazala line, a series of brigade-sized defensive boxes that the British Eighth Army held west of Tobruk. On 14 February 1942 the 1st Free French Brigade took over the box, which was surrounded by 50,000 mines. The brigade had a fighting strength of 3,000 men, with the 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion as its backbone, and by mid-May it had dug 1,200 entrenchments, foxholes and gun emplacements. The Axis plan sent the armour around the box while the Italian 132nd Armoured Division Ariete neutralised it.

On the morning of 27 May an Italian tank battalion of the Ariete Division, with 60 tanks, charged the minefield and wire. It lost 31 tanks and a self-propelled gun, and ten tanks that got through were knocked out by 75 mm anti-tank guns. From 2 June the position was shelled and bombed, and Stuka dive-bombers raided it more than twenty times, but the well-built positions were almost invulnerable. On 6 June the 90th Light Division attacked with pioneers, who cleared passages through the minefields.

From 8 June Rommel directed attacks from the north with part of the 15th Panzer Division, and the perimeter was forced back. On 10 June, with ammunition almost gone, the fort took the largest air raid of the siege, by 100 Stukas. After dark sappers cleared a narrow passage through the mines on the western face. Kœnig left at the head of the column in a car driven by Susan Travers, an Englishwoman serving with the Foreign Legion, and most of the brigade broke through troops of the 90th Light Division to reach lorries and ambulances sent by the British 7th Motor Brigade.

Thomas Buell and Ken Ford give the French losses as 141 dead, 229 wounded and 814 taken prisoner, with 53 guns and 50 vehicles; the Axis lost 3,300 dead or wounded and 227 captured, with 164 vehicles destroyed and 49 aircraft shot down. The defence had lengthened the Axis supply route around the Gazala line and gave the British time to recover from their defeat in the Cauldron, and the delay influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta. Tobruk still fell ten days later. Both sides used the battle for propaganda, and Winston Churchill declared the Free French to be the Fighting French.
battle-of-bitonto: Philip V of Spain had long aimed to recover Naples and Sicily, lost to the Habsburgs after the War of the Spanish Succession, and his wife Elisabeth Farnese had dynastic interests in Italy. When the War of the Polish Succession broke out in 1733, Spain and France signed the Treaty of the Escorial, the first of the Bourbon Family Compacts, to conquer the Habsburg lands in Italy. A Spanish army landed at Genoa and joined Charles of Parma, eldest son of Philip and Elisabeth, and 21,000 men marched through the Papal States. Charles entered Naples almost unopposed and proclaimed himself king of the Two Sicilies on 7 May 1734.

While 6,000 men blockaded the Austrian garrisons of Gaeta and Capua, Montemar pursued the retreating Austrians with 12,000 troops. The viceroy, Guido Visconti, fled by ship from Bari on 21 May, leaving Giuseppe Antonio, Prince of Belmonte, in command. Reinforced from Sicily, Belmonte moved to Bitonto on 24 May to fight before the Spanish grew stronger, holding low walls and two monasteries.

The Spanish arrived at daybreak on 25 May, about 14,000 strong by the reports Belmonte later received, with far more cavalry than the Austrians. After feints meant to draw the defenders out, they attacked. Around 10 am the Austrian cavalry broke and fled towards Bari, followed by Belmonte, and the rest of the army collapsed. The monasteries were taken by storm, and the garrison of the town surrendered the next day for want of ammunition and food. Local tradition holds that the Virgin Mary appeared to Montemar and stopped him from sacking the town, which then made the Immaculate Mary its patron.

At Bari the townspeople sided with the Spanish, and Belmonte surrendered 3,800 men to the local authorities, while several hundred who had escaped northwards reached Pescara. Gaeta held out until August, and Traun defended Capua until 30 November, when his garrison marched out with the honours of war. The Treaty of Vienna, which ended the war in 1738, confirmed the outcome. Charles made Montemar Duke of Bitonto and had Giovanni Antonio Medrano raise an obelisk on the battlefield.
battle-of-blaauwberg: Britain had first taken the Cape Colony from the Dutch East India Company in 1795, during the War of the First Coalition, but handed it back to the Batavian Republic under the Treaty of Amiens of 1802. When the Napoleonic Wars broke out in 1803 the colony again became a strategic concern: it lay midway on the sea route between Europe and India, and holding it, along with Mauritius, would let Britain dominate the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. A fleet was sent to the Cape in July 1805 to forestall French troopships that Napoleon had dispatched to reinforce the Batavian garrison.

The invasion force of around 7,000 veteran soldiers sailed from England in August 1805 with a squadron commanded by Home Riggs Popham, whose flagship was the 64-gun HMS Diadem. The main fleet entered Table Bay on 4 January 1806, and Janssens declared martial law and called up the militia.

After a delay caused by rough seas, Baird landed two brigades at Melkbosstrand on 6 and 7 January; 36 men of the 93rd drowned when their boat capsized. Janssens judged that victory was impossible but that the honour of the fatherland demanded a fight, meaning to strike and then withdraw inland until the French arrived. On 8 January the two armies met on the slopes of Blaauwberg. The Waldeck mercenaries in the Batavian centre fled before the 71st Foot without firing a shot, and the battalions beside them began to give way.

The French sailors and marines resisted longest, and the 71st Highlanders took the central guns only after a hard defence by their Javanese gunners. Janssens ordered a withdrawal. Baird had begun the battle with 5,399 men and lost 15 killed and 189 wounded; Janssens, with 2,049, lost either 337 or 353 in casualties and desertions.

Lieutenant-Colonel Hieronymus Casimir von Prophalow, commandant of Cape Town, sent out a white flag on 9 January, and the Articles of Capitulation for the town were signed on 10 January at a cottage in Papendorp, now Woodstock. Janssens held out in the Hottentots Holland Mountains for another week before signing the final articles on 18 January. Their terms were reasonably favourable: the Batavian troops were not treated as prisoners and were shipped back to the Netherlands in March. The Cape remained British until it became part of the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910.
battle-of-blenheim: By 1704 the War of the Spanish Succession was in its fourth year. Louis XIV of France sought to knock the Holy Roman Emperor, Leopold, out of the war by seizing Vienna and so gain a favourable peace. Maximilian II Emanuel and Marshal Ferdinand de Marsin threatened the city from Bavaria, a large army under the Duke of Vendôme in northern Italy posed a second danger, and Rákóczi's Hungarian revolt pressed from the east. The fall of Vienna would almost certainly have led to the collapse of the Grand Alliance.

The Duke of Marlborough resolved to relieve the danger. Leaving Bedburg on 19 May with about 21,000 men, he marched 400 km to the Danube in five weeks, concealing his destination, and by the time he arrived his army numbered 40,000.

After Marshal Tallard reached the Danube with 34,000 men and joined Maximilian and Marsin, Eugene and Marlborough combined their forces at Donauwörth by noon on 11 August. On 13 August the Allies advanced before dawn and reached Schwenningen, three kilometres from Blenheim, by about 06:00. The marshy Nebel stream fronted the French line. Marlborough would command 36,000 troops against Tallard's 33,000, while Eugene's 16,000 faced Maximilian and Marsin's 23,000.

Lieutenant-General John Cutts attacked the village of Blenheim, but repeated French volleys drove his men back, and Eugene's Prussians and Danes were repulsed at Lutzingen. In the centre Marlborough crossed the Nebel, and five English squadrons under Colonel Francis Palmes pushed back the elite Gens d'Armes. By 16:00 the Allied centre was planted among the French line, and large parts of the Franco-Bavarian army were penned in Blenheim and Oberglau. Marlborough then sent more infantry to storm Blenheim, where the fighting was hand to hand.

French losses were immense, over 27,000 killed, wounded and captured, among them Tallard, who was taken to England. Munich, Augsburg, Ingolstadt, Ulm and the rest of Bavaria soon fell to the Allies, and by the Treaty of Ilbersheim, signed on 7 November, Bavaria was placed under Austrian military rule.

Historians regard the battle as perhaps the most important of the war's early years, since it saved the Habsburg Empire and kept the Grand Alliance together, though it did not win the war. The war continued until 1714.
battle-of-blood-river: On 6 February 1838, two days after Piet Retief and King Dingane signed a land settlement at UmGungundlovu, Dingane invited Retief's party to a farewell, accused them of witchcraft and had them killed. His regiments then attacked Trekker encampments by night, killing an estimated 500 men, women, children and servants, most notably at Bloukrans. A mounted commando failed at Italeni in April, while a wagon laager held off General Ndlela kaSompisi's 10,000 men at Veglaer in August. The Trekkers then called on Andries Pretorius, appointed commander on 26 November 1838 with 64 wagons.

Pretorius backed Prince Mpande, Dingane's half-brother, who had fled with 17,000 followers. On 6 December, after meeting friendly Zulu chiefs at Danskraal, he proposed a vow that the commando and its descendants would celebrate the victory and build a church if they succeeded.

Avoiding the narrow defile at Italeni, Pretorius halted on 15 December and formed a laager beside a deep hippo pool in the Ncome River, which guarded two sides, with open ground in front. Movable barriers closed the gaps between the wheels, and two small cannon, one a 6-pound carronade named Grietjie, fired grapeshot. During the night six Zulu regiments, an estimated 20,000 or more, crossed the river, while Ndlela and his elite troops stayed on the far bank.

At dawn on 16 December the regiments under Dambuza stormed the laager repeatedly but could not break through. After two hours and four waves, Pretorius sent out mounted men, the Zulu scattered, and the Trekkers pursued them for three hours. In the Zulu telling, only the left horn of the army made contact, advancing under the mist. The historian S. P. Mackenzie doubts the reported number of Zulu dead.

UmGungundlovu was found deserted and burnt, and the bones of Retief and his men were buried there. The war went on: eleven days after the battle a Zulu prisoner led a Trekker party into a trap at the White Umfolozi River. Dingane was finally defeated in January 1840 at Maqongqe once Mpande joined the Trekkers, and Pretorius attended Mpande's crowning. For Afrikaner nationalism the battle came to signify God's intervention, and 16 December, once the Day of the Vow, is now the Day of Reconciliation. Monuments to both sides stand on either bank of the river.
battle-of-blue-waters: After the death of its ruler Berdi Beg Khan in 1359, the Golden Horde fell into succession disputes and wars that lasted two decades, and it began to split into separate districts. Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania took advantage of the disorder to campaign into Tatar lands, aiming to secure and extend the southern territories of the Grand Duchy, especially the Principality of Kiev. Kiev had come under semi-Lithuanian control after the Battle on the Irpin River in the early 1320s but still paid tribute to the Horde.

The battle was fought in the autumn of 1362 or 1363 on the banks of the Syniukha River, a left tributary of the Southern Bug. Algirdas first marched between the lower Dnieper and the Southern Bug and took the remaining territories of the Principality of Chernigov. He attacked the fortress of Korshev and is believed to have conquered lands of the former Principality of Pereyaslavl. In autumn his army crossed the Dnieper towards Podolia, where three Tatar beys gathered an army. The armies are believed to have met at present-day Torhovytsia, then called Sinie Vody, or Blue Waters.

The only description of the fighting is in the late and unreliable work of Maciej Stryjkowski, published in 1582. He says Algirdas drew up six groups in a half circle, that Tatar arrows had little effect, and that the Lithuanians and Ruthenians, with spears and swords, broke the Tatar front. Sons of Karijotas attacked the flanks with crossbows, and the Tatars retreated in disorder.

The victory brought Kiev and much of present-day Ukraine, including Podolia, under Lithuanian control and gave Lithuania access to the Black Sea. Algirdas left his son Vladimir in Kiev and entrusted Podolia to four sons of Karijotas. Lithuania now bordered the Grand Duchy of Moscow. The Principality of Moldavia, which supported Lithuania in the battle, asserted its independence from the Golden Horde.

Historians have given the battle little attention, partly for lack of sources. The main one, the Tale about Podolia, was written around the Lithuanian Civil War of 1432–38 and is political propaganda supporting Lithuanian claims to Podolia. Jan Długosz did not mention the battle at all. Interest grew in the 20th century, and a conference marked its 650th anniversary in 2012.
battle-of-boju: Wu was at first a minor state east of Chu, a major power of the Spring and Autumn period often at war with Jin to its north. To check Chu, Jin allied with Wu, trained its army and taught it to use chariots. Wu first defeated Chu in 584 BCE, and in the next 70 years the two fought ten wars, most of them won by Wu. Wu Zixu fled to Wu after King Ping of Chu, urged by the official Fei Wuji, killed his father Wu She and brother Wu Shang, and he helped Prince Guang take the throne as King Helü.

The Zuo Zhuan, compiled in the 4th century BCE, gives the fullest account. In 506 BCE Helü, his brother Fugai and Wu Zixu led the army, joined by the small states of Cai and Tang, up the Huai River and overland to the Han River. The Chu commanders Nang Wa and Shen Yin Shu agreed that Shen would go north to Fangcheng to destroy the Wu boats and block the passes behind them, but after he left, Nang Wa, warned that Shen would take the credit, crossed the river and attacked at once.

After three defeats Chu drew up at Boju. Fugai disobeyed the king and attacked with his own 5,000 men, and the Chu army broke; Nang Wa fled to Zheng. Wu pursued, striking the Chu troops at the Qingfa River as half had crossed, and after five victories took Ying. Shen Yin Shu, returning, won at Yongshi, but wounded three times he had an officer kill him rather than be captured.

In 505 BCE Qin and Chu together defeated Wu in several battles. Fugai went home and declared himself king, forcing Helü to return and defeat him, and King Zhao of Chu came back to Ying. The historian Fan Wenlan counts the war the first large-scale war of the Eastern Zhou. Chu took long to recover, but Wu could not hold its gains and was itself conquered by Yue in 473 BCE. Sun Tzu's command rests on Sima Qian's Shiji; the Zuo Zhuan does not mention him.
battle-of-bosworth-field: In 1471 the Yorkists defeated their rivals at the battles of Barnet and Tewkesbury, and the House of Lancaster was left with no direct claimants. Henry Tudor, whose mother Lady Margaret Beaufort was a great-granddaughter of John of Gaunt, had only a weak claim, and Edward IV regarded him as a nobody. The Tudors took refuge in Brittany under Duke Francis II. Richard III took the throne in 1483, after his twelve-year-old nephew Edward V was declared illegitimate. The boy and his younger brother soon disappeared, and their fate remains a mystery. Henry's first invasion in 1483 foundered in a storm.

Henry sailed from Harfleur with thirty ships and landed at Mill Bay, near Dale, on 7 August 1485, and marched inland through Wales. Richard learned of the landing on 11 August and called his lords to Leicester. The Yorkist army, estimated at 7,500 to 12,000 men, formed on a ridge in three groups under Richard, the Duke of Norfolk and the Earl of Northumberland. Henry's force, estimated at 5,000 to 8,000, was commanded by the experienced Earl of Oxford. Lord Stanley and Sir William Stanley stood nearby with 4,000 to 6,000 men, lending Henry only four knights at first.

Norfolk's vanguard attacked but struggled against Oxford's men, and some of Norfolk's troops fled. Northumberland took no action when signalled to help the king, so Richard gambled on a charge across the field to kill Henry. When the Stanleys saw the king's knights separated from his army, Sir William led his men to Henry's aid and Richard was surrounded and killed. According to Polydore Vergil, Lord Stanley found Richard's circlet, and Henry was proclaimed king on Crown Hill near Stoke Golding.

Henry seized the crown by right of conquest and married Elizabeth of York. Richard was the last English monarch to fall in battle. Henry hired chroniclers to present his reign as a modern age that began in 1485, and Tudor writers depicted Bosworth as a clash of good and evil, as Shakespeare does in his play Richard III. The battle is poorly recorded; contemporary accounts come from the Croyland Chronicle and from the foreigners Vergil, Jean Molinet and Diego de Valera. The site is disputed: surveys by the Battlefields Trust between 2003 and 2009 suggested a place about three kilometres south-west of Ambion Hill, where a silver-gilt boar badge was found among lead shot.
battle-of-bouvines: The battle ended the Anglo-French War of 1213–1214. Ferrand of Flanders wanted back Aire-sur-la-Lys and Saint-Omer, which he had lost to Philip II of France under the Treaty of Pont-à-Vendin, and he joined a coalition that included Emperor Otto IV, King John of England, Duke Henry I of Brabant and Count William I of Holland. John planned the campaign: he would draw the French southward while Otto marched on Paris from the north. The allies in the north moved slowly, and after two encounters with the French John retreated to Aquitaine on 3 July.

Philip had 6,000 to 8,000 men by 23 July, and Otto just under 9,000. Philip offered battle on 27 July on the plain east of Bouvines, and Otto, surprised by his speed, attacked what was then the French rearguard. On the allied left the Flemish knights fought for three hours until Ferrand was captured and their morale collapsed.

In the centre allied infantry with hooked pikes pulled Philip from his horse, but his armour turned a lance and a knight gave him a fresh horse. French knights then nearly captured Otto, who fled, and they took the imperial standard of eagle and dragon. On the allied right William Longespée was unhorsed and captured. The last stand was Renaud de Dammartin's, with a ring of Brabant pikemen, until a charge overran it. Night was falling, and there was no pursuit.

The counts of Boulogne and Flanders and Longespée were captured, with twenty-five barons and over a hundred knights. Philip returned to Paris in triumph with his prisoners. Otto retreated to Harzburg and was soon overthrown by Frederick II, and John obtained a five-year truce on lenient terms. Renaud was held chained in a small cell and committed suicide in 1227. The battle ended all hope of restoring the Angevin Empire and weakened John so far that he soon had to accept Magna Carta in 1215. Jean Favier called it one of the most decisive and symbolic battles in the history of France.
battle-of-boyaca: In early July 1819 Simón Bolívar's patriot army surprised the Spanish by crossing the Andes through the Páramo de Pisba into the Boyacá region, though the march had weakened it. Viceroy Juan de Sámano ordered Colonel José María Barreiro, commanding the III Division of the Expeditionary Army of Costa Firme, to intercept Bolívar and stop him reaching the capital Santa Fe. The two forces met at the Battle of Vargas Swamp on 25 July, where Bolívar won narrowly. On 3 August he feigned a retreat across the Chicamocha River near Paipa, then countermarched by night and took the Toca road, and on 4 August the patriots occupied Tunja, where they gained 600 rifles and cut Barreiro's line to the capital.

On 7 August Barreiro's army left Motavita at 3:30 a.m. to rejoin the Royal Road at Casa de Teja, near the bridge over the swollen Teatinos River. From a height near Tunja Bolívar saw the royalists and ordered Santander and Anzoátegui to destroy Barreiro wherever they found him. Santander's vanguard drove the Spanish vanguard of Colonel Francisco Jiménez back across the bridge, while Colonel Antonio Béjar forded the river to attack it from the rear. Anzoátegui cut the royalist rearguard off from its vanguard and attacked its flanks with the Barcelona and Bravos de Páez battalions, the British Legion and the Rifles Battalion under Arthur Sandes.

Sandes's charge disrupted the Spanish artillery, which had been carried unassembled, and patriot lancers then broke the royalist infantry. Barreiro and his officers dismounted in trying to stop the rout and were captured. Santander took the bridge with a bayonet charge, and the Spanish commander on it, Colonel Juan Tolrá, was killed. The fighting ended shortly after 4:30 p.m. after little more than two hours. The patriots had about 66 casualties, with 13 dead and 53 wounded; Barreiro's division lost 100 dead, 150 wounded and 1,600 captured.

Viceroy Sámano learned of the defeat at about 10 p.m. on 8 August and left Santa Fe at 9:00 a.m. the next day, disguised as a peasant, leaving behind some 900,000 pesos and the government's archives. Bolívar entered the city on 10 August. On the orders of Santander, Barreiro and 38 others were executed in Bogotá on 11 October 1819, under the Decree of War to the Death. The victory opened the way to the republic of Gran Colombia, created in December 1819, and to the later patriot victories at Carabobo, Pichincha, Junín and Ayacucho. In Colombia 7 August is a national holiday and Army Day.
battle-of-breadfield: Turkish raiders had struck Transylvania and Vojvodina several times in 1474 and 1475, emptying some villages. After the Ottoman–Venetian War ended in the spring of 1479, a large Ottoman army, mostly Akıncı raiders, gathered at Szendrő, today Smederevo. King Matthias ordered Stephen V Báthory, Voivode of Transylvania, and Pál Kinizsi to mobilise. Led by Ali Koca Bey, the Ottomans entered Transylvania on 9 October near Kelnek, taking Hungarians, Vlachs and Saxons captive, and on 13 October camped on the Breadfield near the Saxon village of Alkenyér by the river Maros. The Wallachian prince Basarab cel Tânăr had urged the campaign and brought 1,000–2,000 infantry.

Estimates of the Ottoman force range from 100,000 in Jan Długosz to Matthias's own figure of 43–45,000; a more probable number is between 6 and 20 thousand. The Christian army of Hungarian, Szekler, Serbian and Saxon forces and Vlach volunteers, the last under the former Wallachian ruler Basarab Laiotă cel Bătrân, numbered about 12,000 to 15,000. Báthory waited until the raiders were slowed by their loot and attacked in the afternoon, Kinizsi on the right, Serbian light cavalry under Vuk Grgurević and Demetrius Jakšić on the left and Báthory in the centre.

Báthory fell from his horse and was nearly captured before a nobleman, Antal Nagy, carried him away. The Ottomans had the upper hand until Kinizsi charged with the heavy cavalry and 900 Serbs under Jakšić, forcing Ali Bey back and then breaking Isa Bey in the centre. Survivors fled into the mountains, where local men killed most of them.

Several thousand Ottomans died, among them Isa Bey and Malkoçoğlu, along with about a thousand of their Wallachian allies; the Hungarians lost about 3,000 men. In 1480 Kinizsi raided Serbia and defeated Ali Koca Bey several times. The victory was a great psychological boost for Hungary.
battle-of-breitenfeld-1631: Swedish intervention in the Thirty Years' War began in June 1630, when Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania with nearly 18,000 troops. Hopes of widespread German support largely failed, and by the end of 1630 his only new ally was Christian William, whose capital Magdeburg was besieged by Tilly. The Sack of Magdeburg in May 1631 warned the German princes of the consequences of an Imperial victory. The 1631 Treaty of Bärwalde, provided funds for the Swedes and their Protestant allies, and Gustavus raised his forces to around 36,000. He allied with John George I, Elector of Saxony, and the combined army marched on Leipzig, where Tilly was based.

The battle began at noon on 17 September 1631 with a cannonade of about two hours. The Swedes fired three to five volleys to each Imperial one, and Tilly's tightly packed tercios made easy targets for Torstenson's guns. At two o'clock Pappenheim charged the Swedish right wing on his own initiative, but Swedish musketeers placed among the cavalry broke each attempt. Imperial cavalry meanwhile routed the Saxon centre and left, and the Saxons fled.

Tilly then turned his infantry against the Swedish left under Horn. Dust and the wind disordered the manoeuvre, and Horn bent his line back and held on, with Colonel Caldenbach's regiment sacrificed to delay the attackers. At about five o'clock Gustavus Adolphus led a cavalry charge up the Galgenberg, seized the Imperial guns and turned them on Tilly's infantry, while other Swedish brigades cut off its retreat towards Leipzig.

Imperial and Catholic League losses were between 7,000 and 8,000 killed, with around 6,000 captured, and Tilly lost his artillery, his war chest and 120 banners, which were sent to the Riddarholmen Church in Stockholm. The Swedes lost 3,550 men and the Saxons between 2,000 and 3,000. Captured Imperial soldiers were soon recruited into the Swedish ranks.

It was the first major Catholic defeat in a war then 13 years old, and it sent shockwaves around Europe. A council of war at Halle weighed a direct march on Vienna, but the Saxons were sent towards the Austrian Hereditary Lands and Vienna while the Swedes moved south-west towards the Rhine. Historians have long questioned that choice, though it cannot be known whether a march on Vienna would have brought favourable terms in 1632. The Swedish brigade of mobile battalions had also shown its advantage over the tercio.
battle-of-britain: Germany had rapidly overwhelmed France and the Low Countries in the Battle of France, leaving Britain to face the threat of invasion by sea. The German high command recognised the difficulty of a seaborne attack while the Royal Navy controlled the English Channel, and its primary objective was to compel Britain to accept a negotiated peace. On 16 July 1940 Adolf Hitler ordered preparation of Operation Sea Lion, an amphibious and airborne assault to follow once the Luftwaffe had air superiority over the Channel. Britain officially dates the battle from 10 July to 31 October 1940.

The Luftwaffe first attacked coastal convoys and ports. On 1 August it was directed to achieve air superiority and incapacitate RAF Fighter Command, and twelve days later it shifted its attacks to airfields and infrastructure. The RAF's Hurricanes and Spitfires faced the Bf 109, and Fighter Command relied on the Chain Home radar and a system of reporting chains named for Hugh Dowding. About 20 per cent of the pilots were from outside Britain, among them 145 Poles, 127 New Zealanders and 112 Canadians.

On 7 September the Luftwaffe began the night attacks on London and other cities known as the Blitz. At a conference on 14 September Hitler acknowledged that it had not gained the air superiority that Sea Lion required. On 15 September the Luftwaffe made its largest bombing attack yet, which forced the whole of the RAF to defend London and the south-east and ended in a decisive British victory. In September RAF Bomber Command night raids also disrupted the German preparation of converted barges.

On 19 September Hitler ordered a reduction in work on Sea Lion. The Luftwaffe proved unable to sustain daylight raids, though its night bombing continued until 11 May 1941. By 2 November the RAF fielded 1,796 pilots, over 40 per cent more than in July. The battle was the first major military campaign fought entirely by air forces and the first major defeat of Germany's military forces. Churchill summed it up with the words, Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few, and the pilots have been known as The Few ever since.
