battle-of-brunanburh: After Æthelstan defeated the Vikings at York in 927, Constantine of Scotland, Hywel Dda of Deheubarth, Ealdred I of Bamburgh and Owain of Strathclyde accepted his overlordship at Eamont, near Penrith. He invaded Scotland in 934 with a large military and naval force; John of Worcester gave as the cause Constantine's violation of the treaty of 927. The army harassed the Scots as far as Kincardineshire and the navy as far as Caithness, but was never engaged. It then became clear that Æthelstan could be beaten only by an alliance of his enemies, and Olaf Guthfrithson, king of Dublin, led one with Constantine II and Owain; according to John of Worcester, Constantine was Olaf's father-in-law.

In August 937 Olaf sailed from Dublin to join Constantine and Owain. Æthelstan's army went north through Mercia and met them at Brunanburh. According to the Old English poem in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the English fought all day and finally forced the invaders to flee, pursuing them until nightfall. Olaf escaped by ship to Dublin and Constantine to Scotland; Owain's fate is not mentioned. The Annals of Ulster call the battle great, lamentable and horrible, and record that several thousands of Norsemen fell, among them five kings and seven earls of Olaf's army. Constantine's son died, and so did two of Æthelstan's cousins, Ælfwine and Æthelwine.

More than forty medieval texts mention the battle. Egil's Saga, written in Old Norse in the early 13th century, gives detail found nowhere else, but historians such as Sarah Foot doubt it is a reliable narrative. Later chroniclers differ on matters such as the size of Olaf's fleet, given as 615 ships by Symeon of Durham, and on whether Constantine was killed.

The victory preserved the unity of England, and Michael Livingston calls it the moment when Englishness came of age. Alfred Smyth ranked it above every other single battle in Anglo-Saxon history before Hastings, though he thinks its effects beyond Æthelstan's reign have been overstated. Alex Woolf calls it a pyrrhic victory: the campaign ended in stalemate, and after Æthelstan died in 939 Olaf became king of Northumbria without resistance. The Northumbrians submitted to southern kingship only in 954.

The site is unknown. More than forty places have been proposed, though most historians think northern England most plausible. Bromborough on the Wirral is the only surviving place name derived from Old English Brunanburh, and a local volunteer group found a field there with many artefacts, but others dispute the evidence.
battle-of-brunkeberg: In May 1471 the Riksmöte at Arboga elected Sten Sture the Elder Lord Protector of Sweden. Known as Herr Sten, he favoured Swedish secession from the Kalmar Union and drew his support above all from the peasantry, from Stockholm and from the Bergslagen mining region, whose trade with German cities such as Lübeck often clashed with the Union's Danish foreign policy. Later writers often recast the battle as a national war of liberation against Danish oppressors, but most of the combatants on both sides were Swedish, and the conflict rested chiefly on economic and political interests.

Christian I sailed to Sweden with an army to unseat Sture. He moored his ships off Skeppsholmen and camped on Brunkebergsåsen, a ridge a short distance north of Stockholm, which was then confined to the island of the Old Town.

On 10 October Sten Sture and Nils Bosson Sture led their troops north towards the area of present-day Hötorget. The plan was to catch the king's army in a vice: Sten would attack from the west, Nils from the east, and Knut Posse would sally from the city itself. Early in the fighting Christian was hit in the face by handgonne fire, lost several teeth and had to leave the field.

The battle turned when Nils's men broke out of the forest north of the ridge just as Posse attacked from the town, cutting off a Danish contingent at the Klara monastery. Christian fell back towards the island of Käpplingen, now the Blasieholmen peninsula, but Sture's troops destroyed the makeshift bridge his men had built, and many drowned.

The victory made Sture's power as regent secure for the rest of his life and weakened the Kalmar Union considerably. Legend holds that he prayed to Saint George before the battle; he later commissioned a statue of Saint George and the Dragon from the Lübeck sculptor Bernt Notke for the Storkyrkan church, an allegory of his struggle against Christian, together with an altar to the saint. A Saint George and the Dragon sculpture dedicated to the battle in Stockholm's Köpmantorget was unveiled on 10 October 1912, the 441st anniversary of the battle.
battle-of-bulgarophygon: Under Boris I Bulgaria had become Christian, and the Council of Preslav in 893 replaced Greek with Old Bulgarian as the language of the church and named his third son Simeon as the next prince. Members of Emperor Leo VI's court then moved the market for Bulgarian goods from Constantinople to Thessaloniki, where merchants paid higher taxes. When Leo ignored Simeon's protest, Simeon invaded Byzantine Thrace in what has sometimes been called the first commercial war in Europe, defeating an army under Prokopios Krenites and Kourtikios and cutting off the noses of its captured Khazar guardsmen.

Leo turned to diplomacy. At the end of 894 the Byzantine navy ferried the Magyars across the Danube, and they defeated Simeon in Dobruja and plundered as far as the outskirts of Preslav. Simeon stalled the envoy Leo Choirosphaktes while he allied with the Pechenegs, and in the decisive battle the Magyars suffered a devastating defeat, after which they moved west into Pannonia.

Simeon broke off the talks and invaded Thrace again, encouraged by the death of the general Nikephoros Phokas. The Byzantines brought all their themes and tagmata from the Arab front under the Domestic of the Schools Leo Katakalon. At Boulgarophygon in the summer of 896 his army was routed; the protovestiarios Theodosius, second in command, was killed, and Katakalon escaped with a few survivors. One soldier is said to have left the world to become the ascetic Luke the Stylite. Simeon marched on Constantinople, and according to al-Tabari Leo armed Arab prisoners of war against him before the Bulgarians agreed to negotiate.

The peace lasted formally until about Leo VI's death in 912. In exchange for the tribute, Bulgaria returned allegedly 120,000 captured Byzantine soldiers and civilians, received the land between the Black Sea and Strandzha, and promised not to invade Byzantine territory. Simeon began a building programme in Preslav meant to rival Constantinople and imposed his authority on Serbia by recognising Petar Gojnikovic as its ruler. The lesson of the Magyar invasion served him in 917, when he kept Byzantium from allying with the Serbs or Pechenegs before the Battle of Achelous.
battle-of-buxar: The battle was fought on 22–23 October 1764 at Buxar, a strong fortified town on the banks of the Ganges in Bihar, about 130 kilometres west of Patna. The East India Company force under Major Hector Munro numbered 7,072, about 1,800 British regulars and 5,300 sepoys. Against it stood the combined armies of the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and his allies Mir Qasim, Nawab of Bengal, Maharaja Balwant Singh of Benares and Shuja-ud-Daula, Nawab of Awadh and Grand Vizier to the emperor, estimated at over 40,000 men.

Mirza Najaf Khan commanded the right flank of the Mughal army and advanced first, at daybreak. The Company lines formed within twenty minutes and turned the advance back, and by midday the battle was over. As his forces withdrew, Shuja-ud-Daula blew up large tumbrils and three magazines of gunpowder. Munro pursued him towards the Karmanasa River, and Shuja-ud-Daula destroyed the boat-bridge after crossing, abandoning the emperor and some of his own troops. Mir Qasim fled and was exiled by Shuja-ud-Daula, while Najaf Khan rallied the remaining forces around the emperor.

John William Fortescue gave British casualties as 847 and those of the Indian allies as 2,000 dead; another source counts 69 European and 664 sepoy casualties and 6,000 on the Mughal side. The victors captured 133 guns and over a million rupees. The emperor chose to negotiate with the British, and Shuja-ud-Daula, pursued westward, eventually surrendered. Mir Qasim carried away gemstones worth 3 million rupees but died in poverty in 1777.

The defeated rulers signed the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765, which granted the Company the diwani, the right to collect revenue from Bengal, Bihar and Orissa on behalf of the Mughal emperor. In 1772 the Company abolished local rule and took complete control of the province of Bengal-Bihar. The battle is seen as the beginning of the end of Mughal political control, and as exposing the lack of unity and coordination among the Nawabs and the emperor, which made it easier for the British to defeat them.
battle-of-buyur-lake: In 1387 a Ming campaign forced the Mongol commander Naghachu and his Uriyankhad horde to surrender. Encouraged by this success, the Hongwu Emperor ordered General Lan Yu in December 1387 to lead a campaign against the Northern Yuan khan Tögüs Temür, and Lan set out with an army of 150,000 soldiers.

Lan Yu marched through the Great Wall to Daning and on towards Qingzhou, where spies told him that Tögüs Temür was camped near Buir Lake. The army crossed the Gobi Desert northwards. Within 40 li of the lake it still had not found the horde, and Lan was disheartened, but his subordinate General Wang Bi, Marquis of Dingyuan, reminded him that it would be foolish to return with so large an army and nothing achieved.

Learning that the Mongols were camped north-east of the lake, the Ming approached under cover of darkness and a sandstorm. On 18 May 1388 they attacked and caught the Northern Yuan forces off guard. Many Mongols were taken, but Tögüs Temür escaped.

The Hongwu Emperor praised Lan Yu in a proclamation that compared him with Wei Qing, the general of the Han, made him Duke of Liang with a stipend of 3,000 shi and gave him the honorific of Grand Tutor. Six of his subordinates were made marquises, and the other officers and soldiers were generously rewarded.

Historians give different tallies of the captives. Langlois counts 100 members of the khan's family, among them his younger son, 3,000 princes and their followers, 77,000 people of the camp, seals of office and 150,000 animals, with the khan and his eldest son escaping; Dreyer gives 3,000 notables and 70,000 ordinary Mongols, including the crown prince and his younger brother; Tsai names the khan's second son and General Qarajang. Fleeing, Tögüs Temür reached the Tula River, where the chieftain Yesüder murdered him.
battle-of-cabira: Rome had already fought Mithridates VI of Pontus twice. In the first war, after taking the province of Asia, he had massacred 80,000 Roman and other Italian civilians in the Asian Vespers. When King Nicomedes IV of Bithynia died in 74 BCE and left his kingdom to Rome, Mithridates invaded it in 73 BCE, defeated the governor Marcus Aurelius Cotta and besieged him in Chalcedon. Lucullus, consul with Cotta and newly governor of Cilicia, took command of the Roman forces in Asia Minor.

Mithridates moved on Cyzicus, an ally of Rome, but Lucullus trapped his army on the Cyzicus peninsula, starved it, and defeated his admiral Marcus Varius off Lemnos. Of the 300,000 men who had set out for Bithynia, only 20,000 effective troops returned to Pontus. In 72 BCE, leaving Heraclea Pontica to Cotta, Lucullus marched through Galatia, whose people were glad to supply him, and let his troops plunder the Pontic heartland.

Mithridates rebuilt an army of 40,000 men, 4,000 of them cavalry, near Cabira. Lucullus suffered a setback in a first skirmish and had to withdraw, and further skirmishes followed, as well as an attempt on his life. His supplies now came north from Cappadocia, an ally of Rome. Pontic cavalry attacked a convoy escorted by ten cohorts under the legate Sornatius and suffered heavy losses.

Mithridates then sent some 4,000 cavalry and infantry against a second convoy under Marcus Fabius Hadrianus. In a narrow valley that hampered the horsemen, the Romans counter-attacked and destroyed half the force. The king tried to hide the scale of the defeat, but Hadrianus marched past his camp in full array with the spoils. Talk of retreat spread, and when Mithridates prepared to flee, his army fell apart. Lucullus attacked the fleeing troops, and the Romans took the camp, killed everyone left in it and began to loot.

Mithridates escaped nearly penniless. Before leaving he sent a eunuch, Bacchus, to the royal palace to see to the deaths of his sisters, wives and concubines. Lucullus pressed the sieges across Pontus and organised it as a new Roman province, and sent Appius Claudius to demand that Tigranes hand Mithridates over. Tigranes refused and prepared for war, and in 69 BCE Lucullus marched his legions into Armenia.
battle-of-caishi: The Treaty of Shaoxing of 1142 had fixed the border between the Song and the Jin along the Huai River, and relations were mostly peaceful until 1161. Wanyan Liang, who became Jin emperor in 1150 after killing his cousin Emperor Xizong, aimed to rule all of China. From 1158 he prepared an invasion, drafting Han as well as Jurchen soldiers and building a fleet, while the unpopular draft provoked revolts and a Khitan rising. He left Kaifeng on 15 October 1161, and his armies crossed the Huai on 28 October against little resistance.

Wanyan Liang ordered his army to cross the Yangzi at Caishi, south of modern Nanjing. Yu Yunwen, a civil official who happened to be there to distribute awards, gathered the scattered Song forces into a single command, while the prime minister Chen Kangbo directed the navy. On 26 November the Jin embarked in ships many of which were hastily and poorly built. Song paddle-wheel ships, hidden behind the island of Qibao Shan, attacked from both sides, and their trebuchets threw thunderclap bombs of gunpowder, lime and sulphur. The Jin were beaten again the next day, burned their remaining ships and fell back to Yangzhou.

Figures vary widely. A Song source puts 18,000 Song soldiers at Caishi, one document claims 400,000 to 600,000 Jin, and the historian Herbert Franke argues that the larger figure describes the Jin army before it crossed the Huai. Traditional Chinese historiography ranked the victory with the Battle of Fei River of 383.

Disaffected officers assassinated Wanyan Liang on 15 December 1161; Emperor Shizong had already been enthroned in a coup in his absence. The Jin withdrew in 1162, and a peace treaty of 1165 ended the war with the Huai border unchanged. The battle also shows the growth of the Song navy, whose paddle-wheel ships were built in many sizes between 1132 and 1183.
battle-of-callao: Spain, seeking to recover prestige in its former American colonies, seized Peru's guano-rich Chincha Islands and demanded an indemnity for the murder of two Spanish citizens in Lambayeque. President Juan Antonio Pezet, judging Peru's navy too weak, began handing over guano, and in November 1865 Colonel Mariano Ignacio Prado took power in a coup and organised resistance. After the indecisive Battle of Abtao in February 1866, Méndez Núñez bombarded the undefended Chilean port of Valparaíso and then turned on the well-defended Callao, arriving on 25 April with seven warships and seven auxiliaries carrying 252 guns, led by the ironclad Numancia.

Callao's forts had been reinforced with five British-made 22-ton Blakely rifles and four Armstrong guns in two armoured turrets, Junín and La Merced; in all the Peruvians had 52 guns ashore, 13 more on warships, and two locally built ironclads, Loa and Victoria. American, British and French ships watched. The Spanish entered the bay at 10:00 and Numancia opened fire at 11:50. A shot struck Numancia and wounded Núñez, but her armour held. A Blakely shell wrecked the boilers of Villa de Madrid, which had to be towed away, and an Armstrong shot pierced Berenguela at the waterline.

A shot from Blanca destroyed La Merced, killing or wounding 93 men, among them the Minister of War and Navy, José Gálvez Egúsquiza. Other batteries were silenced, and many of the 3,000 Peruvian troops entrenched outside the forts were hit. By 17:00 Santa Rosa had three guns left firing, and the badly wounded Núñez ordered the fleet to cease fire. The damaged ships spent several days at San Lorenzo island tending their wounded.

In Spain the battle was hailed as a victory; Núñez received the Grand Cross of the Order of Carlos III and was promoted to Lieutenant General, and before the Battle of Lissa the Austrian admiral Wilhelm von Tegetthoff urged his crews to imitate the Spanish at Callao. Peruvians, for their part, counted it a victory, the day they stopped Spain from recolonising South America, and the American eyewitness T. H. Nelson wrote that the damage to the town was barely noticeable. It was the last battle of the war between Spain and Peru; the Spanish expedition ended officially in 1868, but peace was not signed until 1879. A square and a metro station in Madrid bear the name Callao.
battle-of-camperdown: In the winter of 1794–1795 the French Republic overran the Dutch Republic and reorganised it as the Batavian Republic, which gained France the Dutch fleet anchored off the Texel. Britain answered with a force of small, old ships based at Yarmouth under the 65-year-old Admiral Adam Duncan. In the spring of 1797 the Spithead and Nore mutinies paralysed the British fleets, and at one point Duncan was left with only his own Venerable and the Adamant to contain the whole Dutch fleet.

By September the mutinies were over and Duncan's fleet, which had grown to 17 ships of the line, was blockading the Texel. De Winter had abandoned a plan to join the French at Brest for an invasion of Ireland. When the British returned to Yarmouth for supplies in October, he led his fleet into the North Sea, and on its return to the coast Duncan intercepted it.

De Winter formed a line of battle close to the shore. Fearing that the Dutch would reach the shallows, Duncan abandoned his earlier signals and ordered each ship to steer for and engage her opponent; in poor visibility his line broke into two loose groups. At 12:05 he signalled close action, and soon afterwards Onslow's flagship Monarch broke through the Dutch rear, where superior British numbers overwhelmed the ships of the Dutch rearguard.

In the north the fight centred on the flagships, Duncan's Venerable engaging de Winter's Vrijheid. Onslow sent his least damaged ships to help, and Powerful and Director joined the attack on Vrijheid at 14:00. As the unengaged Dutch ships turned away for the shore, the damaged ones struck their colours one by one, until only the flagship remained in action.

Duncan refused de Winter's sword and shook his hand instead. He did not follow the fleeing ships into the shoals, but took his prizes home; his convoy began to reach Yarmouth on 17 October, and on 20 October he was created Viscount Duncan of Camperdown. King George III pardoned 180 men condemned for their part in the Nore Mutiny. The losses of the Batavian Navy gave Britain naval superiority in the North Sea and were a serious blow to French hopes of invading Ireland.
battle-of-cannae: Hannibal crossed the Pyrenees and the Alps in 218 BCE and beat the Romans at the Trebia and at Lake Trasimene. The Romans then appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus dictator, and he avoided pitched battles and cut Hannibal's supplies. The policy grew unpopular, and Rome feared its allies would defect. In 216 BCE the consuls Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus were given a newly raised army of unprecedented size, about 86,000 Roman and allied troops, and told to engage Hannibal.

In the spring Hannibal seized the supply depot at Cannae in Apulia, between the Romans and their supplies. The consuls found him on the left bank of the Aufidus. Roman law made them alternate command daily, and Varro commanded on the day of the battle. The sources, none contemporary, make him reckless, though some historians suggest he was made a scapegoat.

The Romans massed their infantry in a deeper formation than usual to break through Hannibal's centre. Hannibal advanced his centre, held by Hispanics and Celts, into a crescent and kept his African infantry on the flanks. As the Roman centre pressed forward, the Africans wheeled in on its flanks while Carthaginian cavalry closed behind, surrounding most of the army, which was slaughtered.

The figures are uncertain. Polybius gives 70,000 Roman and allied infantry killed and 10,000 captured; Livy gives a considerably lower count of the dead. Among the dead were the consul Paullus and 29 of 48 military tribunes. Only about 15,000 Romans survived, mostly from the camp garrisons.

Rome was gripped by panic. The authorities consulted the Sibylline Books, sent Quintus Fabius Pictor to the Delphic oracle and buried four people alive as a sacrifice. They lowered the draft age and enlisted criminals, debtors and slaves. Capua and other Italian cities went over to Carthage, but Rome refused Hannibal's offer to ransom prisoners and fought on until victory at Zama 14 years later. The defeat led Rome to adopt smaller, more flexible infantry units, and Cannae became the model of a battle of annihilation, studied by later commanders such as Alfred von Schlieffen.
battle-of-cape-matapan: In late March 1941, as the Mediterranean Fleet covered troop movements to Greece, the Bletchley Park cryptanalyst Mavis Batey read the Italian naval Enigma for the first time. Intercepts reported that an Italian fleet under Admiral Angelo Iachino, with one battleship, six heavy and two light cruisers and destroyers, was sailing to attack the convoys supplying British forces. To hide the breakthrough, the British arranged a plausible visible reason for the detection, a directed reconnaissance flight. Admiral Andrew Cunningham also slipped away from a golf club in Alexandria to board his flagship, HMS Warspite, unseen. The Italians had been wrongly told by the Germans that the British had one operational battleship and no carrier.

On 28 March the Italian heavy cruisers met Vice-Admiral Henry Pridham-Wippell's cruisers south of Gavdos and chased them, but their fire scored no significant hits. When Iachino's battleship Vittorio Veneto joined and opened fire, the British cruisers withdrew. Torpedo bombers from HMS Formidable attacked that day. At 15:09 one hit the battleship's outer port propeller and brought her to a halt for a time, and a third attack in the evening hit the heavy cruiser Pola, which drifted to a stop. Zara and Fiume were ordered back to help her.

At about 22:00 British radar detected the Italian ships, which had none and had not prepared their main guns for night action. Cunningham's battleships Barham, Valiant and Warspite closed to 3,800 yards and opened fire. Fiume and Zara were destroyed within minutes, and the destroyers Vittorio Alfieri and Giosue Carducci were sunk. Pola was sunk by torpedoes shortly after 04:00. The Allies rescued 1,015 survivors and the Italian hospital ship Gradisca took another 160. Italian losses were up to 2,303 sailors; the Allies lost one torpedo bomber and its crew of three.

The naval historian Vincent O'Hara called the battle Italy's heaviest defeat at sea but hardly decisive. The Italian fleet did not enter the eastern Mediterranean again until the fall of Crete two months later. Iachino wrote that it showed Italian inferiority in air-naval cooperation and in night-fighting technology. Cunningham regretted that his destroyers had failed to find Vittorio Veneto. The role of codebreaking, kept secret for decades, was an exception to the rule that Bletchley Park rarely learned the effect of its work: Cunningham visited a few weeks later to thank Dilly Knox and his staff. Records were declassified in 1978, and earlier accounts crediting a spy with a codebook were later contradicted.
battle-of-cape-passaro: The Treaty of Utrecht of 11 April 1713 gave the Kingdom of Sicily to Savoy and Naples, Milan and Sardinia to Austria. In Spain, Cardinal Giulio Alberoni rebuilt the royal administration and promised Philip V a chance to recover Sicily and Naples. When Britain and France proposed that Victor Amadeus II of Savoy exchange Sicily for Sardinia, the emperor's arrest of the Spanish Grand Inquisitor José Molinés at Milan gave Spain its pretext. A Spanish fleet took Sardinia in 1717, and on 18 June 1718 another left Barcelona carrying 36,000 infantry and 8,000 horse under the Marquis of Lede to Sicily.

Most of the island fell with little resistance, except Messina. Admiral George Byng, who had sailed from Spithead with twenty ships of the line, carried 2,000 German infantry to Messina. Trusting Alberoni's letters that Byng meant no harm, the Spanish commanders José Antonio de Gaztañeta and José Patiño took their fleet south towards Malta.

The Spanish fleet sailed in disorder and by morning lay in three separate groups. Byng sent Captain George Walton with Canterbury and five other ships after the rear under the Marquis of Mari, who drove his ships ashore off Avola and set them on fire. The main British force overhauled Gaztañeta's six ships of the line, taking Santa Rosa, San Carlos and Príncipe de Asturias. The flagship San Felipe fought for hours against Kent, Superb and Byng's Barfleur and struck only at nightfall, Gaztañeta wounded in the leg. Some ships escaped to Malta; Santa Isabel surrendered the next morning. The British lost no more than 500 killed or wounded.

Walton reported that he had taken and destroyed all the Spanish ships on the coast. The captured San Felipe later blew up by accident, killing 50 Spanish prisoners and 160 of her British prize crew. The Spanish army in Sicily was cut off. Alberoni banned news of the expedition, issued letters of marque and seized British ships in Spanish ports. Britain declared war on 26 December and France on 9 January the following year. Alberoni's answer, a Jacobite expedition to Britain, was scattered by a storm off Cape Finisterre, and about 400 men who landed in Scotland were defeated at Glenshiel.
battle-of-caporetto: Through spring and summer 1917 the Italians launched repeated offensives on the Isonzo front, the most successful being the 11th Battle of the Isonzo. Emperor Karl, expecting a breakthrough as both sides ran out of men, asked Kaiser Wilhelm II for German forces. In August 1917 Paul von Hindenburg and Arthur Arz von Straußenburg agreed to send troops from the Eastern Front, over Erich Ludendorff's opposition. In September experts led by the chemist Otto Hahn found a suitable site for a gas attack in the quiet Caporetto sector, where a good road ran west through a mountain valley to the Venetian Plain. A new 14th Army was formed under Otto von Below.

At 02:00 on 24 October, with no wind and the front misted over, 894 tubes dug into a reverse slope fired gas canisters into the Italian trenches near Bovec. The defenders fled, but 500 to 600 were killed. At 06:41 some 2,200 guns opened fire, and at 08:00 two large mines were exploded and the infantry attacked. Stormtrooper units led the assault with light machine guns, mortars, flamethrowers and grenades, while Alpine troops infiltrated the ridges. The attackers in the valley advanced almost unopposed, some for 25 kilometres on the first day, breaching the Italian Second Army.

Luigi Capello, the Second Army's commander, was bedridden with fever and asked to withdraw to the Tagliamento, but Luigi Cadorna refused. On 30 October Cadorna ordered most of the army to retreat across it, and by 10 November he had established a position on the Piave River and Monte Grappa. The attackers, with stretched supply lines and exhausted soldiers, could not follow up.

Italian losses were 13,000 killed, 30,000 wounded and 265,000 to 275,000 prisoners, most of whom surrendered willingly because of low morale under Cadorna's harsh discipline. The Austro-Hungarians and Germans suffered about 70,000 casualties. The army's strength fell from 1,800,000 to 1,000,000 and Paolo Boselli's government collapsed. Cadorna was forced to resign and was replaced by Armando Diaz. The last Austro-German push was repelled in the First Battle of Monte Grappa. The name Caporetto became in Italy a word for a terrible defeat, and Ernest Hemingway described its aftermath in A Farewell to Arms.
battle-of-carabobo: Venezuela's independence had been won and lost several times. Francisco de Miranda held Caracas from 1810 to 1812 before the Spanish retook it; Simón Bolívar restored the republic with the Admirable Campaign of 1813, lost it again in 1814, and by 1818 had founded a third republic. The Republic of Colombia was formed in 1819 with Bolívar as president, and once it was secure he turned to the liberation of Venezuela. In 1820 he concluded an armistice with the Spanish under General Pablo Morillo, and he regrouped his forces and stationed them on Lake Maracaibo.

The royalists held the road from Valencia to Puerto Cabello. Bolívar, with 6,500 or 8,000 men, including some 340 or 350 of the British Rangers battalion, divided his army and sent half on a flanking march through rough, overgrown country under General José Antonio Páez, while he attacked in the centre. De la Torre split his own force to meet the flank attack, and musket fire at first threw back the Apure Braves Battalion.

The British battalion under Colonel Thomas Ilderton Ferrier, which included many former members of the King's German Legion, took the hills and held them though outnumbered and short of supplies; it lost 119 dead, among them 11 officers and Ferrier himself. Reinforced, the patriots pushed the royalists back, and Pedro Camejo was killed rallying the troops in front of Páez. The royalist llanero cavalry fled, the patriot cavalry under Colonel Munoz broke through the centre, and only some 400 men of one royalist infantry regiment reached Puerto Cabello.

The victory was costly: the division commanders Ambrosio Plaza and Manuel Cedeño were both killed. Bolívar later called the British legionaries the saviours of his fatherland. With the main royalist army in Venezuela destroyed, independence was assured, and the battle led to the establishment of the Republic of Gran Colombia. The independence forces won a naval victory at the Battle of Lake Maracaibo on 24 July 1823, and in November 1823 Páez occupied Puerto Cabello. In Venezuela 24 June is kept as Battle of Carabobo Day, also called Army Day, with a military parade.
battle-of-carchemish: Under its 26th dynasty Egypt had begun to re-establish its influence in the Levant through vassal states, dominating much of the region once controlled by the Neo-Assyrian Empire. The declining Assyrian remnants became allies dependent on Egyptian support. Babylon and its allies the Medes fought the Assyrians for control of Syria, which brought them into conflict with Egypt as well.

After Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BCE, the Assyrians moved their capital to Harran, which was captured in 609 BCE. Ashur-Uballit II fled to Carchemish and asked Necho II of Egypt for help. Necho had become king around 610 or 609 BCE on the death of his father Psamtik I, and marched north. At Megiddo he met Josiah, king of Judah, an ally of the Babylonians, who sought to delay the Egyptians. Josiah was defeated and killed in 609 BCE, and Necho installed Jehoiakim as an Egyptian vassal on the Judean throne. The Siege of Harran then failed. Ashur-Uballit II is never mentioned again in surviving sources, and Necho returned to Egypt.

Around 605 BCE Carchemish, the capital of the Assyrian remnant and a major trading city and crossing of the Euphrates, came under threat from the Babylonians and Medes. Nebuchadnezzar II commanded the allied force, since his father Nabopolassar was still in Babylon. Necho brought an army north to defend the city. The armies met at or near Carchemish and the Egyptian and Assyrian forces were defeated. The numbers on each side and the course of the fighting are not known. Nebuchadnezzar took Carchemish, and the defeat ended Egyptian influence in the Levant.

No Egyptian record of the battle survives, in text or art. The accounts come from Babylonian and Jewish sources. The Nebuchadnezzar Chronicle says the Egyptian army withdrew and was overtaken at Hamath so that not a man escaped to his own country, but it is unlikely that Necho's whole army was destroyed. The Book of Jeremiah also describes the defeat, though it calls Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon while his father still reigned, and the biblical books differ on dates. Josephus, writing about 700 years later, says Necho entered the battle to take advantage of a power vacuum, not to help the Assyrians; historians agree he supported the Assyrian remnants.

Necho's son Psamtik II may have removed his father's name from records, though scholars such as Roberto Gozzoli doubt it, and a later ruler may have done so. The silence may also reflect the loss of influence in the Levant. The defeat let Babylon extend its domain to the borders of Egypt.
battle-of-carillon: After the setbacks of 1757 William Pitt planned three campaigns against New France: against Fort Duquesne, against Louisbourg, and through the Champlain Valley under General James Abercrombie, with the more able George Howe as his second in command. The fort stood on a point between Lake Champlain and Lake George, on the route between the St. Lawrence and the Hudson. Abercrombie gathered his army near the ruins of Fort William Henry, including 6,000 regulars such as the 42nd Highland Regiment and militia from Connecticut, Massachusetts, New York, New Jersey and Rhode Island. It embarked on 5 July and landed unopposed at the north end of Lake George on 6 July.

Marching through thick woods, the British met a French party under Captain Trépezet near Bernetz Brook. About 150 of his men were killed and 150 captured, but Howe was killed by a musket ball. On 7 July the engineer Lieutenant Matthew Clerk viewed the French works from Rattlesnake Hill and judged them incomplete, unaware that brush disguised largely finished defences. Abercrombie attacked the next morning, hoping to strike before the Chevalier de Lévis arrived with reinforcements; Lévis had in fact reached the fort that evening with 400 regulars.

Rogers' Rangers and light infantry drove in the French scouts on 8 July, followed by provincials and three columns of regulars, who assaulted the entrenchment without field artillery. Abercrombie ordered further waves after the first had failed and never tried to turn the French right, from which French militia twice came out to fire into the attackers' flank.

Abercrombie reported 547 killed, 1,356 wounded and 77 missing; the Black Watch lost more than 300 dead. The news dampened British celebrations of the fall of Louisbourg, and Montreal held out until 1760. Jeffery Amherst took the abandoned fort in 1759 and renamed it Ticonderoga. Historians widely regard Abercrombie as an incompetent commander, and Lawrence Henry Gipson wrote that no campaign on American soil involved a greater number of errors of judgment. The battle gave Ticonderoga a reputation for impregnability, yet the Americans surrendered it without much of a fight in July 1777.
battle-of-carrhae: Marcus Licinius Crassus, Pompeius Magnus and Julius Caesar formed the First Triumvirate. After meetings at Ravenna and Luca in 56 BCE, the alliance secured for Crassus the province of Syria, with the evident intention of going to war with Parthia. Ancient writers, particularly Plutarch, put his motive down to greed, while the historian Erich S. Gruen believes he wished to enrich the public treasury. Cicero called the war one with no justification, since Parthia had a treaty with Rome. Crassus left Rome on 14 November 55 BCE despite protests and dire omens. In Parthia, meanwhile, a war of succession had followed the killing of King Phraates III by his sons Orodes II and Mithridates IV.

According to Plutarch, Crassus raised seven legions of about 28,000 to 35,000 heavy infantry, with some 4,000 light infantry and 4,000 cavalry. King Artavasdes II of Armenia twice offered him reinforcements if he marched through Armenia, but Crassus chose the direct route through Mesopotamia. Orodes took most of the Parthian army to punish the Armenians and sent the spahbod Surena with an all-cavalry force to harass the Romans. Surena's force numbered about ten thousand including slaves and vassals, supported by a baggage train of a thousand camels.

The armies met near Carrhae on 9 June 53 BCE. Crassus formed his men in a hollow square, which protected them from being outflanked but cost them mobility. Surena's horse archers surrounded the square and shot from beyond the range of the Roman javelins, while his cataphracts charged whenever the legionaries locked their shields. Crassus sent his son Publius with 1,300 Gallic cavalry, 500 archers and eight cohorts; they were drawn away and destroyed. The Romans retreated to Carrhae, leaving 4,000 wounded to be killed. At a truce meeting the next day violence broke out and Crassus was killed.

Plutarch gives Roman losses as about 20,000 killed and 10,000 captured, with minimal Parthian casualties. The Parthians took several legionary eagles. Gaius Cassius Longinus led about 10,000 survivors back to Syria and held the province against Parthian attack. Orodes II, jealous of Surena's victory, had him executed.

Some historians see the loss of Crassus as weakening the ties that held the First Triumvirate together and so as a step towards Caesar's civil war, though others note the lapse of time between the two. In the longer run the defeat did little lasting harm to Rome: the Parthian invasion of 40 BCE was repulsed by Publius Ventidius Bassus. The modern historian Gregory Hospodor argues that blaming Crassus alone oversimplifies the defeat, which also exposed the limits of the Roman military system of the late Republic.
battle-of-caseros: From 1814 Argentina had been torn by civil wars over the proper form of government. A British and French blockade of the Río de la Plata had kept Rosas and his ally Manuel Oribe from taking Montevideo, but after the Arana–Southern Treaty ended it, Rosas banned the trade with the city that had been tolerated, angering those who lived by it, Urquiza among them. Sent to prepare for war with Brazil, Urquiza suspected the war was a ploy to delay a constitution, took Brazilian loans and issued his Pronunciamiento from Concepción del Uruguay, calling for Rosas to resign.

Allied with Brazil and the Montevideo government, Urquiza and his Corrientes allies crossed into Uruguay while Brazilian troops invaded from the north, and Oribe came to terms without fighting. The allies then declared war on Rosas, and Urquiza's Grand Army crossed Morón creek. Rosas's commander Ángel Pacheco resigned, and Rosas took command himself and waited for the enemy.

Rosas had about 10,000 infantry, 12,000 cavalry and 60 guns; the Grand Army numbered 24,000, among them 3,500 Brazilians and 1,500 Uruguayans, with 50 guns. The armies met near the ranch of the Caseros family, where the National Military College now stands. Urquiza charged the Rosista left, while Brazilian infantry with Uruguayan and Argentine support seized the Palomar, a round pigeon house on the right. When both flanks collapsed, only the centre under Martiniano Chilavert fought on until its ammunition ran out. In six hours about 2,000 men fell, 1,500 of them Rosistas, and 7,000 Rosistas were captured. Chilavert was then executed on Urquiza's orders.

Rosas, wounded in the hand, wrote his resignation in what is now the Plaza Garay and left on the British ship Centaur under the protection of the consul Robert Gore. Buenos Aires was looted until Urquiza sent three battalions on 5 February; the survivors of the Regimiento Aquino were shot without trial, and members of the Mazorca were later tried and executed. Under the San Nicolás Agreement a constituent assembly met to write the constitution, and Urquiza became the first constitutional president in 1854. Civil wars went on until 1880, and Buenos Aires separated from the Confederation.
battle-of-castelfidardo: On 7 September 1860 the Sardinian prime minister Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, sent an ultimatum to the Papal Secretary of State, Cardinal Giacomo Antonelli, demanding the dismissal of the foreign mercenary units in the papal army. When it was refused, the Sardinian army crossed the border on 11 September. General Louis Juchault de Lamoricière aimed to march his field army to the port of Ancona, fortify it and await help by sea from the Catholic powers of Europe; General Manfredo Fanti, in overall command, and Enrico Cialdini sought to intercept him first.

The papal field army of about 10,000 men was largely made up of foreign volunteers from France, Belgium, Austria and Ireland. By 17 September Cialdini's IV Corps blocked the inland road to Ancona, and Lamoricière, outnumbered and outgunned, sent General Georges de Pimodan with the vanguard to hold the Sardinians in the valley of the Musone while the main body slipped along the coast past Monte Conero. On 18 September de Pimodan attacked and took several fortified farmhouses, but Sardinian artillery and infantry retook them.

Lamoricière turned back to save his vanguard, giving up his march to Ancona, and arrived to find the papal lines overwhelmed. De Pimodan was mortally wounded, and the survivors fled over the Conero promontory. The Sardinians lost 61 killed and 184 wounded; the papal army 88 killed, about 400 wounded and around 600 captured.

The papal field army ceased to exist as a fighting force. Lamoricière and the remnants reached Ancona, which surrendered on 29 September after a siege. Plebiscites in the Marche and Umbria in November 1860 approved their annexation, which joined the northern and southern lands held by the Sardinian crown and Giuseppe Garibaldi and prepared the proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy in March 1861. An ossuary built in 1861 holds the dead of both armies, and a national monument by Vito Pardo was unveiled on Monte Cucco in 1912.
battle-of-castillon: After the French took Bordeaux in 1451 the Hundred Years' War seemed over, but its citizens, after three hundred years of Plantagenet rule, saw themselves as subjects of the English king and asked Henry VI to recapture the province. On 17 October 1452 John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, landed near Bordeaux with 3,000 men. He was rumoured to be seventy-five or eighty but was more likely about sixty-six. With the townspeople's cooperation he took the city on 23 October, and by the end of the year the English held most of western Gascony. The French had expected an expedition through Normandy and spent the winter preparing a counterattack.

Charles VII invaded Guyenne with three armies, and the French besieged Castillon on 8 July. Yielding to the town leaders' pleas, Talbot abandoned his plan to wait at Bordeaux for reinforcements. The French ordnance officer Jean Bureau had built an artillery park of ditch and earth wall with up to 300 guns.

Talbot reached Libourne on 16 July with only 500 men-at-arms and 800 mounted archers. On 17 July he defeated a small French detachment at a priory and, told that the French were retreating, pushed on; the dust was in fact raised by camp followers leaving. The English ran into the full French force, and Talbot ordered his men to keep fighting. French guns destroyed the advancing soldiers, and his reinforcements arrived piecemeal to the same fate. After over an hour a thousand Breton cavalry under Peter II, Duke of Brittany, struck the English right flank and the English broke. Talbot and his son were killed.

The survivors took refuge in the castle of Castillon, which surrendered on 19 July. English authority in Gascony eroded, and the French retook Bordeaux on 19 October. The battle is cited as the end of the Hundred Years' War and was the first major European battle won through the extensive use of field artillery. The English crown lost all its continental possessions except Calais, lost in 1558, and the Channel Islands. Henry VI lost his mental capacity in late 1453, and the Wars of the Roses began. Historians differ over the site of the French camp: one hypothesis puts it north of the Dordogne, another in front of the town itself.
battle-of-cer: Relations between Austria-Hungary and Serbia worsened after the Serbian May Coup of 1903, and the Karađorđević government aligned itself with the Russian Empire. After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on 28 June 1914 Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum on 23 July, declared war on 28 July and shelled Belgrade the next day.

The invasion force was about 200,000 men under General Oskar Potiorek, who had called the Serbs pig farmers, and forty percent of it were South Slavs of Austria-Hungary. Serbia could muster some 450,000 men on full mobilization, but the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and Užice Armies numbered about 180,000. The Serbs were short of artillery, rifles and even uniforms, but many were veterans of the Balkan Wars. Field Marshal Radomir Putnik was the de facto commander.

Austro-Hungarian troops crossed the Drina and the Sava from 12 August, and Šabac fell quickly. On 15 August Putnik ordered a counterattack. That night, in a thunderstorm, the Serbian 1st Combined Division met Austro-Hungarian outposts on the slopes of Cer Mountain. Fighting spread to the villages around, including Trojan, Parlog and Kosanin Grad, and the Serbs held out through a night of repeated assaults at Kosanin Grad.

On 19 August the morale of the Austro-Hungarians collapsed and they retreated across the Drina, where many drowned in the panic. Serbian forces encircled Šabac, and on 24 August they entered it to find it abandoned the night before. The first dogfight between aircraft of the war took place during the battle.

Casualty figures vary. Horne and Jordan give about 3,000 Serbs killed and 15,000 wounded, while Glenny gives 3,000 to 5,000 killed. For the Austro-Hungarians, Glenny gives 6,000 to 10,000 killed and almost 30,000 wounded, and David Stevenson says 4,500 were taken prisoner. Horne adds that 46 guns, 30 machine guns and 140 ammunition wagons were lost. The Serbian victory ended the first Austro-Hungarian invasion of Serbia and is regarded as the first Allied victory over the Central Powers in the First World War.
battle-of-cerignola: The Third Italian War flared again late in 1502 over disagreements arising from the secret Treaty of Granada of 11 November 1500, under which Louis XII of France was to take the throne of Naples; he and the Spanish monarchs soon quarrelled over territories between their spheres. Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, El Gran Capitán, avoided contact at first, hoping to make the French complacent. His army of around 9,000 men, with 2,000 Landsknecht pikemen, 1,000 arquebusiers and 20 cannons, was organised in coronelías, the immediate predecessors of the tercios, and fortified the heights of Cerignola with ditches and stakes.

The French under Louis d'Armagnac, Duke of Nemours, also about 9,000 men, relied on the heavy cavalry of the Compagnies d'ordonnance and Swiss mercenary pikemen, with about 40 cannons. Before the battle the Spanish gunpowder reserve exploded, and Córdoba told his men these were the lights of victory.

Two charges of French heavy cavalry against the Spanish centre were driven back by artillery and arquebus fire. A third, against the right flank, ended with many riders falling into the ditch, and Nemours was killed by the arquebus volleys, possibly the first European general to die in action from small-arms fire. The Swiss under Chandieu then attacked without waiting for the rearguard and artillery under Yves d'Alègre. Córdoba moved his arquebusiers to the flanks and put the Landsknechts under Hans von Ravenstein behind the ditch; struck from the front and flanks, the Swiss and Gascon infantry fell back, Chandieu among the dead. A counterattack routed the remaining gendarmes, and d'Alègre withdrew.

The French lost around 2,000 men and their wagons and artillery, the Spanish some 500. Córdoba had the body of Nemours recovered and gave him a military funeral, and his order that three long tones be played and his troops pray for all the fallen was the first call to prayer, or toque de oracion, a practice later adopted by most Western armies. The French retreated to Gaeta, which Córdoba failed to storm. The battle marks the rise of pike and shot tactics and the beginning of 140 years of Spanish dominance on European battlefields, ending with Rocroi in 1643. Bernard Montgomery saw in it the moment when the infantryman with a handgun became the most important fighting man on the battlefield.
battle-of-chacabuco: From 1814 José de San Martín planned to drive the royalists from South America, beginning with Chile, and in under two years he assembled about 6,000 men, 1,200 horses and 22 cannons. He began the crossing of the Andes on 17 January 1817. The royalists, misled into guarding against threats that did not exist, left the passes unchallenged, but the Army of the Andes lost as much as a third of its men and more than half its horses on the way. In Chile San Martín joined forces with Bernardo O'Higgins.

Brigadier Rafael Maroto proposed abandoning Santiago and regrouping in the south, and a council called by the royal governor, Casimiro Marcó del Pont, on 8 February adopted the plan. The next morning the governor reversed it and ordered Maroto to give battle at Chacabuco, a valley near the capital. Maroto's task was to delay the patriots until reinforcements arrived from Santiago, so San Martín chose to attack while he still had the advantage in numbers.

At a war council on 11 February San Martín decided to take the Chacabuco Ranch, the royalist headquarters, with two columns descending by separate roads: the right under Miguel Estanislao Soler and the left under O'Higgins. The troops moved down from midnight. Soler's narrow path took longer than expected, and O'Higgins attacked before him; what happened then is fiercely debated, O'Higgins later claiming that retreat up the path would have destroyed his men. San Martín ordered Soler against the royalist flank. Soler took a key artillery position, the royalists formed a square around the ranch, and with Soler behind them and O'Higgins charging their centre they were overwhelmed.

Five hundred royalists were killed and 600 taken prisoner. The Army of the Andes lost twelve men in the fighting, and another 120 died of wounds. Maroto escaped, slightly hurt. The patriots re-entered Santiago, where an assembly under the interim governor Francisco Ruiz-Tagle chose San Martín as governor; he declined, and a new assembly named O'Higgins Supreme Director, beginning the Patria Nueva. The remaining royalists held out in the south, supplied by sea, and their expulsion was completed the following year at the Battle of Maipú.
battle-of-chaeronea-338-bce: Philip II ended the Third Sacred War in 346 BCE and concluded the Peace of Philocrates with Athens, which made Athens a reluctant ally. The peace was never popular. The orator Demosthenes led the war party, and in 340 BCE persuaded the assembly to ally with Byzantium, which Philip was besieging. Philip took this as a declaration of war.

In 339 BCE a Fourth Sacred War against Amphissa gave him a pretext to march south, and Thebes and Athens allied against him. After months of stalemate Philip marched down the main road from Phocis into Boeotia in August 338 BCE.

Diodorus Siculus gives the Macedonian army as roughly 30,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry. Philip took the right wing and placed his 18-year-old son Alexander on the left, with experienced generals. The allies, mostly Athenians and Thebans, held a line about 2.5 miles long between Mount Thurion and the Kephisos River, the Athenians on the left and the Thebans on the right. Modern opinion holds the armies about equal in size.

Diodorus says the battle was hotly contested for a long time until Alexander broke the allied line and put the right wing to flight while Philip routed the left. Polyaenus, of varying reliability, suggests Philip drew the Athenians forward by withdrawing. Plutarch says Alexander was first to break the Sacred Band of Thebes. Diodorus reports over 1,000 Athenians dead and 2,000 captured. Excavations beneath the Lion of Chaeronea found 254 bodies, generally accepted as the Sacred Band's grave.

The Athenian orator Lycurgus said that with the dead of Chaeronea the freedom of the Greeks was also buried. Philip treated Thebes severely, with a Macedonian garrison and a ransom for its prisoners, but treated Athens leniently, probably wanting its navy against Persia. In 337 BCE a congress he organised formed the League of Corinth, joined by every state except Sparta, and voted him strategos for a war on Persia. Philip was assassinated in 336 BCE, and Alexander conducted the campaigns from 334 to 323 BCE.
battle-of-chaldiran: After his struggle against his brothers for the Ottoman throne, Sultan Selim I turned to the Qizilbash, a Twelver Shi'i warrior-dervish group that had sided with other members of the dynasty against him. He feared they would incite the population against him in favour of their leader, the Safavid ruler Ismail I, whom his partisans believed to be descended from Muhammad and infallible. Selim obtained a jurist's opinion describing Ismail and the Qizilbash as unbelievers and heretics, and before the campaign he ordered the execution of some 40,000 Qizilbash in Anatolia. He also tried to block the import of Iranian silk.

When Selim marched east, the Khanate of Bukhara attacked the Safavids from the other side, and Ismail used a scorched earth policy against the Ottomans. Selim's army was discontented, because supply was hard, the terrain of the Armenian highlands was rough and the men were marching against fellow Muslims. At one point the janissaries fired their muskets at the sultan's tent. Learning that the Safavid army was forming at Chaldiran, Selim moved quickly to fight, partly to quiet this discontent.

The battle took place on 23 August 1514. The Ottomans had a larger army, of 60,000 to 100,000 men, and many heavy artillery pieces. The Safavid army numbered 40,000 to 80,000 and had no artillery. The Ottomans placed their guns and thousands of janissaries with gunpowder weapons behind a barrier of carts. The Safavid cavalry attacked the wings to avoid the guns at the centre, but the artillery was highly mobile and the Safavids suffered disastrous losses. Ismail was wounded and almost captured, and his wives were taken by Selim. Kurdish tribes fought on both sides, since the battle was fought in the Kurdish heartland.

The Ottomans entered the Safavid capital Tabriz on 7 September, pillaged it and left, though the Friday sermon that week was delivered in Selim's name. Selim could not press further because of the janissaries' discontent. The Ottomans annexed Eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia. Control of these regions changed hands several times, was settled in the Peace of Amasya of 1555 and was made firm by the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639. Ismail withdrew from government and never again took part in a military campaign.

The defeat undermined belief in the infallibility of the Qizilbash leader, and Kurdish chiefs shifted their allegiance from the Safavids to the Ottomans. The Safavids made firearms a part of their armies, and Ismail's son Tahmasp I used cannon in later battles. Selim next turned south against the Mamluk Sultanate in 1516 and 1517.
battle-of-chamdo: The campaign took place from 6 to 24 October 1950, when the People's Republic of China moved to capture the Chamdo region from a de facto independent Tibetan state. The Khampas of eastern Tibet and the Tibetans of Lhasa held each other in mutual dislike, and some Khampas resented Lhasa's rule even more than Chinese rule. Khampas such as the Pandatsang clan had led rebellions for autonomy, and in January 1950 the communists offered to aid the Pandatsang brothers in exchange for staying on the sidelines; the brothers instead sent George Patterson to India to seek other aid.

After defeating the Kuomintang in the Chinese Civil War, the People's Liberation Army turned to the hinterland. Its 18th Army reached Ya'an on 12 February 1950 and Kangding in March, and a road from Kangding to Garze was completed in August.

The 18th Army assembled at Garze on 30 July and entered Litang, while the Qinghai Cavalry Detachment entered Gyegu on 22 July, forming a pincer on Chamdo from north and south. In June the PLA and the Tibetan army had fought for the first time at Dengke, where 50 PLA soldiers captured the town and destroyed a radio station. About 800 Khampa militia, 300 of them monks, raided it in July, claiming to have killed 600 PLA soldiers. After months of failed negotiations, the PLA crossed the Jinsha River on 6 or 7 October at five places.

Two PLA units took the town of Chamdo by 19 October. By then 114 PLA soldiers and 180 Tibetan soldiers had been killed or wounded. The governor and commander of the Tibetan forces, Ngabo Ngawang Jigme, surrendered with his 2,700 men. Writing in 1962, Zhang Guohua claimed that 5,738 enemy troops were liquidated and more than 3,000 surrendered peacefully; the Peace Research Institute Oslo estimated 2,000 PLA and 2,000 Tibetans killed, noncombatants included. The PLA took the prisoners' weapons, gave them lectures on socialism and a little money, and let them go home.

The PLA ceased hostilities unilaterally and sent Ngabo to Lhasa to restate its terms. On 21 October Lhasa told its delegation to go to Beijing and to accept the first provision if the status of the Dalai Lama could be guaranteed, but it later rescinded even that after a divination before the Six-Armed Mahakala. Military operations ended on 24 October. Chinese Communist Party broadcasts promised that if Tibet was peacefully liberated its elites would keep their positions. Some Khampa fighters kept up opposition, and local warlords later united as Chushi Gangdruk with CIA help. Melvyn Goldstein says the campaign aimed to capture the Lhasa army at Chamdo, demoralise the government and press Tibetan representatives into negotiating in Beijing.
battle-of-changping: In 265 BCE Qin attacked the State of Han and took Qinyang, cutting off Han's Shangdang Commandery from its southern heartland. Rather than let it fall to Qin, its governor, Feng Ting, offered the region to Zhao. Shangdang lay just west of the Zhao capital, Handan, so King Xiaocheng of Zhao accepted and sent the senior general Lian Po to hold it. In 262 BCE a Qin army under Wang He invaded Shangdang, and Lian Po built three defensive lines south of the Changping Pass.

After early defeats lost him the first line, Lian Po avoided battle in the open and held a fortified line along the Dan River, hoping to exhaust an enemy fighting far from home. By July the two sides faced each other across the river, and the stalemate lasted two years, with around a million combatants by early 260 BCE. Qin spies then spread rumours that Lian Po was old and cowardly, and the king replaced him with Zhao Kuo, son of the late general Zhao She, who had never fought a battle. Qin secretly gave its command to Bai Qi.

In July 260 BCE Zhao Kuo crossed the river to attack. The Qin left fell back to hill forts, drawing him on, while a detachment of 25,000 men swung behind the Zhao lines and 5,000 cavalry cut his army off from its supply depot. King Zhaoxiang of Qin called up every able-bodied man over the age of 15 in Henei to tighten the ring. Besieged for 46 days and starving, the Zhao army surrendered after Zhao Kuo was killed by archers in a last attempt to break out.

Unable to guard or feed so many prisoners, Bai Qi had them executed, presumably by burying them alive, and released only 240 of the youngest to spread terror. The Han historian Sima Qian, writing about 150 years later, is the main source for the death toll. King Zhaoxiang refused Bai Qi's wish to march on Handan at once; Bai Qi later declined command and was forced to kill himself, and a Qin defeat at the Battle of Handan halted its expansion for almost three decades. Zhao never recovered, and Qin unified China in 221 BCE. Zhao Kuo's failure gave the idiom talking wars on paper.
battle-of-chengpu: After the death of Duke Huan of Qi in 643 BCE, the State of Chu steadily extended its influence northward, absorbing half a dozen smaller states as satellites. In 636 BCE Chong'er, a prince of Jin, returned after nineteen years in exile and came to power as Duke Wen of Jin with the help of Duke Mu of Qin. In the winter of 633 BCE King Cheng of Chu attacked the State of Song, Jin's ally, and the following spring Duke Wen marched south and occupied Wey and Cao, both satellites of Chu.

As Duke Wen had promised King Cheng during his exile in Chu, the Jin army withdrew three days' march before camping on the plain of Chengpu, which also joined it with its Qi and Qin reinforcements. Only the Chu centre under the prime minister Ziyu was made up wholly of Chu troops; its right wing came from Chen and Cai, its left from Shen and Xi.

The armies met on the fourth day of the fourth month of 632 BCE. Xu Chen, commander of the Jin left, dressed his chariot horses in tiger skins to panic the Chu horses and scattered the weak Chu right wing. His men then held the Chu centre in place. On the Jin right, Hu Mao's wing skirmished and faked a retreat, carrying off the commander-in-chief's two great banners, while Luan Zhi's chariots dragged branches to raise a cloud of dust that hid them as they wheeled and reformed.

Believing the Jin right beaten, the Chu left pursued and was caught in the flank by Duke Wen's bodyguards and the Song contingent, then struck by Hu Mao's returning wing and destroyed. With both wings enveloped, Ziyu ordered a general retreat, which became a rout when his men found that the Qi and Qin contingents had captured the Chu camp and train in the rear. Duke Wen did not direct the fighting himself.

Chengpu was the first major battle in the long conflict between the states of the Yellow River valley and those of the Yangtze, and one of the biggest of the Spring and Autumn period. On his return north Duke Wen was recognised by the King of Zhou as first among the feudal lords, and a conference of states he led at Jiantu in 631 BCE swore a covenant of alliance. The victory did not, however, restrict the power of Chu in the long term.
battle-of-chester: The reasons for the battle are unknown. Geoffrey of Monmouth states that Æthelfrith's political rival, Edwin of Deira, was living in exile in Gwynedd, and there are some supporting references to Edwin in Reginald of Durham and the Welsh Triads, but no evidence that Æthelfrith was pursuing him. It seems unlikely that he was protecting Anglian settlers in the area, and he may have been planning to attack Powys. The annals and chronicles give a variety of years for the battle.

Æthelfrith destroyed a combined force from Powys and Rhôs, a cantref of the Kingdom of Gwynedd, and possibly from Mercia. Cadwal Crysban of Rhôs and Gwion ap Cyndrwyn of Pengwern were among the dead, and circumstantial evidence suggests that King Iago of Gwynedd may have been killed too. The Brut y Brenhinedd, the Middle Welsh versions of Geoffrey's history, calls the battle Perllan Fangor, Bangor Orchard, which suggests it may have been fought nearer Bangor-on-Dee.

According to Bede, Æthelfrith ordered the praying monks to be attacked first, saying that though they bore no arms they fought against him by their prayers, and about twelve hundred are said to have been killed. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle speaks of 200 priests slain and says their leader, Scrocmail, escaped as one of fifty. The attack on the monks before the army may perhaps be explained as a ruse to throw the defence into disarray.

Excavations at Heronbridge, just south of Chester, in 2004 found post-Roman graves beneath a defensive earthwork, and there is evidence that they hold casualties of the battle. Its strategic significance remains unclear, since Æthelfrith died soon afterwards, at the Battle of the River Idle according to some accounts. It has been suggested that Cearl of Mercia shared in the Britons' defeat, as his overkingship ended until the rise of Penda.

Bede saw the massacre as divine retribution for the Welsh bishops' refusal to join Augustine of Canterbury in converting the Saxons. During the English Reformation scholars such as Matthew Parker argued that Augustine himself had been complicit, relying on an early date in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The charge was rejected by scholars such as Elizabeth Elstob, Henry Spelman, Henry Wharton and Jeremy Collier, and it has no support from modern historians, not least because Æthelfrith and his army were pagan.
battle-of-cissa: In the summer of 218 BCE Hannibal crossed the Ebro and spent July and August subduing the tribes between the river and the Pyrenees at heavy cost, leaving the Greek cities alone. He left a general named Hanno, variously identified as his nephew, his brother or no relation, to hold the conquered land with 10,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, watch the pro-Roman Bargusii, guard the link with Hasdrubal Barca and keep the heavy baggage left in a camp at Cissa. The Roman expedition to Iberia had been delayed when the Boii and Insubres attacked the colonies of Placentia and Cremona and troops were sent to Cisalpine Gaul instead.

The Romans arrived within four to five weeks of Hannibal's departure and took Hanno by surprise, as he had marched south to put down a rebellion. He withdrew inland to Cissa and probably raised Iberian levies, perhaps under Indibilis, chieftain of the Ilergetes, while Hasdrubal marched north from Cartagena with 8,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry.

The Roman army, strengthened by garrisons and Iberian auxiliaries, may have numbered between 20,000 and 25,000, and outnumbered Hanno about two to one. There were no manoeuvres or ambushes: the armies formed up and fought, and Hanno was beaten relatively easily, losing 6,000 men. The Romans took his camp, with all the baggage left by Hannibal, 2,000 more soldiers and Hanno himself, and among the prisoners was Indibilis. They also stormed Cissa, which held no valuable booty.

Hasdrubal arrived too late, but his raiding column caught Roman sailors and marines foraging and reduced the effective Roman fleet in Iberia from 60 to 35 ships. Scipio punished the naval officers for lax discipline, shared out the booty and wintered at Tarraco, while Hasdrubal garrisoned allied towns south of the Ebro and returned to Cartagena. The battle cut Hannibal's overland link with Iberia, and he never received reinforcements from Spain during the war.
battle-of-clastidium: After the campaign of the consuls Publius Furius Philus and Gaius Flaminius against them in 223 BCE, the Insubres sent envoys to the Roman senate to ask for peace. The new consuls, Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, urged that none be granted. Refused, the Insubres hired thirty thousand transalpine Gaesatae as mercenaries. The consuls invaded the territory of the Insubres and besieged Acerrae, near modern Pizzighettone between Cremona and Lodi. Unable to relieve it, the Gauls crossed the Po into the land of the Anares and besieged the town of Clastidium to draw the Romans away.

Marcellus hurried to relieve Clastidium with about 3,200 horsemen, two-thirds of his cavalry, and six hundred of his fittest legionaries, while Gnaeus kept up the siege of Acerrae. The Celts left the siege and drew up for battle. As Marcellus extended his wings to outflank them, his horse panicked and turned away, and he made the moment into a vow to dedicate the finest armour taken from the enemy to Jupiter Feretrius. The Gallic king, called Viridomarus by Florus and Britomartus by Plutarch, then rode out and challenged him to single combat. Marcellus unhorsed him with his lance on the first pass, killed him and stripped his armour.

The Roman cavalry then charged the Gallic horse and foot, attacking from the front and the sides until they broke. Thousands of Gauls were killed in the pursuit, and many drowned in the Po. It was one of the few Roman battles won by the cavalry without the legions.

The Romans soon took Acerrae, and the Gauls fell back to Mediolanum. Gnaeus followed, beat off a sally against his rear, laid waste the country and stormed the city, after which the chieftains of the Insubres surrendered unconditionally. Rome had conquered the largest independent Celtic tribe in Italy and established its hegemony over the Po Valley, then the most productive farmland of the peninsula.
battle-of-clavijo: In the legend, the battle took place on 23 May 844 at the Campo de la Matanza near Clavijo. The Christian troops of King Ramiro I, led by General Sancho Fernández de Tejada, went in search of the Muslims commanded by Abd ar-Rahman II, but near Nájera and Albelda found themselves surrounded by a large army of troops from the peninsula and levies from present-day Morocco, and took refuge in the castle of Clavijo on Monte Laturce.

Ramiro dreamt that the apostle James appeared and promised him victory, and the next day his armies, encouraged by the apostle mounted on a white steed, faced the Muslim army and won. Ramiro then had the Church of the Blessed Santiago built and gave Sancho privileges and the surname Tejada, after the branch of a yew tree he had fought with when his spear broke.

On 25 May, in a year the story does not give, Ramiro was said to have dictated the vow of Santiago at Calahorra, committing the Christians of the peninsula to pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela with offerings. The apostle became a symbol of the fight against Islam, as Santiago Matamoros, the Moor-killer, and the battle came to be treated as an element in the shaping of Spanish national history and as an origin of the pilgrimage of the Way of Saint James. Henry IV and later Spanish monarchs cited it in granting and confirming privileges to the Solar de Tejada.

In his República Mista of 1602 the jurist Tomás Fernández de Medrano, a descendant of Sancho Fernández de Tejada, defended the battle as a foundational tradition of Spain, warning that to deny it was like denying that the apostle had preached in Spain. Saint James's appearance at Clavijo became a major theme in art, painted by Aniello Falcone, Martin Schongauer and Corrado Giaquinto among others.

The historiographical criticism of Juan Francisco Masdeu and the Diccionario de historia de España of 1968 led to the battle being regarded today as a legend, a story mixing data from other battles of different times and places. In 1948 Claudio Sánchez-Albornoz showed that aspects of the historical Battle of Monte Laturce of 859 had been worked into it. Christian and Muslim chronicles agree on fierce fighting in La Rioja, Asturian-Leonese sources tell of Ordoño I, Ramiro's son, besieging Albelda from a base on Mount Laturce, and finds confirm fighting at Albelda, but no source mentions a Battle of Clavijo until centuries after its supposed date.
battle-of-clontarf: Vikings had held Dublin since 838, and by the tenth century the Kingdom of Dublin controlled wide territories around the Irish Sea. Brian Boru of the Dál gCais rose from the kingship of Munster to become undisputed High King of Ireland by 1002, displacing Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill of the Uí Néill. In 999 he and Máel Sechnaill had defeated Sigtrygg Silkbeard, King of Dublin, and Máel Mórda mac Murchada, King of Leinster, at the Battle of Glenmama.

When Dublin and Leinster raided Meath in 1013, Brian camped outside Dublin from September to the end of the year. Sigtrygg sought help overseas from Sigurd Hlodvirsson, Earl of Orkney, and Brodir of the Isle of Man; Njáls saga says he promised each of them the kingship of Ireland. Their fleets reached Dublin in Holy Week 1014.

Contemporary sources give no order of battle. According to the Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib, the foreign Vikings formed the front line, with the men of Dublin and then the Leinstermen behind, while Sigtrygg watched from the walls of Dublin. Brian, in his seventies, stayed behind to pray. The fighting lasted from first light all day. When the Dublin and Leinster forces broke, the incoming tide cut them off from a wood and carried away their ships, and many drowned. Brian's grandson Toirdelbach drowned in the pursuit, his son Murchad killed Sigurd and then fell, and Brodir found Brian in his tent and killed him.

Between 7,000 and 10,000 men are estimated to have died. Brian was buried at Armagh, and Máel Sechnaill was restored as High King until his death in 1022. The loss of both Brian and his heir Murchad opened a succession struggle among his sons Donnchad and Tadc. Dublin was reduced to a lesser power, and in 1052 Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, King of Leinster, captured it. Historians have long debated the battle: the popular view sees a war of Irish against Vikings, while revisionists see an Irish civil war with Vikings on both sides.
battle-of-copenhagen-1801: In 1801, during the French Revolutionary Wars, Britain's main advantage over France was its navy, and the Royal Navy searched and seized neutral ships trading with French ports. The Russian tsar Paul, once a British ally, formed a League of Armed Neutrality of Denmark, Sweden, Prussia and Russia to enforce free trade with France. The British saw it as a threat to their supply of timber and naval stores from Scandinavia. They also feared that, once the ice melted, the Russian fleet would join the Danish and Swedish fleets, together up to 123 ships of the line.

A fleet under Admiral Sir Hyde Parker, with Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson as second-in-command, sailed from Yarmouth on 12 March 1801 and learned at the Skaw on 19 March that the Danes had rejected an ultimatum. Parker was cautious, and Nelson persuaded him to attack the Danish fleet off Copenhagen.

The Danes had used the delay to prepare. Old hulks and ships not fitted for sea were moored along the shore of Amager as floating batteries, and the Tre Kroner fort at the northern end had 68 guns. Parker gave Nelson twelve ships of the line with the shallowest drafts and the smaller vessels. On 2 April three British ships ran aground, Agamemnon, Russell and Bellona, which weakened the northern end of the line. The Danish batteries opened fire at 10:05 am, and by 11:30 the battle was general.

At 1:30 pm Parker, who could see only distress signals through the smoke, hoisted the signal of recall. Nelson, who is said to have put his telescope to his blind eye, did not obey; only Captain Edward Riou withdrew and was killed. By about 2:00 pm much of the Danish line had fallen silent. Nelson then sent a note under a flag of truce to Crown Prince Frederik, and a ceasefire was agreed.

Of the 18 Danish ships engaged, two had sunk, one had exploded and twelve were captured. The Danish flagship Dannebroge blew up at 4:30 pm, killing 250 men. British losses were returned as 274 killed and 737 wounded; Danish casualties are uncertain, Olfert Fischer estimating at least 1,600 to 1,800 killed or wounded. The next day Nelson secured an armistice, and the news of Tsar Paul's assassination, which reached the Danes before the British, led to the League's dissolution. A final peace was signed on 23 October 1801, and Parker was recalled in May.
battle-of-coronea-394-bc: The Corinthian War began in 395 BCE, when Thebes, Argos, Corinth and Athens, with Persian support and money, united against Spartan intervention in Locris and Phocis. Agesilaus II was then campaigning against the Persians in Ionia. Recalled, he marched overland through Thrace and central Greece, and on entering Boeotia found his way blocked on the plain near the foot of Mount Helicon by an army of Boeotians, Athenians, Argives, Corinthians, Euboeans and Locrians, probably about 20,000 hoplites against his 15,000. He had substantially more peltasts, and the cavalry of the two sides was roughly equal.

Some of his troops were troubled by an omen: some days earlier the sun had appeared crescent-shaped. Agesilaus reminded them of the recent Spartan victory at Nemea and told them the navarch Peisander had died winning a battle against the Persian fleet, though he knew Peisander had been killed in a crushing defeat at Cnidus.

Agesilaus commanded the Spartans on his right, with the veterans of the Ten Thousand under the Spartiate Herippidas and the Asian Greeks beside them and the Orchomenians on the far left; the Argives faced the Spartans and the Thebans the Orchomenians. The veterans and the Asian Greeks routed the troops facing them, and the Argives fled to Mount Helicon before the Spartans reached them. On the other wing, however, the Thebans broke the Orchomenians and reached the baggage train with its loot from Asia.

Agesilaus wheeled his phalanx and placed it directly in their path rather than striking their flank or rear, perhaps out of his long hostility to Thebes. Xenophon described how, shield pressed upon shield, they killed and were killed in turn. A few Thebans broke through to Mount Helicon, but many others were killed on the way.

Agesilaus was wounded and carried back to his phalanx. When some 80 of the enemy took refuge in a nearby temple, he ordered that they be spared. The next morning he gave out awards for valour and let a Theban delegation collect their dead, then withdrew to Phocis and invaded Locris, where the polemarch Gylis was killed. According to Diodorus Siculus, more than 600 Boeotians and their allies fell and the Spartans lost 350 men.
battle-of-cortenuova: In 1235 Frederick II resolved to renew the struggle with the Lombard communes, which Pope Gregory IX supported diplomatically; the dispute turned on how far the rights recognised in the Peace of Constance could coexist with imperial jurisdiction. In 1236, helped by Ezzelino III da Romano, he stormed and sacked Vicenza. He returned in September 1237 with around 2,000 German knights, joined by troops from Tuscany and the Kingdom of Sicily, among them Muslim archers from Lucera, and contingents from Cremona, Pavia, Parma and other allies. Mantua submitted, and Montichiari surrendered on 21 October after almost three weeks.

The League army, probably about 15,000 men under Pietro Tiepolo, podestà of Milan and son of the Venetian doge, held a position near Manerbio protected by rivers, marshes and autumn rain. After weeks of stalemate Frederick began withdrawing across the Oglio on 23 November, keeping a mobile force at Soncino, and the League set off for winter quarters.

In heavy rain the Lombard column became stretched out, its baggage several kilometres behind. Bergamese patrols shadowed it, and smoke signals passed from Cividate al Piano through a chain of towers to Soncino. Imperial propaganda later presented the operation as a planned trap, though Frederick's own early account called the opportunity accidental. His troops fell first on the rearguard, which resisted for about an hour. Tiepolo then formed a line near Cortenuova, the carroccio at its centre, infantry in close ranks behind shields and spears, protected by a shallow ditch.

Frederick, with probably more than 10,000 men, combined Saracen archery, Cremonese infantry with long axes and repeated cavalry charges.
