A Lombard cavalry counterattack broke into his position, but the infantry was pressed back to the carroccio, and darkness ended the fighting. In the night retreat towards Treviglio the army fell apart; men drowned crossing the swollen Serio or were captured, and Tiepolo was taken. Contemporary estimates of the League's losses differ widely, from a Milanese tradition of at least 500 cavalry and 2,000 infantry killed or captured among Milan's forces alone to imperial claims of about 10,000.

Frederick entered Cremona with the carroccio drawn by his elephant and Tiepolo in chains upon it; Tiepolo was later executed at Trani. The carroccio was displayed on the Capitoline Hill with an inscription celebrating Caesar's triumph, a spectacle that humiliated Gregory IX in his own city. Lodi, Vercelli and Novara submitted, but Milan refused unconditional surrender, Frederick's siege of Brescia failed in 1238, and his renewed excommunication in 1239 followed from the altered balance.
battle-of-corupedium: The battle, also called Koroupedion, was the last between the Diadochi, the rival successors of Alexander the Great. Lysimachus had ruled Thrace for decades and parts of western Asia Minor since the Battle of Ipsus, and he had recently gained control of Macedon. Seleucus I Nicator ruled the Seleucid Empire, which covered lands in present-day eastern Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Iraq and Iran.

The two men had long been rivals, Lysimachus wishing to extend his influence east and Seleucus west. The event that started the war was the murder of Agathocles, the eldest son of Lysimachus and his first wife Nicaea and heir to his father's realm. Lysimachus's third wife, Arsinoe, wanted her own children on the throne and conspired with Ptolemy Keraunos. They accused Agathocles of plotting with Seleucus, and Lysimachus put his son to death. Many cities of Asia Minor then revolted against the rule of Lysimachus.

Agathocles's widow and their children fled to Seleucus, who saw an opportunity to attack Lysimachus while he was weak. He invaded and fought at Corupedion, the plain of Kyros or Koros. Almost nothing is known about the battle itself except that Seleucus won and that Lysimachus died in the fighting. According to Memnon of Heraclea, in his History of Heraclea Pontica, a javelin thrown by Malacon, a soldier from Heraclea serving under Seleucus, killed Lysimachus.

The victory gave Seleucus nominal control over nearly every part of Alexander's empire except the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, but it was short-lived. Not long after the battle he crossed the Hellespont to take possession of the European holdings of Lysimachus. There Ptolemy Keraunos assassinated him, and Macedon quickly became independent again.
battle-of-covadonga: Texts written by Mozarabs in northern Hispania in the late ninth century say that the Visigoths elected a nobleman named Pelagius as their princeps in 718. He was the son of Favila, a dignitary at the court of King Egica, and he set up his headquarters at Cangas de Onís. Since the start of the Muslim invasion, refugees and fighters from the south had moved north, and some took refuge in the mountains of Asturias, where Pelagius recruited his band. Remnants of the Hispano-Gothic aristocracy supported him and, with the local leaders, formed a new aristocracy. The mountain population included Astures, Galicians, Cantabri and Basques.

Pelagius refused to pay the jizya to the Muslims and attacked small Umayyad garrisons, eventually expelling a provincial governor named Munuza. At first the revolt posed no threat to the new rulers of Hispania, who held power at Córdoba, and their forces were occupied with raids on Narbonne and Gaul. A Muslim defeat at the Battle of Toulouse on 9 July 721 probably set the stage for Covadonga.

In 722 the Umayyad commanders Alqama and Munuza were sent to Asturias, and according to legend Bishop Oppas of Seville went with them and tried without success to persuade his fellow Christians to surrender. Pelagius retreated deep into the mountains to a narrow valley that could not be attacked on a broad front.

Alqama came to Covadonga and sent an envoy to demand surrender, which Pelagius refused. Alqama then ordered his best troops into the valley. The Asturians shot arrows and stones from the slopes, and at the decisive moment Pelagius led some of his men out of a cave where they had been hiding. Christian accounts describe a horrific slaughter of the Muslims, while Umayyad accounts call it a mere skirmish. Alqama fell, and his soldiers withdrew.

Afterwards the people of the villages emerged with their weapons and killed hundreds of Alqama's retreating troops. Munuza gathered survivors and later met Pelagius and his enlarged force near the modern town of Proaza, where Pelagius won again and Munuza was killed. Pelagius soon founded the Kingdom of Asturias, which became a Christian stronghold against further Muslim expansion.

The battle is traditionally regarded as the foundational event of that kingdom and so as the starting point of the Christian Reconquista of Iberia after the Umayyad conquest of 711. It is commemorated at the shrine of Our Lady of Covadonga.
battle-of-crannon: When the Athenians learned of the death of Alexander the Great in June 323 BCE, they turned against Macedonian hegemony in Greece. Recruiting mercenaries and joined by many other city-states, they at first outnumbered Antipater, the Macedonian viceroy in Europe, whose troops were depleted by the campaigns in the east. Antipater took refuge in Lamia and called for reinforcements from Asia. Leonnatus, the first to come, was defeated and killed in a battle with the Athenian cavalry, but Antipater was able to leave Lamia with his own and Leonnatus' remaining troops. The arrival of a third army under Craterus gave the Macedonians the larger numbers.

Antipater and Craterus marched south to force a battle, and the allies, having gathered their scattered forces, met them near Crannon in Thessaly. Trusting the reputation of the Thessalian horse, the Athenian general Antiphilus sought to win with his cavalry, as against Leonnatus, and the battle opened with a cavalry clash. With the horsemen of both sides engaged, Antipater sent his more numerous infantry against the enemy line. The allied infantry fell back to high ground, where it could hold off any assault, and when their cavalry saw it withdraw, they too left the field, conceding the victory.

The allied army was still intact, but after conferring with his cavalry commander, Menon of Pharsalus, Antiphilus sent envoys to Antipater the next day to ask for terms. Antipater would make no general peace with the alliance and insisted that each city send its own ambassadors. The allies at first refused, but when the Macedonians took several Thessalian cities, one city after another sought a separate peace. Abandoned, Athens surrendered unconditionally, and its democracy was replaced by an oligarchy led by Phocion.
battle-of-crecy: English monarchs had held lands in France since the Norman Conquest of 1066, which made them vassals of the kings of France. On 24 May 1337 the Great Council of Philip VI in Paris agreed that Edward III's lands in France should be taken back into the king's hands because he had breached his obligations as a vassal, and the Hundred Years' War began. Eight years of costly and inconclusive fighting followed. In 1345 Henry, Earl of Derby, led a rapid campaign in Gascony, defeating two large French armies at Bergerac and Auberoche. Edward landed at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue in Normandy on 12 July 1346, achieved complete strategic surprise and stormed Caen on 26 July, where more than 5,000 French soldiers and civilians were killed.

The English burned a path to within 2 miles (3 km) of Paris, then marched north hoping to meet an allied Flemish army. Edward chose a sloping hillside facing south-east at Crécy-en-Ponthieu, with Wadicourt anchoring the left flank and Crécy and the River Maye protecting the right. His men dug pits in front of their positions and set up several primitive gunpowder weapons. The English army, estimated by modern historians at between 7,000 and 15,000, was substantially smaller than the French, which Clifford Rogers puts at twice to three times its size.

Late on 26 August the French advanced, unfurling the oriflamme, the sacred banner that meant no prisoners would be taken. A rainstorm broke. Genoese crossbowmen engaged the longbowmen, who outranged them and shot more than three times as fast, and the crossbowmen fled. The French then charged uphill in a series of cavalry attacks, disordered by the fleeing crossbowmen, the mud and the pits, and broken up by archery that killed or wounded many of the unarmoured horses. By the time the charges reached the dismounted English men-at-arms they had lost much of their impetus. They continued late into the night, each ending in fierce fighting and a French retreat.

English losses were very low; a roll-call after the battle gave about forty dead, though some modern historians think around three hundred. The English heralds counted 1,542 bodies of French noble men-at-arms on the field, perhaps not including those killed the following day, and no count was made of lower-born foot soldiers. Edward then besieged Calais, which fell after eleven months and stayed in English hands until 1558. The battle was reported to the English parliament on 13 September as a sign of divine favour. Rogers calls it a total English victory, and Andrew Ayton says England's reputation as a military power was established in an evening's hard fighting. It confirmed the longbow as a dominant weapon of Western European warfare.
battle-of-cuito-cuanavale: The Angolan Civil War was fought against the backdrop of the Cold War, with the Soviet-backed MPLA government and its armed wing FAPLA supported by Cuba, and UNITA under Jonas Savimbi backed by the United States and South Africa. In August 1987 eight FAPLA brigades mustered for Operation Saluting October, a two-pronged drive on Mavinga, a major UNITA stronghold, and then on its headquarters at Jamba. The Soviet Union supplied over a billion dollars' worth of new equipment, and the operations were directed by Lieutenant General Petr Gusev, head of the Soviet military mission. South Africa, determined to keep the People's Liberation Army of Namibia out of the region, launched Operation Moduler on 4 August 1987.

The armies met at the Lomba River on 6 September. Through September and October the SADF repulsed FAPLA's attempts to cross and destroyed most of its bridging equipment, and the 61 Mechanised Battalion Group annihilated FAPLA's 47 Brigade, forcing the rest to withdraw east of Cuito Cuanavale. In Operation Hooper the SADF and UNITA tried in vain to destroy the retreating units, which concentrated in the Tumpo Triangle between the Cuito, Tumpo and Dala rivers, protected by minefields and reinforced by Cuban armoured units.

Over two months the SADF and UNITA made six unsuccessful assaults on the triangle under Operation Packer, the last on 23 March 1988, slowed by minefields and artillery fire. They disengaged after laying minefields south-east of the town, and a small force went on shelling Cuito Cuanavale and its airstrip with G-5 artillery until the end of August.

South Africa announced 31 dead and 90 wounded; later reports settled on 43 dead. UNITA lost around 3,000 dead. FAPLA and the Cubans claimed victory because they had held Cuito Cuanavale, while the SADF and UNITA claimed it because the offensive on Mavinga had been shattered. Fidel Castro called it an overwhelming victory, and Nelson Mandela a turning point for the liberation of the continent, while Peter Vanneman and Fen Osler Hampson judged that neither side won decisively. The battle is credited by some with opening the talks, mediated by the United States, that removed Cuban and South African troops from Angola and Namibia by 1991.
battle-of-culloden: Charles Edward Stuart landed in the Western Isles on 23 July 1745 to reclaim the British throne for the exiled House of Stuart. After a victory at Prestonpans in September the Jacobites controlled much of Scotland, and their invasion of England reached Derby before retreating. Recruitment brought their strength to more than 8,000, and on 17 January 1746 they repulsed a government force under Henry Hawley at the Battle of Falkirk Muir. When the Duke of Cumberland took over command, the Jacobites abandoned the siege of Stirling Castle and withdrew to Inverness.

A Royal Navy blockade left them short of money and food. When Cumberland resumed the campaign on 8 April, Charles and his advisers agreed their best option was a set-piece battle. On the night of 15 April Lord George Murray led a march to attack the government camp at Nairn, but it was slow and confused, and he turned back before reaching it, leaving the army tired and hungry.

On 16 April the Jacobites, about 5,400 strong, formed on Drummossie Moor with the Highland regiments in the first line and the River Nairn about a kilometre to their right. Cumberland's army marched across country and formed line within about 500 metres. The artillery of both sides opened fire at about 1:30 pm, though accounts differ on how long the Jacobites waited under bombardment.

When Charles ordered the advance, government gunners switched to canister shot, and the Highland regiments came on into heavy fire. In the centre and on the right the regiments swerved and became entangled. Many reached the government lines, where the brunt fell on Barrell's 4th Foot and Dejean's 37th Foot, but a second line counterattacked and surrounded them on three sides. The Jacobite first line collapsed, French regulars covered the retreat, and the fleeing Highlanders were pursued by dragoons. Jacobite losses were between 1,500 and 2,000 killed or wounded, many in the pursuit. Cumberland reported 50 dead and 259 wounded.

The army was ordered to disperse until Charles returned with French support, and by 18 April most of it had disbanded, though at least a third had missed the battle. Of 3,471 prisoners, only one in twenty was tried; about 1,200 were transported, 905 were released under the Indemnity Act 1747, 362 were exchanged with France, and 120 were executed. The defeat effectively ended Jacobitism as a significant element in British politics.

Commemoration was slight before the 1840s. A cairn was raised on the battlefield in 1881, and the Gaelic Society of Inverness began an annual ceremony in 1925. The site is now protected, with a visitor centre opened in December 2007 and the farmhouse of Leanach standing where a cottage probably served as a government field hospital.
battle-of-cunaxa: Cyrus the Younger revolted against his elder brother Artaxerxes II for control of the Achaemenid throne. He gathered Greek mercenaries, 10,400 hoplites and 2,500 light infantry and peltasts under the Spartan general Clearchus, and a large force of levied troops under his second-in-command Ariaeus. The main source for the campaign is Xenophon, a Greek who took part and was probably a mid-level officer. The battle was fought in the late summer of 401 BCE at Cunaxa, 70 kilometres north of Babylon on the left bank of the Euphrates.

Cyrus placed the Greeks on his right, beside the river, and himself stood in the centre with 600 bodyguards. He asked Clearchus to move into the centre to attack Artaxerxes, but Clearchus refused for fear of his unprotected right flank, which showed how little control Cyrus had over his army. Artaxerxes, with a far longer line, placed himself in the centre with 6,000 cavalry.

The Greeks charged the left flank of Artaxerxes' army, which broke and fled before they came within arrowshot. On the other side the fight was harder, and Cyrus personally charged his brother's bodyguard and was killed by a javelin. The rebels retreated, but the Greeks, who had not heard of his death, held firm, and Clearchus drove back the larger right wing. Meanwhile Artaxerxes' troops took the Greek camp and destroyed their food supplies.

The Greeks learned only after the battle that Cyrus was dead, which made their victory irrelevant. They offered to make Ariaeus king, but he refused as he was not of royal blood. The satrap Tissaphernes supplied them and led them northwards, then invited their senior officers to a feast, where they were taken prisoner, brought to the king and beheaded. The Greeks elected new officers and marched north through Corduene and Armenia to the Black Sea, the march of the Ten Thousand that Xenophon recorded in the Anabasis.
The physician Ctesias, a native of Caria, was with Artaxerxes at the battle and treated the king's wound. He later wrote a history of Assyria and Persia in 23 books, the Persica.
battle-of-curupayty: Curupayty was a fortified line of trenches in the Paraguayan defences around the fortress of Humaitá. It was held by about 5,000 men and 49 cannon under General José Eduvigis Díaz, some of the guns placed where an attacker could not see them. The allied armies of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, with about 20,000 men for the assault, planned to break it with the support of the Imperial Brazilian Navy, whose ships had to keep their distance from the guns of Humaitá.

The attack of 22 September began at 07:00 with a bombardment by Admiral Tamandaré's fleet, including the Brasil, Barroso, Tamandaré and Ipiranga, which lasted until noon. Despite the firing of 5,000 bombs and shells, only one Paraguayan gun was damaged, and a decoy trench drew much of the fire while the defenders waited elsewhere. Assuming that the positions had been destroyed, Bartolomé Mitre ordered the land advance.

Argentine columns under Generals Emilio Mitre and Wenceslao Paunero formed the right wing, Brazilian columns under General Albino de Carvalho and Colonel Augusto Caldas the left, and Brazilians under Colonel Lucas de Lima the centre. Advancing in dense formations through mud, the troops crossed two ditches and came under grape, canister and shell fire as they reached the wall. Only about 60 men got close to it, and they were soon killed. By 14:00 the attack had been abandoned, and by 17:00 the army was back at Curuzú.

Around a fifth of the attackers were lost, while Paraguay lost fewer than a hundred men. Francisco Solano López did not counterattack, and the allied retreat was orderly, covered by the guns of Tamandaré's squadron. The defeat changed the allied command, led to tensions within the Triple Alliance and was followed by open revolt against the war in Argentina by January 1867. In Paraguay the victory became a symbol of national unity, and political opponents were pardoned. It did not change the outcome: after the Siege of Humaitá and the fall of Asunción in 1868, Paraguay's position became desperate.
battle-of-curzola: The battle was one of many fought in the 13th and 14th centuries between Pisa, Genoa and Venice in a long series of wars for the control of Mediterranean and Levantine trade. The Venetian fleet was led by Admiral Andrea Dandolo, son of Doge Giovanni Dandolo, and the Genoese by Lamba Doria.

The fighting took place in the channel between Curzola and the mainland peninsula of Sabbioncello, now Pelješac, and also ashore, where Venetian troops had been landed on the far side of the island. The Venetians ran their galleys aground while trying to capture the Genoese ships, and Doria, showing the better strategy, turned this into a resounding defeat. His own son was killed in the fighting, and Doria was said to have ordered him thrown overboard into the deep sea, asking what better resting place they could give him.

The two fleets had apparently been equal in number, yet Venice lost 83 of its 95 ships, and about 7,000 men were killed. Andrea Dandolo was taken prisoner by the Genoese and soon afterwards took his own life.

Although the defeat was a disaster, Venice at once equipped another 100 galleys and sought peace terms that would not seriously hamper its power and prosperity. According to a later tradition of the 16th century, recorded by Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Marco Polo was among the Venetian prisoners and dictated his book during his few months of captivity. Whether he was in fact captured in this battle or in an earlier minor engagement near Laiazzo is unclear.
battle-of-custoza-1848: In March 1848 the city of Milan rose against Austrian occupation. Charles Albert of Piedmont-Sardinia supported the Milanese revolt and declared war on Austria, and Venice declared its independence from Austria. The Austrian Field Marshal Radetzky withdrew his forces from Milan to defensive positions based on the four fortresses known as the Quadrilateral: Verona, Mantua, Peschiera and Legnago. The Piedmontese took Peschiera after a short siege, but Radetzky received substantial reinforcements.

By July the Piedmontese army was widely dispersed, from the Rivoli plateau in the north to Governolo in the south. On 23 July Radetzky attacked the Piedmontese II Corps under General Ettore Gerbaix De Sonnaz and forced it back first before Peschiera and, after a second attack on the 24th, behind the River Mincio, which split the Piedmontese army in two.

The Piedmontese high command reacted slowly and uncertainly. It decided to attack the Austrian rear towards the village of Staffalo with the bulk of I Corps under General Eusebio Bava. The attack began on the afternoon of the 24th and succeeded, forcing back the single brigade covering the area. This lulled the Sardinian commanders into complacency and led Radetzky to halt his advance beyond the Mincio and turn on these forces.

For the 25th the Piedmontese were ordered to attack the enemy further on, with II Corps to support from the Mincio, but De Sonnaz refused to obey the order, claiming his troops were too tired. What was meant to be an offensive became a struggle to hold the advancing enemy. All day the outnumbered Piedmontese faced attacks by two Austrian army corps, and by evening the whole line had been pushed back, though in good order and with the men still fighting.

The battle was not a total victory for the Austrians: they suffered higher losses, and all major Piedmontese units kept their cohesion and equipment. It was nonetheless a considerable reversal. On the 26th the Piedmontese failed to stop the Austrians crossing the Mincio at Volta Mantovana and suffered a decisive defeat. They fell back first behind the River Oglio and then to Milan. After a small battle on the outskirts of the city an armistice was signed, and the army retreated into the Kingdom of Sardinia. An attempt to renew the war the next year brought another victory for Radetzky and effectively ended the First Italian War of Independence. Johann Strauss I's Radetzky March was commissioned to commemorate his victories.
battle-of-custoza-1866: In June 1866 Prussia declared war on the Austrian Empire. The recently formed Kingdom of Italy allied with Prussia, intending to annex Venetia and so unite the peninsula. The Italians quickly raised a force twice the size of the Austrian troops defending Venetia, and divided it into two armies: the Army of the Mincio, of eleven divisions under General Alfonso La Marmora and accompanied by King Vittorio Emanuele II, and the five-division Army of the Po under Enrico Cialdini. The Austrians, with the advantage of interior lines and the protection of the Quadrilateral forts, concentrated against the Army of the Mincio and left a covering force against the Army of the Po.

Archduke Albrecht marched west from Verona to the north of the Italians, hoping to get behind them. On 24 June La Marmora turned his front towards the same heights, so that the armies collided head on near Villafranca. At 7:00 a.m. the Austrian cavalry attacked the Italian I Corps without orders; the charge was ineffectual but caused panic in the Italian rear and kept three divisions on the defensive all day. In the morning fighting broke out at Oliosi, San Rocco, Custoza and San Giorgio. Brignone's division took Belvedere Hill, but a counterattack led by the king's younger son Amadeo failed and left the prince wounded, and Brignone was forced back.

By 1:00 p.m. La Marmora thought the battle lost and ordered a retreat, although Govone's division had in fact taken Belvedere Hill. At 2:00 p.m. General Rodich attacked Monte Vento and Santa Lucia; when Sirtori's division gave way, a hole opened in the Italian line. General Maroicic committed the two Austrian reserve brigades without orders and attacked Govone's flank, and after a bombardment by 40 guns the Austrians drove the Italians out of Custoza at 5:00 p.m.

The Italians were driven back across the Mincio out of Veneto, but the defeat was not decisive. Albrecht did not pursue, thinking his troops exhausted and his cavalry mauled, and he moved his headquarters back to Verona on 26 June, so the demoralised Army of the Mincio was not destroyed. After the Austrian defeat at Königgrätz on 3 July, one corps was moved to cover Vienna. The Italians resumed the offensive in mid-July, Cialdini occupying Rovigo, Padua, Vicenza and Udine, but they suffered a naval defeat at Lissa on 20 July. By the armistice of Nikolsburg on 26 July Austria agreed to cede Veneto to Italy through French mediation.
battle-of-cutanda: After taking the city of Zaragoza in 1118, Alfonso the Battler pressed on against the Almoravids in the lands of the former Taifa of Zaragoza. In May 1120, together with the Duke of Aquitaine, he laid siege to Calatayud, the second city of that territory, while part of his forces moved south along a tributary of the Jalón River to besiege the fortified town of Daroca.

When news came that an Almoravid relief army under Ibrahim ibn Yusuf was marching towards Calatayud, Alfonso and the duke took most of their troops to intercept it. Alfonso's army was also joined by soldiers of the former ibn-Hūd ruler of Zaragoza, which brought it, by one estimate, to as many as 15,000 men.

The Almoravid army advanced north through the valley of the Jiloca River towards Daroca. It included contingents from Sevilla, Murcia and Lérida and has been estimated at 5,000 mounted knights and 10,000 foot soldiers. Alfonso is believed to have known of its approach and to have known the terrain, and to have prepared his ground accordingly.

The two armies met on 17 June 1120 at a place called Cutanda, near Calamocha in Teruel. The Christian army, drawn mainly from Aragon and Navarre, appears to have taken the Almoravids by surprise, and the result was a complete rout. The Almoravid army was destroyed and its general, Ibrahim, was killed, and among the dead was also the scholar Abu Ali al-Sadafi. With no further hope of relief, both Calatayud and Daroca surrendered, and Alfonso went on with his campaign in the lands of Zaragoza.
battle-of-cynoscephalae: The Second Macedonian War followed an uneasy peace after the First Macedonian War, which had begun because of an alliance between Macedon and Carthage in the Second Punic War. Philip V's moves against Thrace, the Dardanelles, Rhodes and the Kingdom of Pergamum alarmed Rhodes and Pergamum, which sent envoys to Rome. When Philip would not give up further conquests, the Roman Senate and Assembly declared war. Titus Quinctius Flamininus took command in Macedonia in 198 BCE and demanded that Philip withdraw from all of Greece outside the Macedonian homeland; Philip stormed out of the talks. By the start of 197 BCE he had lost most of his earlier conquests.

In the spring of 197 BCE the armies camped near Pherae, and Philip then marched west towards Scotussa for grain, with the Romans following on the other side of the Cynoscephalae Hills. Flamininus had about 26,000 men, among them Aetolian allies and war elephants from Numidia. Philip had about 25,500, of whom 16,000 were phalangites. In a heavy fog the light infantry and cavalry of both sides collided on the hills, and each general reinforced his men. Philip, misled by reports that the Roman force was routed, attacked with 8,000 phalangites and 4,000 peltasts before his left wing was formed.

Flamininus sent his elephants against the disordered Macedonian left, which broke and fled. An unnamed tribune then took 20 maniples, about 2,500 men, into the rear of the Macedonian right, and the rigid phalanx disintegrated. According to Polybius and Livy 8,000 Macedonians were killed, and Flamininus took 5,000 prisoners; Roman losses were between 700 and 750. Philip escaped with a few cavalry.

The peace of 196 BCE let Philip keep his kingdom but required him to leave his conquests, withdraw his garrisons from Greece, pay 1,000 talents of silver, give up all but five to ten decked ships and keep an army of no more than 5,000 men. It is often held that this battle, with the later Battle of Pydna, showed the superiority of the Roman legion over the phalanx. Some scholars challenge that view, pointing out that the Romans won because the Macedonian left was not yet formed.
battle-of-cynoscephalae-364-bce: Alexander took power in Pherae in 369 BCE after murdering his uncle Polyphron, became tagos of the Thessalian League and extended his city's dominance over the other cities of Thessaly, whose leaders appealed to Thebes. Pelopidas negotiated with him in 369 without result, and in 368 Alexander took Pelopidas and Ismenias prisoner; a force under Epaminondas secured their release. In 364, after Alexander had seized Achaia Phthiotis and Magnesia, the Theban assembly voted Pelopidas an army of seven thousand, but it was disbanded after a solar eclipse on 13 July was taken as a bad omen.

Pelopidas set out anyway, against the advice of the priests, with volunteer cavalry and mercenaries, and gathered Thessalian allies at Pharsalos into what the classicist James Romm calls a rough, untrained phalanx, with some three hundred Theban horsemen. Diodorus Siculus gives Alexander around 20,000 troops; Plutarch says his infantry outnumbered Pelopidas's two to one.

The two armies met in the Cynoscephalae Hills, where Alexander's men had reached the Thetideion, a temple of Thetis on a ridge. Both sides sent light infantry to seize the high ground between them, and Alexander's more experienced troops won it, while Pelopidas's cavalry won the plain to the south. An attempt to retake the heights with hoplites failed with heavy losses. Pelopidas recalled his cavalry, re-equipped himself as a hoplite and reorganised his infantry, with the Thessalians in a deep formation on the left and the Thebans on the right.

After several failed attacks Alexander's troops withdrew to avoid being outflanked by the cavalry. Seeing Alexander on the enemy right, Pelopidas charged towards him, got ahead of his men in the disordered downhill rush and was killed by javelins. His hoplites reformed and, with the cavalry, broke Alexander's army; according to Plutarch, 3,000 of its men were killed.

According to Plutarch, the Thessalians piled captured weapons around Pelopidas's body. Their cities granted lands to his children and raised a bronze statue of him by Lysippos. Alexander, possibly after a second battle, gave up the cities he had taken, accepted an alliance with Thebes and agreed, in the words Diodorus reports, to rule over Pherae alone, making Thebes the hegemon of Thessaly. He was assassinated in 358 or 357 BCE by his wife Thebe and her brothers.
battle-of-dandanaqan: The Seljuks were forced out of Transoxiana in 1034 by the Kara-Khanids and settled in Khwarazm under the protection of the Ghaznavid governor Harun. After his murder in 1035 they fled across the Kara Kum Desert towards Merv, but turned instead to Nasa on the edge of Khurasan. The Ghaznavid sultan Ma'sud I sent Iltughdi with a large army to Nasa, and it at first drove off the Seljuk forces. Then it began squabbling over the spoils. The Seljuks, led by Chaghri, returned, fell on the disorganised Ghaznavids and defeated them. Ma'sud then granted the Seljuks three cities in Khurasan, Dihistan, Nasa and Farawa, and after raids as far as Balkh all of Khurasan fell to them.

During Ma'sud's march to Sarakhs, Seljuk raiders harassed his army with hit-and-run tactics. Swift and mobile, the Turkmens were better suited to fighting in steppe and desert than the heavily laden and conservative Ghaznavid army. They also destroyed its supply lines and cut it off from the nearby wells, which seriously reduced its discipline and morale. On 23 May 1040 around 16,000 Seljuk soldiers fought a starving and demoralised Ghaznavid army at Dandanaqan, near Merv, and destroyed a large part of it. Ma'sud fled to India, was overthrown and was finally murdered in prison.

The victory brought down Ghaznavid domination in Greater Khorasan. The Seljuks took Herat, Sistan, Pushang and Ghur, put Musa Yabghu bin Seljuk in charge, and besieged Balkh. By 1047 Tughril had coins minted at Nishapur that called him al-Sultan al-Mu'azzam and Shahanshah. The Seljuks lost Khurasan to the Khwarazmian Empire in 1138, which in turn lost it to the Ghoris in 1173.
battle-of-delium: In 424 BCE the Athenian generals Demosthenes and Hippocrates planned a two-pronged invasion of Boeotia. Demosthenes sailed too early and landed at Siphae, where his plans were betrayed by a Phocian named Nicomachus, and he had to withdraw. Hippocrates then arrived with 7,000 Athenian hoplites, 1,000 cavalry and some 10,000 metics and other non-citizens, and fortified the temple at Delium in five days. He left a garrison and sent the rest of the army home. Many Boeotians saw no point in attacking a departing enemy, but Pagondas of Thebes urged them on, knowing the Athenians would use Delium as a base.

The Boeotians had 7,000 hoplites, 1,000 cavalry, 500 peltasts and 10,000 light troops, with the Thebans on the right wing, the men of Haliartus, Coronea and Copiae in the centre, and Thespiae, Tanagra and Orchomenus on the left. The two armies were hidden from each other by a hill, and the Boeotians charged while Hippocrates was still addressing his men. The longer Athenian line surrounded the Boeotian left, where only the Thespian contingent stood firm, but in circling them some Athenians killed one another by mistake, the first documented incident of friendly fire.

Pagondas sent his cavalry to support the left, the Athenians there broke, and when the Theban right also prevailed the Athenian centre fled. About 500 Boeotians and 1,000 Athenians were killed. Plato has Alcibiades describe Socrates retreating calmly beside Laches, so plainly ready to defend himself that pursuers left him alone.

The survivors held the fort at Delium and answered a Boeotian herald's demand to leave sacred ground by claiming the land as their own. After two weeks, joined by 2,000 hoplites from Corinth and other allies, the Boeotians used a device that Thucydides describes, apparently a kind of flamethrower, to set the fort alight; about 200 Athenians died and the rest escaped. Demosthenes arrived too late and was defeated near Sicyon. Pagondas's use of deep ranks, reserves, cavalry, skirmishers and changing tactics marked one of the first planned tactical battles in recorded history.
battle-of-delville-wood: Delville Wood, a thick tangle of beech and hornbeam with hazel thickets cut by grassy rides, lay east of the village of Longueval. In the general offensive that began on 14 July 1916, the Battle of Bazentin Ridge, General Douglas Haig meant to take the German second position between Delville Wood and Bazentin le Petit. The divisions of XIII and XV Corps of General Sir Henry Rawlinson's Fourth Army attacked at 3:25 a.m. after a five-minute hurricane bombardment, which gained a measure of surprise. Longueval could not be held safely without the wood, which overlooked the village and offered the Germans a starting point for counter-attacks.

The 1st South African Infantry Brigade, fighting its first battle on the Western Front with the 9th (Scottish) Division, took the wood on 15 July. The village and wood formed a salient that German artillery could fire on from three sides. A South African attack on 17 July failed, and in the night the German 3rd Guards Division advanced behind a creeping barrage and drove the brigade from its forward trenches. On 20 July troops of the 76th Brigade broke through, and Lieutenant-Colonel E. F. Thackeray marched out with two wounded officers and 140 other ranks, the last of the brigade.

For the rest of July and August British attacks and German counter-attacks continued. Wet weather, ammunition shortages and heavy losses reduced both sides to piecemeal attacks on narrow fronts, most of them stopped by defensive fire and mud. The fighting went on for seven weeks, until just before the Battle of Flers–Courcelette.

The 9th (Scottish) Division lost 7,517 men from 1 to 20 July, 2,536 of them from the South African brigade, and the 3rd Division lost 6,102 from 11 to 27 July. Holding Longueval and the wood let the divisions to the north take High Wood, and the Battle of Flers–Courcelette, with the first use of tanks, began from there in September. The wood, replanted with oak and birch by the South African government, keeps the remains of trenches, a museum and the South African National Memorial.
battle-of-dhi-qar: In the 6th century the Lakhmid kingdom, a client of the Sasanian Empire, projected Persian power into Arabia and shielded it from nomadic raids. Seeking direct control, the Persians deposed the Lakhmids in 602. King al-Nu'man III travelled from the Lakhmid capital, al-Hira, to the court at Ctesiphon, where he was seized and sent to prison at Khanaqin; he died there of plague. The Persians made Iyas ibn Qabisa, leader of the Tayyi tribe, governor of the region, which soon brought them into conflict with the Banu Bakr, a large tribal confederation of south-western Iraq and eastern Arabia.

Persian sources do not mention the battle, and its story comes from two later Arabic versions. One goes back to Ibn al-Kalbi, who died in 819: the fall of the Lakhmids opened the way to Bakri raids, and when rival members of the Shayban kept raiding despite an agreement, the Persians imprisoned the Shaybani leader and demanded Bakri hostages, which were refused. The other, held to be more fanciful, goes back to Abu Ubayda, in which the Shaybani chief refused Khosrow II's demand to hand over the former king's family and armour.

The Bakris won despite poor coordination among their tribes. Traditional sources put the Persians and their Arab auxiliaries at 2,000 and 3,000, and the clash may have been no more than a skirmish. Muslim traditions date it anywhere from 602 to 624, a range modern scholars have narrowed to 604 to 611.

The battle, also called the War of the Camel's Udder, is remembered as a turning point in Arab-Persian relations and a blow to Persian control over eastern Arabia. It is sometimes seen as part of a longer Arab revolt against Persia that culminated in the early Muslim conquests a few decades later. Its classical account is in al-Tabari's History of the Prophets and Kings, and it appears earlier in the Khuzistan Chronicle.
battle-of-didgori: On the complaints of the Muslim merchants of Tbilisi, Ganja and Dmanisi, Sultan Mahmud II of Baghdad sent an expedition into Georgia under Ilghazi ibn Artuq of Mardin. Ilghazi had pillaged the County of Edessa and defeated Roger of Antioch at the battle of Ager Sanguinis in 1119. He joined a Muslim coalition that included Tughan-Arslan, the Mazyadid Dubays ibn Sadaqa and Toghrul. In the first half of 1121 the Georgians twice attacked the Seljuks in the Emirate of Ganja, so that the ruler of Arran could not take part.

The size of the coalition is debated. Walter the Chancellor and Matthew of Edessa give 600,000 and 560,000, while modern Georgian historians estimate 100,000 to 250,000, and the higher numbers are held to be exaggerated. The Georgian army numbered 56,000, including 500 Alans, about 200 Franks and 15,000 Kipchaks. King David IV had formed the mona-spa, a royal servant host of about 5,000 heavy horsemen.

The Muslim army entered Trialeti and encamped near Didgori and Manglisi on 10 August 1121. David led his army from Mtskheta along the Nichbisi valley on 11 August and divided it, keeping a smaller group under his son Demetrius hidden behind the heights. The battle was fought on 12 August. According to Ibn al-Athir, a Kipchak detachment feigned desertion and attacked the Seljuk commanders at a meeting. David then sent his Frankish knights against the vanguard, and the cavalry charged downhill on both flanks.

Ilghazi was injured and withdrew, leaving the army leaderless. The battle was decided in about three hours, and a Georgian chronicler says the pursuit lasted three days. Matthew of Edessa writes that the corpses filled the rivers and covered the valleys and cliffs. Fugitives were hunted down for several days so that they could not regroup.

The victory allowed the Georgians to liberate the region from Muslim influence and to contest territory within the Seljuk Empire. David captured Tbilisi in 1122 and soon moved the capital there from Kutaisi. The Georgian Chronicles celebrate Didgori as a miraculous victory, and it began the medieval Georgian Golden Age. Georgians still mark 12 August as the festival of Didgoroba.
battle-of-dien-bien-phu: By 1953 the First Indochina War had defeated a succession of French commanders, who had been unable to suppress the Viet Minh insurrection. In 1952 and 1953 the Viet Minh overran much of Laos. Navarre looked for a way to protect it, and Colonel Louis Berteil formulated the hedgehog concept: a fortified airhead, supplied by air, beside Viet Minh supply lines to Laos.

In June 1953 Major General René Cogny proposed Dien Bien Phu, which had an old airstrip built by the Japanese. Navarre chose it, and every major subordinate officer protested; Cogny warned of a new Nà Sản under worse conditions. Operation Castor began on 20 November 1953, when the French dropped or flew about 9,000 troops into the area in three days.

The French had assumed that the Viet Minh had no anti-aircraft capability. Under General Võ Nguyên Giáp the Viet Minh surrounded the camp and hauled heavy artillery, anti-aircraft guns among it, up the rear slopes of the mountains, where tunnels let them pull the guns out, fire and withdraw. Their attack began on 13 March 1954 against the outpost Béatrice. On 14 March the airstrip was put permanently out of commission, so supplies had to come by parachute. On 17 March most of the Tai troops defending Anne-Marie left or defected.

Fighting then centred on the strong points Eliane and Dominique, and from 5 April Giáp changed to entrenchment and sapping. By the end of April the outpost Isabelle was nearly out of water and ammunition. On 6 May the Viet Minh used Katyusha rockets for the first time and exploded a mine under Eliane 2. The garrison was overrun, and the survivors surrendered on 7 May.

Dien Bien Phu was the decisive battle of the First Indochina War, and the loss of the garrison cost roughly one-tenth of the French Union manpower in Indochina. The Viet Minh counted 11,721 prisoners on 8 May, of whom 4,436 were wounded. The able-bodied were force-marched over 600 km to prison camps, and hundreds died of disease on the way.

The Geneva Conference opened on 8 May, and its agreement in July partitioned Vietnam into a communist North and the State of Vietnam in the south, temporarily, with elections in 1956 that were never held. The last French forces left Vietnam in 1956. The defeat did not significantly alter the strategic situation, but it brought a profound psychological shock to France.
battle-of-diu-1509: The Portuguese found that trade of the kind they had practised in West Africa was impossible in India, because Muslim merchant elites on the west coast incited attacks on them and led the massacre of the Portuguese at Calicut in 1500. In 1505 Dom Francisco de Almeida sailed from Lisbon as the first viceroy of India, with orders to curb hostile Muslim shipping. The disruption of the spice trade threatened Venetian interests, and Venice supplied the Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri with ships and gunners. The expedition under Amir Hussain al-Kurdi reached Diu in September 1507, where the governor, Malik Ayyaz, supported it only cautiously.

In March 1508 the fleets of Hussain and Ayyaz fought the Portuguese in the harbour of Chaul, and among the dead was the viceroy's son Lourenço. Almeida resolved on revenge. Afonso de Albuquerque arrived with orders to replace him, but Almeida refused to give up office, razed Dabul on his way and sailed for Diu. On 2 February 1509 the Portuguese sighted the port. Hussain had lashed his carracks and galleys together near shore under the fortress and waited for the attack.

The battle began about 11:00 on 3 February with a general bombardment, in which the Portuguese fired directly at the water so that the cannonballs bounced like skipping stones. Hussain's flagship was grappled by the Espírito Santo, and the arrival of the Rei Grande tipped the balance. The oar ships of Calicut, held back in the channel, were blocked by the viceroy's flagship Flor do Mar, which fired over 600 shots, and they retreated to Calicut. The last great carrack was sunk by continuous bombardment at dusk.

Malik Ayyaz returned the prisoners of Chaul. Almeida signed a trade agreement with him and opened a feitoria but declined to take Diu. The Mamluk captives were treated brutally: Almeida ordered most of them hanged, burned alive or torn to pieces, in retaliation for his son's death. Hussain fled with 22 other Mamluks and was later murdered on the Red Sea by his Turkish second-in-command. Almeida handed the viceroyalty to Albuquerque and left in November 1509; he was killed in December in a skirmish with the Khoikhoi near the Cape of Good Hope.
Historians regard the battle as one of the most important in naval history. According to Michael Adas, it established European naval superiority in the Indian Ocean for centuries to come.
battle-of-dogali: After unification in 1861 Italy sought a colonial empire to secure its standing as a great power, and its occupation of coastal Eritrea brought it into conflict with Ethiopia. Moving inland, the Italians seized the villages of Ua-à and Zula and the town of Sahati, where they built a redoubt commanding the water supply of the caravans. Ras Alula Engida, governor under Emperor Yohannes IV, returned to Asmara from a campaign against the Dervishes and warned that the Italians were breaking the treaty between Abyssinia, Egypt and Britain, and that any further move towards Sahati would be treated as hostile.

The Italians reinforced the post instead. By 25 January it was held by 167 Italians and 1,000 native troops. Ras Alula attacked it on his own initiative, losing hundreds of men to cannon and rifle fire while only four Italians were wounded, and pulled back. The garrison asked for more ammunition and supplies.

On 26 January a battalion of about 550 men, 500 Italians and 50 Eritrean irregulars with two machine guns, under Lieutenant-Colonel Tommaso De Cristoforis, set out for Sahati and was ambushed by about 10,000 warriors under Ras Alula. The Gatling guns soon jammed, and once their ammunition was spent De Cristoforis and most of his men were killed in hand-to-hand fighting. McLachlan gives Italian losses of 23 officers and 407 soldiers killed and 1 officer and 81 men wounded; the Italians estimated that 1,000 of Ras Alula's men had died.

Italy abandoned Sahati and nearby posts, but the defeat stirred revanchist feeling, and the new cabinet of Francesco Crispi sent 18,000 troops with modern weapons. After clashes from March to May 1888, the Ethiopians, short of supplies and facing Mahdist incursions in the west, withdrew, and Italy founded its colony of Eritrea in 1890. The historian Haggai Erlich notes that the battle also led the Italians to encourage Menelik of Shewa against the emperor.

In Rome the Piazza dei Cinquecento in front of Termini station is named after the 500 Italian dead, and the cruiser Dogali took the battle's name. For the centenary in January 1987 the Ethiopian government of Mengistu Haile Mariam put up a monument topped with a red star on the battlefield; it was blown up after Eritrean forces took the area in 1989.
battle-of-dorylaeum-1097: The crusaders left Nicaea on 26 June 1097, distrusting the Byzantines, who had taken the city without their knowledge after a long siege. To ease supplies the army split in two. The weaker vanguard was led by Bohemond of Taranto, his nephew Tancred, Robert Curthose, Robert of Flanders and the Byzantine general Tatikios. Godfrey of Bouillon, Baldwin of Boulogne, Raymond IV of Toulouse, Stephen II of Blois and Hugh of Vermandois followed in the rear, about 5 km behind.

Bohemond's force probably numbered about 10,000, mostly on foot. The Turkish army of Kilij Arslan and his ally Gazi Gümüshtigin numbered 6–7,000 cavalry, including Danishmendid troops. Chroniclers gave far higher figures, which modern historians consider impossible. On the evening of 30 June Bohemond camped on the north bank of the river Thymbres near the ruined town of Dorylaion.

At dawn on 1 July the Turks surrounded the camp and shot arrows into it, taking the crusaders by surprise and cutting down non-combatants and unarmoured foot soldiers. Bohemond ordered his knights to dismount and form a defensive line, with the foot soldiers and non-combatants gathered in the centre, where the women carried water. Turkish horse archers charged, shot and withdrew, doing little harm to the armoured knights but killing many horses and foot soldiers.

Godfrey arrived just after midday with 50 knights, and small groups of reinforcements came through the day. After about seven hours Raymond's knights struck the Turkish flank. In mid-afternoon a force led by Bishop Adhemar of Le Puy, the papal legate, came round through the hills and fell on the Turkish camp from the rear. Seeing the camp in flames, the Turks fled. Albert of Aix claimed 4,000 crusader and 3,000 Turkish casualties.

The crusaders captured Arslan's treasury and became rich, at least for a time. Arslan turned to other concerns in the east and, as a punishment, took male Greek children from the region between Dorylaeum and Iconium, sending many as slaves to Persia. The crusaders marched virtually unopposed across Anatolia, which took almost three months, and began the Siege of Antioch in October.

Emperor Alexios I Komnenos gained part of what he had sought, the recovery of imperial lands in Asia Minor, and John Doukas restored Byzantine rule in Chios, Rhodes, Smyrna, Ephesus, Sardis and Philadelphia in 1097–1099. His daughter Anna ascribed this to his diplomacy, but Latin historians of the crusade blamed his treachery.
battle-of-dumlupinar: After the Battle of Sakarya in August and September 1921, the Greek Army of Asia Minor under General Anastasios Papoulas fell back to a defensive line running from İzmit to Eskişehir and Kara Hisâr, present-day Afyonkarahisar. The line formed an arc of some 700 km over hilly ground. A single-track railway ran from Kara Hisâr through Dumlupınar to Smyrna on the coast and was the main supply route of the Greeks. Greek morale was low: many men had been under arms for years, and no quick end to the war was in sight.

Mustafa Kemal, Commander-in-Chief of the government at Ankara, resisted pressure to attack and used the pause to strengthen his forces and draw French and Italian sympathy towards the Turks, which isolated the pro-Greek British. For the offensive he reinforced the First Army under Nureddin Pasha against the southern flank of the Greek salient at Kara Hisâr. The Greek army under Lieutenant General Georgios Hatzianestis numbered about 220,000 men but was short of heavy artillery; the Turkish Western Front had about 208,000.

On the night of 25 to 26 August the Turkish V Cavalry Corps passed through the Kirka gorge behind the Greek lines and cut the telegraph and the railway to Smyrna. On 26 August a heavy artillery barrage was followed by an attack of seven Turkish divisions on two Greek ones, and on 27 August the Turkish IV Corps broke through at the peak of Erkmentepe. The Greek I Corps ordered a withdrawal and Kara Hisâr was evacuated. With communications broken, the Greek headquarters at Smyrna issued orders that no longer matched the situation, and a gap opened between the groups of Major General Frangou and Major General Nikolaos Trikoupis.

The Trikoupis Group was encircled and fought all day on 29 August without breaking through. On 30 August near Alıören Turkish artillery inflicted heavy losses on its crowded columns, and the Turks counted over 2,000 Greek dead on the field the next day. Trikoupis surrendered with 5,000 to 6,000 men on 2 September; brought before Mustafa Kemal, he learned that he had been appointed commander-in-chief of the Greek army in Asia Minor.

By 7 September the Greek army had suffered 50,000 casualties, 35,000 killed and wounded and 15,000 captured, while Turkish casualties between 26 August and 9 September were 13,476. The last Greek troops left Anatolia from Erdek and Biga on 18 September. The Armistice of Mudanya was signed on 11 October 1922, and Greece was forced to accede to it on 14 October.
battle-of-dun-nechtain: During the 7th century the Northumbrians extended their territory northward, and Bede's evidence points to the Picts being subjugated under King Oswald and his successor Oswiu. Soon after Ecgfrith succeeded Oswiu in 670, the Picts rebelled and were crushed at the Battle of Two Rivers; the king of Fortriu, Drest mac Donuel, was deposed and replaced by Bridei. By 679 the Northumbrian hegemony seems to have begun to fall apart, with a Mercian victory over Ecgfrith in which his brother Ælfwine of Deira was killed.

Sieges at Dunnottar in 680 and Dundurn in 682, most probably by Bridei's forces, threatened Ecgfrith's hold on the southern Picts. Bridei, who was closely involved with the church of Iona, is also unlikely to have welcomed the new Northumbrian-sponsored see at Abercorn, whose bishop Trumwine was consecrated Bishop of the Picts.

Ecgfrith attacked Fortriu against the counsel of his advisers, among them Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne; the consensus is that he meant to reassert control over the Picts. Bede gives the fullest account, though a brief one, with further detail in the annals of Ulster and Tigernach and in Nennius's Historia Brittonum. The Picts feigned retreat and drew the Northumbrians into an ambush at a lake in the mountains, where their army was defeated.

The site is uncertain. Bede says only that the battle took place in straits of inaccessible mountains, Nennius calls it Gueith Linn Garan, the Battle of Crane Lake, and the Irish annals name Dún Nechtain, Nechtan's Fort. Since George Chalmers in the early 19th century it has been placed at Dunnichen in Angus, but in 2006 the historian Alex Woolf pointed to the absence of inaccessible mountains in mid-Angus and argued for Dunachton, on Loch Insh in Badenoch, a name of the same origin.

Bede recounts that the Picts recovered the lands held by the Northumbrians and the Dál Riatan Scots, and that the Northumbrians who did not flee were killed or enslaved. The diocese of the Picts was abandoned, Trumwine and his monks fleeing to Whitby, which stalled Roman Catholic expansion in Scotland. Battles between Northumbrians and Picts went on, as in 697, when Berhtred son of Beornhæth was killed, but Pictish independence from Northumbria was permanently secured.
battle-of-dunbar-1296: King Edward I of England invaded Scotland in March 1296 to punish King John Balliol for refusing to support English military action in France. After the sack of Berwick-upon-Tweed he stayed a month in the town to strengthen its defences, and on 5 April received John's renunciation of his homage. The next objective was the Earl of March's castle at Dunbar, 29 miles up the coast. March was with the English, but his wife, Marjory Comyn, sister of the Earl of Buchan, let the Scots occupy the castle. Edward sent John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, Balliol's own father-in-law, with a strong force of knights to besiege it.

The garrison appealed to King John at Haddington, and his army, or a large part of it, marched to its relief without him. The battle seems to have been fought between two bodies of mounted men-at-arms: one of the four formations of the English cavalry against most of the Scottish cavalry, led in part by the Comyns. The Scots held high ground to the west.

As Surrey's men crossed a gully cut by the Spott Burn their ranks broke up, and the Scots, believing the English were leaving the field, charged downhill in disorder. They found Surrey's force reformed on Spottsmuir and were routed in a single charge. The action was brief and probably not very bloody: the only casualty of note was Sir Patrick Graham, though about 100 Scottish lords, knights and men-at-arms were captured. An English report of over ten thousand Scottish dead probably confuses Dunbar with Berwick.

The next day Edward arrived and the castle surrendered, giving up John Comyn, Earl of Buchan, the earls of Atholl, Ross and Menteith and 130 knights and esquires, all sent into captivity in England. The rest of the campaign was a mopping-up. James, the High Steward, gave up Roxburgh without a fight, Edinburgh Castle held out for a week, and Stirling was found deserted but for a porter. At Montrose on 8 July Antony Bek, Bishop of Durham, tore the arms of Scotland from Balliol's surcoat, giving him the nickname Toom Tabard, empty coat. The battlefield was added to the Inventory of Historic Battlefields in Scotland in 2012.
battle-of-dunbar-1650: After the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649, the Rump Parliament set up a republican Commonwealth in England. The Scottish Parliament, which had not been consulted, declared his son Charles king of Britain, but required him first to sign both Covenants, recognising the authority of the Kirk in religion and of parliament in civil affairs. He accepted with the Treaty of Breda on 1 May 1650 and landed in Scotland on 23 June. The English sent the New Model Army under Oliver Cromwell, which crossed the border near Berwick on 22 July with over 16,000 men.

David Leslie's new army never reached its intended 36,000. A commission purged it of men suspected of supporting the Engagement or thought sinful, against the objections of much of the nobility and of Leslie himself, leaving it largely raw recruits. The Scots withdrew to Edinburgh and stripped the land of provisions, and at the end of August Cromwell, his army weakened by disease and hunger, fell back to Dunbar. Leslie followed and took a strong position on Doon Hill.

Doon Hill was exposed to foul weather and hard to supply, and on 2 September a Scottish council of war resolved to advance; the idea that the clerics present pressed Leslie into it is, according to the historian Royle among others, a myth. At about 4:00 am on 3 September English cavalry cleared the Scottish pickets from the crossings of the Brox Burn, and at first light Lambert's cavalry brigade crossed at the road ford and scattered the Scottish cavalry, some still in their tents. Hemmed in by the terrain, Leslie could not reinforce the fighting, while Cromwell used his last reserve to outflank the Scots, whose cavalry broke and fled.

Estimates of the Scottish dead range from fewer than 300 to Cromwell's claim of near 4,000; about 1,000 were wounded, and all accounts agree that about 5,000 prisoners were marched south. English losses were low: Cromwell put their dead at not twenty men, or at 30–40. Leslie rallied his army at Stirling, while the English took Edinburgh and Leith, and Edinburgh Castle held out until December. Parliament struck the Dunbar Medal for the combatants, claimed to be the first campaign medal given to all ranks. Historic Environment Scotland lists the site in its Inventory of Historic Battlefields as a battlefield of national importance.
battle-of-durbe: The Livonian Order had been fighting the Samogitians since 1253, when Mindaugas was crowned King of Lithuania and transferred parts of Samogitia to the order. The Samogitians did not recognise the transfer. For the knights the region was strategically important, since it separated their Prussian and Livonian branches. After the Samogitians killed 12 knights at the Battle of Memel in 1257, a two-year truce followed. Once it expired they invaded Courland and defeated the knights at the Battle of Skuodas in 1259, which encouraged the Semigallians to rebel. The knights then built fortresses at Dobele and at Georgenburg in Samogitia, and the Samogitians cut Georgenburg off from its supplies.

The Livonian master Burkhard von Hornhausen raised a large army and on 25 January 1260 obtained a papal bull from Pope Alexander IV blessing the crusade. The Prussian and Livonian forces and their allies gathered at Memel Castle, meaning to reinforce the besieged Georgenburg. Learning that a large Samogitian force was raiding Courland, they marched into present-day Latvia and met the Samogitians on the southern shore of Lake Durbe on 13 July 1260.

The knights were divided. Danes from Estonia refused to dismount from heavy horses that were ill suited to the swampy ground. When the fighting began, the local Curonians abandoned the knights because the knights refused to release Curonian captives from the Samogitian camp, and Peter von Dusburg even alleged that the Curonians attacked from the rear. The Estonians and other local people fled soon afterwards. The knights were surrounded, and some 150 of them died, among them Hornhausen and the Prussian land marshal Heinrich Botel, along with hundreds of secular knights and soldiers. No contemporary source names the Samogitian leader: a chronicle of about 1517 to 1526 says Treniota, while Inga Baranauskiene argued that it was Alminas, an elder.

It was by far the largest defeat of the knights in the 13th century; in the second largest, at Aizkraukle, 71 knights were killed. It inspired the Great Prussian Uprising, which lasted from 1260 to 1274, and revolts by the Semigallians, Curonians and Oeselians. The battle undid some 20 years of Livonian conquest, and it took about thirty years for the order to restore its control. Treniota is alleged to have persuaded his uncle Mindaugas to renounce Christianity and break the peace with the order, and in 1263 Treniota killed Mindaugas and took the throne.
battle-of-dybbol: After King Christian IX annexed the Duchy of Schleswig in November 1863, Prussia and Austria invaded Jutland in January 1864. The Dybbøl fortifications, built between 1861 and 1864, stood on a short peninsula guarding the ferry across the Alssund to Sønderborg on the island of Als and consisted of seven large and three smaller redoubts. Too much effort had gone into the Danevirke, and the position was ill-prepared: it lacked safe shelters in the forward line and had too little depth, and long-range rifled guns across the southern inlet could rake the line along its length. The Danes did command the sea, and the ironclad Rolf Krake shelled the Prussians from its turret guns.

On 18 April the Prussians took up their positions at 02:00, and at 10:00 the bombardment stopped and they charged. Within thirteen minutes they held the first line of redoubts. A counterattack by the Danish 8th Brigade, which historians note came only after half an hour, checked the advance near Dybbøl Mill and let the remnants of the 1st and 3rd Brigades escape to the pier opposite Sønderborg; it cost the brigade 1,399 of its 3,000 men. The last resistance at the bridgehead collapsed at 13:30. Around 3,600 Danes and 1,200 Prussians were killed, wounded or missing. Louis Appia and Charles van de Velde watched the battle for the Red Cross, the first it monitored.

The Danes withdrew to Als, which the Prussians attacked in late June. A truce from 12 May to 26 June brought talks in London, where Denmark's demand for a border on the Eider was rejected, and the war ended with the peace of 30 October 1864. After the defeat the returning army met no cheering crowds in Copenhagen. Germans built the Düppel-Denkmal on redoubt 4, read as a victory monument; after the plebiscites that followed the Treaty of Versailles the site returned to Denmark, and it became a national park in 1924. The monument was destroyed in 1945. A national commemoration is held at Dybbøl each 18 April, and German soldiers have joined it since 1998.
battle-of-dynekilen: The battle was part of the Great Northern War. After Sweden's defeat at the Battle of Poltava, Frederik IV of Denmark declared war on Sweden on 28 October 1709. In 1716 Charles XII invaded Norway, and his army there depended on supplies brought by sea. A Swedish transport fleet of 44 ships under Olof Strömstierna was carrying troops, ammunition and stores from Gothenburg and lay in the harbour of Dynekilen, a fjord just north of Strömstad on the west coast of Sweden.

Peter Tordenskjold attacked with a light force of seven ships, among them the barge Hjælper, the frigates Hvide Ørn and Vindhund and three galleys. His flotilla first overcame and destroyed a small island fort armed with six 12-pounder guns at the harbour entrance. The largest Swedish vessel, Stenbock, a former ship of the line converted into a cannon barge, surrendered, after which the Swedes ran the lighter ships aground and tried to destroy them.

The Dano-Norwegian crews put out fires and saved as many vessels as they could, while Swedish troops fired muskets at them from the surrounding hills. In the end Tordenskjold was forced to leave, but he took 30 captured ships with him; 14 galleys and transports had been destroyed by the Swedes. By his own report, several galleys sunk in the harbour, among them Wreden, Castor and Schelpaden, were later salvaged by the Swedes. The Dano-Norwegian force had 76 casualties, 19 killed and 57 wounded.

Without its transport fleet the Swedish army in Norway could not be supplied, and Charles XII had to abandon the invasion and withdraw his troops to Sweden. There he was soon occupied with preparing defences against an expected combined Danish and Russian invasion.
battle-of-dyrham: The only evidence for the battle is a single annal of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, in the common stock on which all its manuscripts build, which was edited into its present form in the later 9th century. The earliest manuscript, the Parker Chronicle, names the three British kings killed as Coinmail, Condidan and Farinmail. Scholars agree that the place-name Deorham survives in Dyrham, on the Cotswold escarpment a few miles north of Bath, and that the three cities were the Roman Corinium, Glevum and Aquae Sulis. Saint Aldate, a British bishop, is said to have been killed in the battle.

The annal gives no details, and the accounts of the fighting are modern reconstructions. In 1929 the antiquarian Welbore St Clair Baddeley supposed that the Saxons seized the hill fort of Hinton Hill Camp near Dyrham, which commanded the Avon valley, forcing the Britons of the three towns to unite in a failed attempt to dislodge them. The military historian Lieutenant-Colonel Alfred Burne instead imagined Ceawlin advancing methodically towards the Severn, the British forces drawn up on two ridges with the fort behind them, and a last stand in the fort that would explain why none of the three leaders escaped.

In an influential lecture of 1849 Edwin Guest presented the battle as the decisive blow that sealed the fate of southern Britain, a view that historians such as Frank Stenton, John Morris, H. P. R. Finberg and J. N. L. Myres maintained into the 1980s.

Patrick Sims-Williams then argued that the Chronicle shows no sign of being a contemporary record for the sixth century and may draw on oral tradition, perhaps a Welsh triad, or on later West Saxon claims against Mercia in the Severn valley. Other scholars hold that the weight given to the towns reflects the polities of the ninth and tenth centuries. Roger Collins and Barbara Yorke questioned the battle's importance and dating without denying it took place, and Guy Halsall wrote that the named kings may have fought at Dyrham, though it is much less likely that they ruled the three cities.
battle-of-edessa: Before the battle, Shapur I had penetrated deep into Roman territory several times and had conquered and plundered Antioch in Syria, in 253 or 256. Valerian, having defeated the usurper Aemilianus and taken imperial power, reached the eastern provinces in 254 or 255 and gradually restored order. He then faced a naval Gothic invasion of northern Asia Minor, in which the Goths ravaged Pontus and moved south into Cappadocia. An attempt by Valerian and his army at Antioch to intercept them failed because of plague. While the Roman army was in that weakened state, Shapur invaded northern Mesopotamia in 260, probably in early spring.

Valerian, then in his sixties, marched east to the Sasanian borders. According to Shapur's inscription at the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht, his army contained men from almost every part of the Roman Empire as well as Germanic allies. The armies met between Carrhae and Edessa, and the Romans were thoroughly defeated.

Roman sources are unclear. They report that the army was beaten and besieged, that Valerian tried to negotiate and was captured, and that his army may have surrendered after that. Some say Shapur broke his word and seized the emperor after agreeing to truce talks, but such accounts are typical of Roman descriptions of defeat, which blame the incompetence of generals and the treachery of foreigners. According to Ian Hughes, the Romans lost about 10,000 in battle, and the rest of the army retreated to Edessa and surrendered to save their lives.

Accounts of Valerian's fate differ. Some scholars hold that Shapur sent him and part of his army to Bishapur, where they lived in relatively good conditions and worked as engineers, and Band-e Kaisar near Shushtar is counted among the remains of their work. Lactantius says Shapur used the former emperor as a stepstool to mount his horse, Aurelius Victor says he was kept in a cage, and later stories say his body was skinned and stuffed as a trophy. Other accounts say he was treated with respect and that tales of torture were invented by Christian historians to show what befell persecutors of Christianity.

Shapur then divided his army into at least five groups to raid Anatolia, ravaging Cilicia, Cappadocia, Pamphylia and Lycaonia. He took Tarsus and Caesarea Cappadocia, deporting the latter's people, claimed to number 400,000, to the southern provinces of his empire. Valerian's defeat set off revolts that led to the temporary fragmentation of the Roman Empire, including the Gallic Empire of Postumus in the west.
battle-of-edington: Viking raids on England became sustained from the 830s, and the arrival of the Great Heathen Army in 865 to 866 began a stage of conquest and settlement. By 870 the Northmen had conquered Northumbria and East Anglia, and in 871 they attacked Wessex. Alfred succeeded his brother Æthelred. In 875 Guthrum's army slipped into Wareham and later went to Exeter, where in autumn 877 it made a firm peace with Alfred and then withdrew to Gloucester in Mercia. The Danes attacked Chippenham in midwinter after Twelfth Night, probably on the night of 6 to 7 January 878, and forced Alfred to retreat with a small force into the Somerset marsh of Athelney.

Around Easter 878 Alfred built a fortress at Athelney. Between 4 and 7 May he called a levy at Egbert's Stone, where men of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire who had not fled rallied to him. The host moved to Iley Oak and then to Edington, where it fought the Danes. According to the Life of King Alfred, he put them to flight and pursued them to their stronghold, which the West Saxons besieged for two weeks. The Danes then gave hostages and oaths that they would leave the kingdom and promised that Guthrum would be baptised.

Most historians place the battle at Edington near Westbury in Wiltshire, which belonged to Alfred's family estate. Other sites have been proposed since early times, among them Edington Hill in the Polden Hills in Somerset, argued by Charles Whistler and Albany Major in 1913.

Three weeks after the battle Guthrum was baptised at Aller in Somerset with Alfred as his sponsor, and took the name Athelstan. Under the Treaty of Wedmore he returned to East Anglia; the army went to Cirencester in 879 and settled in East Anglia the following year. This allowed Alfred to stabilise Wessex, establish fortified towns known as burhs and reorganise the fyrd. A later treaty between Alfred and Guthrum defined the boundaries of their kingdoms. Guthrum reigned in East Anglia until his death in 890, and minted coins on the Alfredian model under his baptismal name. By 896 the Vikings had given up their attacks on Wessex.
battle-of-elchingen: In September 1805 the Austrian army of Karl Mack von Lieberich and Archduke Ferdinand of Austria-Este invaded Bavaria and gathered on the Iller near Ulm. Napoleon's Grande Armée crossed the Rhine on 24 and 25 September and wheeled round to the north of it, crossing the Danube east of Ulm and cutting the road to Vienna. On 11 October Mack tried to break out on the north bank, but Pierre Dupont's lone division held him at Haslach-Jungingen. On 12 October Mack sent Johann Sigismund Riesch along the Danube to destroy the bridges, and Riesch camped at Elchingen.

Napoleon ordered Michel Ney's VI Corps back to the north bank. Riesch held the heights around Ober- and Unter-Elchingen with about 8,000 men, though Scott Bowden gives him nearly 15,000. At 8:00 am on 14 October the elite companies of Eugene-Casimir Villatte's brigade crossed the partly dismantled bridge and overpowered its guard, and engineers repaired the span behind them. Led by Ney himself, the 6th Light Infantry took Elchingen Abbey and most of Ober-Elchingen. François Roguet's brigade drove the Austrians into the Grosser Forest, and the French dragoons broke an Austrian square as Riesch, threatened from the east and north-east, fell back.

The French admitted 56 officers and 737 men killed or wounded and took 4,000 prisoners and 4 cannon; Austrian killed and wounded may have reached 2,000. Riesch's survivors were trapped in Ulm with Mack, who capitulated with 23,500 troops and 60 cannon on 20 October. Joachim Murat's pursuit then mopped up most of the rest, forcing Franz von Werneck to surrender 15,000 men at Trochtelfingen on 18 October, and only a few commanders and 12 squadrons escaped into Bohemia. Napoleon made Ney Duke of Elchingen in 1808.
battle-of-ellendun: Through the 8th and early 9th centuries the kings of Mercia held a shifting hegemony over the kingdoms of southern England, at times ruling them directly. Wessex had once had to recognise the overlordship of Æthelbald of Mercia but seems to have escaped Mercian dominance afterwards. Ecgberht's father Ealhmund had been king of Kent in the 780s, which set the family against Offa of Mercia, and Ecgberht was driven into exile by Offa with the co-operation of Beorhtric of Wessex. His accession in 802 was followed at once by a violent clash with Mercia.

Beornwulf had seized the Mercian throne from Ceolwulf, brother and successor of the powerful Coenwulf. His war with Wessex may have been an effort to establish his own authority and Mercia's after this upheaval, and he may have hoped to profit from Ecgberht's campaigns against the Britons of Cornwall: in the autumn of 825 Ecgberht was fighting them at Gafulford.

The battle was fought in September 825, and little is known of its course. Sir Frank Stenton called it one of the most decisive battles of English history. The exact site is unknown. William Camden placed it near Wilton, west of Salisbury; Charles Oman argued for Wroughton, 4 miles south of Swindon; T. Spicer has suggested the grounds of Lydiard Park in Swindon.

Ecgberht at once sent his son Æthelwulf with an army into the south-east, and the West Saxons took Sussex, Kent and Essex, roughly doubling the size of Wessex. The East Angles revolted against Mercia in alliance with Wessex; Beornwulf was defeated and killed by them, and his successor Ludeca met the same fate the next year. In 829 Ecgberht occupied Mercia and was recognised by the Northumbrians, briefly becoming overlord of all England. Wiglaf restored Mercian independence the following year, but Mercia never regained the primacy it had held before Ellendun.
battle-of-ergeme: The forces of the Livonian Confederation, under Philipp Schall von Bell, Land Marshal of the Livonian Order and Commander of Riga, had gathered near the settlement of Trikāta to meet the Russian armies invading Livonia. On 2 August thirty knights rode out to collect fodder and, across a river, came upon a Russian guard of 500 men. After an exchange of fire the Russians fell back to their main army. Eighteen knights returned for reinforcements while twelve followed the enemy, then turned back on sighting the main Russian force, losing several men on the way.

Expecting to meet about 500 Russians, Schall von Bell sent his 300 horsemen to attack. They overran a Russian outpost and drove its men back to their main body, only to find themselves surrounded on all sides. Prince Kurbsky gave Barbashin's main force as 12,000 men; modern historians consider this overstated and put it at no more than 1,000. Many of the German soldiers and mercenaries were killed or captured, and those left in the camp at Trikāta fled.

A German chronicle puts the knights' losses at 261. Russian losses are unknown, though it was said that 14 carts were needed to carry their dead to be burned. The prisoners included the land marshal, called the last hope of Livonia, and ten other commanders. Questioned in Moscow by Ivan the Terrible, Schall von Bell answered so haughtily that the tsar had him executed with his senior commanders, among them his brother Werner Schall von Bell, Komtur of Goldingen. Some other prisoners were executed or kept in Russia as serfs. Hermann II Wesel, Bishop of Dorpat, a captive since 1558, was allowed to bury the dead by Catholic rite. After the battle the Order could only defend its fortresses.
battle-of-fakhkh: Many Alids, chiefly of the Zaydi and Hasanid branches, rejected the Abbasids as usurpers, and al-Mansur had faced the revolt of Muhammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya in 762 to 763. Al-Husayn ibn Ali was a close relative of that rebel: his father Ali al-Abid, famed for his piety, died in al-Mansur's prisons in 763. The historian Laura Veccia Vaglieri describes Husayn's upbringing as an atmosphere of extreme piety and secret hatred for the Abbasids, though he was on friendly terms with Caliph al-Mahdi.

After al-Mahdi died in July 785, the Abbasid governor of Medina, al-Umari, had three men, among them Abu'l-Zift, a son of Muhammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya, flogged for drinking alcohol, and quarrelled with the Alids when Abu'l-Zift fled. The revolt had been planned for some time, with Kufans waiting secretly in the city and hopes of help from pilgrims to the Hajj.

On the morning of 16 May 786 about 26 Alids and their supporters gathered at the Prophet's Mosque, where Husayn, dressed in white, received oaths as caliph and imam under the title al-Murtada. Musa ibn Ja'far al-Kazim, the seventh imam of the Twelver Shi'a, refused his support. The rebels drove off about 200 men of the garrison, but, in al-Tabari's words, the people of Medina locked their doors. Penned into the mosque, Husayn left the city with about 300 men on 28 May.
