Caliph al-Hadi entrusted the response to Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn Ali, who gathered the armed retinues of the Abbasid princes returning from the pilgrimage. On 11 June the armies met in the wadi of Fakhkh, about 4 kilometres north-west of Mecca. After Muhammad ibn Sulayman won on his wing he led the right and centre against the massed Alid army, which was routed. Husayn refused an offer of clemency and fought until he was killed; his head was sent to al-Hadi, who sent it on to Khurasan as a warning.

Over a hundred rebels fell and lay unburied for three days. Abu'l-Zift surrendered but was killed, and several Alid prisoners were executed at Mecca and Baghdad. Yahya ibn Abdallah and his brother Idris escaped among the pilgrims; Idris founded the Idrisid dynasty in 789, and Yahya rose in Daylam in 792. The wadi became known as al-Shuhada, the Martyrs, second only to Karbala in Shi'a martyrology for the number of Alids killed. Husayn's oath, modelled on that of Zayd ibn Ali in 740, later shaped Zaydi practice, and the Alids who scattered carried their loyalties to the Maghreb and northern Iran.
battle-of-falkirk-1298: After the Battle of Stirling Bridge, William Wallace led a Scottish army south from November 1297 until January 1298, raiding the countryside from Newcastle upon Tyne to Carlisle. Edward I made a truce with the French king Philip the Fair in October 1297 and returned to England on 14 March 1298. He moved the centre of government to York, where it stayed for six years, and declared the Scottish magnates traitors when none came to a council of war there. His army assembled at Roxburgh on 25 June and may have included about 2,000 armoured cavalry and some 12,000 paid infantry, though one estimate puts the infantry at only 8,000.

Edward was about to fall back on Edinburgh when he learned that the Scots were at Torwood, near Falkirk. On 22 July he placed his army south of the town. The Scots were chiefly spearmen drawn up in four great schiltrons, with archers between them and about 500 mounted knights at the rear. The Comyns and Robert Bruce were absent, and Andrew Moray, who had shared the victory at Stirling Bridge, had died of wounds from that battle.

The English cavalry advanced in four divisions. They routed the Scottish cavalry and overran the archers under Sir John Stewart, but the schiltrons held, and 111 English horses were killed against the spears. Edward's archers, crossbowmen and slingers then shot into the packed, poorly armoured spearmen, who could neither retreat nor attack. When the ranks were thin and disordered, the English cavalry and infantry broke the schiltrons.

Scottish leaders were not lost in great numbers, but the dead included Wallace's second-in-command Sir John de Graham, Sir John Stewart and Macduff of Fife. Wallace resigned as Guardian of Scotland shortly afterwards. Edward occupied Stirling and raided Perth, St Andrews and Ayrshire, but was back at Carlisle by 9 September, and he invaded again in the summer of 1300. The historian Stuart Reid judged that Wallace, a good partisan leader, was not suited to leading a conventional army. The exact site of the battle is uncertain, with three proposed locations. The Falkirk Roll, a list of the arms of English bannerets present, is the oldest known English occasional roll of arms.
battle-of-fehrbellin: Sweden and Brandenburg had been allies against the Kingdom of Poland, but when Elector Frederick William joined Emperor Leopold I's expedition to Alsace against Louis XIV in the Franco-Dutch War, France persuaded an isolated Sweden to attack Brandenburg while its army was away. The Swedes under Count Waldemar von Wrangel invaded from Pomerania and occupied much of the electorate. Hearing of it in December 1674, Frederick William left the coalition, wintered at Marktbreit in Franconia, then, leaving his supply wagons and much of his infantry behind, marched 250 kilometres to Magdeburg in two weeks, a feat counted among the great marches in military history.

Finding the Swedes dispersed in the marshy Havelland, he sent Field Marshal Georg von Derfflinger to take Rathenow and split them. A banquet arranged by a bribed local official left the Swedish officers drunk, and Derfflinger, posing as a Swedish officer, had the gates opened. Wrangel fell back, his way blocked by marshes and by parties under Colonel Joachim Hennings, until he was cornered at Fehrbellin.

With the bridge over the Rhin destroyed and marshes on both flanks, Wrangel had to fight south of the village of Hakenberg while his engineers repaired it. About 6,000–7,000 Brandenburgers with 13 cannons faced 7,000 Swedes with 28 guns, but Wrangel failed to secure the nearby heights, where the Brandenburgers placed their guns. Their fire caused heavy losses on the Swedish right, and Brandenburg cavalry beat back every attempt to take the hills. The Swedish cavalry finally fled, and the infantry brigade of Generalmajor Henrik von Delwig was routed, but the bridge was repaired in time for Wrangel to bring much of his army across before dark.

The Brandenburgers lost about 500 men and the Swedes some 500–600 killed, wounded and captured, but the retreating Swedes lost many more to pursuit and to local peasants; of Delwig's 1,200 men all but 20 were killed or captured. The Holy Roman Empire and Denmark now declared war on Sweden, and Frederick William invaded Swedish Pomerania, though the Peace of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 1679 largely restored the status quo. In Sweden the defeat was laid against the Privy Council aristocrats at the Riksdag of 1680. Frederick William was known thereafter as the Great Elector, and Heinrich von Kleist made the battle the setting of his drama The Prince of Homburg.
battle-of-fei-river: Under Fu Jian the Di-led Former Qin conquered the Former Yan in 370, took modern Sichuan and Chongqing from the Jin in 373 and Xiangyang in 379, and by 381 held all of north China. After a Jin attempt to retake Xiangyang failed in May 383, Fu Jian conscripted six of every ten able-bodied men. His brother Fu Rong, who had opposed the campaign, led an advance force of 300,000, and Fu Jian set out from Chang'an with 270,000 cavalry and 600,000 infantry. Many of these troops, levied from conquered peoples, had little loyalty to the Former Qin and little training.
Emperor Xiaowu of Jin gave the Huai front to Xie Shi and Xie Xuan with the 80,000-strong Beifu Army, whose officers brought their own hereditary troops and who were trained as a professional force.

In October 383 Fu Rong took the Jin city of Shouyang, and Fu Jian hurried ahead with 8,000 light cavalry. He sent the captured Jin official Zhu Xu to urge Xie Shi to surrender, but Zhu told him the Qin army had not yet fully arrived. Xie Xuan and Liu Laozhi then attacked the advance force with 5,000 men and killed 15,000. In November the armies faced each other across the Fei River. Xie Xuan asked the Qin to draw back so that the Jin could cross; Fu Jian agreed, meaning to strike them in midstream. As the Qin pulled back, Zhu Xu shouted that the Qin army was defeated, panic spread, Fu Rong was killed when his horse fell, and the whole army collapsed.

An estimated 70 to 80 per cent of the Qin troops died in the fighting and the flight, from combat, hunger and exposure, while Jin losses were minor. Fu Jian withdrew to Luoyang under the protection of Murong Chui, who rebelled in early 384. Chang'an fell to the Western Yan in 385, and Fu Jian was killed that year by his former general Yao Chang. The Jin advanced to the Yellow River, and the south stayed independent of the north until the Sui dynasty in 589.
battle-of-fleurus-1794: The battle belonged to the War of the First Coalition and was the most significant battle of the Low Countries theatre. In May 1794 Jean-Baptiste Jourdan was given about 96,000 men and the task of taking the fortress of Charleroi, which French forces on the Sambre had tried and failed three times to capture. He crossed the Sambre a fourth time on 12 June and was driven back at Lambusart on 16 June, but the defeat did little damage. He crossed for a fifth time on 18 June and began the third siege of Charleroi the next day.

The garrison of 2,800 men could not delay him, and its commander, Colonel Reynac, asked for terms on 25 June. The representative Louis-Antoine Saint-Just refused them and demanded immediate surrender.

Prince Josias of Coburg marched from Tournai with 12,000 men in blazing heat to relieve the siege, bringing the Allied force to about 52,000. Jourdan, who overestimated it at 70,000, chose to receive the attack within fortifications, with some 75,000 men available. Coburg planned five columns, the main blow under Archduke Charles against the French right, with another against the left beyond the river Pieton.

Fighting began on 26 June, and the Allies gained ground on both French flanks in the morning. The French held their line and counterattacked in the afternoon. Count Radetzky then brought word that Charleroi had fallen. With no siege to relieve and the French defences strong, Coburg ordered a withdrawal around 3 pm. The battle was tactically indecisive.

The Allied defeat led to the permanent loss of the Austrian Netherlands and to the dissolution of the Dutch Republic. The battle marked a turning point for the French army, which remained ascendant for the rest of the War of the First Coalition.
battle-of-flodden: The Treaty of Perpetual Peace of 1502 between James IV of Scotland and Henry VII of England had formally ended centuries of intermittent warfare. Relations soured through border raids, the death of the Scottish privateer Andrew Barton in 1511 and Henry VIII's claim to be overlord of Scotland. James declared war to honour the Auld Alliance with France, diverting Henry from his campaign against Louis XII in the War of the League of Cambrai. On 5 August 1513 border reivers under Lord Home pillaged Northumberland, and on 13 August Sir William Bulmer's archers ambushed them on Milfield Plain and killed as many as 600 in the so-called Ill Raid.

James invaded England with about 34,000 men, reduced by sickness and desertion from 42,000, and took Flodden Edge, a strong hill south of Branxton, outnumbering the English by 8,000. Surrey marched round to the rear of the Scottish camp, and the Scots moved to the adjacent Branxton Hill. At about 4 p.m. on 9 September, in wet and windy weather, James opened with an artillery duel in which his heavy guns, poorly sited, did badly. His infantry then advanced downhill with 18-foot pikes supplied by the French, a weapon that needed training, discipline and suitable terrain.

An area of marshy ground lay in their path and broke up the formations, giving the English the close-quarter fight for which their bills were better suited. The Scots had placed their officers in the front line in the medieval manner, and their loss left no one to organise a retreat. James IV was killed, the last monarch of Great Britain to die in battle, along with a large part of the nobility. Surrey's army lost about 1,500 men; accounts of Scottish losses range from 5,000 to 20,000.

Lord Dacre found the body of James IV, which was embalmed and taken to Newcastle, York and Sheen Priory. A General Council of thirty-five lords met at Stirling on 19 September to rule in the name of Margaret Tudor and her son James V, who was crowned at Stirling on 21 October at 17 months old. Margaret remained his guardian but was not made regent. Thomas Howard was restored to the title of Duke of Norfolk, and his family's arms carry an augmentation for Flodden. British historians sometimes use the battle to mark the end of the Middle Ages in the British Isles, and it has been called the last great medieval battle there.
battle-of-formigny: Charles VII of France used the Treaty of Tours of 1444 to reorganise his armies, while the English, divided by the struggle for power that would lead to the Wars of the Roses, left their forces in Normandy scattered and weak. The French broke the truce in June 1449 and by October occupied much of Normandy; the Bureau brothers took Rouen in October, Harfleur in December and Honfleur in January 1450 before investing Caen. An English expeditionary force assembled at Portsmouth under Sir Thomas Kyriell, a relatively unknown commander.

Lack of money lowered morale, and in January 1450 the troops lynched an official sent to negotiate their pay. Kyriell landed at Cherbourg on 15 March with some 2,500 men, joined by another 1,800 collected by the Duke of Somerset.

Rather than relieve Caen, Kyriell took Valognes on 27 March and marched on Carentan, which he reached on 12 April. The French commander, the Count of Clermont, refused battle, so Kyriell marched toward Bayeux and halted near Formigny on 14 April, followed by 3,000 men under Clermont. Arthur de Richemont, Constable of France, reached Saint-Lo the same day with a Breton force of 2,000.

On 15 April the armies faced each other on the Carentan-Bayeux road. The English, under 4,000 men of whom 2,900 were archers, stood with their backs to a stream and had no time to make the usual defence of sharpened stakes. Clermont's dismounted men-at-arms attacked and were repulsed, as were two cavalry probes; he then had two culverins fire from beyond bowshot, and the archers left their positions to try to seize them. Around 7 p.m. Richemont's 1,200 cavalry arrived from the south.

Caught in the open by the Breton cavalry and enveloped by Clermont and Pierre de Breze, the English were broken into small groups, and most were killed or captured, Kyriell among them. A French writer claimed that about 500 captured archers were massacred afterwards.

Kyriell's army was effectively destroyed, the last significant English field army in Normandy. French records claim 3,744 bodies were buried, though that count seems to include both sides, and put the prisoners at 1,200 to 1,400; other historians suggest 2,500 killed and 900 captured. Caen fell on 12 June and Cherbourg on 12 August. Formigny is notable as one of the first recorded uses of field artillery on a European battlefield, though accounts are unclear how effective the guns were; the noise of their firing alerted Richemont to the battle and brought him onto the field.
battle-of-fort-sumter: South Carolina adopted an ordinance of secession on 20 December 1860, soon after Abraham Lincoln's victory in the presidential election, and by February 1861 six more Southern states had done the same. The seceding states seized federal property. President James Buchanan protested but took no action.

In Charleston Harbor the garrison under Major Robert Anderson held Fort Moultrie, whose defences against land attack were feeble. On 26 December 1860 Anderson secretly moved his command by small boat to Fort Sumter, a substantial fortress controlling the harbour entrance. South Carolina's governor, Francis Wilkinson Pickens, considered this a breach of faith. An attempt to resupply the fort with the unarmed ship Star of the West failed when shore batteries fired on it on 9 January 1861. Brigadier General P. G. T. Beauregard took command of Confederate forces in Charleston, and the garrison of 85 men reported only six weeks of rations left.

Lincoln, inaugurated on 4 March, faced the crisis as his first. Both he and Jefferson Davis preferred that the other side be seen as the aggressor, since each believed the side that used force first would lose support in the border states. Lincoln informed Pickens that he was sending supply ships, which brought a Confederate ultimatum for immediate evacuation, and Anderson refused.

At 4:30 am on 12 April a single mortar round fired from Fort Johnson signalled a bombardment by 43 guns and mortars around the harbour, fired in sequence under Beauregard's orders. Anderson held fire until daylight, and of his 60 guns he could safely use only the 21 on the lowest level. The fort had been designed against naval attack, and the high-arcing fire of land-based guns reached parts of it that ships' guns could not.

On 13 April the flagpole was shot down. Anderson, short of ammunition with fires burning and his men exhausted, agreed to a truce at 2 pm after enduring over 3,000 rounds, 34 hours after the first shot. No one on either side died in the fighting, although a gun explosion during the surrender ceremony on 14 April killed two US Army soldiers.

The bombardment was the first military action of the American Civil War. Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers for 90 days, and four more slave states then declared secession and joined the Confederacy; the governors of Missouri and Kentucky refused to send troops. The war lasted four years, effectively ending in April 1865 with Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House.

Charleston Harbor stayed in Confederate hands almost throughout, and the Confederates evacuated Fort Sumter and Charleston in February 1865. On 14 April 1865 Anderson returned to the ruined fort to raise the flag he had lowered.
battle-of-fraga: From the second half of the 11th century the kings of Aragon and the counts of Barcelona and Urgel sought again and again to conquer the towns and frontier fortresses of the Marca Superior held by the Muslims. Their aim was the lowland around the Segre and Cinca rivers down to the mouth of the Ebro, a prosperous region with direct access to the Mediterranean Sea, whose chief towns were Lleida, Mequinenza, Fraga and Tortosa.

Alfonso the Battler, known to the Muslims as Ibn Rudmir or al-Farandji, laid siege to Fraga in July 1134 with an army from Aragon, fighting alongside Viscount Centule VI of Béarn. The Almoravid response was swift: the Emir of Cordoba, son of the caliph, equipped 2,000 horsemen, the Emir of Murcia and Valencia 500, and the governor of Lleida another 200, and the combined force marched to relieve the town.

The relief army, led by the governor of Lérida, Ibn ‘Iyad, arrived on 17 July 1134. Seeing it, the defenders of Fraga sallied out, while Alfonso, still confident of his numbers and his tactics, rallied his troops. His entourage clashed with the cavalry of the emir of Murcia, Yahya ibn Ghaniya, which cut down many of the Aragonese. The townspeople then fell on the Aragonese camp, killing most of the soldiers there and carrying the army's provisions back into the town. A final charge by the cavalry of the emir of Cordoba broke the Christian army.

Having lost most of his men, Alfonso fled towards Zaragoza, and he died on 7 September 1134. The losses at Fraga were heavy, and many notable members of Aragonese society were among the dead or captured. The French knights killed included Aimery II of Narbonne, Centule VI of Béarn and Bertrán de Risnel, while Guy of Lescar, who fought with the Christian forces, was taken by the Almoravids and imprisoned at Balensiyya.
battle-of-france: France and Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after the German invasion of Poland. The French army began the limited Saar Offensive but by mid-October had withdrawn to its start line, and a period of inaction known as the Phoney War followed. In the 1930s the French had built the Maginot Line along the border with Germany, intended to divert a German invasion into Belgium, where the best French divisions would meet it. The hills and woods of the Ardennes were thought to cover the area to the north of the line.

The German plan, Fall Gelb, was reshaped on the advice of Manstein and Heinz Guderian, who proposed concentrating most of the armour at Sedan. The invasion began on 10 May 1940 with attacks on Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and the French sent their best forces north into Belgium. German armour advanced through the Ardennes, crossed the Meuse and raced down the Somme valley, cutting off the units that had gone into Belgium. British, French and Belgian forces were pushed back to the sea, and the British and French navies evacuated much of the British Expeditionary Force and the French and Belgian armies from Dunkirk in Operation Dynamo.

The Germans began Fall Rot on 5 June against the Somme and Aisne, where the French resisted strongly but were beaten by German air superiority and armoured mobility. Italy declared war on 10 June. Paris was declared an open city and occupied by German forces on 14 June. Paul Reynaud resigned as Prime Minister on 16 June and was succeeded by Philippe Pétain, who asked for an armistice.

The armistice was signed at Compiègne on 22 June 1940, the site Hitler chose because the 1918 Armistice had been signed there. France was divided into a German occupation zone in the north and west and a zone libre in the south. Pétain's Vichy government replaced the Third Republic, and De Gaulle refused to accept its legitimacy; his Appeal of 18 June was the beginning of Free France. German losses are commonly put at 27,074 killed, 111,034 wounded and 18,384 missing, little more than a third of those at Verdun in the First World War.
battle-of-frankenhausen: Unrest in and around Frankenhausen, in the County of Schwarzburg, became open revolt on 29 April 1525. Many of the townspeople joined the rising, occupied the town hall and stormed the castle of the Counts of Schwarzburg. Insurgents from the surrounding Thuringian and Saxon lands gathered in growing numbers, and when Thomas Müntzer arrived from Mühlhausen with 300 fighters on 11 May, several thousand peasants were camped in the fields around the town.

Landgrave Philip I of Hesse and his father-in-law Duke George of Saxony had first made Mühlhausen their objective, but on hearing that Müntzer had gone to Frankenhausen they turned their Landsknecht troops there. The princes had great difficulty recruiting these mercenaries. The peasants carried a mix of farming tools, polearms, breastplates and handguns, which many had from service in the local militia bands, the Landwehr.

On 14 May the peasants drove off a scouting party and its reinforcements but did not pursue it, while the main Hessian and Brunswick column rested after a night's march. Late that day the rebels withdrew into a wagon fort on the hill above the town. A truce followed, though it is unclear who proposed it, and it gave the princes time to join George of Saxony's army coming from the east and to encircle the wagon fort.

Around midday on 15 May, once it was clear that Müntzer would not be handed over, the truce was broken. An artillery barrage was followed by waves of horsemen and foot soldiers. Caught off guard, the peasants fled in panic into the town, pursued by the mercenaries, and the battle became a massacre. Casualty figures are unreliable: peasant losses have been estimated at more than 7,000, and those of the mercenaries at as few as six. Müntzer was captured in the town, tortured and executed on 27 May 1525.

The battle was the final act of the war in Thuringia. At Frankenhausen it is depicted in Werner Tübke's Early Bourgeois Revolution in Germany, a painting 120 metres long and 14 metres high in a museum built for it. East Germany's socialist leadership, which regarded Müntzer as a revolutionary forebear, commissioned it, and Tübke worked on it from 1975 to 1987, setting the battle in the wider context of Reformation Germany rather than on its own as the state had wished.
battle-of-fyrisvellir: In the Old Norse accounts Styrbjörn the Strong was the son of the Swedish king Olof Björnsson, who had died by poisoning, and suspected his uncle Eric, his father's co-king, of the deed. Denied the crown by the Swedish Thing, he made himself ruler of the Jomsvikings and pillaged Denmark until Harald Bluetooth gave him his daughter Tyra in marriage. He then returned with 1000 longships, forced the Danes to give him 200 more and to send whoever he chose, the king included, and sailed for Sweden.

The fullest account is the short story Styrbjarnar þáttr Svíakappa in Flateyjarbók. When the fleet entered Mälaren, Eric sent the fiery cross through the land and gathered the levy at Uppsala, and Torgny the Lawspeaker advised him to block the waterway with stakes. Styrbjörn burned his ships so that his men would fight to the death. On the plain the Swedes drove a herd of cattle armed with spears and swords into the Jomsvikings, and the fighting lasted two days.

In the story Styrbjörn sacrificed to Thor, while Eric went to Odin's hof and promised himself to Odin after ten years. A tall man in a low hat gave Eric a reed to throw over the enemy with the words Óðinn á yðr alla, May Odin have you all; Styrbjörn's men were struck blind and buried by an avalanche, and Harald fled. Other sources differ: in Eyrbyggja saga some Jomsvikings escaped through the forest, in Knýtlinga saga Harald left before the battle, and neither they nor Saxo Grammaticus mentions Odin. After the victory Eric rewarded the Icelandic skald Þórvaldr Hjaltason with a golden bracelet for a poem about it.

Four runestones may name men who died in the battle. The Hällestad and Sjörup stones in Skåne commemorate men who did not flee at Uppsala, and the Karlevi stone on Öland may have been raised by Danish warriors returning from there. Two men buried in ship graves at Uppsala in the late 900s, with sword wounds to the head and raised in western Scandinavia or England, may have died in it.

The battle's historicity is disputed. Lauritz Weibull rejected the sagas as sources; his brother Curt Weibull read the runestones and Þórvaldr's verses as evidence that Eric repelled mainly Scanian Vikings under Tóki Gormsson, while Lis Jacobsen dated the stones after Eric's reign. Later historians have doubted whether the battle took place at all.
battle-of-gaixia: Since 205 BCE Xiang Yu, Hegemon-King of Western Chu, and Liu Bang, King of Han, had worn each other down in a war of attrition on the Central Plain, while the Han general Han Xin conquered the State of Qi, an ally of Chu. Xiang Yu offered Han Xin a three-way division of China; his adviser Kuai Tong urged him to accept, predicting that Liu Bang would one day execute him, but Han Xin stayed loyal. With his supplies cut by the warlord Peng Yue and by the loss of Qi, Xiang Yu agreed in August 203 BCE to divide China along the Honggou Canal and returned Liu Bang's captive father and wife.

The peace was a ploy devised by the Han advisers Zhang Liang and Chen Ping. Liu Bang broke it and pursued the withdrawing Chu army, but when Han Xin and Peng Yue failed to join him at Guling, Xiang Yu defeated him. Only after Liu Bang promised to make Han Xin King of Chu and Peng Yue King of Liang did they commit their forces.

Under Han Xin's overall command, armies from the north-east, the west and the south-east converged on Chu territory in winter. After defeating Xiang Yu outside the former Chu capital of Chen, the coalition met him again at Gaixia. Han Xin's centre advanced, then withdrew, and his flanks under General Gung and General Pi attacked from both sides, probably in a double envelopment resembling Hannibal's at Cannae.

Surrounded in his camp, Xiang Yu fled by night with only 800 cavalry, pursued by Han horsemen under Guan Ying. At the Wu River, ashamed of how many of his soldiers from Wu had died, he made a last stand rather than return home. He reportedly killed hundreds of pursuers before cutting his own throat, and five soldiers who pieced his body together shared the reward of 1,000 catties of gold and a fief of 10,000 households.

Han Xin then took the cities of Lu and Huling, Lu surrendering when shown Xiang Yu's head, and Jin Xi conquered the pro-Chu kingdom of Linjiang, whose king Gong Wei was executed. A few months after the battle Liu Bang took the throne as Gaozu. Folklore credits Xiang Yu, Liu Bang or Han Xin with inventing xiangqi, whose board is divided by the Chu River and Han Border, but the first written rules date from the Tang dynasty. Some historians place the battlefield in Lingbi County, others in present-day Luyi County.
battle-of-gallabat: By the Treaty of Adowa of 3 June 1884, Yohannes IV let the Egyptian garrisons cut off by the Mahdist rising withdraw to Massawa through Ethiopian territory, and the Khalifa Abdallahi ibn Muhammad came to treat Ethiopia as an enemy. The twin towns of Gallabat and Metemma, on the trade route from the Nile to Gondar, became the base from which the Mahdists raided Ethiopia. In January 1887 Tekle Haymanot attacked Gallabat with 30,000 men and sacked the Gedaref region; in revenge a Mahdist army under Abu Anga defeated him at Sar Weha on 18 January 1888 and plundered Gondar, burning churches and enslaving hundreds of women and children.

Yohannes, distrustful of Menelik II of Shewa, at first held back, but his clergy and officers pressed him to deal with the Mahdists first. After Ras Gobana Dacche defeated a Mahdist force at Guté Dili in Welega on 14 October 1888, the emperor accepted their advice and prepared to march on Metemma.

In late January 1889 Yohannes gathered 130,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry in Dembiya. The Mahdist army of 85,000, commanded after Abu Anga's death by Zeki Tummal, fortified Gallabat behind a zariba of thorn bushes. The attack began on 9 March. When Ras Haile Maryam Gugsa, commanding the left wing, was shot, the emperor took personal command, and the Ethiopians broke through the Mahdist lines and poured into the town, killing women and children. Yohannes was hit in the hand and then in the chest, and died that night after naming his son Ras Mengesha as successor.

The demoralised Ethiopians retreated with what loot they could carry, and the exhausted Sudanese did not pursue at first. On 12 March Zeki Tummal caught the rearguard of Ras Alula near the Atbara River, inflicted heavy losses and seized the emperor's body; his head was sent to Omdurman and displayed at the Khalifa's court.

The victors' losses were heavy: Zeki Tummal's army, at least 87,000 before the war, could raise only 10,000 men in the spring of 1890, and they never again put so great a force in the field. In Tigray, torn by famine and feuding chiefs, Mengesha did not claim the throne, and within weeks Menelik II was recognised as emperor. Menelik later sought friendly ties with the Mahdists before seizing Bani Shangul, which was part of Ethiopia by 1897.
battle-of-gammelsdorf: The dispute turned on who would act as guardian of the underage children of the late dukes of Lower Bavaria, and so command the great economic power of that region. One claimant was their Upper Bavarian cousin Duke Louis, the future Emperor Louis IV, whose right rested on agreements among the branches of the House of Wittelsbach and who had the backing of the burghers of the Lower Bavarian towns. The other was Duke Frederick I of Austria, called the Fair, also a cousin of Louis; the two had been raised and educated together in Vienna.

After Louis occupied Landshut and Straubing, then the two most important towns of Bavaria, the ducal widows called on their children's Austrian cousin for help, although Lower Bavaria had fought Austria bitterly over land and sovereignty in the decade before.

Louis led the Upper Bavarians and troops sent by the Lower Bavarian towns. Frederick commanded the Austrians and the nobility and knighthood of Lower Bavaria, which probably outnumbered their opponents. The decisive engagement, more a skirmish than a battle, was fought at Gammelsdorf on 9 November 1313. A thick fog lay over the field and hid Louis's real strength from Frederick. Louis's town militias fought on foot, while others of his troops were mounted, and by the end of the day his smaller force had won.

Louis did not pursue and destroy Frederick's beaten men, and no names of fallen nobles were recorded. Frederick had to give up his claim to the guardianship of the Lower Bavarian dukes, and the victory checked Habsburg hopes of annexing parts of Bavaria for a long time. A monument to the battle stands near the battlefield.
battle-of-gangut: Peter I had begun his offensive in Finland in the spring of 1713, and the Russian armies advanced to Åbo (Turku). After the Russian victory at the Battle of Storkyro on 19 February 1714 southern Finland was fully in Russian hands. The Russian governor, Prince Mikhail Galitzine, could not be supplied by sea, because a Swedish fleet under Admiral Gustav Wattrang had blockaded the coastal route past the Hanko Peninsula since 24 April. The blockade also kept the Russian coastal fleet from raiding the Swedish coast.

Admiral Apraksin brought a galley fleet of 80 ships to the peninsula on 29 June 1714 and met 16 ships of the line and seven smaller ships. He withdrew to the eastern side and called for reinforcements. Peter I, finding his battle fleet ill-prepared, abandoned its use and reached the coastal fleet on 20 July.

A first attempt to haul galleys across the peninsula on ox skins was abandoned after the second galley was damaged. A second attempt used calm weather on the morning of 26 July: the small galleys were easily manoeuvred, while the heavy Swedish ships were hard to turn. Apraksin sent 20 galleys past the blockade, then 15 more, and on 27 July the Russians ran the cleared sea route along the cape.

Only the small coastal squadron of Rear Admiral Nils Ehrenskiöld then stood in their way. He formed a defensive line between two islands, with the pram Elefanten broadside-on. After he refused to surrender, the Russians attacked at 14:00 on 27 July 1714. They boarded the galley Tranan, which capsized, opened a gap in the line and boarded the remaining ships. Fighting lasted three hours and ended with the capture of Elefanten and Ehrenskiöld himself.

The loss of the small squadron mattered less than the fact that over 70 Russian galleys had passed the blockade and reached the Archipelago Sea. Apraksin sailed from Rilax on 1 August, reached Åland by 8 August and had the whole of Åland under Russian control on 13 August. Russian galleys razed the Swedish town of Umeå on 18 September, and the Swedish army in Finland withdrew to the Torne River.

Swedish accounts of repeated Russian attacks and heavy Russian losses were disputed in 1996 by the Russian historian Paul A. Krotov, who found one massive attack and 127 men killed and 347 wounded. The victory is commemorated in Russia as a Day of Military Honour, and a stone cross at Riilahti manor, which replaced a wooden one of 1869, commemorates it.
battle-of-garni: Jalal al-Din Mangburni, the last sultan of the Khwarazmian Empire, had been driven from his realm by the Mongol Empire and was trying to recapture lost territories. He sent Queen Rusudan of Georgia a letter demanding that her kingdom submit to him, while assembling a large army from his allies and nobles. The Georgian court had reports of a possible attack but did not take the threat seriously, and the nobility answered by reminding Jalal al-Din of his defeat by the Mongols. In 1225 a large Khwarazmian army crossed the Georgian border.

Messengers went out to every region of the kingdom to gather troops. Georgia could raise around 100,000 men with mercenaries, but kept some forces back, leaving about 60,000 to 70,000 for the battle. Estimates of the invading army vary: the Georgian chronicler Jamtaaghmtsereli gives 140,000 men, Alexander Mikaberidze 200,000 Turkmen and mercenaries, and Richard G. Hovanissian a more modest 60,000.

A Georgian vanguard of about 20,000 men under the brothers Shalva Akhaltsikheli and Ivane Akhaltsikheli took the plateaus above the Khwarazmians, who stood on lower, flat ground, while General Mkhargrdzeli waited behind with more than 50,000 men. Jalal al-Din's left wing attacked the vanguard and his main force soon followed. The brothers sent several messengers asking Mkhargrdzeli to strike the enemy's rear, but his troops did not move; personal enmity between him and the brothers is believed to have been the reason. The vanguard was overrun, and Mkhargrdzeli ordered a full retreat.

Ivane was killed while retreating into the mountains. Shalva, badly wounded, was captured and at first treated with some honour, but was later executed; accounts link his death to his refusal to renounce Christianity and to letters he sent from the enemy camp warning the Georgians of its plans. Jalal al-Din captured Dvin and moved on Tbilisi, and Rusudan left the capital for Kutaisi, entrusting its defence to Botso and Memna Botsodze.

A quarter of the Georgian army had been destroyed, leaving the country poorly prepared for the Mongol invasions that followed. The battle is remembered in Georgian history as a disaster brought about by betrayal, and the failure of the feudal elite to unite at the critical moment is seen as a sign of the divisions that weakened the kingdom.
battle-of-gaugamela: Darius III had lost the Battle of Issus to Alexander in November 333 BCE, and his wife, mother and two daughters were captured. Alexander then took the Levant after the Siege of Tyre and Egypt, whose satrap Mazaces surrendered peacefully. Ancient historians report that Darius tried diplomacy three times, finally offering land west of the Euphrates, joint rule, a daughter in marriage and 30,000 talents of silver. The accounts differ in detail. Diodorus Siculus has Parmenion say he would accept, and Alexander reply that so would he, if he were Parmenion. Alexander refused, insisting there could be only one king of Asia.

In the summer of 331 BCE Alexander crossed the Euphrates and followed a northern route, easier for foraging and cooler. He crossed the Tigris with great difficulty, and captured scouts told him that Darius waited at Gaugamela, where the ground was being levelled. Calculations put the battle on 1 October 331 BCE.

Modern scholars reject the very high ancient figures for Darius's army and accept Arrian's for Alexander's: 7,000 cavalry and 40,000 infantry. Darius cleared the ground for scythed chariots and placed himself at the centre with his best infantry, with Bessus commanding the left flank and Mazaeus the right. Alexander took the right wing himself with the Companion cavalry and left Parmenion to hold the left.

Alexander led the Companions toward the right, drawing the Persian cavalry to the flanks and forcing Darius to attack. A long cavalry battle followed, in which the outnumbered Macedonians held on by careful use of reserves. The scythed chariots were intercepted by javelin-throwers, and those that got through were let pass between gaps in the ranks. Alexander then formed a wedge and struck the weakened centre, and Arrian says Darius was the first to turn and flee.

Alexander went first to help Parmenion, whose wing was encircled, and the fiercest fighting of the day followed against the Persian right. Babylon was surrendered by Bagophanes, and 4,000 talents and the war elephants were captured. Darius escaped east with a small force, but Bessus murdered him. Alexander gave him a full burial at Persepolis and executed Bessus the next year. The Achaemenid Empire is traditionally considered to have ended with Darius's death. The site of the battlefield is uncertain, and the most commonly accepted location is Karamlesh in the Nineveh Plains.
battle-of-geok-tepe: The battle was the main event of the Russian campaign of 1880 and 1881 against the Teke tribe of Turkmens. It is also called Denghil-Tepe or Dangil Teppe: Denghil-Tepe seems to have been the name of the fort and of a small hill in its northwest corner, while Geok Tepe, meaning Blue Hill, refers to the wider area. The fort lay in the Akhal Oasis, where streams from the Kopet Dagh watered irrigated fields, and its mud walls were said to be 5.5 m thick.

After a Russian defeat in 1879, Mikhail Skobelev was put in charge of the Trans-Caspian region in March 1880. He chose a slow, massive advance, made Bami his base by 11 June and decided to take the fort by siege rather than by storm. Supply was the main problem, since the oasis was surrounded by several hundred kilometres of semi-desert and camels were short.

In December Skobelev moved up to a fort a few kilometres west of Geok Tepe, and on 27 December Aleksey Kuropatkin arrived with five companies after a march across the desert from Khiva. By the end of the month Skobelev had 4020 infantry, 750 cavalry, artillery, rockets, several machine guns and heliographs, against about 40000 Tekkes thought to be in the area. On 1 January 1881 he occupied Yanghi-Kala to control the water supply and chose the southeast corner as the point of attack.

Siege lines were dug from 4 January, and the Tekkes made sorties on the 9th, 11th and 16th. A mine was loaded with 1,200 kg of powder. On 24 January it blew a 43-metre breach; Kuropatkin's companies took it while other columns stormed the south breach and scaled the west wall. Skobelev then ordered a general advance, and the cavalry pursued the fleeing Tekkes for 16 kilometres until nightfall.

Skobelev's official report gave 6,500 bodies buried inside the fortress and 8,000 people of both sexes killed in the pursuit; Tekke losses were estimated at 20,000. The Russians spared about 5,000 women and children and freed about 600 Persian slaves. Skobelev was removed from command, probably because of the excessive slaughter of civilians.

On 30 January the Russians took Ashgabat. Transcaspia became an oblast of the Russian Empire on 6 May 1881, and in September Persia signed the Treaty of Akhal, fixing the Atrek River as the border. In Turkmenistan the battle is remembered as a national day of mourning, and a mosque built in the 1990s commemorates the siege and its defenders.
battle-of-gettysburg: After the Confederate victory at the Battle of Chancellorsville, General Robert E. Lee decided on a second invasion of the North. It would upset the Union's plans for the summer, might reduce the pressure on the besieged Confederate garrison at Vicksburg, and would let his army live off Northern farms while Virginia rested. His army of about 72,000 men could also threaten Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington and might strengthen the growing peace movement in the North. Lee began to move north from Fredericksburg on 3 June, and on 28 June President Abraham Lincoln replaced Major General Joseph Hooker with Major General George Meade as commander of the Army of the Potomac.

On 1 July the armies met northwest of Gettysburg. Brigadier General John Buford's Union cavalry delayed the Confederates until infantry arrived, but two large Confederate corps broke the hastily formed Union lines, which fell back to the hills south of the town. On 2 July the Union line stood in a fishhook shape. Lee attacked the Union left, with fierce fighting at Little Round Top, the Wheatfield, Devil's Den and the Peach Orchard, and assaulted Culp's Hill and Cemetery Hill on the right, but the Union held its lines.

On 3 July around 1 p.m. 150 to 170 Confederate guns opened what was probably the largest bombardment of the war, which did little to the Union position. About 3 p.m. between 10,500 and 12,500 Confederate soldiers advanced three-quarters of a mile towards Cemetery Ridge in the assault known as Pickett's Charge. Union artillery and rifle fire devastated them, and the few who briefly reached the ridge were driven back. On 4 July Lee began his retreat.

Union casualties were 23,055, of whom 3,155 were killed, and the Confederates lost 23,231 by one recent count, though many authors give as many as 28,000. Nearly a third of Lee's general officers were killed, wounded or captured. On 4 July the Vicksburg garrison surrendered to Major General Ulysses S. Grant, and news of Gettysburg ended lingering hopes of European recognition of the Confederacy.

Historians often call Gettysburg the turning point of the war, usually together with Vicksburg, since Lee conducted no more strategic offensives afterwards, though it was not seen as decisive at the time and the war went on for almost two years. On 19 November 1863 Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery, now Gettysburg National Cemetery, in his Gettysburg Address of 271 words.
battle-of-grahovac: On 10 May 1858 the Ottoman commander Hussein Pasha took the villages of Vilusi and Grahovo and advanced on Grahovac, a small village on a plateau a little above them. In the Montenegrin plans Grahovac was the main bastion of the defence, and the core of the resistance gathered there.

The fighting began early on 11 May, when the Ottomans attacked and the Montenegrins held their ground, determined not to retreat. Most of the 3,000 Ottoman and 1,000 Montenegrin casualties fell on that day. On 12 May Hussein Pasha offered a truce, which Grand Duke Mirko Petrović-Njegoš refused, though he gave the Ottomans time to bury their dead and would not cut off their water, which he considered dishonourable.

On 13 May, as the Ottomans received support from Bosnia, the Montenegrins took the offensive and forced them back in successive retreats. Their chief difficulty was the Ottoman artillery, which shelled their positions without pause, and they resolved to charge across the field and take the guns. When the Serdar Đuro Kusovac and the priest Luka Jovović were killed in the charge, the rest of the troops, the guardsmen among them, rushed forward to avenge them, and the capture of the Ottoman cannon decided the battle.

The victory was soon told in the songs and literature of the South Slavs, above all among the Serbs of Vojvodina. It led the Great Powers to demarcate the border between Montenegro and the Ottoman Empire, in effect recognising its long independence, and Montenegro gained Grahovo, Rudine, Nikšići, more than half of Drobnjaci and other districts. Prince Danilo gave every survivor the Grahovo medal, and Mirko was proclaimed Grand Duke of Grahovo. In 1864 Nicholas I built the Church of the Ascension on the site of Hussein Pasha's headquarters, and an obelisk to the battle was unveiled in 2008.
battle-of-grandson: In 1475 the Old Swiss Confederacy, led by the Canton of Bern, had taken the town of Grandson in Vaud, which belonged to Charles the Bold's ally Jacques of Savoy. When talks on returning Vaud failed in January 1476, Charles left Lorraine with the bulk of his army, about 12,000 men, crossed the Jura and seized Yverdon. He took the town of Grandson on 21 February and besieged its castle, which surrendered on 28 February.

Swiss sources agree that the garrison gave up only after Charles promised to spare it. Panigarola, who was with the duke, wrote that the men had thrown themselves on his mercy. Charles ordered all 412 to be hanged from trees or drowned in the lake, an execution that lasted four hours and that Panigarola called shocking and horrible.

Opposition among the other cantons to Bern's campaign of 1475 delayed the Confederate reinforcements. Unaware of the garrison's fate, 18,000 troops from the eight cantons and their allies gathered at Bevaix on 1 March and attacked Vaumarcus Castle, which Charles held to block the road to Neuchâtel. On 2 March his army of about 20,000 met the Swiss vanguard near Concise in an unfavourable position. When his cavalry could not hold it, Charles ordered a pull-back to better ground, and the arrival of the larger Swiss body during the manoeuvre threw his army into confusion. The retreat became a rout that Charles could not stop.

Lacking cavalry, the Swiss could not pursue far, and few were killed on either side. They took Charles's artillery and his treasure: carpets said to have belonged to Alexander the Great, the 55-carat Sancy diamond, the Three Brothers jewel, his silver bath and his ducal seal. Part of the booty survives in Swiss museums, some guns at La Neuveville. The victors then found their countrymen still hanging at Grandson, a scene the eyewitness Peterman Etterlin described. The killings united the Swiss as never before, and at the Battle of Morat in June 1476 they annihilated his army.
battle-of-grauholz: France had already encroached on the associates of the Swiss Confederation, seeking control of the alpine passes and a buffer against the monarchies of Europe. Part of the bishopric of Basel was absorbed in 1793, and in 1797 Napoleon annexed the Valtellina to the new Cisalpine Republic and invaded the rest of the bishopric. In 1798 the republican faction of Vaud, led by Frédéric-César de La Harpe, invited the French in. Vaud was ruled by Bern, whose government often spoke another language, and when it revolted and declared a republic the French had a pretext to invade.

French troops entered the Lemanic Republic on 24 January 1798. Bern raised about 20,000 men and the rest of the Confederation 4,100, against about 35,000 French in two wings under Balthazar Alexis Henri Schauenburg. On 1 March the French invaded Bern and Solothurn, and on 2 March the battles of Lengnau, Twann, Grenchen and Bellach ended in French victories and the capitulation of Solothurn.

The Bernese army of about 6,400 men under Karl Ludwig von Erlach first met some 18,000 French at the Battle of Fraubrunnen and was driven back to Grauholz, a wooded hill in what are now the municipalities of Urtenen-Schönbühl and Moosseedorf. By then Erlach had about two battalions left. Many women, older men and even children of the countryside joined the fighting; an eyewitness described many people of the village of Bolligen coming to the army, and 27 of its farmers died. The Bernese held out for about two and a half hours before they broke and left the woods in small groups.

A report of 1804 put the Swiss losses at 2,000 and the French dead at about 1,600, while a later estimate gave Bern's total losses in the fighting of 2 to 5 March as about 700; French losses in the campaign are unknown. On the same day General Johann Rudolf von Graffenried defeated the southern French wing at Neuenegg, but the government's surrender and the defeat at Grauholz ended Bernese resistance. Erlach failed to hold the approaches to the city and set off for the Bernese Oberland to organise resistance, but at Wichtrach he was murdered by Bernese soldiers or farmers who believed him a traitor.
battle-of-graus: Graus was the northernmost Muslim outpost in the valley of the Cinca. Ramiro I of Aragon first tried to take it in 1055, probably in response to the defeat of García Sánchez III of Navarre at Atapuerca the year before, which had left Ferdinand I of León and Castile in a commanding position on Ramiro's western border and over the Taifa of Zaragoza to his south. That expedition failed, and in 1059 Ferdinand forced Zaragoza to pay him parias, or tribute.

Ramiro marched on Graus again in the spring of 1063, traditionally on 8 May. This time the Zaragozans had with them 300 Castilian knights under the infante Sancho the Strong. The presence of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar rests on a single source, the generally reliable Historia Roderici, which makes him Sancho's alférez; given how rarely his name appears in documents of the early 1060s, historians think this unlikely.

The fighting itself is obscure. The Fragmentum historicum ex cartulario Alaonis records only that Ramiro was killed by the Moors in war near Graus, without mentioning the Castilians. The Chronica naierensis tells a story, generally regarded as legend, that an illegitimate son of García Sánchez III eloped with the infante Sancho's fiancée and took refuge in Zaragoza and Aragon, and that Sancho marched against them to avenge the insult. According to the Arab historian al-Turtushi, Ramiro was assassinated by a Muslim soldier who spoke the Christians' language and had slipped into the Aragonese camp.

Historians such as Pierre Boissonnade linked the defeat to the War of Barbastro of the next year. In the summary of Charles Bishko, Boissonnade saw the Barbastro expedition as a French crusade, inspired by Cluny and launched through the papacy of Alexander II, to save an Aragonese kingdom threatened with invasion after Ramiro's death, with Graus serving as an Iberian Manzikert. Graus itself was finally taken in 1083 by Ramiro's successor, Sancho Ramírez.
battle-of-gravelotte: On 16 August 1870 the German Second Army under Prince Friedrich Karl met the right wing of Marshal François Achille Bazaine's French Army of the Rhine at the Battle of Mars-la-Tour, and both sides claimed victory. Bazaine's four corps retreated in bad weather along the road towards Verdun, with the Germans pressing hard to stop them linking up with French forces at Sedan. Their pressure forced Bazaine to take the crests east of the Moselle, with his left flank at Rozerieulles and his right at St. Privat. Bazaine regarded the position as virtually impregnable, with the defenders sheltered behind hedges and low walls and anchored in villages and farmhouses.

King Wilhelm I's combined forces, the Prussian First and Second Armies, numbered 188,332 officers and men with 732 heavy cannons. At 8:00 a.m. on 18 August Wilhelm, whose chief of staff was Moltke, ordered an advance. General Manstein, with artillery of the Hessian 25th Infantry Division, advanced on Amanvillers. The Germans met murderous fire from the French Chassepot rifle and the mitrailleuse before their shorter-ranged needle-guns could reply. Steinmetz's VII and VIII Corps attacked repeatedly across the Mance Ravine and failed with enormous casualties; by 18:30 a large part of them panicked and withdrew.

At 16:50 the Prussian Guards of the Second Army attacked St. Privat, held by Marshal Canrobert, and were pinned down on the slopes by French fire. After a mass artillery barrage, the Guards, the II Corps and the Saxon XII Corps attacked again and took St. Privat by 20:00, forcing the decimated French back. General Bourbaki refused to commit the Old Guard, having judged the situation a defeat, with ammunition spent and a quarter of his men lost.

The Army of the Rhine retreated into Metz on the morning of 19 August, and its last chance of retreating west to Verdun was gone. After a siege of over two months it surrendered on 27 October 1870. The Prussian and Hessian force lost 20,163 killed, wounded or missing, including about 8,000 of 18,000 men of the Guards Corps; the French lost 12,275, though the record is incomplete. Most Prussians fell to the Chassepot, most French to the shells of Krupp's steel breech-loading guns. It was the largest battle of the Franco-Prussian War.
battle-of-grunwald: In 1230 the Teutonic Order, a crusading military order, moved to Chełmno Land and launched the Prussian Crusade, conquering and converting the pagan Prussians by the 1280s. It then turned on the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania and for about 100 years raided its lands, particularly Samogitia, which separated the order's lands in Prussia from its branch in Livonia, but gained very little territory. In May 1409 an uprising began in Teutonic-held Samogitia, which Lithuania and Poland supported. Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen declared war on both on 6 August 1409.

The Polish and Lithuanian troops gathered at Czerwińsk and crossed the Vistula over a pontoon bridge between 24 and 30 June 1410. They then marched towards Marienburg (Malbork), the capital of Prussia, and crossed the Prussian border on 9 July. No contemporary source gives reliable troop counts; the highest estimates, 39,000 Polish–Lithuanian and 27,000 Teutonic men, are often cited as commonly accepted. The Teutonic army was outnumbered but had advantages in discipline, training and equipment.

On 15 July the armies met between the villages of Grünfelde, Tannenberg and Ludwigsdorf. Vytautas attacked the Teutonic left flank, and after more than an hour the Lithuanian light cavalry retreated. Heavy fighting between Poles and Teutons followed, and Jungingen led 16 banners to the Polish right flank. The Lithuanians returned and struck from the rear, Jungingen was killed, and the leaderless Teutonic forces retreated to their camp, where the defence was broken. The battle lasted about ten hours.

The victors delayed three days on the battlefield and reached Marienburg only on 26 July, which gave Heinrich von Plauen time to organise its defence. Many Teutonic fortresses surrendered, but the siege of Marienburg failed, and the Peace of Thorn of 1411 cost the order minimal territory. The order never recovered its former power, and the burden of war reparations caused internal conflicts and an economic downturn in its lands.

The battle shifted the balance of power in Central and Eastern Europe towards the Polish–Lithuanian union. It is regarded as one of the most important victories in the history of Poland and Lithuania and is also commemorated in Ukraine and Belarus. In 1914 Germany named a victory over Russia the Battle of Tannenberg and framed it as revenge for 1410.
battle-of-guandu: Conflict between Cao Cao and Yuan Shao had become apparent by 196. Yuan Shao held the lands north of the Yellow River, the Hebei region, while Cao Cao controlled most of the land to the south after defeating Lü Bu at the Battle of Xiapi in 199, and kept Emperor Xian with him in the new capital at Xu. Each saw the other as the obstacle to his ambition to rule China. In the autumn of 199 Cao Cao stationed troops at Guandu, which lay on the road to Xu near the Yellow River. In 200 Yuan Shao, whose army numbered up to 110,000, including 10,000 cavalry, marched to Liyang, after his adviser Tian Feng had urged him not to and been imprisoned.

Yuan Shao's general Yan Liang besieged the fort at Boma, but Cao Cao feinted towards Yan Ford on the advice of Xun You and then struck east; Yan Liang was killed by Guan Yu. Cao Cao then abandoned his forward bases to hold Guandu, still outnumbered. Both armies dug earthworks, and Yuan Shao's archers on high platforms were answered by Cao Cao's traction trebuchets. When supplies ran short, Cao Cao considered retreat, but Xun Yu wrote to dissuade him, and in the ninth month raiders under Xu Huang burned grain carts at Gushi.

In the tenth month Yuan Shao's adviser Xu You, dissatisfied with his lord, defected and told Cao Cao that the depot at Wuchao, under Chunyu Qiong, was lightly guarded. Cao Cao led 5,000 infantry and cavalry there at night, disguised as Yuan Shao's reinforcements, and burned almost all the food supplies. Yuan Shao sent his main army under Zhang He and Gao Lan against Guandu instead, but it failed, and the two generals surrendered. Yuan Shao fled north across the Yellow River with about 800 cavalry. Cao Cao had captured men buried alive, and claimed to have killed 70,000 enemy troops.

Yuan Shao died in June 202, and his sons Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang fought each other, which Cao Cao exploited. By 207 most of northern China was under his control. Sima Guang blamed Yuan Shao's obstinacy for the defeat, while Carl Leban credits Cao Cao's choice of ground and Rafe de Crespigny doubts that Yuan Shao held a real advantage. Mao Zedong cited the battle as an example of a weaker side yielding at first and then defeating a stronger one.
battle-of-guningtou: After the People's Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 October 1949, the government of Chiang Kai-shek withdrew its forces to Taiwan but kept garrisons on Kinmen and the Matsu islands off Fujian, which the People's Liberation Army saw as stepping stones to Taiwan. The PLA 10th Corps under Ye Fei, part of Chen Yi's 3rd Field Army, had no experience of naval warfare and no air or naval cover. Ye Fei chose to take Kinmen and Xiamen at once; Xiamen fell on 17 October, and the attack on Greater Kinmen was given to the 28th Army with regiments of the 29th.

Kinmen had had no defences before mid-June 1949, when a fortress headquarters began building fortifications, chiefly along the flat western part and the sandy northern shore. Hu Lien's 12th Army Corps was still on its way by sea when the attack came.

At about midnight on 25 October a Nationalist sentry accidentally set off a landmine, and the alerted defenders' searchlights exposed an advancing landing party. Near Lungkou three M5A1 Stuart tanks, one of which had broken down on the beach the evening before, opened fire on the landing craft; the tanks, later nicknamed the Bear of Kinmen, were said to have crushed attackers when their ammunition ran out. A second wave early on 26 October was scattered by wind and heavy seas, and only ten platoons landed, lit up by flares dropped from C-47 aircraft.

By the early morning of 27 October the PLA troops had no food or ammunition left. Over 1,300 were trapped on the beaches below the cliffs north of Kuningtou; after a four-hour assault more than 400 were dead and about 900 had surrendered by 10:00. The commander of the 253rd Regiment, Hsu Po, hid in a cave near Mount Taiwu until his capture in February 1950.

Ye Fei apologised to Mao Zedong, blaming a shortage of landing craft, the failure to secure beachheads and the lack of unified command, but was not punished. Nationalist records give 1,267 of their own killed and 1,982 wounded, and 7,364 PLA soldiers and civilian workers captured; many prisoners were later drafted into the Nationalist army, and about 900 were returned to the mainland in 1950. Hu Lien then fortified Kinmen and developed its roads, forests, schools and Kaoliang liquor production. The Kuningtou Battle Museum opened in 1984, and in May 2025 the Legislative Yuan made 25 October a national holiday.
battle-of-hafrsfjord: According to Snorri Sturluson's saga, Harald Fairhair already controlled much of south-eastern Norway before the battle, though other sources hold that the east was under the Danish king. The opposition he faced at Hafrsfjord came from the south-west, mainly Rogaland, with chieftains from the Sognefjord area. The battle may well have been the largest fought in Norway up to that time and for a long time afterwards.

The victory ended resistance in the south-west and allowed Harald to subdue the country and collect taxes from much of it. After it he proclaimed himself king of the Norwegians, and later historiography regarded him as the first legitimate king of Norway. Many of the defeated who would not accept his rule emigrated to Iceland. It was long believed that the battle was the decisive event of the unification, but most scholars now see the making of the kingdom as a process lasting centuries, though the battle keeps a large place in the Norwegian popular imagination.

The year is unknown, since the sagas count winters passed since an event rather than years of the Christian calendar. In the 1830s the historian Rudolf Keyser counted back from the Battle of Svolder in Snorri's Heimskringla and arrived at 872, a date popularised by P. A. Munch and chosen for the millennial celebration of 1872. In the 1920s Halvdan Koht, more critical of the sagas, dated the battle to about 900, and in the 1970s Ólafia Einarsdóttir argued for 870 to 875. Most scholars now place it in the 880s.
The national monument of Haraldshaugen was raised in 1872 to mark the battle, and in 1983 Fritz Røed's Swords in the Rock was set up at Hafrsfjord in its memory.
battle-of-haldighati: The siege of Chittorgarh in 1568, under Udai Singh II, had cost Mewar its fertile eastern belt, but the wooded hills remained in Sisodia hands. Akbar wanted Mewar to secure a route to Gujarat, and after Pratap Singh was crowned in 1572 he sent four envoys, Jalal Khan Qurchi, Man Singh of Amber, Raja Bhagwant Das and Todar Mal, to make him a vassal. All failed. Pratap set up his base at Gogunda, and Man Singh marched from Mandalgarh. The pass of Haldighati, named for rocks that crush into yellow sand like turmeric, lay between Gogunda and the village of Khamnor.

Figures differ. Mewari tradition sets 20,000 against 80,000, which Jadunath Sarkar thinks exaggerated; al-Badayuni, who witnessed the battle, gives the Rana 3,000 horsemen and some 400 Bhil archers under Rana Punja, against about 10,000 under Man Singh. The Rajputs had no firearms, while the Mughals used muskets. The battle began three hours after sunrise. The Rana's charge broke the Mughal wings and centre, but they rallied, Man Singh led in the rear guard, and Mihtar Khan spread word with kettle-drums that the emperor's army was arriving. Musket fire broke the charge of the Mewari elephants.

As the Rana's men began to desert, his nobles persuaded the wounded Rana to leave the field. Jhala Man Singh put on his royal emblems and was killed in his place, giving him time to escape. Abul Fazl gives 150 Mughal and 500 Mewari dead; later Rajasthani chroniclers raised the toll to 20,000.

Man Singh did not pursue, and Akbar suspended him from court for a time. The Mughals briefly took Gogunda and, in a sustained campaign, most of Mewar, but after 1585 their attention turned elsewhere and Pratap recovered much of his kingdom except Chittor and Mandalgarh. The historian Satish Chandra called the battle at best an assertion of local independence. Mainstream historians, among them D. N. Jha, Tanuja Kothiyal and Rima Hooja, reject as ahistorical later claims that Pratap won it.
battle-of-haliartus: In 396 or 395 BCE Timocrates of Rhodes, an envoy of the Persian satrap Pharnabazus, arrived in Greece and promised Persian money and support to the leading states if they would make war on Sparta. Sparta's aggressive and unilateral conduct had angered many of its allies, and the offer was enough to bring several states, Thebes above all, to war.

The Thebans chose to start the war indirectly. They persuaded the Locrians to raid Phocis, an ally of Sparta; Thebes was bound to support Locris, and Phocis appealed to Sparta. The Spartans saw a chance to discipline the restive Thebans and prepared a major campaign, while Thebes sought help from Athens, and a perpetual alliance was concluded between the Athenians and the Boeotians.

The Spartan plan called for two armies to meet at Haliartus for a combined attack: one under King Pausanias of the Agiad dynasty with Spartan and Peloponnesian troops, the other under Lysander with Phocians and allies from north-western Greece. Pausanias lingered for several days in the Peloponnese, and Lysander reached Haliartus first. Unwilling to wait, he tried to take the city by subversion and, when that failed, assaulted its walls.

A large Theban force nearby, perhaps unknown to Lysander, hurried to help the defenders. In the fighting beneath the walls Lysander's army was routed and he was killed. The Thebans pursued too far into rough and steep ground, where the fleeing troops turned and drove them back with heavy losses. The next day Lysander's army broke up, each contingent going home.

When Pausanias arrived days later, the Thebans let him recover the bodies only if he left Boeotia, and he agreed. At Sparta, Lysander's faction put him on trial for arriving late and not attacking, and expecting to be condemned to death, he went into exile. With Lysander dead and Pausanias gone, Agesilaus was left to direct Spartan policy for years. The war that began here lasted until 387 BCE, with battles at Nemea and Coronea the next year.
battle-of-halidon-hill: In 1332 Edward Balliol, son of King John I of Scotland, led the Scottish nobles disinherited after the Treaty of Northampton in an invasion of Scotland, quietly supported by Edward III. He crushed a Scottish army at Dupplin Moor and was crowned at Scone, granting Edward lands that included Berwick, but supporters of the five-year-old David II ambushed him at Annan in December and he fled to England. Edward then openly recognised Balliol and chose Berwick-upon-Tweed as his target: the most successful trading town in Scotland, whose wool duties were the Crown's largest source of income, and a place the Scots could hardly abandon.

Balliol reached Berwick in late March 1333 and Edward joined him on 9 May. The guardian, Sir Archibald Douglas, gathered an army that the historian Clifford Rogers puts at around 15,000. When the town's governor, Sir Alexander Seton, broke a truce, Edward hanged his son Thomas, a hostage, in sight of the walls; a new truce required the town to surrender if not relieved by sunset on 19 July.

Edward placed his army on Halidon Hill, a rise of some 600 feet north-west of Berwick, with dismounted men-at-arms and spearmen in three divisions and longbowmen on each flank. After a stalemate Douglas ordered an assault a little after noon. The Scots had to cross marshy ground and climb the slope under dense arrow fire, and arrived tired, having marched 60 miles in 48 hours. Two of their three schiltrons broke almost at once; the third fought on before it too collapsed.

English men-at-arms mounted and pursued the fleeing Scots for 8 miles. Most who surrendered were killed on Edward's orders, and about a hundred prisoners were beheaded the next morning. English chronicles claimed 35,000 to 60,000 Scottish dead and Scottish ones 10,000; Rogers suggests about 2,900. Six of the nine most senior Scots present died, while English losses were reported as 14 or 7.

Berwick surrendered on 20 July. Balliol held a parliament at Perth in October 1333 and in 1334 ceded eight counties of south-east Scotland to England by the Treaty of Newcastle, but he was deposed, restored and deposed again by 1336. The outbreak of the Hundred Years' War in 1337 let David II consolidate his position. The battlefield is on Historic England's Register of Historic Battlefields, and a rough stone monument stands near the top of the hill.
battle-of-halmyros: The Catalan Company, veterans of the War of the Sicilian Vespers, had been hired by the Byzantine Empire against the Turks in Asia Minor. Quarrels led to war with their employers, and after their eviction from Gallipoli in 1307 they fought and plundered their way west through Thrace and Macedonia, entering Thessaly in early 1309. There the Greek ruler John II Doukas, aided by Byzantium and Epirus, defeated them, and they agreed to move on towards the Frankish principalities of southern Greece.

Walter of Brienne, chosen Duke of Athens in 1309 after Guy II died childless, had fought the Catalans in Italy and spoke their language. He hired the company for six months against the Greeks, and it took Domokos and some thirty other fortresses. Walter then refused the remaining four months' pay, kept 200 horsemen and 300 Almogavar infantry in his service and ordered the rest to give up their conquests and leave. When they offered to recognise him as lord in return for some land, he refused and gathered his vassals and allies to expel them.

Every source gives different numbers, and modern scholars consider them exaggerated, but the Athenian army clearly outnumbered the Catalans, whose cavalry were mostly Turks under their own leaders, Halil and Malik. The company took a defensive position behind a swamp. On the eve of battle the 500 Catalans in Walter's service asked leave to rejoin their comrades, and the Turks camped apart, suspecting a plot against them. Confident in his heavy cavalry, Walter led a charge against the Catalan line. It failed, the duke and most of his knights fell, and the Turks then came down on the Athenian army and routed it.

With the Frankish elite of Athens dead or captive, the Catalans met little resistance. Livadeia surrendered, Thebes was plundered, and Walter's widow Joanna of Châtillon gave up Athens. The victors divided the duchy, often marrying the widows of the men they had killed. They offered the leadership to Boniface of Verona, who declined, then to Roger Deslaur, and later accepted Frederick II of Sicily, who named his son Manfred duke. Under Alfonso Fadrique they added the Duchy of Neopatras in 1319. Nerio I Acciaioli took Athens in 1386-1388, and the capture of Neopatras in 1390 ended Catalan rule in Greece.
battle-of-hamel: After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk took Russia out of the war, the Germans moved up to 48 divisions to the Western Front and on 21 March 1918 opened the Spring Offensive. Its advance towards Amiens was checked at the First Battle of Villers-Bretonneux in April, and in June the Allies began small advances known as peaceful penetrations. Hamel, on a spur about 3 km north-east of Villers-Bretonneux, gave the Germans observation over the sector and stood in the way of a later Allied advance.

It was John Monash's first battle as commander of the Australian Corps, and his first plan was rejected after his subordinates opposed it. The official war historian Charles Bean had conspired with the journalist Keith Murdoch to have him removed, and Prime Minister Billy Hughes arrived two days before the attack ready to replace him, but changed his mind after hearing senior officers praise their commander.

The attack was made by the 4th, 6th and 11th Australian Brigades, with ten American companies attached to give the American Expeditionary Force experience, six of which were withdrawn before the fighting; it was the first time units of the AEF served under non-American command. The 15th Brigade made a feint north of the Somme. The 5th Tank Brigade's new Mark V tanks moved up under the noise of a harassing bombardment that began at 03:02 on 4 July, and German defenders put on gas masks expecting gas.

The objectives were taken in 93 minutes, three minutes over Monash's plan. Tanks and parachute drops from aircraft brought up supplies, and wireless sets were used for the first time from captured positions. A German counter-attack that night broke into the 44th Battalion's line but was thrown back on 6 July.

Allied losses were about 1,400 killed or wounded; around 2,000 Germans were killed and 1,600 captured. The Australians Thomas Axford and Henry Dalziel received the Victoria Cross, and fourteen Americans were decorated by the British. Georges Clemenceau toured the field and praised the result, and the methods tried at Hamel succeeded on a much larger scale at the Battle of Amiens.
battle-of-hanau: After his defeat at the Battle of Leipzig, Napoleon withdrew westwards at speed to regroup his forces on the Rhine. The coalition armies had suffered such losses that they could not pursue him effectively, and he reorganised his army at Erfurt from 23 October before sending his corps towards Frankfurt and Mainz. Bavaria's change of sides allowed the coalition to send an Austro-Bavarian army of 45,000 to 50,000 men under Karl Philipp von Wrede into the French rear. It occupied Würzburg without a fight, and Wrede's advance guard took Hanau on 28 October, blocking the road to Frankfurt.

Wrede probably expected to meet only about 20,000 men, believed the French army to be disorganised and thought the main coalition army close behind it. None of this was true. At Hanau he had at least 42,000 men and 94 guns in an Austrian and a Bavarian corps, deployed along the Kinzig with the river behind much of his army. Napoleon, with little more than 30,000 men fit for combat, committed about 20,000 of them.

Dense forest east of Wrede's position let the French approach almost unseen. On 30 October Napoleon attacked the allied left with all the troops he had. By midday Marshal Victor and MacDonald had cleared the woods in front of the allied centre, and General Drouot found a track through the forest along which cannon could be moved. Once Old Guard grenadiers had cleared the ground, Drouot brought up 50 guns, which quickly silenced Wrede's 28.

French cavalry under Sébastiani and the Guard drove back the allied horse on the left and struck the flank of the centre, which fell back along the Kinzig with heavy losses. Troops of the right wing trying to cross the single bridge to help it drowned in numbers. Wrede rallied a line from Lamboy Bridge to Hanau, but the allies abandoned the town in the night, and the French occupied it on 31 October.

Wrede lost 9,000 men. French losses were fewer, though some 10,000 stragglers were taken prisoner between 28 and 31 October. Napoleon reached Frankfurt and soon came within 20 miles of Mainz, so that his army could recover before the invasion of France in 1814. Beethoven's Symphony No. 7 was first performed in Vienna on 8 December 1813 at a charity concert for soldiers wounded at Hanau. The battle is listed on the Arc de Triomphe.
battle-of-hansan-island: Yi Ŏkki joined Yi Sun-sin at Yeosu on 10 August 1592, and on 12 August they met Wŏn Kyun at Noryang, bringing their combined fleet to 56 warships. At Dangpo they learned that a Japanese fleet was sailing west from Busan. Wakizaka Yasuharu's 73 ships entered the narrow Gyeonnaeryang Strait. Yi's fleet gave chase to a Japanese scout vessel and broke off on sighting the main Japanese fleet there.

Rather than fight in the strait, Yi Sun-sin sent a small detachment forward as bait. The Japanese followed it into open water off Hansan Island, where the Korean fleet stood in a U-shaped crane formation, with large warships, among them two turtle ships, in the centre and lighter ships on the wings. Most of the Japanese ships were destroyed, while the Koreans reported few losses. The fighting lasted all day, until the Koreans tired of the chase. Fourteen Japanese ships that had not engaged escaped, and Wakizaka withdrew to Gimhae.

News of the defeat reached Busan within hours, and the commanders Kuki Yoshitaka and Kato Yoshiaki sailed with 42 ships to the port of Angolpo, hoping to meet the Koreans close to shore. This time the Japanese refused to follow the Koreans into open water, so Yi's fleet moved in and bombarded the anchored ships for hours until their crews retreated inland. Both commanders survived. In the two encounters the Koreans destroyed roughly 100 Japanese ships.

Wŏn Kyun, left behind to deal with Japanese soldiers marooned on a small isle, fled on a false report that a large Japanese fleet was approaching, and the stranded men drifted ashore on rafts made from the wreckage. On 23 August Hideyoshi Toyotomi halted naval operations at Busan and ordered Todo Takatora to reinforce Japanese operations in Korea. The British vice admiral George Alexander Ballard later called the battle Yi's crowning exploit, and the historian Hulbert compared it to the Battle of Salamis.
battle-of-hastings: King Edward the Confessor died childless on 5 January 1066, leaving several claimants to the throne. Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex, was elected king by the Witenagemot and crowned by Ealdred, the Archbishop of York. Duke William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to agree, and the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada also made a claim.

Hardrada and Harold's exiled brother Tostig Godwinson defeated an English army at the Battle of Fulford on 20 September 1066, and Harold defeated them at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Three days later William landed at Pevensey. Harold marched about 200 miles south in roughly a week and camped on Caldbec Hill on the night of 13 October.

The armies met on Saturday 14 October 1066 about 7 miles north of Hastings, near the present town of Battle. The fighting began at 9 am and lasted until dusk. The numbers are unknown; most modern historians argue for 7,000 to 8,000 English troops. The English were almost entirely infantry, in a shield wall at the top of a steep slope, with few archers. About half of William's army was infantry, and the rest was split between cavalry and archers.

Norman arrows shot uphill had little effect, and attacks by infantry and then cavalry failed to break the shield wall. A retreat began on William's left, and a rumour spread that he was dead; he rode through his men showing his face and led a counter-attack. The Normans then used the tactic of feigned flight. Accounts of Harold's death conflict, and the traditional arrow in the eye is first mentioned in the 1080s. He appears to have died late in the battle, and most of his army then retreated.

Some historians estimate that 2,000 invaders died, along with about twice that number of Englishmen. Harold's body was identified the day after the battle.
