William was crowned king on Christmas Day 1066. Rebellions and resistance continued, but Hastings effectively marked the culmination of his conquest of England. William founded a monastery on the site, with the high altar of the abbey church said to mark the spot where Harold died.
battle-of-hatfield-chase: Edwin, the most powerful ruler in Britain at the time, seems to have defeated Cadwallon a few years before the battle. Bede describes Edwin extending his rule over what he called the Mevanian islands, one of them Anglesey, and another source tells of Cadwallon being besieged on the island of Priestholm off the coast of Anglesey. Cadwallon later drove the Northumbrians from his lands and allied with Penda, Cadwallon being the stronger partner. Penda's standing in Mercia at the time is uncertain: Bede suggests he became king soon after Hatfield, while the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he became king in 626.

The battle, called Hæðfeld in Old English and Meigen in Old Welsh, was fought on 12 October 633. Its site is usually placed in a marshy area about 8 miles (13 km) northeast of Doncaster on the south bank of the River Don. Edwin was killed together with his son Osfrith, and his other son Eadfrith was captured by Penda and later killed.

The location has been disputed. The Battle of Hatfield Investigation Society has proposed Cuckney in Nottinghamshire, at a place known locally as High Hatfield. In the 1950s workmen underpinning St Mary's Church there uncovered a mass grave thought to predate the church of the 1100s. The group received £15,600 from the Heritage Lottery Fund in 2016 for ground-penetrating radar surveys; the Diocese of Southwell refused permission to excavate in November 2017, and in April 2018 a further £58,000 was awarded for LIDAR scanning and trenches in the fields around the church land.

The defeat was a disaster for Northumbria, which was divided between its constituent kingdoms. Eanfrith, a son of the former king Æthelfrith, returned from exile to take power in Bernicia, while Edwin's cousin Osric took over Deira. Cadwallon went on waging war against the Northumbrians until Oswald defeated him at the Battle of Heavenfield, also known as Deniseburna.

The historian D. P. Kirby suggested that Edwin's fall was the work of a wide alliance of interests opposed to him, including the deposed Bernician line of Æthelfrith. Given the later hostility between Cadwallon and Æthelfrith's sons, any such alliance cannot have lasted long after the battle.
battle-of-hattin: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was divided. Guy of Lusignan became king in 1186 in right of his wife Sibylla, and his court faction, which included Raynald of Châtillon, Gerard of Ridefort and the Knights Templar, was opposed by a nobles' faction led by Raymond III of Tripoli. Saladin, who had become vizier of Egypt in 1169, had taken Damascus in 1174 and Aleppo in 1183 and controlled the southern and eastern flanks of the crusader states. In 1187 Raynald raided a Muslim pilgrim caravan while a truce was in force. Saladin's son al-Afdal and the emir Gökböri then raided around Acre, and in May 1187 they heavily defeated the Templars at the Battle of Cresson.

Saladin assembled about 40,000 men and crossed the Jordan on 30 June. On 2 July he stormed Tiberias, where Raymond's wife Eschiva of Bures held out in the citadel, hoping to draw the Crusader army away from its well-watered camp at La Saphorie. Raymond advised against marching, but Gerard and Raynald accused him of cowardice, and Guy resolved to advance.

On 3 July the Crusaders marched under constant attack by mounted archers and found the springs inadequate. They were forced to camp on a dry plateau near Meskenah, surrounded overnight, while Muslim troops set fire to dry grass. On 4 July, blinded by smoke and tormented by thirst, they were blocked from the water. Raymond broke through to the lake with two charges and escaped to Tyre. Most of the infantry fled onto the Horns of Hattin. The knights made three charges on Saladin's position and were broken when Guy's tent fell.

Guy, Raynald and other barons were captured. Saladin had Raynald killed for breaking the truce, assuring Guy that kings do not kill kings. About 200 captive Templar and Hospitaller Knights were beheaded, except the Grand Master of the Temple, and the captured turcopoles were executed. Other prisoners were sold into slavery, while the high-ranking barons were treated well; Guy was released in 1188.

Having sent most of their men to the field, the Crusaders had little left to defend their castles. Fifty-two towns and fortifications fell, among them Acre, Nablus, Jaffa and Beirut, and Queen Sibylla, Patriarch Heraclius and Balian negotiated the surrender of Jerusalem on 2 October. Tyre held, saved by Conrad of Montferrat. The defeat led Pope Gregory VIII to call a new crusade, and the Third Crusade began in 1189. Crusader military power in Outremer finally collapsed at La Forbie in 1244.
battle-of-heavenfield: An alliance between Cadwallon of Gwynedd, a Christian king of Brythonic descent, and King Penda of Mercia, a pagan king of Anglian descent, invaded Northumbria and killed King Edwin at the Battle of Hatfield Chase on 12 October 633. The kingdom split into its two parts. Eanfrith, exiled under Edwin, took Bernicia, and Osric, Edwin's cousin, Deira. According to Bede, Cadwallon killed Osric when he tried to besiege him and then ruled both as a tyrant. He killed Eanfrith too, when Eanfrith came to negotiate peace. Eanfrith's brother Oswald returned from seventeen years of exile, possibly partly in Dál Riata, to claim Bernicia.

The Welsh army seems to have advanced north from York along Dere Street. Oswald took up a defensive position beside the Roman Wall, about 4 miles (6 km) north of Hexham, facing east, with Brady's Crag on his northern flank and the Wall to the south. It was claimed that the night before, Oswald saw Saint Columba in a vision foretelling his victory, and Bede says he raised a cross and prayed with his troops.

The Welsh, believed to be more numerous, had to attack on a narrow front where they could not outflank the Northumbrians. Their line broke, and many were cut down in the flight south. Bede says Cadwallon was caught and killed at Denisesburna, now identified as the Rowley Burn near Whitley Chapel.

Oswald reunited Deira with Bernicia and ruled all Northumbria for eight years, until he was killed at the Battle of Maserfield; his brother Oswiu succeeded him. Bede saw the battle's importance in the restoration of Christianity to Northumbria, and the field became a place of pilgrimage. A wooden cross beside the B6318 east of Chollerford marks the site, with St Oswald's Church, Heavenfield, on the hill to its north, though Max Adams places the fighting near Devil's Water.
battle-of-hohenlinden: From April to July 1800 Jean Victor Marie Moreau's army drove the Austrians from the Rhine to the Inn, and an armistice was agreed on 15 July. Emperor Francis II removed the commander, Pál Kray, and, after his brother Archduke Charles refused the post, appointed the 18-year-old Archduke John. Franz von Lauer was named his second-in-command, and Colonel Franz von Weyrother his chief of staff. The armistice lapsed on 12 November. Weyrother's ambitious plan was converted into a direct advance on Munich, and the Austrians pushed back part of the French left at Ampfing on 1 December.

Believing the French were fleeing, John and Weyrother launched a pursuit, but Moreau chose to stand near Hohenlinden, with about 56,000 men against some 64,000 Austrians and Bavarians. The Austrians advanced west in four columns through heavily wooded terrain in snow, over bad roads and with poor staff work, so that the columns could not support one another.

On 3 December Kollowrat's column on the main highway met Grouchy's division in the forest and was thrown back when the French counterattacked as it emerged. The divisions of Latour and Riesch fell behind and split into small groups. Antoine Richepanse's division marched through the forest and struck the rear of Kollowrat's column, and Ney and Grouchy attacked from the front. Kollowrat's column disintegrated, and Archduke John escaped on a fast horse.

The Austrians reported 798 killed, 3,687 wounded and 7,195 prisoners, and the Bavarians lost 1,754 prisoners. The French admitted 1,839 casualties. Moreau's army advanced 300 km in 15 days and captured 20,000 Austrians. On 17 December Archduke Charles replaced his brother, and on 25 December he asked for an armistice, which Moreau granted. The Treaty of Lunéville followed in February 1801, and the victory made Moreau a potential rival to Napoleon Bonaparte. Thomas Campbell wrote a poem on the battle, and the towns of Linden in Alabama and Tennessee are named after it.
battle-of-holowczyn: Having dealt with Saxony-Poland, Charles XII turned on Russia. Rather than the easier route from Grodno through Minsk and Smolensk, he chose a straighter but harder one across the Berezina and Drut rivers, and in June 1708 moved his army from its winter camp near Radoszkowice through bad roads and weather. Unsure of his intentions, and with Peter I away, the Russian command, in which Field Marshal Boris Sheremetev had to contend with the rivalry of Alexander Menshikov, decided to hold a line by the Dnieper and moved its army piecemeal to the marshy Vabich, a tributary of the Drut.

The main Russian force stood around Vasilki, behind fortified bridges, while General Anikita Repnin, in his first independent command, held a long, thin and half-fortified line three kilometres to the southeast. Between the two camps lay marsh that could not be fortified, and the Russians had no overall commander and little contact with each other. Charles saw the gap and planned a night attack through it to split the enemy in two.

At midnight on 4 July the Swedes moved towards the river with fascines, leaving behind pontoon bridges that heavy rain had made too heavy to carry. The Russian alarm was raised at 02:30, when Swedish artillery opened fire, and Charles led the crossing himself, wading in front of his men. Repnin saw the danger of a wedge between the Russian positions and ordered his men north towards Sheremetev, but Swedish battalions kept the two forces apart, and Repnin was driven east and south while Swedish cavalry scattered the Russian horse.

Sheremetev's forces, still across the river from Holowczyn, had been on full alert for hours in the belief that the attack on Repnin was a feint. Sheremetev moved against the almost undefended Swedish camp to the west, but when news of Repnin's setback reached him he began retreating towards Shklov on the Dnieper rather than wait for an attack on his rear. Only 9,000 Russians took part in the battle.

The victory gave the Swedes a line along the Dnieper and a base around Mogilev, but so many Russians escaped that it was not a decisive strategic victory. Repnin and Heinrich von der Goltz were tried for the failures of the Russian command and later released. Official Swedish and Russian reports gave 1,293 Swedes and 1,655 Russians killed and wounded, while each side's other sources claimed far higher losses for the enemy. It was reportedly Charles's favourite victory.
battle-of-hormozdgan: Around 208 Vologases VI succeeded his father Vologases V as king of the Arsacid Empire, but from 213 he fought a dynastic struggle with his brother Artabanus IV. By 216 Artabanus held most of the empire and was acknowledged as supreme ruler by the Roman Empire. He contained the forces of the Roman emperor Caracalla at Nisibis in 217, and the peace of the following year left the Arsacids most of Mesopotamia, though Vologases went on minting coins and challenging him.

Meanwhile the Sasanian family had risen to prominence in its native Pars, and under Ardashir I it began conquering neighbouring regions and more distant lands such as Kirman. Artabanus at first paid little heed, and only later chose to confront him.

The site of the battle has not been found. The Arabic chronicle Nihayat al-arab names a place that has been read as Golpayegan, which is improbable, while Bal'ami placed it at Khosh-Hormoz, another name for Ram-Hormoz near Ahvaz, on a plain well suited to cavalry. According to al-Tabari, whose work probably drew on Sasanian sources, the two kings agreed to meet at Hormozdgan at the end of the month of Mihr.

Ardashir arrived early, took an advantageous position on the plain, dug a ditch to protect his forces and seized a spring. He had 10,000 cavalry, some in flexible chain armour like that of the Romans; Artabanus led more men, hampered by heavier lamellar armour. Ardashir's son and heir Shapur also fought. The battle was fought on 28 April 224, and Artabanus was defeated and killed.

Ardashir executed Dad-windad, the dead king's chief secretary, took the title shahanshah and began the conquest of the lands that would be called Iranshahr. At Ardashir-Khwarrah, present-day Firuzabad, he had two rock reliefs carved: one of combats, with Shapur impaling Dad-windad with his lance and Ardashir ousting Artabanus, the other of Ardashir receiving the badge of kingship from Ahura Mazda.

Vologases VI was driven out of Mesopotamia soon after 228. The great Parthian noble families, the Seven Great Houses of Iran, kept their power under their new Sasanian overlords and supplied much of their cavalry, so that the state has been called the empire of the Persians and Parthians. Attempts to restore Arsacid rule by Bahram Chobin and Vistahm in the late 6th century failed.
battle-of-hulao: As the Sui dynasty's authority collapsed under Emperor Yang, local governors and magnates rose to claim power. Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, took Chang'an in 617 and proclaimed himself first emperor of the Tang in 618, and in 618-620 his son Li Shimin defeated the dynasty's rivals in the north-west. Two regimes held the north-eastern plain: Wang Shichong, a former Sui general who had declared himself emperor of Zheng at Luoyang, and Dou Jiande, a one-time bandit leader who ruled Hebei as King of Xia.

In August 620 Li Shimin marched on Luoyang with 50,000 men and ringed it with fortified camps; most of Henan went over to the Tang, and two breakout attempts by Wang failed. By March 621 people in the city were eating cakes of rice and mud. Wang appealed to Dou, who in April marched west with an army that the sources put at 100,000 or 120,000 men.

Against the advice of his older generals, Li Shimin left the siege to his brother Li Yuanji and the general Qutu Tong and took 3,500 men to the Hulao Pass, some 97 km east of Luoyang, which he occupied on 22 April. For about a month Dou camped at Banzhu and offered battle, while Li Shimin waited in his strong position. Dou's official Ling Jing urged him to cross the Yellow River and strike at the Tang heartland in Shanxi, but the Xia generals refused.

Li Shimin feigned sending part of his cavalry away, and on the morning of 28 May Dou drew up his army along the Sishui river. The Tang held back until noon, when the Xia troops grew thirsty and broke ranks to fetch water. A probing attack of 300 horsemen under Yuwen Shiji found them in confusion, and a general assault followed. When Li Shimin and his cavalry broke through to the eastern escarpment, the Xia army collapsed: 3,000 men fell and more than 50,000 were captured, among them Dou Jiande himself.

Wang Shichong surrendered on 4 June after Li Shimin showed him the captured Dou and his generals, and the Xia surrendered on 10 June. Dou was executed in Chang'an, and Wang was killed on his way into exile in Sichuan. The historian David A. Graff called the battle the single most decisive engagement of the civil wars after the fall of the Sui. The last rebel leader, Liang Shidu, was defeated in June 628.
battle-of-hwangsanbeol: King Muyeol of Silla had won the support of Emperor Gaozong of Tang China for the conquest of Baekje, whose King Uija had let the state decline as his parties and dissipation led him to neglect its affairs. In 660 Kim Yu-sin set out with fifty thousand troops to join a Tang army of perhaps 122,711 to 130,000 men that was coming by sea. By the time King Uija learned of the danger he had lost the support of his ministers and could raise only five thousand men, whom he placed under General Gyebaek.

The Baekje army reached Hwangsanbeol first and made camp. Gyebaek rallied his soldiers with a speech recalling how in antiquity Goujian had defeated a force said to number seven hundred thousand with only five thousand men. When the Silla army arrived and attacked in full, the Baekje troops, fighting to the death, drove it back five times.

As Silla's morale sank, General Kim Pumil sent his young son Gwanchang, a hwarang, to fight the enemy alone. Gyebaek captured him and let him go; Gwanchang charged again, and when he was taken a second time Gyebaek, out of respect for his young enemy, had him executed and sent his body back to the Silla camp. His death restored Silla's spirit, and Kim Yu-sin ordered a full attack on the dwindling Baekje force. Gyebaek died in the fighting, and Kim later said that his enemy had been a man of honour and bravery.

Baekje fell soon afterwards, when Kim Yu-sin and the Tang general Su Dingfang closed in and King Uija surrendered. The battle is the subject of the Korean comedy war film Once Upon a Time in a Battlefield, and the television dramas Gyebaek and Queen Seondeok follow Kim Yu-sin and Gyebaek towards the war. It was re-enacted in 2008 at a park in Nonsan during the Baekje festival.
battle-of-idistaviso: Arminius, a Germanic chief, had been instrumental in organising the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, in which three Roman legions on their way to winter quarters were ambushed and annihilated by allied Germanic forces. That defeat haunted the Romans, and revenge and the removal of the threat of Arminius drove the campaign of Germanicus. In 15 CE he marched against the Chatti and then the Cherusci under Arminius, buried the bones of the Roman soldiers still lying in the Teutoburg Forest region, and recovered the eagle of the annihilated nineteenth legion. Skirmishes were constant, but the Romans could not draw the Germans into open battle.

Ancient sources name the site Idistavisus. Its precise location is unknown, except that it lay on the right bank of the Weser, somewhere between Minden and Hamelin. Repeated Roman incursions deep into Germanic territory forced Arminius, at the head of a large but fractious coalition, to respond. The Romans, with Chauci fighting as auxiliaries, defeated the allied Germans and inflicted heavy losses. Arminius and his uncle Inguiomer were wounded but escaped.

Many of the retreating Germans were cut down; some tried to swim the Weser and died under missiles or in the current, and others climbed trees, where Roman archers shot them down. Tacitus writes that from nine in the morning to nightfall the Germans were slaughtered and ten miles were covered with arms and dead bodies.

The Roman soldiers hailed Tiberius as imperator and raised a pile of arms as a trophy, inscribed with the names of the defeated tribes. The sight enraged the Germans, who attacked the Roman positions at the Angrivarian Wall and were routed again. Germanicus stated that he wanted no prisoners, seeing extermination of the tribes as the only end to the war.

He then forced Mallovendus, leader of the Marsi, to reveal where another of the lost eagles lay, and withdrew behind the Rhine for the winter. According to Tacitus, it was thought that one more summer's campaign would end the war, but Tiberius advised Germanicus to return to Rome, writing that the vengeance of Rome had been satisfied and the Germans could be left to their internal feuds. Germanicus was granted a triumph on 26 May 17 CE.
battle-of-ilerda: Having driven the Optimates from Italy, Caesar turned in March 49 BCE against the Pompeian army in the Iberian provinces. On the way he was held up by the rebellion of Massilia under Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, and he left the siege to Gaius Trebonius and Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus. His legate Fabius had already secured passes through the Pyrenees and, reinforced to six legions, faced Lucius Afranius and Marcus Petreius, who were camped on a hill south of Ilerda on the western bank of the Sicoris, the modern Segre, with a stone bridge giving them access to the land beyond.

Fabius built two wooden bridges upstream and crossed to the western bank. When one bridge was swept away, Afranius attacked the two legions it had cut off under Lucius Plancus, who held out on a hill until Fabius brought up help.

Caesar took command two days later and fortified a camp close to the Pompeians. He then tried to seize a rise in the plain between their hill and Ilerda, which would have cut them off from the town, its bridge and their stores. The Pompeians reached it first and drove back his detachment. Caesar led the ninth legion forward and pushed the enemy to the walls, but the legion pursued too far onto a narrow slope beneath the town, where it fought for five hours before breaking free. Caesar's own account puts his losses at about seventy killed and over six hundred wounded.

Spring floods then swamped the Caesarian camp and cut off its foraging, and famine and disease followed. When the waters fell, Caesar dug channels to divert the river, and Afranius and Petreius abandoned Ilerda to retreat towards Marcus Terentius Varro's army. Caesar's legions crossed in shoulder-high water, overtook them and blocked their route. As soldiers of the two camps began to fraternise, Petreius had the Caesarians found in his camp killed.

Driven back towards Ilerda, the Pompeians were besieged and completely surrounded by 30 July, and Caesar accepted the surrender of their five legions in front of both armies. Varro in Hispania Ulterior then submitted without a fight, giving up two more legions. Caesar left Quintus Cassius Longinus in command of Hispania with four legions and returned to the siege of Massilia, free to face Pompey himself at Pharsalus in 48 BCE.
battle-of-ilipa: After the Carthaginian defeat at the Battle of Baecula and the departure of Hasdrubal Barca for Italy, new reinforcements reached Iberia from Carthage at the beginning of 207 BCE under Hanno, who joined Mago Barca, Hannibal's younger brother. Scipio sent a detachment under Marcus Junius Silanus against Mago, whose camp was attacked by surprise and scattered, and Hanno was captured. In 206 BCE Hasdrubal Gisco and Mago, still reeling from a series of defeats, joined their Iberian and Numidian allies at Ilipa, near present-day Seville. They assembled about 70,000 infantry, 4,000 cavalry and 32 elephants. Scipio fielded 45,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry, Romans and allied Iberians.

Mago attacked the Roman camp with most of the cavalry, including King Massinissa's Numidian horsemen, but the Roman cavalry charged his flank. For several days both armies lined up in the same formation, Scipio with the legionaries in the centre and Iberians on the flanks, the Carthaginians mirroring him with their elite African infantry in the centre. Then Scipio prepared his troops overnight, and at dawn sent the velites and cavalry against the enemy camp. The Carthaginians came out in disorder, many still asleep, and took their usual positions. Scipio had reversed his formation, placing the legionaries on the flanks and the Iberians in the centre.

The cavalries clashed, the legionaries fought the Iberians in the Carthaginian line, and the velites used javelins and trumpets to drive the elephants into a frenzy, so that they trampled much of the Carthaginian cavalry. Scipio's Iberians in the centre held back, and the African infantry could not help their comrades without exposing their own centre. They lost heart and began an orderly retreat, which became a rout when the Iberians pursued. The army was virtually annihilated, and Hasdrubal and Mago took refuge in Gades.

That night Iberian mercenaries deserted the Carthaginian camp, and Hasdrubal tried to slip away in the dark. Scipio pursued and left him with 6,000 men on a mountain top without water, who soon surrendered. Hasdrubal Gisco went to Africa to visit the Numidian king Syphax, where Scipio also met him, and Mago fled to the Balearics and sailed to Liguria to attempt an invasion of northern Italy. Scipio returned to Rome and was elected consul in 205 BCE. Many regard Ilipa as his most brilliant victory. It permanently broke the Carthaginian grip on Iberia, denied any further land invasion of Italy and cut off the Barca family's source of silver and manpower.
battle-of-immae: During the Crisis of the Third Century Rome lost its ability to defend its eastern provinces against Sassanid invasion. Septimius Odaenathus, a chieftain of Palmyra, raised an army that repelled the Sassanid onslaught, and Gallienus made him king and protector of the east. After his death his widow Zenobia took direct control, through her son, of the provinces under Palmyrene protection, extended her rule into Egypt and won over much of Asia Minor. In public she kept up a partnership with Rome, placing her son below Aurelian on documents and coins.

Aurelian regarded her move into Egypt, a province held personally by the emperor, as a declaration of war, but Germanic invasions kept him busy. Only after defeating the Alamanni, building city walls and abandoning Dacia did he turn east. He sent a general with a fleet against the Palmyrene garrison of Egypt and marched on Antioch, while Zenobia had her son declared augustus and sent an army under her general Zabdas to meet him.

The armies met at Immae, close to present-day Reyhanli in Turkey, with infantry in the centre and cavalry on the wings. Zabdas relied on his cataphracts and on the heat, to which the Romans were not used. Aurelian adopted a tactic Claudius Gothicus had used against the Goths. When Zabdas ordered a cavalry charge, the Roman light cavalry met it, then broke and fled. The heavily armoured Palmyrene horsemen gave chase until men and horses were worn out by the long pursuit in the sun, and at a chosen point the Romans turned and attacked them. Very few of the Palmyrene cavalry returned.

With his cavalry lost, Zabdas ordered his infantry back to Antioch, and he and Zenobia led their resupplied forces out of the city by night to Emesa. Abandoned and fearing Aurelian's reputation for savage retribution, the leaders of Antioch opened their gates. Aurelian neither executed them nor let his troops sack the city, but granted a general amnesty. The news spread through the east, and city after city accepted peaceful reincorporation into the Roman Empire.
battle-of-imphal: In late 1941 and early 1942 the Imperial Japanese Army overran Burma, driving British, Indian and Chinese defenders into India and Yunnan. Imphal, the capital of Manipur, was held by IV Corps under Lieutenant General Geoffry Scoones, part of the Fourteenth Army under Lieutenant-General William Slim. Because the Allies planned to take the offensive, the corps' divisions stood almost at the Chindwin River, widely separated and open to isolation.

The Japanese commander Mutaguchi planned to take Imphal and then advance to the Brahmaputra Valley, cutting the lines to northern Burma, where the Ledo Road was being built, and the airfields supplying Nationalist China over the Hump. His plan, named U-Go, won approval from Prime Minister Hideki Tojo and Imperial General Headquarters. A failed Japanese attack in the Arakan in February, the Battle of the Admin Box, showed that Allied aircraft could supply cut-off troops, but U-Go was too far advanced to change.

Slim and Scoones planned to withdraw their forward divisions into the Imphal plain and make the Japanese fight at the end of long supply lines, but they misjudged the date and strength of the attack. The Japanese began crossing the Chindwin on 8 March 1944, and the forward divisions were ordered back on 13 March. The 17th Indian Division was cut off by the Japanese 33rd Division, and the 50th Indian Parachute Brigade was roughly handled at Sangshak. The Japanese 60th Regiment cut the main road a few miles north of Imphal on 28 March. The Indian National Army's Subhas Brigade also operated in the Chin Hills.

From April the Japanese attacked the plain from several sides. At Bishenpur their advance halted for lack of supply about 10 miles from Imphal. At the Shenam Saddle heavy fighting for five peaks lasted from 8 to 22 April. On 13 April the 5th Indian Division retook Nungshigum Ridge with air strikes, artillery and Lee tanks. By 1 May all Japanese attacks had stopped, and Slim and Scoones began a slow counter-offensive through the monsoon, with the garrison supplied by air.

The Japanese saw as early as May that the operation should be broken off, but Imperial Headquarters urged that it be fought to the end. The defeat at Kohima and Imphal was the Japanese army's largest up to that time, with 54,879 casualties including 13,376 dead, mostly from starvation, disease and exhaustion. The Allies suffered 12,603 casualties. The Japanese lost almost all of their 12,000 pack animals and 30,000 cattle, which crippled several divisions the next year. Mutaguchi and Kawabe were both relieved of command. In December Slim and three corps commanders were knighted at Imphal by the viceroy, Lord Wavell. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission established Imphal and Kohima war cemeteries.
battle-of-ipsus: After the Second War of the Diadochi, Antigonus I Monophthalmus held undisputed control of the Asian lands of Alexander's empire, and his growing power led the other successors to unite against him. A war from 314 to 311 BCE ended in compromise, and the Babylonian War of 311 to 309 BCE left Seleucus in control of Babylonia and the lands to its east. In 307 BCE Antigonus's son Demetrius took Athens, and he later defeated Ptolemy's fleet off Cyprus; after this Antigonus and Demetrius took the title of king, and the others did likewise.

Cassander offered terms, but Antigonus rejected them and demanded his complete surrender. Cassander then joined Lysimachus in a joint plan and asked Ptolemy and Seleucus to take part. In 302 BCE Lysimachus crossed the Hellespont into Asia Minor, and Antigonus marched north from Syria to meet him.

Seleucus brought an army from the eastern satrapies, with Indian war elephants. Plutarch gives Antigonus 70,000 infantry, 10,000 cavalry and 75 elephants, and the allies 64,000 infantry, 10,500 cavalry, 400 elephants and 120 scythed chariots. The battle was fought on an open plain near the village of Ipsus, but its exact site is unknown, and the ancient accounts do not give a coherent narrative.

The fighting seems to have begun with a clash of elephants. Demetrius led the Antigonid cavalry round them and routed the allied cavalry under Antiochus, but he pursued too far. The allies then placed their elephants in his path, and he could not return to the battlefield. Seleucus rode round the exposed Antigonid phalanx, whose morale collapsed, and some of its troops defected or fled. Antigonus, in the centre, was surrounded and killed by javelins thrown by skirmishers.

Demetrius escaped with 5,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry to Ephesos, then sailed for Greece, where Athens refused to admit him. The empire was divided among the victors: Ptolemy kept Egypt, Seleucus expanded into eastern Asia Minor, and Lysimachus received the rest of Asia Minor. The last chance of reuniting Alexander's empire had already passed when Antigonus lost the Babylonian War, and Ipsus confirmed the failure. Seleucus defeated Lysimachus at Corupedium in 281 BCE.
battle-of-iquique: In 1879 the Bolivian government threatened to confiscate and sell the Antofagasta Nitrate & Railway Company, a mining enterprise with Chilean and British investors, and Chile seized the port of Antofagasta on 14 February. Bolivian President Hilarión Daza declared war, Peru was bound by a secret treaty of 1873 with Bolivia, and Chile declared war on both on 5 April.

The Chilean naval commander Juan Williams Rebolledo sailed north with his main ships to seek out the Peruvian Navy at Callao, leaving the old wooden corvette Esmeralda under Captain Arturo Prat and the schooner Covadonga under Captain Carlos Condell to blockade Iquique. Meanwhile the Peruvian monitor Huáscar under Rear Admiral Miguel Grau and the armoured frigate Independencia under Captain Juan Guillermo More steamed south from Callao undetected.

On the morning of 21 May 1879 the Peruvian ships came out of a dense fog, and Covadonga fired a warning shot to alert Esmeralda. Prat placed his ship close to the shore, so that Huáscar had to fire with care to avoid hitting the town, where crowds had gathered to watch. The Peruvian gunners, inexperienced with the monitor's Coles turret, missed for an hour and a half, while Chilean shot could not pierce Huáscar's armour. Grau then rammed the corvette, and Prat leapt aboard the Huáscar with Petty Officer Juan de Dios Aldea and was shot dead.

After two more rammings and a failed boarding by Sublieutenant Ignacio Serrano and eleven men, Esmeralda sank at 12:10 p.m. with her flag still flying, and Grau had the survivors picked up; reports indicate that 57 were saved. To the south, in an action sometimes counted as the separate Battle of Punta Gruesa, Independencia ran aground while chasing Covadonga. Condell, pointing to the Peruvian flag still flying, ordered fire on the men left aboard, a contrast with Grau's conduct often drawn by Peruvian maritime historians.

Grau returned Prat's diary, uniform and sword to his widow with a letter praising his courage, and came to be known as the Gentleman of the Seas. The battle lifted the blockade of Iquique, but the loss of Independencia was a strategic setback for Peru, while Chile had lost only one of its oldest wooden warships. In Chile news of Prat's death led thousands to enlist, which Chilean historians count among the causes of the country's eventual victory, and since 1905 the date has been kept as Día de las Glorias Navales, a national holiday.
battle-of-isandlwana: In 1877 Sir Henry Bartle Frere was appointed High Commissioner for Southern Africa to bring about a confederation in South Africa, as had been done in Canada. The independent South African Republic and the Kingdom of Zululand stood in the way, and the British Empire meant to overcome both by force. On 11 December 1878 Bartle Frere, on his own initiative and without the approval of the British government, presented the Zulu king Cetshwayo with an ultimatum he could not possibly meet. When it expired a month later he ordered Lord Chelmsford to invade Zululand. Chelmsford planned a five-pronged invasion, then settled on three columns, the centre one under his own command. It crossed the Buffalo River at Rorke's Drift on 11 January 1879.

On 22 January Chelmsford was in the field looking for the Zulu army, which had outmanoeuvred him. About 20,000 Zulu warriors, commanded by Ntshingwayo kaMahole Khoza and Mavumengwana kaNdlela Ntuli, attacked part of the main column, some 1,800 British, colonial and native troops with about 350 civilians, at Isandlwana. The Zulus carried mainly assegais and cow-hide shields, with some muskets and old rifles. The British had Martini-Henry rifles, two 7-pounder guns and a rocket battery.

Scouts under Lieutenant Charles Raw found the main Zulu force at about 11:00 am, and it at once attacked. Attacked on the flanks by the Zulu formation known as the horns and chest of the buffalo, the British could not concentrate. A solar eclipse occurred at 2:30 pm. More than 1,300 troops were killed, including all those on the forward firing line. Evidence shows several last stands, one by about 150 men, and no quarter was given to the wounded. Zulu dead are estimated at 1,000 to 3,000.

The victory ended the first British invasion of Zululand, and the British Army had suffered its worst defeat by an indigenous force with far inferior weapons. It led to a more aggressive approach, a heavily reinforced second invasion and the end of Cetshwayo's hopes of a negotiated peace. Chelmsford blamed Colonel Anthony Durnford, though there is no evidence that he disobeyed an order; Wolseley thought the aim was to protect Chelmsford. Recent historians such as Lock and Quantrill place responsibility with Chelmsford.
battle-of-isly: After the French invasion of Algiers in 1830, Abd al-Qadir led the tribes of the Mascara region against the French from 1832. The Treaty of Tafna of 1837, signed by Bugeaud, recognised his authority over much of Algeria in return for his recognition of French sovereignty, but in November 1839, supported by Sultan Abd al-Rahman of Morocco, he declared war again. Bugeaud, governor from 1840, undertook a systematic conquest, and after the Battle of the Smala in 1843 Abd al-Qadir was driven into the desert and took refuge in Morocco.

Border fighting followed in 1844. On 30 May a Moroccan force attacked the French camp at Lalla Maghnia and was repulsed by General Lamoricière; on 19 June French troops occupied Oujda, and on 6 August French ships under François d'Orléans, a son of the French king, bombarded Tangier. Bugeaud brought on the battle without a declaration of war, to force the sultan to give up his support for Abd al-Qadir.

Bugeaud marched 11,000 men on the Moroccan camp at Djarf el-Akhdar, on the right bank of the Isly a short distance from Oujda. Expecting to face cavalry, he formed his infantry into a great diamond of small squares with the cavalry inside. At daybreak 20,000 to 25,000 Moroccan horsemen charged but could not break the lines and were split by the advancing squares. French cavalry then attacked in echelons: six squadrons of spahis under Colonel Joseph took a Moroccan camp and its eleven guns before the gunners could reload, while a second echelon under Colonel Morris engaged the cavalry on the right, and the Moroccan infantry scattered into ravines.

The French took eleven guns, eighteen flags and all the Moroccan tents, among them the commander's tent and umbrella, the equivalent of a captured standard. About 800 Moroccans and 27 French were killed, with 99 French wounded. The bombardment of Mogador began the next day, and Bugeaud was made Duke of Isly. Morocco sued for peace and declared Abd al-Qadir a mufsid, a corrupter, rather than a holy warrior; relations between them worsened into open conflict over the border regions, and after three more years of guerrilla warfare Abd al-Qadir surrendered to Lamoricière in 1847.
battle-of-issus: Alexander the Great crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and defeated the Persian satraps of Asia Minor at the Battle of the Granicus. He then occupied most of Asia Minor and took the coastal settlements, in order to negate the power of the superior Persian fleet. While he was at Tarsus he heard that Darius III was massing a great army at Babylon. Alexander sent Parmenion ahead to occupy the coast around Issus. Darius took a northern route and captured Issus without opposition, cutting off the hands of the sick and wounded Alexander had left there. In doing so he put his army behind Alexander's and cut his supply lines.

The two armies met on either side of a small river, the Pinarus, on a coastal plain only 2.6 kilometres wide between the sea and the mountains, where Darius could not use his superior numbers. Ancient writers gave Persian totals from 250,000 to 600,000, but most modern historians estimate no more than 100,000. Alexander's army may not have exceeded 40,000. The fighting is dated to 5 November 333 BCE.

The Persian cavalry charged first against Parmenion. In the centre the Macedonian phalanx suffered severely crossing the river against the Greek mercenaries. Then Alexander's hypaspists broke through the Persian line, and Alexander led the Companions in a direct assault on Darius and his bodyguard, who fled. Alexander then turned on the rear of the Greek mercenaries, who also gave way. The Persians, seeing their king gone, fled in rout, and the cavalry pursued them while the light lasted.

The battle was a decisive victory for Alexander and marked the beginning of the end of Persian power. It was the first time the Persian army had been defeated with the king present. The Macedonians captured Darius's wife, his daughters and his mother, who had accompanied the campaign. Alexander, who later married the younger daughter Stateira, treated the women with great respect. The Spartan king Agis III later recruited 8,000 of the Greek mercenary survivors, and in 331 BCE he defeated a Macedonian general but was finally beaten at the Battle of Megalopolis.
battle-of-isted: Under pressure from the major European powers, Schleswig-Holstein stood alone in the summer of 1850. The Danish High Command had no overall plan for the campaign, but in July it received reports that the Schleswig-Holsteinian army had taken up positions north of the town of Schleswig, and it saw a chance to defeat the rebels in a last, decisive battle. The Schleswig-Holsteinian High Command likewise hoped to lure the Danes into battle at Isted. The Danish army was considerably larger, but its opponent held a strong defensive position.

On 24 July the Danish vanguard clashed with the Schleswig-Holsteinian outposts and pushed them back along the line, with a larger engagement at the Helligbæk stream. The Danish main force attacked that night. In the early hours of 25 July warm weather gave way to heavy mist and pouring rain, and officers on both sides lost their overview of the field. Two Schleswig-Holsteinian brigades counter-attacked at Stolk and Isted, where General F. A. Schleppegrell fell and the fighting turned to house-to-house combat.

Alarming messages from Colonel Baggesen led General Krogh to call off a flanking manoeuvre west of the battlefield. Around noon Krogh ordered a general advance, which struck as the Schleswig-Holsteinian artillery was being withdrawn. By the afternoon the Schleswig-Holsteinian centre gave way and retreated towards Schleswig, which the Danes occupied by late afternoon. The Danes took 1,483 prisoners, 411 of them wounded.

The victory was not as decisive as the Danish command had hoped, and Danish losses exceeded those of Schleswig-Holstein. Its army escaped, attacked at Mysunde in September and besieged Frederiksstad in October, until the Great Powers pressed both sides to end the war in January 1851 and the provisional government and its army disbanded. Baggesen and General Flindt, whose cavalry pursued half-heartedly, were later criticised, though such criticism likely rests on hindsight.

Isted remained the largest battle in the Nordic countries until the Winter War of 1939-1940. The Isted Lion was raised in the cemetery of Flensburg, where many of the fallen were buried, and 25 July is a military flag day in Denmark.
battle-of-ivankovac: In the 1790s Sultan Selim III granted the Serbs of the Sanjak of Smederevo the right to run their own affairs in exchange for cooperation with the governor of Belgrade, Hadži Mustafa Pasha. After the Slaughter of the Knezes in February 1804, a revolt led by Karađorđe Petrović broke out against the janissary junta, the Dahije. The Serbs at first had Selim's support and defeated the janissaries by the end of the year.

In the negotiations that followed, the Serbs demanded the restoration of their autonomy and made contact with Serbs in other parts of the Ottoman Empire. Alarmed, Selim appointed the governor of Niš, Hafiz Mustafa Agha, known in historiography as Hafiz Pasha, as the new governor of Belgrade and ordered him to destroy the insurgents. For the first time a regular Ottoman force was sent against the rebels.

Hafiz Pasha gathered his army in the Sanjak of Niš and marched north in the summer of 1805. At the village of Ivankovac near Ćuprija it was ambushed by a much smaller Serbian force under Milenko Stojković, who had designed fortifications of three earth and palisade fortresses and two redoubts. Karađorđe arrived with guns and reinforcements, and the Ottoman army was defeated and driven back to Niš. Hafiz Pasha, seriously wounded in the battle, died there of his wounds.

The battle was the first full-scale confrontation between the Serbian revolutionaries and regular Ottoman forces in the First Serbian Uprising, and the first defeat of a regular Ottoman unit by them. After it the Serbian forces took full control of the Belgrade Pashaluk. Smederevo was captured in November and became the first capital of the Serbian revolutionary government, and Belgrade was taken the following year. The defeat prompted Selim to declare jihad against the Serbian revolutionaries fighting to expel the Turks from Serbia.
battle-of-iwo-jima: After the American capture of the Marshall Islands in early 1944, Japanese commanders expected a drive toward the Marianas and set up an inner line of defences running north to Japan through the Volcano Islands. The American invasion, called Operation Detachment, aimed to capture Iwo Jima and its two airfields. In June 1944 Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi took command of the defence. He knew his garrison could not win, but hoped to inflict such casualties that the Americans would reconsider invading Japan.

The Japanese positions were heavily fortified, with bunkers, hidden artillery and 18 kilometres of tunnels. Major General Harry Schmidt, commanding the Marine landing force, asked for a ten-day bombardment, but Rear Admiral William H. P. Blandy insisted on three days, a decision the Marines resented.

The landings began on 19 February 1945. After about an hour, once men and equipment crowded the beach, the Japanese opened fire with machine guns, mortars and heavy artillery. Loose volcanic ash stopped the amphibious tractors, and the Marines had to go forward on foot. The 28th Marines crossed the island at its narrowest, about 800 metres, and isolated Mount Suribachi. Kuribayashi had forbidden banzai charges as a waste of resources, and the Japanese fought from their fortifications.

On 23 February six Marines raised a flag on Suribachi, in the second flag-raising there that day, and Joe Rosenthal's photograph of it won a Pulitzer Prize. The north was harder: rocky terrain favoured the defenders, and the Motoyama Plateau became what the Marines called the meatgrinder. Flamethrowers were used to clear pillboxes and caves.

Of some 21,000 Japanese on the island, only 216 were taken prisoner, and 3,000 or more kept fighting in the caves until they were hunted down. The 36-day assault cost more than 26,000 American casualties, including 6,800 dead. It was the only Marine battle in which American casualties exceeded Japanese. Two Japanese soldiers held out until January 1949. The value of the island remains disputed: William V. Pratt, a retired Chief of Naval Operations, called it useless to the Army and the Navy, though its airfield served escort fighters and emergency landings of B-29s. Lessons from it guided the Battle of Okinawa.
battle-of-jamrud: After consolidating his empire in the Punjab, Maharaja Ranjit Singh had taken advantage of the Afghan civil war to conquer long-held Afghan lands, and the Durrani Empire lost the Punjab, Multan, Kashmir, Derajat, Hazara, Balakot and Attock. Peshawar was seized from the Peshawar Sardars in 1834. Towards the end of 1836 Hari Singh Nalwa, commander-in-chief of the Khalsa Army, captured the small fortified village of Jamrud at the mouth of the Khyber Pass, bringing the Sikh frontier up to Afghanistan.

In 1837 the best Sikh generals and troops, including those of Peshawar, were recalled to Lahore for the wedding of Kanwar Nau Nihal Singh, the Maharaja's grandson. Dost Mohammad Khan seized the moment and sent his sons with 7,000 cavalry, 2,000 matchlock men, 9,000 irregulars and 20,000 Khyber tribesmen. Finding no Sikh army at Jamrud, Wazir Akbar Khan began to demolish the fort's defences, until Nalwa charged and threw the Afghans into disarray. Shams al-Din Khan countercharged, and Akbar Khan rallied his men and drove the Sikhs back into the fort.

Accounts of Nalwa's death differ. The Afghan chronicle Siraj al-Tawarikh says he and Akbar Khan fought a duel without recognising each other, while the historian Hari Ram Gupta writes that he was struck by two bullets and carried into the fort, where he ordered his death kept secret until help came. The garrison held out until reinforcements arrived from Lahore, and the Afghans withdrew to Jalalabad. Historians disagree over the result: some count it a Sikh victory, others stress Nalwa's death, and James Norris calls it inconclusive.

Dost Mohammad wrote to the Maharaja that his sons had acted without authority, sent horses as gifts and proposed that Peshawar be entrusted to him, warning that otherwise he would resort to arms. The Sikh court refused. Ranjit Singh reorganised the government of Peshawar: General Paolo Avitabile became its governor, the surrounding districts went to the Barakzai Sardars and local chiefs, and a strong garrison was posted at the new fort of Shabkadar.
battle-of-jemappes: In the summer of 1792 Charles François Dumouriez, French foreign minister and commander of the Armée du Nord, had wanted to forestall invasion by striking into the Austrian Netherlands, but the Allies moved first. After the Duke of Brunswick withdrew from Valmy on 20 September, Dumouriez was free to turn north, relieve Lille and begin his invasion. Short of the resources for a three-pronged attack, he gathered most of his men before Valenciennes at the end of October and marched on Mons and the road to Brussels.

Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen, governor of the Austrian Netherlands, had more than 20,000 men but fought with about 11,600 infantry, 2,170 cavalry and 56 guns along the Cuesmes ridge between Mons and Jemappes. Franz von Lilien held the right at Jemappes, the Count of Clerfayt the centre and Johann Peter Beaulieu the left; a retreat could be made only across a single bridge. Dumouriez brought 32,000 infantry, 3,800 cavalry and 100 guns, a mixture of royal army, volunteer and national guard units, and planned to turn both flanks.

The French attacks of the morning were enthusiastic but ill-coordinated. At noon the Duke of Chartres, the future King Louis-Philippe, sent a large column against the centre of the ridge and won a foothold the Austrians could not retake, while other troops threatened their right and rear. Saxe-Teschen withdrew into Mons, with Beaulieu covering the retreat.

The French reported about 650 dead and 1,300 wounded; the Austrians 305 dead, 513 wounded and 423 men captured. Mons surrendered the next day, Brussels fell on 14 November and Namur on 2 December. The victory of volunteers over regulars raised the confidence of the National Convention and its taste for aggressive war; the historian J. Holland Rose wrote that at Valmy the French had merely stood their ground, while at Jemappes they learnt to conquer. The occupation alienated the population, and after his defeat at Neerwinden on 18 March 1793 Dumouriez fled into exile.
battle-of-jena-auerstedt: Napoleon began his campaign against the Fourth Coalition by thrusting a force of 180,000 through the Franconian Forest. The Prussian army awaited him with about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons. Its command was bloated and inefficient: the post of chief of staff was held by three officers, there was no courier system, and five competing plans of battle were debated until the initiative passed to the French. Prussian doctrine had barely changed in over fifty years, and the Prussian musket of 1806, the 1754 model, was called the worst in Europe by one authority. The French army, by contrast, had been reorganised into the corps system.

At Jena on 14 October 1806 Napoleon's troops met the force of Prince Hohenlohe, who remained disoriented about the enemy's strength throughout. Marshal Michel Ney attacked without orders and was nearly cut off, but Napoleon held the centre with the Imperial Guard until he was relieved. Around 1 p.m. Napoleon ordered his flanks forward and broke the Prussian line. The Prussians lost 10,000 killed or wounded, 15,000 prisoners and 150 guns.

Further north, at Auerstedt, Marshal Louis-Nicolas Davout's III Corps ran into the Prussian main force of 64,000, which included King Frederick William III and the Duke of Brunswick. Outnumbered more than two to one, Davout held Hassenhausen, and the Duke of Brunswick was carried from the field mortally wounded shortly before 10 a.m. Davout counter-attacked at 11 a.m., and by noon the Prussian centre was broken and the King ordered a withdrawal. Davout lost 7,052 men killed or wounded, against 13,000 Prussian casualties. Marshal Bernadotte, within earshot, took no part, because he kept to the last orders he had received.

Napoleon at first doubted that one corps had beaten the Prussian main body, and he made Davout Duke of Auerstedt. Murat's cavalry pursued the beaten army, and the Capitulation of Erfurt on 16 October gave up a large body of troops with hardly a shot fired. Davout entered Berlin on 25 October, and Blücher surrendered at Lübeck on 7 November after the city was stormed.

The defeat showed the need for reform in a Prussian state and army that was still largely feudal. Gerhard von Scharnhorst, August Neidhardt von Gneisenau and Carl von Clausewitz, all of whom served in the battle, were among the later reformers. Their work, with civil reforms in the following years, began Prussia's transformation into a modern state, and the memory of Prussia as a French vassal became a part of German nationalism. Napoleon named a bridge in Paris after the battle, and a Metro station there bears the same name.
battle-of-jersey: Only 14 miles off the coast of France, Jersey was a base for British privateers that harried French merchant shipping, some as far as the coast of America. Contemporary British newspapers also saw the attack as an attempt to draw British attention and resources away from the Great Siege of Gibraltar. The island had a militia of some 3,000 men and about 6,250 troops of all kinds in all, and a French landing at St Ouen's Bay had been beaten off on 1 May 1779.

The French military thought an attack futile, but the government approved a plan by Baron Philippe de Rullecourt, an adventurer and colonel. The expedition was officially private, though the government supplied money, transport and troops. Some 2,000 soldiers sailed from Granville on 5 January 1781; a storm scattered the ships, and about 1,400 landed at La Rocque, unnoticed by guards who had left their post to go drinking.

The French reached Saint Helier between six and seven in the morning, surprised the guard in the market, later the Royal Square, and seized the lieutenant-governor, Major Moses Corbet, in bed. Rullecourt convinced Corbet that thousands of French troops had overrun the island and, threatening to burn the town, made him sign a capitulation. The garrison of Elizabeth Castle refused to surrender and fired on the French.

Command passed to the 24-year-old Major Francis Peirson, who gathered about 2,000 men on the Mont ès Pendus, sent the 78th Highlanders to block the French retreat and attacked into the town. Most of the fighting lasted a quarter of an hour. Peirson was shot through the heart, and Rullecourt was mortally wounded, after which many French soldiers fled.

The British took 600 prisoners. The regulars lost 11 dead and 36 wounded, the militia four dead and 29 wounded; the French had 78 killed and 74 wounded. Corbet was tried by court-martial and dismissed, with a pension of 250 pounds a year. Between 1781 and 1814 nineteen more round towers and three Martello towers were built on the island. Peirson's death is remembered through a painting by John Singleton Copley.
battle-of-julu: After defeating Xiang Liang of the insurgent state of Chu at the Battle of Dingtao, the Qin general Zhang Han crossed the Yellow River, defeated the rebel state of Zhao and captured its capital, Handan. His deputies Wang Li and She Jian besieged Julu, where the Zhao ruler Zhao Xie had retreated, while Zhang Han kept the supply route open from the south. Zhao Xie asked King Huai II of Chu for help. The king sent Song Yi, with Xiang Yu as his deputy, to relieve Julu, and Liu Bang to attack the Qin heartland of Guanzhong.

Song Yi halted at Anyang for 46 days. As his soldiers suffered from rain, cold and hunger, Xiang Yu killed him in his tent, claimed a secret order from the king, and took command; King Huai II was forced to approve it.

Xiang Yu first sent Ying Bu and Zhongli Mo across the river with 20,000 men, then followed with the rest of the army, carrying three days of supplies and destroying everything else. His troops defeated the Qin forces in nine consecutive engagements and cut Wang Li's supply lines. Qin casualties rose to over 100,000; the Qin general Su Jiao was killed, Wang Li was captured, and She Jian threw himself into a fire. Other rebel armies had gathered outside Julu but watched from their camps, and afterwards joined Xiang Yu.

Zhang Han fell back to Jiyuan and asked the court for reinforcements, but the eunuch Zhao Gao accused him of conspiring with the rebels and Qin Er Shi refused. Surrounded, Zhang Han surrendered with 200,000 men in the summer of 207 BCE. At Xin'an Xiang Yu had the surrendered soldiers buried alive, sparing their three generals, who later ruled the Three Qins. In 1912 workers building the Longhai Railway found large amounts of human remains at Yima, the site of the burial. The battle gave Chinese the idiom breaking cauldrons and sinking boats, for a point of no return.
battle-of-junin: The battle was fought in the Peruvian War of Independence. In February 1824 the royalists had regained control of Lima, and Simón Bolívar, having regrouped in Trujillo, led his forces south in June to confront the Spanish army of Field Marshal José de Canterac. Bolívar hurried some 8,000 soldiers forward to cut the royalist retreat towards Cusco and sent his 1,000-strong cavalry ahead to hold the Spanish on the Plain of Junín, a marshland near Junín Lake at around 4,100 metres above sea level. Canterac sent out some 1,300 riders to give his infantry time to withdraw.

The Spanish charge struck the patriots while they were still forming and drove them back in confusion. The Colombian Grenadiers under General Necochea checked it for a time, but Necochea was wounded and taken prisoner, and General Miller, who was to outflank the Spanish right with 250 Hussars of Peru, was forced into a frontal melee. Bolívar, watching from a hill as defeat seemed near, rode to the rear to hurry the infantry forward.

The pursuing Spanish squadrons lost their formation and did not notice that the First Squadron of the Hussars of Peru, under Lieutenant Colonel Isidoro Suarez, was still hidden behind a hill. Major Jose Andres Razuri brought Suarez a false order to charge, and the attack on the exposed Spanish flank and rear took the royalists completely by surprise. The rest of the patriot cavalry rallied under Miller and returned to the fight, and the Spanish broke and fled. The whole action lasted about 45 minutes and was fought with lance and sabre, without firearms.

About 250 royalist and 150 pro-independence fighters were killed, and the patriots took over 400 Spanish horses. The victory, their first in Peru, raised the patriots' morale; Canterac's retreat was relentless, defections from the royalist ranks grew, and Viceroy José de la Serna e Hinojosa had to take command himself. The final Spanish capitulation followed the Battle of Ayacucho on 9 December 1824.

General José de la Mar later reprimanded Razuri for inventing the order, telling him that he deserved execution but that the day's victory was owed to him. Bolívar renamed the regiment the Hussars of Junín. The poet José Joaquín de Olmedo wrote a poem on the battle, and Jorge Luis Borges wrote one on his ancestor Suarez.
battle-of-jutland: The German High Seas Fleet had 16 dreadnought-type battleships against the Royal Navy's 28 and stood little chance of a head-on clash, so the Germans planned to lure out and destroy parts of the British fleet. In January 1916 Vice-Admiral Reinhard Scheer took command. His plan was to use Vice-Admiral Franz Hipper's five battlecruisers to draw Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty's battlecruisers into the path of the main fleet, with submarines across the likely British routes. The British, however, held a copy of the German codebook, taken in 1914 from the cruiser SMS Magdeburg, and usually knew of German activities. Admiral Sir John Jellicoe sailed with the Grand Fleet on 30 May 1916 to meet Beatty.

On the afternoon of 31 May Beatty met Hipper earlier than the Germans expected, and in the exchange he lost two battlecruisers. When at 16:40 he sighted the German battleships, he turned back north, drawing the Germans towards Jellicoe. At 18:30 the main fleets engaged for the first time, with Jellicoe crossing the T of Scheer's line. Scheer, taken by surprise and hampered by poor visibility, ordered a turn away at 18:33. Jellicoe crossed his line again at 19:15, and the leading German battleships were badly damaged.

At 21:00 Jellicoe, aware of the fleet's weakness in night fighting, chose to avoid a major engagement until dawn and moved south to block Scheer's escape. Scheer instead crossed Jellicoe's wake and escaped by Horns Reef, and most of the British light forces failed to report their night encounters with the Germans. Fourteen British and eleven German ships were sunk.

Both sides claimed victory, and historians have not agreed on who won, or whether anyone did. The British lost more ships and far more sailors, but the German fleet had not broken the blockade. By the end of 1916 the German navy accepted that its surface ships had been contained and turned to unrestricted submarine warfare, which together with the Zimmermann Telegram led to the United States declaring war in April 1917.

Jellicoe was criticised for caution in letting Scheer escape, became First Sea Lord, and was replaced as commander of the Grand Fleet by Beatty. His supporters blamed Beatty for the failure to achieve a complete victory. The Admiralty's own review found that British armour-piercing shells often exploded outside German armour instead of penetrating it.
battle-of-kadesh: After expelling the Hyksos around 1550 BCE, the rulers of the Egyptian New Kingdom reclaimed their borders and fought as far north as the Orontes, but Egyptian influence in Syria declined in the late Eighteenth Dynasty, as the Amarna letters show. In the Nineteenth Dynasty Seti I set out to restore the empire. He reoccupied abandoned posts, made an informal peace with the Hittites and captured Kadesh and Amurru, with his son Ramesses II campaigning beside him. In his fourth year Ramesses marched into Syria, and in the spring of his fifth year, in May 1274 BCE, he set out from his capital Pi-Ramesses. The Hittite king Muwatalli II gave the recovery of Amurru as his reason for marching south.

Ramesses led four divisions, named Amun, Re, Set and Ptah, together with Sherden troops and a contingent called the Ne'arin. Muwatalli had gathered allies, and Ramesses recorded nineteen of them. Two captured nomads, who were Hittite spies, told Ramesses that the Hittite army was far off at Aleppo, and he hurried towards Kadesh with the Amun division while the others were strung out behind him. Hittite chariots then crossed the river and struck the Re division in the open, scattering it, and went on to attack the Egyptian camp.

Ramesses, by his own account abandoned and surrounded, rallied his bodyguard and the survivors and led several charges. The Hittites stopped to plunder the camp and were driven back towards the Orontes. Muwatalli sent another thousand chariots, but the Ne'arin arrived suddenly and the Ptah division threatened the Hittite rear. After six unsuccessful charges the Hittites were pinned against the river, and many drowned trying to swim it. They kept Kadesh itself.

Unable to besiege the walled city, Ramesses went south and then back to Egypt, proclaiming victory. Hittite records tell a different story, and modern historians regard the battle as a draw. Muwatalli went on to capture the Egyptian province of Upi. Ramesses took Dapur and Tunip in his eighth and ninth years, but they returned to Hittite control within a year. A peace treaty with Hattusili III was signed in the twenty-first year of Ramesses's reign, about 1258 BCE. It was inscribed on a silver tablet; a clay copy was found at Hattusa and an Egyptian version survives on papyrus.

More texts and wall reliefs record this battle than any other in the Ancient Near East, almost all from the Egyptian side. The main sources are the Poem and the Bulletin, repeated in temples at Abydos, Luxor, Karnak, Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, and the bombastic nature of Ramesses's version is recognised.
battle-of-kambula: On 28 March 1879 the mounted part of Colonel Evelyn Wood's force had been routed at the Battle of Hlobane, and Wood prepared for an attack by the whole Zulu impi. King Cetshwayo had sent the main army to help the abaQulusi against Wood's raids, ordering it not to attack fortified positions but to draw the British into the open; the order was ignored. By late morning on 29 March Wood learned that nearly 21,000 men were coming, among them regiments that had won at Isandlwana, many armed with rifles taken from British dead.

The camp combined a hexagonal laager of locked wagons, a separate cattle kraal on the southern edge of the ridge and a stone redoubt, joined by trenches, earth parapets and a palisade, with four 7-pounder guns between redoubt and laager and two more in the redoubt. Wood had about 2,000 men, 88 of them sick.

At 1:30 p.m. Lieutenant-Colonel Redvers Buller's horsemen provoked the Zulu right horn into a premature attack, and some 11,000 warriors charged into rifle and artillery fire. When the right horn drew back, the left horn and centre attacked from a ravine below the redoubt around 3:00 p.m., and Zulu riflemen drove the defenders out of the cattle kraal. Two companies of the 90th Light Infantry under Major Hackett retook it with the bayonet but lost forty-four men killed or wounded to fire from the flanks. Repeated charges were broken by volleys and case shot, and at about 5:30 p.m. the Zulu began to retire.

Buller's 600 horsemen pursued the retreating Zulu until dusk. Captain Cecil D'Arcy of the Frontier Light Horse told his men to give no quarter and remember Hlobane, and infantry and African auxiliaries killed the wounded and hiding on the field. Burial parties counted 785 Zulu dead near the camp, and the historian Ian Knight estimated that perhaps as many as 2,000 died; the official British figure was 18 killed and 65 wounded. In four hours the British fired 138,000 rounds and 1,077 shells.

Kambula is regarded as the decisive battle of the war. Many warriors went home instead of returning to Ulundi, and no impi again attacked a prepared position with such resolution. Four days later the Zulu were defeated at Gingindlovu and the siege of Eshowe was raised, and the war ended with the Battle of Ulundi on 4 July 1879.
battle-of-karbala: After the assassination of the third caliph Uthman ibn Affan in 656, Ali ibn Abi Talib was proclaimed caliph, but Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, denounced his legitimacy. After Ali was assassinated in 661, his son Hasan handed power to Mu'awiya by treaty, on condition that Mu'awiya rule justly and let his successor be chosen by consultation. After Hasan's death in 670 his brother Husayn became head of the Banu Hashim clan. Before his death in 680, Mu'awiya named his son Yazid successor, making the caliphate hereditary.

Husayn declined to pledge allegiance to Yazid and went to Mecca. There the people of Kufa sent him many letters inviting him to overthrow Umayyad rule, and his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil reported favourably on their support. Husayn set out for the city on 9 September 680 with about fifty men and his family.

On the way Husayn learned that Muslim ibn Aqil had been executed in Kufa, and told his followers they could leave. Most who had joined him on the road did, and his companions from Mecca stayed. A force of 1,000 sent by the caliph intercepted his caravan, and he camped at Karbala on 2 October, where a further 4,000 Umayyad troops arrived. The governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad refused safe passage unless Husayn submitted to his authority, which Husayn rejected.

On 10 October 680 Husayn addressed his opponents, reminding them that he was Muhammad's grandson. Al-Hurr ibn Yazid al-Tamimi went over to his side. Husayn was struck by an arrow and then surrounded and killed. Seventy or seventy-two died on his side, and the surviving women and children were taken to Kufa and then Damascus.

Kufan supporters felt guilty at having abandoned Husayn and formed the Tawwabin movement, with the slogan Revenge for Husayn, which was crushed in January 685. Mukhtar al-Thaqafi then ruled much of Iraq for eighteen months, killing several of those responsible for Husayn's death. Heinz Halm writes that there was no religious aspect to Shi'ism before 680 and that the deaths at Karbala created it. Shia commemorate Husayn's martyrdom in the ten days of Muharram, ending on Ashura, and the Imam Husayn Shrine at Karbala is a holy site of Shia Islam, the destination of the Arba'in pilgrimage.
battle-of-karnal: News that Kabul had fallen in June 1738 reached Delhi in early July, yet the Mughal court did little for months. Only on 2 December 1738 did Muhammad Shah send his leading nobles, the wazir Qamar-ud-Din Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk and Khan Dauran, against the invader, and they spent a month camped outside Delhi. Appeals to the Rajput chiefs, among them Sawai Jai Singh, and to the Peshwa Baji Rao brought no help in time. Nader Shah crossed the river at Attock in January 1739. Rustam Ali put his army at Karnal at about 55,000 horsemen, in a camp of some 160,000 people.

The emperor dug in behind a canal built by Ali Mardan Khan, near Karnal, 110 km north of Delhi. Rather than attack this position, Nader moved east of the town towards the Jamuna and threatened to cut the road to Delhi through Panipat, forcing the Mughals to come out or be trapped.

Saadat Khan, who had marched from his province of Oudh with 20,000 cavalry, reached the Mughal camp at midnight, but his baggage train trailed far behind, unguarded, and Persian scouts found it. When the Mughal army came out of its lines, Nader's forces defeated it within three hours. Estimates of the Mughal dead ran up to 30,000, most contemporaries agreeing on about 20,000 and the historian Axworthy suggesting about 10,000, among them some 400 officers and many of the army's best leaders. Recent scholarship puts Persian losses at about 1,100, including 400 killed. Outdated Mughal cannon, elephants that made easy targets and better Persian musketry decided the day.

Nizam-ul-Mulk negotiated with Nader, who demanded an indemnity, and Muhammad Shah then came to the Persian camp in state. In Delhi a rumour that Nader had been murdered led a crowd to kill five Persian soldiers at a granary, and an uprising followed. Nader's troops answered with a mass killing: men were beheaded by the Yamuna, houses plundered and burned, and many people killed themselves and their families rather than fall into their hands. The campaign left the Mughal dynasty critically weakened and showed the British East India Company how frail the empire had become.
battle-of-keren: After the Italian declaration of war on 10 June 1940, Italian forces from Eritrea took Kassala and other border posts in Sudan. The British built up more than two divisions in Sudan under Lieutenant-General William Platt, which invaded Eritrea through Kassala on 18 January 1941 and by 1 February had taken Agordat. Keren was not fortified, but steep granite mountains and ridges surrounded it. The road and railway to the town ran through the narrow Dongolaas Gorge, overlooked by Fort Dologorodoc on one side and Mount Sanchil on the other, and the Italians had blocked the gorge by blowing down its crags.

The 11th Indian Infantry Brigade attacked on 5 February. The Cameron Highlanders took the ridge in front of Sanchil, later called Cameron Ridge, and held it under constant fire, but the Savoia Grenadiers drove the Indians back from Brig's Peak and Sanchil. An attack on Acqua Col on 12 February also failed, and Richhpal Ram was awarded a posthumous Victoria Cross for his part in it. Platt paused to regroup and train, while Briggsforce, including two Free French battalions, broke through the Mescelit pass north-east of Keren on 1 March.

By March some 25,000 defenders faced more than 13,000 attackers. On 15 March the 4th Indian Division attacked towards Sanchil without success, while the 5th Indian Division took Pinnacle that night and captured Fort Dologorodoc on the morning of 16 March, holding it for ten days against Italian counter-attacks. Major-General Lewis Heath then judged that the key to the gorge lay in two small features overlooking the roadblock. On 25 March troops advancing from the railway tunnel took them by surprise, the engineers reopened the road by midday on 26 March, and on 27 March the Italians withdrew towards Asmara.

Estimates of the losses differ. The 4th Indian Division's history of 1948 gave 3,273 British casualties, and Raugh in 1993 wrote of 536 British killed and 3,229 wounded and 3,000 Italians killed. With the route to Asmara and Massawa open, the 4th Indian Division was sent back to Egypt. At Massawa Rear-Admiral Mario Bonetti surrendered in April, and 9,590 prisoners were taken; scuttled ships blocked the harbour, but the British had the port in use by 1 May. On 11 April President Franklin D. Roosevelt lifted the Red Sea's status as a combat zone, opening it to US merchant ships.
battle-of-keresztes: Sultan Mehmed III led the Ottoman army out of Constantinople on 23 June 1596, reaching Belgrade on 9 August by way of Edirne, Plovdiv, Sofia and Niš. A war council at Slankamen chose to besiege Eger, a fort on the routes between Habsburg Austria and Transylvania. Meanwhile the Austrians took the castle of Hatvan and killed all the Ottomans inside, women and children included. The siege of Eger began on 21 September and the castle gave in on 12 October; in retaliation for Hatvan its defenders were all executed. When a mixed Austrian and Transylvanian army was reported advancing, the sultan wished to withdraw and was persuaded only with great difficulty to give battle.

The Ottomans, worn out by the siege and a long march through marshy country, met the enemy on the plain known in Turkish as Haçova. The Christian army, under the joint command of an Austrian archduke and Prince Sigismund Bathory of Transylvania, held trenches around an old ruined church and threw back the Ottoman assaults with musket fire and 100 cannon. The English diplomat Edward Barton reported large numbers of Crimean Tatar auxiliaries on the Ottoman side.

According to the 17th-century Ottoman historian İbrahim Peçevi, Christian soldiers broke into the camp, killed the guards of the treasury and danced on its chests of gold. Mehmed III wanted to flee, but his tutor, the cleric Hoca Sadeddin Efendi, urged him to fight on. The camp servants' attack on the plunderers spread the cry that the enemy was fleeing, and an Ottoman artillery barrage and a cavalry attack on the flank then routed the Habsburg-Transylvanian army.

The Christians lost 23,000 or over 30,000 men and the Ottomans 20,000 to 30,000. Grand Vizier Damat Ibrahim Pasha, absent from the fighting, was dismissed at Sadeddin's instigation, and Cigalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha took his place. Mehmed III, now called the Conqueror of Eger, returned to Constantinople in November to a triumphal procession and streets hung with costly cloth. The sipahis stripped of their timars rose against the government, and an Ottoman official, Karayazıcı, became a leader of the Celali rebels.
battle-of-kesselsdorf: Two Prussian columns, one under King Frederick and the other under Leopold, the Old Dessauer, converged on Dresden, capital of Saxony, then an ally of Austria. Leopold entered Saxon territory on 29 November and advanced on the Saxon and Austrian army of Field Marshal Rutowsky at Leipzig, which fell back towards Dresden. On 12 December Leopold reached Meissen and joined a corps under Hans von Lehwaldt. Rutowsky, reinforced by Austrians under Grünne, took up a position at Kesselsdorf, 5 miles west of Dresden, along a ridge running to the Elbe behind a stream and marshy ground. There was a wide gap in the centre of the line between the Saxons and the 7,000 Austrians on the right.

Leopold, then sixty-eight, came up on 15 December over a field of snow and ice. His 32,000 men faced 35,000 on stronger ground. He saw that taking Kesselsdorf, defended by twenty-four heavy cannon, would turn the enemy's flank. Two attacks by picked infantry and grenadiers failed, the first costing the life of General Hertzberg, and the Prussians lost some 1,500 of the 3,500 men engaged. The Saxon grenadiers then left their position to pursue and were broken by a massed charge of Prussian dragoons, which drove them back through the town. Leopold's son, Prince Moritz, led a regiment through the Saxon centre. With its flank turned the Saxon line collapsed, and the army fled at nightfall.

Prussian losses were over sixteen hundred killed and more than three thousand wounded. The Saxons lost fewer than four thousand killed and wounded, but almost seven thousand prisoners, forty-eight cannon and seven standards. The Austrians on the right never fired a shot, and Charles of Lorraine, who had reached Dresden with 18,000 men and could hear the guns, did not come to his ally's aid. Frederick joined Leopold and embraced him, and the two occupied Dresden on 18 December. France, Prussia's ally, was left to fight the rest of the War of the Austrian Succession alone.
battle-of-khanwa: After defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat, Babur held Delhi and Agra. According to the Baburnama, Rana Sanga had offered to help him against Ibrahim and then made no move; Rajput sources claim instead that it was Babur who proposed the alliance. Historian Satish Chandra suggests that Sanga expected Babur to withdraw like Timur, and that once he saw Babur meant to stay he built a coalition to drive him out. More than 120 Rajput chieftains answered his call, joined by Mahmud Lodi with Afghan horsemen and by Khanzada Hasan Khan Mewati, the ruler of Mewat.

Sanga's forces defeated the detachment Babur sent to Bayana and took Bhusawar, cutting Babur's supply line from Delhi and Kabul. Fear spread in Babur's army, and to restore its morale he gave the war a religious colour, renounced wine, broke his drinking cups and poured out his stores of liquor.

The battle was fought on 16 March 1527. Babur built a fortified line of carts fastened by iron chains, with gaps for his horsemen and ditches on the flanks, and placed musketeers, falconets and mortars behind them. Sanga charged in the traditional manner, and his men were shot down in great numbers, while the noise of the muskets frightened the Rajput horses and elephants into trampling their own side. For three hours the Rajputs attacked the Mughal flanks, able to strike back only at close quarters.

Silhadi of Raisen went over to Babur during the fighting, though some historians hold that this betrayal is a later invention.
