Sanga was shot and fell unconscious, and a Jhala chieftain called Ajja led the army in his place. When Babur saw the weak Rajput centre he ordered an attack, and many Rajput commanders were killed as they rushed to the front. A last charge on the flanks failed, and the battle ended in the defeat of the Rajputs.

Both sides suffered heavy losses, and the exhausted Mughals did not pursue; Babur gave up the idea of invading Mewar. He had a tower of enemy skulls built, a practice of Timur's that Chandra sees as meant to terrorise his opponents. Sanga, carried from the field by Prithviraj Kachwaha and Maldev Rathore, vowed not to return to Chittor until he had beaten Babur, but was poisoned by his own nobles and died at Kalpi in January 1528. Pradeep Barua notes that Babur's cannon ended outdated trends in Indian warfare.
battle-of-kharistan: The Umayyads had conquered Transoxiana under Qutayba ibn Muslim in 705-715, but from about 720 the Türgesh attacked their rule there, joined by uprisings of the native Sogdians. After the Battle of the Defile in 731 the caliphate lost most of the region, and from 734 the rebellion of al-Harith ibn Surayj spread across Khurasan itself. Asad ibn Abdallah al-Qasri, who returned as governor with 20,000 Syrian troops, put the revolt down, but in 737 his campaign into Khuttal ended in disaster when Suluk came south with some 50,000 men and captured the Umayyad baggage train on 30 September.

Asad withdrew to Balkh and, as the Arabs did not campaign in winter, demobilised his men. Urged by Ibn Surayj, Suluk invaded Lower Tokharistan with most of the native princes of Sogdiana and Tokharistan, hoping to raise the population in revolt. On 7 December Asad learned that some 30,000 of them were at the fortress of Jazzah. He paid each Syrian soldier twenty dirhams to fight and gathered 7,000 men. The Türgesh seized the capital of Juzjan and dispersed to raid and forage, but the ruler of Juzjan sided with Asad.

Al-Tabari's account of the battle is confused. It appears Asad caught Suluk with only 4,000 men. Ibn Surayj's wing reportedly reached Asad's tent, but an attack from the rear broke the Türgesh, who abandoned their camp and spoils, including 155,000 sheep and many Muslim captives. Suluk escaped when Ibn Surayj rescued him, and the raiding bands left behind were destroyed one by one.

The orientalist H. A. R. Gibb judged that the fate of Arab rule in Transoxiana, and possibly in Khurasan, hung on what was little more than a skirmish. The caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik is said to have doubted the first news of the victory. Suluk was assassinated early in 738, more directly through Türgesh rivalries fanned by the Chinese court, and the khaganate fell into infighting. Asad's successor Nasr ibn Sayyar recovered most of Transoxiana by about 743. The heavy Syrian losses of 737, however, weakened the main pillar of the Umayyad regime in Khurasan and opened the way, eventually, for the Abbasid Revolution.
battle-of-khotyn-1621: At the turn of the 17th century Polish-Lithuanian magnates intervened in Moldavia, an Ottoman vassal, and the Ottomans were angered by constant raids from Ukrainian Cossacks, then nominal subjects of the Commonwealth. King Sigismund III Vasa sent the mercenary Lisowczycy to aid his Habsburg allies in the Thirty Years' War, and they defeated George Rakoczi of Transylvania in 1619. Gabriel Bethlen, Prince of Transylvania, asked Sultan Osman II for help. On 20 September 1620 an Ottoman army under Iskender Pasha routed the Commonwealth army at the Battle of Cecora, captured Stanisław Koniecpolski and beheaded Stanisław Żółkiewski. In April 1621 an Ottoman army of 120,000 to 160,000 men, depending on the source, advanced under Osman II.

The Commonwealth's Sejm raised taxes and recruited Cossacks. Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, Grand Hetman of Lithuania, crossed the Dniester in September with 20,000 to 35,000 soldiers, joined by 10,000 more under Prince Władysław Vasa, and an allied Cossack army under Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny. Around 24 August the army began entrenching near Khotyn Fortress in a semicircle of field works with the river behind it, built to allow cavalry counterattacks. The main Ottoman army arrived on 2 September, and a series of assaults on the Cossack camp and the main lines failed. On 7 September janissaries stormed into the Polish entrenchments and cut down about a hundred infantrymen before being driven out.

Chodkiewicz himself led a counterattack of between 600 and 650 cavalry that routed a force of Sipahi. Cossacks raided the Ottoman camp on the nights of 18 and 21 September. Chodkiewicz died on 24 September, and Stanisław Lubomirski took command and drew the defenders into a shorter line. The final assault was stopped on 28 September. The late season, heavy losses estimated at 40,000 to 80,000 men and shortages of supplies led Osman II to accept talks.

The Treaty of Khotyn was signed on 9 October. There were no territorial changes: the border stayed at the Dniester and the Commonwealth recognised Ottoman control of Moldavia. Many sources call the battle a Polish-Lithuanian-Cossack victory, others a stalemate. Osman II blamed the janissaries and wanted to modernise the army; the opposition of the janissaries led to the revolt of 1622 in which he was deposed and killed. Konashevych-Sahaidachny died several months later of his wounds.
battle-of-kinsale: By the end of 1599 the rebellion of Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, and his allies had left the English little beyond the walled towns and garrisons of Ireland. Spain, at war with England, saw a chance to open a new front. After two armadas were wrecked by storms, Philip III sent Don Juan del Águila with 6,000 men in 1601; bad weather turned back nine ships, and the remaining 4,000 landed at Kinsale on 2 October 1601. Charles Blount, Lord Mountjoy, the Lord Deputy, stripped the garrisons of the Pale and besieged the town with an army that reached 12,000, though illness left about 7,500 fit to fight.

O'Neill and Red Hugh O'Donnell hesitated for weeks before making a 300-mile winter march south, abandoning their successful guerrilla tactics for open battle. Meanwhile the English took the outer forts of Ringcurran and Castle Ny-Parke, cutting the Spanish off from the sea, while dysentery and fever thinned the besiegers. On the night of 24 December the Irish, over 6,000 men in two columns, marched for the ridge at Ardmartin overlooking the English camp, but O'Neill drew back towards the Millwater when he saw the English advance.

English cavalry found a crossing of the bog and outflanked the Irish line. O'Neill's formation, drawn up in the Spanish manner, repelled the first charge, but when the Irish horse broke and fled back into it the English charged home and routed it. The Spanish company under Alonzo Del Campo was surrounded and overwhelmed, and O'Donnell's rearguard arrived late and withdrew without fighting.

Águila surrendered Kinsale on honourable terms and sailed home, giving up the Spanish garrisons of Dunboy, Baltimore and Castlehaven. O'Donnell went to Spain and died a few months later. O'Neill submitted at Mellifont on 30 March 1603 and four years later left for Spain in the Flight of the Earls, after which the English administration divided Ulster in the Plantation of Ulster. The defeat broke the old Gaelic order. James's Fort was later built on the site of Castle Ny-Parke.
battle-of-kircholm: The battle took place on 27 September 1605 (17 September in the old style) near Kircholm, now Salaspils in Latvia, about 18 kilometres south-east of Riga, during the Polish-Swedish War of 1600 to 1611. A Swedish expedition under Charles IX was besieging Riga. His force had 10,868 men and 11 cannon, and included two western commanders, Frederick of Lüneburg and Count Joachim Frederick of Mansfeld, with a few thousand German and Dutch mercenaries. The Polish Crown declined to raise funds or send troops, so the relief army of Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, Great Hetman of Lithuania, was tired and hungry. He promised to pay the wages from his own fortune, which brought an influx of recruits.

Chodkiewicz had about 1,000 infantry, 2,600 cavalry and five cannon, a disadvantage of roughly one to three. His cavalry were mostly superbly trained winged hussars armed with lances, while the Swedish cavalry carried pistols and carbines on poorer horses and were tired after a night march in torrential rain. The Swedes stood in four lines on a ridge, the infantry in squares of 30 by 30. Chodkiewicz skirmished for hours, then feigned a withdrawal, and the Swedes advanced to the foot of the slope.

The hussars charged: about 1,000 shattered Mansfeld's reiters on the Swedish right, and 650 under Jan Piotr Sapieha attacked on the left. After Charles committed his reserve of 700 cavalry, Chodkiewicz committed his own. Within 30 minutes the Swedish cavalry was in full retreat, exposing the infantry. The Swedes lost at least 5,000 killed and 500 captured, perhaps up to 8,000 killed, captured or dispersed; the Commonwealth lost about 100 dead and 200 wounded. Charles IX's horse was shot under him, and the officer Henrik Wrede gave the king his own and was killed.

Charles IX abandoned the siege of Riga and withdrew by sea to Sweden, giving up control of northern Latvia and Estonia. The Commonwealth could not exploit the victory, because its troops had not been paid for months and many trained horses had been lost. A truce was signed in 1611, war resumed in 1617, and in 1621 Gustavus Adolphus landed near Riga and took the city after a brief siege, which in Swedish eyes wiped away much of the shame of Kircholm. The battle is commemorated on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Warsaw.
battle-of-kirina: By the late twelfth century the Ghana Empire, once the dominant power of the region, had collapsed after internal strife and the political intervention of the Almoravids in the eleventh century. A number of smaller neighbouring states moved to fill the gap, among them the Sosso people of the Kaniaga kingdom and the Mandinka people of the Upper Niger. Under Sumanguru Kanté the Sosso seized Koumbi Saleh, the former capital of the Ghana Empire, and expanded outward, conquering the Mandinka among others.

Sundiata Keita, an exiled Mandinka prince, organised a coalition of smaller kingdoms to oppose the growing power of the Sosso. The opposing armies met in about 1235 in what is now the Koulikoro Region of Mali, in an engagement also known as the Battle of Krina or the siege of Karina. Sundiata's forces roundly defeated those of Sumanguru Kanté and then marched on to raze Sosso. The victory guaranteed the pre-eminence of the new Mali Empire over West Africa.

The date of the battle is often cited as the beginning of the Mali Empire, which went on to control most of West Africa for the next two centuries. The story of the battle is retold in the Epic of Sundiata, widely considered the national epic of Mali.

In the epic Sumanguru Kanté appears as an evil sorcerer-king who oppresses the Mandinka people. When Sundiata discovers that the sorcerer's sacred animal is the rooster, he is able to wound him with an arrow tipped with a cock's spur. The Sosso king then flees the field and disappears into the Koulikoro mountains. A version of the story was recounted by Maximilien Quenum in his Légendes africaines.
battle-of-kleidion: The conflict began in the 7th century, when the Bulgars under Khan Asparukh set up a state along the Danube inside a Byzantine province. After the fall of Preslav in 971, eastern Bulgaria came under Byzantine rule, but the western lands stayed autonomous under the Comitopuli brothers, including Samuel. Basil II took the throne in 976 intent on destroying independent Bulgaria, and Samuel's army annihilated his in the Gates of Trajan pass in 986.

Samuel was defeated at the Battle of Spercheios in 996 after invading southern Greece. From 1000 Basil took Vidin in 1003 and defeated Samuel at Skopie the next year, campaigning every year and slowly depriving the Bulgarians of their strongholds. In 1014 Samuel resolved to stop the Byzantine army before it entered the Bulgarian heartland.

Samuel dug ditches and fortified the passes, above all the pass of Kleidion on the Struma river, and he gathered a large army, which some claimed numbered as many as 45,000. A thick wooden wall, defended by 15,000 to 20,000 Bulgarians, stopped Basil's army near the village of Klyuch, and its first assault was repulsed with heavy losses.

Basil kept attacking the wall while the general Nikephoros Xiphias led troops along a steep path around Belasitsa mountain. On 29 July Xiphias fell on the Bulgarians from behind, trapping them in the valley. Basil broke through and destroyed the wall. Thousands were killed in the rout. Samuel barely escaped when his son Gabriel Radomir put him on his own horse and took him to Prilep.

John Skylitzes records that Basil took 15,000 prisoners, though modern historians such as Vasil Zlatarski consider such numbers exaggerated. Basil blinded 99 men in each group of 100 and left one with a single eye to lead the others home, partly in retaliation for the death of his favourite general Theophylact Botaneiates, who was ambushed and killed soon after the battle. Basil gained the name Boulgaroktonos, the Bulgar-slayer. Samuel died of a heart attack on 6 October 1014, reportedly on seeing his blinded soldiers.

The war continued for four more years, and some modern historians doubt that the defeat was as complete as Skylitzes and Kekaumenos describe. Others stress that Samuel's death mattered more. His heirs Gabriel Radomir and Ivan Vladislav could not resist Basil, and many governors surrendered voluntarily. Bulgaria was defeated in 1018 and remained a Byzantine province until the uprising of the Asen brothers in 1185. The Byzantine frontier returned to the Danube for the first time since the 7th century.
battle-of-klokotnitsa: Around 1221 to 1222 Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria made an alliance with Theodore Komnenos Doukas, ruler of Epirus. Secure on that side, Theodore took Thessalonica from the Latin Empire and lands in Macedonia including Ohrid, and established the Empire of Thessalonica. When the Latin emperor Robert of Courtenay died in 1228, Ivan Asen II was thought the likeliest regent for the young Baldwin II. Theodore saw Bulgaria as the last obstacle on his road to Constantinople and invaded it early in March 1230 without a declaration of war.

Theodore gathered a large army that included western mercenaries and was so sure of victory that he brought his whole court, his wife and children among them. His army moved slowly, plundering villages on its way. Ivan Asen II raised a small force of a few thousand men, Cumans among them, and marched south so fast that in four days he covered three times the distance Theodore had travelled in a week. It is said that he carried the broken treaty fixed to his spear as a banner. The Bulgarians surrounded the surprised enemy, and the fighting went on until sunset. Only a small force under Theodore's brother Manuel escaped.

Ivan Asen II released the captured soldiers without conditions and took the nobles to Tarnovo. His name as a merciful ruler went before him, and the lands Theodore had recently won in Thrace and Macedonia passed to Bulgaria without resistance, while Thessalonica became a Bulgarian vassal under Manuel. In the Church of the Holy Forty Martyrs at Tarnovo the tsar had an inscription carved on a marble column recording that he had defeated the Greek army and captured their Tsar, Kyr Teodore Komnenos, together with all his boyars, and conquered his land from Adrianople to Dyrrhachium. Bulgaria emerged once again as the strongest state of south-eastern Europe.
battle-of-klushino: The battle belonged to Russia's Time of Troubles. In response to the Polish-Lithuanian advance, Russia and Sweden allied in the De la Gardie Campaign, and a Russian army under Prince Dmitry Shuisky marched to relieve the besieged fortress of Smolensk. Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski first trapped an advance force of 8,000 under Grigory Valuyev in its fortified camp at Tsaryovo-Zaymishche. Knowing that Shuisky's main force was only days away, and that the besieged troops had not warned him, Żółkiewski left part of his army to hold the camp and on 3 July led his most mobile units against Shuisky.

Żółkiewski had about 6,500 to 6,800 men, some 5,500 of them hussars, and two cannon, against about 30,000 Russians under Shuisky, Andrey Galitzine and Danilo Mezetsky and about 5,000 mercenaries under Jacob De la Gardie. The Russian infantry stood behind a high village fence that let the hussars charge only through a narrow gap; Samuel Maskiewicz, a hussar, said his company charged eight or ten times. A counterattack by Russian reiters failed when the hussars closed to melee, the Russian left broke and the army fell back to its camp. The mercenaries held for several hours until Polish infantry and guns arrived, then retired in good order to their own camp.

Żółkiewski negotiated with the surrounded mercenaries, who were allowed to leave on condition that they would not fight for Russia against the Commonwealth again; several hundred joined the Polish side. Shuisky retreated, leaving all 11 Russian guns. The historian Sikora puts the Russian losses at about 2,000 and the Polish at 80 killed and 100 wounded. Valuyev then surrendered, Tsar Vasili IV was ousted by the Seven Boyars, and Żółkiewski entered Moscow. The boyars proclaimed Prince Władysław IV Waza tsar, but he never took the throne. The battle is commemorated on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Warsaw.
battle-of-ko-chang: The Franco-Thai War was going badly for the French on land, and Admiral Jean Decoux, Governor General of Indochina and commander of its naval forces, decided to strike at the Thai fleet and coastal cities to clear the way for bombardments in support of a counter-offensive along the Cambodian frontier. On 9 December 1940 he formed a small squadron, the Groupe Occasionnel, at Cam Ranh Bay under Capitaine de Vaisseau Régis Bérenger: the light cruiser Lamotte-Picquet, built in 1923, the modern avisos Dumont d'Urville and Amiral Charner, and the older avisos Tahure and Marne.

The Royal Thai Navy had recently acquired ships from Japan and Italy. Its core was two Japanese-built armoured coast defence ships, HTMS Thonburi and Sri Ayudhya, each with four 8-inch guns, and the Royal Thai Air Force had over 140 aircraft. Decoux ordered attacks on the coast from Rayong to the Cambodian frontier. When Loire 130 seaplanes from Ream reported one coastal defence ship and one torpedo boat at Ko Chang, Bérenger chose a dawn attack there, the weaker of the two Thai anchorages.

The French closed on the anchorage at 05:30 on 17 January and split into three groups to cover the channels between the islands. A last air reconnaissance found two torpedo boats instead of one, HTMS Chonburi having arrived in the night, and the aircraft's attempt to bomb them cost the French their surprise. Lamotte-Picquet soon sank both torpedo boats with gunfire. At 06:38 Thonburi was sighted heading northwest, and a running fight followed among the islets. An early French shot killed her captain, Commander Luang Phrom Viraphan; by 07:15 she was on fire, and she reached shallow water listing heavily. As the squadron headed home from 08:40, Thai aircraft attacked, and one bomb hit Lamotte-Picquet but failed to explode.

Thonburi, with about 20 dead, was taken in tow by the transport HTMS Chang and run aground on purpose at Laem Ngop, where she capsized; Chonburi lost two men and HTMS Songkhla fourteen. Fearing that further French action might turn back the Thai invasion, Japan offered to mediate, and the settlement confirmed Thailand's annexation of territory it had lost to France in the late 19th century. After World War II Thailand had to return these gains. Thonburi was raised, repaired in Japan and used as a training ship, and her guns and bridge are preserved at the Royal Thai Naval Academy at Samut Prakan.
battle-of-kohima: The Japanese plan to invade India, codenamed U-Go, began as a spoiling attack on the British IV Corps at Imphal in Manipur. Lieutenant General Renya Mutaguchi, commanding the Fifteenth Army, enlarged it into an invasion of India itself, and Imperial General Headquarters approved it on 7 January 1944. The Japanese 31st Division under Lieutenant General Kōtoku Satō was to take Kohima, which cut off Imphal's supplies, and perhaps push on to the railhead at Dimapur. Satō had misgivings and thought Mutaguchi a blockhead. His division crossed the Chindwin from 15 March with only three weeks' food and ammunition.

Kohima lay at the summit of a pass and on the road between Dimapur and Imphal. Its ridge held the home of the Deputy Commissioner, Charles Pawsey, with its garden and tennis court. A small force of British and Indian troops, with the 1st Battalion of the Assam Regiment and the paramilitary Assam Rifles, held it when the Japanese reached the outskirts of the Naga village on 3 April. Fighting continued on the ridge until the garrison was relieved on 18 and 20 April, with some 300 wounded brought out under fire.

The British 2nd Division then counter-attacked, and monsoon mud made the steep slopes very difficult. Japanese bunkers were deeply dug in and mutually supporting, and the progress was slow. The decisive factor was Japanese supply. By mid-May Satō's troops were starving, and a British long-range penetration brigade cut his supply lines behind him. The Allies depended entirely on aircraft for resupply until the road from Dimapur was cleared.

The battle ended on 22 June when troops from Kohima and Imphal met at Milestone 109. Satō ignored army orders for several weeks and was removed in July; he refused to commit seppuku and demanded a court martial, but was declared mentally unfit to stand trial. The Japanese offensive was broken off, and the losses at Imphal and Kohima, mostly through starvation and disease, crippled their defence of Burma in the following year. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission maintains the war cemetery of 1,420 Allied dead on the old tennis court, where the Kohima Epitaph is carved.
battle-of-kolin: Frederick II of Prussia had won the bloody Battle of Prague against Austria on 6 May 1757 and was besieging the city. The Austrian Marshal Daun arrived too late to fight but picked up 16,000 men who had escaped from the battle, and with this army he moved slowly to relieve Prague. Frederick halted the bombardment and left the siege under Duke Ferdinand of Brunswick, then marched against the Austrians on 13 June with the troops of Prince Moritz of Anhalt-Dessau.

Frederick took 34,000 men to intercept Daun. Daun knew the Prussians were too weak both to besiege Prague and to keep him away, or to fight his army if it were reinforced by the Prague garrison, so on the night of 17 June his forces took defensive positions on hills near Kolín. At noon on 18 June, Frederick attacked an Austrian force of 35,160 infantry, 18,630 cavalry and 154 guns, on gently rolling hill slopes.

Frederick planned to envelop the Austrian right wing with most of his army, keeping only enough troops along the rest of the line to hide the concentration on his left. His main force turned towards the Austrians too early and attacked their positions from the front. Austrian Croatian light infantry played a large part, harassing the Prussian infantry under Generals Christopher Hermann von Manstein and Joachim Christian von Tresckow and provoking a premature attack.

Austrian musket and artillery fire stopped the advance. A counterattack by the Austrian right was beaten by Prussian cavalry, and Frederick poured more troops into the gap, but this assault was halted and then crushed by Austrian cavalry. After about five hours the Prussians were disoriented and Daun's troops were driving them back. The cuirassiers of Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz, promoted to major-general that day, arrived late, and there were many charges and counter-charges on the Křečhoř Hill. A Guard battalion under General Friedrich Bogislav von Tauentzien covered the retreat. Frederick is quoted as asking the hesitating Guards whether they would live forever.

The Prussians lost 13,733 men and the Austrians 8,100, with 54,000 Austrians defeating 34,000 Prussians in about five and a half hours of combat. It was Frederick's first defeat in the war. He abandoned his planned march on Vienna, raised the siege of Prague on 20 June and fell back to Litoměřice. The Austrians, reinforced by the 48,000 troops in Prague and 100,000 strong, followed and inflicted a severe check on Prince August Wilhelm of Prussia at Zittau. The king withdrew from Bohemia to Saxony. Maria Theresa founded the Military Order of Maria Theresa afterwards, a street in Vienna was named after the victory in 1870, and memorials stand at Křečhoř and Nová Ves I.
battle-of-kolubara: After Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia on 23 July, designed to be unacceptable, and declared war on 28 July. Oskar Potiorek commanded the first invasion of Serbia in August with far fewer troops than the 308,000 intended, since much of the 2nd Army had gone to the Russian front. The Serbian army was led by Crown Prince Alexander, with Radomir Putnik as his deputy and de facto military leader.

A third invasion was authorised in early October by Emperor Franz Joseph after Austro-Hungarian troops found in a bookshop a map, The New Division of Europe, showing Austria-Hungary abolished. Rain and snow had swamped the valleys of north-western Serbia, and Putnik remarked that his whole strategy was to place the Serbian national mud between the enemy's fighting line and his supplies. The invasion began on 6 November, and the outnumbered Serbs, short of ammunition, retreated. Putnik ordered the abandonment of Valjevo and a stand on the Kolubara. Nikola Pašić telegraphed abroad for urgent help, and France supplied munitions.

The Austro-Hungarians reached the Kolubara on 16 November and attacked the next day. For five days both armies fought in heavy rain and snow, and many soldiers died of frostbite and hypothermia. By 19 November the Austro-Hungarians had gained a foothold at Vrače Brdo and the Serbian 1st Army was forced back.

On the night of 26 to 27 November the Austro-Hungarian 6th Army attacked along the whole front. The Serbian command abandoned Belgrade on 29 and 30 November, and the Austro-Hungarians entered on 1 December, to celebrations in Vienna. Potiorek wrote that he was laying Belgrade at the emperor's feet.

But supply lines were overextended, and Potiorek paused. Živojin Mišić withdrew the Serbian 1st Army to rest, and supplies reached the Serbs by the Niš to Salonika railway. On 2 December Putnik ordered a counterattack along the whole front, and King Peter I took a rifle to the front. The attack caught the Austro-Hungarians holding a parade in Belgrade, with their artillery well behind the line. Valjevo and Užice were retaken on 8 December, and the Austro-Hungarians abandoned Belgrade on 14 and 15 December.

It was a decisive Serbian victory. It failed to knock Serbia out of the war, to bring Bulgaria into the Central Powers or to keep Romania neutral, and Austro-Hungarian historians judged it a serious loss of prestige. Potiorek and Liborius Ritter von Frank were relieved of command on 22 December. Austro-Hungarian casualties are given as about 225,000, and the Serbs lost 22,000 killed, 91,000 wounded and 19,000 missing or captured. Western correspondents reported atrocities by Austro-Hungarian troops against Serbian civilians, and William Shepard of the United Press saw at least 11 towns abandoned.
battle-of-komaki-and-nagakute: In 1583 Hashiba Hideyoshi, who would take the name Toyotomi in 1586, backed Oda Nobukatsu, the second son of Oda Nobunaga, and defeated Shibata Katsuie at the Battle of Shizugatake. When Hideyoshi then invited Nobukatsu and other generals to pay homage at his new Osaka Castle, Nobukatsu refused. Rumours that his chief retainers Tsugawa Yoshifuyu, Okada Shigetaka and Azai Nagatoki supported Hideyoshi led Nobukatsu to have them executed on 17 March 1584. This gave Hideyoshi his reason to attack, and Nobukatsu called on Tokugawa Ieyasu, so that the war became one between Hideyoshi and Ieyasu.

At Haguro, Mori Nagayoshi, eager to match the achievements of his father-in-law Ikeda Tsuneoki, advanced beyond Inuyama Castle and was surprised by Sakai Tadatsugu, retreating with 300 casualties. Ieyasu fortified Mount Komaki and Hideyoshi built forts of his own, and the two armies faced each other in a stalemate. Ikeda Tsuneoki then set out with an army numbering 20,000 to raid Mikawa Province. His forces took Iwasaki Castle, where Niwa Ujitsugu lost 300 killed, among them his brother Niwa Ujishige.

Ieyasu's troops surprised and wiped out the force of Miyoshi Hidetsugu resting in Hakusan Forest, and Hori Hidemasa, who came to its aid, was forced back when the main Tokugawa army of some 9,000 arrived. In the final battle at Nagakute, Ii Naomasa's musketeers repeatedly broke the charges of Tsuneoki and Nagayoshi for over two hours. Nagayoshi was shot dead, Tsuneoki was killed by the spear of Nagai Naokatsu, and Tsuneoki's son Ikeda Motosuke also fell.

Hideyoshi withdrew to Osaka, and the war moved to sieges such as that of Kanie Castle. Nobukatsu made a separate peace with Hideyoshi in November 1584 and became his vassal, after which Ieyasu no longer had a clear justification for continuing the war. During the Edo period the Tokugawa records called the fighting the Battle of Komaki. The Nagakute Battlefield Historic Site was designated a National Historic Site of Japan in 1939.
battle-of-koniggratz: At the start of the war in June the Prussian armies stood along the Prussian border: the Army of the Elbe under Karl Herwarth von Bittenfeld, the First Army under Prince Friedrich Karl, and the Second Army under Crown Prince Frederick William in Silesia. Benedek's Austrian army was gathered at Olmütz and left it reluctantly on 18 June. Moltke ordered the two armies under his command to Jitschin, a daring move meant to keep the war short.

Benedek was indecisive and did not use his larger numbers to beat the Prussian armies one by one. On 29 June Prince Friedrich Karl won at Jitschin over General Clam-Gallas. Benedek asked Emperor Franz Josef to make peace and, when this was refused, drew up his army against the Elbe between Sadová and Königgrätz.

The Prussians sighted the Austrians on the eve of 2 July. The telegraph to the Second Army was down, so two mounted officers rode 32 kilometres through the night and reached it at 4 am. The battle began at dawn on 3 July in rain and mist. The Prussian 7th Division under Fransecky advanced into the Swiepwald and held there while the Austrian artillery pinned the Prussian right. Benedek refused to order a cavalry charge that later writers argue might have won the day.

The Prussian needle gun fired much faster than the Austrian muzzle-loaders and could be used lying down. At 2:30 pm the Crown Prince arrived with nearly 100,000 men and struck the Austrian right flank, and the Army of the Elbe broke the left. The 1st Guard Division took Chlum behind the centre. Benedek ordered a general retreat at 3 pm, covered by cavalry charges that cost 2,000 men and almost as many horses, and crossed the Elbe near 6 pm.

The Prussians lost nearly 9,000 men killed, wounded or missing. The Austrians and their allies lost roughly 31,000, among them 9,291 prisoners, with 187 cannon and 51 colours. Austrian medical staff withdrew with the army, because Austria had refused to sign the First Geneva Convention, leaving the wounded on the field; the Saxon nurse Marie Simon tended them for 17 weeks and went on with Carola of Vasa to found the Albert Association, a precursor of the German Red Cross.

The last skirmish was fought at Blumenau on 22 July, as the Peace of Prague was being signed. The victory cleared the way to the Little German solution and the North German Confederation. The French public demanded revenge for Sadová, which formed part of the background to the Franco-Prussian War of 1870.
battle-of-konotop: The battle belongs to the Ruin, the years of struggle within the Cossack elite after the death of Bohdan Khmelnytsky. His successor, Ivan Vyhovsky, faced growing interference from Moscow and turned to Poland, concluding the Treaty of Hadiach on 16 September 1658, which planned a Grand Principality of Rus' within the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Moscow sent Prince Grigory Romodanovsky to Ukraine, backing Vyhovsky's rivals under Ivan Bezpaly. In spring 1659 a further army, 28,600 men according to the records of the Razryadny prikaz, came under Prince Aleksey Trubetskoy, defeated Vyhovsky at Romny and Lokhvytsia, and besieged Konotop, held by 4,000 Cossacks under Hryhoriy Hulyanytsky.

The garrison threw back an assault on 21 April. Trubetskoy then shelled the town and filled its moat with earth, but the defenders used the earth at night to strengthen their walls and held out for 70 days, giving Vyhovsky time to gather the Crimean khan Mehmed IV Giray with 30,000 men and a Polish detachment of 4,000.

On 27 June Vyhovsky raided Trubetskoy's camp and drove off many of its horses, then fell back across the Sosnivka river. Trubetskoy sent Prince Semen Pozharsky after him with 4,000 noble cavalry and 2,000 of Bezpaly's Cossacks. During the night of 28 June Stepan Hulyanytsky's men, their horses' hoofs muffled with cloth, seized and dismantled the bridge behind Pozharsky and dammed the river, flooding the valley. On 29 June Vyhovsky drew Pozharsky into a pursuit with a feigned flight; three cannon shots signalled the Tatars, and the heavy cavalry, bogged down in the flooded ground, was cut to pieces. Pozharsky was captured and, after insulting the khan, beheaded.

Trubetskoy lifted the siege and retreated, losing most of his artillery, his banners and his treasury. Archive documents of the Ambassadors' Chancellery put Russian losses at 4,769 men, far below the 30,000 to 50,000 of Polish and Ukrainian narrative sources. Vyhovsky gained little: Ivan Sirko's Zaporozhian Cossacks attacked Crimean outposts, the khan went home, and towns rebelled. By the end of the year Vyhovsky had resigned and fled to Poland, where the Poles executed him in 1664.
battle-of-koppam: From his accession Rajadhiraja Chola I sought to subdue the Chalukyas, who ruled parts of northern Karnataka and the south of present-day Maharashtra, and to add their lands to the Chola Empire. His first invasion, in 1047–48, had failed. On the second expedition he led a large army north and plundered the province of Rattamandalam, with his brother and heir-apparent Rajendra Chola II following in the rear.

According to the Chola sources and the Thiruvalandur copper plate, Rajadhiraja had personally led the attack on Kalyanapura, also called Kalyani, the modern Basavakalyan. Someshvara I fled when the city was attacked, returned with an army and was beaten again, and the Chola king then withdrew towards Kollapura. The copper plate says that Someshvara gathered a huge army and called out for battle as the Chola withdrew, and that the Chola turned to meet him at the place called Koppam.

The copper plate describes columns of foot soldiers, horses and elephants engaging their counterparts, with Rajadhiraja fighting from his elephant until a downpour of Chalukya arrows killed him. The Chola troops, who had been holding the upper hand, panicked and began to retreat. Rajendra II, commanding the reserve, took over the army, rallied it and inflicted heavy losses, forcing Someshvara to flee. Chola sources record that the elephants, horses and camels of the Chalukyas, a large booty and the queens of Someshvara fell into Chola hands. Rajendra is reported to have set up a victory pillar at Kolhapur before returning to his country.

The battle is known chiefly from the Chola side: an inscription dated to 1054 and Rajendra Chola II's Manimangalam record of 1055. The latter gives the victory to Rajendra and says that Ahavamalla, as it calls the Chalukya king, became afraid, incurred disgrace and ran away. The year is given as 1054, or as 1052 by the historian Sen. The site is also uncertain. The Manimangalam inscription places Koppam on the bank of the great river; the scholar Fleet identified it with Khidrapur, 30 miles south-east of Kolhapur, taking the river to be the Krishna, while other historians have put it near Maski.
battle-of-kose-dag: After the Seljuk Turks defeated the Byzantine Empire at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, Suleiman ibn Qutalmish founded the Sultanate of Rum, which controlled large parts of Anatolia over the next 150 years. By the 1230s it had gained maritime and commercial strength through the ports of Antalya and Sinope.

The Mongols reached Rum's frontier in the early 1230s by conquering western Iran. Under their general Chormaqan they subdued Transcaucasia and made the Kingdom of Georgia a vassal. Relations with Rum worsened after Kaykhusraw II became sultan in 1237, and Mongol raids began in 1240. In 1242 Baiju, who had replaced the disabled Chormaqan, captured and pillaged Erzurum, which opened a war.

Kaykhusraw hired mercenaries from the Latin Empire, the Greek remnants of the Byzantine Empire, the Ayyubids of Aleppo and the Arab tribes of Iraq. The Khwarazmian troops and the Turkomans who had joined the Babai revolt refused to fight for him, and several capable commanders had been eliminated by his adviser Sa'd al-Din Köpek. The Mongol core numbered about 30,000, with Georgian and Armenian auxiliaries. Chroniclers put Kaykhusraw's army at 160,000 or 200,000, but the historian Bayarsaikhan Dashdondog estimates 80,000.

The army gathered at Sivas. Experienced nobles urged a defensive stand, but younger nobles accused them of cowardice, and on 26 June the army attacked at the pass of Köse Dağ, about 80 kilometres north-west of Sivas. Baiju assembled a vanguard of the best soldiers of every unit and met the army of Rum in a narrow ravine.

For most of the day the army of Rum seemed slightly superior, but its formation collapsed in the evening. Sources differ on why: the Armenian historian Grigor of Akanc credited a Georgian prince, Aghbagha, while Josef Matuz favoured accounts of a feigned Mongol retreat followed by arrow fire and a charge. The army fled that night. Baiju suspected a trap in the deserted camp and lost the chance to capture the sultan.

The Mongols took Kayseri, Sivas, Erzincan and Ankara. The vizier Muhezzibeddin negotiated surrender terms: a yearly tribute of 12 million silver coins, 500 bolts of silk, 500 camels and 5,000 sheep, and a Mongol overseer, or daruyachi. The Empire of Trebizond submitted, and Cilician Armenia did so in 1244. After Kaykhusraw died in 1246 the realm split among factions of his three young sons. Seljuk power declined until it ended in 1308, and its lands passed to the Mongol Ilkhanate.
battle-of-kosovo: After the death of Stefan Uroš V in December 1371 and the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Maritsa earlier that year, the Serbian Empire had broken into virtually independent principalities. Prince Lazar, ruler of Moravian Serbia, the northern part of the former empire, prepared for a campaign against the Ottomans. After Ottoman defeats at Pločnik in 1386 and Bileća in 1388, Sultan Murad I moved his troops through Kratovo and Kumanovo to Pristina, where he arrived on 14 June 1389. Lazar gathered troops near Niš and moved to Kosovo, a crossroads that let him control the routes Murad could take. Lazar's army included his own troops, a contingent under his son-in-law Vuk Branković and Bosnian forces under Vlatko Vuković sent by King Tvrtko I.

Reliable accounts are scarce, and no first-hand account from a participant exists. The army sizes are disputed; the leading estimate accepted by Western scholars is 15,000 to 20,000 for Lazar and 27,000 to 30,000 for Murad. Murad's son Bayezid commanded the right wing and his son Yakub the left. It is believed that the battle began with Ottoman archers shooting at the Serbian cavalry, which broke through the Ottoman left wing, but light Ottoman cavalry and infantry then counterattacked and the Serbian heavy armour became a disadvantage. Bayezid led a counterattack and the Ottomans routed the Serbian infantry.

Lazar was captured and Murad was killed. Murad's death is attributed to a Serbian knight named Miloš Obilić, and accounts of how he did it differ. In popular tradition Vuk Branković betrayed Lazar by fleeing, a theory first presented by Mavro Orbini in 1601 that is largely seen as unfounded. Both armies were largely destroyed, and the battle is the only time an Ottoman sultan was killed in battle.

Bayezid killed his brother Yakub on hearing of their father's death and became sole heir. The Serbs had too few men left to field large armies, while the Ottomans could draw on reserves from the east. Hungary tried to expand in northern Serbia, and the Ottomans renewed their campaign in the south in 1390 to 1391. Some Serbian principalities that were not already vassals became so in the following years, and Lazar's daughter married Bayezid. Serbia became an Ottoman province, and the capture of Smederevo on 20 June 1459 marks the end of medieval Serbian statehood.

The battle was mythologised soon afterwards, and the Kosovo Myth became central to Serbian folklore. In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić collected the epic poems of the Kosovo cycle. The battle is seen in Serbian public discourse as important to Serbian history, tradition and national identity, and Vidovdan commemorates it.
battle-of-kousseri: The battle was the climax of French plans to occupy the Chari-Baguirmi region of present-day Chad. In 1899 the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr could field about 10,000 infantry and cavalry with rifles, most of them obsolete, besides many auxiliaries with lances or bows, and he held fortified garrisons at Baggara and Karnak Logone. Talks at Dikoa with the French representative Ferdinand de Béhagle broke down, and Béhagle was arrested. On 17 July 1899 Rabih destroyed Lieutenant Bretonnet's force at Togbao on the Chari, taking three cannons, and ordered his son Fadlallah to hang Béhagle.

France sent three columns, from Congo, from Niger and from Algeria. Émile Gentil's column from Gabon, supported by the steamboat Leon Blot, was pushed back by Rabih at Kouno at the end of 1899 but went on to Kousséri. There it met Lamy's column from Algeria and the former Voulet–Chanoine Mission from Niger, now under Joalland-Meynier after news of the mission's brutality had reached the European press. The columns joined on 21 April 1900, and Lamy took command.

On 22 April the French, 700 troops with 600 riflemen and 200 cavalry from their Baguirmian allies, left Kousséri in three columns and attacked Rabih's camp. Lamy was killed in the fighting, but Rabih's forces were overwhelmed. As Rabih tried to flee across the Chari he was shot in the head by a skirmisher, who, hearing of a bonus for the body, went back and brought in his head and right hand. The French lost 28 dead and 75 wounded; Rabih's side lost 1,000 to 1,500 dead and more than 3,000 wounded, among them women and children who accompanied the army.

The victory secured French control over most of Chad, which became part of the French colonial empire, and linked France's three most stable possessions in Africa: Senegal and the Upper Niger valley, Gabon and Congo-Brazzaville, and Algeria. The marches of the columns helped define the practical borders between French and British rule. French colonial histories usually treat Kousséri as the end of the Scramble for Africa and the beginning of the pacification phase of French West and Equatorial Africa.
battle-of-krbava-field: After the fall of the Kingdom of Bosnia to the Ottomans in 1463, raids by the Akıncı, irregular light cavalry, grew more frequent. They plundered the countryside in spring and summer and avoided fortified towns, driving the local population from the land. A raid of September 1491 ended when the Croatian ban Ladislav of Egervár and Count Bernardin Frankopan defeated the Ottomans at the Battle of Vrpile, and the raids stopped in 1492. They resumed once Hadım Yakup Pasha became sanjak-bey of Bosnia.

In the summer of 1493 Hadım Yakup Pasha raised 8,000 light cavalry, failed to take Jajce, and raided Carniola and Styria. A war between the new ban of Croatia, Emerik Derenčin, and the Frankopans over Senj was set aside because of the Ottoman raid. The Croatian nobles gathered about 3,000 cavalry and 8,000 infantry, part of them peasants, to meet the Ottomans returning from sacking Modruš. Ivan Frankopan Cetinski urged an ambush in the ravines, but Derenčin accused the Croats of cowardice and chose open battle on the Krbava plain.

On 9 September the Ottomans feigned a retreat and drew the Croatian army towards a hidden force of about 3,000 cavalry in the woods, which struck its rear while the main Ottoman army attacked the front. Most of the Croatian infantry was surrounded and only a few reached the fortified town of Udbina. The battle lasted from about nine in the morning into the afternoon.

Derenčin was captured and died in captivity, and his brother and son Pavao were killed. Ivan Frankopan Cetinski, Petar II Zrinski and Juraj Vlatković were among the nobles killed. Nikola VI Frankopan was ransomed, and Bernardin Frankopan and Franjo Berislavić survived. Older historians called the defeat the first dissolution of the Croatian Kingdom, and local tradition named the plain the Field of Blood.

The Ottomans made no territorial gains from the victory, and a peace with Croatia and Hungary was signed in April 1495. In the following decades, under constant attack, the Ottomans gradually expanded into southern Croatia. Older sources exaggerate the numbers involved, since the reports were written under the impression of the heavy loss.
battle-of-kressenbrunn: The Babenberg dynasty died out in 1246, leaving Austria and Styria without a prince. In 1251 King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia made his son Ottokar Margrave of Moravia and installed him as duke of both lands, and in 1252 Ottokar married Duchess Margaret of Austria, sister of the last Babenberg duke and about 26 years his senior, to legitimise his claim. When Ottokar became King of Bohemia in 1253, Béla IV of Hungary, wary of his growing power, claimed Styria.

A settlement reached with the help of Pope Innocent IV in 1254 gave Béla large parts of Styria, where he later installed his son Stephen as duke. In 1260 the Styrian nobility revolted against the Árpáds, Ottokar reclaimed the duchy, and Béla, allied with Daniel of Galicia and Bolesław V the Chaste of Poland, marched against him. Hungary had not recovered from the Mongol invasion of 1240 and 1241, in which historians estimate up to half of its population of about 2,000,000 perished.

Ottokar's army drew on Bohemian-Moravian, German, Polish, Carinthian, Carniolan and Styrian forces, while Béla gathered Hungarian, Cuman, Russian, Bulgarian, Wallachian, Croatian, Serbian, Szekler and other contingents. The armies faced each other for some time across the Morava, neither daring to cross. Ottokar proposed to withdraw so that the Hungarians could reach the other bank. As his troops pulled back, Stephen attacked, crossed the river and caught the retiring Bohemian cavalry at Kressenbrunn. Ottokar recalled his forces and drove Stephen back, seriously wounded, and the returning Bohemian forces then routed Béla's army, many of whose men drowned in the river as they fled. Scholars doubt that armies as large as those reported could have been supplied.

Béla renounced Styria and in 1261 arranged the marriage of his granddaughter Kunigunda of Slavonia to Ottokar, though his successors went on challenging Bohemia. A memorial at the eastern edge of the Groissenbrunn municipality, designed by Vladislav Plekanec, was unveiled in 2010 for the 750th anniversary.
battle-of-krtsanisi: Eastern Georgia had been under Iranian suzerainty since the 1510s, but after Nader Shah's death in 1747 its kings declared de facto independence, and in 1762 Heraclius II united Kartli and Kakheti. In 1783 he placed his kingdom under Russian protection by the Treaty of Georgievsk. A small Russian force reached Tbilisi in 1784 but was withdrawn in 1787, and in 1792 General Gudovich told Heraclius he would receive only diplomatic support against any Iranian attack.

Agha Mohammad Khan, head of the Qajar dynasty, regarded Georgia as a province of Iran like Khorasan and resolved to bring the Caucasus back under Iranian rule. He demanded that Heraclius renounce the treaty with Russia and accept Iranian suzerainty. Heraclius asked Empress Catherine II for at least 3,000 Russian troops, was not heeded, and still rejected the ultimatum.

In August 1795 Agha Mohammad Khan crossed the Aras with a 70,000-strong army. After forcing the khans of Ganja, Erivan and Karabakh into submission, he marched on Tbilisi with about half of it. Abandoned by several of his nobles, Heraclius mobilised some 5,000 men, including about 2,000 from Imereti under King Solomon II, and held fortified positions on the southwestern edge of the city, where the Georgians beat back a series of Persian attacks.

Early on 11 September Agha Mohammad Khan led an all-out offensive. His troops crossed the Kura and outflanked the Georgians, and by nightfall Heraclius's army had been almost destroyed; the last Georgian guns held off the Persians long enough for the king and some 150 men to escape to the mountains. Tbilisi was sacked and its population massacred, the archbishop Doistheus among the dead, and the Persian army marched home with some 15,000 captives. The Georgians lost 4,000 men, the Iranians 13,000.

Agha Mohammad was crowned Shah in the Mughan plain in 1796. Catherine II sent an army under Valerian Zubov against Iran that year to restore Russian prestige, but her successor Paul I soon recalled it. The shah was assassinated at Shusha in 1797 while preparing a second expedition against Georgia, and Heraclius died early in 1798. Russian troops entered Tbilisi in 1799, and the battle led directly to the Russo-Persian wars of 1804–1813 and 1826–1828, by which Iran ceded Transcaucasia and Dagestan to Russia.
battle-of-kulikovo: After the Mongol invasion of Rus' in the 13th century the Russian principalities became vassals of the Golden Horde. Moscow grew in power and often challenged its neighbours, and in 1300 it seized Kolomna from Ryazan. After the killing of Khan Berdi Beg in 1359 the Golden Horde fell into what were called the Great Troubles, and the commander Mamai, Berdi Beg's son-in-law, took power in its western part and enthroned khans of his own. He was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, so his hold on power was tenuous, and he had to fight both for supremacy and against separatism while Lithuania, Moscow and Ryazan rose as new powers.

In August 1380 Dmitry of Moscow learned that Mamai's army was approaching. Mamai's envoys demanded a tribute raised to the level of the time of Khan Jani Beg, and Dmitry agreed only to the amount of his earlier agreement. He gathered an army at Kolomna and marched south, reaching the Don on 6 September. Jogaila of Lithuania was marching to join Mamai. On the morning of 8 September, in thick fog, the Russian army crossed the Don.

The early sources give few details of the fighting. The fullest account, The Tale of the Rout of Mamai, dates from the 16th century, and it is unknown whether it rests on an earlier source. It describes six regiments, with an ambush regiment hidden in an oak grove and Dmitry exchanging his coat and helmet with a boyar so as to fight unrecognised. The main forces clashed at about 10.35 in the morning, and Russian sources agree that a long and cruel melee followed in which many died on both sides. A third of the commanders of the banners were killed. Dmitry survived, wounded and exhausted, and was found among the corpses.

Jogaila turned back on hearing of Mamai's defeat. Dmitry made Prince Oleg of Ryazan accept him as his older brother. Mamai escaped to the Genoese stronghold of Caffa in Crimea and raised a new army, but without a legitimate khan his nobles went over to his rival Tokhtamysh, who gained full power and ended the twenty-year split of the Golden Horde. Mamai fled to Caffa again and was killed.

The victory did not end Mongol domination, but it is traditionally regarded as the turning point at which Mongol influence began to fade and Moscow's power to rise. Only five primary sources survive, none from the Tatar side, yet the battle produced a larger body of medieval Rus' literature than any other event, the Kulikovo cycle, which includes the epic Zadonshchina.
battle-of-kunersdorf: The battle belonged to the Third Silesian War and the wider Seven Years' War. By 1759 Prussia had reached a strategic defensive position, with Russian and Austrian troops around it. After a Prussian corps was defeated at the Battle of Kay on 23 July, Pyotr Saltykov's Russians occupied Frankfurt an der Oder on 31 July and entrenched near Kunersdorf, and an Austrian corps under Ernst Gideon von Laudon joined them on 3 to 5 August. By 9 August Frederick the Great had 49,000 to 50,000 men. The Allies numbered about 41,000 Russians and 18,500 Austrians, and the terrain suited defence better than attack.

Frederick crossed the Oder and marched round the Russian flank, a trek of up to eight hours, sending no reconnaissance. Saltykov had meanwhile reversed his line. At 11:30 on 12 August the Prussian artillery opened fire. Frederick's troops took the Mühlberge, but against the advice of his brother Prince Henry and other generals, who pointed to heat and exhaustion, he chose to press on.

A cavalry charge led by Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz against the Russian centre failed and Seydlitz was badly wounded. Laudon led the Austrian cavalry in a counterattack, and fresh Austrian infantry joined the fight at about 7 pm. The Prussians broke and fled, throwing away their weapons.

That evening Frederick wrote a despairing letter in a peasant hut at Reitwein and named his brother as generalissimo. Allied losses were 16,332, some 27 percent. Sources differ on Prussian losses: Duffy gives 6,000 killed and 13,000 wounded, and others 18,609 or 21,000. The Prussians lost 172 of their own cannon, their horse artillery and 60 percent of their cavalry. Only 3,000 men stayed with Frederick at first, but within days most of the scattered survivors returned, and his army recovered to 32,000 men and 50 guns. Saltykov and Laudon disagreed and did not march on Berlin, 80 kilometres away. Military historians generally regard Kunersdorf as Frederick's worst defeat.
battle-of-kursk: After Stalingrad the Red Army moved to a general offensive in the south, and by February 1943 the southern sector of the German front was in strategic crisis. Kursk was retaken by the Soviets on 8 February. Short of infantry and artillery, the Germans would have to rely chiefly on their panzer divisions for any offensive in 1943. On 10 March Manstein presented a plan to pinch off the Kursk salient. Hitler believed that a victory would reassert German strength and improve his prestige with allies he thought were considering withdrawing from the war.

The Soviets had foreknowledge of the German plans through the Lucy spy ring in Switzerland and the spy John Cairncross at Bletchley Park. Georgiy Zhukov and other officers recommended a strategic defensive before going on the offensive. The Germans delayed the attack to build up their forces, which gave the Red Army time to construct a series of deep defensive belts and a large reserve.

Operation Citadel began on 5 July 1943, with attacks from north and south on the base of the salient. In the north, Model's 9th Army attacked the Central Front, and the fighting around Ponyri and Olkhovatka became a battle of attrition that troops called a mini-Stalingrad. In the south, Hoth's 4th Panzer Army advanced against the Voronezh Front, and the Soviets committed their strategic reserves, including the 5th Guards Tank Army, which advanced to Prokhorovka, where a large armoured clash took place from 12 July.

The Western Allies invaded Sicily on 10 July, and on 12 July Hitler decided to stop the offensive and move forces to Italy, though Manstein objected that his forces were on the verge of breaking through. The same day the Soviets launched Operation Kutuzov against the Orel salient, and on 3 August they began Operation Polkovodets Rumyantsev, liberating Belgorod by 5 August.

For the first time a major German offensive was stopped before it broke through; the Germans advanced at most 8 to 12 kilometres in the north and 35 kilometres in the south. The Soviet victory was costly, but the Soviet Union's industry and manpower allowed it to replace its losses. The battle was the last strategic offensive the Germans were able to launch on the Eastern Front, and the Red Army held the strategic initiative for the rest of the war. It is the single largest battle in the history of warfare and the single deadliest armoured battle.
battle-of-la-forbie: The capture of Jerusalem by the Khwarezmians in August 1244 alarmed Christian and Muslim states alike. Al-Mansur, Emir of Homs, and an-Nasir Dawud of Kerak joined the Templars, the Hospitallers, the Teutonic Knights, the Order of Saint Lazarus and the remaining forces of the Kingdom of Jerusalem against the Egyptian sultanate. The armies met near Forbie, a small village north-east of Gaza. Overall Christian command lay with Walter IV of Brienne, Count of Jaffa and Ascalon, with Robert of Nantes, Patriarch of Jerusalem, and Philip of Montfort, Constable of Jerusalem, also present.

The Christians fielded about 1,000 cavalry and 6,000 foot soldiers, Al-Mansur about 2,000 cavalry with troops from Damascus, and the Transjordanian contingent about 2,000 mounted Bedouin. The Egyptian army, led by the Mamluk officer Rukn al-Din Baybars al-Salihi, was slightly weaker. Al-Mansur advised a fortified defensive camp, expecting the undisciplined Khwarezmians to disperse, but Walter would not refuse battle while he held the rare advantage of numbers.

On 17 October the Christian knights charged repeatedly along the line, but the Egyptians held. The next morning Baybars threw the Khwarezmians against the Damascene centre, which broke, and they then cut the Bedouin on the left to pieces. Al-Mansur's cavalry stood firm until nearly destroyed, and he left the field with 280 survivors. The Crusaders on the right charged the Mamluks and at first drove them back, but the Khwarezmians attacked their rear and flanks, and after several hours their resistance collapsed. Over 5,000 Crusaders died and 800 were captured, among them Walter of Brienne; only 33 Templars, 27 Hospitallers and three Teutonic Knights survived, and the Master of the Temple, Armand de Périgord, was killed.

Pope Innocent IV called for the Seventh Crusade at the First Council of Lyon in 1245, but the Franks never again mustered major power in the Holy Land. The Kingdom of Jerusalem had not put so large an army into the field since the Battle of Hattin and could never again undertake offensive operations. The victory brought the Ayyubids no lasting gain: the Khwarezmians fell out with Egypt and were defeated near Homs by Al-Mansur Ibrahim in 1246, and Baybars, accused of siding with them, was arrested by as-Salih Ayyub and died in prison.
battle-of-lade: The Ionian Revolt began in 499 BCE, after the Milesian tyrant Aristagoras, whose joint expedition with the Persian satrap Artaphernes against Naxos had failed, incited the Ionian cities to rise against Darius the Great. Persia had sponsored a tyrant in each Ionian city, and the tyrants were the revolt's primary grievance. In 498 BCE Athens and Eretria sent twenty-five triremes, and the Ionians took the lower city of Sardis but were routed at Ephesus. The revolt spread to Caria and Cyprus. By 494 BCE the Persian army and navy had regrouped and made for Miletus. The Ionians left the defence of its walls to the Milesians and gathered their fleet at the island of Lade to fight for Miletus at sea.

According to Herodotus the Persian fleet numbered 600 ships, provided by the Phoenicians, Egyptians, Cilicians and Cypriots. The Ionians were joined by the Aeolians of Lesbos. The Persians, uncertain of victory, had the expelled Ionian tyrants offer each contingent lenience if it deserted, and threaten enslavement if it did not. The Phocaean general Dionysius trained the fleet for seven days, until the Ionians, unused to hard work, refused to obey and stayed in camp. According to Herodotus the Samians then accepted the Persian offer. Some modern historians reject this, since his account derives from the Samians, who may have invented the dissent to excuse their treachery.

When the fleets met, the Samian contingent hoisted sails and left, as agreed, though eleven Samian ships stayed and fought; the Samians later raised a pillar in their marketplace for those crews. The Lesbians fled, and the western wing collapsed. Only the large Chian fleet stood its ground and suffered huge casualties before it sailed home.

With the defeat the revolt was effectively over. The Persians besieged Miletus, mining its walls, and according to Herodotus most of the men were killed and the women and children enslaved. Archaeology partly supports this, showing widespread destruction. Darius settled the captive Milesians near the mouth of the Tigris. Many Samians emigrated to Sicily. In 493 BCE the Persians took Chios, Lesbos, Tenedos and the remaining cities of Ionia. Darius then resolved to punish Athens and Eretria for their support of the revolt, and the first Persian invasion of Greece began in 492 BCE.
battle-of-lagos-1759: In 1759 the ministers of Louis XV planned a direct invasion of Britain, gathering an army of 17,000 at Vannes and nearly 100 transports near Quiberon Bay. After the British took Guadeloupe, whose governor surrendered on 1 May, Paris decided to send the Mediterranean Fleet under Admiral Jean-François de La Clue-Sabran to reinforce Maximin de Bompart in the West Indies. La Clue left Toulon on 5 August with twelve ships of the line and three frigates, meaning to pass the Strait of Gibraltar by night. Boscawen had brought the British Mediterranean fleet into Gibraltar on 4 August for urgent repairs, with orders to stop any French breakout.

The frigate HMS Gibraltar sighted the French late on 17 August. The British left port in confusion, many captains ashore and sails being fitted in the dark; by 11:00 pm eight ships of the line were at sea, the rest following under Vice-Admiral Thomas Brodrick. Knowing he had been seen, La Clue turned west for the open Atlantic instead of the rendezvous at Cádiz, but the French navy had no effective system of night signals and eight of his fifteen ships held on for Cádiz. At dawn on 18 August he had only seven ships, and the British overhauled them in the afternoon.

The rearmost French ship, Centaure, fought five British ships for five hours before surrendering. Boscawen in Namur engaged La Clue's flagship Océan, which had nearly 200 men killed or wounded, La Clue among the wounded, and escaped when Namur lost a mast. In the moonlit night Souverain and Guerrier slipped away. La Clue took the other four into neutral Portuguese waters west of Lagos, where Boscawen attacked regardless: Océan and Redoutable, run ashore, were burned and blew up, and Modeste and Téméraire were taken.

The French had 500 men killed, wounded or captured, the British 56 killed and 196 wounded. The five French ships at Cádiz were blockaded by Brodrick and later returned to Toulon. Britain placated Portugal over the breach of its neutrality, which the Spanish and French governments cited three years later among their pretexts for invading Portugal. Five of Boscawen's ships were with Admiral Edward Hawke when he destroyed the Brest fleet in Quiberon Bay in November, and the run of victories made 1759 an annus mirabilis for Britain. Olaudah Equiano, then a young slave, served on the British side and described the battle in his autobiography.
battle-of-laings-nek: After the Boers declared the independence of the Transvaal in 1880, the British suffered a series of defeats trying to regain it. On 20 December 1880 Lieutenant-Colonel Philip Robert Anstruther, marching elements of the 94th Regiment from Lydenburg to Pretoria, was stopped at Bronkhorstspruit; when he refused to turn back, an ambush cut down 155 of his 259 men. Colley did not wait for reinforcements. He gathered his force at Newcastle in Natal, sent the Boers an ultimatum and, when it was rejected, advanced on Laing's Nek, a ridge blocking the road from Newcastle to Standerton.

The Natal Field Force numbered around 1,216 officers and men: five companies each of the 58th Regiment and the 3rd Battalion, 60th Rifles, about 150 men of the Mounted Squadron, Royal Navy sailors with two 7-pounder guns and Royal Artillery with four 9-pounders. Commandant-General Joubert had about 2,000 Boers in the area, at least 400 of them fortifying the heights. At about half past nine the guns bombarded the Boer positions on Table Hill, and ten minutes later the 58th advanced over broken ground.

The Mounted Squadron charged Brownlow's Kop but was met by entrenched Boers on the reverse slope and had to withdraw. At 11:00, as the 58th reached the summit of Table Hill, concealed Boers fired on them from trenches 150 m away, killing both commanding officers, Major Hingeston and Colonel Deane. Lieutenant Lancelot Baillie, carrying the Regimental Colour, was mortally wounded. Two companies of the 60th Rifles covered the retreat, and by noon the battle was over.

The British lost 84 killed, 113 wounded and 2 captured, most of them from the 58th, which lost about 35% of its strength; several of Colley's staff were among the dead. The Boers reported 14 killed and 27 wounded. Lieutenant Alan Richard Hill, who had carried the Queen's Colour, and Private John Doogan of the 1st King's Dragoon Guards, who gave his horse to the dismounted Major William Vesey Brownlow, received the Victoria Cross. A month later Colley was killed at the Battle of Majuba Hill, which ended the war.
battle-of-lake-george: In 1755 General Edward Braddock and the provincial governors planned four campaigns against New France, and Sir William Johnson, who had no experience of war, was given the task of taking Fort St. Frédéric at Crown Point. His army of colonial volunteers from Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and New York reached the southern end of the Lac du Saint Sacrement on 28 August 1755, and he renamed it Lake George in honour of George II.

Baron Dieskau, learning from a prisoner that only 500 men held Fort Lyman, later Fort Edward, set out on 2 September with a column of 1,500 to cut Johnson's supplies. His Abenaki allies would not attack a fort they expected to have cannon, so on the morning of 8 September he turned towards Lake George instead.

Johnson sent Colonel Ephraim Williams south with 1,000 provincial troops and 200 Mohawks under Hendrick Theyanoguin. Warned by a deserter, Dieskau laid an ambush in a ravine, which was set off early when Christian Iroquois on the French side saw relatives in the column and fired warning shots. The column collapsed in what became known as the Bloody Morning Scout: Williams was killed, Hendrick was bayoneted after his horse was shot, and the French lost Jacques Legardeur de Saint-Pierre, commander of their Canadians and Indians.

The survivors fled to Johnson's camp, where he threw up barricades of wagons, overturned boats and felled trees. Dieskau led his grenadiers along the lake road, but the Caughnawagas would not attack a camp defended by hundreds of their Mohawk kinsmen, and the Abenakis and Canadians held back with them. Johnson's three cannon, firing grapeshot, broke the advance, and Dieskau was shot while calling the Canadians forward. Around 4 pm the French withdrew, and that evening a detachment from Fort Edward under Nathaniel Folsom attacked them near Bloody Pond.

Dieskau, left on the field, was carried to Johnson's tent, and Johnson protected him from Mohawks who wished to burn him for Hendrick's death. Accounts of the losses conflict: Ian K. Steele gives 331 killed, wounded and missing on the British side and 339 on the French. Johnson received a baronetcy and £5,000, while Dieskau was censured and spent much of his life in captivity. Before the battle Williams had made a will at Albany for the foundation of Williams College.
battle-of-lake-poyang: The battle was part of the Red Turban Rebellion that brought down the Yuan dynasty. Nanchang guarded Lake Poyang, which connected the Yangzi with other river basins, and in the early 1360s Zhu Yuanzhang held key garrisons on the lake, governing them from Nanjing, 560 kilometres downriver. Chen Youliang of Chen Han brought his troops to Nanchang in tower ships, but the city wall no longer stood on the shore, so they could not land on it from the ships as at other cities. His assault on the gates was driven back by cannon fire, and he set up a blockade to starve the defenders out. A small fishing boat slipped through and reached Nanjing in time to warn Zhu.

Zhu's fleet reached Hukou on 24 August, relieved Nanchang on the 28th and met Chen's fleet on the lake the next day, with forces only a third the size of his enemy's. A Ming source lists fire bombs, fire guns, fire arrows, fire lances, iron bombs and rockets among his arms, showing older gunpowder weapons in use beside guns. On 30 August Zhu deployed eleven squadrons, ordered to fire gunpowder weapons first, then bows and crossbows, then close in. They burned twenty or more vessels, but his own flagship caught fire and ran onto a sandbar, and Chen's ships drove his line back into the shallows.

When the wind shifted towards Chen's fleet, Zhu sent burning ships into it and destroyed several hundred vessels; incendiary weapons rather than guns decided the battle. On 2 September Zhu's ships isolated and destroyed larger enemy warships, and then held Chen under blockade for a month. Chen's attempted breakout on 4 October was scattered by fire ships set adrift, and in the fighting he was killed by an arrow to the head.

Chen Youliang's son Chen Li succeeded him and surrendered to Zhu in 1364. The victory made Zhu's Western Wu the leading rebel group. Five years later it overthrew the Yuan, and Zhu Yuanzhang became the first emperor of the Ming dynasty as the Hongwu Emperor.
battle-of-lake-regillus: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the seventh and last King of Rome, had been expelled in 509 BCE, and the battle was the last attempt of the Tarquins to win back the throne. The threat from Rome's former allies in Latium led to the appointment of Aulus Postumius Albus as dictator. The year has been uncertain since antiquity: Livy gives 499 BCE but notes sources that place it in Postumius's consulship of 496 BCE, Dionysius of Halicarnassus gives 496 BCE, and some modern authors suggest 493 or 489 BCE. The lake lay in an old volcanic crater between Rome and Tusculum and was drained in the fourth century BCE. Livy says Volscian troops coming to aid the Latins arrived too late.

Postumius led the infantry, with Titus Aebutius Elva as Master of the Horse, while the elderly Tarquin fought alongside his last surviving son, Titus. In the opening fighting the king was wounded attacking Postumius, and Aebutius and Mamilius wounded each other. The exiles pressed the Romans hard and killed Marcus Valerius Volusus, until Postumius brought up fresh men from his bodyguard.

Titus Herminius Aquilinus, who had fought beside Horatius at the Sublician bridge, killed Mamilius but was struck by a javelin while stripping the body. With the outcome in doubt, Postumius ordered the cavalry to dismount and fight on foot, and the Latins were driven back and their camp taken. Postumius returned to Rome and held a triumph.

Legend held that the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, fought for Rome as two young horsemen, and Postumius ordered a temple to them in the Roman Forum where they were said to have watered their horses. Plutarch records the battle as the first engagement of the young Coriolanus, who won an oak garland. In the 19th century Thomas Macaulay told the story in his Lays of Ancient Rome.
battle-of-lake-trasimene: Carthage and Rome had fought the First Punic War from 264 to 241 BCE. Afterwards the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca expanded Carthaginian Iberia into an autonomous territory ruled by the Barcid family, which gave Carthage silver mines, manpower and shipyards. Hannibal succeeded to its rule in 221 BCE. In 219 BCE his army besieged and sacked Saguntum, which had a treaty with Rome, and Rome declared war.

Hannibal marched from New Carthage through Gaul in May 218 BCE and crossed the Alps in October with 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and elephants. He beat the consul Publius Scipio at the Battle of Ticinus and then destroyed most of a Roman army at the Battle of the Trebia. In Rome the consuls Gnaeus Geminus and Gaius Flaminius were elected, and the Romans fielded twenty-two legions in 217 BCE, ten more than the year before.

In spring 217 BCE the Carthaginians crossed the Apennines by a difficult but unguarded route and moved into Etruria, plundering, razing villages and killing every adult man they met. Flaminius, commanding the Roman army at Arretium, set off in pursuit. The historian Adrian Goldsworthy notes that his troops, marching through devastated land, would have felt humiliated and provoked. The Romans thought the Carthaginians were fleeing and pursued so fast that they could not scout properly. On 20 June the Carthaginians marched along the north shore of Lake Trasimene, and Hannibal decided to turn and fight there.

On 21 June 217 BCE, probably in poor visibility, the Romans were attacked from the flank and rear and had no chance to form even a rudimentary line. After three hours of hard fighting some 15,000 were killed. About 6,000 at the front of the column escaped the trap but were surrounded later that day and surrendered. Nearly all of Flaminius's army of about 25,000 was killed or captured. The destruction of a whole army by an ambush is widely considered unique. Several days later the Carthaginians wiped out the cavalry of the second Roman army, which did not yet know of the disaster.

News of the defeat caused panic in Rome, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus was elected dictator. The Carthaginians marched towards southern Italy, hoping to win over Greek and Italic city-states. Impatient with the Fabian strategy of avoiding major battles, the Romans elected Lucius Paullus and Gaius Varro as consuls the next year. They fought Hannibal at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE, a third and worse disaster, and thirteen more years of war followed.
battle-of-lalakaon: Arab raids into Byzantine Asia Minor had come almost every year through the 8th and 9th centuries. After 842 the threat from the Abbasid Caliphate waned, but semi-independent frontier emirates remained dangerous, above all Melitene, whose position west of the Anti-Taurus gave direct access to the Anatolian plateau. In 860 Umar al-Aqta and the Paulician leader Karbeas raided deep into Asia Minor. In the summer of 863 Umar joined the Abbasid general Ja'far ibn Dinar al-Khayyat in a raid into Cappadocia and then pressed on alone. Ya'qubi gave him 8,000 men; the Byzantinist John Haldon puts the combined Arab forces at 15,000 to 20,000.

Emperor Michael III met the raiders at Bishop's Meadow, north of Nazianzus, in a bloody battle, but they escaped north into the Armeniac Theme and sacked Amisos. Michael then gathered a large force, al-Tabari claims 50,000 men, under Petronas, Domestic of the Schools, and Nasar, governor of the Bucellarian Theme. Three armies, from the northeastern themes, from the south and from the west under Petronas, converged on the Arabs and met on 2 September. Their position was most likely near the Halys, about 130 kilometres south-east of Amisos.

During the night the Byzantines won the hill that commanded the only way out. The next day Umar threw his whole force against Petronas, whose men held firm while the other two armies struck the Arab rear and flanks. Most of the Arab army fell. Umar's son escaped with a small force and was captured by Machairas, commander of Charsianon.

That autumn another Byzantine army defeated and killed Ali al-Armani in Arab-held Armenia, and the power of Melitene was destroyed for good. Constantinople hailed the victory as revenge for the sack of Amorium in 838; Petronas was made magistros and Charsianon became a full theme. Al-Tabari reports grief and riots in Baghdad. Freed from the eastern threat, the empire invaded Bulgaria in 864, and its ruler Boris accepted Byzantine missionaries and was baptised with the name Michael. Henri Grégoire held that these victories inspired the Song of Armouris.
battle-of-langensalza-1075: Henry IV inherited his quarrels with the Saxons from his father, Emperor Henry III, whose long and costly stays at the Imperial Palace of Goslar had annoyed the local nobles. Attempts to restore royal rights over the Harz forests, to extend the crownlands and to raise the demands of the fisc met opposition, and a policy of building castles held by loyal, mainly Swabian officials bred resentment. The great Harzburg became a symbol of imperial tyranny.

In 1070/71 Henry seized the title and property of Otto of Nordheim, Duke of Bavaria, and kept Magnus Billung prisoner at Harzburg Castle. In 1073 bishops and princes organised a resistance, and in February 1074 Henry made concessions at Gerstungen. Saxon freedmen then sacked the Harzburg and scattered the bones of members of the royal family, which shocked the religious authorities and gave Henry a pretext for renewed war.

The two sides met at Homburg on 9 June 1075. The Saxon army of several thousand men was mostly on foot, made up of nobles and their vassals, freedmen and some serfs, many of them poorly trained. Henry's army advanced in five ranks over the open ground south of the River Unstrut, and the Saxons rode out of their castle at Homburg, apparently leaving their foot soldiers behind.

The engagement was less a battle than a rout. A charge by the Swabians under Duke Rudolf almost at once broke the Saxon centre. The Saxon leaders fled on horseback, while the foot soldiers were slaughtered, and several thousand were reported drowned in the Unstrut.

Henry's army ravaged the Saxon and Thuringian countryside, bringing starvation. The Archbishop of Magdeburg asked for terms, and Henry demanded a short imprisonment for the leaders and the confiscation of their fiefs. The rebel bishops, nobles and peasants walked barefoot between the ranks of the royal army to submit. At Goslar at Christmas Henry freed Otto of Nordheim and made him his viceroy in Saxony.
battle-of-langensalza-1866: When war between Prussia and Austria approached in 1866, most of the kingdoms around Prussia sided with Austria for fear of losing their autonomy. King George V of Hanover lost time trying to negotiate separately with both powers, and his foreign minister declared that Bismarck would never break the rule of a six-week interval before an invasion.
