On 15 June 1866 Wilhelm I ordered Hanover, Saxony and Kassel to disarm at once, and the next day Prussian troops, those of General August Karl von Goeben among them, moved against all three.

The Hanoverian army happened to be mobilised for its summer exercises. George sent its 19,000 men under General Alexander von Arentschildt marching south to join their Bavarian allies, while some 40,000 Prussians entered Hanover in four detachments. Falckenstein took the undefended capital, and Helmuth von Moltke closed a box around the Hanoverians, with Beyer to the south and Flies, with 9,000 troops, to the west. Ordered to hold fast and stop any breakout, Flies instead attacked. After a feint towards Thamsbruck he struck at Merxleben, but the larger Hanoverian force and its artillery drove his men back towards Langensalza, routing them and taking more than 900 prisoners.

The victory nevertheless halted the Hanoverian march and let the Prussian forces from north and south converge. Pushed east, further from their allies, and pinned against the Harz Mountains, the Hanoverians surrendered at Nordhausen two days later.

The quick occupation of Hanover, together with Kassel and Saxony, took the Austrians by surprise and weakened their position, since the small states could together have given Austria more than 100,000 troops. The Royal Hanoverian Army ceased to exist. Langensalza also saw the first actual combat mission of the Red Cross, created under the First Geneva Convention of 1864: 30 trained volunteer nurses from Gotha, with Prussian medical personnel wearing the sign of the Red Cross on their arms, tended the wounded on the Prussian side.
battle-of-largs: From the turn of the 12th century the Hebrides and Mann, which the Norwegians called the Southern Isles, were ruled by local dynasties that recognised the overlordship of the kings of Norway. Alexander II, King of Scots, tried to buy the Isles from Haakon and in 1249 campaigned deep into Argyll and the Hebrides, but died suddenly. His son Alexander III, after another failed attempt to purchase them, sent forces against Skye in 1262. Haakon answered with an expedition that the Icelandic Annals describe as the largest force ever to sail from Norway, and it reached the Isles in the summer of 1263.

Alexander drew out the negotiations over the islands of the Clyde, buying time while the season turned. When talks broke down, Haakon sent Islesmen to raid Loch Lomond and Lennox and placed his main fleet between the Cumbraes and the Ayrshire coast.

In the stormy nights before the battle a merchantman and four other vessels were driven aground on the mainland, where Scots armed with bows harassed their crews. On 2 October, while the Norwegians were salvaging the ships, the main Scottish army arrived, probably from the south, under Alexander of Dundonald, Steward of Scotland. The chief source, Hakonar saga Hakonarsonar by Sturla Thordarson, places 200 Norwegians on a mound under Ogmund Crouchdance and 700 to 800 on the beach, though its numbers may be exaggerated.

As the Scots advanced, Ogmund's men ran from the mound to rejoin those on the beach, who took this for a retreat and fled towards the ships with substantial losses. A detachment under Sir Robert Boyd held the mound for the Scots, but late in the day the Norwegians retook it and withdrew to their ships, returning on 3 October to collect their dead and burn the beached vessels.

Haakon fell ill in Orkney and died at the Bishop's Palace in mid December. The saga called the campaign a triumph, but it had achieved nothing, and Alexander III prepared expeditions against the lords who had aided Haakon until King Magnus of Mann and the Isles agreed to become his vassal. In the 14th and 15th centuries the battle was told as an epic defence of the realm, and 19th-century antiquarians made it a conflict of international importance; most modern historians see it as one part of a failed campaign. A stone tower known as The Pencil was unveiled at Largs on 12 July 1912.
battle-of-las-navas-de-tolosa: In 1195 the Almohads defeated Alfonso VIII of Castile at the Battle of Alarcos. León and Navarre then allied with the Almohad ruler Yaqub al-Mansur and attacked Castile in 1196 to 1197, and Yaqub signed a ten-year truce with Alfonso in 1197. When it expired Alfonso resumed raiding the frontier. In 1211 Yaqub's successor, Muhammad al-Nasir, brought a large army from Morocco and captured Salvatierra Castle, stronghold of the knights of the Order of Calatrava.

Pope Innocent III called Christian knights to a crusade. Alfonso was joined in person by Peter II of Aragon and Sancho VII of Navarre, by the religious orders and by volunteers from across Europe. Alfonso IX of León stood aloof, and Afonso II of Portugal, busy with civil war, sent a contingent of town militiamen and Templars.

The army gathered at Toledo in May 1212. French and other European knights disliked Alfonso's merciful treatment of defeated Jews and Muslims at Malagón and Calatrava la Vieja, having already assaulted and murdered people in Toledo's Jewish quarter. The Christians went south in mid-June, taking castles including Calatrava and Alarcos. Led by a local shepherd, Martín Alhaja, they crossed the mountains through the Despeñaperros Pass and, on 16 July 1212, took the Almohad camp by surprise. Alhaja received the hereditary title Cabeza de Vaca.

The fight was at close quarters, with no room for archers, and the Christian knights proved superior. Knights of the Order of Santiago broke the Almohad line, and Sancho VII led his Navarrese knights through the gaps to the caliph's tent, defended by a densely packed bodyguard of black warriors. A story that they were chained together is thought to come from a mistranslation. The caliph escaped but his army was routed. His tent and standard were sent to Pope Innocent III. Christian losses were about 2,000, among them the Portuguese Templar master Gomes Ramires.

Muhammad al-Nasir withdrew to Marrakesh, shut himself in his palace and died a year later. Soon after the battle the Castilians took Baeza and Úbeda. Alfonso VIII's letter to the pope claims 60,000 Muslims killed at Úbeda, with many enslaved, and the Latin Chronicle of the Kings of Castile gives almost 100,000 captured. The defeat hastened the Almohad decline in Iberia and the Maghreb and gave new impetus to the Christian conquest. Alfonso's grandson Ferdinand III took Córdoba in 1236, Jaén in 1246 and Seville in 1248, while James I of Aragon took Valencia in 1238. By 1252 the Almohad empire was almost finished. The Emirate of Granada, under the Nasrid dynasty, survived as a vassal of Castile until 1492.
battle-of-las-salinas: The quarrel between the Pizarro brothers and Diego de Almagro grew out of a dispute over the possession of Cuzco during the first Spanish partition and administration of Peru. Both camps claimed to act for the Spanish Crown: Pizarro's forces held the province of Nueva Castilla, Almagro's that of Nueva Toledo. Almagro had held Cuzco since 1537, having taken it by a coup de main, but Pizarro's forces were by far the strongest in the region. Weakened by a debilitating disease, Almagro left the campaign to his lieutenant, Rodrigo Orgóñez.

Almagro's men failed to secure the Guaitara pass guarding the approach to Cuzco, and the Pizarros' army crossed the mountains. At a war council in Cuzco Almagro still considered negotiating; Orgóñez is said to have answered that it was too late, since Almagro had freed Hernando Pizarro and nothing remained but to fight him. Orgóñez marched his 500 men to the old salt mines of Cachipampa, about 5 km south of the city.

His choice of ground has been criticised: the broken terrain hampered his cavalry, more than half his force, and many of his infantry carried only pikes, though a battery of six falconets gave him an advantage. Pizarro's army of about 700 was mostly infantry, with veteran conquistadors and a contingent of Imperial arquebusiers recently arrived from Santo Domingo.

Both armies placed their infantry in the centre and cavalry on the wings, with Alonso de Alvarado and Hernando Pizarro commanding Pizarro's two cavalry corps. Gonzalo Pizarro led the infantry across the small river between the armies. Orgóñez's guns threw his column into disorder, but the swampy ground kept Orgóñez's horsemen from exploiting it, and the Imperial arquebusiers, once across, opened a heavy fire of double-headed shot.

With the infantry locked in combat in the marshes, each side gathered its cavalry into a single column, and the two met at full gallop, the men shouting for the king and for Almagro or for Pizarro. Orgóñez was shot, unhorsed and killed while offering to surrender, and his cavalry fell back in confusion despite its superiority. After an hour Almagro's outgunned infantry scattered towards Cuzco. Almagro, who had watched from a litter on a hill, rode off on a mule to the fortress of Cuzco, and the Pizarros took the city. Juan de Málaga, the husband of the conquistadora Inés Suárez, reportedly died in the battle.
battle-of-laupen: The free imperial city of Bern had expanded at the expense of the feudal lords around it and came into competition with Fribourg, its ally since 1241, which had been sold to the House of Habsburg in 1277. Fribourg joined a league with the County of Neuchâtel, the County of Savoy, the Prince-Bishop of Basel and other lords, raising some 17,000 men, among them about 1,000 heavy cavalry under Rudolf von Nidau and Gérard de Valengin, and besieged Laupen Castle. Bern raised 6,000 men, with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, allied to it since 1323, and other allies.

The Bernese arrived on the afternoon of 21 June and drew up on the Bramberg hill, about 3 km from the castle, the Forest Cantons on one flank. Late in the afternoon the Freiburgers attacked. Their cavalry struck the Forest Cantons, who formed an all-round hedgehog, while their infantry climbed the hill. As the Bernese skirmishers fell back, up to 2,000 men at the rear fled into the forest, but the rest held, and the Freiburg infantry broke and fled towards Laupen. Part of the Bernese army then turned to relieve the Forest Cantons and routed the cavalry. At least 80 nobles fell, including the Counts of Nidau, Valengin and Aarburg.

A Habsburg force gathered in Aargau by the Duke of Austria and the Count of Kyburg dispersed on hearing the news. Bern became one of the Eight Cantons of the Confederacy in 1353, and Fribourg, after renewing its alliance with Bern in 1403, joined the Confederacy as an associate by 1454 and in full in 1481. Like Bannockburn 25 years earlier, the battle foreshadowed the decline of heavy cavalry before infantry. It is also the first battle at which the white cross is documented as a field sign of Swiss combatants, and the first open-field victory of the Confederacy over Habsburg.
battle-of-lechfeld: In 953 a rebellion in Francia under Otto I's son Liudolf, Duke of Swabia, and his son-in-law Conrad, Duke of Lorraine, led them in 954 to call in the Hungarians, who then plundered the Rhineland. The year 955 began badly for Otto, with the archbishop of Salzburg joining the enemy and Bavarian counts taking up arms. Otto defeated the rebellion at Mühldorf and besieged Regensburg, but raiders from the Polabian principalities still troubled Saxony. In early July he received Hungarian envoys, whom the Germans suspected of assessing the outcome of the rebellion.

Soon afterwards couriers from his brother Henry I, Duke of Bavaria, told him of a Hungarian invasion. The Hungarians, said to number 8,000 to 10,000 horse archers, ravaged the land between the Lech and the Iller and besieged Augsburg, which Bishop Ulrich defended. The Magyars preferred to fight at a distance with light armour, while Otto's army, perhaps 7,000 to 9,000 strong, was divided into eight legions, among them Bavarians, Swabians, Frankish troops under Conrad, a Bohemian legion and Otto's own royal legion.

After failed assaults on the city, the Hungarians learned on 9 August that Otto's army was near. As it approached Augsburg on 10 August, a Hungarian force crossed the river and attacked the Bohemian legion on the flank, routing it and damaging the two Swabian legions. The Hungarians stopped to plunder the baggage train, and Conrad led a counterattack that shattered them, preventing the army from being encircled.

Otto then led his army against the main Hungarian force, which was defeated in close combat, though it retreated in good order. The sources are brief about how the fighting went. Otto did not pursue far, since three legions in the rear had been decimated and the heat weighed on his armoured men. He ordered the river crossings held, and on 11 and 12 August heavy rain and flooding slowed the retreating Hungarians, who were hunted down by troops operating from nearby fortifications. Conrad died in the battle, struck in the throat by an arrow.

The Hungarian leaders Bulcsú, Lél and Súr were captured and hanged, and captives were executed or sent back to their prince Taksony without ears and noses. Otto's army proclaimed him father of the fatherland and emperor, and he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962. Many came to regard him as a new Charlemagne.

The Magyars ceased their campaigns westwards after 955. The Hungarian historian Gyula Kristó calls the result a catastrophic defeat, and Paul K. Davis writes that it convinced survivors to settle down, creating the basis for the state of Hungary. The battle has also been viewed as a symbolic victory of knightly cavalry over the nomadic light cavalry of the early Middle Ages.
battle-of-legnano: In the eleventh and twelfth centuries the communes of northern Italy built governments able to raise taxes and militias independently of older bishops and nobles, while remaining formally within the Empire. Frederick Barbarossa's expeditions sought to enforce imperial jurisdiction. Milan was destroyed in 1162, which frightened other cities, and after the disaster that struck his army at Rome in 1167 the Lombard League took shape as a coordinated alliance of communes. The League founded Alessandria, named for Pope Alexander III. In his fifth campaign, from 1174, Frederick besieged it from October 1174 to April 1175 and failed.

On 29 May 1176 Frederick was marching from Como towards Pavia with about 3,000 heavy cavalry, leaving his infantry behind to move faster. The League moved north from Milan with perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 cavalry and 10,000 to 12,000 infantry, mostly Milanese. A small League detachment met an imperial advance body near Borsano, and the imperial cavalry then drove much of the League cavalry from the field.

The Milanese infantry formed lines with shields and long spears around the carroccio, the wagon that carried Milan's standard, and held for hours against repeated attacks. When the League cavalry reorganised and returned, the imperial army was attacked from several sides. The imperial standard-bearer was killed and the standard lost, and Frederick, whose horse was killed or disabled, disappeared from view; contemporaries thought him dead. The retreat became a rout, and many men were killed, captured or drowned crossing the Ticino.

The battle did not end imperial authority in Italy. Frederick survived, but he had lost the field army needed for a military solution. Talks resumed in 1176 and led to the Peace of Venice of 1177, which reconciled Frederick with Alexander III and gave the League a six-year truce. The Peace of Constance of 1183 recognised extensive communal rights while keeping formal imperial supremacy.

Alberto da Giussano and his Company of Death first appear in the fourteenth-century chronicler Galvano Fiamma, not in any account from the time. In the Risorgimento the battle became a symbol of Italian resistance to foreign rule, and it is commemorated in the Italian national anthem and in the Palio di Legnano.
battle-of-legnica: The Mongols considered the Cumans their subjects, but the Cumans fled west into the Kingdom of Hungary. After Béla IV of Hungary rejected Batu Khan's ultimatum to surrender them, Subutai planned the invasion of Europe. Batu and Subutai were to attack Hungary, while a third army under Baidar, Orda Khan and Kadan struck Poland as a diversion. Baidar and Kadan sacked Sandomierz, defeated Polish armies at Tursko and Chmielnik, and burned Kraków on 24 March. They failed to take Wrocław, and when they heard that Wenceslaus I of Bohemia was two days away with an army more than twice the size of Henry's, they turned to intercept Henry before the two could unite.

Henry II the Pious of Silesia commanded Poles and Moravians, with Bavarian miners from Goldberg, conscripts from Greater Poland, an army from Opole under Mieszko II the Fat and a small contingent of Templars. Estimates of his army range from 2,000 to as many as 25,000 men, and the Mongol force was at most 25,000 horsemen, perhaps far fewer. The Mongols used feigned retreats to draw the Polish cavalry away from its infantry and then attacked from the flanks, with a smokescreen to hide their movements.

Henry's army was almost destroyed, and Henry was killed while trying to flee. The Mongols paraded his head on a spear before the town of Legnica. Estimates of European casualties range from 2,000 to 40,000. Mongol losses are unknown.

Wenceslaus I fell back to gather reinforcements on hearing of the defeat. His much larger force routed the Mongol vanguard that overtook it at Kłodzko, but since Baidar and Kadan had orders only to divert, they avoided a clash with the Bohemian army and sacked small towns. They then headed south to join Batu and Subutai, who had defeated the Hungarians at the Battle of Mohi. Later raids reached Poland in 1259–1260 and 1287, the second unsuccessfully. The battle is commemorated on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Warsaw with the inscription LEGNICA 9 IV 1241.
battle-of-leipzig: Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in disaster, and in June 1813 the Duke of Wellington routed the French at Vitoria in Spain. The allies regrouped as the Sixth Coalition, which included Prussia, Russia, Sweden, the United Kingdom and smaller German states whose rulers no longer felt loyal to the French emperor. Napoleon raised another large army, but it consisted largely of teenagers and inexperienced conscripts, and his cavalry was weak. The Coalition followed the Trachenberg Plan, defeating his marshals with weaker forces while wearing out his own corps in chases across Germany.

Two attempts to take Berlin failed, at Großbeeren and Dennewitz. Napoleon withdrew westward and gathered his army around Leipzig to protect his supply lines, while the Coalition armies converged on the city. He was outnumbered but held Leipzig and its bridges, which let him shift troops between sectors faster than the Allies could.

The fighting lasted from 16 to 19 October 1813. On the first day the French won small victories at Lindenau and Wachau and had a reverse at Möckern, and the day ended in a draw. Reinforcements then favoured the Allies: 145,000 arrived by 17 October, against 14,000 for the French. On 18 October Napoleon offered to surrender his fortresses on the Oder and Vistula in return for an armistice and a withdrawal behind the Saale. Alexander I, Francis I and Frederick William III declined.

On 19 October the Allies attacked the retreating French, while Marshal Oudinot's rearguard of 30,000 fought street by street in Leipzig. A corporal blew up the only bridge over the Elster while it was crowded with retreating troops, and the rout cost thousands of French lives and 30,000 prisoners. Prince Józef Poniatowski drowned.

Leipzig was the bloodiest battle of the Napoleonic Wars, with estimates of 80,000 to 110,000 killed, wounded or missing. It ended French power east of the Rhine and brought Baden, Saxony and Württemberg over to the Coalition. Napoleon told the Senate that a year before all Europe had marched with him and now all Europe marched against him. The Coalition invaded France in 1814, and Napoleon abdicated in May and was exiled to Elba. A 91-metre Monument to the Battle of the Nations was completed in Leipzig in 1913.
battle-of-lepanto: Pope Pius V promoted the Christian coalition to rescue the Venetian colony of Famagusta on Cyprus, which the Turks were besieging in early 1571. On 1 August the Venetians surrendered after being promised they could leave freely, but the Ottoman commander Lala Kara Mustafa Pasha broke his word, imprisoned them and had Marco Antonio Bragadin flayed alive. The Holy League included Venice, the Spanish Empire, the Papal States, Genoa and other states. Its banner reached Naples on 14 August 1571, where it was consigned to John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II of Spain, the overall commander.

The Holy League fleet had 206 galleys and six galleasses, large Venetian galleys with heavy artillery. The Ottoman admiral Ali Pasha commanded 211 war galleys and 63 galliots; the oarsmen were virtually all slaves, many of them captured Christians. The Christians had an estimated 1,815 guns against 750 Ottoman guns with insufficient ammunition, and their arquebusiers faced Ottoman composite bowmen.

On the morning of 7 October 1571 the Christian fleet formed up in four divisions on a north–south line, with the Venetian Agostino Barbarigo on the left, John of Austria in the centre and the Genoese Gianandrea Doria on the right, and met the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras. John of Austria had the galley slaves freed from their chains. The battle was in essence an infantry battle on floating platforms, and the Ottoman fleet was almost completely destroyed.

It was the largest naval battle in Western history since classical antiquity, with more than 450 warships, and the last major engagement fought almost entirely between rowing vessels. The Ottomans, who had not lost a major naval battle since the fifteenth century, rebuilt quickly, with about 250 ships built within six months. The League failed to capitalise, since friction among the Christian leaders ended further operations and it regained none of the territories lost earlier. The loss of qualified crews led to a sharp decrease in Ottoman naval initiative after 1580.

The victory confirmed the de facto division of the Mediterranean between an Ottoman east and a west under the Spanish Crown and its Italian allies. The League credited the victory to the Virgin Mary, and Pius V instituted the feast of Our Lady of Victory, now kept as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary.
battle-of-leuctra: The King's Peace of 386 BCE, which ended the Corinthian War, guaranteed the autonomy of Greek cities not under Persian control. Sparta used that clause to force the Boeotian League, dominated by Thebes, to disband, and in 382 BCE the Spartan general Phoebidas seized the Theban acropolis, the Cadmea. In late 379 BCE an anti-Spartan faction of Theban exiles overthrew the pro-Spartan oligarchs, and the Boeotian War began in 378 BCE.

In 371 BCE both Sparta and Athens were ready for peace. The Theban ambassadors wished to sign for the whole Boeotian League, but the Spartans demanded that each Boeotian city sign separately, and the Thebans refused. With Thebes isolated, Sparta sent King Cleombrotus I into Boeotia, where his army met a hastily repositioned Boeotian force at Leuctra, a village in the territory of Thespiae.

Ancient sources disagree on the numbers. The modern consensus is that Cleombrotus led about 10,000 Peloponnesian infantry, including 700 Spartiates, and 1,000 cavalry, against 7,000 Boeotian infantry and 700 cavalry under Epaminondas, with Pelopidas commanding the 300-strong Sacred Band. Greek phalanxes were usually about eight ranks deep with the best troops on the right. Cleombrotus's was at most twelve deep with the Spartans on the right. Epaminondas, breaking with tradition, massed the Thebans at least fifty shields deep on the left, opposite the Spartans, and held back the other Boeotians in a shallower line.

The ancient accounts differ in detail, and Xenophon, the only contemporary, gives reasons for the Spartan defeat more than a narrative. He reports that the Spartan cavalry was beaten and fled through their own infantry just as the Thebans charged. Plutarch instead has the Spartans opening out their right wing to envelop the Thebans, and the Sacred Band charging before the line was closed. The massed Theban column drove back the Spartan right, Cleombrotus was mortally wounded, and the Spartan left gave way when it saw the right pushed back. Xenophon records almost 1,000 Lacedaemonian dead, about 400 of them Spartiates.

A truce let both armies collect their dead, and the Thebans set up a victory trophy. More than a quarter of Sparta's full citizens had been lost, and Aristotle called the battle the single blow that ended Spartan dominance. Democratic factions revived in the Peloponnese, and in the winter of 370/69 BCE a Theban-led army invaded Laconia and Messenia, freeing the helots of Messenia. Within a decade Sparta had lost the Peloponnesian League and half its territory.

The years 371 to 362 BCE are known as the Theban hegemony, which ended at the Second Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE, where Epaminondas died. Epaminondas's tactics are commonly thought to have influenced Philip II of Macedon, who lived in Thebes as a hostage between 368 and 365 BCE.
battle-of-leuthen: The rivalry of Frederick II of Prussia and Maria Theresa of Austria dated from 1740, when Frederick annexed Silesia, which the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle of 1748 awarded to Prussia. When the Seven Years' War broke out in 1756 Frederick overran Saxony and defeated the Austrians at Prague in May 1757. On 5 November he beat a combined French and Austrian force at Rossbach, but meanwhile Prince Charles had taken Schweidnitz and Breslau. Frederick and 22,000 men covered 274 km in 12 days and joined Prussian survivors at Liegnitz. The army of about 33,000 men and 167 cannons arrived near Leuthen to find 66,000 Austrians.

Frederick had learned the country by heart on earlier manoeuvres. On 5 December, in fog, he left a cavalry unit and some infantry in front of the Austrian right and moved the bulk of his army in four columns behind a line of low hills. Prince Charles, watching the diversion, moved his reserve to his right and stretched his front. The Prussians passed beyond the Austrian left and formed a line at nearly a right angle to its weakest point. The Württemberg troops of the first Austrian line held until the mass of Prussians emerged through the smoke, then ran.

The Prussian infantry reached Leuthen in 40 minutes, and hand-to-hand fighting raged in the village and its church. Prussian heavy cannon on the Butterberg laid down a barrage, which some participants thought won the battle more than the infantry. Austrian cavalry hurried from the right, but Hans Joachim von Zieten's squadrons and others charged them in front, flank and rear. The Austrian infantry broke and retreated toward Breslau.

Of about 66,000 men the Austrians lost 22,000, including 3,000 dead, 7,000 wounded and 12,000 captured, and 116 of their 250 cannons. The Prussians lost 6,344, among them 1,141 dead. Frederick laid siege to Breslau on 7 December, and the city surrendered on 19 and 20 December. Maria Theresa replaced Prince Charles with Count Leopold Joseph von Daun. After Rossbach the French had refused to take part further, and after Leuthen Austria could not continue the war alone. Napoleon, half a century later, called the battle a masterpiece of movements, maneuvers and resolution. A victory column at Heidau, put up in 1854, was dynamited during or after the Second World War.
battle-of-levounion: After the defeat of Romanos IV Diogenes by the Seljuk Turks at Manzikert on 26 August 1071, Turkoman tribesmen moved into Anatolia while the empire's strength went into civil wars; by 1080 it had lost 78,000 square kilometres, with much of its manpower and grain. Alexios Komnenos, a nephew of Isaac I Komnenos who had fought the Turks since the age of fourteen, took the throne on 4 April 1081. In the spring of 1087 news came of an invasion from the north by Pechenegs of the north-western Black Sea region, reported at 40,000 men, who plundered the northern Balkans and moved towards Constantinople. Around 1090 or 1091 Emir Chaka of Smyrna proposed an alliance with them.

Lacking troops after years of civil war and neglect, Alexios won over the Cumans, another Turkic nomadic people, with gold. Their forces arrived in late spring 1091, and on 28 April the combined army reached the Pecheneg camp at Levounion near the Hebros. Alexios feared until the end that the Cumans might join the Pechenegs, but they kept faith. He took the centre with the infantry; George Palaiologos led the right wing and Constantine Dalassenos the left, and Constantine Humbertopoulos commanded the Western knights.

The battle the next morning was practically a massacre. The Pechenegs, probably outnumbered and caught by surprise, had their women and children with them in a wagon laager. The cavalry wings advanced faster than the infantry centre and encircled them, and the defence soon collapsed. Anna Comnena wrote that the victors grew weary of striking. Survivors were captured; men of fighting age were taken into imperial service and settled in depopulated areas.

Levounion was the most decisive Byzantine victory in more than half a century and gave rise to the saying that "all because of one day the Scyths never saw May". It marked the first decisive success of the Komnenian restoration. With its European lands more secure, the empire under Alexios and his descendants returned to Asia Minor and, after the First Crusade, recovered much lost territory, a revival that lasted until the end of the 12th century.
battle-of-leyte: Japan had conquered the Philippines in 1942, and holding them mattered to it because they secured the sea routes to Borneo and Sumatra, from which rubber and petroleum were shipped to Japan. For the United States the islands were a key step in isolating Japanese holdings in China and the Pacific, and a matter of personal pride for General Douglas MacArthur, whom President Franklin D. Roosevelt had ordered out of the Philippines in 1942 to prevent his capture; MacArthur had vowed to return.

In March 1944 the Joint Chiefs of Staff ordered him to plan an attack on the southern Philippines by the end of the year, and in July Roosevelt, MacArthur and Chester Nimitz decided in Hawaii to invade, so that land air bases could be used.

American forces and Filipino guerrillas faced the Japanese army under General Tomoyuki Yamashita. Preliminary operations began on 17 October 1944, when the 6th Rangers took Suluan, Dinagat and Homonhon, and the 21st Infantry Regiment landed on Panaon Strait on 20 October. The 1st Cavalry Division took the provincial capital, Tacloban, on 21 October, and on 23 October MacArthur presided over a ceremony to restore civil government to Leyte. In the drive through the Leyte Valley the 24th Infantry Division inflicted nearly 3,000 casualties; by 2 November only Ormoc City on the west coast was left to Japan.

Yamashita, who had 432,000 soldiers in the Philippines, made Leyte the main effort and reinforced it through Ormoc Bay, so that the Sixth Army had to prepare for extended combat in the mountains. Fighting at Breakneck Ridge, the Yamashita Line, began on 7 November. The defence of Shoestring Ridge ended on 29 November, and the Japanese attack on the airfields from 6 December was contained by 9 December. The 77th Infantry Division landed south of Ormoc on 7 December, under kamikaze attack, and entered Ormoc on 10 December. Patrols met on 21 December, closing the pincer on the Ormoc Valley.

Leyte was the first operation in the American reconquest of the Philippines, and proved the most decisive. The Japanese army lost four divisions and several combat units, and the navy lost 26 major warships, 46 large transports and hundreds of merchant ships. Land-based Japanese air capability in the Philippines fell by more than 50%. About 250,000 troops remained on Luzon, but Yamashita was reduced to a passive defence there. In 1998 it was claimed in Australia that Allied estimates of Japanese strength on Leyte had been passed to Tokyo through the Soviet consulate in Harbin.
battle-of-lincoln-1141: King Stephen's forces had been besieging Lincoln Castle when they were themselves attacked by a relief force loyal to Empress Matilda, commanded by her half-brother Robert, 1st Earl of Gloucester. His army was made up of Robert's own men, those of Ranulf, Earl of Chester, and knights whom Stephen had disinherited, with a mass of Welsh troops on the flank under Madog ap Maredudd, Lord of Powys, and Cadwaladr ap Gruffydd. Cadwaladr's brother Owain, King of Gwynedd, supported neither side in the Anarchy. Stephen's army, which included William of Ypres, Simon of Senlis, Gilbert of Hertford, William of Aumale, Alan of Richmond and Hugh Bigod, was markedly short of cavalry.

As Stephen's lieutenant Baldwin fitz Gilbert addressed the royal troops, the disinherited Angevin knights charged the cavalry of the king's five earls. On the left William of Aumale and William of Ypres broke the poorly armed Welsh division, but were routed in turn by Earl Ranulf's well-ordered men. Outnumbered, the earls fled, and most of the leading magnates deserted the king as soon as the battle was joined.

Stephen and his knights were quickly surrounded. In the account of Roger de Hoveden, writing in the late 12th century, the king fought on with a battle-axe until it broke and then with his sword until that broke too, when the knight William de Keynes seized him by the helmet. Barons of respected families were taken with him, among them Baldwin fitz Gilbert, Bernard de Balliol, Roger de Mowbray, William Peverel of Nottingham, Gilbert de Gant and Ilbert de Lacy.

After fierce fighting in the streets of the city, Stephen's forces were defeated. The king was taken to Bristol and imprisoned, and was effectively deposed while Matilda ruled for a short time. He was exchanged for Robert of Gloucester after Robert was captured at the Rout of Winchester the following September, which ended Matilda's brief ascendancy in the war.
battle-of-lindanise: The battle was part of the Northern Crusades, fought between the invading Kingdom of Denmark and the non-Christian Estonians. King Valdemar II of Denmark had undertaken his crusade into Estonia in response to calls from the Pope. At the beginning of June 1219 he sailed to the northern Estonian province of Revalia with Archbishop Anders Sunesen of Lund, Bishop Theoderich von Treyden and his vassals Count Albert of Nordalbingia and Vitslav I of Rügen. The army camped at Lindanise and built a castle named Castrum Danorum. The Estonians sent negotiators, but only to gain time while they assembled an army large enough to fight the Danes.

On 15 June 1219 the Estonians attacked the Danes near the castle, right after supper, advancing from five directions. The crusaders were completely surprised and fled in all directions, and the Estonians killed Bishop Theoderich, believing he was the king. The Danes were saved by their Wendish vassals: Witslaw led a quick counterattack that stopped the Estonian advance, giving the crusaders time to regroup, and the Estonians were routed. The victory helped Valdemar II to claim northern Estonia afterwards, at the site of the later Hanseatic city of Reval, now Tallinn.

The battle is still well known among Danes and Estonians because of the legend of the Dannebrog, the Danish flag. According to the legend, as the Danes were hard pressed, Archbishop Sunesen raised his hands in prayer and the defenders held while they stayed raised; when he tired and lowered them, the Estonians neared victory, and a red flag with a white cross fell from the sky and gave the Danes the win.

The account builds on two versions of the early 16th century, both from an older source. An edition of the Gesta Danorum published in 1514 placed the flag's appearance in a battle in Livonia in 1208, and the Franciscan friar Peder Olsen, about 1527, corrected the year to 1219. The red flag with a white cross did originate as a crusader symbol.
battle-of-lipany: The battle, also called the Battle of Český Brod, was fought at Lipany, 40 km east of Prague. The army of the moderate Hussite nobility and the Catholics, the Bohemian League, faced the radical Taborites and Orphans, or Sirotci, under Prokop the Great as overall commander and Jan Čapek of Sány as cavalry commander. The radicals set up a Wagenburg, a fortified ring of wagons, on a hill that gave them a strong position, and the two armies stood facing each other for some time. An attempt by the Utraquists to settle the conflict by negotiation failed because the two sides' positions could not be reconciled.

Three days after the failed talks the Leaguers advanced on the radicals' camp. An exchange of cannon fire did little harm at that distance, and then, to the radicals' surprise, the Leaguers began to retreat with all their wagons. Taking this for flight, the radical commanders opened the Wagenburg and attacked. The retreat was a trick: the Leaguers halted and opened fire from their wagons, while their heavy cavalry, hidden near the radical camp, struck from the side and broke into the open Wagenburg.

The radical army quickly collapsed, and Čapek of Sány fled with all his men to the nearby town of Kolín. The battle became a massacre of the lightly equipped radical forces. Prokop the Great and Prokop the Lesser were both killed in a last stand at the wagons. Jan Roháč of Dubá and other leaders were captured, and about 700 ordinary soldiers who surrendered on promises of renewed military service were burned to death in nearby barns.

The Taborite army was much weakened, and the Orphans virtually ceased to exist as a military force. The Compacts of Basel were signed at Jihlava on 5 July 1436, and the next month all major factions accepted Sigismund as King of Bohemia. Sigismund remarked that the Bohemians could be overcome only by Bohemians. The last Taborite force, under Roháč, was besieged in his castle Sion near Kutná Hora; when it fell, Roháč, still refusing to accept Sigismund as king, was hanged in Prague on 9 September 1437.
battle-of-lissa-1866: The Kingdom of Italy allied with Prussia to seize the last parts of the Apennine Peninsula held by Austria. War broke out in mid-June 1866, and the Italian army, though larger, was defeated at Custoza on 24 June. Admiral Carlo Pellion di Persano had been told to clear the Adriatic of Austrian ships and make Ancona his base, but his passivity drew criticism, and in July the Italian navy minister ordered him to act. It was decided to occupy the island of Lissa as a base for a later landing in Dalmatia.

The Italian fleet had twelve armoured ships, including Re d'Italia, Re di Portogallo and the turret ship Affondatore, but both fleets had technical deficiencies and the Italian officers were divided by rivalries. Rear Admiral Wilhelm von Tegetthoff, regarded as one of the most experienced and creative naval commanders in Europe after the naval battle at Heligoland, had seven ironclads armed with obsolete muzzle-loading guns and made up for it with training.

Persano sailed on 16 July and from 18 July bombarded the island's forts, but the batteries stood too high for his guns, and by 19 July the landing had not been made. Tegetthoff, warned by telegraph, sailed from Pula on 19 July and sighted the Italians at 06:40 on 20 July. His armoured ships formed a wedge, with orders to break through the Italian line, ram and concentrate fire.

Persano meanwhile moved his flag from Re d'Italia to Affondatore without signalling the fleet, and this left a gap in the line. Tegetthoff broke through at 10:50. The Austrian ships were painted black and the Italians light grey, and his order was, Ram everything that is gray. An Austrian shot tore away the rudder of Re d'Italia, and Tegetthoff's Erzherzog Ferdinand Max rammed her at full speed. She sank within three minutes. By 12:20 the fleets had separated.

That evening Tegetthoff telegraphed Vienna: Lissa relieved. The Italians lost 38 officers and 574 sailors killed, the Austrians three officers and 35 sailors. Persano was removed and dishonourably dismissed from the navy. Tegetthoff was promoted to vice admiral by Emperor Franz Joseph and awarded the Military Order of Maria Theresa.

It was the first naval engagement in European warfare in which ironclads were used on a major scale. Too much emphasis was put on ramming, since the Austrians attacked a disorganised fleet and sank only one ship with the ram, and longer-range guns soon made the tactic obsolete.
battle-of-lodi: The battle was one of the key engagements of the Italian Campaign. French forces under Napoleon Bonaparte were pursuing the retreating Austrian army across the Adda River. Lodi lay in Lombardy, then part of the Habsburg monarchy. The French had about 15,500 infantry and 2,000 cavalry, with an advance guard under Claude Dallemagne and a division under André Masséna. The Austrian commander at Lodi was Karl Philipp Sebottendorf, who commanded a rear guard of some 6,577 men, most of them exhausted after a hasty forced march. The Austrian army's commander, Beaulieu, was not present.

The French advance guard caught up with the Austrian rear guard at about 9 am on 10 May 1796 and followed it to Lodi. The town's defences were weak and the French entered it and reached the bridge, a wooden span of about 200 yards. It was defended from the far bank by nine battalions in two lines and fourteen guns. Sebottendorf judged it unwise to retire by day and chose to hold the crossing until nightfall. French artillery arrived that afternoon and bombarded the Austrian positions for several hours, while Marc Antoine de Beaumont's cavalry was sent to ford the river upstream.

At about 6 pm the 2nd battalion of carabiniers stormed out of the town gates onto the bridge. An Austrian salvo caused numerous casualties and the column wavered, until officers including Masséna, Louis Berthier, Jean Lannes, Jean-Baptiste Cervoni and Dallemagne rushed to its head and led it forward. Some carabiniers climbed down the pilings and waded the river. Austrian morale collapsed and the defenders retreated towards Crema under the gathering dark, some units fighting a rear-guard action in which Count Attems of the Terzi regiment was killed.

The battle was not decisive, since the bulk of the Austrian army escaped, but it cleared the way for Napoleon to occupy Milan five days later. It became a central element of the Napoleonic legend and convinced Napoleon himself, it is said, that he was destined for great things. His soldiers nicknamed him the Little Corporal; a story that this arose from his directing the guns at Lodi has no contemporary evidence.
battle-of-lutter: As Duke of Holstein, Christian IV of Denmark belonged to the Lower Saxon Circle, whose Protestant members feared by 1625 that Emperor Ferdinand II meant to reclaim former Catholic lands in north-west Germany. In May 1625 Christian was made commander of the circle forces, and the Treaty of The Hague of December 1625 brought English and Dutch subsidies. His plan for 1626 failed in part at once: Ernst von Mansfeld was beaten at Dessau Bridge in April, and Christian of Brunswick's attack collapsed before he died of disease in June. With Albrecht von Wallenstein drawn away to the Peasants' War in Upper Austria, Christian believed he outnumbered Tilly.

Leaving Wolfenbüttel in late July, Christian did not know that Tilly had received over 4,000 men from Wallenstein. Rain turned the roads to mud, and Tilly took the Protestant fortresses of Münden, Northeim and Göttingen. Christian withdrew, his rearguard fighting off attacks for three days, and on 27 August made a stand behind the Neile and Hummecke rivers. Around midday Count Anholt seized the bridge. Taking a counter-attack for a general advance, Philipp von Hesse-Kassel charged without orders and the whole line followed; Tilly's guns held fire until the attackers were 100 metres away. Fuchs von Bimbach and Hesse were killed, and after 17:00 Tilly attacked across the river and into the Danish rear.

Christian, who had four horses shot from under him, fled to Wolfenbüttel, leaving 3,000 dead or wounded; another 2,500 surrendered at Burg Lutter, while Tilly lost around 700. The Danes lost their whole artillery train and two wagons of gold. Christian wintered at Stade, abandoned by most of his German allies. Mansfeld, stranded in the Tatra Mountains with a starving army, died in November 1626. By October 1627 the Danes had been driven from the Empire, and the Treaty of Lübeck ended the war in June 1629.
battle-of-lutzen-1632: Swedish intervention in the Thirty Years' War began in June 1630, when nearly 18,000 troops under Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania. Backed by French subsidies and by Saxony and Brandenburg-Prussia, he defeated Imperial armies at Breitenfeld in September 1631 and at Rain in April 1632. This drew him deep into southern Germany, where Albrecht von Wallenstein established himself at Fürth. After an assault on the Imperial camp was bloodily repulsed on 3 September, Wallenstein attacked Saxony and took Leipzig in early November. When the Swedes learned that Pappenheim's corps of 5,800 men had been sent to Halle, leaving Wallenstein with 13,000 to 15,000 men, Gustavus, with 19,000, advanced from Naumburg to attack.

On 16 November 1632 the Swedish advance was slowed by morning mist and by the Flossgraben canal, so the attack began only at 11:00, which gave Pappenheim time to arrive with 2,300 cavalry. Gustavus overran musketeers holding the ditch along the Lützen–Leipzig road and moved to outflank the Imperial left. Pappenheim's charge drove the Swedish infantry back across the road, and some elite units lost up to 65 per cent of their strength. Pappenheim was fatally wounded. While trying to rally his infantry, Gustavus lost his way, met an Imperial cavalry unit and was shot three times; his body was found only after the fighting.

The Swedish reserve under Knyphausen held the line. Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar then overran Lützen around 16:00 and seized the Imperial battery by the windmills. By 17:00, with dusk falling, Wallenstein ordered a retreat, abandoning his guns and baggage.

Imperial casualties of 5,160 killed or wounded were slightly lower than the Swedish losses of about 6,000, but amounted to nearly a third of the Imperial army. Wallenstein left Leipzig, withdrew into Bohemia and abandoned over 1,200 wounded, who were taken prisoner. Most historians accept a Swedish victory, though it can also be seen as a marginal Imperial one. Gustavus was succeeded by his six-year-old daughter Christina, and Axel Oxenstierna, appointed Chancellor in January 1633, directed Swedish policy. On 27 April 1633 Sweden and its German Protestant allies formed the Heilbronn League, and in July they defeated an Imperial army at Oldendorf. Rumours that Wallenstein might change sides led to his assassination by Imperial agents in February 1634.

A granite boulder, the Schwedenstein, was placed near where Gustavus fell the day after the battle. Sweden still marks Gustavus Adolphus Day on 6 November, the date by the Julian calendar. In 2011 a mass grave of 47 soldiers was found.
battle-of-madagascar: Diego-Suarez, a large bay with a fine harbour at the northern tip of Madagascar, passed to France in a protectorate signed by Queen Ranavalona III on 17 December 1885. In March 1942 Japanese carriers raided Colombo and Trincomalee in Ceylon and drove the British Eastern Fleet back to a new base at Kilindini Harbour, Mombasa. The British feared that Japanese submarines, some with a range of more than 10,000 miles, might use Madagascar and threaten Allied shipping from Australia to the Middle East.

Winston Churchill at first doubted Britain had the resources, but by 12 March 1942 he had agreed that planning should begin. The Free French were explicitly excluded, after the experience at Dakar in 1940. Force 121 under Major-General Robert Sturges and a naval force under Rear-Admiral Edward Syfret assembled at Durban.

Operation Ironclad began on 5 May 1942 with landings at Courrier Bay and Ambararata Bay, west of Diego-Suarez. The Vichy forces under Governor General Armand Léon Annet had about 8,000 troops, most of them Malagasy. The landings met little resistance, but a frontal assault on the Joffre line near the naval base failed on 6 May, and ten of twelve tanks were lost. The deadlock was broken when the destroyer HMS Anthony ran past the harbour defences and landed fifty Royal Marines in the town. Antisarane surrendered that evening. The British lost 109 killed and 283 wounded in three days, the French about 700 casualties.

On 29 May Japanese midget submarines reached Diego-Suarez and damaged the battleship HMS Ramillies. The rest of the island was taken in Operations Stream, Line and Jane, with landings at Majunga on 10 September and Tamatave on 18 September; Tananarive fell on 23 September. An armistice was signed at Ambalavao on 6 November, and Annet surrendered two days later.

This was the first large Allied operation combining sea, land and air forces, and it put the island's deep-water ports beyond the Axis. Free French General Paul Legentilhomme became High Commissioner in December 1942. Madagascar later saw the Malagasy Uprising of 1947 to 1948 and became independent on 26 June 1960.
battle-of-magenta: From 1 to 3 June 1859 the French and Piedmontese pursued the Austrian 2nd Army to the Ticino River, the border between Lombardy and Piedmont. The Austrians under Marshal Ferenc Gyulay set up a defensive position at Magenta, using the Naviglio Grande, a canal that could be crossed only at four bridges. Gyulay had 68,000 men in the I, II, III and VII Korps. The French had about 50,000, and Manfredo Fanti added another 12,000. After the Battle of Turbigo, Camou crossed the Ticino, followed by MacMahon, and with Espinasse they crossed the canal on bridges at Bernate Ticino and Boffalora sopra Ticino, which placed them north of Magenta.

The country was confined, a spread of orchards cut by streams and irrigation canals, and it prevented elaborate manoeuvre. The Austrians turned every house into a miniature fortress. At noon on 4 June 1859 MacMahon met elements of Liechtenstein's II Korps, and the Imperial Guard made contact with the Austrians from Buffalora to Magenta. At 2 pm the Guard Zouaves crossed the canal in boats and established a bridgehead. Gyulay, told of the French attack by Eduard Clam-Gallas, sent Schwarzenberg's III Korps from Robecco sul Naviglio against the French right flank, but Canrobert arrived in time to reinforce the Guard.

From 3.30 to 5.30 pm MacMahon attacked the Austrian I and II Korps. By 6.30 pm the Austrians began a fighting withdrawal while the French advanced into Magenta and beyond. By 10 pm the Austrian 2nd Army was retreating towards Abbiategrasso. The brunt of the fighting fell on 5,000 grenadiers of the French Imperial Guard, still mostly in First Empire uniforms. It was not a particularly large battle but was a decisive victory for the Franco-Sardinian alliance.

Napoleon III and Victor Emmanuel II entered Milan on 8 June and Brescia a few days later. Gyulay withdrew to the Chiese River east of Milan and resigned on 16 June. Patrice de MacMahon was created Duke of Magenta for his part in the battle and later served as President of the French Third Republic. A dye discovered in 1859 was named magenta after the battle, apocryphally because its colour matched the blood-stained red trousers of French soldiers, and a Paris boulevard, the Boulevard de Magenta, bears the name as well.
battle-of-magersfontein: Early in the war the Boers laid siege to Kimberley, and Lord Methuen's 1st Division advanced along the railway from the Orange River to relieve it, driving the Boers from their positions at Belmont, Graspan and the Modder River at a cost of a thousand casualties. While Methuen waited for the Modder railway bridge to be repaired, the Boers brought their force up to some 8,500 men. De la Rey, who had just buried his son Adriaan, persuaded President Martinus Theunis Steyn of the Orange Free State to move the defence forward to Magersfontein, and to dig the trenches in front of the kopjes rather than on their slopes, where British artillery expected to find them.

Unable to reconnoitre the position and without serviceable maps, Methuen believed the Boers held the crests. He planned a bombardment on the evening of 10 December, followed by a night march of the Highland Brigade under Major General Wauchope for a frontal attack at dawn.

The bombardment fell on the empty slopes and only warned the Boers. In torrential rain, which also upset the compasses, the Highlanders marched in quarter column, 3,500 men packed into a block 45 yards wide. At first light they were still in that formation, and they were about 400 yards from the trenches when the Boers opened fire. Wauchope was killed by almost the first volley, and according to Conan Doyle 700 of the British casualties fell in the first five minutes.

The survivors lay pinned down under the summer sun for most of the day while the Boers tried to encircle them. The Seaforth Highlanders overran the Scandinavian Corps, a company of foreign volunteers whose stand Cronje later credited, next to God, with the victory. In the late afternoon the remaining Highlanders broke and fled, and Methuen withdrew his army to the Modder River camp during the night.

The British lost 22 officers and 188 men killed and 46 officers and 629 other ranks wounded, 747 of their losses falling on the Highland Brigade; Boer losses are disputed. Lord Roberts was made Commander in Chief in South Africa, relieved Kimberley on 15 February 1900 and forced Cronje to surrender at Paardeberg on 27 February. Typhoid, spreading from the camps at Modder River and Paardeberg, killed more British soldiers in the war than enemy action.
battle-of-magnesia: After campaigns in Bactria and India, Antiochus III took Coele-Syria in the Fifth Syrian War of 198 BCE and then turned to Asia Minor. In 196 BCE he used the death of Attalus I to attack cities held by the Attalid dynasty, and began rebuilding Lysimachia on the European side of the Hellespont. A Roman delegation there demanded that he leave Europe and restore the autonomy of the Greek cities of Asia Minor. Hannibal fled to his court at Ephesus. Encouraged by the Aetolian League, Antiochus crossed to Greece in 192 BCE, but the Romans defeated him at Thermopylae in 191 BCE, and a Roman fleet beat his at Corycus and, with the Rhodians, at Myonessus in 190 BCE.

The battle took place late in 190 BCE or early in 189 BCE. The consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus led the Roman army, joined by Eumenes II of Pergamon, and faced Antiochus III the Great northeast of Magnesia ad Sipylum, in modern Manisa. For several days the armies lined up without fighting. Scipio could not assault the fortified camp but risked having his supplies cut by the enemy cavalry, and he wished to win before a new consul replaced him. Livy and Appian give the Romans about 30,000 men and the Seleucids about 72,000, though some modern historians think each had about 50,000.

Eumenes opened the battle by sending archers and slingers against the Seleucid scythed chariots, which fled and threw the cataphracts behind them into disorder, and his cavalry broke the Seleucid left. On the right Antiochus's cavalry drove the Roman infantry back to their camp, but the tribune Marcus Aemilius Lepidus rallied them. In the centre the Macedonian phalanx could not drive off the archers and slingers who bombarded it. When its war elephants panicked, the phalanx broke. According to Livy 53,000 Seleucids died and the Romans lost 349 men; modern estimates give 10,000 and 5,000.

A truce signed at Sardes in January 189 BCE had Antiochus give up all claims west of the Taurus Mountains and pay a heavy indemnity. The terms were put into effect with the Treaty of Apamea in the summer of 188 BCE. Lycia and Caria went to Rhodes, and Thrace and most of Asia Minor west of the Taurus to the Attalids. Antiochus had to hand over Hannibal and twenty hostages and destroy his fleet apart from ten ships. The defeat also marked the end of the Macedonian phalanx's dominance on Hellenistic battlefields.
battle-of-maipu: In 1817 José de San Martín had led an army across the Andes, won the Battle of Chacabuco and taken Santiago. The viceroyalty answered by sending an army under General Mariano Osorio, which defeated San Martín at the Second Battle of Cancha Rayada. The patriots regrouped within two days. Bernardo O'Higgins gathered weapons from civilians and merchants, hurried supplies from Los Andes and set up a training camp at Ochagavía, while resistance in towns and countryside slowed the royalist advance. By 2 April the patriot army stood in three infantry divisions of about 5,000 men.

On the night of 4 April the royalists camped at Lo Espejo, about seven kilometres from the patriots. The next morning San Martín drew up on the low hills with the divisions of Las Heras and Alvarado in front and Quintana's behind. The artillery opened fire about 11:30 to little effect, and San Martín then sent his infantry forward. The grenadiers under Zapiola beat off the royalist cavalry on the right, and Colonel Ramón Freire's Cazadores scattered the Spanish horse on the other flank, a charge in which Colonel Santiago Bueras died.

In the centre the Ordóñez division, reinforced by the Burgos and Arequipa battalions, pushed the patriot line back until three battalions sent by San Martín split the Burgos battalion and broke the Arequipa battalion. Osorio left the field, and Ordóñez made a last stand in the houses of Lo Espejo, where the artillery of Blanco Encalada and Borgoño shelled the position until his men surrendered.

About 1,500 Spaniards were killed and 2,289 captured; the patriots lost 800 killed and 1,000 wounded. The battle ended major Spanish operations in Chile and opened the way for attacks along the Pacific coast that led to the liberation of much of Peru. The embrace of O'Higgins and San Martín after the battle is remembered as the Abrazo de Maipú, and every 5 April a civil and military parade is held in Maipú.
battle-of-majuba-hill: Major General Sir George Pomeroy Colley occupied the summit of Majuba, near Volksrust, on the night of 26-27 February 1881. His motive is uncertain: he may have feared that the Boers, whose trenches he had seen being dug towards the hill, would soon take it themselves, while the Boers believed he meant to outflank their positions at Laing's Nek. Most of his 405 men came from the 58th Regiment and the 92nd Gordon Highlanders, with a small naval brigade from HMS Dido. Against the advice of several subordinates he brought no artillery to the summit and did not order his men to dig in, expecting the Boers to withdraw.

The summit's slopes were convex, so that a man kneeling on the rim could seldom see more than 50 yards below him. The Boers, at least 450 volunteers under Nicolaas Smit, used this dead ground. Older marksmen at the foot of the hill kept up accurate fire on British soldiers silhouetted against the sky, while storming parties under Field Cornet Stephanus Roos, Commandant D.J.K. Malan and Commandant Joachim Ferreira climbed almost unseen. At 12:45 Ferreira's men took Gordon's Knoll. Lieutenant Ian Hamilton reported the Boer advance four times, but Colley ordered neither a counter-attack nor reinforcement.

According to Piet Joubert, the British rifles were sighted at 400 to 600 yards while the fighting took place at 50 to 100, so their shots passed over the attackers' heads. Once the Boers held the rim, the reserves in the central hollow came under fire from above, and fleeing men from the front line ran into them. The line collapsed, the Gordons holding longest. Colley was killed trying to organise a fighting retreat, and 285 British were killed, wounded or captured.

The battle led to a peace treaty and to the Pretoria Convention of 1881, under which the Transvaal became self-governing under British suzerainty, a legal fiction soon replaced by the London Convention of 1884. After the defeats at Laing's Nek and Schuinshoogte, Majuba left a lasting memory in Britain, and in the Second Boer War Remember Majuba became a rallying cry. Some British historians have seen it as the start of the empire's decline; others note that the war went largely unnoticed by the public.
battle-of-maling: The battle belongs to the Warring States period. When the State of Wei attacked the State of Han, Han turned to its ally Qi. Sun Bin advised King Wei of Qi to promise aid but to send troops only once Wei had worn itself down in prolonged fighting, so that Qi would keep its own strength while winning Han's respect. Han, believing it could rely on Qi, fought without reserve, and after a year of resistance asked for help a second time.

Rather than relieve Han directly, Sun Bin proposed a march on Daliang, the Wei capital. King Hui of Wei recalled his general Pang Juan, who was only days from taking the Han capital, named Prince Shen of Wei chief commander with Pang Juan under him, and mobilised an army of 100,000 against Qi.

Mindful of his ambush at the Battle of Guiling, Pang Juan took his troops around the Qi army and hurried on. Sun Bin let most of his own men rest and move slowly back into Qi to prepare an ambush, while a smaller force met Pang Juan and at once retreated. As the cooking fires dwindled and Qi abandoned some of its heavy equipment, Pang Juan pursued with a small elite cavalry unit.

At Maling Sun Bin chose a heavily wooded, narrow pass, stripped the bark from a tree and carved on it that Pang Juan would die there, a saying of Guiguzi, who had taught them both. Pang Juan arrived at nightfall and ordered the words scraped off. Qi crossbowmen then shot down many Wei soldiers in the darkness before the rest charged in. By one account Pang Juan killed himself; in others he was among the first shot dead.

Prince Shen was captured, and the power of Wei declined considerably after the battle. The ruse of the dwindling cooking fires became known as the Tactic of Missing Stoves, an example of leading an enemy to underestimate one's strength.
battle-of-malplaquet: By early 1709 the French state was bankrupt and the Great Frost of 1709 had caused widespread famine and mutiny in garrisons. Louis XIV opened peace talks with the Grand Alliance at The Hague and accepted most of its terms, but he could not agree to use French troops to remove his grandson Philip V from the Spanish throne, and the talks broke down at the end of April. The Allies then besieged Tournai, which surrendered on 3 September, and marched on Mons. Louis ordered Marshal Villars to prevent its loss at all costs. Villars could not, but decided to give battle, telling the king his army would dissolve if he did not fight.

The Allies delayed their attack for a day to await 21 battalions from Tournai, which gave Villars time to build earthworks and entrenchments. At Malplaquet the French had 75,000 to 90,000 men and the Allies 86,000 to 110,000. Marlborough used his plan from Blenheim, Ramillies and Oudenarde: flank assaults to draw troops from the centre, then a mass cavalry charge. The Allied artillery opened at 07:00 on 11 September, and Prince Eugene's wing assaulted the Bois de Sars while Dutch infantry attacked the French right, taking Blairon Farm at the cost of over 5,000 casualties before being forced back.

Villars was badly wounded around midday and handed command to Marshal Boufflers. The centre was overrun by the infantry of the Earl of Orkney, and the largest cavalry action of the 18th century followed. As the French left crumbled under pressure, Boufflers ordered a general retreat towards Le Quesnoy at 15:00, and the Allies were too exhausted to pursue.

Most commentators put Allied losses at 21,000 to 25,000 killed or wounded and French losses at 11,000 to 14,000. Contemporaries and most modern historians regard it as an Allied victory. Boufflers reported to Louis a defeat accompanied by great glory, and Villars wrote that if God granted the grace to lose such a battle again the king's enemies would be destroyed. Mons surrendered on 21 October, and the Allied advance resumed in 1710, but the losses sharpened divisions within the Alliance. Marlborough's domestic opponents used them against him, and the Tories won the British general election of October 1710. Historians argue that Villars, by saving his army, helped Louis obtain better terms at Utrecht in 1713 than were available in 1709.
battle-of-manila-bay: Tension between Spain and the United States grew over Spain's conduct in the Cuban War of Independence, and the explosion of the cruiser USS Maine in Havana harbour, which killed 261 sailors, inflamed American opinion. On 25 February 1898 the Asiatic Squadron was ordered to Hong Kong, and the United States declared war on 25 April. Counter-admiral Patricio Montojo y Pasarón had obsolete ships and crews who had not trained for over a year. He gave up a stand at Subic Bay when its mines and batteries proved unready, and anchored in shallow water off Cavite, outside the range of the coastal guns, apparently to spare Manila and let survivors swim ashore.

Informed by Oscar F. Williams, the United States consul in Manila, Commodore George Dewey led his squadron aboard USS Olympia into the bay at midnight on 30 April, through the unmined south channel. At 5:41 a.m. he told Olympia's captain, "You may fire when ready, Gridley." The American ships passed the Spanish line five times, closing from 5,000 to 2,000 yards. Montojo's flagship Reina Cristina charged and was shot to pieces, with more than 200 of her crew of 400 among the casualties, Montojo included. A garbled report on ammunition led Dewey to withdraw at 7:45 a.m., and the crews had breakfast. Action resumed at 10:40 a.m., Montojo ordered his remaining ships scuttled, and the Spanish colours were struck at 12:40 p.m.

Of 5,859 shells fired, 145 hit the seven engaged Spanish ships. American sources counted nine men injured and one death, from a heart attack; the Spanish naval historian Agustín Rodríguez González suggests heavier losses, citing Spanish estimates of 13 killed. Marines landed at Cavite on 2 May. Dewey cabled that he would need 5,000 more men to take Manila, and President William McKinley sent troops. Meanwhile Dewey returned Emilio Aguinaldo from exile in Hong Kong. Dewey was later promoted to the special rank of Admiral of the Navy, and Olympia survives as a museum ship in Philadelphia.
battle-of-manzikert: Byzantine strength in the east weakened under Constantine IX Monomachos, who about 1053 disbanded the Iberian Army of 50,000 men, a step that contemporaries judged catastrophic for the eastern defences. A truce with the Seljuks lasted until 1064, when Alp Arslan took Ani. Romanos IV Diogenes came to power in 1068 and campaigned against the Seljuks, retaking Hierapolis but winning no decisive victory in 1069.

While Alp Arslan besieged Aleppo, Romanos led a large army into Armenia to recover lost fortresses. It numbered around 40,000, with professional troops from the western and eastern provinces, Frankish and Norman mercenaries under Roussel de Bailleul, Turkic and Bulgarian mercenaries, Georgian and Armenian troops and part of the Varangian Guard. Andronikos Doukas, son of his rival John Doukas, commanded the rear guard. Romanos took Manzikert on 23 August 1071 but had detached part of his army to Khliat, halving his force.

Alp Arslan was nearby with a large cavalry force, and his scouts knew exactly where Romanos was. Seljuk horse archers harassed the Byzantines, some Turkic mercenaries deserted, and Romanos rejected a Seljuk peace emissary. On 26 August the Byzantines advanced against a Seljuk crescent whose wings moved to surround them. They captured Alp Arslan's camp, but the Seljuk cavalry avoided a pitched battle.

At nightfall Romanos ordered a withdrawal. The right wing misunderstood, and Doukas ignored the order to cover the retreat and marched back to camp. The Seljuks attacked the confused army, the right wing and then the left broke, and the emperor and the Varangian Guard were surrounded. Romanos was wounded and taken prisoner.

Alp Arslan treated Romanos with considerable kindness and, after about a week, agreed terms. Back in the empire Romanos was defeated three times by the Doukas family, deposed, blinded and exiled, and died of an infection from the blinding. Modern scholars think Byzantine losses in the battle were relatively low, and that the civil war that followed did more harm. By 1080 the Seljuks had gained 78,000 square kilometres of Anatolia. Byzantine writers such as Anna Komnene saw the battle as a disaster, and historians date the loss of Anatolia from it.
battle-of-marathon: Athens and Eretria had each sent a force to support the Ionian cities in their revolt against Persian rule, and the Athenians and Eretrians captured and burned Sardis before retreating with heavy losses. Darius I swore to burn down the two cities. After the Persian victory at the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE crushed the revolt, he began planning to subjugate Greece. In 490 BCE he sent a naval force under Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean, which captured Eretria and then landed at the bay of Marathon, about 27 kilometres north-east of Athens.

Under Miltiades, the Athenian general with most experience of fighting the Persians, the Athenian army marched to block the two exits from the plain. The Spartans, in the middle of a religious festival, said they could not march until the full moon, but 1,000 hoplites from Plataea joined the Athenians.

Ancient sources give the Athenians and Plataeans as about 10,000 men, a figure modern historians generally accept. Modern estimates for the Persian infantry run from 20,000 to 100,000, with a consensus of perhaps 25,000. The Athenians, probably outnumbered at least two to one, had no need to seek battle, since each day brought the Spartans closer, and the marshes and mountains kept the Persian cavalry from joining the infantry.

Miltiades ordered a general attack. The Greeks thinned their centre, perhaps so that their line was as long as the Persian line, and ran for the last stretch under the Persian arrows. The Persian centre prevailed against the thin Greek centre, but on both wings the Athenians and Plataeans routed the Persian levies and turned inwards to surround the Persian centre. The Persians broke in panic towards their ships, and some ran into the swamps, where an unknown number drowned. The Athenians captured seven ships.

Herodotus records 6,400 Persian bodies counted on the battlefield and 192 Athenian dead, among them the war archon Callimachus. The Persian fleet then sailed towards Athens, but the Athenian army marched back quickly and arrived in time to prevent a landing, and the Persians returned to Asia. The Spartan army reached Marathon the next day and agreed that the Athenians had won a great victory. Darius's son Xerxes I began the second invasion in 480 BCE.

The defeat barely touched the resources of the Persian Empire, yet it was the first Greek victory over the Persians and showed that resistance was possible. It also showed that Greeks could win without the Spartans, and it raised Greek esteem for Athens.
battle-of-marengo: Bonaparte led his Army of the Reserve over the Alps in mid-May 1800, almost before the passes were open, and took Milan on 2 June. He cut the main Austrian supply route along the south bank of the Po. He hoped the siege of Genoa, held by General André Masséna, would keep Michael von Melas occupied, but Genoa surrendered on 4 June. On 9 June Jean Lannes beat Peter Karl Ott von Bátorkéz at Montebello. Melas gathered his army at Alessandria and planned to fight his way east. Through a double agent, usually known as François Toli, he tried to make Bonaparte believe the Austrians would march north, and Bonaparte sent large forces north and south.

On 14 June about 30,000 Austrians with 100 guns faced 22,000 French with 15 guns. The Austrians had to file through a narrow bridgehead over the Bormida, and their first two assaults across the Fontanone stream near Marengo village were repelled. At 11:00 Bonaparte realised the true situation and recalled the detachment of Louis Desaix. Melas renewed the assault and broke the French centre, and by 2:30 pm the French were withdrawing.

Desaix arrived at around 5:30 pm with 6,000 men. Tradition holds that he told Bonaparte the battle was lost but there was time to win another. A surprise charge by François Étienne de Kellermann's cavalry, hidden by musketry and artillery fire, threw the pursuing Austrians back into Alessandria in disorder, with about 14,000 killed, wounded or captured. French casualties were considerably fewer but included Desaix.

Within 24 hours Melas began negotiations, the Convention of Alessandria, by which the Austrians evacuated north-western Italy west of the Ticino. The victory strengthened Bonaparte as First Consul after his coup of the previous November. Marengo was mythologised in an army bulletin and three increasingly glamorous official reports; Napoleon's bulletin set a charge by Jean-Baptiste Bessières against Kellermann's, although Melas and Murat both credited Kellermann. A department of 1802 and several French ships were named Marengo, as was Napoleon's horse, and chicken Marengo is said to have been devised by his army's chef Dunan on the evening of the battle.
battle-of-marignano: The campaign of Marignano followed years of Swiss success in northern Italy. After their victory at the Battle of Novara in 1513 the Swiss controlled Milan and restored Maximilian Sforza to the ducal throne, making the duchy a Swiss protectorate. In 1515 Francis I led a French army across the mountains by the Col d'Argentière, hauling 72 large cannon over newly made roads. At Villafranca a French cavalry raid captured the papal commander Prospero Colonna, which stunned the allies. The Swiss then agreed to terms that gave Milan back to France, but fresh troops arrived who refused the treaty, and the cardinal of Sion, Matthäus Schiner, tricked the Swiss into battle by exaggerating a minor skirmish.

About 22,000 Swiss marched out of Milan in three columns of pikemen with almost no artillery or cavalry. Near sunset they met the French, who had a mixed force of pikemen, arquebusiers, cavalry and heavy guns, and who were not expecting battle because a treaty had been signed. The Swiss charged the French guns and at first drove back the German landsknechts and took some pieces, but cavalry under Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, counter-attacked their flank. Night fighting in smoke and moonlight left the outcome in the balance, and many French commanders were wounded or killed.

The battle resumed in the morning. The French guns had been reassembled, and their massed fire tore into the Swiss as they charged. Only the mid-morning arrival of the Venetian forces of Bartolomeo d'Alviano turned the tide. The Swiss then withdrew in a single large square, keeping discipline. The Swiss command was also divided: each captain could decide whether his company would continue, and the troops of Uri, Schwyz and Glarus attacked despite the agreement not to, hoping for plunder.

Francis had a medal struck with the words "I have vanquished those whom only Caesar vanquished", and he was knighted on the field by the Chevalier Bayard. The French took Milan and its Castello Sforzesco, and Maximilian Sforza went into exile with a French payment of 100,000 écus. The battle ended Swiss ambitions in Milan. By the Treaty of Fribourg of 29 November 1516, the "Perpetual Peace", the Swiss gave up all claim to Milan in return for 700,000 gold crowns, and the peace lasted until the French invasion of Switzerland in 1798. In 1521 a service pact made Swiss mercenary regiments a regular part of the French army.
battle-of-maritsa: The Ottomans crossed into Europe in 1354 and took Gallipoli, then advanced through Thrace, capturing Demotika, Philippopolis and, by 1369, Adrianople. Ottoman writers saw these campaigns as a holy war. By 1370 most of Thrace was under Ottoman control, bringing them into direct contact with the lands of the Serbian lords. The Serbian Empire had been in decline since the death of Emperor Stefan Dušan in 1355, and his successor Stefan Uroš V could not hold it together as vassals asserted independence. Despot Uglješa of Serres tried to form a coalition against the Ottomans, but Byzantine and Bulgarian support failed and only his brother Vukašin joined him.

In the summer of 1371 Vukašin was at Skadar, helping a relative in Zeta, when Uglješa called him away. Believing Ottoman control weak while Sultan Murad I was in Asia Minor, Uglješa planned a surprise attack on Adrianople. The two brothers marched east across the Thracian plain and met the Ottoman force on the Maritsa River near Chernomen, now Ormenio in Greece. It was a provincial contingent under Lala Şahin Pasha and Hacı İlbey, not an imperial army.

Estimates of the armies are unreliable. A 14th-century Serbian monk claimed 60,000 Serbs, which historians treat as exaggeration, and John Fine thinks the coalition was large by the standards of the time but nowhere near that number. Aleksandar Shopov suggests the forces did not exceed ten thousand. The Ottomans attacked the Serbian camp at night, while most of the soldiers slept, and the army was massacred along with its commanders. Donald Nicol calls it a catastrophic blow to the Serbs and to eastern Christendom, and a later account said the river ran red with blood.

Both Vukašin and Uglješa were killed, and Ottoman troops advanced into Macedonia and parts of central Serbia. Several regional lords, among them Vukašin's son Prince Marko, became Ottoman vassals, owing tribute and military service. Ion Grumeza holds that the Serbian Empire lost a large part of its ruling aristocracy. Emperor Uroš V died childless later that year, ending the Nemanjić line, and nobles such as Prince Lazar, the Balšići and the Brankovići set up principalities of their own. Fragmented resistance continued until Prince Lazar's stand at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389.
battle-of-marj-ardabil: In 726 the Umayyad caliph removed al-Jarrah ibn Abdallah from his post as governor of Armenia and Azerbaijan and appointed Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, a general with a reputation for effectiveness. Maslama campaigned successfully against the Khazars but failed to halt their raids altogether, and in 729 the caliph removed him and reappointed al-Jarrah. In 730 the Khazars launched a counterattack. An army of 30,000 men under the khagan, Barjik, advanced to the town of Warathan and laid siege to it.

Al-Jarrah marched to relieve Warathan but failed to dislodge the Khazars. As his army was outnumbered, a local man advised him to fall back to Ardabil and take up a defensive position on Mount Sabalan. He chose instead to give battle on the plain of Ardabil. His army was in a weak position, many of its troops being irregulars and levies, while the Khazars were in high morale.

The fighting began on 7 December, and the next two days were fierce and bloody. By the end of the second day the greater numbers of the Khazars had told, and most of the Arab veterans had been killed.
