That night the surviving levies escaped to Ardabil, leaving al-Jarrah with few men. At dawn on the third day the Khazars attacked again. The remaining Arabs chose to fight to the death; al-Jarrah was killed and beheaded, and the Khazars took a great amount of booty from his camp. His army had numbered 25,000, and Agapius of Hierapolis reports that the Arabs lost 20,000 dead.

The Khazars followed their victory by attacking Ardabil itself. They captured and sacked the town, massacred its men and enslaved its women and children, around 40,000 civilians in all. They went on to ravage the whole of Azerbaijan and reached Mosul in northern Iraq.

The disaster led Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik to appoint Sa'id ibn Amr al-Harashi to meet the threat, and he gave him 100,000 dirhams to recruit men from across the caliphate. Sa'id marched to Azerbaijan, intercepted the Khazars, drove them out of Armenia and Azerbaijan and rescued some of the prisoners they had taken.
battle-of-marj-dabiq: The battle belonged to the war of 1516–17 between the Ottoman Empire and the Mamluk Sultanate. Sultan al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri spent the winter and spring preparing an army. Before it marched, Selim I sent an embassy promising to meet Mamluk requests over the buffer state of Dulkadir and to reopen the frontier to trade. Al-Ghawri left Cairo on 18 May with 5,000 of his own royal Mamluks, fifteen emirs of a Thousand, militia conscripts, the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil III and courtiers, but little artillery. He entered Damascus on 9 June and moved on towards Aleppo.

At Aleppo a second Ottoman embassy brought gifts under the pretence of peace. The Mamluk chancellor Mughla Bey was sent back with counter-gifts, and the Ottomans returned him with his head and beard shaved.

At Aleppo the Mamluk governor Khai'r Bey had secretly sided with the Ottomans. The governor of Damascus told the sultan, who discredited the report. On 20 August the Mamluks camped on the plain of Marj Dabiq, a day's journey north of Aleppo, with the sultan in the centre, Sibay of Damascus on the right and Khai'r Bey on the left. The battle was fought on 24 August 1516.

At first the veterans under Sibay did well, killed several thousand Ottoman soldiers and took some guns, and Selim considered a retreat or truce. Then a rumour spread that al-Ghawri had ordered the recruits to avoid combat. When Sibay and the marshal Sûdûn Adjami were killed, panic broke out on the right, and Khai'r Bey, whose forces were the first to leave the field, called a retreat. This was taken as proof of his betrayal.

Accounts differ on how al-Ghawri died. Ibn Iyas says he fell from his horse and died, adding that some said it was a ruptured gallbladder and others poison. In another version he was found alive and beheaded, and the Ottoman account says a soldier killed him. Selim entered Aleppo, welcomed as a deliverer from Mamluk misrule. Discord among the emirs paralysed the remaining forces, which fled or went over to him, and he entered Damascus in mid-October. The victory gave him control of Syria and opened the way to the conquest of Egypt.
battle-of-marj-rahit-684: After the death of Mu'awiya I in 680, the succession of his son Yazid I was contested, chiefly by Husayn ibn Ali, killed at the Battle of Karbala in October 680, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who denounced Umayyad rule from Mecca. Yazid's death in November 683 ended a siege of Mecca, and his son Mu'awiya II died a few weeks into his reign. Umayyad authority then collapsed. Most of the Muslim world recognised Ibn al-Zubayr as caliph, including the Qaysi tribes of northern Syria and the Jazira, the governor of Homs, Nu'man ibn Bashir, and Natil ibn Qays in Palestine.

The pro-Umayyad Banu Kalb under Ibn Bahdal, dominant in the district of Jordan, held an assembly of the loyal tribes at Jabiya, which recognised Marwan ibn al-Hakam, a distant cousin of Mu'awiya I and once an aide of Caliph Uthman, as caliph. The Qays rallied to the governor of Damascus, al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Fihri, who declared for Ibn al-Zubayr.

A revolt led by the Ghassanid noble Yazid ibn Abi al-Nims secured Damascus for Marwan. The armies first met in mid-July 684 at Marj al-Suffar, and the Qays were pushed back to Marj Rahit, about 17 kilometres north-east of Damascus. Twenty days of skirmishing ended in the decisive battle on 18 August. The traditions give different numbers but agree that the Umayyads were considerably outnumbered. The course of the fighting is unclear, but al-Dahhak and the main Qaysi leaders fell. Nikita Elisséeff explains the victory by defections from the Qays and by Umayyad control of the treasury in Damascus. The survivors fled to Qarqisiya under Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi.

Marwan was proclaimed caliph at Damascus and recovered Egypt later that year. His son Abd al-Malik, caliph from April 685, brought Zufar's tribes back in 691, defeated Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr, and in October 692 Ibn al-Zubayr was killed after another siege of Mecca. The battle hardened the rivalry between Qays and Yaman, which divided the caliphate's tribes into two blocs and helped bring on the Third Fitna. Julius Wellhausen judged that Marj Rahit brought the Umayyads victory and at the same time shattered the foundations of their power.
battle-of-markellai: In the last quarter of the 8th century Bulgaria overcame the political crisis that had followed the end of the rule of the Dulo, as the khans Telerig and Kardam strengthened central authority and ended the quarrels among the nobility. The Bulgarians then stepped up their campaigns in Slavic-populated Macedonia, and in 789 they defeated the Byzantines in the valley of the Struma, killing Filites, the strategos of Thrace. To draw them away from Macedonia, Constantine VI campaigned in northern Thrace in April 791; the armies met near the fortress of Provat and the Byzantines withdrew, though their defeat was not decisive.

In the summer of 792 Constantine VI marched north and found Kardam's army near the border castle of Marcellae, behind ramparts blocking the roads to the Rish Pass and the capital Pliska. For several days the emperor did not attack, until, according to the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes the Confessor, false astrologers convinced him that the stars promised victory. Kardam meanwhile hid part of his cavalry behind the hills around the battlefield.

On the rugged ground the advancing Byzantine army broke its order, and Kardam's counter-attack routed it. The Bulgarian cavalry went round the Byzantines and cut off their way back to the fortified camp and the fortress, seized the supplies, the treasury and the emperor's tent, and pursued Constantine to Constantinople, killing many soldiers. Many commanders and officers fell, among them Michael Lachanodrakon. The Bulgarians used the arkani, a long pole with a lasso-like loop at one end for pulling riders from the saddle.

Constantine VI had to make peace with Kardam and pay tribute. Four years later he stopped the payments, which led to a new war in Thrace that ended without a decisive battle, and hostilities went on under Kardam's successor Krum. The victory marked the end of Bulgaria's decades of crisis: the state entered the 9th century united and stronger, which helped Krum win his string of victories over Byzantium.
battle-of-maserfield: Since the death of Oswald's uncle Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield Chase in 633, the Mercians under Penda had stood in the way of Northumbrian power south of the Humber. Oswald defeated Cadwallon ap Cadfan of Gwynedd, Penda's ally at Hatfield, at Heavenfield in 634 and re-established Northumbrian hegemony across much of Britain. Penda is thought to have recognised Oswald's authority in some form, but may still have been hostile to it, or have been seen by Oswald as a threat.

The cause of the war is unknown. Bede, writing in the next century and portraying Oswald as a saintly figure, says only that he died fighting for his country, and may have left out Oswald's aggressive warfare. If the battle was fought at Oswestry, which was probably still in the territory of Powys, Oswald was in enemy country and on the offensive; the site is still debated, and in 2020 Andrew Breeze suggested Forden in Powys.

Penda had Welsh allies. Welshmen from Pengwern took part according to the Canu Heledd, probably on the Mercian side, and the poem Marwnad Cynddylan may refer to Cynddylan ap Cyndrwyn of Powys answering Penda's call. Bede tells that Oswald prayed for the souls of his soldiers when he saw that he was about to die. His body was cut into pieces and his head and arms mounted on poles, and his brother and successor Oswiu recovered them the next year. According to the Historia Brittonum and the Annales Cambriae, Penda's brother Eowa, also said to have been a king of the Mercians, was killed in the battle too, possibly fighting as Oswald's ally.

Deira chose a king of its own, Oswine, while Bernicia was ruled by Oswiu, and Northumbria stayed divided and weakened until after the Battle of the Winwaed, despite Oswine's murder on Oswiu's orders in 651. Frank Stenton judged that the battle left Penda the most formidable king in England. He raided Bernicia and once besieged Bamburgh, until he was killed fighting the Bernicians at the Winwaed in 655. Bede reports miracles attributed to Oswald's bones and to the spot where he died.
battle-of-maysalun: Emir Faisal's Arab forces, backed by the British Army, captured Damascus from the Ottomans on 30 October 1918, although the Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916 had divided the Ottoman Arab provinces between the British and French governments. The Syrian National Congress proclaimed the Kingdom of Syria on 8 March 1920 with Faisal as king, and in April the San Remo Conference gave France the mandate over Syria. General Henri Gouraud, whose forces had landed at Beirut in November 1919, issued an ultimatum on 14 July 1920 demanding that Faisal disband the Arab Army and submit to French authority. On 18 July Faisal and all his cabinet but the war minister, Yusuf al-Azma, accepted. Al-Azma opposed surrender and asked to confront the French.

Gouraud then demanded that French troops advance to Maysalun, where water wells were abundant. This convinced Faisal's cabinet that he meant to take Syria by force, and it rejected the ultimatum. Al-Azma set out from Damascus on 23 July with remnants of the army and civilian volunteers, around 4,000 by some estimates. They had rifles discarded by Ottoman soldiers, a number of machine guns and about 15 artillery pieces, with little ammunition.

The French Army of the Levant under General Mariano Goybet numbered 9,000 to 12,000 troops, mostly Senegalese and Algerian, with tanks and aircraft. It attacked at about 5:00 on 24 July. The Syrians resisted at first but lacked coordination. By 8:30 the French had broken the central trench, and by 10:00 the battle was effectively over. French forces reached al-Azma's headquarters at 10:30, where he was shot down by a French tank unit, in one account. Intermittent clashes continued until 13:30.

The French Army claimed 42 of its soldiers killed, 152 wounded and 14 missing, and about 150 Syrian fighters were killed and 1,500 wounded. French troops entered Damascus on 25 July. Faisal left Damascus on 27 July and reached Haifa on 1 August. The French took control of the territory that became the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon, and divided it into smaller states, among them Greater Lebanon, the Jabal al-Druze State, the Alawite State and the states of Damascus and Aleppo.

The Iraqi historian Ali al-Allawi writes that the battle has gone down in Arab history as a synonym for heroism and hopeless courage against huge odds. It is commemorated annually by Syrians, thousands of whom visit al-Azma's grave at Maysalun.
battle-of-mbwila: Kongo and Portugal had been trading partners in the sixteenth century, but the founding of the Portuguese colony of Angola in 1575 strained the relationship. In 1622 a Portuguese army invaded southern Kongo and won the Battle of Mbumbi; King Pedro II of Kongo crushed the invasion at Mbanda and proposed an alliance with the Dutch. In 1641 Dutch forces took Luanda with an army from Kongo, but the Portuguese drove the Dutch out in 1648.

Angolan governors then pursued an aggressive policy to avenge themselves on Kongo and support the slave trade, attacking the Dembos, small semi-independent states between Angola and Kongo that both claimed. King António I negotiated with Spain for a renewed anti-Portuguese alliance and sent envoys to win over the Dembos. In 1665 a succession struggle in one of them, Mbwila, led its factions to appeal to both sides, and both sent armies.

The core of the Portuguese force under Luís Lopes de Sequeira was 450 musketeers and two light guns, with soldiers from Brazil and about 15,000 Imbangala and other African troops. The Kongo army had probably about 15,000 peasant archers, some 5,000 heavy infantry with shields and swords, and 380 musketeers. The armies met in the valley of the Ulanga River just south of the capital of Mbwila, where the musketeers formed a diamond in the centre around their artillery.

Kongo's archers swept most of the opposing African archers from the field and then attacked the musketeers, but the formation held, and António was killed in a final assault. Most of his army broke; the survivors escaped thanks to a rearguard under the Duke of Bengo. More than 400 heavy infantry died, with many more archers and the royal chaplain, Francisco de São Salvador. The king's head was buried by the Portuguese in a chapel on the Bay of Luanda, and the crown and sceptre were sent to Lisbon.

Portugal obtained an act of vassalage from D. Isabel, the regent of Mbwila, but could not hold the region once its forces withdrew. In Kongo the lack of an immediate heir began a civil war of half a century. Nobles and members of the royal family were captured, and some were enslaved and taken to Brazil. Ganga Zumba and Ganga Zona, sons of princess Aqualtune, who had led a battalion in the battle, later led a rebellion on a plantation in Pernambuco and founded the Maroon kingdom of Quilombo dos Palmares, which Zumbi led until he was killed in 1695.
battle-of-meloria-1284: In the 13th century Genoa founded the colony of Caffa in Crimea, and its alliance with the restored Byzantine Empire of the Palaiologos dynasty, which granted it most of its free trading rights, increased Genoa's wealth and power while decreasing Venetian and Pisan commerce. In 1282 Pisa tried to take control of Corsica when Sinucello, judge of Cinarca, rebelled against Genoa and asked for Pisan help. A Genoese squadron blockaded Pisan trade near the Arno that August, and in 1283 both sides prepared for war. Pisa gathered soldiers from Tuscany, while Genoa built 120 galleys, sixty owned by the Republic and the rest rented out, needing at least 15,000 to 17,000 rowers and seamen.

Early in 1284 part of the Genoese merchant fleet defeated a Pisan force on its way to the Byzantine Empire. In the same year the Genoese attacked Porto Torres and Sassari in Sardinia and blockaded Porto Pisano, and Benedetto Zaccaria took thirty ships to support the siege of Sassari.

The Pisan fleet, which carried members of every leading family and most officers of state, came out of the Arno in a single body under the Podestà Morosini and his lieutenants Ugolino della Gherardesca and Andreotto Saraceno. According to Agostino Giustiniani, the first Genoese line had fifty-eight galleys and eight panfili, with the admiral Oberto Doria in the centre, the Spinola galleys on the right and the Doria galleys on the left. Zaccaria's twenty galleys stood so far behind that the Pisans could not tell whether they were warships or tenders. The Pisans fought the first line by ramming and boarding until Zaccaria's squadron fell on their flank. Their fleet was nearly annihilated, the Podestà was captured and Ugolino fled with a few vessels.

Pisa, attacked also by Florence and Lucca, never recovered. Two years later Genoa took Porto Pisano, the city's access to the sea, and filled up the harbour, and in 1406 Florence conquered Pisa. Count Ugolino was later starved to death with several of his sons and grandsons, a fate recounted in the 33rd canto of Dante's Inferno. Among the prisoners was Rustichello da Pisa, who co-wrote Marco Polo's account of his travels.
battle-of-mentana: Rome was declared capital of the Kingdom of Italy on 27 March 1861, but a French garrison kept there by Napoleon III protected Pope Pius IX. Garibaldi's first attempt on the city, under the slogan Roma o Morte, was stopped by Italian troops at Aspromonte in 1862. By the September Convention of 15 September 1864 Italy undertook to protect the Papal States and moved its capital from Turin to Florence, while France was to withdraw its garrison within two years. After Italy gained Mantua and Veneto in 1866, the last French battalions left Civitavecchia that December.

At a congress in Geneva on 9 September 1867 Garibaldi denounced the papacy, and he was left free to raise about 10,000 volunteers to march on Rome while a rising broke out inside it. His open preparations gave Napoleon III time to send a relief force.

In October 1867 the volunteers invaded Lazio. On 22 October revolutionaries in Rome seized the Capitoline Hill and Piazza Colonna, and a mine exploded under the Serristori barracks of the Papal Zouaves, killing 27 people, but the rising was put down. Enrico Cairoli was mortally wounded at Villa Glori and his brother Giovanni severely wounded. Garibaldi, with about 8,100 men, took Monterotondo and waited for an insurrection that never came, while a French force landed at Civitavecchia.

Early on 3 November papal troops under General Hermann Kanzler and French troops under General Balthazar de Polhès advanced along the Via Nomentana. The volunteers had almost no artillery or cavalry. Driven from a position south of Mentana, they held the fortified village against repeated attacks until three companies of Zouaves seized the road to Monterotondo. Garibaldi could not stop the rout; survivors held out in the castle, and some surrendered the next morning.

On 4 November Garibaldi withdrew to the Kingdom of Italy with 5,100 men. The Ara dei Caduti at Mentana stands over the mass grave of his fallen. A French garrison stayed at Civitavecchia until August 1870, when the Franco-Prussian War recalled it, and the Italian Army took Rome on 20 September 1870.
battle-of-midway: Japan had quickly won its first goals in the Pacific, taking Hong Kong, the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies. After the Doolittle air raid on Tokyo in April 1942, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto planned Operation MI, an attack on Midway Atoll meant to draw out and destroy the American Pacific Fleet, above all its carriers. The plan was complex, scattered its forces over hundreds of miles of sea, and assumed that only two American carriers were available.

The United States had an advantage in intelligence. Cryptanalysts under Commander Joseph Rochefort had partly broken the Japanese naval code JN-25b and learned of an operation against a target called AF. To confirm that AF was Midway, the base broadcast an uncoded message that its water supply had failed, and a Japanese message soon reported AF short of water. Admiral Chester Nimitz sent forces under Frank Jack Fletcher and Raymond Spruance, and the carrier Yorktown, damaged at the Coral Sea, was made battle-ready in 72 hours.

On 4 June 1942 Japanese aircraft bombed Midway. Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, who had kept half his aircraft in reserve, ordered them rearmed with bombs for land targets, and then received a report of an American fleet. American carrier aircraft reached his force while his carriers were rearming and refuelling. Akagi was set ablaze by a single hit that exploded among armed and fuelled aircraft, and Kaga and Sōryū were also sunk.

The last carrier, Hiryū, counterattacked and hit Yorktown with three bombs, but that afternoon American dive bombers left her unable to operate aircraft. All four Japanese fleet carriers were sunk, as was the heavy cruiser Mikuma. Japan lost 3,057 men, including many pilots hard to replace. The United States lost Yorktown and the destroyer Hammann.

American forces withdrew once pursuit became too hazardous, and returned to Pearl Harbor after 10 June. Three American airmen captured during the battle were killed by their captors. After Midway and the Solomon Islands campaign, Japan could not replace its losses in ships and trained men, while American industrial and training capacity grew. The depth of the sea made the wrecks hard to find: Robert Ballard located Yorktown in 1998, and in 1999 an expedition found wreckage of Kaga. In 2000 the atoll was designated the Battle of Midway National Memorial.
battle-of-mikatagahara: In 1571 Aoyama Tadamon, a vassal of Tokugawa Ieyasu, resisted a Takeda invasion of Mikawa by building a series of palisades, but he was later killed by a gunshot. In October 1572 Takeda Shingen, having made alliances with the Later Hōjō clan of Odawara and the Satomi clan of Awa and waited for snow to close the northern passes against Uesugi Kenshin, led 30,000 men south from Kōfu into Tōtōmi Province. Yamagata Masakage led a second force of 5,000 into eastern Mikawa, and the Takeda quickly took Yoshida Castle and Futamata Castle.

Ieyasu held Hamamatsu Castle with 8,000 men and 3,000 reinforcements sent by Oda Nobunaga. Shingen's aim was to save his strength for an attack on Nobunaga and a march to Kyoto, not to fight Ieyasu. Ieyasu nevertheless refused advice from Nobunaga's officers and his own generals to let the Takeda pass, and drew up his army on the plain of Mikatagahara, just north of Hamamatsu. The historian Kawai Atsushi argued that this was a necessity, since refusing to fight would have cost Ieyasu the respect of the Mikawa samurai.

At about four in the afternoon, as snow began to fall, Tokugawa arquebusiers and peasant stone-throwers opened fire. Naitō Masatoyo's cavalry overran Honda Tadakatsu's section on the Tokugawa right, and the Takeda horsemen then routed the Oda reinforcements, killing the officer Hirate Hirohide. An attack on the Tokugawa left was held. Shingen then rested his vanguard and sent forward fresh cavalry under Takeda Katsuyori, Obata Masamori and Saegusa Moritomo, followed by the infantry of his main body, and the Tokugawa line broke.

Ieyasu wished to rescue his trapped general Mizuno Tadashige but was persuaded by his retainer Natsume Yoshinobu to flee. Natsume led a last charge to cover the retreat and was killed, as were Matsudaira Koretada, Naruse Masayoshi and others. Ieyasu reached Hamamatsu Castle with five men and ordered the gates left open and braziers lit. The Takeda vanguard under Baba Nobuharu and Yamagata Masakage suspected a trap and camped for the night.

That night about one hundred Tokugawa foot soldiers and 16 matchlock gunners under Ōkubo Tadayo and Amano Yasukage raided the Takeda camp. Uncertain of Tokugawa strength, and worried that Nobunaga or Uesugi Kenshin might send help, Shingen withdrew. The tale that the Tokugawa laid a cloth across a gorge to imitate a bridge appears only in later records compiled by the Tokugawa shogunate, not in contemporary sources, though the site was made a Shizuoka Prefecture Historic Site in 1952.
The battle was Ieyasu's most decisive defeat. Shingen was fatally wounded at the siege of Noda Castle in February 1573 and died in May, so no attack on Hamamatsu followed.
battle-of-minatogawa: The battle was part of the Nanboku-chō Wars. In February 1336 a defeat forced Ashikaga Takauji to flee Kyoto for the island of Kyushu. From this position of strength the imperial general Kusunoki Masashige tried to persuade Emperor Go-Daigo to seek peace with the Ashikaga, but Go-Daigo, believing their threat could be eliminated, refused and ordered Nitta Yoshisada to assemble a force against them.

Yoshisada was drawn into a long siege of Shirahata Castle in Harima Province when Akamatsu Norimura sided with the Ashikaga. Meanwhile the Ashikaga regrouped in Kyushu, defeated imperial loyalists at the Battle of Tatarahama in April and advanced into Honshu by land and sea. Yoshisada ended the siege and fell back to Hyogo.

Go-Daigo ordered Kusunoki to reinforce Yoshisada in Settsu Province. Kusunoki proposed instead that the emperor and his forces withdraw to Mount Hiei, let the Ashikaga enter Kyoto and then trap them there while harassing their supply route, but Go-Daigo refused to leave the city. Kusunoki sent his eldest son, Kusunoki Masatsura, back to his domain to carry on the war and joined Yoshisada near the Minato River. The imperial side had no naval force to stop a landing.

On 5 July 1336 the Ashikaga set out to encircle the imperial army. Ashikaga Tadayoshi attacked from the west with the main land force, Shoni Yorihisa from the south and Shiba Takatsune from the north. A landing by Hosokawa Jozen further east forced Yoshisada to pull back, and Takauji landed his own force between the two imperial armies. Kusunoki's men were surrounded and overwhelmed, and he, his brother Kusunoki Masasue and all his clansmen were killed.

Kyoto was abandoned as undefendable and Go-Daigo withdrew to Mount Hiei. The Ashikaga entered the city and enthroned Emperor Kōmyō. The Taiheiki, a historical epic that is the main source for the period, records the battle with drama and exaggeration. In the Edo period Kusunoki became a figure of loyalty for sacrificing himself for the imperial family; Tokugawa Mitsukuni wrote his epitaph, and Minatogawa Shrine was consecrated on 24 May 1872. The battle was taught as a morality tale until the end of World War II.
battle-of-minden: In 1757 the French invaded Hanover, won the Battle of Hastenbeck and tried to impose the Convention of Klosterzeven, which Prussia and Britain refused to ratify. In 1758 Ferdinand drove the French back across the Rhine and beat them at Krefeld, and Britain sent 9,000 troops to reinforce him. In April 1759, however, the duc de Broglie held off his attack at the Battle of Bergen, and the reinforced French advanced and took the fortress of Minden on 10 July.

Contades held a strong position along the Weser around Minden. When Ferdinand split his force to threaten the French supply lines, Contades believed it over-extended and, on the night of 31 July, moved his army onto the plain west of the town. The French had 42,000 infantry, 10,000 cavalry and 162 cannon; the Allies 45,000 men and 170 cannon, among them a British contingent of 10,000 under Lord George Sackville.

Unusually for the time, Contades placed his artillery in the centre, protected only by his cavalry, with his infantry on the flanks. The decisive action came there through a misunderstanding: the British infantry of Friedrich von Spörcken's division, ordered to advance on the beating of drums, took it as an order to advance at once. Under constant artillery fire, the six British regiments, soon supported by two Hanoverian battalions, kept their ranks closed and drove off repeated cavalry charges with musket fire. Contades reportedly said he had seen a single line of infantry break through three lines of cavalry.

Supported by the British and Hanoverian artillery, the whole Allied line then advanced and sent the French fleeing from the field, with only de Broglie's troops forming a rear guard. The Allies lost nearly 2,800 men killed and wounded and the French about 7,000. The French retreated south to Kassel.

Sackville was accused of ignoring repeated orders to bring up his cavalry, and a court martial declared him unfit to serve. In Britain the victory was counted part of the Annus Mirabilis of 1759, and George II gave Ferdinand £20,000 and the Order of the Garter. In France Contades was replaced by de Broglie. The successors of the British units, known as the Minden Regiments, mark 1 August as Minden Day by wearing roses, in memory of those the soldiers picked in German gardens on their way to the battle.
battle-of-mingtiao: In the traditional account, Xia power was already declining when Jie came to the throne. He is described as corrupt and irresponsible, and as having built the Qing Palace, the tilt palace, over seven years with great sums of money and tens of thousands of slaves. The Shang, whose ancestor Xie had served Yu the Great and been given the territory of Shang, grew stronger through farming and trade. Tang allied with neighbouring tribes and won the support of Yi Zhi, once a slave of his father-in-law, who became his chef and then his minister, Yi Yin.

Tang outwardly obeyed Jie while preparing to overthrow him. He moved his people to Bo, from where flat country led to the Xia capital, and conquered one by one the tribe of Ge and vassals of the Xia such as the Youluo, Jing, Wen, Gu and, after repeated wars, Kunwu. The Shuo Yuan records that when Tang withheld tribute, Jie summoned the Nine Barbaric Tribes of the Dongyi against him, and Tang paid it again.

When several tribes rebelled against the Xia, Tang attacked. Before the armies met at Mingtiao he gave the speech known as the Oath of Tang. His troops attacked from Er, while Jie's men ignored his commands and surrendered or fled. Tang drove Jie to Kunwu and, after taking it, into exile at Nanchao, where Jie stayed until his death. The Rong Cheng Shi, a Warring States text first published in academia in 1994, divides the war into three defeats of Jie: at Yousong, at Mingtiao at Lishan, and finally at Nanchao.

Tradition counts Tang's rising as the first noble revolution in Chinese history and the Shang as China's second dynasty. Its history is uncertain: the Xia appear only in records written after the Shang, and no direct archaeological evidence for them has been found, though some scholars place them in the Erlitou culture. Most sources put Mingtiao near Xia County in southern Shanxi, but only on the evidence of names in the classical texts, and two scholars, reasoning from the burial site of Emperor Shun, have proposed Jingzhou.
battle-of-misar: The battle was fought from 13 to 15 August 1806, a year after the insurgents had repulsed an Ottoman force at Ivankovac. As an Ottoman army advanced towards rebel-held Belgrade, Karađorđe met his commanders at Mišar and chose a position on the field on top of Mišar Hill, between the river Sava, a wood and the villages of Žabar, Jelenča and Mišar. There the rebels built a square earthwork of about 300 by 280 metres, with a palisade, surrounding trenches and four cannons.

Karađorđe kept the infantry inside the fortification, with sharpshooters in two lines on the parapet and loaders in the trench beside them, while the cavalry under Luka Lazarević and Miloš Obrenović waited in reserve near Žabar. The battle opened with a charge of Ottoman sipahi cavalry, followed by infantry under the Bosnian captain Mehmed-beg Kulenović of Zvornik. Serbian fire broke the first line of horsemen, who fell back into their own infantry, but the Ottomans regrouped, and at one point Karađorđe drove panicking men back to their posts with his sabre.

At his signal of two cannon shots the Serbian cavalry charged from opposite ends. Lazarević broke the Ottoman line, and part of the cavalry overran the Ottoman artillery and reached the headquarters of the commander, Sulejman Pasha Skopljak. The Ottoman centre collapsed and Kulenović was killed, in a duel with Lazarević according to some Serbian sources. The Bosnian army fled, and fugitives were ambushed in the Kitog forest by Stojan Čupić, Miloš Pocerac and the archpriest Nikola Smiljanić, who freed Serb captives.

Many Bosnian beys and aghas fell, and the victory raised the morale of the Christian lower classes of Ottoman Bosnia, strengthening their sense of identity and resistance. The insurgents went on to take the citadels of Šabac and Belgrade. The guslar Filip Višnjić made the victory the subject of the epic poem Boj na Mišaru, in which Kulenović's wife waits for news brought from the battlefield by two ravens. The Russian painter Afanasy Ivanovich Sheloumov painted a large composition of it, and a monument stands in the village of Mišar.
battle-of-miyajima: In 1551 Sue Harukata revolted against his lord Ōuchi Yoshitaka in the Tainei-ji incident and forced him to commit seppuku. Sue installed Ōuchi Yoshinaga, a younger brother of Ōtomo Sōrin, as the next lord of the clan, but himself led the Ōuchi family and its armies. In 1554 Mōri Motonari, a vassal of the Ōuchi, rebelled against Sue, intending to avenge Yoshitaka, and defeated him at the Battle of Oshikibata. He then built Miyao Castle on Itsukushima, while lamenting in public that it could not hold out long against an attack.

The castle stood on a hill near Itsukushima Shrine, facing the mainland, a visible and tempting target. Sue gathered a fleet of merchant vessels and in the early hours of 15 October attacked it from the sea. Mōri used his absence to seize Sakurao Castle, Sue's castle on the mainland, and enlisted the Noshima Murakami, local pirates led by Murakami Takeyoshi, to ferry his troops to the island.

In a driving thunderstorm Motonari and his sons Kikkawa Motoharu and Mōri Takamoto landed on the east side of the island, behind the Sue force, while his third son, Kobayakawa Takakage, made a feint toward the castle. At dawn Takakage's 1,500 men rushed the front gate as the main force struck from behind. Many Ōuchi troops scattered, hundreds drowned trying to swim to the mainland and many committed seppuku. By 18 October resistance had ended, at a cost of about 4,700 dead. Sue Harukata, unable to escape, also committed seppuku.

The Sue forces are estimated at about 20,000 to 30,000 men, while estimates of Mōri's range from 4,000 to 10,000. Because the whole island is considered a Shinto shrine where no birth or death is allowed, Motonari had the bodies removed to the mainland, buildings scrubbed and blood-soaked soil taken away, and extensive purification rituals followed. The victory established the Mōri reputation for strategy and naval tactics.
battle-of-mobei: Under Modu Chanyu the Xiongnu had become a powerful nomadic empire, and after Emperor Gao of Han was encircled in 200 BCE the Han bought peace through the heqin marriage alliance, while raids continued for seven decades. Emperor Wu abandoned this policy. After an aborted ambush at Mayi in 133 BCE, Wei Qing won the first proper Han victory with a raid on the Xiongnu holy site of Longcheng in 129 BCE, and over the next ten years he and his nephew Huo Qubing recaptured the Hetao and Hexi regions.

On the advice of Zhao Xin, the Yizhixie Chanyu withdrew north of the Gobi, hoping the desert would shield him. In early 119 BCE Emperor Wu sent two columns of 50,000 cavalry each, supported by over 140,000 infantry and auxiliaries. Misled by a prisoner, he switched their routes so that Huo Qubing's elite troops would meet the Chanyu's main force.

Huo Qubing, marching over 1,000 miles from Dai Prefecture, overran the forces of the Worthy Prince of the East, killing 70,443 men and capturing three Xiongnu lords and 83 nobles at a cost of a fifth of his own men. He resupplied from what he captured, held rituals at the Khentii Mountains and pursued as far as Lake Baikal.

Wei Qing instead met the Chanyu's main force of 80,000 cavalry at the edge of the desert after a march of over 800 km. He ringed his armoured Wu Gang chariots into mobile fortresses, and the battle stood in stalemate until a sandstorm at dusk let his reserve cavalry encircle the Xiongnu from both flanks. The Chanyu fled with a few hundred men, and the Han razed the Fortress of Zhao Xin in the Orkhon Valley. The general Li Guang, whose division had lost its way in the desert, killed himself rather than face a court martial.

The wars of 129-119 BCE cost the Han almost 80% of their horses, and new taxes, famine and falling registered population followed. The Xiongnu lost millions of livestock and were driven to the cold north. A truce held seven years, until a raid at Wuyuan in 112 BCE. The Xiongnu never regained their former strength and a century later split into northern and southern branches.
battle-of-mogadishu-1993: The United Nations sent forces to Somalia to relieve the famine of 1992, which followed the collapse of Siad Barre's regime in early 1991 and a severe drought. In March 1993 the Security Council authorised a second mission, UNOSOM II, to establish a secure environment and promote national reconciliation. On 5 June 1993 fighters of the Somali National Alliance (SNA) and civilians attacked Pakistani troops inspecting an arms cache at Radio Mogadishu, and the UN blamed the SNA leader Mohamed Farah Aidid.

On 12 July, in the raid Somalis call Bloody Monday, US helicopters attacked a house where clan elders were meeting. UNOSOM said it had struck an SNA command centre, an account disputed by Somalis, journalists and human rights groups. After bombs killed American soldiers in August, President Bill Clinton sent Task Force Ranger, including 400 Rangers and Delta Force operators, to capture Aidid.

On the morning of 3 October a local informant told the CIA that two of Aidid's advisors, Omar Salad Elmi and Abdi Hassan Awale, would meet near the Olympic Hotel in the Bakara market area. At 13:50 sixteen helicopters took off from the airport for the target. About 40 minutes into the assault a rocket-propelled grenade struck the Black Hawk Super 61, which crashed about 300 yards from the target, killing both pilots.

At about 16:40 another grenade hit the tail rotor of Super 64, piloted by Michael Durant, which crashed into tin shacks. Some 90 Rangers and Delta Force soldiers were trapped overnight around the first crash site, fighting at close quarters and occupying four houses.

A first relief convoy led by Lieutenant Colonel Lawrence Casper turned back under heavy fire at the KM4 junction. A larger UNOSOM II convoy of Pakistani, Malaysian and American troops pushed into the city and rescued the survivors the next morning, taking further casualties.

Eighteen American soldiers were killed and 73 wounded, one Malaysian soldier was killed and seven wounded, and two Pakistani troops were injured. Somali dead, a mixture of fighters and civilians, are variously estimated at between 133 and 700; the Red Cross estimated 200, and Aidid claimed 315. Crowds dragged the bodies of several American dead through the streets, an act shown on American television. A captain of the SNA said it was done by enraged civilians who had lost relatives, and pointed to Bloody Monday.

On 6 October Clinton ordered a halt to all US action against Aidid except in self-defence and announced that US forces would leave Somalia by 31 March 1994. The last UN forces withdrew by early 1995. The wariness of large interventions that followed is often called the Somalia Syndrome. Mark Bowden's book Black Hawk Down appeared in 1999, and Ridley Scott's film of it in 2001.
battle-of-mohacs: After the death of King Matthias Corvinus in 1490, the Hungarian magnates secured the accession of the weak-willed Vladislaus II, who gave away most royal estates and revenues. The nobility cut its own taxes by 70 to 80 per cent, the Black Army of Matthias was dissolved and border garrisons went unpaid. A peasant rebellion under György Dózsa in 1514 was crushed by the nobles under John Zápolya, leaving the country divided. In 1521 the Ottomans took Nándorfehérvár, present-day Belgrade, the strongest Hungarian fortress on the Danube.

King Louis II married Mary of Habsburg in 1522, and the Ottomans saw the alliance as a threat. After Suleiman I came to power in 1520 they offered peace at least once, and Louis refused for reasons that are unclear. Help from Europe was scarce, since the western powers were absorbed in the Italian wars. Francis I of France, defeated at Pavia in 1525, asked Suleiman to make war on the Habsburgs, and the road lay across Hungary. An Ottoman army left Constantinople on 16 April 1526.

The Hungarian nobles were slow to answer their king's call. The army that took the field numbered around 25,000 to 30,000 men, with 85 cannons against about 300 for the Ottomans. The battle was fought on the afternoon of 29 August 1526 on a waterlogged plain near Mohács. Pressed by nobles who wanted immediate battle, the Hungarians relied on heavy cavalry to break the Ottoman line.

Archbishop Pál Tomori led a charge that at first drove back the Ottoman front line. The grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha drew his centre back into a crescent, exposing the flanks of the cavalry, and Ottoman cavalry and light infantry attacked from both wings while Janissaries and artillery fired from prepared positions. The Hungarian army was encircled, and its lines collapsed within two hours. King Louis and much of the aristocracy were killed.

Suleiman did not at first grasp the scale of his victory. During four more days on the field about 2,000 captured nobles were executed. Queen Mary fled Buda, and the Ottomans pillaged the abandoned castle and left. The nobility elected two kings, John Zápolya and the Habsburg Archduke Ferdinand, and the Ottomans occupied Buda in 1541, dividing Hungary into Habsburg, Ottoman and Transylvanian parts. Many Hungarians regard Mohács as the turning point of their history, and the saying More was lost at Mohács is still used for any great loss.
battle-of-mohi: The Mongols attacked central Europe with three armies. Two crossed Poland and defeated Duke Henry II the Pious of Silesia at Legnica, a southern army attacked Transylvania, and the main army under Batu Khan and Subutai entered Hungary through the Verecke Pass. On 12 March 1241 it annihilated the army of the count palatine, Denis Tomaj. Hungary was weakened by its own politics. Kings had forbidden nobles to build private stone castles, so few stood along the Mongol routes.

Béla IV had taken back the lands his father Andrew II had given away and expelled his advisers, which angered the nobles. He also sheltered some 40,000 Cuman refugees, but the Cuman khan was murdered in a riot at Pest, and the Cumans, believing themselves betrayed, left the country, pillaging as they went.

The Mongol vanguard reached Pest on 15 March. After a week of forced marches the Hungarians reached the flooded Sajó and built a camp of wagons. A Ruthenian slave of the Mongols warned them of a night attack on the bridge, and the king's brother Coloman and Archbishop Ugrin Csák, with the Templar master, beat the Mongol vanguard there, returning to camp at about 2 am. At dawn Batu attacked the bridge with seven stone throwers, Shiban crossed at a ford to the north, and Subutai built a makeshift bridge to the south and attacked the Hungarian rear.

Confined in the camp, the Hungarians were bombarded by stones and flaming arrows. The Mongols left a gap open, and those who fled through it were almost all slaughtered. Ugrin was killed with another archbishop and three bishops, and Béla escaped, though Coloman died soon afterwards of his wounds.

A near-contemporary source reports 10,000 Hungarians killed, almost the entire army. The Mongols burnt Pest, killed most of Esztergom's population and occupied the Great Hungarian Plain, Transylvania and the northern Carpathian slopes. Nearly half of the inhabited places were destroyed, and 15 to 25 per cent of the population was lost. Béla fled to Austria, where Duke Frederick arrested the royal family and extorted a ransom and three western counties, and then to the Adriatic coast at Trogir, where he stayed until the Mongols withdrew. Among the Mongols, Batu blamed Subutai for the heavy losses, while Güyük and Büri accused Batu of incompetence, and he sent them back to Karakorum.
battle-of-mollwitz: The death of Charles VI in 1740 and the succession of his daughter Maria Theresa, allowed by the 1713 Pragmatic Sanction, sparked the War of the Austrian Succession. The Habsburg monarchy was the most powerful element of the Holy Roman Empire, and France, Prussia and Saxony challenged it by nominating Charles of Bavaria as emperor. In December 1740 Frederick II invaded Silesia, a province of over one million people whose mining, weaving and dyeing industries produced 10 per cent of imperial income.

Under Kurt Christoph Graf von Schwerin the Prussians overran most of the province but failed to take the southern fortresses of Glogau, Breslau and Brieg. Maria Theresa sent about 20,000 men under Wilhelm Reinhard von Neipperg to recover it. Neipperg slipped past Frederick and reached Neisse, which a small Prussian force was besieging, before him, leaving Frederick's army cut off from its supplies and communications.

Fog and snow let the Prussians approach to within 2000 paces of Neipperg's camp unseen. Frederick, who had never fought a battle, chose to deploy in a battle line; he misjudged the distance to the river on his right, so several units stood behind a bend where they could take no part. The two hours this took let the Austrians, who had been cooking food in three villages facing the wrong way, form a line. The Prussians had the larger army and three times as many field guns, but the Austrian cavalry outnumbered theirs two to one.

Six regiments of Austrian cavalry, some 4,500 to 5,000 men, charged the Prussian right without orders and shattered the Prussian horse. Frederick was swept up in the rout and left the field on Schwerin's advice, and Schwerin took command. Asked whether the Prussians would retreat, he is said to have answered "Over enemy bodies". The drilled Prussian infantry held, killing the Austrian cavalry commander, General Römer. Using the iron ramrod, they fired four or five shots a minute, three times the rate of other European armies, and advanced in oblique order. The Austrian line, with many raw recruits, collapsed.

Neipperg retreated to Neisse without being pursued. Frederick returned the next morning, restored his communications and brought the siege of Brieg to a successful end. He later wrote that Mollwitz had educated him and his army, and he set about training the cavalry in coordinated action. The victory raised his prestige and showed Maria Theresa that Silesia would not easily be regained. It also encouraged other rulers to reject the Pragmatic Sanction, and within a few months France, Spain, Bavaria, Saxony, Savoy and Prussia formed the League of Nymphenburg, widening the conflict.
battle-of-molodi: The battle was one of the key engagements of the reign of Ivan the Terrible. While the Tsardom of Russia was tied down in the Livonian War, the Crimean khan hoped to profit from the weakness of its southern borders. In the course of three expeditions Devlet I Giray devastated southern Russia, defeated the Russian army and set Moscow on fire in 1571.

On 26 July 1572 the Crimean army, numbering around 30,000 cavalrymen, marched towards Russia once more. The historian Spencer Tucker held that the Tatar force also carried cannons, was reinforced by janissaries, and badly mauled the Russian vanguard while crossing the Oka River near Serpukhov.

Prince Mikhail Vorotynsky held the supreme command of the Russian and Cossack forces, with Prince Repnin on the left flank and Prince Odoevsky on the right. On 30 July the armies clashed near the Lopasnya River without much prior reconnaissance. The fighting went on for several days and reached its peak on 8 August.

Much of it was close melee with sabres and spears, which left the Tatars' skill in archery of little use, while the Russians used artillery and arquebuses to great effect. Lacking gunpowder weapons of their own, the Tatars could not break through the fortified Russian positions, nor could they draw the Russians into a pitched battle in the open field. With a second Russian army on its way to reinforce Vorotynsky, they called off the campaign and marched back to Crimea without suffering much harm on the way.

The size of both armies is disputed. Contemporary chronicles give very large and unreliable figures for the Tatars: the Novgorod Second Chronicle speaks of 120,000 men and the Moscow Chronicle of about 150,000. Modern Russian historians think the khan's army most likely numbered 40,000 to 60,000, two thirds of them the Crimean army proper and the rest Nogai, Circassians and janissaries sent by the Ottoman Sultan.
Estimates of the Russian forces range from 20,000 to 70,000 men. The Russian historian Vitaly Pensky puts the whole Moscow army at 35,000 and regards the other estimates as overstated.
battle-of-mons-en-pevele: After the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302 the Flemish retook Douai and Lille, and Philip IV sought revenge. By early 1304 he was ready to attack. The French army, led by the king and by Foulques du Merle, marched north against the force of William of Jülich, while the French navy sailed to Zeeland to join the army of Hainault and Holland. That northern force struck first, defeating the army and fleet of Guy of Namur at the Battle of Zierikzee on 10-11 August. Guy was captured, and the Flemish conquest of Holland was halted. Philip of Chieti, a son of Guy, Count of Flanders, had meanwhile taken up a position on Mons-en-Pévèle with a strong Flemish army.

After a day of fighting the outcome was still undecided, and negotiations were opened between 17:00 and 18:30. When a French force under Guy de Saint-Pol tried to surround the Flemish, it was driven back, and the Flemish then launched a frontal attack that surprised the French, who believed the fighting over for the day. They reached the royal tent and attacked Philip IV, who escaped only because knights around him covered his flight with their lives. Helped onto his horse, the king counterattacked and had the horse killed under him; William of Jülich was killed in this counterattack. The oriflamme, the French royal banner, was lost in the struggle.
Only the Flemish right wing had joined the attack. When the left wing under John I, Marquis of Namur, began to leave the field, the right withdrew as well, and the French did not pursue.

The French held the battlefield while the Flemish marched back to Lille, and the French went on to take Douai and Orchies and burn Seclin. By the treaty signed on 23 June 1305 Flanders kept its place within the kingdom but lost Lille, Douai and Béthune to the French royal domain and paid heavy fines. Bruges has held the Brugse Belofte procession on 15 August every year since 1305, in memory of the return of most of its militiamen.
battle-of-mons-graupius: Tacitus, whose father-in-law Gnaeus Julius Agricola was Roman governor of Britain, is the source of nearly everything known of the battle. The Romans were often outnumbered in Britain but found it hard to make their enemies fight in open battle. The Caledonii were the last unconquered British tribe, and were never entirely subdued. After many years of avoiding battle they were forced to fight when the Romans marched on their main granaries just as the harvest had filled them, leaving them to fight or starve over the winter. Agricola had sent his fleet ahead to cause panic and reached the site with light infantry reinforced by British auxiliaries, finding it occupied by the enemy.

In Tacitus's account the Roman centre was formed by 8,000 auxiliary infantry, with 3,000 cavalry on the flanks and the legionaries held in reserve in front of the camp. Estimates for the Roman army range from 17,000 to 30,000. The Caledonians, said to number over 30,000 and led by Calgacus, who is mentioned only as giving a speech that was probably fictitious, stood on rising ground in a horseshoe, with chariots on the plain below.

After a brief exchange of missiles Agricola sent forward auxiliaries, four cohorts of Batavians and two of Tungri swordsmen, in a frontal attack. The Caledonians were cut down on the lower slopes, and those who tried to outflank the Romans were outflanked in turn by cavalry. The Caledonians fled to nearby woodland. Tacitus reports 10,000 Caledonian dead against 360 auxiliaries, and says 20,000 retreated into the woods and fared better there. Scouts could not find them next morning.

The location is debated. In the 19th century it was linked with almost every Roman site in Perth and Kinross, but aerial photography of marching camps has moved attention to the north-east, with Bennachie in Aberdeenshire and high ground near the Raedykes camp among the suggestions. Historic Environment Scotland excludes the battle from its inventory of battlefields because of this uncertainty. Tacitus wrote after the death of Domitian in 96, and historians have long suspected exaggeration, though Agricola was given triumphal honours. Soon after the battle he was recalled and replaced by Sallustius Lucullus. Within a few years Roman forces withdrew to the Forth-Clyde line, and Tacitus's remark that Britain was completely conquered and immediately let go reflects his disapproval of Domitian.
battle-of-mons-lactarius: In 540 the Gothic capital Ravenna surrendered to Belisarius, bringing most of Italy under Byzantine control. After he was recalled to Constantinople, corruption among Byzantine commanders and harsh taxation revived Gothic resistance. The new king Totila gained support by treating Italian civilians more fairly than some Byzantine officials did, and after nearly a decade he had recaptured much of Italy. The emperor Justinian I sent his chamberlain Narses, who assembled an army at Salona that included Lombards, Heruls and Gepids. Totila was mortally wounded at Taginae and his army scattered. The Goths gathered at Ticinum and chose Teia as king; the Franks refused his plea for an alliance, preferring to let the Goths and Byzantines wear each other down.

Narses took Narni and Spoleto and recaptured Rome in July, with its keys sent to Justinian. The Goths then executed their hostages, among them senators with their families and 300 children Totila had taken from leading families, and carried out widespread killings of the Italian population. Narses besieged Cumae, where Totila's war chest was kept and Teia's brother commanded the garrison.

Teia marched south by long detours that took nearly thirty days. Narses intercepted him near Mount Vesuvius, and Teia camped at the foot of the mountain on the left bank of the Sarno, the two armies facing each other across a small stream with a single bridge. The standoff lasted nearly two months, with skirmishes and single combats at the bridge, until Narses brought up his fleet and the Gothic admiral surrendered the Gothic ships, cutting off supply.

Teia withdrew toward Mount Lactarius and launched a surprise attack on 1 or 30 October. Both armies fought on foot in deep formations, and the Byzantines held. Throwing spears were aimed at Teia, whose companions kept supplying him with new shields, until he died. His head was fixed on a stake to discourage the Goths, who nevertheless fought on for two more days.

The Goths sent an envoy to ask to leave Italy with their money, and Narses agreed on strict conditions on the advice of John. The survivors swore to leave Italy, but a thousand Goths under Indulf broke away, and Aligern held Cumae and Ragnaris Conza della Campania. The Goths failed to choose a new king. Franks under the Alamannic dukes Lothar and Buccelin entered Italy with 75,000 men, and in October 554 Narses defeated them at the Battle of the Volturnus. Campsa fell in 555 and Verona in 561.
battle-of-montaperti: In the mid-13th century the Guelphs, nominally the papal party, held Florence and the Ghibellines, nominally the imperial party, held Siena. In 1258 the Florentine Guelphs expelled the last Ghibellines of any power and murdered Tesauro Beccharia, Abbot of Vallombrosa, accused of plotting their return. Two years later Florence and its Tuscan allies, among them Bologna, Prato, Lucca, Orvieto, San Gimignano and Volterra, marched on Siena with some 35,000 men. Siena called on King Manfred of Sicily, who sent German mercenary heavy cavalry; Pisa and Cortona also sent help. Even so, the army Farinata degli Uberti led numbered fewer than 20,000.

The Ghibellines formed four divisions, one of them 200 German knights and 200 Sienese crossbowmen under Count d'Arras sent round the Monselvoli-Costaberci Ridge to lie in ambush. According to Sienese tradition, the day before the battle their army marched three times round a hill in view of the Guelphs, changing uniforms each time to seem larger. The cautious Florentines had begun to withdraw when the Sienese crossed the Arbia early on 4 September.

The battle opened around 10:00 with a charge of the German knights against the Guelph right, about six kilometres east of Siena. The weight of Florentine numbers told until about 15:00, when the Sienese rearguard under Niccolò da Bigozzi restored the line. At about the same time Bocca degli Abati, a Florentine knight with Ghibelline sympathies, cut off the hand of the Florentine cavalry's standard-bearer. Around 18:00 the cry of "San Giorgio" brought d'Arras's knights out of ambush; they killed the Florentine commander, whose name the chronicles give differently, and the rout began.

It was the bloodiest battle of medieval Italy. Some 10,000 men are estimated to have died on the Guelph side, 4,000 went missing and 15,000 were captured, while about 600 Ghibellines died; the Florentine carroccio was taken. The German soldiers founded the Church of San Giorgio in Siena with part of their pay. Dante placed Bocca degli Abati in the ninth circle of Hell, and Farinata in Hell too, for his alleged adherence to the philosophy of Epicurus.
battle-of-montgisard: In 1177 King Baldwin IV of Jerusalem and Philip of Alsace, who had recently arrived on pilgrimage, planned an alliance with the Byzantine Empire for a naval attack on Egypt, but nothing came of it. Philip instead joined Raymond III of Tripoli's expedition against Harim in northern Syria, and a large Crusader army, the Knights Hospitaller and many Knights Templar followed him. This left the Kingdom of Jerusalem with few troops.

Saladin, who was planning his own expedition from Egypt, invaded on 18 November. Baldwin, still recovering from malaria, rode out with Raynald of Châtillon and, according to William of Tyre, only 375 knights, and issued an arrière-ban calling up all able-bodied men. Saladin's army looted the kingdom as it advanced, and many of the men it captured were sold into slavery.

Saladin reached Ascalon on 22 November 1177. Baldwin led his troops out, but seeing how greatly he was outnumbered withdrew into the city. Believing the king no threat, Saladin went on towards Jerusalem and probably let his army spread out to forage. Baldwin ordered the Templars to leave Gaza and join him, and he and Raynald broke out of Ascalon along the coast with them. Saladin sent no scouts to watch the city. The two forces met at Mons Gisardi, near Ramla; its exact location is disputed, and Malcolm Barber identifies it with the mound of al-Safiya.

Saladin's supply train may have been delayed at a river crossing, and his army was caught unprepared. Baldwin, ill and fighting with bandaged hands, was said to have knelt before the relic of the True Cross before attacking. Saladin's nephew Taqi ad-Din held effective command on the Egyptian side, and his son Ahmad died in the early fighting. The army was quickly overwhelmed, and Saladin escaped, according to Ralph de Diceto, on a camel.

Only a tenth of the sultan's army returned to Egypt with him; Saladin reached Cairo on 8 December. Saladin's army was pursued for twelve miles. The victory was costly for the Christians: Roger de Moulins, Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, reported 1,100 men killed and 750 wounded. Baldwin founded a Benedictine monastery on the battlefield, dedicated to St. Catherine of Alexandria, whose feast day fell on the day of the battle.

The defeat prevented Saladin from relieving his Syrian vassals during the siege of Harim, which lasted into 1178. Saladin beat Baldwin at the Battle of Marj Ayyun in 1179, but Muslim historians judged Montgisard so severe a defeat that it was redeemed only by the victories of Cresson and Hattin and the capture of Jerusalem in 1187.
battle-of-morgarten: Toward the end of the 13th century the House of Habsburg coveted the area around the Gotthard Pass, which offered the shortest passage to Italy. Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, which had formalised the Swiss Confederacy in 1291, held imperial freedom letters granting them local autonomy. In 1314 Louis IV of Bavaria and the Habsburg prince Frederick the Handsome each claimed the imperial crown, and the Confederates supported Louis. War broke out after men of Schwyz under Werner Stauffacher raided the Habsburg-protected Einsiedeln Abbey on the night of 6 January 1314, following a dispute over land that settlers had cleared. The bishop of Constance excommunicated Schwyz, and then Uri and Unterwalden.

Frederick's brother Leopold led a large army against the Confederates. The chronicler Johannes von Winterthur puts it at 20,000, probably an exaggeration, while Hans Delbrück estimated only 2,000 to 3,000 men, mainly well-trained and well-equipped knights. The size of the Confederate force is unknown, with estimates from 1,500 to 3,000 or 4,000. Leopold sent diversionary detachments and then chose to march to Sattel from the north. According to Konrad Justinger's chronicle of about 1430, the lords of Hünenberg warned Schwyz with arrows carrying a message, beware near Morgarten.

The men of Schwyz, supported by 600 men of Uri and Unterwalden, prepared an ambush between Lake Ägeri and Sattel, where a narrow path ran between a steep slope and a swamp. The Habsburg column was stretched out for about 2 km and its vanguard met a roadblock near Schafstetten. The Confederates attacked, throwing rocks from above to frighten the horses and fighting the mounted knights with halberds. About 1,500 men were said to have been killed, not counting those drowned in the lake.

In December 1315 the Confederates renewed the oath of 1291, and in March 1316 Louis IV confirmed the rights of the Forest Cantons. A truce of ten months was agreed with the Habsburgs in 1318. By 1323 the Forest Cantons had allied with Bern, and within 40 years Lucerne, Zug and Zürich had joined the Confederacy. The peace with the Habsburgs lasted until the Battle of Sempach in 1386.

As the Confederacy's first military success, Morgarten became a staple of Swiss patriotism. A chapel at the site is recorded in 1501, and the present one dates to 1604. A monument was inaugurated in 1908 at Hauptsee, which was renamed Morgarten. A target shooting event, the Morgartenschiessen, has been held every year since 1912.
battle-of-muhlberg: After 1517 the Reformation obstructed Charles V's aim of restoring religious and political unity in Germany. In 1531 Philip I of Hesse and John Frederick, Elector of Saxony, opposed his attempt to revive the Edict of Worms, and the Schmalkaldic League was formed, a defensive alliance named after Schmalkalden in Thuringia. The Treaty of Crépy in 1544 ended Charles's conflicts with Francis I of France, and the League lost French support. Martin Luther died in 1546 and the Turkish threat paused. The opportunity came from the rivalry between John Frederick and his cousin Maurice of Saxony, who in 1546, with the help of Ferdinand I, invaded John Frederick's lands. Charles joined the war in 1547, occupied Ulm and Württemberg and marched toward Saxony.

John Frederick sent a large part of his troops to Bohemia in the hope of encouraging an uprising, and marched north toward Wittenberg. At the end of April he camped at Mühlberg, leaving few guards on the bank of the Elbe, which he thought too wide to cross. Charles reached the Elbe on the evening of 23 April, against the advice of his generals. At dawn on 24 April, helped by surprise and dense fog, small groups of Spanish and Italian veterans swam across and killed the Saxon guards. With the help of a local farmer, troops found a ford, and others saved a pontoon bridge from demolition, which the imperial cavalry crossed.

John Frederick deployed along the edge of a forest. The imperial army of 16–20,000 men had the Duke of Alba commanding its right wing, while Charles, suffering from gout, was carried in a litter. The battle began in the evening. The Saxon army, mainly peasants, repelled the first assaults of the Hungarian cavalry, but the imperial cavalry beat its wings and the tercios broke its centre. John Frederick was wounded in the face and captured.

Saxon losses are estimated at 2,000 to 3,000 men, against about fifty killed on the imperial side. John Frederick was condemned as a heretic and his life was spared in exchange for the capitulation of Wittenberg. He gave up the electoral privilege to Maurice, and was released in 1552. The surrender of Philip of Hesse soon afterwards ended the Schmalkaldic War. The Augsburg Interim of 1548 did not settle the Protestant question, and only the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed each ruler to choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism. Some sources report that Charles commented on the victory, I came, I saw, and God won. The town of Mühlberg has a small museum dedicated to the battle.
battle-of-muhldorf: In the early 14th century the dynasties of Habsburg, Luxembourg and Wittelsbach competed for rule over the Holy Roman Empire, and the prince-electors were anxious that no family should make the crown hereditary. After the death of Emperor Henry VII in 1313 the electors passed over his son John of Bohemia and favoured Louis of Wittelsbach and Frederick of Habsburg, but they could not agree between the two.

In 1314 a double election was held at Frankfurt. Cologne, the Electorate of the Palatinate, Bohemia and the Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg voted for Frederick as Rex Romanorum; Mainz, the Archbishopric of Trier, Brandenburg and Elector John II of Saxe-Lauenburg chose Louis. A long and violent conflict followed in which both sides sought the support of the Imperial estates. Louis also had to settle a dispute with his brother, Count Palatine Rudolf I, which ended only with Rudolf's death in 1319, while Frederick repeatedly ravaged Bavaria without meeting much resistance.

Encouraged by these expeditions, Frederick allied in 1322 with the Bishop of Passau and the Archbishopric of Salzburg. Their forces gathered on 24 September near Mühldorf on the Inn, where Frederick expected further troops from Further Austria under his brother Leopold. Louis, allied with John of Bohemia and Burggrave Frederick IV of Nuremberg, arrived on 28 September with a large army that included 1,800 knights and 500 to 600 mounted Hungarian archers.

Leopold's relief force was kept from reaching the field in time, yet Frederick chose to give battle at once. His army was beaten by Louis's larger force, with heavy losses on both sides. More than 1,000 noblemen from Austria and Salzburg were taken prisoner, together with Frederick himself and his younger brother Henry the Friendly.

The victory did not end the dispute over Louis's royal title, which Pope John XXII and Frederick's brother Leopold continued to contest. After three years Louis released Frederick, reconciled with him and even offered him a joint rule and the royal title in return for his support in gaining the imperial crown. In the end neither Wittelsbach nor Habsburg could hold the crown: after Louis died in 1347 it passed to Charles IV of the House of Luxembourg.
battle-of-munda: The republican cause had been led by Pompey until the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE, and Caesar destroyed their army at Thapsus in April 46 BCE. Resistance then centred on Hispania. In the spring of 46 BCE two legions in Hispania Ulterior, largely former Pompeian veterans, declared for Gnaeus Pompeius and drove out Caesar's proconsul. They were joined by the brothers Gnaeus and Sextus Pompeius, Publius Attius Varus and Titus Labienus, a trusted general of Caesar in the Gallic Wars, and raised four legions. Caesar travelled from Rome to Obulco in less than a month, arriving in early December.

The campaign took Caesar past Ulia, Corduba and Ategua, which he besieged through the winter and which surrendered in early 45 BCE, damaging Pompeian morale. After a skirmish near Soricaria on 7 March, many Romans in the Pompeian camp began planning to defect, and Gnaeus Pompeius gave up his delaying tactics and marched south towards Munda.

On 17 March 45 BCE Caesar, with eight legions and 8,000 horsemen, faced thirteen legions, 6,000 light infantry and about 6,000 horsemen on a hill less than a mile from the walls of Munda. Many Pompeian soldiers had surrendered before and rejoined, and fought desperately. The fighting lasted eight hours, and Caesar later said that at Munda he had fought for his life. His Tenth Legion began to push back the Pompeians. Gnaeus Pompeius weakened his right wing to reinforce his left, and King Bogud's Mauretanian cavalry broke through. The Pompeians took Labienus's move for retreat and fled.

About 30,000 Pompeians were reported dead on the field, while Caesar claimed to have lost only 1,000, though his real losses were probably higher. Labienus and Attius Varus died and Caesar had them buried. Gnaeus Pompeius escaped the field and was later cornered and killed. Corduba surrendered and paid a heavy indemnity, and Munda yielded with 14,000 prisoners. Sextus Pompeius remained at large, but no conservative army challenged Caesar again. Plutarch says his triumph for the victory displeased the Romans, as it marked the destruction of the family of one of Rome's great men. He was murdered on 15 March the next year. The site of Munda remains disputed, with Ronda, Montilla and the area near Osuna proposed.
battle-of-muret: Simon de Montfort led the Albigensian Crusade, aimed at destroying Catharism and bringing Languedoc under Capetian control. He invaded the County of Toulouse and drove Count Raymond VI into exile. Raymond turned to his brother-in-law, King Peter II of Aragon, who felt threatened by Montfort's conquests and crossed the Pyrenees. Peter's army reached Muret, 25 km south of Toulouse, on 10 September 1213, where contingents of Languedoc under Raymond and other southern lords joined him. He placed his army between the Saudrune River and a marsh and set the militia of Toulouse to assault the town's walls.

Estimates of the armies vary widely. According to Laurence Marvin, Montfort had 900 cavalry, 260 of them knights, with his infantry left to hold Muret. Pierre des Vaux de Cernay, the main contemporary source, gave the allies an impossible 100,000 men; modern figures run from 4,000 to 8,000 in Clifford J. Rogers to Charles Oman's 15,000 to 20,000 infantry. Montfort led his horsemen out in three lines, the first under his half-brother William of Barres. It broke the first allied line under the Count of Foix and reached the second, where Peter fought in borrowed armour, while Montfort's own line struck the allied cavalry in the flank. Peter was killed, and news of his death turned the retreat into a rout.

Montfort kept his own line in reserve and returned to Muret. The Toulouse militia, learning of the king's death, fled their camp towards the Garonne River and were slaughtered. The heavy losses among the Aragonese nobility had lasting consequences: Aragonese influence over Languedoc ended, and the French Crown was able to extend its royal domain to the south. Muret was the last major battle of the crusade, which formally ended only with the Treaty of Paris of 1229.
battle-of-muye: Much of the history is written from the viewpoint of the victorious Western Zhou and of later rulers, and accounts of Di Xin grew steadily more hostile, so a neutral account is difficult. By the 12th century BCE Shang influence reached the Wei River valley, home of the Predynastic Zhou. Di Xin gave King Wen of Zhou the title Overlord of the West, to guard the Shang rear while he campaigned in the east against the Renfang, Linfang and Hufang, wars that were costly to the Shang.

Di Xin allegedly killed the daughter of Marquess Jiu and then the marquess himself, and King Wen was imprisoned after a sigh was reported to Di Xin. Wen died in 1050 BCE, leaving King Wu to lead the revolt.

King Wu waited some years, since he believed the heavenly order to conquer the Shang had not yet been given and following the advice of Jiang Ziya. According to the sources, the Zhou had only 45,000 men and a few hundred wagons, while Di Xin organised some 170,000, many allegedly slaves, as most of his forces were fighting in the east.

The majority of the Shang troops fled or joined the Zhou. Loyal troops fought on in a very bloody battle, described in the Shijing, and King Wu broke the Shang line in a chariot charge. Di Xin fled to his palace. The Zhou showed little mercy, shedding enough blood to float a log.

The Yi Zhou Shu portrays the conquest in a more brutal light, saying that King Wu took prisoners, massacred civilians as he entered Yin and killed Di Xin with an axe; Mencius and other scholars condemned it. The location of Muye is unclear, and excavations have found no remains of the battle.

In the traditional narrative Di Xin gathered his treasures, climbed the Deer Terrace Pavilion and burned it with himself inside. The imperial grain store was opened to feed the population, and Shang officials were released, some later serving the Zhou. Wu Geng was allowed to continue the Shang state religion, and King Wu set his brothers over the Shang as the Three Guards.

After King Wu's death Wu Geng joined them in the Rebellion of the Three Guards against the Duke of Zhou, and King Cheng of Zhou then relocated the Shang people from Yin to Wey, Luoyi and Lu. The year is in doubt: earlier chronologies proposed at least 44 dates between 1130 and 1018 BCE, and the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project settled on 20 January 1046 BCE, which other scholars have criticised.
battle-of-mycale: After the Greek naval victory at Salamis, Xerxes I retreated to Asia with a minor portion of his army and left his general Mardonius to finish the campaign the following year. The Persian fleet was stationed at Samos to defend Ionia and prevent an Ionian revolt. Its morale was breaking, and its commanders waited anxiously for news of Mardonius's land army.

Herodotus gives 300 ships and 60,000 soldiers for the Persians, but Charles Hignett and others think both figures far too high, and estimates of the Persian army range from about 4,000 to 10,000 men. The Greek fleet is usually put at about 110 ships, with perhaps 3,300 marines.

When the Persians learned that the Greek fleet was approaching, they sailed from Samos to Mycale on the mainland, possibly because they judged a sea battle hopeless. They beached their ships behind rocks, built a palisaded camp of cut wood with stakes on the ramparts, and expected a siege.

The Greek commander Leotychides decided to attack anyway and landed the fleet's marines. The Athenians and Corinthians formed the left wing along the shore, while the Spartans and others were still crossing the hills on the right. The Persians came out and set up a shield wall. The Greek left engaged first, and the right wing broke the wall by shoving. Tigranes and Mardontes were killed. The Persians fled to their camp, the Ionian contingents defected, and the ethnic Persian troops who held out were attacked in the rear when the Greek left outflanked the camp.

With Plataea and Mycale the second Persian invasion of Greece was over. The Greek fleet sailed to the Hellespont to break down the pontoon bridges, found them already destroyed, and the Peloponnesians went home. The Athenians stayed and besieged the Persians at Sestos, which fell after a long siege and began a new phase of the war, the Greek counterattack. Chios, Lesbos and Samos joined the Hellenic alliance, and Thrace and Macedonia broke away from the Persians.

Some historians treat the fighting itself as minor. George Cawkwell called it a very minor affair whose results were major because it led to an Ionian revolt. The ancient accounts also differ on the ships: Herodotus has them burned, and Iain McDougall argues that the burned vessels were mostly Ionian and too damaged to salvage. Spoils from the campaign were displayed at Delphi and, according to Vitruvius, Persian masts and spars were used in the roof of the Odeon of Pericles at Athens.
battle-of-myeongnyang: Admiral Yi Sun-sin had been impeached at the Joseon court, tortured and demoted to common soldier, and his rival Wŏn Kyun took over a fleet that had grown under Yi from 63 heavy warships to 166. At the Battle of Chilcheollyang the Japanese, under Tōdō Takatora, virtually wiped it out and killed Wŏn Kyun, and the second invasion began. The Japanese army took Namwon and planned a push on Hanyang, supplied by a navy that now meant to enter the Yellow Sea.

Reinstated as Supreme Commander of the Regional Navies, Yi had the ships Pae Sŏl had saved and two brought by Kim Ŏkch'u. When King Seonjo ordered the navy disbanded and its men sent to General Kwon Yul, Yi replied that as long as he lived the enemy would not dare to look down on it. His fleet drove off Japanese scouting attacks on 8 and 17 October, and on 25 October he withdrew to Usuyeong, north of the strait.

Yi chose the strait because its currents of about 10 knots reversed every three hours: the narrows kept him from being outflanked, the current broke up the Japanese formations, and the turning tide would carry the enemy back. Korean sources put the ships that fought at 120 to 133, out of as many as 330. Because the larger atakebune could not enter the shallows, the Japanese sent in middle-sized sekibune.

For a time Yi's flagship fought alone against the vanguard of Kurushima Michifusa while his shaken crews held back, until ships under An Wi and Kim Ŭngham came to his aid and the rest followed. When the tide shifted, the Japanese ships drifted back and collided, and the Koreans pressed in with cannon fire. At nightfall Yi withdrew to Dangsa island. Claims that he stretched iron ropes across the channel find no support in his war diary.

Kurushima was killed and Tōdō Takatora wounded twice in the hand, and a prisoner reported half the Japanese killed or wounded. Still outnumbered, Yi withdrew to resupply, and survivors of Chilcheollyang rejoined him. The victory persuaded the Ming to send a fleet to his aid in early 1598. On 23 November 1597 the Japanese burned Yi's home village of Asan in revenge and killed his youngest son, Yi Myon. Japanese historians of the imperial era and of today have generally called the battle a decisive Korean victory.
battle-of-myonessus: Antiochus III the Great expanded into Asia Minor and, in 196 BCE, across the Hellespont into Europe, where he rebuilt Lysimachia. Rome demanded that he leave Europe and respect the autonomy of the Greek cities of Asia Minor. Encouraged by the Aetolian League, he landed in Greece in 192 BCE, but after his defeat at the Battle of Thermopylae on 26 April 191 BCE he returned to Ephesus. To invade Asia Minor the Romans had to cross the Aegean, and both sides hurried to build ships and draft seamen.

In September 191 BCE a Roman and Pergamene fleet defeated the Seleucids at the Battle of Corycus. In spring 190 BCE Polyxenidas, himself a Rhodian exile, destroyed a Rhodian squadron at Samos by pretending he would surrender his fleet to its admiral Pausistratos, whom he killed. In August the Rhodians under Eudamus destroyed half of Hannibal's fleet at the Battle of the Eurymedon. When Lucius Aemilius Regillus sent part of his fleet to the Hellespont in September, Polyxenidas chose to attack.
