The allied fleet of 58 Roman and 22 Rhodian warships had sailed from Samos for grain and to relieve Notion, besieged by Antiochus. Polyxenidas, with 89 warships and less experienced crews, hid behind the island of Makris to ambush it as it left the narrow northern harbour of Teos, but a Tean peasant warned Aemilius, who moved to the southern harbour.

The Seleucids attacked as the allies put to sea between Myonessus and the Corycus peninsula. Aemilius formed his line and counterattacked the Seleucid right-centre, exposing his seaward flank. Eudamus led the Rhodians behind the centre to reinforce it, and their fire baskets spread panic, while Aemilius broke through and struck the Seleucid seaward wing from behind. The Seleucids lost 29 ships sunk and 13 captured, the allies two sunk and one captured.

Polyxenidas took his remaining 47 ships to Ephesus. Aemilius told the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus that the Aegean was secure and sent 30 Roman ships and the Rhodian squadron to help the army cross the Hellespont, while other Rhodians blockaded Hannibal at Megiste. Antiochus withdrew from Thrace and offered to pay half of Rome's war costs and accept the demands of 196 BCE, but the Romans pressed on.
battle-of-myriokephalon: A series of Byzantine campaigns between 1158 and 1161 ended in a treaty in which the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan II accepted a form of subordination to Manuel I Komnenos, and he visited Constantinople. The long peace let Manuel concentrate on the west and the east, defeating Hungary and reducing the Principality of Antioch to vassal status, but it also let Kilij Arslan eliminate his internal rivals. After the death of Nur ad-Din Zangi in 1174 he destroyed the Danishmend emirates and drove out his brother Shahinshah, Manuel's vassal. The peace collapsed in 1175 when he refused to hand over the Danishmend lands as the treaty required.

Manuel gathered a very large army at Lopadion and rejected a new offer of peace from Kilij Arslan. A force under Andronikos Vatatzes sent towards Amasia was destroyed in an ambush. The Turks destroyed crops and poisoned water supplies, and harassed the main army towards the Tzivritze Pass, near the ruined fortress of Myriokephalon. Manuel decided to force the pass despite the danger, perhaps because the army lacked forage and water and dysentery had broken out. Modern estimates of its size run from 25,000 to 35,000 men.

The vanguard and main division passed with few casualties, but the following divisions did not secure the heights or keep close order. The Turks closed the trap and fell especially on the right wing, whose commander Baldwin was killed, and then on the baggage and siege trains. A dust storm added to the confusion. Manuel is said to have sat down and awaited his fate before his officers roused him. The army fought free of the pass and camped with the divisions that had gone ahead, repelling attacks through the night.

Both sides had casualties, but Manuel's siege equipment was lost and he could not attack Konya. Kilij Arslan sent an envoy to negotiate; under the truce Manuel was to demolish his forts at Dorylaeum and Sublaeum, and he destroyed only Sublaeum's. Manuel compared the defeat to Manzikert in a message to Constantinople. The Byzantines won a victory over the Seljuks on the Meander the following year, and Manuel made a peace in 1179. Myriokephalon nevertheless proved that the empire could not destroy Seljuk power in central Anatolia, and it marked the end of Byzantine attempts to recover the plateau.
battle-of-nafels: A few weeks after the Battle of Sempach on 9 July 1386, the Old Swiss Confederation captured the Habsburg village of Weesen on the Walensee. The next year Glarus rose against the Habsburgs and destroyed Burg Windegg, and on 11 March 1387 its valley council declared itself free of Habsburg control. The battle was the last of the conflicts between the Swiss and the Duchy of Austria that ran through most of the 14th century.

On the night of 21–22 February 1388 an Austrian army attacked Weesen and drove off the Swiss. At the start of April two Austrian armies set out to cut Glarus off from the rest of the Confederation. The main army, about 5,000 men under Count Donat von Toggenburg and the knight Peter von Thorberg, marched on Näfels, while a column of about 1,500 under Count Hans von Werdenberg-Sargans advanced over the Kerenzerberg Pass.

On 9 April the main army captured the fortifications, known as the letzi, around Näfels. Their garrison of about 400 men of Glarus and a few dozen from Schwyz and Uri held out briefly, then withdrew into the hills. As the Austrians spread out to plunder villages and farms, the Glarners came out of the snow and fog and took them by surprise.

After a short fight the disorganised Austrians fled towards Weesen, and when the bridge over the Maag or Weeser Linth collapsed, many fell into the river and drowned. Seeing the main column destroyed, Werdenberg-Sargans retreated to Beglingen. The Swiss lost 54 men, buried at the parish church of Mollis; Habsburg losses are estimated at between several hundred and 1,700 killed. On 29 November 1389 Abbot Bilgeri had about 180 bodies moved from the battlefield to Rüti Abbey.

In 1389 a seven years' peace signed at Vienna left the Confederation in undisputed possession of all the territory it had gained in the war. The first Näfelser Fahrt, a pilgrimage to the battlefield, was held in the same year. It is still held on the first Thursday in April and played an important part in the making of the unified canton of Glarus.
battle-of-nagashino: The Takeda and Tokugawa clans had been at war since the lifetime of Takeda Shingen, and the Takeda forces were far stronger. Several leading families of the north-eastern part of Mikawa joined the Takeda side. Tokugawa Ieyasu had a powerful ally in Oda Nobunaga, but Nobunaga was by no means an equal partner and used Ieyasu as a bulwark against the Takeda.

When Shingen fell ill on campaign in Mikawa in May 1573, the Takeda army withdrew to Kai Province and tried to conceal his death while power passed to Takeda Katsuyori. Ieyasu then regained northern Mikawa, and Honda Tadakatsu and Sakakibara Yasumasa captured Nagashino Castle, which became his base. Katsuyori, with his succession complete, led the main Takeda army into Okumikawa.

In June 1575 Katsuyori surrounded Nagashino Castle, held by 500 defenders, with 15,000 men. Ieyasu could raise about 8,000 troops and asked Nobunaga for help. Nobunaga left Gifu on 21 June with about 30,000 men and joined Ieyasu at Okazaki the next day. On 26 June he halted at Shitaragahara, about 4 kilometres west of the castle, and had his men build positions with horse fences and earthworks.

His camp lay in a hollow, so the Takeda could not see how large his force was. During the siege Torii Suneemon, sent to Ieyasu for help, was captured on his return and crucified after he shouted to the castle that reinforcements would come.

On 28 June Katsuyori marched east of Shitaragahara with 12,000 men, leaving 3,000 at the siege. In the night Sakai Tadatsugu led about 4,000 men in a surprise attack on the fort on Mount Tobigasu, which was taken early on 29 June, and the detachment joined the castle's garrison. With its retreat cut off, the Takeda army charged the Oda and Tokugawa lines, where matchlock guns and fences blocked each attack. By midday the Takeda were routed, and the fighting ended around 2 pm.

The Shinchō Kōki records Takeda losses of 10,000 men, two thirds of the besieging force, and several of the Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen died, among them Baba Nobuharu, Yamagata Masakage and Naitō Masatoyo. Katsuyori withdrew to Kai, and the Takeda clan was not destroyed until 1582. The traditional account of Oda guns firing in three rotating stages of 1,000 comes from a 1903 army staff history based on a later war tale.

It is now widely seen as a later invention, since the Shinchō Kōki does not mention it. Research since the 2010s holds that both armies had similar structures and numbers of guns, and that Oda superiority lay in supplies of lead and powder and in the placing of his forces.
battle-of-najera: Castile's fleet, far stronger than those of France or England, drew both powers into the civil war. After the Treaty of Brétigny of 1360, Charles V of France and Pope Urban V sent the idle free companies to Spain, and France and the Crown of Aragon paid them to fight for Henry of Trastámara. When Peter I fled Castile, he met the Black Prince and Charles II of Navarre at Bayonne in August 1366 and promised to pay for an army and to cede Castilian lands to Aquitaine. The prince raised Gascon, Poitevin and English nobles and the best-known mercenary captains, probably 8,000 to 10,000 men.

Charles II of Navarre had also agreed with Henry to block the Pyrenean pass. When Hugh Calveley's English mercenaries changed sides and raided Navarre in February 1367, he opened the way and then faked his own capture to avoid the battle. Henry wore the invaders down with light cavalry, and in the third week of March his vanguard destroyed a detachment under Sir Thomas Felton at Aríñez.

Pedro López de Ayala, who was in Henry's camp, gave Peter's side more than 10,000 men and Henry's 4,500; Jean Froissart's far larger figures are judged unreliable. Leaving the cover of the River Najerilla against the advice of du Guesclin, Henry was surprised at dawn by the prince's army, which according to the Chandos Herald had marched round by night. Some Castilian horsemen and infantry defected. Du Guesclin's vanguard charged and drove back the English under the Duke of Lancaster and John Chandos, but Gascon companies outflanked it, while English archers cut down Don Tello's light cavalry and Henry's own charges. The main body fled for the narrow bridge of Nájera, where many were killed.

Henry's losses probably exceeded half his army, and the victors sacked Nájera and killed most of its inhabitants. Told that Henry had escaped, the Black Prince is reported to have said, "non ay res fait" (nothing then is done). Henry crossed the Pyrenees and fought on, and his captured supporters ransomed themselves. Peter never paid the prince or ceded the promised lands, and the English alliance broke down. In Castile, France gained an ally against England that lasted a century, and the Castilian fleet destroyed an English fleet at La Rochelle five years later.
battle-of-nancy: Charles the Bold had besieged Nancy, the capital of Lorraine, since 22 October 1476, after René II recaptured it earlier in the year. Despite the harsh winter he wanted to end the siege quickly, knowing that René would arrive with a relieving army when the weather improved. Contemporary observers put the Burgundian numbers between 2,000 and 8,000. By late December René had gathered some 10,000 to 12,000 men from Lorraine and the Lower Union, besides a Swiss army of 8,000 to 10,000. He reached Nancy early on 5 January 1477.

Charles drew up the bulk of his army south of the city on a wooded slope behind a stream, at the narrowest part of the valley the Swiss would have to descend. His infantry and dismounted men-at-arms formed a large square with about 30 field guns in front, with mounted knights on either flank.

The allied scouts judged a frontal assault disastrous. A vanguard of 7,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry was to attack from the right, while the centre, 8,000 infantry and 1,300 cavalry, marched in a circuit round the left flank over snow-covered wooded slopes. After about two hours it emerged to the rear of the Burgundian position and formed a wedge. Swiss horns sounded three times and the Swiss charged downhill. The guns could not be trained on the centre, and one volley killed two men.

The Burgundians began to break apart. Charles is thought to have said that he struggled against a spider that was everywhere at once. He and his staff were carried along by the fleeing army until a halberdier struck a deadly blow to his helmet. His death went unnoticed, and his stripped body was found two days later and carried into Nancy.

Most of Charles's army was killed in the battle and the retreat. Only the few who reached Metz, over 50 kilometres away, survived, and chronicles say the killing went on for three days. The battle was the final and decisive one of the Burgundian Wars.

René II built the church of Notre-Dame-de-Bonsecours on the site, and the basilica of Saint-Nicolas-de-Port. Nancy took the motto non inultus premor and a thistle for its arms. Walter Scott's novel Anne of Geierstein, published in 1829, ends at the battle, and Eugène Delacroix painted it in 1831.
battle-of-narva-1700: Peter the Great of Russia wanted an adequate opening to the Baltic and so sought the Swedish Baltic provinces that Russia had lost during the Time of Troubles. Sweden, by contrast, had a professional army, one of the largest and most disciplined in northern Europe. Russia, Denmark-Norway and Augustus the Strong of Poland-Lithuania allied against Sweden, but Charles XII landed at Humlebæk north of Copenhagen and forced Denmark-Norway out of the alliance in August 1700. He then took part of his army across the Baltic to Estonia.

The Russian army was poorly drilled. In spring 1700 Peter retired or reassigned most of his officers, leaving up to 70 percent of company posts vacant, and filled them with young Moscow noblemen with no command experience. In November Russian troops besieged Narva. Peter left the camp the day before the battle, and the new commander, Charles Eugène de Croÿ, had never commanded a Russian unit.

Charles XII approached Narva on 29 November 1700 and the next morning positioned his army before the Russian siege lines. The Russians, stretched over four miles between two ramparts, outnumbered the relief force three or four to one. The Swedes moved forward at 2 pm, just as a snowstorm blew into the Russian faces. Charles ignored officers who wished to wait, and the Swedes attacked in two dense columns and, within 15 minutes, had filled the ditches with fascines and broken in.

The Swedes rolled up the Russian line to north and south, shattering inexperienced regiments one by one. Panic followed, and de Croÿ hurried to surrender. The Kamperholm Bridge, the only one across the Narva River, collapsed under retreating troops. Only the Preobrazhensky and Semyonovsky regiments held, in a square behind improvised barricades of wagons.

The Russian high command lost its morale and capitulated. The Swedes captured ten generals and ten colonels, 4,050 muskets and 173 artillery pieces. Regimental rolls of January 1701 show a loss of about 25 percent of personnel. Charles kept the senior Russian commanders as prisoners, explaining that he had not received the army's treasury.

The battle was not followed by a Swedish advance into Russia, and Charles turned south against Augustus the Strong in Livonia and Poland-Lithuania. Peter took Narva in a second battle in 1704. A Russian memorial to the fallen was begun in 1900, and a Swedish one reading Svecia memor was inaugurated in 2000.
battle-of-naseby: Parliament's victory at Marston Moor in July 1644 was offset by defeat at Lostwithiel and indecision at the Second Battle of Newbury. The Self-denying Ordinance introduced by Henry Vane the Younger led to the creation of the New Model Army, a centralised, professional force under Sir Thomas Fairfax, with Philip Skippon over the infantry and Oliver Cromwell commanding the cavalry on a temporary commission. The Royalist command was divided. In May 1645 the main Royalist field army of 8,600 men under Charles I and Prince Rupert moved north, and on 31 May the Royalists stormed Leicester.
Parliament told Fairfax to leave Oxford and engage them. The day before the battle Cromwell's cavalry had brought his numbers to 14,000, and the Royalists decided to stand and fight.

On the foggy morning of 14 June 1645 Rupert advanced to take the Naseby ridge. Cromwell advised Fairfax to withdraw to a hill from which he might provoke a charge, and Fairfax moved back slightly. Cromwell also sent a regiment of dragoons under Colonel John Okey into the Sulby Hedges to fire on Rupert's flank.

The Royalist centre attacked first, and the infantry had time for one volley before fighting hand to hand. Rupert's cavalry beat Henry Ireton's wing and pursued it as far as Naseby and the baggage, which was defended. On the other wing Cromwell routed Marmaduke Langdale's Northern Horse. He then turned his reserves on the Royalist centre, while Okey's dragoons charged it as well. The Royalist infantry was trapped, and the Earl of Carnwath seized the bridle of the king, who had tried to lead his lifeguard against Cromwell, with the words Would you go upon your death, Sire?

The Royalists suffered over 1,000 casualties, and over 4,500 of their infantry were captured and paraded through London. They lost all their artillery and stores. Parliamentarian troops reportedly killed at least 100 female camp followers, probably Welsh women taken for Irish.

The king's baggage held correspondence revealing his intention to seek help from the Irish Catholic Confederation and Catholic powers in Europe. Parliament published it as The King's Cabinet Opened, which won it support. The Royalists never again fielded an army of comparable quality, though Charles did not surrender until May 1646.
battle-of-navarino: The Greeks rose against Ottoman rule in 1821, and by 1825 neither side could win. The sultan then persuaded Muhammad Ali Pasha, the wali of Egypt, to send his Western-trained army and navy, promising the Peloponnese as a hereditary fief to Ali's eldest son Ibrahim. Ibrahim landed with 16,000 men in February 1825 and overran the western Peloponnese. By 1827 the Greek government was almost bankrupt and its forces far weaker than those of its enemies. Tsar Nicholas I, who succeeded Alexander in December 1825, was more willing to act, and Britain, France and Russia signed the Treaty of London on 6 July 1827. It called for an armistice and Greek autonomy within the Ottoman Empire, and they sent squadrons to enforce it.

The British admiral Edward Codrington was to impose the armistice and cut the flow of supplies to Greece, using force only as a last resort. The Ottomans rejected the treaty on 29 August, and the Greek government accepted the armistice on 2 September. The Ottoman and Egyptian fleet lay at anchor in Navarino Bay in a horseshoe of three lines, so that small vessels could fire through gaps in the front line. On 20 October 1827 the Allied ships entered the bay in two lines, with Codrington's flagship HMS Asia in the lead. He had a band play on deck to show peaceful intent, and the captains were to fire only if attacked. Fighting broke out, and Codrington claimed the Ottomans started it.
It was the last major naval battle fought entirely with sailing ships, though most vessels fought at anchor. The Allies won through superior firepower and gunnery and destroyed the Ottoman armada.

The sultan still had some 40,000 troops in central and southern Greece, so independence was not yet secure. Russia declared war in April 1828, and a French expeditionary force landed in the Peloponnese at the end of August. The Egyptians left in October 1828, a year after the battle. In Britain, Codrington was a hero to the public, but ministers thought he had exceeded his instructions, and King George IV called the battle an untoward event. He was relieved of his command in June 1828. Pylos holds Three Admirals' Square with a monument to Codrington, Van Heiden and Rigny, and the battle is commemorated there each year on 20 October.
battle-of-nedao: After the death of Attila, his son Ellac struggled with his brothers Ernak and Dengizich for supremacy over the Hunnic realm. The peoples subject to the Huns, led by Ardaric, king of the Gepids, gathered against the Hunnic forces of Ellac. The battle was fought in Pannonia in 454, at a place named after the Nedao, believed to be a tributary of the Sava.

The main account is that of the 6th-century historian Jordanes. He describes a clash of many nations in which the Goths fought with pikes, the Gepids with swords, the Rugii broke their spears in their own wounds, the Suavi fought on foot, the Huns used bows, the Alani drew up a battle-line of heavy-armed warriors and the Heruli light-armed ones.

After many fierce clashes Jordanes says victory fell to the Gepids, through the sword and the planning of Ardaric, who killed nearly thirty thousand men, Huns and the tribes that came to their aid. Attila's eldest son Ellac, whom his father was said to have loved above his other sons, was killed in the fighting.

Jordanes names the Ostrogoths among the fighters against the Huns, but modern historians disagree about this. Herwig Wolfram and Hyun Jin Kim reject it, and Kim believes the Ostrogoth king Valamir fought alongside the Huns. J. R. Martindale and Franz Altheim accept that the Ostrogoths were among the victors, and many others, including Otto J. Maenchen-Helfen, think they did not take part at all. Medieval Hungarian chronicles told the story differently, as a quarrel between Attila's sons Csaba and Aladar in which Dietrich of Verona played a treacherous part, but the Chronicon Pictum's account is far from the modern reconstruction.

The battle broke Hunnic dominance in Central and Eastern Europe. The exact course of events is hard to reconstruct, but by the early 460s the Hunnic Empire had dissolved. The Gepids, Rugii, Heruli, Suebi and Ostrogoths gained independence and in time became federates of the Eastern Roman Empire. The Huns, reorganised under Dengizich, moved east, where they attacked the Eastern Roman Empire and were decisively defeated in 469. After that the Huns disappear from European history.
battle-of-nesjar: After Olav Tryggvason was defeated at the Battle of Svolder, Norway was divided between Sveinn Hákonarson and his brother Eiríkr Hákonarson. When Eiríkr joined his brother-in-law Canute the Great in the conquest of England, the power of the brothers weakened, and Olav Haraldsson, a claimant of the line of Harald Fairhair, began to gather support in Eastern Norway.

Sveinn, based in Trøndelag, sailed south along the coast when he learned of this, joining forces on the way with several of Norway's farmer-chieftains, the most prominent of them Erling Skjalgsson. Olav, having raised his own forces, was already moving north to meet him.

The fleets clashed off the coast on Palm Sunday, 25 March 1016. Tradition places the battle at the west end of the Oslofjord; the exact place is unknown but lies somewhere in the Langesundfjorden inlet in present-day Larvik Municipality, Vestfold. Few accounts survive, but it is generally regarded as a fierce battle with heavy casualties. None of the leaders was killed. Sveinn was chased off and retreated to Sweden, where he died of illness before he could raise a force to retake Norway.

The victory opened the way for Olav to establish a unified rule over Norway, but he was later forced into an uneasy alliance with Erling Skjalgsson. It ended violently: Erling was killed in connection with the Battle of Boknafjorden in Rogaland in 1028, and two years later his followers took revenge when Olav himself was killed at the Battle of Stiklestad.

The Icelandic skald and court poet Sigvatr Þórðarson composed the poem Nesjavísur in memory of the battle. A monument was raised on its 1000th anniversary in the village of Helgeroa in Larvik Municipality, where the battle is believed to have been fought.
battle-of-nevilles-cross: The battle belonged to the Second War of Scottish Independence and to the Hundred Years' War. When Edward III of England prepared to invade France in 1346, King Philip VI of France called on the Scots to honour the Auld Alliance and open a northern front, describing northern England as a defenceless void. By the time a truce expired on 29 September, the French had been beaten at Crécy and the English were besieging Calais.

On 7 October some 12,000 Scots crossed the border, many with weapons and armour supplied by France. They stormed Liddell Peel and massacred its garrison, sacked Hexham Abbey and camped at Beaurepaire Priory outside Durham. Because Edward III had exempted the counties north of the River Humber from his levy, an army could be raised at Richmond under William de la Zouche, Archbishop of York; joined by the Yorkshire contingent, it numbered 6,000 to 7,000 men under Lord Ralph Neville.

The Scots discovered the English only on the morning of 17 October, when a raiding party under William Douglas stumbled on them in the mist. David II drew up his army on broken ground west of Durham, cut by ditches and walls, in three divisions. Both sides stood on the defensive until the afternoon, when English longbowmen came forward and provoked the Scots into attacking. The Earl of Moray's division was slowed by the obstacles and repulsed, the division of the Earl of March and Robert Stewart fled, and the king's division was shot at, attacked by the English men-at-arms and routed.

Scottish chroniclers put the Scottish dead at a thousand; modern historians have estimated about 3,000. More than 50 Scottish barons were killed or captured, among them the Constable, the Marischal, the Chamberlain and the Chancellor.

David II, twice shot in the face with arrows, was found hiding under a bridge over the River Browney and taken by John de Coupland, who was knighted for it. Edward III refused to ransom or parole the captured nobles, and the Earl of Menteith was executed as a traitor. The Black Rood of Scotland was given to the shrine of Saint Cuthbert in Durham Cathedral. The battle freed English resources for the war in France, and the truce that came with the king's ransom brought peace to the border for four decades. The site is a registered battlefield.
battle-of-nicopolis: After the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 the Ottomans had conquered most of the Balkans and reduced the Byzantine Empire to the area around Constantinople, which they blockaded from 1394. In 1393 the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Shishman lost his temporary capital Nicopolis, and his brother Ivan Stratsimir held Vidin only as an Ottoman vassal. Hungary now formed the frontier between the two religions in Eastern Europe. In 1394 Pope Boniface IX proclaimed a new crusade, although the Western Schism had split the papacy.

Philip, Duke of Burgundy, withdrew from the planned leadership and named his 24-year-old son John, Count of Nevers, to nominal command, with the experienced Enguerrand VII, Lord of Coucy, as chief counsellor. The crusade left Dijon on 30 April 1396 and joined King Sigismund of Hungary at Buda, where the French rejected his advice to let the Ottomans make the long march to them.

The crusaders besieged Nicopolis, whose governor Doğan Bey was prepared for a long siege. They had brought no siege machines, and the steep slope and strong fortifications made an assault impossible. On the morning of 25 September 1396 Sigismund asked Nevers to postpone the advance for two hours while scouts reported on the Turkish forces. Coucy and Jean de Vienne agreed, but the Constable of France, D'Eu, declared that Sigismund wished to keep the honour for himself, and the argument ended when D'Eu decided to advance. The army was routed. Estimates of the numbers are heavily contested.

Sigismund later told the Master of the Hospitallers: "We lost the day by the pride and vanity of these French." On 26 September Bayezid had the prisoners assembled. Nevers, Coucy, D'Eu and a few other nobles were spared for ransom, those under 20 were taken as slaves, and the rest, thought to number several thousand, were killed in front of the sultan. Accounts of the number killed that day range from 300 to 3,000.

Western Europe made no further move to halt the Turkish advance in the Balkans until the 1440s. In 1402 Bayezid was defeated and captured by Timur. Nicopolis is widely regarded as the end of the Second Bulgarian Empire, and Ivan Stratsimir was captured and killed in Bursa. The Turks tightened their control of the Balkans and became a greater threat to Central Europe.
battle-of-nieuwpoort: The battle, also called the Battle of the Dunes, set the military leaders of the two Netherlands against each other. Over the previous five years Maurice, Count of Nassau, son of William of Orange, had reformed the Dutch army with new drill, standard commands and careful bookkeeping. The Spanish army of the Habsburg Netherlands was as experienced, but long unpaid, and mutiny had become commonplace. Maurice used this to take border forts, among them Crevecoeur in May 1600.

The Dutch government then ordered a strike at Dunkirk, the main Spanish port in the north, whose raiders harmed Dutch merchants and fishermen. The army was to sail to Ostend, take Nieuwpoort and Fort Albert, and march on. Maurice and his officers would have preferred Sluis, but were overruled.

Maurice gathered some 12,000 foot and 2,000 horse, reached Nieuwpoort on 1 July and learned that night that the Archduke's field army had cut him off from Ostend. Ernst Casimir of Nassau-Dietz, sent to delay it at the Leffinghen bridge, was routed, and over 600 Scots were killed. Urged on by mutineers promised free plunder, the Archduke advanced along the coast until the rising tide forced his army up into the dunes.

English regiments under Francis Vere held the dunes in the Dutch first line. The Spanish vanguard was repulsed, but the veteran tercios of Monroy and Villar drove the English from their hill at push of pike. A small reserve of Dutch cavalry then charged the tired and disordered Spanish, Vere rallied his men, and a last charge under Maurice's cousin Louis drove the Spanish cavalry from the field. The Spanish infantry broke and fled, leaving their guns, while an Anglo-Dutch fleet offshore bombarded their positions.

Spanish losses were 2,500 to 4,000 killed and wounded, including some 600 prisoners, with the artillery train and 90 standards; the allies lost 1,700 to 2,700. Maurice stayed at Nieuwpoort fourteen days, never invested Dunkirk and withdrew, as the Flemish stayed loyal to the Spanish monarchy. The lesson drawn was that sieges paid better than open battle, and they increasingly marked the war thereafter. The battle is considered the first challenge to the dominance of the tercios, though it was Maurice's cavalry, not his reformed infantry, that saved him.
battle-of-nihawand: When the Prophet Muhammad died in 632, the religion he led dominated the Hejaz in western Arabia. Under the first two caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar, Islam expanded into Palestine and Mesopotamia, where it confronted the East Roman and Persian empires. Both were exhausted by warfare and internal dissent. After the East Roman defeat at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636, the Muslim Arabs were free to turn east, and in November 636 a Sasanian army was defeated at the Battle of Qadisiya, which cost the Sasanians Iraq. Yazdegerd III later abandoned his capital at Ctesiphon and withdrew to the southern plateau of Iran.

By 642 Yazdegerd III had assembled an army to replace the one lost at Qadisiya. At Nahavand the Arab commander, An-Numan ibn Muqarrin, had an estimated 30,000 warriors. The Sasanian army is estimated at between 50,000 and 150,000 men, mostly farmers and villagers rather than veteran soldiers. Many Sasanian nobles and officials had deserted the empire even before the battle began.

Accounts of the fighting differ. In one version the Persian cavalry mounted an ill-prepared pursuit of Arabs who had retreated to a more secure position; the Arabs then rallied, surrounded the Persian force and assaulted it from all sides. In another, the Arab commander outmanoeuvred his Sasanian counterpart Firuzan by drawing the Persians out of a strong defensive position, and the Sasanian army, caught between two mountain defiles, fought for two days and three nights. Both commanders reportedly died.

The battle marked the near dissolution of the Sasanian imperial army, with the fall of the last of the grand marshals and the rise of warlordism among the Persians. Yazdegerd fled east, where several provincial governors received him badly; in Merv the governor Mahoye openly showed hostility. He appealed to the princes of Tukharistan and Sogdia and sent his son Peroz III to the Tang court, without success. Yazdegerd was assassinated by a local miller in Merv in 651, and Peroz, who tried to re-establish the empire, died in China.

The former Sasanian provinces, in alliance with Parthian and White Hun nobles, resisted for about a century in Tabaristan, south of the Caspian Sea, even after the Rashidun Caliphate was replaced by the Umayyads. They thus kept alive Sasanian court styles, the Zoroastrian religion and the Persian language.
battle-of-nineveh-627: After Emperor Maurice was murdered by the usurper Phocas, Khosrow II declared war under the pretext of avenging his benefactor. The Persians conquered much of the Levant, Egypt and even some of Anatolia, but the resurgence of Heraclius forced them onto the defensive. Allied with the Avars, they failed to take Constantinople. During that siege Heraclius allied himself with the Western Turkic Khaganate under Tong Yabghu, whom Byzantine sources call the Khazars under Ziebel. The Turks sent 40,000 men into the Caucasus in 626, and joint operations focused on besieging Tiflis.

In mid-September 627 Heraclius left Ziebel at the siege and invaded the Persian Empire with between 25,000 and 50,000 troops and 40,000 Göktürks. The Göktürks soon deserted him because of the strange winter conditions. Khosrow appointed Rhahzadh to confront him, with an army of 12,000. Heraclius evaded him, entered Mesopotamia and took food and fodder from the countryside, leaving Rhahzadh to follow through stripped land. On 1 December he crossed the Great Zab and camped near the ruins of Nineveh.

Heraclius chose a plain west of the Great Zab where his lances and hand-to-hand fighting counted for most, and fog reduced the Persian advantage in missile troops. On 12 December Rhahzadh attacked in three masses. Heraclius feigned retreat to draw them onto the plain, then turned on them. After eight hours the Persians withdrew to the foothills, with 6,000 dead. Nikephoros says Rhahzadh challenged Heraclius to single combat and was killed by him with one thrust, and Theophanes supports this, though doubt has been cast on it. 3,000 Persian reinforcements arrived too late.

The Byzantines could not capture the Persian camp, but no Persian army remained to oppose them. Heraclius plundered Khosrow's palace at Dastagird and recovered 300 captured standards. He could not attack Ctesiphon because the Nahrawan Canal was blocked by a fallen bridge. The Persian army rebelled and overthrew Khosrow II, raising his son Kavad II, also called Siroes, and Khosrow died in a dungeon, shot slowly with arrows on the fifth day.

Kavad at once sent peace offers. Heraclius, knowing that his own empire was near exhaustion, imposed no harsh terms. The Byzantines regained all their lost territories, their captured soldiers, a war indemnity and, of great spiritual significance, the True Cross and other relics lost at Jerusalem in 614. It was the last conflict of the Roman–Persian Wars. The Sasanian civil war that followed weakened the empire and contributed to the Muslim conquest of Persia.
battle-of-nordlingen-1634: By 1634 the Swedes and their German allies occupied much of southern Germany and blocked the Spanish Road, the overland supply route from Italy to Flanders. Sweden had intervened in 1630 under Gustavus Adolphus, who died at Lützen in November 1632, and Sweden and its allies formed the Heilbronn League in April 1633. Emperor Ferdinand II dismissed Albrecht von Wallenstein, who was assassinated in February 1634, and became more reliant on the Spanish. The Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand recruited an army in Italy and crossed the Alps in May. Ferdinand of Hungary took Regensburg on 26 July and then besieged the Swedish-held town of Nördlingen. The Imperial and Spanish armies linked up on 2 September.

Gustav Horn and Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar marched to relieve Nördlingen with around 26,000 men, 8,000 of them poorly trained Württemberg militia. Horn wanted to wait for reinforcements, but Bernhard urged an immediate attack, claiming the Spanish reinforcements numbered under 7,000. The true figure was over 18,000, so the combined Spanish-Imperial army exceeded 33,000. On 5 September the Protestant army seized hills south of the town, and Swedish assaults on the Heselberg were repulsed. At 5:00 on 6 September the Swedish artillery opened fire and a general assault on the Albuch followed. Veterans of the Tercio of Idiáquez counter-attacked, and by 6:00 the Imperial forces were back in control.

Horn ordered further assaults, all of which failed, and around 10:00 told his troops to hold until nightfall and then withdraw. Seeing this, the Spanish-Imperial troops advanced. Bernhard's cavalry was routed, Croat light cavalry outflanked his infantry and Imperial cavalry charging out of the woods cut off Horn's retreat. His army disintegrated, with between 12,000 and 14,000 casualties against 3,500 for the victors, including 4,000 prisoners. Horn was held in custody until 1642.

Nördlingen effectively destroyed Swedish power in southern Germany, and some commentators call it arguably the most important battle of the war. The Imperial army retook most of Württemberg and moved into the Rhineland. The Swedish Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna said the defeat was so terrible it could not have been worse. In December Saxony and Hesse-Darmstadt negotiated peace with the emperor, formalised in May 1635 as the Treaty of Prague. France then intervened: in February 1635 Cardinal Richelieu agreed a joint offensive with the Dutch in the Spanish Netherlands, in April France allied with Sweden, and in May it declared war on Spain.
battle-of-noryang: Setbacks on land and at sea had driven the Japanese armies back to their fortresses, the wajō, on the south-eastern coast of Korea. Toyotomi Hideyoshi died unexpectedly at Fushimi castle on 18 September 1598, and the new Council of Five Elders ordered the forces in Korea home. The westernmost fortress, Sunch'on, held 14,000 troops under Konishi Yukinaga, and Yi Sun-sin and the Ming admiral Chen Lin blockaded it. Konishi sent Chen gifts to have the blockade lifted, and Chen at first agreed, but Yi refused to leave.
On 15 December about 20,000 Japanese troops from the fortresses of Sach'on, Goseong and Namhae boarded 500 ships and massed east of the Noryang Strait under Shimazu Yoshihiro to break the blockade.

The allies had 82 Joseon panokseon and a Ming fleet of war junks and lighter ships, almost 16,000 men in all, outnumbered in ships but with greater firepower and sturdier hulls. Warned by scouts and fishermen, Yi waited at the western end of the strait, and the battle began around 2:00 am on 16 December. Japanese ships could not answer the allied cannon, but when Chen closed to melee the Japanese boarded his flagship. The Ming commander Deng Zilong, rowing to his aid in a panokseon, was fired on by Ming ships that took it for Japanese, and was killed when the Japanese boarded it.

By dawn half of Shimazu's fleet had been sunk or captured, and the rest retreated along the south coast of Namhae Island. During the pursuit an arquebus bullet struck Yi near the left armpit. Only his eldest son Yi Hoe, his adjutant Song Hui-rip and his nephew Yi Wan saw him die; Yi Wan wore his armour and beat the war drum until the fighting ended.

An estimated 200 of Shimazu's ships reached Busan, though other Joseon records put the survivors at only 50. Konishi slipped out of his fortress on 16 December by the southern end of Namhae Island, and the last Japanese ships sailed for Japan on 24 December. Yi was buried in his home town of Asan, given the posthumous rank of Minister of the Right and in 1643 the title chungmugong. A Ming force of three to four thousand stayed in Korea until 1601.
battle-of-notium: In 407 BCE Lysander was appointed navarch of the Spartan fleet in place of Mindarus, who had been killed. He made his base at Ephesus with 70 triremes, raising the number to 90 by building ships there. He formed a personal friendship with the Persian prince Cyrus, who agreed to raise the pay of Spartan rowers from 3 to 4 obols a day out of his own purse, so that the Spartan fleet could attract experienced rowers away from the Athenians.

Alcibiades brought the Athenian fleet to Notium to watch the Spartans across the water and force a battle, but Lysander would not come out. Alcibiades then sailed north with a few troopships to help Thrasybulus besiege Phocaea, leaving the 80 ships at Notium under his helmsman Antiochus, a choice that ancient and modern writers have widely criticised, since a fleet of that size would normally have been led by generals or at least a trierarch. Antiochus was ordered not to attack Lysander's ships.

Antiochus disobeyed. He sailed towards Ephesus with 10 triremes to lure the Spartans into pursuit, intending the rest of the fleet to ambush them, a plan resembling the one that had won the Athenian victory at Cyzicus. A sudden Spartan attack sank his ship and killed him, and the other nine fled back to Notium with the whole Spartan fleet behind them, catching the main Athenian force unprepared. The Athenians lost 15 triremes captured and seven sunk before the Spartans returned to Ephesus.

Alcibiades lifted the siege of Phocaea and rejoined the fleet, but could not draw Lysander out again. His political enemies seized on the defeat and he was removed from command; he went to his land in the Thracian Chersonese and never returned to Athens. His friends Thrasybulus and Theramenes fell with him, and Conon took command. Donald Kagan has argued that the loss of Thrasybulus was the battle's most important effect for Athens. Lysander, replaced by Callicratidas under the navarch's term limit, returned in 405 BCE to destroy the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami.
battle-of-novara-1513: The battle, also known as the Battle of Ariotta, belonged to the War of the League of Cambrai. The French had won the Battle of Ravenna in 1512, but the following month the Holy League drove the army of King Louis XII out of the city of Milan. Swiss mercenaries then installed Maximilian Sforza as Duke of Milan on 29 December 1512.
By June 1513 the French had occupied most of the western part of the duchy. An army of more than 20,000 under Louis de La Trémoille laid siege to Novara, which was held by Swiss troops.

After marching to Novara during the night, the French were surprised at dawn by a Swiss relief army of some 12,000 men. The German Landsknechte serving France, armed with pikes like the Swiss, formed heavy squares and resisted stiffly, and the French managed to bring some of their artillery into action. The Swiss, however, had reached the camp by forced marches and closed on it from several directions. They took the French guns, pushed back the Landsknecht infantry and broke their squares. Caught unprepared, the French heavy cavalry could not deploy properly and fled, leaving the baggage train to the Swiss.

The battle was particularly bloody. The French side lost at least 5,000 men, and the Swiss about 1,500, most of them to French artillery fire during the advance. After the fighting the Swiss executed the hundreds of Landsknechte they had captured. They also took 22 French guns.

Lacking cavalry, the Swiss could not pursue closely, although several contingents followed the French retreat as far as Dijon, until France paid them to leave. The defeat forced Louis XII to give up Milan and withdraw from Italy altogether.
battle-of-okehazama: In 1560 Imagawa Yoshimoto, a powerful warlord who controlled Suruga, Tōtōmi and Mikawa Provinces, assembled an army of 25,000 men to march on Kyoto and challenge the increasingly weak Ashikaga shogunate. The army followed the Tōkaidō highway and crossed from Mikawa into Owari Province, which had recently been united by the local warlord Oda Nobunaga. The Imagawa overran Oda's border fortress of Washizu, Matsudaira Motoyasu took Marune fortress, and Yoshimoto camped at Dengaku-hazama in the village of Okehazama, just outside what is now Nagoya.

Nobunaga could field only about 2,000 to 3,000 men, roughly a tenth of the Imagawa army. Some of his staff urged withdrawal to Kiyosu Castle, but he knew it could not withstand a siege. He said that only a strong offensive policy could make up for the enemy's greater numbers. He and his scouts knew the ground well, having used it for war games disguised as falconry hunts. The next morning he recited a passage from the song Atsumori, ate a bowl of rice porridge standing, and rode out.

He led his men to the fortified temple of Zenshō-ji, near Okehazama, and set up many flags and banners to suggest a larger force. The actual sequence of events is much embellished by legend and historically unclear. Tradition holds that on 12 June 1560 the Oda hid at Kamagatani and attacked the camp from the north, but many modern historians think it was a frontal assault, by design or by accident.

The Imagawa were celebrating their recent easy victories, and in the heat of the afternoon many had taken off their armour. Using a thunderstorm to cover their movements, the Oda struck the heart of the camp, in a narrow valley, and the Imagawa panicked. Yoshimoto was not, as is popularly believed, killed in his camp. He fled to where the fighting was, fought off the spearman Mōri Shinsuke, and was tackled by Hattori Koheita, who took his head. With their leader and all but two senior officers dead, the rest surrendered or fled.

The battle is regarded as one of the most significant turning points in Japanese history. The Imagawa clan was greatly weakened and soon destroyed by its neighbours, while Nobunaga gained great prestige. Many samurai and minor warlords pledged fealty to him, among them Yoshimoto's former retainer Matsudaira Motoyasu, the future Tokugawa Ieyasu. At the battle Nobunaga first noticed the sandal-bearer Kinoshita Tōkichirō, who became Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The battlefield is now a park and a National Historic Site.
battle-of-okinawa: The battle, codenamed Operation Iceberg, followed a long campaign of island hopping. The Allies planned to use Kadena Air Base on Okinawa as a staging point for Operation Downfall, the invasion of the Japanese home islands 550 kilometres away. The United States formed the Tenth Army, combining Army and Marine divisions, with its own tactical air force. Against it stood Lieutenant General Mitsuru Ushijima's Thirty-Second Army, a mixed force of regular troops, naval infantry and conscripted local Okinawans, about 100,000 Japanese troops in all at the start.

The 77th Infantry Division captured the Kerama Islands from 26 March 1945. On 28 March, 394 civilians on Tokashiki island were forced by Japanese soldiers to kill themselves after American troops landed. The main landing took place on 1 April on the Hagushi beaches on the west coast, and the Tenth Army quickly took the Kadena and Yomitan airbases. The 6th Marine Division cleared the north, while two Army divisions turned south and met fierce resistance at fortified outposts guarding the Shuri Line. The Japanese fought from prepared cave positions, and the advance cost many lives on both sides. The land battle lasted about 81 days.

At sea, Japanese attacks came in waves. Between 1 April and 25 May seven major kamikaze attacks involved more than 1,500 planes. In April the battleship Yamato and nine other warships sailed from Japan on a suicide sortie, Operation Ten-Go; American carrier aircraft sank Yamato and five other warships before they reached Okinawa.

The Americans suffered some 48,000 casualties, more than 12,000 of them killed or missing. Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr., the commander of the Tenth Army, was killed by artillery fire four days before the campaign ended, the highest-ranking American officer killed by enemy fire in the war. Okinawa had a large civilian population, and about 40,000 of the Okinawans killed had been drafted or impressed by the Japanese army. The Cornerstone of Peace at Mabuni, erected in 1995, lists the names of all the known dead, civilian and military, Japanese and foreign.

Japan surrendered soon after, so the planned invasion of the home islands never took place. Some military historians hold that the cost of Okinawa led American planners to seek an alternative in the atomic bombings, while others point to the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and Japan's depleted resources.
battle-of-opis: Opis stood on the Tigris about 80 kilometres north of Baghdad and is thought to have been a favoured crossing point; Xenophon describes a bridge there. It also lay at one end of the Median Wall, a defensive barrier north of Babylon built decades earlier by Nebuchadnezzar II, so its capture would open the road to the capital. The invasion may have been timed for early autumn, when the rivers are at their lowest.

Babylonia, bordered by the Persian empire to the north, east and west, suffered severe economic problems made worse by plague and famine, and King Nabonidus was said to be unpopular for his unconventional religious policies. Cyrus is said to have won over Gobryas, governor of the frontier region of Gutium, which served as the starting point of the invasion. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that Nabonidus had cult statues brought into the capital beforehand, so the fighting may have begun in the winter of 540 BCE.

The Nabonidus Chronicle places the battle in the month of Tashritu at Opis on the bank of the Tigris, between Cyrus and the army of Akkad, but gives no detail of its course, the forces or the casualties. The Babylonian commander is not named: some assume it was Belshazzar, son of Nabonidus, while Paul-Alain Beaulieu holds that Nabonidus himself led. The defeated army is not mentioned again, which suggests a rout. The Persians took plunder, and most translations mention a massacre of the people of Akkad, though translators disagree on who was killed and by whom; Amélie Kuhrt sees a probably hard-won victory, while W. G. Lambert argues there was no massacre at all.

According to the chronicle, Sippar was captured without battle on 6 October and Nabonidus fled. On 12 October Ug/Gubaru, governor of Gutium, entered Babylon with the army of Cyrus without a battle, and Nabonidus was captured on his return. The chronicle notes that the rites of the Esagila and the other temples were not interrupted. Cyrus entered Babylon on 29 October and was proclaimed king.

The Cyrus Cylinder does not mention the battle and presents Cyrus as liberating Babylon peacefully, but Opis shows that the Babylonian regime resisted the invasion. The later Greek accounts of Herodotus and Xenophon tell of a siege and the diverting of the Euphrates, which neither the cuneiform sources nor the city's archaeology support.
battle-of-oriskany: In June 1777 the British Army launched a two-pronged attack from Quebec under General John Burgoyne, aiming to split New England from the other colonies by taking the Hudson Valley. While Burgoyne came south across Lake Champlain, Brigadier General Barry St. Leger led about 1,800 regulars, Jäger, Loyalists of the Royal Yorkers and the British Indian Department, and Indigenous warriors down the Mohawk Valley. His force besieged Fort Stanwix, a Continental Army outpost, from 2 August. Nicholas Herkimer, head of Tryon County's Committee of Safety, raised about 800 militiamen, mostly poorly trained farmers of Palatine German descent, joined by 60 to 100 Oneida warriors under Han Yerry.

Warned by a message from Molly Brant to her brother Joseph Brant, St. Leger sent Sir John Johnson's men and about 400 warriors and rangers to intercept the column. Herkimer wished to wait for a cannon signal from the fort, but his captains accused him of being a Tory, and he marched on. About 10 km from the fort the road dipped into a marshy ravine, where the Seneca chiefs Sayenqueraghta and Cornplanter laid the ambush.

At about 10 am the warriors opened fire too early, yet the Patriots were taken by surprise. Herkimer's leg was shattered; propped against a beech tree, he kept directing his men. The rear of the column fled, and within 30 minutes only about half his men were still fighting. After a thunderstorm halted the battle for an hour, Herkimer had his men fight in pairs. Meanwhile Lieutenant Colonel Marinus Willett led 250 men out of the fort and looted the nearly deserted enemy camps, and the warriors withdrew to protect them.

The Americans lost around 465 dead, wounded or captured, Johnson's force 93. Herkimer's leg was amputated and he died on 16 August. Discontent among Britain's Indigenous allies, who had done most of the fighting and lost belongings in the sortie, helped St. Leger's expedition fail: when Benedict Arnold's relief column approached, the besiegers withdrew.

The battle began a war within the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Brant's Mohawks burned the Oneida settlement of Oriska, and the Oneidas plundered the Mohawk strongholds of Tiononderoge and Canajoharie. Haudenosaunee oral histories call the site A Place of Great Sadness. A monument went up in 1883, and the battlefield became a National Historic Landmark in 1962.
battle-of-orsha: At the end of 1512 the Grand Duchy of Moscow began a new war for the Ruthenian lands of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. The fortress of Smolensk, the easternmost outpost of Lithuania, fell to a Muscovite army in July 1514, and Grand Prince Vasili III then ordered his forces into present-day Belarus, where they occupied Krichev, Mstislavl and Dubrovna. Sigismund I the Old gathered some 35,000 troops, mostly well-trained cavalry, of whom 57 per cent were Poles. The main force of around 30,000 under Hetman Konstanty Ostrogski moved to face the Muscovites, who had camped between Orsha and Dubrovno. Their commander Ivan Chelyadnin split his forces to guard the Dnieper crossings, but Ostrogski crossed farther north on two pontoon bridges.

On 8 September Chelyadnin ordered an attack. The Muscovites tried to outflank the Polish and Lithuanian wings, failed and withdrew. Chelyadnin, preoccupied with his own wing, lost track of the other sectors, and the Lithuanian light and Polish heavy cavalry, held in reserve, counter-attacked. The Polish cavalry seemed to waver and retreat, and the Muscovite cavalry pursued, only to meet artillery hidden in the forest as Lithuanian forces appeared from both sides and surrounded them. The retreat became panicked, and the Muscovites were pursued for five kilometres.

Sigismund von Herberstein reported 40,000 Muscovites killed, while Polish chronicles speak of 30,000 killed and 3,000 captured, among them Chelyadnin and eight other commanders. The victors seized the Muscovite camp and 300 cannons. The sizes of the armies are disputed. Herberstein gave 80,000 Muscovites against under 30,000, but some modern historians estimate 40,000 or fewer, and the Russian historian A. Lobin put the number at Orsha at perhaps 12,000.

Ostrogski retook most of the strongholds the Muscovites had taken, including Mstislavl and Krichev, and the Muscovite advance was stopped for four years. His exhausted army did not reach Smolensk until late September, which gave Vasili III time to prepare its defence. In December Ostrogski entered Vilnius in triumph, and two Orthodox churches, the Church of the Holy Trinity and the Church of Saint Nicholas, were built to commemorate the victory. Accounts of the battle were sent to Rome as propaganda for Poland-Lithuania.
The war lasted until 1520. By the peace of 1522 Lithuania ceded about a quarter of its lands of the former Kievan Rus' to Moscow, Smolensk among them, and Smolensk was not retaken until 1611.
battle-of-ostia: Muslim forces began the conquest of Sicily in 827, and from 835 the Aghlabids also campaigned on the Italian mainland. Their invasions of Calabria and Apulia, and their attacks on other islands of the central Mediterranean, were probably an extension of the conquest of Sicily, meant to weaken Byzantine positions in the region. In 846 a Muslim force raided the outskirts of Rome, although it is not certain that the raiders came from Aghlabid territory. The attack of 849 was the next approach on the city.

Early in 849 news reached Rome that Muslim ships were gathering off Sardinia. A Christian fleet was assembled off the recently refortified port of Ostia under the command of Caesar, son of Sergius I of Naples, and Pope Leo IV came out to bless it and celebrate mass for the troops. When the Muslim ships appeared, battle was joined with the Neapolitan galleys in the lead.

Midway through the fight a storm separated the two sides. The Christian ships were able to return to port, but the Muslim fleet was scattered far and wide, with many ships lost and others driven ashore. Once the storm had passed, its remnants were easily picked off and many prisoners were taken.

Much wreckage washed ashore and was plundered by the local people under the right of shipwreck, jus naufragii. The prisoners were made to work in chain gangs on the Leonine Wall, which was to enclose the Vatican Hill. No Muslim army approached Rome again. The battle is one of the few ninth-century events of southern Italy still remembered today, largely through the walls named after Leo and the Renaissance painting Battaglia di Ostia by Raphael.
battle-of-otlukbeli: The Republic of Venice opened negotiations with Uzun Hasan in the autumn of 1463, and from 1464 he intervened in the affairs of central Anatolia. Mehmed II occupied Karaman in 1468 but could not subdue the Turkoman tribes of the mountains reaching to the Mediterranean coast, who rose from time to time around pretenders to the Karamanid throne. Uzun Hasan then turned more aggressive. He allied with the Venetians, made contact with the Knights of Rhodes, the Kingdom of Cyprus and the Bey of Alaiye, and in 1472, with Karamanid forces, drove the Ottomans from Karaman and marched on Bursa before Mehmed repulsed him.

When Uzun Hasan demanded Cappadocia and Trabzon, Mehmed answered with open defiance and, against his habit of secrecy, announced when he would march. The sultan reached Yenişehir on 11 April 1473; joined by Prince Mustafa, governor of Karaman, and Prince Bayezid, governor of Amasya, the army reached 85,000 men. Beyond Sivas it crossed mountains in a snowstorm. Turahanoğlu Ömer Bey defeated an Aq Qoyunlu force of 5,000 near Erzincan, but on the Euphrates the young Has Murad Pasha was drawn forward by a feigned retreat and his force was destroyed, a blow that badly demoralised the army.

On Wednesday 11 August the Ottomans were caught in a narrow pass when Aq Qoyunlu troops appeared on the Otlukbeli ridge. Davud Pasha held off the commander Gavur İshak and engaged the right wing under Uzun Hasan's son Zeynel Mirza; Prince Mustafa then fell on Zeynel, who was killed. Another son, Uğurlu Mehmed, withdrew before Prince Bayezid almost without fighting. When Mehmed brought his 25,000 janissaries into action, Uzun Hasan fled, leaving a lookalike, Pir Mehmed Bey, in his place, and the battle turned into a rout.

Mehmed went on to take Şebinkarahisar, whose lord surrendered, and announced his victory in a series of letters, among them a decree in the Uyghur language to the Turkomans of Anatolia, dated 30 August 1473. The Ottomans had nearly broken Aq Qoyunlu power in the east; the dynasty was later destroyed by Ismail I, founder of the Safavid Empire, which became a new rival of the Ottoman Empire in the east.
battle-of-oudenarde: The War of the Spanish Succession followed the death of the childless Charles II of Spain in November 1700. He left his monarchy undivided to Philip, a grandson of Louis XIV, and the Grand Alliance of England, the Holy Roman Empire and the Dutch Republic backed Charles, younger son of Emperor Leopold I. After the French defeats at Blenheim and Ramillies the war settled into stalemate. In 1708 the two French commanders, the Duke of Burgundy and the Duke of Vendome, quarrelled over their plan, and the one adopted on Louis XIV's orders was to attack Flanders.
On 5 July the French suddenly moved west and took Bruges and Ghent, leaving Oudenaarde as the only Allied fortress; its loss would have cut Marlborough off from the coast and from England.

Marlborough guessed the French plan and made a forced march that took Lessines on 10 July. He sent eleven thousand men under his quartermaster general William Cadogan to hold the main crossing of the Scheldt, and Cadogan's men built five pontoon bridges. French foragers discovered the Allied presence around 9 a.m. on 11 July. Cadogan's cavalry pushed back the French vanguard under the Duke of Biron, and Eugene crossed with twenty squadrons of Prussian cavalry.

Burgundy then launched an attack over Vendome's protests; Vendome led twelve infantry regiments himself, so neither commander directed the whole field. Half the French forces were held in reserve, and their left wing stayed inactive.

Dutch field deputies thought Marlborough unsteady and asked Eugene to take supreme command, which he partly did, commanding the right flank. Marlborough ordered a double encirclement with 25,000 fresh Dutch troops under Lord Overkirk, who arrived at about 6 p.m. after a delay at the bridges. Sicco van Goslinga and the Prince of Orange then led some 10,000 infantry down the slope and swept aside the French infantry. Dutch cavalry cut off the retreat to Kortrijk, and in the dark the Allied wings briefly fired on each other before Eugene and the Prince of Orange stopped them.

The French army retreated in disorder toward Ghent, its commanders blaming one another; only nightfall and some broken pontoon bridges saved it from total destruction. It lost some fourteen to fifteen thousand men, about eight thousand of them prisoners, and 25 guns, while the Allies lost roughly three thousand. The victory restored the strategic initiative to the Allies, who besieged Lille. The town surrendered on 22 October and the citadel yielded on 10 December. The French were driven out of almost all the Spanish Netherlands. Marlborough wrote that he and Eugene would never differ over their share of the laurels.
battle-of-ourique: After the Battle of Sao Mamede in 1128, Afonso Henriques wrested the County of Portugal from the regent-countess Teresa and moved his court from Guimaraes to Coimbra, which let him concentrate on the southern frontier. His seizure of the county brought conflict with his suzerain Alfonso VII of Leon, and peace was signed at Tui in 1137.

Almoravid forces had besieged Coimbra in 1117 and destroyed the frontier castle of Leiria in 1137, and a Portuguese force was destroyed by the river Nabao. The Almoravid ruler Ali Ibn Yusuf faced a revolt by the Almohads in Morocco, and in 1138 his heir Tashfin was recalled from al-Andalus. Troops were gathered in May 1139 and set out south in the summer. The Portuguese probably numbered 800 to 1,000 knights and 1,600 to 2,000 footmen.

The campaign seems to have been timed with the Leonese siege of Oreja, which drew Almoravid forces from the garrisons of Cordoba and Seville. Afonso crossed the Tagus, threatening Silves, and met little resistance. The governor of Cordoba, Muhammad Az-Zubayr Ibn Umar, whom Christian chronicles call King Ismar, called up forces from Badajoz, Evora, Elvas, Seville and Beja and pursued the Portuguese, who were slowed by spoils and prisoners. The two armies sighted each other near Ourique on 24 July. Afonso set up a camp on a hill fortified with trenches. Shortly before dawn on 25 July he was lifted on a shield and hailed as king by his troops.

The Muslims struck first, trying to breach the camp. The Portuguese then sallied out in a vanguard, two wings and a rearguard, and a heavy cavalry charge shattered the Muslim vanguard; Afonso himself killed an enemy with his lance. The fighting became a disorganised melee, but the Portuguese had heavier armour. Most of the Muslims withdrew and many were killed in the rout, while Ismar fled. The exact site of the battle is uncertain.

Afonso had a number of prisoners beheaded and buried on the spot, and the army marched back to Coimbra three days later. Ismar regrouped at Santarem and sacked Trancoso, but was routed near it by Afonso. After April 1140 Afonso's documents were usually signed rex Alfonsus. A legend says that Christ crucified appeared to him the night before the battle and revealed the coat of arms of Portugal, whose five escutcheons stand for five vanquished Muslim kings. The oldest accounts do not mention it, but by the 14th century the tradition was well established, and in the 19th century Alexandre Herculano judged it a pious fraud.
battle-of-paardeberg: Lord Methuen's advance to relieve Kimberley had been halted by Piet Cronjé and Koos de la Rey at the Battle of Magersfontein. Field Marshal Lord Roberts, appointed to command in South Africa in December 1899 in succession to General Buller, gathered reinforcements between the Orange and Modder rivers and from 11 February 1900 sent Major General John French's cavalry around the Boer left. After exhausting marches across the Riet and the Modder, French reached Kimberley on the evening of 15 February, but his horses were worn out.

The same day Cronjé, with some 5,000 Transvaalers and Free Staters and many of their families in slow ox-wagons, left Jacobsdal for Bloemfontein. On 17 February, as the convoy began crossing the Modder at Paardeberg Drift, 1,500 of French's mounted troops opened fire on it from the north. Instead of brushing them aside, Cronjé formed a laager and dug in on the river bank, letting the British gather about 15,000 men with far more artillery.

With Roberts ill, his chief of staff Lieutenant General Herbert Kitchener overruled Lieutenant General Thomas Kelly-Kenny's plan for a siege and on 18 February launched uncoordinated frontal assaults. By nightfall 24 officers and 279 men had been killed and 59 officers and 847 men wounded, the most severe British reverse of the war, known as Bloody Sunday. Christiaan De Wet seized the lightly held Kitchener's Kopje to the south-east, opening a way out for Cronjé.

Roberts arrived on 19 February and refused Cronjé a truce to bury the dead. The British then shelled the laager with more and more guns, killing almost every horse, mule and ox, while Cronjé refused to break out. De Wet finally abandoned the kopje shortly before Roberts had planned to withdraw. On the night of 26 February the Royal Canadian Regiment, helped by Royal Engineers, dug trenches close to the Boer lines, and on 27 February Cronjé surrendered with some 4,019 men and 50 women.

The surrender, on the nineteenth anniversary of the British defeat at Majuba, was the first major British victory of the war, and about a tenth of the Boers' whole army were now prisoners. Thomas Pakenham judged that Cronjé's blunders had outmatched those of Kitchener and Roberts; the South African historian J. H. Breytenbach replied that Cronjé's 4,000 men with five cannons had been trapped by about 40,000 soldiers with 100. In Canada, 27 February was kept as Paardeberg Day until Armistice Day replaced it after the First World War.
battle-of-panium: In 202 BCE Ptolemy son of Thraseas, the Ptolemaic governor of Coele-Syria, went over to Antiochus III the Great. By the autumn of 201 BCE Antiochus had occupied most of the province, including Gaza, before returning to winter quarters in Syria, and during that winter the Ptolemaic commander Scopas of Aetolia won back parts of it. Antiochus then gathered his army at Damascus and in the summer marched to meet the Ptolemaic army at the stream of Panium near Mount Hermon.

The Ptolemaic line was four kilometres wide. Its left wing on the plain held the kingdom's best troops, a phalanx of 25,000 to 32,000 Macedonian settlers under Ptolemy son of Aeropus, while Scopas, in supreme command, brought 6,500 Aetolian mercenaries. Antiochus probably had around 70,000 men, including cataphracts, the elite cavalry agema, Tarentines, phalangites, hypaspists and war elephants, as Polybius records.

In the night his eldest son, Antiochus the Younger, seized the foothill of Tel Hamra with the cataphracts, and at the opening of the battle they routed the Ptolemaic cavalry. In the centre the Ptolemaic phalanx pushed back its Seleucid counterpart until elephants charged through gaps in the Seleucid line and halted it. The cataphracts then broke off their pursuit and charged the phalanx from the rear, and, pressed from two sides, it was almost annihilated where it stood.

Scopas fled from the right wing with 10,000 men to Sidon, while other contingents escaped to Jerusalem, Phoenicia, Samaria and the Decapolis; all had surrendered by the end of 198 BCE, and the Ptolemies made peace in 195 BCE. Judged by the losses of phalanxes at Magnesia and Pydna, the Ptolemaic phalangites may have lost 17,500 to 20,825 men killed or captured. The Ptolemaic Kingdom never recovered as an independent great power and reduced the role of its settler phalanx, while Antiochus turned to the coming conflict with the Roman Republic. Some biblical commentators link the battle to Daniel 11:15.
battle-of-passchendaele: The Third Battle of Ypres was fought from July to November 1917 for control of the ridges south and east of Ypres in West Flanders, as part of a strategy decided by the Entente in November 1916 and May 1917. Passchendaele lies on the last ridge east of Ypres, 8 kilometres from Roulers, whose station was on the main supply route of the German 4th Army. The campaign was controversial from the start. David Lloyd George and Ferdinand Foch opposed it, and Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig did not receive the War Cabinet's approval until 25 July. The first stage was the Battle of Messines in June, after mines filled with nearly 454 tonnes of explosives were fired under the ridge.

The first Allied attack was the Battle of Pilckem Ridge on 31 July. General Hubert Gough's offensive was not planned as a breakthrough. The Germans held the Gheluvelt Plateau in August, though their casualties worsened a manpower shortage. On 25 August Haig shifted the main effort to the Second Army, whose commander Plumer planned to take the plateau in four limited steps at six-day intervals. Unusually wet weather in August and the autumn rains in October turned the ground to mud. The campaign ended in November when the Canadian Corps captured Passchendaele, and a British night attack towards Westroosebeke on 1 and 2 December failed.

Casualty figures have been published with acrimony. James Edmonds put British casualties at 244,897 and estimated German losses at 400,000, while A. J. P. Taylor, who rejected Edmonds's calculations, gave 300,000 British and 200,000 German. The British claim of 24,065 prisoners is undisputed. Lloyd George later called Passchendaele one of the worst disasters of the war, while a German General Staff publication wrote that Germany had been brought near to certain destruction by the Flanders battle. Jack Sheldon argued that it pinned the German army to Flanders and caused unsustainable casualties. The German submarine bases on the coast had not been captured. The Menin Gate Memorial commemorates Commonwealth dead of the Ypres Salient who have no known grave.
battle-of-pavia: The French had held Lombardy at the start of the Italian War of 1521 to 1526 but lost it after the Battle of Bicocca in 1522. A French invasion in late 1523 under Guillaume Gouffier, Seigneur de Bonnivet, was defeated at the Battle of the Sesia. An imperial invasion of Provence then stalled at the Siege of Marseille and withdrew when Francis I arrived at Avignon with the main French army. In mid-October 1524 Francis crossed the Alps, entered Milan and advanced on Pavia, where Antonio de Leyva held out with about 9,000 men, paying them by melting the church plate.

The French besieged the city from late October. An assault on 21 November was beaten back, and Francis decided to starve the garrison. He then divided his forces, sending the Duke of Albany south to aid Pope Clement VII, while about 5,000 Grisons Swiss left for home. In January 1525 Georg Frundsberg arrived with 15,000 fresh landsknechts, and Charles de Lannoy renewed the offensive. Short of supplies, the imperial commanders decided on 21 February to attack, Pescara arguing that battle was their only way.

On the night of 23 February the imperial engineers breached the wall of the Visconti Park at the Porta Pescarina. By 5:00 am some 3,000 arquebusiers under Alfonso d'Avalos, Marquis of Vasto, were inside and advancing on Mirabello Castle. A full infantry battle developed by 7:00 am, when Frundsberg's landsknechts met Swiss pikemen. Around 7:40 am Francis led his gendarmes in a charge that scattered Lannoy's cavalry, but it carried him away from his infantry and masked the fire of his own artillery.

By 8:00 am imperial pikemen and arquebusiers had surrounded the French cavalry in the wooded ground and killed them systematically. The Black Band of landsknechts was exterminated, and Richard de la Pole and François de Lorraine were killed. Francis's horse was killed under him and he was taken prisoner. By 9:00 am the battle was over.

Many leading French nobles died, among them Bonnivet, La Trémoille and La Palice, and Anne de Montmorency was captured. Who took Francis is uncertain: candidates include Lannoy, three Spanish soldiers, the Count of Salm and the condottiero Cesare Hercolani, and Charles V in his autobiography credited his principal captains. Francis was held at Pizzighettone and taken to Spain, and under the Treaty of Madrid he gave up his claims in Milan and Burgundy. The peace was broken in the same year, and a new war lasted from 1526 to 1529.
battle-of-pavon: After the secession of Buenos Aires Province on 11 September 1852, in the aftermath of the Battle of Caseros, Argentina was divided between the Argentine Confederation and the State of Buenos Aires. The Battle of Cepeda in 1859 and the Pact of San José de Flores of 1860 set the conditions for Buenos Aires to rejoin. When the province elected its deputies to the National Congress under its own electoral laws, Congress rejected them, and President Santiago Derqui annulled the elections. Buenos Aires then declared the pact null.

Congress treated this as sedition, and Derqui named Justo José de Urquiza commander in chief of the national army. The federal army numbered about 17,000 men, mostly cavalry. Mitre's army had 22,000 men and 35 artillery pieces, supplied by the British with trained British crews.

The armies clashed by the Pavón creek, 40 km south of the city of Rosario. Urquiza formed a defensive line east of the Domingo Palacios ranch, with cavalry on the wings, and his artillery opened gaps in the porteño infantry. In about two hours of fighting his left wing under Juan Saá routed the First Cavalry of Venancio Flores, and his right wing under Miguel Galarza overran the small porteño cavalry facing it.

The federal centre, made up of untrained militia, was forced back by the better trained porteño infantry. Seeing it collapse, Urquiza left the field without committing the 4,000 men of Entre Ríos he held in reserve, and did not return even after learning of his cavalry's success.

Over the following months the porteño advance met no serious resistance, as Urquiza did not act and almost dismantled his army. Derqui resigned and took refuge in Montevideo, and Vice-President Juan Esteban Pedernera declared the national government dissolved. Nearly all the federal governors were deposed, and Mitre was elected in new elections from which federal candidates were barred. The capital, moved to Paraná by Urquiza, returned to Buenos Aires.
battle-of-pelagonia: After the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, the Empire of Nicaea and the Despotate of Epirus competed to recover it. When the Nicaean emperor John III Vatatzes died in 1254, Michael II Komnenos Doukas of Epirus invaded Nicaean Macedonia. He bound Manfred of Sicily to him by marrying his daughter Helena to Manfred with Albania and Corfu as her dowry, and gave his daughter Anna to William of Villehardouin, Prince of Achaea. Facing this coalition, Michael VIII Palaiologos sent an army into Europe in the autumn of 1258 under his brother, the sebastokrator John Palaiologos, and Alexios Strategopoulos. In spring 1259 it advanced along the Via Egnatia and drove Michael II back across the Pindus.

Manfred sent 400 German knights, and William led a levy of the Frankish states of Greece. The allies probably outnumbered the Nicaeans, whose army included Cuman, Turkish, Hungarian and Serbian mercenaries. The Byzantine and Western sources differ widely on date, place and events. George Akropolites describes a campaign of attrition: the heavy troops held the hills while light horsemen struck at the allies' horses and supply trains. The Epirote army lost heart, Michael II withdrew, and his bastard son John Doukas went over to the Nicaeans. George Pachymeres adds that William had insulted John Doukas for his birth, while Nikephoros Gregoras credits a false deserter sent by John Palaiologos.

When the Latins found the Epirotes gone, they tried to withdraw, but were attacked and many killed. Gregoras reports that the 400 Germans surrendered, and William, found hiding near Kastoria, was taken with some thirty of his senior barons.

The Nicaeans briefly overran Thessaly and took Arta, but Michael II reversed these gains the next year and captured Strategopoulos. For Achaea the defeat was the first heavy one in its history. In early 1262 William bought his freedom by handing over Monemvasia, Mystras and the district of Mani, an agreement ratified by the so-called Parliament of Ladies. This foothold grew into the Despotate of the Morea, and the weakened Frankish states later turned to the Angevins of Naples through the Treaty of Viterbo of 1267.
battle-of-pelusium: Most accounts of the war come from Greek historians, above all Herodotus. He tells that Pharaoh Amasis II, asked by Cambyses II for a daughter in marriage, sent instead Nitetis, a daughter of the former pharaoh Apries, and that Cambyses vowed revenge when she revealed the deceit. Herodotus also names Phanes of Halicarnassus, a former adviser of Amasis who escaped to Persia and helped shape the king's resolve. The King of Arabia, an enemy of Amasis, granted Cambyses safe passage on the desert road from Gaza to Pelusium and supplied troops. Gaza, according to Polybius, alone resisted, and fell after a long siege.

Amasis died six months before Cambyses reached Egypt, and his son Psamtik III gathered the army. His hope of Greek allies failed, as the Cypriot towns and Polycrates of Samos, who sent 40 triremes, joined the Persians. Herodotus says Psamtik had the sons of Phanes killed and their blood mixed with wine and drunk before the battle. Near Pelusium, an important city on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta 30 km south-east of modern Port Said, the Egyptians were routed. Ctesias puts the Egyptian dead at fifty thousand and the Persian at seven thousand. The survivors fled to Memphis and were besieged there.

According to Herodotus, the Egyptians at Memphis killed the crew of a ship sent with a Persian herald, and after the siege two thousand Egyptians died, ten for every Mytilenean killed. Psamtik was captured and allowed to live under watch, but later killed himself after attempting a revolt.
