Herodotus says Cambyses then had the mummy of Amasis burned, though the historian Pierre Briant judges this account false. Polyaenus, writing about 700 years later, told the story that Persian soldiers carried sacred animals such as cats before them. Herodotus saw the bones of the dead still lying on the field.
battle-of-petrovaradin: In the summer of 1715 the Ottoman Empire began to reclaim the Peloponnese, which the Treaty of Karlowitz had ceded to the Republic of Venice in 1699, and easily retook the Venetian Kingdom of the Morea. Austria allied with Venice in April 1716 and demanded full Ottoman withdrawal and compensation to Venice. The Ottoman grand vizier, confident that he could defeat the Habsburgs and even regain Hungary, declared war on 15 May 1716. He left Constantinople with a 120,000-strong army that took nearly three months to reach Belgrade, where he consolidated a force of between 60,000 and 150,000, including 41,000 Janissaries and 30,000 Sipahi cavalry. They crossed the Sava at Zemun on 26 July and moved toward Sremski Karlovci.

Prince Eugene of Savoy decided to meet the Ottomans at Petrovaradin, the so-called Gibraltar on the Danube. He reached the fortress on 9 July, where 8,000 men, mostly Serbs, formed the garrison. On 2 August Field Marshal Janos Palffy's reconnaissance ran into over 10,000 Turkish cavalry, the Austrians lost 700 men and Field Marshal Siegfried Breuner was captured. The vizier demanded the fortress's surrender; Eugene answered, We will attack. His army crossed the Danube on 4 August by two pontoon bridges, under cover of an unusual summer snowstorm. It stood with one flank on the river and the other on the fortifications, with 64 battalions, 187 cavalry squadrons and 80 guns.

At seven in the morning on 5 August Eugene attacked. The left wing took the first Ottoman positions and a ten-gun battery, but in the centre the Janissaries drove back Guido Starhemberg's troops into their entrenchments. When the Janissaries pushed on, they exposed both their flanks. Eugene sent cavalry against the left and Alexander of Wurttemberg's battalions against the right, while the fortress's cannon fired into the Turkish lines. The grand vizier was killed in a desperate charge with his bodyguard, along with 20,000 men. Imperial losses were 3,695 soldiers and 469 officers. The battle was over by 2 p.m., and Eugene reported the capture of 172 cannon and 156 banners.

Pope Clement XI sent Eugene a consecrated sword. Within 20 days Eugene entered the Banat with the help of Serbian irregulars and besieged Temesvar, in Ottoman hands since 1552; it surrendered on 16 October after 43 days. Belgrade fell on 18 August 1717. A pilgrimage church was built at Tekije on the hill overlooking the battlefield, and a monument of 1902 by Hermann Bolle stands on Vezirac hill.
battle-of-pharsalus: After the war began, Caesar captured Rome, forced Pompey and his allies out of Italy and defeated Pompey's legates in Spain. In 48 BCE he crossed the Adriatic and besieged Dyrrachium but was defeated there. He then withdrew east into Thessaly, partly to relieve a legate threatened by Metellus Scipio's forces arriving from Syria, and besieged Gomphi after it resisted him. Pompey pursued, seeking to end the war on Greek soil and spare Italy invasion. His overconfident allies pressed him, accusing him of prolonging the war to extend his command.

Caesar's army, by his own account, had 22,000 legionaries in eight understrength legions, most of them veterans of the Gallic Wars, with 1,000 Gallic and Germanic cavalry. Pompey had about 45,000 Roman infantry according to Caesar, Appian and Plutarch, and between 5,000 and 7,000 cavalry, besides thousands of archers, slingers and light infantry from the east. Both armies formed in three lines, with Pompey's right and Caesar's left resting on the river Enipeus. Pompey massed his cavalry on his left under Labienus, intending it to sweep round Caesar's flank and rear. Caesar, thinning his ranks to six men deep, secretly formed a fourth line on his right.

Pompey ordered his men to wait rather than charge. Caesar's infantry advanced under Mark Antony and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus. Labienus's cavalry pushed back Caesar's, but Caesar's hidden fourth line, ordered to thrust with their pila rather than throw them, surprised the horsemen, who panicked and fled to the hills. Caesar's third line then broke Pompey's exposed left wing. Seeing his cavalry and legions give way, Pompey retreated to his camp and then fled, and the camp fell after brave resistance by seven cohorts of auxiliaries.

Caesar claimed to have lost about 200 soldiers and 30 centurions and put Pompeian losses at 60,000; Appian gives 1,200 and 6,000, and the larger figures seem exaggerated. Caesar captured Pompey's camp, burned his correspondence and announced that he would forgive all who asked for mercy. Marcus Junius Brutus sought his pardon, and Cato regrouped with supporters and went to Libya. Pompey fled to Mytilene and Cilicia, then to Egypt, where he was assassinated on arrival on the order of Ptolemy XIII; Caesar reached Alexandria on 2 October 48 BCE. The battle did not end the civil war, but it gave Caesar legitimacy, and former allies of Pompey began to align themselves with him.
battle-of-philippi: After the assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BCE, Brutus and Cassius, known as the Liberators, left Italy and took control of the eastern provinces from Greece to Syria and the allied eastern kingdoms. In Rome the three main Caesarian leaders, Antony, Octavian and Lepidus, established the Second Triumvirate and crushed the Senate's opposition. They declared a civil war ostensibly to avenge Caesar, though the underlying cause was a long conflict between the Optimates and the Populares.

Lepidus stayed in Italy while Antony and Octavian moved to northern Greece with 28 legions, sending an advance force of eight legions along the Via Egnatia. The Liberators, with the Republican admiral Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus commanding 130 ships, wished to avoid a decisive battle and to use their naval superiority to cut the triumvirs' supplies from Italy. They took a fortified position about 3.5 kilometres west of Philippi, Brutus to the north of the Via Egnatia and Cassius to the south.

Each side probably had only 40,000 to 50,000 legionaries. After Antony cut a causeway through the southern marshes, Cassius built a transverse wall against him, and a general battle began on 3 October 42 BCE. Brutus's troops attacked without waiting for orders, routed Octavian's army and captured its camp, though Octavian himself was not found in his tent. To the south Antony stormed Cassius's fortifications. Unable to see what had happened on Brutus's wing, and believing the day lost, Cassius ordered his freedman Pindarus to kill him. Brutus called him the last of the Romans.

On the same day the Republican fleet destroyed a convoy of reinforcements led by Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus. Over the next three weeks Antony advanced south, forcing Brutus to extend his line. Brutus attacked on the afternoon of 23 October. After close combat his thinned centre gave way, the triumvirs turned on his flank and rear, and his army could not re-form. Brutus retreated into the hills with the equivalent of four legions and took his own life.

Antony covered Brutus's body with a purple garment, according to Plutarch. Many young aristocrats died in the battle or by suicide, among them Marcus Porcius Cato, the son of Cato the Younger, and the father of Livia. About 14,000 survivors were enrolled in the triumvirs' army, and some veterans settled at Philippi, which became the Roman colony Colonia Victrix Philippensium. Antony stayed in the East and Octavian returned to Italy to find land for the veterans. Sextus Pompey still held Sicily, but Republican resistance had been crushed.
battle-of-pichincha: The struggle for the Presidencia de Quito began on 9 October 1820, when the port of Guayaquil proclaimed its independence after an almost bloodless revolt. A first Patriot advance into the highlands was beaten at the First Battle of Huachi on 22 November 1820. From February 1821 Simón Bolívar, President of the Republic of Colombia, sent men and supplies, and in May Antonio José de Sucre arrived to take command. Bolívar wanted every province of the Real Audiencia, Guayaquil included, joined to Colombia. Sucre's second campaign also ended in defeat at Huachi, on 12 September 1821, and an armistice followed.

In January 1822 Sucre took an indirect route through the southern highlands. At Saraguro on 9 February he was joined by about 1,500 men of the Peruvian Division under Andrés de Santa Cruz, and on 21 February he retook Cuenca without a shot. After a cavalry clash at Tapi, near Riobamba, on 21 April, he flanked the Royalist positions along the slopes of the Cotopaxi volcano, and the Royalists fell back on Quito.

On the night of 23 to 24 May the Patriot army of 2,971 men climbed Pichincha, slowed by rain that turned the trails to mud. Royalist sentries saw them at dawn, and Aymerich sent his 1,894 men up the mountain. On steep, broken ground the fighting went badly for the Patriots until the Albión battalion of British volunteers, arriving with the reserve ammunition, stopped the veteran Aragón battalion as it was about to strike their rear. The Colombians of the Alto Magdalena then broke the Royalist line, and at midday Aymerich ordered the retreat. The fighting had lasted no more than three hours.

Sucre reported 1,100 prisoners and 14 guns taken, with four hundred Royalist and two hundred Patriot dead. Lieutenant Abdón Calderón, who stayed in the fight after four wounds, became with Sucre a symbol of the battle for Ecuador. Bolívar entered Quito on 16 June 1822, and Guayaquil was proclaimed part of Colombia on 31 July. In 1830 the southern departments seceded to form the Republic of Ecuador. A monument and museum, La Cima de la Libertad, now stand on the battlefield, where a parade is held every 24 May.
battle-of-plassey: Siraj-ud-Daulah, who succeeded his maternal grandfather Alivardi Khan as Nawab of Bengal in 1756, ordered the British to stop extending their fortifications. He attacked British-controlled Calcutta, an episode that included the Black Hole massacre. The British sent reinforcements from Madras under Colonel Robert Clive and Admiral Charles Watson, recaptured Calcutta, and then seized the French fort at Chandannagar. The conflict took place during the Seven Years' War, and a small French contingent fought against the British. The Nawab also feared attack from the Afghans under Ahmad Shah Durrani in the north and from the Marathas in the west, so he could not commit his whole army against the British.

The British formed a conspiracy with Siraj-ud-Daulah's demoted commander-in-chief Mir Jafar, with Yar Lutuf Khan, Rai Durlabh and others. Clive promised to make Mir Jafar Nawab. He marched on Murshidabad with about 3,000 men, and the Nawab's army, about 50,000 strong with 40 cannons and 10 war elephants, took position at Plassey by 21 June 1757.

On 23 June the Nawab's artillery opened fire at 8:00, and Clive withdrew into a grove sheltered by an embankment. After a heavy rainstorm, in which the British covered their ammunition and the Nawab's army did not, Mir Madan Khan led a cavalry charge that was driven back with grapeshot. Siraj, disturbed, appealed to Mir Jafar, who sent word of it to Clive, and on the advice of Rai Durlabh the Nawab withdrew and left for Murshidabad. Clive's troops took the French position at 15:00. Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh and Yar Lutuf Khan had made no move to join the battle, which lasted about eleven hours.

On 24 June Clive greeted Mir Jafar as Nawab of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, and on 29 June he placed him on the throne at Murshidabad. The French were no longer a significant force in Bengal. By 1759 Mir Jafar resented his subordination to the British and encouraged the Dutch to send ships from Java; Clive defeated them at the Battle of Chinsura on 25 November 1759, and the British then deposed Mir Jafar and installed Mir Qasim. The British used the revenue and concessions they gained to increase their military strength, and historians judge Plassey one of the pivotal battles in the colonial control of the subcontinent.
battle-of-plataea: Xerxes I began preparing an invasion of Greece soon after his accession in 486 BCE, and a congress of city states, probably at Corinth, formed an alliance known as the Allies in 481 BCE. In August 480 BCE a small Allied army under the Spartan king Leonidas I held the pass of Thermopylae for three days before being outflanked. The Persians then occupied the evacuated city of Athens. The Allied navy won a decisive victory at Salamis, and Xerxes retreated to Sardis with a small part of his army, leaving his general Mardonius to finish the conquest the following year.

Mardonius retreated into Boeotia, hoping to draw the Greeks onto ground suited to his cavalry, and built a fortified camp on the north bank of the Asopos river. The Greek army, commanded by Pausanias, the regent of Sparta, crossed Mount Cithaeron and took positions on high ground opposite. According to Herodotus the Spartans sent 45,000 men, among them 5,000 full citizens and 35,000 helots. Estimates of the Persian army, drawn from the size of its camp, range from about 70,000 to 120,000, though modern historians differ widely.

The Greeks refused to descend to the plain, and a stalemate lasted eleven days. Persian cavalry then cut the Greek supply lines. On the thirteenth day the Greeks tried to withdraw, and their line broke up. Mardonius took this for a full retreat and ordered a pursuit. The Spartans, Tegeans and Athenians turned and fought, routed the lightly armed Persian infantry and killed Mardonius. Much of the Persian army was trapped in its camp and killed.

According to Herodotus the Battle of Mycale was fought on the same day, destroying what remained of the Persian fleet. After the two victories the second Persian invasion was over, and the Persian desire to conquer Greece gradually diminished. The sale of the loot paid for buildings such as the Athenian Treasury at Delphi.

A bronze column of intertwined snakes, the Serpent Column, was made from melted Persian armour and set up at Delphi, listing the 31 city-states that fought; most of it now stands in the Hippodrome of Constantinople. The poet Simonides of Ceos wrote an elegy and an encomium on the battle, and in Spartan tradition the victory avenged Thermopylae.
battle-of-poitiers-1356: English kings had held lands in France as vassals of the French crown since 1066, and by the early 14th century only Gascony remained. On 24 May 1337 Philip VI's Great Council agreed to take back Edward III's lands in France, which began the Hundred Years' War. In 1356 Edward III's son, the Black Prince, left Bergerac on 4 August with about 6,000 Anglo-Gascon fighters and devastated the countryside in three divisions. His aim was to force the French to attack him on ground of his choosing. King John II pursued with a large and unusually mobile army, and on 18 September the Anglo-Gascons took a strong position on a wooded hill 5 miles south of Poitiers, where they dug pits and trenches.

On 19 September about 14,000 to 16,000 French faced 6,000 Anglo-Gascons, who fought on foot as nearly all the French did. The first French attack, begun when a movement in the English lines was taken for a withdrawal, was driven back, and a second attack under the Dauphin Charles was also repulsed. Philip, Duke of Orléans, then led about half the third division off the field with three of John's four sons. John led the fourth division forward and had the Oriflamme unfurled, the signal that no prisoners were to be taken. A mounted force of 160 Anglo-Gascons appeared behind the French, and believing themselves surrounded the French collapsed. John II and his 14-year-old son Philip were captured, and about 2,500 French men-at-arms died.

France fell into near anarchy, and the peasant revolt known as the Jacquerie broke out in 1358. Two treaties of London were rejected in France. After a campaign in 1359 the Treaty of Brétigny was agreed in 1360, ceding large areas of France to England, and John was ransomed for three million gold écus. The French resumed hostilities in 1369 and recaptured most of the lost territory, and the war ended in a French victory in 1453.
battle-of-poltava: King Charles XII of Sweden had defeated most of the anti-Swedish coalition, and Tsar Peter I was the only enemy still fighting. Peter offered to return the Baltic provinces Russia had occupied since 1703, except Ingria, where he had begun to build St. Petersburg, but Charles refused. In the autumn of 1707 Charles marched towards Moscow with almost 44,000 men. Russian scorched-earth tactics and harsh weather forced him south into Ukraine, where he hoped for help from Ivan Mazepa, the Cossack hetman who had decided to rebel against Peter. The winter of 1708 to 1709 was the coldest in Europe in over 500 years.

By spring 1709 Charles had about 20,000 soldiers and 34 cannons. He besieged the fortress of Poltava on the Vorskla on 2 May, and Peter marched to relieve it with about 80,000 men and built a fortified camp north of the town. On 20 June Charles was shot in the foot, so Field Marshal Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld took operational command. Peter had built ten redoubts across the corridor between two woods.

The Swedish attack began before dawn, but the cavalry arrived late and the Russians sounded the alarm. The Swedes overran the first two redoubts, but a column under General Carl Gustaf Roos became isolated at the third and surrendered at 9:30 a.m. At 9:45 the Swedes advanced on Peter's 42 battalions and nearly broke the first line, but their cavalry could not reform in time and the infantry on the left flank fled. The Russians filled the gap, and Aleksandr Menshikov's cavalry outflanked the Swedes.

Charles retreated south that evening. Lewenhaupt led the survivors towards the Dnieper but, pursued by Russian cavalry and Kalmyk auxiliaries, was forced to surrender at Perevolochna on 11 July. Peter sent many Swedish prisoners to Siberia. Charles and Mazepa escaped with about 1,500 men to Bendery in Moldavia, then controlled by the Ottoman Empire, where Charles stayed five years.

The battle revived the anti-Swedish coalition, which attacked the weakened Swedish Empire on several fronts. It was the largest battle of the Great Northern War, and Sweden lost its dominant position in the Baltic, which the Russian Empire took over.
battle-of-ponte-novu: Ponte Novu is a Genovese bridge over the Golo in Castello-di-Rostino, on the road through the mountains to Corte, the capital of the fourteen-year-old Corsican Republic. The French planned to land at Bastia, follow the Golo valley over the passes and seize Corte, the centre of Pasquale Paoli's power. The Comte de Vaux was a seasoned professional soldier with an expert on mountain warfare on his staff.

The Corsicans meant to block the choke point where the road crossed the bridge. Gaffori was posted above the road at Lento and Grimaldi at Canavaggia, with militia on the road before the bridge, while Paoli raised troops nearby and left the defence to his second-in-command, Carlo Salicetti. His forces included a company of Corsican women under a captain named Serpentini.

Historians give rather different pictures of the battle. The bridge was held by Prussian mercenaries who had worked for the Genoese before Paoli hired them. They opened fire on Corsican troops retreating over the bridge under French pressure, and in the crossfire the river ran red and the rest of the army retreated in disorder. In the most flattering account, 2,000 Corsicans crossed to attack a much larger force, tried to fall back and were cut down by the Prussians, who may have thought they were stopping an unauthorised retreat. A less flattering version accuses Grimaldi of taking French money and Gaffori of cowardice, with the militia fleeing before French bayonets and fired upon by the Prussians in self-defence.

The battle effectively ended the Corsican Republic and opened the way to annexation by France. Napoleon testified to the defence behind a rampart of the dead and is known to have gone over the battlefield with Paoli in 1790, and Voltaire praised the courage of the Corsicans in his Précis du Siècle de Louis XV. Historians conclude that Corsica was not united enough for an effective defence: senior officers defected, troops lacked motivation and Paoli depended on mercenaries of questionable loyalty.
battle-of-posada: In a diploma of 26 July 1324 King Charles I of Hungary called Basarab "our voivode of Wallachia", a sign that Basarab was then his vassal. By 18 June 1325 another diploma named him "unfaithful to the king's Holy Crown": Basarab's growing power and his own policy to the south were unacceptable in Hungary. Encouraged by the Voivode of Transylvania, Charles took the long-disputed citadel of Severin in 1330. Basarab offered 7,000 marks in silver, Severin and his own son as a hostage for peace. According to the Illuminated Chronicle, Charles answered that he would drag Basarab out of his mountains by his beard.

Against his councillors' advice, Charles led his 30,000-strong army deeper into Wallachia without proper supplies or reconnaissance. It included Székelys, Transylvanian Saxons, mercenaries and many Cumans, under Stephen Lackfi; the Saxons of Sibiu sided with Basarab. Charles reached Curtea de Argeș, but Basarab withdrew into the mountains. After days of hard marching the two agreed an armistice, Basarab to provide guides back to the Hungarian plain by the shortest route.

In a ravine the Wallachians, probably fewer than 10,000 cavalry, infantry, archers and local peasants, attacked from all sides with arrows, trees and stones, and the last two days brought heavy hand-to-hand fighting. Charles gave his royal robes and insignia to one Desev, who died under the missiles, and escaped to Visegrád in civilian clothes. Historians still debate where the battle was fought: in the Olt Defile at Loviștea, or, according to Neagu Djuvara, on the border between Oltenia and Severin.

The Illuminated Chronicle records that the Wallachians took many captives, weapons, horses and purses of coins and gave them to Basarab. The historian Sălăgean writes that the victory sanctioned Wallachia's independence from the Hungarian crown. Relations stayed tense until 1344, when Basarab sent his son Alexandru to restore ties. In a charter of 13 December 1335 Charles recalled how Nicholas, son of Radoslav, had saved his life.
battle-of-pressburg: In 900 the advisers of the new East Francian king, Louis the Child, led by the regent Hatto I, Archbishop of Mainz, refused to renew the alliance with the Hungarians that had ended with the death of Arnulf of Carinthia. The Hungarians then took Pannonia from the Duchy of Bavaria, starting a war that lasted until 910. Margrave Luitpold of Bavaria allied with Mojmir II of Moravia, but in 902 Hungarian armies, probably led by Kurszán, defeated Great Moravia and took its eastern area, which cut Bavaria's trade routes to northern and eastern Europe.

Luitpold's forces won minor battles at Laibach in 901 and the Fischa River in 903, and in 904 the Bavarians killed Kurszán after inviting him to negotiate a peace. When the Hungarians then ceased attacking Bavaria, Luitpold concluded that they feared him and that the time had come to expel them.

In 907 Luitpold called out a large army from all over Bavaria, gathered around Ennsburg, and the Bavarian leaders met there on 15 June. Louis the Child, nominally in command, went with the army as far as St Florian Monastery and stayed there. The hope was to repeat Charlemagne's success against the Avars in 803. The battle was fought from 4 to 6 July 907 and the Bavarian army was annihilated. Contemporary sources give little detail; the fullest account is by Johannes Aventinus, writing about 600 years later from lost tenth-century documents. Many historians think the Hungarians were led by Árpád, though there is no proof.

The Hungarians probably evacuated the border lands and used scorched earth. The exact site is unknown. The Annals of Salzburg name Brezalauspurc, which some place at Zalavár near Lake Balaton and most historians in the vicinity of Bratislava, the traditional assumption. No Hungarian chronicle mentions the battle.

Luitpold's son Arnulf, the new Bavarian prince, made a peace in which he accepted the loss of Pannonia and Ostmark, the Enns as the border and the payment of tribute, and let Hungarian armies cross his lands. East Francia could not regain the March of Pannonia, and almost fifty years of Hungarian raids on the East Francian duchies and West Francia followed, from 908 to 955. Louis the Child was defeated at Augsburg and the Rednitz in 910 and also had to pay tribute. The battle is regarded as marking the end of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin.
battle-of-preveza: In 1537 Hayreddin Barbarossa, commanding a large Ottoman fleet, took several Aegean and Ionian islands from the Republic of Venice, including Syros, Aegina, Paros, Tinos and Naxos, which ended the Duchy of Naxos. He failed to take Corfu and ravaged the Spanish-held coast of Calabria. In February 1538 Pope Paul III assembled a Holy League of the Papal States, Habsburg Spain, Genoa, Venice and the Knights of Malta, under Andrea Doria, the Genoese admiral in the service of Emperor Charles V. Doria joined the papal and Venetian fleets on 22 September 1538. The Christian side was divided by old rivalries, above all between the Venetians and the Genoese and Spanish, while the Ottoman fleet had a single command.

Barbarossa's fleet lay in the Gulf of Arta, near Preveza, where the Battle of Actium had been fought in 31 BCE. Doria stationed his armada at the mouth of the gulf on 25 September, and the fleets watched each other. He could not enter the narrow mouth, and winds threatened to drive his sailing ships onto the hostile coast. On the night of 27 September he sailed south towards Sessola to draw Barbarossa out, and Barbarossa formed his fleet into a Y shape.

Accounts of the battle on 28 September are highly divergent, and Roger Merriman wrote that it is almost impossible to reach the truth. Venetian and papal sources blame Doria, who they say held back out of caution or deliberately. Imperial sources blame Grimani and Cappello for refusing his orders. All agree that the wind dropped and left the sailing ships becalmed, where Barbarossa attacked them with his galleys. Spanish galleons beat off the attackers with their guns, and the huge Venetian galleon was damaged but not captured. Doria withdrew at nightfall. Italian and Spanish sources state that the Christians lost two galleys and five ships, while Turkish sources claim 128 ships sunk, destroyed or captured.

The Holy League's fleet came out mostly unscathed but quarrelled. Cappello accused Doria of sabotaging the battle to spare Genoese and Spanish ships, and the papal captain Virginio Orsini accused him of collusion with Barbarossa. The League took Castelnuovo, but Venetians and Spaniards disputed who would garrison it, and Barbarossa retook it the next year. In October 1540 Venice made peace with the Ottomans, surrendering possessions in the Peloponnese, Dalmatia and the Aegean and paying 300,000 ducats. The Ottomans stayed the dominant naval power until Lepanto in 1571.
battle-of-pteria: Croesus saw in the Persian rising against the Medes, his longtime rivals, a chance to push the eastern frontier of Lydia forward. He made alliances with Chaldea, Egypt and several Greek city-states, Sparta among them, and asked the Oracle of Delphi for advice. The oracle replied that if he crossed the Halys River a great empire would be destroyed, and he took the answer as favourable. The war it encouraged ended his own kingdom, not the Persian Empire.

Croesus opened the campaign by invading Cappadocia, crossing the Halys and capturing Pteria, then the capital of the district and a strong fortress. The city was sacked and its people enslaved. Cyrus advanced to halt him, taking in northern Mesopotamia on the way and receiving the submission of Armenia, Cappadocia and Cilicia.

The two armies met near the fallen city. Cyrus is said to have had only 25,000 men against close to 100,000, though this is likely an exaggeration. The fighting moved into the streets of the abandoned city, and both kings are said to have led troops in person. Cyrus's leadership and the refusal of the Persian Immortals to give way when pressed are credited with holding the Lydian army off. The fighting went on until nightfall without a decision, and both sides lost heavily.

Croesus then withdrew across the Halys, meaning to use the winter to wait for reinforcements from the Babylonians, the Egyptians and above all the Spartans. The decision proved a mistake. His army dispersed, and Cyrus marched on into Lydia despite the season, following him almost at once. The two kings fought again before Sardis at the Battle of Thymbra, a decisive victory for Cyrus.
battle-of-puebla: The French intervention in Mexico was at first backed by the United Kingdom and Spain. It followed President Benito Juárez's two-year moratorium on loan-interest payments to French, British and Spanish creditors from July 1861. A Spanish fleet took the port of Veracruz in December 1861, and French and British forces arrived in January 1862.

An agreement ratified on 23 January moved the forces inland for a conference at Orizaba and recognised the Juárez government and Mexican sovereignty. On 9 April 1862 the allies' agreements broke down, as France made clear that it meant to invade and interfere in Mexico's government. The British left, and France went on alone. It defeated a small Mexican force at Escamela and captured Orizaba, and the Mexican generals Porfirio Díaz and Ignacio Zaragoza withdrew towards Puebla.

General Charles de Lorencez led 6,000 French troops towards Puebla, certain of a quick victory. The Mexican generals who had joined the French, Juan Almonte and Antonio de Haro y Tamariz, advised him either to attack an orchard opposite the heights or to bypass Puebla and march on the capital, but he did neither. The Mexican army reached Puebla on 3 May, and on the 4th Miguel Negrete's division occupied the forts of Guadalupe and Loreto on the hills above the city.

On 5 May the French shelled the forts for two hours and sent zouave battalions up the hill towards Guadalupe. The French rifles were better than the Mexicans' older muskets, and many French soldiers underestimated the defences. Zaragoza reinforced the forts, and the French assaults from the north and east were driven back, with Mexican cavalry charging the remnants. After three failed attacks uphill the French drew back, and by seven in the evening they had returned to camp. On 8 May they retreated to Orizaba to await reinforcements.

The victory inspired Mexico and surprised a world that had expected a rapid French success. Zaragoza received the thanks of congress, and the city was renamed Puebla de Zaragoza. He died of typhoid fever four months later. On 9 May 1862 Juárez declared the anniversary a national holiday.

Napoleon III dismissed Lorencez and sent more troops, and the French won the Second Battle of Puebla on 17 May 1863 and went on to Mexico City. Juárez's government went into exile, and the Habsburg Archduke Maximilian became Emperor of Mexico. Cinco de Mayo is marked chiefly in the state of Puebla, and in the United States it has become a celebration of Mexican heritage.
battle-of-pydna: The Third Macedonian War began in 171 BCE, after acts by King Perseus of Macedon led Rome to declare war. Perseus won the Battle of Callinicus and regained most of his early losses, then took an unassailable position on the river Elpeus. The next year command passed to the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus, who sent Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum on a feint to the coast and then over the mountains to attack the Macedonians from the rear. A deserter warned Perseus, whose force under Milo was driven back, and Perseus moved north to a level plain near Katerini, well suited to the phalanx.

The Romans camped in the foothills of Mount Olocrus. The night before the battle a lunar eclipse occurred, which, according to Plutarch, the Macedonians took as a sign of their king's fall. Fighting began on the afternoon of 22 June, probably when Roman foragers were attacked by Thracians in Perseus' army. The Romans had at least 28,600 men and perhaps up to 37,000, and the Macedonians about 30,000 by then, after detachments were sent away.

The centres engaged at about three o'clock. As the phalanx pushed into the foothills the uneven ground broke up its line, and Paullus ordered the legions into the gaps to strike the phalangites on their exposed flanks, where the longer Roman sword and heavier shield prevailed. The Roman right routed the Macedonian left, and Perseus fled with the cavalry on his right. The 3,000-strong guard fought to death. Nearly 11,000 Macedonians were captured, and Livy reported that his sources claimed up to 20,000 dead.

The battle is often considered a victory of the flexibility of the Roman legion over the rigidity of the phalanx, though the guard's staying power suggests that training also mattered. It broke the back of Macedonian power and marked the effective end of Macedonian independence, although formal annexation came some years later.

Perseus later surrendered to Paullus and was paraded in chains in Rome in triumph, then imprisoned and held under house arrest at Alba Fucens. Many of the king's friends were deported to Italy. The Macedonian kingdom was dissolved and replaced by four republics, heavily restricted in contact and trade with one another, and in time Macedonia became a Roman province. In 167 BCE Paullus was ordered to attack Epirus because the Molossians had sent aid to Perseus, and 150,000 Epirotes were enslaved and 70 cities sacked. Athens passed a decree honouring Calliphanes, who had brought the news of the victory.
battle-of-qarqar: The battle was fought during the Assyrian conquest of Aram, which lasted from 854 to 846 BCE. It is notable for having more combatants than any previous battle and for the first recorded appearance of some peoples, such as the Arabs. It is recorded on the Kurkh Monoliths, and a different recension of the Assyrian Eponym List would put its date at 854 BCE.

According to Shalmaneser III's own inscription, he left Nineveh on the 14th day of Iyar, crossed the Tigris and Euphrates without incident and received the submission and tribute of several cities, Aleppo among them. Past Aleppo he met resistance from Irhuleni, king of the Luwian state of Hamath, whom he defeated, plundering the palaces and cities of his kingdom. After sacking Qarqar he met the allied army near the Orontes. Qarqar is generally identified with Tell Qarqur in the Hama Governorate of north-western Syria.

The inscription lists the allies' forces. Hadadezer, called Adad-idir in Assyrian and possibly King Benhadad II of Aram-Damascus,commanded 1,200 chariots, 1,200 horsemen and 20,000 soldiers; Irhuleni of Hamath 700 chariots, 700 horsemen and 10,000 soldiers; Ahab of Israel 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers; and Gindibu of Arabia 1,000 camel cavalry. Smaller contingents came from Quwe, Irqanata, Arwad, Ammon and other lands.

Scholars doubt Ahab's figure, which exceeds Aram-Damascus's: Nadav Na'aman suggests a scribal error for 200 chariots, while excavated stables at Megiddo, dated to the 9th century BCE, housed 150 chariots. Shalmaneser's account says he defeated them from Qarqar to Gilzau, felled 14,000 troops with the sword and blocked the Orontes with their corpses.

Royal Assyrian inscriptions of this period never directly acknowledge defeats, and sometimes claim victories won by predecessors. If Shalmaneser won a clear victory, it did not lead at once to further conquests in Syria. He campaigned there several more times in the following decade and fought Hadadezer six times, the latter supported by Irhuleni at least twice. His opponents kept their thrones. Ahab died soon afterwards in an unrelated battle, and Hadadezer was king of Damascus until at least 841 BCE.
battle-of-qatwan: The Khitans were the people of the Liao dynasty of northern China, who moved west after the Jin dynasty destroyed the Liao in 1125. Their remnants under Yelü Dashi took Balasagun, the capital of the Eastern Karakhanids, and in 1137 defeated the Western Karakhanids, vassals of the Seljuks, at Khujand. The Karakhanid ruler Mahmud II appealed to his Seljuk overlord, Sultan Sanjar. In 1141 Sanjar arrived at Samarkand with his army. The Kara-Khitans came too, invited by the Khwarazmians, themselves Seljuk vassals, and answering an appeal from the Karluks, who were in conflict with the Karakhanids and Seljuks.

Sources give widely varying figures for the Kara-Khitan army, from 20,000 to 700,000, and 100,000 for the Seljuks, while some contemporary Muslim authors said the two forces were of equal size; the Kara-Khitans were said to have been joined by 30,000 to 50,000 Karluk horsemen. On 9 September 1141, on the Qatwan steppe north of Samarkand, they attacked from all sides at once, encircled the Seljuks and drove their centre into a wadi called Dargham, about 12 km from the city. The Seljuk army was destroyed. Figures for the dead range from 11,000 to 100,000, and Seljuk commanders and Sanjar's wife were among the captured.

According to the chronicle of Sadr al-Din al-Husayni, Sanjar's emirs were divided and his troops soon began to retreat. Abu'l Fadl advised the sultan to put an ordinary soldier in his place and save himself; Sanjar escaped, while Abu'l Fadl stayed with the stand-in and was captured. Al-Husayni says Yelü Dashi later freed him unransomed and let Sanjar retreat towards Balkh unhindered.

Yelü Dashi spent ninety days in Samarkand, accepting the loyalty of Muslim nobles and making Mahmud's brother Ibrahim its ruler, while letting the Burhan family keep Bukhara. Khwarazm became a Kara-Khitan vassal, and after a raid in 1142 its ruler Atsiz agreed to pay 30,000 dinars a year in tribute. Stories of the battle, reaching the Holy Land during the Second Crusade, helped inspire the legend of Prester John.
battle-of-quatre-bras: Napoleon planned to cross into the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, drive a wedge between Wellington's Anglo-allied army and the Prussians under Field Marshal von Blücher, and beat each in turn. The crossroads of Quatre Bras lay on the Nivelles–Namur road by which Wellington could reach the Prussians at Ligny. Wellington, unsure of Napoleon's route, ordered his army towards the Prussians only near midnight on 15 June. Against Wellington's order to gather at Nivelles, Major-General Jean Victor de Constant Rebecque, chief of staff to the Prince of Orange, sent Prince Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach's Nassau brigade to hold the crossroads and then reinforced it.

Marshal Michel Ney spent the morning of 16 June massing his corps. When the real attack began around 14:00, his 18,000 men faced about 8,000 infantry and 16 guns under William, Prince of Orange. The Dutch and Nassauers were pushed back to Grand-Pierrepont farm and Gemioncourt but held the Bossu wood. From about 15:00 Picton's British 5th Division arrived and Wellington, back from meeting Blücher at the Windmill of Bussy, took command. The Duke of Brunswick was mortally wounded leading a charge.

At 17:00 Alten's 3rd Division tipped the numbers towards the allies, and Ney learned that d'Erlon's I Corps had marched east towards Ligny without his order. Kellermann's cuirassiers caught Halkett's brigade in line and took the King's colour of the 69th, but were driven back from the crossroads. The Guards Division then retook the Bossu wood at heavy cost, and by 21:00 the French had given up all their gains.

Ney lost 4,000 men and Wellington 4,800. The allies held the field, but the French had kept them from aiding the Prussians at Ligny, and when Wellington learned of the Prussian defeat he withdrew north along the Brussels road while the Prussians fell back towards Wavre. Historians have long debated what d'Erlon's corps might have done had it fought at either battle. Holding the crossroads slowed the French advance and let Wellington take position at Waterloo two days later. King William I of the Netherlands later made Wellington Prince of Waterloo, with lands covering much of the battlefield.
battle-of-quiberon-bay: The battle, called the Bataille des Cardinaux by the French, was fought on 20 and 21 November 1759 in Quiberon Bay, near Saint-Nazaire. By 1759 France was spending more than 60% of its revenue on its debt, and its navy was overstretched and more than 9,000 men short of full crews. Louis XV's ministers planned a direct invasion of Britain: an army of 17,000 gathered at Vannes and nearly 100 transports near Quiberon Bay, to be escorted by the fleet from Brest.

In August the British under Edward Boscawen broke the French Mediterranean Fleet at the Battle of Lagos, but Choiseul still contemplated a landing in Scotland. When a westerly gale in early November drove Sir Edward Hawke's blockading fleet back to Torbay, Hubert de Brienne slipped out of Brest on the 14th to collect the transports.

On the morning of 20 November de Brienne chased Robert Duff's small squadron off Belle-Isle and was still scattered when Hawke's 24 ships of the line came into sight. In a very violent wind and high seas he made for the shelter of the bay, behind its maze of shoals and reefs. Hawke signalled a general chase and followed under full sail. As the French rounded Les Cardinaux, the rocks at the end of the Quiberon peninsula, the British caught their rear.

Formidable surrendered just before 4 pm. Thésée capsized with only 22 survivors when water poured through her open lower gunports, Superbe also capsized, and Héros struck her flag and ran aground. With darkness falling Hawke signalled his fleet to anchor. During the night eight French ships escaped to Rochefort and others jettisoned their guns to cross the bar of the river Vilaine. De Brienne's flagship Soleil Royal was wrecked on the Four Shoal and burned. The French lost 2,520 men killed, the British about 300 killed or wounded.

The power of the French fleet was broken for the rest of the war, and with Lagos the invasion threat was removed. Alfred Mahan called the battle the Trafalgar of this war: Britain's fleets were free to act against the French colonies, and France could not reinforce New France after Sainte-Foy the next spring. France defaulted on its debt. The battle was part of Britain's annus mirabilis of 1759.
battle-of-ramillies: The Grand Alliance of Austria, England and the Dutch Republic had followed an indecisive campaign in 1705. Although the Allies captured Barcelona that year, they abandoned their campaign on the Moselle, stalled in the Spanish Netherlands and were defeated in northern Italy. King Louis XIV of France wanted peace, but on reasonable terms, and so the French took the offensive in 1706. In April Marshal Vendôme defeated the Austrians at the Battle of Calcinato, and Louis urged Villeroi to attack in the Spanish Netherlands to win a fair peace.

Marlborough had hoped to take his army to Italy or back to the Moselle, but the monarchs of Denmark, Prussia and Hanover refused to let their contingents march that far, and the Dutch would commit none of their own troops. He left The Hague on 9 May, writing that he had little hope of doing anything considerable unless the French chose to fight.

Villeroi marched from Leuven with about 60,000 men, and Marlborough assembled some 62,000 near Maastricht. The armies met on dry ground between the rivers Mehaigne and Petite Gheete. Villeroi held Taviers, Ramillies, Offus and Autre-Eglise, with cavalry on the open plain between Taviers and Ramillies. At about 13:00 the batteries opened, and Dutch troops took Franquenée and then Taviers in close fighting.

The Earl of Orkney led English troops against Offus and Autre-Eglise, and Villeroi shifted battalions from his centre to meet them. Marlborough then moved Orkney's second line south, hiding the move behind a fold in the land, and pressed the attack on Ramillies. Around 16:30 the weight of the Allied cavalry began to tell. Danish squadrons under the Duke of Württemberg swept round the French right and into the flank of the Maison du Roi. The French and Bavarian army broke in under four hours, and Marlborough halted the pursuit after midnight near Meldert, 19 km from the field.

Villeroi lost 52 guns and his pontoon train. Casualty figures vary widely between authorities. Chandler gives about 12,000 French dead and wounded and some 7,000 prisoners, while Voltaire says the French lost twenty thousand men. Marshal Villars called the defeat the most shameful, humiliating and disastrous of routs. Leuven fell on 25 May and Brussels three days later. Bruges, Ghent, Oudenaarde and, on 6 June, Antwerp followed, each proclaiming the Archduke Charles as sovereign. Louis XIV recalled Vendôme from Italy to command in Flanders. With Prince Eugene's success at the Battle of Turin, 1706 brought the largest loss of territory and resources Louis suffered in the war.
battle-of-rancagua: The British-brokered Treaty of Lircay had set up a truce between the patriot government of Chile and the royalist Viceroyalty of Peru, and some factions of the independence movement saw this approach to Spain as treason. On 25 July 1814 radicals overthrew the Supreme Director, Francisco de la Lastra, and made Jose Miguel Carrera head of a provisional junta. When the Viceroy of Peru, José Fernando de Abascal, heard of the revolt, he sent an expedition of Spanish soldiers and royalists to put down the rebellion.

Bernardo O'Higgins, whose position towards the revolt was unclear, took his army of 1,000 patriots to reinforce the troops of Juan Carrera at Rancagua, which the Chilean forces held because of its strategic importance for the defence of Santiago. Outnumbered and short of supplies, he did not retreat. On the morning of 1 October the forces of Mariano Osorio surrounded the town; among them were the Talaveras, an elite force of veterans of the Napoleonic Wars in Europe.

The fighting was fierce and went on into the evening, when the Spanish set fire to the town. With casualties growing, the Chilean forces asked for reinforcements from Santiago, 87 kilometres to the north, but the request failed, and the army was forced to disperse and flee into the countryside.

The Spanish army went on to Santiago, which it captured within a few days, and crushed the Chilean government, the decisive step of the military reconquest of Chile. Many people fled as refugees to other parts of South America to escape the violence they feared the Spanish would inflict on the rebels. Known in Chile as the Disaster of Rancagua, the battle remained a stain on the national memory, recalled as a time when the nation was lost and the struggle for independence seemed in vain.
battle-of-raphia: The two largest Hellenistic kingdoms of the 3rd century BCE, Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucid Empire, repeatedly fought for Syria in the Syrian Wars. The Fourth Syrian War began in 219 BCE under Ptolemy IV Philopator and Antiochus III the Great. In 217 BCE the armies met near Rafah and camped a few hundred metres apart. Theodotus the Aetolian, once an officer of Ptolemy, crept into the Ptolemaic camp to assassinate the king, but Ptolemy was absent and the plot failed.

Ptolemy had just completed a recruitment and retraining plan. According to Polybius he had 70,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and 73 African elephants, including 20,000 Egyptians trained to fight in the Macedonian way. Antiochus had 62,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 102 Indian elephants.

The battle was fought on 22 June 217 BCE, after five days of skirmishing. Both kings put their phalanxes in the centre and the elephants and cavalry on the wings, Ptolemy on his left and Antiochus on his right. Ptolemy's smaller elephants fled from the larger Indian ones and ran through their own infantry, causing disorder. Antiochus routed the cavalry opposite him and pursued it, believing he had won.

Meanwhile the Ptolemaic phalanx, strengthened by the Egyptians, drove back the Seleucid phalanx. By the time Antiochus returned his troops were routed. According to Polybius the Seleucids lost a little under 10,000 infantry, about 300 horse and 5 elephants, with 4,000 captured, and the Ptolemaic losses were 1,500 infantry, 700 horse and 16 elephants. It is the only known battle in which African and Asian elephants fought each other.

The victory secured Coele-Syria for Egypt, but Antiochus recovered it at the Battle of Panium in 200 BCE. The Egyptian phalanx had solved Ptolemy's manpower problem, and Polybius credits the self-confidence it gave the Egyptians as one cause of the secession of Upper Egypt from 207 to 186 BCE under the pharaohs Hugronaphor and Ankhmakis. Native Egyptians grew in influence in Ptolemaic administration and culture. A stele recording a priestly convocation at Memphis in November 217 BCE was inscribed in Greek, hieroglyphic and demotic, and for the first time gave Ptolemy full pharaonic honours in the Greek text as well.
battle-of-red-cliffs: By the early 3rd century the Han dynasty was crumbling, and Emperor Xian, who had come to the throne in 189 at the age of eight, was a figurehead with no control over the regional warlords. Cao Cao held the emperor at his capital at Ye. In 208 he was appointed Chancellor on his own recommendation. His southern campaign began in the autumn of 208, aimed at the naval base of Jiangling and the Yangtze through Jing Province. Liu Cong, who had succeeded his father Liu Biao as governor, surrendered to him, giving him a sizeable fleet.

Zhuge Liang, Liu Bei's chief advisor, went to Sun Quan to arrange an alliance. Cao Cao had written claiming an army of 800,000 and hinting at surrender, but Zhou Yu and Lu Su argued for resistance and Sun Quan agreed. Zhou Yu estimated Cao Cao's force at about 230,000, including between 70 and 80 thousand impressed men of doubtful loyalty, against about 50,000 allied marines.

Cao Cao's attempt to establish a bridgehead across the Yangtze failed, and both sides drew back to opposite banks. His men, weakened by disease and forced marches, had lost a skirmish with the allied vanguard at Red Cliffs and retreated to Wulin. Cao Cao had chained his ships together, possibly to reduce seasickness among his northern troops. Huang Gai sent him a letter feigning surrender and prepared ships filled with kindling, dry reeds and oil.

As his squadron reached mid-river the sailors set the ships alight and took to small boats, and a south-east wind carried the burning ships into Cao Cao's fleet. Many men and horses burned or drowned. Zhou Yu then attacked with a lightly armed force and the northern army was routed.

Cao Cao retreated along Huarong Road, where heavy rain made the marshes so treacherous that sick soldiers carried bundles of grass to fill the road and many drowned in the mud or were trampled. He reached Huarong Pass and escaped.

Jiangling fell to Zhou Yu by the end of 209, and Cao Cao's territory shrank by about 160 kilometres. Liu Qi died within months and Liu Bei took control of four commanderies south of the Yangtze. Cao Cao never again commanded so large a fleet. The battle confirmed the division of southern China from the northern heartland and prepared the states of Shu Han and Eastern Wu.

Cao Cao himself blamed the sickness among his men and said it was unreasonable for Zhou Yu to claim the credit. The battlefield's location is unsettled: candidates include Chibi City, formerly Puqi, and sites near Wuhan and in Jiayu County.
battle-of-rhandeia: In 51 CE a Parthian campaign deposed Mithridates, Rome's client king of Armenia, and installed his brother Tiridates I in his place. Rome would not accept a weakened eastern border, and in 58 Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo was sent with three legions; after a one-year campaign the Romans set Tigranes VI on the throne. In 61 Tigranes made an ill-advised probing attack into Parthia, and Vologases I answered by besieging Tigranocerta. The city was well supplied and its attackers were not, so both sides agreed to withdraw.

After a Parthian declaration of war, Lucius Caesennius Paetus, governor of Cappadocia, invaded Armenia in 62 with only two legions, IV Scythica and XII Fulminata, hoping to make a military reputation. He took only a few minor forts and lack of supplies drove him west for the winter. Corbulo, in Syria strengthening the Euphrates frontier, did not march at once, and some accused him of waiting to win more glory from a rescue. When the calls for help came he set out with half the Syrian army and provisions on camels, but before he arrived Paetus had been defeated by the Armenian and Parthian army near Rhandeia, northeast of Melitene, and had surrendered.

The terms were humiliating. The Romans were to leave Armenia, give up their forts and build a bridge over the Arsanias so that Vologases could cross in triumph on an elephant. The Armenians plundered the army of weapons and clothing, and according to rumours reported by Tacitus the Romans were made to pass under the yoke.

The two Roman forces met on the Euphrates near Melitene amid mutual grief. Paetus urged a new invasion, but Corbulo refused, saying he lacked the authority and that the troops were worn out. Envoys of Vologases then asked Corbulo to give up his bridgehead over the Euphrates, and he demanded the Parthian evacuation of Armenia in turn. Both sides withdrew, leaving Armenia nominally independent but in practice under Parthian control until a Parthian delegation could travel to Rome. The later treaty, signed at Rhandeia itself, made Tiridates king and founded the Arsacid dynasty of Armenia.
battle-of-riade: The Magyars had served as mercenaries under Emperor Arnulf, and after his death in 899 they campaigned in the Kingdom of Italy and East Francia, breaking up Great Moravia in 906 and destroying a Bavarian army under Margrave Luitpold at the Battle of Pressburg a year later. In 924 a Magyar army invading Saxony defeated Henry in the field, but the capture of an Árpád prince, probably Zoltán, near Pfalz Werla allowed him to negotiate, and a truce with annual tribute was declared in 926.

Henry used the truce to reorganise the defences of Saxony and subdue the Polabian Slavs. A 926 assembly approved new castles and a new garrison duty: soldiers were grouped in nines of agrarii milites, farmer-soldiers, one on guard while the other eight worked the fields, and all nine manned the castles in an invasion. In 932, with the support of the church at the Synod of Erfurt, Henry stopped paying the tribute; he allegedly had a dead dog thrown down before the Magyar envoys.

Henry levied mounted contingents from every stem duchy, though only the chronicler Flodoard of Reims records the Bavarian presence. Widukind of Corvey calls the Thuringian contingent inermes, probably meaning poorly armed, and says Henry could not fully trust his Saxon horsemen. The Magyars, who had besieged an unknown town, tried to withdraw by night when Henry camped nearby at Riade. He sent ahead a screen of foot soldiers with a few horsemen, then met the Magyar light cavalry and archers with lightly armoured troops followed by a massed heavy cavalry attack. According to Widukind the Magyars fled at the approach of Henry's horsemen, and the victorious troops proclaimed Henry emperor on the battlefield.

The exact site is unknown. Several places in Central Germany claim it, among them Kalbsrieth at the confluence of the Unstrut and Helme and the Hunnenfeld near Riethgen, and the Riade named by Widukind probably denotes Henry's camp rather than the battlefield. The Magyars invaded Germany again in 954, during a rebellion instigated by Duke Liudolf of Swabia, and were finally defeated by Henry's son and successor Otto I at the Battle of Lechfeld.
battle-of-ridaniya: Sultan Tuman bay II at first resolved to march out as far as Salahia and meet the Ottomans there, while they were still worn out by the desert crossing. In the end he gave way to his emirs, who preferred to entrench themselves at Ridaniya, a short way outside Cairo. The Ottomans crossed the Sinai Peninsula, reached Arish and marched unopposed by way of Salahia and Bilbeis to Khanqah. On 20 January 1517 they reached Birkat al Hajj, a few hours from the Mamluk capital.

Two days later the main Ottoman body faced the Egyptian entrenchments while another party, crossing Mocattam Hill, struck them in the flank. Tuman bay and a band of devoted followers threw themselves into the Ottoman ranks and reached the tent of the grand vizier, Hadım Sinan Pasha, whom the sultan killed himself, believing him to be Selim. The Egyptians were nevertheless routed and fled two miles up the Nile.

The Ottomans entered Cairo unopposed, took the Citadel and killed its entire Circassian garrison, and the city's streets saw plunder and killing for days. Tuman bay returned one night with Bedouin allies, retook the weakly held city and had the Friday prayer said in his name again, but the Ottomans came back in overwhelming force and he fled across the Nile to Giza and on to Upper Egypt.

Selim I proclaimed an amnesty from which the Mamluks were excluded: anyone sheltering them was threatened with death, and 800 who were found were beheaded. Many townspeople were spared at the plea of the Caliph Al-Mutawakkil III, who had followed in Selim's train and led prayers in his name. The amnesty was later extended to the hidden emirs, who were held in the Citadel; Janbirdi al-Ghazali, who had fought at Ridaniya, alone was received with honour and given a command.

When Janbirdi went over to the Ottomans is disputed; the presumption is that he stayed loyal up to the battle and changed sides about the end of January. The head of Tuman bay, the last Mamluk sultan of Egypt, was later hung over an entrance gate in the Al Ghourieh quarter of Cairo; by another account he was hanged from the gate and buried after three days.
battle-of-rio-salado: After Alfonso XI's victory in the Teba campaign of 1330, Muhammed IV of Granada turned to the Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan 'Ali, who in 1333 sent a fleet and 5,000 troops that helped Granada take Gibraltar. Abu al-Hasan then gathered a great army to reverse the Christian advances of the previous century. His fleet of 60 war galleys and 250 other ships under Muhammad ibn Ali al-Azafi destroyed the Castilian fleet at the Battle of Getares on 8 April 1340, killing Admiral Alfonso Jofre de Tenorio. The sultan crossed the straits on 14 August, and with Yusuf I laid siege to Tarifa on 22 September.

Believing Castile would need months to rebuild its fleet, Abu al-Hasan laid up most of his galleys. Afonso IV of Portugal sent a fleet under Manuel Pessanha and paid for 15 Genoese galleys under Micer Gil Bocanegra, and with new ships from Seville the Christians cut the sultan's supply route from Morocco in October.

Alfonso XI left Seville on 15 October with a relief army, joined the Portuguese king and crossed into enemy territory with about 20,000 men. The sultan lifted the siege and took up a position on a hill between Tarifa and the sea, with Yusuf on a neighbouring hill. Contemporary chronicles gave the Muslim armies hundreds of thousands of men, figures the historian Joseph O'Callaghan considered greatly exaggerated. During the night Alfonso slipped 1,000 horse and 4,000 foot into Tarifa, but the sultan was told no Christians had entered the town.

On the morning of 30 October the Castilians forced the crossing of the Salado and broke into the sultan's camp, while the troops hidden in Tarifa struck it at the same time. When Alfonso was nearly drawn into hand-to-hand fighting, Archbishop Gil Álvarez Carrillo de Albornoz seized his reins. Attacked from front and rear, the Marinid army fled, and the Granadan contingent broke before the Portuguese. The battle lasted three hours.

The pursuit showed little mercy. Several of the sultan's wives were killed, among them Fatimah, daughter of the Sultan of Tunis, and his son Abu Umar Tasufin was captured. Abu al-Hasan crossed to Ceuta that night. Control of the straits passed to Castile and the Genoese. Algeciras fell after a two-year siege in 1344, but an attempt on Gibraltar failed; peace came in 1350 after Alfonso XI died in his camp during the Great Plague, and Castile captured Gibraltar only in 1462.
battle-of-rocroi: Since 1618 the Thirty Years' War had raged in Germany, with the Catholic Austrian and Spanish Habsburgs fighting the Protestant states. In 1635 France intervened directly, declaring war on the Habsburgs and Spain, though an initial invasion of the Spanish Netherlands failed. Cardinal Richelieu died in December 1642, and Louis XIII died on 14 May 1643, leaving his four-year-old son Louis XIV on the throne. The new chief minister, Cardinal Mazarin, did not want to end the war and pressed France's forces on Franche-Comté, Catalonia and the Spanish Netherlands.

The Spanish Army of Flanders advanced through the Ardennes into northern France with 27,000 men, hoping to relieve pressure on Catalonia and Franche-Comté. Under Francisco de Melo it laid siege to the fortified town of Rocroi.

The Duke of Enghien, aged 21, commanded a French army of 23,000 at Amiens. He learned of the king's death on 17 May but kept it secret from his troops, and against the advice of his older officers he advanced through a defile between woods and marshes that the Spanish had not blocked. De Melo drew up his army before Rocroi, with the infantry in tercio squares in the centre, and the two armies traded fire on 18 May.

On the morning of 19 May the French cavalry on the right under Jean de Gassion pushed back the Spanish horse, and Enghien charged the exposed Spanish left. His own left and centre were meanwhile hard pressed. He swept his cavalry round behind the Spanish lines and struck the rear of the infantry and the cavalry of the Spanish right. The Germans and Walloons deserted, but the Spanish tercios held, repulsed several attacks and accepted surrender terms. When some of them fired as Enghien rode forward, the French attacked again without quarter.

French losses were about 4,000. Estimates of Spanish dead range from 4,000 to 8,000, and of 7,000 Spanish infantry only 390 officers and 1,386 men escaped to the Spanish Netherlands. The French lifted the siege but could not carry the war into Flanders, and the Spanish regrouped quickly.

The battle was of great symbolic weight, because of the high reputation of the Army of Flanders, and it made the name of Enghien, later known as the Great Condé. Military predominance in Europe passed slowly from Spain to France. Mazarin later allied with England, won the Battle of the Dunes and took Dunkirk in 1658, and the Treaty of the Pyrenees followed in 1659.
battle-of-roncevaux-pass: In 778 Sulayman al-Arabi, the pro-Abbasid governor of Barcelona and Girona, sent a delegation to Charlemagne at Paderborn. He offered his submission and that of Husayn of Zaragoza and Abu Taur of Huesca in return for military aid against Abd ar-Rahman I, the Umayyad emir of Córdoba. Charlemagne crossed the Pyrenees that year, some forces through Vasconia in the west and others through Catalonia, and besieged Zaragoza. Husayn refused to surrender the city, claiming he had never promised allegiance, and Charlemagne put Sulayman al-Arabi in chains. After more than a month a deal was struck by which Husayn paid gold and freed prisoners and the Franks withdrew.

Before leaving, Charlemagne tried to secure Basque territory, believing many Basques were allied with the Moors. He ordered the walls of their capital, Pamplona, torn down, and some sources say he destroyed the city altogether. Roland, military governor of the Breton March, and Eggihard, Mayor of the Palace, were placed in the rearguard, probably to protect the baggage train. On the evening of 15 August the Basques, who had followed in anger at the destruction, attacked the rearguard in the mountain pass. They held the high ground and knew the terrain, and cut off the rearguard and baggage from the rest of the army.

Roland and the others held for a considerable time before being massacred, which let Charlemagne and the main army reach safety. The Basques looted the baggage and used the darkness to disappear. The revised Annales Regni states that the Franks were superior in arms and courage but weaker because of the terrain and the style of fighting. Einhard wrote that the men were massacred to the last man, and the Vita Karoli names Eggihard, Roland and Anselmus, the count palatine. Einhard and Pierre de Marca suggest that Lupo II of Gascony was responsible. The exact site is disputed, though the mainstream view puts it not far from Roncevaux.

It was the only significant defeat of Charlemagne's military career, and he never again led an army in Spain himself. He later established the Marca Hispanica, and the Franks took Barcelona a decade later. Over time the battle was romanticised into a conflict between Christians and Muslims, although the Basques of the period were mainly pagans and Charlemagne had been allied to some Muslims. The Song of Roland, by an unknown poet of the 11th century, is the earliest surviving chanson de geste and replaces the Basques with a force of 400,000 Saracens. A second battle in the same pass in 824 saw a Frankish force under Count Aeblus trapped and routed.
battle-of-roosebeke: Ghent had rebelled against Count Louis II of Flanders. When the besieged citizens asked for terms, Louis demanded that all men between 15 and 60 present themselves with halters around their necks, so that he could decide whom to pardon and whom to execute. The men of Ghent chose to fight, and on 3 May 1382, under Philip van Artevelde, they smashed the count's army at the Battle of Beverhoutsveld. Louis then called on the French king. Philip the Bold, who ruled France during the childhood of his nephew Charles VI, was married to Margaret of Flanders, the count's only surviving child and heiress.

The French assembled about 10,000 men south of Arras in early November, with the king and the dukes of Burgundy, Bourbon and Berry, and the Oriflamme was carried for the first time since the Battle of Poitiers in 1356. Artevelde had 30,000 to 40,000 men, mostly urban levies. On the Lys near Comines, Olivier de Clisson ferried 400 knights across the broken bridge and the French forced the crossing.

Artevelde camped on the Goudberg, a hill between Oostnieuwkerke and Passendale, with the French on its far side. On the morning of 27 November he planned to use the dense fog to attack, and ordered his men forward in a tight square formation to guard against cavalry. Mindful of the Battle of the Golden Spurs, the French first sent in a wave of infantry, which Artevelde repelled before advancing himself. Clisson answered by striking the unsecured Flemish flanks with heavy cavalry. Panic spread to the Flemish rear, which fled, and the main body was forced into a circle, pushed back and defeated. Artevelde was killed and his corpse put on display.

Philip the Bold could gain little from the victory. He became Count of Flanders in late January 1384 and needed the economic power of Ghent, which went on resisting until the Peace of Tournai was signed on 8 December 1385.
battle-of-rorkes-drift: Rorke's Drift, called kwaJimu in Zulu, was a mission station of the Church of Sweden and the former trading post of James Rorke, beside a ford on the Buffalo River, then the border between Natal and the Zulu Kingdom. On 9 January 1879 Lord Chelmsford's No. 3 Column encamped there and on 11 January crossed into Zululand. The station became a supply depot and hospital, garrisoned by B Company of the 2nd Battalion, 24th Regiment under Lieutenant Gonville Bromhead. Chelmsford's column marched to Isandlwana on 20 January. After Major Henry Spalding left around noon on 22 January, Lieutenant John Chard of the Royal Engineers was in temporary command, and two survivors of Isandlwana arrived with news of the defeat.

Chard, Bromhead and James Dalton of the Commissariat agreed that a column burdened with hospital patients would be overtaken in the open, and decided to stay. The garrison built a perimeter of mealie bags and biscuit boxes round the storehouse, hospital and stone kraal. The Zulu force of 3,000 to 4,000 men was a reserve that had not fought at Isandlwana. Under Prince Dabulamanzi kaMpande it acted against King Cetshwayo's order not to carry the war over the border. Native horsemen and a Native Contingent company withdrew as it approached, leaving about 154 to 156 defenders.

The attack began at about 4:30 p.m. The Zulus could not climb the wall and fought hand to hand at it. At 6:00 p.m. Chard abandoned the north wall, and the burning hospital was evacuated, with Privates John Williams, Alfred Hook and Robert and William Jones cutting through walls to bring patients out. By 10:00 p.m. the garrison held a small bastion round the storehouse. The attacks ended by 2:00 a.m., and only 900 of 20,000 rounds remained. The Zulus had gone by dawn, and Chelmsford's relief column arrived at about 8:00 a.m.

Seventeen British and colonial troops were killed and 351 Zulus lay dead on the field, though estimates of Zulu dead run to at least 500 or 600, including wounded killed after capture by the defenders and the relief force. Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded, seven of them to the 2nd/24th Foot, with four Distinguished Conduct Medals, the most Victoria Crosses for a single battle. Some have interpreted the awards as a way to draw attention from the defeat at Isandlwana, and Sir Garnet Wolseley thought them excessive, while other historians hold that the defence stands on its own merits. Elizabeth Butler and Alphonse de Neuville painted it, and the film Zulu of 1964 made it widely known.
battle-of-route-coloniale-4: In the First Indochina War the Việt Minh at first struggled against the better trained and equipped French. Their position improved in 1949, when the People's Liberation Army of Mao Zedong defeated the Nationalist army led by Chiang Kai-shek and the new People's Republic of China offered a safe haven, arms and supplies. The Việt Minh called the 1950 operation the Autumn-Winter Border Campaign; its aim was to open the border with China to that supply flow.

Route Coloniale 4 supplied the French base at Cao Bằng and had suffered ambushes since 1947. On 25 May 1950 the Việt Minh overwhelmed the fort at Đông Khê, which French paratroops retook two days later. By September their regular army numbered roughly 100,000 combatants. On 16 September they attacked Đông Khê again, and on 18 September the fort fell, with only 12 survivors escaping. General Marcel Carpentier then ordered Cao Bằng evacuated.

The plan was for Groupement Bayard, 3,500 men under Colonel Le Page, to fight north from Thất Khê and retake Đông Khê long enough to meet the Cao Bằng garrison under Colonel Charton, 2,600 troops and 500 civilians. Bayard set out on 30 September but was thrown back by Võ Nguyên Giáp's concentrated battalions and artillery. Charton left Cao Bằng on 1 October, against orders taking his heavy equipment, which ambushes forced him to abandon before the two groups met near Đông Khê on 5 October.

Driven into the Coc Xa gorge, the French forces were annihilated by 7 October. Reinforcements parachuted into Thất Khê on 8 October were destroyed over the following week. Only 23 men of the Foreign Legion's 1st Parachute Battalion, the first French parachute battalion lost in combat, reached French lines.

Of more than 6,000 French soldiers and civilians in the operation, only 700 reached French lines. Lạng Sơn was abandoned on 17 October, panic spread in Hanoi, and General Jean de Lattre de Tassigny replaced Carpentier late in 1950. The Việt Minh now controlled a large part of the border and had far greater access to their socialist allies.
battle-of-rovine: The battle opposed the Wallachian army of Voivod Mircea the Elder to an Ottoman invasion led in person by Sultan Bayezid I, called the Thunderbolt, whose force heavily outnumbered the Wallachians. A legend tells that on the eve of the battle Mircea, dressed as a peace emissary, spoke with Bayezid, asked him to leave Wallachia and offered him safe passage home, and that the sultan proudly insisted on fighting. The site is uncertain: the Ottoman historian Idris Bitlisi called it a mountainous and dangerous place, but most sources place the battle near the Argeș River.

Wallachian archers played a key part, thinning the Ottoman ranks during their first attack. Among Bayezid's Serbian vassals, Stefan Lazarević fought with great courage, and the Dečani chronicle reports that Prince Marko Mrnjavčević, his brother Andreja Mrnjavčević and Constantine Dragaš died fighting. Some historians hold that the fighting lasted a week rather than a day, beginning as a war of positions.

Both sides suffered heavy casualties. The Wallachians pushed the enemy back, but the Ottomans held a defensive position resting on the sultan's personal guard of Janissaries, the same kind of position they would hold a year later at the Battle of Nicopolis; this became a basic element of Ottoman tactics until the 18th century. Mircea's army could not break the defence of the sultan's camp.

Historians disagree on the result. Some record a Wallachian victory, while Tony Jaques, Halil İnalcık, Şerif Baştav and Jean Sedlar count it an Ottoman one, and others think it inconclusive. Because the Ottomans could not conquer Wallachia at this time, Rovine is counted among the most important battles of Romanian history. News of a Wallachian victory reached King Sigismund of Luxembourg in Buda, who spread his own version through Europe as though he had been the victor, though he had sent no troops. When word reached Charles VI of France from Venice in July 1395, he attended a Te Deum in Notre Dame in thanks, as the monk Michel Pintoin recorded. Mihai Eminescu told the battle in his poem The Third Letter.
battle-of-rozgony: After the senior line of the Árpád dynasty died out in 1301, the throne of the Kingdom of Hungary was contested by several foreign monarchs and other claimants. Charles Robert of Anjou, the Pope's champion, drove out his foreign rivals over several years, but central power was weak, and in many parts of the kingdom his rule remained nominal because powerful magnates, local dukes and princes did not recognise him. His chief adversary, Máté Csák, who held several counties in the west and north, eventually allied himself with the Aba family, which ruled the east of the kingdom.

In 1312 Charles besieged Sáros Castle, held by the Abas. When they were reinforced, according to the Chronicon Pictum by almost all of Máté's forces and 1,700 mercenary spearmen, Charles withdrew to the loyal county of Szepes, whose Saxon inhabitants joined his army. The Abas then turned on the town of Kassa, today Košice, both for its strategic importance and because Kassa's German colonists had killed Palatine Amade Aba a few months earlier, on Charles's orders.

The rebels abandoned the siege and took up a position on a hill near the Tarca river, forcing Charles to deploy on the flat farmland below. His army, of uncertain size, included his own men, an Italian unit of Knights Hospitaller and 1,000 infantry of the Zipser Saxons. The rebels opened with a surprise attack during or just after Mass in the royal camp, and a bloody mêlée followed with heavy losses among the knights of both sides. At one point the king's standard was lost and Charles fought under the standard of the Knights Hospitaller. Reinforcements from Kassa arrived at the crucial moment, and the rebel army, having lost its commanders, was routed.

Several leaders of the Aba family died in the battle, and part of their lands was divided between the king and his followers. Charles gained control of the northeast of the country. Máté Csák kept much of his territory until his death in 1321, but his power declined from the battle onwards and he never again launched a major offensive against the king. The Chronicon Pictum called it the most cruel battle since the Mongol invasion of Europe.
battle-of-rudau: The Teutonic Knights had waged a crusade against pagan Lithuania since the 1290s, and each side answered the other's expeditions with raids of its own. In August 1369 the Knights burned a Lithuanian fort at the mouth of the Nevėžis River, and 109 people died in the fire. During truce negotiations Kęstutis warned the Prussian Marshal Henning Schindekop that he would retaliate, which gave the Knights time to gather their army at Königsberg.

Kęstutis and Algirdas led an army of Lithuanians, Samogitians, Ruthenians and Tatars into Prussia earlier than the Knights expected, and took and burned Rudau Castle, north of Königsberg. Winrich von Kniprode marched out to meet them. Contemporary Teutonic sources, unusually, give no details of the fighting; the battle plans told later by Jan Długosz rest on unknown sources. After the defeat Algirdas took his men into a forest behind hastily built wooden barriers, while Kęstutis withdrew into Lithuania. Schindekop pursued the retreating army but was wounded by a spear and died before reaching Königsberg. The Lithuanian noble Vaišvilas is presumed to have died in the battle.

The chroniclers Wigand of Marburg and Hermann de Wartberge describe a great Lithuanian defeat, and Teutonic sources claim that 1,000 to 5,500 Lithuanians died of wounds, freezing weather and starvation. Those figures appear exaggerated: in the same year Lithuania raided Ortelsburg, advanced in the Galicia-Volhynia Wars and raided Moscow a second time. The Order lost its marshal and two komturs, and a local legend tells of the apprentice shoemaker Hans von Sagan raising the fallen standard at a critical moment. Kniprode credited the Virgin Mary with the victory and founded the Augustinian convent at Heiligenbeil in her honour. It was the last serious Lithuanian threat to Prussia in the 14th century.
battle-of-rusokastro: In 1328 Emperor Michael Asen III of Bulgaria and Andronikos III Palaiologos signed a secret treaty against Serbia. While Michael Asen III was fighting the Serbs in 1330, the Byzantines invaded Thrace and captured its Bulgarian towns. The new Bulgarian emperor, Ivan Alexander, expected a decisive confrontation with Byzantium and improved his relations with Serbia. In 1332 he made a peace with the Serbs that lasted until his death, sealed by the marriage of his sister Elena to the Serb king Stefan Dushan.

In the summer of 1332 the Byzantines, without a declaration of war, advanced towards Bulgaria, plundering villages on their way and seizing several castles while Ivan Alexander was dealing with the rebellion of his uncle Belaur in Vidin. After failed negotiations, his cavalry covered 230 km in five days to reach Aitos and face the invaders.

Ivan Alexander had 8,000 men against 3,000 Byzantines. He drew out talks with Andronikos while he waited for reinforcements, and when 3,000 cavalry reached his camp on the night of 17 July he resolved to attack the next day.
