The Byzantine army of 16 squads formed a wide front in two lines in a crescent, with the protostrator on the right, the megas papias Alexios Tzamplakon on the left and the emperor in the centre, beside John Kantakuzin and Manuel Komnenos Raoul Asen.

The battle began at six in the morning and lasted three hours. The Byzantines tried to stop the Bulgarian cavalry from surrounding them and failed: the horsemen rode round the first Byzantine line, left it to the infantry and charged the rear of the flanks. Defeated, the Byzantines took refuge in Rusokastro, which the Bulgarians surrounded, and at noon Ivan Alexander sent envoys to resume negotiations.

Bulgaria recovered its lost territory in Thrace and strengthened its position. The peace was sealed by the marriage of the Bulgarian emperor's eight-year-old son and successor, Michael Asen, to Andronikos's daughter Maria. Medieval Bulgarian historians regarded the battle as a great triumph of Ivan Alexander. The two empires' rivalry for the Balkans ended soon after with their fall under Ottoman rule.
battle-of-sagrajas: After a civil war, the Umayyad caliphate of al-Andalus broke up into small independent states, the taifas, of which Seville under the Banu Abbad was the strongest. Alfonso VI of Castile, with Sancho of Aragon and Navarre and Count Berengar Raymond of Barcelona, pressed them hard after the fall of Toledo, took Coria, raided as far as Tarifa and besieged Zaragoza. The taifa kings paid tribute, and Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad of Seville wrote for help in 1082 to Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the leader of the Almoravids, a Sunni Maliki reform movement of Sanhaja tribes, who had founded Marrakesh and united the western Maghreb. Yusuf promised to come once he had taken Ceuta.
Alfonso sent mocking letters to Ibn Abbad while besieging him. Ibn Abbad wrote to Yusuf again, and agreed to give him the Green Island and Algeciras as a base for his troops.

The armies camped facing each other across the Wadi Bira near Badajoz, the Andalusians in one camp and the Almoravids in another. Yusuf offered Alfonso the usual three choices of Islam, tribute or war, and Alfonso refused. The two sides agreed on a Monday for the battle, but the Muslims suspected an attack on Friday, their holy day, and set scouts to watch. Alfonso is said to have attacked first, with a force under Count García and Count Zodric sent against Ibn Abbad's camp.

On 23 October 1086 this force met the Almoravid knights under Dawud ibn Aisha, whose archers helped repel the first assault. The turning point came when Yusuf ordered 4,000 cavalry from Takrur, with large shields and javelins, to charge, destroying the Christian cavalry. One of them is said to have wounded Alfonso severely in the thigh, leaving him with a limp. Towards sunset Alfonso retreated to a hill with a small company and escaped in the dark to Coria.

Alfonso, who had reportedly come with an army of 60,000, left with only about 300 knights. The battle preserved al-Andalus from Alfonso's conquests and lifted the sieges of major cities, though he kept up his offensives. Yusuf stayed near Seville for three days and returned to Morocco on the death of his son Abu Bakr. The taifa rulers soon returned to their quarrels, and the Castilians resumed raids and took the fortress of Aledo.
battle-of-saint-quentin-1557: The battle was a decisive engagement of the Italian War of 1551–1559 between the Kingdom of France and the Spanish Empire. Emmanuel Philibert, with 7,000 English allies, had laid siege to Saint-Quentin in Picardy. Anne de Montmorency, together with Louis de Gonzague, marched to relieve the town with a force of around 26,000 men.

The armies met on 10 August, the feast day of Saint Lawrence. Facing an enemy twice their number, the French tried to bring help into Saint-Quentin by way of a marsh. Their withdrawal came too late, which allowed the Spanish to defeat them and take Montmorency prisoner. During the fighting the town's collegiate church was badly damaged by fire. Among those who fought on the Spanish side was the Frenchman Martin Guerre, later impersonated in his home village, who lost a leg at Saint-Quentin.

According to one account, the sight of the battlefield gave Philip II a permanent distaste for war. He did not press his advantage but withdrew to the Spanish Netherlands, which he had governed since 1555. The Habsburgs won again at the Battle of Gravelines in 1558, and the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis ended the war in 1559.

Philip, a deeply pious king, knew that 10 August was the feast of Saint Lawrence, the Roman deacon who was roasted on a gridiron for his faith. To commemorate the victory he ordered a great palace in the shape of a gridiron to be built in the Guadarrama Mountains northwest of Madrid. Known as El Escorial, it was completed in 1584. The battle also lives on in a Spanish saying, se armó la de San Quintín, used of a great quarrel.
battle-of-sainte-foy: New France had suffered heavy setbacks in the Seven Years' War. Louisbourg fell to a siege in 1758 and Fort Duquesne was abandoned; in 1759 Fort Carillon and Fort Niagara were taken, and Quebec fell after a long siege and the Battle of the Plains of Abraham on 13 September. The French army regrouped at Montreal, while the British garrison left in Quebec after the fleet sailed suffered from hunger and scurvy in a city it had largely destroyed.

In April 1760 Lévis marched back on Quebec with regulars and Canadien militia, hoping to besiege the town until a French fleet arrived. Murray judged his army too small to hold the walls, which had not been improved since the capture, and took 3,886 men and more than twenty cannon out to the position Montcalm had held in 1759, choosing to attack rather than wait.

About 5,000 French soldiers with only three cannon were on the field. Seeing them still deploying, Murray advanced. His light infantry drove French grenadiers out of a windmill on the right but were scattered by the French left, and a bitter fight for the windmill went on. On the left the British took some redoubts before Lévis counterattacked with his right wing. Murray sent in his last reserves, but his left gave way after heavy losses and the line collapsed from left to right.

The British guns held the French back at first, but they began to run out of ammunition, and the ammunition carts were bogged in the snow and mud. The British spiked and abandoned their guns as they retreated. They lost 292 killed and the French 193; three quarters of the officers of the Fraser Highlanders were killed or wounded.

The British withstood a weak siege behind the walls until naval reinforcements arrived in May. No French fleet came: French naval hopes had been ended at Quiberon Bay, and the few supply ships were lost in the Battle of Restigouche. Lévis raised the siege and fell back to Montreal. In 1863 the Monument des Braves in Quebec commemorated the battle, the start of a wave of commemorations across Canada meant to bring Anglophones and Francophones closer together.
battle-of-sakarya: In July 1921 a Greek feint towards Eskişehir drew off İsmet Pasha while the main blow fell at Kara Hisar, and Eskişehir fell on 17 July. On Mustafa Kemal's advice İsmet broke off with heavy losses and fell back to the Sakarya River, about 80 km from Ankara. The river's great loop, with steep banks and few bridges and barren ridges rising beyond it, made strong defensive ground. The Greek command chose to advance and try to destroy the nationalist army, while the Turkish leadership prepared to move the government to Kayseri if the line broke.

King Constantine I committed his army to the assault on 10 August. After nine days of hard marching through country short of food and water, the Greeks made contact south of the Gök River on 23 August and attacked along the whole line on 26 August, storming one entrenched ridge after another. By 2 September they held the heights of Mount Çal, and in the centre they broke through the Turks' second line, some units coming within 50 km of Ankara. Turkish cavalry raids cut their supplies, while fresh Turkish draftees kept arriving.

Mustafa Kemal took personal command and on 8 September led a counterattack near Mount Çal that won only limited success. Fearing a larger outflanking move as winter approached, Anastasios Papoulas ordered a general retreat towards Eskişehir and Afyonkarahisar. The Greeks crossed back over the river unmolested, blowing up railways and bridges and burning villages as they went.

The Grand National Assembly also made Mustafa Kemal a field marshal. In Turkey the battle is called the Officers' Battle for its officer losses of 70 to 80 per cent. Freed by the Treaty of Kars with the Russians and the Treaty of Ankara with the French, the nationalists turned their strength west and opened their offensive at Dumlupınar on 26 August 1922. Historians still debate the Greek failure: Roderick Beaton holds the battle was very nearly won by the Greeks, and George Sayen blames an overcautious plan and reserves left unused.
battle-of-salamis: Athens and Eretria had supported the Ionian Revolt against the Persian king Darius I, and a Persian force destroyed Eretria in 490 BCE but was defeated by the Athenians at Marathon. In 480 BCE Xerxes I invaded Greece with a vast force. A small Greek force held Thermopylae, where the Spartan rearguard was annihilated, while the allied fleet fought at Artemisium and retreated with heavy losses. The Persians took Phocis, Boeotia, Attica and Euboea. The allies prepared to defend the Isthmus of Corinth, and the fleet withdrew to Salamis.

The Persians needed to finish the conquest in one campaigning season, since so large a force could not be supplied for long. To outflank the Isthmus they needed their navy, so destroying the allied fleet offered Xerxes the best hope. Herodotus has Queen Artemisia of Caria warn him that fighting at sea was an unnecessary risk.

The Athenian general Themistocles persuaded the allies to fight at sea again. By a ruse, a message telling Xerxes that much of the Greek fleet lay at Salamis, he drew the Persian navy into the straits to block both entrances. Herodotus gives the Greek fleet as 378 triremes, while Aeschylus, who fought there, says 310. Herodotus puts the Persian fleet at 1,207 ships at the outset, but most modern historians favour 600 to 800 at Salamis.

Ancient sources describe the fighting poorly. In the cramped waters Persian numbers became a hindrance, as ships struggled to manoeuvre and fouled their own lines. The Persian admiral Ariabignes, a brother of Xerxes, was killed early, and the Phoenician squadrons were pushed against the coast, many running aground. In the centre a wedge of Greek ships split the Persian fleet in two.

Xerxes tried to build a causeway across the straits, but the Greek fleet now patrolled them. He retreated to Asia with much of his army and left Mardonius to complete the conquest. The next year the Persians lost at Plataea and Mycale and made no further attempt on the Greek mainland, and over thirty years Thrace, the Aegean islands and Ionia were removed from their control. Many historians count Salamis among the most significant battles in history. In 2017 archaeologists announced the discovery of the anchorage used by the Greek warships before the battle.
battle-of-salsu: In 612 Emperor Yang of Sui invaded Goguryeo with 1,138,000 men. Held up by the defence of Yodong Fortress and other strongholds in Liaodong, he sent 300,000 troops to march directly on Pyongyang, the Goguryeo capital. The advance was hampered by discord among the Sui commanders and a poor supply line: the soldiers had been loaded with supplies meant to last the whole march, and many exhausted men abandoned them along the way.

The Goguryeo general Ŭlchi Mundŏk feigned surrender and toured the Sui camp to judge its morale. The Sui commander Yu Zhongwen had orders from the emperor to seize him, but another general, Liu Shilong, urged his release so that he could negotiate surrender terms with King Yeongyang. Once free, Ŭlchi lured the Sui troops deep into Goguryeo territory, wearing them down further.

When the army neared Pyongyang it was in no condition to besiege the fortified city. The naval force under Lai Hu'er that was to supply it had already been ambushed and defeated within Pyongyang by Go Geonmu, the king's younger half-brother. Goaded by a poem from Ŭlchi urging them to withdraw, the Sui commanders turned back towards Liaodong. Goguryeo forces harried the retreat in a series of attacks that ended at the river, where they cut down the Sui troops as they crossed. The Korean nationalist historian Sin Chaeho and modern popular accounts speak of a dam used against the Sui, but no contemporary source mentions a dam or a water attack.

The survivors fled to the Liaodong Peninsula, and many died of disease or hunger on the way. Of 305,000 men, all but 2,700 were lost. With no progress in Liaodong either, Emperor Yang withdrew. Yu Zhongwen and Yuwen Shu were put in chains and reduced to commoners, and Liu Shilong was executed for defying the order to capture Ŭlchi. Further invasions in 613 and 614 also failed, and the human and financial cost of the wars fed rebellions that brought down the Sui, who were replaced by the Tang.
battle-of-samara-bend: In 1221 Genghis Khan gave Subutai and Jebe two tumens, 20,000 men, to reconnoitre the lands west of the Caspian Sea, on condition that the campaign take no more than two years and that on the way back they join his son Jochi against the Volga Bulgars. The two generals defeated George IV of Georgia, crushed the Cumans and their allies, and on the Kalka River destroyed a combined Cuman and Rus army in 1223 before turning east.

The Volga Bulgars, apparently of Turkic origin, had settled in the Volga-Kama region and embraced Islam in 922, becoming a trading centre between the Islamic world and Europe. In the 12th century the principality of Vladimir-Suzdal, expanding on the middle Volga, had taken several of their towns, including Osel, and forced them to move their capital to Bilar, leaving the state weakened.

A messenger from the khan ordered Subutai and Jebe to find Jochi on the Volga and return with him to Mongolia. Jochi brought a single tumen of 10,000 men, and the army subdued the Bulgars on the west bank of the river before moving further north. The only record of what followed is a short passage by the Muslim historian Ibn al-Athir, writing in Mosul. In it the Bulgars laid ambushes in several places, drew the Mongols past them and attacked from behind, killing most of them. A second version in the same chronicle mentions no encounter with the Bulgars at all. The historian A. H. Halikov names the Bulgar commander as Ilgam Khan.

Historians disagree about the battle. Morgan, Chambers and Grousset hold that the Mongols in fact defeated the Bulgars, and Chambers suggests the Bulgars made up the story of their victory. In Peter Jackson's reading, the figure of about four thousand in Ibn al-Athir's second version refers to the size of the whole Mongol army, not to survivors. Afterwards the Mongols skirted the Urals, defeated the Saxin and the Kanglis and took a large tribute, which would hardly have been possible had their force been badly damaged. Jebe died of a fever on the Imil River on the way home.
battle-of-san-jacinto: Antonio López de Santa Anna had favoured federalism when he helped oust President Anastasio Bustamante in December 1832, but after his election in April 1833 he adopted centralist policies. His abrogation of the Constitution of 1824 and abolition of local authority in Coahuila y Tejas became a flashpoint with Tejano and Anglo citizens in Texas. In February 1836 Santa Anna led the Mexican Army of Operations, numbering 6,019 soldiers, into Texas and took Béxar and the Alamo. The Texian army under Sam Houston then retreated eastward, followed by civilians in the Runaway Scrape, and by 28 March it had retreated 120 miles. Some troops grumbled that Houston was a coward.

Houston's army of around 800 men reached Lynch's Ferry on Buffalo Bayou on the morning of 20 April 1836, and Santa Anna's force of 700 arrived a few hours later. The Texians camped in woods that gave cover but left no room to retreat. Against the advice of several officers, Santa Anna camped on an exposed plain near the San Jacinto River, which Colonel Pedro Delgado later said was against all military rules. Two brief skirmishes took place that day.

On 21 April the Texian army defeated Santa Anna's army in a fight that lasted just 18 minutes. Both Santa Anna and Cos escaped. Santa Anna fled towards Vince's Bridge, found it destroyed, hid in the marsh and was captured the next day, wearing a private's jacket until other prisoners recognised him. Houston, shot in the ankle, was surrounded by soldiers calling for his execution. Cos was captured on 24 April.

Santa Anna ordered the remaining Mexican troops to retreat to Béxar. Filisola, now the senior Mexican officer, did not wish to risk another disaster, and rain had ruined ammunition and roads. The Treaties of Velasco required Mexican troops to withdraw south of the Rio Grande and release prisoners, and Santa Anna secretly promised to press the Mexican Congress to recognise Texas. Mexican authorities rejected any agreement signed by a prisoner and refused to recognise the republic. Houston became the first president of the Republic of Texas, and voters asked for annexation to the United States. Hundreds of Tejano families moved to Mexico after Tejanos between the Guadalupe and Nueces rivers were ordered to leave.
battle-of-santiago-de-cuba: From 1895 relations between the United States and Spain worsened over Spain's suppression of the Cuban War of Independence, during which General Valeriano Weyler interned rural Cubans in camps where many died of disease and malnutrition. The publication of a letter by the Spanish minister Enrique Dupuy de Lôme critical of President William McKinley, and the explosion of the USS Maine in Havana harbour in February 1898, which killed 266 sailors and which the yellow press blamed on Spain without proof, pushed American opinion towards war.

Counter-admiral Pascual Cervera y Topete, recalled from retirement, had warned Spanish officials of the navy's weakness. He sailed from Cape Verde on 29 April, evaded the American fleet for several weeks and took refuge in Santiago harbour. From 29 May an American squadron blockaded its mouth, and by early July about 16,000 American soldiers and 3,000 Cuban insurgents were closing on the city by land.

The American force under Rear Admiral William T. Sampson and Commodore Winfield Scott Schley had four battleships and two armoured cruisers against four armoured cruisers and two destroyers. With American land forces driving on the city, Governor-General Ramón Blanco y Erenas wanted a sortie, holding that it was better for Spain's honour that the squadron perish in battle. On 3 July Cervera steamed out, his crews in full dress uniform, and made a desperate run for the open sea with the Americans in pursuit. The Spanish lost 343 killed and 151 wounded; the Americans pulled 1,889 Spaniards from the water, Cervera among them.

Credit for the victory became a quarrel. Sampson, in overall command, had been absent when the Spanish came out, while Schley directed the fight from the bridge of USS Brooklyn. Sampson cabled Navy Secretary John D. Long offering the nation the whole fleet as a Fourth of July present without naming Schley, and the dispute among naval officers and the public reached Theodore Roosevelt.

Unwounded Spanish prisoners were held at Camp Long on Seavey's Island in Maine from July to September 1898 and then returned to Spain on American ships. Cervera won American respect for his conduct during and after the battle. The terms agreed in the 1898 Treaty of Paris settled the fate of the Spanish troops and vessels and the question of Cuba's sovereignty.
battle-of-sao-mamede: In 1096 King Alfonso VI of León granted the County of Portugal to Henry, a brother of the Duke of Burgundy, who married Alfonso's daughter Theresa. After Henry's death in 1112 Theresa ruled as regent and, from 1117, signed as queen, seeking independence from León and from her sister, Queen Urraca. Her involvement in the quarrels of Galicia made the Galician noble Fernão Peres de Trava her close associate and, by 1123, her equal in power; clerical writers called the relationship adulterous, and the pair had a daughter.

Disgruntled Portuguese nobles gathered around her son Afonso Henriques, among them Archbishop Paio Mendes of Braga and the Moniz brothers of Ribadouro. In 1125 his tutor Egas Moniz took him to Zamora to be knighted by his cousin Alfonso VII.

In September 1127 Alfonso VII, now king of León and Castile, invaded Portugal to force Theresa and Afonso to acknowledge him as overlord. During the siege of Guimarães Egas Moniz won his withdrawal by standing surety for his pupil's loyalty. The six-week invasion reduced Portugal to a province and cost the lands north of the Minho, and Theresa and Fernão Peres were blamed. The charters show the break: on 31 March 1128 mother and son still signed together, but by 27 April Afonso confirmed the charter of Guimarães without her. Shortly before the battle Theresa and Fernão Peres came into the district of Braga with an army and were defeated near Guimarães. Both were captured, but only expelled.

Afonso still had to submit as a vassal of León, and he was at war with Alfonso VII from 1128 to 1137. Theresa died in Galicia two years after the battle, and Fernão Peres became one of Alfonso VII's generals. Afonso cultivated the Archbishop of Braga and, after a revolt led by his brother-in-law Bermudo Pérez in 1131, moved his capital from Guimarães to Coimbra, near the frontier with al-Andalus. He declared himself king after the Battle of Ourique in 1139; León recognised him in the Treaty of Zamora of 1143, and the Holy See in 1179.
battle-of-sardarabad: After the October Revolution of 1917 in Russia, newly forming Armenian detachments replaced Russian forces retreating from the Caucasian Front. The Ottoman government set out to regain the territories the Russian Army had occupied and to invade Eastern Armenia and the South Caucasus, intending to seize Russian Transcaucasia and the oil wells of Baku. The German government, its ally, objected and refused to help. The Ottoman Third Army attacked in February 1918, took the fortress of Kars on 25 April and Alexandropol on 15 May, leaving only a small area unconquered, into which hundreds of thousands of Armenian refugees fled.

In Yerevan the city council voted on 18 May to hand the city over without resistance. The Special Committee headed by Aram Manukian overturned the decision and had the defences fortified, with the help of as many as 1,500 residents. Catholicos George V refused to leave Etchmiadzin and encouraged resistance.

The Ottoman 36th Division, with cavalry and 1,500 Kurdish fighters, numbered 7,500 to 10,000 men with 40 cannons. The Armenian forces formed part of the Yerevan detachment under Major-General Movses Silikyan; Colonel Daniel Bek-Pirumyan commanded the troops at Sardarabad itself.

On 21 May the Ottoman 108th Infantry Regiment attacked from the Araks railway station. The Armenians withdrew, and that evening a detachment under Zihni Bey took Sardarabad and advanced to within 20 km of Yerevan. The Ottoman advance along the railway threatened to cut off the Armenian troops and as many as 100,000 Western Armenian refugees, but the artillery battery of Captain Khoren Igitkhanyan at Artashar pinned the Ottomans in place. Silikyan and his chief of staff, Colonel Alexander Vekilyan, drew up a plan to drive the Ottomans out of Sardarabad by counter-attack.

The Ottoman forces were routed and thrown back 50 to 65 km. Silikyan wished to press on to Alexandropol and Kars, but was ordered to stop because of negotiations between the Ottoman leadership and the Armenian National Council in Tiflis; ammunition was nearly exhausted and the Ottomans had received reinforcements. Together with the battles of Bash Abaran and Karakilisa, the victory allowed the Armenian National Council to declare the First Republic of Armenia. The Treaty of Batum of 4 June 1918 was harsh, but the republic held out until the Ottomans withdrew at the end of the First World War.

The battles are known in Armenian historiography as the Heroic battles of May. Soviet historians gave Sardarabad little attention until after Stalin's death. A monument and park near the battlefield was completed in 1968.
battle-of-sarhu: Before the battle Nurhaci had unified the Jurchen people, except the Yehe, and had turned against the Ming, whom he accused of favouritism and of meddling in the affairs of the Jurchen tribes. In 1618 he proclaimed his Seven Grievances against the Ming to Heaven and declared war, occupying Fushun, Qinghe and other cities. In 1619 he attacked the Yehe. The Ming answered by sending expeditionary forces under the Military Commissioner Yang Hao to converge on the Later Jin capital, Hetu Ala, by four routes, with allied troops from Joseon.

Du Song led the western column out of Shenyang and pressed on despite snow. At the Hun River he crossed with 10,000 men, leaving 20,000 with the artillery and baggage; halfway over, Nurhaci's bannermen broke dams they had prepared. While Hong Taiji and Daišan held Du at Jilin Cliff, Nurhaci took six banners against his camp at the Sarhu pass, then surrounded Du's own camp. Du Song and the generals Wang Xuan and Zhao Menglin were killed.

Ma Lin fortified three camps at Xiangjiayan, but the Jin banners came on so fast that his gunners fired only one volley; half his troops were killed or captured. Liu Ting, on the eastern route, never received Yang Hao's order to retreat. Deceived by a false letter from Jin spies posing as Du Song's messengers, he hurried into the Abudali Pass, where the charges of Daišan and Hong Taiji destroyed his army and he died fighting. The Joseon commander Gang Hong-rip surrendered, and Li Rubai withdrew from the south with few losses.

Yang Hao was arrested by the Embroidered Uniform Guard and executed after ten years in prison. Li Rubai, accused over his personal ties to Nurhaci, killed himself before his trial, and Ma Lin was killed when the Later Jin took Kaiyuan a few months later. Two-thirds of the 13,000 men of the Joseon force were killed. Gang Hong-rip, kept for his knowledge of the Jurchen language, later urged the Jin to invade Joseon, which led to the First Manchu invasion of Korea in 1627.

The battle is noted for the Later Jin's heavy use of cavalry against forces armed with hand cannons, cannons and matchlocks. After Sarhū the Joseon army revised its doctrine so that spearmen supported its musketeers.
battle-of-saule: The Livonian Brothers of the Sword were established at Riga in 1202 to conquer and convert the pagan Baltic tribes, and were the first Catholic military order in the Baltic lands. By the 1230s, under Master Volkwin, the order had strained finances, falling numbers and a poor reputation.

On 19 February 1236 Gregory IX issued a bull declaring a crusade against Lithuania. Volkwin was reluctant, since the order lacked the strength and knew little of the lands south of its territory, and he delayed for a whole summer. In the autumn a party of crusaders from Holstein arrived in Riga and demanded to be led into battle. Volkwin gathered a large force of troops from the Pskov Republic, Livonians, Latgallians, Curonians and Estonians.

The crusaders marched south through Semigallian lands, which the order did not control, and raided Samogitian settlements, giving the locals only a few days to gather troops. On the way back north the knights met a determined group of Samogitians at a river crossing. The Holsteiners, unwilling to risk their horses in the swampland, refused to fight on foot, and the army camped for the night.

On the day of Saint Maurice, 22 September 1236, the main pagan force, possibly led by Duke Vykintas, arrived. Lithuanian light cavalry threw javelins at short range, which told heavily against the unwieldy Livonian heavy cavalry, and the swamp favoured the lightly armed. The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle says the Master and his Brothers resisted until their horses were killed and then fought on foot. Volkwin and almost all the members of the order died. Those who fled towards Riga were allegedly killed by Semigallians, and only one crusader in ten reached the city.

Between 48 and 60 knights were killed. It was the earliest large-scale defeat suffered by the orders in the Baltic lands. The remnants of the Sword-Brothers accepted incorporation into the Teutonic Order in 1237. The battle inspired rebellions among the Curonians, Semigallians, Selonians and Oeselians, tribes the order had conquered, and some thirty years of conquests on the left bank of the Daugava were reversed.

The exact site is unknown. It has traditionally been placed at Šiauliai or at Vecsaule near Bauska, and in 1965 Friedrich Benninghoven proposed the village of Jauniūnai, where the Lithuanian government sponsored a memorial in 2010. In 2000 the Lithuanian and Latvian parliaments declared 22 September Baltic Unity Day in commemoration.
battle-of-savra: The battle is also called the Battle of the Vjosë, and in Serbian the battle on the Saurian field. In 1372 Balša II married Comita Muzaka, daughter of Andrea II Muzaka, and gained as her dowry Vlorë, Berat, Kaninë and Himarë, the Principality of Vlorë. He later took Durrës, presumably from Karl Thopia, and styled himself Duke of Durrës in a charter for Ragusa. His expansion towards Epirus put him on the front line against the Ottomans, and aware of their designs on his lands he asked the Venetians on 8 August 1385 for the help of four galleys.

Karl Thopia invited the Ottomans to support him against Balša, and Hayreddin Pasha brought his forces from the region of Ohrid to the Savra field near Lushnjë. Balša heard of the incursion into the region of Berat while he was in Durrës. According to Mavro Orbini, he gathered 1,000 men and, against the advice of his nobles, marched out against the much larger Ottoman force. His small army had little success, and he was killed; Orbini writes that his body was beheaded and the head taken to Hayreddin Pasha.

Orbini alone names Ivaniš Mrnjavčević among the combatants, and some scholars doubt that he existed, while others see him as a loyal member of the Balša family. Orbini also tells of Balša's voivode Đurađ Krvavčić, a brave warrior who died in the battle. His work The Realm of the Slavs is one of the main sources for the battle but contains much that is wrong or imprecise; Marin Barleti, the other, describes Balša as brave and idealistic.

Most of the local Serbian and Albanian lords became Ottoman vassals. Thopia recaptured Durrës at once, probably under Ottoman suzerainty. The Ottomans took Krujë, Berat and Ulcinj but soon withdrew, keeping only Kastoria. The historian Stojan Novaković held that for these lords the battle mattered as much as the battles of Marica and Kosovo together, and it brought an influx of Albanians into the Ottoman forces.
battle-of-sedan-1870: After the costly Battle of Gravelotte on 18 August, Marshal François Achille Bazaine's Army of the Rhine retreated to Metz, where Prussian forces besieged it from 19 August. Napoleon III and Marshal Patrice de MacMahon formed the Army of Châlons to relieve him and marched north-east towards the Belgian border. The march depleted the French and left both flanks exposed, and Helmuth von Moltke took the Prussian Third and Fourth Armies north to catch them. At the Battle of Beaumont on 30 August MacMahon lost 7,500 men and 40 cannons and fell back on the obsolete fortress of Sedan to rest and resupply. He refused General Félix Douay's request to dig trenches, saying the army would not stay long.

Moltke divided his forces into three groups, one to hold the French where they were, one to catch them if they retreated and a smallest to hold the river bank. By 09:00 on 1 September the Prussian V and XI Corps had completed the encirclement to the north-west. The fighting opened at Bazeilles, where French marines held stone houses before Bavarian artillery shelled the village into rubble.

MacMahon was wounded early. General Auguste-Alexandre Ducrot, who took command, ordered a retreat, but General Emmanuel Félix de Wimpffen overruled him and attacked at La Moncelle, which gave the French a brief rally. By 11:00 German artillery had taken a heavy toll. A cavalry attack led by General Jean Auguste Margueritte, who was mortally wounded, was beaten back by infantry fire. French troops were driven into the Bois de la Garenne, which the Prussian Guards took at 14:30, and the troops inside it surrendered. Napoleon III then raised a white flag over the fortress, although Wimpffen launched one more failed attack.

Wimpffen signed the surrender of the army and the fortress at 11:30 on 2 September. Moltke had refused him an honourable capitulation, pointing to the French lack of ammunition and food. The Germans counted 9,860 casualties, while the French lost 3,220 killed, 14,811 wounded and 104,000 captured, with 558 guns. Napoleon III left for captivity at Schloss Wilhelmshöhe near Kassel on 3 September.

On 4 September protesters stormed the imperial palace and the Second French Empire collapsed in a bloodless revolution. A Government of National Defense, which later became the French Third Republic, carried on the war for five more months. The German armies besieged Paris from 19 September. Because of the battle's part in German unification, many Germans marked 2 September as Sedantag, the Day of Sedan, until 1919, though the Kaiser did not make it an official holiday.
battle-of-sekigahara: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's heir, Toyotomi Hideyori, was only five years old when Hideyoshi died, which left a power vacuum. After the Imjin War, factional disputes arose between Ishida Mitsunari and seven former Toyotomi generals including Katō Kiyomasa. Tokugawa Ieyasu won over Kiyomasa and Fukushima Masanori to challenge Mitsunari, who claimed to fight for the Toyotomi clan. Mitsunari met Ōtani Yoshitsugu, Mashita Nagamori and Ankokuji Ekei to raise an anti-Tokugawa army, with Mōri Terumoto as overall commander. This became the Western Army. Terumoto captured Osaka Castle while the main Tokugawa army was on its way to suppress Uesugi Kagekatsu. Mitsunari had hoped to hold Gifu Castle and Ōgaki Castle, but the Eastern Army, the Tokugawa-led coalition, captured Gifu Castle first.

On 21 October 1600, in what is now Gifu Prefecture, the Tokugawa advance guard stumbled into Ishida's army in dense fog. Ii Naomasa, commanding his 3,600 crimson-clad troops, attacked the Western Army's centre, and Fukushima Masanori engaged Ukita Hideie's troops. The fighting then reached a deadlock, which the chronicler Ōta Gyūichi describes as friends and foes pushing each other.

Several Western commanders defected. The most notable was Kobayakawa Hideaki, Hideyoshi's nephew. The conventional account says he hesitated until around noon, when Ieyasu supposedly ordered arquebuses fired at his position. Modern historians such as Jun Shiramine and Stephen Turnbull doubt this and think he had already agreed to defect. Ukita's ranks broke, and Ōtani Yoshitsugu, outnumbered, killed himself. Mitsunari began to retreat as Shima Sakon fell, and Shimazu Yoshihiro's men escaped encirclement with only 200 soldiers. Large forces on both sides never reached the field, among them Tokugawa Hidetada's 38,000 held up at the Siege of Ueda.

Authority to assign ranks and redistribute land passed from the Toyotomi to Ieyasu, who immediately redistributed domains worth 6.8 million koku, mostly to the allies who had made his victory. Katō Kiyomasa's domain rose from 195,000 to 515,000 koku. The battle is generally regarded as the beginning of the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled Japan until 1868. Jakob Meckel, a Prussian general advising Meiji Japan, judged from a map that the Western Army's greater numbers and higher ground should have won. Japanese historians point instead to resentment of Mitsunari among powerful daimyo, particularly veterans of the invasions of Korea.
battle-of-sellasia: In 229 BCE Cleomenes III began hostilities against the Achaean League, then the dominant power of the Peloponnese, by seizing several Arcadian cities. Achaean attempts to recover them under the strategos Aratus of Sicyon largely failed, and the League's armies were defeated at the Battle of Mount Lycaeum and the Battle of Ladoceia in 226 BCE and again at the Battle of Dyme. Ptolemy III of Egypt, who had subsidised the Achaeans against Macedon, shifted his financial backing to Sparta.

When peace talks failed, Aratus asked Antigonus III Doson for help. Antigonus demanded the citadel of Acrocorinth in return, a condition that angered many Achaeans, and Cleomenes used the anger to occupy Corinth and Argos. Aratus accepted the terms and also surrendered Orchomenus and Heraia. Antigonus marched south through Euboea with 20,000 infantry and 1,300 cavalry, but was held at the Isthmus of Corinth by Spartan fortifications until Argos revolted and Cleomenes fell back to Arcadia.

Antigonus revived the Hellenic League of Philip II of Macedon as the League of Leagues. When Ptolemy stopped paying his subsidies, Cleomenes sold helots their freedom to pay his mercenaries, sacked and razed Megalopolis after its citizens refused to join him, and raided the territory of Argos. Antigonus recalled his army, which Polybius puts at 29,200 men, among them 10,000 Macedonian phalangists, Illyrians under Demetrius of Pharos and Greek allied contingents. Cleomenes mustered 20,650 men and held the hills of Olympus and Euas at the pass of Sellasia, with the Oenous River between them.

Eucleidas held Euas with the perioeci and allies. The allied right wing advancing there was attacked in the flank and hard pressed until the Arcadian cavalryman Philopoemen, disregarding his orders, charged; the Illyrians and other light infantry then drove the Spartans from the hill and killed Eucleidas. On Olympus the two phalanxes fought longer, until troops from Euas struck the Spartan flank. According to Plutarch, only 200 of 6,000 Spartiates survived.

Cleomenes left the field with a handful of companions, took ship at Gythium and joined his mother and sons in Alexandria, where he lived in exile until his death three years later. Antigonus became the first non-Spartan general to occupy Sparta. After the battle he praised Philopoemen's initiative and reproved his own cavalry commander, Alexander.
battle-of-sempach: In 1383 and 1384 the expansion of the Old Swiss Confederacy collided with Austrian interests, and in 1385 forces of Zürich, Zug and Lucerne attacked Austrian strongholds such as Rapperswil, Rothenburg and Wolhusen without any declaration of war. On 6 January 1386 Lucerne extended its citizenship to the people of Sempach and made pacts with towns and valleys, under Austrian control, among them Meienberg, Reichensee and Willisau; these moves were the immediate cause of war. Duke Leopold III gathered vassals from Swabia, Alsace and Tyrol at Brugg, and 167 noblemen sent declarations of war to the Swiss diet. Instead of attacking Zürich, as the confederates expected, Leopold marched south, burned Willisau and moved on Sempach on 9 July.

The troops of Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden had marched back from Zürich; Zürich's own forces stayed home and Bern ignored the call. The two armies met around noon about 2 km outside Sempach, to the surprise of both. The Swiss held wooded high ground near Hildisrieden. Judging the ground unsuited to cavalry, the Austrian knights dismounted and cut the long tips off their shoes. The confederates attacked them in the flank, but the wider Austrian line threatened to surround them.

How the battle turned is debated. Some point to the July heat, which wore out the heavily armoured knights, others to the nobles' contempt for the small Swiss force; Tschudi says they took the front ranks themselves rather than leave the work to their mercenaries. The Swiss broke through and routed the army, killing Leopold, Otto I, Margrave of Baden-Hachberg, and many nobles. The story of Arnold von Winkelried throwing himself onto the enemy pikes first appears in the Lucerne Chronicle of 1513.

An armistice followed on 12 October. With many of the local elites loyal to Habsburg dead, Habsburg control of the lands west of the Rhine collapsed. By 1389 Lucerne had consolidated its control over the towns around Lake Sempach, Willisau and the Entlebuch, and Bern began the conquests that formed its canton. A peace of 1 April 1389 was extended to 20 years in 1394. The battle chapel, built by the Habsburg side for its dead in 1387, became a Swiss place of worship after Sempach passed to Lucerne in 1415.
battle-of-sentinum: The Third Samnite War began when envoys from Lucania asked Rome for help against a Samnite attack. In 297 BCE Quintus Fabius defeated the Samnites at the Battle of Tifernum and Publius Decius beat a Samnite force near Maleventum. In 296 BCE the Samnite commander Gellius Egnatius led an army north into Etruria and pressed the Etruscan council into a joint war, which Umbrian groups also joined, while large sums were reportedly offered to the Gauls.

Facing such a coalition for the first time, Rome elected Fabius and Decius consuls again for 295 BCE and sent them into Etruria with four legions and allied troops, 40,000 men in all, while Lucius Volumnius Flamma Violens kept up the war in Samnium. The allies planned for the Samnites and Senones to fight the Romans while the Etruscans and Umbrians took the Roman camp. Deserters from Clusium revealed the plan, and Fabius sent the reserve legions to ravage the land of Clusium, drawing the Etruscans away from Sentinum to defend it.

After two days of waiting, the Romans attacked. Fabius on the right fought defensively, waiting for the enemy to tire. Decius on the left ordered cavalry charges that twice drove back the Senone horse, but his men were routed by Senone chariots and his infantry line was broken. Decius then performed the devotio, offering prayers to the gods and launching himself into the enemy lines, as his father had done at the Battle of Vesuvius in 340 BCE. The act rallied the Roman left, which Fabius reinforced with two reserve contingents.

On the right, Fabius sent his cavalry round the Samnite flank and pushed his infantry forward, and the Samnites broke and fled. The Senones formed a testudo with their shields, and Fabius had 500 Campanian lancers attack them from the rear while the rest of his army stormed the Samnite camp. Livy gives the Senone losses as 20,000 and the Roman losses as 8,700.

Livy noted that some earlier writers had exaggerated the battle's size. Of the Samnites who escaped, 5,000 crossed the land of the Paeligni, who killed 1,000 of them. Fabius held a triumph in Rome and later defeated the Perusini, who fought on. The Etruscans, Umbrians and Senones left the war, and five years later the Samnites capitulated.
battle-of-sepeia: The fertile plain of Thyrea had long been disputed between Sparta and Argos. Sparta won it at the Battle of the 300 Champions in 546 BCE, and nearly two generations later Argos took it back. The Agiad king Cleomenes I sent envoys to the Oracle of Delphi and announced that it foretold a Spartan victory, which won him the support of the Spartan people; the Argives were told of their own defeat. The nearest thing to a contemporary account is the Histories of Herodotus, written about fifty years later.

Cleomenes first led his army to the Erasinos River on the border of the Argolid but, receiving bad omens at his sacrifice, withdrew. He then arranged with the Aeginetans and Sicyonians to ship his forces to the district of Tiryns and Nauplia, which caught the Argives off guard and made them camp close to the Spartans at Sepeia.

According to Herodotus, the cautious Argives copied the commands of the Spartan herald so that they took their meals at the same time as the Spartans. Cleomenes noticed, told his men to attack at the next call to eat, and fell on the unprepared Argives. Plutarch instead tells of a seven-day truce broken on the third night. The surviving hoplites fled into the Sacred Grove of Apollo. Cleomenes called out names as if their ransom had been paid and killed each man who came out, at least fifty, until one climbed a tree and saw what was happening. Cleomenes then set fire to the grove.

Herodotus puts the Argive dead at six thousand, Pausanias at five thousand; modern historians widely accept the higher figure. The date of about 494 BCE rests on a prophecy linking the fall of Argos with that of the Milesians, fulfilled at the end of the Ionian Revolt. Argos lost most of its young and middle-aged men, and slaves married into the city's political and administrative positions until noble men born in Argos came of age.
battle-of-seven-oaks: The Forks of the Red and Assiniboine rivers had long been a meeting place of the fur trade, home to Ojibwe newcomers, Cree traders and Métis buffalo hunters. The North West Company built Fort Gibraltar there in 1810, and from 1812 Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk, settled Scottish colonists nearby at Fort Douglas. The Métis saw the colony as a threat to their way of life.

On 8 January 1814 the colony's governor, Miles MacDonell, issued the Pemmican Proclamation, forbidding the export of pemmican for a year. The North West Company and the Métis who supplied it saw a ploy to monopolise the commodity. MacDonell resigned in 1815 and was replaced by Robert Semple, who had no experience of the fur trade, and in March 1816 the Hudson's Bay Company seized and destroyed Fort Gibraltar.

In June 1816 Cuthbert Grant led about 60 mounted Métis and First Nations freighters to escort pemmican to Lake Winnipeg, seizing an HBC pemmican flotilla and the Brandon House post on the way. Semple went out on foot with 26 to 28 men to confront them at Seven Oaks, which the Métis called la Grenouillère, Frog Plain. A gunfight broke out when the settlers tried to arrest François-Firmin Boucher, sent to speak with Semple. The Métis, sharpshooters who outnumbered their opponents nearly three to one, dropped to reload after the first volley; the colonists thought them dead and were surprised when they rose and fired again. The fighting lasted no more than 15 minutes, and 16-year-old Joseph Letendre dit Batoche was the Métis dead.

The settlers left for Norway House the next day. Pierre Falcon wrote La Chanson de la Grenouillère, and the Métis flew their flag as la Nouvelle Nation, the New Nation. The Royal Commissioner William Bachelor Coltman, whose report reached the House of Commons on 24 June 1819, found that the first shot came from Semple's side. Selkirk's prosecutions of North West Company men ended in acquittals, and the two companies merged in 1821. The site became a National Historic Site of Canada in 1920.
battle-of-shamkor: The battle was one of several conflicts between the Atabegs of Azerbaijan, known after their ruling dynasty as the Eldiguzids, and the Kingdom of Georgia. The consolidation of Eldiguzid power had coincided with a revival of Georgian expansion, and the territories of both met in Muslim Shirvan and Arran.

A dynastic war in the Eldiguzid lands from 1191 to 1195 preceded the battle. Abu Bakr, the victor, had his elder brother Qutluq Inandj assassinated and forced his younger brother, Amir Mihran, to take refuge at the court of his brother-in-law, Shirvanshah Akhsitan I. The two went to Tbilisi and appealed to Queen Tamar of Georgia, an official protector of Shirvan. Received with great honours, they were given the support they asked for, and a Georgian army marched to Shirvan.

Abu Bakr, reinforced by his client Muslim emirs, met the Georgians at the well-fortified city of Shamkor on 1 June 1195. The Georgians sent a relatively small force to break through the city gates while the main body raided deep in the enemy's rear. Poor roads and difficult country slowed them, and the atabeg held the city for a while, but the manoeuvre proved decisive and his army was severely defeated. The Georgians took Shamkor and pursued the fleeing soldiers to Ganja, which also fell to them.

The victors took numerous prisoners and a huge amount of booty, including the Caliph's standard, which Queen Tamar donated to the Khakhuli Monastery. At Ganja the noblemen, merchants, the qadi and the scholars came out to meet the Georgians, opened the gate and spread gold-brocaded carpets up to the door of the sultan's palace, where an assembly and a feast were held. Shamkor and its surroundings were handed to Amir Mihran on terms of vassalage. Abu Bakr was able to return to his capital, from where he had his brother Amir Mihran poisoned.
battle-of-shanghai: Armed conflict between China and Japan had continued without a declaration of war since the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931 and the attack on Shanghai in 1932, and it escalated into a full-scale war after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of July 1937. Shanghai was China's largest and most cosmopolitan city and its main commercial hub and port. By starting a major battle there, the Chinese leadership is believed to have aimed to divert Japan to the Yangtze delta, to gain time to move industry inland and to draw Western powers to its side, though there is no consensus on whether this succeeded. The last negotiations in Nanjing failed over Japan's demand for a Chinese withdrawal from the city.

The battle lasted from 13 August to 26 November 1937 and involved around one million troops. In the first stage, to 22 August, the Chinese army besieged the Japanese Naval Landing Force in street fighting. On 23 August the Japanese 3rd and 11th Divisions landed at Chuanshakou, Shizilin and Baoshan on the northeast coast, which stretched the Chinese front. The armies then fought house to house in the creek country north of the city, around Luodian and Dachang, while the fighting in the city became a stalemate.

After Dachang fell the Chinese began withdrawing from the city on the night of 26 October, leaving one battalion of the 88th Division to hold the Sihang Warehouse. Japanese landings at Jinshanwei on Hangzhou Bay, planned since 12 October, forced the Chinese to retire from the whole front, and a general retreat was ordered on 8 November. The Japanese army began its advance on Nanjing on 11 November, covering nearly 400 kilometres in about a month.

The Japanese took Shanghai after over three months of fighting, a campaign they had expected to finish in days. China lost a large part of its best troops, the elite divisions trained and equipped by the Germans, and no foreign power intervened. A Chinese historian of the time called it the bloodiest battle since Verdun, though estimates of casualties differ. According to Iwane Matsui's diary, all 500 Chinese prisoners taken near Wusong were shot. Both sides accused each other of using chemical weapons, and Japanese forces are confirmed to have used poison gas at least thirteen times. Peter Harmsen argues that the battle presaged urban combat in the rest of the century.
battle-of-shaykan: After Muhammad Ahmad, the self-proclaimed Mahdi, withdrew into Kordofan in 1881, he raised an army there and in Darfur. A force of 4,000 sent to capture him was ambushed near El Obeid and destroyed, and its equipment taken. By 1883 British sources put the Mahdi's army at 200,000, almost certainly an overestimate.

Against the advice of his British advisers, the Egyptian governor, Rauf Pasha, raised an army and placed it under European officers commanded by William Hicks, a retired colonel with experience in India and Abyssinia. Most of the soldiers were Egyptians imprisoned after the Urabi Revolt and released for service in Sudan, and they showed little will to fight. They beat off Mahdist forces near the fort of Kawa on the Nile on 29 April 1883. When word came that the Mahdi was besieging El Obeid, officials planned an expedition from Duem on the Nile, about 200 miles away, despite Hicks's reluctance.

The expedition had about 8,000 Egyptian regulars, 1,000 bashi-bazouk cavalry, 100 tribal irregulars and 2,000 camp followers, with supplies for 50 days carried by 5,000 camels, some ten mountain guns, four Krupp field guns and six Nordenfeldt machine guns. El Obeid had fallen before it set out, but it went on to relieve Slatin Bey, the governor of Darfur. Winston Churchill later called it perhaps the worst army that has ever marched to war: unpaid, untrained and undisciplined.

Whether by mistake or design, the guides led the column astray, and the troops began to desert in large numbers. On 3 November the whole Mahdist army fell on them, and they formed a defensive square, which reports published in Britain soon after said held for two days before it collapsed. All the officers were killed, Hicks among them, and only about 500 Egyptian troops made it back to Khartoum. The journalists Edmund O'Donovan of The Daily News and Frank Vizetelly of The Graphic also died.

The Mahdi's forces had taken El Obeid, a town the Egyptians had founded some years earlier as the capital of Kordofan, before the expedition set out, and after the battle they made it a centre of operations for some time. The victory also emboldened Osman Digna, whose Hadendoa followers joined the rebellion from their lands on the Red Sea coast.
battle-of-shelon: Novgorod traditionally recognised the authority of the Russian grand princes, but Lithuanian influence grew there in the 15th century. Its leaders had sided with Dmitry Shemyaka in the Muscovite Civil War, and after a defeat in 1456 the Treaty of Yazhelbitsy barred Novgorod from an independent foreign policy. In 1470 the pro-Lithuanian faction invited the Lithuanian prince Mikhailo Olelkovich, who stayed four months, and drafted a treaty recognising the limited suzerainty of Casimir IV; it was probably never approved by him.

After Archbishop Jonah died in November 1470, the same faction sought to have his successor ordained by Metropolitan Gregory rather than by Philip I in Moscow. Ivan III and the metropolitan accused Novgorod of treachery and of abandoning Orthodoxy. On 23 May 1471 Ivan went to war, joined by Pskov and Tver, and the Moscow chronicle of 1479 likened his campaign to Dmitry Ivanovich's war against Mamai; the historian Hélène Carrère d'Encausse wrote that it had features of a crusade.

The battle was fought on the morning of 14 July on the left bank of the Shelon. The Novgorodian army, at least 10,000 strong under Dmitry Boretsky and Vasily Kazimer, was drawn largely from citizens without military experience, probably the militias of the city's five ends. Daniil Kholmsky led 4,000 to 5,000 Muscovite troops across the river and its tributary, the Dryan, and a surprise attack by Tatars from Kasimov put the Novgorodians to flight, pursued as far as the Mshaga River. The Novgorodian Fourth Chronicle blames disorder, saying the archbishop-elect Feofil had ordered his cavalry to attack only the men of Pskov.

The 1479 chronicle's figure of more than 12,000 Novgorodian dead is thought exaggerated; 1,700 to 2,000 were taken prisoner. On 24 July Ivan III had Dmitry Boretsky executed; his clan, led by Marfa Boretskaya, had headed the opposition to Moscow. Under the Treaty of Korostyn Novgorod recognised itself as the grand prince's patrimony and the metropolitan's sole right to appoint its archbishop, though it kept its republican government. Ivan returned several times in the 1470s to arrest leading boyars, and took direct control in January 1478.
battle-of-sheriffmuir: John Erskine, 6th Earl of Mar, mustered Highland chiefs and on 6 September 1715 declared James Francis Edward Stuart, the Old Pretender, King of Scots. With about 12,000 men he took Perth and controlled much of the northern Highlands. After unsuccessful skirmishes against John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll, who was based at Stirling, Mar was persuaded on 10 November to lead his whole army south. Warned by spies, Argyll moved his army of about 4,000 to Sheriffmuir, a remote plateau of moorland on the northern fringe of the Ochil Hills.

The Jacobite army, somewhat smaller than before, still greatly outnumbered Argyll's, and his left wing under General Thomas Whetham was far shorter than the Jacobite right opposite it. Argyll's right attacked and drove the Highlanders back, but Whetham's men were overpowered, and Argyll came to their aid. By evening both armies were badly reduced. Mar, though he still had a great advantage in numbers, would not risk his whole army and let Argyll withdraw.

Both sides claimed victory. Jacobite losses in killed, wounded and captured have been put at between two hundred and eight hundred, among them John Lyon, 5th Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne; the government side lost upwards of six hundred, including Archibald Douglas, 2nd Earl of Forfar.

In strategic terms Argyll had halted the Jacobite advance. The outcome demoralised the Jacobites, who felt their numbers should have won, and Mar's French and Spanish supporters withdrew. The Old Pretender landed at Peterhead on 23 December but could not rouse the army at Perth. As Argyll advanced north, the Jacobites fled to Montrose, the Pretender returned to France and the army dispersed at Ruthven. The battle inspired the Jacobite song Sheriffmuir fight and Robert Burns's The Battle of Sherramuir, in which two shepherds disagree over who won.
battle-of-shizugatake: In June 1582 Oda Nobunaga, the most powerful daimyō in Japan, and his eldest son and heir Oda Nobutada were killed in the Honno-ji Incident after being betrayed by Akechi Mitsuhide. Their deaths opened a succession crisis within the Oda clan, as Nobunaga's sons Oda Nobukatsu and Oda Nobutaka quarrelled over who would succeed him. Hashiba Hideyoshi, as Toyotomi Hideyoshi was then known, summoned a council to Kiyosu Castle, which declared Nobutada's 3-year-old son Oda Hidenobu the rightful heir.

Having defeated Akechi Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki, and with the heir an infant, Hideyoshi was well placed to succeed Nobunaga in all but name. Shibata Katsuie, one of Nobunaga's trusted generals, challenged him by moving his support from Hidenobu to Nobutaka's claim to the lordship.

Katsuie ordered simultaneous attacks on Shizugatake, a series of forts in northern Ōmi Province, in present-day Nagahama, Shiga Prefecture, held by Hideyoshi's generals, among them Nakagawa Kiyohide and Takayama Ukon. Katsuie's nephew Sakuma Morimasa took Iwasaki-yama and killed Nakagawa, but the defences of Shizugatake held. Hearing that Hideyoshi had camped at Ōgaki with 20,000 mounted men, Katsuie ordered Sakuma to withdraw to Ōiwa. Sakuma ignored the order, reckoning that the castle would fall before a relieving army, thought to be at least three days away, could arrive.

Meanwhile the force of Maeda Toshiie on the Shibata side, posted on Mt. Shige, abruptly left the front. Hideyoshi marched his men through the night, covering nearly 50 miles in 6 hours, and joined the defenders of Tagami. His army drove Sakuma's forces into a rout, and as the troops of Fuwa Naomitsu and Kanamori Nagachika also fell back, he pursued them to Kitanosho Castle in Echizen Province. The castle fell after three days. Before it did, Katsuie killed members of his household, including his wife Oichi, Nobunaga's sister, set the keep on fire and committed seppuku. Sakuma was captured and beheaded.

Oichi's young daughters by Azai Nagamasa left the castle unharmed and became Hideyoshi's adoptive daughters. In June 1583, pressed by Hideyoshi and Nobukatsu, Oda Nobutaka committed suicide, leaving a death poem that cursed Hideyoshi. Hideyoshi still faced Nobukatsu, now allied with Tokugawa Ieyasu, until the Battle of Komaki and Nagakute in 1584. The historian George Sansom counted Shizugatake among the decisive battles of Japanese history.

Hideyoshi's seven chief generals in the battle became known as the Seven Spears of Shizugatake (shichi-hon yari). Among them were Katō Kiyomasa, later one of Hideyoshi's closest retainers, Fukushima Masanori and Wakizaka Yasuharu.
battle-of-siffin: After the third caliph Uthman was killed in 656 CE by Egyptian rebels, the Basrans, Kufans and most of the Ansar supported Ali for the caliphate. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the Umayyad governor of Syria, refused to pledge allegiance and sent Ali a formal declaration of war, charging him with Uthman's murder and demanding that the killers be surrendered. Ali answered that he was innocent and that Mu'awiya should first pledge allegiance and then bring his case to Ali's court.

Modern authors often regard Mu'awiya's call for revenge as a pretext to keep his rule over Syria or to seize the caliphate. Mu'awiya won the support of Amr ibn al-As, who was promised the governorship of Egypt for life.

Siffin lay on the right bank of the Euphrates, near Raqqa in present-day Syria. Ali's army, which drew on Kufa, reached it early in the summer of 657, and found Mu'awiya's forces already there and holding the watering place. The size of the armies is uncertain, with reports ranging from 100,000 to 150,000 on each side.

The main battle seems to have begun on Wednesday, 26 July 657 and continued to Friday or Saturday morning. Ali probably did not initiate the fighting. Mu'awiya fared better on the first day, but by the second the Iraqis began to gain the upper hand. Before noon some Syrians raised pages of the Quran on their lances, calling for the Book of God to judge between them, and the fighting stopped. Ali is said to have urged his men to continue, calling it a deception, but the majority of his army wanted a truce, and he agreed under pressure. By this point Ali may have lost 25,000 men and Mu'awiya 45,000.

A minority in Ali's camp opposed the arbitration, and about 12,000 are said to have seceded outside Kufa. Some later left for al-Nahrawan and became the Kharijites, who fought Ali at the Battle of Nahrawan in 658. The arbitration itself was inconclusive, and the accounts of it are highly tendentious. The arbitrators could not agree on the next caliph.

The Syrians recognised Mu'awiya as caliph at Jerusalem, and in July 658 Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt from Ali's governor. Ali was assassinated by the Kharijite Ibn Muljam in January 661. That summer Mu'awiya invaded Iraq and compelled Ali's son Hasan to give up the caliphate, and his rule was acknowledged throughout the caliphate. The battle is regarded as a major step towards the Umayyad Caliphate.
battle-of-sirmium: The battle is also called the Battle of Semlin or of Zemun. From the mid 11th century the Kingdom of Hungary had expanded southwards towards Dalmatia and Croatia and allied with the Serbian principalities, which Constantinople saw as a threat to its dominance in the Balkans, and the two powers fought repeatedly in the 1150s and 1160s. Manuel I Komnenos sought a dynastic settlement: in 1163 King Stephen III's younger brother Béla was sent to Constantinople, became a Despotes and the fiancé of Manuel's daughter, and in 1165 was named heir to the throne as Alexios.

In 1167 Stephen refused to hand over the former Byzantine lands allotted to Béla, and war followed. Manuel, kept from the field by ill health, gave command to his nephew Andronikos Kontostephanos, the Megas Doux.

The fullest account is that of the historian John Kinnamos. The Byzantine army, a third of it foreign, included Turks, Cumans, the Varangian Guard, Lombard lancers, 500 armoured Serbian infantry and German mercenaries, drawn up in three divisions with the river Sava behind them and a reserve of infantry and archers. The Hungarian commander, Dénes, count of Bács, formed his army, with German allies, in one broad line led by heavily armoured cavalry.

Byzantine horse archers goaded the Hungarians into charging. Most of the Byzantine left gave way towards the river, perhaps in feigned flight, and quickly reformed, while the centre and right held. The right counter-charged, the left returned, and Andronikos Lampardas drove at the troops around Dénes, where heavy cavalry fought with iron maces. Kontostephanos then committed his reserves and sent the infantry forward along the whole front, and the Hungarian army broke and fled.

The Byzantines took the main Hungarian standard on its ox-drawn wagon, five commanders with the title Župan and 800 other soldiers; a flotilla on the river killed or captured many fugitives. Hungary sued for peace, recognised imperial rule over Bosnia, Dalmatia, Croatia south of the Krka River and the Fruška Gora, and agreed to give hostages, pay tribute and supply troops. When Manuel's own son was born Béla lost his place as heir, but in 1172, with Manuel's help, he took the Hungarian throne.
battle-of-slivnitsa: The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 and the Congress of Berlin left Bulgaria divided: the lands north of the Balkan Mountains and Sofia became an autonomous principality, while Eastern Rumelia, between the Balkan and Rhodope mountains, was semi-autonomous under an Ottoman-appointed Christian governor. Relations between the principality and Russia cooled after 1883, and Russia came to oppose reunification.

When a rebellion broke out in Eastern Rumelia in September 1885, Prince Alexander Battenberg chose to lead the national movement rather than lose his throne. Russia recalled all its officers, leaving the Bulgarian Army almost without commanders above the rank of captain. Bulgaria massed its forces in Eastern Rumelia against an Ottoman attack that never came; the threat came instead from King Milan's Serbia, which demanded compensation for the change in the Balkan balance of power.

Serbia declared war on 13 November 1885 and crossed the lightly defended border in three columns, aiming to concentrate four divisions before Sofia. Alexander moved his army west by every means available, one regiment marching 95 km in 32 hours, while light forces slowed the Serbs in the mountains. Reinforcements gathered at a prepared position at Slivnitsa, 30 km north-west of Sofia: nearly 4 km of trenches and redoubts on a ridge, commanded by Major Guchev.

On 17 November a Bulgarian advance on the right surprised the Danube division, and the main Serbian attack on the centre, poorly supported by artillery, was driven back with some 1,200 casualties. On the 18th two battalions of the Preslav Regiment arrived in time to hold the weaker left. On the 19th a Serbian flanking attack near Karnul failed, since Captain Popov's battalions had held the Morava division in the Visker Hills, and Alexander's counterattack pushed the Serbs back on both flanks.

Slivnitsa decided the war. The Serbs were back in Serbia by 24 November, and on 27 November the Bulgarians, with Alexander leading the final attack, defeated them at Pirot. Austrian and Russian intervention brought a ceasefire on the 28th. Serbian casualties are given as 6,800 against 2,300 Bulgarian, though Serbian sources give other figures. The Treaty of Bucharest of 1886 effectively confirmed the unification, but Russia continued to oppose Alexander, and Russophile officers deposed him in August 1886.
battle-of-sluys: The war began after disagreements between Philip VI of France and Edward III of England. By 1337 English monarchs held only Gascony and Ponthieu in France, and on 24 May 1337 Philip's Great Council agreed that the Duchy of Aquitaine should be taken back into Philip's hands because Edward had breached his obligations as a vassal. At sea the French began with the advantage. Their galleys, partly hired from Genoa and Monaco, raided the English coast and razed Portsmouth in 1338, while Edward owned only three warships and relied on merchant cogs fitted with wooden castles at bow and stern.

The balance shifted in 1340. Genoese crews had mutinied in 1339, and in January 1340 an English raid on Boulogne destroyed 18 galleys and 24 other ships. Philip then assembled a Great Army of the Sea of about 200 ships, most of them requisitioned merchantmen, under Hugues Quiéret and Nicolas Béhuchet. It reached Sluys on 8 June 1340 and cut English communications with Edward's allies in Flanders.

Merchants had been reluctant to supply ships, but after an angry council Edward assembled between 120 and 150 ships at the River Orwell, carrying 1,300 men-at-arms and 1,000 longbowmen. He sailed on 22 June. The French chained their ships in three lines across the estuary of the Zwin. Pietro Barbavera, who commanded the galleys, advised putting to sea, but Béhuchet insisted on blocking the inlet.

On 24 June Edward entered at high tide with the wind and tide in his favour. The French ships had drifted eastward and become entangled. The English attacked in groups of three, two ships of archers flanking one of men-at-arms, and the longbowmen outshot the crossbowmen, according to the historians Jonathan Sumption and Robert Hardy. At night the rear line tried to break out, and apart from the galleys only 17 ships escaped. The English captured 166 merchant ships and sank or burned 24. French losses are put at 16,000 to 20,000 dead.

The victory let Edward land his army, which went on to besiege Tournai without success. It gave the English naval supremacy in the Channel, but Philip's greater resources allowed him to rebuild his navy quickly, and French raids continued, including attacks on the Isle of Wight, Plymouth and the Channel Islands later in 1340. In 1341 French, Castilian and Portuguese squadrons cut English communications with Gascony. Edward later issued a gold noble showing himself seated in a ship, inscribed with a line from the Gospel of Luke used as a protection in battle.
battle-of-sobraon: The First Anglo-Sikh War began in late 1845, when growing disorder in the Sikh Empire after the death of Ranjit Singh in 1839, together with provocations by the East India Company, led the Khalsa Army to invade British territory. The British won the first two major battles helped by the treachery of the Sikh commanders Tej Singh and Lal Singh. The Governor General, Sir Henry Hardinge, was dismayed by the head-on tactics of the commander-in-chief, Sir Hugh Gough, but no successor could arrive for months, and British spirits revived after Sir Harry Smith's victory at the Battle of Aliwal and the arrival of heavy artillery and two battalions of Gurkhas.

After their defeat at the Battle of Ferozeshah the Sikhs had withdrawn most of their forces across the Sutlej. Reinforced, they moved into a fortified bridgehead at Sobraon, encouraged by the veteran leader Sham Singh Attariwala, but the position was linked to the far bank by a single pontoon bridge, and three days of rain had swollen the river.

Early on 10 February 1846, once the fog lifted, 35 British heavy guns and howitzers opened a two-hour bombardment that did little harm. Divisions under Smith and Sir Walter Gilbert made feint attacks on the Sikh left while Robert Henry Dick attacked the weaker right, where the defences were of soft sand; Dick was killed and his men driven back. Renewed attacks along the whole front broke through, and engineers blew a breach for cavalry and horse artillery.

Tej Singh had left the field early. The bridge broke, many Sikh accounts holding that he weakened it and British accounts that the swollen river and the weight of men broke it, trapping nearly 20,000 Sikh soldiers on the east bank. None tried to surrender; many, Sham Singh among them, fought to the death, and British guns fired into the crowds in the river. The Sikhs lost between 8,000 and 10,000 men and 67 guns.

British units crossed the river that evening, and by 13 February Gough was 30 miles from Lahore. By the Treaty of Lahore the Sikhs ceded the Jullundur Doab, accepted a British Resident and owed an indemnity of 1.2 million pounds. Unable to pay it, they let Gulab Singh of Jammu acquire Kashmir by paying 750,000 pounds to the Company.
battle-of-solferino: The early weeks of the Second Italian War of Independence went well for the Piedmontese and French, who largely pushed Austria out of northern Italy, took Milan and marched east to finish Austria off before Prussia could become involved. On 22 June the allied army, 96,000 French and 37,000 Piedmontese, advanced from the Chiese to the Mincio. The Austrian Emperor Franz Joseph moved his 1st Army of 57,000 men and 2nd Army of 45,500 across the Mincio, and both sides converged on Medole, Solferino and San Martino.

It was the last major battle in which all the armies were under the personal command of their monarchs, and the largest since Leipzig in 1813. Napoleon III led the French and Victor Emmanuel II the Sardinians, while the Austrian high command was hindered by rivalry between its chief of staff, Heinrich von Heß, and the emperor's adjutant general, Karl Ludwig von Grünne.

With no fixed plan, the fighting was uncoordinated and fell into three engagements, at Medole in the south, Solferino in the centre and San Martino in the north. At Medole, from around 4 am, General Niel's 4th Corps held a thin line and kept three Austrian corps from helping the 2nd Army at Solferino. At Solferino the Austrians held their positions all day against repeated French attacks, until Napoleon III fed in the Imperial Guard.

Near 3 pm the French reserves attacked Cavriana, occupying it at 6 pm and breaking the Austrian centre, which forced both Austrian armies to retreat. In the north the Sardinians fought Benedek's VIII Corps from 7 am, and San Martino changed hands three times before a fourth assault took it at 8 pm.

The battle lasted over nine hours. Austrian losses were 2,386 killed, 10,634 wounded and 9,290 missing, and the Allies lost 2,313 killed, 12,102 wounded and 2,776 captured or missing. The Austrians retreated to the fortresses of the Quadrilateral.

Napoleon III, moved by the losses, ended the war with the Armistice of Villafranca on 11 July 1859. The Piedmontese won Lombardy but not Venetia, and Cavour resigned. The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861. Henry Dunant, who toured the field afterwards, was horrified by the suffering of the wounded and began the campaign that led to the Geneva Conventions and the International Red Cross, which he described in A Memory of Solferino. Memorials, ossuaries and museums mark the field, among them the 70-metre Tower of San Martino della Battaglia, built in 1893.
battle-of-solicinium: After the death of Julian in Persia in 363, the Alamanni set aside the truce he had imposed after his campaigns beyond the Rhine in 357, 358, 359 and 360 and renewed their raids into Gaul, complaining that the ministers of Valentinian I had failed to pay the customary tribute. They crossed the Rhine in 366 and returned with plunder. The next year they defeated Valentinian's generals in two battles and captured several standards, until Jovinus beat two of their detachments along the Moselle and routed their united forces at Chalons-Sur-Marne, with losses put at up to 10,000 against no more than 1,200 Romans.

Early in 368 the chieftain Rando fell without warning on Moguntiacum, put its defenceless inhabitants to the sword and withdrew over the river. Valentinian resolved to forestall further raids by a campaign in their own territory beyond the Rhine. Count Sebastian was sent to encircle the enemy from the south by way of Rhaetia, while the emperor advanced from Gaul with the forces of the west. The Alamanni, unable to defend their fields and villages, withdrew into the mountains and camped on a hill called Solicinium, in the area of Württemberg.

While reconnoitring their position, Valentinian was nearly captured by an advanced party lying in ambush, and lost his helmet and his standard-bearer as he retreated. Little is known of the battle itself. It appears that the Romans carried the height by a general assault up the slope, and that the Alamanni, driven from the summit, fled down the far side into the hands of Sebastian, who had been placed in their rear.

The site of the battle is unknown, and no archaeological evidence has been found. Proposed sites include Sulz am Neckar, Heidelberg, Schwetzingen, Rottenburg (Sülchen), Glauberg and the Spitzberg near Tübingen, spread over an area roughly 200 km across. The most recent research places the battle in the north of present-day Hechingen, with Solicinium where the town's Roman museum now stands.
battle-of-solway-moss: When Henry VIII of England broke with the Roman Catholic Church, he asked his nephew James V of Scotland to do the same. James ignored the request and further insulted him by refusing to meet him at York. Angered by the defeat of his forces at Hadden Rig, Henry sent troops under Thomas Howard, 3rd Duke of Norfolk, on a major raid into Scotland. In reply James gave Robert, Lord Maxwell, the Scottish Warden of the West March, the task of raising an army, and an order survives for a muster at the Kirk of Morton before dawn on 22 November.

On 24 November 1542 an army of 15,000 to 18,000 Scots advanced into England. Accounts of its command differ. A report by George Douglas of Pittendreich, who was not present, and some later chronicles say that Oliver Sinclair, the king's favourite, declared himself commander and the other leaders refused to accept him; the English commander Sir William Musgrave reported that Maxwell was still in charge.

Lord Wharton met the Scots near Solway Moss with 3,000 men. The fight was uncoordinated and may be called a rout. The Scots found themselves penned in south of the Esk, between the river and the peat bog of the Moss, and after intense fighting surrendered with their 10 field guns. Several hundred may have drowned in the marshes and river. James, who had stayed at Lochmaben, withdrew to Falkland Palace ill with fever and died there at the age of thirty.

Gervase Phillips has estimated that only about seven Englishmen and 20 Scots were killed, but 1,200 Scots were taken prisoner, among them Sinclair and the Earls of Cassilis and Glencairn. The prisoners were mostly well treated in England, in the hope that after their ransoms they would further the English cause, and many were released in exchange for hostages called pledges. The historian Marcus Merriman sees the battle as the culmination of James V's war rather than the beginning of the Rough Wooing.
battle-of-sphacteria: The Battle of Pylos left over 400 Spartan soldiers stranded on Sphacteria. Sparta arranged an armistice, handing over the ships of the Peloponnesian fleet as security, and sent envoys to Athens, but the talks failed and the Athenians refused to return the ships. Demosthenes, commanding at Pylos, meant to starve the garrison out, yet Helots promised freedom and free men offered money ran food across at night, some swimming underwater towing bags. The Athenians themselves were short of rations and had a single spring for water.

At Athens Cleon, who had led the rejection of Sparta's offer, claimed the reports from Pylos were wrong. His rival Nicias offered to stand aside and let him take command, and the assembly held him to it. Cleon promised to kill or capture the Spartans within twenty days and named Demosthenes his colleague.

A fire started by Spartan sailors cooking a meal had stripped the island of vegetation, letting Demosthenes see the defenders' positions. One night he landed 800 hoplites near the southern end, where only thirty Spartans stood guard, and they were killed before they understood.
