At dawn some 2,000 light troops and archers and about 8,000 rowers came ashore. Whenever the Spartans under Epitadas charged, the lightly armed men ran out of reach, and ash from the fire hid them. The Spartans withdrew to a fort at the northern end until the Messenian commander Comon led his men along the shore through ground thought impassable and appeared in their rear.

Epitadas had been killed, and his third in command, Styphon, sought advice from the mainland. The last message told him that the Spartans ordered him to decide for himself, so long as he did nothing dishonourable, and of the 440 Laconians who had crossed to the island 292 surrendered. The historian Donald Kagan wrote that the outcome shook the Greek world. Athens threatened to execute the prisoners if Attica were invaded, a Messenian garrison at Pylos raided Spartan land, and Cleon was honoured with meals in the prytaneum. Thucydides wrote that only the victory at Mantinea in 418 BCE removed the reproach of the disaster on the island.
battle-of-st-jakob-an-der-birs: In 1443 the seven cantons of the Old Swiss Confederacy invaded the canton of Zürich and besieged the city. Zürich had allied with Holy Roman Emperor Frederick III, who appealed to King Charles VII of France for an army to relieve it. Charles, eager to rid himself of the écorcheurs, troops left idle by the truce with King Henry VI of England in the Hundred Years' War, sent the Dauphin with about 30,000 of them, most of them Armagnacs.

When the French entered Swiss territory at Basel, the Swiss commanders at Farnsburg sent an advance troop of 1,300, mainly young pikemen, which reached Liestal on the night of 25 August and was joined there by a local force of 200.

Early the next morning the Swiss surprised and routed the French vanguard at Pratteln and Muttenz. Against strict orders, they then crossed the Birs to meet the main French army, which stood ready for battle. Formed in three pike squares, they repulsed charge after charge of Armagnac cavalry for several hours. Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, described Swiss fighters pulling crossbow bolts from their bodies and charging on after losing their hands.

As the squares weakened, the commander withdrew his men into the small hospital of St. Jakob. A relief force from Basel was driven back and its leader, Henman Sevogel, killed. Armagnac artillery bombarded the hospital, and the Swiss refused to surrender; when the attackers broke in, the defenders were pressed into the hospital garden and killed within half an hour.

The defeat was a heavy blow to Bern, which had supplied the force, but heavy French losses led the Dauphin to abandon the march on Zürich, where a Swiss army of 30,000 waited. He made peace with the Confederacy and Basel at Ensisheim on 28 October and left Alsace in the spring of 1445; the Church Council then meeting at Basel helped bring this about. The battle also showed the weakness of pike formations against artillery.

In the 19th century, after the fall of the Helvetic Republic, the battle was cast as a Swiss Thermopylae. It was named in Rufst du, mein Vaterland, the national anthem from the 1850s to 1961, and Ferdinand Schlöth's monument on the site dates from 1872.
battle-of-st-matthews-day: By 1217 the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, based in Riga, with Bishop Albert and their Latgalian and Livonian allies, had forced the elders of Ugandi, Sakala, Järvamaa and Soontagana to recognise their authority. The princes of the Novgorod Republic and the Principality of Pskov, who regarded Ugandi as part of their sphere, then took the stronghold of Otepää after a long siege, and the forces of the order and the bishop had to withdraw from Ugandi. In August the Estonians sent gifts to the Russians and asked them to join a new campaign, and Svjatoslav Mstislavich, the new prince of Novgorod, agreed.

At the call of Lembitu, elder of Sakala, about 6,000 men from Sakala, Läänemaa, Harjumaa, Järvamaa, Revala and Virumaa gathered by the Navesti river around 6 September; of the larger counties only Ugandi and Saaremaa stayed away. They waited 15 days, but the promised Novgorodian troops never came. Riga quickly raised an army of 3,000, probably led by the Master of the Order, Volkwin, with Count Albert of Lauenburg and Caupo among its leaders.

The army camped near Viljandi castle on the evening before St Matthew's Day and next day pursued the Estonians until they came out of the woods ready for battle, probably in the area between Vanamõisa, Karuse and the former Madi farm. The Germans in the centre advanced slowly in formation and broke the Estonian centre, the largest division. The Sakalians on the Estonian right had held the Latgalians, but fled when the centre collapsed, and in the rout Lembitu and the leaders Vottele, Manivalde and Vytamas were killed. The Livonians on the other flank at first fell back under a hail of spears, then joined the pursuit.

Henry of Livonia counts about 1,000 Estonian dead and 2,000 horses taken, the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle 1,400 dead. The victors camped for three days at Lembitu's village, pillaging the area, until his brother Unnepewe and other surviving elders of Sakala renewed peace and gave hostages. Many scholars regard the battle as effectively the final battle of the Ancient Estonian War for Freedom, while Enn Tarvel, Artur Vassar and Sulev Vahtre see a heavy blow rather than a decisive turn. A Danish tradition recorded by Petrus Olai in 1527 tells of a flag descending from the sky during a battle near Viljandi, and some historians have linked it with this battle.
battle-of-staffarda: By 1690 the Nine Years' War was in its third year, and neither side could gain a decisive advantage in the Spanish Netherlands or along the Rhine, which left Northern Italy as the one area where the Allies might strike at France. Louis XIV regarded Savoy as a French dependency, a view backed by French control of the fortresses of Pinerolo, annexed in 1631, and Casale, acquired in 1681 from Ferdinand Charles, Duke of Mantua and Montferrat.

Early in 1690 the French demanded that Victor Amadeus send troops to the Spanish Netherlands or join Nicolas Catinat against the Duchy of Milan, and hand over the citadel of Turin and Verrua. The intimidation proved counter-productive. Victor Amadeus sought the return of Pinerolo and the razing of Casale as his price for joining the Grand Alliance, negotiated subsidies from England and Spain, and declared war on France on 4 June.

Catinat took command in Piedmont in July with some 12,000 men and was ordered to burn and tax large parts of the country; peasants found carrying arms were hanged. The Marquis de Saint-Ruth overran most of the Duchy of Savoy, leaving only the fortress of Montmélian in ducal hands. Against the advice of Prince Eugene of Savoy, Victor Amadeus resolved to engage the French.

When Catinat marched south from Cavour towards Saluzzo, the duke moved to stop him, and the armies met at the abbey of Staffarda. Marshes and hedges sheltered the Savoyard line, but the French broke it; only Eugene's handling of the cavalry in the retreat averted disaster. Victor Amadeus lost 2,800 casualties, 1,200 prisoners and 11 of his 12 cannon, against French losses of between 1,000 and 2,000.

Catinat went on to take Saluzzo, Savigliano and Fossano, levying supplies and taxes, and looted towns such as Ceresole that refused to pay. The Imperial troops achieved little, Eugene blaming Spanish reluctance. Susa, which controlled communications with Briançon, capitulated in November, but sickness, supply problems and a shortage of men prevented an attack on Turin, and the French wintered in Savoy, the Dauphiné and Provence.
battle-of-stalingrad: By the spring of 1942 the Wehrmacht held Ukraine, Belarus and the Baltic republics, and Adolf Hitler chose the south of the Soviet Union as the target of the summer campaign. Germany's fuel supplies had dwindled, and the plan, code-named Fall Blau, aimed to seize the Soviet oil fields in the Caucasus. Stalingrad was one of the largest industrial centres of the Soviet Union and a transport hub on the Volga River, and controlling it would block Soviet shipments along the river. The city also carried the name of the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. Hitler split the army group, sending one part south to the Caucasus and the other, including Paulus's 6th Army, east towards the Volga.

German forces first met the Red Army's Stalingrad Front on 17 July 1942. On 23 August the 6th Army and part of the 4th Panzer Army began their offensive, supported by Luftwaffe bombing that reduced much of the city to rubble. The fighting became house-to-house. The Soviet commander Chuikov kept his front line as close to the Germans as possible, so that German artillery and aircraft could not strike without risking their own men, and used small units moving through the city's sewers. After 27 September the struggle moved to the factory district, and by November the Germans held 90 per cent of the ruined city, with the Soviet defenders confined to two narrow pockets on the Volga's west bank.

On 19 November the Red Army launched Operation Uranus against the Romanian armies guarding the German flanks. The flanks were overrun and about 330,000 Axis troops were trapped. Hitler forbade a breakout; attempts to supply the army by air failed, and Manstein's relief attempt, Operation Winter Storm, did not reach it. On 7 January 1943 Soviet envoys offered terms of surrender, which Hitler refused to let Paulus accept. On 2 February 1943 the 6th Army, out of ammunition and food, capitulated, the first of Hitler's field armies to do so.

The Axis suffered between 800,000 and 1,500,000 casualties, killed, wounded or captured, among the German armed forces and their allies. Of the troops trapped in the pocket, 105,000 eventually surrendered and 60,000 died. The German public was told of the disaster only at the end of January 1943; on 31 January state radio broadcast the Adagio of Anton Bruckner's Seventh Symphony before announcing the defeat. On 18 February Joseph Goebbels gave his Sportpalast speech calling for total war.

The defeat ended Germany's 1942 summer offensive and passed the strategic initiative on the Eastern Front to the Soviet Union. It is generally regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe. Stalingrad was named a Hero City in 1945, and the monument The Motherland Calls was erected on Mamayev Kurgan in 1967.
battle-of-stamford-bridge: The death of the childless King Edward the Confessor in January 1066 set off a struggle for the English throne among contenders from across north-western Europe, among them Harald Hardrada of Norway. The Norwegian army, with reinforcements from Orkney, most likely numbered between 7,000 and 9,000 men. Hardrada was joined by forces Tostig Godwinson had recruited in Flanders and Scotland. Tostig, exiled in 1065 after being ousted as Earl of Northumbria, was at odds with his brother Harold, who had been elected king. On 20 September the invaders defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar at the Battle of Fulford and received the surrender of York.

Harold was in southern England awaiting an invasion by William, Duke of Normandy. On hearing of the Norwegians he marched north with his housecarls and as many thegns as he could gather, covering about 185 miles from London to Yorkshire in four days. On 25 September he took the Norwegians completely by surprise at Stamford Bridge, where they had gone to collect hostages and supplies. According to Snorri Sturluson's saga, Harold himself rode up beforehand and offered Tostig his earldom.

A Norwegian with an axe was said by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Henry of Huntingdon to have blocked the narrow bridge alone and cut down more than 40 Englishmen. The delay allowed the Norse to form a shield wall, but they had left their armour behind. The battle raged for hours and went far beyond the bridge. When the shield wall broke, Hardrada was killed by an arrow in the throat and Tostig was slain. Eystein Orre's men ran 16 miles from the ships at Riccall and briefly checked the English, but were overwhelmed.

Harold granted a truce to the survivors, among them Hardrada's son Olaf and Paul Thorfinnsson, Earl of Orkney, who pledged not to attack England again. Only 24 ships of a fleet of over 300 were needed to carry them home. Three days later, on 28 September, William landed at Pevensey, and Harold marched south and was defeated and killed at Hastings on 14 October. The battle has traditionally marked the end of the Viking Age, although major Scandinavian campaigns in Britain followed, such as Sweyn Estrithson's in 1069–1070 and Magnus Barefoot's in 1098.
battle-of-stiklestad: Harald Fairhair created a unified Norwegian state at the end of the 9th century, but the union came apart after his death, and the jarls of Lade and Harald's descendants spent the next century in feuds over power. In 1015 Olaf Haraldsson returned from Viking trips and was elected king, and in June 1016 he won the Battle of Nesjar against the jarls of Lade. In 1028 Cnut the Great allied himself with the Lades and Olaf went into exile in Kievan Rus'. After the last Lade jarl, Haakon Ericsson, drowned in 1029, Olaf prepared an expedition, supported by the Swedish king Anund Jacob, who gave him 400 men and guides.

According to saga sources, Olaf crossed the mountains with 3,600 men into the valley of Verdalen, about 80 km north of Trondheim, and at the farm of Stiklestad met an army led by Hárek of Tjøtta, Thorir Hund and Kálfr Árnason, who had once served him. Snorri Sturluson, writing in the Heimskringla about 200 years later, gives Olaf's war cry as Forward, men of Christ, men of the cross, men of the king, and the farmers' as Forward, farmers. According to Snorri, Olaf received three wounds: in the knee, in the neck and, as he leaned against a large stone, a spear thrust into his belly.

Snorri names Thorir Hund and Kálfr Árnason among those who gave the lethal wounds. Dagr Hringsson fought on after the king's death, until Kálfr and Thorir forced him and the rest of Olaf's army to retreat. Olaf's half-brother Harald, fifteen years old and later King Harald Hardrada, was wounded and hidden by locals. The king's body was buried secretly in the sandy banks of the Nidelva River.

According to Snorri, the grave was opened the year after the battle and the body was found incorrupt. It was moved to St. Clement's Church in Trondheim, and Bishop Grimketel began the beatification of Olaf on 3 August. The rule of Cnut's wife Ælfgifu of Northampton and their son Svein proved harsh, and the church came under pressure. Olaf's status as a martyr grew, and the common people revolted against Danish rule. When Olaf's son Magnus the Good claimed the throne, Cnut had to yield. About a century after the battle Nidaros Cathedral was built on the site of Olaf's first burial.

Historians treat Snorri's account with caution. The sizes of the armies are probably impossible to determine, and archaeology has found little at Stiklestad. Olaf became Rex Perpetuus Norvegiae, the eternal king of Norway, and his cult helped complete the conversion of the country. The Saint Olav Drama has been staged at Stiklestad every year since 1954.
battle-of-stirling-bridge: In 1296 John de Warenne, 6th Earl of Surrey, defeated the Scots at the Battle of Dunbar, King John Balliol surrendered to Edward I on 10 July, and the Scottish landholders were made to acknowledge Edward's overlordship. In 1297 Andrew Moray began a revolt in northern Scotland and by late summer controlled Urquhart, Inverness, Elgin, Banff and Aberdeen. William Wallace joined him in September near Dundee, and they marched to Stirling, traditionally regarded as the key to Scotland. Surrey and Edward's treasurer in Scotland, Hugh de Cressingham, had both reached Stirling by 9 September, by which time the Scots held Abbey Craig.

The Forth was crossed near Stirling Castle by a long causeway and a narrow wooden bridge wide enough for only two horsemen abreast. Surrey saw the risk and delayed for several days to negotiate. Walter of Guisborough reports that Wallace answered the envoys that the Scots were there not to make peace but to fight and free their kingdom. A Scots knight, Sir Richard Lundie, offered to cross at a ford two miles upstream, but Cressingham persuaded Surrey to order a direct attack over the bridge.

Wallace and Moray waited until, by one estimate, about 2,000 English troops had crossed. Their spearmen then came down from the high ground, held off the heavy cavalry and cut off the bridge. Most of those trapped in the loop of the river were probably killed. Marmaduke Thweng fought his way back across. Surrey ordered the bridge destroyed and retreated towards Berwick, leaving Stirling Castle isolated.

Walter of Guisborough recorded English losses as 100 cavalry and 5,000 infantry. Scottish losses are unrecorded except for Moray, who was mortally wounded and was dead by November. The Lanercost Chronicle says Wallace had a strip of Cressingham's skin made into a sword belt. The Scots raided as far south as Durham, and Wallace was appointed Guardian of Scotland. Edward was already planning another invasion, which led to the Battle of Falkirk. Wallace's later fame rests largely on the poet Blind Harry, writing about 1470, whose account of the battle is a blend of fact and fiction and is highly improbable in its details.
battle-of-strasbourg: During the 3rd century the small tribes of free Germany coalesced into large, loose confederations: the Franks, the Alamanni and the Burgundians. The Alamanni colonised the Agri Decumates after the Romans evacuated it in the mid-3rd century and formed small cantons, mostly along the east bank of the Rhine. In 350 the usurper Magnentius killed the emperor Constans, and Constantius II made a truce with Persia to deal with him. The Franks and Alamanni used the absence of the best Roman forces to overrun much of eastern Gaul and Raetia. They captured many Roman forts on the Rhine and set up permanent camps on the west bank, and more than 20,000 Roman civilians were reported to have been abducted.

Julian came to Gaul with a small escort of 360 men and learned on the way that Cologne had fallen to the Franks. In 356 he joined the main Gaul army at Reims and decided to march to Alsace. At Dieuze his army was ambushed, and two legions were rescued only when other regiments heard the uproar. A deserter told Chnodomar that Julian had 13,000 men at Saverne, and Libanius implies 15,000. Ammianus puts the Alamanni at around 35,000, a figure several historians regard as unrealistically high; about 25,000 is considered the most likely.

The army marched 21 Roman miles from probably Saverne. Ammianus reports that Julian urged a postponement, but his officers and men demanded battle at once. Chnodomar held the Alamannic left with his cavalry and mixed light infantry among the horsemen to stab the horses of the Roman cataphracts. His nephew Serapio, still a teenager, commanded the right. When the German ranks demanded that Chnodomar and the chiefs dismount and lead the foot, he complied and so lost control of the battle. The Roman cavalry initially performed poorly, but the Roman infantry won the day and drove the Alamanni beyond the Rhine, with negligible Roman losses. About 6,000 Alamanni were counted dead on the field.

After the battle Julian was acclaimed Augustus by his troops but refused the title, which only the ruling Augustus, Constantius, could bestow. All Alamanni families who had settled in Alsace were rounded up and expelled from imperial territory. The battle was the turning point in Julian's effort to restore the Rhine frontier. Until then he had campaigned largely inside Gaul, with the barbarian bands holding the initiative. Afterwards he invaded the lands beyond the Rhine each year, devastated them and imposed tributary status on the tribes, and repaired Rome's line of forts.
battle-of-suomussalmi: The Soviet objective was to advance to Oulu and cut Finland in half. On 30 November 1939 the Soviet 163rd Rifle Division under Zelentsov crossed the border near Juntusranta and at Raate and advanced towards Suomussalmi. Finnish battalions fought it from 4 December, but Suomussalmi was captured on 7 December. Colonel Hjalmar Siilasvuo's Regiment JR 27 arrived by 9 December and stopped the Soviet advance towards Hyrynsalmi, and by the 11th it had cut the Soviet road link at Raate.

Over the next two weeks Siilasvuo contained the Soviets while Finnish artillery arrived, and on 25 December his forces became the 9th Division. On 21 December Finnish raiding parties attacked the Soviet 44th Division on the Raate road. Surrounded, Zelentsov tried to break out on 24 and 25 December and was stopped. On 27 December Siilasvuo attacked from several sides, and on 28 December Soviet resistance collapsed: the 163rd Division was reduced to a few hundred men who fled towards the border. The battle lasted until 8 January 1940.

On the Raate–Suomussalmi road the Finns captured 43 tanks, 70 field guns, 278 trucks, 1,170 horses, 29 anti-tank guns, 300 machine guns and 6,000 rifles. Had the Soviet Union taken Oulu, Finland would have had to fight on two fronts and a rail link to Sweden would have been cut. Estimates of Soviet casualties vary: Allen Chew gave 22,500, David Campbell 22,500 to 27,000 and Brian Best 27,000 killed and 2,100 captured. Alvar Aalto sculpted a memorial to the Finnish dead.

The battle is often cited as an example of a small force fighting on familiar ground and defeating a larger enemy. Finnish troops on skis and sleds were more mobile, while Soviet heavy equipment kept to roads in forested marshland, where the network was mostly logging trails. The Finns targeted Soviet field kitchens and intercepted Soviet telephone communications, and were better equipped for the cold.
battle-of-surabaya: Sukarno and Hatta declared Indonesia's independence in Jakarta on 17 August 1945. On 19 September Dutch internees raised the Dutch flag at the Hotel Yamato in Surabaya; nationalist militia overran them and tore off the flag's blue stripe, making it the Indonesian flag. The senior Japanese commander, Vice Admiral Shibata Yaichiro, backed the Republicans and let them take Japanese arms, which they did not hand over to the Dutch.

In late October and early November the Muslim organisations Nahdlatul Ulama and Masyumi declared the defence of the homeland a holy war, kyai and their students streamed into the city, and Bung Tomo stirred it by radio. British Indian troops of the 49th Infantry Brigade arrived on 25 October to evacuate European internees. Brigadier A. W. S. Mallaby agreed with Suryo, the Republic's governor of East Java, that the Indonesians would not be asked to give up their weapons.

On 27 October a British plane from Jakarta dropped leaflets ordering the Indonesians to surrender their arms. Taking this as a breach of the agreement, they attacked the British Indian troops on 28 October. The British flew in Sukarno, Hatta and the minister Amir Sjarifuddin, and a ceasefire was agreed on 30 October. That day Mallaby, spreading news of it, was killed near the Jembatan Merah, the Red Bridge, in confused circumstances: Captain R. C. Smith reported that a young Republican shot him, other accounts that a grenade explosion killed him.

General Robert Mansergh demanded surrender by 6.00 am on 10 November, and the demand was rejected. Two more brigades of the 5th Indian Division, with tanks, two cruisers and three destroyers, then advanced methodically under naval and air bombardment, clearing buildings room by room. Half the city fell in three days, but the fighting lasted until 29 November.

Estimates of Indonesian deaths range from 6,300 to 15,000, and perhaps 200,000 people fled the city; British Indian losses were 295 killed and missing. The loss of weapons hampered the Republicans for the rest of the revolution, but the resistance became its rallying cry. It persuaded the Dutch that the Republic had popular support and made Britain wary of being drawn into the war; within a few years Britain supported the Republican cause at the United Nations. The Heroes Monument in Surabaya commemorates the battle.
battle-of-svolder: Norway had long been divided into petty kingdoms, and its unification, traditionally traced to Harald Fairhair in the ninth century, was contested by regional rulers such as the Jarls of Lade and by Danish kings who claimed the south. The spread of Christianity was also a political issue. In 995 the pagan Haakon Sigurdsson, Jarl of Lade, was deposed and Olaf Tryggvason came to the throne. Olaf set out to convert Norway, using threats, torture and executions, and made enemies. The most prominent were Eirik Jarl, Haakon's son, and Svein Forkbeard of Denmark, who each felt that Olaf had deprived them of a share of Norway. Olaf Tryggvason had also taken control of Viken, an area long under Danish overlordship.

The Norse sagas, written about two centuries later and historically unreliable, blame the quarrel on Olaf's marriage to Thyri, Svein's sister, whose dowry Svein refused to pay. They say Olaf was lured into an ambush, with Jarl Sigvaldi as a traitor, while he was in Wendland. The sources disagree about where the battle was fought: Adam of Bremen places it in the Øresund, Icelandic sources off an unidentified island called Svolder, and modern historians are divided between the Øresund and Rügen. The sagas agree that Olaf had only eleven ships against far larger fleets.

The sagas say Olaf lashed his ships together, with the Long Serpent in the middle, as a floating fort. The Danes and Swedes were repulsed at the front, while Eirik Hákonarson forced his iron-plated ship against the end of the line and cleared the ships one by one until only the Long Serpent was left. In the best-known episode Einarr Þambarskelfir's bow was split by an arrow, which Olaf was told meant Norway breaking from his hands. Danish sources say Olaf threw himself overboard in armour; Norwegian and Icelandic accounts suggest he may have escaped.

Heimskringla says the victors divided Norway in three. Olaf of Sweden took districts in Trondheim and Møre, which he gave to Jarl Svein Hákonarson, his son-in-law, to hold as a vassal. Svein Forkbeard took Viken, and Eirik ruled the rest as Svein's vassal. The jarls ruled prosperously and, most sources say, allowed religious freedom, leading to a backlash that undid much of Olaf Tryggvason's mission. The same interests divided Norway until Magnus the Good became king of an independent, Christian Norway in 1035. The battle became one of the best-known battles of the Viking Age and inspired Icelandic rimur cycles and, around 1830, a Faroese ballad, Ormurin langi.
battle-of-sybota: Corcyra, modern Corfu, was an old Corinthian colony that no longer wished to remain under Corinthian influence, and the two cities had fallen out over the Affair of Epidamnus. Corcyra, which had the third largest navy in Greece, allied itself with Athens, an enemy of Corinth, which was allied with Sparta. Athens sent ten ships under Lacedaimonius, the son of Cimon, Diotimus and Proteas, with orders not to fight unless the Corinthians tried to land on the island.

Corinth assembled 150 ships under Xenoclides. The Corcyraean fleet of 110 ships, led by Miciades, Aisimides and Eurybatus, made the Sybota islands its base. The Corcyraeans formed their line with the Athenians on the right, while the Corinthians placed the Megarians and Ambraciots on their right and their own ships on the left. Both sides carried hoplites, archers and javelin-throwers and fought in a manner Thucydides calls old-fashioned, boarding enemy ships instead of ramming them, so that the fight was essentially a land battle at sea.

The Corcyraean left routed the Corinthian right and chased it back to its camp on the coast, which it burned. The Corinthian left was more successful, and the Athenians, who had held back, were forced to come to their allies' aid. The Corinthians still won, and sailed through the wreckage killing survivors, among them, unknowingly, some of their own defeated allies, though they also took prisoners.

The Corcyraeans and Athenians withdrew to defend Corcyra, but when the Corinthians arrived they pulled back at once, as 20 more Athenian ships under Glaucon were approaching. The next day the new squadron threatened a second battle if the Corinthians tried to land, and the Corinthians withdrew altogether. Both sides claimed victory: Corinth for winning the battle, Corcyra for escaping occupation. Soon afterwards Athens and Corinth fought again at the Battle of Potidaea, which led to Sparta's formal declaration of war.
battle-of-tacna: After the Tarapacá campaign the Chileans paused, expecting Peru to accept a truce that would leave them the conquered territory. Their army grew with civilian volunteers, and saltpetre exports from Antofagasta paid for its supplies. In Peru and Bolivia the reverses brought down the presidents Mariano Ignacio Prado and Hilarión Daza, replaced by Nicolás de Piérola and General Narciso Campero, while the loss of Tarapacá cut off the allies' saltpetre income.

In February 1880 four Chilean divisions landed at Ilo. Manuel Baquedano González, a veteran of the war against the Peru-Bolivian Confederacy, replaced Erasmo Escala as commander after Escala quarrelled with War Minister Rafael Sotomayor, who died of a stroke on 20 May. The allied army at Tacna, about 10,000 men, was weakened by disease and armed with mixed, often obsolete rifles, while the Chileans carried Comblain and Gras rifles firing the same ammunition. An allied attempt to ambush the Chileans at Quebrada Honda on the night of 25 May was foiled by darkness and mist.

The allies stood on the Intiorko plateau in a defensive line about 3 km long but dug no trenches. Baquedano adopted Colonel Velasquez's plan of a simultaneous attack along the whole front, so that the shallow allied line could not shift troops to its weak points. After an artillery duel in which shells buried themselves in the sand, Santiago Amengual's division attacked the allied left at about 10 a.m. When the Chileans ran short of ammunition, an allied counter-attack drove them back.

A charge by the Granaderos a Caballo was repulsed but bought time for the Chileans to rally and resupply, and Amunátegui's division came up to break the allied centre. Orozimbo Barbosa's division then outflanked Lizardo Montero on the right, and after five hours the allied front collapsed. Amengual entered Tacna around 18:30.

Chile lost about 2,200 men; allied losses are estimated at 3,500 to 5,000. The Bolivian Colorados and Aroma battalions fought on rather than retreat. Campero withdrew to Bolivia and Montero to Puno. With Bolivia out of the war, the Chilean government concluded that the war would end only with Peru's complete surrender. Tacna remained under Chilean control until the Treaty of Lima of 1929.
battle-of-taginae: After the murder of Amalasuntha in 535 Justinian used her death as a pretext to invade Italy, and Belisarius took Ravenna in May 540. Byzantine misrule strengthened the Goths, and under their king Totila they held much of southern and central Italy by 544. Totila captured Rome in December 546. Justinian assigned his cousin Germanus to raise an army, but Germanus died in 550, and in mid-551 Justinian appointed his chamberlain Narses. The force assembled at Salona in Dalmatia included Lombards, Heruls and Bulgars. The Franks controlled the land route through Venetia, so Narses marched along the Adriatic coast while a fleet ferried troops across river mouths, and he reached Ravenna.

In July 552 the armies met at Busta Gallorum, near the village of Taginae, north of modern Gualdo Tadino. Totila waited there for 2,000 men under Teia. Narses deployed defensively, with dismounted Germanic mercenaries in a dense centre, 4,000 foot-archers on each wing and a detachment of 1,500 cavalry behind a hill on the left. The next day the Armenian bodyguard Anzalas killed the Goth Coccas in single combat, and Totila rode out in shining purple and gold armour, tossing his lance, to delay the battle. When Teia's men arrived, Totila withdrew his troops for lunch, hoping to relax the Byzantines, but Narses kept his army in position.

Totila then formed his cavalry in a single body, with the infantry behind, and charged the Byzantine centre with orders to use spears over any other weapon. Narses turned his two archer detachments half round into a crescent, so that they shot at the Gothic cavalry from both sides. The charge faltered with heavy losses, and by evening the cavalry gave way. The Gothic infantry, which had not fought, fled with it. As many as 6,000 were slain by nightfall, many prisoners among them put to death, and Totila was mortally wounded.

Narses dismissed his Lombard allies after their arson and rape, and entered Rome in July 552. The Goths proclaimed Teia king, and he was defeated and killed at Mons Lactarius near Vesuvius in October. In October 554 Narses defeated a Frankish army at the Battle of Volturno. Taginae was not the last engagement, but it broke the ability of the Goths to field a viable army.

Charles Oman called it the first experiment in the combination of pike and bow. Philip Rance rejects that reading, arguing that infantry remained the core of Byzantine armies, and that Totila had lost strategically before the battle began, because he had to intercept Narses's numerically superior army before it reached Rome. The main source is Procopius, whose account emphasises mounted combat.
battle-of-tagliacozzo: The Hohenstaufen emperors, who had inherited the Kingdom of Sicily from its Norman rulers in 1194, also sought to consolidate their claims to northern Italy, against the opposition of many northern Italian states and the Papacy. The struggle split Italians into the factions of Guelphs and Ghibellines. After the death of Emperor Frederick II in 1250, Sicily was ruled by his illegitimate son Manfred of Sicily, first beside his half-brother Conrad IV and, after Conrad died of malaria in 1254, as regent for Conrad's son Conradin. In 1258 Manfred declared himself king.

Pope Clement IV, continuing the policy of Pope Urban IV, excommunicated Manfred and backed Charles of Anjou, who entered Italy in 1265 with papal support, including a crusading tithe, and defeated and killed Manfred at the Battle of Benevento the next year. When Conradin entered Italy with an army in September 1267, Clement appointed Charles papal vicar to oppose him.

The armies met on the Palentine Plains near Scurcola Marsicana, each in three divisions. Conradin's army, the larger, had Spanish and Italian knights under Henry of Castile, a mainly Italian division under Galvano Lancia, and most of the German knights under Conradin himself with his friend Frederick I, Margrave of Baden. Charles placed an Italian and Provençal division and a French division under Marshal Henri de Cousances in front, and on the advice of the veteran crusader Erard of Valery hid his third division of veteran French knights behind a hill.

Conradin's men routed the first two divisions, and Henry of Castile killed a man wearing Charles's armour, who was in fact Henri de Cousances. Believing the day won, the Hohenstaufen troops scattered to pursue and to plunder the Angevin camp. Charles's hidden reserve then attacked and cut them to pieces.

Conradin fled towards Rome but was captured, imprisoned and executed. The battle was the last act of Hohenstaufen power in Italy, and his death marked the fall of the family from the imperial and Sicilian thrones. For the Papacy, which still saw the Hohenstaufen as the main threat, the victory carried a risk of its own: the Angevins might in turn try to dominate the north as well as the south, despite Charles's explicit promises that he would claim nothing in northern Italy.
battle-of-taillebourg: By his will Louis VIII had left the title of Count of Poitou to his younger son, Alphonse of Poitiers. In June 1241 Louis IX held a plenary court at Saumur and announced that Alphonse, now of age, would take possession, then installed him at Poitiers. The Lusignans opposed Capetian authority in the region, and Isabella of Angoulême resented that her son Richard of Cornwall, brother of Henry III of England, had not received the title. Her husband, Hugh X of Lusignan, Count of La Marche, raised an army, and talks failed.

In April 1242 Louis gathered a force at Chinon, put at around 50,000 by some contemporaries and at 25,000 by modern historians, and took many rebel castles. Henry III landed at Royan on 20 May and joined the rebels, forming an army that modern estimates place at around 30,000 men.

On 21 July the armies faced each other across the bridge over the Charente, a strategic crossing on the route between northern and southern France. Louis and Alphonse held the Château de Taillebourg above it. The English and the rebels attacked to take the bridge, but a massive charge by French knights sallying from the castle drove them back toward Saintes. Henry and Hugh fled separately, leaving their army without leaders, and on 22 July a prolonged melee north of Saintes ended in a second defeat.

After a short siege the citizens of Saintes handed Louis the keys of the city. A blockade of La Rochelle by sea failed, and in January 1243 Henry told Emperor Frederick II that he had given up hope of retaking his French possessions. A five-year truce was signed at Pons on 1 August, and a lasting peace came at Paris on 4 December 1259, under which Louis restored Guyenne to Henry. Hugh's Poitevin castles were confiscated. The battle ended Henry's hopes of restoring the Angevin Empire, and Eugène Delacroix painted it for the Salon of 1837.
battle-of-talas: Tang China and the Arab caliphates had met in Central Asia since the early eighth century. In 715 a Tang force defeated a Tibetan-Arab army at the Battle of Namangan and restored the king of Fergana, and in 717 Tang troops and Karluks defeated the Umayyads and Tibetans at the Battle of Aksu. In 747 the Tang general Gao Xianzhi established control over the Gilgit region, and in 750 the Abbasids took power after the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate.

The immediate cause was a quarrel over Shash, the region of modern Tashkent. Gao Xianzhi led Tang and Karluk soldiers against its king, who surrendered and was taken to the Tang capital Chang'an and executed. His son then appealed to the Abbasids, and the Abbasid commander Ziyad ibn Salih received reinforcements from Abu Muslim in May 751.

In July 751 the armies met on the Talas River, near the present border of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, though the exact site is unconfirmed. According to the Chinese account, the two sides fought to a stalemate for five days, with crossbowmen and archers behind a shield wall of infantry. On the fifth day the Karluk mercenaries, who made up two thirds of the Tang army, attacked it from the rear while the Abbasids attacked from the front.

Gao Xianzhi escaped with some of his regulars, helped by his officer Li Siye, but most of his troops were captured. Numbers are uncertain. Chinese sources put the Tang dead at 20,000 to 30,000, and Arabic sources at 45,000 to 50,000 with 20,000 to 25,000 captured. Sources also differ on whether the Karluks changed sides during the battle or were Abbasid allies from the start.

Historians judge the battle differently. One view holds that it ended Tang influence in Transoxiana and secured Abbasid control of the region and the spread of Islam among the Turkic peoples. Another holds that it was little more than a border clash: borders barely moved, Arab envoys visited the Tang court four times in 752 and 753, and the Tang kept considerable influence in eastern Central Asia until the An Lushan rebellion of 755 forced them to withdraw troops from the Protectorate General to Pacify the West.

Chinese prisoners taken at Talas are said to have introduced papermaking to West Asia, but several findings dispute this. The Arabic historian al-Maqdisi reports that Abu Muslim took 5,000 Chinese prisoners. The battle is recorded in both Chinese and Arabic sources, which differ in their accounts of it.
battle-of-tali-ihantala: After the Siege of Leningrad was lifted in January 1944, the Stavka planned an offensive to push Finland out of the war. It opened on the Karelian Isthmus on 9 June 1944, broke the Finnish front at Valkeasaari the next day and the VT-line on 14 June, and took Viipuri on 20 June. The Finnish army, though driven back, was not destroyed and gathered on the VKT-line. Marshal Mannerheim asked for German help on 12 June; the air unit Detachment Kuhlmey arrived on 16 June, followed by the 303 Assault Gun Brigade and Panzerfaust anti-tank weapons.

On 22 June the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop obtained from President Ryti a personal guarantee that Finland would fight on. The battle was fought over about 100 square kilometres between the northern tip of Vyborg Bay and the River Vuoksi, the only ground suited to armour leading out of the isthmus.

On 25 June, after an hour of bombardment, the Soviet 21st Army attacked from Tali village. Finnish reserves and the armoured division threw back the attack west of Lake Leitimojärvi, but an attempt to encircle four Soviet divisions at Talinmylly failed. 29 June was the hardest day for the Finns, and on 30 June they withdrew from Tali. At Ihantala, Finnish artillery, using the fire correction method of General Vilho Petter Nenonen, could bring as many as 21 batteries, some 250 guns, onto one target. From 9 July the Soviets no longer tried to break through, and troops began moving to the Narva front.

Finnish sources estimate Soviet losses at about 600 tanks. The Finnish army reported 8,561 men killed, wounded or missing; Soviet reports, according to the Finnish historian Ohto Manninen, give about 18,000 to 22,000 killed or wounded. Several historians hold that the battle, with other Finnish victories of that summer, convinced the Soviet leadership that conquering Finland was not worth the cost. Ryti resigned on 28 July, freeing Finland from his pledge to Germany, and the cease-fire began on 4 September 1944.
battle-of-talikota: For about twenty years Aliya Rama Raya profited from the wars among the successors of the Bahmani Sultanate, allying with one sultan or another as it suited him. His efforts to keep hold of Kalyan and diplomatic dealings with the sultans laden with insulting gestures eventually united four of them: Hussain Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar, Ali Adil Shah I of Bijapur, Ali Barid Shah I of Bidar and Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah Wali of Golkonda, drawn together by marriage alliances.

The battle is hard to reconstruct, since its chroniclers disagree. They include the Ahmadnagar court historian Tabataba, Ferishta and Rafi-ud-Din Shirazi at Bijapur, the Portuguese record-keeper Diogo do Couto and the Dakhni poet Hasan Shauqi. The site is given as Talikota, Rakkasagi-Tangadigi or Banahatti, all on the Krishna, and accounts of its length range from hours to days. Muslim troops of the Vijayanagara army under the Gilani brothers are said to have changed sides, and the sultanates' artillery proved superior.

Rama Raya was beheaded, either by Hussain Nizam Shah himself or on his orders, although Adil Shah, who had been on friendly terms with him, was against it. His brother Tirumala deserted with the army, and another brother, Venkatadri, was blinded and probably killed.

The sultanates' armies plundered Vijayanagara unopposed. Older scholarship describes the whole city burned and left in ruins, still called Halu Hampi, but present-day historians and archaeologists find little evidence of damage beyond the Royal Center and note that sites tied to royal power were singled out. Tirumala founded the Aravidu dynasty, which ruled fragments of the empire, from Vijayanagara for two years and then from Pengonda, until it broke up in the late 1640s.

Kulke and Rothermund wrote that Vijayanagara was winning until two generals defected, but many scholars treat the treachery story as speculation by the Venetian merchant Cesare de Federici and point instead to a gap in military skill, above all in gunpowder. Colonial and nationalist historians saw the battle as a clash between Hindus and Muslims; Richard M. Eaton, Romila Thapar and others reject this, citing Rama Raya's many Muslim allies and the Persian Islamate culture of his court.
battle-of-tampere: In the 1910s Tampere, with about 60,000 people, was the third largest and most industrialized town in Finland and was considered the capital of the Finnish labour movement. Its working-class population and railway links made it the main base of the Red Guards, who held it completely from 27 January 1918. The Whites opened their operation against it on 15 March, broke the Red front in battles at Länkipohja and Orivesi, and reached the town on 23 March with 17,000 men, the largest military operation of the war, against about 15,000 Red fighters. The siege was closed on 26 March when the Whites took the Siuro railway station.

On 28 March, later called Bloody Thursday, the Whites attacked around the Kalevankangas Cemetery and the Hippodrome and suffered their worst daily losses of the war so far. Their conscript battalions, led by Jäger officers, lacked experience, and the Swedish Brigade, dressed in white snow camouflage where there was hardly any snow, made an easy target. The Red leader Hugo Salmela was killed when a grenade exploded by accident in his headquarters, and Verner Lehtimäki took his place.

The decisive assault began at 2:30 am on 3 April and took the working-class districts of Tammela and Kyttälä, fighting block by block, while 1,700 people sheltered in Tampere Cathedral. A unit under Gunnar Melin took the Näsilinna Palace and shot 20 surrendered Reds there. On 4 April the Whites crossed the Tammerkoski rapids, and on 5 April the City Hall, the last Red stronghold in the centre, surrendered. A white flag rose on the Pyynikki Tower on the morning of 6 April.

The dead are usually estimated at 600 to 820 Whites and 600 to 1,000 Reds. The Whites began executions as soon as the Reds surrendered, shooting up to 1,000 of them and about 200 Russians. More than 10,000 prisoners stood for nearly 24 hours in the Central Square before going to a camp in the Kaleva district, where 1,228 died of execution, disease or hunger in the next five months.
battle-of-tannenberg-line: After defending the Narva bridgehead for six months, the German forces fell back on 26 July 1944 to the Tannenberg Line in the Blue Hills, three hills running east to west and rising 20–50 m above the land around them: Orphanage Hill, Grenadier Hill and Tower Hill. Felix Steiner's III SS Panzer Corps dug in there, with the Nederland brigade on the northern flank, units of the 20th Waffen Grenadier Division of the SS (1st Estonian) in the centre and the Nordland division in the south. The Soviet Estonian Operation aimed to reoccupy Estonia as a base for invading Finland and East Prussia.

The defenders were few and had no reserves. Anton Grasser, commander of Army Detachment Narwa, warned that the Soviets would break through without reinforcements, and Ferdinand Schörner told Adolf Hitler repeatedly that almost no German division was left on the line, but Hitler's answer remained to stand or die. The Soviets held massive superiority in the air.

On 26 July Soviet troops attacked before the Germans had dug in and seized the eastern side of Orphanage Hill. On 29 July a barrage of 25,000 shells destroyed the forest on the hills, and 6,000 Soviet infantry with nearly 100 tanks, most of them heavy IS-2s, reached the top of Grenadier Hill. German and Estonian counterattacks retook it, and eight Soviet attempts to win it back that afternoon failed, while the political commissar's report to the Soviet High Command falsely claimed the hill was still held.

Ordered by Stalin to break through to Tallinn at all costs, Marshal Leonid Govorov reinforced the front and massed 1,913 assault guns on a nine-kilometre stretch. Soviet intelligence greatly overestimated the defenders, who in fact had one tank and 70–80 guns left. Attacks on 2 and 3 August again reached Grenadier Hill, and each time Estonian battalions counterattacked and cleared it.

Soviet sources gave no losses in Soviet times. Of the 109th Rifle Corps, which carried the main weight of the attack of 29 July, 225 men survived, while the Germans lost 600 that day. On 14 September the Soviet Riga Offensive began, and Hitler finally agreed to the evacuation of Estonia; the exhausted III SS Panzer Corps fought its way back from the Tannenberg Line, and Tallinn was abandoned on 22 September. Some Estonian soldiers stayed behind and joined the Forest Brothers, guerrilla groups that fought the Soviet occupation.
battle-of-tarawa: Tarawa was part of the Gilbert Islands, then a Japanese-occupied British colony, and the battle was part of Operation Galvanic, the American invasion of the Gilberts. It was the first American offensive in the Central Pacific. American planners wanted forward air bases to reach the Marianas, for which the Marshall Islands were the nearest base. The Marshalls were cut off from direct communication with Hawaii by a Japanese garrison and air base on Betio, on the western side of Tarawa atoll, so that garrison had to be neutralised first. Betio is about 2 miles long and at most 800 yards wide, and a shallow reef 500 metres wide surrounds it.

The invasion force was the largest yet assembled for one Pacific operation, with 17 aircraft carriers, 12 battleships and 36 transports carrying about 35,000 troops of the 2nd Marine Division and the Army's 27th Infantry Division. On 20 November 1943 the island's four 8-inch guns opened fire before dawn, and the battleships Colorado and Maryland silenced three of them. The Japanese fought almost to the last man. Marine losses grew from a miscalculation of the tide and the height of the reef, shortcomings of the landing craft and a bombardment that failed to damage entrenched defences, since high-explosive shells often went off before penetrating them.

On 21 November the Marines took Green Beach at the western end, while fighting on Red Beaches 2 and 3 was harder. By 22 November they had formed a continuous line across the island, and artillery broke up an expected Japanese counterattack that night. At 03:00 on 23 November a large banzai charge killed 45 Americans and wounded 128, and the Marines killed 325 attackers with support from destroyers. Betio was declared secure at 13:30 on 23 November, about 76 hours after the landing.

The 2nd Marine Division lost 894 killed in action, with 84 more dying of wounds, and 2,188 wounded. Only one officer and sixteen enlisted men of the Japanese garrison and 129 of the 1,200 Korean labourers survived. The heavy losses on so small an island prompted public protest, and General Holland Smith likened them to Pickett's Charge. The lessons shaped the Marshalls campaign, where bombardments lasted a month, used armour-piercing shells, and landing craft were armoured. The remains of 36 Marines were recovered in 2015 from a cemetery whose location had been lost.
battle-of-tegyra: An insurrection in 379/8 BCE ended Spartan control over Thebes, and the city set about restoring its control over the Boeotian League. Over several years of campaigning the Thebans drove Spartan garrisons out of every city in Boeotia but Orchomenus. Learning that the garrison of Orchomenus had gone on an expedition to Locris, Pelopidas set out with the Sacred Band of Thebes and a small force of cavalry to seize the city while it was unguarded. On the way he learned that a sizable force from Sparta was coming to reinforce the garrison, and he turned back. Before reaching safety at Tegyra, the Thebans met the original garrison returning from Locris.

The Sacred Band numbered some 300 hoplites, while the Spartan garrison of two companies (mori) held between 1,000 and 1,800. Plutarch reports that one Theban, on seeing the enemy, said to Pelopidas that they had fallen into their enemies' hands, and that Pelopidas asked why the enemy had not fallen into theirs. Pelopidas sent the cavalry to charge while the infantry formed an unusually dense formation. When the phalanxes met, the compact Theban column broke through the Spartan line at the point of contact and turned on the exposed flanks to either side. The Spartans fled, though the nearness of Orchomenus limited the pursuit.

The victory had little immediate military effect beyond the survival of Pelopidas's force: once regrouped inside Orchomenus, the Spartans were too strong for him to press his advantage. Its weight was symbolic. Diodorus Siculus records that it was the first time the Thebans had set up a trophy of victory over a Spartan force, their earlier successes having come in much smaller skirmishes. Plutarch saw in it a prelude to the Battle of Leuctra four years later, when a similarly outnumbered Theban phalanx dealt Sparta a blow from which it never recovered.
battle-of-telamon: Rome had been at peace with the tribes of Cisalpine Gaul since skirmishing ended in 238 BCE, but its partition of the formerly Celtic territory of Picenum in 234 BCE, and a law of 232 BCE giving large areas of former Celtic land to poorer citizens, angered the Boii and the Insubres. In 225 BCE they paid large sums to the Gaesatae, mercenaries from beyond the Alps led by the kings Aneroëstes and Concolitanus. Rome made a treaty leaving Hispania to the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal the Fair and called on its allies in Italy for troops.

The consul Lucius Aemilius Papus stationed most of his army at Ariminum, while his colleague Gaius Atilius Regulus was in Sardinia. The Celts overran Etruria and marched on Rome. Near Clusium they feigned a retreat, drew the Roman force on the Etruscan border into an attack at Faesulae and killed six thousand men. When Papus arrived, Aneroëstes persuaded the Celts to withdraw along the coast with their booty.

Regulus, who had landed at Pisa, met the Celtic advance guard near Telamon in an area called Campo Regio, with Papus following behind them. The Celts formed their infantry facing both ways: the Gaesatae and Insubres against Papus, the Boii and Taurisci against Regulus, with wagons and chariots guarding their flanks. In a fierce cavalry fight for a hill above the road Regulus was killed and his head brought to the Celtic leaders, but the Roman horsemen took the hill.

Roman velites showered the Gaesatae, who fought naked with narrow shields, with javelins. The Insubres, Boii and Taurisci then held firm against the hastati and the principes until the Roman cavalry rode down from the hill into their flank. Around 40,000 Celts were killed and 10,000 captured, Concolitanus among them; Aneroëstes escaped with a few followers, who took their lives with him.

Papus led the combined armies on punitive raids into Liguria and the land of the Boii and was awarded a triumph. In 224 BCE two Roman armies forced the Boii to submit, and after further victories in 223 and 222 BCE the Celts surrendered large tracts of land, on which Roman citizens were settled. Their resentment helped bring them over to Hannibal when he crossed the Alps in 218 BCE.
battle-of-tenmokuzan: The war between the Takeda clan and Oda Nobunaga began in 1572 with the Battle of Mikatagahara, where Takeda Shingen, lord of Kai, Shinano and Suruga, defeated the combined forces of Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu. Shingen's heir Takeda Katsuyori was decisively defeated at the Battle of Nagashino in 1575, losing more than 10,000 men and most of his generals, but because Nobunaga was occupied on other fronts, chiefly against the Ikko-Ikki, Katsuyori kept his domain until 1582.

Early in 1582 some Takeda retainers in Shinano defected to Nobunaga, and his son Oda Nobutada invaded the province as Takeda garrisons surrendered or changed sides. The only real fighting was at Takato Castle, taken by storm in a single day. Ieyasu meanwhile took Suruga, and Hojo Ujimasa marched on Kai from the east.

The fall of Takato caused panic in Katsuyori's army of 10–15,000 at Shinpu Castle, the capital of Kai. With enemy armies of 40–50,000 closing in, the army dispersed, leaving no more than 500 to 600 samurai. At dawn Katsuyori set fire to Shinpu Castle and fled east with his family, leaving many hostages from noble families to die in the flames. Nobutada occupied Kōfu and had Katsuyori's family, relations and house elders hunted down and executed.

Katsuyori sought refuge with the old retainer Oyamada Nobushige, who turned him away although he had promised support a week before. His followers deserted until only 41 warriors and about 50 women were left, who fortified a manor house at the village of Tano. Search parties of the Oda general Takikawa Sakon found and attacked the camp. The last samurai killed their wives and children and came out fighting, causing many losses; the Shinchō Kōki praises Katsuyori's young lover Tsuchiya Uemon and his 16-year-old son Takeda Nobukatsu.

The Shinchō Kōki, written by Ota Guyuchi, an old retainer of Nobunaga, shows open admiration for the last Takeda samurai despite its sympathy for the Oda. Oyamada Nobushige went over to the Oda camp but was executed by Nobunaga's officer Horio Yoshiharu.
battle-of-tertry: Pepin of Herstal had made peace with his Neustrian counterpart, the mayor Waratton, in 680/681, with hostages exchanged to secure it. Waratton's successors renewed the conflict between Austrasia and Neustria. King Theuderic III, born and raised in Neustria, joined the nobles of Neustria and Burgundy under their mayor Berchar in invading Austrasian territory. The historian Michael Frassetto sees the war as the outcome of a long-standing feud between Austrasian and Neustrian leaders and of civil strife within Neustria itself.

Berchar and Theuderic were routed at Tertry, in the modern department of the Somme, and the Austrasians held the field. The battle is told as a heroic account in the Annales mettenses priores, probably written at the monastery of Chelles, which credits Pepin with leading the Austrasians to victory. Through it, in the annals' telling, he extended his family's control and influence over Neustria, and from then on the Austrasians dictated the political future of the Neustrians.

The victors forced Berchar out of office, and Pepin appointed Nordebert to act for him in Neustria. The king had to recognise Pepin as mayor over Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy. Rather than alienate the defeated, Pepin betrothed his son Drogo to Anstrudis, Berchar's widow and Waratton's daughter, drawing the Neustrian kin group into his own and into the foundation of Arnulfing power.

Royal authority in Neustria was reduced, and Austrasia gained supremacy over the rest of the realm. Pepin took the title dux et princeps Francorum and spent the following years forcing the Frisians, Saxons, Alemanni, Thuringians and Bavari to acknowledge Frankish overlordship. From Tertry onwards a mayor of his clan remained the senior figure in Francia, among them his son Charles Martel. The historian Rosamond McKitterick counts the battle among the decisive moments of the Carolingian house, though two generations passed before Pepin the Short claimed the Frankish kingship.
battle-of-thapsus: After Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus and his murder in Egypt, the remaining Optimates regrouped in Africa under Cato the Younger and Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio, with Titus Labienus, Lucius Afranius, Marcus Petreius, Publius Attius Varus and Pompey's sons among them. King Juba I of Numidia was a valuable local ally. Caesar sailed from Sicily and landed near Hadrumetum on 28 December, but a storm had scattered his transports and left him with only 3,000 infantry and 150 cavalry. Harassed by Numidian cavalry on the way to Ruspina, he made it his base, and as reinforcements arrived he went on the offensive. In early February he reached Thapsus and besieged it by land and sea.

Scipio marched round the Marsh of Moknine to the eastern approach and began building a camp opposite Caesar's, while his army stood in battle formation to cover the workers. Caesar, who had twelve legions and perhaps 60,000 to 70,000 men against an Optimate army of some 90,000 with 60 elephants, drew up his well-rested army in three lines against tired troops. A trumpeter of Legio VII sounded the attack and Caesar ordered a general advance.

His archers drove the elephants on one flank back into their own men. On the other, five cohorts of Legio V Alaudae held a charge, stabbing at the elephants' eyes and weak points, and the legion was afterwards awarded an elephant as its symbol. Scipio's left broke first and the rest followed. Juba's troops abandoned their position. Caesar's soldiers, once the Optimate camp was stormed, ignored his orders to spare the beaten, and around ten thousand of the enemy were killed. Plutarch reports, according to some sources, that Caesar had an epileptic seizure just before the advance.

Afranius and Faustus Cornelius Sulla were caught by Publius Sittius, an ally of Caesar, and executed. Juba and Petreius, according to the account known as the African War, fought each other in a duel and Juba had a slave kill him.

Cato killed himself at Utica when he heard the news, and Caesar is reported by Plutarch to have said that he grudged Cato his death. Scipio took ship for the Iberian Peninsula but was driven back, was caught off Hippo Regius by Sittius, and killed himself after losing the naval engagement. Labienus, Sextus Pompeius and Varus escaped to Gnaeus Pompeius on the Iberian Peninsula. Caesar returned to Rome on 25 July, but the civil war was not over and the Battle of Munda followed. Thapsus is generally regarded as the last large-scale use of war elephants in the West.
battle-of-the-aegates: The First Punic War began in 264 BCE and by 248 BCE the Carthaginians held only Lilybaeum and Drepana in Sicily, both on the west coast. The Romans had won the earlier large naval battles with the help of the corvus, a boarding device, but lost fleets to storms. Carthage then let its navy run down. By 243 BCE both states were exhausted, and Rome was almost bankrupt. The Senate asked its wealthiest citizens for loans to build one ship each, repayable from reparations, and a fleet of about 200 quinqueremes was built, modelled on a captured Carthaginian vessel. The corvus was abandoned, so that the Romans would have to be better sailors rather than better soldiers.

Gaius Lutatius Catulus and Quintus Valerius Falto led it to Sicily in 242 BCE and blockaded both cities, drilling their crews. Carthage took nine months to ready 250 warships and many transports, but could not train the crews properly.

The Carthaginian fleet, under a commander named Hanno, gathered off Hiera in early March 241 BCE, planning to reach Lilybaeum on a following wind, unload grain and embark soldiers as marines. Roman scouts saw it. Catulus took soldiers from the besieging army as marines and anchored off Aegusa. On 10 March a strong west wind blew, and Hanno set sail. Catulus decided to attack against the wind and had his ships stripped of masts and sails. Injured, he left command to Falto.

The fleets met west of Phorbantia. The Carthaginian ships were laden with supplies, short of marines and crewed by hurriedly levied men, while the Roman ships were light and better handled. The Romans sank 50 Carthaginian ships and captured 70 with 10,000 men, losing 30 ships sunk and 50 damaged. A change of wind let the rest flee, as the Romans had no sails to pursue.

Hanno was crucified at Carthage. Catulus and Falto each received a triumph, and Catulus built a temple to Juturna in the Campus Martius. The Carthaginian Senate was reluctant to build another fleet, and Carthage sued for peace. By the Treaty of Lutatius it surrendered Sicily to Rome and paid substantial reparations, and Rome became the leading military power of the western Mediterranean.
battle-of-the-allia: The Senones were one of the Gallic tribes that had invaded northern Italy, settling on the Adriatic coast around what is now Rimini. According to Livy, they were called to the Etruscan town of Clusium by Aruns, a young man seeking revenge on Lucumo. The Clusians asked Rome for help, and the Romans sent the three sons of Marcus Fabius Ambustus as ambassadors. A quarrel broke out; the ambassadors joined the fighting, and one killed a Senone chieftain, breaking the rule that ambassadors stay neutral.

Ancient sources give forces of 24,000 to 40,000 for each side, none of them reliable. Jeremy Armstrong suggests about 5,000 men on each side, while Max Cary and H. H. Scullard placed some 15,000 Romans against a Gallic army of thirty to seventy thousand.

Only Livy and Diodorus Siculus describe the battle in detail. The armies met where the Allia brook joins the Tiber, 11 Roman miles north of Rome. According to Livy, the Romans did not set up camp, build a rampart or take the auspices. They stretched their wings to avoid being outflanked, which thinned the line, and placed reserves on a hill on the right. Brennus, the Senone leader, suspected a ruse and attacked the hill.

The Romans panicked. The left wing threw down its arms and fled to the Tiber, where many drowned in their armour, though most reached Veii. The right wing fled to Rome. The Gauls, surprised by the ease of the victory, reached Rome before sunset to find the gates open and the walls unmanned. The Romans withdrew to the Capitoline Hill, and Plutarch says the siege lasted seven months.

The accounts were written centuries after the events. Many modern historians see the rescue of Rome by Camillus as an addition, since Diodorus Siculus and Polybius do not mention him. Peter Cornell notes that no archaeological trace of the sack has been found, and suggests the Senones ransacked the city for booty and left after being bought off. A few years later Rome began building new walls 11 km long in yellow Grotta Oscura tuff from a quarry in the territory of Veii.

The Day of the Allia, 18 July according to Tacitus, was regarded as ill-omened and treated as a day on which public and ritual activity was avoided. Livy presents this as a lasting civic taboo, but the tradition is attested only from the 1st century BCE and may be a later reconstruction. Modern dates for the battle vary, with c. 387 BCE considered most probable by modern historians.
battle-of-the-atlantic: At its core was the Allied naval blockade of Germany, announced the day after the declaration of war, and Germany's counterblockade. The United Kingdom was an island highly dependent on imports and needed more than a million tons of imported material a week to survive and fight, so the battle became a tonnage war. The Germans targeted merchant shipping, and from 1942 the Axis also sought to stop the build-up of Allied supplies in Britain for an invasion of occupied Europe. The name came into use in 1941, when the First Lord of the Admiralty, A. V. Alexander, asked Parliament on 5 March for more ships and men to fight the Battle of the Atlantic.

The Kriegsmarine lacked the strength in 1939 to challenge the British and French navies directly, and relied on commerce raiding. The German occupation of Norway and France in 1940 gave U-boats bases on the Atlantic coast, and from June to October 1940 over 270 Allied ships were sunk, a period U-boat crews called the Happy Time. The British answered with permanent escort groups, and the Royal Canadian Navy grew from a handful of destroyers into a large escort force. United States ships and aircraft began to aid convoys on 13 September 1941.

In February 1942 the U-boats changed to a new four-rotor Enigma key that the Allied codebreakers could not read for ten months, and the Germans read about 80 per cent of the Admiralty messages sent in Naval Cipher 3 from March 1942 to June 1943. Against this the Allies developed shipborne direction-finding radio, the Leigh Light for night attacks by aircraft and long-range B-24 Liberator aircraft that closed the mid-Atlantic gap. In March 1943, 120 ships were sunk and 12 U-boats destroyed; by mid-1943 the U-boats had been defeated, although losses continued until the end of the war.

The German tonnage war failed, and the supplies and troops needed for the D-Day landings were built up in Britain. Between 1939 and 1945, 72,200 Allied naval and merchant seamen died. The Germans lost about 30,000 U-boat sailors, three quarters of a force of 40,000. United States yards built 2,710 Liberty ships of 38.5 million tons, far more than the 14 million tons the U-boats sank in the whole war.

Historians disagree about which measures mattered most. Max Hastings holds that in 1941 alone Ultra saved between 1.5 and two million tons of shipping, while a former U-boat commander writing for the Admiralty after the war attributed the defeat first to Allied radar developments.
battle-of-the-berezina: Napoleon had fought his way out of Russia in the battles of Maloyaroslavets, Vyazma and Krasnoi. He planned to cross the Berezina River at Borisov to join his Austrian ally, Field Marshal Schwarzenberg, at Minsk. His battered force was reduced to 49,000 men under arms and 40,000 stragglers, and Russian troops supported by Cossacks moved to block it.

On 21 November the Russians captured the French garrison at Borisov with its bridge, and they destroyed the bridge when a French force tried to retake it on 23 November. Field Marshal Wittgenstein with 30,000 men tracked Napoleon from the north, Admiral Chichagov with 35,000 advanced from Minsk, and General Miloradovich with 32,000 pursued from the east.

A French cavalry brigade found a crossing at the hamlet of Studienka, eight miles north of Borisov. A temporary thaw and muddy banks meant bridges had to be built. General Jean Baptiste Eblé, commander of the pontoon builders, had disobeyed an earlier order to destroy the bridge-building equipment. Diversions and the movements of General Nicolas Oudinot's corps led Chichagov to move his main body south, and on the morning of 26 November the French found the Russian camp on the west bank abandoned.

By 1 p.m. the smaller bridge was complete, and Oudinot led 7,000 infantry across; the larger bridge for the artillery was finished later but collapsed twice. By midday on 27 November Napoleon and the Imperial Guard were across, followed by the corps of Marshal Davout and Prince Eugene. Marshal Victor's IX Corps stayed on the east bank to hold off Wittgenstein, and one of its divisions surrendered over 8,000 men.

On 28 November the Russians attacked on both banks. Marshal Ney took command on the west bank when Oudinot was wounded, and a cavalry charge ended the fighting there. On the east bank, Russian artillery fired on the bridges and the stragglers crowding them. Victor's corps crossed at about 10 p.m.

On the morning of 29 November General Eblé burned the bridges at 8:30 a.m., an hour and a half after Napoleon's ordered time, and tens of thousands of stragglers and civilians were left behind. David G. Chandler wrote that the cost in lives would never be known accurately, but probably 20-30,000 French combatants became casualties, besides perhaps as many as 30,000 non-combatants. The Russians lost at least 10,000 killed.

Napoleon could claim a strategic success, having saved about 40,000 of his army, with his generals, 200 guns and the war chest; without this core of experienced men he could not have rebuilt his army for the War of the Sixth Coalition. The battle also showed that Europe could be rallied against him. In French historiography the Berezina is associated with disaster.
battle-of-the-boyne: The battle was part of James II's attempt to regain the thrones of England and Scotland after the Glorious Revolution, and it had wider European roots in the League of Augsburg and the Grand Alliance against the ambitions of Louis XIV of France. In Ireland the war was also a sectarian and ethnic conflict. Catholic landowners had lost almost all their lands after Cromwell's conquest, and under Richard Talbot, Earl of Tyrconnel, they raised an army for James and by 1690 controlled all of Ireland except Derry and Enniskillen. Protestants feared for their lives and property under a Catholic king.

William, a seasoned commander who had yet to win a major battle, saw Ireland as one front in the war against France, while James could count on Louis XIV, who sent 6,000 French troops. The Duke of Schomberg, aged 74, had been sent to Ireland in 1689 with 20,000 men, but fever and Jacobite blocking forces left the campaign static. William landed at Carrickfergus on 14 June 1690 and marched south.

The Williamite army numbered about 36,000, of whom only about half were British; its best infantry were 7,000 Danish infantry and 6,000 Dutch with flintlock muskets, plus 3,000 French Huguenots. James had 23,500 men, mostly Irish Catholics with some French regiments. His Irish cavalry were good troops, but many of the infantry were pressed peasants, some armed only with scythes, and those with firearms had obsolete matchlocks.

On 1 July 1690 William sent about a quarter of his men west to cross at Roughgrange as a diversion, led by Schomberg's son Meinhardt. James sent much of his army, including his best French troops, to meet it, but a swampy ravine kept the two forces apart. At the main ford near Oldbridge the Dutch Blue Guards crossed and held off Jacobite cavalry under the Duke of Berwick with platoon fire. The Jacobites retired in good order, and about 2,000 of some 50,000 participants died, three quarters of them Jacobites.

William's forces entered Dublin two days later. James fled to France and never returned, and his Irish supporters nicknamed him Séamus a' chaca. The war ended only after Aughrim in 1691 and the Treaty of Limerick. On the continent the battle was treated as the first real victory of the League of Augsburg. The Twelfth of July was first a commemoration of Aughrim, and the two battles were combined in the late eighteenth century after the founding of the Orange Order in 1795.
battle-of-the-bulge: After the breakout from Normandy at the end of July 1944, the Allies advanced toward Germany faster than expected, leaving troops tired and supply lines stretched thin. They captured Antwerp intact in September, but it was not operational until 28 November. Adolf Hitler believed that a blow in the west could split the Allies and force the Americans and British to a separate peace, giving Germany time to produce new weapons and concentrate in the east. After the war this was generally judged unrealistic given Allied air superiority.

The offensive aimed to stop Allied use of Antwerp and to split their lines. The Germans called it Unternehmen Wacht am Rhein, a name implying a defensive posture. The name Battle of the Bulge came from the press, from the way the Allied line bulged inward on wartime news maps.

At 5:30 on 16 December 1944 the Germans opened with a 90-minute barrage along a front of 130 kilometres. They achieved total surprise, through Allied overconfidence, poor air reconnaissance in bad weather and faulty intelligence. The region was a rest area held thinly by tired troops and inexperienced replacements. In the north the 2nd and 99th Infantry Divisions held Elsenborn Ridge and forced the German spearhead onto less favourable routes. Waffen-SS troops under Joachim Peiper shot American prisoners near Malmedy.

In the centre the Germans encircled two regiments of the 106th Division at the Schnee Eifel, the most serious American reverse of the campaign. Bastogne was surrounded, and the farthest German advance, to Foy-Notre-Dame, was stopped by the 2nd Armored Division on 24 December. The weather improved from 23 December, letting Allied aircraft strike, and on 26 December the lead element of George S. Patton's Third Army reached Bastogne from the south.

The offensive was effectively broken by 27 December, but fighting went on for another month as Patton attacked north and Bernard Montgomery south to reduce the bulge. On 1 January 1945 the Luftwaffe attacked Allied airfields in Operation Bodenplatte, destroying about 465 aircraft but losing 277, and was left ineffective for the rest of the war. It was the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in the war. German casualties are put at 81,000 to 103,900 by Allied estimates. The battle destroyed much of Germany's armoured strength and set back the Allied advance into Germany by several weeks.
battle-of-the-camel: Many senior companions of Muhammad, Ali among them, criticised the third caliph Uthman for nepotism and for deviating from the Quran and the Sunna. Discontented groups from the provinces came to Medina, and Ali mediated between them and Uthman. Uthman was assassinated by Egyptian rebels in June 656, and Ali had played no part in the attack. The Ansar and the Basrans and Kufans favoured Ali as the next caliph, and he accepted at last, though he preferred to be a minister. Talha and Zubayr pledged to him but then left for Mecca on the pretext of performing the lesser pilgrimage. Aisha, who had opposed Uthman, also blamed Ali for the assassination.

The opposition demanded that Ali punish Uthman's killers, and also called for his removal and a Qurayshite council to choose a successor. In October 656 some six to nine hundred rebels led by Aisha, Talha and Zubayr marched on Basra, where they killed many people and took control of the city and its treasury. Ali gathered an army at Kufa and marched to Basra, and negotiations in a tent between the armies failed after three days. Ali ordered that the wounded and captives were not to be killed and that fugitives were not to be pursued.

The fighting took place on a December day in 656, from noon to sunset, and was mostly hand-to-hand combat. Aisha rode a red camel in an armoured palanquin, and the fiercest fighting was around it. Talha was killed, reportedly by Marwan ibn al-Hakam. Zubayr left the field and was later killed near Basra. Ali's troops killed Aisha's camel and captured her. The lowest estimate of the dead is 2,500 on Aisha's side and 400 to 500 on Ali's.

Aisha was treated with respect, reprimanded for causing loss of life, and sent back to Mecca or Medina with her half-brother Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. Her defeat ended her political ambitions. Ali announced a general pardon, freed prisoners, forbade the enslavement of women and children, and returned seized property. Some of his soldiers objected, and the orders later became a rallying cry for the Kharijites. He then moved to Kufa, which became his main base, and the Medinan elite permanently lost authority over the community. Kufa remained the main centre of Shia Islam until Baghdad was founded in the mid-eighth century.
battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains: By 450 the Romans had restored their authority in much of Gaul, though control of the provinces beyond Italy was diminishing. Germanic peoples occupying Roman territory were bound by treaty as foederati under their own leaders: the Visigoths on the Garonne were restive, the Burgundians awaited an opening for revolt, and the Alans on the Loire were more loyal. When Attila invaded, the general Flavius Aetius moved his army rapidly from Italy to Gaul and tried to persuade the Visigothic king Theodoric I to join him. Theodoric hesitated, and Aetius turned to the former Praetorian Prefect of Gaul, Avitus, who according to tradition persuaded the Visigoths and other wavering peoples.
