The coalition assembled at Arles and Toulouse and marched to Orléans, reaching it on 14 June. Jordanes lists among Aetius's allies Franks, Burgundians, Alans and other Celtic or German tribes; Peter Heather suggests the Visigoths may have fielded about 25,000 men.

Attila was leaving Gaul with most of his objectives achieved when Aetius and his allies pursued him from Orléans. The armies met on the Catalaunian Plains on or about 20 June. The exact site is uncertain; scholars place it near Châlons-en-Champagne or Troyes, and the ridge at Montgueux, west of Troyes, is the most thoroughly researched proposal.

The account of Jordanes, who wrote long afterwards and is described as notoriously unreliable on Gothic history, tells of a struggle for the ridge, with the Alans in the centre. Theodoric was killed on the right, and his son Thorismund attacked the Hunnic centre and nearly killed Attila. Darkness fell in confusion, and neither side knew the outcome until morning. Hydatius says almost 300,000 men are said to have fallen. Attila withdrew.

From Cassiodorus in the early sixth century the battle was increasingly seen as a Roman allied victory. Edward Gibbon called it the last victory achieved in the name of the Western Roman Empire, and Edward Shepherd Creasy called it a triumph of Christian Europe. Most modern authors have moved away from this view. J. B. Bury held that its significance had been enormously exaggerated, since the decisive moment was the defence of Orléans and the battle was fought as Attila retreated, though it damaged his prestige and weakened his forces.

In 452 Attila invaded Italy and razed Aquileia after a three-month siege; Pope Leo I took part in an embassy that brought a treaty, and Attila retreated, most likely because of famine and disease in his army. Attila died in 453, and after the Battle of Nedao in 454 the coalition of the Huns and their Germanic vassals gradually disintegrated.
battle-of-the-caudine-forks: In Livy's account, Gaius Pontius learned that the Roman army was near Calatia and sent ten soldiers disguised as herdsmen to tell the same story, that the Samnites were besieging Lucera in Apulia. The Roman commanders believed it and took the quicker road to Lucera, along the line of the later Appian Way, through the Caudine Forks (Furculae Caudinae), a mountain pass near Benevento in Campania. The valley could be entered only by two defiles. The Romans found the far one barricaded and, turning back, found the first held by the Samnites.

Modern historians doubt Livy's geography. Neither defile is as narrow and steep as he suggests: the western one, near Arienzo, is over a kilometre wide, and the Samnites would hardly have had time to block it while the Romans crossed the 4.5 km of plain to the eastern defile near Arpaia and back. Horsfall suggests that Livy's picture may owe something to accounts of the campaigns of Alexander the Great.

Unsure how to use their success, the Samnites consulted Pontius's father, Herennius. His first letter advised letting the Romans go unharmed, his second killing them to the last man. Summoned in person, he explained that freeing them would win Rome's friendship and killing them would cripple Rome for generations, and that any middle way would leave the Romans eager for revenge without weakening them. Pontius rejected his advice and demanded that the Romans surrender and pass under the yoke, which the two consuls accepted as their army faced starvation.

Livy describes at length the Romans' humiliation and their wish to avenge it, which underlines the wisdom of Herennius's counsel. He contradicts himself on the peace that followed: in one place the Senate rejected its terms, in another Rome honoured the Caudine Peace until fighting broke out again in 316 BCE. The episode was political rather than military, with magistrates on both sides seeking the best terms within the accepted rules of war and peace, and the Romans were held back in their later campaign by considerations of religion and honour.
battle-of-the-chernaya: Tsar Alexander II ordered his commander-in-chief in the Crimea, Prince Michael Gorchakov, to attack the allies besieging Sevastopol before they were reinforced further, hoping that a victory would win Russia better terms. Gorchakov doubted an attack could succeed but judged the best chance to lie against the French and Piedmontese positions on the Chernaya. At the war council many senior commanders opposed the offensive: Dmitri Osten-Sacken proposed leaving Sevastopol altogether, while Stepan Khrulev urged a mass storming of the allied lines by every man available. The attack was set for the morning of 16 August, in the hope that the French and Piedmontese would be tired after celebrating their feast days.

Some 58,000 Russians faced about 36,000 French and Sardinian troops under General Aimable Pélissier and General Alfonso Ferrero La Marmora, with six Ottoman battalions under Władysław Kościelski. Under cover of fog the Russians advanced on the Traktir Bridge, with General Pavel Liprandi on the left and General Nikolay Read on the right. A note from Gorchakov reading Let's start it was taken as an order to attack, although reserves were still on the way.

Liprandi pushed the Sardinian posts off Telegraph Hill but got no further. Read crossed near the bridge without cavalry or artillery and was stopped on the Fedyukhin Heights, where 2,000 Russians died in 20 minutes; he then fed his reserve division in piecemeal and was killed in the retreat. Battalions sent from the left were driven back by the Sardinians, and at 10 in the morning Gorchakov ordered a general retreat.

The Russians suffered almost five times the allies' casualties, and their soldiers lost trust in their commanders. Leo Tolstoy, who took part, blamed the slaughter on incompetent generals and wrote a satirical song about staff officers who forgot the ravine they had to cross; one of its lines became a Russian catch phrase. The Sardinian general Rodolfo Gabrielli di Montevecchio died of his wounds.
battle-of-the-colline-gate: In the spring of 83 BCE Lucius Cornelius Sulla returned to Italy with a veteran army fresh from his victory over King Mithridates of Pontus in the First Mithridatic War, and in 83 and 82 BCE he and his allies beat the government's forces in several major battles. Fearing they would be next, the Samnites and Lucanians joined the war. The Samnite leader Pontius Telesinus raised an army of 70,000 men and marched to break the siege of Praeneste, where the consul Gaius Marius the Younger was shut in.

Sulla's earthworks around Praeneste proved too strong, so Telesinus made a night march on Rome. Sulla sent his cavalry ahead to harass him and force-marched his army after it. The Samnites arrived first, at daybreak, and drove off a cavalry force sent out from the city, but Sulla's main army came up at noon and camped near the temple of Venus Erucina.

Appian is the only source who gives details of the fighting. Against the advice of his commanders, who wanted the tired troops to rest overnight, Sulla allowed only a meal and a few hours' rest, and the battle began at four in the afternoon. His left wing was driven back against the city wall, where the defenders dropped the portcullis on men seeking shelter; Sulla's own efforts to rally it failed, and he and most of the left ended up in their camp.

Then messengers came from Marcus Licinius Crassus, commanding the right, to report that he had routed the enemy facing him. Sulla used the news to restore his men's spirits and counter-attacked. The fighting went on through the night. Telesinus was killed and his camp taken, and the Lucanian commander Marcus Lamponius fled. The dead were estimated at 50,000, with 6,000 to 8,000 prisoners.

Sulla had the Marian leaders Marcius and Carrinas killed and their heads shown before Praeneste, which surrendered; Marius the Younger hid in a tunnel and killed himself, and his head was displayed in Rome. At Praeneste the inhabitants were divided into Romans, Samnites and Praenestians: the Romans were pardoned and the men of the other two groups killed. The town of Norba, which still held out, was taken by treachery. On 3 November Sulla began the proscription of his enemies.
battle-of-the-cosmin-forest: In 1484 the Ottomans conquered Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi and Kiliia, the last Moldavian ports on the Black Sea. Stephen the Great turned to the Kingdom of Poland, which sent 3,000 cavalry, and the joint army defeated the Ottomans at the Battle of Cătlăbuga. King Casimir IV Jagiellon won papal approval for a crusade against the Ottomans, and after his death his successor John I Albert took up the plan. He entered Moldavia claiming to help Stephen recover the lost forts, but his main aim was to put his brother Sigismund on the Moldavian throne.

Stephen asked his neighbours for help, the Ottomans, Crimeans and Wallachians among them. John besieged Suceava from 24 September to 19 October 1497 while the Moldavians and their allies waged a guerrilla war on the Polish camps and supply lines, impaling Polish captives. Stephen gathered 18,000 Moldavians, 12,000 Transylvanians, 8,000 Wallachians, 5,000 Ottoman Akinji and some thousands of Crimean Tatars. After negotiations the Poles left Suceava, apparently promised safe passage if they went home by the road they had come, but John chose another route through Bukovina towards Sniatyn.

The allies let the orderly Greater Poland column pass and struck the rest. The rear under Stanisław Chodecki held out, but as the baggage train entered the forest the Moldavians felled large trees onto it, and about half its guards were killed or taken. The unarmoured Lesser Poland column, attacked from the left and pressed against rocky slopes, collapsed and lost about 7,500 men. A countercharge by the court companies under Jan Teczynski drove the allies back, but the pursuit failed and Teczynski was captured by the Ottomans.

The Polish army lost 11,000 men, a fifth of its strength, and the Teutonic Knights with it lost all their cannon. The defeat dissuaded the king from challenging Ottoman supremacy on the Black Sea. In 1498 the Ottomans and Crimeans began raiding Poland and sacking its cities, and in 1499 Poland sued for peace.
battle-of-the-crocus-field: The Third Sacred War broke out after the Phocian Confederation refused to pay a fine imposed in 357 BCE by the Amphictyonic League, the religious body that governed the Temple of Apollo at Delphi; the Thebans, who controlled the council, probably expected it to go unpaid. The Phocians under Philomelos seized Delphi and used the temple treasury to hire mercenaries. After Philomelos fell at Neon, Onomarchos carried on the fight.

The war spread into Thessaly, where the Thessalian Confederation supported the League and the city of Pherae sided with Phocis. Called in by the nobles of Larissa, Philip II repulsed a Phocian force under Phayllos, but Onomarchos then defeated him twice and Philip withdrew to Macedon for the winter. He is said to have remarked that, like a ram, he had pulled back to butt again harder. He returned the next summer with, according to Diodorus Siculus, 20,000 infantry and 3,000 cavalry.

Philip seems to have been besieging Pagasae, the harbour of Pherae, when Onomarchos came north again, while Athens sent Chares with a fleet to support its Phocian allies. The armies met near the sea before the Athenians arrived; the Crocus Plain near modern Almyros is the most likely site, though it has never been firmly identified. Philip's men wore laurel crowns, the sign of Apollo, as avengers of sacrilege. Superior numbers and the valour of Philip's cavalry won what is called the bloodiest recorded battle in ancient Greek history. The fleeing Phocians ran for Chares' ships, and many were cut down or drowned. Some 6,000 died.

Onomarchos was hanged or crucified, punishments meant to deny an honourable burial. Philip, now leader of the united Thessalian army and master of its revenues, marched to Thermopylae, but an Athenian force held the pass and he did not risk forcing it. Under Phayllos the Phocians paid doubled wages from the temple treasure to rebuild their army, and the war dragged on until 346 BCE. The sources for it are scant: the main account is that of Diodorus Siculus, written in the 1st century BCE, supplemented by the speeches of Demosthenes and Aeschines.
battle-of-the-defile: Transoxiana had been conquered by Qutayba ibn Muslim under Caliph al-Walid I, but its Iranian and Turkic inhabitants remained restless, and from 720 the Türgesh attacked while the Sogdians rose in revolt. By 728 the Caliphate had lost most of the region except the area around Samarkand. Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik appointed Junayd governor of Khurasan in early 730. Junayd recovered Bukhara, but rebellions in Tokharistan drew 28,000 of his men south. When the Türgesh besieged Samarkand in early 731 and its governor, Sawra ibn al-Hurr al-Abani, appealed for help, Junayd marched at once, against the advice of Khurasani leaders to wait for 50,000 men.

Unable to use the Royal Road, Junayd went to Kish and took the short, steep Takhtakaracha Pass with 28,000 men. The Türgesh, a wholly mounted army of horse archers, attacked while the Arabs stopped to eat, supported by troops from Sogdia, Shash and Ferghana. Junayd deployed his men by tribe behind hurried earthworks, and as losses mounted they dismounted to form a spear wall. The stragglers and baggage train near Kish were almost wiped out.

Besieged in camp, Junayd ordered Sawra to make a diversionary attack. Sawra led 12,000 men over the mountains, but the Türgesh set fire to the dry grass, and all but a thousand died, Sawra with them. Junayd broke through, and after almost three days of fighting, in which he promised slaves their freedom if they fought, reached Samarkand. The fullest account is in al-Tabari's History of the Prophets and Kings, drawing on al-Mada'ini.

Khalid Yahya Blankinship calls it a Pyrrhic victory at best, estimating Arab losses at 25,000 to 30,000. Junayd later raised a Türgesh siege of Bukhara, but by his death in early 734 the Muslims held little north of the Oxus beyond Bukhara, Kish and al-Saghaniyan. Some 20,000 Iraqis were sent to Khurasan, followed by Syrian troops. Only after Suluk's murder and the Türgesh collapse did Nasr ibn Sayyar restore the Caliphate's position in 739 to 741. The strain on the Syrian army helped bring down the Umayyads in the Abbasid Revolution, which began in Khurasan.
battle-of-the-downs: Spain's main route for troops to the Army of Flanders was the Spanish Road overland from Italy, since Dutch naval superiority made the sea dangerous. In December 1638 a French-backed army under Bernard of Saxe-Weimar captured Breisach in Alsace and cut the road. Encouraged by successes elsewhere, the chief minister Olivares assembled by August 1639 a fleet of about 50 warships manned by 6,500 sailors and 8,000 marines, with 30 transports carrying 9,000 reinforcements and three million escudos. Breaking with the Spanish policy since 1621 of avoiding the Dutch fleet, its commander Antonio de Oquendo was ordered both to deliver the reinforcements and to bring the Dutch to battle.

The fleet entered the Channel on 11 September and met Maarten Tromp's squadron near Calais. In the Fight in the Channel Oquendo gave his captains no adequate instructions and sought only to board Tromp's flagship; his half-moon formation broke up, and the outnumbered Dutch escaped. Oquendo then took refuge in The Downs, an anchorage between Dover and Deal, near an English squadron under Vice-Admiral John Pennington. Thirteen fast Dunkirk frigates slipped north round the Goodwin Sands with 3,000 troops and all the bullion, and the Spanish later reckoned that 6,000 troops had been landed.

Tromp blockaded the anchorage while the Dutch admiralties hired every large armed merchant ship they could find, and by the end of October he had 95 ships and 12 fireships. On 21 October, with an easterly wind giving him the weather gage, he sent 30 ships under Witte de With to keep Pennington out, blocked the northern and southern exits and attacked with fireships. Some large Spanish ships ran themselves aground and were plundered by English onlookers. The Portuguese flagship Santa Teresa was set on fire and burned with great loss of life, while Oquendo escaped in fog with about ten ships to Dunkirk.

Estimates of the losses differ widely: the historian de Boer puts the Spanish losses at about 40 ships and 7,000 men, while Dutch sources mention the loss of one Dutch ship and about a hundred dead. With the defeat of another Spanish expedition against Dutch Brazil a few months later, the battle contributed to the climate in which the Portuguese revolted against the Spanish king. Tromp was rewarded with 10,000 guldens and De With with 1,000, and De With answered with anonymous pamphlets presenting himself as the real hero of the battle.
battle-of-the-eurymedon: The Delian League was formed under Athenian leadership after Sparta withdrew from the war with Persia that followed the invasions of Greece in 492–490 and 480–479 BCE. According to Thucydides its aim was to avenge the wrongs the Greeks had suffered by ravaging the territory of the king. Through the next decade its forces expelled the remaining Persian garrisons from Thrace and extended the League's control in the Aegean.

The date of the battle is disputed, most authorities placing it in 469 or 466 BCE. The surest fact is that it came before the revolt of Thasos in or just before 465/4. The sources are thin: Thucydides gives only a brief, undated digression, Plutarch wrote six centuries later, and Diodorus Siculus is regarded as a poor guide for this period.

The Persians gathered a large army and fleet at Aspendos near the mouth of the Eurymedon River. One suggestion, from the historian Cawkwell, is that they meant to move along the southern coast of Asia Minor, taking each city in turn, to regain naval bases from which to operate in the Aegean again. Plutarch says the Athenian general Cimon sailed from Cnidus with 200 triremes to Phaselis, which refused him admittance. He ravaged its land, and with Chian mediation Phaselis agreed to join the League, to send troops and to pay ten talents.

On Plutarch's account the Persian fleet lay off the river mouth awaiting 80 Phoenician ships from Cyprus. It withdrew into the river, then accepted battle when Cimon pressed on. Its line was quickly breached, and the crews grounded the ships and fled to the army nearby. Cimon landed his marines and attacked the Persian army, which held at first but was routed by the heavily armoured hoplites. The Greeks took the Persian camp. Thucydides says 200 Phoenician ships were captured and destroyed. Plutarch adds that Cimon then took the 80 ships from Cyprus, a claim Thucydides does not mention and some doubt.

One tradition recorded by Plutarch held that the Persian king agreed a humiliating peace after the battle, but other authors denied it, and modern historians generally think no treaty was made. The victory probably ended the threat of another Persian invasion of Greece and prevented any Persian attempt to reconquer the Asian Greeks until at least 451 BCE. More cities, particularly from Caria, probably joined the League afterwards. The Greeks did not press their advantage, perhaps because of the revolt of Thasos if the later date is right, and the next major League campaign against Persia came in 460 BCE in support of a revolt in Egypt.
battle-of-the-frigidus: On 15 May 392 the western emperor Valentinian II was found dead at Vienne in Gaul. His magister militum, Arbogast, told Theodosius, the eastern emperor and Valentinian's brother-in-law, that the young emperor had killed himself, but Theodosius came to believe he had been murdered, partly because his wife Galla was convinced that her brother had died by treachery. On 22 August Arbogast raised Eugenius, a respected scholar of rhetoric and the western court's magister scrinii, to the western throne. Eugenius removed most of the high officers Theodosius had left in the West, and when western ambassadors came to Constantinople Theodosius gave them presents and vague promises. In January 393 he declared his eight-year-old son Honorius western augustus and resolved to invade.

Over the next year and a half Stilicho and Timasius restored discipline and numbers to the eastern army, which had declined after the Battle of Adrianople. The army left Constantinople in May 394 with over 20,000 Visigoth federates and forces from Syria, and its commanders included Alaric and Bacurius the Iberian. Arbogast, hoping to keep his Franks, Alemanni, Gallo-Romans and Gothic auxiliaries united to defend Italy, left the Alpine passes unguarded. The eastern army descended towards the Frigidus, east of Aquileia, and found the western camp in the first days of September.

On 5 September Theodosius attacked at once with little reconnaissance, sending his Gothic allies in first, perhaps to thin their ranks. Some 10,000 Goths are reported to have died, and Bacurius was killed. Arbogast sent men to close the passes behind Theodosius, but they proved ready to desert to him. On 6 September a fierce wind, apparently the bora, blew down the valley, and Arbogast's lines broke. Eugenius was captured and beheaded. Arbogast fled into the mountains and killed himself after a few days. The site is uncertain: it is usually placed in the Vipava Valley, with the Frigidus as the Vipava, and recent research suggests a place between Col and Sanabor.

Church historians attributed the victory to divine intervention, and Rufinus compared its importance to Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge. Alan Cameron argues that the idea that Eugenius and Arbogast were pagans was created to justify the campaign, and Eugenius was not a pagan. The earliest source for the wind, Ambrose of Milan, says it blew before the battle and demoralised the enemy, and the poet Claudian moved it to the decisive moment. A contemporary historian said Theodosius won two battles, one against Eugenius and one against the Goths, who suffered most. He died four months later, leaving his sons Honorius and Arcadius. The losses weakened the western legions and increased reliance on foederati.
battle-of-the-garigliano-1503: From mid-November 1503 the French and Spanish armies faced each other across the Garigliano, some 60 km north of Naples, both camped in marshy, unhealthy ground. The French army was commanded by Ludovico II, Marquis of Saluzzo, and was based at the river's mouth near the ruins of Minturnae (Traetto), with a supply base in the nearby port of Gaeta. Several Spanish attempts to cross on a makeshift bridge failed. While he weighed attack against retreat, Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba received reinforcements from Naples under Bartolomeo d'Alviano and Orsini, and he moved some units to make the French believe he was falling back towards the Volturno.

Diego de Mendoza held the rearguard with 300 men-at-arms and 5,000 to 6,000 infantry, while bridges of boats and barrels, built in the castle of Sessa Aurunca, were brought on the night of 27 to 28 December to a point near the castle of Suio, out of French sight. Construction began at dawn, and by 10 am some 3,500 Spaniards had crossed. The 300 Norman crossbowmen at Suio noticed nothing; Gonzalo followed with 2,000 German pikes and 200 horsemen under Prospero Colonna, and d'Alviano occupied Castelforte.

With many sick men in the Traetto camp, the French captain Alegri destroyed the bridge and ordered a retreat to Gaeta, abandoning the sick and nine cannon. Colonna's horsemen caught the French at Scauri, where Chevalier Bayard's defence of a bridge covered their withdrawal, and again at Mola, until the arrival of the main Spanish force forced the Marquis of Saluzzo to retreat once more.

The French army's offensive capacity was destroyed. After some days of siege, the French in Gaeta surrendered, and the survivors made their way to Milan by sea or on foot. Many died at the hands of civilians or of hunger, and the Marquis of Saluzzo himself died on reaching Genoa. In the Treaty of Blois of 1504 France recognised Spain's authority over Naples.
battle-of-the-golden-spurs: The battle belongs to the Franco-Flemish War of 1297–1305. King Philip IV of France hoped to reassert control over the County of Flanders, a semi-independent polity notionally part of his kingdom, and perhaps to annex it. The French invaded in 1297 and again in 1300, and by May 1300 they controlled the county; Guy of Dampierre was imprisoned.

After Philip left, unrest returned in Bruges against the new governor, Jacques de Châtillon. On 18 May 1302 rebels who had fled the city came back and killed every Frenchman they could find, an act known as the Bruges Matins. Most towns joined the rising, though Ghent did not, and most of the Flemish nobility took the French side.

Philip sent a force under Count Robert II of Artois, built around a core of 2,500 noble cavalry. The Flemish army, led in the field by William of Jülich, was mostly town militia organised by guild, between 8,000 and 10,000 infantry. They carried pikes, crossbows and the goedendag, a thick wooden shaft topped with a steel spike. The Flemish besieged the castle of Courtrai from 26 June and fought the French on 11 July beside the Groeninge stream.

The ground was crossed by ditches and streams that the Flemish had dug and in places hidden, which robbed the French charge of momentum. Artois sent his heavy cavalry across the brooks. The Flemish pikemen did not flinch, and many knights were knocked from their horses and killed with the goedendag. Artois ordered his rearguard forward, but it turned back to protect the baggage. The count was cut down, and the surviving knights were driven into the marshes and slaughtered. The Flemish took few prisoners for ransom.

Courtrai castle surrendered on 13 July. The patrician regimes in Ghent and Ypres were overthrown and the guilds were officially recognised. The Annals of Ghent put French losses at more than 1,000 men, including 75 important nobles. The 500 pairs of spurs taken from the dead were given to the Church of Our Lady. The French soon reversed the result, winning at Mons-en-Pévèle in 1304, and the Peace of Athis-sur-Orge in 1305 made the Flemish pay substantial tribute.

Later writers saw the battle as an early sign of an infantry revolution, copied or adapted at Bannockburn, Crécy and Agincourt. In the 19th and 20th centuries it became the centre of a cult in Flanders: Hendrik Conscience's 1838 novel The Lion of Flanders made it known, and in 1973 its date was made the official holiday of the Flemish Community.
battle-of-the-granicus: After winning the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip II of Macedon forced most Greek states into the Hellenic League, whose aim was war on the Achaemenid Empire to avenge the Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. The Persian empire had been in crisis since the murder of Artaxerxes III in 338 BCE, and in spring 336 BCE Philip sent an expeditionary corps to the western coast of Asia Minor.

In early spring 334 BCE Alexander marched to the Hellespont with around 32,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry. Darius left the defence of Asia Minor to his satraps, perhaps because Alexander had not yet proved himself abroad. The satraps, led most probably by Arsites, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia, and including Spithridates and Memnon of Rhodes, were camped near Zeleia when Alexander crossed.

The battle was fought in May 334 BCE at the crossing of the Granicus, now called the Biga River, on the road from Abydus to Dascylium. Arrian's account, the longest, describes Alexander's army as 18,100 men, and gives the Persians almost 20,000 Greek mercenary infantry and 20,000 cavalry. Diodorus and Justin give far higher figures, which modern historians regard as exaggerated.

In Arrian's account Alexander first sent Amyntas against the Persian left, but the Persians held the higher bank and threw back the attack with javelins. Alexander then charged with the Companion cavalry and fought personally against Persian nobles, among them Rhosaces and Spithridates. The Persian cavalry broke, the Foot Companions crossed the river and the Persian infantry routed, except the Greek mercenaries, who withdrew to higher ground and fought hard.

Arrian gives 115 Macedonian dead. Arsites escaped to Phrygia but later killed himself after being blamed for the defeat. Arrian says 1,000 cavalry were killed and 2,000 Greek mercenaries taken prisoner, and Alexander sent the prisoners to Macedon to work the land as slaves, because they had fought for Persia against fellow Greeks.

Alexander sent 300 suits of Persian armour to Athens as an offering to Athena, with an inscription that left out the Spartans. He also set up at Dion a bronze group by Lysippus of twenty-five of his companions who had died in the first cavalry charge; it was later taken to Rome by Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus in 146 BCE. The Persians were forced onto the defensive in the cities they still held. Sardis surrendered to Alexander, and Miletus, which resisted, was besieged.
battle-of-the-great-plains: Scipio, who had driven the Carthaginians out of Iberia, was elected consul in 205 BCE and given Sicily, with permission to cross to Africa. He spent about a year training his army, built around the legions formed from the survivors of Cannae, and in 204 BCE landed at Cape Farina, north of Utica, with a force that modern historians estimate at 25,000–30,000 men. Masinissa, the Numidian rival of Syphax, joined him, while Syphax had been drawn to the Carthaginian side by Hasdrubal Gisco and by his new wife, Hasdrubal's daughter Sophonisba.

Scipio besieged Utica but was blockaded in his camp, Castra Cornelia, by the armies of Hasdrubal and Syphax. During peace talks he sent junior officers disguised as slaves to study the Numidian camp, built largely of reeds and thatch. In a night attack the Romans set fire to both camps and inflicted heavy casualties, and Hasdrubal fled to Carthage with 2,500 survivors.

Carthage decided to fight on with the resources at hand. Reinforced by 4,000 Iberian warriors and fresh local troops, and rejoined by Syphax, Hasdrubal gathered about 30,000 men within 30–50 days on a flat plain of the Bagradas River near modern Souk el Kremis, about 120 kilometres from Utica. Scipio marched there quickly without a baggage train, with a smaller army that the historian Brian Carey puts at about 20,000. After three days of skirmishing, both commanders formed up their full armies on the fourth.

Hasdrubal placed the Iberians in the centre, the Carthaginian infantry and cavalry on the right and Syphax's Numidians on the left. The Carthaginian cavalry broke at the first charge, and the Carthaginian and Numidian infantry, many of them survivors of Utica, fled with little resistance. The Iberians fought fiercely against the hastati, and Scipio sent the second and third ranks of each legion round in columns to strike them in the flank and rear. Enveloped, they fought to the death.

Hasdrubal was demoted and exiled. Syphax was pursued, defeated again outside his capital, Cirta, and captured, and Masinissa took over his kingdom. As Scipio moved his army to Tunis, within sight of Carthage, the city opened peace negotiations and recalled Hannibal and Mago Barca from Italy, but it repudiated the draft treaty once Hannibal had arrived. The war ended after Hannibal's defeat at Zama in October 202 BCE.
battle-of-the-hydaspes: After Alexander the Great defeated the last Achaemenid forces under Bessus and Spitamenes in 328 BCE, he began a campaign towards India in 327 BCE. He entered India through the Khyber Pass, and a smaller force under his own command took the fortress of Aornos. In the early spring of the next year he allied with Taxiles, king of Taxila, against his neighbour Porus, who had refused to surrender and was preparing for war.

Alexander had to subdue Porus to keep marching east, since leaving a strong opponent on his flank would have been dangerous, and he could not show weakness to the Indian princes already subdued. Porus chose the ground well.

Alexander camped on the north bank of the Hydaspes, now the Jhelum, and in the spring of 326 BCE Porus drew up on the south bank. The river was too deep and fast for a direct crossing, so Alexander moved his cavalry up and down the bank each night with Porus shadowing him. He found a crossing about 27 km upstream, where a wooded island divided the river, and left Craterus in camp with most of the army to make feints. According to Arrian he took 6,000 foot and 5,000 horse. A storm that night drowned the noise of the crossing. Porus's son, sent to meet them, was routed and died.

Porus came with the best of his army, with cavalry on the flanks, chariots in front and elephants before the infantry. Alexander attacked the flanks with cavalry first, and the Indian horsemen were routed. The elephants then advanced against the Macedonian phalanx and caused heavy losses, but were driven back and trampled their own side. The phalanx advanced while the cavalry charged from the rear, and Craterus, who had crossed, pursued the fleeing army.

Porus, who had fought on, finally dismounted and was taken to Alexander. Asked how he wished to be treated, he is said to have replied, treat me as a king would treat another king. Alexander let him keep his lands and made him a satrap. He founded two cities, Nikaia at the site of the battle and Boukephala across the river in honour of his horse Bucephalus, which died during or after the battle.

Alexander then marched east to the Hyphasis, now the Beas, where his troops, who had campaigned nearly eight years, refused to go on. He turned south along the Indus. The battle exposed the Indian subcontinent to Greek political and cultural influence.
battle-of-the-java-sea: The Japanese invasion of the Dutch East Indies advanced rapidly, with troop convoys screened by destroyers and cruisers and covered by aircraft from captured bases. Opposing them was a small force of Dutch, American, British and Australian warships, many of World War I vintage. On 19 February 1942 Japanese air raids rendered Darwin useless as a supply and naval base, and an Allied attack off Bali that night resulted in the Battle of Badung Strait. On 27 February Rear Admiral Karel Doorman sailed from Surabaya to intercept a Japanese convoy approaching from the Makassar Strait. His force, drawn from several navies, had little experience of each other's methods, and a language barrier separated the Dutch-speaking Doorman from the English-speaking ships.

The Allied force comprised two heavy cruisers, three light cruisers and nine destroyers. It was sighted at 15:48 and the first shots were fired at about 16:00. Gunfire on both sides missed at first, and the Japanese fired 43 torpedoes at long range without effect. The heavy cruiser Haguro then crippled HMS Exeter by gunfire and sank the destroyer HNLMS Kortenaer with a torpedo, and the destroyer HMS Electra was sunk in a destroyer action. After almost two hours Doorman had not come near the convoy and withdrew towards Surabaya.

After dark his ships turned back. A floatplane from Haguro had been shadowing them, and Haguro and Nachi, low on gun ammunition, attacked with torpedoes shortly before midnight. One struck the light cruiser Java, which blew apart and sank in about fifteen minutes with only 19 survivors. Another hit the flagship De Ruyter, which sank over several hours, killing Doorman. The destroyer HMS Jupiter was lost to a Dutch mine.

In the following days the cruisers USS Houston and HMAS Perth were sunk in the Battle of Sunda Strait on the night of 28 February, and on 1 March the damaged Exeter and the destroyers Encounter and Pope were sunk in a second battle of the Java Sea.

The Allied fleet was dissolved, 50 Dutch ships were scuttled at Surabaya to prevent capture, and the Dutch surface fleet was practically eradicated from Asian waters. The four American destroyers that had survived the battle escaped to Fremantle. ABDA forces surrendered on 9 March. The wrecks of the Java, De Ruyter, Electra, Kortenaer, Exeter and Encounter were found between 2002 and 2007, and by 2017 all eight ships sunk in the two battles had been reduced to remnants or removed by illegal salvage.
battle-of-the-kalka-river: After Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarezmian Empire in 1219, the generals Jebe and Subutai pursued the Khwarezmian sultan and then asked leave to continue their conquests for a year or two, returning to Mongolia by way of the Caucasus. With an army of 20,000, each general commanding a tumen, they sacked Rey, Zanjan and Qazvin and raided the Kingdom of Georgia. Crossing the Caucasus at heavy cost, they met a league of Lezgians, Alans and Cherkesses joined by the Cumans. The Mongols persuaded the Cumans to leave the alliance by appealing to Turkic-Mongol friendship and promising booty, then routed the others and turned on the Cumans themselves.

The Cuman Khan Koten fled to his son-in-law Mstislav Mstislavich of Galicia, known as Mstislav the Bold. He warned him that the Mongols had taken the Cuman land that day and would take his the next. Mstislav gathered the Rus' princes, among them Mstislav III of Kiev, but no commander-in-chief was appointed, so each prince could act as he pleased. The Mongols sent envoys saying they had no quarrel with the Rus', but Mstislav of Kiev had them executed.

The Mongols drew the Rus' forces eastward in a feigned retreat for nine days, then turned to face them on the Kalka River, whose exact location is unknown. Mstislav the Bold crossed and attacked with his Cuman allies without waiting for the rest. According to the chronicles the Cumans broke and ran through the Rus' ranks, causing confusion and a rout that began very quickly. Mstislav the Bold cut his way out with part of his army, while Mstislav of Kiev withdrew with some 10,000 men to a stockaded camp on a hill by the Dnieper.

After three days Mstislav of Kiev surrendered on a promise of safe conduct. The Mongols then killed his men and executed him and the Kievan nobles by burying and suffocating them under a victory platform, in the traditional Mongol manner of killing royalty without shedding blood. The number present is disputed, since no primary source gives it: estimates of the Rus' army range from 8,000 to 80,000. The Novgorod First Chronicle, the most reliable, gives no figures but says that only one soldier in ten returned home.

The Mongols did not stay. They plundered a few towns in the south and marched east, were defeated by the Volga Bulgars at Samara Bend, and rejoined Genghis Khan east of the Syr Darya. Their raid is described as history's longest cavalry raid, with 5,500 miles (8,900 km) ridden in three years. In 1237 Subutai and Batu returned and conquered the Kievan Rus'.
battle-of-the-little-bighorn: The battle belonged to the Great Sioux War of 1876 and was fought on land the Lakota had taken from other tribes since 1851, without the consent of the Crow, who had a treaty claim there. The Lakota had been displaced by the United States around Fort Laramie and reacted to white encroachment into the Black Hills, which they consider sacred. Around 5 June 1876, during a Sun Dance on Rosebud Creek, Sitting Bull, the spiritual leader of the Hunkpapa Lakota, reportedly had a vision of soldiers falling into his camp like grasshoppers from the sky.

The army sent three columns to force the Lakota and Cheyenne back to their reservations, one of them under Alfred Terry, which included the 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer. Plans rested on the Indian agents' figure of no more than 800 hostiles, which was correct until several weeks before the battle, when thousands of reservation Indians joined Sitting Bull for the summer buffalo hunt.

On 25 June, after Custer's Crow scouts reported that the village was being alerted, Major Marcus Reno's detachment of three troops was ordered to charge. His force crossed the Little Bighorn around 3:10 p.m. and found the Lakota and Northern Cheyenne present in force. The details of Custer's own fight are largely conjectural, because none of the men who went forward with his five companies survived. Lakota accounts say far more of their casualties occurred in the attack on Last Stand Hill than anywhere else, and that the command structure broke down rapidly, though smaller last stands were made by several groups.
The Lakota and Northern Cheyenne then turned on Reno and Benteen, and the fight continued until dark and for much of the next day. On 27 June Terry's column approached and the warriors drew off.

The 7th Cavalry had 16 officers and 242 troopers killed or dead of wounds, and Custer's two brothers, nephew and brother-in-law died with him. Estimates of Native casualties range from 36 to 300. Six women and four children are known to have been killed at the start of the battle, among them two wives and three children of Gall.

Congress authorised an increase in the size of the army, and the Indian Appropriations Act of 1876 cut off rations for the Sioux until they ended hostilities and ceded the Black Hills; the Agreement of 1877 took their land. Custer's widow Libbie Custer worked to burnish his memory, and his heroic image began to tarnish after her death in 1933. An army court of inquiry in 1879 found Reno's conduct without fault. The battlefield was renamed the Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument in 1991.
battle-of-the-masts: In the 650s the Rashidun Caliphate completed its conquest of the Sasanian Empire and went on expanding into Byzantine territory. In 645 Caliph Uthman appointed Abd Allah ibn Sa'd governor of Egypt, replacing the semi-independent Amr ibn al-As. Uthman let Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, raid Cyprus in 649, and the success of that campaign set the stage for naval activity from Egypt. Abd Allah built a strong navy and proved a skilled commander, and under him the Muslim navy won a number of victories, including repulsing a Byzantine counterattack on Alexandria in 646.

The campaign that led to the battle was the earliest attempt by Mu'awiya to reach Constantinople. He led an expedition into Cappadocia while his fleet advanced along the southern coast of Anatolia, and Emperor Constans II embarked against it with a large fleet.

The fleets met off Mount Phoenix in Lycia, near the harbour of Phoenix, modern Finike. Theophanes the Confessor, a Byzantine chronicler of the 9th century, tells that Constans dreamed the night before that he was in Thessalonica. An interpreter read the name as thes allo nike, give victory to another. In rough seas, al-Tabari says, the ships were arranged in lines and lashed together so that the men could fight hand to hand. The Arabs won, though losses were heavy on both sides, and Constans barely escaped to Constantinople, according to Theophanes by exchanging uniforms with one of his officers.

Traditional Arabic sources record no further attacks, and the respite granted to the Byzantines is usually put down to the Arab fleet retreating amid conflict over Uthman's authority, the first stirrings of civil war. The Armenian historian Sebeos reports instead that the fleet went on to attempt a siege of Constantinople, which a fierce storm defeated by sinking the ships carrying siege machines. On this account Mu'awiya's land force, which had reached Chalcedon, returned to Syria without its artillery.

Both fleets suffered major casualties. The battle is described as the first decisive conflict of Islam on the deep sea. The Mediterranean, long a Roman lake, became contested between the caliphate and the Eastern Roman Empire, and Muslim naval power later reached Sicily and cleared the way for uncontested expansion along the coast of North Africa.
battle-of-the-monongahela: General Edward Braddock came to the Thirteen Colonies as the first Commander-in-Chief, North America, with the 44th and 48th Regiments from Ireland, and recruited provincial troops until he had roughly 2,200 men when he left Fort Cumberland, Maryland, on 29 May. His expedition, one of four attacks planned against the French, was to take Fort Duquesne at the forks of the Ohio and then go on to Fort Niagara. Scornful of the need for Indian scouts, he took only eight Mingo guides, and the road had to be widened constantly for artillery and wagons. He split his army and pushed ahead with a flying column of 1,300.

Fort Duquesne had just been reinforced. Its commander, Claude-Pierre Pecaudy de Contrecœur, sent Captain Daniel Liénard de Beaujeu with about 800 men, 108 Troupes de la Marine, 146 militia and 600 Indians, to check the British advance.

The column crossed the Monongahela on 9 July and met the French force head on. The advance guard under Lieutenant-Colonel Thomas Gage opened fire and killed Beaujeu, but Captain Dumas rallied the French, while Odawa, Ojibwe and Potawatomi warriors spread through the woods on both flanks. Gage's men fell back into the main body on the narrow road, and the regulars, keeping tight formations, made easy targets; several platoons fired on each other and on provincials sheltering behind trees. Only the Virginia rearguard fought effectively from cover.

After three hours Braddock was shot in the lung, possibly by one of his own men, and resistance collapsed. George Washington, who held no official command, formed a rear guard that let the survivors escape. That night about a dozen captured soldiers were tortured and burned to death, as the prisoner James Smith witnessed.

Of about 1,300 men, 456 were killed and 422 wounded; of 86 officers, 26 were killed and 37 wounded; the French and Canadians reported 23 killed and 20 wounded. Braddock died on 13 July and was buried on the road near Fort Necessity. Colonel Thomas Dunbar burned about 150 wagons and retreated towards Philadelphia. The defeat led the British to make far better use of skirmishers, often armed with rifles, and historians still debate whether Braddock lost by keeping to European methods or by failing to apply them. The French held the Ohio Country until the Forbes Expedition forced them out of Fort Duquesne in 1758.
battle-of-the-muthul: Metellus, assisted by Gaius Marius and Publius Rutilius Rufus, led his army into the part of Numidia that Adherbal had received at the partition of the kingdom. The Muthul has been identified with the Wäd Mellag in south-east Numidia, though Mannert and Forbiger identified it with the river Ubus in the west. Between the river and a barren range of mountains about twenty miles away lay a dry plain, crossed by a hill covered with wild olive and myrtle.

Jugurtha drew up his army in a long line on that hill, at a right angle to the Roman road. He gave Bomilcar the elephants and part of the infantry, and kept the cavalry and the best infantry with himself nearer the mountain, reminding his men that they had sent the Romans under the yoke at the Battle of Suthul.

Descending the mountain, Metellus spotted the hidden Numidians, halted, and re-formed his army with a triple reserve and cavalry on the flanks. Fearing thirst, he sent Rutilius ahead with light cohorts and cavalry to secure a camp by the river, while he advanced slowly with Marius commanding the rear. Once the Roman rear had passed, Jugurtha sent about 2,000 men to seize the hill behind them and attacked from all sides. His cavalry scattered when pursued and closed in again, and for a quarter of the day the fighting was confused and indecisive.

As the Numidian attacks slackened in the heat, Metellus rallied his men and sent four legionary cohorts against the infantry on the high ground, and towards evening the Romans stormed the hill, though its defenders escaped. By the river, Bomilcar attacked Rutilius's camp, but his men gave way once the elephants were caught in the trees and surrounded. In the darkness the two Roman forces nearly fought each other until scouts discovered the truth.

Jugurtha disbanded most of his troops and turned to guerrilla warfare. At Rome, according to Sallust, the news was greeted with joy and public thanksgivings were decreed. Metellus was later checked at Zama, and Marius, elected consul against the Senate's wishes, enlisted volunteers from the capite censi, Romans without property, and went on to capture Jugurtha in 106 BCE. The Senate nonetheless gave Metellus the title Numidicus.
battle-of-the-nile: After Napoleon Bonaparte's victories in northern Italy, Britain remained the only major European power still at war with the French Republic. The French Directory considered invading Britain or Ireland but found British control of northern waters an obstacle, and the French navy was dominant only in the Mediterranean. Bonaparte proposed an invasion of Egypt as a first step in a campaign against British India.

His fleet sailed from Toulon on 19 May 1798, took Malta from the Knights of St. John of Jerusalem in June, and reached Alexandria. The Royal Navy sent a squadron under Rear-Admiral Sir Horatio Nelson to find out the purpose of the expedition and defeat it. He pursued the French for more than two months and several times missed them by hours.

Vice-Admiral François-Paul Brueys d'Aigalliers anchored his line in Aboukir Bay, a shallow anchorage about 32 km north-east of Alexandria, and believed his position was strong. His crews were needed ashore to find provisions, so he had no scouts out. Nelson's fleet was sighted on 1 August and attacked at once. His ships split into two divisions, one passing between the French line and the shore and the other engaging its seaward side, so the leading French ships were caught in a crossfire.

The French vanguard surrendered during the evening. At 21:00 fire was seen on the lower decks of the flagship Orient, and at 22:00 it reached the magazines and the ship exploded. Brueys had been killed. Fighting resumed at dawn on 2 August, and the surviving French ships of the line gradually pulled away to the east. Only two ships of the line and two frigates escaped.

British losses were recorded as 218 killed and about 677 wounded. French losses are harder to calculate; estimates range from 2,000 to 5,000, with a suggested median of 3,500, and about half the dead died on Orient. Nelson was wounded in the battle.

The victory reversed the strategic position in the Mediterranean and left Napoleon's army trapped in Egypt. British naval dominance off the Syrian coast contributed to the French defeat at the siege of Acre in 1799, before Napoleon left Egypt. The result also encouraged other European states to turn against France and was a factor in the outbreak of the War of the Second Coalition. Nelson was made Baron Nelson of the Nile and Burnham Thorpe, though he was privately dissatisfied with the reward.
battle-of-the-olive-grove-of-koundouros: After the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople on 12 April 1204, Boniface of Montferrat founded the Kingdom of Thessalonica and that autumn campaigned south, driving the local magnate Leo Sgouros back to Nauplia and Acrocorinth. Geoffrey I of Villehardouin, whose ship had been blown off course to Modon on his way from the Holy Land, met Boniface at the siege of Nauplia and urged the conquest of the rest of the Morea.

Villehardouin joined his fellow Champenois William of Champlitte, promising to recognise him as his lord, and with Boniface's leave the two set out with around a hundred knights and some soldiers. Patras and Andravida fell without a struggle, and the Franks moved down the west coast with a fleet, taking Pontikon, Modon, Coron and Kalamata while bypassing the strong fortress of Arkadia.

The Greeks of Laconia and Arcadia, under a certain Michael, tried to stop the Franks at the olive grove in north-eastern Messenia. Scholars have traditionally identified him with Michael I Komnenos Doukas, founder of the Despotate of Epirus, but Raymond-Joseph Loenertz questioned this. The Chronicle of the Morea gives the Greeks 4,000 men and notes that most of the infantry came from the Melingoi, the Slavic tribe of Mount Taygetos; the elder Geoffrey of Villehardouin, uncle of Geoffrey I, puts Michael's army above 5,000. Neither source describes the fighting. The exact site is unknown.

The battle was the last general effort of the local Greeks to resist, and the historian William Miller called it a Hastings of the Morea. In late 1205 or 1206 the Franks took Arkadia after a long siege and the fortress of Araklovon, defended by Doxapatres Voutsaras. Champlitte then ruled the north and west of the peninsula, though Leo Sgouros held out in his fortresses and Laconia and the Taygetos remained unsubdued. In a letter of Pope Innocent III of 19 November 1205 Champlitte is styled prince of all Achaea.
battle-of-the-plains-of-abraham: The battle was the culmination of a three-month British siege of Quebec during the Seven Years' War. In 1758 the British had taken Louisbourg, opening the sea route up the St Lawrence. In 1759 James Wolfe expected to lead 12,000 men but was given about 7,000 regulars, supported by a fleet of 49 ships under Vice-Admiral Charles Saunders. James Cook surveyed the river channel for the fleet. Troops landed on the Ile d'Orleans on 28 June and at Point Levis, where a battery nearly levelled the lower town. Illness spread through the British camps and Wolfe, frustrated by Montcalm's defensive stance, resolved to land upriver of the city to cut his supply line to Montreal.

Montcalm had sent Bougainville and some 3,000 men upriver to Cap-Rouge but did not think an upstream landing serious. On the night of 12 September British boats were challenged by sentries who expected a French supply convoy, and a French-speaking officer of the 78th Fraser Highlanders answered in excellent French. At L'Anse-au-Foulon 24 volunteers under Colonel William Howe climbed a slope and captured the small camp of Captain Vergor from behind. Wolfe followed, and by sunrise his army held the top of the cliffs.

Montcalm chose to confront it at once, though he might have awaited Bougainville. The British formed a thin line two ranks deep across the plain, while Canadian militia and native sharpshooters fired from scrub on their left. The British held their fire until the French column was within about 30 yards, then fired a heavy volley, advanced a few paces and fired again. The French broke. Wolfe, struck by two shots, died as the French began to retreat, and Montcalm died the next morning.

Governor Vaudreuil abandoned Quebec and marched his forces west, leaving a garrison under Jean-Baptiste Nicolas Roch de Ramezay, who signed the Articles of Capitulation with Townshend and Saunders on 18 September. In the spring of 1760 the French forced the British back into the city at the Battle of Sainte-Foy but failed to retake it, and in 1763 France ceded most of its North American possessions to Britain in the Treaty of Paris. In 2009 a planned re-enactment for the 250th anniversary was cancelled after threats of public disorder, as some separatist leaders called it an insult to francophone Quebecers. A cannonball believed to date from the siege was found in the Old City in 2017.
battle-of-the-pyramids: After landing in Ottoman Egypt and capturing Alexandria on 2 July 1798, General Napoleon Bonaparte marched his army across the desert towards Cairo. His aim was to break the power of the Mamluk beys who dominated Egypt and to secure the capital before Ottoman reinforcements could arrive. Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey, two Georgian Mamluks who commanded the country's military forces, prepared to resist, with elite heavily armoured cavalry supported by fellahin militia as infantry. On 13 July French scouts found Murad's camp near Shubra Khit. French artillery destroyed the Mamluk flagship on the Nile and forced a retreat, an early demonstration of how concentrated firepower could stop cavalry.

On 21 July, after marching all night, the French reached the village of Embabeh. Napoleon formed each of his five divisions into a hollow rectangle with cavalry and baggage in the centre and cannon at the corners. He told his troops that forty centuries looked down on them from the pyramids, from which he named the battle. The divisions of Louis Desaix, Jean-Louis-Ébénézer Reynier, Charles-François-Joseph Dugua, Honoré Vial and Louis André Bon advanced in echelon, with the Nile on their left.

Murad anchored his right on the Nile at Embabeh, which was fortified with infantry and artillery, and his left on Biktil, planning to hold the flanks and strike the French centre with cavalry. Across the river Ibrahim Bey's army watched but could not cross. At about 15:30 Murad ordered his defterdar, Ayyub Bey, to lead a mass assault. The squares of Desaix, Reynier and Dugua repelled the horsemen with musketry and artillery. Meanwhile Bon's division formed attack columns and stormed Embabeh. The garrison broke, and many fled into the Nile, where hundreds drowned. The chronicler ʻAbd al-Raḥmān al-Jabartī wrote that the fighting lasted about three-quarters of an hour.

French reports listed 29 killed and 260 wounded. Murad's losses were far heavier, with thousands killed or wounded, including Ayyub Bey and perhaps 3,000 of the elite cavalry. Wounded in the cheek, Murad escaped to Upper Egypt, where he fought a guerrilla campaign until Desaix defeated him in late 1799. Napoleon entered Cairo on 24 July and set up a French administration, putting down later rebellions by force. The battle marked the beginning of the end of seven centuries of Mamluk dominance in Egypt. Its strategic effect was brief, because ten days later Admiral Horatio Nelson destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile, cutting Napoleon's army off from France.
battle-of-the-sabis: In the winter of 58–57 BCE Caesar heard that the Belgae were forming a union under Galba, king of the Suessiones, out of fear of Roman interference. He raised two new legions in Cisalpine Gaul, won the Remi to his side and, after defending their oppidum of Bibrax and winning an action at the Aisne, saw the union break up for lack of provisions. Tribe after tribe surrendered, but the Nervii, Atrebates, Aduatuci and Viromandui refused. The Nervii, who allowed no luxuries into their land, were said to be the most hostile to Roman rule. Caesar had eight legions, perhaps 30,000–45,000 fighting men; the Remi reckoned the Nervii alone at 50,000.

Hidden in woods across the shallow river, the Belgae waited for the Roman baggage train to appear, then rushed across and charged the legions as they fortified their camp, giving them no time to form up. On the left Legions X and IX drove the Atrebates into the river, and in the centre VIII and XI pushed back the Viromandui. A column of Nervii under Boduognatus poured through the gap this opened, attacking the camp and surrounding Legions XII and VII on the right. Camp followers fled, and the Treveri cavalry rode home to report a disaster.

Caesar took a shield, went to the front line of the hard-pressed Legion XII, called his centurions by name and had the ranks open out. The two legions on the right were brought back to back, the new Legions XIII and XIV arrived with the baggage, and Labienus, having taken the Belgic camp, sent Legion X back across the river against the Nervii's rear. The Nervii fought on from the bodies of their dead until the last few fled.

The Nervian elders told Caesar their council had fallen from 600 to three and their 60,000 fighting men to barely 500; Caesar says he spared them. He gives no Roman losses, and his account is almost the only source. The Aduatuci turned home and were later defeated, some 53,000 of them sold into slavery. The Nervii fought again in the revolt of Ambiorix in 54 BCE.
battle-of-the-somme: The Chantilly Conference of December 1915 agreed on simultaneous offensives in 1916 by the Russian, Italian, British and French armies. The Somme offensive was the Franco-British share, with the French army to take the main part, supported on the northern flank by the British Fourth Army. When the Germans began the Battle of Verdun on 21 February 1916, French commanders diverted many of the divisions intended for the Somme, and the British attack became the principal effort. The British force was a mixture of wartime volunteers from the Territorial Force and Kitchener's Army with the remains of the pre-war army.

A five-day artillery bombardment preceded the attack, which began on 1 July 1916. The French Sixth Army and the right wing of the British Fourth Army inflicted a considerable defeat on the German Second Army, but from the Albert–Bapaume road north to Gommecourt, where the Germans had made their main defensive effort, the British attack was a disaster. British casualties on the first day were 57,470, including 19,240 killed, the worst in the history of the British Army.

Douglas Haig abandoned the attack north of the road to reinforce the success in the south, and the offensive became the capture of fortified villages and woods that offered observation for artillery. The Battle of Flers–Courcelette on 15 to 22 September saw the first use of tanks on the Somme and the debut of the Canadian Corps and the New Zealand Division. The battle is dated to 18 November.

More than three million men fought in the battle, and more than one million were wounded or killed. The Anglo-French operational objectives were not achieved, since they failed to capture Péronne and Bapaume. In March 1917 the Germans made a strategic retreat of about 25 miles to the Hindenburg Line in Operation Alberich.

In the United Kingdom and Newfoundland the Somme became the central memory of the First World War, commemorated on 1 July each year at the Thiepval Memorial to the Missing of the Somme. Some historians see it as the beginning of modern all-arms warfare, in which Kitchener's Army learned to fight a mass-industrial war. Debate continues over the necessity, significance and effect of the battle.
battle-of-the-teutoburg-forest: Julius Caesar conquered most of western Europe in the Gallic Wars and twice crossed the Rhine, but his engagements with Germanic tribes were inconclusive. Rome then neglected the continent for two decades, and the Gauls rebelled when troops left in 31 BCE. Publius Quinctilius Varus, appointed by Augustus to command in Germania in 7 CE, had been consul and governor of Africa and Syria. The historian Michael McNally judges that he was sent for his political skill in handling the Germanic factions rather than for military ability.

Arminius of the Cherusci had been taken to Rome as a hostage as a boy, received an aristocratic education, joined the Roman cavalry and commanded auxiliaries. He then returned home, still nominally loyal to Rome. His Roman training let him anticipate Roman tactics and deceive Varus.

Varus planned a simple campaign for 9 CE: the army would cross the Rhine and set up a summer camp in nominally pacified Cherusci territory. Sources say he took little military action that summer and held court instead, though the only contemporary account comes from Velleius Paterculus, who had reason to dislike him. In late summer Arminius invented reports of a local rebellion. Others advised Varus that there was too little time to suppress it, but Arminius proposed a shorter route through the territory of the Angrivarii, and Varus took it.

The army set out on 8 September, strung out for 15 to 20 kilometres on forest tracks, and Arminius meant to lead it toward Kalkriese, where the Angrivarii lay in ambush. In the late morning his Bructerii allies attacked along the line in a brief skirmish aimed at tiring the Romans. A torrential downpour began, and Varus ordered a camp. The fighting went on between 8 and 11 September.

Suetonius records that Augustus struck his head against the palace walls, shouting for Varus to give him back his legions. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used for Roman legions again. Tiberius took effective control, and Germanicus raided Germania in 14 CE. Arminius was poisoned by fellow Germans in 21 CE. Since the 15th century the battle has been seen as the event that ended Roman expansion at the Rhine, and in the 19th century it became part of German nationalist mythology. Recent scholars point to other reasons for the frontier, such as supply from the Mediterranean by river and the greater wealth of the Rhine lands.
battle-of-the-thames: British and Indigenous forces under Major General Isaac Brock and Tecumseh had taken Detroit in August 1812, and in January 1813 Henry Procter's Right Division and the Wyandot war leader Roundhead defeated James Winchester's Americans at Frenchtown on the River Raisin. On 10 September 1813 Oliver Hazard Perry captured all six ships of Robert Heriot Barclay's squadron at the Battle of Lake Erie, cutting Procter's supply line and taking much of Fort Amherstburg's artillery, which had been mounted on the ships.

Without consulting his senior officers, Procter decided to abandon the Detroit frontier and withdraw up the Thames valley towards Burlington Heights. Tecumseh, who knew a retreat would end British support for his confederacy, tried in vain to dissuade him. On 27 September, after burning Detroit and Amherstburg, 880 British regulars marched from Sandwich, followed by Tecumseh with 1,200 warriors and their families.

The retreat was slow in rain and on bad roads, and Procter rarely shared his plans. William Henry Harrison landed below Amherstburg on 27 September and gave chase on 2 October. By the time he caught up west of Moraviantown on 5 October, half of Tecumseh's warriors had drifted away, and Procter had only about 450 regulars and about 500 warriors against roughly 2,500 Americans, many of them Kentucky militia.

The British formed two lines in open woodland between the river and the Backmetack Marsh, without tools to build defences, while Tecumseh's warriors waited in the marsh. Lieutenant Colonel James Johnson's mounted infantry charged shouting Remember the Raisin, broke both lines and took most of the British prisoner; Procter narrowly escaped. In the marsh Richard Mentor Johnson led a forlorn hope of 20 men against Tecumseh's flank, and Tecumseh was killed. His followers held for about 30 minutes before withdrawing.

Harrison reported seven killed and 22 wounded and 601 prisoners, counting those taken before and after the battle. He burned Moraviantown and returned to Detroit. Tecumseh's alliance dissolved, though some tribes fought on. Johnson, usually credited with killing Tecumseh, later became vice president of the United States. A court martial at Quebec found Procter erroneous in judgment and deficient in energy, ending his career.
battle-of-the-trebia: The Second Punic War followed the First Punic War of 264 to 241 BCE, in which Carthage was defeated by Rome. Hamilcar Barca then expanded Carthaginian Iberia into a quasi-monarchical territory ruled by his family, the Barcids, which gave Carthage silver mines, manpower and the means to resist Roman demands. In 218 BCE Hannibal led an army from Iberia through Gaul and across the Alps, reaching northern Italy in October with 38,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry.

The Gallic tribes of Cisalpine Gaul had risen against the Romans after colonists were settled at Placentia and Cremona. At the Battle of Ticinus, Publius Scipio led the Roman cavalry and light infantry against the Carthaginian cavalry, was beaten and wounded, and the Romans withdrew to a fortified camp near Placentia. The Senate ordered the second consul, Sempronius Longus, whose army in Sicily had been meant for an invasion of Africa, to march north. Because Scipio was partly incapacitated, Sempronius took overall command.

After a day of heavy skirmishing in which the Romans gained the upper hand, Sempronius was eager for battle. Hannibal had his brother Mago take 1,000 cavalry and 1,000 infantry in the night to hide in an old brush-filled watercourse beside the flood plain where he meant to fight. His Numidian cavalry then lured the Romans out of their camp onto ground of his choosing. The armies were each about 40,000 strong, the Carthaginians stronger in cavalry and the Romans in infantry.

Fresh Carthaginian cavalry routed the outnumbered Roman cavalry, and light infantry outflanked the Roman infantry. Hannibal had also placed his elephants on either side of the infantry to discourage the Romans from approaching the flanks, and he thinned his line, especially the Gauls in the centre, to match the Roman length. The hidden force then struck the Roman infantry in the rear. Most Roman units collapsed, but about 10,000 under Sempronius kept formation and fought their way out to Placentia.

Historians disagree about Roman losses. Paul Erdkamp puts them at 20,000 killed, half the force, not counting prisoners. Carthaginian losses were several thousand, mostly Gallic infantry in the centre, and several elephants. News of the defeat caused panic in Rome at first, but this calmed when Sempronius arrived to preside over the consular elections. Gnaeus Servilius Geminus and Gaius Flaminius were chosen, and the new consuls raised fresh legions and built a fleet of 60 quinqueremes.

Gallic recruits flocked to Hannibal, whose army grew to 60,000. In spring 217 BCE he crossed the Apennine Mountains and won the Battle of Lake Trasimene, and in 216 BCE the Battle of Cannae, the last of what modern historians call the three great military calamities of the Romans in the first three years of the war.
battle-of-the-vorskla-river: In 1395, after losing his war with Timur, Tokhtamysh, Khan of the Golden Horde, was dethroned by the party of Khan Temür Qutlugh and Emir Edigu, who were supported by Timur. He fled to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and asked Vytautas for help in retaking the Horde, in exchange for surrendering his suzerainty over Ruthenian lands. Vytautas gathered Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Poles, Moldavians and Wallachians, and signed the Treaty of Salynas, surrendering Samogitia to the Teutonic Knights. Expeditions into Tatar territory followed in 1397, 1398 and 1399. The first reached the Black Sea and Crimea. In May 1399 Vytautas declared a crusade against the Tatars and received the blessing of Pope Boniface IX.

In 1399 the army moved against the Horde along the Dnieper from Kiev, and on 5 August it met the Tatars at the Vorskla, just north of Poltava. Temür Qutlugh proposed a three-day ceasefire, a trick to win time while Edigu's reinforcements arrived. Vytautas planned a great wagon fort to stop charging horsemen, which he would then destroy with cannons. His army was well equipped but smaller. On 12 August Temür Qutlugh feigned a retreat, and Vytautas left the wagon fort to pursue him. Edigu's units appeared from behind and surrounded the Lithuanian army. Tokhtamysh judged the battle lost and fled. The Tatars used their own artillery against the Lithuanian cavalry and captured the wagon fort.

Vytautas barely escaped alive. About 50 princes fought under his banners and about 20 of them were killed, among them his cousins Demetrius I Starszy and Andrei of Polotsk and Stephen I of Moldavia. The Tatars besieged Kiev, which paid a ransom, and pillaged as far west as Lutsk in pursuit of Tokhtamysh, who was assassinated in 1407 or 1408. The defeat blocked Lithuanian expansion into southern Ruthenia and cost the state its access to the Black Sea. Smolensk, Novgorod and Pskov revolted against Lithuanian rule.

Vytautas gave up his plans to break the Union of Kreva and allied himself again with his cousin Jogaila, King of Poland. It has been suggested that he learned the staged retreat during this battle and used it at Grunwald in 1410. The Lithuanian historian Edvardas Gudavičius judged that Vytautas took an unjustified risk and lost terribly.
battle-of-the-winwaed: Penda of Mercia had come to dominate England through a series of victories over the Northumbrians. Allied with Cadwallon ap Cadfan of Gwynedd, he defeated and killed Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield Chase in 633, and he killed Oswald of Northumbria at the Battle of Maserfield in 642. In the years that followed the Mercians apparently campaigned into Bernicia and at one point besieged Bamburgh, and in 655 the Northumbrian sub-kingdom of Deira supported Penda's invasion.

Oswiu, Oswald's brother, had succeeded him only in Bernicia, the northern part of Northumbria. Penda, with allies from East Anglia and Wales and a force led by thirty warlords, besieged him at a place called Urbs Iudeu. Bede says Oswiu offered treasure for peace and was refused, but also that Oswiu's young son Ecgfrith was a hostage among the Mercians, perhaps as part of a deal; the Historia Brittonum says Penda shared the treasure among his British allies.

Penda's army may then have been marching home when the two armies met by the river Winwæd, which has never been identified. Since Oswiu ended his campaign in the district of Loidis, the river is usually placed near Leeds; Andrew Breeze argued for the River Went, north of Doncaster, and others for Cock Beck. Bede calls the Northumbrian force very small and says Oswiu vowed to make his daughter a nun and give twelve estates for monasteries if he won.

Penda's army was weakened by desertions: according to the Historia Brittonum, Cadafael ap Cynfeddw of Gwynedd left with his men and was remembered as the battle-shirker, and Bede says Aethelwald of Deira withdrew to watch from safety. Penda was killed, with the East Anglian king Aethelhere and thirty leaders of warbands. The battle was fought in heavy rain, and Bede writes that more drowned in the flight than fell by the sword.

Northumbrian dominance was restored. Oswiu took northern Mercia outright, and the southern part went to Penda's Christian son Peada, who was murdered in 656; Northumbrian authority over Mercia was overthrown within a few years. Bede saw the battle as the effective end of Anglo-Saxon paganism, and every later Mercian king, Penda's sons Peada, Wulfhere and Æthelred among them, was Christian.
battle-of-the-yarmuk: Emperor Heraclius had defeated the Sasanian Empire in 627 and restored the True Cross to Jerusalem in 629. The Muslims had seized Emesa, a march from Aleppo and from Antioch, where Heraclius resided. Alarmed, he prepared a counteroffensive, and in 635 Yazdegerd III of Persia sought an alliance, planning a simultaneous attack in Iraq. When Heraclius launched his offensive in May 636, Yazdegerd could not coordinate with it. The Muslims learned of the preparations from Byzantine prisoners, and on Khalid ibn al-Walid's advice Abu Ubayda pulled the army back from Palestine and Syria and concentrated it on the plain near Jabiyah and the Yarmuk River.

Estimates of the armies are uncertain. Early accounts give the Muslims 36,000 to 40,000 men and the Byzantines 60,000 to 70,000, while some modern estimates put the Byzantine army at 40,000 at most or even 15,000 to 20,000, and Warren Treadgold suggests 80,000 to 100,000 or more. The only early Byzantine source is Theophanes, who wrote a century later. Heraclius had told his commander Vahan to avoid battle until diplomacy was exhausted, and negotiations delayed the fighting for a month.

The battle began on 15 August 636 and lasted six days. On the first days the Byzantines tried limited attacks and then thrusts against the Muslim right wing and centre, which fell back, but Khalid used his mobile guard of cavalry to counterattack and the Byzantines made no breakthrough. On 20 August, with some 8,000 cavalry massed, Khalid rode round the Byzantine left wing and drove the Byzantine cavalry from the field. The infantry was left exposed and was forced towards the ravine to the west.

Khalid pursued the survivors towards Damascus. Vahan, who had escaped the fighting, was probably killed there, and Khalid entered Damascus, where he was welcomed. When news reached Heraclius at Antioch, he accepted that the defeat was God's decision and a result of the sins of the people, himself included. Lacking men and money to defend Syria, he sailed for Constantinople by night and, according to tradition, bade farewell to Syria.

The battle effectively ended Byzantine rule in Syria and is regarded as one of the most decisive in military history. It marked the culmination of the first great wave of early Muslim conquests after the death of Muhammad, which saw the Rashidun Caliphate advance into both the Sasanian and the Byzantine empires. It was also the most important victory of Khalid ibn al-Walid.
battle-of-thermopylae: Athens and Eretria had aided the Ionian Revolt against Darius I in 499–494 BCE, and Darius vowed to punish them. His first invasion of Greece ended in 490 BCE with the Greek victory at the Battle of Marathon. A decade later his son Xerxes had assembled a very large land and naval force to conquer Greece. The Athenian general Themistocles proposed that the allied Greeks block the Persian army at the pass of Thermopylae while the fleet held the Straits of Artemisium. The Spartans sent an advance force under King Leonidas I, with the 300 men of the royal bodyguard, to block the pass.

The Greek force numbered approximately 7,000. Ancient authors gave the Persian army in the millions; modern scholars estimate between 120,000 and 300,000. Xerxes attacked on the fifth day after the Persians reached the pass, first with 5,000 archers, whose arrows the Greeks' shields and bronze helmets deflected, then with waves of about 10,000 men. The Greeks fought at the narrowest part of the pass in a phalanx of overlapping shields, and the Persians could make no headway on the first day or the second.

On the second day Ephialtes, a local man motivated by the desire for a reward, told Xerxes of a mountain path around the pass. His name came to mean nightmare in Greek and to stand for the archetypal traitor. On the third day a Persian column bypassed the Phocians guarding the path. Leonidas, aware that he was being outflanked, dismissed most of the Greek army and stayed to guard the retreat with 300 Spartans and 700 Thespians; up to 900 helots and 400 Thebans are also reported to have remained. Most of the Thebans reportedly surrendered, and the others fought to the death.

The Persians now held the pass, and the Greek fleet at Artemisium withdrew to Salamis. The Persians overran Boeotia and captured the evacuated city of Athens, but the Greek fleet defeated them at the Battle of Salamis in late 480 BCE. Xerxes withdrew to Asia with much of his army, leaving Mardonius, who was decisively defeated at the Battle of Plataea the following year. Writers ancient and modern have used Thermopylae as an example of an army defending its native soil.
battle-of-thymbra: Cyrus conquered the Kingdom of Media in 550 BCE, which brought him into conflict with the neighbouring Lydian Kingdom of Croesus. After the drawn Battle of Pteria, Cyrus pursued Croesus into Lydia and hoped to catch the Lydian king unprepared. Croesus had partly disbanded his army, but he armed his reserves and marched out to meet the Persians before his allies could arrive, and they never did. The two armies met on the plain north of Sardis.

The size of the armies rests on Xenophon. He gives Cyrus 196,000 men, including Persian infantry, peltasts, pikemen, Arabians, Armenians and Medians, together with 300 camel cavalry, 300 chariots and siege towers that each held 20 men. He gives Croesus 420,000, among them Babylonians, Lydians, Phrygians, Cappadocians, peoples of the Hellespont and 120,000 Egyptians.
