His figures, even if untrue, are considered within the realm of possibility, though less than half of the men may have taken part in the fighting. The Lydian army was about twice the size of the Persian one.

Cyrus drew up his troops in a square formation with the flanks held back and covered by chariots, cavalry and infantry. Baggage camels formed a barrier around his archers, and their smell disturbed the Lydian horses and broke up the cavalry charge while the archers shot into the Lydian ranks. As Cyrus had expected, the Lydian wings wheeled inward to envelop the square, and gaps opened at the hinges of the turning wings.

Fire from the archers and the mobile towers inside the square added to the disorder. Cyrus then ordered his flank units forward, and they struck the disorganised Lydian wings. The Lydian cavalry lost many men and retreated, and most of the infantry surrendered. Croesus escaped with a small part of the infantry to his capital. Herodotus gives no numbers, but his account of the course and outcome of the battle agrees with Xenophon's.

The Lydians were driven within the walls of Sardis, which fell after a siege of 14 days, reportedly because the defenders had left unguarded a part of the wall they thought too steep to attack. Croesus was captured, and Lydia, with the Greek cities of Ionia and Aeolis, became part of the Persian empire. The Egyptian soldiers who had fought for Croesus surrendered and joined Cyrus's army. Herodotus says Cyrus treated Croesus with respect, while the Babylonian Nabonidus Chronicle appears to report that Cyrus killed the Lydian king, though which king it means is unclear. The conquest brought Greece and Persia into the contact that led to the Persian Wars of Cyrus's successors.
battle-of-tinchebray: Henry invaded Normandy in 1105, in the course of a long dynastic dispute with his brother. He took Bayeux and Caen but broke off the campaign because of political problems arising from an investiture controversy. With these settled, he returned to Normandy in the spring of 1106, quickly took the fortified abbey of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives near Falaise, and turned south to besiege Tinchebray Castle, on a hill above the town.

Tinchebray, today in the Orne département of France, lay on the border of the county of Mortain in the south-west of Normandy. It was held by William, Count of Mortain, one of the few important Norman barons still loyal to Robert. Duke Robert brought up his forces to break the siege, and after some unsuccessful negotiations he decided that a battle in the open was his best option.

Henry's army was organised in three groups. Ranulf of Bayeux, Robert de Beaumont, 1st Earl of Leicester, and William de Warenne, 2nd Earl of Surrey, commanded the two main forces, while a reserve under Elias I of Maine waited out of sight on the flank. Alan IV, Duke of Brittany, William, Count of Évreux, Ralph of Tosny, Robert of Montfort and Robert of Grandmesnil also fought on Henry's side. William of Mortain and Robert of Bellême, 3rd Earl of Shrewsbury, supported Robert Curthose.

The battle lasted an hour. Henry dismounted and ordered most of his knights to do the same, which was unusual in Norman warfare and gave the infantry a decisive part. William of Évreux charged the front line with men from Bayeux, Avranches and the Cotentin, and Henry's reserve decided the day.

Most of Robert's army was captured or killed. Among the prisoners were Robert himself, Edgar Ætheling, the uncle of Henry's wife, and William of Mortain. Robert of Bellême, commanding the duke's rear guard, led the retreat and escaped. Most prisoners were released, but Robert and William of Mortain were held for the rest of their lives. Henry kept his brother first in Devizes Castle and later in Wales, where Robert died at Cardiff Castle in 1134. Robert's legitimate son, William Clito (1102–1128), pressed claims to the duchy that fed several rebellions through the rest of Henry's reign.
battle-of-tippecanoe: William Henry Harrison became governor of the newly formed Indiana Territory in 1800 and sought land for settlement. By the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne the Miami, Potawatomi, Lenape and other tribes ceded about 3 million acres to the United States. Tecumseh opposed the treaty, holding that land was owned in common by all tribes and could not be sold without the agreement of all. He built a resistance at Prophetstown, near the meeting of the Tippecanoe and Wabash rivers, while his brother Tenskwatawa preached a return to ancestral ways.

Meetings with Harrison at Grouseland, his home in Vincennes, in 1810 and again in the summer of 1811 settled nothing. In 1811 Tecumseh left to recruit among the Muscogee and Choctaw. Harrison gathered about 1,000 men, among them Kentucky cavalry volunteers under Joseph Hamilton Daveiss and regulars under Colonel John Parker Boyd, built Fort Harrison at Terre Haute in October and marched on Prophetstown, where Tenskwatawa had perhaps 500 warriors of the Kickapoo, Potawatomi, Winnebago, Shawnee, Wyandot and other nations.

Harrison camped on Burnett's Creek on 6 November and arranged to meet Tenskwatawa the next day. Accounts of how the fighting began differ; Tenskwatawa later blamed the Ho-Chunk warriors, and a Kickapoo chief said the shooting of two Winnebago warriors by sentries provoked the attack. Around 4:30 a.m. on 7 November the soldiers woke to find themselves nearly surrounded. The warriors, having lost the element of surprise, attacked in many small, uncoordinated assaults from every side.

Daveiss was killed leading a counter-charge of dragoons, and Captain Spier Spencer's Indiana Yellow Jackets lost all but one officer before reserves under Captain Robb closed the gap with Ensign John Tipton. After about two hours the warriors ran short of ammunition and withdrew into the woods. Harrison lost 37 killed in action and 25 mortally wounded, with 126 others wounded; historians estimate that as many as 50 warriors were killed and 70 to 80 wounded. On 8 November his men burned the deserted town and 5,000 bushels of corn and beans, and dug up its cemetery.

Secretary of War William Eustis asked why Harrison had not fortified his camp. Harrison claimed a decisive victory, but the historian Alfred Cave found no confirmation of that in contemporary reports. The Shawnee partly rebuilt Prophetstown, and attacks on settlers increased after the New Madrid earthquakes of December 1811, which many tribes took as a sign of Tenskwatawa's powers. In the War of 1812 Tecumseh's warriors fought beside the British until his death at the Battle of the Thames on 5 October 1813. The Whigs later used the slogan Tippecanoe and Tyler too in Harrison's 1840 presidential campaign.
battle-of-toba-fushimi: On 3 January 1868 the restoration of imperial rule was proclaimed. Shōgun Tokugawa Yoshinobu had resigned his authority to the emperor, but his apparatus of state continued and the Tokugawa family held a domain around Edo valued at more than 2 million koku, which hard-liners from Satsuma and Chōshū found intolerable. Saigō Takamori is said to have physically threatened members of the fifteen-year-old Emperor Meiji's assembly into ordering the confiscation of Yoshinobu's lands.

Yoshinobu at first agreed, but on 17 January declared that he would not be bound by the proclamation. On 24 January, after provocation by Satsuma rōnin in Edo, he prepared from Osaka Castle to send an army to Kyoto, ostensibly to dislodge the Satsuma and Chōshū elements dominating the court.

The shogunal army of 15,000 outnumbered the Satsuma–Chōshū force three to one, but it was spread out, with about 8,500 men engaged, and some of its front-line troops carried pikes and swords and had empty rifles. The Satsuma and Chōshū troops had Armstrong howitzers, Minié rifles and one Gatling gun. On 27 January the shogunate advanced along the Toba and Fushimi roads. At about 17:00 its vanguard reached a Satsuma barrier at the Koeda Bridge in Toba and was refused passage; the Satsuma opened fire, the first shots of the Boshin War, and the column fell into panic. Fighting at Fushimi, around the Bungo Bridge, was inconclusive.

On 28 January Iwakura Tomomi obtained orders from the emperor declaring Yoshinobu and his followers enemies of the court, and the imperial brocade banners were brought out. Prince Yoshiaki was named nominal commander, turning the Satsuma–Chōshū forces into an imperial army, so that anyone firing on it became a traitor. When the banner appeared on 29 January at Tominomori, the shogunal troops were thrown into confusion and retreated. The daimyō of Yodo refused them entry to Yodo Castle, and the daimyō of Tsu changed sides two days later.

On 30 January Yoshinobu told his advisers that he would take the field himself, but that evening he slipped away from Osaka Castle with the daimyō of Aizu and Kuwana, taking refuge on the American warship USS Iroquois until the Kaiyō Maru arrived. His men then left Osaka Castle, which was surrendered without resistance. The battle weakened the shogunate's prestige, led many neutral daimyō to declare for the emperor, and silenced those in the new government who favoured a peaceful settlement.
battle-of-tolbiac: The Franks were two neighbouring and allied peoples: the Salian Franks, whose king was Clovis, and the Ripuarian Franks, whose capital was Cologne and whose king was Sigebert the Lame. Bordering Sigebert's kingdom were the Alemanni, a confederation of Germanic tribes. Border incidents, looting and punitive raids between the Alemanni and the Ripuarian Franks multiplied until Sigebert suffered a real invasion and called on his ally Clovis, who raised an army. The date is traditionally given as 496, though some accounts place the battle earlier or later. The site, Tolbiacum, is usually identified as Zülpich in North Rhine-Westphalia, and there may have been two battles.

Little is known about the battle. The Ripuarian Franks were probably of no help after the first battle. Clovis saw his warriors being killed and, moved to tears, called upon the God of his wife Clotilde, whom she had preached to him since their marriage in 493. Gregory of Tours records his prayer: if he were given victory he would believe and be baptised, since his own gods had failed to help him. At these words the Alemanni began to flee, as their leader had been killed with an axe, and they submitted to Clovis, saying that they were now his. The Franks subdued or killed the remaining Alemanni.

Gregory was the first to mention the vow, which has shaped later readings of Tolbiac as a climax of European history. He then tells how the queen asked Remigius, bishop of Reims, to urge Clovis to believe, and how Clovis was baptised at Reims on Christmas 496, calling him another Constantine. A surviving letter from Avitus of Vienne congratulating Clovis on his baptism makes no mention of a battlefield conversion.

The Alemanni abandoned the Lower Rhine and left the Ripuarian Franks alone. Clovis, who profited only a little, allowed his ally to keep the territory, and later relied on Sigebert's help in conquering the northern part of the Visigothic kingdom. The conversion brought him the support of neighbouring Christians and of the influential clergy, and allowed him to undertake conquests and crusades to Christianise new territories or expunge Arianism.

Further clashes with the Alamanni followed. Some researchers hold that a third battle, possibly near Strasbourg, led to the northern Alamanni coming under Frankish rule, while the southern Alamanni placed themselves under the protection of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great.
battle-of-tolentino: Tolentino was the decisive battle of the Neapolitan War, which Murat, the Napoleonic King of Naples, fought to keep his throne after the Congress of Vienna. By the end of April 1815 he had lost all his early gains, as two Austrian corps under Generals Bianchi and Neipperg drove the Neapolitans south-east to a base at Ancona. The two corps had become separated on either side of the Apennine Mountains, and Murat hoped to defeat Bianchi to the west before turning on Neipperg.

Sending a small force under General Michele Carrascosa to delay Neipperg, Murat moved his main army against Bianchi. On 29 April Hungarian hussars routed the small Neapolitan garrison of Tolentino, and Murat camped at Macerata to the north-east. Bianchi, seeing the plan, set out to delay him, with a defensive line based on the Tower of San Catervo and troops at Rancia Castle, the church of Maestà and Saint Joseph.

The battle opened at dawn on 2 May with artillery fire on the valley leading north to Sforzacosta. Neapolitan troops surrounded and captured Bianchi near Sforzacosta, but Hungarian hussars freed him almost at once. Rancia Castle changed hands many times during the day, and by nightfall the Neapolitans had made slight gains, including Monte Milone, though the Austrians still held a strong position.

On the second day fog delayed the fighting until 7:00 a.m. The Neapolitans took Rancia Castle and the hills of Cantagallo, and two infantry divisions, among them Murat's Guard Division, descended from Monte Milone against the Austrian left. Expecting a cavalry counter-attack that never came, they formed square, and Austrian volleys and artillery fire cut into them. General Mohr repulsed an attack on the Austrian right, and the Neapolitan line fell back to Pollenza. Murat then learned that Neipperg had beaten Carrascosa at the Battle of Scapezzano, and heard false rumours that a British fleet had landed a Sicilian army in the south. He ordered the retreat.

The Neapolitans lost over 4,000 men and the Austrians 800. Hungarian cavalry beat the Neapolitans again at Castel di Sangro, and the remains of the army were destroyed at San Germano, while the whole Neapolitan fleet surrendered to the Royal Navy to spare the capital a bombardment. Murat fled to Corsica disguised as a Danish sailor. On 20 May 1815 Austria and Naples concluded the Treaty of Casalanza, which restored Ferdinand IV to the throne.
battle-of-tondibi: The Songhai had been the dominant power of West Africa for more than a century, controlling the Western Sudan from the headwaters of the Senegal River to what is now Niger, but succession conflicts after the death of Askia Al-Hajj in 1586 had weakened the empire. To the north the Saadi dynasty of Morocco was at the height of its power after repelling a Portuguese invasion at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578, yet the cost of its defences had brought it close to bankruptcy.

Seeking new resources, Sultan Ahmad I al-Mansur turned to the Songhai, wrongly believing that their wealth came from gold mines. Many advisers warned that war on another Muslim nation was unlawful, but he set their objections aside and in October 1590 sent an army under Judar Pasha, a Spanish eunuch captured as a child.

The expedition travelled with 8,000 camels, 1,000 packhorses and eight cannons, reached the Niger on 28 February 1591 after a four-month journey, and razed the salt mines at Taghaza. Judar's army of 1,500 light cavalry and 2,500 infantry, many armed with arquebuses, faced a Songhai force estimated at 18,000 cavalry and 9,700 foot soldiers by the Tarikh al-fattash and at up to 80,000 men by other accounts, strong in cavalry but without firearms.

The armies met at Tankondibogho, near Tondibi, just north of Gao. A stampede of 1,000 cattle meant to break the Moroccan lines was turned back by the noise of the guns. The Songhai infantry and then their cavalry were cut down by arquebus and cannon fire, and the rearguard fought hand to hand until it was killed. The battle took about two hours; according to the Tarikh al-Sudan, some Songhai soldiers sat on their shields rather than flee and were killed.

Judar sacked Gao, already evacuated by its residents, and moved on to Timbuktu and Djenné. Morocco could not hold the vast region, and after a decade of sporadic fighting it splintered into dozens of smaller kingdoms. The Songhai moved east to their surviving province of Dendi and kept their tradition alive there for two and a half centuries.
battle-of-torvioll: Skanderbeg, son of the prince Gjon Kastrioti, had served the Ottoman Empire as a sipahi, a cavalry commander. After the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Niš he deserted with 300 other Albanians and, by forging a letter from Murad II to the governor of Krujë, became lord of the city in November 1443. On 2 March 1444 he gathered Albania's nobles in the Venetian-held town of Alessio (Lezhë), among them George Arianiti, Pal Dukagjini, Andrea Thopia and Lekë Zaharia, who formed the League of Lezhë and chose him as its captain.

Murad II, seeking to end the movement at once, sent Ali Pasha, one of his most favoured commanders, from Üsküp (Skopje) in June 1444 with 25,000 to 40,000 troops along the Drin towards Krujë. Skanderbeg raised 10,000 to 15,000 men from the League, 8,000 of them on horseback; most were feudal levies, but over 2,000 were paid permanent troops.

Skanderbeg chose the battlefield himself, a plain in Lower Dibra north of Peshkopi, thought to be the Plain of Shumbat: 11.2 kilometres long and 4.9 kilometres wide, surrounded by hills and forests. He placed 3,000 men under five commanders, among them Hamza Kastrioti, in the woods with orders to attack the Ottoman wings and rear only on a signal. On the night before the battle the Ottomans rejoiced in advance, certain of victory, while the Albanians put out their campfires and rested, ignoring Ottoman parties that came to provoke them.

On the morning of 29 June the Albanian army, divided into three parts, feigned a retreat and dispersed into the mountains and forests, drawing the Ottomans into the gorge of Torvioll. As Ali Pasha prepared to declare his victory, the Albanians regrouped and attacked, and at Skanderbeg's signal Hamza's hidden horsemen surrounded and defeated the Ottoman forces.

Between 7,000 and 10,000 Ottoman troops died and around 500 to 2,000 were taken prisoner, while 3,800 to 4,000 Albanians were killed or wounded. The victory was praised in the rest of Europe, raised the morale of Skanderbeg's followers and strengthened his position as leader of the League. It also encouraged Pope Eugenius IV and John Hunyadi to organise a new crusade against the Ottomans in the autumn of 1444.
battle-of-tours: The Umayyad troops under Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani, governor-general of al-Andalus, overran Septimania by 719 and made Narbonne their capital from 720. Duke Odo the Great broke the siege of Toulouse, taking them by surprise, and Al-Samh ibn Malik was mortally wounded, but the Umayyads raided into Burgundy in 725. When Odo was later defeated, he appealed to the Franks for help, which Charles Martel granted only after Odo agreed to submit to Frankish authority.

In 732 the Umayyad advance force under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was heading north towards the Loire, having outpaced its supply wagons and part of its army. It was caught off guard to find a large Frankish force sitting directly in its path to Tours. Charles chose not to attack but to take up a defensive formation, and according to Arab sources the Franks drew up in a large square with hills and trees in front of them to break up cavalry charges. For a week the armies skirmished.

The battle was fought on 10 October 732 at a site between Poitiers and Tours that the sources do not fix exactly. Abd al-Rahman trusted in his cavalry and had it charge repeatedly through the day. According to Arab sources the cavalry broke into the Frankish square several times, but the Franks did not break. Al-Ghafiqi was killed in combat, and the Umayyad army withdrew.

The Umayyad army retreated south over the Pyrenees, and Charles continued to expand southwards. The Umayyads remained in control of parts of Septimania for another 27 years; Charles failed to take Narbonne in 737, and his son Pepin the Short forced its surrender in 759. Ninth-century chroniclers gave Charles the nickname Martel, the hammer.

Historians disagree about the battle's importance. Edward Gibbon and others held that it halted the spread of Islam in Western Europe. Alessandro Barbero writes that historians now tend to play down its significance, since the Muslim force aimed to pillage the monastery of St-Martin of Tours rather than conquer the Frankish kingdom. Arab historians who mention it at all present it as a minor skirmish. Most historians agree the battle helped lay the foundations of the Carolingian Empire.
battle-of-trafalgar: In 1805 Napoleon Bonaparte's First French Empire dominated the European continent by land, while the Royal Navy held the seas through blockades. Napoleon renewed his determination to invade Britain, and to bring his invasion flotilla across the English Channel he needed to wrest control of it from the Royal Navy. Vice-Admiral Villeneuve's fleet evaded Horatio Nelson's blockade of Toulon, joined the Spanish fleet at Cádiz and sailed for the Caribbean. Nelson pursued it across the Atlantic and missed it by a few days. Villeneuve returned to Europe and ended at Cádiz, where Napoleon ordered him in September to sail to Naples.

Villeneuve changed his mind several times, and on 18 October he ordered the combined fleet to sail, though the winds were very light. On 21 October, off Cape Trafalgar, it met Nelson's fleet of 27 ships of the line, against Villeneuve's 33. Nelson sailed at the flank of the Franco-Spanish line in two columns, hoping to break it up and force a melee in which his well-trained crews could fight ship to ship, instead of the usual parallel lines of battle.

At 11:45 Nelson signalled to the fleet, England expects that every man will do his duty. The light winds meant the leading British ships were under heavy fire for almost an hour before their own guns could bear. Nelson's flagship HMS Victory led one column and was almost knocked out of action; Nelson was shot by a French marksman and died shortly before the battle ended. The columns split the Franco-Spanish fleet into three groups and isolated the rear, which was overwhelmed. The British lost no ships, and Villeneuve was captured.

A storm followed the battle and wrecked or sank several of the captured ships. On 4 November 1805 a British squadron under Sir Richard Strachan captured four French ships that had escaped the battle. The victory confirmed Britain's naval supremacy and ended any real effort by Napoleon to invade Britain; Britain's command of the sea was not tested for over a century. Nelson's death in victory secured his place as a British national hero.
battle-of-tricamarum: After the Byzantine victory at the Battle of Ad Decimum on 13 September 533, Belisarius took Carthage, and Gelimer fell back to Bulla Regia in Numidia. He recalled his brother Tzazo from Sardinia, where Tzazo had restored Vandal rule, offered the local Punic and Berber peoples a reward for every Byzantine head, and sent agents to win over the people of Carthage and the Hun mercenaries of Belisarius. The Huns, fearing they would be kept in Libya, chose to wait and join the winning side. Early in December the reunited brothers marched on Carthage and cut the aqueduct that supplied most of its water.

With the city walls not yet repaired and the Huns unreliable, Belisarius chose to force a battle. He sent John the Armenian ahead with most of the cavalry to Gelimer's camp by the Medjerda River, where the Vandals had gathered their wives, children and property. On 15 December the Vandals stood behind a small stream, Tzazo with about 5,000 picked men in the centre and Moorish allies in reserve; the historian Ilkka Syvänne puts their whole force at 15,000–20,000. Belisarius faced them with 8,000–11,000 cavalry, his infantry still a day's march behind.

Tzazo's men threw back John's first two attacks. In the third nearly all the Byzantine cavalry of the centre closed with the Vandals, Tzazo and several nobles were killed, and the line collapsed. The Huns now joined the pursuit and Gelimer fled. The Byzantines lost fewer than 50 men and the Vandals about 800. When the camp was stormed, the soldiers broke ranks to plunder it, and Belisarius needed a day to restore order.

Hippo Regius opened its gates and the royal treasure was taken. Gelimer, deserted by his nobles, tried to flee to Spain, was cut off, and took refuge with the Moors in the mountains, where Pharas the Herulian besieged him through a hard winter. Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearic Islands passed to Justinian. Gelimer was brought to Constantinople for Belisarius's triumph, and Procopius records him repeating, Vanities of vanities, all vanities. North Africa became the base for the invasion of Italy.
battle-of-tsushima: The Russo-Japanese War began on 8 February 1904, when Japanese destroyers made a surprise attack on the Russian Far East Fleet at Port Arthur. Japan needed to neutralise Russian naval power in order to secure its supply lines to the mainland and fight a ground war in Manchuria. After the Russian First Pacific Squadron fell inactive and Port Arthur came under siege, the Tsar agreed to form a Second Pacific Squadron from the Baltic Fleet, including 11 of its 13 battleships. The voyage lasted over seven months and covered 18,000 nautical miles. In the Dogger Bank incident the squadron mistook British fishing trawlers for Japanese torpedo boats, killing several fishermen.

Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky revealed his choice of the Tsushima Strait, the shortest route, only on 25 May 1905. The fleet approached in radio silence, but a Japanese ship located it early on 27 May and reported by wireless, and Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō sailed with the Combined Fleet. In the afternoon Tōgō turned his line in sequence across the Russian course. The Russian gunnery proved surprisingly good, but Rozhestvensky was wounded and knocked unconscious, and four Russian battleships were sunk by sunset.

At night 21 destroyers and 45 torpedo boats attacked for three hours without a break, and the Russians dispersed into small groups. On the morning of 28 May the Japanese surrounded the squadron of Admiral Nebogatov, who ordered the four remaining battleships to surrender. Tōgō's greater battle experience, extensive Japanese gunnery practice, high-explosive shells, wireless telegraphy and British help with guns, ships and intelligence are all credited with the result.

All 11 Russian battleships were lost, seven sunk and four captured. Only a cruiser and two destroyers reached Vladivostok. Russian losses were 216 officers and 4,614 men killed, with about 6,000 taken prisoner. Japan lost three torpedo boats and 117 men killed, and none of its heavy ships.

The loss forced Russia to seek peace, and the Treaty of Portsmouth was signed in September 1905. In Japan Tōgō was revered as a national hero, and his flagship Mikasa is preserved as a museum ship at Yokosuka. It was the only decisive engagement ever fought between modern steel battleship fleets and the first in which wireless telegraphy played a critical role. It showed that faster battleships with long-range big guns were superior to mixed batteries, which led to the dreadnought arms race. Russia's prestige was badly damaged and the defeat was a blow to the Romanov dynasty.
battle-of-turckheim: From 1672 the campaign of Louis XIV against the Netherlands provoked Austria, which controlled the Holy Roman Empire, and Brandenburg, whose intervention carried the Franco-Dutch War to the upper Rhine and threatened French territory. In 1674 Turenne, the French commander in that sector, failed to prevent part of the Imperial Army from invading Alsace. At the end of the year the Imperials went into winter quarters around Colmar, a few miles south of the French barracks at Haguenau.

By the conventions of war at the time, operations should have halted until spring. Turenne broke with the custom: using the Vosges mountains as cover, he marched west and then south, reappeared at Belfort, south of his opponents, on 27 December 1674, and reached Mulhouse unopposed on the 29th. The surprised Imperials fell back hastily on Turckheim.

On the afternoon of 5 January 1675 Turenne, with 30,000 troops, found the Imperial army of 30,000 to 50,000 men under Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, well positioned but not yet fully ready for battle. He feigned an attack in the centre and another on his right, then led a third of his army round his left flank, hidden from view by the ground along the mountains, and took the small village of Turckheim. Frederick William tried to retake it but was beaten off by French guns and an infantry charge. Turenne then fell on the enemy's extreme right without preliminary artillery fire, and the defenders broke after 3,400 casualties.

With their winter quarters threatened, the Elector's forces left Alsace, abandoning three thousand sick and wounded men at Colmar, and fell back on Strasbourg, where they crossed the Rhine the following week. The brief winter campaign is considered one of the most brilliant of the 17th century: by one strategic and one tactical indirect manoeuvre, Turenne had saved France from invasion at small cost.
battle-of-ucles-1108: Tamim ibn Yusuf set out from Granada for Jaén in early May 1108 with the forces of Granada. There he was joined by those of Córdoba, and at Chinchilla by the forces of Murcia and Valencia under their governors, Muhammad ibn Aysa and Abdallah ibn Fatima. Uclés offered no resistance and was taken on 27 May, its garrison shutting itself in the alcázar, while the Almoravids spread out to sack the Christian settlements of the Tagus valley.

According to the Historia Compostelana, the counter-attack was led by the heir, Sancho, who already held the rule of Toledo while his father Alfonso VI was in the north. His army included eight Leonese counts and Castilian magnates, the eight counts of legend, and with townsmen from Calatañazor, Alcalá and Toledo and the baggage train it numbered about 2,300 men by the estimate of the historian Bernard Reilly.

The Christians camped near Uclés on 28 May. Tamim placed the Córdobans under Muhammad ibn Abi Ranq in front, his own Granadans behind them, and the Valencians and Murcians on the flanks. The battle opened the next day with a Christian cavalry charge that at first drove back the Córdobans but was then surrounded while engaging the Granadans. As the main force fell back on its camp, the Murcians and Valencians attacked the baggage. The infantry scattered and the cavalry was trapped in its own camp and slaughtered.

Sancho, his horse killed, escaped with seven of his men towards Belinchón but was killed by his Muslim subjects, who had risen in revolt. Of the counts only Álvar Fáñez got away, leading a large body of horsemen north to organise the defence of the upper Tagus.

The Almoravids lured the garrison of Uclés out of the alcázar and defeated it, then took the castles of Huete and Ocaña and a few smaller ones, but they could not follow up their victory in the field by taking Toledo. Arabic sources speak of 3,000 Christian heads piled before Uclés to terrify its people. Seven counts died in the fighting or were beheaded afterwards; their names must be pieced together from several chronicles, which record among them García Ordóñez, count of Nájera, and Martín Laíñez.
battle-of-uhud: After the Muslims migrated to Medina, hostilities with the Quraysh of Mecca grew, largely because of Muslim raids on Meccan caravans. In 624 the Muslims defeated a more numerous Meccan force at Badr, where several Quraysh leaders were killed, including Amr ibn Hisham. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, chosen as their leader, vowed revenge, and wealthy Meccans who had lost relatives gave money for another expedition. He mobilised more than 3,000 men against Medina.

Muhammad had meant to stay in Medina and use its fortifications, but many Muslims who had missed Badr wanted open battle, and he gave way. Shortly before the battle Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, chief of the Khazraj, withdrew with 300 men. The Muslim force of around 700 took position on the slopes of Mount Uhud, which protected its rear. Muhammad posted 50 archers on a nearby hill to guard the flank against the Meccan cavalry and ordered them not to leave their places.

The battle took place on 23 March 625. It opened with duels in which the Meccan standard-bearer Talha ibn Abi Talha was killed by Ali ibn Abi Talib, and others of his family who took up the banner fell one after another. In the general engagement the Muslims swept through the Meccan ranks. Believing the battle won, most of the archers left the hill to collect spoils. Khalid ibn al-Walid, commanding the Meccan cavalry, attacked the few who stayed and then struck the Muslim flank and rear.

Many Muslims were killed, among them Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad's uncle. Rumour spread that Muhammad had died, but he had been wounded in the face. Umar ibn al-Khattab rallied the troops, and a counter-charge drove Khalid's men from the slopes. The Meccan cavalry could not climb the slope, and Abu Sufyan returned to Mecca without attacking the wounded Muslims again.

Scholars differ on the result. Chase F. Robinson writes that a disheartening Muslim defeat is clear enough, while William Montgomery Watt notes that the Meccans failed to destroy Muhammad and his followers. The Qur'an, in a verse revealed soon after, attributes the setback to disobedience and desire for loot and treats it as a test. Abu Sufyan then sought alliances with nomadic tribes, and the Quraysh returned in 627 with a larger confederate force at the Battle of the Trench. Khalid ibn al-Walid's leadership at Uhud was an early sign of the career that made him one of the best-known Arab generals of the later conquests.
battle-of-ulai: Assyria struggled to hold its neighbour Babylonia, which had joined Chaldeans and Elamites against Sennacherib at Halule in 691 BCE. Ashurbanipal took the throne at Nineveh while his brother Shamash-shuma-ukin claimed the kingship in Babylon, a kingdom Ashurbanipal treated as a vassal. Elam was Babylonia's ally. Teumman, a known enemy of Assyria, had usurped the Elamite throne and forced the sons of Urtaki to flee to Nineveh; Ashurbanipal refused his demand that they be handed over. Teumman also pushed Assyrian influence out of the Sealand and placed Nabo-usalim on the throne at Ur.

The armies met on the banks of the Ulai, the river known today as the Karkheh. Assyrian forces specialised in siege warfare rather than pitched battle, but here their cavalry outflanked the Elamites while the foot soldiers attacked the centre and drove the enemy into the river. Teumman and his son Tammaritu were killed, and the king's head was carried to Nineveh and displayed at Ashurbanipal's court.

Ashurbanipal later fought a four-year campaign against Babylonia and replaced his brother with Kandalanu. Susa, the Elamite capital, was sacked in 647 BCE, and Elam did not regain its power before the Persians conquered it a century later.

The battle is known above all from the relief carvings of Ashurbanipal's palace at Nineveh, crowded scenes of the torture and death of enemy soldiers. Teumman's severed head appears in nearly every panel, even the one showing the king's victory banquet, in keeping with Assyrian propaganda meant to make viewers fearful and in awe of Assyrian might. As an innovation in Assyrian relief art, the cycle was modelled on Egyptian depictions of the Battle of Kadesh, more than 600 years older.
battle-of-ulundi: After the Zulu victory at the Battle of Isandlwana in January 1879, reinforcements poured into Natal and Chelmsford prepared a second invasion of Zululand. By mid-June he knew that Sir Garnet Wolseley had superseded him, but he ignored the government's order to subordinate his plans to Wolseley and turned down several peace offers from Cetshwayo, hoping to restore his reputation by a victory before he was removed. His main force numbered 1,000 regular cavalry, 9,000 regular infantry and 7,000 other men with 24 guns, among them the first British Army Gatling gun battery.

The advance on Ulundi began on 3 June and met no opposition, as Cetshwayo, his army weakened at the Battle of Kambula, did not attack the long supply convoys. Messages from Wolseley ordering Chelmsford to undertake no serious operations went unanswered. Cetshwayo's envoys brought oxen and elephant tusks, but Chelmsford rejected the terms as not fully met.

On 3 July Colonel Redvers Buller's cavalry, reconnoitring across the White Umfolozi River, narrowly escaped an ambush by 3,000 Zulus. The next morning the infantry crossed and formed a hollow rectangle of 5,317 men with artillery and Gatling guns at its faces, mounted troops covering its sides and no laager or trenches, so as to show that a square could win in the open. A Zulu army of about 12,000 to 15,000 under umNtwana Ziwedu kaMpande formed a horseshoe around it.

From about 9:00 a.m. the infantry opened fire at 2,000 yards. Rifle volleys, Gatling fire and canister at close range stopped every charge, and no warrior came within 30 yards of the ranks. When the Zulu reserve broke against the south-west corner, Chelmsford sent out his cavalry, and the pursuit went on until no living Zulu remained on the Mahlabatini plain; Natal auxiliaries killed the Zulu wounded in revenge for Isandlwana.

The British lost 13 killed and the Zulus about 1,500 casualties. The royal kraal burned for days. Chelmsford handed over command on 15 July and was awarded a Knight Grand Cross of the Bath, but never served in the field again. Wolseley divided Zululand into thirteen districts under pro-British chiefs. Cetshwayo, exiled to Cape Town, was restored to a reduced central Zululand in January 1883, shortly before his death in 1884.
battle-of-val-es-dunes: William had succeeded to the duchy in 1035 as the seven-year-old illegitimate son of Duke Robert I. Several of his kinsmen, among them his cousin Guy of Burgundy, believed they had a better claim, but William had the support of the French king Henry I and other influential nobles. In 1046 his enemies tried to ambush him near Valognes on the Cotentin Peninsula. When that failed, Guy, Nigel of the Cotentin, Rannulf of the Bessin, Ralph Tesson of Thury, Grimoald of Plessis and Hamon Dentatus raised an army put at about 25,000 men. William rode to the king's court at Poissy and reminded him that a revolt against his faithful vassal was a revolt against himself, and Henry raised about 10,000 men.

The king's army joined William's much smaller Norman force near Caen, in the heart of rebel territory. Early on Ralph Tesson changed sides and attacked the rebels from the rear. The next day the armies fought on the plain of Val-ès-Dunes, near the present-day town of Conteville, in a series of cavalry skirmishes. The rebels had the greater numbers but lacked coordination. Hamon Dentatus unhorsed King Henry but was killed before he could harm him.

After losing several skirmishes the rebel army broke, panicked and fled west and was driven into the Orne, where, an observer recorded, the bodies blocked the mill of Barbillon. The battle is traditionally dated 10 August; David Douglas argued for winter or spring, while David Bates holds that it almost certainly took place in summer.

Guy escaped to his castle of Brionne, which William could not force to surrender until 1050, and the eastern third of the duchy beyond it remained outside his authority. In October 1047 the Norman nobles were made to declare a Truce of God at Caen, banning private wars from Wednesday evening to Monday morning, from which William and the king were exempt. In 1851 a memorial was built on the battlefield at Vimont under Arcisse de Caumont.
battle-of-valdejunquera: The battle was part of the Córdoban expedition known as the Campaign of Muez, which was aimed chiefly at the southern line of defence of the Kingdom of León, the County of Castile along the Duero river. When the Muslim army reached Muez and threatened the Kingdom of Pamplona, its king, Sancho Garcés I, asked Ordoño II of León for help.

The earliest account is the Chronicon of Sampiro, a Leonese cleric writing probably in the late 980s, who calls the Muslims Agarenes, descendants of Hagar. According to him, Ordoño met them in the Valdejunquera, the valley of Iuncaria, and was routed. Other sources show that the Muslim army was commanded by the emir himself. Two of Ordoño's bishops, Dulcidio and Ermogio, were taken captive to Córdoba. Ordoño ransomed Dulcidio, while Ermogio's nephew Pelagius, later venerated as a martyr, went into captivity in exchange for his uncle's freedom.

As a further result of the defeat, the fortified site of Clunia, which the Castilian count Gonzalo Fernández had repopulated in 912, had to be abandoned; it was still in Muslim hands as late as 1007-10.

The exact place of the battle is unknown. The late eleventh-century Historia Silense put it in Sancho Garcés's territory, between Estella and Pamplona. The seventeenth-century Navarrese historian José de Moret placed it north of Irujo and south of the sierra of Andía, and claimed that the Basques of his day still called the region Iuncadia.

The bishops' sees are also uncertain. Pelayo of Oviedo, continuing Sampiro in the twelfth century, made them bishops of Salamanca and Tuy, but neither is possible: Salamanca then lay in the depopulated Desert of the Duero, and Tuy had a bishop named Nausto. The historian Justo Pérez de Urbel concluded that Dulcidio was Bishop of Zamora and Ermogio Bishop of Oporto, with roots in the region of Tuy.
battle-of-valea-alba: In 1475 an Ottoman winter attempt to bring Moldavia under control with Rumelian levies ended in defeat at the Battle of Vaslui. For the next campaigning season the Ottomans gathered a large army under Mehmed II himself, which entered Moldavia in June 1476. Contemporary western sources put it at about 90,000 to 150,000 men, but the historian Kármán Gábor regards these figures as exaggerated, noting that Ottoman military records of the time put the army at close to 30,000.

Groups of Tartars from the Crimean Khanate, recent allies of the Ottomans, were also sent against Moldavia. Stephen the Great avoided open battle and followed a scorched-earth policy, but his forces were dispersed across the country, leaving him a small army to face the main Ottoman attack.

Forests, swamps and the lack of roads made conventional tactics and the movement of artillery difficult. For about forty days Mehmed advanced without finding Stephen, supplied by the Ottoman fleet on the Danube, while the Moldavians ambushed small detachments. On 26 July Stephen, surrounded in the White Valley near Cetatea Neamțului, attacked the vanguard of Hadım Süleyman Pasha. As Mehmed fed in more units and arrived with the main army, Stephen fell back to a position with a wooded hill behind it, fortified with trenches, felled trees and wagons, his artillery in front.

Moldavian fire pinned down the Janissaries until Mehmed charged forward with his shield to rally them. According to Turkish military histories and Selahattin Tansel, forces under Gedik Ahmed Pasha finally broke the Moldavian front, and as darkness fell the exhausted Moldavians retreated. The same accounts say Stephen escaped with only a few men, his camp was plundered and Mehmed ordered the execution of 7,000 to 8,000 prisoners.

Stephen withdrew to the north-west of Moldavia, or perhaps into the Polish Kingdom, and raised another army. The Ottomans could not take Suceava, Neamț or Hotin, were harassed by small Moldavian attacks and suffered starvation and plague. Faced with forces gathering in Transylvania under Stephen V Báthory and Stephen's counterattack, they left most of Moldavia in August 1476, returning in 1480.
battle-of-valmy: The battle came early in the War of the First Coalition, when the monarchies of Europe sought to stop the French Revolution or contain it to France. King Frederick William II of Prussia, supported by Great Britain and Austria, sent the Duke of Brunswick towards Paris with a large army. Longwy fell on 23 August and Verdun on 2 September 1792. About 54,000 French troops in the Army of the North under Charles Dumouriez and the Army of the Centre under François Kellermann faced Brunswick's coalition army of about 84,000, which included Hessians and French royalist émigrés. Just over half of the French infantry were regulars of the old Royal Army, as were nearly all the cavalry.

Dumouriez abandoned his plan to attack the Austrian Netherlands and approached the invaders from the rear. Kellermann joined him at Sainte-Menehould on 19 September, which put the French east of the Prussians and behind their lines. Brunswick, troubled by bad weather and sickness, turned back to fight. On 20 September Kellermann took position on slopes near Valmy, around an old windmill that he had razed, and his artillery opened what is called the Cannonade of Valmy.

Kellermann had about 36,000 men and 40 cannon, Brunswick about 34,000 and 54 cannon. The French batteries proved superior, and the Prussian infantry made a cautious, fruitless advance under fire. Kellermann is said to have raised his hat and cried Vive la Nation, and the troops sang La Marseillaise and Ça Ira. To general surprise Brunswick broke off the action. Casualties were no more than three hundred French and two hundred Prussians. Brunswick withdrew towards Germany on 30 September without being attacked.

Historians have never settled why the Prussians withdrew. Most point to the strong French position, growing reinforcements and the unexpected spirit of the volunteers, together with Prussian worries about the Russian invasion of Poland. Stories of a secret plea by Louis XVI or of bribery are doubted; Munro Price finds no convincing proof of bribery.

Beset by food shortages and dysentery, the Prussians retreated beyond the Rhine, and French troops took Mainz in October. On the day of the battle the Legislative Assembly had transferred its power to the National Convention, which then abolished the monarchy and proclaimed the French Republic. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who was with the Prussian army, later wrote that a new epoch in the history of the world had begun. Kellermann was ennobled by Napoleon in 1808 and became Duke of Valmy.
battle-of-varna: The Hungarian kingdom fell into crisis after the death of King Sigismund in 1437, and his successor Albert died in 1439. Hungarian nobles then called the young Władysław III of Poland to the throne, expecting help against the Ottomans, and he ruled beside the nobleman John Hunyadi. The sultan Murad II signed a ten-year truce with Hungary and in 1444 resigned the throne to his twelve-year-old son Mehmed II.

Cardinal Julian Cesarini insisted that Władysław should break the truce, arguing that it was invalid because it had been made with infidels. Hungary worked with Venice and Pope Eugene IV to raise a new crusader army under Hunyadi and Władysław. Çandarlı Halil Pasha recalled Murad II, who commanded the Ottoman army. The crusaders numbered some 20,000, mainly Hungarian, Polish, Bohemian and 4,000 Wallachian troops.

An Ottoman army of around 40,000 or 60,000 approached Varna on 9 November. Cesarini first urged withdrawal, then a defence behind the Hussite Wagenburg until the fleet arrived. The young Władysław and Hunyadi rejected defensive tactics, and Hunyadi declared: "To escape is impossible, to surrender is unthinkable."

On 10 November Hunyadi drew up the army in an arc 3.5 kilometres long between Lake Varna and the Franga plateau. Ottoman light cavalry assaulted the Croats, and when the Christians pursued them in disorder, the Anatolian cavalry ambushed them. The right wing fled into the marshland, where Cesarini met his end. Against Hunyadi's advice, Władysław led 500 Polish knights at the Ottoman centre and almost reached Murad, but in front of his tent the king's horse fell or was stabbed.

Hunyadi organised the retreat of the remains of the army, which had suffered thousands of casualties. The king's head and body were never found. Turkish chroniclers say a mercenary beheaded him, but Murad II's own memorandum says he survived the battle and was executed later in captivity. Hunyadi became Governor of Hungary on 5 June 1446.

Hungary passed to the four-year-old Ladislaus the Posthumous, while Poland had a three-year interregnum before Casimir IV Jagiellon. The Ottoman victories at Varna and at the Second Battle of Kosovo in 1448 deterred European states from sending help to the Byzantines in 1453. The fallen king was given the name Ladislaus of Varna (Władysław III Warneńczyk), and the battle is commemorated on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Warsaw.
battle-of-vaslui: Stephen III of Moldavia and Sultan Mehmed II quarrelled over southern Bessarabia and its ports of Chilia and Akkerman, essential to Moldavian trade on the route from Caffa through Suceava to Lwow. Stephen took Chilia in 1465 and, after beating Matthias Corvinus at the Battle of Baia in 1467, tried to free Wallachia from Ottoman control, fighting Radu the Handsome and backing rival claimants to its throne. In 1473 he stopped paying tribute. He refused Mehmed's ultimatum to give up Chilia and come to Constantinople, and in November 1474 asked the Pope for help.

Mehmed sent Suleiman Pasha from the siege of Shkodër with an army of Janissaries, sipahis, akinci and Tatar cavalry, joined in Wallachia by 17,000 men under Basarab Laiotă. Stephen's army, reinforced by 1,800 Hungarians, 2,000 Polish horsemen and 5,000 Székely soldiers, included some 30,000 peasants of the Great Army. As the invaders entered Moldavia in December 1474, Stephen burned the land, poisoned the wells and sent people and livestock into the mountains.

He chose to fight at the wooden bridge of Podul Înalt over the Bârlad River, in a marshy valley ringed by wooded hills. On the foggy morning of 10 January, musicians in the valley drew the Ottomans forward into fire from cannon, archers and handgunners on three sides, and the bridge collapsed under their cavalry. Then Stephen attacked from all sides while buglers behind the Ottoman lines spread confusion. Suleiman lost control and retreated, pursued for three days to Obluciţa. Jan Długosz writes that the prisoners were impaled.

Pope Sixtus IV named Stephen Athleta Christi but sent no help, and King Casimir of Poland did nothing. Mehmed invaded in person in 1476 and defeated Stephen at the Battle of Valea Albă, but failed to take Suceava and Neamț. In 1484 Bayezid II took Chilia and Cetatea Albă. Stephen built the Voroneț Monastery in 1488 to commemorate the victory.
battle-of-vedrosha: The First Lithuanian–Muscovite War ended in 1494 with a perpetual peace between Grand Duke Alexander of Lithuania and Grand Duke Ivan III of Moscow, both descended from the Gediminids. Alexander's marriage in 1495 to Elena, daughter of Ivan III, did not bring lasting peace. Ivan declared war again on 3 May 1500, aiming to join Lithuania's eastern lands to Muscovy. The pretext was the flight of Duke Simeon Ivanovich Belsky to Moscow in 1499; Moscow also presented itself as the defender of the Eastern Orthodox in Lithuania and claimed there had been attempts to convert Elena to Catholicism by force.

After the declaration the princes of Chernigov and Novgorod-Seversk went over to Muscovy. The main fighting was on the Smolensk front, and after the Muscovites took the fortress of Dorogobuzh a Lithuanian vanguard of about 3,500 horsemen moved toward Smolensk, joined by 500 horsemen of its regent, Stanisław Kiszka.

The Grand Hetman of Lithuania, Konstanty Ostrogski, underestimated the enemy and decided to attack first with 4,000 men against a Muscovite force of at least 20,000. The Lithuanians struck the camp of the central Muscovite forces on the Vedrosha, a tributary of the Dnieper, but were drawn by the vanguard into an ambush by the main army of about 40,000 under the boyars Daniil Shchenya and Yakov Koshkin-Zakharyin. Little is known of the fighting itself. The entire Lithuanian command was captured, among them Grigalius Astikas and Jonas Liutauras Chreptavičius; Ostrogski escaped from Moscow in 1507.

The defeat deeply affected Lithuanian society, though the Muscovites did not use it to the full: the road to Smolensk lay open, yet they did not try to take the city. Alexander, with the rest of the army about 200 kilometres away, sought in vain to bring the Crimean Khanate under Meñli I Giray and Moldavia under Stephen III into the war against Muscovy. The only help came from the Livonian Order, whose attack on Pskov failed because of dysentery.
battle-of-velbazhd: From the 1280s the Kingdom of Serbia expanded south into northern Macedonia, lands that Bulgaria had lost to the Byzantines. During the Byzantine civil war of 1320 to 1328 the Serbian king Stefan Uroš III, known as Stefan Dečanski, backed the old emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos, while the Bulgarian ruler Michael Shishman backed his brother-in-law Andronikos III. In 1324 Michael had divorced Stefan's sister Anna Neda and married Andronikos III's sister Theodora. The Serbs took Prosek and Prilep and besieged Ohrid in 1329.

Alarmed by Serbia's growth, Bulgaria and the Byzantine Empire concluded an anti-Serb treaty on 13 May 1327 and in 1329 agreed to invade. The plan was to partition Serbia between them. Michael drew on his ally Basarab of Wallachia and on Ossetian and Tatar detachments, and contemporaries put his army at 15,000. Stefan's army of 17,000 included Catalan and German mercenaries, about 1,000 of each.

Coordination between the allies was weak. Andronikos III invaded Macedonia in July 1330 but halted after taking Prilep and five small fortresses. Michael left Tarnovo on 19 July and advanced through Sofia into the Struma valley, while his brother Belaur, setting out from Vidin, took no part in the fighting. Stefan marched south from the Morava and camped near Velbazhd. From 24 July the two sides negotiated and agreed a one-day truce, during which the Bulgarians, short of food, scattered to find supplies.

Reinforced in the night by 1,000 Catalan horsemen led by his son Stefan Dušan, the Serbian king broke the truce and attacked early on 28 July. The main fighting took place at Bozhuritsa, between the village of Shishkovtsi and the Spasovitsa heights. The outnumbered Bulgarian units were crushed, though some resisted stubbornly. Michael was badly wounded and captured, and probably died of his wounds in the Serbian camp on 31 July; other accounts say he died on the field or was killed on Dušan's order. He was buried at Staro Nagoričane.

Bulgaria lost no territory. At Mraka the Bulgarian boyars agreed with Stefan that his nephew Ivan Stefan, son of Anna Neda, would rule Bulgaria, but he was deposed in 1331 in favour of Ivan Alexander. Stefan Dušan overthrew his father the same year and took northern Macedonia in 1333 to 1334, then Albania, Epirus and Thessaly during the Byzantine civil war of 1341 to 1347. On 16 April 1346, in Skopje, he was crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks, with the support of the Bulgarian Patriarch Simeon. The battle is believed to be depicted in the Serbian epic song Ban Milutin and Duka Hercegovac.
battle-of-vercellae: In 113 BCE a migrating Germanic-Celtic alliance headed by the Cimbri and the Teutons entered Noricum, and at the Battle of Noreia overwhelmed a Roman army sent under the consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo. They then moved into Gaul and defeated Roman armies several times, most seriously at Arausio in 105 BCE. There the quarrel between the patrician Quintus Servilius Caepio and the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus left the two Roman armies unwilling to support each other, and the defeat was on a scale not seen since Cannae.

In 104 BCE the Romans sent Gaius Marius against the invaders. In 102 BCE he defeated the Ambrones and Teutons near Aquae Sextiae, while his colleague Quintus Lutatius Catulus, charged with keeping the Cimbri out of Italy, retreated near Tridentum with his army intact. In July 101 BCE the Cimbri were moving west along the Po, and the armies of Marius and Catulus, joined near Placentia, were under Marius, now consul for the fifth time. Negotiations over land for the Cimbri came to nothing, and Marius displayed captured Teuton nobles to their envoys.

Marius agreed the time and place with the Cimbric king Boiorix, choosing the Raudine Plain near Vercellae. The site is traditionally placed near modern Vercelli, though some historians suggest the Polesine near Rovigo or Roddi in the province of Cuneo. The sources give the Romans about 52,000 to 54,000 men and the Cimbri 120,000 to 180,000, figures modern historians treat with scepticism. On 30 July the Romans formed up facing west, so that the Cimbri fought with the morning sun in their eyes and the dust blowing toward them. Marius took the left wing, Catulus the centre and Sulla the cavalry on the right.

The Cimbri advanced in a great square, their cavalry in front. Marius's wing marched into a dust cloud and missed the fighting, which took place around Catulus's centre. The Cimbric cavalry were thrown back by Sulla's horsemen into their own infantry, and Catulus's legionaries advanced with javelins and swords while the other wings closed in. The summer heat added to the Cimbri's trouble. The rout ended against their wagons at the rear and became a massacre that stopped when the Cimbri began to surrender in numbers. Boiorix and his nobles died fighting.

Marius claimed to have killed 100,000 and to have enslaved many thousands more, including women and children. Marius and Catulus quarrelled over credit, and held a joint triumph, with Marius receiving most of the praise. Marius then granted citizenship to his Italian allied troops without consulting the Senate. The war's end also began a growing rivalry between Marius and Sulla, which would lead to the first of Rome's great civil wars.
battle-of-verdun: By late 1914 the war of movement on the Western Front had ended, and offensives gained little ground at heavy cost. According to his memoirs, the German Chief of the General Staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, believed that the French army could still be defeated if it suffered enough casualties. He offered five corps for an offensive at Verdun, but only on the east bank of the Meuse. Verdun, a town that had played an important part in the defence of France for centuries, was ringed by a double line of 28 forts, but in 1915 guns and ammunition had been removed from many of them.

Bad weather delayed the German attack from 12 to 21 February 1916. It began with a ten-hour bombardment by 808 guns, which fired about 1,000,000 shells, and German stormtroopers followed with flamethrowers and grenades. The Germans captured Fort Douaumont four days later. Philippe Pétain ordered that there be no retreat and that German attacks be counter-attacked. The Germans extended the offensive to the west bank of the Meuse to eliminate the French artillery there, but the attacks failed to reach their objectives.

The Germans captured Fort Vaux in June and came within 4 kilometres of the Verdun citadel, but the Brusilov Offensive and the opening of the Battle of the Somme on 1 July forced them to transfer artillery from Verdun. In September and December French counter-offensives recaptured much ground on the east bank, including Fort Douaumont and Fort Vaux. The battle lasted 302 days, the longest of the First World War.

In 2000 Hannes Heer and Klaus Naumann calculated that the French suffered 377,231 casualties and the Germans 337,000, a total of 714,231. Rain and constant bombardment turned the clay soil into mud full of debris and human remains, and forests were obliterated. Accounts of men breaking down with insanity and shell shock were common.

In France, Verdun came to symbolise the determination of the French Army and the destructiveness of the war, and it has become for the French the representative memory of the First World War, as the Somme is for the British. In 1920 a ceremony was held in the citadel of Verdun to choose the body for the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Arc de Triomphe.
battle-of-versinikia: After Krum's victory over Nikephoros I at the Battle of Pliska in 811, the emperor's son Staurakios was left paralysed, and on 2 October 811 senior officials, among them Patriarch Nikephoros I, forced him to abdicate in favour of his brother-in-law Michael I Rangabe. Bulgaria resumed its attacks the next year in Thrace and the Struma valley. In the autumn of 812 a Bulgarian delegation led by Dobromir offered peace, but Michael refused, possibly over the clause of the Treaty of 716 on handing back refugees. Krum then took Mesembria with siege machines built by an emigrant from Arabia, capturing 36 copper siphons for throwing Greek fire and much gold and silver.

When Bulgarian scouting raids in February 813 pulled back after several clashes, Michael took the retreat for a victory and called for a counter-attack. He summoned troops from every theme, including the guards of the Syrian passes, and after delays caused by unrest in the army left Constantinople in May, seen off outside the walls by the people of the city and Empress Prokopia.

A solar eclipse on 4 May shook the soldiers' morale, and the army plundered settlements around Adrianople. In June the two armies camped close together near the fortress of Versinikia; John Skylitzes says the Byzantines were ten times as many. After thirteen days of waiting, the strategos of Macedonia, John Aplakes, attacked with the right wing and pushed back the Bulgarian left, but the centre and left did not follow.

Krum sent Slavic infantry and Bulgar horse archers and heavy cavalry against Aplakes, who was killed with most of his men. The Anatolian theme withdrew first, then the whole army, with Michael and Leo the Armenian among the first commanders to go. The later chroniclers Genesius and Theophanes Continuatus blamed Leo for ordering the flight; J. B. Bury and Steven Runciman agree, while Vasil Zlatarski disputes it.

Michael withdrew to a monastery. On 17 July 813 Krum camped before Constantinople, sacrificed to the god Tangra and offered peace. During the talks the Byzantines shot at his delegation, killing the kavkhan; in reply Krum destroyed the churches, monasteries and palaces outside the walls and razed fortresses around the Sea of Marmara. He forced Adrianople to surrender and resettled 10,000 people north of the Danube. The site of Versinikia is unknown, though an inscription of Krum's reign found at Malomirovo describes the Bulgarian army's dispositions in 813.
battle-of-vertieres: The battle was the last major engagement of the Saint-Domingue expedition, the French attempt to regain control of the colony. In 1802 French forces arrested Governor-General Toussaint Louverture, who said from the ship that took him to prison that they had cut down only the trunk of the tree of black liberty, which would spring back from its many deep roots. In October 1802 Jean Jacques Dessalines rose against the French, rightly fearing that they meant to restore slavery, and defeated them many times. By the end of October 1803 the rebel Indigenous Army held most of Saint-Domingue; the French kept only Môle St. Nicolas, under Noailles, and Cap-Français, where General Donatien de Rochambeau was at bay with 5,000 troops.

During the night of 17 to 18 November 1803 the rebels placed their few guns to fire on Fort Bréda. When French trumpets sounded the alarm, Clervaux fired the first shot. François Capois led his half-brigade up a long ravine under the guns of Vertières; the columns lost men to French fire but closed ranks and climbed past their dead, singing. Capois's horse was shot under him, and he rose, drew his sword and ran on shouting Forward.

Rochambeau, watching from the rampart, had the drums roll a cease-fire, and a staff officer rode out to carry the captain-general's compliments to the general who had covered himself with such glory. Then the fighting resumed. Dessalines sent in his reserves under Gabart, the youngest of the rebel generals, and Gabart, Capois and Clervaux threw back a last French charge. Under cover of a sudden thunderstorm Rochambeau withdrew from Vertières, knowing the colony was lost.

The next morning Rochambeau sent Duveyrier to negotiate, and by evening the terms were settled: the French had ten days to embark and leave. The wounded French soldiers left behind were drowned by the rebels a few days later. In 1826 King Charles X demanded 150 million gold francs before France would recognise Haiti's independence; Louis-Philippe reduced the sum to 90 million in 1838. Haiti celebrates 18 November as a Day of Victory.
battle-of-vienna-1683: Capturing Vienna had long been an Ottoman aim, because the city controlled the Danube and the trade routes to Germany. Suleiman's advance had been stopped at Szigetvár in 1566, and Vienna was not threatened again until 1683. Under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha the Ottomans made extensive preparations. In Habsburg Hungary, unrest against Leopold I's Counter-Reformation had grown into rebellion, and in 1681 the Ottomans reinforced the forces of Imre Thököly. A peace had held between the two empires for twenty years.

The Ottomans laid siege to Vienna on 14 July 1683. Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg, commanding the garrison, refused to surrender, having heard of the massacre at Perchtoldsdorf, where townspeople who had surrendered were killed. The Viennese demolished houses near the walls, and the Ottomans dug trenches and mines towards the city.

Delays in the siege gave a relief force time to arrive. Poles and Imperial troops assembled in only six days under King John III Sobieski, with money from bankers, noblemen and the Pope. Kara Mustafa left his rear to the Khan of Crimea, who refused to attack the relief force as it crossed the Danube. The Wallachian prince Șerban Cantacuzino, sympathetic to the Christian side, also proved unreliable.

On 12 September the Ottomans attacked at 4:00 in the morning to disturb the deployment. Charles of Lorraine's Imperial troops counterattacked and took the villages of Nussdorf and Heiligenstadt, and ten Ottoman mines under the walls were found and disarmed. In the afternoon Polish infantry advanced on the Ottoman right and took Gersthof, and as the Imperial troops closed in, the Polish cavalry charged, in what is noted as the largest cavalry charge in history.

Ottoman losses in the battle itself are put at 8,000 to 15,000 dead, and the relief force lost about 3,500 killed and wounded. The Ottoman raiding of 1683 in the Austrian and Hungarian border zone took 57,220 people as slaves. Kara Mustafa was executed in Belgrade on 25 December. The war continued until 1699, when the Treaty of Karlowitz ceded most of Ottoman Hungary to the Habsburgs. Historians see the battle as the end of Ottoman expansion into Europe, and Pope Innocent XI extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church in commemoration.
battle-of-villalar: In late March 1521 the royalists moved to unite their armies against the rebel stronghold of Torrelobatón. The Constable of Castile marched southwest from Burgos with about 3,000 infantry and 600 cavalry, including soldiers recently moved from the defence of Navarre, to join the Admiral's forces near Tordesillas. He could leave Burgos because the comunero-aligned Count of Salvatierra was tied down in the siege of Medina de Pomar.

The comuneros, weakened by desertions, neither struck the Constable before the armies joined nor harried his march. Their commander, Juan de Padilla, considered falling back to Toro for reinforcements in early April but put off the decision until the early hours of 23 April, by which time the royalists had united at Peñaflor.

The royalists, with 6,000 infantry and 2,400 cavalry, pursued Padilla's 7,000 infantry and 400 cavalry. Heavy rain slowed the rebel foot and made the firearms of their 1,000 arquebusiers nearly useless, and Padilla gave battle at Villalar before he could reach Toro. The rebel artillery failed to stop the cavalry and by some reports did more harm to its own side. Pedro de Alcocer, a friend of the Padillas, claimed the gunners and some 300 soldiers had been bought by the royalists; others blame the rain or panic. The cavalry charges scattered the rebels, with an estimated 500 to 1,000 casualties. The three leaders were beheaded in the Plaza of Villalar before many royalist noblemen.

The rebel cities of Old Castile soon surrendered, and Madrid was retaken. A French invasion of Navarre called the royal army north before it could take Toledo, which held out for some months more. From the 1820s Spanish liberals saw Villalar as the end of Castilian liberties, and Juan Martín Díez, El Empecinado, led an expedition to exhume the three leaders. In 1986 Castile and León made 23 April its official day, and the town calls itself Villalar de los Comuneros.
battle-of-vimy-ridge: Vimy Ridge is an escarpment about 8 km north-east of Arras, some 7 km long and rising to 145 m, with an unobstructed view for tens of kilometres. It fell under German control in October 1914. In 1916 the sector became a theatre of mine warfare, with British tunnelling companies countering German mining in the chalk, and an estimated 150 French, British and German charges were fired between October 1915 and April 1917. The Canadian Corps relieved the British IV Corps on the western slopes in October 1916, and Lieutenant-General Sir Julian Byng, its commander from 28 May 1916, was given the ridge as the objective of the Arras offensive.

Planning drew on lessons from the French at Verdun. The corps was reinforced to about 170,000 men, of whom 97,184 were Canadian, and given a density of one heavy gun for every 20 m and one field gun for every 10 m of its front, three times the heavy guns of the Somme. Battalions rehearsed on full-scale models of the battlefield behind the lines, objectives were assigned down to the platoon, and the corps carried out 55 trench raids in the four months before the attack. The Royal Flying Corps deployed 365 aircraft along the Arras sector, outnumbering the German air service two to one.

The attack began at 5:30 am on Easter Monday, 9 April 1917, in sleet and snow that blew into the defenders' faces. Every gun opened at once, and thirty seconds later engineers fired mines under no man's land. Supported by a creeping barrage, the Canadians took most of the ridge on the first day. Thelus and the crest fell on the second day, and the last objective, a fortified knoll near Givenchy-en-Gohelle, on 12 April. The German 6th Army retreated to the Oppy-Mericourt line.

By nightfall on 12 April the Canadian Corps held the ridge, having suffered 10,602 casualties, of whom 3,598 were killed. Later sources put German casualties at around 20,000, with some 4,000 prisoners. Four members of the corps won the Victoria Cross. Historians attribute the success to technical and tactical innovation, planning, artillery and training, and to the German failure to apply their new defence-in-depth doctrine. Although not generally considered the corps' most important achievement in strategic results, the battle became a symbol of Canadian national achievement and sacrifice. France granted Canada perpetual use of land at the ridge in 1922, and a 100-hectare park surrounds the Canadian National Vimy Memorial, Canada's largest overseas war memorial.
battle-of-vitkov-hill: On 1 March 1420 Pope Martin V issued a papal bull ordering Sigismund and the princes of the east to organise a crusade against the followers of Jan Hus, John Wycliffe and other heretics. On 15 March, in Breslau, Sigismund had Jan Krása, a Hussite leader of the Wrocław uprising of 1418, executed. The Utraquist Hussites concluded that no agreement with him was possible and joined the Taborites to resist.

The crusaders gathered at Schweidnitz and crossed into Bohemia in late April, taking Hradec Králové in early May, while the Taborites won at Mladá Vožice and took Sedlice, Písek and Strakonice. On 22 May Taborite forces entered Prague, and the siege of the city began on 12 June. Chroniclers of the time put the crusading army at 100,000 to 200,000 men; the modern historian Victor Verney thinks it was probably only about 8,000.

Unable to storm the walls, the crusaders planned to encircle Prague by taking the fortifications around it. Vítkov Hill dominated the area east of the city and overlooked roads the crusaders needed for supplies. Its defences were of timber reinforced with stone and clay, with moats around the base and a steep cliff on the northern flank. Tradition holds that 26 men and 3 women held it; the garrison was probably larger, and it is unclear whether Žižka himself was on the hill.

Austrian and Meissen cavalry under Heinrich of Isenburg, governor of Meissen, attacked from the south an hour before sunset, but the terrain forced them onto a narrow path. As the defenders were slowly pushed back, reinforcements from the New Town struck the knights in the flank through the vineyards. Trapped against the cliff, the crusaders panicked, and many drowned in the Vltava as they fled.

The crusaders lost between 400 and 500 knights, gave up hope of starving the city into submission, and their army disintegrated. The castles of Vyšehrad and Hradčany, still held by Sigismund's troops, soon capitulated, Sigismund had to withdraw from Prague, and the crusaders fell back to Kutná Hora. The hill was renamed Žižkov in honour of Jan Žižka.
battle-of-vittorio-veneto: After the Battle of Caporetto in 1917 General Armando Diaz replaced Luigi Cadorna as Italian Supreme Commander and stabilised the front on the Piave with defence in depth and mobile reserves. The Austro-Hungarian offensive of June 1918 ended in heavy defeat. Diaz then waited until success was assured. His plan was for three of the five armies between Monte Grappa and the Adriatic to cross the Piave towards Vittorio Veneto and cut communications between the two Austro-Hungarian armies facing them. The Allies fielded 57 infantry divisions, including 52 Italian, three British, two French and a US regiment, with 7,700 guns to the Austro-Hungarian 6,030. Both sides were ravaged by influenza and malaria.

On the night of 23 October British and Italian troops, rowed across the river by Italian engineers, seized the island of Grave di Papadopoli. In the early hours of 24 October, the anniversary of Caporetto, the Italian Fourth Army attacked on Monte Grappa to draw in reserves. Flooding of the Piave delayed two of the three central armies, but Lord Cavan's Tenth Army won a foothold on the far bank on 27 October. Its bridgehead was about 4 km deep, and the British took 3,520 prisoners and 54 guns. That day General Boroevic ordered a counter-attack, but his troops refused to obey.

Political collapse followed. On 28 October a group of Czechs declared Bohemia's independence, the Austro-Hungarian command ordered a general retreat, and on 31 October the Hungarian Parliament withdrew from the union. The Italian Eighth Army entered Vittorio Veneto on 30 October. Trieste was taken by an amphibious expedition on 3 November. The Armistice of Villa Giusti was signed on 3 November at 15:20 and took effect at 15:00 on 4 November.

The Italians took 448,000 prisoners, about a third of the Austro-Hungarian army, with about 5,600 cannon and mortars. Italian casualties in the ten days were 37,461 killed and wounded, 24,507 of them on Monte Grappa, with 2,139 British and 778 French. The armistice required evacuation of South Tyrol, Trieste, Istria and Dalmatia among other territory, and Italian troops occupied North Tyrol by the end of November. Austria-Hungary dissolved, and less than a week later the German Empire asked for an armistice. Erich Ludendorff wrote that the Austro-Hungarian army had completely dissolved in the fighting, while Ernst Nolte called the battle merely the coup de grace to an army abandoned by an already crumbling state.
battle-of-vlaardingen: Frisia, the most remote part of the duchy of Lower Lotharingia, fell under Adalbold, bishop of Utrecht, and under Count Dirk III, to whom the defence of the western coast had been delegated. Dirk had his power base at Vlaardingen, where the Merwede met the Meuse. He forced sailors on the Merwede to pay a heavy tribute, endangering the trade route between Tiel and England and the emperor's tax income, and he had occupied lands claimed by the bishop of Utrecht and built a castle there.

At a diet in Nijmegen at Easter 1018 Emperor Henry II heard the complaints of the Tiel merchants and Bishop Adalbold II of Utrecht. Dirk refused to change his ways and left. An army gathered at Tiel to sail down the Waal and Merwede, with troops supplied also by Baldrick II of Liège, Gerhard of Cambrai and Archbishop Heribert of Cologne. Baldrick fell ill on the way and died on the day of the battle.

The fleet moored at Vlaardingen and the army marched toward the castle. To avoid the many ditches, Duke Godfrey led his men toward a flat field, and during this manoeuvre the Frisians attacked from an ambush. A cry that the duke had been killed set off a panic; the imperial troops ran for their ships, which the falling tide had left in mid-stream, and sank in the soggy bank or drowned, while others were finished off with javelins. Dirk rode out late in the fight and captured Godfrey, saving his life.

Godfrey was soon released and reconciled the bishop and the count, perhaps because both saw that defending the coast against Viking attacks mattered more. Knowledge of the battle comes from three chronicles written soon afterwards: those of Alpertus of Metz, Thietmar of Merseburg and the bishops of Cambrai. The Cambrai Chronicle's claim that a thousand routed twenty thousand is very likely a borrowing from Deuteronomy, and Kees Nieuwenhuijsen concluded in 2018 that a few hundred fought. The battle is seen as the start of the later County of Holland's greater de facto autonomy.
battle-of-vouille: The battle was fought at Vouillé, near Poitiers, around the spring of 507 in the Franco-Gothic War, between the Franks under Clovis and the Visigoths under Alaric II. Clovis had already defeated the Alemanni east of the Rhine and the Burgundians in the Rhone Valley, and the growing power of the Franks threatened Alaric's territory in Aquitaine and Hispania. Theodoric the Great tried to broker peace between the two kings, but Clovis began a campaign to seize Aquitaine and Alaric's centre of power at Toulouse. Alaric marched north with his army and an Auvergnat militia commanded by Apollinaris of Clermont.

Clovis's army was slowed by the rain-swollen Vienne River, but it still engaged the Visigoths south of Vouillé. He kept his missile troops at the rear and sent the rest of the army forward to fight hand to hand. Although Alaric's army was larger and better equipped, his soldiers wavered after all the Auvergnat commanders except Apollinaris were killed. In the melee Clovis allegedly killed Alaric himself, whereupon the Visigothic army broke and fled. Clovis's army then went south and plundered Alaric's treasure at Toulouse.

The Franks conquered Gallia Aquitania, and the Visigoths withdrew to Septimania, which they continued to hold. The Byzantine emperor Anastasius made Clovis an honorary consul and patrician. Alaric's illegitimate son Gesalec tried to organise a counterstroke at Narbonne but was deposed and eventually killed when Narbonne was taken by the Burgundian allies of the Franks. Clovis later drove the Goths out of Angoulême, and his son Theuderic I defeated them in Hispania.
