battle-of-wadi-al-khaznadar: In 1260 Hulagu Khan invaded the Middle East as far as Palestine, but he was recalled to Mongolia and left two tumens under the general Kitbuqa, which were defeated at the Battle of Ain Jalut. A renewed invasion was delayed when Hulagu's cousin Berke of the Golden Horde allied with the Mamluks. Nearly 20 years after the Mongol defeat at the Second Battle of Homs, Ghazan Khan crossed the Euphrates, the border between the two powers, in 1299 with an army of Mongols, Georgians and Armenians, seized Aleppo and advanced to a few miles north of Homs.

The Mamluk sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad, who was in Syria at the time, marched north from Damascus with 20,000 to 30,000 Mamluks, more according to some sources. The armies met at Wadi al-Khaznadar, north-east of Homs, early on the morning of 22 December 1299. The Mamluk cavalry charged first; the Mongol heavy cavalry answered while Mongol archers, standing behind their horses, shot into the Mamluk ranks, and the fighting soon became hand-to-hand.

In the afternoon the Mongols broke through the Mamluk right flank. Messages could take hours to cross the battlefield, and the Mamluk army began to rout when news of the breakthrough reached it. Mamluk sources claim that only 200 of their soldiers died against 5,000 to 10,000 Mongols, figures that are considered false given the collapse of the Mamluk right; since the Mongols held the field and went on to take Damascus, the Mamluks are assumed to have suffered a serious reverse.

The Mamluks fled south towards Damascus, harassed on the way by 12,000 Maronite and Druze bowmen, and a Mongol force under the general Mulay pursued them as far as Gaza and back into Egypt. The Mongols sacked Damascus and besieged its citadel, and raiding parties reached Jerusalem and ranged across Palestine. In 1300 the Mongol army withdrew, needing fodder for its horses and having to repel an invasion by the Chagatai Khanate. No Christian effort followed to build on the victory, and the Mamluks soon took back Syria and Palestine. The Georgian and Armenian part in the campaign was unrelated to the crusades of the West.
battle-of-wagram: In 1809 Napoleon had moved a number of soldiers from the Confederation of the Rhine to the Peninsular War. The Austrian Empire saw its chance to recover some of its former sphere of influence and invaded the Kingdom of Bavaria, a French ally. Napoleon beat the Austrian forces and occupied Vienna at the beginning of May 1809, but Archduke Charles of Austria-Teschen salvaged an army and retreated north of the Danube, so the war went on.

Towards the end of May, Napoleon suffered a surprise defeat at the Battle of Aspern-Essling, which cost some 53,000 casualties, almost equally divided between the two armies. It took him six weeks to prepare his next offensive, for which he gathered a French, German and Italian army of over 150,000 men near Vienna.

The battle began after Napoleon crossed the Danube with the bulk of his forces during the night of 4 July and attacked the Austrian army, which had over 130,000 men. On the first day he tried for an early breakthrough with a series of evening attacks. The Austrians were thinly spread in a wide semicircle but held a naturally strong position, and the attacks failed. Napoleon knew by that night that he had sustained high losses.

At dawn on 6 July Archduke Charles launched attacks along the whole line, hoping to take the French in a double envelopment. The offensive failed against the French right but nearly broke Napoleon's left. He redeployed IV Corps under Masséna to steady that wing and set up a grand battery, while Marshal Davout attacked the Austrian left. With his flank collapsing and no reserves left, Charles ordered an orderly retreat.

Napoleon was the uncontested winner but did not secure an overwhelming victory. With more than 300,000 combatants, it was the largest battle in European history up to that time, and with at least 72,000 casualties it was the bloodiest engagement of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars thus far. The cause was an unprecedented concentration of artillery on a flat battlefield; each army fired at least 90,000 roundshot. French casualties numbered 34,000, including over thirty generals.

On 7 July Napoleon made General MacDonald a Marshal of the Empire on the field, the only man so raised, and later gave Louis-Alexandre Berthier the title of 1st Prince of Wagram. The Treaty of Schönbrunn meant the loss of one sixth of the Austrian Empire's subjects.
battle-of-warsaw-1920: Poland fought after the First World War to keep its newly regained independence and to fix its eastern borders. In April 1920 Józef Piłsudski allied with the Ukrainian leader Symon Petlyura, and their forces entered Kiev on 7 May. A Soviet counter-offensive then forced the Poles back, and the Red Army's 1st Cavalry Army under Semyon Budyonny broke through in early June. On 4 July Mikhail Tukhachevsky's Western Front began an assault from the Berezina River, and by the end of July it had reached Białystok.

Vladimir Lenin viewed Poland as a bridge to Central and Western Europe, and Bolshevik speeches held that the shortest route to Berlin and Paris lay through Warsaw. Foreign observers expected Poland to collapse.

On the night of 5-6 August Piłsudski conceived a plan in which Polish armies would hold Warsaw while a strike group of about 20,000 men, under his own command, attacked northward from the Wieprz River into the weak point between the Soviet fronts. Many officers called it amateurish, and Piłsudski himself called it a gamble. Tukhachevsky meanwhile planned to cross the Vistula north-west of Warsaw and encircle the city.

The Soviet assault on Warsaw began on 12 August, and Radzymin, east of the city, fell on 14 August. Polish forces retook it on 15 August. Budyonny's army, influenced by command quarrels, marched on Lwów rather than Warsaw. On 16 August Piłsudski's group advanced 45 kilometres against almost no opposition and cut the communications of the Soviet 16th Army. Polish radio units also broke Soviet ciphers. On 18 August Tukhachevsky ordered a retreat, but by 21 August organised resistance had ceased.

Three Soviet armies and a cavalry corps largely disintegrated, and between 25,000 and 30,000 Soviet troops crossed into East Prussia, where they were briefly interned. Polish victories followed at the Battle of Komarów on 31 August and at the Niemen River in September. A ceasefire was signed on 12 October under pressure from France and Britain, and the Treaty of Riga was signed on 18 March 1921.

The name Miracle on the Vistula was coined by the deputy Stanisław Stroński, who disapproved of Piłsudski's Ukrainian campaign. Prime Minister Wincenty Witos replied that this was the miracle of 1920. Many participants credited the Virgin Mary, since 15 August is the feast of the Assumption. The Soviet defeat ended plans for revolutions in Germany and elsewhere, and cancelled a planned Soviet move against Lithuania.
battle-of-waterberg: From the start of the Herero uprising in January 1904 until 11 June, the German campaign was directed by the colonial governor, Colonel Theodor Leutwein, who combined military pressure with talks aimed at a settlement. After a series of skirmishes the Germans cornered the Herero at the Waterberg Plateau, but the German government replaced Leutwein with Lieutenant General Lothar von Trotha, expecting him to end the revolt with a decisive victory.

The plateau lay 100 km east of the railhead, and Trotha spent nearly three months bringing troops and supplies forward by ox cart. His force of just over 1,500 men had 1,625 modern rifles, 30 artillery pieces and 14 machine guns. Under Samuel Maharero the Herero, expecting peace negotiations, had gathered some 3,500 to 6,000 warriors with their families and their cattle, living on scarce grass and water.

On the eve of the battle the Germans stood in six columns around the Waterberg, with Trotha's headquarters in the south. His plan was to squeeze the Herero south of the plateau with columns from the east and west while two more columns sealed the escape routes to the south and south-east. The south-eastern column failed to reach its position in time and did not report the failure, and the western column pressed on past its appointed line, driving the Herero through the gap.

Herero mounted infantry and irregulars holding the Waterberg military station were quickly beaten by German artillery and Maxim guns, but the bulk of the Herero and their cattle escaped eastwards into the Omaheke Desert. At the end of a long supply line, the Germans could not pursue at once. Trotha reported a complete victory to Berlin.

Trotha then ordered the pursuit of the Herero into the desert, denying them pasture and water holes, and on 2 October issued his extermination order: any Herero found within the German borders would be shot. Tens of thousands died of thirst, starvation or disease; German patrols later found skeletons around holes 8 to 16 m deep dug in search of water, and those who tried to surrender were shot. After Berlin countermanded the order, captured survivors were sent to the concentration camp on Shark Island. Samuel Maharero and about 1,000 of his men crossed the Kalahari Desert to asylum in the Bechuanaland Protectorate.
battle-of-waterloo: When Napoleon I returned to power in March 1815, at the start of the Hundred Days, the powers at the Congress of Vienna declared him an outlaw, and the United Kingdom, Russia, Austria and Prussia mobilised armies as the Seventh Coalition. Critically outnumbered, Napoleon judged that his only chance was to attack before the coalition was ready. Wellington's and Blücher's armies were cantoned close to the north-eastern border of France, and he planned to strike them separately. On 16 June he defeated the bulk of the Prussian army at the Battle of Ligny, while a smaller French force fought the Battle of Quatre Bras. The Prussians withdrew in good order, and Wellington fell back in parallel to the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean near Waterloo.

On Sunday 18 June the French army of around 74,500 men and 254 guns faced a multinational army under Wellington. Napoleon had sent a third of his forces after the Prussians, and they were held at the Battle of Wavre. The French attacked the farm of Hougoumont in the morning, then bombarded the centre with the 80 guns of the grande batterie and sent infantry columns forward. British heavy cavalry charged in support of the hard-pressed infantry. Around 16:00 Marshal Ney, mistaking the movement of wounded to the rear for a retreat, led massed cavalry, about 9,000 horsemen, against Wellington's centre, but they could not break the infantry squares. The French later captured the farm of La Haye Sainte.

At about 13:15 Napoleon had seen Prussian columns approaching his right flank, and from about 16:30 Prussian corps under Bülow, Zieten and Pirch arrived in strength and fought through Plancenoit. At about 19:30 Napoleon committed his last reserve, the Imperial Guard. Wellington's line repulsed it, the Prussians broke through on the French right, and the French army was routed.

Wellington lost around 17,000 killed or wounded and Blücher some 7,000. Napoleon lost between 24,000 and 26,000 killed or wounded, including 6,000 to 7,000 captured, and about 15,000 more deserted in the following days. Wellington called the battle the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life. Napoleon abdicated four days later, and coalition forces entered Paris on 7 July. The defeat ended the Hundred Days and the First French Empire.

Later generations in Europe saw Waterloo as the turning point that ended the wars convulsing Europe since the French Revolution and ushered in the Concert of Europe, a period of relative peace often called the Pax Britannica. The battlefield lies about 15 kilometres south of Brussels. In 1820 King William I of the Netherlands ordered a monument there, and the Lion's Mound, a hill built from 300,000 cubic metres of earth taken from the ridge, now dominates the site.
battle-of-wesenberg-1268: Before the battle the Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Dorpat had promised Novgorod not to interfere in its war against Danish Estonia. In 1267 a Novgorodian army, which Russian chronicles say was led by Yury of Suzdal and first meant to march against the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, turned instead beyond the Narva River, ravaged the land around Wesenberg and failed to take its castle. The posadnik of Novgorod, Mikhail Fyodorovich, then pressed for a new offensive, and in 1268 the forces of several Russian princes raided northern Estonia.

The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle, the only contemporary source on the battle that survives unaltered, says the Russians invaded in January 1268 and looted the countryside. The Danish vassals called for help and received 34 Brothers of the Order from Weissenstein, Leal and Fellin, with lesser troops, and men of the Bishopric under Bishop Alexander of Dorpat, who fell early in the fighting. Estonian troops held the left, the Danish king's men the right. Two Russian formations were driven back and routed, but Prince Dmitry regrouped about 5,000 men; the chronicle claims that after a fight at a bridge over a deep river 5,000 Russians lay dead.

The Chronicle of Novgorod, rewritten several times, above all in the 15th century, tells it otherwise. The Russians left for Wesenberg on 23 January, besieged Estonians hiding in a cave by channelling water into it, and met the German force at the river Kegola, whose iron troops advanced in a great wedge. Many boyars were killed and Prince Yury fled, but the Germans were pushed back to the town, and before dawn after the fighting of 18 February they withdrew from the field.

Among the Russian dead was the posadnik Mikhail Fyodorovich. Some see a Livonian victory as more plausible, since the Russians left Danish Estonia and the Livonian Knights attacked Izborsk and Pskov in June 1269; Russian historiographic tradition counts the battle a Russian victory, noting the loot brought home. On 30 May 1268 the Teutonic Order and the merchants of Lübeck stopped trade with Novgorod. The Livonian siege of Pskov failed, peace with Novgorod followed in 1269, and in 1270, at war with the Lithuanians, the Livonians gave up their claims to north-western Russia in a treaty with Yaroslav of Novgorod.
battle-of-white-mountain: Most Bohemian estates, though under the Holy Roman Empire, had large Protestant populations and rights granting them religious and political freedom. In 1617 Ferdinand, a devout Catholic and supporter of the Counter-Reformation, was named successor to Emperor Matthias as emperor and King of Bohemia. Protestants feared for their property and their semi-autonomy, under which the king was elected, and Rudolf II's 1609 Letter of Majesty seemed violated.

In May 1618 two imperial representatives and their scribe were thrown from a high window at the royal castle in Prague, the Third Defenestration of Prague, which began the Bohemian Revolt. In November 1619 the Calvinist Frederick V, Elector Palatine, was chosen King of Bohemia.

In 1620 Ferdinand II set out to conquer Bohemia. Frederick's commander Christian of Anhalt had raised an army of 30,000, reduced to about 15,000 by earlier reverses. Ferdinand's force of about 25,000 included Imperial troops under the Count of Bucquoy and Catholic League troops under Field Marshal Tilly. Anhalt reached the White Mountain, in fact a low plateau, just ahead of the Imperial army but had little time to build defences.

On 8 November a small Imperial force probed the Protestant flank and the Bohemians retreated. Anhalt's son Christian II led a cavalry charge that routed several regiments, but Tilly's cavalry drove it back. The Bohemian infantry fired one volley at extreme range and retreated, most companies without entering the battle. The fighting lasted about an hour. Some 4,000 Protestants were killed or captured, against about 700 Imperial losses.

Tilly entered Prague and the revolt collapsed. Frederick fled with his wife Elizabeth after a year on the throne, earning the nickname the Winter King. Of forty-seven leaders tried, twenty-seven were executed in the Old Town Square. An estimated five-sixths of the Bohemian nobility went into exile and their properties were confiscated. In 1621 the emperor ordered Calvinists and other non-Lutherans to leave or convert, and in 1626 Lutherans too. Most Bohemians converted. The battle began two centuries of recatholicization of the Czech lands.
battle-of-white-wolf-mountain: The warlord Yuan Shao had allied with the Wuhuan in the 190s against their common enemy Gongsun Zan, giving their chieftains seals as chanyus and marrying his subordinates' daughters to their leaders. After Yuan Shao's defeat by Cao Cao at the Battle of Guandu and his death, his sons fought over the succession. Yuan Tan was killed fighting Cao Cao, and Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi, driven out of You Province by a mutiny, fled north to the Wuhuan.

The Wuhuan were then united under Tadun, who was rumoured to seek a hegemony over the northern tribes like that of Modu Chanyu of the Xiongnu. Their raids across the border in Yuan Shang's name were said to have carried off over 100,000 Chinese families. Cao Cao had Dong Zhao dig the Pinglu and Quanzhou canals to carry supplies north, and against generals who feared an attack from Liu Biao in the south, his strategist Guo Jia urged a swift campaign.

In the summer of 207 Cao Cao advanced to Wuzhong, where the local leader Tian Chou submitted to him. Monsoon rains flooded the coastal route towards the Wuhuan base at Liucheng, and the Wuhuan held the river crossings. On Tian Chou's advice Cao Cao feigned a retreat, leaving signs saying he would wait for autumn, and following Guo Jia's maxim that swiftness is the key in war, he left the baggage behind and led a light force over the hills of Xuwu, through Lulong Pass and over 500 li of difficult country, outflanking Tadun's positions.

Tadun, Yuan Shang, Yuan Xi and the chanyus Louban and Wuyan gathered tens of thousands of men and met Cao Cao at White Wolf Mountain. Seeing from a slope that the Wuhuan were not in order, Cao Cao attacked at once; Cao Chun's brigade captured Tadun, who was killed with many of his men, and over 200,000 Chinese settlers and Wuhuan surrendered.

The Yuan brothers fled to Gongsun Kang in Liaodong. Cao Cao declined to pursue, predicting that Gongsun Kang would kill them, and he did, sending their heads to Liucheng. The march home was hard, and Guo Jia died during the campaign. The Wuhuan cavalry became known as the finest in the empire, and in 208 Cao Cao took the title of Imperial Chancellor. The scattered Wuhuan were gradually absorbed, most into the Xianbei.
battle-of-wilkomierz: When Vytautas the Great died without an heir in October 1430, the Lithuanian nobles elected Švitrigaila, brother of Jogaila, as Grand Duke without consulting Poland, in breach of the Union of Horodło of 1413. Sigismund Kęstutaitis deposed him in a coup on 31 August 1432, and Švitrigaila rallied the Slavic lands of the Grand Duchy from Polotsk. Secretly backed by the Teutonic Knights through their Livonian branch, he lost the Battle of Ashmyany in December 1432 but kept raiding; with Livonia he organised six raids into Lithuania, the last of which ended at Wiłkomierz.

Švitrigaila led about 11,000 men: Lithuanians and Orthodox Ruthenians from Polotsk, Vitebsk, Smolensk, Kiev and Volhynia, Livonian knights and their mercenaries, at least 500 Tatars of the Golden Horde and his nephew Sigismund Korybut, a veteran of the Hussite Wars. Sigismund's probably smaller army was commanded by his son Michael, with 4,000 Polish troops under Jakub Kobylański. The armies faced each other for two days across Lake Žirnajai and a marshy creek about 9 kilometres south of Vilkmergė.

When Švitrigaila and the Livonian Grand Master Franco Kerskorff moved north, their army was split by a rivulet and Sigismund attacked. The banner of the Livonian marshal Werner von Nesselrode fell first, and panic followed. Kerskorff, his marshal and several komturs were killed; Korybut was captured and died days later. Švitrigaila escaped to Polotsk with about 30 followers, while the victors hunted survivors for 15 days.

The damage to the Livonian Order is often compared to that of the Battle of Grunwald on the Teutonic Order. By the peace signed at Brześć Kujawski on 31 December 1435, the Orders promised not to interfere in the internal affairs of Lithuania or Poland. The Livonian Confederation agreement was signed on 4 December 1435, and the Order lost its crusading character. Švitrigaila retreated to Moldavia in 1438, and Sigismund ruled unchallenged until his assassination in 1440. He built a church on the battlefield, around which the town of Pabaiskas grew.
battle-of-wimpfen: In the Bohemian Revolt the Protestant nobility of Bohemia refused to confirm the Catholic Ferdinand II as king and offered the crown to Frederick V of the Palatinate. Frederick was crowned in 1619 but lost the kingdom to Catholic League troops under Tilly at the Battle of the White Mountain in 1620. Divided, the Protestant Union declared its neutrality in the Treaty of Ulm in 1620 and dissolved the next year.

Georg Friedrich of Baden-Durlach, one of the Union's generals, kept the mercenary army he had raised. When Tilly moved from Bavaria towards the Palatinate in April 1622, the margrave declared for Frederick and joined Count Mansfeld shortly after Mansfeld's victory over Tilly at Mingolsheim on 27 April. While Mansfeld crossed the Neckar at Heidelberg to join Christian of Brunswick, Georg Friedrich pursued Tilly towards Wimpfen, unaware that Córdoba had reinforced him with several thousand men.

Late on 5 May the Protestants crossed the Böllinger Bach near Obereisesheim and formed their lines. On 6 May both sides, each behind a wagenburg with strong artillery, made cautious and unsuccessful attacks until about 11 o'clock. Tilly kept Córdoba's troops in reserve, fearing that another Protestant army would arrive, and when the Catholic lines began to give way his elite regiments held in a tight pike formation that drove off the margrave's cavalry. In the afternoon a Catholic assault on the Protestant right flank put its cavalry to flight. At about six o'clock a cannon shot blew up the Protestant powder magazine, the wagenburg fell, and many died trying to escape across the creek.

Georg Friedrich, wounded in the face, escaped to Stuttgart and abdicated in favour of his eldest son. Catholic troops devastated his lands, and in August a large part of them went to William, Margrave of Baden-Baden, of the rival Catholic branch; the margraviate stayed divided until 1771. Tilly won again at Höchst in June and took the Palatinate's fortified towns one by one. In 1623 the Diet of Regensburg gave Frederick's lands and electoral seat to Duke Maximilian of Bavaria.
battle-of-worringen: Duke Waleran IV of Limburg died without male heirs in 1279, and his daughter Ermengarde's husband, Count Reginald I of Guelders, claimed the duchy and had his title recognised by King Rudolf I in 1282. When Ermengarde died childless in 1283, Count Adolf VIII of Berg, Waleran's nephew, put forward his own claim and sold it in September 1283 to Duke John I of Brabant, who wanted to rebuild the old Duchy of Lower Lorraine. Limburg also lay along the Via Regia trade route to Aachen and Cologne. Archbishop Siegfried II of Westerburg, wary of Brabant's growing power, allied with Reginald in 1284, joined by Count Henry VI of Luxembourg and Count Adolf of Nassau.

After years of indecisive clashes, Reginald sold his rights to Henry of Luxembourg in May 1288, just before peace talks. John of Brabant marched with the troops of Berg and Mark to besiege the archbishop's castle of Worringen on the Rhine, supported by Cologne's citizens, who wanted to be free of the archbishop's rule. Siegfried and Henry gathered their forces at Neuss and set out for Worringen early on 5 June.

Early in the fighting John and Henry met in a fierce clash in which Henry and two of his brothers were killed. Siegfried's advance pushed back the Berg troops and the Cologne militia, but his reserves gave too little support. In mid-afternoon the men of Berg, Mark and Cologne rallied and attacked again. Daniel van Bouchout captured Reginald, and John took the archbishop prisoner and handed him to Adolf of Berg.

Deaths are estimated at 1,100 on the Guelders side and 40 on Brabant's. Siegfried spent over a year at Schloss Burg before paying a ransom, and Worringen Castle was demolished. On 14 August 1288 Adolf granted city rights to Düsseldorf. Limburg passed to Brabant in 1289, and Cologne became a free imperial city in 1475. Jan van Heelu wrote a chronicle of the battle.
battle-of-worth: After part of the French army was beaten at the Battle of Wissembourg, Marshal MacMahon took up a position along the western bank of the Sauer, from Morsbronn and the Niederwald to the heights west of Wœrth and the woods northeast of Frœschwiller. The German Third Army under Crown Prince Frederick William, directed by his chief of staff General Leonhard Graf von Blumenthal, was moving south towards Haguenau, and its cavalry found the French on 5 August. A false alarm that evening kept the French in bivouac rather than in camp; without it, the battle would probably not have been fought.

At dawn on 6 August Prussian outposts shelled French stragglers in Wœrth, and although German orders forbade a general engagement, the firing drew in the II Bavarian Corps under Jakob von Hartmann. When the Bavarians fell back, General Hugo von Kirchbach brought the Prussian V Corps and 84 guns into action, while units of the XI Corps under General Julius von Bose crossed the Sauer and fought a stubborn battle for the Niederwald against General Lartigue's division.

The decisive move came when General von Schkopp ignored an order and led his brigade on Morsbronn, turning the French right. French cavalry charges failed at heavy cost; 700 cuirassiers were trapped in Morsbronn and shot down within minutes. By 15:00 the Germans held the Niederwald, and after repeated French counter-attacks were broken by artillery fire, a final rush took Frœschwiller. The Prussian cavalry division arrived only late at night, and the French escaped in the darkness.

MacMahon received no help from neighbouring French troops, and the battle was won by weight of numbers: 71,000 German rifles and 234 guns came into action against 32,000 French rifles and 101 guns. The French chassepot made nearly twice as many hits as the Prussian needle gun, but the French had no answer to the German artillery. The Germans lost 103 officers and 1,483 men killed, 383 officers and 7,207 men wounded, and 1,373 missing. The French lost 5,884 killed and wounded and perhaps 9,212 captured, about a third of their force; the 2nd Turcos lost 93 per cent.
battle-of-wuzhang-plains: In the spring of 234 Zhuge Liang, the chancellor of Shu, led more than 60,000 troops out of Xie Valley and camped on the southern bank of the Wei River near Mei County. Worried that his long supply line could not feed the army, he applied the tuntian policy, setting his soldiers to farm alongside the local people and forbidding them to take the civilians' crops.

The Wei emperor Cao Rui sent General Qin Lang with 20,000 men to reinforce Sima Yi, his commander in the region. Sima Yi crossed the river and camped with the Wei behind him, judging that the south bank, where many civilians had gathered, would be hotly contested.

In the first clashes Shu crossbowmen beat off Sima Yi's cavalry, while Guo Huai, foreseeing that Zhuge Liang would try to seize the plains north of the river, occupied them and drove off a Shu attack. Guo Huai also saw through a feint in the west and held Yangsui when the Shu attacked it at night, and Zhuge Liang fell back to the Wuzhang Plains. The Book of Jin's account of a Wei night raid that killed 500 Shu soldiers is disputed by historians.

Cao Rui then ordered Sima Yi not to give battle. When Zhuge Liang sent him a woman's ornaments as a taunt, the minister Xin Pi used the imperial sceptre to keep him in camp. Asking a Shu envoy about Zhuge Liang's habits, Sima Yi heard that he ate little and managed almost everything himself, and predicted that he would soon die. Sometime between 11 September and 10 October 234 Zhuge Liang fell gravely ill; he named Jiang Wan and then Fei Yi as his successors and gave secret orders for the retreat.

After more than 100 days Sima Yi learned of the death and pursued, but turned back when the Shu army under Yang Yi formed to resist, which gave rise to the saying that a dead Zhuge scares away a living Zhongda. During the retreat the general Wei Yan quarrelled with Yang Yi, each accusing the other of treason, and Wei Yan was killed by Ma Dai. Jiang Wan, Zhuge Liang's successor, put domestic affairs before expansion, and Sima Yi's rise prepared the way for his grandson Sima Yan's Jin dynasty.
battle-of-xiaoting: In late 219 Lü Meng, a general serving Sun Quan, invaded Liu Bei's territories in southern Jing Province while Guan Yu, who guarded them, was away at the Battle of Fancheng; Guan Yu was captured in an ambush and executed. Cao Pi founded the state of Wei in December 220, Liu Bei declared himself emperor of the Han on 10 May 221, and on 23 September 221 Sun Quan became a vassal of Wei with the title King of Wu. Zhao Yun and the official Qin Mi advised against war, Zhang Fei was assassinated by his own subordinates while mobilising, and peace talks through Zhuge Jin came to nothing.

In August 221 Wu Ban and Feng Xi took the Wu positions at the Wu Gorge, and the Shu army of over 40,000 troops advanced to Zigui County. Sun Quan gave Lu Xun 50,000 troops as Grand Chief Controller. In February 222 Liu Bei moved along the southern bank of the Yangtze, leaving Huang Quan to guard the northern bank against Wei, and built about 10 fortified garrisons at the border of Yiling. Lu Xun refused his officers' calls to attack and saw through a lure in which 8,000 Shu troops lay in ambush in the valleys.

When he struck, Lu Xun had each man carry straw for a fire attack and followed it with an all-out assault. Feng Xi, Zhang Nan, Ma Liang and the tribal king Shamoke were killed, and over 40 Shu camps were destroyed. Liu Bei fell back to the Ma'an Hills, where landslides cost him thousands more, and escaped at night through the mountains to Yufu County, which he renamed Yong'an. His boats, equipment and supplies were all captured.

Huang Quan's army on the northern bank was cut off and defected to Wei. On the advice of Lu Xun, Zhu Ran and Luo Tong, who distrusted Cao Pi's intentions, Sun Quan did not pursue Liu Bei to Baidicheng, and Cao Pi soon invaded Wu from three directions. Before his death on 10 June 223 Liu Bei named his son Liu Shan as successor, with Zhuge Liang and Li Yan as regents. Zhuge Liang made peace with Wu and restored the Wu–Shu alliance against Wei.

The campaign is told in chapters 81–84 of the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms by Luo Guanzhong, which adds fictitious episodes; according to the Sanguozhi, Huang Zhong died in 220 and Zhao Yun took no part in the battle.
battle-of-yamama: After the death of Muhammad in June 632, many Arab tribes rebelled against the State of Medina. Caliph Abu Bakr organised 11 corps to deal with the rebels. One was commanded by Ikrima ibn Amr, who was ordered to make contact with the forces of Musaylima, a self-proclaimed prophet, at al-Yamama, but not to engage him. Abu Bakr meant to tie Musaylima down so that Khalid ibn al-Walid could deal with the rebels of north-central Arabia.

Ikrima grew impatient as news arrived of Khalid's victories and attacked at the end of October 632, and Musaylima defeated him. Shurahbil ibn Hasana, told to wait, made the same mistake and was also defeated. Abu Bakr then ordered Khalid to destroy Musaylima's forces, giving him Shurahbil's corps as well as his own. Musaylima was encamped on the plain of Aqraba with an army of 40,000, whose confidence had grown with the two victories.

The battle was fought in December 632 in the region of al-Yamama, south of Riyadh in present-day Saudi Arabia. On Khalid's orders the Muslims attacked along the whole front. The worst slaughter took place in a gulley, which became known as the Gulley of Blood. The battle hung in the balance, and the warriors withdrew to rest. The next phase is clouded by legend, but the accounts show that the enemy force largely disintegrated.

Only about a quarter of Musaylima's army was still fit to fight. It withdrew to a walled garden, and a little over 7,000 rebels, Musaylima among them, took shelter inside and shut the gate. A Muslim soldier, al-Bara' ibn Malik, climbed the wall and opened it.

Fighting in the garden became increasingly vicious. Musaylima was struck by a javelin thrown by Wahshi ibn Harb, who had earlier killed Hamza, uncle of Muhammad, at Uhud, but accounts of who killed him conflict. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan claimed the blow, a claim the Umayyads supported, while others named Wahshi, Abd Allah ibn Zayd or Abu Dujana. After his death his forces broke, and about 7,000 rebels died in the garden, which became known as the Garden of Death.

The rebellion within the Rashidun Caliphate was crushed. In Medina there was relief, but also sorrow, since almost every house had lost a martyr. About 360 huffaz, Muslims who had memorised the Qur'an, died at al-Yamama. At Umar's urging, Abu Bakr then ordered what is called the first standardisation of the Qur'an, and Zayd ibn Thabit collected the scattered pieces into one copy.
battle-of-yamazaki: In the Honnō-ji Incident, Akechi Mitsuhide, a retainer of Oda Nobunaga, attacked his lord as he rested at the temple and forced him to commit seppuku, then took over Nobunaga's power around Kyoto. Hideyoshi was then fighting the Mōri clan at the Siege of Takamatsu. Mitsuhide wrote to the Mōri proposing an alliance to crush him, but Hideyoshi's men intercepted the messenger and the plot was revealed.

Keeping Nobunaga's death secret, Hideyoshi made peace with the Mōri, demanding the seppuku of Shimizu Muneharu, the commander at Takamatsu. From 25 June his army made a forced march from the Chugoku region towards Kyoto, covering up to 40 km a day and stopping at his Himeji Castle, and reached Amagasaki on 29 June. Niwa Nagahide and Oda Nobutaka joined him as he passed through Osaka. The episode is known as the Great Chugoku retreat.

Mitsuhide held the castles of Shōryūji and Yodo but, unwilling to be trapped inside a castle with his forces divided, chose to fight at Yamazaki, where a river and a mountain created choke points. He drew up his army behind the Enmyōji-gawa. Hideyoshi saw that the wooded Mount Tennōzan controlled the road to Kyoto and sent Nakagawa Kiyohide to take it. On the night of 1 July ninja sent by Hideyoshi's generals Nakamura Kazuuji and Horio Yoshiharu set fires in the Akechi camp.

On the morning of 2 July some of Mitsuhide's samurai under Matsuda Masachika and Nabika Kamon crossed the river towards Tennōzan and were driven back by arquebus fire. Hideyoshi then sent his right wing under Kato Mitsuyasu and Ikeda Tsuneoki across the river, followed by the left wing with support from the mountain. Most of Mitsuhide's men fled; 200 under Mimaki Kaneaki charged and were destroyed. The pursuit reached Shōryūji, whose garrison collapsed, and Mitsuhide was killed by bandits near the town of Ogurusu.

The battle is also called the Battle of Mt. Tennō, after the hill that decided it. By avenging his lord, Hideyoshi took over much of Nobunaga's authority. On 7 July, when the Oda clan learned that the Hōjō clan had defeated Takigawa Kazumasu at the Battle of Kanagawa, he authorised Tokugawa Ieyasu to secure Kai and Shinano provinces against the Hōjō and Uesugi, which began the Tenshō-Jingo war.
battle-of-yamen: In 1276 the Southern Song court fled the capital Lin'an and left Emperor Gong behind to be captured. Hopes of resistance centred on his two young brothers, and the older, Zhao Shi, was declared emperor. When Fuzhou fell in 1277 the court fled to Quanzhou, where the merchant Pu Shougeng refused to lend boats. The Grand General Zhang Shijie confiscated his property and fled on stolen boats, and Pu slaughtered imperial clansmen and officials in Quanzhou and surrendered to the Yuan, strengthening their navy.

Zhao Shi fell ill after his boat capsized in a storm and died, and his younger brother Zhao Bing, aged seven, succeeded him. Zhang Shijie took the new emperor to Yamen. In 1278 the captured general Wen Tianxiang removed Song land forces from the area.

In 1279 Zhang Hongfan of the Yuan attacked, reinforced by Li Heng. Zhang Shijie rejected advice to secure the mouth of the bay and had the palaces, houses and forts on land burned, so that his soldiers would not flee. He chained about 1,000 ships together with Zhao Bing's boat at the centre. Fire ships sent by the Yuan failed because the Song ships were painted with fire-resistant mud, but the Yuan blockaded the bay and cut off the fresh water and wood on land. The Song side, with many non-combatants, ran short of supplies and had to drink sea water. Zhang Hongfan kidnapped Zhang Shijie's nephew and three times asked him to surrender.

On 19 March Zhang Hongfan split his fleet in four. After a repulsed northern attack the Yuan played festive music, and at noon he attacked from the front, with soldiers hidden under cloth. The chained Song ships could neither support the centre nor retreat. Zhang Shijie cut about a dozen ships free in an attempt to break out with the emperor. The Yuan reached Zhao Bing, and Prime Minister Lu Xiufu jumped into the sea with the boy, and both drowned. Many officials and concubines followed.

The History of Song records that thousands of corpses floated up seven days later. The emperor's body was reportedly found near Shekou in Shenzhen, though his grave has not been found. Dowager Yang killed herself at sea when she heard of his death, and Zhang Shijie, who had escaped, was assumed drowned in a tropical storm, though some suggest his death was Mongol propaganda. With the death of the last Song emperor the House of Zhao lost power and the Yuan under Kublai Khan held all China. Temples to Wen Tianxiang, Lu Xiufu and Zhang Shijie were built nearby, a memorial to Zhao Bing was built near Shekou in the 1980s, and a museum complex stands east of the battle site.
battle-of-yique: By 294 BCE the State of Qin under King Zhaoxiang had become a major military power, and its conquests began with its neighbours Wei and Han. The two states had long been enemies and paid little attention to Qin until Bai Qi attacked Han and took an important fortress. Alarmed, Wei and Han joined forces and gathered 240,000 troops across a wide front of five fortresses, cities and defensive positions along rivers and mountain ranges. Bai Qi had only 120,000 men, but the allies feared Qin's better trained and equipped troops and stayed on the defensive, and the campaign stood in stalemate until 293 BCE.

Seeing that Wei and Han were still hostile to each other, Bai Qi chose to divide and conquer. He scouted the allied lines for weaknesses, drew the attention of the main Han forces with small ambushes and threw the main Qin army against the weakly held Wei positions. Wei officers believed Han had failed them on purpose, and Han, to preserve its own forces, stopped supporting its ally. Over the following months Bai Qi took the Wei positions one by one without having to fight the Han army.

He then turned on the Han troops, who were trapped and tried to break out, but the Qin cavalry let none escape. The allied general Gongsun Xi was captured, and five Han and Wei cities, Yique among them, fell to Qin.

The battle brought Qin influence into central China for the first time. With their armies destroyed, Wei and Han ceded land to Qin in return for a temporary peace, but their end was only delayed: Qin conquered Han in 230 BCE and Wei in 225 BCE. The site of the battle, Yique, is the place now known as Longmen, in the city of Luoyang.
battle-of-yungay: Chile declared war on the Peru-Bolivian Confederation in 1837 and sent an expedition under Admiral Manuel Blanco Encalada, whom Andrés de Santa Cruz surrounded at Paucarpata and forced to sign a treaty on 17 November. The Chilean Congress and public opinion thought the outcome humiliating, and it was believed that Santa Cruz was behind the assassination of Diego Portales. A second expedition followed under General Manuel Bulnes, with 5,400 Chileans and 600 Peruvian exiles under General Agustín Gamarra.

Bulnes defeated General Orbegoso at Portada de Guias on 21 August 1838 and entered Lima, and the Chilean fleet won command of the sea at the Battle of Casma. Local hostility, lack of supplies and disease drove him north, and Santa Cruz followed. An indecisive clash at Buin on 6 January 1839 was followed by Santa Cruz's occupation of Yungay on 13 January, meant to cut Bulnes's supply lines and force his surrender.

Each army had about 6,000 men. Bulnes first sent troops to clear the Punyán Hill, then a column of 400 under Jerónimo Valenzuela up the Pan de Azúcar Hill under heavy fire. Valenzuela and all his officers were killed, one company being led at the end by Sergeant Candelaria Perez, but the hill was taken with the bayonet and its defenders, Colonel Anselmo Quiroz among them, were killed.

Bulnes then attacked Santa Cruz's trenches across the Ancash River. The Confederates held, and a bayonet charge by General Pedro Bermúdez broke the Portales Battalion. Bulnes rallied his men, and in a third charge Baquedano's cavalry broke the Confederate left, after which the whole front collapsed. Santa Cruz left the field around 15:00.

Santa Cruz lost around 3,000 dead, about half his force; the Restorer Army lost one general, 39 officers and 622 soldiers. On 25 August 1839 Gamarra, now president, declared the Confederation dissolved and Peru reunified. Santa Cruz went into exile and died in France in 1865, while Bulnes served as President of Chile from 1841 to 1851. In Santiago the Barrio Yungay was named after the victory.
battle-of-zama: In 218 BCE, at the start of the Second Punic War, Hannibal invaded Italy and campaigned there for 16 years. In 210 BCE Scipio took command of the Roman war effort in Iberia and cleared the peninsula of Carthaginians in five years. He was elected consul in early 205 BCE at the age of 31, though the minimum age was 42, and had made an ally of the Numidian leader Masinissa. In 204 BCE his army landed near Utica. Scipio attacked the Numidian and Carthaginian camps at night, setting fire to the Numidian reed barracks, and inflicted heavy losses on both. Carthage opened peace talks and recalled Hannibal from Italy. The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but Carthage repudiated it when Hannibal arrived.

Scipio probably had 29,000 or 30,000 men, including 4,000 Numidian cavalry under Masinissa; the Carthaginians had 40,000 or 50,000 and 80 war elephants. The battle opened with a charge by the elephants, which was repulsed. Some fled through the Carthaginian cavalry on the wings and disordered it, and the Roman cavalry routed their opponents and chased them from the field.

The heavy infantry of both armies stood in three lines. The first lines fought hard until the Carthaginians broke, and their second line then drove back the Roman first line until Scipio committed his second. After a pause, in which the Romans formed one long line to match Hannibal's veterans, the two lines charged each other fiercely, and for some time neither gained the advantage. The Roman cavalry then returned and attacked the Carthaginian line from behind, and it was destroyed.

Polybius states that 20,000 Carthaginians were killed and as many taken prisoner, and that the Romans lost 1,500 dead. Hannibal reached Hadrumetum and advised the Carthaginian Senate to make peace on whatever terms it could. The peace treaty dictated by Rome stripped Carthage of its non-African territories and some of its African ones, and it was clear that Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.

Masinissa later raided and seized Carthaginian land, and Rome always backed him. In 149 BCE Carthage sent an army against him, in breach of the treaty, and Rome used this as a pretext for the Third Punic War. In 146 BCE the Romans destroyed the city and sold 50,000 survivors into slavery.
battle-of-zenta: After the Battle of Vienna of 1683 the Habsburgs and their allies took Ottoman lands, and by 1688 Belgrade and most of the Pannonian Plain were in Habsburg hands. Belgrade was recaptured in 1690, and the campaigns that followed were indecisive. Sultan Mustafa II then won victories at Lugos in 1695 and at Ulaş and Cenei in 1696. On 18 April 1697 he left Edirne with about 100,000 men to invade Hungary and reached Belgrade on 11 August.

On 5 July Emperor Leopold I appointed Prince Eugene of Savoy commander-in-chief. The war chest was empty, so Eugene borrowed money to pay wages and to set up a medical service. After gathering troops he had about fifty thousand German, Austrian, Hungarian and Serbian soldiers.

The Ottomans left Belgrade on 18 August and marched north along the Tisza. They reached the neighbourhood of Zenta on the morning of 11 September and began to ford the river, unaware that Eugene's army had followed them. Jovan Popović Tekelija, commander of the Serbian Militia, reported their movements and led the Imperial army over swamps to the rear of the Ottoman camp. A courier from Vienna ordered Eugene to act with extreme caution, but he did not wish to let the Ottomans cross during the night and went on.

Two hours before sunset, after a ten-hour forced march, the Habsburg army fell on the Ottomans mid-crossing. The sultan, the baggage and the artillery were on the far bank, while most of the infantry stood with the grand vizier on the near one. Guido Starhemberg's wing pushed between the Ottoman left and the bridge, and Charles-Thomas de Vaudémont's forces broke through the trenches. The bridge, crowded and under fire, collapsed, and thousands fell into the river. Mustafa II left for Temeşvar. The grand vizier was killed on the battlefield by mutinous Janissaries, and the Holy League reported only 429 casualties.

The victors took 87 cannon, 9,000 baggage carts, 6,000 camels, 15,000 oxen, a treasure chest of three million piastres and the sultan's state seal, which no enemy had captured before. On 22 October Eugene raided Ottoman Bosnia with six thousand cavalry, and Sarajevo was plundered and burned.

The battle led to peace negotiations at Sremski Karlovci, supervised by the English ambassador William Paget. By the Treaty of Karlowitz, signed on 26 January 1699, Austria gained Hungary, apart from the Banat of Temesvár and a small area of eastern Slavonia, together with Transylvania, Croatia and Slavonia. The Ottomans kept Belgrade and Serbia, and the Sava became the northern limit of their empire.
battle-of-zhovti-vody: In 1646 King Władysław IV Vasa secretly asked Cossack officers to raise forces for a sea campaign against the Crimean Khanate, but the Senate and the Sejm opposed his war plans. Bohdan Khmelnytsky, then a company commander of the Chyhyryn Regiment, kept up the preparations; Daniel Czapliński raided his estate at Subotiv, and Khmelnytsky was later arrested and released on bail. At the end of January 1648 he drove the Polish garrison from Khortytsia, and on 15 March he won Khan İslâm III Giray to an alliance. On 19 April the Cossacks elected him hetman.

Grand Crown Hetman Mikołaj Potocki and Field Crown Hetman Marcin Kalinowski sent a vanguard of 3,500 under Stefan Potocki, in practice led by Commissioner Szemberg and Stefan Czarniecki, without waiting for Prince Jeremi Wiśniowiecki. Registered Cossacks went down the Dnipro by boat to join it. Facing 4,000–5,000 Zaporozhian Cossacks and 3,000–4,000 Crimean Tatars under Tugay Bey, whose presence surprised them, the Poles fortified a camp in tabor formation and beat off repeated assaults from 1 May.

On 4 May, near Kamianyi Zaton, the river force mutinied and killed its officers; Ivan Barabash, who stayed loyal, was cut down. The mutineers reached the battlefield on 13 May, and the next day the registered Cossacks in Stefan's camp also went over, leaving him about 1,000 men. The Poles gave up their cannons in exchange for safe passage, but Khmelnytsky broke the agreement and held their deputies. On 16 May the Poles broke out towards Kryliv and were overwhelmed near Kniazhi Bairaky.

Most of the Commonwealth's soldiers died in the battle or soon afterwards. Stefan Potocki was wounded, taken prisoner and died of his wounds; Czarniecki was also captured but soon escaped. Mikołaj Potocki, who had learned of his son's plight on 3 May, came no closer than about 100 km and was himself defeated at the Battle of Korsun.

For the 350th anniversary of the uprising a monument bearing the arms of Khmelnytsky and İslâm III Giray was put up near Zhovto-Oleksandrivka. The 1999 film With Fire and Sword by Jerzy Hoffman reduced the 18-day battle to a failed charge of hussars.
battle-on-the-ice: The origins of the conflict are unclear and disputed. Novgorodians had tried to subjugate, raid and convert the pagan Estonians since 1030, when they founded the outpost of Yuryev, modern Tartu. The Livonian Brothers of the Sword captured Yuryev in 1224, and it became the capital of the Bishopric of Dorpat. Yaroslav, a son of Prince Vladimir Mstislavich of Pskov, gained Pskov in September 1240 with the help of his brother-in-law, bishop Hermann of Dorpat.

In winter 1240 to 1241 the Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek launched a campaign in Votia, which may properly be called a crusade. It provoked a delayed Novgorodian counterattack in 1241, in which Alexander retook Votia and Pskov. In spring 1242 the Teutonic Knights defeated a detachment of his army about 20 kilometres south of Dorpat, and Alexander took position at Lake Peipus.

The sources differ. The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle, written in the 1290s, says the Rus' had many archers, that the Brothers' army was surrounded, and that twenty Brothers were killed and six captured; it says the dead fell on the grass. The Novgorod First Chronicle says 400 Germans and countless Estonians fell. The Life of Alexander Nevsky, from the mid-15th century, was the first to say the battle itself took place on the ice.

David Nicolle estimates the crusader force at around 2,600 men and the Novgorodian at around 5,000. In a scholarly reconstruction the knights charged across the lake but were held up by the Novgorodian militia infantry. After a little more than two hours Alexander ordered both wings, including the cavalry, to enter the battle, and the exhausted crusaders retreated deeper onto the ice and then fled in panic.

Traditional accounts hold that the defeat prevented the crusaders from retaking Pskov and halted the eastward expansion of the Teutonic Order, making the Narva and Lake Peipus a stable boundary between Eastern Orthodoxy and Western Catholicism. In 1983 John Fennell argued that the battle was neither as large nor as important as portrayed, and whether it should be called a crusade is disputed.

The Russian Orthodox Church canonized Alexander Nevsky in 1547. Sergei Eisenstein's 1938 film Alexander Nevsky created a popular image of knights drowning through the breaking ice, but Donald Ostrowski argues that no primary source mentions this and that it first appeared in the film. Underwater searches in 1958 and 1959 found no artefacts of the battle.
battle-on-the-marchfeld: After the death of Emperor Frederick II in 1250, the Holy Roman Empire fell into crisis. In that year Ottokar II, son of King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia, moved into the Duchies of Austria and Styria, which had no duke, and was proclaimed duke by the estates. He became king of Bohemia in 1253, defeated Béla IV of Hungary at Kressenbrunn in 1260, and acquired Carinthia and Carniola through an inheritance contract with Ulrich III of Carinthia. At the height of his power he aimed at the imperial crown, but the electors chose Rudolph of Habsburg as King of the Romans on 29 September 1273.

Ottokar did not acknowledge Rudolph and failed to appear before the diet at Würzburg in 1275, so he was placed under the imperial ban. Rudolph gathered allies, among them Meinhard II of Gorizia-Tyrol and King Ladislaus IV of Hungary. Besieged in Vienna in 1276, Ottokar renounced his acquisitions and held only Bohemia and Moravia. In 1278 he invaded Austria again, with Henry I of Lower Bavaria, who had switched sides, and besieged Laa an der Thaya.

Ottokar fielded 6,000 cavalry, of whom 1,000 were heavily armed. Rudolph had 300 heavy and 4,000 light cavalry together with 5,000 Cuman horse archers. On 26 August the armies met near Dürnkrut. Cuman archers harassed the Bohemian left wing from the early morning, but in the main clash Ottokar's larger force seemed to gain the upper hand, and Rudolph, then sixty, was unhorsed and narrowly escaped. After three hours the Bohemian knights in heavy armour suffered in the summer heat.

At noon Rudolph sent a fresh heavy cavalry force hidden behind hills and woods against Ottokar's right flank. Such ambushes were regarded as dishonourable, and its commander Ulrich von Kapellen is said to have apologised to his men beforehand. The attack split the Bohemians. When Ottokar tried to bring up a reserve behind von Kapellen's men, his own troops took the move for flight, and the army collapsed. Ottokar's camp was plundered and he was found slain. No exact casualty figures exist, but his losses were far higher than Rudolph's.

Rudolph had Ottokar's body displayed in Vienna and secured Austria and Styria. At the 1282 Diet of Augsburg he installed his sons Albert and Rudolf II as dukes of Austria, and their descendants held the title until 1918. In Bohemia he acted cautiously, agreeing with the nobility and Ottokar's widow Kunigunda of Slavonia that her son Wenceslaus II would succeed. The influence of the Přemyslid kings was confined to Bohemia and Moravia, and the battle marked the beginning of Habsburg ascendancy in Central Europe.
battleford: Battleford lies on the North Saskatchewan River near the mouth of the Battle River, across the river from the city of North Battleford; together the two are known as the Battlefords. Fur traders were active in the area from the 1770s. William Holmes ran a North West Company post just above the meeting of the Battle and Saskatchewan rivers in 1784, and the Hudson's Bay Company opened its Battle River post around 1868. The Swift Current–Battleford Trail ended here.

The town was founded in 1875 as a fur trading post and a North-West Mounted Police fort, Fort Battleford, and its post office opened in 1877. As capital of the North-West Territories, a territory then reaching over what are now Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nunavut and the Northwest Territories, it housed the territorial government in Old Government House, built in 1878 and 1879. In 1883 the Battleford Industrial School opened, the first residential school run by the Government of Canada with the aim of assimilating Indigenous people into settler society; it was run by an Anglican minister and operated until 1914.

On 30 March 1885, during the North-West Rebellion, a party of Cree, short of food as the bison declined, came to Battleford. The 500 residents fled into Fort Battleford, and the Cree took food and supplies from the empty stores and houses. Two people died. Crooked Leg was accused of killing John Payne and Man Without Blood of killing a farmer named Tremont; both were convicted of murder and hanged later that year. The Canadian Pacific Railway reached the area in 1888.

Battleford is a town whose economy rests mainly on agriculture; it had about 4,400 people in 2021, nearly a quarter of them Indigenous. Fort Battleford, the Battleford Court House and the site of Old Government House, which burned in 2003, are National Historic Sites of Canada, and the Land Registry Office of 1877 to 1878 is the last building of the territorial era on Government Ridge.
battles-of-kawanakajima: Takeda Shingen of Kai Province began his conquest of Shinano in 1541, and by 1553 he had driven out Ogasawara Nagatoki and Murakami Yoshikiyo, who turned to Uesugi Kenshin of Echigo for help. The plain they contested lay between the Sai and Chikuma rivers, in what is now the city of Nagano. The five clashes are named Fuse in 1553, Saigawa in 1555, Uenohara in 1557, Hachimanbara in 1561 and Shiozaki in 1564. In 1553 Kenshin turned Shingen back at Fuse; in 1555 the armies faced each other for months near the Zenkō-ji temple until Imagawa Yoshimoto mediated a peace; in 1557 Shingen took Katsurayama but withdrew from Iiyama.

The fourth battle, on 18 October 1561, cost both sides a greater share of their forces than any other battle of the Sengoku period. Kenshin had camped with 13,000 men on Saijoyama, above Shingen's Kaizu castle. Yamamoto Kansuke planned for Kōsaka Masanobu to climb the mountain by night with 8,000 men and drive the Uesugi down onto Shingen's main force waiting in crane's wing formation. Kenshin guessed the plan and led his army down in silence, so that at dawn the Takeda found it ready to attack.

The Uesugi struck in rotating waves. Shingen's brother Takeda Nobushige was killed, and Kansuke, seeing his plan fail, died charging the enemy. Kenshin himself is said to have burst into Shingen's headquarters, where Shingen parried with his signalling fan until a retainer, Hara Osumi-no-Kami, speared Kenshin's horse. The Takeda main body held, and Kōsaka's force, finding Saijoyama empty, came down and struck the Uesugi from the rear. Accounts give losses of 62 per cent for the Uesugi and 72 per cent for the Takeda, though more conservative estimates put them around 20 per cent.

In September 1564 the two met a fifth time and skirmished for 60 days before both withdrew, and neither ever held the plain. The battles became favourite subjects of woodblock prints in the Edo period, partly because both clans had died out, so praising them posed no threat to the Tokugawa shogunate. The 1561 battle forms the climax of the 1969 film Fūrin Kazan.
battles-of-khalkhin-gol: After the Japanese occupation of Manchuria in 1931, Japan turned its military interests to the Soviet territories bordering it. The Soviet Union and the People's Republic of Mongolia signed a Mutual Assistance Pact in March 1936, allowing Soviet troops into Mongolia, and Japan signed the Anti-Comintern Pact in response. After Japan's full invasion of China in July 1937 the Soviet Union sent the 57th Special Corps under Ivan Konev to Mongolia. The first major Soviet-Japanese border incident, the Battle of Lake Khasan, took place in 1938 in Primorye, and clashes along the border of Manchuria were frequent.

The fighting began on 11 May 1939, when Manchu cavalry drove back a Mongolian unit of 70 to 90 men that had entered the disputed area in search of grazing. On 28 May Soviet and Mongolian forces surrounded and destroyed a Japanese force under Lieutenant Colonel Yaozo Azuma, which lost 63 per cent of its men. Georgy Zhukov arrived on 5 June as corps commander with more motorised and armoured forces. On 27 June the Japanese 2nd Air Brigade struck the Soviet airbase at Tamsak-Bulak, on an order from the Kwantung Army that Tokyo had not approved.

Fearing war in Europe, Zhukov planned an offensive to end the fighting, and on 20 August 1939 attacked with a force supplied by at least 4,000 trucks from Chita, 600 km away. It had around 498 BT-5 and BT-7 tanks and over 550 fighters and bombers, with two Mongolian cavalry divisions. The offensive was a simultaneous three-pronged attack by aircraft, tanks and infantry, the first of its kind in modern warfare, and similar tactics were later used in Operation Uranus at Stalingrad.
Japanese records report about 20,000 casualties, 162 aircraft lost in combat and 42 tanks disabled. The Soviets at first claimed 29,085 Japanese casualties and later raised the figure to 61,000.

The battle earned the Kwantung Army the displeasure of officials in Tokyo, chiefly because it had started and escalated the fighting without government authorisation. With Chinese resistance and the German-Soviet non-aggression pact, the defeat moved the Imperial General Staff away from the North Strike policy of seizing Siberia as far as Lake Baikal. Japan favoured the Nanshin-ron, or strike south, strategy, and the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact followed in April 1941. Zhukov earned his first Hero of the Soviet Union award, and Japan raised tank production from 500 a year to 1,200 in 1939.
battles-of-lexington-and-concord: The British Army occupied Boston in 1768. After the Boston Tea Party, Parliament passed the Coercive Acts of 1774, which colonists called the Intolerable Acts, and in response leaders in Suffolk County adopted the Suffolk Resolves, which the First Continental Congress endorsed on 17 September 1774. The colonists formed the Massachusetts Provincial Congress, which effectively controlled the colony outside Boston, and called on local militias to train. General Thomas Gage, military governor and commander of about 3,000 troops in Boston, planned small, secret strikes to remove military supplies, and in February 1775 the British government declared Massachusetts in a state of rebellion.

On 14 April 1775 Gage was instructed by the Earl of Dartmouth to disarm the rebels and imprison their leaders. On 18 April about 700 regulars under Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith, with Major John Pitcairn as his second, were ordered to seize and destroy supplies at Concord. The Patriots had learned of the plan and moved most of the supplies. On the night of 18 April Paul Revere, William Dawes and Samuel Prescott rode to warn the militias.

At sunrise on 19 April Pitcairn's advance guard reached Lexington, where about 80 militiamen under Captain John Parker stood on the Common without blocking the road. Shots were fired, and eight militiamen were killed and ten wounded, while one British soldier was wounded. The accounts of who fired first remain contested. The regulars went on to Concord and split into companies to search for supplies. At the Old North Bridge at about 11:00 am about 400 militiamen engaged 100 regulars, with casualties on both sides.

The British then began the march back to Boston. Militia from neighbouring towns gathered along the road and fired from cover at places such as Meriam's Corner and Brooks Hill. Smith's column was reinforced at Lexington by Earl Percy's force, and the combined British force of about 1,700 reached Charlestown after heavy losses. The militias then blockaded the land approaches to Boston and Charlestown, beginning the siege of Boston.

The expedition failed, since the fighting it was meant to prevent had begun and few weapons were seized. By the next morning more than 15,000 New England militiamen surrounded Boston, and the Second Continental Congress later adopted them as the beginnings of the Continental Army. Americans later told the events as British aggression, and Ralph Waldo Emerson's 1837 Concord Hymn spoke of the shot heard round the world.
battles-of-saratoga: In 1777 the British planned a three-way advance to divide New England from the other colonies and meet near Albany, New York. Lieutenant General John Burgoyne moved south from Quebec in June, but his campaign was slowed by supply problems after the capture of Fort Ticonderoga. Nearly 1,000 of his men were killed or captured at the Battle of Bennington on 16 August, and the expedition under Barry St. Leger turned back after the failed Siege of Fort Stanwix. General William Howe took his army to Philadelphia instead of moving north. Burgoyne chose to advance and crossed the Hudson River between 13 and 15 September.

On the American side, Major General Horatio Gates took command from Philip Schuyler on 19 August. Militia turned out in growing numbers, and by the end of the battles the effective American force was about 12,000, against Burgoyne's 5,791.

The first battle, at Freeman's Farm on 19 September, began when Burgoyne tried to flank the American position on Bemis Heights. Benedict Arnold anticipated the move and placed forces in his way. Burgoyne held the field at heavy cost. He then waited for help from Sir Henry Clinton in New York City, who did not come in time.

Gates and Arnold quarrelled, and Gates stripped Arnold of his command. On 7 October Burgoyne attacked again in the Battle of Bemis Heights, but he lost the battle and his earlier gains, while Arnold rallied the American troops and was wounded charging the redoubt of Heinrich von Breymann. Burgoyne retreated to what is now Schuylerville. He had lost over 1,000 men and was outnumbered roughly three to one. On 13 October he held a council of war, and after several days of talks he surrendered his army to Gates on 17 October.

Burgoyne returned to England and never again held a command. When news of the surrender reached France, Louis XVI entered negotiations that produced the Franco-American alliance, which made the war a global conflict and forced Britain to divert resources to the West Indies and Europe. France had already been secretly supplying arms, among them the de Vallière cannon. The battlefield is now the Saratoga National Historical Park. Its Saratoga Monument has an empty niche where a statue of Arnold would stand, and the Boot Monument marks the spot where he was shot without naming him.
battus-i-of-cyrene: What is known of the family of Battus comes from Herodotus. His father, Polymnestus, was a nobleman of Thera of the Minyan family of the Euphemidae. The people of Cyrene named his mother as Phronima, daughter of Etearchus, king of Oaxus on Crete. Falsely accused by her stepmother, she was to have been thrown into the sea, but the Therean merchant Themiston lowered her into the water on a rope, hauled her back and took her to Thera, where she became the mistress of Polymnestus.

Pindar gives his birth name as Aristotle, and Justin calls him Aristaeus, the name under which he was later worshipped. In Greek battus means a stammerer, but Herodotus says that in the Libyan language it meant king, and that he was not called Battus until he left for Libya.

In c. 639 BCE King Grinus of Thera, whom Battus accompanied, consulted the oracle at Delphi during a drought of seven years. The priestess told him to found a city in Libya, and the aged king passed the task to Battus, though neither knew where Libya was. Corobius, a fisherman of Itanus on Crete, guided a small party to Platea, an island off the Libyan coast. A larger party, drawn by lot from the seven villages of Thera, followed under Battus in two penteconters; when he turned back, the Thereans drove the ships away from their harbour.

The settlers lived two years on Platea, then, after consulting the oracle again, six years at Aziris on the mainland on friendly terms with the Libyans. The Libyans then led them west through the farmland of Irasa to Apollo's Fountain, saying that there the sky had a hole in it, perhaps a reference to the rainfall. Battus named the new settlement Cyrene after the fountain Cyre and made the colonists swear an oath, which a 4th-century BCE inscription claims to record.

Little is known of his reign, though he appears to have governed with moderation. After his death Battus was worshipped as a hero; his grave lay by the marketplace, on the road he had built to the temple of Apollo. The people of Cyrene dedicated a statue of him at Delphi, showing him in a chariot driven by the nymph Cyrene while a figure of Libya crowned him. His son Arcesilaus I succeeded him.
batu-khan: Batu was a son of Jochi and so officially a grandson of Genghis Khan, although Jochi's paternity is highly uncertain. After Jochi died, Genghis Khan divided his lands between Batu and his older brother Orda and installed Batu as khan. Orda's White Horde ruled the lands between the Volga and Lake Balkhash, while Batu's Golden Horde ruled the lands west of the Volga. According to Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Batu was kind enough to his own people but greatly feared by them, and most cruel in fight.

At a kurultai after the war against the Jin, the Great Khan Ögedei ordered Batu to conquer western nations. In 1235 he was given an army of possibly 130,000, which was actually commanded by the general Subutai. It crossed the Volga and invaded Volga Bulgaria in 1236. In November 1237 Batu demanded the allegiance of Yuri II of Vladimir-Suzdal. When Yuri refused, the Mongols besieged Ryazan, which was destroyed after six days and never restored to its former glory. They took Vladimir after a siege that began on 4 February 1238 and burned it, and on 4 March destroyed the army Yuri had raised on the Sit' River. Kiev was stormed in December 1240, and the Rus' principalities became vassals of the Mongol Empire.

The Mongols then invaded central Europe in three groups. One devastated Poland and defeated Henry II the Pious, Duke of Silesia, and the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order at Legnica. Batu's own army defeated King Béla IV of Hungary and his allies at the Battle of Mohi on 11 April. Plans to invade Austria, Italy and Germany were under way when news came of Ögedei's death in December 1241, and the Mongols withdrew in late spring 1242 as the princes were recalled to Karakorum for the kurultai.

Batu made his camps on the Volga and, as one of the oldest of the descendants of Genghis Khan, became viceroy over the western parts of the empire. He controlled routine affairs among the Rus' princes, among them Yaroslav II of Vladimir, whom he confirmed as suzerain, while Michael of Chernigov was put to death for refusing to bow before the tablets of Genghis Khan. Danylo of Halych submitted to him at Sarai. Batu delayed the election of Güyük, who became Great Khan in 1246, and in 1250 he called a kurultai on his own territory that offered the throne to him; he nominated Möngke instead, who was proclaimed Great Khan in 1251.

Batu died in 1255 and left affairs of state to his son Sartaq. His brother Berke inherited the Golden Horde after a brief regency. The Golden Horde ruled the steppes of what is now Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan, and Batu's line held the throne until 1360.
batumi: Batumi stands on the site of an ancient Greek colony in Colchis called Bathus or Bathys, from the Greek for deep harbour. Under Hadrian it became a fortified Roman port and was later deserted in favour of the fortress of Petra, founded in the time of Justinian I. It was possessed by the kingdom of Lazica, which fell to the Kingdom of Abkhazia in 780 through a dynastic union. From 1010 it was governed by a viceroy of the king of Georgia, and in the late 15th century it passed to the princes of Guria, a western Georgian principality under the kings of Imereti.

In 1444 a Burgundian flotilla, after a failed crusade, raided the Black Sea coast until its men under the knight Geoffroy de Thoisy were ambushed while landing at Vaty, as Europeans then called Batumi.

The Ottomans conquered the town in the 15th century in the reign of Kakhaber Gurieli but did not hold it, and returned a century later to defeat the Georgian armies at Sokhoista. Georgians recaptured Batumi in 1546 and in 1609, under Mamia II Gurieli. In 1703 it again became part of the Ottoman Empire, and in its one and a half centuries of Ottoman rule it grew into a provincial port serving the eastern fringes of the Black Sea. Islamization of the hitherto Christian region began, then was largely reversed after Russia annexed the area following the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78.

Russia occupied the town on 28 August 1878 and declared it a free port until 1886. The Transcaucasus Railway to Tiflis and Baku was completed in 1883 and the Baku–Batumi pipeline opened in 1907, making Batumi the chief Russian oil port on the Black Sea. The population doubled in twenty years, from 8,671 in 1882 to 16,000 by 1902. More than 7,400 Doukhobor emigrants sailed from Batumi for Canada. After 1918 the British held the city until July 1920, when it passed to the Democratic Republic of Georgia, and in 1921 Atatürk ceded it to the Bolsheviks on condition that Adjara be granted autonomy for its Muslims.

Batumi is the capital of the Autonomous Republic of Adjara, in south-western Georgia, 20 kilometres north of the border with Turkey. It lies in a subtropical zone at the foot of the Caucasus. It remains an important seaport, with shipbuilding, food processing and light manufacturing, and its economy draws heavily on tourism.
bauchi-state: Bauchi State lies in north-eastern Nigeria and covers 49,119 square kilometres. It borders Jigawa, Yobe, Gombe, Taraba, Plateau, Kaduna and Kano. It spans two vegetation zones, Sudan savanna in the south and semi-desert Sahel savanna in the north, with a mountainous south-west where the Bauchi Plateau continues. Rainfall falls from about 1,300 millimetres a year in the south to about 700 in the far north. The Gongola River crosses the south and east, and the Jama'are River runs through the north. Farming and livestock are the base of the economy, with cotton, groundnuts, millet and yams, and tin and columbite mining.

According to tradition the city of Bauchi was named after a hunter called Baushe, who settled in the region before the arrival of Yakubu, first traditional ruler of the Bauchi emirate. In the early 1800s the Fulani jihad seized much of the area and formed the Bauchi Emirate under the Sokoto Caliphate. About 90 years later a British expedition occupied it and made it Bauchi Province in the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. Nigeria became independent in 1960, and the area passed from the Northern Region to the North-Eastern State in 1967.

Bauchi State was formed on 3 February 1976, when the North-Eastern State was divided and ten other states were created. It then included the area of today's Gombe State, which became a separate state in 1996. The Ajawa language, once spoken there, became extinct by 1940 as speakers shifted to Hausa.

The state takes its name from its capital, the historic city of Bauchi, and has twenty local government areas. It has 55 tribal groups, among them the Bolewa, Fulani, Kanuri, Karai-Karai, Jarawa and Gerawa, and most of its people are Muslim, with Christian and traditionalist minorities. The Durbar Festival is a major annual event, and there are twenty traditional institutions, nineteen emirates and one chiefdom. Yankari National Park in the south is a large wildlife park with a population of hippopotamus, buffalo and roan antelope, and its Wikki Warm Springs attract visitors. Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, the first and only Prime Minister of Nigeria, is among the state's notable people.
baudouin-of-belgium: Baudouin was born on 7 September 1930 at Laeken, north of central Brussels, the elder son of Prince Leopold and Princess Astrid of Sweden. His grandfather King Albert I was killed in a climbing accident in 1934, and Leopold became king. His mother died in a car accident in 1935, and in 1941 his father married Mary Lilian Baels. Germany invaded Belgium in May 1940, and Leopold surrendered on 28 May and stayed under house arrest. After the Normandy landings the family was deported to Germany and then Austria, and was freed in May 1945.

The Royal Question, over whether Leopold had collaborated, kept the family out of Belgium. It rested on his surrender, his refusal to join the government in exile, his visit to Adolf Hitler in November 1940 and his marriage to Lilian. Prince Charles served as regent, and the family lived in Switzerland.

A referendum in March 1950 narrowly favoured Leopold's return, but parliamentary dissent and public protests forced him to delegate his powers to Baudouin on 11 August 1950 and then to abdicate. Baudouin took the oath on 17 July 1951. In 1960 he declared the Belgian Congo independent. At the ceremony he praised Leopold II as a genius, and the prime minister Patrice Lumumba answered with a speech citing the killings, insults and slavery the Congolese had suffered under Belgian rule.

Katanga Province seceded with Belgian support, and Lumumba was executed there on 17 January 1961. A Belgian parliamentary investigation of 2001 concluded that Baudouin knew of the plot against Lumumba and did nothing to oppose it, though it found no conclusive evidence that he ordered its details. Baudouin married Doña Fabiola de Mora y Aragón in 1960; they had no children. In 1990 he refused to sign a law liberalising abortion, and the government declared him temporarily unable to reign for a day so that it could sign the bill.

Baudouin died of a heart attack on 31 July 1993 at Motril in Spain, after a reign of 42 years. About 500,000 people came to see his body in Brussels. He was buried at the Church of Our Lady of Laeken, and his brother succeeded him as Albert II. The King Baudouin Foundation, formed in 1976 on his silver jubilee, works to improve living conditions in Belgium.
bauhaus: Walter Gropius founded the school on 1 April 1919 by merging the Grand Ducal Saxon Academy of Fine Art with the Grand Ducal Saxon School of Arts and Crafts. Gropius was strongly influenced by William Morris and the British Arts and Crafts Movement, and his pamphlet for an exhibition in April 1919 declared the aim of creating a new guild of craftsmen without the class distinctions that raise an arrogant barrier between craftsman and artist. The name joins the German words for building and for the Bauhütte, a premodern guild of stonemasons.

The first faculty was Johannes Itten, Lyonel Feininger, Gerhard Marcks and Gropius. Oskar Schlemmer joined in 1920 to head the theatre workshop, and Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky came in 1922. The first major joint project was the Sommerfeld House, built in 1920–1921.

The school moved to Dessau in 1925, and its new buildings, designed by Gropius, opened in late 1926. It offered no classes in architecture until 1927. Gropius resigned in February 1928 and Hannes Meyer became director; under him the school won commissions for five apartment buildings in Dessau and for the ADGB Trade Union School at Bernau bei Berlin, and it turned its first profit in 1929.

In 1930 the mayor of Dessau, Fritz Hesse, dismissed Meyer after a scandal over alleged use of school funds for communist causes, and appointed Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. Nazi writers had labelled the Bauhaus un-German, and the Dessau school was closed in 1932 after the Nazi party took over the local government of the Free State of Anhalt. Mies rented a derelict factory in Berlin and ran the school there for ten months. In 1933 the Gestapo closed it; Mies protested and obtained permission to reopen, but he and the faculty chose to shut it voluntarily.

The Bauhaus became one of the most influential currents in modern design and architecture. Many of its artists fled or were exiled by the Nazi regime, and it had a major effect in Western Europe, Canada, the United States and Israel in the following decades. German Jewish architects who emigrated to the British Mandate of Palestine built more than 4,000 buildings in the Bauhaus or International Style in Tel Aviv, whose White City UNESCO proclaimed a World Heritage site in 2003. In 1996 four major Bauhaus sites in Germany were inscribed on the World Heritage List, and two more in 2017.
