According to legend the sage Veda Vyasa, author of the Mahabharata, created it from its source lake, the Beas Kund and gave it his name. Another legend tells that the sage Vashishta tried to drown himself in the river, which turned to a sandbed and broke his cords, so that he called it Vipasa, the cord-breaker.

The Beas marks the easternmost limit of the conquests of Alexander the Great. In 326 BCE his troops mutinied at the river and refused to march further east. Alexander shut himself in his tent for three days, and when the mutiny did not cease he gave way and raised twelve colossal altars to mark the limit of his expedition. Their location and fate are unknown, although one historian has suggested that they were later reused in some of the Pillars of Ashoka. According to the Kavyamimansa of Rajasekhara, the lands of the Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Mahipala I reached the upper course of the Beas.

The river has changed its course. It once ran from its present junction with the Sutlej towards Lahore and joined the Chenab near Shujabad, and by 1245 it occupied the old bed of the Chenab that passed Dipalpur. An older channel flowed south of the site of Harappa. Between 1750 and 1800 the Sutlej captured its flow, after many earlier shifts.

In the 20th century the Beas Project developed the river for irrigation and hydroelectric power. The Pandoh Dam diverts water to the Sutlej through tunnels and channels, and the earth-fill Pong Dam in Kangra district was completed in 1974. The Harike Barrage, at the confluence of the Beas and Sutlej, feeds canals that irrigate Punjab and Rajasthan. Under the Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan, the waters of the Beas are allocated to India.
beatrice-i-countess-of-burgundy: Beatrice was the only surviving child of Reginald III, Count of Burgundy, and Agatha of Lorraine, and was named after her grandmother. When her father died in 1148 she inherited the County of Burgundy and became countess palatine, which made her one of the most desired brides in the Empire. Her uncle William III of Macon, acting as her regent, tried to deprive her of her rights and had her imprisoned until Emperor Frederick I stopped him by proposing a marriage. The emperor may have been attracted by an alternative to the Brenner Pass, a strategic position against Milan and Burgundian knights for his wars. They married at Wurzburg on 9 June 1156.

Frederick took control of Burgundy as co-ruler by right of his wife, though Beatrice's name seldom appears in its charters before 1166. She accompanied him on campaigns, and in July 1159 she brought reinforcements of 1,200 knights from Burgundy to the Siege of Crema. When Milan was destroyed in 1162, the Annals of Genoa say that at her suggestion the lives and property of the Milanese were spared. She was crowned empress in Rome by the antipope Paschal III on 1 August 1167. On the retreat, a plague struck the army and she was attacked at Pontremoli, escaping the arrows, and then stayed in hostile Susa until 1168.

After the Peace of Venice of 1177 her imperial coronation, performed by an antipope, was declared void, and she was crowned queen of Burgundy at Vienne on 15 August 1178. She then seems to have governed Burgundy by herself, issuing nine charters of her own between 1181 and her death, many witnessed by her younger son Otto, her designated heir. She still called herself empress in them. Contemporaries called her a litterata, learned in Latin. The early minnesang is associated with the troubadours she brought to court, including Guyot de Provins, and Gautier d'Arras dedicated a version of his Ille et Galeron to her.

In 1184 Beatrice fell ill with an unknown illness at Jouhe and died quickly, aged about 40. She was buried in Speyer Cathedral and her heart in the old Benedictine abbey at Jouhe. Frederick grieved. They had eleven children, among them the emperor Henry VI, Philip, king of Germany from 1198, and Otto I, Count of Burgundy. Sources for her political activity are scarce compared with those for earlier empresses, but recent research holds her role was more important than once estimated: contemporaries sought to influence the emperor through her, and she intervened for people connected to her and for churches, monasteries and hospitals.
beatrice-of-provence: Beatrice was the fourth and youngest daughter of the Count of Provence, Ramon Berenguer, and Beatrice of Savoy. Her three older sisters all married titles: Margaret became Queen of France as wife of Louis IX, Eleanor Queen of England as wife of Henry III, and Sanchia titular Queen of Germany as wife of Richard, Earl of Cornwall. In his will of 20 June 1238, however, Ramon Berenguer unexpectedly left Provence and Forcalquier to Beatrice, still unmarried. After his death on 19 August 1245 she became Countess in her own right, with her mother keeping the usufruct of Provence for life.

As a rich heiress Beatrice drew suitors. Raymond VII of Toulouse and James I of Aragon, who invaded Provence, made claims, and Emperor Frederick II sent the imperial fleet. Her mother sheltered with her at Aix and appealed to Pope Innocent IV. At a secret meeting at Cluny in December 1245, Innocent, Louis IX, Blanche of Castile and Louis's youngest brother Charles agreed that in return for Louis's military support of the Pope against Frederick, Charles would marry Beatrice. They married at Aix-en-Provence on 31 January 1246.

Charles refused to share the counties with his sisters-in-law, who felt cheated by their father's will. He also brought in French lawyers, took castles and fees from nobles and shut his mother-in-law out of government. Revolts followed at Arles and Avignon, and by July 1252 he had defeated them. Beatrice sided with her husband. She went with him on the Seventh Crusade in 1248 and bore a first child at Nicosia, who lived only a few days.

In 1259 her sister Margaret publicly slighted her by refusing to seat her at the family table, saying Beatrice was not a queen. When Pope Clement IV granted Charles the Kingdom of Sicily, Beatrice helped raise his army, calling on her knights and, according to the historian Angelo di Costanzo, selling her jewels. Charles was invested as King of Sicily at Rome on 28 June 1265. They were crowned on 6 January 1266, and she held Rome while he fought at Benevento.

Beatrice died on 23 September 1267, at Nocera Inferiore or Naples. The cause is unrecorded, though complications after a pregnancy are suspected. She was buried first in Naples, and in 1277 Charles moved her remains to Aix-en-Provence. As the last ruling Countess of Provence and Forcalquier of the House of Barcelona, she left the counties to her husband. Their children included Charles II, later King of Naples.
beatus-of-liebana: Apart from his writings, almost nothing is known about Beatus. He was a monk, and probably abbot, at Santo Toribio de Liébana in the Kingdom of Asturias, the only region of Spain left outside Muslim control, and he was probably one of the many monastic refugees who moved north after the Muslim conquest of southern and central Spain. He corresponded with the scholar Alcuin and was a confidant of Queen Adosinda, daughter of Alfonso I of Asturias and wife of Silo of Asturias. He was present when she took her vows as a nun in 785, the last record of his life. A Life of Beatus has been shown to be a 17th-century fraud.

The Commentary on the Apocalypse, revised in 784 and again in 786, is a work of learning rather than originality, made up mainly of extracts from Augustine of Hippo, Tyconius, Ambrose, Irenaeus and Isidore of Seville. Beatus drew most heavily on the lost commentary of Tyconius, and later versions added Jerome's commentary on the Book of Daniel. Unusually for a work of theology, Beatus seems to have meant it to be illustrated from the start, and the first designs are attributed to him. For him, reading such a book was a sacred act akin to communion.

The second book of the Commentary held a world map that showed, besides Europe, Asia and Africa, a fourth, unknown continent, with the apostles preaching in every part of the world. The original is lost, but the surviving copies face east and show paradise with four rivers. Beatus also opposed the Adoptionism of Elipandus and Bishop Felix of Urgell, fearing with Alcuin and Paulinus II of Aquileia that it divided the person of Christ. In 794 Elipandus called him a pseudo-prophet who had falsely foretold the end of the world; the Council of Frankfurt condemned Adoptionism that year, and Pope Leo III confirmed it as heresy in 798.

The Commentary was read in Iberia until about the 13th century and survives in at least 32 manuscripts from the 9th to the 13th century, some of them only fragments; no copy from Beatus's own time remains. Most are lavishly decorated, among them the Morgan Beatus and the Saint-Sever Beatus. A lasting influence of Beatus seems to have been the idea, established in Spain, that the Apostle James had converted Iberia.
beatus-rhenanus: He was born Beatus Bild on 22 August 1485 in Schlettstadt (Sélestat), the son of Anton Bild, a butcher whose family came from Rhinau and who served on the town council and as mayor; Beatus Latinised the town's name as Rhenanus. His two elder brothers died in childhood and his mother, Barbara Kegler, died when he was very young, so he was raised by his father and his uncle Reinhart Kegler, a priest. From 1491 to 1503 he attended the Latin school of Schlettstadt, where his classmates included Basilius and Bruno, sons of the printer Johann Amerbach.

In May 1503 he reached Paris and entered the College du Cardinal Lemoine, where he came under the influence of the Aristotelian Jacobus Lefèvre Stapulensis and helped him publish works of Aristotle with the printer Henri Estienne.

Back in Alsace in 1507, he worked in Strasbourg for the printer Mathias Schürer and came to know the humanists Jakob Wimpfeling, Johann Geiler von Kaisersberg and Sebastian Brant. In July 1511 he moved to Basel to study Greek with Johannes Cuno, who later left him his library. His first known edition there was the Decretum Gratiani of 1512, and he took an active part in the publishing of Johann Froben. He brought out the first edition of Tertullian in 1521 and an edition of Velleius Paterculus in 1520, based on the only surviving manuscript, which he found in the Benedictine monastery of Murbach.

In 1528 he returned to Schlettstadt for a life of learned leisure. There he edited Tacitus, published by Froben in 1533, and Livy, wrote the Rerum Germanicarum Libri III of 1531, and supervised the printing of many of Erasmus's most important works.

He fell ill around Pentecost 1547 and went to Wildbad for a cure, which failed; still gravely sick, he reached Strasbourg on 14 July and died six days later. Four years after his death Johannes Sturm wrote his biography. His books passed to his home town and can still be seen in their entirety in the Humanist Library of Sélestat.
beaufort-castle-lebanon: Beaufort, Old French for beautiful fortress, was the name the crusaders gave the castle; its Arabic name, Qalʿat al-Shaqīf, means Castle of the Steep Cliff. Little is known of the site before 1139, when Fulk, King of Jerusalem, captured the fortification there and gave it to the lords of Sidon. The medieval historian Hugh Kennedy suggests that the crusader castle was begun soon after.

After the Battle of Hattin in 1187 Beaufort was one of the last castles to resist Saladin. Arab sources tell how its lord, Reynald of Sidon, asked for three months to bring his family out of Tyre and used them to repair and stock the castle. The siege that followed ended in August 1189, when Saladin lifted it to defend Acre. In April 1190 the garrison handed the castle over in return for Reynald's release. A treaty negotiated by Theobald I of Navarre returned it to the crusaders in 1240, Julian of Sidon sold it to the Knights Templar in 1260, and in 1268 the Mamluk sultan Baibars captured it.

The castle stands on a cliff 300 metres high that falls steeply eastwards to the Litani River, about one kilometre south-south-east of the village of Arnoun in southern Lebanon. It is roughly triangular, about 150 metres by 100, and divided into two wards, one on the lower ground to the east. A square keep of about 12 metres a side stands against the west wall of the upper ward and, as is usual in Syria, is entered from the ground floor.

After the Ottoman conquest of Syria in 1516 the castle was held for the Ottomans by the Shiite Sa'b family. Fakhr-al-Din II took it in the early 17th century, and the Ottomans, after defeating him, destroyed its upper parts. Jazzar Pasha, governor of Acre, besieged it in 1782 and destroyed many of its remaining fortifications, and the earthquake of 1837 added to the damage. Surveys began in 1880 and 1881, and Paul Deschamps studied it from 1927.

Its view over southern Lebanon and northern Israel made it a strongpoint in later conflicts. The Palestine Liberation Organization held it from 1976, and Israeli forces took it on 8 June 1982; the Israeli army used it as a base until 2000. In 2026 Israeli forces struck the remains during the war in Lebanon and captured the castle on 31 May; the Israeli military said it wanted to control the area around a tunnel it said Hezbollah used. In July 2026 UNESCO designated the Mount Amel Castles, Beaufort among them, a World Heritage Site and classified them as endangered.
beaumaris-castle: Beaumaris Castle was built as part of Edward I's campaign to conquer north Wales after 1282. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 divided Wales into shires on the English model, and plans were probably made then for a castle and town near Llanfaes on Anglesey, but the cost of the other castles postponed them. In 1294 Madog ap Llywelyn rebelled, and once Edward had reoccupied Anglesey in April 1295 he moved at once. The site was called Beaumaris, "fair marsh", about a mile from Llanfaes. The Welsh population of Llanfaes was moved some 12 miles south-west to a new settlement, Newborough, to make way for an English town.

The architect was Master James of St George, whose chief responsibility from 1295 was Beaumaris. Historian Arnold Taylor called it Britain's "most perfect example of symmetrical concentric planning". It is built of local stone. A moated outer ward with twelve towers and two gatehouses is overlooked by an inner ward with two large D-shaped gatehouses and six massive towers, designed to hold buildings for two major households. First-floor passages in the inner walls link the towers, and the chapel was built into one of them. The south gate could be reached by ship, so the castle could be supplied by sea.

In the first summer an average of 1,800 workmen, 450 stonemasons and 375 quarriers worked on the site, at a cost of about £270 a week, and officials fell so far behind that they issued leather tokens in place of coin. Edward's wars in Scotland drew away money, and work stopped by 1300 with about £11,000 spent. It resumed after an invasion scare in 1306 and ended around 1330, when £15,000 had been spent. The castle was never finished.

Welsh forces under Owain Glyndŵr captured it in 1403, and royal forces retook it in 1405. In the English Civil War it was held for Charles I until it surrendered to Parliament in 1646, and it was briefly held again by royalists in 1648. It fell into ruin after 1660. Thomas Bulkeley, 7th Viscount Bulkeley, bought it in 1807 for £735 and made it part of his park. In 1925 it passed into state care and was restored. UNESCO declared it part of a World Heritage Site in 1986.
beaune: Beaune stands on a plain beside the hills of the Côte d'Or and is served by a small river, the Bouzaise, whose source lies in a public park on the north-east edge of the town. The name derives from the Latinised Gaulish Belena, the name of a spring around which the settlement grew, itself derived from Belenos, a god of fast-flowing water. The climate is semi-continental with an oceanic influence, with frequent rain in every season.

A Roman fort was built at the site in the first century CE, and the town has features from pre-Roman and Roman times through the medieval and Renaissance periods. The region was already a wine-growing area in the 13th century, and the cellars of producers have stood in the historic centre since Roman times. Beaune is a walled city: much of its battlements, ramparts and moat survives in good condition, and the old town inside the walls is extensive. Historically it is closely connected with the Dukes of Burgundy.

The Hospices de Beaune were founded in the 15th century by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of the Duke of Burgundy, who was encouraged by his wife Guigone de Salins. They are a charity running hospitals and other services for the needy, and through the gifts of benefactors they own vineyards in Burgundy. At the end of the First World War the American Expeditionary Forces University was established in Beaune under Brigadier General Robert I. Rees, with its own chapter of Phi Beta Kappa.

Beaune is a commune and sub-prefecture of the Côte-d'Or department, in the region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, and is regarded as the wine capital of Burgundy. Many major négociants have their houses there, and the appellation Beaune was created in 1936. An annual charity wine auction is held for the Hospices. Landmarks include the Hospices, the old market, the Beffroi clock tower and the collegiate church of Notre Dame, and the town is the main centre of the polychrome Burgundian tile roofing of the Renaissance. In 2015 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Climats, terroirs of Burgundy.
beauvais: Beauvais is a town and commune in northern France, the prefecture of the Oise département in the Hauts-de-France region, 75 kilometres north of Paris. It lies at the foot of wooded hills on the left bank of the Thérain at its confluence with the Avelon. Its ancient ramparts have been destroyed and it is now surrounded by boulevards. The region around it is called the Beauvaisis.

The Romans knew it by the Gallo-Roman name Caesaromagus, the capital of the Belgic tribe of the Bellovaci. Some hold that it was the fortified town of Bratuspantium that surrendered to Julius Caesar, as De Bello Gallico reports, while others identify that town with Vendeuil-Caply or Bailleul sur Thérain. In the ninth century it became a county, which passed in about 1013 to the bishops of Beauvais, who became peers of France from the twelfth century. At royal coronations the Bishop of Beauvais wore the royal mantle and, with the Bishop of Langres, raised the king from his throne to present him to the people.

The town defended itself against the English in 1346 and was besieged by them again in 1433. The siege by the Duke of Burgundy in 1472 was noted for the heroism of the town's women under Jeanne Hachette, remembered in a procession on 27 June in which women take precedence over men. Beauvais was extensively damaged in World War I and again in June 1940; much of the older part was all but destroyed, and the cathedral was badly damaged before British forces liberated the town on 30 August 1944.

The cathedral of Saint-Pierre, begun in 1247 under Bishop William of Grès, was raised an extra 5 metres to make it the tallest cathedral in Europe, and the vaulting of the interior exceeds 46 metres. Work stopped in 1284 when the vaulting of the choir collapsed, and the fall of a too-ambitious central tower in 1573 halted it again. The building consists only of a transept and choir with an apse and seven apse chapels; a small Romanesque church of the 10th century, the Basse Oeuvre, occupies the site meant for the nave. Its stained glass of the 13th, 14th and 16th centuries includes work by Engrand Le Prince.

The state tapestry manufactory dates from 1664. The church of Saint-Étienne is a Romanesque and Gothic building of the early 12th to late 16th centuries, and a former episcopal palace of the 16th century houses the departmental museum. Beauvais–Tillé Airport, dating from the 1930s, serves as a gateway to Paris.
beaver-wars: In the 17th century the Haudenosaunee, a confederacy of the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, lived in what is now Upstate New York. The traditional explanation of the wars is the fur trade: George T. Hunt argued that the Haudenosaunee, dependent on European goods, had exhausted their beaver by the 1630s and fought to seize hunting grounds and become the middlemen of the trade. Bruce Trigger and others criticised this view as Eurocentric. Two other explanations have gained acceptance: a need to replace people lost in the epidemics of the 1630s, and a wish to impose the Great Law of Peace on other Iroquoian-speaking peoples.
In the summer of 1609 Samuel de Champlain joined the Innu, Algonquin and Wendat in an attack on the Mohawk on the shores of Lake Champlain. The battle began almost a century of conflict.

From the late 1630s the Mohawk ambushed Wendat trading parties and in time blocked the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers. In 1642 they began raiding French settlements, including the new outpost of Montreal. In the 1640s the Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga raided the Wendat on a larger scale. Peace talks in 1647 failed against the opposition of the Seneca and Mohawk, and the Wendat Confederacy collapsed. Late in 1649 the Haudenosaunee attacked the Petun, and in 1650 and 1651 the Neutral, many of whose survivors were adopted into Haudenosaunee society while others fled. The Erie fell afterwards, and the Susquehannock were defeated around 1674.

Against New France the Mohawk besieged Trois-Rivières in 1653 with 600 warriors and were held off for nine days. Louis XIV sent the Carignan-Salières regiment to defend the colony. After the English took New Netherland in 1664 the Haudenosaunee lost their Dutch allies. Fighting with the French resumed, and Lachine was burned on 4 August 1689.

The Great Peace of Montreal was signed in 1701 by the French and 39 Indigenous leaders. The Haudenosaunee agreed to stop raiding and to let refugees from the Great Lakes return east, and the Shawnee, Miami, Potawatomi and Illinois went back to their lands in the Ohio country, Indiana, Michigan and Illinois. The Haudenosaunee had become the dominant power of the region and had greatly extended their territory.

Scholars disagree on whether the wars were genocide. Some point to the brutality of the fighting. Others argue that the mass adoption of captives, meant to replenish a declining population, is the opposite of an intent to destroy, and that what was destroyed was the political independence of peoples such as the Wendat.
bec-abbey: The abbey, formally the Abbey of Our Lady of Bec, takes its name from the bec, or stream, that runs nearby, a word from the Scandinavian root bekkr. It lies in the Bec valley in the Eure département, midway between Rouen and Bernay. Its founder Herluin was a Norman knight who in about 1031 left the court of Gilbert, Count of Brionne, for a religious life; the village of Le Bec-Hellouin keeps his name. Building began in 1034 and continued into 1035, further lands were added up to 1040, and 136 monks made their profession while Herluin was abbot.

Lanfranc of Pavia, already known for his lectures at Avranches, came to Bec as prior and master of the school, which made the abbey a focus of 11th-century intellectual life. He left in 1062 to become abbot of St. Stephen's Abbey at Caen. Anselm, abbot from 1078, and the fifth abbot, Theobald of Bec, also became archbishops of Canterbury. The future Pope Alexander II and Saint Ivo of Chartres were probably educated there. Unusually, the first abbots received individual biographies, gathered by the monk Milo Crispin and printed at Paris in 1648.

The followers of William the Conqueror gave the abbey large estates in England, among them the land of Tooting Bec, now a London suburb, and Bec held St Neots Priory and Goldcliff Priory in Monmouthshire, founded in 1113. The Empress Matilda was first buried at Bec, though her bones were later moved to Rouen Cathedral. The abbey was damaged in the Wars of Religion and left in ruins after the French Revolution; the 15th-century Tower of Saint Nicholas still stands.

In 1948 Olivetan monks led by Dom Paul Grammont re-established monastic life on the site and carried out some restorations. The community is known for its links with Anglicanism: successive archbishops of Canterbury have visited it, and its library holds the John Graham Bishop deposit of 5,000 works on Anglicanism. The monks are also known for the pottery they make.
bechara-el-khoury: Bechara Khalil El Khoury was born on 10 August 1890 in Rechmaya, a town in the Aley district of the Mount Lebanon governorate, to Lebanese Maronite Christian parents. He studied law. In 1922 he married Laura Shiha, the sister of the banker and intellectual Michel Shiha, who helped El Khoury financially and introduced him to ideas about confessional power-sharing and a free market economy. His son Michel El Khoury later served as governor of the Lebanese central bank. The Maronite Patriarch of Antioch, Paul Peter Meouchi, was his second cousin.

El Khoury served two short terms as prime minister, from 5 May 1927 to 10 August 1928 and from 9 May to 11 October 1929. He founded the Constitutional Bloc Party and was a cabinet minister before his election as president on 21 September 1943. A strong nationalist who opposed the French Mandate, he was arrested by Free French troops on 11 November 1943 and held for eleven days in the Rashaya Tower, together with Prime Minister Riad Al Solh, Camille Chamoun and others who were to dominate politics in the following generation. Massive demonstrations forced the release of the prisoners on 22 November 1943, a date now observed as Lebanon's national independence day. His presidency was interrupted for those eleven days only.

He is remembered for the National Pact, an agreement between Christian and Muslim leaders. Christians accepted Lebanon's affiliation with the Arab League and agreed not to seek French protection, while Muslims accepted the state within its existing boundaries and promised not to seek union with Syria. Seats in the National Assembly were divided six Christians to five Muslims, following the 1932 census, and the offices of president, prime minister and speaker went to a Maronite, a Sunni Muslim and a Shi'a Muslim. The pact was not written into the constitution until the Taif Agreement of 1989.

His years in office saw great economic growth, but the 1948 Arab-Israeli War strained the economy through its cost and the arrival of some 100,000 Palestinian refugees. His administration had a reputation for major corruption, and he faced opposition from traditional za'im leaders whose powers his policies were beginning to limit. In 1951 Camille Chamoun, Pierre Gemayel, Raymond Edde, Kamal Jumblatt and others formed the National Socialist Front, and on 18 September 1952, amid widespread demonstrations, it forced his resignation. He died on 11 January 1964. He is widely regarded in Lebanon as a national hero of independence, though he has been criticised for corruption, nepotism and electoral fraud.
bede: Almost everything known of Bede's life comes from the last chapter of his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in about 731. He gives his birthplace as the lands of the twin monastery of Monkwearmouth and Jarrow. Bede says nothing of his origins, but his connections with men of noble ancestry suggest that his family was well-to-do.

At the age of seven he was sent to Monkwearmouth to be educated by Benedict Biscop and later by Ceolfrith. Jarrow was founded by Ceolfrith in 682, and Bede probably moved there with him that year. In 686 a plague broke out at Jarrow, and the Life of Ceolfrith records that only two surviving monks could sing the full office, one of them a young boy, almost certainly Bede. In about 692 he was ordained a deacon by John, Bishop of Hexham, and in about 702 he became a priest.

Bede began writing in about 701 with two classroom works, De Arte Metrica and De Schematibus et Tropis, and eventually completed over 60 books, most of which survive. He wrote on music, metrics, chronology, history and theology, knew some Greek, and read Pliny the Elder, Virgil, Ovid and Horace. In his own time he was as well known for his biblical commentaries as for his history.

The Ecclesiastical History opens with Caesar's invasion and a brief account of Christianity in Roman Britain, then tells of Augustine's mission of 597, the progress of the faith in Kent and Northumbria, the reigns of Oswald and Oswy, and the Council of Whitby. He also studied computus, the calculation of calendar dates, above all the date of Easter, a subject of controversy, and helped to popularise dating forward from the birth of Christ.
His last surviving work is a letter to Ecgbert of York, written in 734. He died on 26 May 735. A cult formed around him by the 10th century and was widespread in England by the fourteenth.

His body was moved to Durham Cathedral in 1020 and placed in the tomb of Saint Cuthbert, then in 1370 to a shrine of its own. The shrine was demolished during the English Reformation, and Bede was reburied in the cathedral. In 1899 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church, the first native of Great Britain to hold the title.
bedia-cathedral: The church was built at the close of the 10th century and consecrated in 999 at the wish of King Bagrat II of Abkhazia, who went on to rule a united Georgia as Bagrat III. According to the Georgian chronicler, he made it the seat of a bishop. He and his mother, Queen Gurandukht, are buried there. Within the Catholicate of Abkhazia, Bedia was the centre of a diocese, and over the centuries the see was an important ecclesiastical, cultural and educational centre. Services ceased in the 17th century and resumed in the second half of the 19th.

The complex stands in Bedia, in the Tkvarcheli district of Abkhazia, a disputed region on the Black Sea coast. Its main building, the church of the Virgin, stands in the middle of a walled courtyard and was much rebuilt between the 13th and 15th centuries. It is a cross-in-square church built of cleanly trimmed sandstone, with a dome of 14 facets and as many windows resting on two free-standing pillars in the west and on the apses in the east. A bell tower of the 12th to 14th centuries rises over the gateway, and to the west lie the ruins of a two-storeyed bishops' palace.

Three layers of murals survive inside, dating from the 10th and 11th, the 13th and 14th, and the 16th and 17th centuries; those of the southern wall include portraits of the king and of members of the Dadiani family. Inscriptions in the Georgian Asomtavruli script record the church's building and repairs.

In the 16th century Archbishop Anton Zhuanisdze built the bishops' palace and set up a rich library, where old manuscripts were restored and theological works translated. By the end of the 19th century the church stood abandoned and overgrown, though most of the dome survived; early in the 20th century Russian monks and nuns, intending to renovate it, removed the damaged dome entirely. The palace's floors were repaired in the restoration of 1968-69.
bedouin: The English word bedouin comes from the Arabic badawī, desert-dweller, traditionally contrasted with ḥāḍir, a sedentary person. The Bedouin originated in the Syrian Desert and Arabian Desert and spread across the rest of the Arab world in West Asia and North Africa after the spread of Islam. They were called Arabaa by the Assyrians. According to tradition, the Arabian Bedouin descend from two groups: the Qahtanis, or Yaman, from south-western Arabia, who claim descent from an ancestral figure, Qahtan, and the Adnanis, from north-central Arabia, who claim descent from Adnan, a descendant of the biblical Ishmael.

The Bedouin are described as having engaged in nomadic herding, agriculture and sometimes fishing in the Syrian steppe since 6000 BCE. By the time the Roman Empire was founded they were recognisable as a single people, though often at war among their families, clans and tribes. A major source of income was taxing caravans and collecting tribute from settlements, and they also carried goods and people across the desert in camel caravans. In 1326 Ibn Battuta reported that Egyptian authorities at Qatya on the Sinai coast used Bedouin to guard the road.

From the 11th to the 15th centuries nomadic Bedouin tribes moved into the Maghreb in great numbers: the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym, from central and north Arabia, moved west in the 11th century and were joined by the Ma'qil, who had roots in south Arabia. In the late 18th century rivalry between the Shammar and Anizah confederations, together with the rise of the Wahhabi movement, led a Shammar faction under the Al Jarba family to migrate across the Euphrates into Upper Mesopotamia. Raiding was still part of Bedouin life in the early 20th century, when Saudi Arabia began a policy of settling the tribes.

The Bedouin are divided into tribes or clans. A widely quoted adage runs, I am against my brother, my brother and I are against my cousin, my cousin and I are against the stranger, which grades loyalties by closeness of kin; disputes are settled by self-help and collective responsibility. Traditional livelihoods were herding goats, sheep and dromedary camels for meat, dairy products and wool. Camels, regarded as a gift from God, were the main food source and means of transport, and were raced at weddings and religious festivals.

Oral poetry is the most popular art form, and a poet in the tribe was highly regarded; it also carried news and served as social control. Raiding, known as ghazw, was a regulated habit. Coffee prepared before the guest is a major part of hospitality. Many Bedouin have since adopted an urban life, while others keep the clan structure, music, poetry and dances.
bedrich-smetana: Smetana was born on 2 March 1824 in Litomyšl, east of Prague near the traditional border between Bohemia and Moravia, then provinces of the Habsburg Empire. He was the third child, and first son, of František Smetana, a brewer in the service of Count Waldstein, and his third wife Barbora Linková. German was the official language of Bohemia, and the children did not learn correct Czech until much later in their lives.

He gave his first public performance at the age of six. He came to Prague in the autumn of 1839 and soon began missing classes at his school in favour of concerts and the opera, convinced after hearing Franz Liszt that he wanted a musical career. His father saw music only as a pastime. Smetana later studied under Josef Proksch, and in 1848 he helped man the barricades on the Charles Bridge as a member of the Citizens' Army, where he met the writer Karel Sabina.

After failing to establish himself in Prague, Smetana left for Gothenburg, where within weeks he gave a recital, opened a music school that was soon overwhelmed by applications and became conductor of the Gothenburg Society for Classical Choral Music. A visit to Liszt at Weimar in the summer of 1857 shaped his later orchestral work and led to the three Gothenburg symphonic poems, Richard III, Wallenstein's Camp and Hakon Jarl.

The announcement in 1861 of a Provisional Theatre for Czech opera drew him back to Prague. The conductorship went to Jan Nepomuk Maýr, because the conservative faction considered Smetana a dangerous modernist in thrall to Liszt and Wagner. His first two operas, The Brandenburgers in Bohemia and The Bartered Bride, were premiered there in 1866, and he then became the theatre's principal conductor, though his years in the post were marked by controversy.

By the winter of 1882–83 Smetana suffered depression, insomnia and hallucinations. By the middle of February 1884 he had ceased to be coherent, and on 23 April his family removed him to the Kateřinky Lunatic Asylum in Prague, where he died on 12 May 1884.

Most commentators agree that he created a canon of Czech opera where none had existed and a musical style matching the emergent Czech national spirit. Relatively few of his works are in the international repertory, and most foreign commentators regard Antonín Dvořák as the more significant Czech composer.
beemster: Around 800 the area was covered in peat. Its name derives from Bamestra, the name of a small river there. Between 1150 and 1250 peat-digging and storm floods enlarged that river into an inland sea, a lake connected with the Zuiderzee. Private investors set about draining the lake. In 1610 the work was almost complete, but the lake filled again after a breach in the Zuiderzee dikes. It was decided to raise the ring-dike to a metre above the surrounding country, and by 1612 the polder was dry and the land was divided among the investors.

In its early days farmers there grew the crops needed for the long sea journeys of the VOC to the East Indies. The farmland was so good that the project was considered an economic success, in contrast to the drainage of Heerhugowaard. In 1901 a co-operative, CONO Kaasmakers, was formed to make cheese from the milk of the polder; it sells the Beemster brand.

The original landscape of fields, roads, canals and dykes survives intact. A grid of canals runs parallel to the grid of roads, with the larger feeder canals offset from the larger roads by about a kilometre. The villages are Middenbeemster, Noordbeemster, Westbeemster and Zuidoostbeemster, and the painters Carel Fabritius and Barent Fabritius were born in Middenbeemster. The former municipality merged into Purmerend on 1 January 2022.

UNESCO inscribed the polder as a World Heritage Site in 1999. It cited the polder as a masterpiece of creative planning that applied the ideals of antiquity and the Renaissance to a reclaimed landscape, with a lasting impact on reclamation projects in Europe and beyond. Five fortresses of the Stelling van Amsterdam, another World Heritage Site, also stand in the Beemster.
beer-hall-putsch: After the Treaty of Versailles, Germany declined as a European power. Hitler, who had fought in the German Army but still held Austrian citizenship, shared the common belief that the country had been stabbed in the back by its own government. He remained in the army in Munich and was sent to infiltrate the small German Workers' Party, which he joined on 12 September 1919 and soon led. He also took the political lead of the Kampfbund, a group of Bavarian patriotic associations, with about 15,000 members of the Sturmabteilung (SA). The coup was inspired by Benito Mussolini's March on Rome.

Hitler came to realise that Gustav Ritter von Kahr, the Minister-President of Bavaria, sought to control him and was not ready to act against Berlin. On the evening of 8 November 1923, 603 SA men surrounded the Bürgerbräukeller, where Kahr was speaking to 3,000 people, and a machine gun was set up in the auditorium. Hitler fired a shot into the ceiling, jumped on a chair and shouted that the national revolution had broken out. He declared the Bavarian government deposed and announced a new government with Erich Ludendorff.

The state police seized the central telegraph office and the telephone exchange and warned Major-General Jakob von Danner, the army's commandant in Munich, who alerted all units. Around 23:00 Danner and other generals compelled Otto von Lossow to repudiate the putsch. The next day Archbishop Michael von Faulhaber and Rupprecht persuaded Kahr to do the same, and a march on the Feldherrnhalle by about 2,000 Nazis met a police cordon.

Hitler escaped immediate arrest but was arrested two days later, and he, Ludendorff, Ernst Röhm and others were charged with high treason. The Nazi newspaper, the Völkischer Beobachter, was banned. The trial lasted 24 days and was widely publicised, giving Hitler a platform. He was sentenced to five years in Landsberg Prison, where he dictated Mein Kampf to Emil Maurice and Rudolf Hess, and was released on 20 December 1924 after about nine months. Afterwards he sought power by legal means. The Nazi dead were later treated as the party's first blood martyrs, and their bloodstained flag became the Blutfahne.
beeston-castle: The castle stands on Beeston Crag, 107 m above the Cheshire Plain, in the southern part of the Mid Cheshire Ridge, a chain of low sandstone hills. Pits of the 4th millennium BCE show that the site was used in the Neolithic, and archaeologists have also found flint arrowheads, the remains of a Bronze Age community with a rampart dated to around 1270–830 BCE, and an Iron Age hill fort. It may have been a specialist metalworking site.

Known in medieval documents as Castellum de Rupe, the Castle on the Rock, Beeston was one of three castles Ranulf built after the Fifth Crusade, with Bolingbroke and Chartley. It has no keep: an inner bailey on the summit, cut off by a rock ditch up to 9 m deep, and an outer bailey whose walls reused the Iron Age rampart and carried D-shaped towers, then an innovation in English castles. One of its two wells, 113 m deep, is among the deepest castle wells in England.

Henry III enlarged it during his wars with Wales and held Welsh captives there, and in 1254 gave it to his son Prince Edward. During the rebellion of Simon de Montfort it was retaken for the crown in 1265 by James de Audley and Urian de Saint Pierre. By the 16th century it was thought of no military use and in 1602 was sold to Sir Hugh Beeston.

In the English Civil War, Parliamentary forces under Sir William Brereton seized it on 20 February 1643; on 13 December Captain Thomas Sandford and eight Royalist soldiers surprised the governor, Captain Thomas Steele, who surrendered and was later shot for it. The Royalists held out against a siege from November 1644 until hunger forced them to surrender in November 1645.

In the 18th century the grounds were quarried and the outer gatehouse demolished for a track. John Tollemache, 1st Baron Tollemache, bought the castle in 1840, and in the mid-19th century an annual fete there drew more than 3,000 visitors a day. A legend that Richard II buried treasure at Beeston in 1399 has prompted many searches, none successful.

The ruins are a Scheduled Ancient Monument owned and managed by English Heritage, with a small museum and visitor centre. The outer bailey walls and the inner bailey's gatehouse and curtain walls are Grade I listed buildings. Enough of the walls and towers remain to show how the castle looked in its prime, and the views from the crag stretch across eight counties.
begum-hazrat-mahal: Begum Hazrat Mahal was named Mohammadi Khanum and was born at Faizabad, the former capital of Oudh State, around 1820. She was sold by her parents and became a tawaif by profession. Sold to royal agents, she entered the royal harem as a Khawasin and was promoted to a pari.

She became a junior wife of Wajid Ali Shah, the last Tajdaar-e-Awadh, after being accepted as a royal concubine, and the title Hazrat Mahal was bestowed on her after the birth of their son, Birjis Qadr. In 1856 the British annexed Awadh and Wajid Ali Shah was exiled to Calcutta. She remained in Lucknow with her son.

When the Indian Rebellion of 1857 broke out, her supporters, including Raja Hanumant Singh, rebelled against the British. Forces under Raja Jailal Singh seized control of Lucknow, and she took power as guardian of her young son, whom she declared Wali, or ruler, of Awadh. As regent she took a leading part in the rebellion against the East India Company.

One of her chief complaints was that the Company had casually demolished temples and mosques to make way for roads. In a proclamation issued in the final days of the revolt she mocked the British claim to allow freedom of worship, listing the destruction of the temples and mosques of Hindus and Mussalmans, the building of churches and the sending of clergymen into the streets to preach the Christian religion. She worked in association with Nana Saheb, and later joined the Maulavi of Faizabad in the attack on Shahjahanpur. When British forces recaptured Lucknow and most of Oudh, she was forced to retreat.

She withdrew to Nepal, where the Rana prime minister Jung Bahadur at first refused her asylum but later allowed her to stay. She died there in 1879 and was buried in an unmarked grave in the grounds of Kathmandu's Jama Masjid. After the jubilee of Queen Victoria in 1887 the British government pardoned Birjis Qadr, who was allowed to return home.

Her role in the rebellion has given her heroine status in the post-colonial history of India. On 15 August 1962 she was honoured at the Old Victoria Park in Hazratganj, Lucknow, which was renamed and given a marble memorial. In 1984 the Government of India issued a stamp in her honour, and a national scholarship for girls from minority communities bears her name.
behanzin: Béhanzin, whose name before he took the throne was Kondo, succeeded his father Glele after Glele's suicide. His people saw him as intelligent and courageous. Watching the Europeans encroach on the West African coast, he tried to keep them at a distance, and as prince he declined to meet the French envoy Jean Bayol, pleading ritual and ceremonial obligations. He was the last ruler of Dahomey to come to power through its traditional structures.

In March 1889 Dahomey attacked a village on the Ouémé whose chief was under French protection; the chief was beheaded and his head wrapped in the tricolour. The French fortified Cotonou, and on 4 March 1890 a Dahomey army of several thousand charged its stockade and was driven off with the loss of several hundred men. At the Battle of Atchoukpa, 350 French soldiers in infantry squares, with King Toffa I's men of Porto-Novo, repelled Béhanzin's force of 9,000. By a treaty of 3 October 1890 Dahomey recognised Porto-Novo as a French protectorate and ceded Cotonou.

Both sides bought arms, and in 1892 Dahomey's raids near Grand Popo and Porto-Novo led France to declare war. The French justified annexation by calling the Dahomeans savages, citing the human sacrifice of slaves at the annual customs and the women soldiers they called Amazons. General Alfred Dodds advanced up the Ouémé valley from Porto-Novo, and the French lost 85 men to an estimated 2,000 to 4,000 Fon killed. After a failed truce mission on 5 November 1892, Béhanzin burned and abandoned Abomey, which the French entered on 17 November, installing his brother Agoli-agbo as king. Unable to rebuild his army, he surrendered on 15 January 1894.

His remains were returned to Abomey after his death. His throne and his sculptures of wood, copper, iron and silver are in the Musée du Quai Branly, and their return to Benin has been widely discussed. In royal art he is represented by the shark guarding the coast, an egg held in a hand, a pun on his name in Fon, and the smoking pipe.
behbeit-el-hagar: The village and the site lie in Gharbia Governorate along the Damietta branch of the Nile, 7 kilometres north-east of Sebennytos and 8 kilometres west of Mansoura. In antiquity the place belonged to the nome of Sebennytos, the Twelfth Lower Egyptian Nome. Its Egyptian name, Pr-ḥꜣbyt(.t), means house of the festival hall, and the name lived on in Coptic and Greek forms. Egyptian texts mention it as early as the New Kingdom, though it may have been an offshoot of Sebennytos rather than a town in its own right.

Texts as early as the Pyramid Texts of the Fifth Dynasty link Isis with the region of Sebennytos, and her cult may have begun there. Yet major temples were dedicated to her only under the Thirtieth Dynasty, when building started both at Philae and at Behbeit El Hagar. The two were counterparts: Philae was her main cult centre in Upper Egypt, the Iseion at Behbeit El Hagar its equivalent in Lower Egypt.

The Iseion was begun under Nectanebo II (360–342 BCE) and finished under Ptolemy III (r. 246–222 BCE). Most Egyptian temples were built of limestone or sandstone, with granite kept for statues, obelisks or doorways, but this temple was built entirely of granite.

Only scattered blocks of the temple remain on the site. In 2026 rescue excavations by Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities found the remains of two colossal royal statues. The first is of Ramesses II: its head, about 1.6 metres high, shows him in the double crown, and archaeologists estimate the whole statue stood about 8.5 metres tall with its base. The second, about 2.4 metres long, may also show Ramesses II, and a pink granite block bore two of his royal titles.
behistun-inscription: The inscription stands on a limestone cliff at Mount Behistun, near Kermanshah, some 100 metres above an ancient road linking Babylon and Ecbatana. The Old Persian text has 414 lines in five columns, the Elamite 260 lines in eight columns and the Babylonian 112 lines; a copy in Aramaic from the reign of Darius II was found in Egypt. It opens with Darius's ancestry from Achaemenes through Teispes, Ariaramnes, Arsames and Hystaspes, and he says that eight of his dynasty were kings before him and he is the ninth. A list of twenty-three subject lands follows.

Later the text tells of the upheaval after the death of Cambyses II, in which Darius says he fought nineteen battles in a year, ending in December 521 BCE. He states that several impostors, each falsely proclaiming himself king, orchestrated the revolts, declares himself victorious in every battle and credits the grace of Ahura Mazda.

A life-sized relief shows Darius holding a bow, his left foot on a figure lying on its back who is reputed to be the pretender Gaumata. Nine one-metre figures with hands tied and ropes round their necks stand for conquered peoples.

The text was composed between Darius's coronation in the summer of 522 BCE and his death in autumn 486 BCE. The Achaemenid inscriptional tradition is thought to derive from those of Elam, Lullubi, Babylon and Assyria, and the relief resembles that of the Lullubi king Anubanini, dated to about 2300 BCE, which its sculptors may have seen. The campaigns are described with formulaic brevity, and, as in earlier inscriptions, victories are tied to divine approval.

After the end of Old Persian cuneiform the nature of the inscription was forgotten and fanciful explanations took its place. Robert Sherley saw it in 1598, and his party wrongly took it for Christian. Carsten Niebuhr published a copy in 1778, which Georg Friedrich Grotefend used to decipher ten of the 37 Old Persian symbols by 1802.

From 1835 Henry Rawlinson, an officer of the East India Company army, scaled the cliff with the help of a local boy and copied the Old Persian text, sending a full and accurate copy to Europe in 1847; the Elamite and Babylonian texts were out of easy reach and left for later. Expeditions in 1904 and 1948 obtained photographs and casts. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006.
beijing: Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of the municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. The highest point of the municipality is Mount Dongling, at 2,303 metres, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

The name Beijing means 'Northern Capital' and was applied to the city in 1403, during the Ming dynasty, to distinguish it from Nanjing, the 'Southern Capital'. The older English spelling Peking was used by the Jesuit missionary Martino Martini in an atlas published in Amsterdam in 1655. Over the past 3,000 years the city has had numerous other names.

The earliest traces of human habitation in the municipality were found in the caves of Dragon Bone Hill near the village of Zhoukoudian, where Peking Man lived. Homo erectus fossils from the caves date to 230,000 to 250,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens lived there more recently, about 27,000 years ago. Neolithic settlements have been found throughout the municipality, including in Wangfujing in central Beijing.

The first walled city in the area was Ji, the capital of the state of Ji, located around the present Guang'anmen area in the south of Xicheng District. During the early Zhou period the settlement was conquered by the state of Yan, which made it its new capital. Its original capital lay 45 kilometres to the southwest in Fangshan District. Yan eventually became one of the seven major states of China in the Warring States period.

Beijing is the capital of China and is governed as a provincial-level municipality with 16 districts. In 2024 its population was about 21.8 million. Its traditional housing consists of siheyuans, courtyard houses, and the narrow alleys between them called hutongs. It has eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, the Ming Tombs, the Zhoukoudian Peking Man Site and parts of the Great Wall and the Grand Canal. Beijing opera is its best-known traditional form of theatre.
beit-shean: Beit She'an, also called Beth-Shean and, in Arabic, Beisan or Baysan, lies about 120 m below sea level in the Beit She'an Valley. Its position at the junction of the Jordan River Valley and the Jezreel Valley made it strategically important, since it controlled access from Jordan and the interior to the coast and from Jerusalem and Jericho to the Galilee. Its ancient mound holds remains beginning in the Chalcolithic period, and excavations have revealed 18 successive ancient towns.

After Pharaoh Thutmose III conquered it in the 15th century BCE, as an inscription at Karnak records, Beit She'an became the centre of Egyptian administration in the region. Fire destroyed the site around 1150 BCE, and the Egyptians did not rebuild. The Hebrew Bible says the Philistines hung the body of King Saul on its walls, though no archaeological evidence of Philistine occupation has been found. The Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel burned the city in 732 BCE.

In the Hellenistic period it was reoccupied as Scythopolis, perhaps named for Scythian mercenaries who settled there as veterans. After Pompey made Judea part of the Roman Republic in 63 BCE, Gabinius refounded the town, and it became the leading city of the Decapolis and the only one west of the Jordan. It had a theatre, a hippodrome and a cardo. In 409 Scythopolis became capital of Palaestina Secunda, a mainly Christian city with Jewish and Samaritan communities, which reached about 40,000 people in the 6th century. After the Arab conquest of 634 it took the name Baysan, and an earthquake on 18 January 749 devastated it.

Beit She'an is a city in the Northern District of Israel with about 20,000 people and is the regional centre for the towns of its valley. Its Muslim and Christian inhabitants fled or were expelled between 1948 and 1950, and Jewish immigrants then settled it. The ancient ruins are protected within Beit She'an National Park.
beiteddine-palace: Emir Bashir II of the Shihab dynasty, later ruler of the Mount Lebanon Emirate, raised the palace on the site of a Druze hermitage. An engraving after a painting by William Henry Bartlett, published in Fisher's Drawing Room Scrap Book in 1839 with a poem by Letitia Elizabeth Landon, recorded a gathering of troops there for an incursion into Syria under Ibrahim Pasha.

After 1840 the Ottomans used the palace as a government building, and under the French Mandate it served as a local administrative office. In 1943 it was declared the official summer residence of the President of Lebanon. It was heavily damaged during the Lebanese Civil War. During the Israeli invasion of Lebanon in 2024 UNESCO placed it under enhanced protection, as one of 34 cultural sites so protected. Parts of the palace are now open to the public, while the rest remains the president’s summer residence; it houses the Beiteddine Palace Museum and hosts the annual Beiteddine Festival.

The palace is regarded as a fine example of early 19th-century Lebanese architecture with Italian influences. The main entrance opens onto a courtyard 107 by 45 metres, along one side of which runs Al-Madafa, a two-storey wing once used to receive guests. A double stairway at the western end leads to the central section, Dar El Wousta, where the austere outer court gives way to arcades, balconies, fountains and rooms of carved and painted cedar wood with Arabic calligraphy, inlaid marble and mosaics, which served as offices and reception rooms.

Beyond lie the private apartments, Dar el Harim, with the upper and lower harems, the selamlik and the kitchens, and the hammam at their northern edge. Past the baths is the shaded tomb of Bashir II and his first wife.
beiyang-army: The Qing dynasty's traditional forces, the Manchu Banners and the Green Standard Army, had declined so far that in the 1890s much of the army still carried bows, swords, spears and old matchlocks. After the Nian and Taiping Rebellions, provincial officials raised private armies of braves, such as Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army and Li Hongzhang's Huai Army. The Beiyang Army grew from the Dingwu Army, formed in 1894 and trained at Tianjin by Hu Yufen with German officers. Yuan Shikai took it over in late 1895 as the New Field Army, and with Zhang Zhidong's Self-Strengthening Army it became the core of the New Army.

Yuan's division was the only unit of the Wuwei Corps not destroyed in the Boxer Rebellion, and from 1901 he was put in charge of rebuilding the forces around Beijing under the New Policies of Empress Dowager Cixi's court. His divisions grew until by 1911 they were China's strongest force. Prince Chun dismissed Yuan in January 1909 and placed the military under Manchu princes, but when the Wuchang Uprising began on 10 October 1911, Beiyang corps were sent against it. Yuan then used the army's strength to negotiate both the emperor's abdication and Sun Yat-sen's surrender of the presidency.

As provisional president from 10 March 1912, Yuan made the Beiyang Army the national army to curb the provincial military governors. After his death in 1916 it split between Duan Qirui's Anhui clique and Feng Guozhang's Zhili clique, and with Zhang Zuolin's Fengtian clique these factions fought for northern China.

The Kuomintang's National Revolutionary Army, led by Chiang Kai-shek, advanced north from 1926, and Zhang Zuolin's National Pacification Army was pushed back into Manchuria. The National Revolutionary Army entered Beijing on 6 June 1928, ending the Beiyang Army, though many warlord forces were absorbed or kept their commands under nominal Nationalist control until 1949. Its officers came largely from the Baoding Military Academy, its recruits mostly from the peasantry.
beiyang-fleet: The fleet began in 1871, when four ships from the southern provinces were moved north to patrol the northern waters. At first it was the weakest of the four regional navies, but Li Hongzhang, Viceroy of Zhili and a trusted servant of Empress Dowager Cixi, steered most naval funds to it. In 1884 it was second only to the Nanyang Fleet at Shanghai, and by 1890 it was the largest. Before 1888 its budget was two million taels; once it came under the Navy Yamen this fell to 1.3 million, and new construction almost stopped.

The fleet guarded the coast from the mouth of the Yalu River to Jiaozhou Bay and the approaches to Tianjin and Beijing. Its headquarters was at Tianjin, with the Dagu shipyards, the Tianjin Arsenal and the naval college; Weihaiwei, on the Shandong Peninsula, became a base in 1887; and Lushunkou, built by a French syndicate between 1880 and 1890 for about three million taels, had the only dock able to repair the two battleships. Besides them the fleet had eight cruisers acquired between 1881 and 1889, the coastal battleship Pingyuan, six British gunboats and torpedo boats.

Officers came mainly from the Fuzhou academy and from the Beiyang naval college founded in 1880, and 35 cadets trained in Britain, at Greenwich, Woolwich and in the Royal Navy. Command went to Ding Ruchang, an army officer without naval training. Foreign advisers included Captain William Lang, who resigned after the Flag-hoisting incident, the German gunnery expert Constantin von Hanneken, and the American Philo Norton McGiffin.

In the Sino-French War of 1884 to 1885 the fleet kept out of reach of Admiral Amédée Courbet's squadron. On 3 July 1884 Ding withdrew it to Pei-ho, where it stayed almost idle, and the French persuaded Germany to delay delivery of Dingyuan, Zhenyuan and Jiyuan until after the war. In February 1885 Li recalled two cruisers sent to help the Nanyang Fleet break the blockade of Formosa, and in the war with Japan the Nanyang Fleet did little to help the Beiyang. Lack of funds left ships unmaintained and training at a standstill; when Dingyuan fired its 10-inch guns at the start of the Battle of the Yalu River, its flying bridge collapsed, throwing Ding and the adviser William Ferdinand Tyler with it.
beiyang-government: The Beiyang Army arose from the New Army reforms that followed the First Sino-Japanese War of 1895, headed by Li Hongzhang. Commanded by Yuan Shikai, it grew into the largest and most modernised of China's New Armies. After the Wuchang Uprising of October 1911 the Qing recalled Yuan, and the national assembly elected him premier on 8 November. Sun Yat-sen, made president of the provisional government at Nanjing on 1 January 1912, privately offered the presidency to Yuan, who held greater military resources. Emperor Puyi abdicated on 12 February 1912, and the National Council elected Yuan provisional president the next day. Yuan refused to move to Nanjing, and the government settled in Beijing.

The Kuomintang, led by Song Jiaoren, emerged as the leading party from the elections of January 1913. Song was assassinated in Shanghai in March; Yuan was suspected but never officially implicated. After the Second Revolution was suppressed, Yuan forced parliament to elect him president for five years, expelled Kuomintang members, and dissolved parliament in January 1914. A constitutional compact of May 1914 gave the president unlimited power. After Yuan died in 1916, Li Yuanhong succeeded him and reinstated the 1912 provisional constitution. In June 1917 the general Zhang Xun occupied Beijing and restored Puyi as emperor, a restoration that rival generals ended within weeks. Sun Yat-sen and his followers then set up a rival government at Guangzhou under the Constitutional Protection Movement.

Power then passed between cliques. The Zhili clique, under Wu Peifu, defeated Zhang Zuolin's Fengtian clique in the First Zhili–Fengtian War, which began on 28 April. In November 1924 Huang Fu was made acting president, the 1923 constitution was set aside and Puyi was expelled from the Forbidden City. Duan Qirui then headed a provisional government with the combined powers of president and premier, though he was at the mercy of Feng Yuxiang and Zhang Zuolin.

The government kept diplomatic recognition, foreign loans and access to tax and customs revenue. Its foreign ministry, with diplomats such as Wellington Koo, secured the return of German concessions in Shandong in 1922, and China was a founding member of the League of Nations. The Kuomintang launched the Northern Expedition in July 1926 and quickly defeated Wu Peifu and Sun Chuanfang. In June 1927 Zhang Zuolin was declared Generalissimo and formed a military government, the only time the regime was explicitly one. Feng Yuxiang's Guominjun and Yan Xishan's Shanxi army swore allegiance to Chiang Kai-shek's government in Nanjing in mid-1927. The name Beiyang government is a retronym popularised by the Nationalist government, and some historians prefer Beijing government.
bejaia: Béjaïa owes its existence to its port. It stands in a sickle-shaped bay on the Gulf of Béjaïa, protected from the swell by Cape Carbon, and is backed by Mount Gouraya, with the Babors range behind. It is also the outlet of the Soummam valley. Its position between Grande and Petite Kabylie has not given it a firm hinterland, since both regions turn towards inland centres. The name is a transliteration of the Berber Bgayet, probably from a word meaning wild brambles and blackberries; Ibn Khaldun instead derived it from the tribe called the Bedjaïa.

Prehistoric people lived around Béjaïa, and the Afalou caves hold some of the oldest burials of modern humans, of the Iberomaurusian culture. The Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax mentions the site in the 5th century BCE, and the region belonged to Numidia and later to Rome. Umayyad conquerors from Kairouan called the surrounding mountains el 'adua, the enemy, for the stubborn resistance there; the city seems to have been conquered relatively late, around 708. Its prosperity, tied to trans-Saharan and Mediterranean trade, declined around the turn of the 15th century as world trade moved to new sea routes.

Pedro Navarro took the city for the Spanish from Sultan Abdelaziz in 1510, ending the kingdom of Bougie. The harshness of the Spanish caused the local population to flee, and Abu Bakr, Abdelaziz's brother, failed to retake the city in 1512. The beylerbey Salah Raïs entered it after the Battle of Béjaïa in 1555, with the help of the Kabyles of Koukou, and it became part of the Regency of Algiers. The French took it in 1833 after fierce resistance, but kept to a limited occupation until 1846. In 1959 it was Algeria's most important oil port, at the end of the pipeline from Hassi Messaoud.

Béjaïa is the capital of Béjaïa Province in Algeria, with 177,988 inhabitants at the 2008 census. The old town, nestled against the Gouraya massif, keeps Moorish houses, the Casbah and the Sea Gate, and Roman remains such as a cistern. Spanish and French building removed many medieval structures, among them the Hammadid Palace of the Star. The port exports oil, iron ore, phosphates and wine.
bela-i-of-hungary: Béla descended from a younger branch of the Árpád dynasty, and his baptismal name was Adalbert. Modern historians hold that he and his brothers Levente and Andrew were the sons of Vazul and a concubine. When King Stephen's only surviving son Emeric died on 2 September 1031, Vazul had the strongest claim, but Stephen suspected him of inclining to paganism, favoured his own nephew Peter Orseolo and had Vazul blinded. The three brothers fled. They settled first in Bohemia, then in Poland, where King Mieszko II Lambert received them warmly. Béla married his daughter, named Richeza or Adelaide, around 1033.

In 1046 a rebellion dominated by pagans dethroned Peter Orseolo, and Andrew was proclaimed king. Levente died that year, and Andrew, still childless, invited Béla home. In 1048 Béla returned and received one third of the kingdom with the title of duke, including large territories along the eastern and northern borders such as Nyitra and Bihar. He kept royal prerogatives, among them coinage, and his half-denars bear the inscription BELA DUX. Their relations soured after Andrew had his young son Solomon crowned in 1057 or 1058. Andrew offered Béla a choice between a crown and a sword, planning to have him killed if he chose the crown. Béla chose the sword and went to Poland.

Béla returned in autumn 1060 with Polish troops provided by Duke Boleslaus the Bold and defeated Andrew in two battles, at the Tisza and at Moson. He was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 6 December 1060. He reformed the coinage, introducing large coins of purest silver, fixed maximum prices and moved the weekly markets from Sunday to Saturday. In 1061 a crowd of commoners at Székesfehérvár demanded the restoration of paganism, and he put down the uprising within three days. In 1063 German princes decided to restore Solomon. Béla was fatally injured when his throne broke beneath him at Dömös, and he died on 11 September 1063. His sons Géza and Ladislaus later became kings.
bela-iii-of-hungary: Béla was the second son of King Géza II of Hungary and Euphrosyne of Kiev. Around 1161 his father granted him a duchy that included Croatia and central Dalmatia, and possibly Sirmium. After Géza died in 1162, Stephen III succeeded him. In 1163 a peace treaty with the Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos sent Béla to Constantinople, where he was renamed Alexios and given the title of despotes and a betrothal to the emperor's daughter Maria.

Manuel named Béla-Alexios his heir in 1165, and Béla accompanied Byzantine campaigns against Hungary. When the emperor's son Alexios was born in 1169, the betrothal was dissolved and Béla was reduced to the rank of kaisar. In 1170 he married Agnes of Antioch, the emperor's sister-in-law.

Stephen III died on 4 March 1172. Béla promised the emperor that he would never make war on the Byzantine Empire and returned to Hungary. Archbishop Lucas of Esztergom refused to crown him, accusing him of simony, so the Archbishop of Kalocsa crowned him on 18 January 1173 with Pope Alexander III's approval. He held his brother Géza in captivity for more than a decade.

After Manuel died on 24 September 1180, Béla restored his rule in Dalmatia within six months and later occupied Syrmium. In 1185 he made peace with Emperor Isaac II Angelos, who married Béla's daughter Margaret. In the summer of 1186 Béla married Margaret of France. He occupied the Principality of Halych in 1188 but lost it within two years. He invited Cistercian monks from France and began a royal castle and cathedral at Esztergom.

He had learnt the value of organised administration in Constantinople. In 1181 he ordered that a charter be issued for every transaction made in his presence, and later chronicles credit him with founding the Royal Chancery.

Béla died on 23 April 1196, aged about 49 according to studies of his bones. He was described as the wealthiest European monarch of his time on the evidence of a list of his revenues, though the list's reliability is questioned. The royal palace built in Esztergom during his reign is the first example of Gothic architecture in Central Europe.
bela-iv-of-hungary: Béla was the eldest son of King Andrew II of Hungary and his first wife, Gertrude of Merania, and was born in the second half of 1206. Noblemen murdered his mother in 1213, and in 1214 a group of lords had the eight-year-old Béla crowned against his father's wishes. Andrew refused him a province until 1220, when he became Duke of Slavonia and married Maria, daughter of Theodore I Laskaris, Emperor of Nicaea. From 1226 he governed Transylvania, where he supported Dominican missions among the Cumans, and in 1233 he adopted the title King of Cumania.

Béla succeeded his father on 21 September 1235 and set out to restore royal authority. Commissions revised the land grants made since 1196 and he reclaimed royal estates, which alienated many nobles and prelates. When the Mongols under Batu Khan reached Hungary in 1241 the lords he had alienated gave poor support, and the Cumans, his most valuable allies, left after a mob in Pest killed their chieftain Köten. His army, of fewer than 60,000, was destroyed at Mohi on 11 April 1241, and the Mongols ravaged the lands east of the Danube until they withdrew in March 1242.

Béla returned in May 1242 to a ruined country, at least half the villages east of the Danube depopulated, and famine followed. He abandoned the royal monopoly on castle-building, and nearly 100 new fortresses were raised by the end of his reign, among them one he founded at Visegrád. He settled colonists from the Holy Roman Empire, Poland and neighbouring lands, and made Buda a royal town. With Ruthenian and Polish princes he formed a defensive alliance against the Mongols, and he held the Duchy of Styria from 1254 to 1258.

From the early 1260s Béla quarrelled with his eldest son and heir, Stephen, who suspected his father of favouring Béla's younger son, also named Béla, and his daughter Anna. A civil war followed in which Stephen routed his father's army at Isaszeg in March 1265, and it ended in 1266 with Hungary divided along the Danube. Béla died on 3 May 1270 on Rabbits' Island and was buried at Esztergom. He died as a Franciscan tertiary, and his daughters Kunigunda, Yolanda and Margaret were later venerated as saints. Posterity called him the second founder of the state. The Illuminated Chronicle called him a man of peace, but the least fortunate in the conduct of armies.
bela-kun: Béla Kun was born Béla Kohn on 20 February 1886 in the village of Lele, in the Kingdom of Hungary, now part of Romania. His father was a lapsed Jewish village notary, and his mother, a Hungarian, had converted to Judaism on marriage. He studied law at Franz Joseph University in Kolozsvár from 1904, the year he began to be called Kun rather than Kohn, and befriended the poet Endre Ady, who introduced him to Budapest's left-wing intelligentsia. He worked as a journalist until the First World War, served in the Austro-Hungarian Army and was captured by the Russian army in 1916.

The Russian Revolution freed him from a prisoner-of-war camp. In March 1918 in Moscow he co-founded the Hungarian Group of the Russian Communist Party and came to know Lenin, though he stood with the ultra-radical left, which wished to continue the war against the Central Powers. He fought for the Bolsheviks in the Russian Civil War and returned to Budapest on 16 November 1918 with Soviet money. On 24 November he founded the Party of Communists from Hungary and campaigned against the government of President Mihály Károlyi.

The Hungarian Soviet Republic was proclaimed on 21 March 1919, after his release from prison. Sándor Garbai was its nominal head, but power rested with Kun, officially People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs and from April also for Defence. Social Democrats held most commissariats but accepted the leadership of the smaller Communist Party. Four months later the regime collapsed before an offensive by the Kingdom of Romania.

Kun went into exile in Vienna, where he was interned until July 1920. In Russia he led the Crimean Revolutionary Committee and took part in the Red Terror in Crimea in 1920-1921. He advised the German Communists in the failed March Action of 1921, which Lenin blamed him for. During the Great Purge he was arrested by the NKVD on 28 June 1937, accused of Trotskyism and sentenced to death after a brief secret trial. He was shot at Kommunarka on 29 August 1938. After his rehabilitation in 1956 the Soviet party told the Hungarians that he had died in prison in 1939; only in 1989 did the Soviet government acknowledge the true date.
belagavi: Belagavi lies in north-western Karnataka, near the borders with Maharashtra and Goa, near the foothills of the Sahyadri range of the Western Ghats. It stands at an average elevation of 770 metres, about 100 kilometres from the Arabian Sea, with the Markandeya river flowing nearby. It is 502 kilometres from Bangalore and 500 kilometres from Mumbai, and is the administrative headquarters of the Belagavi division and district.

The town was founded in the late 12th century by the Ratta dynasty, who moved from nearby Saundatti. A Ratta official named Bichiraja built the Jain temple of Kamal Basadi, dedicated to Neminatha, in 1204. Its original name was Venugram, a Sanskrit name meaning village of bamboo. In the early 13th century it passed to the Yadava kingdom, as an inscription of 1261 attests. The Khalji dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate invaded the region in the 14th century, after which Belgaum came under the Vijayanagara Empire.

The Bahmani Sultanate conquered it in 1474 with an army led by Mahmud Gawan. After the Bahmani state split in 1518 the town became part of the Bijapur Sultanate. In 1686 the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb overthrew Bijapur, and the Mughals called the town Azamnagar. Mughal control collapsed after Aurangzeb's death in 1707, and the Maratha confederacy took the area under the Peshwas. Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan overran it in 1776, but the Peshwa regained it after Tipu was defeated. The British annexed Belgaum in 1818. In 1824 Kitturu Chennamma, queen of Kittur, led an unsuccessful armed rebellion against them.

Belgaum hosted the 39th session of the Indian National Congress in December 1924 under the presidency of Mahatma Gandhi. It was a major British military installation, partly because of its proximity to Portuguese Goa, and in 1961 the Indian government used forces from Belgaum to end Portuguese rule in Goa. In 1956 the States Reorganisation Act transferred Belgaum and ten taluks of Bombay State to Mysore State, which was renamed Karnataka in 1973. Maharashtra claims the city on linguistic grounds, a dispute taken to the Supreme Court. The Maharashtra Ekikaran Samiti, formed in 1948 to campaign for the merger, marks 17 January as martyrs' day for activists shot by police in 1956.

On 1 November 2014 the Karnataka government changed the name from Belgaum to Belagavi. Kannada and Marathi are the predominant languages, with Urdu, Konkani, Hindi and Telugu also spoken. The Suvarna Vidhana Soudha, an administrative building inaugurated in 2012, hosts the annual winter session of the Karnataka Legislative Assembly.
belarus: Belarus is a landlocked country of 207,600 square kilometres, lying between latitudes 51° and 57° N and measuring 560 kilometres from north to south and 650 from west to east. It is relatively flat, with large tracts of marshy land, about 40% forest, and 11,000 lakes.

Three major rivers run through it: the Neman flows west toward the Baltic Sea, the Pripyat flows east to the Dnieper, and the Dnieper flows south toward the Black Sea. The highest point is Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, at 345 metres. About 70% of the radiation from the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighbouring Ukraine entered Belarusian territory, and about a fifth of the land was affected by fallout.

Baltic tribes first permanently settled the region in the 3rd century, and around the 5th century the Slavs took it over, and the gradual assimilation of the Baltic settlers into Slavic culture was peaceful. In the 9th century it became part of Kievan Rus', a vast East Slavic state ruled by the Rurikids, which split into independent principalities on the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054.

The Battle on the Nemiga River in 1067 is considered the founding date of Minsk. The lands avoided the brunt of the 13th-century Mongol invasion and joined the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; the annals affirm an alliance and united foreign policy between Polotsk and Lithuania for decades. The duchy fought alongside Poland against the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410.

By the 14th century the lands had come fully under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, a period lasting 500 years until the partitions of 1792–1795 placed Belarus within the Russian Empire for the first time. The Byelorussian SSR, formed after the Russian Revolution, became a founding republic of the Soviet Union in 1922. After the Polish-Soviet War (1918–1921) Belarus lost almost half its territory to Poland, and in the Second World War it lost about a quarter of its population and half of its economic resources. Many prominent Belarusian intellectuals were exiled or killed in Stalinist purges in the 1930s.

Belarus proclaimed its sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and gained independence on 25 August 1991. Belarus and Russia signed a treaty in 2000 forming the Union State. The official languages are Russian and Belarusian. Francysk Skaryna's Bible, published between 1517 and 1525, was the first book printed in Belarus or anywhere in Eastern Europe.
