belarusians: Balts historically inhabited most of the territory of present-day Belarus, and many ancient place names there are of Baltic origin. Slavic settlement began around the 6th and 7th centuries, and the Balts were gradually absorbed, a process that ended in eastern and central Belarus around the 12th century. In the 8th and 9th centuries most of the land was held by three tribal unions, the Kryvichs, Dryhavichs and Radzimichs. The Kryvichs were the most important, and Polotsk and Smolensk, which they founded, were the chief cultural and political centres. The principalities formed there belonged to Kievan Rus'.

Beginning with Mindaugas and Gediminas, Lithuania expanded rapidly east and south, and by the mid-14th century most of modern Belarus, including Polotsk, Vitebsk, Minsk, Turov and Pinsk, belonged to the Lithuanian state. These lands kept their Orthodox Christian and East Slavic traditions, and the Ruthenian nobility took full part in Lithuania's political life. Polish influence grew after the Union of Lublin in 1569 and the Union of Brest in 1596, and Polish replaced Ruthenian in official use in the late 17th century. A modern Belarusian national identity did not yet exist.

After the Third Partition of 1795 the Russian Empire took most of these lands. In 1839 Tsar Nicholas I banned the word Belarus and replaced it with Northwestern Krai. A short-lived Belarusian Democratic Republic was declared in March 1918. By the Peace of Riga in 1921 the territory was split between the Second Polish Republic and Soviet Russia, which created the Belarusian Soviet Socialist Republic. More than two million people, about a quarter of the population, were killed in Belarus during the three years of German occupation.

Before 1991 Belarusians were known as Ruthenians, Litvins and White Ruthenians, and in the Soviet era as Byelorussians. The name White Rus' was first used in the Middle Ages for the area of Polotsk. The Republic of Belarus has existed since the Belovezha Accords ended the Soviet Union in 1991. Belarusians form the majority of its population, with minorities in Ukraine, Poland, Russia and Lithuania, and many emigrated to the United States, Brazil and Canada in the early 20th century. Most are Eastern Orthodox.
belek-ghazi: Nur al-Dawla Belek bin Bahram Ghazi was the son of Behram and a grandson of Artuk Bey, an important figure of the Seljuk Empire in the 11th century. He was briefly governor of Suruç, a city captured during the First Crusade in 1098. He took part in the failed Seljuk expedition to recover Antioch from the Crusaders and was present during the Crusade of 1101, which ended in a Seljuk victory.

In 1112 Belek captured Harput from the Mengüceks and founded a beylik there, now known as the Harput branch of the Artukids, beside the Hasankeyf branch of Sökmen and the Mardin branch of Ilghazi. The next year he married Ayşe Hatun, widow of the Anatolian Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan, which tied him to the Seljuk family. In 1120, with the Danishmends, he defeated a coalition of the Mengüceks and Constantine Gabras of the Byzantine Empire.

After the death of Ilghazi in 1122, Belek became the leader of the Artukids. His capture of Joscelin I that year and of Baldwin II of Jerusalem in 1123 made him known both in the Muslim world and in Europe. He served as emir of Aleppo from 1123 to 1124.

In 1124 Belek was invited to defend Tyre, the only port the Muslims still used in Syria, against the Crusaders. At the time he was besieging Manbij, whose emir, Hassan al-Ba'labakki ibn Gümüshtigin, had pledged allegiance to Joscelin and been imprisoned by Belek. He took the city, but the castle held out under Hassan's brother Isa. Belek drove a relief force under Joscelin back to Turbessel and kept up the siege until he was killed by an arrow on 6 May 1124. His cousin Husam al-Din Timurtash ibn Ilghazi carried his body to Aleppo. Harput was soon annexed by the Artukids of Hasankeyf, though another Artukid beylik was founded there in 1185.
belem: Belém lies about 100 km upriver from the Atlantic Ocean, on the Pará River, which belongs to the greater Amazon River system and is separated from the larger part of the Amazon delta by Marajó Island. It is the gateway to the Amazon, with a busy port. The climate is tropical rainforest, with more than 60 mm of rain on average in every month and a wetter season from December to May. The city is called the City of Mango Trees because of the many mango trees in it, and it is named after Santa Maria de Belém in Lisbon.

In 1615 the Portuguese captain-general Francisco Caldeira Castelo Branco led a military expedition, sent by the Governor General of Brazil, to check the trading excursions of French, Dutch and English up the Amazon. On 12 January 1616 he anchored in Guajará Bay, where the Pará and Guamá rivers meet. Mistaking the bay for the main channel, he built a wooden fort covered with straw, which he called Presépio, meaning nativity scene, now known as Forte do Castelo. The colony it formed was named Feliz Lusitânia and became the beginning of Belém. The fort failed to suppress Dutch and French trading but did ward off colonisation. Belém was the first European colony on the Amazon, and was given city status in 1655.

Sugar was important in the region until the end of the 17th century, followed by cattle ranching and, in the 18th century, rice, cotton and coffee. Belém then became the main exporting centre of the Amazon rubber industry, and its position was further enhanced in 1866 when the Amazon, Tocantins and Tapajós rivers were opened to navigation, although the Port of Manaus upriver reduced its importance somewhat. The rubber era ended after the boom of 1910–12, but Belém remained the main commercial centre of northern Brazil.

Belém is the capital and largest city of the state of Pará, in northern Brazil. Its colonial quarter keeps tree-filled squares, churches and traditional blue tiles. On the second Sunday in October it holds the Círio of Nazaré, described as the largest religious event in Brazil, a procession that follows a statue of the Virgin and Child and is regarded as the Christmas of the Amazon; its river pilgrimage honours the water men, who regard the Virgin of Nazareth as their patron saint. The Federal University of Pará and the State University of Pará are in the city.
belfast: Belfast stands on the banks of the River Lagan and is connected to the open sea through Belfast Lough and the North Channel. Its name comes from the Irish Béal Feirste, "mouth of the Farset", a river whose name means a sandbar or tidal ford. The Farset flowed into the Lagan, until it was culverted in the late 18th century, along what is now High Street, and the early settlement developed at the low-water crossing near the present Queen's Bridge. The site has been occupied since at least the Neolithic, and the Giant's Ring, a 5,000-year-old henge, lies near the city.

In 1613, under a commission from King James VI, Sir Arthur Chichester undertook the Plantation of Belfast and its surroundings, building a new castle and attracting mainly English and Manx settlers. Scottish Presbyterians followed, and in 1649 an English Parliamentarian army temporarily expelled them in the town's only recorded siege. Their descendants' disaffection with Ireland's Anglican establishment contributed to the rebellion of 1798 and the union with Great Britain in 1801.

From the 1820s Belfast expanded rapidly in industry. After a cotton boom and bust it became the global leader in linen goods, earning the name Linenopolis, and shipbuilding led to heavier industry. When it was granted city status in 1888 it was the world's largest centre of linen manufacture, and by the 1900s its shipyards were building up to a quarter of all United Kingdom tonnage.

New industry drew large numbers of Catholics from rural districts to a largely Protestant town, and sectarian tensions grew. They erupted in sustained violence in 1920–22, as Belfast became the capital of the six north-eastern counties that kept the British connection.

In the spring of 1941 the German Luftwaffe attacked the city four times, damaging or destroying more than half its housing and killing more than a thousand people, the heaviest loss of life in any air raid outside London. The Troubles began in the late 1960s, and the British Army was on the streets from August 1969 in the longest continuous deployment in its history.

Belfast is the capital, largest city and main port of Northern Ireland, the second largest city on the island of Ireland after Dublin, with 345,418 people recorded in 2021. A division of working-class Protestant and Catholic districts by barriers remains a legacy of the conflict. The port still has commercial and industrial docks and a reduced Harland and Wolff shipyard, and the Titanic Quarter has been developed on former dockland. Ulster University and Queen's University Belfast are in the city.
belfort-gap: The gap marks the watershed between the drainage basins of the Rhine to the east and the Rhône to the west, and so forms part of the European Watershed between the North Sea and the Mediterranean. Its elevation runs from 315 metres in the Doubs valley at Montbéliard to 651 metres on Mont Salbert. The corridor, put at about 40 kilometres wide or by others at 20, links the Haut-Rhin department with the Territoire de Belfort. It lets warm Mediterranean air flow north-eastwards into the Upper Rhine Plain, and it carries the A36 autoroute, the Basel to Paris railway and the LGV Rhin-Rhône high-speed line.

The gap is first recorded in a military role in 58 BCE, when Julius Caesar marched through it to confront the Germanic chieftain Ariovistus. After the Western Roman Empire collapsed in the 5th century, the Alemanni settled east of it and the Burgundians to the west. Both were conquered by the Kingdom of Francia early in the 6th century, but the gap remained the border between Germanic and Romance languages.

When the Carolingian Empire broke up, the gap again divided East Francia from the Kingdom of Burgundy-Arles, both part of the Holy Roman Empire by 1033. The House of Habsburg acquired the Sundgau in 1324 and the County of Burgundy in 1493. The Sundgau passed to France under the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, and the Franche-Comté under the Treaties of Nijmegen in 1678.

During the Franco-Prussian War the Prussian army laid siege to Belfort, hoping to break through the gap into central France; the siege dragged on for months until an armistice. When Alsace was ceded to the new German Empire in 1871, the language border was used to draw the line, so France kept Belfort, which was then heavily fortified. At the outbreak of the First World War French troops invaded Germany through the gap, and in November 1944 the French I Corps under General de Lattre advanced through it.
belgian-revolution: After the defeat of Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, the Congress of Vienna combined the United Provinces of the Netherlands with the former Austrian Netherlands under the House of Orange-Nassau, creating a buffer state north of France. The southern provinces were mainly Flemish and Walloon and traditionally Catholic, while the north was dominated by the Dutch Reformed. King William I was a supporter of the German Lutheran tradition and wished to influence the appointment of bishops.

The southerners held about 62% of the population but 50% of the seats in the General Assembly. Only one minister in four was Belgian, and the administration had four times as many Dutch officials as Belgian. Grievances included state control of schools, a language reform of 1823 that favoured Dutch, a free trade policy that hurt southern industry, high unemployment and the limits on freedom of the press and assembly.

On 25 August 1830, at the Théâtre Royal de la Monnaie in Brussels, a performance of Daniel Auber's opera La Muette de Portici was followed by riots, as members of the audience joined a crowd already in the streets. Uprisings spread, factories were occupied and machinery destroyed. The Crown Prince William, sent to Brussels, was persuaded that an administrative separation of north and south was the only solution, but his father rejected it.

About 8,000 Dutch troops under Prince Frederik failed to retake Brussels in street fighting from 23 to 26 September, and many southern recruits deserted. A National Congress was summoned and a Provisional Government formed under Charles Latour Rogier. The London Conference of the five major powers, Austria, the United Kingdom, France, Prussia and Russia, eventually accepted Belgian independence, and none sent troops to aid the Dutch.

The National Congress decided on a constitutional monarchy, and the Belgian Constitution was proclaimed on 7 February 1831. It refused any candidate from the House of Orange-Nassau and eventually offered the throne to Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, who took his oath as king on 21 July 1831, the date now kept as Belgian National Day.

On 2 August 1831 William invaded in the Ten Days' Campaign and defeated the Belgian army at Hasselt, but French troops under Marshal Étienne Maurice Gérard crossed the border on 9 August, and the Dutch agreed to an armistice. The Treaty of London of 19 April 1839 recognised Belgium as independent and neutral, with half of Luxembourg and Limburg. A movement for reunion with the Netherlands, Orangism, was active in Flanders and Brussels and was banned from public expression in 1834.
belgium: Belgium covers 30,689 square kilometres in the Low Countries, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, France and the North Sea. It has three main geographical regions: the coastal plain in the northwest, with sand dunes and polders; the central plateau, a slowly rising landscape of fertile valleys and the sandy plain of the Campine; and the forested, rugged Ardennes in the southeast. The highest point is the Signal de Botrange, at 694 metres. The climate is maritime temperate, with significant precipitation in all seasons.

In his account of the conquest of Gaul, Julius Caesar described the Belgae as inhabiting northern Gaul between the Seine and Marne rivers and the Rhine, and as the bravest of the Gauls. The northernmost tribes, including the Menapii, Nervii and Atuatuci, held most of modern Belgium. After Caesar's conquests the Roman province of Gallia Belgica covered most of northern Gaul, and the eastern part of modern Belgium lay in Germania Inferior. As Roman central government collapsed, the provinces were inhabited by Romanised populations and Germanic-speaking Franks, who came to dominate military and political life.

The region was later part of the Carolingian Empire, the Holy Roman Empire and the Burgundian Netherlands, and was ruled by Habsburg Spain (1556–1714), the Austrian Habsburgs (1714–1794) and Revolutionary France (1794–1815). Most of it joined the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after the Congress of Vienna in 1815. Being contested by so many powers gave Belgium the name the Battlefield of Europe.

An independent Belgium was established in 1830 after the Belgian Revolution. It was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, and mining and steelmaking in Liège Province and around Charleroi made it one of the three most industrialised nations in the world from 1830 to 1910, although Flanders suffered famine from 1846 to 1850.

Belgium is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a federal state of three regions, Flanders, Wallonia and the Brussels-Capital Region, with Dutch-speaking, French-speaking and small German-speaking communities. Tensions between Dutch-speakers and French-speakers rose in the second half of the twentieth century and led to reforms that turned a unitary state into a federal one between 1970 and 1993. After the 2010 federal election the country went a record 589 days without forming a government. Brussels hosts the seats of several European Union institutions, and the country's colonies, the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi, became independent between 1960 and 1962.
belgium-luxembourg-economic-union: The treaty was signed on 25 July 1921, although a referendum in Luxembourg had first favoured closer ties with France rather than Belgium. It came into force when the Luxembourg Chamber of Deputies ratified it on 22 December 1922. For Luxembourg the union had several advantages over the German customs union. Belgium could change its tariffs or conclude trade treaties only after consulting the Luxembourg government, whereas before 1918 Luxembourg had had to accept German decisions, and only Luxembourg's own customs officers worked in the country, where Prussian officials had once served.

The economic frontier between the two countries was lifted, and in 1929 the Belgian and Luxembourg francs were fixed at a set parity, revised in 1935 and 1944. The union was run by a board of directors of two Belgian members, one of them the chairman, and one Luxembourg member, and by the Higher Council of the Union, with three Belgian and two Luxembourg members. Until 1999, when European Community rules required separate figures, international trade statistics were published for the two countries only as one combined entity.

The original treaty ran for fifty years and was later extended, and on 18 December 2002 the two countries signed a new convention. The union has been seen as the forerunner of the Benelux Union, founded with the Netherlands as the Benelux Customs Union by the London Customs Convention of 1944. Many of its aims passed to Benelux and later to the European Union, but it keeps some role in deciding more precise measures between the two states.
belgrade: Belgrade lies 116.75 m above sea level at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers, at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkan Peninsula. Its historical core, Kalemegdan, stands on the right banks of both rivers. Since the 19th century the city has expanded to the south and east, and after World War II New Belgrade was built on the left bank of the Sava, connecting Belgrade with Zemun. The name in Serbian, Beograd, means White City.

Chipped stone tools found in Zemun show that nomadic foragers lived around Belgrade in the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic eras. The first farmers belonged to the Neolithic Starčevo culture, which flourished between 6200 and 5200 BCE, and the Vinča culture (5500-4500 BCE) grew out of their settlements and is known for very large settlements. In antiquity Thraco-Dacians inhabited the region, and after 279 BCE Celts settled the city and named it Singidūn. The Romans conquered it under Augustus and awarded it city rights in the mid-2nd century.

Slavs settled the city in the 520s. It then changed hands several times between the Byzantine Empire, the Frankish Empire, the Bulgarian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary before becoming the seat of the Serbian king Stefan Dragutin in 1284. It was the capital of the Serbian Despotate under Stefan Lazarević, and his successor Đurađ Branković returned it to the Hungarian king in 1427. Noon bells rung in support of the Hungarian army during the siege of 1456 against the Ottoman Empire remain a widespread church tradition.

After the Serbian Revolution Belgrade was named capital of Serbia again in 1841. Northern Belgrade remained the southernmost Habsburg post until 1918, when former Austro-Hungarian territories joined the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Belgrade was the capital of Yugoslavia from its creation to its dissolution. Placed in a strategic position, it has been battled over in 115 wars and razed 44 times, and has been bombed five times and besieged many times.

Belgrade is the capital and largest city of Serbia and the seat of its central government. The 2022 census counted 1,197,114 people in the city proper and 1,682,720 in its administrative area. The University of Belgrade, founded in 1808 as the Velika škola, is the oldest institution of higher learning in Serbia. The author Ivo Andrić wrote The Bridge on the Drina in the city, and it hosted the first Non-Aligned Movement Summit in 1961.
belisarius: Belisarius was born around 500, probably in Germaneia, a fortified town within the borders of Thrace and Paeonia. His ancestry is unknown. By 526 he was a senior guardsman of Justinian, nephew of Emperor Justin I, though how he reached that post is unrecorded. In the war against Persia over Iberia his early record was mixed: he and Sittas raided Persian territory, but he lost his first independent command, fled with his troops at Tanurin after his colleagues were lured into a trap, and lost at Mindouos. He was promoted soon after, so he was probably not held to blame.

During the Nika riots of 532, in which the Blues and Greens rose against Justinian and declared Hypatius emperor, Belisarius, Mundus and Narses were called in. Belisarius led his troops into the crowd in the Hippodrome while Narses blocked the other exits, and the revolt ended in a massacre in which between 30,000 and 60,000 people died, mostly unarmed civilians.

In June 533 Belisarius sailed for North Africa with about 17,000 soldiers and a fleet, against the Vandal king Gelimer, who had deposed Justinian's guest friend Hilderic in 530. He landed at Caput Vada rather than at Carthage, defeated the Vandals at Ad Decimum and took Carthage, and Gelimer was compelled to surrender after Tricamarum. In 535 Justinian sent him against the Ostrogoths in Italy. He took Sicily, entering Syracuse on 31 December 535, and from March 537 to March 538 held Rome against the far larger army of Vitiges. By late 539 he had surrounded Ravenna.

In 559 Justinian called him from retirement to meet the Kutrigur Bulgars under Khan Zabergan, who had crossed the Danube and approached Constantinople. With 300 veterans and a host of civilians he camped near them, had a trench dug and many torches lit to exaggerate his numbers, and placed his men in a narrow defile where the Kutrigurs could not use their numbers.

In 562 Belisarius was tried in Constantinople on a charge of conspiring against Justinian, found guilty and put under house arrest, but he was soon pardoned and restored to favour. He died in March 565. A later legend that he was blinded and reduced to begging near the Pincian Gate of Rome is thought apocryphal by most modern scholars. Procopius's Secret History, whose reliability is debated, portrays him as a cuckolded husband dependent on his wife Antonina, and recent work reads that portrait as invective. Historians generally rate him highly, chiefly for Dara, Ad Decimum and Tricamarum.
belize-city: Belize City stands at the mouth of Haulover Creek, a distributary of the Belize River, which empties into the Caribbean Sea eight kilometres from the city. The city proper is usually divided into two areas: Northside, bounded by Haulover Creek and ending in the east at the Fort George area, and Southside, which includes downtown and the port. Four bridges, among them the Swing Bridge at Market Square, link the divisions, and the main canals are Haulover Creek, Burdon Canal and Collet Canal. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a long wet season from May through February, and the city is susceptible to flooding in the rainy season.

The city was founded as Belize Town in 1638 by English lumber harvesters, on the site of a small Maya settlement called Holzuz. The place suited the English as a central post because it was on the sea and was a natural outlet for the local rivers and creeks down which they shipped logwood and mahogany. It also became the home of the thousands of African slaves brought in by the English, and later the British from 1707, to work in the forestry industry.

Belize Town was the coordination site for the Battle of St. George's Caye in 1798, which the British won against would-be invaders, and the home of the local courts and government officials until the 1970s. For this reason historians often say that the capital was the colony, since the centre of British control lay there. Antonio Soberanis Gómez, George Price and Evan X Hyde all lobbied to take their movements outside the city, but people continued to look to it for guidance.

Belize City was directly struck by hurricanes in 1931 and 1961, and fires have burnt out stretches of housing at various times. Hurricane Hattie swept ashore in October 1961 and almost entirely destroyed the city. The government was moved to the new capital, Belmopan, in 1970.

Belize City is the largest city in Belize, with a population of 63,999 at the 2022 census, and it is the country's principal port and its financial and industrial hub. It has branches of all the major banks and the Central Bank, and the Supreme Court of Belize still sits there.

St John's Cathedral, begun in 1812 and completed in 1820 of orange bricks that came on British ships as ballast, is the oldest Anglican church in Central America and the only Anglican cathedral outside England where kings have been crowned.
bella-ciao: The origins of the song are unclear. One hypothesis is that it began as Alla mattina appena alzata, sung with different words by the seasonal workers of the rice fields of Italy's Po Valley from the late 19th century to the first half of the 20th. The work, weeding the flooded fields from the end of April to the beginning of June, was done mainly by women called mondine, recruited from the poorest classes, who spent the day barefoot in water up to their knees. Poor conditions, long hours and low pay led to discontent and, at times, riots in the early 20th century. The earliest written version, dated 1906, comes from near Vercelli in Piedmont.
A possible source for the melody is a Yiddish tune, the Koilen song, recorded in 1919 in New York by the klezmer accordionist Mishka Ziganoff, according to the researcher Fausto Giovannardi.

As a partisan song, Bella ciao is dedicated to the fighters of the Italian Resistance against Nazi German occupation and the collaborationist fascist forces. Its place in the war itself is disputed. There is no documentary trace of the partisan version before its text was first published in 1953 in the magazine La Lapa, and then in L'Unità in 1957, and it is absent from important songbooks of the time. The partisan and journalist Giorgio Bocca said he never heard it sung in twenty months of the partisan war, and historians such as Antonio Virgilio Savona and Michele Straniero agree that it became popular only after the war. A few, including Cesare Bermani and Ruggero Giacomini, claim that some version was sung by some brigades.

The song spread after Yves Montand recorded it in 1963 and the group Il Nuovo Canzoniere Italiano presented it at the Festival dei Due Mondi at Spoleto in 1964, as both a song of the mondine and a partisan hymn. Its message was inclusive enough to hold together the currents of the Resistance, Catholic, Communist, Socialist and Liberal, and it was sung at the end of the Christian Democracy congress of 1975. Many singers have recorded it, among them Milva, Quilapayún, Mary Hopkin, Sandie Shaw and Manu Chao, in dozens of languages. It has come to stand for liberation from tyranny in many places.
bellapais-abbey: The site stands at 220 metres above sea level on the northern side of the village of Bellapais, about 5 kilometres from Kyrenia, with a long view down to the sea. Its older name, Episcopia or Piscopia, suggests it may have served the Bishop of Kyrenia as a residence and a refuge from Arab raids in the 7th and 8th centuries. The first known settlers were Canons Regular of the Holy Sepulchre, who fled Jerusalem after it fell to Saladin in 1187. Aimery de Lusignan founded the monastery, consecrated as the Abbey of St. Mary of the Mountain, and the White Canons took it over in 1206.

The main building was raised under King Hugh III (1267–1284), and the cloister and refectory under Hugh IV between 1324 and 1359; Hugh IV lived there in apartments of his own. The Genoese stripped it of everything portable in their raid on Kyrenia in 1373. By the Venetian period the canons had abandoned their rule and reportedly took wives. After the Ottoman conquest of 1571 the abbey was given to the Church of Cyprus and fell into disrepair, though its church served the village that grew round it. Under British rule soldiers used the refectory as a hospital from 1878, and George Jeffery, Curator of the Ancient Monuments of Cyprus, repaired the abbey in 1912.

A fortified gate on the south leads to a forecourt and the 13th-century church, the best preserved part, with a nave and two aisles, a carved pulpit and a bishop's throne. The cloister has 18 arches; under one, two Roman sarcophagi served the canons as basins. The Gothic refectory, 30 by 10 metres, has a pulpit projecting from its north wall, a rose window in the east wall and bullet holes left by British soldiers, and its doorway carries the arms of Cyprus, Jerusalem and the Lusignans. The chapter house keeps a carving of figures, beasts, sirens and a canon. The refectory is now used for concerts and lectures.
bellerophon: Bellerophon, a hero of Corinth, was in most accounts the son of Poseidon and the mortal Eurynome and the foster son of Glaukos. His earlier name was Hipponous, or in another version Leophontes. The name Bellerophon is explained as meaning slayer of Belleros: according to the Scholia of Homer, he killed a Corinthian citizen of that name by accident while practising knife-throwing, and was exiled. In another account he murdered his own brother. In the Iliad, however, his grandson Glaucus tells the story and names the hero's father as Glaucus, king of Potniae and son of Sisyphus.

To atone for the killing he sought out Proetus, king of Tiryns, who cleansed him. Proetus's wife, Anteia or Stheneboea, made advances to him, and when he refused her she accused him of making advances to her. Proetus would not kill a guest and instead sent Bellerophon to his father-in-law Iobates in Lycia, carrying a sealed tablet asking that the bearer be put to death.

Iobates feasted Bellerophon for nine days before reading the tablet. Fearing the Erinyes if he killed a guest, he sent him to kill the Chimera, a fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, a goat's body and a serpent's tail. The seer Polyeidos told him that he would need the winged horse Pegasus. Bellerophon slept in the temple of Athena and found a golden bridle beside him on waking. He caught Pegasus as it drank at the spring of Pirene at Corinth. Unable to wound the Chimera, he mounted a block of lead on his spear and thrust it into the creature's throat, where its fiery breath melted the lead and suffocated it.

Iobates then set further tasks. Bellerophon defeated the Amazons by dropping boulders from Pegasus, and in some versions the Solymi before them. He killed the men sent to ambush him. When Poseidon flooded the plain behind him, the women of the palace came out and bared themselves, and he withdrew. Iobates relented, showed him the letter and gave him his daughter Philonoe and half his kingdom. She bore him Isander, Hippolochus and Laodamia. In one version he took revenge on Stheneboea by taking her up on Pegasus and throwing her into the sea off Milos.

As his fame grew, so did his pride, and he sought to fly to Olympus on Pegasus. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse, and Bellerophon fell to earth and died, while Pegasus reached Olympus and carried Zeus's thunderbolts. In other accounts he was blinded by a thorn bush and lived out his life in misery on the Plain of Aleion in Cilicia. Euripides wrote a tragedy, Bellerophon, of which about thirty quotations survive. Its passage doubting the gods' existence apparently led Aristophanes to accuse the poet of atheism.
bellovesus: The Gaulish name Bello-uesus literally means Worthy of Power. It joins the stem bello-, strong or powerful, to uesus, worthy, good or deserving, which goes back to Proto-Celtic *wesus, excellent or noble. In the legend told by the Roman historian Livy, Bellovesus and his brother Segovesus were the sons of the sister of King Ambigatus of the Bituriges, then the most powerful of the Gallic peoples. Because the Bituriges were suffering from overpopulation, the king sent his two nephews to find new lands to settle.

By lot Segovesus was assigned the Hercynian highlands, while to Bellovesus, in Livy's words, the gods proposed a far pleasanter road, into Italy. Taking the surplus people of the Bituriges, Arverni, Senones, Haedui, Ambarri, Carnutes and Aulerci, he marched with great numbers of infantry and cavalry into the country of the Tricastini. The Alps at first seemed impassable, and only after helping the Greeks who had founded Massalia did his followers cross by the Taurine passes and the pass of the Duria.

Livy sets the invasion of the Po Valley in the reign of Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome. The settlers took a district later called Insubria, and Bellovesus named his new city Medhelanon. A group of Cenomani led by Etitovius followed by the same pass with his approval and settled around the present-day cities of Brescia and Verona.

The story is anachronistic: the historical Celtic invasion of Italy took place between the end of the 5th century and the middle of the 4th century BCE, in the context of the Battle of the Allia in 387 BCE. Its core was probably inspired by real events. The historian Venceslas Kruta regards it as the construction of a myth of origins, likely Insubrian, combining Celtic, Cisalpine, Transalpine, Massaliote and Etrusco-Italian elements, and the tribes it names were probably drawn from names current in Livy's own day.
belmopan: Belmopan stands in Cayo District, 76 metres above sea level, just east of the Belize River and about 80 km inland from the Caribbean coast. It lies near the Belize River Valley with a view of the foothills of the Mountain Pine Ridge. The name joins two words: Belize, the name of the longest river in the country, and Mopan, one of the rivers of the area, which empties into the Belize River.

Hurricane Hattie in 1961 destroyed about 75 per cent of the houses and business premises in low-lying, coastal Belize City. The government proposed a new capital on better terrain, which would need no costly reclamation of land and would have room for an industrial area, and in 1962 a committee chose the site now called Belmopan. In 1964, when Belize was the British colony of British Honduras, Premier George Cadle Price led a delegation to London to seek funds. The British government did not commit itself but saw the logic of a capital on high ground safe from storm surges.

The site was dedicated by Lord Greenwood, the Secretary of State for the Commonwealth and Colonies, on 9 October 1965. The estimated cost was 40 million Belize dollars, but only 20 million were available. Work began in 1967, and the first phase was completed in 1970 at a cost of 24 million. The government moved there in 1970, and until 2000 the Reconstruction and Development Corporation, known as Recondev, ran the city. Foreign governments were at first reluctant to move their embassies, and the British High Commission opened in 1981, when British Honduras became independent as Belize.

Belmopan is the capital of Belize and the second-largest settlement in the country after Belize City, with 20,754 inhabitants in 2022, which makes it the smallest capital city in the continental Americas by population. The city is laid out around the Ring Road, just under 4 km in circumference, with most government buildings within or around it. The National Assembly Building, of grey stone with broad steps, is designed to resemble a Maya temple.
belovezha-accords: In the 1980s Mikhail Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika were meant to revive the Soviet system but instead hastened its unravelling. Nationalist, democratic and liberal movements gained strength in the republics and the Communist Party's control weakened. Proposals for a new Union Treaty were made, and on 14 November 1991 Gorbachev and the heads of seven union republics pre-agreed a political union to be called the Union of Sovereign States, to be signed in December. Stanislav Shushkevich later said that by December the union had already been broken up by the putschists who tried to remove Gorbachev in August 1991, and that the three leaders sought to avoid what had happened in the breakup of Yugoslavia.

The agreement was signed at the state dacha near Viskuli in Belovezhskaya Pushcha on 8 December 1991. For Belarus the signers were Shushkevich and the prime minister Vyacheslav Kebich, for Russia Boris Yeltsin and Gennady Burbulis, and for Ukraine Leonid Kravchuk and Vitold Fokin. Its preamble stated that the USSR, as a subject of international law and a geopolitical reality, was ceasing its existence. It has fourteen articles guaranteeing equal rights to citizens, protecting national minorities, and providing for territorial integrity. Article 6 set up a common military and strategic space. It also invited other republics to join.

Legally it rested on the 1922 Treaty on the Creation of the USSR, whose three surviving signatories were present, together with the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. A statement by the heads of state adopted at the same time declared the formation of the Commonwealth of Independent States, and the three governments issued a statement on coordinating economic policy.

The Ukrainian and Belarusian parliaments ratified it on 10 December, and the Russian Supreme Soviet on 12 December, which also withdrew from the 1922 treaty. Gorbachev called the document illegal, saying the fate of a multinational state could not be decided by three republics' leaders. On 21 December representatives of eleven of the remaining twelve republics, all except Georgia, signed the Alma-Ata Protocol, which repeated that the Soviet Union had ended and the Commonwealth of Independent States existed. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December, and on 26 December the Soviet of Republics voted the Union out of existence. Russia took over the Soviet seat at the United Nations.
belozersk: Belozersk lies on the southern bank of Lake Beloye, from which it takes its name, 214 kilometres north-west of Vologda. Until 1777 it was known as Beloozero, meaning white lake. On several occasions the settlement was moved from one bank of the lake to the other. The Belozersky Canal, part of the Volga–Baltic Waterway, passes through the town, bypassing the lake to the south.

The Primary Chronicle first mentions Beloozero in 862, among several towns that later became part of Kievan Rus', and says that Rurik's brother Sineus became its prince. Sineus and his brother Truvor most likely never existed. In the 11th century the region was inhabited mainly by Finnic peoples who resisted Christianization. In 1071 local pagan priests rose in rebellion and were put down by the Kievan commander Yan Vyshatich. From the 10th to the 13th century the territory was controlled by the Novgorod Republic.

Beloozero was the seat of a small principality, governed by the Belosselsky-Belozersky princes, between 1238 and the 1370s, and between 1380 and 1384 it became subordinate to the Grand Duchy of Moscow. On 10 July 1612 Polish and Lithuanian raiders known as the Lisowczycy captured the town without a fight and looted it. Under the reform of Peter the Great in 1708 it joined the Ingermanland Governorate, and in 1727 it became the seat of Belozersk Province in the Novgorod Governorate.

In June 1918 Belozersky Uyezd was placed in the new Cherepovets Governorate. In 1927 the uyezds were abolished and Belozersky District was created, and in 1937 the district was transferred to the newly established Vologda Oblast.

Belozersk is the administrative centre of Belozersky District in Vologda Oblast and had 8,464 inhabitants in the census of 2021. Its economy rests on the timber and food industries. The Ministry of Culture of Russia classifies it as a historical town. The monuments of the centre include the Assumption Church of 1552, the Transfiguration Cathedral of 1668 and the wooden shrine of St. Elijah of 1690, and the neighbourhood has old monasteries, among them Kirillo-Belozersky and Ferapontov. Two medieval icons, the Virgin of the White Lake and Saints Peter and Paul, were made in the town in the 13th century.
belshazzar: Belshazzar, in Babylonian Bēl-šar-uṣur, meaning "Bel, protect the king", was the son and crown prince of Nabonidus. Through his mother he might have been a grandson of Nebuchadnezzar II, though this is not certain, and the claim may come from royal propaganda.

Belshazzar played a central part in the coup that overthrew King Labashi-Marduk and brought Nabonidus to power in May 556 BCE. As the main beneficiary, inheriting the estates of Labashi-Marduk and of the family of Neriglissar, he was probably the chief orchestrator. Afterwards he appears as a prominent businessman and head of a wealthy household, owning lands throughout Babylonia.

Nabonidus left Babylon in May 553 BCE to campaign in the west, made Tayma in Arabia his provisional seat and did not return until 543 or 542 BCE. Belshazzar administered Babylonia in his absence. He could grant royal privileges, command part of the army and receive offerings. Yet he was always styled crown prince, never king, documents were dated by Nabonidus's years, and he was not allowed to preside over the New Year festival, which was not held while Nabonidus was away.

The main sources are the Nabonidus Chronicle, the Cyrus Cylinder and the Verse Account of Nabonidus, all written after the Persian conquest and biased in favour of Cyrus. When Cyrus invaded Lydia in 546 BCE, Belshazzar took up a defensive position but sent no aid. On his return Nabonidus removed him from his administrative duties and dismissed officials he had appointed.

Belshazzar helped defend Babylon against Cyrus in 539 BCE. After the Persian victory at Opis the army entered Babylon without a fight on 12 October. His fate is not recorded. It is often assumed that he was killed when the city fell, but he may have died at Opis, or been captured and executed, or exiled with his father.

In the Book of Daniel, which scholars regard as historical fiction written about four centuries after his time, Belshazzar is king of Babylon and holds a feast using the vessels of the temple of Yahweh. A hand writes on the wall, Daniel reads it as a judgment, and Belshazzar is killed that night. The book errs in calling him king and a son of Nebuchadnezzar, and its Darius the Mede is unknown to history. The later authors of the Talmud and the Midrash presented him as a tyrant who oppressed his Jewish subjects.
belvedere-vienna: The Belvedere stands in Vienna's third district, Landstraße, and consists of two Baroque palaces, the Upper and Lower Belvedere, with an Orangery, stables and a formal garden. It was built when Vienna was the imperial capital of the Habsburg monarchy, after Prince Eugene of Savoy's successful campaigns against the Ottoman Empire. On 30 November 1697 Eugene bought a plot south of the Rennweg and chose Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt as chief architect rather than Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach. Dominique Girard, who had trained at Versailles, laid out the gardens in the formal French manner over three terraces, with sculpture linking Eugene to the god Apollo.

The Lower Belvedere served as a Lustschloss, a pleasure palace tied closely to the gardens. Marcantonio Chiarini of Bologna began painting the quadratura in its central hall in 1715. The Upper Belvedere was begun in the late 1710s and finished in 1723, conceived less as a private residence than as a building for ceremonies, receptions and display. Eugene received the Turkish ambassador Ibrahim Pasha there in 1719, while the interior was still being decorated. Carlo Innocenzo Carlone painted the ceiling fresco of the Marble Hall between 1721 and 1723.

Prince Eugene died on 21 April 1736 without a legally binding will, and his niece Maria Anna Victoria of Savoy inherited the estate and soon tried to sell it. Maria Theresa bought it in 1752. In 1776 she and Joseph II decided to move the Imperial Picture Gallery to the Upper Belvedere to make the imperial collection accessible to the public. It is often described as one of the world's first public art museums, with the opening dated to 1777 or 1781. The Moderne Galerie opened in the Lower Belvedere in 1903, and on 15 May 1955 the Austrian State Treaty was signed at the Upper Belvedere. The Upper Belvedere holds a major group of works by Gustav Klimt, including The Kiss.
belz: Belz lies on a fertile plain near the border with Poland, between the Solokiya River, a tributary of the Bug, and the Richytsia stream. In ancient times the plain was settled by peoples of Indo-European origin: the Celtic Lugii, later Germanic Goths, Slavized Sarmatians and finally the Slavic Dulebes, who became part of Kievan Rus' in 907, according to the usual account.

The town has existed since at least the 10th century as one of the Cherven Cities, which were under Polish rule in the 970s. In 981 it was incorporated into Kievan Rus', and in 1170 it became the seat of the Duchy of Belz. During the Wars of the Galician Succession the city and its surroundings were plundered by the army of Prince Daniel of Galicia and his brother Vasylko Romanovych. From 1234 it belonged to the Duchy of Galicia–Volhynia, and from 1340 it came under Lithuanian rule.

Belz was under Polish rule from 1366 to 1772, first as a fief and from 1462 as the capital of the Belz Voivodeship. On 5 October 1377 Władysław Opolczyk, governor of Red Ruthenia, granted the town Magdeburg rights, which a charter of 10 November 1509 confirmed.

The First Partition of Poland in 1772 brought it into the Habsburg Empire, where it lay in the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria, and a railway reached it in 1884. After 1918 it was briefly part of the Western Ukrainian People's Republic, then Poland from 1919. Germany occupied it from 1939 to 1944, and a border readjustment passed it from Poland to the Soviet Union in 1951.

Belz is a small town in Lviv Oblast with 2,191 inhabitants in a 2022 estimate, part of independent Ukraine since 1991. Its Jewish history is central to its fame. An Ashkenazi community was established around the 14th century, and Shalom Rokeach (1779–1855) became the first Belzer Rebbe in the early 19th century. At the start of the First World War Belz had 6,100 inhabitants, among them 3,600 Jews. On 2 June 1942 about 1,000 Jews were deported to Hrubieszów and from there to Sobibor extermination camp.

The fourth Rebbe, Aharon Rokeach, escaped to Israel in 1944 and re-established the dynasty there. The town is also remembered as the place where the Black Madonna of Częstochowa resided until 1382, when Władysław Opolczyk took it to his own principality.
belz-hasidic-dynasty: The founder, Rabbi Shalom Rokeach, known as the Sar Shalom, was a disciple of the Seer of Lublin, whose own line of teachers ran back through Rabbi Elimelech Lipman of Lizhensk and Dovber, the Maggid of Mezeritch to the Baal Shem Tov, the founder of Hasidism. He helped build the town's synagogue, dedicated in 1843, a fortress-like building with walls three feet thick and a castellated roof that could seat 5,000 worshippers. On his death in 1855 he was followed by his youngest son, Yehoshua Rokeach, then by Yissachar Dov Rokeach from 1894 and by Aharon Rokeach from 1926.

After the German invasion of Poland in 1939 Belz was occupied as part of the General Government. The Germans tried to destroy the synagogue by fire and dynamite and then forced Jewish men to take it apart brick by brick. Aharon Rokeach, high on the Gestapo's list of wanted rabbis, escaped with his brother Rabbi Mordechai of Bilgoray, helped by money from Belzer Hasidim abroad, through the Kraków and Bochnia ghettos. Disguised as captured Russian generals, they were driven into Hungary by Major General István Újszászy, head of Hungarian counter-intelligence.

After eight months in Budapest they took the Orient Express to Istanbul. Most of the Belz Hasidim, and Aharon's wife, children and grandchildren, were murdered in the Holocaust. He re-established his court in Tel Aviv, moved it to Jerusalem in 1950 and died in 1957, soon after a large yeshiva and study hall there was completed. His nephew Yissachar Dov, son of Mordechai, was nine; for nine years the movement had no active Rebbe, until he took up the leadership in 1966.

Belz grew from a few hundred families in 1966 to more than 10,000 by 2024, with communities in Israel, the United States, Canada and Europe. Its largest community outside Israel is in Borough Park, Brooklyn, and in London it is centred in Stamford Hill. It runs yeshivas, the Bnos Belz and Beis Malka girls' schools, and self-help bodies including a free medical counselling centre. Its Great Synagogue, the Beis HaMedrash HaGadol, was dedicated in 2000, with an ark that can hold 70 Torah scrolls.
belz-voivodeship: Belz, on the Zaloka river, was one of the oldest gords, or fortified settlements, of the Czerwien Land. In 981 the area was seized by Vladimir the Great; Bolesław Chrobry recovered it in 1018, but after his death it passed back to Rus'. In the early 14th century the Land of Belz was inherited by Boleslaw Jerzy II of Mazovia, and after his death on 7 April 1340 King Casimir III the Great seized Red Ruthenia together with Belz.

In 1387 King Wladyslaw Jagiello gave the Land of Belz as a dowry to his sister Alexandra of Lithuania on her marriage to Siemowit IV, Duke of Masovia. It stayed with the sons and grandsons of Siemowit IV until the grandsons died childless early in 1462, when it became property of the Crown and was turned into a voivodeship.

Together with the Ruthenian Voivodeship, Belz formed part of Red Ruthenia within the Lesser Poland Province, and it was the smallest of the Lesser Poland voivodeships, slightly smaller than the Lublin Voivodeship. It sent four senators to the Senate of the Commonwealth: the Voivode and the Castellan of Bełz and the Castellans of Lubaczów and Busk. The local sejmik at Belz elected five deputies to the Sejm, while the general sejmik for all the Ruthenian lands met at Sądowa Wisznia.

At first the voivodeship was made up of three counties, Lubaczów, Horodło and Szewlock; in 1767 it was divided into the counties of Bełz, Grabowiec, Horodło and Lubaczów and the Land of Busk. In the 17th century it had 483 villages and 33 towns. Nobles from Mazovia, Lesser Poland and Greater Poland settled in the region: in 1570–1580, among noble families of known origin, 79% were Polish, 15% Ruthenian and 4% Wallachian, while the peasantry was little touched by migration from the west. Its voivodes included Rafał Leszczyński, Jakub Sobieski and Adam Mikołaj Sieniawski.

In the First Partition of Poland in 1772 almost the whole voivodeship passed to the Habsburg Empire as part of Galicia. Only the towns of Dubienka and Korytnica, with some villages, remained in Poland, and after the Second Partition in 1793 these were joined to the newly created Chełm and Włodzimierz voivodeships. The historian Zygmunt Gloger described the voivodeship in his Historical Geography of the Lands of Old Poland.
belzec-extermination-camp: Bełżec was a village in the Second Polish Republic, between Lublin, 76 kilometres to the north-west, and Lwów to the south-east, the two cities of the region with the largest Jewish populations. After 1939 it lay in the German zone of occupation. In 1940 Jewish forced labour was brought in to build military defences, including an anti-tank trench, along the Nazi-Soviet frontier. The SS chose the site for the camp because it lay on the border between the Lublin District and the new District of Galicia, so it could serve the Jews of both, with a railway junction at nearby Rawa-Ruska and the highway between Lublin and Lwów.

Construction began around 1 November 1941 under Richard Thomalla, using local builders overseen by Trawniki guards, and the gassing installation was fitted in February 1942. Daily gassing began on 17 March 1942, using staff from the Aktion T4 euthanasia programme. Christian Wirth, the first commandant, proposed using the exhaust gas of an engine as the killing agent. The camp had two sections, joined by a narrow corridor, and arriving Jews were told they were at a transit camp. In the first phase, to the end of June 1942, small wooden gas chambers killed about 80,000 people. From July 1942 new brick chambers, which could hold over 1,000 victims at a time, were used; the design was copied at Sobibor and Treblinka.

Between 430,000 and 500,000 Jews are believed to have been murdered. A telegram sent by Hermann Höfle on 11 January 1943 records 434,508 Jews deported to Bełżec through 31 December 1942. Later the graves were opened, and the bodies burned on open-air pyres as part of Sonderaktion 1005; the ashes were mixed with crushed bone to hide the evidence. The last Sonderkommando prisoners were sent to Sobibor in 1943, the camp was dismantled and planted with trees, and the site was disguised as a farm.

Only seven Jews who worked in the Sonderkommando survived the war, and only Rudolf Reder gave a full account, in his official testimony of January 1946 and in his book Bełżec. Chaim Hirszman, the other escapee to testify, was assassinated in March 1946. The graves were plundered by robbers after the war, and the site was fenced off and given its first monuments in the 1960s. In 1997–1998 archaeologists led by Andrzej Kola and Mieczysław Góra found 33 mass graves, the largest 480 square metres in area and 4.8 metres deep. Of the SS personnel, only Josef Oberhauser was tried, in Munich in 1964, and was sentenced to four and a half years.
ben-jonson: Jonson was born in June 1572, possibly on the 11th, in or near London. His father, a Protestant who had lost his property and been imprisoned under Queen Mary, became a clergyman after his release and died a month before his son's birth; what is known of him comes from the poet's own account. His widow married a master bricklayer two years later. A family friend paid for his studies at Westminster School, where the antiquarian William Camden was one of his masters; their friendship and Camden's wide scholarship left a lasting mark on Jonson's style until Camden's death in 1623.

A play he wrote with Thomas Nashe, The Isle of Dogs, was suppressed in 1597 after causing great offence, and Jonson was jailed in Marshalsea Prison. In 1598 he killed the actor Gabriel Spenser in a duel on 22 September and was imprisoned in Newgate; he pleaded guilty to manslaughter but was released by benefit of clergy, forfeiting his goods and being branded on the left thumb.

His public plays were mainly comedies, among them Every Man in His Humour, Volpone, The Alchemist and Bartholomew Fair; his two tragedies, Sejanus and Catiline, largely failed to impress audiences. His comedies show a keen eye for absurdity and hypocrisy. When James VI and I came to the throne in 1603 he quickly adapted to the demand for masques and entertainments encouraged by the king and Anne of Denmark, and enjoyed the patronage of Elizabeth Sidney and Lady Mary Wroth, which led to his country house poem To Penshurst.

According to a contemporary letter, Jonson died in London on 18 August 1637, and his funeral was attended by all or the greater part of the nobility then in town. He is buried in the north aisle of the nave of Westminster Abbey, with the inscription O Rare Ben Johnson over his grave; John Aubrey records that a passer-by, John Young, paid a workman eighteen pence to cut it. The upright burial was taken as a sign of his reduced circumstances.

Younger poets such as Robert Herrick, Richard Lovelace and Sir John Suckling called themselves the Sons or Tribe of Ben. After the Restoration his comedies and his theory of humour characters were the blueprint for many Restoration comedies, and his work, with Shakespeare's and Fletcher's, formed the core of the repertory when the theatres reopened. He has been called the first poet laureate, and many critics since the 18th century have ranked him below only Shakespeare among English Renaissance dramatists. Of Shakespeare he wrote in Timber that he was not of an age, but for all time.
ben-youssef-madrasa: The madrasa takes its name from the adjacent Ben Youssef Mosque, the original main mosque of Marrakesh, founded by the Almoravid sultan Ali ibn Yusuf, who ruled from 1106 to 1142. According to historical sources, notably al-Ifrani, the first madrasa on the site was founded under the Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan, who reigned from 1331 to 1348. Madrasas in the Maghreb trained ulama in Maliki law, jurisprudence and the variant readings of the Qur'an.

The present building was commissioned by the Saadian sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib, who reigned from 1557 to 1574. Its construction probably began soon after he took power, and an inscription records its completion in 1564 to 1565 (972 AH). It followed a style established under the Marinid dynasty, although the Saadian dynasty, as sharifs, depended less on madrasas than their predecessors to win the support of the ulama.

The plan is nearly square, about 40 by 43 metres. A single street entrance, fronted by a muqarnas vault, leads through a corridor and a vestibule to the central courtyard, which is arranged to open suddenly on the visitor. A shallow pool about 3 by 7 metres stands at its centre, and a prayer hall with a richly stuccoed mihrab lies at the south-eastern end. Around the courtyard, on two levels, are 130 student rooms grouped around six small courtyards, which housed up to 800 students.

The decoration follows earlier Moroccan and Andalusi traditions: zellij tilework on the lower walls, calligraphic friezes at eye level, carved stucco above and carved wooden eaves, with arabesques, sebka, inscriptions, muqarnas and the pine cones that are more distinctly Saadian. The cedar lintel over the bronze-plated doors names and praises Abdallah as the builder. Many inscriptions are Qur'anic, and the Kufic band around the mihrab arch gives verse 36 and the start of verse 37 of the Surah an-Nur.

It was the largest madrasa in the Maghreb. The college was closed in 1960 and reopened to the public as a historical site in 1982. It closed for restoration in November 2018 and reopened in April 2022. A carved marble ablutions basin made at Madinat al-Zahra between 1002 and 1007 and dedicated to 'Abd al-Malik, son of al-Mansur, stood in the madrasa for centuries. Mariam Rosser-Owen has suggested that Ali ibn Yusuf brought it to Marrakesh. After study it was kept at the Dar Si Said Museum and now stands in the prayer hall.
benazir-bhutto: Benazir Bhutto was born on 21 June 1953 in Karachi, the eldest of four children of the barrister and politician Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and Begum Nusrat Ispahani, who was born in Isfahan of Persian and Kurdish descent. The Bhuttos were wealthy landlords from Sindh. From 1969 to 1973 she studied at Radcliffe College, entering at sixteen, and graduated cum laude in comparative government. She then studied at the University of Oxford, where she became President of the Oxford Union.

In 1977 her father was ousted in a military coup and later executed. Benazir and her mother took control of the Pakistan People's Party and led the Movement for the Restoration of Democracy. She was repeatedly imprisoned by Zia-ul-Haq's military government and lived in self-exile in Britain from 1984, returning in 1986. She chaired the party from 1982 until her death and moved its platform from socialist to liberal. After Zia died in an air crash in August 1988, she led the party to victory and became Pakistan's first female prime minister.

Her attempts at reform were stifled by conservative and Islamist forces, including President Ghulam Ishaq Khan and the military, and her administration, accused of corruption and nepotism, was dismissed in 1990. She was sworn in again on 19 October 1993, after the party won 86 seats. In this term she established a Ministry of Women's Development and a Women's Development Bank and sought to privatise industries nationalised in the 1970s. Her brother Murtaza was killed, and on 5 November 1996 President Farooq Leghari dismissed her government on grounds of corruption and incompetence.

She lived in exile between Dubai and London from 1998 and was convicted by a Swiss court in 2003. She returned to Pakistan in October 2007, after negotiations with President Pervez Musharraf, to contest the 2008 elections.

On 27 December 2007 she spoke at a party rally in Rawalpindi's Liaquat National Bagh. As she left in a bulletproof vehicle and stood up through its escape hatch to wave, a man fired three shots and detonated a suicide vest. Twenty-two others also died. She was buried beside her father at Garhi Khuda Bakhsh. Al-Qaeda claimed responsibility, though other involvement was also suggested. Opinions of her were deeply divided: critics called her inexperienced and corrupt, and Islamist and conservative forces opposed her secularist, modernising agenda. After her death she came to be regarded as an icon for women's rights.
bendigo: Bendigo, formerly known as Sandhurst, lies in the Bendigo Valley in north-central Victoria, near the geographical centre of the state and about 150 kilometres north-west of Melbourne. The Dja Dja Wurrung (Djaara) people are the traditional owners of the area, which they called Leanganook. They used its rich hunting grounds. The city is surrounded by parts of the Greater Bendigo National Park and by the Bendigo Box-Ironbark Region, an Important Bird Area identified for swift parrots and other woodland birds. Its climate is dry and temperate, with warm, variable summers and cool, cloudy winters.

White settlers established the first of a number of vast sheep runs in 1837 and displaced the Dja Dja Wurrung, who experienced two waves of settlement and dispossession, from the south from 1837 and from the north from 1845. Introduced animals also rooted up the nutritious moon-nar tuber, the yam daisy, which became scarce within a year.

Gold was officially discovered in October 1851, just after the finds at neighbouring Castlemaine, and some diggers moved from there, bringing the population to 40,000 in less than a year. A number of them were Chinese, and their descendants still live in the region. The discovery on Bendigo Creek turned a sheep station into one of colonial Australia's largest boomtowns, intensified the Victorian gold rush and drew migrants from around the world, particularly Europe and China. In 1852 William Swan Urquhart surveyed the goldfields under the Surveyor General of Victoria, Robert Hoddle. From 1853 to 1891 the town was officially named Sandhurst.

Bendigo was declared a city in 1871. Its rapid growth caused a water shortage, partly solved by a viaduct from the Coliban River. The architect William Charles Vahland left a mark on it, designing more than 80 buildings, among them the Alexandra Fountain, and giving his name to a popular cottage design. A tram network existed by 1890. The boom lasted until the early 20th century, and after a temporary decline in population and employment, growth resumed from the 1930s as Bendigo became a manufacturing and regional service centre.

The wealth of the gold rush is reflected in the city's late Victorian colonial architecture. Several buildings are on the Victorian Heritage Register, including the Bendigo Town Hall, the Old Post Office and the Old Bendigo Law Courts, which are in the Second Empire style. Sacred Heart Cathedral, completed in 1977, is the largest church building in provincial Australia. The Bendigo Art Gallery is one of Australia's oldest and largest regional art galleries. Tourism centres on the gold-rush history, with attractions such as the Central Deborah Gold Mine, the Bendigo Tramways and the Golden Dragon Museum. The first women's cricket match in Australia was played in Bendigo in 1871.
benedetta-of-cagliari: Benedetta was born around 1194, the daughter and heiress of William I of Cagliari and Adelasia, a daughter of Moroello Malaspina. On her father's death she was consecrated by Riccus, Archbishop of Cagliari, before the higher clergy and the grandees, and swore not to diminish the territory of the giudicato, alienate its castles or make foreign alliances without their consent. On 14 June 1214 she married Barisone III of Arborea, who took the dynastic name Torchitorio V, and the two ruled their giudicati jointly.

Benedetta favoured natives over Pisans in her government and the Sardinian economy over that of the Republic of Pisa, and Pisa turned against her. Lambert Visconti, judge of Gallura, landed a large army near Cagliari and fortified the hilltop of S. Gilla, forcing her to flee to the interior. In 1217 his brother Ubald I Visconti made her surrender Cagliari and take it back as a fief from the consul of Pisa. She and Barisone then allied with Comita III of Torres and Genoa to expel the Pisans.

Pope Honorius III supported her, annulling in February 1217 the election of the Pisan Marianus to the see of Cagliari. After Barisone's death that spring, Ubald arranged her marriage to the widowed Lambert, married on 9 April 1220, which the pope at once annulled. In December 1224 she renewed her homage to the Holy See, promising a yearly tribute of twenty pounds of silver, no marriage without papal approval, and Cagliari to the pope should she die without heirs.

War resumed in 1226 with Lambert's heir, Ubaldo II. To protect herself she married twice more without papal permission, first Enrico di Ceola, a Pisan of the Capraia family, in 1227, then Rinaldo de Glandis. Violence drove her to the castle of Santa Igia and then to Massa, her ancestral home, where she died. Her son William reigned but never ruled, under the regency of her sister Agnes and Marianus of Torres, and by February 1233 Pope Gregory IX had granted Massa away while Cagliari was divided between the Pisan families of the Visconti, Capraia and Donoratico.
benedetto-antelami: Little is known of his life. He probably came from Lombardy, perhaps from Val d'Intelvi near Como, or from Genoa, where a group of artists from the Intelvi Valley worked in the 12th century. Antelami is not a surname but a place-name used for skilled sculptors and stone workers from the Intelvi Valley north of Como. The Provençal style of his art has led to the belief that he served an apprenticeship at the Church of St. Trophime in Arles.

His earliest recorded work, the Deposition from the Cross in Parma Cathedral, was originally part of the ambo; his name and the date are inscribed on it, and besides its Provençal element it shows classical and Byzantine influence. Between 1196 and 1214 he carved the lunettes of the three portals of the Parma Baptistery. Those outside show the Adoration of the Magi, the Last Judgement and an allegory of life; those inside, the Flight into Egypt, the Presentation at the Temple and David playing the harp. The high-relief figures of the months and seasons inside were probably meant for a portal of the cathedral's facade, a project cut short by his death.

He presumably travelled in his fifties. At Fidenza Cathedral, dedicated to Saint Domninus, the lower and middle parts of the facade are definitely his, and his plan, which also included the two side towers, was a French one. Much of the facade's sculpture was made by his workshop, and he completed his part of the work in 1207.

His style is described as springing from north Italian traditions that can be traced back to late antiquity. His trademark is relief carving that stresses design through drapery on elongated figures and tight compositions, and his figures show close similarities with those on the outer arch of the north porch of Chartres Cathedral of 1213. Some attribute the main west door of St. Mark's Basilica in Venice to him or his school, and the present replacement of the Holy Face of Lucca, the Volto Santo, is ascribed to his circle.
benedict-biscop: Benedict Biscop, also known as Biscop Baducing, was born into a noble Northumbrian family and served for a time as a thegn of King Oswiu of Bernicia. At about the age of 25, around 653, he set out for Rome with his friend Wilfrid. Wilfrid was detained at Lyon, and Benedict completed the journey alone; on his return he was said to be full of fervour for the good of the English Church. It has been suggested that he is the Biscop Beding named in the Anglian Collection of royal genealogies as a son of Beda Bubbing, King of Mercia.

A second journey to Rome followed about twelve years later. Alchfrith of Deira, a son of Oswiu, wished to go with him, but the king refused permission. On the way home Benedict stayed at the island monastery of Lérins off the coast of Provence from 665 to 667, where he took monastic vows and the name Benedict. On a third visit Pope Vitalian asked him to accompany Archbishop Theodore of Tarsus to Canterbury in 669, and Theodore made him abbot of the monastery of SS. Peter and Paul at Canterbury for two years.

King Ecgfrith of Northumbria granted him land for a monastery in 674. Benedict recruited masons on the Continent able to build in the Pre-Romanesque style, and on his last journey to Rome in 679 he brought back books, relics, stonemasons, glaziers and a grant of privileges from Pope Agatho. The monastery was the first church building in Britain constructed in stone, and its glass was a novelty in 7th-century England. In 682 he named Eosterwine as his coadjutor, and at Jarrow he set Ceolfrid over the sister house of Saint Paul, who took 20 monks from Wearmouth to found it.

He drew up a rule for the community based on that of Saint Benedict and on the customs of seventeen monasteries he had visited, and he engaged Abbot John, arch-cantor of Saint Peter's in Rome, to teach Roman chant. His library, mostly service books but also scripture and classical works, is estimated at about 250 titles. Manuscripts copied there were prized across Europe, among them the Codex Amiatinus, the earliest surviving complete Latin Vulgate Bible.

Benedict was bedridden for the last three years of his life and died on 12 January 690. A sermon of Bede points to an early cult, which spread more widely after his relics were moved to Thorney under Ethelwold around 980. The Catholic Church, the Church of England and the Eastern Orthodox Church keep his feast on 12 January, and the parish church of Wombourne in Staffordshire is the only one in England dedicated to him.
benedict-of-aniane: According to Ardo, his biographer, Benedict was the son of a Visigoth, Aigulf, Count of Maguelonne, and was given the Gothic name Witiza. He was educated at the Frankish court of Pippin the Younger and entered royal service as a page. He later served at the court of Charlemagne and took part in the Italian campaign of 773, during which he nearly drowned in the Ticino River near Pavia while trying to save his brother.

The experience led him to renounce the world. He left the court and was received into the monastery of Saint Sequanus, the Abbey of Saint-Seine, where he was made cellarer and then elected abbot. Realising that the monks would never conform to his strict practices, he left and returned to his father's estates in Languedoc, where he built a hermitage.

Around 780 he founded a monastic community at Aniane in Languedoc, based on Eastern asceticism, but it did not develop as he had intended. In 782 he founded another monastery on the Benedictine Rule at the same location. His success there gave him considerable influence, which he used to found and reform a number of other monasteries, and he became the effective abbot of all the monasteries of Charlemagne's empire. Louis the Pious, King of Aquitaine from 781, asked him to reform the monasteries of his territory and, as emperor, later entrusted him with coordinating practices among the monasteries of his domains.

In 814 Louis had him found a monastery on the river Inde, near the court at Aachen. It was first called the Monastery of the Redeemer on the Inde but came to be known as Kornelimünster Abbey. In 817 Benedict headed a council of abbots at Aachen that drew up a code of regulations, the Codex regularum, binding on all their houses.

Benedict sought to restore the primitive strictness of monastic observance wherever it had been relaxed. Shortly after the council he compiled the Concordia regularum, which gives sections of the Benedictine Rule in order, with parallel passages from other rules in the Liber regularum, to show their agreement of principles and so enhance respect for the Benedictine Rule.

He died at Kornelimünster Abbey on 11 February 821 and was buried the next day, which is why his feast day is given as either the 11th or the 12th. His new codes fell into disuse shortly after the deaths of Benedict and of Louis the Pious, but they had lasting effects on Western monasticism.
benedict-xiv: Prospero Lambertini was born into a noble family of Bologna, the third of five children of Marcello Lambertini and Lucrezia Bulgarini. At thirteen he began attending the Collegio Clementino in Rome, where he studied rhetoric, Latin, philosophy and theology, and he often read the works of Thomas Aquinas, his favourite author. In 1694, at nineteen, he received the degrees of Doctor of Sacred Theology and of both ecclesiastical and civil law.

As Promoter of the Faith from 1708 he secured the canonization of Pope Pius V and wrote a treatise on the process of beatification and canonization of saints. Created a cardinal in 1726, he was named Archbishop of Bologna in 1731 and wrote there a three-volume treatise on the diocesan synod, De synodo dioecesana.

After Clement XII died in February 1740 the conclave lasted six months. Lambertini arrived late and was not among the favourites of any faction; he was put forward as a compromise and is reported to have said, 'If you wish to elect a saint, choose Gotti; a statesman, Aldrovandi; an honest man, me.' He was elected on the 255th ballot on 17 August 1740.

His pontificate began amid disputes with Catholic rulers over their demand to nominate bishops, and he settled the quarrels of the Holy See with Naples, Sardinia, Spain, Venice and Austria. The papal government was heavily in debt, by 56,000,000 scudi, and he cut the army and the pay of its officers and soldiers, though the administration still ran a deficit at his death. He encouraged agriculture and free trade, revived anatomical studies at the University of Bologna and added about 3,300 of his own books to the Vatican Library.

On 22 December 1741 the bull Immensa Pastorum Principis excommunicated anyone who enslaved the indigenous peoples of Brazil, though it went unenforced. In the bulls Ex quo singulari of 1742 and Omnium sollicitudinum of 1744 he condemned the accommodation of Chinese and Indian customs by the Jesuit missions, and many converts left the Church.

Benedict XIV had suffered from kidney problems for years. After a battle with gout he died on 3 May 1758, at the age of 83, lucid to the end, and was buried in Saint Peter's Basilica. He was noted for his modesty and humour and was also an avid gambler who used profane language.

His intellectualism and advocacy of science education earned him the nickname the Enlightenment Pope. Horace Walpole described him as a pope without nepotism and an author without vanity, a man whom neither intellect nor power could corrupt.
benedicto-kiwanuka: Benedicto Kagimu Mugumba Kiwanuka was born on 8 May 1922 in Kisabwa, a member of the Baganda people and of the Roman Catholic Church. After a law course in Lesotho in 1950–52 he went to London to study for the Bar at University College, and he was called to the Bar by Gray's Inn in February 1956.

Kiwanuka led the Democratic Party in the transition from British colonial rule to independence. After the Uganda Constitutional Conference held in London in September 1961, the country gained internal self-government on 1 March 1962, and he headed the new government in the National Assembly. In the elections of April 1962 his party lost to the alliance of Milton Obote's Uganda People's Congress and the Buganda traditionalist party Kabaka Yekka. His Catholicism had made him unpopular among the mainly Protestant Baganda. Uganda became independent on 9 October 1962 with Obote as prime minister.

Obote's government imprisoned Kiwanuka in 1969. He was one of 55 political detainees freed by Idi Amin immediately after the coup that brought Amin to power, and on 27 June 1971 Amin made him chief justice, the first Ugandan and first black holder of the office. He soon clashed with Amin's disregard for the rule of law, countermanding some of the regime's harshest orders from the bench, and he had secretly agreed to support Obote's return on condition that he took part in constitutional reform.

In the immediate aftermath of Obote's invasion of Uganda in 1972, Amin's men arrested Kiwanuka at gunpoint while he presided over the High Court. He was killed on 22 September 1972 at Makindye Military Prison. Western accounts, citing eyewitnesses, described a prolonged execution with mutilation before he was burned; other sources said Amin shot him himself. Amin publicly blamed Obote's supporters and even ordered a police investigation. The killing was the first of a series aimed at leading figures of the Baganda and Ankole. A monument to him was dedicated in 2018.
benelux: The name Benelux is a syllabic abbreviation formed from the initial syllable of each country's name, first used for the customs agreement signed in 1944 that began the union. Before the First World War Luxembourg had formed part of the Zollverein with the German Empire. Its collapse led in 1921 to the Belgium-Luxembourg Economic Union, a customs union and limited monetary union between the two states. In 1944 exiled representatives of Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed the London Customs Convention, which established the Benelux Customs Union. It was ratified in 1947 and in force from 1948.

The treaty establishing the Benelux Economic Union was signed on 3 February 1958 in The Hague and came into force on 1 November 1960. Its purpose was to end customs barriers and ensure free movement of persons, capital, services and goods among the three countries. It was the first example of international economic integration in Europe after the war, and the three countries provided the model for later European integration, from the European Coal and Steel Community to the European Economic Community. They also launched the Schengen process, which came into operation in 1985.
The 1958 treaty was limited to fifty years, and a revising treaty was signed on 17 June 2008. It has no time limit, and the Benelux Economic Union became the Benelux Union.

Under the 2008 treaty there are five institutions. The Committee of Ministers is the supreme decision-making body, with the presidency rotating yearly among the three countries. The Council, made up of senior officials, prepares its dossiers. The Benelux Parliament, officially the Interparliamentary Assembly, was created in 1955 and has 49 members from national parliaments. The Benelux Court of Justice promotes uniform application of Benelux legislation. The General Secretariat is based in Brussels. About 80 percent of the population of the three countries speaks Dutch as a first language and around 20 percent French.
benes-decrees: Edvard Beneš, elected president of Czechoslovakia in 1935, resigned after the Munich Agreement in 1938. After the occupation he and other Czechoslovak politicians emigrated to France and in November 1939 set up the Czechoslovak National Committee.
