After the fall of France the committee moved to London, where it became the Interim Czechoslovak Government, recognised by Great Britain on 21 July 1940.

The 1920 constitution gave the power to make laws to the National Assembly, which could not meet in exile, so the president's office was the only body with limited legislative power. Beneš returned to his post on the premise that his 1938 resignation under duress was invalid. Later decrees were proposed by the government in exile and co-signed by the prime minister or a minister, and their validity depended on ratification by the National Assembly.

The decrees were issued from 21 July 1940 to 27 October 1945 and ratified by the Interim National Assembly on 6 March 1946. They covered the restoration of Czechoslovakia's legal system, denazification and reconstruction. The term Beneš decrees is also used for the decrees and the ordinances of the Slovak National Council concerning ethnic Germans, Hungarians and others, which provided the legal framework for the expulsion of Germans.

Czech resistance groups, especially after Nazi reprisals for the assassination of Heydrich, demanded the deportation of ethnic Germans, and the government in exile sought Allied support for this from 1943. The decrees removed citizenship and confiscated the property of Germans and Hungarians, with exemptions for those who proved loyalty to Czechoslovakia or had been victims of Nazi or fascist terror. For Hungarians they also allowed dismissal of civil servants, banned the use of Hungarian in public offices and church services and the publication of Hungarian books, and excluded students from universities.

The decrees are associated with the deportation in 1945–47 of about 3 million ethnic Germans and Hungarians. The relevant decrees omit any mention of deportation, whose basis was Article 12 of the Potsdam Agreement. About 250,000 Germans remained. A joint Czech-German commission found that over 20,000 German speakers died during the expulsion. A number of historians and legal scholars consider it ethnic cleansing.

The decrees were never repealed and remain controversial in the Czech Republic and Slovakia. In 1995 the Czech Constitutional Court held that a decree it reviewed was legitimate and had fulfilled its purpose. In 2005 the European Court of Human Rights refused the application of Josef Bergauer and 89 others. Slovakia's parliament adopted a resolution in 2007 rejecting revision of postwar decisions, and Germany and the Czech Republic signed a declaration of mutual apology in 1997.
benevento: Benevento stands on a hill 130 metres above sea level at the confluence of the Calore and the Sabato rivers in Campania. As Maleventum it was one of the chief cities of Samnium, on the Appian Way 51 kilometres east of Capua. Ancient writers ascribed its foundation to Diomedes after the Trojan War, a legend its inhabitants adopted, and in the time of Procopius they claimed to display the tusks of the Calydonian Boar as proof. Another tradition names Auson, a son of Ulysses and Circe, as founder.

The city first appears in history as a Samnite town, strong enough that the Romans did not attack it in their first two wars with the Samnites. Its theatre, completed under Caracalla between 200 and 210, reflects its growing importance after the Via Appia Traiana opened. After Totila sacked it and razed its walls in 545, Benevento became the seat of a powerful Lombard duchy, whose creation is disputed. Arechis I, who died in 640, captured Capua and Crotone. After his reign the Eastern Roman Empire held only Naples, Amalfi, Gaeta, Sorrento, the tip of Calabria and the maritime cities of Apulia in the south.

Benevento passed peacefully to the papacy when Emperor Henry III ceded it to Leo IX in exchange for the pope's consent to the founding of the Diocese of Bamberg. In 1806 Napoleon gave the principality to Talleyrand, who never ruled it, and in 1815 it returned to the papacy. It was united with Italy in 1860. A Jewish community lived there from at least the fifth century, and was expelled in 1569 under Paul IV.

Benevento is the capital of its province and the seat of an archbishop. Its Lombard church of Santa Sofia, a circular building of about 760, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2011 as one of seven buildings called Longobards in Italy. The Arch of Trajan, the Roman theatre and the castle called the Rocca dei Rettori also survive. Allied bombing in the summer of 1943 killed 2,000 people, destroyed half the town and almost all of the cathedral, which was rebuilt by 1965.
bengal-army: The Bengal Army began with the raising of a European Regiment in 1756, after the small force of Dutch and Eurasian mercenaries the East India Company had kept in Bengal was destroyed when the Nawab of Bengal captured Calcutta on 30 June that year. In 1757 the first locally recruited unit of Bengal sepoys, the Lal Paltan battalion, was formed from men who had served in the Nawab's army; drilled and armed on British lines, it served at the Battle of Plassey, and 20 more Indian battalions were raised by 1764.

By 1796 the establishment stood at three battalions of European artillery, three regiments of European infantry, ten regiments of Indian cavalry and twelve two-battalion regiments of Indian infantry. A reorganisation in 1824 grouped the regular infantry into 68 single-battalion regiments numbered by their date of raising. On the eve of the First Afghan War (1839–42) it had 74 battalions of regular infantry, against 52 from Madras and 26 from Bombay. In the 1840s it added irregular infantry and cavalry with less formal drill and fewer British officers. In 1857 it numbered 151,361 men, 128,663 of them Indians.

During the rebellion of 1857, 64 regular infantry and cavalry regiments rebelled or were disbanded as doubtful. The Government of India Act 1858 transferred the presidencies to the Crown. Unification of the three presidency armies began in 1895, and in 1903, under the Kitchener reforms, their regiments were numbered in a single sequence; the Bengal infantry units became the senior regiments, 1st Brahmans to 48th Pioneers, of the unified army.

Before 1857 the sepoys came mainly from high-caste Brahmins, Bhumihars and Rajputs of Bihar and Oudh, known collectively as Purbiyas, while the regular cavalry were mostly Muslim sowars. The Company kept recruiting stations at Buxar, Bhagalpur, Monghyr and elsewhere, and in 1810 Francis Buchanan-Hamilton counted 4680 men from Shahabad serving in the army. Regiments designated Volunteers accepted overseas service for a special allowance, or batta. After 1858 recruitment turned to Punjabi Muslims, Sikhs, Gurkhas, Baluchis and Pathans, with a largely unspoken aim that an army of diverse origins was unlikely to unite in rebellion.
bengal-subah: The Mughal absorption of Bengal began under Babur, who defeated Sultan Nasiruddin Nasrat Shah at the Battle of Ghaghra in 1529, and Humayun briefly held the Bengali capital Gaur before Sher Shah Suri drove him out. Akbar's army defeated Daud Khan Karrani at the Battle of Tukaroi on 3 March 1575, and after the Battle of Rajmahal Akbar made Bengal one of the original twelve subahs. Local chiefs, among them the Baro-Bhuyans and Isa Khan, resisted for years; the historian Tapan Raychaudhuri dates the real pacification of the province from 1594.

The capital moved several times, from Tanda to Rajmahal, renamed Akbarnagar, and in 1610 to Dhaka, renamed Jahangirnagar, which the Mughals built up with forts, gardens, palaces and mosques. Man Singh founded a coastal navy to contain Arakanese raids, Cooch Behar and Kamrup were annexed in 1609 and 1612, and the conquest of Chittagong in 1666 took the port from the Kingdom of Arakan. Governors were often princes: Shah Shuja proclaimed himself emperor in Bengal during the war of succession, lost to Aurangzeb and was killed in Arakan, while Shaista Khan consolidated Mughal control of eastern Bengal.

Murshid Quli Khan, the finance minister, gained control of the revenues and moved his office to Murshidabad; in 1717 his post became the hereditary title of nawab, and in 1740 Alivardi Khan seized power after the Battle of Giria. Maratha raids between 1741 and 1751 killed 400,000 Bengali civilians, among them weavers and silk winders, and ended with Alivardi agreeing to pay the chauth, an annual tribute of Rs. 1.2 million, while Orissa passed to the Marathas.

A Mughal subahdar governed with his own cabinet and diwans, and deputies known as naib nazims ruled Bengal proper, Bihar and Orissa. Todar Mal's settlement of 1582 divided the province into 24 sarkars, and a landed aristocracy of jagirdars collected the revenue. Under the early nawabs Bengal supplied more than half the funds reaching the imperial treasury in Delhi. The state cleared forest in the Bhati region for farmland, settled farmers in the delta and adapted the Bengali calendar for harvests and taxes, and peasants took up mulberry cultivation and silk. Islam was the official religion, while most of the population was Hindu; an estimated 30 million people lived there before the famine of 1770, which reduced them by as much as a third.
bengaluru: Bengaluru lies in the south-east of Karnataka on the Mysore Plateau, part of the Deccan Plateau, at an average elevation of 900 m. The topography is generally flat, with small hills of granite and gneiss to the south. No major river runs through the city, though six rivers rise at the Nandi Hills about 60 km to the north, and most of its water comes from the Kaveri. Because of its elevation the climate is moderate, with distinct wet and dry seasons. The city is known as India's Garden City because of its parks and greenery.

Stone Age artefacts indicate human settlement around 4000 BCE, and Roman coins of the first century CE show that the region took part in trans-oceanic trade. The earliest known reference to the name Bengaluru is an Old Kannada hero stone of 890 CE at Begur. In 1537 Kempe Gowda I, a local chieftain aligned with the Vijayanagara Empire, built a mud-brick fort that became the centre of the modern city. He divided the town into pētēs and built tanks such as Kempambudhi for water storage. In 1638 an Adil Shahi army defeated Kempe Gowda III, and the Mughals later sold the city to the Maharaja of Mysore. Hyder Ali seized the kingdom after 1759, and the city passed to his son Tipu Sultan.

After the Anglo-Mysore Wars the city returned to the Maharaja of Mysore, and in 1809 the British formed a military garrison and set up the cantonment outside the old city. By the late 19th century Bengaluru was essentially two cities, the Pete and the Cantonment. A plague epidemic in 1898 claimed nearly 3,500 lives and led to better sanitation. The two settlements merged under one urban administration in 1949, and the city became the capital of Mysore State, renamed Karnataka in 1973.

Bengaluru is the capital and largest city of Karnataka, with 8.4 million inhabitants at the 2011 census. Its official name was Bangalore until 1 November 2014. Kannada is the official language of the state and the mother tongue of 42.1 percent of the city's people at that census, and many other languages are spoken. The city was among the first in India to have electric power, in 1905. Lal Bagh, established in the 1760s, is a botanical garden of 97 hectares with a glass house of 1889 modelled on the Crystal Palace in London.
benguela: Benguela was founded in 1617 as São Felipe de Benguela by the Portuguese under Manuel Cerveira Pereira, who had been the eighth governor of Angola from 1604 to 1607. It was long the centre of an important trade, especially in slaves sent to Brazil and Cuba. Ships anchored about 1.6 kilometres off the shore, in depths of 7 to 11 metres, and transferred their loads to smaller boats that used five or six jetties in the town. The nearby sheltered deep-water harbour of Lobito was a much larger port.

Besides the churches of São Felipe and S. António, the hospital and the fortress, there were only a few stone-built houses in 1911. A short way beyond the town is Baía Farta, where salt was made and sulphur extracted.

In the early 20th century Portugal built the Benguela Railway to link the city and Lobito with the interior, and it was highly successful once connected to the Copperbelt of Katanga in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. The sisal and fishing industries expanded, and the financial, construction and service markets boomed until 1974. Angola became independent in 1975, after the Carnation Revolution of April 1974 in Lisbon. The Angolan Civil War, which lasted from 1975 to 2002, closed the railway except for the 30 kilometres between Benguela and Lobito. In 1983 the city had a population of 155,000, and it grew as refugees came in from the countryside. Restoration of the railway between Benguela and Huambo began in the mid-2000s.

Benguela is the capital of Benguela Province in western Angola and has a population of 555,124 in the city, according to the 2014 census. Its Umbundu name is Luombaka. It remains an important commercial link between western and eastern Angola, trading coffee, corn, sisal, sugarcane, tobacco and manganese from the interior. Local industries include fish processing and sugarcane milling, and the city also produces pottery, soap and tools. Foreign trade passes through the deep-water port of Lobito, 29 kilometres to the north. The Universidade Katyavala Bwila was founded in 2009.
beni-hasan: Beni Hasan is an ancient funerary site cut into the limestone cliffs on the eastern edge of the Nile Valley, on the east bank about 20 kilometres south of Minya in Middle Egypt. During the Middle Kingdom it was the main cemetery of the sixteenth nome of Upper Egypt, the Oryx nome, whose capital was the town of Hebenu. Burials were made from the late Old Kingdom to the Middle Kingdom, between the end of the third millennium and the start of the second millennium BCE. The upper cemetery has 39 rock-cut tombs, chiefly of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties, and a lower cemetery of about 900 graves, mainly shaft tombs, lies below.

Provincial governors, conventionally called nomarchs, were buried in the rock-cut tombs. In the Old Kingdom and the first half of the Middle Kingdom the office often appears to have been hereditary, with local dynasties holding the same province for generations, though the nomarch remained the king's representative. Under Senusret III the great families seem to have stopped building immense funerary complexes; one scholar, Connor, cautions that this may reflect the surviving evidence or a change in how power was expressed rather than a decline of the families.

Of the upper tombs, twelve bear inscriptions: eight belonged to governors of the Oryx nome. The Archaeological Survey of Egypt recorded the paintings and inscriptions in four volumes published between 1893 and 1900, and John Garstang excavated 888 tombs of the lower cemetery in 1902–1904.

Twelve of the 39 upper tombs keep painted scenes of farming, crafts, hunting, games, fighting and the arrival of foreign groups. The tomb of Khnumhotep II, Overseer of the Eastern Desert under Senusret II, has an inscription of 222 columns telling his life. On its north wall fifteen Aamu are shown, while the inscription records 37; their leader Abisharie bears the title "ruler of the hill-lands".

The tomb of Baqet III has a wrestling cycle of 220 pairs, and that of Khety shows 122 pairs of wrestlers, military training and an assault on fortified places. Four tombs are open to visitors: those of Amenemhat, Khnumhotep II, Baqet III and Khety. South of the cemetery Hatshepsut built a rock-cut temple to the goddess Pakhet, known as the Speos Artemidos.
benin-bronzes: The Benin Bronzes decorated the royal palace of the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Edo State, Nigeria. The metal plaques, called Ama in the Edo language, were produced by the Guild of Benin Bronze Casters, now located in Igun Street, and depict scenes and themes from the history of the kingdom. Despite the name, the pieces are mostly brass, an alloy of copper, zinc and lead in varying proportions, made by lost-wax casting.

Others are of wood, ceramic, ivory, leather or cloth. The brass came partly from manillas, brass bracelets bought from the Portuguese, whose metal is now thought to have come from the Rhineland. Two golden ages of the craft are placed under the obas Esigie, around 1550, and Eresoyen, in 1735–1750.

Property in bronze and ivory was reserved to the highest ranks. In general only the oba could own objects of bronze or ivory, though he could allow high-ranking people to use items such as hanging masks and cuffs. Coral was also a royal material, and coral neck rings, granted by the oba, marked nobility. The plaques were fixed to the palace pillars, and a Dutch visitor described galleries on wooden pillars covered with cast copper engraved with pictures of war exploits.

2 mm thick, and the backgrounds of most are incised with the ebe-ame, or river leaf, design, whose leaves were used in healing rites by priestesses of Olokun, the god of the sea. The descendants of the casters still revere Igue-Igha, who introduced casting to the kingdom.

In January 1897 a party of unarmed British envoys and many African bearers was massacred, and British forces took most of the plaques in the Benin Expedition of that year, which British sources presented as retaliation. The British Museum received a large share, about 900 objects today, and others went to museums in Germany, France, the Netherlands and the United States. Before then Europeans had described African works as curiosities of pagan cults, and the late 19th-century scholars O. M. Dalton and Charles Hercules Read mistakenly thought the knowledge of metalworking came from the Portuguese.

Nigeria has sought the return of the bronzes since independence in 1960. In 2021 the German government declared it would return looted bronzes in its public collections, and in November 2022 the Horniman Museum became the first museum in the United Kingdom to return bronzes. On 19 June 2025 the Netherlands returned 119 bronzes, the largest single return to that date, and in November 2022 the Digital Benin database was launched, listing more than 5,000 artefacts held by over 130 institutions in 20 countries.
benin-city: The indigenous people of Benin City are the Edo, also called the Benin people, who speak the Edo or Bini language. By tradition they were first ruled by kings called the Ogiso, who named the land Igodomigodo, and the elders later asked Oduduwa of Ife to rule. He sent his son Oranmiyan, whose son Eweka I became the first Oba of the present line; Yoruba and Edo traditions differ on details but agree that Oduduwa sent Oranmiyan to found the Oba dynasty. The city was called Ubinu, which the Portuguese took as Benin, and around 1470 Ewuare changed the name of the state to Edo.

The Portuguese reached Benin City about 1485. The city grew rich in the 16th and 17th centuries through trade within southern Nigeria and with Europeans, mostly in pepper and ivory. In the early 16th century the Oba sent an ambassador to Lisbon, and the King of Portugal sent Christian missionaries. A Portuguese captain, Lourenco Pinto, described it in 1691 as larger than Lisbon, with straight streets and a richly decorated royal palace. In a letter of 1701 or 1702 the Dutch East India Company merchant David van Nyendael called it a mere village of half-ruined houses, though he praised the palace with its turreted roofs decorated with brass snakes.

On 17 February 1897 British forces captured, sacked and burnt Benin City. The force of 1,200, under Admiral Sir Harry Rawson, acted after all but two men of a British delegation led by Acting Consul General James Robert Phillips had been ambushed and killed. The capture paved the way for British colonisation, and the monarchy was permitted to return in 1914, with real power in colonial hands. The Benin Bronzes, portrait figures and groups of brass, ivory and iron, were looted from the palace, and some were auctioned to meet the expedition's costs; most are now in museums abroad.

Benin City is the capital and largest city of Edo State in southern Nigeria, and it was the fourth-largest city in Nigeria in the 2006 census. It became capital of the Mid-Western Region in 1963, of Bendel State in 1976 and of Edo State in 1991. Its monarchy is one of the oldest still continuing in the world, and its attractions include the Oba Palace, the National Museum, Igun Street, known for bronze casting, and the remains of the Benin moats.
benin-expedition-of-1897: In the late 19th century the Kingdom of Benin had kept its independence through the Scramble for Africa, and the Oba's control of trade in his territories was seen as a threat by the Royal Niger Company. In 1892 Captain Henry Lionel Gallwey obtained a treaty from Oba Ovọnramwẹn Nọgbaisi granting free trade to British merchants, but the Oba went on requiring customs duties, which the Protectorate authorities treated as a hostile act. Some historians stress humanitarian motives for British policy; others, such as Philip Igbafe, see the annexation as driven largely by economic designs.

In March 1896 the Oba halted the supply of palm produce to Itsekiri middlemen, bringing trade on the Benin River to a standstill, and British merchants urged that Benin be opened up and the Oba exiled. In late December the Acting Consul-General, James Robert Phillips, set out for Benin City with about 250 people before London had answered his request. The Oba, celebrating the Igue festival, asked the party to wait about a month, but Phillips pressed on, and on 4 January 1897 his party was attacked near Ugbine. Most of the British officials and many African porters were killed, and over 100 Itsekiri porters were taken to Benin.

The Foreign Office authorised what the British called a punitive expedition, and Rear-Admiral Harry Rawson was appointed to lead it. On 9 February about 1,200 Royal Marines, sailors and Niger Coast Protectorate troops advanced in three columns, supported by warships and gunboats. After ten days of fighting, and the use of rockets, the city fell on 18 February. Eight of the British force were recorded as killed in action; Benin's losses were not estimated but are thought to have been very high. Members of the expedition reported human sacrifices, an account the historian Robin Law suggests the British exaggerated to justify intervention.

Houses, sacred sites and chiefs' palaces were looted and many buildings burned, the palace itself on 21 February. Ralph Moor deposed Ovonramwen and exiled him to Calabar, and six chiefs were hanged in the marketplace. Some 2,500 objects officially went to Britain, about 40% of them to the British Museum, and the Admiralty auctioned others from May 1897 to pay for the expedition. Their dispersal influenced early European modernism, and later demands for their return led Jesus College, Cambridge, and the University of Aberdeen to hand pieces to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments in October 2021.
benito-juarez: Benito Pablo Juárez García was born on 21 March 1806 in the village of San Pablo Guelatao, Oaxaca, in New Spain, a settlement of about two hundred people. He came from a poor rural Indigenous family and was orphaned as a child. At the age of 12 he moved to Oaxaca City, where he worked as a domestic servant.

His employer, a lay Franciscan, sponsored him, and he enrolled for a time in a seminary before switching to law, becoming active in liberal politics. As a lawyer he took cases of Indigenous villagers and was imprisoned after helping villagers of Loxicha accuse a priest of abuses. He sat in the Oaxaca state legislature from 1832, married Margarita Maza on 31 October 1843, and later became governor of Oaxaca.

After the Plan of Ayutla ousted Antonio López de Santa Anna, President Juan Álvarez made Juárez his Minister of Justice. He was instrumental in the Juárez Law, part of the reforms known as La Reforma, which ended the separate courts of clerics and soldiers. As head of the Supreme Court he succeeded to the presidency when Ignacio Comonfort resigned early in the Reform War, and he led the Liberals to victory after three years. Liberal troops entered Mexico City on Christmas Day 1860.

The Second French Intervention followed at once. French troops took Puebla on 17 May 1863 and entered Mexico City on 10 June 1863, and Juárez moved his government north to San Luis Potosí, Monterrey and Chihuahua City. The Second Mexican Empire collapsed after the last French troops left on 12 March 1867. Maximilian and his generals were captured at Querétaro on 14 May 1867, and Juárez re-entered the capital on 15 July.

In his last years Juárez faced opposition from Liberals who thought him autocratic. He stood for re-election in 1871, and when he lacked the required majority, Congress decided for him on 12 October 1871. Porfirio Díaz rebelled against him in the Plan de la Noria. Juárez died of a heart attack in 1872 and was given a state funeral.

He is seen as a symbol of Mexican nationalism and resistance to foreign intervention, and his policies favoured civil liberties, equality before the law and the authority of civilian power over the Church and the army. After his death the city of Oaxaca added "de Juárez" to its name, and his birthday, 21 March, is a national holiday.
benito-mussolini: Benito Amilcare Andrea Mussolini was born on 29 July 1883 in Dovia di Predappio, in Romagna. His father, Alessandro, was a blacksmith and socialist, and his mother, Rosa Maltoni, a devout Catholic schoolteacher. He was named after the Mexican president Benito Juárez, and his middle names honoured the Italian socialists Amilcare Cipriani and Andrea Costa. He became a journalist for the Italian Socialist Party newspaper Avanti! and was expelled for advocating military intervention in the First World War. He served in the army from 1915 until wounded in 1917, and during the war turned to nationalism.

On 23 March 1919 Mussolini founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in Milan, often considered the world's first fascist movement. It became the National Fascist Party in 1921, and after fascist militants marched on Rome King Victor Emmanuel III appointed him prime minister in 1922. He founded the secret police OVRA in 1927, outlawed strikes and, through measures such as the Acerbo Law, turned a parliamentary democracy into a one-party state. By the end of 1925 press censorship had tightened and appointed podestàs had replaced elected mayors. He signed the Lateran Treaty in 1929, establishing Vatican City, and ordered the Pacification of Libya, which some scholars characterise as a genocide.

His invasion of Ethiopia brought condemnation from the League of Nations, which isolated Italy and pushed him towards Adolf Hitler and the Rome-Berlin Axis of 1936. The Pact of Steel followed in 1939. In June 1940, believing a German victory imminent, he joined the Second World War on Germany's side.

After defeats and the Allied landing in Sicily, the Grand Council of Fascism voted the Grandi motion, and in July 1943 the king dismissed Mussolini and placed him in custody. After the armistice of September 1943 German forces rescued him, and Hitler made him figurehead of the Italian Social Republic, a collaborationist puppet state in German-occupied northern Italy. In April 1945 he and his mistress Clara Petacci tried to flee to Switzerland, were captured by communist partisans and were summarily executed on 28 April 1945.
benjamin-constant: Henri-Benjamin Constant de Rebecque was born in Lausanne on 25 October 1767, into a family descended from French Huguenots who had fled to Switzerland. His mother died soon after his birth, and his father was a high-ranking officer in the Dutch States Army. He studied at the University of Erlangen and the University of Edinburgh. In Paris he met the Dutch woman of letters Isabelle de Charrière, with whom he wrote an epistolary novel. In September 1794 he met Germaine de Staël, and their collaboration between 1795 and 1811 made them one of the best-known intellectual couples of the time.

A committed republican from 1795, Constant backed the coups of 18 Fructidor and 18 Brumaire. After 18 Brumaire Napoleon Bonaparte, with grave reservations, appointed him to the Tribunat, and in 1802 forced him to withdraw because of his speeches and his connection with Madame de Staël. He became the leader of the Liberal opposition in 1800. In 1814, after the Restoration, he proposed a constitutional monarchy on the Council of State, and during the Hundred Days he helped draft the Charter of 1815.

He was elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1818 and remained a deputy until his death. As head of the parliamentary bloc first called the Independents and later the liberals, he was one of the most eloquent orators of the Chamber and an opponent of Charles X. He supported the accession of Louis Philippe I in the July Revolution, and died in Paris on 8 December 1830.

Constant distinguished the Liberty of the Ancients, the right to take direct part in politics through votes in a public assembly, which rested on slavery and on small, homogenous societies, from the Liberty of the Moderns, based on civil liberties, the rule of law and freedom from excessive state interference. He criticised the French revolutionaries for applying ancient liberties to a modern state, and held that commerce is preferable to war. He opposed imperialism and colonial racism.

He developed a theory of constitutional monarchy in which royal power is a neutral power balancing the executive, legislature and judiciary, while ministers accountable to Parliament hold the executive. This made four powers rather than Montesquieu's three. The theory was applied literally in Brazil in 1824 and in Portugal in 1826, where the monarch was given Moderating Powers. He also wrote on religion for forty years, and published the novella Adolphe in 1816.
benjamin-disraeli: Benjamin D'Israeli was born on 21 December 1804 at Bedford Row in Bloomsbury, London, the eldest son of Isaac D'Israeli, a literary critic and historian, and Maria Basevi. The family was of Sephardic Jewish mercantile background. His father left Judaism after a dispute at his synagogue, and Benjamin became an Anglican at the age of 11. He later romanticised his origins, claiming grand Spanish and Venetian descent for his father's family. In November 1821 he was articled as a clerk to a firm of solicitors in the City of London. In 1830–31 he travelled widely in southern Europe and beyond, a tour that biographers count among the formative experiences of his career.

After several unsuccessful attempts, Disraeli won a seat at Maidstone in July 1837. In 1846 Prime Minister Robert Peel split the Conservatives by proposing to repeal the Corn Laws, and Disraeli's clashes with Peel made him a leading figure in the party. When Lord Derby formed governments in the 1850s and 1860s, Disraeli served as Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons. In 1867 he persuaded a majority of the cabinet to agree to a Reform bill, which Derby called a leap in the dark.

Derby's ill health led to his resignation in February 1868, and Disraeli became prime minister, remarking that he had climbed to the top of the greasy pole. He lost that year's election to William Ewart Gladstone, led the party to a majority in 1874, and served until 1880. His government passed the Public Health Act 1875 and the Elementary Education Act 1876. Queen Victoria made him Earl of Beaconsfield in 1876. He arranged the purchase of a major interest in the Suez Canal Company and, at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, worked for terms favourable to Britain. Wars in Afghanistan and South Africa then undermined his support, and the Liberals won the 1880 election.

Disraeli wrote novels throughout his career, beginning in 1826, among them Henrietta Temple, Venetia, Lothair (1870), a bestseller, and Endymion, his last completed novel, published shortly before he died on 19 April 1881. He is remembered for what has been called one-nation conservatism or Tory democracy. B. H. Abbott stressed in 1972 that Lord Randolph Churchill, not Disraeli, invented the term Tory democracy, and Parry wrote in 2007 that the myth did not survive detailed study, though he still sees Disraeli, rather than Peel, as founder of the modern Conservative Party.
benjamin-durban: Benjamin D'Urban was born in Halesworth on 16 February 1777, the youngest and only surviving son of Benjamin D'Urban. He joined the British Army in 1793 as a cornet in the Queen's Bays at the age of sixteen and rose quickly, distinguishing himself in the Peninsular War.

Assigned to the Portuguese army, he was quartermaster general and chief of staff to William Carr Beresford, 1st Viscount Beresford. As a brigadier general he commanded a Portuguese cavalry brigade, whose troopers performed well at the Battle of Salamanca on 22 July 1812 but were routed at Majadahonda on 11 August, losing 108 men. He received the Army Gold Cross with five clasps and was made a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath.

D'Urban became Governor of Antigua in 1819 and Lieutenant Governor of Demerara Essequibo in 1824. In 1831 he carried out its amalgamation with Berbice to form British Guiana, of which he was the first governor. In January 1834 he took office as governor and commander in chief of the Cape Colony, where his administration was complicated by the Great Trek and by war on the frontier with the Xhosa, whom he drove back. Slavery was abolished and municipal and legislative councils established while he was in office, and in 1835 Port Natal was renamed Durban.

D'Urban was popular with the white colonists, but his treatment of the Xhosa and other Africans disturbed the missionary John Philip, who gave evidence before a parliamentary committee in England and roused opinion against him. In a despatch of 1 May 1837 the colonial secretary, Charles Grant, 1st Baron Glenelg, dismissed him, though he stayed until his successor arrived and served in South Africa as a soldier until 1846.

In 1842 he declined a high military post in India offered by Sir Robert Peel. In January 1847 he accepted command of the British forces in British North America and set up his headquarters in Montreal, where he died on 25 May 1849. His remains now rest at the Last Post Fund National Field of Honour in Pointe-Claire, under an obelisk bearing a plaque from the City of Durban.
benjamin-franklin: Benjamin Franklin was born on Milk Street in Boston on 17 January 1706 and baptised at the Old South Meeting House. His father, Josiah Franklin, born at Ecton in Northamptonshire, was a tallow chandler and soap and candle maker. Benjamin was his fifteenth child and tenth and last son. His mother, Abiah Folger, was born in Nantucket, and both parents were pious Puritans.

His father could afford to send him to school for only two years, and he continued to educate himself by reading. At 12 he became an apprentice to his brother James, a printer. When James founded The New-England Courant, Franklin wrote letters in the name of Silence Dogood, a middle-aged widow, and neither the readers nor his brother knew the author. He later left the apprenticeship without permission and so became a fugitive.

Franklin became a successful printer and editor in Philadelphia, publishing The Pennsylvania Gazette at 23 and Poor Richard's Almanack under the pseudonym Richard Saunders. In 1736 he created the Union Fire Company, and in 1743 he founded the American Philosophical Society. In 1749 he printed Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania and was appointed president of the Academy, which opened in 1751.

His electrical research began in the 1740s. He proposed that vitreous and resinous electricity were one fluid under different pressures, was the first to call them positive and negative, and discovered the principle of conservation of charge. He invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove and bifocal glasses and never patented them. As an agent in London he led the repeal of the Stamp Act, and as the first United States ambassador to France he secured French support for the Revolutionary War. He served as President of Pennsylvania from 1785 to 1788.
Franklin owned at least seven slaves from 1735 and advertised slaves for sale in his newspaper, but by the late 1750s he had begun to argue against slavery and later became an active abolitionist.

Franklin died of a pleuritic attack at his home in Philadelphia on 17 April 1790, aged 84. About 20,000 people attended his funeral, and the assembly of revolutionary France went into mourning for three days. He left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia, to gather interest for 200 years. He is the only person to have signed the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris with Britain and the Constitution.
benjamin-hornigold: Hornigold's early life is unrecorded. Some claim he was born in the English county of Norfolk, where the surname Hornigold or Hornagold appears; if so, he may have first served aboard ships from King's Lynn or Great Yarmouth. His first documented acts of piracy took place in the winter of 1713, when he used periaguas, which were sailing canoes, and the sloop Happy Return, alongside Daniel Stillwell, John Cockram and John West, to menace merchant vessels off New Providence and its capital Nassau, where he had established a privateers' or pirates' republic.

Hornigold himself sailed a ship named the Marianne. After a mutiny in the summer of 1716 he and his supporters were left with a captured sloop. By 1717 he commanded a thirty-gun sloop, the Ranger, probably the most heavily armed ship in the region, which let him seize other vessels with impunity. His second-in-command was Edward Teach, later known as Blackbeard, to whom he delegated his earlier sloop. In the spring of 1717 the two captains seized three merchant ships in quick succession: a Spanish ship carrying 120 barrels of flour bound for Havana, a Bermudian sloop with a cargo of spirits and a Portuguese ship from Madeira carrying white wine.

In September 1717 Hornigold and Teach met Major Stede Bonnet, who, wounded in battle, ceded command of his ship Revenge to Teach. Hornigold took care not to attack British-flagged ships, apparently to keep the legal defence that he was a privateer acting against England's enemies in the War of the Spanish Succession. His lieutenants disliked this restraint, and the combined crews voted to attack any vessel they chose. Hornigold opposed the vote and was replaced as captain of the Marianne by Samuel Bellamy.

Hornigold accepted a royal pardon, sailing to Jamaica with the Ranger and another sloop to receive it from the governor there. He then became a pirate hunter for Woodes Rogers, the new Governor of the Bahamas, who commissioned him to pursue pirates who had refused to give up the trade, among them his former lieutenant Teach. In December 1718 Rogers wrote to the Board of Trade in London commending his efforts to remedy his reputation.

In late 1719 Rogers commissioned Hornigold and other trusted captains to help trade with the Spanish. His ship was caught in a hurricane between New Providence and New Spain and wrecked on an uncharted reef. Captain Charles Johnson's A General History of the Pyrates records that five of his men escaped in a canoe. The location of the reef remains unknown.
benjamin-kallay: Kállay was born in Pest, today part of Budapest, on 22 December 1839, into an old, untitled Hungarian noble family. The family took its name from its estates at Nagykálló in Szabolcs and claimed descent from the gens Balogsemjén, which had settled parts of Borsod, Szabolcs and Szatmár in the late 9th century. Under King Matthias Corvinus an ancestor, Mihály Kállay, received estates at Mezőtúr for his defence of Jajce in Bosnia.

His father, Stephan von Kállay, a senior official of the Hungarian government, died in 1845. His mother, Amalie von Kállay née Blašković de Ebetske, who was of Serbian descent and spoke Serbian, turned his education towards Slavic studies and Serbian history and engaged as his teacher Mihály Táncsics, a populist and revolutionary writer imprisoned by the Austrians. As a young man Kállay travelled in Russia, European Turkey and Asia Minor and learned Greek, Turkish and several Slavic languages.

In 1867 Kállay entered the Diet of Hungary as Conservative deputy for Mühlbach (Szászsebes). In 1869 he was appointed consul-general at Belgrade, and in 1872 he visited the Vilayet of Bosnia for the first time. His views on Balkan questions strongly influenced Count Andrássy, the Austro-Hungarian minister for foreign affairs. After leaving Belgrade in 1875 he returned to the Diet and founded the journal Kelet Népe (People of the East), in which he defended Andrássy's policy.

After the Russo-Turkish War he served at Plovdiv as Austro-Hungarian envoy extraordinary on the International Eastern Rumelian Commission, and in 1879 he became a departmental chief at the foreign office in Vienna. On 4 June 1882 he was appointed minister of finance and administrator of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an office he held for 21 years. He died in Vienna on 13 July 1903.

Kállay was an honorary member of the academies of science of Budapest and Vienna. He translated John Stuart Mill's On Liberty into Hungarian with an introductory critique, and his version of Galatea, a play by the Greek dramatist Spiridion N. Basiliades, was a success on the Hungarian stage. His monograph on Serbian history, Geschichte der Serben, was translated into Serbo-Croatian by Gavrilo Vitković, and his study Die Orientpolitik Russlands appeared at Leipzig in 1878. He himself counted as his best work an academic oration on Hungary's position as a link between East and West.
benjamin-mkapa: Benjamin William Mkapa was born on 12 November 1938 in Lupaso, near Masasi, Tanganyika. He graduated from Makerere University in Uganda in 1962 with a Bachelor of Arts in English. The following year he went to Columbia University, where he earned a master's degree in International Affairs.

He worked as an administrative officer in Dodoma and served as Minister for Science, Technology and Higher Education. He headed the Tanzanian mission to Canada in 1982 and to the United States in 1983 and 1984, and he was Minister of Foreign Affairs from 1977 to 1980 and again from 1984 to 1990.

In 1995 Mkapa was elected president on a popular anti-corruption campaign and with the strong support of the former president Julius Nyerere. He chaired Chama Cha Mapinduzi, the Revolutionary State Political Party. His anti-corruption measures included an open forum, the Presidential Commission on Corruption, known as the Warioba Commission, and increased support for the Prevention of Corruption Bureau.

His second five-year term ended in December 2005. In it he privatized state-owned corporations and instituted free market policies, which his supporters argued would promote growth by attracting foreign investment. These policies won the support of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and led to the cancellation of some of Tanzania's foreign debts. He was criticized for the limited effect of his anti-corruption efforts and for lavish spending, including £15 million on a private presidential jet and almost £30 million on military aviation equipment from BAE Systems.

After he left office under the two-term limit, Mkapa faced accusations of corruption, among them that he and his former finance minister Daniel Yona had improperly taken over the Kiwira coal mine in the southern highlands. In 2007 he joined the African Union's Panel of Eminent African Personalities, with Graça Machel and Kofi Annan as chair, which was sent to Kenya to resolve the violence that followed disputed election results. Its mediation led to the National Accord and Reconciliation Act of 2008.

Mkapa was a trustee of the Aga Khan University from 2007 to 2012. He was treated for malaria on 22 July 2020 and died of a heart attack in Dar es Salaam in the early hours of 23 July, at the age of 81. He was laid to rest in his hometown of Lupaso. Kenya's president declared three days of national mourning in recognition of his role in resolving the violence of 2007 and 2008.
benjamin-of-tudela: Little is known of Benjamin's personal life. He was a native of Tudela in the Kingdom of Navarre and lived in the second half of the 12th century, and his father's name was Jonah. Non-Jewish sources often call him Rabbi, but there is no reliable evidence that he held that title. He is credited with a broad education and a knowledge of many languages.

Benjamin set out from the north-east of the Iberian Peninsula around 1165, in what may have begun as a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. He may also have had a commercial motive, since he shows interest in the coral trade, or he may have meant to list Jewish communities on the way to the Land of Israel as a guide to where travellers could find hospitality. Scholars do not agree on his exact route. He began at Zaragoza, went down the Ebro to Tarragona, Barcelona and Girona, and then north to France before sailing from Marseille.

After visiting Genoa, Lucca, Pisa, Florence and Rome he went to Greece and Constantinople, then crossed Asia through Syria, Lebanon, the Land of Israel and northern Mesopotamia, which he called Shinar, to Baghdad. From there he went to Persia, then crossed Arabia to Egypt and North Africa and returned to the Iberian Peninsula in 1173. He visited some 300 cities, including Susa, Sura and Pumbedita, and gathered information on places he only heard of, such as China and Tibet. His visit to the ruins outside Mosul is one of the earliest accurate descriptions of the site of ancient Nineveh.

Benjamin described his journey in a book written in Hebrew, The Travels of Benjamin, also called the Book of Travels. It describes the countries he visited with an emphasis on Jewish communities, giving their populations and the names of notable leaders, and it describes local customs, Jewish and non-Jewish, with an emphasis on urban life. He wrote of Baghdad with great enthusiasm and often notes the respect and mixing between Judaism and Islam. He also describes the Al-Hashishin, and a significant Jewish community somewhere around modern Ethiopia, which scholars have struggled to locate.

Historians generally regard him as trustworthy and he cites his sources, though some claims rely on earlier writers, such as his identification of Laish, Tel Dan, with Baniyas. His account preceded Marco Polo's descriptions of western Asia by a hundred years. It was translated into Latin and later most major European languages, and drew much attention from Renaissance scholars in the 16th century.
bennachie: Bennachie has several tops, the highest of which is Oxen Craig at 528 metres. The hills are not high by Scottish standards, but their isolation and the flatness of the land around make them very prominent, and they dominate the skyline from many viewpoints, as far north as Longman Hill. Most of the tops lie along an east to west ridge; Millstone Hill (409 m) is a spur to the south. Unlike many hilltop forts in the area, the fort on the Mither Tap shows no sign of vitrification in its stone.
The origin of the name is uncertain. One suggestion is Beinn a Cioch, the hill of the nipple or pap; another reads it as the mountain of Ce, a king named in a list of the kings of Pictland.

From 1800 to 1859 common land on the east side of Bennachie was home to a community of squatters known locally as the Colony. A few families lived as crofters and often did skilled work, such as dyking and quarrying, for local landowners. After 1859 the common land was broken up and divided among the local estates and the Colony dwindled, though the last of the original colonists, George Esson, lived on the hill until his death in the 1930s.
The early Scottish archaeologist Christian Maclagan surveyed the Mither Tap and excavated there in 1876 and 1881, and the University of Aberdeen's Northern Picts Project dug on the summit in 2019.

Most of the range is owned by Forestry and Land Scotland, which keeps paths, car parks and a visitor centre at its eastern foot. The Gordon Way runs along the southern flank, and the Bailies of Bennachie, a volunteer conservation charity founded in 1973, help with environmental and archaeological work on the hill, where the remains of the Colony can still be seen.
benno-of-meissen: Little is known of Benno's early life. He was born in Hildesheim and is reported to have come from a Saxon noble family, perhaps the Woldenburgs, and he may have been educated at the monastery of St. Michael in Hildesheim. It is certain that he was a canon of the chapter at Goslar, and in 1066 King Henry IV nominated him to the see of Meissen.

Benno appears as a supporter of the Saxon rebellion of 1073, although the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld and other contemporaries gave his part little weight. Henry IV exiled him in 1075 but let him return the following year. In the Investiture Controversy he backed Pope Gregory VII and allegedly took part in the election of the antiking Rudolf of Rheinfelden in 1077, then turned to the next antiking, Hermann of Salm.

The Synod of Mainz of 1085 excommunicated him and deprived him of his bishopric. Benno went to Archbishop Guibert of Ravenna, Henry's antipope Clement III, and by a penitent acknowledgment of his offences obtained absolution and a letter to Henry that restored him to his see. He apparently promised to work for peace with the Saxons, but in 1097 he returned to the papal party and recognised Urban II. Nothing supports the later stories of his missionary work and church-building. He died on 16 June 1106. In his diocese he carried out reforms on the Hildebrandine model.

Benno was venerated in Saxony from the 13th century, and Adrian VI issued the bull of his canonisation. Once a saint he became a symbol for both sides of the reforming debate: Luther reviled him in early tracts against the cult of saints, Catholic reformers made him a model of orthodoxy, and after Protestant mobs desecrated his tomb in Meissen in 1539 the Wittelsbach dynasty made him patron saint of Munich and Old Bavaria. The English Protestant John Foxe repeated the charges Benno had made against Henry IV.

His feast day is 16 June, and he is the patron saint of anglers and weavers. He is shown with a book and a fish holding keys, after a legend that he had the cathedral keys thrown into the Elbe when Henry IV was excommunicated and a fisherman later found them inside a fish.
bentheim-castle: The castle stands on an outcrop of Bentheim sandstone, the Bentheimer Höhenrücken, the last protrusion of the nearby Teutoburger forest. The stone supplied the castle's own building material and was also a valued export. Its height above an otherwise very flat landscape gives a wide view and made the site a strong strategic position. It was raised on the remains of an earlier refuge castle, whose history is largely unknown.

In 1116, in the war between Lothar of Süpplinburg, later Lothar III, and Heinrich V, the castle was destroyed; the Annalista Saxo records that Lothar besieged and burned Binithem, a fine and strong city. It was soon rebuilt, this time in stone, by Otto von Salm, Lothar's brother-in-law. In 1146 Otto von Rheineck was defeated near Ootmarsum in a war with the Bishop of Utrecht over Twente, and the castle became a fief of the Diocese of Utrecht.

Through Sophie von Salm-Rheineck's marriage to Dirk VI, Count of Holland, castle and county passed to the Counts of Holland, whose line of Bentheim-Holland held them until 1421, when they went to Eberwin IV von Götterswick. The independent county troubled the bishops of Münster and Utrecht, who both attacked the castle in 1374. In 1486 Eberwin II received the county as a fief from Frederick III, making it an independent political entity, and work on the Pulverturm began in 1489.

Between 1588 and 1593 Arnold II took the side of the Reformation, following Calvin and Zwingli, and in the Thirty Years' War the county was repeatedly sacked by Spanish troops and much of the castle destroyed. In the Seven Years' War it was besieged and taken several times by French and British troops, and in 1795, while serving as a field hospital, it was set ablaze and captured by General Dominique Vandamme.

Bentheim Castle, an early medieval hill castle in the town of Bad Bentheim, belongs to the Prince of Bentheim-Steinfurt, who lives at Steinfurt Castle. It is home to some of his siblings and is open to the public as a family museum, and its gardens have hosted Knight Games since 2006.
bentivoglio-family: The family's presence in Bologna is first recorded in 1323. It took its name from the castle of Bentivoglio near the city and claimed descent from Enzio, King of Sardinia, an illegitimate son of the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. Belonging to one of Bologna's workers' guilds, the Bentivoglio gained power in the 14th century as pro-papal Guelph leaders.

Amid the faction conflicts of the commune, Giovanni I declared himself signore and Gonfaloniere di Giustizia on 14 March 1401 with the help of Gian Galeazzo Visconti. The Visconti turned against him, and he was killed at the Battle of Casalecchio on 26 June 1402. His son Anton Galeazzo, a lecturer in civil law, held power briefly in 1420 before being overthrown, became a condottiero and was assassinated by papal officials in 1435.

In 1438 Annibale I, a putative son of Anton Galeazzo, led a revolt against papal rule. Imprisoned by the Visconti condottiere Niccolò Piccinino in 1442 and freed by Galeazzo Marescotti, he returned to be given the powers of government, but was assassinated in 1445. His successor Sante I, of doubtful parentage and once an apprentice in the wool guild of Florence, was advised by Cosimo de' Medici and brought a short period of calm, with closer ties to Venice, Milan and Florence. Annibale's son Giovanni II then ruled as virtual tyrant until his expulsion.

Giovanni II's son Annibale II, who married Lucrezia d'Este, daughter of Duke Ercole I of Ferrara, retook Bologna with French help during a rebellion against Julius II in 1511, but ruled only a year before he was assassinated. He was the last ruler of his line.

In exile the family settled in Ferrara, where it produced prelates such as Cardinal Guido Bentivoglio, a papal diplomat and historian of the war in Flanders who was among the inquisitors who signed the condemnation of Galileo. In Bologna the Church of San Giacomo Maggiore was the centre of their power; it holds the tomb of Anton Galeazzo by Jacopo della Quercia and the family chapel, with paintings by Lorenzo Costa.
benzoin-resin: Benzoin resin, also called benzoin, gum benzoin or benjamin, is a balsamic resin obtained from the bark of several species of trees in the genus Styrax. Its primary active ingredient is benzoic acid. It is distinct from the chemical compound benzoin, which is ultimately derived from the resin. In India it is called sambrani or loban, though loban is, via Arabic lubān, a generic term for frankincense-type incense. The name comes from the Arabic lubān jāwī, meaning frankincense from Java, and reached the language in the mid 16th century through French benjoin. It is sometimes called storax, not to be confused with the balsam of that name from the Altingiaceae family.

There are two common kinds. Benzoin Siam is obtained from Styrax tonkinensis, found across Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, and its aroma is described as sweet, vanilla, balsamic, woody and powdery. Benzoin Sumatra comes from Styrax paralleloneurus and Styrax benzoin, which grows mainly on the island of Sumatra. It contains cinnamic acid in addition to benzoic acid and smells sweet, spicy, vanilla and balsamic.

Benzoin is a common ingredient of incense and perfumery because of its sweet vanilla-like aroma and its fixative properties. Gum benzoin is a major component of the church incense used in Russia and some other Eastern Orthodox societies, as well as in Latin Catholic churches. It is burned on charcoal as incense on the Arabian Peninsula and in Hindu temples of India, and it goes into bakhoor and mixed resin incenses in Arab countries and the Horn of Africa. It also appears in blended Japanese and Indian incense, in Chinese incense known as Anxi xiang, in Papier d'Arménie and in incense sticks.

In perfumery it slows the dispersion of essential oils and other fragrance materials into the air. It is used in cosmetics, veterinary medicine and scented candles, and as a flavouring in drinks, baked goods, chewing gum, frozen dairy, gelatins, puddings and soft candy. In anaesthesia and surgery it serves as an adhesive to secure wound and catheter dressings, and it is available as a sterile preparation.
beopheung-of-silla: Beopheung was the son of King Jijeung of Silla, who reigned from 500 to 514, and of Lady Yeonje of the Park clan. His name appears on the Bongpyeong Silla Stele and the Cheonjeonri Petroglyphs as Mojeukji, and Chinese writers recorded it as Mojin. He was said to be tall, generous and sociable. Buddhism was already fairly common in Silla when he came to the throne, having been brought in much earlier by monks from Goguryeo during the reign of King Nulji.

After his accession Beopheung restructured the administration and favoured central management to strengthen royal authority. His Yullyeong law of 520 codified Silla's bone-rank system, and in 536 he proclaimed his own era name, Geonwon, a sign of royal authority and independence at home and abroad. In 523 he sent a tribute mission to Emperor Wu of Liang; it travelled with the help of Baekje, which presented Silla as its subordinate, a status Silla accepted because it needed Baekje against Goguryeo and Japan.

Silla went on expanding. In 522 Daegaya sought to avoid conquest through a marriage alliance, and Beopheung gave the sister of Minister Bijobu in marriage to its ruler. When King Guhyeong of Geumgwan Gaya surrendered in 532, Beopheung made him a high official over the conquered lands. Silla also annexed Ara Gaya, gaining access to the Nakdong river basin.

The king himself was drawn to Buddhist teaching, but most of his ministers opposed it. His minister Ichadon, a convert who had taken the tonsure, offered to die for the faith and, when the king refused to execute him, deliberately insulted the other ministers. He was beheaded in public, and according to the Samguk yusa his blood flowed milky white, as he had foretold, which horrified the court. Beopheung then chose Buddhism as the state religion, though full freedom for Buddhism in Silla came only under King Jinheung.

In his later years Beopheung became a monk under the name Beobun, and according to the Samguk yusa his wife, Lady Bodo of the Park clan, became a nun named Myobeop and had a temple built. The Samguk sagi records that he was buried at Aegongsa temple; his burial place is now Historic Site 176. His daughter, Queen Jiso, married Galmunwang Ipjong, and their son became his successor, King Jinheung.
beorhtric-of-wessex: The names of Beorhtric's parents are unknown, but the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle claims that he was descended from Cerdic. In 786 Cynewulf, king of Wessex, was killed by Cyneheard, brother of the former king Sigeberht, and Cyneheard died soon afterwards. Beorhtric became king in the same year.

Beorhtric came to the throne either with the help of his close ally Offa of Mercia or by quickly coming under his influence. He still had to contend for the throne with Ecgberht, whom he and Offa drove into exile. In 787 he held the Synod of Chelsea jointly with Offa, and in 789 he married one of Offa's daughters, Eadburh. Land on the traditional borders of Mercia and Wessex was administered by the Mercian court, and a trail of Offa's pennies runs from the Upper Thames to Wareham, a site connected with Beorhtric.

In 789 the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle recorded the first Viking raids in England. The Vikings landed on the Dorset coast near the Isle of Portland and killed a royal official, the shire reeve Beaduheard, who is said to have taken them for traders.

After Offa died in 796, Mercian power weakened and Beorhtric may have acted more independently. The only two West Saxon coins surviving from his reign date from this time, which suggests that he established a new mint. Within a few years Offa's successor Coenwulf restored Mercia's position, and after 799 Beorhtric's relationship with the Mercians seems to have resembled that before Offa's death.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that Beorhtric was buried at Wareham in 802, possibly at the church of Lady St Mary. Asser, a scholar at the court of Alfred the Great, later recorded a story that he died from being accidentally poisoned by his wife Eadburh, who fled to a nunnery in Francia; the origin of the story is doubtful. Ecgberht was recalled from exile and succeeded him.
beornwulf-of-mercia: Beornwulf's family and most of his background are unknown. His name comes from the Old English beorn, man or warrior, and wulf, wolf. He may have been distantly related to the earlier Mercian king Beornred and to two later rulers, Beorhtwulf and Burgred, the so-called B-dynasty or group, but this is speculation resting on the alliterative names common in Anglo-Saxon royal families. Before he became king he witnessed a charter of King Coenwulf in 812 and one of Ceolwulf I in 823, where his place among the witnesses suggests he was not of especially high rank.

Beornwulf rebuilt the Abbey of St. Peter, later Gloucester Cathedral, and presided with Archbishop Wulfred of Canterbury over two synods at Clofesho, an unidentified place believed to be near London, in 824 and 825. Coins from his reign are very rare, with only around 25 known examples.

In 825 he marched against the West Saxons and met them at Ellandun, now Wroughton near Swindon in Wiltshire. The details of the battle are unknown, but historians see the Mercian defeat there as the end of the Mercian Supremacy. That same year Ecgberht's son Æthelwulf invaded Kent and drove out its pro-Mercian king, Baldred, Essex and Sussex turned to Ecgberht, and the East Anglians asked for his protection against Mercia.

A Kentish charter, S1267, shows that Beornwulf still had authority in Kent on 27 March 826, dating itself to the third year of his reign. Later that year he was killed in battle by the East Anglians while trying to put down their rebellion. His short reign saw Mercia's supremacy over the other kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy collapse.
beowulf: Beowulf is an epic in the tradition of Germanic heroic legend, composed in alliterative verse by an anonymous author called the Beowulf poet. The only certain dating is that of its manuscript, produced between 975 and 1025, and scholars disagree about when the poem was composed. Some place it in the 8th century, J. R. R. Tolkien among them, since he held that it keeps too genuine a memory of Anglo-Saxon paganism to be much later than the Christianisation of England. Others link it with the courts of King Alfred the Great or King Cnut the Great, and some suggest a 7th-century origin at Rendlesham in East Anglia.

The story is set in pagan Scandinavia in the 5th and 6th centuries. Beowulf, a hero of the Geats, helps Hrothgar, king of the Danes, whose mead hall Heorot has been attacked for twelve years by the monster Grendel. He kills Grendel with his bare hands, and then kills Grendel's mother, who has taken revenge by killing Hrothgar's advisor Æschere, with a giant's sword found in her lair.

Beowulf returns home and becomes king of the Geats. Fifty years later a slave steals a golden cup from a dragon's lair, and the dragon burns the land. Beowulf resolves to fight it alone, but only his young Swedish relative Wiglaf stays to help him. They kill the dragon, but Beowulf is mortally wounded, and his body is cremated and a barrow visible from the sea is raised for him. Digressions on the Swedish–Geatish wars, the fight at Finnsburg and biblical tales give the poem historical depth.

The poem survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, now British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.XV, copied by two scribes. It has no title in the manuscript and takes its name from its hero. A fire at Ashburnham House in London in 1731 charred its margins and cost some readings. Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin made the first transcriptions in 1786, which are prized because the manuscript has crumbled since. Some verses were first translated into modern English in 1805, and nine complete translations followed in the 19th century. Tolkien's 1936 lecture argued that its literary value had been overlooked in favour of its historical content.
beqaa-valley: The Beqaa Valley lies about 30 km east of Beirut, between Mount Lebanon to the west and the Anti-Lebanon Mountains to the east. It is the northern continuation of the Jordan Rift Valley, part of the Great Rift Valley, and is about 120 km long and 16 km wide on average. The region broadly corresponds to the Coele-Syria of classical antiquity. Mount Lebanon casts a rain shadow, so rainfall averages 230 mm a year in the north and 750 mm in the central valley. Two rivers rise here: the Orontes, which flows north into Syria and Turkey, and the Litani, which flows south and then west to the Mediterranean.

Baalbek has evidence of habitation going back almost 8,000 to 9,000 years, and Ard Tlaili, dated to around 5780 to 5710 BCE, has the southernmost pottery of the Halaf Culture. In the Middle Bronze Age the valley, known as Amqu, was a highway between Qatna in the north and its vassal Hazor in the south, and belonged to the Amorite kingdoms of Amurru and Qatna. The city of Enišasi, southwest of Baalbek, appears in the Amarna letters of 1350 to 1335 BCE. By the early Iron Age Phoenician and Aramaic speakers dominated the valley, and many scholars place the Aramaean kingdom of Aram-Zobah, mentioned in the Bible, here, though its exact location is debated.

In the time of Alexander the Great the valley was reportedly inhabited by the Itureans, possibly an Arab or Aramaean people. They later broke away from the weakened Seleucid Empire to form the Kingdom of Chalcis, expanded to include the Phoenician coastal cities and came close to Damascus. Their territory was absorbed into Roman Syria. The Roman Empire valued the valley as one of the important agricultural regions of its eastern provinces, and from the 1st century BCE it supplied grain to the Roman provinces of the Levant. It was known for its many temples. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra built the Canalizations of Zenobia, linking the valley with her city.

The valley makes up about 40 percent of Lebanon's arable land and is the country's most important farming region. The north is used mostly for grazing, and farther south the soils support wheat, maize, cotton and vegetables, with vineyards and orchards centred on Zahle, the valley's largest city. The valley accounts for the majority of Lebanon's wine production. Landmarks include the Roman ruins of Baalbek and the Umayyad ruins of Anjar.
bera-count-of-barcelona: Bera's origins are mostly unknown, though it seems certain that he was a Visigoth. In 790 he was given the governorship of the counties of Razès and Conflent, possibly by William of Gellone, Count of Toulouse and cousin of Charlemagne. In 796 Sa'dun al Ruayni, the Wali of Barcelona, tried to break his allegiance to Al-Hakam I, emir of Córdoba, and in April 797 he travelled to Aachen to offer the city to Charlemagne in return for help.

An assembly at Toulouse in the spring of 800 agreed to send Louis the Pious to Barcelona, but Sa'dun changed his mind and the Franks laid siege to the city. Starving, its Visigoth population surrendered on 3 April 801 and handed over the new wali, Harun; Louis entered the next day. Bera, who had served in the besieging army, was soon invested as count.

Bera took part in the Frankish campaigns of 804, 808 and 809 to push the border of the Marca Hispanica to the River Ebro. In 804 he, Adhemar of Narbonne and Borrell of Ausona covered the western flank of Louis's army, while Louis besieged Tortosa without success. In 808, according to the biographer known as the Astronomer, the garrison of Tortosa was alerted when horse dung from Bera's river crossing floated past the town, and he was forced to retreat. In 809 Tortosa was besieged for forty days.

Bera was probably the strongest promoter of peace with Córdoba, urged on by his mother and by the people of Barcelona, and the Frankish court signed a three-year treaty in 812. In 811 he had witnessed Charlemagne's will. When war resumed in 815, a mercenary Visigothic army beat back an attack on Barcelona led by Ubayd Allah Abu Marwan, and a new three-year truce was concluded in February 817.

Gaucelm, Count of Roussillon, and his brother Bernard argued that Bera's truces hindered attempts to force the Basques and Aragón to recognise the empire's authority. At a general assembly in Aachen in February 820, Gaucelm's Visigoth lieutenant Sanila accused Bera of infidelity and perfidy, and the case was settled, as was customary, by a duel in the palace. Bera lost and was deprived of his counties, but Emperor Louis I, who did not believe him a traitor, commuted the death penalty to exile in Rouen. He was succeeded as count of Barcelona by Rampon.
berat: Ceramic finds of the seventh century BCE attest a settlement of the rocky hill, and Berat has been identified with ancient Antipatrea. In 200 BCE, as Livy reports, the Roman legatus Lucius Apustius stormed it, killed the men of military age, demolished the walls and burned it. In the early Byzantine period it was known as Pulcheriopolis. The First Bulgarian Empire under Presian I took it in the ninth century and gave it the Slavic name Beligrad, White City, from which Berat comes. The Bulgarian governor surrendered it to Basil II in 1018, and the Second Bulgarian Empire retook it in 1203.

In 1274 Michael VIII Palaiologos recaptured Berat from Charles I of Naples. In 1280 and 1281 Sicilian forces under Hugh the Red of Sully besieged it, and in March 1281 a relief force from Constantinople drove them off. The town passed to the Serbian Empire in 1345 and was captured by the Ottomans in 1385. By 1396 the Albanian Muzaka family held it as the capital of the Principality of Berat, and in 1417 it became part of the Ottoman Empire.

Under early Ottoman rule Berat declined, with only 710 houses by the end of the sixteenth century, but it recovered in the seventeenth and became a major centre of wood carving. From 1670 it was Muslim-majority. In the nineteenth century it took a leading part in the Albanian national revival, and revolts in 1833 and 1839 besieged the Ottoman forces in its castle. The Council of National Liberation of Albania held its second session there in October 1944.

Berat is the seat of Berat County, on the Osum river, surrounded by mountains including Tomorr, a national park. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 for an architecture combining the influences of several civilisations, with an old fortified city of churches and mosques decorated with murals and frescoes.
berber-languages: Modern Berber languages are relatively homogeneous, so the Proto-Berber language from which they derive was probably comparatively recent, comparable in age to the Germanic or Romance subfamilies of Indo-European. The split of the group from other Afroasiatic branches is much earlier and is sometimes associated with the Mesolithic Capsian culture. The earliest text possibly written in Berber or Proto-Berber is an Egyptian papyrus in Hieratic, in the extinct Kehek language, from the New Kingdom era.

The Berber languages have a level of variety similar to the Romance languages, and apart from Zenaga, Tetserret and Tuareg they form a dialect continuum. Most follow verb-subject-object word order. They are primarily oral languages. Historically they were written with the Libyco-Berber script, whose oldest known variations date from around 600 BCE and appear on rock art and in sepulchres. Its form Tifinagh remains in use among the Tuareg. After the spread of Islam some scholars used the Arabic script, and the Latin alphabet, introduced in the nineteenth century, is now the most widespread.

After independence the Maghreb countries pursued policies of Arabisation, aimed partly at displacing French, and under them the use of Berber languages was suppressed or even banned. Morocco carried this through from 1956 until 1981, and riots among the Amazigh population called for Tamazight to be made an official language. It became one in Morocco's constitution on 29 July 2011. Algeria, independent in 1962, also pursued Arabisation, which led to unrest among speakers, about a quarter of the population. Tamazight was recognised as a national language in 2002, after the riots of the Black Spring.
berber-revolt: Berbers had done much of the fighting in the Umayyad conquest of Hispania, yet they received a smaller share of the spoils and the harsher duties. The governor Yazid ibn Abi Muslim branded the hands of his Berber guard and was assassinated in 721, and under Ubayd Allah ibn al-Habhab Muslim Berbers were still enslaved, with girls sent to the caliph in Damascus. Kharijite preachers of Sufrite and later Ibadite persuasion, arriving from the 720s, promised an order in which all Muslims would be equal regardless of ethnicity. When Omar ibn al-Moradi, deputy governor at Tangier, declared the Berbers a conquered people and seized their property, the tribes of western Morocco rose.

Led by Maysara al-Matghari, the Ghomara, Berghwata and Miknasa took Tangier while the Ifriqiyan army was away on an expedition against Byzantine Sicily, killed al-Moradi, and swept Umayyad garrisons from the Strait of Gibraltar to the Sous. Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik sent Kulthum ibn Iyad al-Qushayri with 30,000 men raised in Syria and Egypt, but the army was destroyed at the Battle of Bagdoura in 741, and about 10,000 survivors under Kulthum's nephew Balj ibn Bishr were besieged in Ceuta.

The revolt spread east and north. Hanzala ibn Safwan, governor of Egypt, saved Kairouan, the capital of Ifriqiya, against the Berber leaders Uqasha ibn Ayub al-Fezari and Abd al-Wahid ibn Yazid al-Hawwari. In al-Andalus the Berber garrisons north of the Douro mutinied in October 741 and marched on Toledo, Córdoba and Algeciras. The Andalusian governor Abd al-Malik ibn Qatn al-Fihri let Balj's Syrians cross the strait, and in 742 they crushed all three Berber columns, after which Balj deposed Abd al-Malik and had him tortured to death.

The Umayyads kept Ifriqiya and al-Andalus but never recovered the rest of the Maghreb, where independent Berber states arose, among them the Barghawata state in Tamesna, the Emirate of Tlemcen and the Midrarid emirate of Sijilmasa. In Iberia, Alfonso I of Asturias seized the abandoned northwestern forts and emptied the Douro valley into a frontier zone. The loss of Syrian troops in North Africa weakened the army on which Marwanid rule rested, and historians count the revolt among the causes of the Abbasid Revolution less than a decade later.
berbera: Berbera lies on the coast of northern Somaliland, about 160 km from Hargeisa. It has the only sheltered harbour on the southern side of the Gulf of Aden, and the surrounding coastal lowlands are semi-arid. The climate is hot and arid, with about 52 millimetres of rain a year. The name is traced by one account to the Somali phrase beri-beri, meaning occasionally, because the place was a seasonal settlement occupied in the cooler months; the Royal Asiatic Society suggested instead an Arabic word meaning talking much or shouting.

Berbera is believed to be the port of Malao described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant's guide of the first century CE, which lists exports of myrrh, frankincense and cinnamon. In the Middle Ages it was a harbour for the Adal and Ifat sultanates, and with Zeila one of the two main ports of Adal. Ludovico di Varthema, Duarte Barbosa and Leo Africanus described its trade with Aden and Cambay in the early 16th century, and a Portuguese fleet sacked it and Zeila between 1516 and 1518.

In the 18th and 19th centuries it was the most important port of the Somali Peninsula. An annual fair between October and April drew Isaaq clans, caravans from Harar and the interior, and Indian merchants. In the 1833 season the town swelled to 70,000 people, and in 1848 duties on goods from Berbera supplied 80% of the revenue of Aden. Somali merchants brought coffee grown near Harar to Mokha and Aden as Berbera coffee. After a British ship was attacked in 1825 and a blockade followed, the Habr Awal were defeated in a battle in 1827 and ordered to pay 15,000 Spanish dollars.

After treaties with the clans between 1884 and 1886 the British made Berbera the capital of the protectorate of British Somaliland, until Hargeisa replaced it in 1941. In August 1940 the British evacuated about 7,000 people through the port before Italy occupied the territory, and they recaptured it in March 1941. After independence in 1960 Berbera was the Somali Republic's main livestock port, and the Soviet Union built port facilities and a military base there that were completed in 1969.

Berbera is the capital of the Sahil region of Somaliland and its main sea port, linked by road to Hargeisa and Burco. Its exports have included livestock, gum arabic, frankincense and myrrh, and goods from Ethiopia also pass through it. The port has been expanded under an agreement made in 2016 with DP World, and the city has an airport with a very long runway.
berchtesgaden: Berchtesgaden lies in the Berchtesgaden Alps in Bavaria, near the border with Austria, 30 km south of Salzburg and 180 km south-east of Munich. The Berchtesgaden National Park, established in 1978, stretches south of the town along three parallel valleys. The Kehlstein mountain, 1,835 m high, carries the Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest. The name was recorded in 1121 as Perehtgeresgadem, from a personal name and the word gadem, meaning a one-roomed house.

The first known record of the area, from 1102, mentions its rich salt deposits. Salt mining began in 1517 and produced much of the town's wealth. The town belonged to the Berchtesgaden Provostry, an independent state of the Holy Roman Empire ruled by the prince-provost of the Augustinian monastery, until 1803. In 1805 the Treaty of Pressburg ceded the area to Austria, and in 1810 it passed to the Kingdom of Bavaria. The Wittelsbach royal family often visited the Königssee and kept a hunting residence in the former monastery, and artists came to the area. In the 1760s several anonymous toy symphonies, among them the Toy Symphony often attributed to Haydn or Leopold Mozart, were composed here, when the town manufactured toy instruments.

Adolf Hitler began holidaying here in the 1920s and bought a house on the Obersalzberg, which he renovated as the Berghof. Other leading Nazis frequented the area, and the town became an outpost of the Reich Chancellery. Hitler met Neville Chamberlain there in 1938 before the Munich Agreement. American troops received the town's surrender on 4 May 1945.

Tourism centres on the national park, the Königssee, the salt mine and the Dokumentationszentrum Obersalzberg, a museum of the area's history. The Königssee track has hosted international bobsleigh, luge and skeleton competitions, and the town is home to the International Luge Federation.
