berdibeg: Berdi Beg, also written Berdibek or Birdibek, was born around 1310 and descended from Genghis Khan through Jochi, Batu Khan and Uzbeg Khan. When his father Jani Beg conquered the Chupanid kingdom in Azerbaijan and northwestern Iran in 1357, he left Berdi Beg as viceroy in Tabriz. Jani Beg fell seriously ill on the way home, and his officer Tughluq Beg secretly sent word to the son, who hurried back with only ten companions. The khan recovered and grew suspicious of his son's intentions, although Berdi Beg's mother, Toqai Toghlu Khatun, assured him that their son was no threat.

Jani Beg died on 22 July 1357 and Berdi Beg was declared khan. The Russian princes came to congratulate him, and when Vsevolod, prince of Kholm, travelled to Sarai to contest his uncle Vasily's place as prince of Tver, the khan arrested him without judgement and sent him back. On Tughluq Beg's advice he had at least twelve of his closest kinsmen executed; he killed his eight-month-old brother himself, despite the pleas of their grandmother Taydula Khatun.

He kept his father's administrators, three of the four emirs named in Jani Beg's treaty with the Venetians of 1347 reappearing in his own treaty of 1358, and raised the number of emirs to six. That treaty, made after tensions with the Venetians in the Crimea, allowed them to trade at Soldaia (Sudak) and lowered the tax owed to the khan on their transactions. A yarliq of November 1357 restored to the Russian Orthodox Church, under Metropolitan Aleksej, rights that Jani Beg had taken away: it freed Church homes from taxes and restored the independence of the Church courts. Azerbaijan, however, slipped from his control and reverted to survivors of the Chupanid regime.

After Berdi Beg's death in 1359 Qulpa became khan, and later accounts hold that by killing so many of his kinsmen Berdi Beg had brought the line of Batu to an end. The Golden Horde then entered its time of troubles, in which no fewer than 25 khans rose to the throne in 20 years. Berdi Beg left a daughter, probably Tulun Beg Khanum, who reigned in 1370 and 1371 and was married first to Mamai and then to Tokhtamysh, who executed her in 1386.
berengar-i-of-italy: Berengar's family was called the Unruochings after his grandfather Unruoch II of Friuli. He was a son of Eberhard of Friuli and Gisela, a daughter of Louis the Pious and his second wife Judith, and was probably born at Cividale. He married Bertila, daughter of Suppo II. When his older brother Unruoch III died in 874, he succeeded to the March of Friuli, which bordered the Croats and other Slavs who were a constant threat to Italy.

After the nobles of East Francia deposed Charles in November 887, Berengar was acclaimed king in Italy, and charter evidence places his reign at Pavia around the turn of 887 and 888. His rival Guy of Spoleto defeated him at the Battle of the Trebbia in early 889 and made himself sole king, although Berengar kept Friuli. Arnulf of Carinthia backed Berengar, and in 894 they defeated Guy at Bergamo. In 898 Berengar was captured by Guy's son Lambert at Borgo San Donnino, but Lambert died within days and Berengar became sole ruler.

The Magyars invaded Italy in 899, and Berengar's army was routed near the Brenta River on 24 September 899. Nobles then supported Louis of Provence, who defeated him in 900. In 902 Berengar struck back, and when Louis returned in 905 he captured him at Verona and ordered him blinded on 21 July. Berengar made Verona his seat and fortified it. In December 915 Pope John X crowned him emperor in Rome.

Dissatisfied nobles, led by Adalbert of Ivrea and many bishops, invited Rudolph II of Upper Burgundy to take the throne in 921. On 29 July 923 Rudolph's forces defeated Berengar at the Battle of Fiorenzuola near Piacenza. He was murdered at Verona by one of his own men, possibly at Rudolph's instigation, and left two daughters, Bertha and Gisela, but no sons. An imperial interregnum of 38 years followed, until Otto I was crowned emperor in 962.

His reign of 36 years is usually characterised as troubled, with seven other claimants to the Italian throne. Some historians have called him incompetent and noted that he is not recorded as having won a pitched battle against his rivals, and his part in beginning the incastellamento, the building of castles, in the following decades is hardly disputed.
berengar-ii-of-italy: Berengar was a son of Margrave Adalbert I of Ivrea and Gisela of Friuli, a daughter of King Berengar I of Italy, after whom he was named. He belonged to the Anscarid and Unruoching dynasties. He succeeded his father as margrave of Ivrea about 923 and married Willa, a daughter of Margrave Boso of Tuscany and a niece of King Hugh of Italy. The chronicler Liutprand of Cremona, who was raised at Berengar's court at Pavia, gives vivid accounts of her character.

About 940 Berengar led a revolt of Italian nobles against his uncle Hugh. Warned by the king's young son Lothair, he fled to the court of Otto I of Germany, who avoided taking sides. In 945 Berengar returned to Italy with hired troops and was welcomed by the local nobility. Hugh was defeated and retired to Arles. From then on all real power in the Kingdom of Italy lay with Berengar, while Lothair remained titular king until his early death in 950, presumably by poison.

Berengar took the royal title and had his son Adalbert crowned as co-ruler in the Basilica of San Michele Maggiore at Pavia. To legitimise his rule he tried to force Lothair's widow Adelaide to marry Adalbert. She refused and was imprisoned at Garda Castle, where Willa allegedly mistreated her. She escaped with the help of Count Adalbert Atto of Canossa and appealed to Otto, who was himself a widower. Otto invaded Italy in 951, received the homage of the Italian nobles, married Adelaide and took the title King of the Lombards.

At the Reichstag of Augsburg in 952 Berengar paid homage to Otto, and he and Adalbert remained kings as Otto's vassals. They had to cede the former March of Friuli, which Otto gave to his brother Henry I of Bavaria as the March of Verona. When Otto faced the revolt of his son Liudolf in 953, Berengar attacked the Veronese march and besieged Canossa.

In 960 Berengar invaded the Papal States, and Pope John XII appealed to Otto, who wanted the imperial crown. Berengar's troops deserted him, and by Christmas 961 Otto held Pavia and declared him deposed. Otto was crowned emperor at Rome on 2 February 962 and then besieged Berengar at San Leo. Berengar surrendered in 964 and was imprisoned at Bamberg, where he died on 4 August 966. His wife Willa spent the rest of her life in a German nunnery.
berengaria-of-castile: Berengaria was born in Burgos, in 1179 or 1180, and was nicknamed the Great. As the eldest child of Alfonso VIII and Eleanor, and the heir presumptive for several years because many of her younger siblings died in infancy, she became a sought-after bride. In 1187 Conrad, a son of Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa, asked for her hand, and the marriage contract provided that she would inherit Castile and that it would not become part of the Empire. They never saw each other again. By 1191 she asked the pope to annul the engagement, and Conrad was assassinated in 1196.

In 1197 Berengaria married her cousin Alfonso IX of León at Valladolid to secure peace between Castile and León, receiving castles and lands in León, mostly along the border. From 1198 Pope Innocent III objected to the marriage on grounds of consanguinity and threatened to excommunicate Alfonso. The pope refused a dispensation, but the couple secured the legitimacy of their children, and the marriage was dissolved in 1204. She returned to Castile and cared for her children. She kept authority over some of her lands in León, and treaties of 1205, 1207 and 1209 extended her control of them.

When her father died in 1214, her brother Henry I was ten and her mother Eleanor, regent for 24 days, died as well. Berengaria replaced her as regent but the House of Lara, led by Count Álvaro Núñez de Lara, forced her to give up the guardianship. Henry died on 6 June 1217 after a loose tile struck his head. Berengaria concealed this from Alfonso IX and had her son Ferdinand III acclaimed king on 31 August. Historians differ on whether this was an abdication, as Georges Martin holds, or whether, as her biographer Miriam Shadis argues, she continued to rule.

Through her son's reign Berengaria negotiated and arranged marriages. She secured the Pact of Toro in 1218 between Ferdinand and his father, and in 1230, when Alfonso IX died naming his daughters as heirs, she obtained the Treaty of Las Tercerías, by which they renounced the throne for money. This reunited León and Castile under Ferdinand, after their division in 1157. She died on 8 November 1246 and was buried at Las Huelgas near Burgos.
She was a patron of the Abbey of Las Huelgas, the Order of Santiago and the Basilica of San Isidoro, and she had Lucas de Tuy write a chronicle of the kings of Castile and León.
berengaria-of-navarre: Berengaria was born in Navarre around 1165 as the eldest daughter of Sancho VI of Navarre and Sancha of Castile. In 1185 her father gave her the fief of Monreal in Navarre. Eleanor of Aquitaine, mother of Richard the Lionheart, promoted her engagement to Richard. An alliance with Navarre meant protection for the southern borders of Eleanor's Duchy of Aquitaine and better relations with neighbouring Castile, whose queen was Richard's sister Eleanor. Navarre had also assimilated the troubadour culture of Aquitaine.

In 1190 Eleanor met King Sancho VI in Pamplona, where he hosted a banquet in her honour at the Royal Palace of Olite. The betrothal could not be made public, because Richard had long been betrothed to Alys, half-sister of King Philip II of France. Richard ended that betrothal in 1190 at Messina.

Eleanor brought Berengaria to Richard, who was already on the Third Crusade. They reached Messina in Sicily during Lent, when a marriage could not take place, and Berengaria was left in the custody of Richard's sister Joan, the widowed queen of Sicily. On the way to the Holy Land the ship carrying Berengaria and Joan ran aground off Cyprus, and the island's ruler, Isaac Comnenus, threatened them. Richard captured the island and overthrew him. Berengaria married Richard on 12 May 1191 in the Chapel of St George at Limassol and was crowned the same day by the archbishop of Bordeaux and the bishops of Évreux and Bayonne.

She accompanied Richard for the first part of the crusade, which was unusual, but returned well before he left the Holy Land. While he was imprisoned on his way home, she stayed in Europe, based at Beaufort-en-Vallée, trying to raise money for his ransom. Afterwards Richard spent most of his time in France. Pope Celestine III ordered him to reunite with her, and he obeyed. The marriage was childless, and Richard spent less than six months in England while they were married.

After Richard died in 1199, King John failed to pay Berengaria the pension due to her, despite the intervention of Eleanor and the threat of an interdict from Pope Innocent III. He still owed her more than £4,000 when he died, and the payments were eventually made under Henry III. She became Lady of Le Mans, one of her dower properties, and settled there. She founded L'Épau Abbey in 1229 and was buried there after her death on 23 December 1230. She did not visit England as queen, hence the tradition that she was the only English queen never to set foot in the country.
berenice-ii: Cyrenaica had been incorporated into the Ptolemaic realm in 323 BCE by Ptolemy I Soter. Around 300 BCE he entrusted it to Magas, son of his wife Berenice I by an earlier marriage, and after Ptolemy I's death Magas asserted his independence and fought Ptolemy II Philadelphus. Around 275 BCE Magas married Apama of the Seleucid dynasty, enemies of the Ptolemies, and Berenice II was their only child. When Ptolemy II sought a settlement in the late 250s BCE, it was agreed that she would marry his heir, her half-cousin, the future Ptolemy III.

Coins show Berenice hailed as basilissa, queen, even in her father's lifetime, and their evidence places her accession as queen of Cyrene in 258 BCE. After Magas died around 250 BCE, Apama refused to honour the agreement and invited the Antigonid prince Demetrius the Fair to marry Berenice. Allegedly he and Apama became lovers, and Berenice discovered them and had him assassinated. Cyrene then fell into civil unrest and was governed by a republican council until Berenice's wedding to Ptolemy III in 246 BCE.

As queen of Egypt, Berenice took an active part in government and was granted the title of vizier. Around 244 or 243 BCE she and her husband were incorporated into the Ptolemaic state cult as the Theoi Euergetai, the Benefactor Gods, and she was also worshipped on her own as Thea Euergetis. She was often equated with Aphrodite and Isis and associated with protection against shipwreck. Her marriage brought Cyrenaica back into the Ptolemaic realm, where it stayed until Ptolemy Apion left it to the Roman Republic in his will in 96 BCE.

According to the story of Berenice's Lock, she vowed to sacrifice her long hair if Ptolemy III returned safely from the Third Syrian War. She placed it in the temple at Cape Zephyrium, but it disappeared by morning, and the court astronomer Conon of Samos declared it a constellation, still called Coma Berenices. The court spread the story, and the poet Callimachus wrote a poem on it. She also entered a chariot team in the Nemean Games, and Callimachus wrote another poem on its victory.

Ptolemy III died in late 222 BCE and was succeeded by their son Ptolemy IV Philopator. Berenice died early in 221 BCE. Polybius states that she was poisoned as part of a purge of the royal family by the new king's regent Sosibius. Her cult continued, and by 211 BCE she had her own priestess, the athlophorus, who walked in Alexandria's processions. The city of Euesperides, now Benghazi, was renamed Berenice in her honour, a name it kept until the Middle Ages.
berenice-troglodytica: Berenice lies on the western shore of the Red Sea, about 825 km south of Suez, 260 km east of Aswan and 140 km south of Marsa Alam. Ptolemy II Philadelphus founded it in 275 BCE and named it after his mother, Berenice I of Egypt. A high mountain range separates the Nile Valley from the coast, and the city stood on a narrow rim of shore at the head of a south-facing bay, the Sinus Immundus. The harbour is marginal but was improved by engineering. The name Troglodytica refers to the native people of the region, the Troglodytai or cave dwellers, though older Ptolemaic inscriptions read Trogodytai.

Berenice prospered through the patronage of the Ptolemaic kings, a safe anchorage and its position at the eastern end of the main road from Upper Egypt. The road ran to Coptos on the Nile, 258 Roman miles or eleven days' journey, with watering stations along it. With Myos Hormos, Berenice was one of the two main shipping centres for trade between Egypt and Aethiopia on one side and Syria, Tamilakkam and Tamraparni on the other. Nearby mines and the island of Ophiodes, now Zabargad Island, supplied gemstones then called topaz and emerald.

From the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE it was a critical way-station for trade between the Indian subcontinent, Arabia and Upper Egypt, and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes the trade along this coast. The Via Hadriana joined it to Antinoöpolis in 137 CE. In the 4th century it was again an active port, forming a district under its own prefect. After the 6th century the port was abandoned, and the bay has since nearly filled with sediment.

Giovanni Battista Belzoni identified the ruins in 1818, measuring the city at 1,600 feet from north to south and 2,000 feet from east to west, and estimating its ancient population at 10,000. The chief ruin is an temple in the Egyptian style whose sculptures preserve the name of Tiberius. Excavations began in 1994 under Steven E. Sidebotham of the University of Delaware, and teams from Delaware and the Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology of the University of Warsaw resumed work in the winter of 2007–2008.

The finds show strong links with India: 7.55 kg of black peppercorns, Indian pottery, sail cloth and basketry, teak, coconuts, beads and a Tamil Brahmi graffito mentioning Korra, a South Indian chieftain. A fortress about 2,300 years old was found in 2019, and remains of monkeys, cats and dogs from about 2,000 years ago were found in 2020–2021 in what has been called the oldest pet cemetery in the world. In March 2022 excavators of the Isis temple uncovered a marble statue of a Buddha.
berga: Berga takes its name from the Bergistani, an Iberian tribe that lived there before the Roman conquest. Hannibal subdued them in 218 BCE, and they rebelled twice against the Romans and were twice defeated; after the second uprising much of the tribe was sold into slavery. Livy mentions their principal town, Castrum Bergium, probably the forerunner of Berga. Muslim forces occupied the area in the eighth century, and local tradition holds that Berga was destroyed then. The Franks conquered and repopulated it before 835, and Berga Castle is first recorded around 855.

In the ninth century the Country of Berga developed within the County of Cerdanya, gaining a more independent character in the early tenth century with Berga as its capital. The viscount Branduí administered it in 905, and the town had its own counts from 988. It was sold to Peter II of Aragon in 1199, and in 1254 a synod held there condemned 168 people accused of heresy. In 1309 it was sold to James II of Aragon and became a royal town. Its walls were built in the fourteenth century, and it had a Jewish quarter with a synagogue.

Carlist forces captured Berga on 12 July 1837 in the First Carlist War, and the Carlist junta moved there from Solsona, making it the capital of Catalan Carlism. Carlist coins were issued there between 1838 and 1840. Berga received the official title of city in 1877. Textile production there is recorded from the medieval period, and around 1790 Ramon Farguell developed the multi-spindle berguedana, which helped make Berga one of Catalonia's leading cotton-manufacturing centres. The Portal de Santa Magdalena is the only surviving late-medieval gate of the walls. Each year the Patum, a traditional festival in which locals dress as symbolic figures to the rhythm of a drum, the tabal, is held in the city.
bergedorf: Bergedorf lies in the south-east of Hamburg, on the river Bille, a right tributary of the Elbe. The borough covers 154.8 square kilometres and comprises the districts of Allermöhe, Altengamme, Bergedorf, Billwerder, Curslack, Kirchwerder, Lohbrügge, Moorfleet, Neuallermöhe, Neuengamme, Ochsenwerder, Reitbrook, Spadenland and Tatenberg. It is the largest of Hamburg's seven boroughs and is nicknamed the Garden of Hamburg.

Bergedorf received town privileges in 1275, when it belonged to the younger Duchy of Saxony; it passed to Saxe-Lauenburg in 1296. In 1321 Duke Eric conceded Bergedorf with the Vierlande to his brother John II, whose share became known as Saxe-Bergedorf-Mölln. In 1370 John's successor Eric III pawned the lordship of Bergedorf, the Vierlande, half the Saxon Wood and Geesthacht to Lübeck for 16,262.5 Lübeck marks. The pledge included much of the trade route between Hamburg and Lübeck, giving safe passage for freight between the cities.

Eric IV of Saxe-Ratzeburg-Lauenburg seized the pawned areas by force in 1401 without repayment. In 1420 his son Eric V attacked Prince-Elector Frederick I of Brandenburg, and Lübeck and Hamburg opened a second front, conquering Bergedorf, Riepenburg castle and the Esslingen river toll station within weeks. By the Peace of Perleberg of 23 August 1420 the territories were irrevocably ceded to the two cities.

The cities ruled the area as a bi-urban condominium governed by bailiffs, alternately from each city, with terms of four years, six from 1446 and life terms from 1620. In 1542 the bailiff Ditmar Koel introduced the Protestant Reformation there. The area was annexed to the First French Empire between 1811 and 1813. The first railway in northern Germany opened between Hamburg and Bergedorf in 1842, and the condominium issued its own postage stamps between 1861 and 1867. On 1 January 1868 Lübeck sold its share to Hamburg for 200,000 Prussian thaler, and on 1 April 1938 Bergedorf became a borough of Hamburg.

The borough has a station for suburban, local and long-distance trains, and its notable buildings include the church of St. Petri and Pauli, Schloss Bergedorf and the Hamburg-Bergedorf Observatory. Its stamps of the condominium are of note to philatelists, since with a population of 12,468 in 1863 it was by far the smallest German territory to issue them.
bergen: Bergen occupies most of the peninsula of Bergenshalvøyen on the west coast of Norway. The city centre faces the fjord of Byfjorden and is surrounded by mountains, so that Bergen is called the city of seven mountains, though locals debate which seven they are. The highest is Gullfjellet, at 987 metres. The climate is temperate oceanic, with plentiful rain in every season, and the Gulf Stream keeps the winters mild. The Old Norse name Bjǫrgvin combines a word for mountains with vin, a new settlement where a pasture or meadow had been.

The traditional founder of the city was King Olav Kyrre in 1070, but modern research has found that a trading settlement already existed in the 1020s or 1030s. Bergen served as the capital of Norway in the 13th century. It became a bureau city of the Hanseatic League, and until 1789 it had exclusive rights to mediate trade between Northern Norway and abroad. It was the largest city in Norway until the 1830s, when Christiania, now Oslo, overtook it. What remains of the quays, Bryggen, is a World Heritage Site.

Fire marked the city's history. In 1198 the Bagler faction burned it during the civil war with the Birkebeiner. In 1428 the Victual Brothers plundered it, and a drunk trader started the fire that burned down Bryggen in 1476. A fire in 1686 destroyed 231 city blocks. The worst came in 1702, when 90 per cent of the city burned to ashes, and in 1756 a fire at Strandsiden consumed 1,500 buildings.
Bergen became a county of its own in 1831 and a municipality on 1 January 1838. The Norwegian School of Economics was founded there in 1936 and the University of Bergen in 1946.

Bergen is the second-largest city of Norway and the administrative centre of Vestland county. It is an international centre of aquaculture, shipping and the offshore petroleum industry, and its port is the busiest in Norway. Natives speak a distinct dialect known as Bergensk.
bergen-auf-rugen: Bergen auf Rügen lies in the middle of Germany's largest island, Rügen, on the Baltic Sea coast. The town is built on a glacial moraine left when the ice sheets retreated at the end of the last ice age, in hilly country. The Rugard woods rise to 91 metres on its north-eastern edge, and the surrounding land is mostly farmland. Two shallow bays lie near it: the Kleiner Jasmunder Bodden to the north-east and the Greifswalder Bodden to the south-east.

The island was settled in the early Middle Ages by the Rani, a Slavic people who kept a pagan worship site at Cape Arkona, defended by a fort, the Jaromarsburg. A castle stood on the Rugard hill in the area of present-day Bergen. After the Danes subdued the Rani they set up the Principality of Rügen under a local dynasty, and the Rugard became an administrative centre. The principality became Christian and received German settlers in the Ostsiedlung. The town itself was built on the neighbouring hilltop, outside the ramparts of the Rugard. Its name comes from the Slavic word gora, mountain, and is recorded in 1232 as the place Gora.

The Jaromarsburg fell in 1168, and soon afterwards work began on St Mary's as the palace church of Prince Jaromar I. In 1193 it became a Cistercian convent, and the foundation encouraged the first inn, built in 1232. In 1325 the principality passed by inheritance to the Duchy of Pomerania. Fires, such as that of 1445, nearly destroyed the town, the convent and part of the church. The Reformation reached Pomerania in 1534, and the dukes took over the convent. Bergen received Lübeck law town rights in 1613, passed to Sweden in 1648 as part of Swedish Pomerania, and became part of the Prussian Province of Pomerania in 1815.

Bergen auf Rügen is in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and is the administrative seat of its Amt, which has more than 23,000 inhabitants. Railways reached it in 1883. St Mary's, the former convent church, is the oldest surviving brick building in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and has the only complete painting of a church interior in northern Germany. The town museum occupies a restored abbey building and covers the history of Rügen from the Stone Age. The Ernst Moritz Arndt tower, completed in 1877, gives views over much of the island.
bergen-op-zoom: Bergen op Zoom lies in North Brabant, at the border with Zeeland. The city was built where sandy soil meets marine clay. Over centuries the sand pushed against the clay and formed hills, called the Brabantse Wal, literally the ramparts of Brabant. Bergen means hills, and Zoom refers to the border of these ramparts. Marshes and easily flooded polders surrounded the site, which made it a strong natural defensive position, and it could receive reinforcements and supplies by sea.

Bergen op Zoom was probably granted city status in 1212. In 1287 it became a lordship, separated from the lordship of Breda, and in 1559 a margraviate. Several noble families, among them the House of Glymes, ruled it until 1795, though the title was nominal from at least the seventeenth century. During the reign of Jan II van Glymes, who lived from 1417 to 1494, the city grew economically. Large fairs held every spring and autumn drew merchants from all over Europe, and they continued until 1910. A recession in the mid-16th century, caused largely by floods in Zeeland and West-Brabant that harmed the port, left the enlargement of the town church unfinished.

In the early modern period it was a very strong fortress and one of the main armouries of the United Provinces. During the Eighty Years' War Alessandro Farnese besieged it in 1588 and Ambrosio Spinola in 1622; both failed, and the city earned the nickname La Pucelle, the Virgin, because no siege had taken it. In 1747, during the War of the Austrian Succession, the French besieged it. The works built by Menno van Coehoorn had no second line of fortification, and after seventy days the city was taken and thoroughly sacked, and the garrison slaughtered. British forces besieged it unsuccessfully in March 1814.

The municipality has a population of about 70 thousand. The Markiezenhof Palace, built in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, houses a cultural centre and a museum. Hotel De Draak, founded in 1397, is described as the oldest hotel in the Netherlands, and its present building dates from 1500. Among the people born in the town are the composer Jacob Obrecht and the humanist Desiderius Erasmus.
bergpark-wilhelmshohe: Bad Wilhelmshöhe is a district of Kassel in northern Hesse, west of the city centre at the foot of the Habichtswald hills. The park covers about 2.4 square kilometres and rises from Kassel to the Karlsberg at 526.2 metres, which makes it the largest European hillside park. At its summit stands the Hercules monument, a 40-metre pyramid topped by an 8.5-metre copper statue of Hercules. Water from reservoirs behind it runs down through a Baroque water theatre, a grotto, fountains and waterfalls, including a Great Cascade 350 metres long, to a pond with the Great Fountain, which at about 50 metres was the largest in Europe in 1767.

Canons Regular from Mainz founded the Weißenstein monastery on the site of the palace in 1143, and after the Reformation Landgrave Philip I of Hesse used its buildings as a hunting lodge. The park began as a Baroque garden under Landgrave Charles I of Hesse-Kassel, and in 1701 the Italian architect Giovanni Francesco Guerniero started the Hercules monument and the giant cascades. In 1785 Landgrave William IX began a large extension, and the next year Simon Louis du Ry designed the Neoclassical palace. Garden taste shifted to the English style, and Heinrich Christoph Jussow added artificial ruins such as the Löwenburg. The Great Waterfall, ordered in 1826 by William II, Elector of Hesse, was the last large work.

Kassel became the capital of the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1806, and its king Jérôme Bonaparte held court at the palace, renamed Napoleonshöhe, until 1813. Prussia annexed Hesse-Kassel in 1866, ending the dynasty that had made the park. Napoleon III was held at the palace after the Battle of Sedan in 1870. From 1899 Wilhelm II used it as a summer residence, and from November 1918 to February 1919 the Oberste Heeresleitung under Paul von Hindenburg directed the withdrawal of German troops from here.

Allied bombs damaged the palace in the Second World War, and from 1968 to 1974 it was rebuilt as an art museum with Old Master paintings, Graeco-Roman antiques and a wallpaper collection. In 1972 Willy Brandt and Willi Stoph met there for talks between the two German states. The State of Hesse administers the park, which belongs to the Museumslandschaft Hessen Kassel. It was proclaimed a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 23 June 2013 for its Baroque architecture and unusual water features. Georg Dehio called it possibly the most grandiose combination of landscape and architecture that the Baroque had dared.
bergslagen: Bergslagen is a historical, cultural and linguistic region north of Lake Mälaren in northern Svealand. It has no precise borders, but is generally understood to cover part of Västmanland, the southern part of Dalarna and the eastern part of Värmland. Typical towns of the area include Lindesberg, Nora, Fagersta, Sala, Kristinehamn, Filipstad, Grythyttan, Ludvika and Hedemora.

Parts of northern Östergötland around Finspång and of southern Närke are sometimes included, then often under the name South Bergslagen. A wider definition takes in parts of Gästrikland around Hofors and of Uppland, where the former iron manufacturing district centred on Dannemora lay.

The earliest signs of iron making in the region date back to 400 BCE, while industrial-scale working dates from the 17th century. The conflict of interests between iron exports from Bergslagen and territorial wars at Denmark's southern border was a chief cause of the Engelbrekt rebellion of 1434 and of the strife that ended with the dissolution of the Kalmar Union in 1523.

Exports from Bergslagen enriched Swedish merchants such as Birgitta Ingvaldsdotter, who traded in the early 16th century. From the 17th century the region was an industrial powerhouse, and it remained one until the steel crisis of the 1970s. During the 20th century, however, Malmfälten, the mining district of northernmost Sweden centred on Kiruna and Malmberget, became more important.

The area is very rich in minerals. Mining long focused on iron ore, but other ores were worked as well, and most mines are now closed. At Långban, where iron and manganese were mined, 270 mineral species have been reported, and 67 minerals were first found there.
bergueda: Berguedà is an inland comarca in the central region of Catalonia, lying partly in the Pyrenees and Pre-Pyrenees and partly in the Catalan Central Depression. Its capital is Berga. The northern half, Alt Berguedà, takes in the upper Llobregat valley and the mountains around it, and is separated from Cerdanya by a chain of peaks of about 2,000 metres, among them the Cadí, Moixeró, Puig d'Alp and Puigllançada ranges.

The more populous southern half, Baix Berguedà, lies along the foothills of the Pyrenees and includes towns of medieval origin such as Gironella, Casserres and Puig-reig, together with many industrial colonies built along the Llobregat after the Industrial Revolution. The north is rainy and cold by Catalan standards, with forests of Scots pine and oak, while the south has a dry Mediterranean climate.

Berguedà has always been sparsely populated. It had 31,544 inhabitants in 1860, a low of 23,257 in 1887 and 27,217 in 1900. For the next sixty years mining, textiles, forestry, cattle ranching and agriculture brought a slow but steady increase, to 39,600 in 1930, 41,938 in 1950 and 47,953 in 1960. A fall in the local economy, especially in mining, then coincided with greater opportunity elsewhere, and the population fell to 44,446 in 1970 and 42,152 in 1981. Industry later concentrated between Berga and Puig-reig, and agriculture, ranching and forestry proved compatible with tourism, which helped to reduce emigration from the north.

The comarca had 44,632 inhabitants in 2019. It is known for Pedraforca Mountain, traditionally regarded as a meeting place of witches' covens, for its Romanesque churches, medieval bridges and old town centres, notably those of Berga and Bagà, and for the mountain of Queralt, home to a sanctuary of Our Lady of Queralt, the comarca's patroness.

Its best-known festival is the Patum, held each summer in Berga, in which figures of mythological beasts and historical characters are carried through the streets. On Christmas Eve, Bagà and Sant Julià de Cerdanyola hold the Fia-faia, a pre-Christian tradition marking the winter solstice, in which people carry lit bundles of Cephalaria leucantha from a mountain bonfire to the main square.
berke: Berke was born to Jochi, officially the eldest son of Genghis Khan, though Jochi's paternity is highly uncertain. The year of Berke's birth is not agreed. Mamluk ambassadors in 1264 or 1265 described him as 56 years old, which points to 1207-1209, but the Persian chronicler Juzjani says he was born during the Mongol conquest of Khwarezmia, between 1219 and 1221.

In 1236 Berke joined his brothers and cousins in the army under his brother Batu Khan, some 150,000 strong, that marched from Siberia against the Volga Bulgars and the Kipchaks. He was sent to the country north of the Caucasus, and in the winter of 1238-39 defeated the Kipchaks there. He later served under Batu in the invasion of Europe and fought at the Battle of Mohi.

Berke is said to have converted to Islam in 1252 after questioning a caravan from Bukhara about its faith, and he persuaded his brother Tukh-timur to convert as well. After Batu died in 1255, his son Sartaq and then Ulaghchi died within months. Berke accused the regent Boraqchin of treason, and she was executed. He took leadership in 1257.

Under his rule the Mongols defeated the rebellion of Daniel of Galicia, and in 1259 the general Burundai led a second attack on Poland and Lithuania, plundering Lublin, Sandomierz and Kraków. A raid on Bulgaria and Byzantine Thrace followed in 1265. His conversion made the western khanate predominantly Muslim, though animists and Buddhists remained among its people.

Berke was angered by Hülegü's sack of Baghdad and the death of the caliph al-Musta'sim. Rashid al-Din quotes him as vowing to call Hülegü to account for so much innocent blood. The dispute also had territorial and economic causes: Möngke Khan had given Hülegü lands in present-day Azerbaijan that Genghis Khan had given to Jochi, and Berke objected to the Ilkhanate's hold on the wealth of northern Iran.

Berke sought an alliance with the Mamluk sultan Baibars. In 1262 open war began, the first open conflict between Mongols, and it signalled the end of the unified empire. Hülegü was defeated at the Terek River in 1263 by Berke's nephew Nogai. Berke supported Ariq Böke against Kublai in the Toluid Civil War and minted coins in his name. He fell ill and died as he prepared to cross the Kura River against Hülegü's son Abaqa, and was succeeded by his grandnephew Mengu-Timur.
berkshire: Berkshire, officially the Royal County of Berkshire, is a ceremonial county in South East England, with Reading as its county town and largest settlement. The whole county is drained by the Thames. The Berkshire Downs, a chalk upland, lie in the west and are the source of the River Kennet, which flows east through Newbury to meet the Thames at Reading. In the south-east lies Swinley Forest, a remnant of Windsor Forest. The historic county included the parts of Oxfordshire south of the Thames, such as Wantage, where Alfred the Great was born, and the Iron Age Uffington White Horse.

According to Asser's biography of King Alfred, written in 893, the county takes its name from a wood of box trees called Bearroc, a Celtic word meaning hilly, west of Frilsham near Newbury. In the Anglo-Saxon period the region was contested between Mercia and Wessex, and Alfred's campaign against the Danes included the battles of Englefield, Ashdown and Reading. Windsor Castle, built after the Norman Conquest, became the official country residence of the British monarch, since William the Conqueror established Windsor as a royal residence.

The county saw several battles in the First English Civil War, with Reading and Wallingford besieged and two battles fought at Newbury, in 1643 and 1644. A second Battle of Reading, on 9 December 1688, was the only substantial military action in England during the Glorious Revolution. Reading replaced Abingdon as county town in 1867. The county received the title Royal County in 1957 because of Windsor Castle, and its boundaries changed on 1 April 1974, when the northern part passed to Oxfordshire and Slough and Eton came from Buckinghamshire.

Berkshire is divided into six unitary authority areas: Bracknell Forest, Reading, Slough, West Berkshire, Windsor and Maidenhead, and Wokingham. Its population is concentrated in the east, nearest London, while the west is rural and its largest town is Newbury. Proximity to London led to development from the 19th century, when Slough became an industrial centre and Bracknell was designated a new town. Software and high-technology industry dominate the economy in the east, and the west remains agricultural.
berkyaruq: Berkyaruq, whose name is a Turkic word meaning "firm, unwavering light", was the oldest son of Malik-Shah I and the Seljuk princess Zubayda Khatun, and was born at the Seljuk capital of Isfahan. When Malik-Shah died in November 1092 no prince was old enough to inherit the empire, and amirs and court figures each backed one of his young sons. Malik-Shah's wife Terken Khatun and the vizier Taj al-Mulk installed her four-year-old son Mahmud at Baghdad and won the caliph al-Mustazhir over, while the family of the dead vizier Nizam al-Mulk, the Nizamiyya, smuggled Berkyaruq out of Isfahan, and he was crowned at Ray.

In January 1093 Berkyaruq's supporters defeated Mahmud's and captured Taj al-Mulk, whom the Nizamiyya had executed on 12 February. Terken Khatun and Mahmud both died in 1094. Berkyaruq's uncle Tutush then invaded western Iran and seized Ray, but Berkyaruq's forces killed him near the city on 25 February 1095, and the caliph acknowledged Berkyaruq as sultan. In the east, his half-brother Ahmad Sanjar was made ruler of Khurasan after an earlier army failed, and Berkyaruq confirmed the Qarakhanids as vassals in Transoxiana and appointed Qutb al-Din Muhammad governor of Khwarazm, which began the Khwarazmian dynasty. Revolts then spread through his eastern lands.

The gravest challenge was the rebellion of his half-brother Muhammad Tapar in 1098 or 1099, backed by Nizam al-Mulk's son Mu'ayyid al-Mulk. The five-year war was indecisive, and by 1104, with his treasury exhausted, Berkyaruq made a treaty that left him Baghdad and most of Iran. Preoccupied with these conflicts, he did not respond to the First Crusade in Syria in 1097. He died of tuberculosis in 1105 on the road to Isfahan, and his infant son Malik-Shah II succeeded him. Muhammad then captured Baghdad and had the child killed.
berlin: Berlin lies in low-lying marshy woodland on the Northern European Plain, along the Spree, which empties into the Havel in the western borough of Spandau. The Spree follows the Berliner Urstromtal, an ice-age glacial valley between the Barnim Plateau to the north and the Teltow plateau to the south, formed by meltwater at the end of the last glaciation. About a third of the city's area is forests, parks, gardens, rivers, canals and lakes. The name has roots in the language of the West Slavs and may be related to the Old Polabian stem berl-/birl-, 'swamp'. Five of the twelve boroughs bear Slavic-derived names, among them Pankow and Spandau.

The area has been settled for millennia: a deer mask of about 9,000 BCE is attributed to the Maglemosian culture, and dense settlement along the Spree and Havel gave rise to the Lusatian culture around 2,000 BCE. Germanic tribes settled from about 500 BCE, the Burgundians followed the Semnones after about 200 CE, and in the 7th century Slavic tribes, later known as the Hevelli and Sprevane, reached the region.

Berlin was first documented in the 13th century, at the crossing of two important trade routes. It was capital of the Margraviate of Brandenburg from 1417, the Kingdom of Prussia from 1701 and the German Empire from 1871. In 1685 the Edict of Potsdam granted religious freedom and tax-free status to French Huguenot refugees.

The Greater Berlin Act of 1920 raised the population from 1.9 million to 4 million, and in the 1920s Berlin was the third-largest city in the world. It was capital of the Weimar Republic and of Nazi Germany until 1945. After the Second World War it was split into West Berlin and East Berlin, divided by the Berlin Wall, and Bonn became the West German capital. Berlin again became the capital of all Germany after reunification on 3 October 1990.

Berlin covers 891 km2 and is the most populous city proper in the European Union. Since 1990 it has been one of three city-states among the 16 states of Germany, governed by the Senate and the 141-seat Abgeordnetenhaus. The bombing of the Second World War devastated the city, and many surviving buildings were later demolished; after reunification many heritage structures were reconstructed.

Museum Island, designated a district dedicated to art and antiquities by royal decree in 1841, is one of three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Charité hospital traces its origins to 1710, and Robert Koch and Rudolf Virchow worked in Berlin. The city hosted the 1936 Summer Olympics.
berlin-conference: Until the later 19th century European power in Africa was largely confined to the coast, where traders held posts protected by gunboats. In 1876 King Leopold II of Belgium founded the International African Association and invited Henry Morton Stanley to join him; from 1878 to 1885 Stanley returned to the Congo as Leopold's agent.

France answered in 1881 by sending the naval officer Pierre de Brazza, who raised the French flag over Brazzaville, and Portugal made a treaty with Great Britain on 26 February 1884 to block the Congo Society's access to the Atlantic. Germany began expeditions of its own, which alarmed British and French statesmen. With British support and on Portugal's initiative, Otto von Bismarck called representatives of thirteen European nations and the United States to Berlin.

The conference met on 15 November 1884 and closed on 26 February 1885 with the signing of the General Act of Berlin. Fourteen countries sent plenipotentiaries, each with a single vote; the United States reserved the right to accept or decline its conclusions. No African state took part.

Sultan Barghash bin Seyyid of Zanzibar asked to send a representative, but British pressure from the Anti-Slavery Society, which objected to Zanzibar's part in the slave trade, led to refusal. Six of the fourteen countries, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden-Norway and the United States, came home without any zone of interest in Africa.

The General Act confirmed the holdings of Leopold's International Congo Society, and on 1 August 1885 the territory was named the Congo Free State, a name absent from the Act. It decreed free trade among the signatories throughout the Congo Basin and made the Niger and Congo rivers free for shipping. Article 6 called on the powers to strive for the suppression of slavery.

Under the principle of effective occupation a power could acquire rights only if it had treaties with local leaders, flew its flag and set up an administration, and it had to notify the other signatories of any possession or protectorate it took in Africa. The Act concerned lands on the coast, and allowed a state to claim the hinterland after occupying the coast.

The conference is usually seen as formalising the Scramble for Africa, and by 1914 about 90 per cent of the continent was under European control. Some historians, among them Sybil Crowe, Matthew Craven and Simon Katzenellenbogen, caution against overstating its role, pointing to the many bilateral agreements before and after it. The only borders set at the conference were those of the Congo region, and these were later revised.
berlin-declaration-1945: The German Instrument of Surrender of 8 May 1945 provided only for the military capitulation of the German armed forces, and its signatories represented the German High Command. The unconditional surrender of the German state itself therefore had no explicit formal basis. Through the European Advisory Commission the Allies had agreed a full surrender text, meant for a post-Nazi government seeking an armistice, but Nazi power lasted to the end and the Allies rejected the claim of Karl Dönitz, Hitler's nominated successor, to have formed a civil government at Flensburg.

The agreed text was therefore redrafted as a declaration with a longer preamble and adopted by the four powers on their own authority. At the signing in Berlin, Georgy Zhukov at first refused to sign because Article 10 would have required the Soviets to arrest Japanese nationals in Germany although the USSR was not at war with Japan. Dwight D. Eisenhower had the clause removed, and the commanders signed copies in English, French, Russian and German.

The preamble asserted German responsibility for the war and the absence of any German central government, while the articles kept a German people and territory, taken as the borders of 31 December 1937, subject to the four powers' right to fix future boundaries. The Allies stated that their assumption of sovereign powers did not amount to annexation. Of the 15 articles, the first eight dealt with the capitulation of the armed forces. Article 11 provided for the arrest and trial of Nazi leaders and suspected war criminals, and Article 13 gave the powers almost unrestricted authority over German civil, economic and legal structures, later used for de-Nazification, reparations and, in the Soviet zone, land reform.

Zhukov refused Eisenhower's wish to begin acting as a control council at once, since the armies had not yet moved to their own zones. The Allied Control Council was established on 30 August 1945, after the Potsdam Agreement of 1 August had confirmed the zones and set the Oder-Neisse line as the border between Poland and Germany. France and then, in 1948, the Soviet Union walked out of the council, which hampered its work.

Some scholars argued that a state could not legally end without annexation, and that the German state had therefore survived. In 2005 the European Court of Human Rights, hearing claims by descendants of landowners expropriated in the Soviet zone, upheld the legality of the occupation as one sui generis that had conferred powers of sovereignty on the Allies. The occupation formally ended in 1991 with the Treaty on the Final Settlement With Respect to Germany. A monument marks the signing site in the Wendenschloss district of Berlin-Köpenick.
berlin-wall: After the Second World War, Germany west of the Oder-Neisse line was divided into four occupation zones, and Berlin, the seat of the Allied Control Council, into four sectors, although it lay wholly within the Soviet zone. The inner German border was closed officially in 1952, but the border in Berlin, administered by all four powers, stayed far more open, and Berlin became the main route by which East Germans left for the West. Before the Wall, 3.5 million East Germans, 20% of the population, had left the GDR.

Emigrants tended to be young and well-educated, which fed official fears of a brain drain. On 15 June 1961 Walter Ulbricht told a press conference that no one had the intention of erecting a wall. A transcript of a telephone call of 1 August suggests the initiative came from Nikita Khrushchev, though other sources say he was wary of Western reaction and that Ulbricht had pushed for a closure.

Construction began on 13 August 1961. The Wall was more than 140 kilometres long, with guard towers and concrete walls, an outer wall and an inner wall, and between them a wide area later known as the death strip. This held anti-vehicle trenches, a strip of raked sand that showed footprints, beds of nails and clear fields of fire. It went through four versions, from a wire fence and concrete block wall in 1961 to the Grenzmauer 75 of 1975 to 1989.

Eastern Bloc propaganda presented it as the Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart, while West Berlin's mayor, Willy Brandt, called it the Wall of Shame. There were nine official crossings, the best known being Checkpoint Charlie, restricted to Allied personnel and foreigners.

More than 100,000 people attempted to escape, and about 5,000 succeeded. A research group in Potsdam confirmed at least 140 deaths, while others estimate well above 200. In 1989 revolutions in Poland and Hungary and the Pan-European Picnic set off a peaceful development in which the Iron Curtain largely broke. On 9 November 1989 the East German government announced that all GDR citizens could visit West Germany and West Berlin. Crowds crossed and climbed onto the Wall, and souvenir hunters chipped away pieces of it. Full demolition began on 13 June 1990 and ended in 1994, and German reunification took place on 3 October 1990.
bermuda: Bermuda is an archipelago of 181 islands, though the most significant are connected by bridges and appear to form one landmass. Its land area is 54 square kilometres. The nearest land is the coast of North Carolina, about 1,035 kilometres to the west-northwest. The islands lie in the west of the Sargasso Sea and have a tropical climate; a coral reef gives them some protection from tropical cyclones. When discovered, they had no human population and were dominated by forests of Bermuda cedar.

Bermuda was discovered in the early 1500s by the Spanish explorer Juan de Bermúdez and appears on Spanish charts of 1511. Spanish and Portuguese ships used it to take on fresh meat and water. Legends of spirits and devils, now thought to stem from the calls of birds and the noises of introduced wild hogs, together with storms and dangerous reefs, gave it the name Isle of Devils, and neither Spain nor Portugal tried to settle it.

In 1609 a flotilla bound for the Jamestown colony was broken up by a storm, and its flagship, the Sea Venture, was driven onto Bermuda's reef to prevent her sinking, so that all aboard survived. Having heard the true conditions in Jamestown, the settlers were unwilling to move on and made several attempts to rebel and stay. The new settlement became a prison labour camp and built two ships, the Deliverance and the Patience. The Somers Isles Company suppressed shipbuilding, wanting the colonists to farm, but the islanders turned to maritime trades, and in 1684 the company's charter was revoked. The House of Assembly dates from 1620.

After the American Revolution the Royal Navy began improving the harbours, and in 1811 work began on the Royal Naval Dockyard on Ireland Island, guarding the western Atlantic shipping lanes. In the War of 1812 the British attacks on Washington, D.C., and the Chesapeake were planned and launched from Bermuda. In the early 20th century it became a popular destination for tourists, and the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 ended its agricultural export trade to America and encouraged tourism.

Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory and a self-governing parliamentary democracy, with a bicameral parliament in the capital Hamilton; the United Kingdom is responsible for foreign affairs and defence. It is divided into nine parishes. An independence referendum in 1995 produced a large majority against independence. The historic Town of St. George's is a World Heritage Site.
bermudo-ii-of-leon: Bermudo II, called the Gouty, was a son of a King Ordono, traditionally identified as Ordono III of Leon. A charter of the monastery of Carracedo in which Bermudo names his father Ordono and his grandfather Ramiro supports that identification and rules out Ordono IV. His mother is disputed. Tradition makes her Urraca Fernandez, but Bishop Pelagius of Oviedo names a second wife, Elvira, who appears in no other record. Justo Perez de Urbel suggested he was an illegitimate son whose mother was a daughter of Pelayo Gonzalez, count of Deza, because a charter of 999 calls the count Gonzalo Betotez of Deza his ancestor. Others find that evidence lacking.

In 982 the Galician nobility proclaimed Bermudo king against his cousin Ramiro III, and he was crowned in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela on 15 October 982. The usurpation is usually seen as part of succession crises that began in the 950s. Because his support was limited and regional, he needed the protection of the Caliphate of Cordoba, and Almanzor's armies came as conquerors, not allies. Between November 991 and September 992 a revolt of magnates expelled him, but he was soon restored and reconciled with them.

Bermudo recovered Zamora from the Muslims, but this brought reprisals from Almanzor, who set out to destroy Coimbra and then besieged and razed the city of Leon. Bermudo took refuge in Zamora. Almanzor went on to take Astorga in 996 and sack Santiago de Compostela in 997. Pelagius of Oviedo, whose Chronicon covers much of the reign, is highly critical of the king, accusing him of imprisoning Bishop Gudesteus of Oviedo in the 990s and blaming Almanzor's attacks on his sins.

In 999 the gout from which he suffered grew worse and he could no longer ride, so he travelled by litter as military leader of the Christians of north-western Spain. He died that year in Villanueva del Bierzo and was buried in the Monastery of Carracedo; his remains were later moved to the Basilica of San Isidoro. Justo Perez de Urbel described him as the poor king tormented in life by Almanzor's sword and in death by a bishop's vengeful pen. By Velasquita Ramirez he had a daughter, Cristina, who married Ordono Ramirez, son of his rival Ramiro III, and by Elvira Garcia he had Alfonso, later Alfonso V of Leon, Theresa and Sancha.
bermudo-iii-of-leon: Bermudo III was a son of King Alfonso V of León by his first wife, Elvira Menéndez. He was a child when he succeeded his father, and he married Jimena Sánchez, a daughter of King Sancho III of Pamplona. Their only child, a son named Alfonso, was born and died in 1030. Like several of his predecessors Bermudo sometimes carried the imperial title, which appears in charters of 1030, 1029 to 1032 and 1034.

In 1029 Count García Sánchez of Castile was about to marry Bermudo's elder sister Sancha when he was murdered in the city of León by the Velas, a party of Castilian nobles exiled from Castile who had taken refuge there. León and Navarre disputed the succession to the vacant county. Sancho III of Pamplona, whose wife Muniadona was the murdered count's sister, claimed Castile in her name and installed their son Ferdinand as count. He also seized the borderlands between the Cea and Pisuerga rivers, just above León's capital, long disputed between León and Castile.

In 1032 Sancho forced a marriage between Ferdinand and Sancha of León, and the disputed lands passed to Castile as her dowry. In 1034 Sancho took the city of León itself from Bermudo, who withdrew into Galicia. By Sancho's death in 1035 the meseta north of the Duero was dominated by Navarre. Bermudo was immediately received back in León and began a campaign to recover the territory between the Cea and Pisuerga from Castile and his brother-in-law Ferdinand.

Bermudo was killed at the Battle of Tamarón on 4 September 1037. An examination of his remains shows that he may have died from infantry spears or pikes after falling from his horse. As he left no heir, the kingdom of León recognised Sancha and her husband as its rulers, and Ferdinand was anointed king in León on 22 June 1038. The united realm of León and Castile, with Asturias and Galicia at its edges, became the political centre of the Christian north of the Iberian peninsula.
bernabo-visconti: Bernabò was born in Milan, the son of Stefano Visconti and Valentina Doria, and was named after his maternal grandfather Bernabò Doria, once ruler of Genoa. His paternal grandfather Matteo I Visconti was in conflict with the Church, and the whole family was excommunicated on a charge of heresy the year before Bernabò's birth. His father died in 1327, and the children were brought up by their mother. From 1346 to 1349 Bernabò lived in exile, until his uncle Giovanni Visconti called him back to Milan after the death of Luchino. On 27 September 1350 he married Beatrice Regina della Scala, daughter of Mastino II of Verona.

At Giovanni's death in 1354 Bernabò inherited power in Milan with his brothers Matteo and Galeazzo, taking the eastern lands of Bergamo, Brescia, Cremona and Crema. Matteo died in 1355, rumoured to have been poisoned by his brothers, who divided his inheritance. His intrigues kept him almost continuously at war with Pope Urban V, the Florentines, Venice and Savoy. In 1360 Pope Innocent VI declared him a heretic at Avignon, and he was defeated at San Ruffillo on 29 July 1361 by imperial troops under Galeotto I Malatesta. He was excommunicated again on 4 March 1363, and the ban was lifted under the peace of 13 March 1364 in exchange for 500,000 florins.

In 1373 the pope sent two delegates to serve Bernabò and Galeazzo their excommunication papers, a parchment with a leaden seal rolled in a silken cord. The furious Bernabò arrested them and refused to release them until they had eaten the parchment, seal and cord. In 1370 he ordered the Trezzo Bridge, then the largest single-arch bridge in the world. He joined Venice in the War of Chioggia against Genoa, and his troops were defeated in the Val Bisagno in September 1379.

His despotism and taxes enraged the Milanese, and Chaucer's Monk's Tale includes him among tyrants brought down by Fortune. His nephew Gian Galeazzo Visconti deposed him on 6 May 1385. He was imprisoned in the castle of Trezzo, where he died on 19 December of that year, presumably poisoned. Bonino da Campione sculpted his equestrian statue around 1363 for the church of San Giovanni in Conca; it was reused as his funerary monument and is now in the Castello Sforzesco in Milan. He had at least fifteen legitimate children, and several daughters married into the royal and ducal houses of Bavaria, Austria and Cyprus.
bernal-diaz-del-castillo: Bernal Díaz was born around 1492 in Medina del Campo, a prosperous commercial city in Castile. His father, Francisco Díaz del Castillo, was a regidor, or city councillor, which gave the family some prominence. He later showed a knack for languages, learning Taíno in Cuba, Nahuatl in Mexico and Cakchiquel in Guatemala.

In 1514, aged about eighteen, he left home as a common foot soldier in the expedition of Pedrarias Dávila, the largest fleet yet sent to mainland America, with 19 vessels and 1,500 people. At Darien, in present-day Colombia, famine and an epidemic killed more than half of the settlers. In 1517 he joined Francisco Hernández de Córdoba's expedition to Yucatán, and in 1518 he returned to the Yucatán coast under Juan de Grijalva.

Back in Cuba, Díaz enlisted in the expedition of Hernán Cortés and took part in the campaigns against the Mexica, or Aztec Empire. He later described many of the 119 battles in which he fought, ending with the defeat of the Aztecs in 1521. Cortés awarded him an encomienda in 1522, confirmed and added to in 1527 and 1528. He settled in Guatemala in 1541 and in 1551, during a trip to Spain, was appointed regidor of Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala, now Antigua Guatemala.

Like many conquistadors, he was discontent that he had not won the wealth he hoped for and felt that the Spanish government had failed to acknowledge his efforts. He died in Guatemala at the age of 92, in early January 1584.

His Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, finished in 1568, was begun almost thirty years after the events and expanded after he read the biography of Cortés by Francisco López de Gómara. The title answers Cortés's own letters to the king and the claims of Gómara, Bartolomé de las Casas and others who were not on the campaign. Díaz held that Cortés took most of the credit and minimised the sacrifices of the other Spaniards and of Indigenous allies such as the Tlaxcaltecs, and he thought Bernardino de Sahagún too sympathetic to the Aztecs.

The book describes the peoples of New Spain, the Aztec palaces, marketplaces and gardens, and the human sacrifice and cannibalism he says he witnessed. Of the ruined Tenochtitlan he wrote that nothing remained of the wonders he had seen. It was published in 1632. Written decades afterwards and containing inaccuracies and biases, it is one of only two first-hand accounts of the Spanish overthrow of the Aztecs.
bernard-of-clairvaux: Bernard's parents, Tescelin de Fontaine, lord of Fontaine-lès-Dijon, and Alèthe de Montbard, belonged to the highest nobility of Burgundy. He was the third of seven children, six of them sons. At nine he was sent to a school at Châtillon-sur-Seine run by the secular canons of Saint-Vorles, where he was drawn to literature and rhetoric. After his mother died he decided to go to Cîteaux, the abbey founded near Dijon in 1098 by a group led by Robert of Molesme to live by a literal reading of the Rule of St Benedict.

Three years after entering Cîteaux, Bernard was sent with twelve monks to found a new house at the Vallée d'Absinthe in the diocese of Langres, which he named Clairvaux on 25 June 1115. Its beginnings were austere, but candidates flocked to it, and more than sixty abbeys followed in his lifetime. He defended the Cistercians against criticism from the Benedictines of Cluny in his Apology, and Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, answered with admiration and friendship.

At the Council of Troyes in 1128 he traced the outlines of the Rule of the Knights Templar. When Honorius II died in 1130 and the election of Innocent II and the Antipope Anacletus II split the Church, Bernard was chosen at the council of Étampes to judge between them and decided for Innocent, then spent years winning over rulers and cities; the schism ended with Anacletus's death in 1138. In 1141 he secured the condemnation of Peter Abelard at a council at Sens.

In 1146 Pope Eugene III commissioned him to preach the Second Crusade, and on 31 March, with King Louis VII present, he preached to an enormous crowd at Vézelay. He also opposed attacks on Jews in the Rhineland and silenced the monk Radulf, who was inspiring them.

The failure of the Second Crusade saddened his last years and put the whole responsibility on him; he wrote that the sins of the crusaders had caused it. He died on 20 August 1153, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Clairvaux. After his remains were destroyed in 1792 by the French Revolutionary government, they were transferred to Troyes Cathedral.

He was canonized 21 years after his death and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1830. Against the rational approach of the scholastics he preached poetically and stressed personal friendship with Christ, and he helped spread devotion to Mary. His sermons on the Song of Songs are his best known. Bernard appears as Dante's last guide in the Divine Comedy.
bernard-of-sedirac: Bernard was born in Gascony around 1050, at La Sauvetat de Blanquefort near Agen, and is also known as Bernard of Le Sauvetat. He is thought to have belonged to the old family of the viscounts of Sédirac, whose castle still stands southwest of La Sauvetat. An illness turned him from a military career to the monastic life, and he became a monk of the Abbey of Cluny, from which he was sent to Spain with others to assist the reforms of Gregory VII.

In 1080 he was made abbot of St. Facundus at Sahagún in the diocese of León, and Alfonso VI of Castile, a great patron of Cluny, later named him to Toledo. Gregory's plans for Spain included a campaign against clerical marriage, simony and lay investiture, the replacement of the Mozarabic liturgy by the Roman one, and pressure for recognition of obligations of tribute from the Spanish church. By raising Toledo to primatial dignity, Urban II gave Bernard the power to carry on the work of Romanizing.

A devoted adherent of the papacy, Bernard made possible Urban's intervention at the Synod of León in 1091. He filled episcopal sees with Cluniac Benedictines, and Alfonso apparently tried to counterbalance them by appointing a Castilian to Santiago de Compostela. His seizure of the mosque of Toledo by force in his first year and his plans for a crusade against the Saracens of the East recalled his youth as a knight; both Urban II and Paschal II forbade the crusade, given the tasks Spanish knights faced at home. Under him the church of Castile and León emerged from its isolation.

Four of his sermons, on the Salve Regina, are preserved among those of Bernard of Clairvaux. He was satirised in The Treatise of Garcia of Toledo, said to have been written by one of his canons. He is often confused with Bernard of Agen, first bishop of Sigüenza, another Gascon and Cluniac monk.
bernard-of-septimania: Bernard was a son of William of Gellone and a cousin of Charlemagne. He is first recorded as one of four sons named in a document of his father's of 14 December 804 on the founding of the monastery of Gellone. He must have inherited land around Toulouse, from which he built up his power. On 29 June 824 at Aachen he married Dhuoda, perhaps a daughter of Sancho I of Gascony; they had two sons, William of Septimania and Bernard Plantapilosa.

Bernard became count of Barcelona around 826 and first made his name against the revolt of Aisso, a nobleman perhaps loyal to the deposed Count Bera. Aisso sought help from Abd ar-Rahman II, Emir of Córdoba, whose general Ubayd Allah Abu Marwan besieged Barcelona in the summer of 827 but failed to take it. The relief army of Hugh of Tours and Matfrid of Orléans arrived too late, and at the Assembly of Aachen in 828 both lost their counties, while Bernard received the lands of Leibulf of Provence and took the title Duke of Septimania.

In August 829 Louis the Pious called him to court as chamberlain and guardian of the young Charles, later king of West Francia. Within months he had many enemies and was the main cause of Lothair's revolt in 830; rumours of an affair with Empress Judith, which the chronicler Thegan of Trier called lies, set off a riot in the army at Rennes, and Bernard fled to Barcelona. Failing to regain favour, he backed Pepin of Aquitaine's revolt of 831, lost all his offices in 832 and recovered Septimania and Toulouse only in 835.

Bernard kept out of the Battle of Fontenay-en-Puisaye on 25 June 841 and then sent his son William to do homage to Charles the Bald. When Charles took Toulouse from him in 842, he rebelled, allied himself with Pepin II and drove out the new count, Acfred. He was captured either during the assault on Toulouse in 844 or, according to the French historian Pierre Andoque, the year before at Uzès. In May 844 he was brought before Charles, who ordered his execution. His honores passed to Sunifred, while his son William fought on against the king.
bernard-vi-of-armagnac: Bernard was born around 1270, the son of Gerald VI, Count of Armagnac, and Mathe de Béarn; Gaston VII, Viscount of Béarn, was his grandfather. His first wife was Isabella d'Albret, daughter of Bernard Ezy IV, Sire of Albret, and Jeanne de Lusignan. Through this marriage he carried the title of lord of Albret from 1280 until her death on 1 December 1294. In 1298 he married Cecilia de Rodez, heiress of Henri II, Count of Rodez, and all his legitimate children were born of this second marriage.

Bernard spent much of his life in the service of the kings of France. In 1302 he fought in Italy under the command of Charles of Valois, and he then took part in all the campaigns in Flanders directed by Philippe le Bel and his son Louis X, in 1303, 1304, 1313 and 1315. He came to lead large detachments of the royal army and contributed in particular to the victory of Mons-en-Alarcon on 18 August 1304, bringing four hundred armed men and a thousand men on foot.

This service was expensive and left him impoverished: he had to borrow 2500 gold florins to pay for his wife's funeral. In the south he was drawn into a long quarrel with the Counts of Foix. After the death of Gaston VII, a dispute arose over the viscount's will, which favoured the Count of Foix. Bernard refused to accept its legitimacy, and the conflict grew into an undeclared war between the houses of Foix and Armagnac that went on through nearly all of the fourteenth century.

Bernard died in 1319. His son John I (1305–1373) became Count of Armagnac, of Fezensac and of Rodez. His daughter Mathe, who died in 1364, was married in 1321 to Bernard Ezi IV, Sire d'Albret, and another daughter, Isabella, was Lady of Beras.

He also had an illegitimate son, John, the Bastard of Armagnac, called la Guerre, the War. John fought in the wars in Gascony, was captured by the king's men and was released after promising to be faithful and loyal to the king. He then left arms to embrace the ecclesiastical state, became Patriarch of Alexandria and in 1376 took over the administration of the diocese of Rodez.
bernard-vii-count-of-armagnac: Bernard was the son of John II, Count of Armagnac, and Jeanne de Périgord. When his brother John III, who claimed the Kingdom of Majorca, invaded northern Catalonia late in 1389 to seize the kingdom's continental lands in the County of Roussillon, Bernard commanded part of his forces. He succeeded John III in Armagnac in 1391, and after prolonged fighting he also became Count of Comminges in 1412. He married Bonne, daughter of John, Duke of Berry, and widow of Amadeus VII, Count of Savoy.

Bernard first gained influence at the French court through the marriage of Louis I, Duke of Orléans, to Valentina Visconti, daughter of Gian Galeazzo Visconti, Duke of Milan; Bernard's sister Beatrice married Valentina's brother Carlo. After Louis was assassinated in 1407, Bernard stayed loyal to the house of Orléans, and in 1410 he married his daughter Bonne to the young Charles I, Duke of Orléans. As head of the faction opposed to John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, he gave it its name, the Armagnacs. As Constable of France he led the government of the Dauphin, the future Charles VII.

On the night of 28 to 29 May 1418 Burgundian troops under the captain Jean de Villiers entered Paris. Bernard hid in a neighbour's house but was betrayed. On 12 June 1418 he was one of the first victims of the massacres in which between 1,000 and 5,000 of his real or suspected followers were killed over several weeks of that summer. His son John became John IV, Count of Armagnac; his daughter Anne married Charles II of Albret, and his son Bernard, Count of Pardiac, married Eleanor, heiress to La Marche.
bernardino-de-sahagun: Bernardino was born Bernardino de Rivera in 1499 at Sahagún in Spain. He studied at the University of Salamanca, then strongly influenced by Erasmus and a centre of Franciscan intellectual life, and joined the Franciscans. He took the name of his birth town, as Franciscan custom had it, and was probably ordained around 1527. Because of his academic and religious reputation he was recruited in 1529 to join the missionary effort in New Spain, where he spent the next 61 years. He began to study Nahuatl on the voyage, learning from indigenous nobles returning from Spain.

Sahagún helped found the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco in 1536, the first European school of higher education in the Americas, and taught Latin there in its early years. He also served as a missionary in Tlalmanalco, Xochimilco, Tepepulco and Huexotzinco, and translated the Psalms, the Gospels and a catechism into Nahuatl. In 1558 the provincial Francisco de Toral commissioned him to write in Nahuatl on topics he thought useful to the mission.

At Tepepulco he spent two years interviewing about a dozen village elders, assisted by native graduates of the college who knew Nahuatl, Latin and Spanish, and who also painted the illustrations. He asked about ritual and calendar, family, economic and political customs, and natural history, and questioned the elders singly and in groups to test their information. This produced the Primeros Memoriales, the basis of the larger Historia general. Between 1561 and 1575 he returned to Tlatelolco and consulted more elders, and he spent his last fifteen or so years editing, translating and copying.

The Florentine Codex of the Historia general has 2,400 pages in twelve books and about 2,500 illustrations by native artists. Its Spanish and Nahuatl texts face one another, and it records Aztec religion, ritual, society, economy and history. Book 12 tells the conquest of the Aztec Empire from the Tenochtitlan-Tlatelolco point of view. Sahagún drew on a range of informants, women among them, and compared their answers, methods that scholars regard as forerunners of modern ethnography.

Some colonial authorities thought the work dangerous, and the Inquisition was established in Mexico in 1570. In 1575 the Council of the Indies banned scriptures in indigenous languages and forced him to hand over his papers, but he made two more copies. The Florentine Codex was catalogued in the Laurentian Library in Florence in 1793, and in 2015 UNESCO declared his work a World Heritage. He died on 5 February 1590.
bernardino-rivadavia: Bernardino Rivadavia was born in Buenos Aires on 20 May 1780, the fourth son of Benito Bernardino González de Rivadavia, a wealthy Spanish lawyer, and María Josefa de Jesús Rodríguez de Rivadeneyra. He was educated at the Royal College of San Carlos but left without finishing. During the British invasions he served as a lieutenant of the Galicia Volunteers, and on 22 May 1810 he took part in the open Cabildo that voted to depose the viceroy. In 1811 he became the dominant member of the governing triumvirate, whose government aimed at a strong central authority and an organised army until its fall in October 1812.

In 1814 Rivadavia and Manuel Belgrano were sent to Europe to seek support from Spain and Britain for the United Provinces. The mission failed, but in Britain he saw the Industrial Revolution and tried to promote similar development in Buenos Aires. In June 1821 Governor Martín Rodríguez named him minister of government of Buenos Aires province. Over five years he built avenues and schools, paved and lit streets, and founded the University of Buenos Aires, academies of theatre, geology and medicine, and the continent's first museum of natural science.

He also persuaded the legislature to authorise a loan of one million pounds, sold in London through the Baring Brothers; the government received only £552,700, and the debt was transferred to the nation in 1825. Liberal historians praise his work for education, culture and the separation of church and state, while revisionist authors condemn his free-trade policy and the Baring loan.

Rivadavia was named the first President of the United Provinces on 8 February 1826, as war with Brazil over territory in modern Uruguay required a national government. He made Buenos Aires the capital, and the constitution enacted on 24 December 1826 adopted a representative, republican and unitary government. Most provinces rejected it, and Facundo Quiroga defeated Rivadavia's ally Lamadrid at Rincón de Valladares on 6 July 1827.

In May 1827 his envoy Manuel José García signed a preliminary peace with Brazil that contradicted his instructions; the government rejected it. Rivadavia resigned on 27 June 1827. He left for Spain, was refused a landing in 1834 on trying to return, lived in Uruguay and died in Cádiz on 2 September 1845. His remains were repatriated in 1857 and now lie in a mausoleum in the Plaza Miserere.
bernardo-buontalenti: Bernardo Buontalenti, born Bernardo Timante Buonacorsi in Florence and sometimes nicknamed Bernardo delle Girandole, entered the service of the Medici as a youth and stayed with them all his life. He is said to have learnt painting from Salviati and Bronzino, sculpture from Michelangelo, architecture from Giorgio Vasari and miniature painting from Giulio Clovio, and he painted miniatures for Francesco, son of Cosimo I. He was also a skilled mechanic and mathematician, and travelled to Spain in 1562.

His first known work, from 1568, is the Palazzo di Bianca Cappello in Florence. Counted among the most important architects of the Mannerist period, he was much employed on fortifications, villas and gardens. At Pratolino little of his park survives beyond Giambologna's giant Colossus of the Apennines. As a military engineer he fortified the port of Livorno and worked on the city walls of Pistoia, Grosseto, Prato, Portoferraio on Elba and Naples; he also perfected designs for cannon and devised a new type of incendiary grenade. With his pupil Matteo Nigetti he was commissioned in 1592 to build the Palazzo Nonfinito, of which only the first floor was completed.

In the theatre he was court architect when the Theater of Baldracca opened in 1576, a simple hall with a slightly raised stage and a grated box from which high-ranking viewers could watch unseen. From 1576 to 1586 he worked on the Medici Theater for Grand Duke Francesco I, with a sloping floor inspired by ancient theatres, and in 1589 changed its decoration to proclaim the authority of Ferdinando I. He designed stage machinery, allegorical costumes and fireworks for Medici performances, and directed the festivities of the winter of 1585–1586 in the Uffizi.

His extravagance ruined him financially, and in later life he lived on a pension from the Grand Duke of Tuscany. He died in June 1608, after a lifetime in which he had served the Medici grand dukes as painter, architect, engineer and designer of their spectacles. He was also an innovator in the storing of ice and is credited with inventing a forerunner of modern Florentine gelato.
bernardo-de-galvez: Bernardo de Gálvez was born on 23 July 1746 in Macharaviaya, a mountain village in the province of Málaga, the son of Matías de Gálvez and María Josefa de Madrid. A soldier from the age of 16, he served in the Spanish invasion of Portugal, then went to New Spain in 1769, where he fought the Apaches with Opata allies and was badly wounded. He served three years in France with the Royal Cantabria regiment, learning French, and was seriously wounded in Alejandro O'Reilly's disastrous expedition to Algiers in 1775.

He took office as governor of Louisiana on 1 January 1777 and that November married Marie-Félicité de Saint-Maxent d'Estrehan, a Creole widow, which won him local favour.
