On secret orders from Madrid he worked with the American patriot Oliver Pollock to send gunpowder, muskets, uniforms and medicine up the Mississippi to the rebels, and the Continental Congress thanked him in 1778. When Spain declared war on Great Britain in 1779, he intercepted orders for General John Campbell to attack New Orleans and struck first.

His capture of Pensacola on 8 May 1781, by land and sea, left Britain without a base on the Gulf coast, and in 1782 forces under his overall command took Nassau in the Bahamas. Spain made him Count of Gálvez and Viscount of Gálvez-Town, and the Peace of Paris of 1783 returned Florida to Spain. In 1785 he succeeded his father as viceroy of New Spain. He faced a freeze that brought famine in 1786 and a typhus epidemic that killed 300,000 people, gave money to buy maize and beans, began Chapultepec Castle and sponsored the Royal Botanical Expedition to New Spain.

Gálvez fell ill with typhus late in the epidemic and died at Tacubaya on 30 November 1786, aged 40; he was buried beside his father in San Fernando Church in Mexico City. His Instructions for Governing the Interior Provinces of New Spain, which urged selling the Indians rifles and goods to make them dependent and sanctioned war on the Apache, stayed in force until colonial rule ended. Galveston Bay, St. Bernard Parish and Galvez, Louisiana, are among the places named for him. In 2014 his portrait was hung in the United States Capitol and Congress made him an honorary citizen.
bernardo-de-monteagudo: Monteagudo was the son of Miguel Monteagudo, a Spaniard, and Catalina Cáceres Bramajo of Tucumán, and the only survivor of eleven children. He was most likely of mixed race, with African slaves among his ancestors; some historians hold that his mother had been the slave of a canon, and his political enemies later used the colonial statutes of blood purity against him. He studied law in Córdoba and at the University of Chuquisaca, where he graduated in 1808 and began to practise as a defender of the poor.

That year, when news came of Napoleon's invasion of Spain, he wrote the Dialogue between Atahualpa and Fernando VII, which argued that since the King was prevented from ruling, the Indies must rule themselves.

In Buenos Aires from 1811 he defended Castelli in the trial over the defeat of Huaqui, edited La Gazeta de Buenos-Ayres and influenced the drafting of the Provisional Statute. In 1817, a few days after the Battle of Chacabuco, he crossed the Andes to serve José de San Martín as auditor of the Army of the Andes. He wrote the Proclamation of the Independence of Chile in January 1818, though Miguel de Zañartu's claim to it is disputed, and advised Bernardo O'Higgins. After the Battle of Maipú he was involved in the summary execution of the brothers Juan José and Luis Carrera, and probably in the murder of Manuel Rodríguez Erdoíza.

In exile after 1822 he went to Panama and met Simón Bolívar at Ibarra in 1823, then travelled to Guatemala City, where José Cecilio del Valle shared his idea of a continental congress. Defying the ban on his return, he came back to Peru as a colonel under Bolívar and entered Lima after the Battle of Ayacucho on 9 December 1824. By then he believed that all Hispanic America should be a single nation.

At around 8 p.m. on 28 January 1825, Monteagudo was walking from his home in Lima to the house of Juana Salguero when he was stabbed to death, at the age of thirty-five. He is remembered as one of the revolutionaries who served in the independence struggles of the Río de la Plata, Chile and Peru, and as a key figure in the history of people of African descent in the region in the 18th and 19th centuries.
bernardo-houssay: Bernardo Alberto Houssay was born on 10 April 1887 in Buenos Aires, the son of Albert and Clara Houssay, immigrants from France. A precocious youngster, he was admitted to the Pharmacy School of the University of Buenos Aires at 14 and to its Faculty of Medicine at 17, studying there from 1904 to 1910. While a third-year medical student he took a post as research and teaching assistant in the Chair of Physiology.

After graduating he presented a doctoral thesis on the physiological activities of pituitary extracts, published in 1911, a theme he pursued for the rest of his scientific career. He became Professor of Physiology in the university's School of Veterinary Medicine, worked as an assistant physician at the municipal hospital of Buenos Aires, and in 1913 became Chief Physician at the Alvear Hospital. In 1915 he became Chief of the Section of Experimental Pathology at the National Public Health Laboratories. In 1919 he was appointed to the chair of physiology at the university's medical school and held it until 1943, turning the department into a research centre of international standing.

In 1943 the military government deprived him of his university posts because of his liberal political ideas, and he re-established his research and staff at a privately funded Instituto de Biología y Medicina Experimental. The Peronist government dismissed him a second time in 1945. When Perón was ousted in 1955 he was reinstated at the University of Buenos Aires, where he stayed until his death. From 1957 he also directed the National Scientific and Technical Research Council.

Houssay worked in many fields of physiology, but his main contribution was experimental research on the part played by the anterior pituitary gland in the metabolism of carbohydrates, particularly in diabetes mellitus. In the 1930s he demonstrated the diabetogenic effect of anterior pituitary extracts and the lessening of diabetes after removal of the gland. These findings stimulated the study of hormonal feedback control, central to modern endocrinology. The work won him the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, shared with Carl Ferdinand Cori and Gerty Cori.

He published more than 600 scientific papers and several specialised books. With his disciples Eduardo Braun-Menéndez and Miguel Rolando Covian he wrote a textbook of human physiology, published since 1950 in Spanish and Portuguese and used in almost all medical schools of Latin America. Covian became the father of Brazilian neurophysiology at the University of São Paulo's medical faculty in Ribeirão Preto. Houssay was elected to the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1940 and became a Foreign Member of the Royal Society in 1943. He died on 21 September 1971.
bernardo-ohiggins: Bernardo O'Higgins was born on 20 August 1778 in Chillán, the illegitimate son of Ambrosio O'Higgins, a Spanish officer born in County Sligo who became governor of Chile and later viceroy of Peru, and of Isabel Riquelme. His father never acknowledged him, and the two never met in person, though Ambrosio supported him financially. At seventeen he was sent to London, where he met the Venezuelan Francisco de Miranda and joined the Lautaro Lodge, a society dedicated to the independence of Latin America. After his father's death in 1801 he inherited a large estate and returned to Chile in 1802 as a gentleman farmer.

On 18 September 1810 O'Higgins joined the revolt that created the Government Junta of Chile, a date now Chile's Independence Day. The patriots were split between the Carrera family and the circle of O'Higgins in Concepción. In October 1814 O'Higgins garrisoned the main square of Rancagua rather than the gorge he and José Miguel Carrera had agreed on; Carrera did not arrive with reinforcements, and the royalists won. O'Higgins broke out with a few men and spent three years in Argentina, where he met José de San Martín, assembled the Army of the Andes and returned to Chile in 1817 to win at Chacabuco.

He was granted dictatorial powers as Supreme Director on 16 February 1817 after San Martín declined the post, and Chile proclaimed itself independent on 12 February 1818. He founded the Chilean Military Academy and, with Lord Cochrane, the modern Chilean Navy, and sent an expedition to liberate Peru. His proposals to establish democracy and abolish titles of nobility met resistance from landowners, and he offended the Church and then the business community. The government went bankrupt, and Carrera's execution in 1821 damaged his name. A conservative coup deposed him on 28 January 1823.

O'Higgins left Valparaíso in July 1823 and never saw Chile again. Simón Bolívar's government granted him two haciendas in Peru but gave him no command. In 1842 the National Congress of Chile voted to allow his return, but he fell ill with heart trouble at Callao and died in Lima on 24 October 1842. His remains were brought to Chile in 1869 and now lie in the Crypt of the Liberator. A region of Chile, a national park and the main avenue of Santiago bear his name.
bernardo-tanucci: Tanucci was born on 20 February 1698 at Stia, near Arezzo, to a family without wealth, and was educated at the University of Pisa thanks to a patron. He became a professor of law there in 1725 and drew attention by defending the authenticity of the Codex Pisanus of the Pandects of Justinian. When Charles, Duke of Parma, passed through Tuscany on his way to conquer the Kingdom of Naples, Grand Duke Cosimo III de' Medici encouraged him to take Tanucci with him. In 1740 Tanucci married Donna Ricciarda Catanti, daughter of a Pisan nobleman, by proxy.

In Naples Charles made him councillor of state and superintendent of posts, minister of justice in 1752, foreign minister in 1754 and finally prime minister and a marquis. Governing on the principles of enlightened absolutism, he aimed at the kind of control over the church that the Gallican church gave the Bourbons in France. Revenues of vacant bishoprics went to the crown, superfluous convents were suppressed, tithes were abolished and new church property in mortmain forbidden. Papal bulls needed royal assent, appeals to Rome royal permission, and marriage was declared a civil contract. Naples's status as a papal fief was denied.

When Charles became King of Spain in 1759, Tanucci presided over the council of regency for the nine-year-old Ferdinand IV, who left the government in his hands even after coming of age. He kept Naples out of wars, and on his advice a commission was set up to study the Herculaneum papyri found in 1752. His commission of jurists drafted a law code, the Codice Carolino, which never came into force.

After the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767, Pope Clement XIII responded with excommunication, and Tanucci occupied the papal enclaves of Benevento and Pontecorvo, which were returned only after the suppression of the Society of Jesus in 1773. His finance and food tax policies provoked popular revolts on several occasions. His power declined after Queen Maria Carolina joined the Council of State in 1774, and he was dismissed and retired. He died in Naples on 29 April 1783 and was buried in the Basilica of San Giovanni Battista dei Fiorentini.
bernburg: The town centre lies in the fertile Magdeburg Börde lowland on the Saale river, about 40 km downstream from Halle and 45 km upstream from Magdeburg. It is dominated by the huge Bernburg Castle, which holds a museum and a bear pit in its moat. Bernburg is the capital of the Salzlandkreis district and a stop on the Romanesque Road. Near the town, in Lower Triassic deposits, the type fossil of the amphibian Trematosaurus brauni was found.

Archaeological sites in the area belong to the Walternienburg-Bernburg Culture, a mid-Neolithic funnel-beaker culture of about 3200 to 2800 BCE. Around 150 CE a settlement named Luppia appears in Ptolemy's Geography. In the early Middle Ages the Saale marked the border between the German stem duchies in the west and the lands of the Polabian Slavs in the east. Bernburg itself is first mentioned as civitas Brandanburg in a deed of King Otto I of 961. Enemies set fire to the castle, then held by the Ascanian prince Albert the Bear, in 1138, and in 1252 the rebuilt castle became the residence of his great-grandson Prince Bernhard I of Anhalt-Bernburg.

During the Nazi dictatorship a wing of the town's mental hospital was used for the mass murder of an estimated 15,000 people in Action T4 and Action 14f13. The victims included Jews, people with physical and mental illnesses and concentration camp inmates. The site now holds a memorial to them.
bernhard-i-duke-of-saxe-meiningen: Bernhard was born on 10 September 1649, the sixth son but the third to survive of his father and of Elisabeth Sophie of Saxe-Altenburg. On 20 November 1671, at Schloss Friedenstein in Gotha, he married Marie Hedwig of Hesse-Darmstadt, with whom he had seven children. Johann Ernst, Marie Elisabeth and Johann Georg died in infancy and Georg Ernst of smallpox at Meiningen in 1699, aged 18; of the others Ernst Ludwig I and Frederick Wilhelm later became dukes of Saxe-Meiningen, while Bernhard died at Brussels in 1694 aged 20.

After his father's death in 1675 Bernhard and his brothers governed their inheritance jointly, until the division of 1680. Under that treaty he received Meiningen, Wasungen, Salzungen, Untermassfeld, Frauenbreitungen and Ichtershausen, and so founded the Saxe-Meiningen line. Work on a residence at Meiningen began at once; finished in 1692, it was named Schloss Elisabethenburg after his second wife. Like his brother Ernst, he kept his duchy's finances stable, by selling chamber goods and by raising further taxes from its people.

On 25 January 1681, at Schöningen, he married Elisabeth Eleonore of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, daughter of Anthony Ulrich, Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Of their five children, Elisabeth Ernestine became Abbess of Gandersheim Abbey, Wilhelmine Luise married Charles, Duke of Württemberg-Bernstadt, in 1703, and Anton Ulrich also became Duke of Saxe-Meiningen.

Bernhard died on 27 April 1706. His will forbade the division of the duchy but did not establish primogeniture, so that his sons could govern it jointly after his death. Three of them, Ernst Ludwig I, Frederick Wilhelm and Anton Ulrich, bore the title of Duke of Saxe-Meiningen.
bernhard-iii-duke-of-saxe-meiningen: Bernhard was born at Meiningen on 1 April 1851, the eldest son of Georg II, Duke of Saxe-Meiningen, and his first wife, Princess Charlotte of Prussia. He was taught from 1860 by Prof. Rossmann and went to Heidelberg University in 1869, breaking off his studies to serve as an orderly officer in the war against France and resuming them afterwards at Leipzig.

On 18 February 1878 he married, in Berlin, his second cousin Princess Charlotte of Prussia, daughter of Frederick III, German Emperor, and granddaughter of Queen Victoria. Their only child, Princess Feodora, married Heinrich XXX of Reuss-Köstritz in 1898. Queen Marie of Romania, his wife's cousin, wrote that Charlotte never liked him, though he was devoted to her.

From 1873 Bernhard served again in the army and rose to its highest ranks. By 1905 he was Generaloberst and inspector general of the 2nd Army Inspection, covering central Germany, and in 1909 he was given the rank of Generaloberst im Range eines Generalfeldmarschalls before retiring from active service in 1912. Beside soldiering he was a composer, poet and translator, an expert on Modern Greek known for translating German literature into Greek. His historical studies, for which he travelled repeatedly to Greece and Asia Minor, earned him an honorary doctorate from the University of Breslau.

Bernhard became duke on his father's death in 1914. When the First World War began he hoped to be given command of an army, and when he was not, he withdrew from his part in the duchy's government. After Germany's defeat the German Revolution forced him to abdicate on 10 November 1918, and like all the German princes he lost his title and his state. He spent the rest of his life in his former country as a private citizen, died at Meiningen on 16 January 1928, and was buried beside his wife in the park at Altenstein.
bernhard-iii-margrave-of-baden-baden: Bernhard was born on 7 October 1474. He was brought up at the court of Emperor Maximilian I and went to Spain with his friend, Maximilian's son Philip I, who was appointed King of Spain in 1504. In 1515 he inherited part of his father's margraviate of Baden, while his brothers Ernest and Philip received the other parts. When Philip died, Bernhard and Ernest each took half of his share.

Bernhard ruled his part of Baden from 1515 until his death. The division with Ernest created two lines of rulers: the Catholic Bernhardine line in Baden-Baden and the Protestant Ernestine line in Baden-Durlach. Bernhard himself, however, inclined towards Protestantism in his later years and introduced the Reformation into the upper margraviate.

In 1535 he married Franziska of Luxemburg, Countess of Brienne and Ligny, a daughter of Charles I, Count of Ligny; she died on 17 June 1566. They had two sons, Philibert, born on 22 January 1536, and Christopher, born on 26 February 1537, after his father's death. Bernhard also had many children outside marriage, of whom six sons are known: Bernard, Philip, John, George, Caspar and Melchior. In 1532 Emperor Charles V declared George, Caspar and Melchior legitimate princes, and later Bernhard and Philip as well. They could not inherit, but received a maintenance payment after their father died.

Bernhard died on 29 June 1536. The Bernhardine line he founded ruled Baden-Baden until it died out in 1771, when Margrave Charles Frederick of the Ernestine line reunited the Margraviate of Baden. His life was described in the 19th century by Friedrich von Weech in the Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, and earlier by Johann Christian Sachs in his history of the margraviate and house of Baden.
bernhard-of-saxe-weimar: Bernhard was born in Weimar on 16 August 1604, the eleventh son of Johann, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, and Dorothea Maria of Anhalt. He received an unusually good education and studied briefly at the University of Jena before going to the court of Duke John Casimir of Saxe-Coburg. At the start of the Thirty Years' War he fought on the Protestant side under Mansfeld at Wiesloch and under the Margrave of Baden at Wimpfen in 1622, and with his brother William at Stadtlohn in 1623, all defeats.

He then served King Christian IV of Denmark until a severe defeat in Holstein in 1627, and was present at the Siege of 's-Hertogenbosch in the Dutch Republic in 1629. When Gustavus Adolphus landed in Germany he joined him, briefly commanding the Swedish life horse guard, and after the Battle of Breitenfeld led expeditions from the Moselle to Tyrol. At Lützen, after taking command, he killed a colonel who refused to lead a charge and won the victory at sundown.

In 1633, with the Swedish general Gustav Horn, he invaded Bavaria, and he was granted the former bishoprics of Würzburg and Bamberg with the title Duke of Franconia. A stern Protestant, he took heavy contributions from captured Catholic cities, and many German Protestants saw him as the saviour of their religion. Nördlingen in 1634 cost him the best of the Swedish army and his new lands. In French service from 1635 he sometimes followed French policy and sometimes his own. In 1638 he won at Rheinfelden, Wittenweiher and Thann and took Rheinfelden, Freiburg and Breisach, which he meant to make the capital of a duchy in Alsace promised to him by France.

His health was failing, and he died at Neuenburg am Rhein on 18 July 1639, at the start of a new campaign. The governor of Breisach, Johann Ludwig von Erlach, was bribed to hand the fortress to France, and Cardinal Richelieu absorbed his army and lands into the French crown. Bernhard was buried at Breisach for a time, and his remains reached Weimar only 16 years later.
bernhard-rothmann: Rothmann was born at Stadtlohn in Westphalia. In the late 1520s he became the leader of religious reform in Münster, preaching against purgatory, the use of images and the low morals of the priests. Censured by the Catholic bishop in 1531, he denied the authority of the Catholic Church, published an evangelical creed in January 1532 and won the backing of the city authorities. By the treaty of 14 February 1533 Münster was recognised as a Lutheran city.

In the summer of 1533 the Anabaptist disciples of Melchior Hoffman won him over to their rejection of infant baptism, which he preached from his pulpit at St. Lambert's church. The city council censured him, but his popularity with the craft guilds kept him safe. After Hoffman was imprisoned in Strasbourg, Jan Matthys declared Münster the New Jerusalem, and Rothmann was baptised on 5 January 1534. Under Matthys, who died in a failed sortie on Easter Sunday 1534, and then under John of Leiden as King of Münster, Rothmann was probably the most important theological voice of the movement.

His writings of 1534 were A Confession of Faith and Life in the Church of Christ of Münster, A Restitution of Christian Teaching, Faith, and Life in October and Concerning Revenge in December. Unlike many Anabaptists of his time he held immersion to be the proper mode of baptism, arguing from the Dutch words doepen and dumpelen, from the Scriptural passages that describe baptism as a burial or a washing of the body, and from Tertullian, Origen and Gratian's Decretum.

He accepted the whole Bible as the word of God, held the celestial flesh view of Christ taught by Kaspar Schwenkfeld and Hoffman, and saw the church as a gathering of baptised believers only. He first opposed the polygamy that John of Leiden introduced, then wrote in its defence, leaning on the Old Testament.

Rothmann may have died fighting when Münster was retaken in June 1535, or may have escaped in the turmoil. His body was not identified, he was apparently not among the small band of survivors around Heinrich Krechting that contemporary sources attest, and he was never heard from again. Pilgram Marpeck borrowed part of his Vermanung from Rothmann's Bekenntnisse of 1533, carrying his influence to the south German Anabaptists, and his view of the incarnation prevailed among Dutch Anabaptists in their first century.
bernkastel-kues: Bernkastel-Kues lies on the Middle Moselle in the Bernkastel-Wittlich district, roughly 50 km from Trier. It consists of four quarters: Bernkastel and Andel on the right bank of the river, Kues and Wehlen on the left. The Eifel shields the town from west winds, putting it in a rain shadow. Historically the most important economic sector has been winegrowing, mostly on steep slopes, and Riesling is the customary grape.

The earliest evidence of human habitation, from about 3000 BCE, was found at Kues. About 370 CE the Roman poet Ausonius wrote his poem Mosella. Bernkastel is first documented in the first half of the 11th century, when Adalbero von Luxemburg, provost of the monastery of St. Paulin at Trier, became its lord. On 29 May 1291 King Rudolph I granted Berrincastel town rights, which Emperor Louis the Bavarian confirmed in 1332. The castle, built then under the archbishops of Trier, took the name Landshut in the 16th century and burned in 1692, after which it remained a ruin.

Nikolaus von Kues, known as Cusanus, was born in 1401 in the house of the Moselle shipowner Henne Cryfftz, and in 1451 the St.-Nikolaus-Hospital for the poor was built. By the Golden Bull of 1356 Bohemond II became Elector, and legend says he was restored to health from serious illness by a glass of wine, which gave rise to the story of the Bernkasteler Doctor vineyard. From 1794 to 1814 the town was under French rule and in 1815 it passed to Prussia. The town in its present form was created on 1 April 1905 by merging Bernkastel with the winemaking village of Kues. In 1938 the synagogue was destroyed on Kristallnacht.

The medieval marketplace has gabled timber-frame houses of the 17th century, among them the narrow Spitzhäuschen of 1416, a fountain of 1606 and a Renaissance town hall of 1608. The Graach Gate is the only town gate still standing, and the ruins of Landshut castle, once a summer residence of the archbishops of Trier, are now a lookout over the Moselle valley. At Kues the late Gothic St. Nikolaus-Hospital, founded by Cusanus, holds his library, and its chapel holds his heart. About 7,794 people live in the four quarters. The town hosts a wine festival of the Middle Moselle each September.
bernt-notke: Very little is known of Notke's life. He was born in the small town of Lassan in Pomerania into a family from Tallinn; his father was probably the trader and ship-owner Michel Notke, his mother probably Michel's second wife Gertraut, from Visby. He seems to have spent part of his youth in Flanders, probably in the workshop of the tapestry weaver Pasquier Grenier in Tournai, where he learned to work on a large scale and to divide the labour of a workshop.

In the early 1460s he settled in Lübeck, where he first appears in the records of the city council on 14 April 1467, called a painter. In 1479 he bought a stone house on Breite Strasse. He spent 1491 to 1497 in Stockholm, holding for three years the office of mint master of the realm, and left after the end of the regency of Sten Sture the Elder. In 1505 he became Werkmeister of the Church of Saint Peter in Lübeck.

Notke headed a workshop that made tapestries, wooden sculptures and paintings, above all altarpieces combining sculpture and painting. Whether he was chiefly a painter, a woodworker or an organiser is unclear. His first known work, made between 1463 and 1466, was a Danse Macabre at least 26 metres long for St. Mary's Church in Lübeck, lost in the bombing of 1942 and known from a copy of 1701 by Anton Wortmann.

For Lübeck Cathedral he made in 1470–1478 a triumphal cross of 72 oak sculptures, commissioned by Bishop Albert Krummedik. The altarpiece of Aarhus Cathedral, inaugurated in 1479, was at 12 metres the largest in the Nordic countries. The high altar of the Church of the Holy Ghost in Tallinn, finished in 1483, was the first in the Baltic region to show a biblical scene in its central panel rather than a line of saints. The Saint George and the Dragon in Storkyrkan was commissioned by Sten Sture to mark his victory over Christian I of Denmark at the Battle of Brunkeberg in 1471.

Notke died in Lübeck in 1509; his wife had died before him, and they had two daughters, one named Anneke. Philippe Dollinger wrote that if any artist can be called Hanseatic, it is Notke, though others have called him a routine producer of altarpieces. His influence reached as far south as Lüneburg, and his pupils included Heinrich Wylsynck and Henning van der Heide, the most accomplished of his followers.
bernward-of-hildesheim: Bernward came from a Saxon noble family; his grandfather was Athelbero, Count Palatine of Saxony. Orphaned young, he was placed in the care of his uncle Volkmar, Bishop of Utrecht, who entrusted his education to the scholar Thangmar. Under him Bernward studied the sciences and the liberal and mechanical arts, and became skilled in mathematics, painting, architecture and above all in making church vessels and ornaments of silver and gold.

He completed his studies at Mainz, where Archbishop Willigis, Chancellor of the Empire, ordained him priest. He turned down a valuable post in his uncle's diocese to stay with his ageing grandfather. After Athelbero's death in 987 he became a chaplain at the imperial court, and soon afterwards the Empress-Regent Theophano made him tutor to her son Otto III, then six years old.

Bernward was the thirteenth bishop of Hildesheim. His years in office fell in the age of the Saxon emperors, whose family came from the region around Hildesheim and were related to him, and the city was then a centre of power in the Holy Roman Empire. He set out to give it an appearance to match, built many churches and other buildings, and revived a classical practice by having his name stamped on the roof tiles made under his direction.

He also fortified his see. The cathedral district received a strong wall with twelve towers, and further forts in the countryside guarded against raids by neighbouring Slavic peoples and against the pagan Normans, from whose attacks he defended his diocese.

Bernward died on 20 November 1022, a few weeks after the consecration of St Michael's Church, which he had built on a symmetrical plan with two apses typical of Ottonian Romanesque art in Old Saxony. He is buried in its western crypt, and his feast day is 20 November. Thangmar wrote his life, the Vita Bernwardi, though parts of it were probably added in the High Middle Ages.

The bronze doors he commissioned, now at St Mary's Cathedral, show the Fall of Man and the life of Christ and are related in some ways to the wooden doors of Santa Sabina in Rome. St Michael's Church and St Mary's Cathedral, with their treasures, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and churches in Hildesheim and Hanover bear his name.
berry-province: The name of Berry, like that of its capital Bourges, comes from the Gaulish tribe of the Bituriges, who settled in the area before Julius Caesar's armies conquered Gaul. Medieval Latin sources often call the region Bituria. Departments replaced the provinces on 4 March 1790, and Berry was divided between Cher in Upper (eastern) Berry and Indre in Lower (western) Berry, with some communes going to Allier, Creuse, Loiret and Loir-et-Cher.

Around 750 the King of the Franks created the Counties of Berry and Bourges. In 843 the County of Berry became part of the royal domain. It formed part of the County of Auvergne from 878 to 892 and was independent again in 893. In 972 the County of Bourges was reduced to a viscounty, and in 1101 it was annexed by France. The Seigneuries of Châteauroux and Issoudun were annexed into the duchy in 1221.

In October 1360 King John II of France created the title Duke of Berry for his third son, John of Poitiers. It passed to members of the senior royal family, a tradition of the House of Valois, until it merged into the royal domain in 1505 on the death of Duchess Joan of France. It was re-created in 1527 for Marguerite de Navarre, in 1686 for Charles de Bourbon, in 1754 for the future Louis XVI and in 1778 for Charles Ferdinand, Duke of Berry, whose assassination ended the title in 1820.

Under the Ancien Régime the governor of the province was a military commander. The first, Adrien Maurice de Noailles, was appointed on 14 March 1698 at the age of 19. In 1778 Louis XVI convened Berry's provincial assemblies and considered extending them to other provinces, but dropped the idea after the privileged classes of Berry opposed it. The region is known for the illuminated manuscript Les Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, and the writer George Sand lived much of her life at her estate in Nohant. La Brenne, once on the border with Touraine, is a protected natural area of many ponds and a Ramsar wetland.
bertalan-szemere: Szemere was born on 27 August 1812 in Vatta into a poor noble family that traced its descent to the 9th-century chieftain Huba. He studied at Miskolc, Késmárk and Sárospatak and wrote poems, published in the periodical Felső-Magyarországi Minerva, under the influence of Ferenc Kölcsey and Mihály Vörösmarty. After qualifying as a jurist in 1832 he served an apprenticeship in Pressburg, where he joined the Parliamentary Young Members' Group and argued for liberal principles.

In 1835 he travelled abroad, to Berlin, Amsterdam, Dublin, Lausanne, Paris and London among other places, and saw how far Hungary lagged behind other countries. His account, Utazás külföldön (Travelling abroad), finished in 1839 but held back by the censors until 1840, made his name and brought him membership of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences.

From 1841 to 1847 Szemere was a judge in Borsod county, and he sat in the Diet at Pressburg as one of the leaders of the opposition, serving as recorder of the Diet of 1847–1848. As interior minister in the Batthyány government in 1848 he organised the new parliament and founded the government's official newspaper, the Közlöny (Bulletin). He also went to Miskolc to reorganise the Upper-Tisza Legion after its retreat before Franz Schlik's attack.

From 2 May 1849 he was prime minister and minister of the interior under the regent Lajos Kossuth. His government ended martial law, worked on the emancipation of the serfs and on 29 July 1849 passed an act allowing the national minorities free use of their languages in local administration and education, in the hope of winning them to the revolution.

After the surrender at Világos, Szemere buried the Holy Crown with the sceptre, the orb and other regalia at Orsova on 23 August 1849, then fled to Turkey and settled in Paris. Austria sentenced him to death in absentia in 1851. In exile he attacked the revolution's leaders, Kossuth among them, in the pamphlet Magyar Emigráció, and wrote a travelogue, Utazás keleten. His support for the Compromise of 1867 further strained his relations with Kossuth.
He obtained a pardon in 1865 but was by then mentally ill. He died on 18 January 1869; his ashes were interred in Buda and on 1 May 1871 moved to a church in the Avas district of Miskolc.
bertha-of-kent: Bertha, also called Aldeberge, was a Frankish princess who became queen of Kent. She was the daughter of Charibert I and his wife Ingoberga, the granddaughter of King Chlothar I and the great-granddaughter of Clovis I and Clotilde. Her father died in 567 and her mother in 589, and Bertha was raised near Tours. Her marriage in 580 to the pagan Æthelberht of Kent was made on condition that she could practise her religion. She brought her chaplain, Liudhard, to England.

A former Roman church just outside Canterbury was restored for her and dedicated to Martin of Tours. It was her private chapel before Augustine arrived from Rome. The present St Martin's Church stands on the same site and keeps Roman walling in the chancel. UNESCO acknowledges it as the oldest church in the English-speaking world where Christian worship has continued since 580, and with Canterbury Cathedral and St Augustine's Abbey it forms Canterbury's World Heritage Site.

Pope Gregory I asked Bertha to convert her husband and reproached her for not having done so. When he sent the mission under Augustine in 596, he asked her to incline her husband's heart to give it a favourable reception. Augustine arrived in 597 and founded the Abbey of St Peter and Paul on land granted by Æthelberht. Without her support and the king's goodwill, the monastic settlements and the cathedral would probably have arisen elsewhere. In 601 Gregory wrote to Bertha, praising her faith and her knowledge of letters. Anglo-Saxon records give her two children, Eadbald of Kent and Æthelburg of Kent.

The date of her death, possibly 606, is disputed. Her legacy can be seen as the conversion of much of England to Christianity, since her prayers paved the way for the Augustinian mission. Canterbury marks her memory with the Bertha trail, 14 bronze plaques set in pavements from the Buttermarket to St Martin's Church, and with bronze statues of Bertha and Æthelberht by Stephen Melton, installed on Lady Wootton's Green in 2006. St Martin's Church also holds a wooden statue of her.
berthold-i-of-zahringen: Berthold rose quickly to become one of the most powerful counts in Swabia. The Salian emperor Henry III promised his follower the Duchy of Swabia, then held by Otto of Schweinfurt, but when Otto died in 1057, Henry's widow Agnes of Poitou gave Swabia in fief to Count Rudolf of Rheinfelden instead. In compensation for giving up his claim, Berthold received the Duchy of Carinthia and the March of Verona after the death of the Ezzonid duke Conrad III in 1061.

He was the only duke of Carinthia from the house of Zähringen. In Carinthia and Verona, like his Ezzonid predecessor, he was regarded as a foreign ruler and never really accepted by the local nobles; according to the contemporary chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld he was even declared deposed for a time in 1072/1073. During the Investiture Controversy, after Henry IV's Walk to Canossa in 1077, Berthold and Duke Welf I of Bavaria backed the election of his old rival Rudolf as anti-king. Henry IV then held an Imperial Diet at Ulm and gave Carinthia to Liutold of Eppenstein.

Berthold withdrew to his Swabian lands, where he had to fend off constant attacks by the king's forces. He died at Limburg Castle on 6 November 1078 and was buried at Hirsau Abbey, where he had supported the building of the monastery church under Abbot William. He married first Richwara and then Beatrice of Montbéliard, a daughter of Count Louis of Montbéliard.

His sons founded the lasting lines of his house. Herman I, who used the margravial title of Verona, founded the line of the margraves of Baden. Berthold II was Duke of Swabia in opposition to Frederick of Hohenstaufen from 1092 to 1098 and around 1098 reached an agreement with him, keeping the title Duke of Zähringen. Gebhard became Bishop of Constance in 1084. From 1112 Herman I's son Herman II ruled as margrave of Baden.
berthold-iv-duke-of-merania: Berthold was born around 1159, the son of Count Berthold III of Andechs and Hedwig of Wittelsbach. His father, a loyal vassal of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, had received the March of Istria on the death of the Sponheim margrave Engelbert III. The younger Berthold first appears in 1170, is named Count of Andechs in a deed of 1172 and was co-ruler of the march by 1175. He also ruled Carniola, where he counted as Berthold II. About 1180 he married Agnes of Rochlitz, daughter of Margrave Dedi III of Lusatia of the House of Wettin.

After Barbarossa deposed Henry the Lion, Berthold's maternal uncle Otto of Wittelsbach received Bavaria. Berthold took the ducal title of Merania, named for the Kvarner coast his ancestors had conquered in the 1060s. Merania covered the same area as the old Istrian march and was no separate entity, but the title made the Andechs princes of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1186 he went with Henry VI to Italy for his marriage to Constance of Sicily, and on the Third Crusade he was standard-bearer of the imperial army, leading the crusaders with Frederick VI, Duke of Swabia, at the Battle of Philomelion in 1190.

During the crusade it was agreed at Niš in 1189 that a daughter of his would marry Tohu, son of Prince Miroslav of Zahumlje, though the match seems never to have taken place. After Henry VI's death in 1197 he backed Philip of Swabia against Otto IV, whom Pope Innocent III supported. The house then held lands from Franconia to the Adriatic.

Berthold died on 12 August 1204 and was buried at the family monastery of Dießen in Bavaria. His son Otto I succeeded him as duke and became Count palatine of Burgundy; Henry II took Istria and Carniola; Ekbert became Bishop of Bamberg and Berthold Patriarch of Aquileia. His daughter Hedwig, wife of Henry I the Bearded of Silesia, was canonised in 1267.
berthold-iv-of-zahringen: Berthold was the son of Conrad I, Duke of Zähringen, and Clementia of Luxembourg-Namur, and succeeded his father in 1152. He also claimed the title of Duke of Burgundy, which he had agreed with Frederick Barbarossa to receive after the two had conquered the Cisjuran, or French, lands of Burgundy together, and after helping him in his Italian campaign of 1152.

The conquest of Burgundy failed, and in 1156 Barbarossa instead married Beatrice, daughter of the last Count of Burgundy of the House of Ivrea, which undercut Berthold's claims. In return Berthold was given the title of Rector of Burgundy and made overlord of the Transjuran, or Swiss, parts of Burgundy, with Geneva, Lausanne and Sion. His rivalry with Duke Frederick IV of neighbouring Swabia led him to fight on the side of Welf VI in the Feud of Tübingen (1164–1166), and in 1173 he became overlord of Zurich.

Berthold died on 8 December 1186. The necrology of the Abbey of Saint Peter in the Black Forest records that he gave five candles for the memory of John the Baptist. He was married to Heilwig of Frohburg, and they had three children.

His son Berthold V was the last Duke of Zähringen, after whom the counts of Kyburg and Urach inherited the family's possessions. A daughter, Agnes, married Count Egino IV of Urach, though the necrology of Tennenbach Abbey names her as the daughter of Berthold V. Another daughter, Anna, married Count Ulrich III of Kyburg; they were the maternal grandparents of King Rudolf I of Germany.
berthold-v-duke-of-zahringen: Berthold, also known as Bertold or Berchtold, was born in 1160, the son of Berthold IV, Duke of Zähringen, and Heilwig of Frohburg, and succeeded his father in 1186. Early in his reign he reduced the power of the Burgundian nobles and settled the Bernese Oberland and the area of Lucerne. He enlarged Thun, and Bern, founded in 1191, became the focus of his expansion.

After the death of Emperor Henry VI in 1198, Berthold was one of the candidates in the imperial election. He offered his nephews as hostages to the Archbishops of Cologne and Trier to win their support, but when he found that a majority had chosen the Hohenstaufen Philip of Swabia, he renounced his claim. In exchange he received territorial concessions in what is now southern Germany and northern Switzerland, consolidating Zähringen control of the Ortenau, the Breisgau, Schaffhausen, Breisach and All Saints' Abbey, and Philip paid him 3,000 silver marks.

In the same year Berthold crushed a rising of the Burgundian nobles, an event recorded on the gate at Breisach. In 1200 he began rebuilding the parish church of Freiburg in the Romanesque style; continued in Gothic from around 1240, it became Freiburg Minster. His attempt to reach the Valais failed at the Battle of Ulrichen in 1211, and the treaty signed at Hautcret Abbey on 19 October 1211 forced him to accept Savoyard suzerainty over the upper Valais.

Berthold married Clementia, daughter of Stephen III of Auxonne. Their son Berthold died before his father, in 1216, so when Berthold V died at Freiburg im Breisgau on 18 February 1218 the Zähringen line became extinct in the male line. The family's lands partly reverted to the crown, were granted imperial immediacy, or were divided between the houses of Urach, whose members became the counts of Freiburg, Kyburg and Fürstenberg.
bertolt-brecht: Eugen Berthold Friedrich Brecht was born on 10 February 1898 in Augsburg. His mother was a devout Protestant and his father a Roman Catholic who had been persuaded to have a Protestant wedding; his Pietist grandmother influenced him in childhood, and the Bible shaped his writing for life. At school he met Caspar Neher, who designed many of the sets for his dramas. Brecht had his first successes as a playwright in Munich and moved to Berlin in 1924, where he worked as a dramaturg. His collection of poems Devotions for the Home was completed with the help of the assistant Elisabeth Hauptmann and published in January 1927.

He fled Germany in February 1933, just after Hitler took power. After brief spells in Prague, Zurich and Paris, he and Helene Weigel accepted an invitation from the writer Karin Michaëlis to Denmark, and lived for six years in Svendborg on Funen, where guests included Walter Benjamin and Hanns Eisler.

In April 1939 he moved to Stockholm and then to Helsinki, where he co-wrote Mr Puntila and His Man Matti with Hella Wuolijoki. During the war he settled in Southern California as a screenwriter, under FBI surveillance. In September 1947 the House Un-American Activities Committee subpoenaed him; he testified and returned to Europe the next day, eventually settling in East Berlin, where he co-founded the Berliner Ensemble with Weigel.

Brecht developed his epic theatre by synthesising and extending the experiments of Erwin Piscator and Vsevolod Meyerhold, treating the theatre as a forum for political ideas. An epic play should not make the spectator identify emotionally with the characters; it should provoke rational self-reflection and a critical view of the action. Brecht thought that a climactic catharsis left an audience complacent, and he wanted audiences to recognise social injustice and to act on it outside the theatre.

He used techniques that remind the spectator the play is a representation and not reality, in the hope of showing that the audience's own reality is equally constructed and so changeable. He later preferred to call it dialectical theatre. He also wrote hundreds of poems, the last new collection published in his lifetime being the Svendborger Gedichte of 1939, and worked in collaboration with composers, designers and actors.

Brecht died of a heart attack on 14 August 1956, aged 58, and is buried in the Dorotheenstadt Cemetery in Berlin. According to Stephen Parker, he had had rheumatic fever as a child, which left him with chronic heart failure. Helene Weigel managed the Berliner Ensemble, which was devoted mainly to his plays, until her death in 1971. His aesthetic theories strongly influenced radical cinema of the 1960s and 1970s, in the work of Jean-Luc Godard, Rainer Werner Fassbinder and Nagisa Ōshima among others.
bertrada-of-laon: Bertrada was born between 710 and 727 at Laon, the daughter of Count Charibert of Laon. The Annals of St. Bertin suggest a connection through Charibert to the Merovingian dynasty, which would have helped Pepin the Short secure legitimacy after he deposed the Merovingian king Childeric III. She married Pepin, son of the Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel, around 740 or 741. They were too closely related for the marriage to be legal at the time, and the union was not canonically sanctioned until 749, after the birth of Charlemagne.

In 751 Pepin and Bertrada became king and queen of the Franks. In June 754 Pepin was crowned, and Bertrada, Charlemagne and Carloman were blessed by Pope Stephen II, a gesture that underlined the legitimacy of Pepin's rule. Pepin later gave military aid to the pope against the Lombards, and the Donation of Pepin created the legal basis for the Papal States. Pepin and Bertrada had eight children, of whom Charlemagne, Carloman and Gisela survived to adulthood. Gisela became a nun at Chelles Abbey.

After Pepin died in 768 Bertrada lost her title as queen. Charlemagne and Carloman inherited the two halves of the kingdom, and she stayed at court and often tried to stop quarrels between them. Her journeys between their courts and a diplomatic mission to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, show political agency. Against the written urging of Pope Stephen III she arranged for Charlemagne to set aside Himiltrude and marry Desiderata, a daughter of Desiderius. Charlemagne divorced Desiderata soon after Carloman died in 771, the only episode that Einhard says strained relations between mother and son.

After Carloman's death Bertrada retired to Choisy-au-Bac, where Charlemagne had set aside a royal house for her. She died there on 12 July 783 and Charlemagne buried her in the Basilica of St Denis near Pepin.

The nickname Bertha Broadfoot first appears in the 13th century, in Adenes Le Roi's poem Li rouman de Berte aus grands piés, which is probably fictitious; no contemporary source mentions a foot deformity. François Villon used the name in the 15th century, and she was adapted as the character Berthe in the musical Pippin, first staged in 1972.
bertrand-du-guesclin: Bertrand du Guesclin was born at Motte-Broons near Dinan in Brittany, the first-born son of Robert du Guesclin and Jeanne de Malmaines, whose family was minor Breton nobility, the seigneurs of Broons. His date of birth is unknown but thought to be 1320. His native language was Gallo. He first served Charles of Blois in the Breton War of Succession, which lasted from 1341 to 1364, against Jean de Montfort, who was allied with England. He was knighted in 1354, and in 1356–57 he defended Rennes against a siege by Henry of Grosmont with guerrilla tactics, which brought him to the attention of the Dauphin Charles.

When Charles became king in 1364, he sent Du Guesclin against Charles II of Navarre. On 16 May he routed an Anglo-Navarrese army at Cocherel. On 29 September 1364 at Auray, Charles of Blois was defeated and killed by John IV, Duke of Brittany and the English under Sir John Chandos. Du Guesclin broke his weapons to signal surrender and was ransomed to Charles V for 100,000 francs.

In 1366 he persuaded the leaders of the free companies, who had been pillaging France, to join an expedition to Castile in support of Henry of Trastámara against Pedro I. They took Burgos, and Henry was crowned there. Du Guesclin was captured again at Nájera in 1367, where the Black Prince's army beat Henry's, and was ransomed again. Du Guesclin and Henry then defeated Pedro at Montiel in 1369. Du Guesclin was made Duke of Molina.

Charles V recalled him in 1370 and invested him as Constable of France on 2 October, although the post usually went to a great nobleman, and aristocratic leaders were reluctant to serve under him. He defeated English forces at Pontvallain and reconquered Poitou and Saintonge. In 1373 he defeated the English at Chizé. He disapproved of Charles V's confiscation of Brittany in 1378, and his campaign against it was halfhearted.

Du Guesclin died of illness at Châteauneuf-de-Randon during an expedition in Languedoc in 1380. He was buried at Saint-Denis in the tomb of the kings of France, which was destroyed during the French Revolution, and his heart is kept at Saint-Sauveur in Dinan. He was known for avoiding major battles where possible, and of seven pitched battles he won the five that he commanded. Twentieth-century Breton nationalists considered him a traitor to Brittany, and statues of him in Rennes and Broons were destroyed. He appears in Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The White Company.
bertrand-russell: Russell was born on 18 May 1872 at Ravenscroft, a country house in Trellech, Monmouthshire, to John Russell, Viscount Amberley, and Katharine, Viscountess Amberley, both early advocates of birth control. His mother died of diphtheria in June 1874, followed shortly by his sister Rachel, and his father died in January 1876. He was raised by his paternal grandparents at Pembroke Lodge in Richmond Park, chiefly by his grandmother, the Countess Russell, whose progressive views on social justice and standing up for principle remained with him all his life.

He began at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1890 on a scholarship to read for the Mathematical Tripos, graduating seventh Wrangler in 1893 and becoming a Fellow in philosophy in 1895. His first major publication was An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry (1897).

Russell started in British idealism, the dominant philosophy of the time, but his friendship with G. E. Moore led him to analytic philosophy, and the two led a revolt against idealism. With Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica, published in 1910–1913. His article On Denoting has been considered a paradigm of philosophy. In 1916 he was convicted under the Defence of the Realm Act 1914 for his pacifist activity in the First World War and dismissed from Trinity. After a campaign by the Fellows, he was offered reinstatement and accepted it in 1920, but he resigned in 1921.

In August 1920 he visited Soviet Russia as part of a delegation and met Vladimir Lenin, whom he found disappointing. The visit ended his tentative support for the revolution, and he wrote The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism. He opposed rearmament against Nazi Germany, but changed his view in 1940 and in 1943 adopted a position he called relative political pacifism, that war may in extreme circumstances be the lesser of two evils. His History of Western Philosophy (1945) was a best-seller.

Russell is credited as one of the founders of analytic philosophy, and Willard Van Orman Quine named his work as a chief influence on his own. He made language a central part of philosophy and influenced Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gilbert Ryle, J. L. Austin and P. F. Strawson. In lectures of 1918 he set out logical atomism, the view that knowledge can be reduced to atomic propositions and their truth-functional compounds.

He argued that religion is largely harmful and was a member of the advisory council of the British Humanist Association. He became the 3rd Earl Russell in 1931 and held the title until his death on 2 February 1970.
berwick-upon-tweed: Berwick-upon-Tweed lies at the mouth of the River Tweed on the east coast, 4 km south of the Anglo-Scottish border, 90 km south-east of Edinburgh and 105 km north of Newcastle upon Tyne. Its name has the same origin as the word berewick, a portion of farmland detached from a manor for the lord's own use, from the Old English berewíc, meaning corn farm. The earliest recorded spelling, Berewich, dates from 1167, and the medieval town seal showed a bear and a wych tree as a pun on the name.

The town was founded as an Anglo-Saxon settlement in the Kingdom of Northumbria. It remained part of the Earldom of Northumbria until control passed to the Scots after the Battle of Carham of 1018. David I of Scotland, who reigned from 1124 to 1153, made it a royal burgh and county town of Berwickshire, and a mint was present by 1153. In 1174, after the defeat of William I of Scotland, the Treaty of Falaise ceded Berwick to Henry II of England, until the treaty was annulled in 1189 when William paid Richard I 10,000 marks.

By the middle of the 13th century Berwick was prosperous. William Edington, a bishop and chancellor of England, wrote that it was so populous and of such commercial importance that it might be called another Alexandria, whose riches were the sea and the water its walls. Its position on the border led to centuries of raids, sieges and changes of ownership. The last came when Richard, Duke of Gloucester, later Richard III, retook it for England in 1482.

The Treaty of Norham of 1551, ending the Rough Wooing, left Berwick in English hands and declared it a free town independent of either kingdom, although in practice England controlled it. Under Elizabeth I large sums, one source giving £128,648, were spent on fortifications in the Italian style, to which Sir Richard Lee and the engineer Giovanni Portinari contributed. After the Act of Union of 1707 Berwick stayed within the legal system of England and Wales.

Berwick is a market town in Northumberland and the northernmost town in England, with 12,043 inhabitants at the census of 2011. Its medieval walls, the Elizabethan ramparts, the Georgian Town Hall and the barracks built by Nicholas Hawksmoor in 1717 to 1721 survive, as do the ruins of the 13th-century castle and the Old Bridge of 1610 to 1624. Berwick Rangers Football Club and Berwick Rugby Football Club play in Scottish leagues.
bes: Bes, also written Bisu, was an ancient Egyptian deity, paired with a female counterpart, Beset, and probably of Nubian or C-Group origin. People in Upper Egypt venerated him long before those in Lower Egypt, which points to a southern origin. In Nubian the word bes means cat, and the god is regularly shown with feline features. The feathered crown he wears was also common dress in ancient Kush. Donald Mackenzie suggested in 1907 that Bes was a Middle Kingdom import from Nubia, whose cult spread widely only at the beginning of the New Kingdom, but figurines resembling Bes, thirteen of them at Tell el-Farkha, have since been found in deposits of the pre-dynastic Naqada period.

Bes is first mentioned in the Pyramid Texts but seems to have been best known and most widely worshipped in the Middle Kingdom. Evidence of his worship continues into Coptic Egypt, the latest being a jug showing Bes from Tell Edfu, dated to the 10th century CE.

Bes protected households and, in particular, mothers, children and childbirth. His tasks included killing snakes, driving off evil spirits and watching over children, and he was present with Taweret at births. Where Egyptian gods were normally shown in profile, Bes appeared in a full-face portrait, ithyphallic and sometimes in a soldier's tunic, ready to attack any approaching evil. Because he drove off evil, he also came to symbolise the good things in life, music, dance and sexual pleasure. Some modern scholars, among them James Romano, hold that in its earliest form Bes represented a lion rearing on its hind legs.

Images of Bes were kept in homes. From the Middle Kingdom he appears on masks, amulets, infant feeding bottles, magic knives, furniture, toiletries and game pieces, and many jugs and storage jars bear his image. In the New Kingdom dancers, musicians and servant girls wore tattoos of him on the thigh, as a wall painting of the 19th Dynasty from Deir el-Medina shows. In the Ptolemaic period chambers at Saqqara were painted with Bes and Beset, which Egyptologists think were used for curing fertility problems or for healing rituals.

His worship spread abroad. Beset was more popular in Minoan Crete, while Bes found favour with the Phoenicians and the ancient Cypriots. From the end of the 6th century BCE his image spread across the Achaemenid Empire, to which Egypt then belonged, and has been found at Susa and as far off as central Asia. Over time he came to be shown in Persian clothes and headdress. His cult reached Syria and the Balearic Islands as well.
besalu: Besalú is a town in the comarca of Garrotxa, in the province of Girona in Catalonia. Its name derives from the Latin Bisuldunum, meaning a fort on a mountain between two rivers. It was designated a historical national property, a conjunt historicoartístic, in 1966, and its urban layout is almost identical to the original one.

The town was most important in the early Middle Ages, as capital of the county of Besalú. The county had roughly the territory of the present Garrotxa, but sometimes extended as far as Corbières in the Aude, in France. In 894 Besalú became a county with its own dynasty. Wilfred the Hairy, credited with the unification of Catalonia, was Count of Besalú, and the troubadour Raimon Vidal was born in the town.
In 1111 Besalú lost its independence to the county of Barcelona. Centuries later the town entered a period of decline, made worse by wars with the French and the Carlist wars.

The emblem of Besalú is its 12th-century Romanesque bridge over the Fluvià, which has seven uneven arches and two towers, with a gateway at its midpoint. Parts of the old walls survive. The narrow streets nearest the bridge belong to the former Jewish quarter, where a mikveh, a ritual bath dating from the 11th or 12th century, is the only Romanesque one remaining in Spain, and the remains of a medieval synagogue lie near the river.

The church of Sant Pere was consecrated in 1003, and of the Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere only a three-nave church and one apse remain. Other monuments include the Royal Curia, the apse of Santa Maria and a tower of the old counts' castle, and the parish church of Sant Vicenç. Industry and tourism are now the main sources of income.
besame-mucho: The song was written in 1932 by the Mexican songwriter Consuelo Velázquez, and its title means "Kiss Me A Lot". She took her inspiration from a piano piece, "Quejas, o la Maja y el Ruiseñor", from the 1911 suite Goyescas by the Spanish composer Enrique Granados. Granados later included the same music as the "Aria of the Nightingale" in his 1916 opera of the same name. English lyrics for the bolero were written by Sunny Skylar, and Velázquez herself recorded it as a piano instrumental on her album Piano Interpretations in 1955.

The song reached a wide audience in 1944. It was heard in two films that May: Follow the Boys, released on 5 May 1944, in which it was played by Charlie Spivak and his Orchestra, and Cowboy and the Senorita, released on 13 May 1944, with a vocal by Dale Evans. The version by Bob Eberly and Kitty Kallen with Jimmy Dorsey and His Orchestra reached number one in the United States that year, and Andy Russell's recording reached number eight. As the song crossed the Atlantic in 1944, it became one of the most recognisable melodies of the decade.

Later recordings include those of Pedro Vargas, who was inducted into the Latin Grammy Hall of Fame in 2001, and Ray Conniff and His Orchestra and Chorus, who recorded it on 25 March 1960 for the album Say It with Music (A Touch of Latin). The Beatles played it at their Decca audition on 1 January 1962 and again at their first session at Abbey Road Studios on 6 June 1962. Dalida reached number five in France with it in 1976, João Gilberto recorded it for the bossa nova album Amoroso in 1977, and Luis Miguel included it on Romances in 1997. In 1999 it was recognised as the most recorded and covered Spanish-language song of all time.

In 1990 the song played a part in a Brazilian political scandal. A clandestine affair between two government ministers, Bernardo Cabral, the Minister of Justice, and Zélia Cardoso de Mello, the Minister for Economy, Finance and Planning, became public when the couple danced cheek to cheek to "Bésame Mucho" at a birthday party held for her. Cabral, a married father of three, was forced to resign. A few days later the regimental band of the presidential guard, Os Dragões da Independência, struck up the song as Cardoso de Mello received the Order of Military Merit, and its musical director was given three days' detention for insubordination.
besancon: Besançon lies in the north-east of France on the river Doubs, at the edge of the Jura Mountains, about 325 kilometres east of Paris. The old city developed in a natural meander of the Doubs, almost 1,000 metres across, known as la Boucle, closed on the south by a hill, Mont Saint-Étienne, which rises to 371 metres. Because the Alps rise abruptly to its south, the town had military importance from the 1st century BCE onward.

Tribes of Gauls settled the oxbow of the Doubs around 1500 BCE. The city is first recorded in 58 BCE as Vesontio in Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico, and it became an important city of Roman Gaul. It acquired a bishop's see in the 3rd century. The name became Besançon in 1243. The Treaty of Verdun in 843 made it part of Lotharingia.

In the 15th century Besançon came under the dukes of Burgundy, and after the marriage of Mary of Burgundy to Maximilian I it was in effect a Habsburg fief. In 1519 Charles V became its master as Holy Roman Emperor, and in 1526 the city won the right to mint coins, which it kept until 1673, all bearing the name of Charles V. French conquest followed in 1674. The Austrians bombarded the city in 1814, and the Germans occupied the citadel in the Second World War, executing some one hundred resistance fighters there.

Besançon is the capital of the department of Doubs and has about 120,000 inhabitants. Its university was founded in 1423, and it is the historical capital of watchmaking in France. Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban designed most of its fortifications, including the citadel across the neck of la Boucle, which are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site with eleven other sites as the Fortifications of Vauban. The Palais Granvelle, a Renaissance palace built for Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, chancellor of Charles V, now houses the Museum of Time.
bessarabia: Bessarabia is bounded by the Dniester to the north and east, the Prut to the west, and the lower Danube and the Black Sea to the south, and has an area of 45,630 square kilometres. It is mostly hilly plains and flat steppe, very fertile. About two thirds of it lies in modern Moldova, with the Budjak in the south and a small part of the Chernivtsi Oblast in the north in Ukraine. According to the traditional explanation the name derives from the Wallachian Basarab dynasty, who allegedly ruled the south in the 14th century; some scholars argue that it began as an exonym used by Western cartographers and was first used in local sources only in the late 17th century.

In antiquity the region was inhabited by Thracians and, for shorter periods, by Cimmerians, Scythians, Sarmatians and Celts. Greek settlers founded the colony of Tyras in the 6th century BCE, and the Roman Empire defeated the Dacian kingdom in 106 CE. From the 3rd to the 11th century it was invaded in turn by Goths, Huns, Avars, Bulgars, Magyars, Pechenegs, Cumans and Mongols. After the 1360s it was gradually included in the Principality of Moldavia, which by 1392 controlled Akkerman and Chilia. Stephen the Great ruled from 1457 to 1504 and built churches and monasteries near his battlefields, many along the Dniester. In 1484 the Ottomans captured Chilia and Akkerman, and in 1538 more land in the south.

By the Treaty of Bucharest of 28 May 1812 the Ottoman Empire ceded the land between the Prut and the Dniester to Russia, and the whole of it was then called Bessarabia. German settlers arrived from 1814, and Bulgarians and Gagauz settled in the south. The south returned to Moldavia in 1856, and Russian rule over the whole region was restored in 1878, when Romania exchanged it for the Dobruja. On 9 April 1918 its assembly, the Sfatul Țării, voted for union with Romania; the Soviet Union never recognised this. In 1940, under an ultimatum, Romania withdrew; it retook the region in 1941 and lost it in 1944, and the Treaty of Paris of 1947 recognised the border along the Prut.

When the Soviet Union dissolved, the Moldavian and Ukrainian republics declared independence in 1991 and kept the existing division of Bessarabia, so that most of it forms the core of Moldova and its northern and southern fringes lie in Ukraine. Chișinău, the former capital of the Russian Bessarabia Governorate, is the capital of Moldova.
bessarion: Bessarion was born in Trebizond, the Black Sea port in north-eastern Anatolia that was the heart of Pontic Greek culture. His baptismal name was Basil, and he took the name Bessarion on entering a monastery. He was educated in Constantinople and in 1423 went to Mystras in the Peloponnese to study Neoplatonism under Gemistus Pletho, with an emphasis on mathematics, astronomy and geography. His Neoplatonism stayed with him throughout his life, even as a cardinal, and he wrote to Pletho's two sons, Demitrios and Andronikos, on the death of his still-beloved teacher in 1452.

In 1436 Bessarion became abbot of a monastery in Constantinople, and in 1437 Emperor John VIII Palaiologos made him metropolitan of Nicaea and took him to Italy to seek a reunion of the Orthodox and Catholic churches. The emperor hoped to win help from Western Europe against the Ottoman Empire. Although Bessarion had first belonged to the anti-unionist party, he became the most eminent unionist in the Byzantine delegation to the Council of Ferrara-Florence, and on 6 July 1439 he read the Greek declaration of union in Florence cathedral. Some historians doubt his sincerity, but one has defended it from his own Oratio Dogmatica.

On his return East he was bitterly resented. Pope Eugene IV made him a cardinal on 18 December 1439, and from then on he lived in Italy. He was legate at Bologna from 1450 to 1455, was an early candidate at the conclave of 1455, and in 1463 received the ceremonial title of Latin Patriarch of Constantinople. He died at Ravenna on 18 November 1472 and was buried in the basilica of the Santi Apostoli in Rome.

His palazzo in Rome was a virtual academy of humanist learning and a centre for learned Greeks and Greek refugees, for whom he commissioned transcripts of Greek manuscripts and Latin translations. He is known as the original patron of Greek exiles such as Theodore Gaza, John Argyropoulos and Janus Lascaris. He translated Aristotle's Metaphysics and wrote a treatise against George of Trebizond, a vehement Aristotelian, entitled In Calumniatorem Platonis. Though a Platonist, he sought to reconcile the two philosophies. In 1468 he presented his library of 482 Greek and 264 Latin manuscripts to the Senate of Venice, where it became the core of the Biblioteca Marciana.
bessemer-process: Henry Bessemer later wrote that the idea came from a conversation with Napoleon III in 1854 about the steel needed for better artillery, during the Crimean War. At that time steel was used only for small items such as cutlery and tools and was too expensive for cannon. He began work in January 1855, filed his first related patent in October of that year and patented the method in 1856. The American inventor William Kelly had experimented with a similar method in the early to mid-1850s and was awarded a priority patent in 1857; whether both invented the same process remains controversial, and Kelly's version is thought to have been less developed.

Bessemer licensed the process to four ironmasters for £27,000, but they could not make steel of the promised quality, and he bought the licences back for £32,500. The fault lay in impurities in the iron. The English metallurgist Robert Forester Mushet found the remedy: burn off nearly all impurities and carbon, then add carbon and manganese in the form of spiegeleisen. Bessemer acquired Mushet's patent after it lapsed. Commercial production began in Sheffield in 1858, using imported Swedish charcoal pig iron.

Air is blown through molten pig iron in a converter, which oxidises silicon, manganese and carbon. The oxides escape as gas or form slag, and the heat of oxidation keeps the iron molten. The blow lasted about 20 minutes, and its progress was judged by the flame at the mouth of the converter. Carbon was then added back. A converter treated a batch of 5 to 30 tons, and converters usually worked in pairs. Bessemer himself used a ganister sandstone lining, the acid process. In 1878 Sidney Gilchrist Thomas, with his cousin Percy Gilchrist, patented a dolomite or limestone lining that removed phosphorus, giving the basic Bessemer process.

In the United States Alexander Lyman Holley secured a licence in 1863 for John F. Winslow and John Augustus Griswold, and a mill opened at Troy, New York. Andrew Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Steel Works opened in 1875, and most American Bessemer steel went into railroad rails.

Steel rails lasted ten times longer than iron rails and carried heavier locomotives. Quality problems, including brittleness caused by nitrogen in the air blast, kept Bessemer steel out of many structural uses, for which open-hearth steel was suitable. By 1895 observers in the UK judged the process to be in decline. The basic process lasted longer, especially in continental Europe, where ores were rich in phosphorus. Commercial Bessemer production in the United States stopped in 1968, and basic oxygen steelmaking, in essence an improved Bessemer process, replaced it.
bessus: Nothing is known about the background of Bessus except that he belonged to the ruling Achaemenid dynasty. Under Darius III he became satrap of Bactria, a prosperous and populous province in the east that had been under Achaemenid rule since 545 to 540 BCE. From there he ruled Sogdia to the north and the regions bordering India, and he kept the loyalty of the Iranian nomadic groups of Central Asia: the Saka, the Dahae and the Massagetae. The Iranologist Richard Foltz describes the eastern satrapies as practically his personal domain.

After the defeat at Issus in 333 BCE Darius III summoned Bessus to his aid. At Gaugamela in 331 BCE Bessus supplied Bactrians, Sogdians, Indians and Saka and led the cavalry on the Persian left wing. After the defeat he followed Darius to Ecbatana, where he conspired with the chiliarch Nabarzanes and Barsaentes, satrap of Arachosia and Drangiana. They arrested Darius in mid-330 BCE and chose Bessus to lead the forces, probably because of his descent. To gain time they killed Darius near Hecatompylus in July 330 BCE, and Alexander had the body buried at Persepolis.

In the autumn of 330 BCE, at Bactra, Bessus declared himself King of Kings under the name Artaxerxes V. His realm soon fell apart: Nabarzanes surrendered and was pardoned, and Satibarzanes was killed in 329 BCE. According to Diodorus Siculus, Bessus raised 8,000 Bactrians, but many dispersed when Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush, and he fled across the Oxus into Sogdia. At Nautaca his Sogdian officers, among them Spitamenes and Dataphernes, arrested him and handed him to the general Ptolemy. Bessus was flogged, and his ears and nose were cut off, a traditional Persian punishment. He was executed at Ecbatana under the supervision of Oxyathres, the brother of Darius. The Shahnameh tells of him as Janusipar.
bethel: Most scholars identify Bethel with the modern village of Beitin, in the West Bank, 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) northeast of Ramallah. Edward Robinson, in his Biblical Researches in Palestine, was among the first to propose this, on the strength of the location described in ancient texts and the similarity of the names. A minority view equates Bethel with al-Bireh, but those who worked on the excavations have hardly taken it seriously. In the 4th century Eusebius and Jerome described it as a small village 12 Roman miles north of Jerusalem.

The Hebrew Bible first mentions Bethel as lying near the place where Abram pitched his tent, close to Ai. In Genesis 28 Jacob, fleeing his brother Esau, sleeps on a stone and dreams of a ladder between heaven and earth; on waking he anoints the stone and names the place Bethel. Both accounts say its original name was Luz, a Canaanite name, and Genesis 35 makes it the site where Jacob's name was changed to Israel.

Later books show Bethel as a religious centre. In Judges the descendants of Joseph capture it, and the Israelites go there to seek counsel before attacking the tribe of Benjamin. The prophet Samuel is said to have made a yearly circuit of Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah. After the kingdom divided on the death of Solomon, about 931 BCE, Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan. The prophet Amos, about 750 BCE, spoke against the shrine, and its priest Amaziah expelled him.

Excavations by William F. Albright and James L. Kelso at Beitin, begun in 1934, found settlement from the Chalcolithic period. About 1750 BCE the site became a fortified Canaanite town, believed to be biblical Luz, with two city gates and a temple destroyed by an earthquake. The Late Bronze Age city was destroyed in the late 13th or early 12th century BCE. Bacchides the Syrian fortified the place in the time of the Maccabees, and Vespasian captured it in the summer of 69 CE.

Bethel appears on the 6th-century Madaba Map as Louza. A church there fell into ruin after the Rashidun conquest and was rebuilt by the Crusaders in the 12th century, when Baldwin V of Jerusalem gave the village as a fief to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. After Saladin's Ayyubid forces defeated the Crusaders in 1187 the church was destroyed and the village abandoned. The site stayed uninhabited for centuries, until the modern village of Beitin was established in the mid-19th century.
bethlehem: Bethlehem stands in the Judean Mountains at about 775 metres above sea level, some 30 metres higher than Jerusalem, which lies about ten kilometres to the north. The Arabic name Bēt laḥm means house of meat, while the Hebrew Bet Leḥem means house of bread or house of food. Beit Jala and Beit Sahour form an urban cluster with the city, and the refugee camps of Aida and Azza lie within its limits.

A possible earliest reference is in the Amarna correspondence of ancient Egypt, where Abdi-Heba, the Egyptian-appointed governor of Jerusalem, appeals for help in retaking a town near Jerusalem called Bit-Lahmi after attacks by Apiru mercenaries. The reading is uncertain and has met with objections. The Hebrew Bible names Bethlehem as the birthplace of David. In 2012 excavators in the City of David found a clay seal impression reading From the town of Bethlehem to the King, which they date to the 8th or 7th century BCE and take to have sealed a tax shipment.

The Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke place the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, though scholars regard the two accounts as contradictory and are divided on his actual birthplace. Under the Roman Empire Hadrian destroyed the city, and Constantine the Great later commissioned the Church of the Nativity in 327 CE. It was heavily damaged in 529 by Samaritans in revolt and rebuilt by Justinian I. In 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered it demolished, but local Muslims, who were permitted to worship in its southern transept, spared it.

Crusaders took Bethlehem in 1099 and replaced the Greek Orthodox clergy with Catholic ones. The Mamluk Sultanate demolished its walls in the mid-13th century, and the Ottoman Empire rebuilt them in the 16th. From 1517 the Catholic and Greek Orthodox churches bitterly disputed custody of the basilica. Bethlehem was part of Mandatory Palestine from 1920 to 1948, was held by Jordan after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War and was captured by Israel in 1967. Refugees from the 1947–48 war settled near the city and helped turn its Christian majority into a Muslim one.

Bethlehem is the capital of the Bethlehem Governorate and had 28,591 inhabitants in 2017. Its economy is closely tied to tourism and to pilgrimage to the Church of the Nativity at Christmas, and it is known for olive wood and mother-of-pearl carving, a craft said to have been introduced by Franciscan friars from Italy in the 15th century. Bethlehem University, founded in 1973, was the first university established in the West Bank.
betsileo: The Betsileo take their name, meaning the Many Invincible Ones, from King Besilau, who repelled an invasion by the Sakalava-Menabe kingdom in the 1670s. Their land runs from north of the Mania River to the foot of the Andringitra Massif, bounded by the Bongolava chain to the west and by the Eastern Forest of the Tanala to the east. Tradition divides it into the Northern Betsileo or Fisakana, the Central Betsileo or Manandriana, and the Southern Betsileo south of the Matsiatra River.

The Betsileo kingdoms, among them Fandriana, Fisakana, Manandriana and Isandra, existed independently of one another, with oral traditions reaching back to the 17th century. All were conquered and reorganised by Radama I. Many Betsileo were enslaved and traded within the island or sold to European slave traders. Radama made Fianarantsoa the administrative capital of the central and southern Betsileo and attached the north to Antsirabe, so that the Betsileo as a group took shape in the 19th century as an administrative division.

Betsileo society rests on a complex system of kinship, and most people are expected to join relatives in the family occupation; elders often hold more authority than officials. Status follows ancestry and was historically divided between andriana (nobles), hova (free commoners) and andevo (slaves), a term still heavily stigmatised, slavery having been abolished under French colonisation.

About 94% of Betsileo are Christians, mostly Protestant or Catholic, but ancestral traditions remain, among them belief in ancestral and nature spirits and in a creator called Zanahary, still invoked in ceremonies. The famadihana, the turning of the bones, in which ancestors' remains are taken from their tombs and wrapped in new linen, is still held. Diviners and astrologers set dates for ceremonies.

The Betsileo are of mixed Bantu African and Austronesian descent and speak a dialect of Malagasy. Their staple is rice grown in terraced paddies cut into the hillsides around Fianarantsoa, and the size and yield of a family's plot often marks its wealth. They are also known as woodcarvers of large sculptures.
bettino-ricasoli: Bettino Ricasoli, 1st Count of Brolio and 2nd Baron Ricasoli, was born in Florence on 9 March 1809. Left an orphan at eighteen with an estate heavily in debt, he was declared of age by special decree of the grand duke of Tuscany and entrusted with the guardianship of his younger brothers.
