He withdrew from his studies to Brolio and by careful management cleared the family possessions of debt.

In 1847 he founded the journal La Patria and addressed to the grand duke a memorial suggesting remedies for the difficulties of the state. Elected Gonfaloniere of Florence in 1848, he resigned because of the grand duke's anti-Liberal tendencies. He led the Moderate Party.

As Tuscan minister of the interior in 1859 he promoted the union of Tuscany with Piedmont, which took place on 12 March 1860. Elected an Italian deputy in 1861, he succeeded Cavour as premier. He admitted Garibaldian volunteers to the regular army, revoked the decree of exile against Mazzini and attempted a reconciliation with the Vatican, which the pope's non possumus made ineffectual. Disdainful of the intrigues of his rival Rattazzi, he resigned in 1862.

He returned to power in 1866 and refused Napoleon III's offer to cede Venetia to Italy on condition that Italy abandon the Prussian alliance. After French troops left Rome at the end of 1866 he proposed a convention under which Italy would restore to the Church the property of the suppressed religious orders in return for gradual payment of 24,000,000, and he conceded the exequatur to forty-five bishops. The Vatican accepted, but the Italian Chamber proved refractory and returned more hostile after he dissolved it. He resigned without waiting for a vote and thereafter practically disappeared from political life.

Ricasoli died at his Castello di Brolio on 23 October 1880. His private life and public career were marked by integrity and a rigid austerity that earned him the name of the Iron Baron. He is also credited with creating the modern recipe of Chianti wine; a formula of specific grape percentages is often wrongly attributed to him, but his switch of focus to Sangiovese as the lead grape had lasting implications for Tuscan and Italian wine. The firm Ricasoli 1141 still produces wine at Brolio.
betty-friedan: Betty Friedan was born on 4 February 1921 to Harry and Miriam Goldstein, whose secular Jewish families came from Russia and Hungary. Her father owned a jewelry store in Peoria, and her mother wrote for a newspaper's society page when he fell ill, a life outside the home that seemed much more gratifying. As a girl she was active in both Marxist and Jewish circles, and later wrote that her passion against injustice originated in the injustice of anti-Semitism. At Peoria High School, after her application to write a column was turned down, she and six friends launched a literary magazine, Tide.

After leaving Berkeley she became a journalist for leftist and labour union publications. She wrote for Federated Press from 1943 to 1946 and for the United Electrical Workers' UE News from 1946 to 1952, where she reported on the House Un-American Activities Committee. She married Carl Friedan in 1947, and was dismissed from UE News in 1952 because she was pregnant with her second child. She then wrote freelance for magazines including Cosmopolitan. Her biographer Daniel Horowitz argues that her feminism began in the 1940s, though she disputed this.

NOW grew from the failure of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. At a conference of state commissions on the status of women, delegates were not allowed to pass a resolution urging it to act, and they met in Friedan's hotel room, where she wrote the acronym NOW on a paper napkin. With Pauli Murray she wrote its statement of purpose. In 1970 she helped defeat the Supreme Court nomination of G. Harrold Carswell, and she supported the Equal Rights Amendment, which passed the House by 354 to 24 and the Senate by 84 to 8.

Friedan pushed the movement to concentrate on economic issues, such as equality in employment and business and provision for child care, and wished to lessen its emphasis on abortion and on rape and pornography. She opposed equating feminism with lesbianism and coined the term lavender menace at a NOW meeting in 1969. Her later books included It Changed My Life, The Second Stage, The Fountain of Age and Beyond Gender, and her autobiography, Life So Far, appeared in 2000. She died of congestive heart failure at her home in Washington, D.C., on 4 February 2006, her 85th birthday.
betwa-river: The Betwa rises in the Vindhya Range, near Raisen, just north of Hoshangabad, now Narmadapuram, in Madhya Pradesh. It flows northeast through Madhya Pradesh, enters Uttar Pradesh after flowing through Orchha, and meets the Yamuna in Hamirpur district, where the Yamuna flows northward and the Betwa approaches from the south. Nearly half of its course runs over the Malwa Plateau, and the river is not navigable. Of its length of 590 kilometres, 232 kilometres lie in Madhya Pradesh and 358 kilometres in Uttar Pradesh. Its Sanskrit name is Vetravati.

The Mahabharata mentions the river as Vetravati, together with the Charmanwati, both tributaries of the Yamuna. It was also known as Shuktimati, and the capital of the Chedi Kingdom stood on its banks. By an interstate agreement of 1973 between Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, the Betwa River Board was constituted under the Betwa River Board Act of 1976, with ministers of the Union and of both states as members. Dams on the river include Rajghat, Matatila, Parichha, Dhurwara, Halali and Sukma Dukma. The Indian Navy named a frigate, INS Betwa, after the river.

The Ken-Betwa River Linking Project was planned to transfer surplus water from the Ken River in Madhya Pradesh to the Betwa, through the Daudhan Dam and a canal of 2.5 km. The government said it would irrigate 1,060,000 hectares in drought-stricken Bundelkhand, supply drinking water to 6.2 million people and generate 130 MW of power, with completion expected in 2030 and a cost estimated at ₹440 billion.

Environmentalists warned that it would submerge nearly 98 sq km of the 543 sq km Panna Tiger Reserve. A 2019 expert panel appointed by the Supreme Court of India questioned its feasibility. Officials said all environmental clearances had been received. Ten villages were to be submerged and eleven more displaced, affecting over 7,000 families, mainly Gond and Kol, and residents protested.
bevagna: Bevagna lies in the flood plain of the Topino river, in the western part of the Umbrian valley and about 225 metres above sea level. It is 25 km south-east of Perugia, 8 km west of Foligno and 16 km south of Assisi. The Clitunno runs close to its ancient walls, and the Timia waters a fertile, well-cultivated plain. In antiquity Classical authors, among them Columella, Silius Italicus and Lucan, refer to the fertility of this valley.

As Mevania the town was an important Umbrian city on the Via Flaminia, between Carsulae and Fulginium. It was already a significant centre before the Roman conquest, and Umbrian forces were stationed there in 308 BCE when the consul Fabius advanced against them. Strabo lists it among the strongest Umbrian cities, and Pliny records that it was enclosed by brick walls and that its territory produced a prized wine called Irtia. Inscriptions show that it belonged to the tribus Aemilia and had quattuorviri among its magistrates.

The city suffered serious damage in barbarian incursions in the 6th century. After the 11th century it became a free municipality governed by consuls, and in 1249 Pope Innocent IV granted it the right to choose its chief magistrate. In November of that year the imperial vicar Thomas I of Aquino besieged and badly damaged it, in the context of Frederick II's claim to the Duchy of Spoleto.

It was under the Trinci family of Foligno from 1371 to 1439, when Cardinal Giovanni Vitelleschi returned it to the direct rule of the Holy See. From 1562 to 1566 its governor was Cardinal Charles Borromeo.

Under the Roman Republic of 1798 Bevagna was assigned to the Canton of Spello. The papal government was restored on 14 May 1814, Pope Leo XII granted the town the title of city in 1825, and in 1860 it joined the Kingdom of Italy.

Roman remains include a temple of the 2nd century, converted into the church of the Madonna della Neve, and the arcaded substructures of a theatre of the 2nd century, which shaped the later streets. A bath building preserves a floor mosaic in black and white of the same century, showing tritons, hippocamps, octopuses, dolphins and lobsters.

The medieval square holds the church of San Michele Arcangelo, with a façade of the early 13th century, the Romanesque church of San Silvestro, built by the architect Binello, whose plaque is dated 1195, and the Palazzo dei Consoli of the later 13th century, which has housed the Teatro Torti since 1886. Medieval festivals are held each year, including the Mercato delle Gaite in June, in which four quarters of the town compete.
beveridge-report: In 1940, during the Second World War, the Conservative Party entered a coalition with the Labour Party and the Liberal Party. On 10 June 1941 Arthur Greenwood, a Labour MP and Minister without Portfolio, announced an inter-departmental committee to survey the national schemes of social insurance and allied services, including workmen's compensation, and to make recommendations. Its members were civil servants from departments including the Home Office, the Ministry of Health, HM Treasury and the Assistance Board. Beveridge, a Liberal, drafted the report, with research and publicity by the mathematician Janet Philip.

The report set out three guiding principles. Proposals should not be limited by sectional interests, since, in Beveridge's words, a revolutionary moment in the world's history was a time for revolutions, not for patching. Social insurance was only one part of a comprehensive policy of social progress. Social security was to be achieved by co-operation between the state and the individual, leaving room for each person to provide more than a national minimum. Beveridge opposed means-tested benefits, which created high marginal tax rates for the poor. He proposed instead a flat-rate universal contribution in exchange for a flat-rate universal benefit.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Kingsley Wood, called it an impracticable financial commitment, but the Cabinet decided on 26 November 1942 to publish it on 2 December. In a poll in the following fortnight the British Institute of Public Opinion found that 95% of the public had heard of it. Archbishop William Temple of Canterbury praised it as an attempt to embody the Christian ethic in an Act of Parliament.

In the Commons debate of February 1943 the government said it would not implement the report at once, and 97 Labour MPs voted against the government. In a broadcast on 21 March 1943 Winston Churchill promised national compulsory insurance for all classes from the cradle to the grave after the war.

Labour won the 1945 general election promising to address the five giants, while Beveridge lost his own seat. The report was carried out mainly through the National Insurance Act 1946, the National Health Service Act 1946 and the National Assistance Act 1948, though Labour's leaders preferred a state-run health service to Beveridge's local health centres and regional hospital administrations.
beylerbey: Beylerbey, from the Turkic for 'bey of beys', also rendered 'commander of commanders' or governor-general, was a high rank in the western Islamic world in the late Middle Ages and early modern period. It began with the Seljuks, who used it in the Sultanate of Rum for the army's commander-in-chief, and it was also used by the Ilkhanids, the Golden Horde, possibly the Mamluks, and later the Safavids of Iran. Its Arabic equivalent was amir al-umara and its Persian equivalent mir-i miran.

In the early Ottoman state the beylerbey was a commander-in-chief held by princes of the dynasty: Orhan under Osman I, then Alaeddin Pasha and Süleyman Pasha. The change towards a governorship began when Murad I gave the title to Lala Shahin Pasha for capturing Adrianople, with military authority over the Ottoman lands in Europe (Rumelia). In 1393 Bayezid I named Kara Timurtash beylerbey in Anatolia, and the beylerbeyliks of Rumelia and Anatolia, soon joined by Rûm, were the first and most important.

A beylerbey ran a province, termed a beylerbeylik or vilayet, and after 1591 an eyalet. Provinces were divided into sanjaks under sanjakbeys. As the empire grew in the 15th and 16th centuries the number of beylerbeys rose to a peak of 44 by the end of the 16th century; a list of 1609 names 32 eyalets. Their size varied from two sanjaks to twenty. The beylerbey of Rumelia ranked first and, after 1536, held a seat in the Imperial Council.

Within his province the beylerbey acted as a virtual viceroy, with authority over war, justice and administration. It was limited by officials appointed from the centre, chiefly the fiscal secretaries and the kadı, and the Janissary contingents stood outside his command. He kept his own court and divan and could grant timars and ziamets, though after 1530 only the smaller timars. His chief duty was to maintain the sipahi cavalry and lead it on campaign.

From Mehmed II onwards beylerbey was also an honorary court rank, below the viziers; both were pashas, the viziers with three horse-tails and the beylerbeys with two. In the 18th century the Arabic title wali increasingly replaced beylerbey for governors-general, except in Rumelia and Anatolia, and the old titles became honorifics. The vilayet reform of 1864 made wali the only official title, and beylerbey survived only as the honorary rank Rumeli beylerbeysi.
beysehir: Beyşehir is a municipality and district of Konya Province, with an area of 2,054 square kilometres and a population of 77,690 in 2022. The town lies on the southeastern shore of Lake Beyşehir. The steep slopes and forests of the Taurus Mountains mark it to the west and southwest, while a fertile plain, an extension of the lake area, extends to the southeast. Its climate is dry-summer humid continental, bordering on Mediterranean, with very warm, dry summers and cold, snowy winters.

A Hittite monument at Eflatunpınar, a short distance northeast of the town, shows that the Hittite Empire reached this region, and marks the southwestern limit of its extension according to present knowledge. Evidence suggests an earlier settlement at Eflatunpınar, perhaps Neolithic. Another early settlement, Erbaba Höyük, 10 km southwest of the town, was explored by the Canadian archaeologists Jacques and Louise Alpes Bordaz in the 1970s and yielded finds from three Neolithic building layers.

The district corresponds to the Pisidia of classical antiquity. On the site of the town there was probably a Greek city, one view calling it Karallia, which was known as Claudiocaesarea in Roman times and Mistheia in Byzantine times. Another theory identifies it with Casae, the seat of a Christian diocese in the Roman province of Pamphylia, whose bishops appear in documents of church councils held from 381 to 879. Casae is now listed by the Catholic Church as a titular see.

By the first decades of the 13th century the ancient city had fallen into desolation, as the name Viranşehir, the desolate city, given by the Seljuk Turks suggests. The Seljuk Sultans of Rum, based at Konya, still built a summer residence on the southwestern lake shore, about 80 km from Beyşehir, which became known as Kubadabad Palace. It was a seasonal settlement of the sultans already in the late 12th century, and its most precious finds date from the reign of Alaeddin Keykubad, 1220 to 1237.

After the fall of the Seljuks the town was renamed Süleymanşehir for a time, in honour of a bey of the ruling Eshrefid dynasty, who made it his capital. Because the Eshrefid beys lived there, the name Beyşehir was gradually adopted. The dynasty built the Great Mosque, also called the Eşrefoğlu Mosque, between 1296 and 1299, and it is considered one of the masterpieces of the architecture of the Anatolian beyliks between the Seljuk and Ottoman styles.
bezeklik-caves: The Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves lie between the cities of Turpan and Shanshan, at the north-east of the Taklamakan Desert, near the ruins of Gaochang. They are high on the cliffs of the west Mutou Valley, a gorge in the Flaming Mountains in Xinjiang. The complex dates from the 5th to the 14th century, and most of the surviving caves belong to the West Uyghur kingdom, around the 10th to 13th centuries. There are 77 rock-cut caves.

Most caves are rectangular chambers with round arched ceilings, often divided into four sections, each with a mural of the Buddha, so that the whole ceiling seems covered by hundreds of Buddha murals. Some murals show a large Buddha surrounded by Turks, Indians and Europeans. Their quality varies from naive work to masterpieces of religious art.

The best-known are the large Praṇidhi scenes, which show Sakyamuni's promise made in a past life. Sogdians in silk robes appear as donors, as in Scene 6 from Temple 9, and the Uyghurs, who took over Sogdian writing and faiths, looked to the Sogdians as mentors. The painting shows a small Indian influence but owes more to Chinese and Iranian styles, particularly Sasanian Persian landscape painting.

The Buddhist Uyghurs of Qocho and Turfan were converted to Islam by conquest under the Chagatai Khanate ruler Khizr Khoja, who reigned from 1389 to 1399. Their descendants later lost the memory of this heritage and believed that the Kalmuks had built the Buddhist monuments. The murals suffered considerable damage. The local Muslim population destroyed all statues, defaced some paintings and smeared others with mud, often gouging out the eyes and mouths because of a belief that the figures might otherwise come to life at night. Pieces of mural were also broken off for fertilizer.

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries European and Japanese explorers found intact murals buried in sand, and many were removed and dispersed. The German explorer Albert von Le Coq took some of the best-preserved to Germany and was the first to study them, publishing his findings in 1913.

Large pieces, including the Praṇidhi scenes, were fixed to the walls of the Museum of Ethnology in Berlin and could not be removed for safekeeping in the Second World War, so they were destroyed when the museum was hit in bombing. Other pieces are in the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg, the Tokyo National Museum, the British Museum and the national museums of Korea and India.
beziers: Béziers stands on a small bluff above the River Orb, about ten kilometres from the Mediterranean coast and 75 kilometres south-west of Montpellier. It is a subprefecture of the Hérault department. The Canal du Midi crosses the Orb here by the Pont-canal de l'Orb, an aqueduct claimed to be the first of its kind. Its inhabitants are called Biterrois, after Baeterrae, the Roman name of the town.

Béziers is one of the oldest cities in France. Research published in March 2013 dates its ancient Greek colony to 575 BCE. The Romans refounded it as a colony for veterans in 36–35 BCE, as Colonia Julia Baeterrae Septimanorum, and it exported wine to Rome. It was conquered by Muslims and remained part of Islamic Iberia between 720 and 752. From the 10th to the 12th centuries it was the centre of a viscounty, whose rulers controlled the coastal plain and the main east–west route through Languedoc. The Trencavels ruled for 142 years, until the Albigensian Crusade.

Béziers was a stronghold of Catharism, which the Catholic Church condemned as heretical. The crusaders arrived on 21 July 1209 and offered the Catholics of the town the choice of handing over the heretics or leaving; many refused. The town was sacked the next day, and no one was spared, not even priests or those sheltering in the churches. The papal legate Arnaud-Amaury reported to Pope Innocent III that almost 20,000 people were put to the sword. The Cathedral of Saint Nazaire burned and collapsed on those inside. Other accounts give a handful of survivors.

The city was repopulated, and repairs to the cathedral began in 1215. Béziers joined the royal domain in 1247. In 1632 the Edict of Béziers abolished the privileges of Languedoc, restored in 1649. In the 18th century it prospered through vine growing. On 12 May 1907, 150,000 people gathered in Béziers to defend southern winegrowing, and in June soldiers of the 17th regiment, sent to Agde, mutinied and returned to the town.

The Gothic Cathedral of Saint-Nazaire, rebuilt in the 14th century, rises above the town; its nave is 32 metres high. The park of the Plateau des Poètes dates from 1867, and the allées Paul Riquet carry a statue of the creator of the Canal du Midi. Every August the town holds the Feria de Béziers, centred on bullfighting.
bhadarwah: Bhadarwah, also spelled Bhaderwah, is a town and a tehsil in the Doda district of the Jammu division. The name may derive from the Sanskrit Bhadarwasa, or from Bhadarkashi, a name given to the town for the ancient temple of the goddess Bhadrakali in the area. The twelfth-century Sanskrit chronicle Rajatarangini of Kalhana calls the area Bhadar Avkash, meaning a good resting place, and Bhadar Pura. Because its topography resembles the Kashmir Valley it is sometimes called Chota Kashmir, or little Kashmir.

Bhaderwah was ruled by its native rulers until the eighth century. In the tenth and eleventh centuries it came under Ananta and Kalsha of neighbouring Kashmir. Local hill chieftains of the Pal clan, said to be Chanderbansi Baloria Rajputs from Billawar, ruled from the eighth to the sixteenth century, beginning with Raja Radhik Pal, who is credited with building the Bhaderkali temple. According to folk history the ruler Nag Pal impressed the Mughal emperor Akbar with his spiritual prowess, an event commemorated each year at the celebration called Mela Patt on Naga Panchami.

By the end of the sixteenth century Chamba had annexed it. In 1820 Raja Pahadchand fought Chamba forces under Wazir Nathu and won, but Nathu attacked again with Sikh help and captured Bhaderwah. After the Treaty of Amritsar in 1846 the Chamba possessions west of the Ravi, including the principality, passed to Gulab Singh of the Dogra Kingdom of Jammu and Kashmir. In 1886 Maharaja Pratap Singh granted it as a jagir to his prime minister Amar Singh, and it passed to Amar Singh's son Hari Singh in 1912. The jagir ended in 1930, and in 1931 Bhaderwah became a tehsil of the Udhampur district.

The 2011 census counted 75,376 people in the tehsil and 11,084 in the town. Hindus formed 58.02 per cent of the tehsil, and 41.71 per cent were Muslim. Around 53 per cent gave Bhadarwahi as their mother tongue and 33.6 per cent Kashmiri. The town is known for fairs and festivals such as Mela Pat, for Kud dance and Pahari folk songs, and for heritage sites including the Ratangarh Fort, a Jamia Masjid and an ancient Vasuki Nag Temple.
bhadradri-kothagudem-district: Bhadradri Kothagudem is the largest district of Telangana, with an area of 7,483 square kilometres. Within the state it borders the districts of Khammam to the south, Mahabubabad to the west and Mulugu to the northwest. To the north and northeast lie the Bijapur and Sukma districts of Chhattisgarh, and to the east and southeast the Polavaram and Eluru districts of Andhra Pradesh. The district is rich in forest reserves and contains the Kinnerasani Wildlife Sanctuary, and its ground holds important minerals, coal above all.

Prehistoric people probably ranged over the lower Godavari valley around Bhadrachalam, Kothagudem, Pinapaka and Paloncha. Megalithic dolmens have been found at Janampet in Pinapaka, and the villages of Padugonigudem in Gundala have yielded megalithic remains discovered in recent exploration. Buddhist sites are known at Aswaraopeta and at Karukonda near Kothagudem.
The town of Bhadrachalam has a documented history centred on its Rama temple, built around the 17th century by Kancherla Gopanna, a saint-poet better known as Bhakta Ramadasu or Bhadrachala Ramadasu.

The district has two revenue divisions, Kothagudem and Bhadrachalam, 481 gram panchayats and five municipalities, and five constituencies of the Telangana Legislative Assembly. Aswaraopeta, Bhadrachalam, Yellandu and Pinapaka are reserved for Scheduled Tribes; Kothagudem and Aswaraopeta belong to the Khammam Lok Sabha constituency and the other three to Mahabubabad.

Mining and industry shape its economy. The Singareni Collieries Company, a government coal company owned jointly by the Government of Telangana and the Government of India, has its headquarters in Kothagudem. The Kothagudem Thermal Power Station at Palvancha is one of the coal-fired plants of the Telangana State Power Generation Corporation, and the Paperboards and Specialty Papers Division of ITC Limited works at Sarapaka near Bhadrachalam.

At the 2011 census the district had 1,069,261 inhabitants, about a third of them in towns. Scheduled Tribes made up 36.66% of the population and Scheduled Castes 13.42%. Telugu was the first language of 72.34% of the people, followed by Koya, Lambadi, Urdu and Hindi.
bhagadatta: In the Mahabharata Bhagadatta is the son of Naraka, or Narakasura, the king of Pragjyotisha whom Krishna had slain, and he is said to have been born from a limb of the asura Bashkala. He was a friend of Indra and an ally of Jarasandha, and from his father he inherited the Vaishnavastra, a weapon that protected him from being killed in battle. The Kalika Purana, the Harshacharita and other texts name Bhagadatta, Mahasirsa, Madavan and Sumali as sons of Naraka.

The epic also links him with the Yavanas. One passage of the Sabha Parva calls him the mighty ruler of the mlecchas who came with the Yavanas, and another, in K. M. Ganguli's translation, refers to him as the king of the Yavanas. The word Yavana is generally taken to come from Ionian, and in early Indian usage it commonly meant Greeks.

When Arjuna set out on a campaign of conquest before Yudhishthira's rajasuya sacrifice, Bhagadatta was among the first kings he met. After eight days in which Arjuna could not overcome him, Bhagadatta accepted defeat, being fond of Arjuna as the son of Indra despite his grudge against Krishna. He was later defeated by Karna during Karna's campaign of conquest for Duryodhana and forced to pay tribute.

In the Kurukshetra War he fought for the Kauravas, contributing one akshauhini of troops and leading the army of the Kiratas and Chinas. By then he was so old that he went into battle with his wrinkled eyelids tied up with a silken handkerchief. Mounted on his elephant Supratika, he caused Bhima to faint on the fourth day, was driven back by Ghatotkacha's illusory elephants, and on the twelfth day crushed Bhima's chariot and killed King Dasharna and Ruciparvan. Abhimanyu, Satyaki and others failed to stop him as he drove towards Yudhishthira.

Krishna then drove Arjuna against him. Bhagadatta knocked off Arjuna's celestial diadem and loosed the Vaishnavastra at him, but Krishna took the weapon upon himself, and Arjuna killed Bhagadatta. Arjuna then walked around the fallen king in pradakshina to honour his father's friend. Bhagadatta's son Vajradatta succeeded him as king of Pragjyotisha and was later killed by Arjuna; another son, Pushpadatta, was killed by Nakula, according to the Drona Parva.
bhagalpur: Bhagalpur, historically known as Champa Nagari, stands on the southern bank of the Ganges in Bihar, at the convergence of Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal. It is the headquarters of Bhagalpur district and division. The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary lies near the town, and the Kosi and Chanan rivers also cross the district.

The city is historically the capital of Anga, an ancient region. Jain tradition holds that all five auspicious events in the life of Vasupujya, the twelfth Teerthankar, took place at Champapur, and that Mahavira spent three rainy-season retreats there. Its main Jain temple is said to be about 2,500 years old. Champa is also the setting of the story of Behula and Lakhinder, told in medieval Bengali works such as the Mansamangal, many of which were produced between the thirteenth and the eighteenth centuries.

At Antichak village lie the excavated ruins of the Vikramshila Mahavihara. Emperor Dharmapala of the Pala Empire established it as an international centre of learning, with Tantric studies among its fields, and it was considered on a par with Nalanda. Bhaktiyar Khilji destroyed it. The Khanqah-e-Shahbazia, founded in 1577, holds the grave of the saint Maulana Shahbaz Muhammad, and its library includes a Qur'an copied by Murshid Quli Khan, the Nawab of Murshidabad.

Bhagalpur is known as the Silk City, after the silk trade of ancient Champanagari. The 2011 census gave its urban agglomeration 410,210 people, making it the third largest city of Bihar. Hinduism is the majority religion, followed by Islam, and Angika is the main language of the district, with Hindi, Bengali, Urdu and Santhali also spoken. Its festivals include a Kali Puja procession so long that one phase of immersing the images takes 36 hours, and the Manasa or Bishari Puja.
bhagat-singh: Bhagat Singh was born into a Punjabi Jat Sikh family in the village of Banga, in the Lyallpur district of the Punjab, then in British India and now in Pakistan. He was the second of seven children of Vidyavati and Kishan Singh Sandhu. His father and his uncle Ajit Singh took part in progressive politics, including the agitation of 1907 around the Canal Colonisation Bill and later the Ghadar Movement. After the village school he attended the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic School in Lahore, and in 1923 he joined the National College there, which Lala Lajpat Rai had founded two years earlier in response to Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement.

When the Simon Commission visited Lahore on 30 October 1928, Lajpat Rai led a march against it. The superintendent of police, James A. Scott, ordered a lathi charge and personally assaulted Rai, who died of a heart attack on 17 November. Singh, a prominent member of the Hindustan Republican Association, probably did much to change its name to the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. On 17 December 1928 he and Shivaram Rajguru shot John P. Saunders, who had left the District Police Headquarters; the postmortem found eight bullet wounds. Chandra Shekhar Azad shot dead Head Constable Channan Singh, who had given chase. Bhagat Singh escaped by train, with his hair cut and wearing Western dress, passing as a married couple with Durgawati Devi.

In 1929 he proposed a dramatic act to gain publicity: a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly, nominally against the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Dispute Act. After it was thrown on 8 April, he and Batukeshwar Dutt dropped leaflets and were arrested. In the jail he joined Jatin Das in a hunger strike for better conditions, and Das died of starvation in September 1929.

Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were sentenced to death in the Lahore conspiracy case and hanged in the Lahore jail on 23 March 1931, 11 hours ahead of the schedule of 24 March. Their bodies were cremated in secret near Ganda Singh Wala village and the ashes thrown into the Sutlej. He had written that he held human life sacred, but that force used for a legitimate cause was morally justified, and he declined to sign a draft letter for clemency.

An atheist, he read Bakunin, Marx, Lenin and Trotsky, and in his last testament named a Marxist basis for social reconstruction. Jawaharlal Nehru wrote that he became popular because he seemed to vindicate the honour of Lajpat Rai, and that the act was forgotten while the symbol remained. A bronze statue of him was installed in the Parliament of India on 15 August 2008. Communists, Hindu nationalists and others have each claimed his memory.
bhagavad-gita: The Sanskrit title means 'God's song'. Indian tradition attributes the Gita, like the Mahabharata of which it is a part, to the sage Vyasa, and a Hindu legend says that Ganesha wrote it down using one of his broken tusks. Modern scholarship regards it as a composite work by several authors that draws on the Upanishads and the Samkhya school. It is generally dated to the second or first century BCE, though estimates run from 400 to 500 BCE to the first century CE. It stands in the Bhishma Parva, the sixth book of the Mahabharata, and is often studied on its own in eighteen chapters.

The text is a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, just before the Kurukshetra War. Seeing relatives, friends and teachers in the opposing army, Arjuna drops his bow and doubts whether he should fight. Krishna's answers form the rest of the work. He argues that one should follow one's dharma without regarding oneself as the agent of the action, and that action and renunciation are inseparable. The poem offers three disciplines, jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion) and karma (action), and does not exclude any of them. In the eleventh chapter Krishna shows Arjuna his universal form.

The 700 verses are mostly in the anushtubh metre, with eight syllables to each quarter-verse, and the tristubh metre appears at dramatic moments. Its manuscripts exist in many Indic scripts and vary little compared with those of the rest of the Mahabharata.

The Gita is part of the Prasthanatrayi, with the Upanishads and the Brahma Sutras, the foundational texts of Vedanta. The oldest surviving commentary is that of Adi Shankara, about 800 CE, who read it as a text of non-dualism. Ramanuja, in the eleventh and early twelfth centuries, read it as qualified monism, and Madhvacharya, about 1250, as a doctrine of the fundamental difference between the soul, Vishnu and the world. Modern commentators include Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Mahatma Gandhi and Sri Aurobindo.

Persian translations were made under the Mughal Empire in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Charles Wilkins published the first English translation in 1785, and French, German and Russian versions followed. The text has also been debated: B. R. Ambedkar criticised its defence of varna duty and of the warrior's duty to fight, while others read the battlefield as an allegory of the struggle within.
bhagavata-purana: Bhagavata means follower or worshipper of Vishnu, and Purana means ancient or old traditional history. The text calls Krishna Bhagavan, the Blessed One. Many Indologists give no precise date for the Puranas, because their material was passed on orally, and a date applies only to the text as it now stands. Sheridan, in a study of 1986, dated its composition between 500 and 1000 CE and argued that a version must have existed by 1030, when al-Biruni mentions it. Many scholars, Hardy among them, date its final redaction to the 9th or early 10th century. The oldest surviving manuscript dates to c. 1124-25 and is held in Varanasi.

The twelve books consist of interwoven dialogues. The main reciter is Suka, who speaks to King Pariksit and quotes an earlier speaker, Narada, addressing King Yudhisthira; the text says that the first speaker was its composer, Vyasa, whose son Suka is. The first book opens at the onset of the Kali Yuga with sages performing a thousand-year sacrifice in the forest of Naimisaranya. Later books cover creation, genealogies, avatars of Vishnu such as Rama and Parashurama, and the destruction of the Yadu dynasty. The tenth book, of 90 chapters, tells of Krishna's life.

Its theology uses Vedanta and Samkhya in the service of bhakti. Traditions of Vedanta, among them the Advaita of Adi Shankara, the qualified monism of Rāmānujachārya, the dualism of Madhavacharya and the Bhedābheda of Vallabha and Caitanya, have each read its verses through their own commentaries.

The Bhagavata Purana is widely recognised as the best known and most influential of the Puranas and is called the Fifth Veda. It is among the most commented texts in Indian literature: over eighty medieval commentaries in Sanskrit alone are known, and a version exists in almost every Indian language. Its legends are retold in festivals such as Holi and Diwali, it inspired Ras Leela, dramatic enactments of Krishna's pastimes, and it played a significant part in the Krishna-bhakti movement of Chaitanya in Bengal.

A French translation of a Tamil version appeared in 1788, and the Bhagavata was the first Purana translated into a European language. In the 20th century it spread beyond India and was translated into over twenty languages.
bhaja-caves: The caves are cut 400 feet above the village of Bhaja, on an important ancient trade route that ran from the Arabian Sea east into the Deccan Plateau. They belong to the Early Buddhist schools of Maharashtra and share their architectural design with the Karla Caves; the Bedse Caves lie some 9 km to the east. Eight inscriptions survive, some naming donors. Two on a wooden beam date to the 2nd century BCE. The stupas carry the names of the resident monks who died at Bhaja, among them Ampinika, Dhammagiri and Sanghdina, styled Theras, and one is inscribed Stavirana Bhadanta, the venerable reverend.

The chief excavation is the chaitya hall, Cave XII, perhaps the earliest that survives. It is an apsidal hall 59 feet long and 26 feet 8 inches wide, its nave divided from a narrow aisle by 27 octagonal shafts and ending in a stupa 11 feet across. The columns slope inwards in imitation of the wooden posts needed to hold up a roof, and the barrel-vaulted ceiling still holds ancient wooden ribs. A wooden facade, now lost, once fronted it, with a large horseshoe-shaped window over the doorway and a portico carved to look like a many-storeyed mansion with balconies and onlookers.

A group of 14 stupas, five inside and nine outside an irregular excavation, are relics of monks; two have a relic box on top. The smaller caves are mostly viharas with cells and stone benches. Cave VI was the gift of Bodhi, a ploughman's wife, whose name is cut on a cell door, and Cave XIX has guardian figures at its door and reliefs of Surya in a chariot and Indra on an elephant.

The sculptures show elaborate headdresses, garlands and jewellery and may once have been brightly painted before being covered with plaster. As in early Buddhism generally, the Buddha was at first shown by symbols. One carving of about 200 BCE shows a woman playing a drum identified as the tabla, then called pushkara, beside another woman dancing. The inscriptions and the cave temple are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a Monument of National Importance.
bhaja-govindam: Tradition attributes to Adi Shankara the twelve verses that follow the opening stanza, known as the Dvadasa-manjarika-stotram. Fourteen further verses, the Caturdasa-manjarika-stotram, are attributed to fourteen of his disciples. Editions of the poem differ in the number, order, wording and arrangement of the stanzas, though the essential meaning of the verses stays the same.

A traditional story tells how the hymn came to be written. Adi Shankara, walking with his disciples along a street in Varanasi, met an elderly scholar reciting over and over the rules of Sanskrit grammar of Panini. Taking pity on him, Shankara advised the old man not to spend his remaining years on grammar but to turn his mind to God in worship, which alone could save him from the cycle of life and death, and the hymn is said to have been composed on that occasion.

The poem holds that bhakti, devotion, matters alongside jñāna, knowledge, as the bhakti movement emphasised. It urges the renunciation of egotistical differences and surrender to God as the way to spiritual development and to liberation from the cycle of birth and death. C. Rajagopalachari wrote in his commentary that knowledge which has matured is spoken of as devotion, and that knowledge which does not become devotion is useless tinsel.

The core of the composition is in a moraic metre, mātrāchandas, in which each line is measured by syllabic instants rather than by a fixed number of syllables. Scholars identify it as mātrāsamaka; apart from the first verse, every verse has 16 mātrās, fitting the description of the padakulakam in the vrtta-ratnakara.

The poem is a reminder that Adi Shankara, often regarded as the reviver of the jnana marga, the path of knowledge to moksha, also taught the bhakti marga, the path of devotion, towards the same goal. Many scholars hold that it sums up, briefly and simply, the substance of the Vedantic thought of his other works. Because its refrain invokes God in the aspect of Krishna, it is popular not only with the Smarthas, Shankara's immediate followers, but also with Vaishnavas and others.
bhakra-dam: The Bhakra-Nangal multipurpose dams were among the earliest river valley schemes India undertook after independence, though the project had been conceived long before. Sir Chhotu Ram, widely regarded as the father of the dam, conceived the idea in early 1923, and as revenue minister of Punjab he signed the agreement for the project with the Raja of Bilaspur in November 1944. The plan was finalised on 8 January 1945, preliminary works began in 1946 and construction of the dam started in 1948.

Work had first been begun under Sir Louis Dane, Lieutenant Governor of Punjab, but was delayed and restarted after independence under the chief architect Rai Bahadur Kunwar Sen Gupta. When a lack of funds nearly forced the American engineer Harvey Slocum to abandon the project, the contractor Sir Sobha Singh paid for it with his own money and the help of Kamani Engineering.

Most of the builders were Indian, joined by Slocum and many workers from the Bull Shoals Dam project in the United States, for whom a small city was built. On 17 November 1955 Nehru poured the first bucket of concrete into the dry bed of the Sutlej as a symbolic start, calling the dam a gift from its workers to the people of India.

The dam stands in a gorge between the hills of Naina Devi and Ramgarh, where the river once ran through a narrow pass, near the original Bhakra village, now submerged. It is 226 m high and 518.25 m long, and its reservoir, named Gobind Sagar after Guru Gobind Singh, is about 90 km long and stores up to 9.34 billion cubic metres of water. The Nangal Dam, a barrage about 10 km downstream, is a separate structure, though the two are often named together. Four spillway gates are opened only when the reservoir exceeds its maximum level.

The project was meant to prevent floods in the Satluj-Beas valley, irrigate the neighbouring states and generate electricity. Through the Nangal Hydel Channel and the Bhakra Main Line its water irrigates 10 million acres in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, and its two power houses, with generators first supplied by Hitachi and the Soviet Union, have a total capacity of 1325 MW. The Bhakra Beas Management Board, constituted in 1966 and renamed in 1976, runs the dam. The reservoir submerged about 371 villages of Bilaspur district, and fifty years after completion the full resettlement of those displaced remained an open question.
bhaktapur: Bhaktapur lies in the eastern corner of the Kathmandu Valley and is a major Newar settlement. Locally it is called Khwopa, and it was historically known as Bhadgaon. The name Bhaktapur, first attested in an inscription of 928, is widely held to be a Sanskrit rendering of the older Newar name Khōpring, from words meaning cooked rice and village, which appears in a Licchavi inscription of 594. Folklore says the valley was once a lake, drained when the Bodhisattva Manjushri cut a gorge with his sword; the Swiss geologist Toni Hagen showed that it was indeed a lake, which began to drain about thirty thousand years ago.

The 14th-century Gopal Raj Vamshavali credits Ananda Deva, who ruled from 1146 to 1167, with founding the city, probably by joining earlier settlements, and with making it the capital with a royal court, Tripura Rājkula. Shrines of eight Matrikas around the city and that of Tripura Sundari at the centre make the whole town a sacred mandala. As seat of government Bhaktapur attracted invasions, because divisions in the royal family brought in Tirhut and the Khasa Kingdom. Rudra Malla married his sister to the king of Tirhut in the 1310s to end its attacks.

After Nepal Mandala divided into three kingdoms, Bhaktapur stayed a wealthy and powerful Newar kingdom, helped by its place on the India-Tibet trade route. Queen Ganga Devi, the only queen regnant, ruled jointly with her two sons, and under her it reached its territorial zenith. In 1769 the Gorkha Kingdom annexed Bhaktapur, which lost importance to Kathmandu and Lalitpur and stayed isolated. After 1846 Dhir Shumsher Rana, as mayor, had many old palaces demolished and replaced with buildings in British style.

Bhaktapur is predominantly Hindu, and about 90 per cent of its people are Newar. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979. The Nyatapola, a five-roofed pagoda completed in 1702 and commissioned by King Bhupatindra Malla, stands in Taumadhi Square, and Durbar Square holds the palace complex and the stone temples of Vatsala Devi and Siddhi Lakshmi. The city has about 104 hitis, carved water spouts, and 50 artificial ponds, the two oldest built in 1118 and 1168.
bhamo: Bhamo, also spelt Banmaw, is a city in Kachin State in northern Myanmar, 186 km south of the state capital Myitkyina. It stands on the Ayeyarwady River and lies within 65 km of the border with Yunnan Province, China. Its name comes from the Shan place name Man Maw, meaning potter's village or village of jars. It has also been called Hsinkai in Chinese. Its people are mainly of Chinese or Shan descent, with Kachin peoples mostly in the hills round the town. It is the administrative centre of Bhamo District and Bhamo Township.

Bhamo was once called Sampanago, capital of the now-extinct Shan predecessor kingdom of Man Maw. The ruins of the old city walls, dating from the fifth century, lie some 5 km from the modern town. From 1869 to 1879 it was the seat of a British colonial assistant political agent, subordinate to the Resident with the king at Ava. In the early twentieth century its position at the highest navigable point of the river made it part of the caravan routes that carried jade from India to China.

Bhamo is the terminus of river ferries from Mandalay, and there is no ferry between it and Myitkyina. It is one of the official border trading towns between China and Myanmar. Three universities stand there: Banmaw University, the Technological University and the University of Computer Science. The climate lies between tropical savanna and humid subtropical, with a dry season from November to April and a wet season from May to October.
bharatas: The Bharatas lived in the latter half of the second millennium BCE. Their name, of Indo-Aryan and Indo-Iranian origin, means bearers or carriers. The earliest place the hymns associate with them is the Sarasvatī River: two Bharatas, Devaśravas Bhārata and Devavāta Bhārata, are said to have lived near the Āpayā, Sarasvatī and Dr̥ṣadvatī rivers, and Devavāta's son Sṛñjaya Daivavāta defeated the Turvaśas. His victory and Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna's over the Vṛcīvants are placed on the Hariyūpiyā and Yavyāvatī rivers, identified with the modern Hali-āb and Zhob.

Under the chieftain Divodāsa Atithigva the Bharatas moved through the Hindu Kush. Divodāsa, said to have been given by the river goddess Sarasvatī to Vadhryaśva, who adopted him, defeated the mountain chief Śambara in the autumn of the fortieth year of campaigning, after destroying ninety-nine of his forts. He also fought the Yadu-Turvaśas. Several Rigvedic poets describe a patron and client bond between Divodāsa and the Bharadvāja family of poets, who received part of the booty taken from Śambara.

Divodāsa's descendant Sudās Paijavana led the Bharatas across the Vipāś and Śutudrī, the modern Beas and Sutlej, first with the priest Viśvāmitra Gāthina and later with Vasiṣṭha Maitrāvaruṇi. In the Battle of the Ten Kings, fought on the Paruṣnī (Ravi) near Mānuṣa, the Tṛtsu-Bharatas faced a coalition that probably included the Pūrus, once their overlords, along with the Yadu, Matsyas, Druhyus, Anu and others. The hymns stress how outnumbered Sudās was; he won by breaching a natural dyke on the river and drowning many of his enemies, a victory credited to Indra, the patron god of the Bharatas. The fighting probably moved to the Yamunā, where the chieftain Bheda was beaten.

Afterwards the Bharatas held the whole of the Pūru lands around the Sarasvatī, and Sudās marked his victory with the Aśvamedha horse sacrifice. A realignment between Pūrus and Bharatas probably followed, since the core of the Rigveda holds hymns of both sides, and the initial compilation of the Rigveda was carried out after the battle. No descendant of Sudās is clearly named in the Rigveda.

The Bharatas and other Pūru clans eventually formed the Kuru kingdom, the first attested state in Indian history, though the gap between the Rigveda and the later Vedas leaves no record of how this happened. In the Mahabharata the ancestor of the Kurus becomes Emperor Bharata, whose realm is called Bhārata, and Bhārata is today an official name of the Republic of India.
bharatiya-janata-party: The party's origins lie in the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, founded in 1951 by Shyama Prasad Mukherjee in collaboration with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and widely regarded as its political arm. Its aims included protecting India's Hindu cultural identity and countering what it saw as the appeasement of Muslims and of Pakistan by the Congress party under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. The RSS lent it several full-time workers, among them Deendayal Upadhyaya, who became General Secretary. The Jana Sangh won three Lok Sabha seats in 1952 and kept a minor presence in parliament until 1967.

After Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a state of emergency in 1975, thousands of Jana Sangh members were imprisoned in the protests. In 1977 the party merged with the Socialist Party, the Congress (O) and the Bharatiya Lok Dal to form the Janata Party, which won a majority and formed a government under Morarji Desai. The former Jana Sangh supplied 93 of its seats, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee became Minister of External Affairs.

The Janata Party dissolved in 1980, and the former Jana Sangh members formed the Bharatiya Janata Party, with Vajpayee as its first president. It first softened the Hindutva stance of its predecessor and stressed Gandhian socialism, and won only two Lok Sabha seats in 1984, an election held soon after Indira Gandhi's assassination, when the Congress won 414 seats. The party then grew through the Ram Rath Yatra in Uttar Pradesh and victories in several state elections, and in 1996 became the largest party in parliament; its government under Vajpayee lasted 13 days.

After the 1998 election the BJP led a coalition, the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), and Vajpayee returned as Prime Minister. The coalition broke up in May 1999 when J. Jayalalithaa withdrew her support, and fresh elections followed. The next NDA government under Vajpayee served a full term, the first non-Congress government to do so, and lost the 2004 election. In the 2014 general election the BJP won 282 seats, the NDA 336 of 543, and Narendra Modi was sworn in as Prime Minister on 26 May 2014.

The party's official philosophy is integral humanism, first formulated by Deendayal Upadhyaya in 1965. It follows Hindutva, a Hindu nationalist ideology, and keeps organisational and ideological links with the RSS. During its first period in national government it set its Hindutva priorities aside and concentrated on economic growth.

The name means Indian People's Party. Its symbol is the lotus, the national flower of India, which has cultural significance in Hinduism and was used by Indian nationalists during the independence movement. Its flag is mostly saffron with a green stripe, and the lotus is set within the saffron part.
bharavi: Very little is known of his life, and he gives no personal details in his only surviving work. Grant inscriptions of the Ganga dynasty, among them the Gummareddipura inscription, say that the Ganga king Durvinita wrote a Kannada commentary on the fifteenth canto of the Kiratarjuniya; since Durvinita's reign ended around 580, Bharavi lived around or before that time. The Indologist A. K. Warder places his working life around 530 to 550, M. K. Gangopadhyaya around 500 to 550, and Arthur Berriedale Keith thought it wiser to place him around 550 than as early as 500.

Most scholars hold that he came from southern India, and the inscriptions that name him are from the western Deccan. R. R. Bhagawat Sastri argued that his description of the Sahya mountains, the Western Ghats, is more vivid than that of the Himalayas; critics answer that he mentions the Sahya only once against some 52 verses on the Himalayas.

The Avanti-sundari-katha attributed to the 7th-century poet Dandin gives the most plausible account. G. Harihara Sastri reads it as saying that Bharavi was a Shaivite, a great poet and a courtier of a prince Vishnu-vardhana, and that he introduced another poet, Dandin's ancestor Damodara, to that prince. M. Ramakrishna Kavi took Damodara to be another name of Bharavi, but Sastri rejected this as a misreading, noting that Damodara wrote works Bharavi is not known to have written. Later legends, one of a poor poet whose verse against rash acts saved a king from killing his own long-lost son, Gangopadhyaya calls absurd and useless.

The Kiratarjuniya is an epic in eighteen cantos whose story comes from the Mahabharata. Warder considered it the most perfect epic that survives, above Aśvaghoṣa's Buddhacharita, for its force, concentration and polish. Its language is extremely difficult and delights in the finer points of Sanskrit grammar, yet it remains concise and direct, with alliteration and metre matched to the story. As Kalidasa is known for his similes and Dandin for his wordplay, Bharavi is known for his weight of meaning, arthagauravam. The poem is thought to have influenced Magha's Shishupala Vadha in the 8th century.
bharhut: The stupa may have been first built by the Maurya king Ashoka, with its railings and gateways added later. As at Sanchi, the central mound was ringed by a stone railing with four torana gateways; the railings came first and the gateway slightly later. Unusually, each panel is labelled in Brahmi characters saying what it shows. In keeping with the early aniconic phase of Buddhist art, the Buddha appears only as symbols: the Dharma wheel, the Bodhi tree, an empty seat, footprints or the triratana. Every figure wears the Indian dhoti except one foreigner, thought to be an Indo-Greek soldier.

An inscription on a gateway pillar records that the gateway and stone-work were given by Vatsiputra Dhanabhuti during the rule of the Sugas, which may mean the Shungas or the Sughanas, a northern Buddhist kingdom. Since the Shungas were Hindu monarchs and Dhanabhuti is absent from their regnal lists, he was probably a tributary or a neighbouring ruler. Mason's marks in Kharosthi on the gateway suggest builders from Gandhara, while the railings bear Indian marks; Alexander Cunningham concluded that northern artists made the more refined gateways and local artists the railings. The fluted bell capital and flame palmette point to Hellenistic and Persian influence.

The 136 donor inscriptions name people from Vidisha, Pataliputra, Kosambi, Nasik and elsewhere, and 82 label scenes of the Jatakas and the Buddha's life. Buddhism survived at Bharhut until the 12th century: a small temple was enlarged around 1100 and a new statue of the Buddha installed, and a colossal Buddha stood in a medieval monastery there.

Cunningham visited Bharhut in 1873 and excavated it the next year, and his assistant Joseph David Beglar photographed the work. The monuments had long been taken apart by villagers for building stone. Only the foundations of the stupa remain at the site; the railings and the one surviving gateway were reassembled at the Indian Museum in Kolkata, and two panels are in the Freer Gallery of Art in Washington. A shipment of sculptures sent to London on the SS Indus was wrecked in 1885 near Mullaitivu in Sri Lanka; the wreck was found again in 2014.
bharmal: Bharmal was the fourth son of Raja Prithviraj Singh I of Amer and Rani Apoorva Devi, a Rathore princess of Bikaner. After Prithviraj's death in 1527 the throne passed to his eldest son Puranmal, who was killed at the Battle of Mandrail on 19 January 1534 while helping the Mughal emperor Humayun recover the fort of Bayana. As Puranmal's son Sujamal was a minor, the throne went to his brother Bhim Singh and then to Bhim Singh's son Ratan Singh, who was killed by his half-brother Askaran. The nobles of Amer deposed Askaran and on 1 June 1548 chose Bharmal, then about fifty years old.

In 1556 Bharmal helped the Mughal commandant Majnun Khan Qaqshal, who told Akbar of it, and Akbar received Bharmal and his relatives at court with robes of honour. In 1562 the Kachhwahas were in danger when Mirza Muhammad Sharaf-ud-din Hussain, the Mughal governor of Mewat, took up the claim of Sujamal. He led a large army to Amber, drove the Kachhwahas into the forests and hills, and took Bharmal's son Jagannath and two nephews as hostages for a fixed tribute.

Through Akbar's courtier Chaghtai Khan, Bharmal met the emperor at his camp at Sanganer on 20 January 1562, while Akbar was on pilgrimage to the dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chisti at Ajmer. There he offered his eldest daughter in marriage. At Sambhar the hostages were surrendered to Akbar, and on 6 February 1562 the marriage took place. Bharmal was then made commander of 5,000 cavalry, the highest rank open to a noble at the Mughal court, and his son Bhagwant Das and grandson Man Singh went with Akbar to Agra.

Bharmal died in Agra on 27 January 1574 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Raja Bhagwant Das. He had at least thirteen sons and four daughters. The chronicler Nizamuddin Ahmad counted him among the leading rajas of Hindustan who entered the emperor's service, and the Tarikh-i-Salim praised his allegiance and courage. He, Bhagwant Das and Man Singh I each became the highest mansabdar of their times.
bharuch: Bharuch lies at the mouth of the Narmada River in Gujarat and is the administrative headquarters of Bharuch District. It was a shipbuilding centre and seaport on the coastal trade routes of the age before the compass, which used the regular monsoon winds, and it became a terminus of several land and sea routes. Its sheltered position on the Gulf of Khambhat suited coastal navigation, and the Narmada gave access inland to caravan routes to the Ganges valley and the plains of Delhi. In ancient times it was known as Bhrigukachchha or Bharukachchha, and by local tradition the name comes from the sage Bhrigu, whose temple stands on the riverbank. Greek and Roman writers called it Barygaza, and British administration wrote Broach.

Around the sixth century BCE Bharukachchha was a western outlet for the trade of the kingdom of Avanti, ruled from Ujjayini by Chanda Pradyota Mahasena. Strabo records an embassy sent to Caesar Augustus by an Indian king that included Zarmanochegas, a man of Bargosa, who later burned himself alive at Athens. By the first century CE the port lay in the realm of the Western Satrap ruler Nahapana. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes Barygaza as the region's principal port, reached through a difficult tidal estuary where royal pilots met ships. Its imports included wine, copper, tin, lead, coral, raw glass and gold and silver coin, and its exports nard, costus, ivory, onyx, agate, cotton cloth, silk and long pepper.

In the seventh century the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang recorded the city, and Arab forces from Sindh raided it in the early eighth century. In 1547 Portuguese forces under Jorge de Meneses Baroche took it in a night attack, when it belonged to the Sultanate of Gujarat. Between 1500 and 1700 it was a major textile centre famed for bafta cloth. The Nawabs of Bharuch came under Maratha suzerainty in 1685 and ruled independently from 1736. The British attacked in 1771 and placed it under Company rule on 18 November 1772.

The city had 148,391 inhabitants at the 2011 census. It is a pilgrimage site, known in the Puranas as Bhrigu Tirtha, with temples along the river, and its Jami Masjid dates from 1644. According to tradition Guru Nanak crossed the Narmada here on a cloth. The damming of the Narmada closed the city's original port, and the nearest port is now Dahej. The region is heavily industrialised, with chemical plants and textile mills, and the city is known for its salted peanuts and for Bandhni cloth design.
bhaskara-ii: Bhāskara II, commonly called Bhāskarāchārya, belonged to a Deśastha Brahmin family of court scholars, mostly astronomer-astrologers, in western India. Verses in his main work place his birth in 1114 at Vijjadavida, in the Sahyadri ranges of the Western Ghats. Scholars disagree about the exact location; many place it near Patan in Chalisgaon, in present-day Maharashtra, while others have suggested Beed, Bijapur, Bidar or Basar. His father Maheśvara was a mathematician, astronomer and astrologer who taught him, and he in turn taught his son Lokasamudra. He is said to have headed the astronomical observatory at Ujjain, the leading centre of mathematical astronomy in medieval India. He died in 1185.

Bhāskara wrote the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi in 1150, at the age of 36. It is an orthodox work of the Brāhmapakṣa school and did not displace the canonical texts of other astronomical traditions. Its two astronomical parts are the Grahagaṇita, on the motions of the planets, eclipses and related phenomena, and the Golādhyāya, on the celestial sphere, the Earth, instruments and the seasons. The Līlāvatī, on arithmetic, and the Bījagaṇita, on algebra, are sometimes counted as parts of it but were usually copied separately. He also wrote a treatise called Karaṇā Kautūhala.

The Līlāvatī has 13 chapters and covers interest, progressions, plane and solid geometry, the shadow of the gnomon, indeterminate equations and combinations. It is written in compact verse for memorising, and its problems are addressed playfully to an inquisitive young learner, using images such as swans, bees and peacocks. A popular story that it was named after Bhāskara's widowed daughter was first recorded in 1587 and has no contemporary support. The Bījagaṇita, in twelve chapters, is regarded as the earliest surviving Indian treatise wholly devoted to algebra. It sets out rules for positive and negative numbers, zero and surds, and methods for linear, quadratic and indeterminate equations.

His chakravala, or cyclic, method gave the first general solution of equations of the type known in the West as Pell's equation. Bhāskara solved a case that Pierre de Fermat posed as a challenge in 1657, which was not solved in Europe until the time of Leonhard Euler. In the Grahagaṇita he also gave a result that can be read as a forerunner of the idea that the cosine is the derivative of the sine, though he did not develop the notion of a derivative.
bhaskaravarman: Bhaskaravarman was a son of Susthitavarman, who was defeated by Mahasenagupta, the ally of Shashanka. His brother Supratisthitavarman ruled briefly but died without an heir, and Bhaskaravarman took the throne around 600, restoring Varman rule. He was the first king of Kamarupa to claim descent from Narakasura, Bhagadatta and Vajradatta, and he was also the last ruler of the Varman dynasty. His principal rivals were Shashanka, who came to rule Bengal, and Prabhakaravardhana, the father of Harshavardhana.

After Shashanka killed Harshavardhana's brother and successor, Rajyavardhana, Bhaskaravarman sent an envoy, Hangsavega, to Thaneswar to form an alliance, an event recorded by Bana and by Xuanzang. Among his gifts to Harshavardhana were a royal umbrella studded with gems, cane mats, agar essence, musk, paintings and silk. After 648 he supplied the Chinese envoy Wang Xuance, who had returned with an army against Yashovarman; Chinese records call him Sri-Kumara, and he asked Wang for an image of Laozi.

Xuanzang described Kamarupa as low and moist, with regular crops and abundant coconuts and jackfruits, and put its circumference at about 1,700 miles, which Edward Albert Gait took to include the whole Assam valley, the Surma valley and parts of North Bengal. The king followed Hindu traditions, chiefly the worship of Shiva, while respecting Buddhist monks; Buddhists in the kingdom practised quietly. Bhaskaravarman's seal, dated 643, was found at Nalanda in the excavations of 1917–18 beside seals of Harsha, and K. N. Dikshit proposed that it accompanied his letter inviting Xuanzang. His Dubi and Nidhanpur copper plate grants describe him in the customary language of royal praise.

The date and circumstances of his death are unknown. The historian Kanaklal Barua suggests that a revolt of the Mlechhas followed it, in which Salastambha seized the throne from his successor Avantivarman. The Assamese calendar, the Bhāskarābda, is named after him and counted from his accession; it differs by 593 years from the Gregorian calendar. A Sanskrit university in Nalbari and a bridge over the Brahmaputra bear his name.
bheemunipatnam: Bheemunipatnam, also called Bheemili, lies on the Bay of Bengal north of Visakhapatnam city, about 31 km from Visakhapatnam railway station, bordered loosely by Rushikonda to the south, Madhurawada to the west and Bhogapuram to the north. The town is named after Bhima, a hero of the Hindu epic Mahabharata. According to the Imperial Gazetteer of India it was entirely zamindari land belonging to the Vizianagram estate.

Buddhist remains dating back to the 3rd century BCE, among them relic caskets, have been excavated on the hillock of Pavurallakonda in the town, and both Hinayana and Mahayana Buddhism were carried from the port of the Gosthani River to lands further east. On the hill's seaward side stands a temple of Narasimha, built around the 14th century by the Mindi kings, and two more temples, Bheemeswaralayam and Choleswaralayam, date from Chola times.

Known to the Dutch as Bimilipatnam, the town was one of the major settlements of the Dutch Coromandel coast in the 17th century, with a currency mint, and the Portuguese also called there. After Maratha troops plundered it in 1754, the local regent allowed the Dutch East India Company to build a fort, planned by the military engineer Coenraad Pieter Keller; it collapsed twice, and Keller had to defend himself before his superiors in Batavia. The British East India Company later made the town its main trading base on the east coast, and in the British Raj its port ran passenger ships to Madras and Calcutta.

Bheemunipatnam was a municipality of its own until 2017, when it was merged into the municipal corporation of Visakhapatnam; it remains the headquarters of a revenue division. Its surviving monuments include one of the oldest Christian cemeteries on the coast, St. Peter's Church, a clock tower and a lighthouse of 1868, and Buddhist sites such as Bojjannakonda, Bavikonda and Thotlakonda lie nearby.
bhils: The name Bhil is thought by some scholars to come from the word billa or billu, meaning bow in Dravidian vocabulary, which reflects the popularity of the bow and arrow among these groups. The term is also used as a blanket name for the aboriginal peoples of the forests and hills of southern Rajasthan and the surrounding parts of western India. The Bhils now speak Bhili, an Indo-Aryan language, but the aboriginal language they originally spoke is lost. Many speak the dominant language of their region, such as Marathi, Gujarati or Bengali.

The Bhils of what is now Gujarat rebelled several times in the British colonial period, notably in 1846, 1857 and 1868. Under the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 the colonial government designated them, with other groups, a criminal tribe, so that a Bhil could be arbitrarily seized, tortured or killed. Susan Abraham notes that many of the tribes so labelled had earlier rebelled against the East India Company or taken part in the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

In Mewar State the Bhils protested in 1881 against the census classification, the ban on liquor manufacture, the new police and customs and the ban on killing witches. Their campaign was given direction by the social and political leader Govind Guru, who used his missionary work to stop meat and alcohol among them and to press for village councils and an end to forced labour. In 1921 Bhils and peasants united under Motilal Tejawat against forced labour and heavy taxes, and Tejawat drew followers from the Bhils and Girasias of Danta, Idar, Palanpur and Sirohi.

The Bhils live in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra, with smaller numbers in Chhattisgarh, Bengal, Tripura and Sindh in Pakistan. They are divided into endogamous territorial divisions, each with clans and lineages, and a traditional village is led by a headman called the gameti, who decides most local disputes. They are listed as a Scheduled Tribe in several Indian states. Around 10 million people recorded themselves in a census as speaking a Bhili dialect.

Their main crops are maize, onion, garlic and chili, and they gather fruits and vegetables from the forests. Every village has a local deity, and families keep household gods symbolised by stones. According to Victoria R. Williams most Bhils identify as Hindu, while the Dang Bhils follow Christianity and the Nirdhi and Tadivi Bhils follow Islam. Bhil painting is marked by multicoloured dots, and the Bhilala are known for Pithora painting. Ghoomar is a traditional folk dance.
bhilwara: Bhilwara lies at an elevation of about 421 metres in the Mewar region of Rajasthan, between the districts of Ajmer to the north and Chittorgarh and Udaipur to the south. The main rivers of the district are the Banas, Bedach, Kothari, Khari, Mansi, Menali, Chandrabhaga and Nagdi. There is no natural lake, but the many ponds and dams make it the most irrigated district in the state. The city has a small man-made pond, Mansarovar Jheel, near Azad Nagar.

Stone Age tools have been found in the districts of Bundi and Bhilwara. The name has two traditional explanations. By one, the city had a mint that struck coins called Bhiladi, which gave the district its name. By another, the Bheel people who helped Maharana Pratap in his war against the Mughal emperor Akbar lived here, so that the area became Bheel Bada, the Bheel's area. The oldest part of the town dates to the middle of the 11th century, when a Krishna and Radha temple, still standing as the Bada Mandir, was built. Local tradition also places the warrior Arjuna here in the time of the Mahabharata.

Historical records show that the town of Mandal, near Bhilwara, served as the Mughal military camp when they conquered Chittaurgarh, and the ruins of the camp can still be seen. A watchtower built there on a small mound is now a Devi temple.

The city grew as a textile centre. It began with the Mewar Textile Mills, a spinning and knitting company owned by the industrialist Sampatmal Lodha and started in 1938, and in 1961 Laxmi Niwas Jhunjhunwala opened his first synthetic textile unit there. The fabric, mainly the synthetic cloth used for trousers, is exported to many countries. At the 2011 census the municipal corporation had 359,483 inhabitants, and Hindi, Mewari and Rajasthani were the commonest first languages. Bhilwara is also known for Phad painting, the depiction of traditional stories on cloth in natural colours, and for the miniature artist Badri Lal Chitrakar.
bhimavaram: Bhimavaram lies in the Godavari delta region of Andhra Pradesh and is the headquarters of West Godavari district and of Bhimavaram mandal. Its economy rests on agriculture-based businesses such as food processing, aquaculture and rice mills, and it is one of the principal trade centres of paddy in the state. It serves as a distribution and commercial centre for its hinterland, and is a regional centre for higher education and specialised health services. The 2011 census of India recorded a town population of 142,184 and an urban agglomeration of 146,961. The average literacy rate then stood at 83.41 per cent, above the state average of 73.00 per cent.

Along with much of present-day coastal Andhra Pradesh, Bhimavaram was governed by the Chola dynasty. Under Kulothunga Chola I the town was administered by his sons, who served as viceroys, and stone inscriptions from his reign, about 1096 CE, have been found there.

The name means the gift of Bhima in Telugu. According to a legend, an Eastern Chalukya king named Chalukya Bheema built a Shiva temple and laid the foundation of the town in about 890 to 918 CE. It was originally called Bhimapuram, and the name gradually changed to Bhimavaram, since puram means a dwelling place and varam an endowment. An alternative explanation holds that the sound va is preferred to pa in colloquial speech, so that the name shifted from puram to varam over time. The municipality was established in April 1948 and was raised in grade several times, reaching Special Grade in September 1980.

Bhimavaram is a pilgrimage centre and the home of the Gunupudi Someswara (Somarama) temple, one of the five holy Pancharama shrines of Shiva. The Shiva lingam there is said to change colour with the lunar month, black at the new moon and white at the full moon. The town also has the temple of the local deity Mavullamma. According to local folklore, the goddess's idol appeared inside a mango farm, which gave her the name Mamillamma, later altered to Mavullamma. The temple was built around 1880 CE.

National Highway 216 passes through the town, and rail lines connect it with Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam and other cities. Rajahmundry Airport, 80 km away, is the nearest airport. Bhimavaram Junction railway station lies in the South Coast Railway zone, and the Gudivada to Bhimavaram section connects it with the Howrah to Chennai main line.
bhimsen-thapa: Bhimsen Thapa was born in August 1775 at Pipal Thok village in Gorkha district, to Amar Singh Thapa and Satyarupa Maya, in a military family of the Bagale Thapa clan, which had migrated east from Jumla. He had four brothers by his mother and two by his stepmother. In 1798 his father recruited him as a bodyguard for the king. He rose to influence by helping the exiled former king Rana Bahadur Shah plan his return to power in 1804, and Rana Bahadur made him a Kaji, equivalent to a minister, in the new government.

After Rana Bahadur was assassinated in 1806, Bhimsen took the title of Mukhtiyar. As Kaji he had already sent armies west, and the Battle of Khurbura in May 1804 carried Nepal's border to the Sutlej River. In 1805 he planned the Baisathi Haran, the seizure of tax-free land held by temple trusts and Brahmin priests without valid documents, to fill the empty treasury and pay for campaigns in the far west. A Kangra campaign followed, and by early 1809 most of the Kangra lands were taken, though the fort held out and the Nepalese army was forced back by Sansar Chand and Ranjit Singh of Punjab.

He was among the main supporters of war with the East India Company, against the advice of commanders such as Bada Kaji Amar Singh Thapa. The Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–1816 ended with the Treaty of Sugauli, by which Nepal lost almost a third of its land. Edward Gardner arrived in May 1816 as the first British Resident, and Bhimsen cut him off from life in Nepal and from the king. He also built the Thapathali bridge over the Bagmati in 1811 and, in 1824 and 1825, two Dharahara towers.

Bhimsen's position weakened after Queen Tripurasundari died of cholera on 26 March 1832. King Rajendra Bikram Shah and Senior Queen Samrajya Laxmi Devi challenged him, rumour blamed him for the death of the earlier king Girvan, and the British Resident Brian Houghton Hodgson worked against him. The Pande faction, who held him responsible for the death of Damodar Pande in 1804, rose at court. He was imprisoned on a charge connected with the poisoning of an infant prince, and he died by suicide in 1839.

Nepalese tradition counts him a national hero, and historians such as Chittaranjan Nepali call him a patriotic statesman who resisted foreign suzerainty. He is also criticised for the Bhandarkhal massacre of 1806, for eliminating rivals and for concentrating power in his family.
bhimtal: Bhimtal lies at 1,370 metres in the Outer Lesser Himalayas, 22 kilometres east of Nainital, 21 kilometres north of the railway terminus at Kathgodam and 30 kilometres north of Haldwani. It is built around Bhimtal Lake, a natural freshwater lake of 47.8 hectares, the largest by surface area in the Kumaon division. The basin is tectonic in origin: movements along transverse faults in the Quaternary period and ancestral rockslides blocked the streams and impounded the water.

The name joins Bhima, the second Pandava prince of the Mahabharata, to tal, meaning lake. Regional Puranic tradition says that during the twelve years of the Pandavas of forest exile Draupadi grew thirsty, and Bhima struck his iron mace into the rock and opened a spring that filled the hollow. The five brothers are said to have consecrated the Bhimeshwar Mahadev shrine on the southern shore.

From the seventh to the eleventh century the region was ruled by the Katyuri kings from Joshimath and Baijnath, and Bhimtal served as a military and trade outpost on the tracks between the lowlands and the Himalayan valleys. It later passed to the Chand kings of Kumaon, ruling from Champawat and then Almora, for whom it was a staging post on the road between Rohilkhand and Almora. In 1667 Baz Bahadur Chand, who reigned from 1638 to 1678, commissioned the reconstruction of the Bhimeshwar Mahadev Temple and gave tax-free land grants to support its rituals and priesthood.

In 1790 forces of the Gorkha Kingdom of Nepal crossed the Kali River, overthrew the Chand dynasty and held Kumaon for twenty-five years. After the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814 to 1816 and the Treaty of Sugauli of 1815, Kumaon passed to the British East India Company. Bhimtal became a rest camp and dak bungalow station on the way to Almora, Ranikhet and Nainital, and in 1883 the Public Works Department's Irrigation Branch completed the 485-metre Victoria Dam across the lake's outlet to supply the canals of the Bhabar tract.

Bhimtal is a municipal town and the headquarters of a tehsil in the Nainital district of Uttarakhand, with a population of 7,722 at the 2011 census. In October 2023 the state government raised it from a Nagar Panchayat to a Nagar Palika Parishad. The town has the Folk Culture Museum, founded in 1983, the Bhimeshwar temple beside the dam, and the Butterfly Research Centre on the Jones Estate, where Frederick Smetacek Senior and Peter Smetacek recorded 243 butterfly species. It is the seat of the ICAR-Central Institute of Coldwater Fisheries Research, founded in 1987, and of tourism on the lakes of Kumaon.
bhojeshwar-temple: As the temple was never finished, it has no dedicatory inscription, but its attribution to Bhoja rests on the name Bhojpur, on sculptures datable to the 11th century and on a Jain temple in the village that shares its masons' marks and bears an inscription dated 1035 CE. The archaeologist Kirit Mankodi dates it to the later part of Bhoja's reign, around the mid-11th century. It originally stood beside a reservoir formed by three earth-and-stone dams of Bhoja's time, which lasted until Hoshang Shah breached two of them in the 15th century.
