The temple has no mandapa and a rectilinear rather than curving roof. From these features Shri Krishna Deva proposed that it was a funerary monument, and a medieval text found by M. A. Dhaky describes such memorial temples. Mankodi speculates that Bhoja may have begun it for his father Sindhuraja or his uncle Munja.

The sanctum stands on a platform 35 m long, 25 m wide and 4 m high and is a square 20 m a side on the outside. Its doorway is 10 m high, flanked by apsaras, attendants of Shiva and river goddesses. The windowless sandstone walls carry purely ornamental balconies, and four octagonal pillars about 12 m high support the richly carved but incomplete dome.

Why work stopped is unknown; historians suggest a natural disaster, a lack of resources or war. Quarries to the north and east hold half-carved fragments, and plans engraved on their rocks show that a much larger complex was intended. The remains of a sandstone ramp 91 m long survive, and the marks of over 1,300 masons are cut into the building and quarries.

The Archaeological Survey of India took over the weakened building in 1951. In 2006–07 a team led by KK Muhammed added a missing 12-tonne monolithic pillar, raised with pulleys and levers, and closed the roof. The temple is still in worship, and thousands of devotees visit it on Maha Shivaratri.
bhrikuti: Tibetans know Bhrikuti Devi as Bal-mo-bza' Khri-btsun, the Nepali consort, or simply Khri-btsun, the royal lady. Tradition makes her a princess of the Licchavi dynasty of Nepal and the first queen of Songtsen Gampo, king of Tibet from about 622. No reference to her has been found among the documents discovered at Dunhuang, but Tibet and Nepal were certainly in close contact at the time, and some scholars hold that such a marriage is historically likely.

Many Tibetan accounts call her a daughter of Amshuvarma (605–621), co-ruler and successor of Śivadeva I; if so, the marriage must have taken place before 624, although Acharya Kirti Tulku Lobsang Tenzin dates it to 632. Other legends name her father as a king called Go Cha, whom Sylvain Lévi identified as Udayavarman, most likely the Udayadeva who was Amshuvarma's adopted heir. That would make her a sister of Narendradeva, who took refuge in Tibet and, according to the Old Book of Tang, was restored to the throne of Nepal with Tibetan help in 641.

Tibetan tradition holds that Bhrikuti, a devout Buddhist, brought sacred images and skilled Newar craftsmen to Tibet as part of her dowry. The Testament of Ba links her marriage to the building of the temple of Rasa, and she and Songtsen Gampo are credited with the Tsulag Khang, now the Jokhang, built to house the images. They are also credited with the Red Palace on Marpo Ri, built by Nepali craftsmen, which moved the seat of government from the Yarlung Valley to Lhasa and was later rebuilt as the Potala by the Fifth Dalai Lama.

Her statue, the Jowo Mikyo Dorje, also called the Manuvajra, came from Bodhgaya and, according to the 8th Dalai Lama, rested at Swayambhunath for seven months before reaching Tibet. It is now in the Ramoche Temple in Lhasa. It is said that after the Jokhang was gutted in the 1960s the statue's lower half was found in a Lhasa rubbish dump and its upper half in Beijing, and the parts were joined again. In Tibetan iconography Bhrikuti is usually shown as Green Tara, and Princess Wencheng, whom Songtsen Gampo married in 641, as White Tara.
bhubaneswar: Bhubaneswar lies in the Khordha district of Odisha, in the eastern coastal plains along the axis of the Eastern Ghats, in the Mahanadi River Delta, at an average altitude of 45 metres. The Daya River is 4 kilometres to the south and the Kuakhai 4 kilometres to the east. The name is the anglicisation of the Odia Bhubanēśwara, from Tribhubanēśwara, the Lord of the Three Worlds, which in this context refers to Shiva. The old town was historically often called Chakra Khetra and Ekamra Khetra, the area adorned with a mango tree.

Bhubaneswar stands near the ruins of Sisupalgarh. At Dhauli, near the city, the Kalinga War of about 262 to 261 BCE took place, in which the Mauryan emperor Ashoka invaded and annexed Kalinga. One of the most complete edicts of Ashoka, dating from between 272 and 236 BCE, remains carved in rock 8 kilometres southwest of the modern city. After the decline of the Mauryan empire the area came under the Mahameghavahana dynasty, whose best-known ruler is Kharavela; his Hathigumpha inscription is at the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves near the city. Several dynasties followed, including the Satavahanas, Guptas, Matharas and Shailodbhavas.

Cuttack, the capital of British-ruled and independent Orissa, was vulnerable to floods and short of space, and in September 1946 a proposal to build a new capital was introduced in the Legislative Assembly of the Odisha Province. The German architect Otto Königsberger designed the modern city in 1946, and with Jamshedpur and Chandigarh it was one of modern India's first planned cities. The foundation of the new capital was laid on 13 April 1948 and the Legislative Assembly moved from Cuttack in 1949. The first census of independent India, in 1951, counted just 16,000 people. A municipality was established on 12 March 1979, and the Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation on 14 August 1994.

Bhubaneswar is the capital and largest city of Odisha and is called the Temple City. Its temples are built in the Kalinga architectural style, with a curving spire over the sanctum housing the presiding deity and a pyramid-roofed hall where people sit and pray. They include the Lingaraja, Muktesvara, Rajarani and Ananta Vasudeva temples, and the small Kukutesvara Siva Temple, a shrine to Shiva about a thousand years old. At the festival of Ashokashtami the image of Lingaraja is taken in procession to the Mausima Temple. The area formed by Bhubaneswar and Cuttack, often called the twin cities of Odisha, had a population of 1.7 million in 2011. The main language is Odia, and Utkal University is the oldest university in Odisha.
bhuj: Bhuj is the headquarters of Kutch district in the Indian state of Gujarat, and it was the capital of Kutch State, a princely state, until the state joined the Indian Union in 1947. The city lies at an average elevation of 110 metres. On its eastern side is Bhujia Hill, with Bhujia Fort, and the city has two lakes, Hamirsar and Deshalsar. Its climate is hot and arid, with annual rainfall averaging around 370 millimetres but varying greatly: it has been as low as 9.6 millimetres, in 1987, and as high as 1,311.4 millimetres, in 1959. According to legend, the name comes from Bhujanga, the last Naga chieftain of Kutch, who was later worshipped as a snake god.

Rao Hamir occupied Bhuj in 1510, and Rao Khengarji I made it the capital of Kutch in 1549. From 1590, when the Rao was forced to acknowledge Mughal supremacy, Muslims knew the city as Suleiman Nagar. Rao Godji I built the city walls in 1723, and Devkaran Seth built the Bhujia Fort in the time of Rao Deshalji I, who reigned from 1718 to 1741.

Bhuj was attacked six times, successfully defended in two cases and lost in four. Rao Deshalji I repulsed the Mughal viceroy Sarbuland Khan in 1728. During the civil troubles of the reign of Rao Rayadhan III the city was taken three times, in 1786, 1801 and 1808. On 26 March 1819 a British detachment under Sir William Keir captured the hill fort. An earthquake on 16 June 1819 destroyed nearly 7,000 houses and killed an estimated 1,140 people. The British garrison peaked in 1826 at nearly 1,400 British troops supported by over 5,000 Indian soldiers, and Alexander Burnes was based in the city from 1826 to 1829.

Kutch State merged with Bombay state in 1956, and in 1960 Kutch became a district of the new state of Gujarat. Earthquakes struck Bhuj again on 21 July 1956 and on 26 January 2001, and the city has been rebuilt since the second.

Bhuj had a population of 213,514 at the 2011 census, most of whom speak Gujarati. The old city was ringed by a fort wall 35 feet high with five main gates, much of which has fallen or been demolished since the 2001 earthquake. Places of interest include Hamirsar Lake, the Kutch Museum, the Prag Mahal, the Aina Mahal, the Sharad Baug Palace and the Swaminarayan Temple of 1822. The city is a destination for the crafts of Kutch, including bandhni tie-dye, embroidery, Rogan art and leatherwork.
bhumibol-adulyadej: Bhumibol was born on 5 December 1927 at Cambridge Hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the youngest son of Prince Mahidol Adulyadej and his commoner wife Mom Sangwan, later Princess Srinagarindra. His father was enrolled in the public health programme at Harvard University, which made Bhumibol the only hereditary monarch born in the United States. He had an older sister, Princess Galyani Vadhana, and an older brother, Prince Ananda Mahidol. He spent his early life in Switzerland, growing up after the 1932 Siamese revolution that toppled the absolute monarchy of his uncle, King Prajadhipok.

Bhumibol became king on 9 June 1946, when Ananda Mahidol died of a gunshot wound in circumstances that remain unclear. An early government statement called it an accident, but an investigation committee judged that virtually impossible. Three palace aides were convicted of regicide and executed by firing squad on 17 February 1955, after Bhumibol rejected their appeals for clemency. He was crowned on 5 May 1950 in the Grand Palace, the first coronation of a Thai sovereign under constitutional monarchy, pledging to reign with righteousness for the benefit and happiness of the Siamese people.

In his early years, under the military government of Plaek Phibunsongkhram, he held little real political power. In September 1957 he advised the field marshal to resign to avoid a coup; Phibunsongkhram refused, and General Sarit Thanarat seized power that evening. Under Sarit the monarchy was revitalised: the king toured the provinces, patronised development projects and visited the United States and Europe in 1960. In 1973 he announced the resignation and departure of General Thanom Kittikachorn after police killed dozens of students. In 1992 he played a key role in ending the Black May crisis, when the military killed many protesters. He was also a jazz saxophonist and composer, a sailor and a painter, and held patents for a waste water aerator and for rainmaking.

Bhumibol died aged 88 at Siriraj Hospital in Bangkok on 13 October 2016, after a period of declining health. Thousands lined the route as his body was taken to the Grand Palace. His reign of 70 years and 126 days was the longest of any Thai monarch. He was widely revered, and protected by strict lese-majeste laws, under which critics could be jailed for three to fifteen years. His son, Crown Prince Maha Vajiralongkorn, succeeded him as Rama X, and the cremation took place in 2017 at Sanam Luang.
bhumij-people: The name Bhumij means one who is born from the soil, from the word bhūmi, land or soil. N. Ramaswani read it instead as people of the Bhum areas, such as Singhbhum, Dhalbhum, Manbhum and Barabhum, and Dalton held the Bhumij to be the original inhabitants of Dhalbhum, Barabhum, Patkum and Baghmundi. A genetic study of 2010 found that about 70 per cent of their Y haplogroups belong to O2a-M95, common among Austroasiatic speakers and in Southeast Asia, and their mitochondrial lineages to haplogroup M of the Indian subcontinent.

Those living nearer the Chota Nagpur Plateau kept close linguistic links with Mundari, while those further east and south took up Bengali and Odia, and in Dhalbhum they became wholly Hindu in practice. Under British rule, or earlier, many Bhumij became zamindars, some gained the title of Raja and others were called Sardar, and those who rose claimed Kshatriya status, as was the trend in the region.

Bhumij landholders supported the Chuar revolt, a series of peasant risings between 1766 and 1816 in the country around Midnapore, Bankura and Manbhum against the East India Company's land revenue policies. In March 1766 the government sent an expedition west of Midnapore to force payment and demolish strongholds. Among the dispossessed zamindars who backed the rebels were Jagannath Singh of Dhalbhum, Durjan Singh of Raipur, Rani Shiromani of Karnagarh and Ganga Narayan of Barabhum.

Bhumij society combines traits inherited from the Munda with elements of caste society, and colonial writers often called it Hinduised. It is marked by the nuclear family, descent in the male line, marriage outside the clan and hereditary village headship, and it is divided into endogamous groups by ancestral territory and occupation. The Bhumij language, written in the Ol Onal script, is spoken by around 100,000 people and became a second official language of Jharkhand in January 2019. Followers of Sarnaism among them have petitioned for their religion to be recognised in the census. They are a Scheduled Tribe in Odisha, Jharkhand and West Bengal.
bhupinder-singh-of-patiala: Bhupinder Singh was born on 12 October 1891 in Moti Bagh Palace, Patiala, into the Jat Sikh Phulkian dynasty and the Sidhu clan, and was educated at Aitchison College in Lahore. He was sent for a time to the princely state of Dholpur, reportedly because intrigues at the Patiala court threatened his life. He succeeded his father, Maharaja Rajinder Singh, on 9 November 1900 at the age of nine. A Council of Regents ruled until he took partial power in 1909, and the Viceroy, the 4th Earl of Minto, invested him with full powers on 3 November 1910.

He built boldly designed buildings, among them the Shri Kali Devi Temple in Patiala and palaces at Chail, had the Patiala State Monorail Trainways built and founded the State Bank of Patiala in 1917. He represented India at the League of Nations and at the Round Table Conference. As Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes he pressed for the rights of the princely states, though the British rejected his proposals; in one election he defeated his cousin Udai Bhan Singh of Dholpur by using his wealth and his private plane to win votes.

In the First World War he served on the General Staff in France, Belgium, Italy and Palestine and sat on the Imperial War Cabinet in 1918. He played 27 first-class cricket matches between 1915 and 1937, helped found the Board of Control for Cricket in India, donated the Ranji Trophy and presided over the Indian Olympic Association from 1928 to 1938. Chosen to captain India on its first Test tour of England in 1932, he withdrew through ill health.

He collected cars, jewels, medals, paintings and watches, owned a fleet of 44 Rolls-Royce cars and was the first Indian to own a private plane. He married ten times and fathered 88 children, 52 of whom reached adulthood. He died on 23 March 1938 and was succeeded by his son Yadavindra Singh, the last Maharaja of Patiala; five days of hartal marked his death. The Maharaja Bhupinder Singh Punjab Sports University is named after him.
bhutia: The Bhutias call themselves Drejongpas, People of the Rice Valley, and their language, Drejongke, is a Tibetic language descended from Old Tibetan, closer to Dzongkha, the language of Bhutan, than to Standard Tibetan. Small numbers migrated from Tibet to Sikkim from the 8th century, and in the 13th century many clans came with Gyed Bum Sa. Conflicts between the Red Hat and Yellow Hat sects of Tibetan Buddhism drove a series of lamas southwards.

After the final victory of the Yellow Hats in the mid-1600s, Güshi Khan and his Gelug allies persecuted followers of the Red Hat sect, and many fled through the passes of the Himalayas into Sikkim and Bhutan, where Red Hat majorities remain. In North Sikkim, where Bhutias are the majority, they are known as Lachenpas or Lachungpas, after La chen, the big pass, and La chung, the small pass.

Bhutia aristocrats bore the title Kazi, after landlord titles in neighbouring regions, especially present-day Bangladesh. This feudal order was part of the Chogyal monarchy, and the Bhutia Namgyal dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Sikkim until the plebiscite of the mid-1970s. Kazi Lhendup Dorjee, a Bhutia, became the first chief minister of Sikkim in 1975 and held the post until 1979. The Lachenpas and Lachungpas keep their own legal system, the Dzumsa, the meeting place of the people, headed by a village headman called the Pipon. The Bhutias are recognised as a Scheduled Tribe in Sikkim, West Bengal and Tripura.

Traditionally the Bhutias were divided into two groups of clans, the Tondu rus-shi with four rus and the Beb tsen gye with eight, and marriage outside the community is looked down upon. They follow Vajrayana Buddhism, mainly the Nyingma and Kagyu schools. Losar marks the Tibetan New Year, and Losoong, at the end of the tenth lunar month, is their most important festival in India, marked by Cham dancing. The Rumtek Monastery in Sikkim is among their best-known monasteries.

The traditional garment is the kho, a loose cloak fastened at the neck and waist; a married woman wears the pangden, a multicoloured woollen cloth, in front. A house, the khim, is usually rectangular, with a vase-shaped stone sangbum outside for burning incense to the deities. Chhaang, made of fermented barley or millet, is served in a bamboo container called the Tongba.
bi-sheng: Bi Sheng was an artisan and engineer of the Song dynasty (960–1279). Because he was a commoner and not an educated man, little is known about his life apart from his invention. His gravestone was located in Hubei province in 1990, and a park and museum opened on the site in April 2023. A subdistrict of Wenquan, Huanggang, in Hubei is named after him, as is a crater on the far side of the Moon, named after him on 2 August 2010.

His invention is recorded only in the Dream Pool Essays of the scholar-official and polymath Shen Kuo (1031–1095), who places it in the Qingli reign. Bi Sheng cut characters in sticky clay, each as thin as the edge of a coin and each forming a single type, and baked them hard. He laid them in an iron frame on an iron plate coated with a mixture of pine resin, wax and paper ashes, warmed the plate until the paste softened, and pressed the type level with a smooth board.

Shen Kuo notes that the method was neither simple nor easy for two or three copies but extremely quick for hundreds or thousands. Two formes were kept going, so that one could be set while the other was printed. Common characters had twenty or more types each. Types were stored with paper labels, one for each rhyme group, in wooden cases. Bi Sheng also tried wooden type, but it was abandoned because of the grain of the wood and its unevenness after soaking in ink.

Ceramic type may have spread after his death to the Tangut kingdom of Western Xia, where a Buddhist text, the Vimalakirti Nirdesa Sutra, found at Wuwei in Gansu, shows traits of clay type. The method was also passed to his descendants, and Kublai Khan's councillor Yao Shu had his pupil Yang Gu print language primers with it. The official Wang Zhen, active between 1290 and 1333, improved on clay with wooden type. A wealthy printer, Hua Sui, developed bronze type by 1490. Wooden movable type became widespread under the Qing dynasty but did not replace woodblock printing, probably because of the expense of making so many pieces or the low cost of a copyist.
bianca-maria-visconti: Bianca Maria Visconti was born on 31 March 1425 near Settimo Pavese, the illegitimate daughter of Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan and last ruler of the Visconti dynasty, and Agnese del Maino, a lady-in-waiting to his wife Beatrice di Tenda. At six months she was sent with her mother to a castle at Abbiate, where the duke often visited and was reportedly struck by her strong character. She grew up at Abbiategrasso with a humanist education.

In 1430, aged five, she was betrothed to the condottiero Francesco I Sforza, twenty-four years older, to keep him tied to Milan after his contract ended. The contract was signed on 23 February 1432 and her dowry included lands around Cremona. She married Sforza on 24 October 1441 in Cremona.

In 1442, aged seventeen, she was named regent of the Marche while Sforza fought Niccolò Piccinino, and chroniclers record her skill in administration and diplomacy. Filippo Maria died in the night of 13 to 14 August 1447, and Sforza took the post of captain general of the Ambrosian Republic. In May 1448, when Venetians attacked Cremona, she is said to have put on parade armour and fought on the walls for a whole day, which earned her fame as a warrior woman. On 24 February 1450 a revolt in Milan recognised Sforza as lord, the first time a duke's title was given by a city's citizens.

As duchess she ran the duchy while Sforza was at war, and their letters show her opinions when they differed from his. After the Peace of Lodi in 1454 she turned to diplomacy, restoration of ducal residences and public works, among them the Ospedale Maggiore. When Sforza fell ill in 1462 she acted as co-regent and kept the state from crumbling after rebellions encouraged by Venice.

Sforza died on 8 March 1466 and Bianca Maria took the regency, calling back their son Galeazzo Maria from France to succeed. He soon acted against her advice and forced her to leave Milan for Cremona, her dower city. She attended his wedding on 9 May 1468, fell ill at Melegnano and died on 28 October 1468. She was buried in the Duomo of Milan beside her husband, with a funeral oration by the humanist Francesco Filelfo. Bartolomeo Colleoni and others accused Galeazzo of poisoning her, though Bernardino Corio wrote that she died of natural ungratefulness more than poison. Of her ten children, Galeazzo Maria and Ludovico Maria became dukes of Milan.
bias-of-priene: Bias was born at Priene in Ionia and was active in the sixth century BCE. He was the son of Teautames and a younger contemporary of Solon. He is said to have descended from the Thebans who founded Priene, a claim common among the Ionian aristocracy. His dates are unclear, since he is described in connection with the Second Messenian War, the reign of the Lydian king Alyattes and the conquests of the Akkadian Empire. Diogenes Laertius reports that Duris of Samos called him a labourer, while others described him as wealthy. Plato and Diogenes Laertius, among others, name him as one of the Seven Sages of Greece.

Bias worked as an advocate, offering legal services without payment to those who had been wronged. He went to Samos as an envoy for Priene in a territorial dispute, arguing that the Batinetis belonged to Priene because the Cimmerians had taken it before Samos captured it. The mediator ruled for Samos. This episode is the best attested of the stories about him and is the earliest known case of mediation, as opposed to arbitration, ending a conflict in ancient Greece.

According to Herodotus, Bias proposed that the Ionians migrate together to Sardinia and found one settlement safe from Persia, and he is among the earliest to discuss the Ionians as a single group. Herodotus also says that either Bias or Pittacus of Mytilene persuaded King Croesus of Lydia not to build a fleet. Tradition adds that he ransomed kidnapped Messenian girls and tricked Alyattes into abandoning a siege of Priene by showing fattened mules and corn laid over sand. He is said to have died while arguing a case, with his head in his grandson's lap.

His best-known saying, translated as most men are bad, won the praise of Heraclitus, who made him an exception to his scorn of earlier figures. Diogenes Laertius reports that he held persuasion preferable to force, that one should treat friends as possible enemies and enemies as possible friends, and that the inability to bear misfortune is itself a misfortune. He is said to have treated possessions as unimportant, leaving Priene under attack without them because his letters and wisdom were all he owned, and to have counselled piety in fear of the gods.

Priene established a heroic cult for him with a heroon and in the second century BCE minted coins showing him with his tripod. Most of what is known of him comes from Diogenes Laertius, and for figures of this period history and legend are not always distinct.
biberach-an-der-riss: Biberach an der Riß, often called simply Biberach, is the capital of the Biberach district in the Upper Swabia region of Baden-Württemberg, between the river Danube and Lake Constance. It takes its full name from the small river Riß that flows through it, to tell it apart from other towns of similar names. The town has about 32,000 inhabitants.

For many centuries Biberach was an Imperial Free City of the Holy Roman Empire, and in that role it took part in the Reichstag of 1792. During the Reformation it was notable as one of a few mixed imperial cities, with Ravensburg, Augsburg and Dinkelsbühl, where the Peace of Westphalia established a joint Catholic and Protestant government, with posts divided exactly equally between the two confessions.

This status ended in 1803, when the Margraviate of Baden, soon to become a grand duchy, annexed the town. In 1806 it was traded to the Kingdom of Württemberg in exchange for the town of Villingen, and in 1871 it became part of the German Empire on its creation. During the French Revolutionary Wars the town and its surroundings were the site of two sizeable battles, in 1796 and 1800. In World War II two large prisoner-of-war camps stood here: Oflag V-B for officers and the internment camp Ilag V-B for Allied civilians, mainly from the Channel Islands.

Biberach is a significant industrial location in south-west Germany, home to firms such as Liebherr, which began making cranes there in 1954, and Boehringer Ingelheim. The Braith-Mali-Museum, in a building of the 16th century, presents archaeology, history, art and natural history, and the Wieland-Museum, founded in 1907 in the summer house of the writer Christoph Martin Wieland, explores his life and work. The Biberacher Schützenfest is a historic festival for children and the town, held each July for nine days.
bibi-khanym-mosque: After his Indian campaign in 1399 Timur decided to build a gigantic mosque in his new capital, Samarkand. He may have been inspired by the Friday Mosque at Sultaniyeh, built by Uljaytu. When he returned from a military campaign in 1404 the mosque was almost complete, but he was dissatisfied with the progress and had changes made at once, especially to the main cupola. Timur named the mosque after his wife Saray Mulk Khanum, although it was actually commissioned by her. It was meant to gather the entire male population of Samarkand for the joint Friday prayers.

The mosque is a courtyard mosque of the four-iwan type. Its outer walls enclose a rectangle 167 metres long and 109 metres wide. A parade portal about 35 metres high leads into the courtyard, opposite which rises a dome about 40 metres high over a square base. The three domes have a double shell, with a hollow space between the inner ceiling and the outer cupola. This let the interior above the mihrab keep a height of 30 metres while the outer dome was made as impressive as possible.

Open galleries 7.2 metres high once ran round the courtyard, roofed with small flat brick vaults and domes on more than 400 marble columns and buttresses. In the middle of the courtyard stands a huge Quran stand of ornate marble blocks, which dates from Timur's time. The interiors had gilding that imitated local brocade embroidery.

The mosque had problems of structural integrity from the start. The scale of the plans pushed the building techniques of the time to their limit, and the haste of the work made it worse. After a few years the first bricks fell from the dome over the mihrab. In the late 16th century Abdullah Khan II cancelled all restoration, and the building slowly became a ruin, plundered for brick and marble. The inner arch of the portal collapsed in an earthquake in 1897. The government of the Uzbek SSR began a complex reconstruction in 1974, and the decoration of domes and facades was extensively restored. The mosque influenced architecture in Central Asia, Iran and Afghanistan.
biblical-hebrew: Hebrew developed in the latter half of the second millennium BCE in Canaan, between the Jordan and the Mediterranean. In its earliest stages it was not highly differentiated from Ugaritic and the Canaanite of the Amarna letters, and the Northwest Semitic languages formed a dialect continuum in the Iron Age, with Phoenician and Aramaic at either extreme. Hebrew belongs with Phoenician in the Canaanite subgroup, which also includes Ammonite, Edomite and Moabite. The oldest layer, Archaic Hebrew, appears in the poetry of the Bible, such as the Song of the Sea and the Song of Deborah, and in inscriptions of about 1000 BCE.

Biblical Hebrew has the typically Semitic system of roots, usually of three consonants, arranged in patterns to form words. It distinguishes masculine and feminine genders and singular, plural and the uncommon dual numbers. Verbs have two main conjugations, the suffix and the prefix forms, whose meaning for tense and aspect is debated and depends much on context. The usual word order is verb, subject, object. The language of the Bible had other names: the Hebrew Bible calls it the language of Canaan or Judean, and the term Hebrew comes from Greek and Mishnaic Hebrew texts, its origin obscure.

The consonantal text of the Hebrew Bible reflects several stages of the language, with evidence of regional dialects, including differences between the northern Kingdom of Israel and the southern Kingdom of Judah. In the biblical story of Jephthah, his forces from Gilead identified fleeing Ephraimites by their pronunciation of the word shibboleth.

Spoken Hebrew persisted as a first language through the Second Temple period and eventually developed into Mishnaic Hebrew, which was used as a second language until the 5th century. The Samaritans kept the Paleo-Hebrew script, and still use a descendant of it. After the Babylonian captivity the Imperial Aramaic alphabet gradually displaced it and became the source of the present Hebrew alphabet. The early writing systems marked consonants only, and certain letters called matres lectionis came increasingly to mark vowels.

The earliest Hebrew writing yet found, an ink text of five lines on a potsherd from Khirbet Qeiyafa, dates to the 10th century BCE. The consonantal text of the Bible was transmitted in manuscript and revised during the Second Temple period. The Masoretes added the Tiberian vowel marks in the Middle Ages, after 600 CE, and this is the system still widely used.
biblioteca-marciana: On 31 May 1468 the Byzantine humanist and scholar Cardinal Bessarion wrote to Doge Cristoforo Moro and the Senate announcing the donation of his collection of 482 Greek and 264 Latin codices to the Republic of Venice. He stipulated that a public library be established to conserve them for future generations and make them available to scholars. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 he had set about acquiring rare works of ancient Greece and Byzantium to prevent the loss of Greek culture. He chose Venice because of its large community of Greek refugees and its historical ties to the Byzantine Empire.

The Venetian government was slow to house the manuscripts, with decades of discussion and indecision during the military conflicts of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. An earlier attempt at a public library had failed when Petrarch's manuscripts, donated to the republic in 1362, were dispersed after his death.

The library was built as part of the Renovatio urbis, a programme begun under Doge Andrea Gritti (in office 1523–1538) to restore Venetian prestige after the defeat at Agnadello. It would transform Saint Mark's Square from a medieval town centre into a classical forum and present Venice as Rome's true successor. The procurators of Saint Mark commissioned Jacopo Sansovino on 14 July 1536, and the building was constructed between 1537 and 1588. Andrea Palladio called it perhaps the richest and most ornate building since ancient times.

Its upper storey is characterised by a series of Serlians, or Palladian windows. The library occupied the upper floor, while the ground floor was let to shops and later cafes. Its gilded rooms are decorated with paintings by Titian, Tintoretto, Paolo Veronese and Andrea Schiavone.

In 1544 the Council of Ten gave custody of the collection to the riformatori dello studio di Padova, who had it catalogued in 1545; it moved into the new building between 1559 and 1565. After the fall of the Venetian Republic to the French in 1797 the post of librarian ceased to exist. In 1811 the collection was moved to the Doge's Palace when the building became a residence for the viceroy of the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy.

After Venice joined the Kingdom of Italy the library was designated a national library in 1876. The collection moved to the Zecca, the former mint, in 1904, and the historical rooms reopened as a museum in 1929. It is the only official institution established by the Venetian Republican government that survives and still functions.
bibliotheca-palatina: In the 1430s Elector Louis III founded the Stiftsbibliothek in the Heiliggeistkirche, chosen for its good reading light. This library formed the core of the Palatine collection that Elector Ottheinrich established in the 1550s together with the University Library of Heidelberg. At its height the Bibliotheca Palatina held about 5,000 printed books and 3,524 manuscripts, and it was the most important library of the German Renaissance.

Among its manuscripts were the Carolingian Lorsch Evangelary, the falconry book De arte venandi cum avibus commissioned by Frederick II, and the Codex Manesse. Further manuscripts came from the collection of Ulrich Fugger, who died in 1584, among them the illustrated Sachsenspiegel. Joseph Scaliger judged the Fugger library superior to the Pope's, and its manuscripts alone were valued at 80,000 crowns.

In 1622 Heidelberg was sacked by the Catholic League under Count von Tilly, who served Maximilian of Bavaria. Book plundering was a source of both Catholic and Protestant cultural triumph in the war, and the occupiers competed for the library. Maximilian first wanted it for his own library in Munich, while Ferdinand II sent Tilly orders to keep it for Vienna. Many books were torn or dispersed among private hands during the sack, but Pope Gregory XV persuaded Maximilian to present the rest to the Vatican as a sign of loyalty and in support of his claim to the Palatinate's electoral title.

The Greek scholar Leo Allatius was sent from Rome to prepare the transport. The victors meant not only to strip the Calvinist party of one of its chief intellectual symbols but also to remove the records of the library's provenance, and the seizure set a pattern for later confiscations in the war. Each volume taken into the Vatican Library kept a leaf bearing the Wittelsbach arms.

Under the Treaty of Tolentino of 1797 the Pope ceded 37 manuscripts to the French Republic, which placed them in the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris. After the Congress of Vienna ordered the return of works of art taken by the French, these manuscripts went from Paris to Heidelberg rather than to Rome. In 1816 Prince Hardenberg and Ignaz Heinrich von Wessenberg persuaded Pope Pius VII to give the University of Heidelberg 852 manuscripts, mostly in German. The German manuscripts carry shelf-marks beginning cpg and the Latin ones cpl. For the university's jubilee in 1986 some books were lent back from the Vatican and shown in the Heiliggeistkirche.
bibliotheque-nationale-de-france: The library traces its origin to the royal library founded at the Louvre Palace by Charles V in 1368, from manuscripts he had received from his predecessor John II. The first librarian of record was Claude Mallet, the king's valet de chambre, who made a catalogue of the books. After the death of Charles VI the collection was bought by the English regent of France, the Duke of Bedford, who took it to England in 1424, and it was apparently dispersed at his death in 1435.

The invention of printing led to a new collection at the Louvre, inherited by Louis XI in 1461. Later kings added to it: Charles VIII seized part of the collection of the kings of Aragon, Louis XII brought in the library at Blois, and Francis I merged it with his private library at Fontainebleau in 1534.

The collection moved several times in Paris, and many treasures were lost. Under the librarian Jacques Auguste de Thou it became the largest and richest collection of books in the world, and it grew rapidly under Louis XIII and Louis XIV, in great part through the interest of the minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert. The library moved in 1666 to two houses in the Rue Vivienne and opened to the public in 1692. Jean-Paul Bignon reformed its system, and from 1721 the Richelieu site, the main location for 275 years, began to take shape.

After the French First Republic was established in September 1792 the Assembly declared the Bibliothèque du Roi national property and it became the Bibliothèque Nationale. Its collections passed 300,000 volumes as the private libraries of aristocrats and clergy were seized. Napoleon ordered provincial libraries to send it any book it lacked and added spoil from his conquests, some of it returned after his fall. In 1868 it moved into new buildings on the Rue de Richelieu designed by Henri Labrouste, and in 1896 it was still the largest repository of books in the world.

The library is a public establishment under the Ministry of Culture and the national repository of all that is published in France, which by law must be deposited there. President François Mitterrand announced a new library on 14 July 1988; the architect Dominique Perrault designed it, and after cost overruns that earned it the nickname Très Grande Bibliothèque it was inaugurated on 15 December 1996.

Its Manuscripts department houses the largest collection of medieval and modern manuscripts worldwide, including about 5,000 Ancient Greek manuscripts. Gallica, its digital library established in October 1997, makes freely available millions of books, manuscripts, newspapers, images, maps and recordings.
bibracte: Bibracte was one of the most important stone hillforts in Gaul. It stood on Mont Beuvray, which straddles the French départements of Nièvre and Saône-et-Loire in Burgundy, about 25 kilometres from Autun. The material culture of the Aedui matched the Late Iron Age La Tène culture. Bibracte is mentioned only twice in Roman sources, both in Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War, in 58 and 52 BCE. The origin of its name is poorly understood: it may come from a Celtic word for beaver, or from the Latin biffractrus, meaning twice fortified, though excavation shows that two walls did not stand at once.

Dating shows that the oppidum was founded at the end of the 3rd century BCE, within an outer rampart enclosing 200 hectares. An inner rampart of the Murus Gallicus type, about 5 kilometres long, was built later and enclosed 135 hectares, so the city shrank. Before the Roman conquest it had more than thirty thousand inhabitants. Caesar describes the Aedui as allies of Rome, called blood brothers, since at least the 2nd century BCE, and as rivals of the Arverni and Sequani for hegemony over much of Gaul.

Rome helped them defeat an Arverni army in that century and defended them against the Helvetii, whom Caesar's armies defeated in 58 BCE, 26 kilometres from the fort. In 52 BCE Vercingetorix was proclaimed head of the Gaulish coalition at Bibracte. A few decades after the conquest the site was abandoned in favour of Autun, called Augustodunum, and then lay undisturbed until modern archaeology.

Excavation has found a district of specialised metalworkers near the Rebout gate: blacksmiths, bronzeworkers and enamellers, probably also goldsmiths and minters. Houses were mostly of wood and earth, with stone kept for the ramparts. A Roman-style basilica with three naves, dated between 50 and 40 BCE and between 35 and 25 BCE, is the oldest known example of Roman monumental stone architecture in Europe outside the Mediterranean, and it shows that the Romanization of the Aedui was faster than once thought.

Jacques-Gabriel Bulliot identified Bibracte in 1867 and excavated from 1867 to 1895, with funds from Napoleon III. His nephew Joseph Déchelette continued from 1897 to 1907. Work resumed in 1984, and the site was declared of national interest in 1985. Teams from Brno, Sheffield, Kiel, Budapest, Vienna and Leipzig have worked there. The site is now an archaeological park in a protected forest, with a Museum of Celtic Civilization that opened in 1996 and a European research centre at Glux-en-Glenne. It received the Great Site of France designation on 12 December 2007.
bicycle: The dandy horse, also called the Draisienne or Laufmaschine, was invented by the German Baron Karl von Drais, who introduced it to the public in Mannheim in 1817 and in Paris in 1818. It was the first means of human transport to use only two wheels in tandem and is regarded as the first bicycle, though it had no pedals: the rider sat astride a wooden frame and pushed it along with their feet while steering the front wheel. A Scottish blacksmith, Kirkpatrick MacMillan, may have built the first mechanically propelled two-wheeled vehicle in 1839, although the claim is often disputed.

In the early 1860s the Frenchmen Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added a mechanical crank drive with pedals to an enlarged front wheel, the velocipede, which was the first to be mass-produced. In 1869 the Scotsman Thomas McCall built a rod-driven velocipede with rear-wheel drive, and Eugène Meyer of Paris patented a method of tensioning wire spokes that allowed stronger, lighter wheels. The velocipede developed into the penny-farthing, with a metal frame, wire-spoked wheels and solid rubber tyres. Britain's first cycle factory grew from the Coventry Sewing Machine Company's order for a Michaux cycle in 1868, which led to the Coventry Model.

A bicycle is a human-powered or motor-assisted, pedal-driven, single-track vehicle with two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other. The basic shape of the upright or safety bicycle has changed little since the first chain-driven model was developed around 1885. Most have a diamond frame, a truss of two triangles. Historically, women's frames had a top tube joined lower on the seat tube, so that a rider could mount and dismount in a skirt or dress; this is called a step-through or open frame.

It is the most efficient human-powered means of transport in terms of the energy a person must spend to cover a distance. Up to 99 per cent of the energy the rider puts into the pedals reaches the wheels, though gearing may reduce this by 10 to 15 per cent. Cycling takes about four-fifths less energy than walking the same distance.

The bicycle had a considerable effect on society, in both culture and industry. Around the turn of the 20th century it reduced crowding in inner-city tenements by letting workers commute from more spacious suburban homes, and it reduced dependence on horses. It also allowed people to travel into the country for leisure, being three times as energy efficient as walking and three to four times as fast.

Several components that played a key role in the development of the car were first invented for the bicycle: ball bearings, pneumatic tyres, chain-driven sprockets and tension-spoked wheels. The first bicycle sharing scheme was the White Bicycle plan in Amsterdam in 1965.
bidam: Little is recorded of Pidam's birth or early career. As Sangdaedeung he was probably of royal or Jinggol rank. It is said that he and Alcheon were close in age and served under King Jinpyeong, and since Alcheon was a hwarang, Pidam may have been one too. With Alcheon and Kim Yongchun he was said to be among those who supported Seondeok while she was still a princess.

Queen Seondeok appointed him Sangdaedeung in 645, and as her health failed she left most of the work of government to him. Silla was then under attack from the joined forces of Baekje and Goguryeo, which took over 40 fortresses in the west, and the queen's costly temple building, above all Hwangnyongsa, was resented. The Tang emperor held that Silla's neighbours did not fear it because a woman ruled it.

Around 8 February 647 Pidam gathered his supporters at the fortress of Myeonghwalseong against Kim Yushin's army at Wolseong, where the queen lived. A story tells that when a falling star over Wolseong heartened the rebels, Kim Yushin flew a burning scarecrow on a kite to make it seem the star had returned. The rising ended on 17 February; Seondeok died before it was fully suppressed, and her cousin became Queen Jindeok.

On 26 February 647 Queen Jindeok ordered the execution of Pidam and 30 of his men with their entire families. His motives remain debated. By custom a Sangdaedeung could succeed a king who left no legitimate heir, and some historians believe Pidam was a victim of political manipulation by Kim Yushin, allied by marriage with Kim Chunchu. The purge of the rebellious nobles reduced their influence at court and strengthened the monarchy, and Kim Chunchu, as King Taejong Muyeol, later passed over 60 laws for a centralised government.
bidar: Bidar stands on the Deccan plateau at about 2,300 feet, bordering Telangana and Maharashtra. Its name appears to derive from the Kannada word bidiru, meaning bamboo, and it was also called Bhadrakote. Legend links it with the ancient kingdom of Vidarbha, a connection mentioned in the writings of Firishta. Under the Bahmani Sultanate it was known as Muhammadabad. Its monuments earned it the nickname City of Whispering Monuments, since about 30 of the 61 listed by the state archaeology department are tombs.

The recorded history of the city goes back to the third century BCE, when it belonged to the Mauryan Empire. The Satavahanas, Kadamba, the Chalukyas of Badami, the Rashtrakutas and the Chalukyas of Kalyana ruled in turn. A small fort is recorded under Prince Ulugh Khan in 1322, after which it came under the Tughlaq dynasty. Officers of the Delhi Sultan rebelled in the mid-14th century and founded the Bahmani dynasty in 1347 at Gulbarga. Sultan Ahmad Shah moved the capital to Bidar for its better climate, rebuilt the fort and raised madrasas, mosques, palaces and gardens. Mahmud Gawan, prime minister from 1466, is its most notable figure.

Bidar remained under the Barid Shahi dynasty until Bijapur conquered it in 1619. In 1656 Aurangzeb took the fort from the Adil Shahis, and gunpowder stored in the Mahmud Gawan madrasa exploded, destroying about a quarter of the building. In 1724 Bidar passed to the Nizams, and in 1956 it became part of Mysore State, now Karnataka.

Bidar Fort is pentagonal, with five gateways. Inside are the Rangin Mahal, with coloured tiles and mother-of-pearl inlay, the Takht Mahal, where several sultans were crowned, and the Solah Khamba Mosque of 1423 to 1424. The Chaubara is a 22-metre tower in the city centre. Bahmani and Barid Shahi tombs lie around the city, and a karez, an underground aqueduct built in the 15th century, is thought to be the earliest in India. The city gave its name to bidriware, metalwork inlaid with silver.
bidayuh: Bidayuh is the collective name for several indigenous groups of southern Sarawak and northern West Kalimantan, on Borneo, that are broadly alike in language and culture. The name means inhabitants of land; the term Land Dayak was first used in the time of Rajah James Brooke, and they have also been called Klemantan. They are the second-largest Dayak group in Sarawak after the Iban. In Sarawak most live within 40 km of Greater Kuching, in the Kuching and Serian divisions, and in Indonesia mainly in the Sanggau Regency.

Their lands lie mainly in the basin of the Sarawak River, in hilly and mountainous forest traditionally worked by rotational farming and hunting from parent villages set on hills for protection. Almost all the traditional longhouse villages have now given way to individual houses and roads, with some plantation farming and less hill padi. Fruit trees, especially durian, remain markers of property, and the head-house has become a symbol of the people.

About 25 Bidayuh dialects are spoken in Sarawak, grouped into Eastern, Central, Highland and Western clusters. They are not mutually intelligible, so Malay or Malaysian English often serve within the community. The Salako and Lara, though classed as Bidayuh by the Malaysian government, have distinct traditions of descent, and the Salako language belongs to the Malayic Dayak family. Bidayuh music uses ensembles of large bossed gongs and a bamboo tube zither called the pratuokng.

The Bidayuh were traditionally animists, and traces of these beliefs remain. Christian missionaries arrived in the Brooke era from 1848, bringing education and modern medicine, and Catholicism reached Kampung Taee through the Mill Hill Missionaries in the early 1920s. Most villages now have a Roman Catholic or Anglican church, or a mosque. The Bukar Bidayuh once hung the bodies of the dead in trees, and the Nyobeng was a headhunting ritual of thanksgiving in which the skulls of the sacrificed were bathed. Gawai festivals celebrate the harvest.
biebrich-palace: Georg August Samuel of Nassau-Idstein, raised from count to prince in 1688, wanted a more impressive seat than his palace at Idstein in the Taunus. He moved first to Wiesbaden and then to Biebrich, at that time a community separate from Wiesbaden, and began a chateau close to the Rhine, opposite the Biebricher Wörth. Designed by the Baroque architect Julius Ludwig Rothweil and completed in 1702, it survives as the West Pavilion. Four years later a matching pavilion was built 86 metres to the east: the western one was kept for the prince and his entourage, the eastern one for his wife.

From 1707 the architect Johann Maximilian von Welsch joined the two pavilions with a gallery and built a circular ballroom at the exact centre. The Rotunda, completed in 1721, gave the palace its distinctive appearance. When Georg August Samuel died, the House of Nassau-Idstein died out and the palace passed to the line of Nassau-Usingen. Prince Karl of Nassau-Usingen chose Biebrich as his permanent residence, and to house his court and government offices Friedrich Joachim Stengel designed the present eastern wing and, three years later, an identical western wing.

In 1817 the landscape architect Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell laid out the gardens for Duke Wilhelm of Nassau. In 1935 Charlotte, Grand Duchess of Luxembourg, sold the palace to the State of Prussia. Heavily damaged in World War II, it was renovated and partly rebuilt by the State of Hesse between 1980 and 1982. The state government now uses it for official occasions, and it houses the state's historic preservation agency.
biedermeier: The Biedermeier period was an era in the art and culture of the German Confederation between 1815 and 1848, in which the middle classes grew and artists produced works that appealed to them. It began with the end of the Napoleonic Wars and ended with the Revolutions of 1848. Two forces drove it: growing urbanisation and industrialisation, which created a new urban middle class and a new audience for the arts, and the political stability under Klemens von Metternich after the Congress of Vienna. Artists and society concentrated on the domestic and, at least in public, the non-political.

The name comes from the fictional mediocre poet Gottlieb Biedermaier, invented by the country doctor Adolf Kussmaul and the lawyer Ludwig Eichrodt for poems in the Munich satirical weekly Fliegende Blätter in 1850. The verses parodied the depoliticised, petit-bourgeois people of the era. Bieder means plain, and Maier is a common surname. The word has been used as a label for the epoch since around 1900.

The values associated with Biedermeier include affection, sensibility, moderation and modesty, and Gemütlichkeit, a state of cosiness and friendliness. Because of strict control of publication and official censorship, writers turned to non-political subjects such as historical fiction and country life, and political talk stayed at home among close friends. Typical poets were Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, Adelbert von Chamisso, Eduard Mörike and Wilhelm Müller, and Adalbert Stifter wrote the novel Der Nachsommer. Painting preferred the everyday world with few grand gestures, as in Friedrich von Amerling's Portrait of the Arthaber Family of 1837 and the landscapes of Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller. Carl Spitzweg was another key painter.

Biedermeier furniture was the first style to arise from the growing middle class. A simplified reading of the French Empire style, it used local woods such as cherry, ash and oak rather than imported mahogany. Pieces from 1815 to 1830 were the most severe and neoclassical, and Vienna produced unique designs. In music, publications of operatic excerpts, Lieder and symphonic arrangements allowed amateurs to play at home on the piano.

An exhibition at the Vienna applied arts museum in 1896 brought the style new admirers and a revival among European cabinetmakers that lasted until Art Deco. In Wilhelmine Germany, social reformers saw Biedermeier architecture as a model of middle-class domestic reform, and in the Weimar Republic architects such as Paul Schultze-Naumburg and Paul Mebes promoted a neo-Biedermeier style for new housing.

In the Czech lands the period coincided with the Czech National Revival, with writers such as Božena Němcová and Karel Hynek Mácha and painters such as Josef Navrátil. The Polish architectural style Świdermajer was named as a play on the word. The Geymüllerschlössel in Vienna, built in 1808, now houses the Biedermeier collection of the Museum of Applied Arts.
bielefeld: Bielefeld was founded in 1214 by Count Hermann IV of Ravensberg to guard a pass across the Teutoburg Forest. As a minor member of the Hanseatic League it became the city of linen, known for its bleachfields into the 19th century. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 made Ravensberg, from 1719 Minden-Ravensberg, part of Brandenburg-Prussia. When Prussia lost its western territories to French control in 1807, Bielefeld belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia; it returned to Prussia in 1813, and after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 it was incorporated into the Province of Westphalia.

The Cologne-Minden railway opened in 1849, and the Bozi brothers built the first large mechanised spinning mill in 1851. Metal works began to open in the 1860s. Dürkoppwerke, founded in 1867 as a sewing machine repair company, employed 1,665 people in 1892, and the Dürkopp car was produced from 1898 to 1927. In 1923, during the inflation of the Weimar Republic, the town's savings bank printed emergency money on silk, linen and velvet, now collectable as Stoffgeld.

The city's synagogue was burned in 1938 during the Kristallnacht pogrom. In 1944 and 1945 American and British bombers attacked the gas works, marshalling yard and railway viaducts; on 14 March 1945 the RAF wrecked the viaduct at Schildesche in the first use of its 10 tonne Grand Slam bomb. American troops entered in April 1945.

After the war Bielefeld was a headquarters town for the fighting command of the British Army of the Rhine, whose presence continued until the 1980s and ended with a final departure in 2020. On 1 January 1973 the city was merged with the surrounding district, taking in the south side of the Teutoburg Forest; its population rose from 167,000 to 320,000 and its area from 48 to 259 km2.

Bielefeld is in the Ostwestfalen-Lippe region of North Rhine-Westphalia, with 342,952 inhabitants, mostly north of the Teutoburg Forest in the Ravensberg Basin. Its university was founded in 1969, and the sociologist Niklas Luhmann was among its first professors. Companies based there include Dr. Oetker, and the Bethel Foundation is a major employer. Since 1994 the satirical Bielefeld conspiracy has claimed that the city does not exist.
biella: Biella is the capital of the province of the same name in Piedmont, about 80 kilometres north-east of Turin and at about the same distance west-north-west of Milan. It lies in the foothills of the Alps, in an area of springs and lakes fed by glaciers and watered by the streams Elvo, Oropa and Cervo. The first inhabitants were Ligurians and Celts. A Ligurian people, the Victimuli, exploited gold veins near the Elvo on the plain of the Bessa, an activity that continued into the early Middle Ages.

The name appears for the first time as Bugella in a document of 826, recording the donation of Bugella to Count Busone by Louis the Pious. On 12 April 1160 Uguccione, bishop of Vercelli, granted trade privileges to anyone living on the Piazzo hill as a refuge from the warfare between Guelphs and Ghibellines of Vercelli, which was the birth of the Borgo del Piazzo. A revolt destroyed the bishop's castle in the 14th century, and Biella and its dependent communes came under the House of Savoy.

In the 14th and 15th centuries the Visconti family competed with Savoy for the region. The French occupied Biella in 1704, and in 1706 the Biellese soldier Pietro Micca saved nearby Turin from a siege, but died doing so. The French occupied the town again in 1798 and annexed it after the Battle of Marengo, and the Congress of Vienna returned it to Savoy. In 1859 Biella was besieged by the Austrians until Garibaldi ended the siege.

The statutes of Biella already refer to the guilds of wool workers and weavers in 1245, and the region's high pastures and abundant water suited the trade. A silk factory built in 1695 was converted in 1835 into a wool factory with mechanical looms, putting Biella at the forefront of the industry.

Biella remains an important wool processing and textile centre; Ermenegildo Zegna and Cerruti 1881 are among its firms. Its cathedral grew around the Romanesque baptistery of the 10th and 11th centuries, which houses 13th-century frescoes. Nearby, the Sanctuary of Oropa, a site of pilgrimage, became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.
big-bear: Big Bear was born at Jackfish Lake, near the future site of Battleford. His father, Muckitoo or Black Powder, was a minor chief of a band of 80 Plains Cree-Saulteaux people. In the spring of 1837 he survived smallpox, which left his face partly disfigured. On a journey with his father to Bull's Forehead Hill he had a vision of the Bear Spirit, the most powerful spirit in Cree belief, and received his power bundle, his song and his name. He became a warrior before he was a leader, and succeeded his father as chief on Black Powder's death in 1864.

In October 1870 Big Bear's band took part in the Battle of the Belly River near present-day Lethbridge, the largest battle between the Cree and the Blackfoot, in which the Cree lost between 200 and 300 men. As the bison vanished and disease spread in the 1870s, he would not sign Treaty 6, saying: "When we set a fox trap we scatter pieces of meat all around but when the fox gets into the trap we knock him on the head. We want no baits." He signed on 8 December 1882 to save his people from starvation.

In 1885 the government cut off rations to force him onto a reserve, and his influence passed to Wandering Spirit. After news of the Métis victory at Duck Lake, warriors led by Wandering Spirit and Big Bear's son Little Bear killed the agent Thomas Trueman Quinn and nine other men at Frog Lake, although Big Bear tried to stop them. The government held him responsible.

Big Bear surrendered to the North-West Mounted Police at Fort Carlton on 2 July 1885. At his trial, held in English with translation into Cree, the evidence showed he had taken no part in the killings, and his friend Henry Ross Halpin testified that he had been as much a prisoner as Halpin himself. Judge Hugh Richardson nonetheless found him guilty of felony treason and sentenced him to three years at Stony Mountain Penitentiary. Released ill in February 1887, he died on the Little Pine reserve. Many honour him as a chief who resisted with ideas rather than guns.
big-hole: The Big Hole, called Groot Gat in Afrikaans, is the open-pit part of the Kimberley Mine in Kimberley, South Africa. It was long considered the deepest hole excavated by hand, a title it contends for with the Jagersfontein Mine. A researcher reported in 2005 that the hand-dug parts of the Jagersfontein and Bultfontein mines may have been deeper or larger in volume. Its surface covers 17 hectares and its width is 463 metres. It was dug to a depth of 240 metres and then partly filled with debris to about 215 metres. About 40 metres of water has since gathered in it.

The first diamonds were found in 1871 on Colesberg Kopje, on the farm Vooruitzigt, which belonged to the De Beers brothers, by members of the Red Cap Party from Colesberg. The scramble for claims gave the place the name New Rush. From mid-July 1871 to 1914 up to 50,000 miners dug the hole with picks and shovels.

On 13 March 1888 the leaders of the separate diggings agreed to merge them into De Beers Consolidated Mines Limited, with life governors who included Cecil John Rhodes, Alfred Beit and Barney Barnato. By 14 August 1914, when work stopped, over 22 million tons of rock had been taken out. Once surface work became too dangerous and unproductive, De Beers mined the pipe underground to a depth of 1,097 metres.

The diamonds created a heavy demand for black labour, and land dispossession in the 1870s helped produce a large black migrant population in Kimberley. Mining managers built segregated housing, without natural water or waste disposal, and the origins of the apartheid city structure have been traced to these conditions. Between 1897 and 1899 Kimberley Hospital admitted 5,368 black patients to separate wards, and 1,144 died, chiefly of tuberculosis, pneumonia, scurvy, diarrhoea, syphilis and mining accidents.

Most accidents came from rockfalls, rockbursts, trucks, explosives and the cages. Basotho miners answered accidents with strikes or with the Koata strategy, a loud and abusive way of going to work despite fear. Between 24 June 1887 and 28 November 1892 an estimated 5,000 black burials took place at Glastone cemetery, some without coffins.

After mining ceased in 1914 the pit became an attraction for visitors. In 1965 De Beers appointed Basil Humphreys as museum consultant, and an open-air museum of early Kimberley, with streetscapes, dioramas and displays of mining technology, opened during the city's centenary celebrations in 1971. Between 2002 and 2005 De Beers invested R50 million in a tourism facility at the Big Hole. Since the early 2000s there has been an effort to have it listed as a World Heritage Site.
bight-of-benin: The Bight of Benin, also called the Bay of Benin, is a bight in the Gulf of Guinea area on the western coast of Africa. It extends eastward for about 640 kilometres from Cape St. Paul to the Nun outlet of the Niger River. It was named for the Kingdom of Benin in present-day Nigeria. The Republic of Benin, formerly Dahomey, took its name from the bight, not the other way around.

Historical association with the Atlantic slave trade led to the coast becoming known as the Slave Coast. Powerful indigenous kingdoms along the bight relied heavily on a long-established slave trade, which expanded greatly after the arrival of European powers and became a global trade with the colonisation of the Americas. Estimates from the 1640s suggest that Benin took in 1,200 slaves a year. Restrictions made it hard for the volume to grow until new states and different routes made an increase possible.

Slave trading was made illegal for Britons in 1807, and from then on the Royal Navy created the West Africa Squadron to suppress it. The effort was magnified after 1833, when the trade was made illegal throughout the British Empire, and it continued until the 1890s. It cost Britain significant sums of money and cost the Royal Navy hundreds, if not thousands, of sailors' lives from tropical diseases. An old naval rhyme warns, in one version, to beware the Bight of Benin, for few come out though many go in, and it is said to refer to the risk of malaria.

On 1 February 1852 the British established the Bight of Benin protectorate under consuls of the Bight of Benin. On 6 August 1861 it was joined with the Bight of Biafra protectorate into a united British protectorate, which was ultimately merged into Nigeria.
bihac: Bihać stands on the banks of the river Una in northwestern Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Bosanska Krajina region close to the border with Croatia. It is the administrative centre of Una-Sana Canton in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The town was first built on the river's Island of St. Ladislav, and it was the centre of the Pounje, the lands along the Una. Its municipality includes many villages, among them Ripač, Kulen Vakuf and Brekovica.

Medieval towns around the Una began to appear in the middle of the 13th century. Bihać is first mentioned on 26 February 1260 in a charter of King Béla IV, which describes it as a town on the Island of St. Ladislav owned by the Benedictine abbey of Topusko. Two years later, in 1262, Béla proclaimed it a royal free city under the direct authority of the throne, with rights that let it develop independently of local lords. A charter of 1271 confirms the status. At the head of the municipality stood a town elder, often called a judge, and the town had a curia of magistrates and notaries who kept court and civil records.

In 1530 Austria sent troops to defend seven key strongholds in Croatia, among them Bihać. The Ottomans occupied it in 1592 after a siege of ten days, and until the 19th century it was one of the most important forts in Bosnia. Auguste Marmont, governor-general of the Illyrian Provinces, briefly interrupted Ottoman rule on 5 May 1810 and then withdrew. Ottoman rule ended de facto after the Congress of Berlin.

During World War II the town was occupied by Axis troops and included in the Independent State of Croatia. The Ustaše regime committed the genocide of the Serbs and the Holocaust; from July to September 1941 the Ustaše killed some 15,000 Serbs, along with some Jews and Roma, at Garavice, near Bihać. For two months in late 1942 and early 1943 Bihać was the capital of a short-lived territory, the Bihać Republic, until German forces recaptured it. It returned to Bosnian territory on 28 March 1945. The town was besieged for three years from 1992 to 1995 during the Bosnian War.

At the 2013 census the city had 56,261 inhabitants, of whom 88 per cent were recorded as followers of Islam. The 1991 census recorded 46,737 Bosniaks, 12,689 Serbs, 5,580 Croats and 4,356 Yugoslavs in the municipality. The fertile soil makes agriculture significant for its economy.
bihar: Bihar borders Uttar Pradesh to the west, Nepal to the north, the northern part of West Bengal to the east and Jharkhand to the south, and covers 94,163 square kilometres. The Ganges flows west to east through the state and divides its fertile plain into North Bihar and South Bihar. Along with its tributaries, the Gandak and Koshi from the Nepalese Himalayas and the Bagmati, it regularly floods parts of the plain. The name is generally believed to derive from the Sanskrit and Pali vihāra, a monastery or religious dwelling, and medieval Persian and Turkic writers applied it to the area.

Chirand, on the northern bank of the Ganges in Saran district, has an archaeological record from the Neolithic, about 2500 to 1345 BCE. Regions of Bihar such as Magadha, Mithila and Anga are mentioned in the religious texts and epics of ancient India. According to Buddhist tradition the Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, at the Mahabodhi Temple. Early Buddhist centres of learning such as Nalanda and Vikramashila arose in Bihar and drew students and scholars from across Asia, and under dynasties including the Mauryas and Guptas Buddhism received royal patronage and spread from the region to other parts of Asia.

Buddhism in Magadha declined after the invasion of Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji, when many viharas were destroyed together with the universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila. Some historians believe thousands of Buddhist monks were massacred in the 12th century, while D. N. Jha suggests that these incidents resulted from Buddhist and Brahmin skirmishes in a fight for supremacy. After the Pala Empire the Karnat dynasty came to power in Mithila in the 11th century, and the Oiniwar dynasty succeeded it in the 14th.

After the Battle of Buxar in 1764 the British East India Company obtained the diwani rights, the right to administer and collect revenue, for Bihar, Bengal and Odisha. Bihar remained part of the Bengal Presidency until 1912, when Bihar and Orissa were carved out as a new province. In April 1917 Mahatma Gandhi visited Champaran, where Raj Kumar Shukla had drawn his attention to the exploitation of the peasants by European indigo planters, and the Champaran Satyagraha that followed drew support from Bihari nationalists such as Rajendra Prasad.

Bihar is a state of eastern India. The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its official languages are Hindi and Urdu, and the main native languages are Maithili, Magahi and Bhojpuri.
bijapur: Bijapur lies in the interior of the Deccan peninsula in northern Karnataka, some 519 km north-west of Bengaluru. The Krishna is the most important river of the district, which has deep black soil good for jowar, wheat, pulses and sugarcane. Evidence shows the area was inhabited from the Stone Age.

The city was established in the 10th and 11th centuries under the Kalyani Chalukyas and was known as Vijayapura, the city of victory. It passed to the Yadavas, came under the influence of Alauddin Khalji of Delhi towards the end of the 13th century, and was conquered by the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347. When Bahmani authority over its provinces ceased by 1490, the Adil Shahi dynasty arose, and the sultans of the Bijapur Sultanate ruled from 1490 to 1686.

The city owes much of its greatness to Yusuf Adil Shah, the founder of the independent state, to Ali Adil Shah I, who fortified it, and to Ibrahim Adil Shah II. At its peak in the early 17th century it is estimated to have held half a million to a million people. The fort, completed in 1566, has a wall with ninety-six bastions and a moat, and outside the walls lie the remains of a vast city of tombs and mosques.

The Mughal emperor Aurangazeb conquered Bijapur in 1686, having made it a subah two years earlier, and disease and other disasters afterwards greatly reduced its population. Mughal rule lasted until 1723; the Nizam of Hyderabad held it briefly, and in 1760 it passed to the Maratha Confederacy. After 1818 it came under the British, and in 1956 it joined Karnataka.

Bijapur is the headquarters of Bijapur district and is known for the monuments of the Adil Shahi period, among them the Bijapur Fort, the Bara Kaman, the Jama Masjid and the Gol Gumbaz. Its name was changed officially to Vijayapura in November 2014.
bikini-atoll: Bikini Atoll consists of 23 low islands of coral limestone and sand around a central lagoon of about 594 square kilometres, at the northern end of the Ralik Chain, some 850 kilometres north-west of Majuro. The average elevation is only about 2.1 metres above low tide. Its Marshallese name is Pikinni; the English form comes from the name given to it when it was part of German New Guinea. Between the 19th century and 1946 it was also known as Eschscholtz Atoll.

Bikini islanders lived by cultivating plants and fishing, and built double-hulled proas to sail between the atolls. Land was held by clans under chiefs. Japan took the Marshall Islands in 1914 and held them under a League of Nations mandate from 1920, and American forces captured nearby Kwajalein in February 1944.

The United States Navy wanted to learn what a nuclear weapon would do to ships, and chose Bikini. In 1946 the 167 islanders were moved to Rongerik, which could not feed them; by early 1948 they were close to starvation and were taken to Kwajalein, where they lived in tents beside a runway for six months before settling on Kili Island. From 1946 to 1958 the United States detonated 23 nuclear devices there, with a combined yield of about 77 megatons. Three islands were destroyed.
About 100 residents returned in 1972. In 1978 tests found dangerously high strontium-90 in well water and abnormal caesium-137 in the islanders' bodies, and they were removed again in September 1978.

UNESCO named the atoll a World Heritage Site on 3 August 2010, citing the sunken ships, among them the aircraft carrier USS Saratoga and the Japanese battleship Nagato, and the large crater left by the Bravo test. In 1998 an advisory group of the International Atomic Energy Agency recommended that Bikini Island not be permanently resettled. The islanders and their descendants live on other Marshallese islands and in the United States.
biladi-biladi-biladi: The anthem's words were written by Muhammad Yunis al-Qady and its music composed by Sayed Darwish, who kept close ties with early leaders of Egypt's national movement for independence, such as Mustafa Kamel. The chorus derives from one of Kamel's best-known nationalist speeches, delivered in 1907, in which he told his country that his love, his heart, his life and his blood were for it, and that there was no life except with Egypt. The anthem was officially adopted in 1979, and the musician Mohamed Abdel Wahab was involved in preparing it at the direction of President Anwar El-Sadat.

Egypt's first national anthem was an instrumental royal piece with no official lyrics, associated with the reign of Khedive Ismail and played at the opening of the Suez Canal. It was adopted as the first national anthem in 1871, and its melody is most likely the work of Giuseppe Pugioli, an Italian cornetist who stayed in Egypt. It did not become popular inside Egypt, and Ahmad Shawqi won a competition in 1920 to write words for it, but his entry failed to gain traction with the bureaucracy.

Eslami ya Misr, by Mustafa Sadiq Al-Rafei with music by Safar Ali, served from 1923 to 1936. King Farouk restored the royal anthem in 1936, and it continued, renamed the republican anthem, after the monarchy ended in 1953. In 1960 a decree adopted a wordless melody by Kamal El-Tawil as the anthem, and it served until 1979.

Republican Decree No. 149 of 1979 made Bilady, Bilady, Bilady the national anthem. A decree of December 1982 laid down that the words of the first verse accompany the music at popular and national celebrations, while only the instrumental music is played when welcoming presidents and foreign delegations. An unofficial Coptic version, not codified in law, circulates widely online.
bilaspur-himachal-pradesh: Bilaspur is a town and a municipal council in Bilaspur district. It lies on the foot of the Bandla Hills along the left bank of the Sutlej, at an average elevation of 673 m, in a valley that shelters it from the extremes of the surrounding mountains. The Sutlej here forms the Govind Sagar, and the monsoon from July to September brings high rainfall. It is the first major town after entering Himachal Pradesh on the way to Manali, 86 km from Shimla and 405 km from Delhi, on the Chandigarh–Manali highway.

Bilaspur was the capital of a state of the same name, founded in the seventh century and also known as Kahlur. Its ruling dynasty were Chandel Rajputs, who claimed descent from the rulers of Chanderi in present-day Madhya Pradesh. The town itself was founded in 1663. On 13 May 1665 Guru Tegh Bahadur went to Bilaspur for the mourning and funeral ceremonies of Raja Dip Chand. Rani Champa offered him land in her state, which he accepted at a cost of 500 rupees, covering the villages of Lodipur, Mianpur and Sahota. On 19 June 1665 he broke ground on a new settlement, which he named Nanaki after his mother.

The state later became a princely state of British India under the Punjab. It joined the Punjab States Agency in 1932, and the Punjab Hill States Agency was separated from that in 1936. On 12 October 1948 the last ruler, Raja Sir Anand Chand, acceded to the Government of India. Bilaspur became a separate state under a chief commissioner, and on 1 July 1954 an act of the Indian Parliament made it a district of Himachal Pradesh.

When the Sutlej was dammed to create the Govind Sagar, the historic town of Bilaspur was submerged and a new town was built upslope of the old. The 2001 census counted 13,058 people. Most people work in the services sector, and the town is served by buses on the highway, with the nearest major airport at Chandigarh, 141 km away.
bilbao: Bilbao lies in the north-central part of Spain, about 16 kilometres south of the Bay of Biscay. Its urban core is surrounded by two small mountain ranges, and the Nervión and the Ibaizabal join at Basauri to form an estuary some 15 kilometres long. The climate is oceanic, with rain through the year. Basque has two names for the city, Bilbao and Bilbo, and Bilbo is held to be the historical one.

Diego López V de Haro, lord of Biscay, founded the town by a charter dated at Valladolid on 15 June 1300, which King Ferdinand IV of Castile confirmed at Burgos on 4 January 1301. It stood on the right bank of the Nervión and received the fuero of Logroño, a body of rights that proved central to its growth. At first it had three streets inside walls; four more formed the Seven Streets, and the walls were pulled down in 1571 after floods and a great fire in 1569.

The Catholic Monarchs gave Bilbao the title of Noble Town on 20 September 1475. On 21 June 1511 Queen Joanna of Castile ordered the creation of its Consulate of the Sea, which long controlled the estuary and made the port one of the most important of the kingdom. Wool and iron from the Biscayan quarries were exported across Europe. The first printing press arrived in 1577, and in 1596 the first book in Basque was published there. After the siege of the First Carlist War the city received the added title of Unbeaten on 25 December 1836.

In the nineteenth century iron mines, ironworks and shipbuilding brought heavy industrialisation and a population explosion that led the city to annex neighbouring municipalities. The Bank of Bilbao was founded in 1857, the stock exchange opened on 21 July 1890, and an outer port was built at Santurtzi in 1902.

Bilbao is the largest city of the Basque Country and the capital of the province of Biscay, with 347,342 inhabitants and a metropolitan area of 1,037,847. Its renewal as a city of services began with the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. The football club Athletic Club, which fields only Basque players, is a symbol of Basque nationalism.
bilbilis: The Celtiberian settlement stood on the heights of Cerro de Bambola and part of San Paterno, north of ancient Segeda and 60 kilometres south-west of the Roman colony of Caesaraugusta, modern Zaragoza. It was the capital of the Lusones, a Celtic people of Hispania Citerior. Its earliest coins, of the late 2nd to the early 1st century BCE, show a male head with a dolphin and a horseman carrying a spear. The Romans first met the Lusones in the 2nd century BCE, when Quintus Fulvius Flaccus journeyed into Celtiberia.

Under Augustus the town became the municipium of Augusta Bilbilis, whose inhabitants all received Roman citizenship, and the road from Emerita Augusta to Caesaraugusta passed nearby.
