Its mint struck coins under Augustus, Tiberius and Caligula, among them one naming Lucius Aelius Sejanus as consul; after his fall his name was filed or stamped off most of them. The city's heyday was the 1st century CE. It declined rapidly in the 2nd century and was half-deserted by the 3rd.

The hilly ground imposed a terraced layout of steep streets and ramps rather than the usual Roman grid. The forum, practically square, lay before the temple in the upper city, framed by porticos, a basilica, a curia and a crypto-porticus; it was completed under Emperor Tiberius and altered under Trajan. The theatre, linked to the forum by gates and corridors, held around 4,500 spectators, far more than the town's estimated 3,500 inhabitants, so it probably served the region. Baths and a nymphaeum fed by hydraulic tanks gave the city a permanent water supply.

The modern town of Calatayud was founded near the Roman site. Much of the Museum of Calatayud holds finds from Bilbilis: frescoes from the baths and town houses, coins from its mint, and portraits of the Julio-Claudian imperial family found in the theatre area, among them a veiled head of Augustus found in 2009.
bilge-qaghan: Bilge Qaghan was born in 683, in the early years of the Second Turkic Khaganate, and his personal name, recorded in Chinese characters, was Ashina Mojilian. He campaigned beside his father from early childhood. In 697 Qapaghan Qaghan made him Tardush Shad, with command of the western wing of the khaganate. With his brother he destroyed the army of Wei Yuanzhong in 701, and he reconquered the Basmyl tribes in 703. He subdued the Yenisei Kyrgyz in 709 and, after they rebelled, killed their qaghan in 710. At the Battle of Bolchu he killed the Türgesh khagan Saqal.

Qapaghan Qaghan was killed in 716 during a campaign against the Toquz Oghuz, and his severed head was sent to Chang'an. His son Inel Qaghan succeeded him, but Bilge's brother Kul Tigin and Tonyukuk carried out a coup, killed Inel Qaghan and made Bilge qaghan. The title means wise king. Bilge appointed Kul Tigin Left Wise Prince, the second most powerful figure in the khaganate, and made his father-in-law Tonyukuk his master strategist. Reforms and the stabilisation of the regime brought back tribes that had fled.

In 720 the Tang chancellor Wang Jun, suspecting that the Pugu and Xiedie tribes planned to defect to the Turks, massacred their chieftains at a feast and attacked the tribes, nearly wiping them out. Emperor Xuanzong gathered a coalition against the Göktürks, but Tonyukuk struck first and crushed the Baximi in the autumn of 721. The Khitans were defeated later that year and the Xi the year after, while Bilge raided Gansu and took much of its livestock. Tonyukuk died in 726. In 733 Bilge defeated rebellious Khitan tribes.

Bilge once thought of converting to Buddhism and settling in cities. Tonyukuk discouraged him, arguing that the Turks were few and vulnerable to Chinese attacks, that their power rested on mobility, and that Buddhism would bring pacifism, so that keeping to Tengrism was necessary for survival.

Soon after sending an emissary to Xuanzong to seek a heqin alliance, Bilge was poisoned. He did not die at once and had time to punish the family of the man responsible with death. He died on 25 November 734, and his burial ceremony took place on 22 June 735. Several steles were then erected in the capital area by the Orkhon River. These Orkhon inscriptions, which describe his accomplishments, are the first known texts in Old Turkic.
bilhana: The 18th canto of the Vikramanka-deva-charita holds Bilhana's own account of his life. He was born in the village of Khonmusha, the modern Khunmoh, into a Brahmin family of the Kaushika gotra whose ancestors had been brought to Kashmir from Madhyadesha by king Gopaditya. His father Jyeshtha-kalasha was a scholar known for teaching a commentary on Patanjali's Mahabhashya. Bilhana praised the Lohara kings Ananta and Kalasha, and according to Kalhana he left Kashmir during Kalasha's reign, probably around 1063. The scholar P. N. Kawthekar places his birth around 1020.

After leaving Kashmir Bilhana visited Mathura, where he defeated scholars in a shastrartha debate, then Kanyakubja, Prayaga and Varanasi. The Kalachuri king Karna honoured him, and he defeated Gangadhara, a scholar of Karna's court. He went on to Dhara hoping to meet the Paramara king Bhoja, but found that Bhoja had died. In Gujarat, at Patana, the capital of the Chaulukya king Karna, he wrote the play Karna-sundari Natika, which was staged at court.

Some time after 1076 he sought the patronage of Vikramaditya VI and completed the Vikramanka-deva-charita in 1087. He wrote that the king made him Vidyapati and gave him a black umbrella and elephants. Some modern scholars think he later fell out of favour: a verse attributed to him says that even if the king of Kuntala takes all his wealth, he still has the treasure of Sarasvati, and the poem's last verses warn kings to respect the poets who make them immortal.

At the end of the poem Bilhana wished to return to Kashmir under king Harsha, who came to the throne in 1089, and to spend his last days by the Ganga. Kawthekar, noting that he does not mention Harsha's death in 1101, suggests he died around 1094. According to Mankhaka, Bilhana's poetry inspired Kalhana.

Later legends made him the hero of a love story told in the introductions to the Chaura-Panchashika, in which a king has him condemned to death for loving a princess and then pardons him. Modern scholars reject the story, and the attribution of the poem itself is doubtful, since Abhinavagupta quoted its verses a century before Bilhana. The story inspired two Tamil films of 1948.
bilhorod-dnistrovskyi: Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi lies on the right bank of the Dniester Estuary, which leads to the Black Sea, in the historical region of Budjak. Its names almost all mean white castle or white city: Asprokastron in Greek, Album Castrum in Latin, Cetatea Albă in Romanian, Akkerman in Ottoman Turkish and Weißenburg in German. The Genoese, who ruled it in the 14th and 15th centuries, used Moncastro. Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi has been the official name since 1944; Dnistrovskyi was added to tell it apart from Belgorod in Russia.

Milesian colonists founded a settlement named Tyras here in the 6th century BCE, which later came under Roman and Byzantine rule. In the 13th century the Cumans held the site, and from about 1290 it was a centre of Genoese commerce. Saint John the New, patron saint of Moldavia, was martyred in the city in 1330 during a Tatar incursion. Cetatea Albă was the last city on the right bank of the Dniester to join the Principality of Moldavia, for which it was a major port and fortress. The fortress was rebuilt in 1407 under Alexander the Good and in 1440 under Stephen II of Moldavia.

The Ottomans took the city in the 15th century. The citadel surrendered on a promise of safe passage, but most of the inhabitants were slaughtered. As Akkerman it became an Ottoman fortress against Poland-Lithuania and later Russia, and a centre of the Black Sea slave trade. Russia annexed it in 1812 with the rest of Bessarabia. On 25 September 1826 Russia and the Ottomans signed the Akkerman Convention here. The city belonged to Romania from 1918 to 1940 and again from 1941 to 1944, and has been in Ukraine since the Soviet period.

Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi is a port city in Odesa Oblast with a large freight seaport. In 1897 Jews formed 19.9 per cent of its population; in 1905 a pogrom killed eight of them, and during World War II about 800 who remained in the city were shot, and others were deported to Transnistria, where most died.
bill-of-rights-1689: Interest in Magna Carta revived in the 17th century, and Parliament passed the Petition of Right in 1628 and the Habeas Corpus Act in 1679. After the English Civil War and the years of the Protectorate and the Restoration, Parliamentarians who objected to the policies of James II invited the Dutch stadtholder William III of Orange-Nassau to overthrow him. William's invasion led James to flee to France, and in December 1688 the peers appointed William provisional governor. A Convention Parliament convened on 22 January 1689.

On 29 January the House of Commons proposed a statement of the rights James had violated. On 13 February the Marquess of Halifax offered the throne to William and Mary, who accepted, and they were crowned on 11 April under a new oath promising to govern according to the statutes agreed in Parliament.

The Declaration of Right was enacted as the Bill of Rights, which received royal assent on 16 December 1689. It declared illegal the suspension of laws or dispensing with them without Parliament's consent, the commission for ecclesiastical causes, and the levying of taxes without a grant of Parliament. It affirmed the right to petition the king, free elections, freedom of speech in Parliament, and frequent parliaments. It held that a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent was against the law, and that Protestants might have arms for their defence as allowed by law. It also forbade excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments.

The Act listed twelve policies of James II said to subvert the Protestant religion and the laws of the kingdom, including the prosecution of the Seven Bishops, and declared that he had abdicated. It barred Roman Catholics from the throne, and named William and Mary as successors to James, with the crown passing then to Mary's heirs and to her sister, Princess Anne.

The Act of Settlement of 1701 later altered the line of succession. A separate Claim of Right Act of 1689 applies in Scotland. Together they contributed to parliamentary sovereignty and a constitutional monarchy, and William Blackstone described such acts as fundamental laws of England. The Bill influenced the Virginia Declaration of Rights of 1776, and the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution reproduces almost verbatim its ban on excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishment. It was also a model for the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and the European Convention on Human Rights.

The Bill of Rights remains in statute in the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms, and Article 9 on freedom of speech in Parliament is still cited. It restates in statutory form the Declaration of Right that the Convention Parliament presented in February 1689, inviting William III and Mary II to become joint sovereigns.
billy-hughes: William Morris Hughes was born on 25 September 1862 in Pimlico, London, to Welsh parents: a carpenter and joiner at the Palace of Westminster and a domestic servant. His mother died when he was six, and he was raised by relatives in Wales, mostly with an aunt who kept a boarding house in Llandudno. At eleven he entered St Stephen's School, Westminster, and later worked as a pupil-teacher.

At 22 he emigrated to Australia on an assisted passage, arriving in Brisbane on 8 December 1884, and gave his birth year as 1864, a deception not uncovered until after his death. He worked at odd jobs, moved to Sydney about 1886, and settled in Balmain, where he joined the Australian Socialist League. He was elected to the New South Wales Legislative Assembly in 1894.

Hughes won the federal seat of West Sydney in 1901 and was called to the bar in 1903. He served as minister for external affairs in the Watson government of 1904 and as attorney-general in Andrew Fisher's governments, and became deputy leader of the Labor Party in 1907. When Fisher resigned in October 1915 with failing health, Hughes became prime minister. His support for sending conscripted troops overseas split the party, and he and his followers were expelled in November 1916. He stayed in office at the head of the National Labor Party, which soon merged with the Liberals to form the Nationalist Party, and his governments were re-elected in 1917 and 1919.

His government introduced a preferential voting system for the House of Representatives in 1918. In 1919 he went to the Paris Peace Conference with Joseph Cook and signed the Treaty of Versailles for Australia, the first international treaty Australia had signed. He secured Australian control of the former German New Guinea. After the 1922 election the Nationalists needed a coalition with the Country Party, whose price was his resignation, and Stanley Bruce succeeded him in 1923.

Hughes remained in parliament for the rest of his life. In 1928 he and his supporters crossed the floor to bring down Bruce's government, and he later joined the United Australia Party, serving as a minister and warning against Japanese imperialism. He lost the 1939 leadership to Robert Menzies by a handful of votes, and led the party briefly in 1941. He was expelled from the party in 1944 and joined the new Liberal Party in 1945.

He died on 28 October 1952, aged 90, at Lindfield, and some 450,000 people lined the streets for his state funeral in Sydney. Troops called him the little digger. The labour movement considered him a traitor, and historians still debate his legacy.
bilma: Bilma lies protected from the desert dunes under the Kaouar Cliffs and is the largest town along the Kaouar escarpment. It is deep in the Sahara, in the Ténéré, a hyper-arid region of north-eastern Niger and western Chad, with an average of only 12.7 mm of measurable rain a year. Its winter highs pass 27 °C, and temperatures exceed 40 °C from April to September, peaking at 44 °C in June. It is known for its gardens, for salt and natron produced in evaporation ponds, and for date cultivation.

Bilma was the destination of one of the last Saharan caravan routes, the Azalai from Agadez, and was a key stop in the trans-Saharan trade. The mixed population, mostly Kanuri with smaller Toubou, Tuareg and Hausa communities, reflects that role. The poet Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Kanemi was born in Bilma in the 12th century.

During French colonial rule the town was the site of a major but isolated military post at Fort Dromard. After independence its isolation made it a destination for disgraced officials in the time of Seyni Kountché, and the government built a prison there. Political leaders were held there in the 1980s, among them Sanoussi Tambari Djakou. In 1989 UTA Flight 772 crashed into the desert near the town after a bomb exploded on board, killing all 170 people aboard.

Bilma is a commune and the administrative seat of the Bilma Department, which covers some 670,000 square kilometres of north-eastern Niger. It had 4,016 people at the 2012 census. Its salt works still produce salt from large natron salt pans, and this salt is sold for livestock throughout West Africa.
biloxi: Biloxi lies on the Gulf Coast of southern Mississippi in Harrison County, on the Mississippi Sound, with barrier islands off the shore. It is bordered partly on the northeast by Biloxi Bay, across which lie Ocean Springs and St. Martin, and Gulfport adjoins it on the west. The climate is humid subtropical, and tropical storms strike in late summer and autumn. The French name Bilocci transliterates the name of the local Native American tribe in their own language.

In 1699 French colonists under Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville formed the first permanent European settlement in French Louisiana at Fort Maurepas, now in Ocean Springs and called Old Biloxi. The present city's site was first settled in 1720 around Fort Louis, and the capital of French Louisiana moved there from Mobile. In 1722, fearing tides and hurricanes, Governor Bienville moved it to New Orleans. France ceded its colonies east of the Mississippi to Great Britain in 1763; British rule lasted until 1779 and Spanish rule until 1810, yet Biloxi remained mostly French in character. The United States took over the area in 1811, and Mississippi became a state in 1817.

In the 19th century Biloxi became a summer resort. The Biloxi Lighthouse was built in Baltimore and finished on the site in May 1848. Union forces took Ship Island early in the Civil War and with it control of Biloxi, which suffered no direct damage. The first seafood cannery opened in 1881 and drew immigrants from Europe. Keesler Field, built during World War II, became a major training site. In 1959 the physician Gilbert R. Mason led the Biloxi Wade-Ins against the exclusion of black people from the beach; a riot in 1960 killed ten people, and the protests led to desegregation of the beaches. Legal gambling in the 1990s made the city a centre of resort casinos.

Biloxi had a population of 49,449 at the 2020 census and is one of the two principal cities of the Gulfport–Biloxi metropolitan area. It has six historic districts on the National Register of Historic Places, and its Blessing of the Fleet, begun in 1929, takes place each year before the shrimp season. Katrina's storm surge of 30 feet on 29 August 2005 caused massive damage, and the most destructive earlier hurricanes struck in 1855, 1906, 1909, 1947 and 1969.
bima-people: The Bimanese, who call themselves Dou Mbojo, are an Austronesian people native to the eastern part of Sumbawa Island in the province of West Nusa Tenggara, and number close to a million. Their language, Bimanese, belongs to the Austronesian family. It is closely related to the languages of Flores and Sumba further east, and only distantly to the Sumbawa language spoken in the western half of the island.

Before Islam spread to most coastal regions of the Malay Archipelago, several small polities of the Bima area belonged to the sphere of influence of the Majapahit Empire, and later had close cultural and political ties with the Kingdom of Gowa in Sulawesi. Local traditions credit Malay merchants with bringing Islam. In the mountains, the Dou Donggo, the mountain people, and the Dou Wawo held to their own beliefs, helped by the rugged country they lived in, and were granted a semi-autonomous status within the Sultanate of Bima, keeping certain political privileges along with their indigenous practices.

Some Dou Donggo communities converted to Catholicism in the mid-20th century, though their older beliefs remained strong. In the 1980s rapid population growth, following the introduction of medicine, left the land no time to recover, and swidden farming of rice, millet and maize gave way to wet rice in terraced paddy fields and cash crops such as peanuts and soybean for sale in the lowlands.

The Bimanese live in the villages of the regencies of Bima and Dompu and in the city of Bima, and also in Sumbawa Regency, especially in the districts of Empang, Plampang, Lape, Lopok and Taliwang. In the countryside most live by wet rice farming, animal husbandry and fishing, while swidden farming survives among highland communities. Townspeople work in trade, local administration and a wide range of other occupations, and tourism has grown with the nearness of Komodo National Park. Many entrepreneurs descend from marriages with Arab and Chinese immigrant communities. Sunni Islam is the main religion, and the lowlanders are known as fervent adherents of Islam.
bimbisara: Bimbisara was the son of Bhattiya, a chieftain, and belonged to the Haryanka dynasty, which he is said to have established. His first capital was Girivraja, identified with Rajagriha, and the 7th-century Chinese monk Xuanzang credited him with building the city of Rajgir. Jain histories know him as Shrenika or Seniya, Buddhist tradition as Bimbisara. The sources give two competing chronologies for his reign, so his dates are uncertain.

Bimbisara led a campaign against Anga, perhaps to avenge an earlier defeat of his father by its king, Brahmadatta. Anga was annexed, and his son Kunika, later Ajatashatru, was made governor at Champa. The conquest gave Magadha control of the routes to the Ganges delta and its ports. Pukkusati, king of Gandhara, sent him an embassy.

He also built alliances by marriage. His first wife, Kosala Devi, was the daughter of Mahā Kosala, king of Kosala, and sister of Prasenajit; she brought Kashi as dowry, and the marriage ended the hostility between Magadha and Kosala. His second wife, Chellana, was a Licchavi princess of Vaishali, and his third, Kshema, a daughter of the chief of the Madra clan. The Mahavagga depicts him with 500 wives. His court is said to have included the physician Jivaka.

Accounts of his end differ. In Buddhist tradition Ajatashatru assassinated him under the influence of Devadatta, a separatist monk. Jain scripture says instead that Bimbisara killed himself after his son imprisoned him, and that he will be reborn as Mahapadma, the first of the future tirthankaras.

Buddhist scriptures record that he met the Buddha before his enlightenment, became an important disciple and attained sotapannahood. He let the women of his palace visit the Buddha in the evenings, and at their request the Buddha gave a hair-and-nail stupa for veneration. Jain literature records him as a devotee who frequently visited Mahavira.
bin-tepe: Bin Tepe lies on a low limestone ridge on the southern shore of Marmara Lake in Manisa Province, north of Sardis. Its height and its nearness to a major travel route made the mounds conspicuous to ancient travellers, and its closeness to earlier Bronze Age settlement mounds suggests it may have been chosen to give a symbolic link to the past. The burials were laid out in groups, probably of families or estates. There were once at least 149 tumuli; about 115 remain, the rest having been destroyed for farmland.

Each tumulus is a stone burial chamber, built of slabs or cut into the bedrock and usually placed off-centre to deter robbers, under a large earthen mound often ringed by a retaining wall called a crepis. The earliest date from around 600 BCE and seem to have been adapted from the Phrygian royal burials at Gordion. The style outlived the fall of the Lydian Empire in 546 BCE, and many datable examples were built in the Persian period that followed, alongside rock-cut tombs and cist graves.

The largest mound, 63 m high with a volume of 785,000 cubic metres, is generally accepted as the tomb of Alyattes, who died in 560 BCE; building it has been estimated at two and a half years for 2,400 labourers and 600 beasts of burden. Its chamber of limestone and marble shows Greek and Near Eastern influence. The second largest, 53 m tall, was traditionally given to Gyges, but pottery in it is at least forty years later than his reign, and archaeologists have suggested it was built for a queen.

Herodotus wrote that the tomb of Alyattes was built by the men of the market, the artificers and the prostitutes, and that marker stones on its top recorded each group's share of the work. The Prussian consul Ludwig Peter Spiegelthal excavated it in 1853, and work on the other mounds began in 1880. Though looting has destroyed much, the tumuli shed light on Lydian society and on the Persian period, which is better attested here than at Sardis. In 2025 Bin Tepe was listed as part of a World Heritage Site with Sardis.
bindusara: Bindusara's life is not documented as well as those of his father Chandragupta and his son Ashoka. Much of what is known comes from Jain and Buddhist legends written hundreds of years after his death, such as the 12th-century Parishishta-Parvan of Hemachandra, the Mahavamsa and the Ashokavadana. Most sources, including the Puranas and the Mahavamsa, make him the son of Chandragupta, though the Dipavamsa and the Ashokavadana give other parentage. Hemachandra names his mother as Durdhara.

Greek writers called him Amitrochates or Allitrochades, probably from the Sanskrit title Amitraghāta, slayer of enemies, and like Ashoka he bore the title Devanampriya, Beloved of the Gods. Buddhist and Jain texts tell that the minister Chanakya fed Chandragupta small doses of poison to build his immunity, and that when the pregnant queen ate some, Chanakya cut open her body to save the child. The name Bindusara is explained by drops of goat's blood in the Buddhist version and by a drop of poison in the Jain one.

The historian Upinder Singh estimates that he came to the throne around 297 BCE. The 16th-century Tibetan author Taranatha says that Chanakya destroyed the nobles and kings of 16 towns and made Bindusara master of the land between the eastern and western seas. Some historians take this to mean a conquest of the Deccan, while others think it refers only to the suppression of revolts. Sailendra Nath Sen concludes that he kept the territory he inherited, and Alain Daniélou that his achievement was to organise and consolidate it.

The Ashokavadana says he sent Ashoka to besiege Takshashila, whose people said they opposed only his oppressive ministers. Bindusara kept friendly relations with the Greeks: Deimachos of Plateia was the ambassador of the Seleucid king Antiochus I at his court. According to Athenaeus, Bindusara asked Antiochus for sweet wine, dried figs and a sophist, and was told that Greek law forbade the sale of a sophist. Buddhist texts call him a follower of Brahmanism, while the Ajivika sect appears to have enjoyed his patronage.

He died in the 270s BCE, around 273 BCE according to Singh. The Mahavamsa gives him a reign of 28 years and the Puranas 25. All the sources agree that Ashoka succeeded him, but they differ on how. According to the Mahavamsa, Ashoka hurried from Ujjain to Pataliputra and killed his 99 brothers, sparing only Tishya. The Brahmanda Purana says that Bindusara crowned Ashoka himself. Sen believes that a four-year struggle over the succession followed, ending with Ashoka's accession in 269-268 BCE.
bingen-am-rhein: Bingen am Rhein lies in the Mainz-Bingen district of Rhineland-Palatinate. The river Nahe empties into the Rhine here, where the Rhine Gorge begins, and the town forms the southern limit of the UNESCO Rhine Gorge World Heritage Site. The original name was Bingium, a Celtic word that may have meant a hole in the rock, a description of the shoal behind the Mouse Tower, known as the Binger Loch.

The first settlement seems to have been Celtic. In the early first century CE Roman troops were stationed here, building a wooden bridge across the Nahe and a bridgehead fort, and Bingen was the starting point of the Via Ausonia, a military road to Trier. The presbyter Aetherius founded a Christian community between 335 and 360. After the fall of the Limes the town became a Frankish royal estate, and in 983 Otto II gave it to Archbishop Willigis of Mainz.

The inhabitants repeatedly sought independence, and in 1165 disputes between the archbishop and the emperor led to the town's destruction. It belonged to the Rhenish League of Towns in the 13th century and took an unsuccessful part in the German Peasants' War in 1525. The Cathedral Chapter of Mainz acquired it in two halves, in 1424 and 1438. From 1792 to 1813 it was French, and in 1816, after the Congress of Vienna, it passed to the Grand Duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt. A Jewish community is mentioned in the mid-12th century, was expelled in 1507, and was ended by deportations in 1942, after which only four returned.

The Mouse Tower is associated with a legend in which Hatto II, Archbishop of Mainz, was eaten by mice, a tale attributed since the 19th century increasingly to his predecessor Hatto I. Other sights are the Basilica of St. Martin, Klopp Castle and the Drususbrücke. The poet Stefan George was born in Bingen, and the abbess Hildegard of Bingen was born 40 km away at Bermersheim. Three winegrowing areas meet at the town.
bingling-temple: The grottoes lie just north of the point where the Yellow River empties into the Liujiaxia Reservoir, in Yongjing County of the Linxia Hui Autonomous Prefecture, some 100 km southwest of Lanzhou. Caves filled with relief sculpture, Buddha figures and frescoes line the northern side of the canyon for about 200 metres. Each cave is a small temple of Buddhist imagery, and the row ends at a large natural cavern where wooden walkways climb the rock face to cliff-side caves and to a standing Maitreya Buddha more than 27 metres tall.

The first grotto was begun around 420 CE under the Western Qin dynasty, and the work went on for more than a millennium, with caves added under the Wei, Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. The style of each grotto can be matched to the art of its own dynasty. In style as in geography the site stands midway between the monumental Buddhas of Bamiyan in Afghanistan and the great cave temples of central China, the Yungang Grottoes near Datong and the Longmen Grottoes near Luoyang. Over the centuries earthquakes, erosion and looting damaged or destroyed many of the caves and their contents. What remains are 183 caves, 694 stone statues and 82 clay sculptures.

In 2014 the Bingling Temple was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List with other sites of the Silk Road, as part of the Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor. The site is remote: it can be reached only in summer and autumn, by boat across the Liujiaxia Reservoir from docks near the Liujiaxia Dam in Liujiaxia City, the county seat, and for the rest of the year it is cut off, as few roads serve the area.
binh-dinh-province: Bình Định was a northern coastal province of the South Central Coast region of Vietnam, bordering Quảng Ngãi to the north, Phú Yên to the south, Gia Lai to the west and the South China Sea to the east. Most of it is covered by mountains or hills, rising to around 1,200 metres in An Lão district. The largest lowland lies in the south along the lower Côn River, which forms a small delta north of Quy Nhơn and can be used as an inland waterway. Most of the population and economic activity has long concentrated there, and it was the site of Vijaya, one of the major city-states of Champa.

Bình Định was probably one of the places where the Cham first arrived in what is now Vietnam. The favourable geography led to the rise of the Cham port of Thị Nại, where Quy Nhơn now stands, and the city-state of Vijaya grew up around this port and a main city further inland. Its architecture suggests it did not become important until the eleventh or twelfth century. It combined stone and brick, unlike most Cham structures, which used only bricks, which suggests some influence from Angkor. Vijaya fought major wars with Angkor in the 12th and 13th centuries and with Vietnam in 1069 and again in the 15th century.

In 1471 King Lê Thánh Tông won a decisive victory over Champa, ending Vijaya and the kingdom. He annexed its lands and set up the Quảng Nam protectorate with three prefectures, one of them Hoài Nhân, which corresponds to Bình Định. The Tây Sơn dynasty took its name from Tây Sơn district, where its rulers came from, and Quy Nhơn was its capital until the Vietnamese civil war of 1789 to 1802 wracked the province and the dynasty collapsed.

During the Vietnam War, Bình Định was the site of heavy fighting between 1966 and 1968, including Operation Masher, Operation Thayer and Operation Pershing. In February 1976 it was merged with Quảng Ngãi to form Nghĩa Bình, and it was separated again on 30 June 1989.

On 12 June 2025 Bình Định province was dissolved and merged with Gia Lai province. It had 11 district-level subdivisions and its capital was Quy Nhơn. Cham towers are now significant tourist attractions, and the Quang Trung Museum in Tây Sơn district commemorates the Tây Sơn uprising. The traditional martial arts of Bình Định have become a cultural heritage.
binnenhof: Little is known about the origin of the Binnenhof. Count Floris IV of Holland bought the grounds in 1229 from Dirk van Wassenaer and built a hunting lodge. His successor William II is often credited with its foundation after he became King of the Romans in 1248, and presumably began the Ridderzaal, a great hall for receiving guests. The hall was finished under Floris V, when the buildings were also walled in with a gate and the Hofkapel was built. The complex had a public part, including the Ridderzaal, and a private area for residence and private meetings.

After the House of Holland died out in 1299 the county passed to the counts of Hainaut, who barely resided there. Albert I of Bavaria, who reigned from 1358 to 1404, was the first to use it more or less permanently as his primary residence and encouraged The Hague to grow nearby. The Treaty of Delft in 1428 brought the county into the Duchy of Burgundy, whose stadtholders of Holland used the offices.

After the Dutch Republic was proclaimed in 1581 the Ridderzaal was at first a public space used by traders, stallholders and booksellers. In 1584 stadtholder Maurice moved into the stadtholder's quarter, and in the same year the hall became the meeting place of the newly formed States General. Maurice's expansions began a gradual reconstruction that ended with the southern wing built under stadtholder William V in the late 18th century.

The National Assembly of the Batavian Republic first met there in March 1796 in William V's former ballroom, which housed the House of Representatives until 1992. Between 1806 and 1810, under French rule, the administrative centre moved to Amsterdam and the Binnenhof was considered for demolition. It was threatened again in 1848, when the States General wished to demolish the old buildings symbolically, but local residents protested successfully. A full-scale renovation began in autumn 2021.

The Gothic Ridderzaal, literally Knight's Hall, forms the centre of the complex, and on Prinsjesdag, the third Tuesday of September, the King gives the Speech from the Throne there. Other buildings form a rectangle around it, with a large courtyard in front and a smaller square behind. The Stadtholder's Gate dates from 1620. The Senate sits in the western corner, and the lower house now meets in the modern eastern part. The Prime Minister's office has been in the small northern tower, the Torentje, since 1982, and the cabinet meets in the Trêveszaal, built for negotiations during the Eighty Years' War.
biobio-river: The Biobío is the second-longest river in Chile, after the Loa, and flows 380 kilometres from Galletué and Icalma lakes in the Andes to the Gulf of Arauco on the Pacific. Its basin is the third largest in Chile, after those of the Loa and the Baker, and with an average width of one kilometre it is the widest river in the country. Its major tributaries are the Malleco and the Laja, the Laja being the larger in volume of water.

From the east shore of Galletué Lake it flows a few kilometres east, receives the waters of Icalma Lake, and then turns north-west through a broad Andean valley. Its upper course, known as Alto Bío Bío, runs fast through a narrow valley. After reaching the Intermediate Depression it crosses a flat area, widening to between 60 and 120 metres, and the Vergara River joins it near Nacimiento. Near San Rosendo and La Laja it is joined by the Laja, and at its mouth near San Pedro de la Paz in Gran Concepción it is 2 kilometres wide. Four bridges cross it in the Concepción metropolitan area, the oldest the railway bridge of 1889.

The name Biobío comes from Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche. During the later part of the Arauco War the river was the traditional borderline, La Frontera, between La Araucanía, the self-ruled Mapuche lands to the south, and the Spanish-ruled Captaincy General of Chile to the north. The territory south of the river was not incorporated into the Chilean state until the later 19th century, after the campaigns known as the Pacification of Araucanía.

In colonial times the river was navigable up and down, and the river island of Diego Díaz, near Colonia Santa Fe, was the scene of an attack in 1610, during the Arauco War, in which Mapuches killed 13 Spanish soldiers. It was once navigable by ship as far as Nacimiento, but deforestation in the 1900s caused erosion that choked it with silt and closed it to boats. In the early 1980s it was regarded as one of the world's best whitewater rafting rivers; the Pangue Dam, built by the state power company Endesa despite protests, ended that, and the Pehuenche people, who had lived in the area for centuries, were displaced.
biograd-na-moru: Biograd na Moru lies 28 kilometres south of Zadar on a small peninsula between the bays of Soline and Bošana, facing the island of Pašman. Its name means white town on the sea in the local Ikavian dialect, and in Latin it appeared as Alba Maritima. The mid-10th-century chronicle De Administrando Imperio first mentions it, as Biogradon, among the populated towns of christened Croatia, and it was then the centre of the county of Sidraga.

A three-naved basilica was built there in the 9th century under Duke Branimir, on the base of an older 6th-century church, and it later became the cathedral of the bishop of Biograd. The Venetians held the town briefly around the year 1000. By the 1050s it was the seat of the Diocese of Alba Maritima, and King Peter Krešimir IV founded the monasteries of St John the Evangelist and St Thomas in 1059 and 1066. It was a major port in the later 11th century, and the Norman princess Felicia of Sicily landed there in 1096 to marry King Coloman of Hungary. Coloman was crowned there in 1102 by Bishop Bono, as the crown of Croatia passed to the Hungarians.

Rule alternated between Venice and the Árpád family, and the town is called a royal city in surviving documents from this time. Venice destroyed it in 1125, when, according to the Historia Ducum Veneticorum, its citizens alone dared resist the doge. The bishopric was abolished and the population moved to Skradin. In 1202, citizens of Zadar sheltered there during the Fourth Crusade. Venice acquired the town in 1409 and held it until 1797, and it was destroyed and burned in 1521 and 1646 in the Venetian-Turkish wars.

Biograd na Moru is part of Zadar County and has 5,601 inhabitants according to the 2021 census, most of them Croats. It is regarded as another capital of the medieval Kingdom of Croatia, and its rulers included Stephen Držislav and Peter Krešimir IV.
bioko: Bioko lies in the Bight of Biafra on the Gulf of Guinea, 32 km south of the coast of Cameroon and about 160 km northwest of the mainland part of Equatorial Guinea. It covers 2,017 km2 and is about 70 km long. The island is volcanic and mountainous, mostly basalt, and its highest peak, Pico Basilé, rises to about 3,012 m. Only 60 metres of water over the continental shelf separate it from the mainland, to which it was joined until about 10,000 years ago. Rainfall is very heavy in the south, and tropical rainforest covers most of the island.

Bioko had an indigenous population when Europeans arrived: Bantu-speaking ancestors of the Bubi probably settled there before the 7th century BCE. The Portuguese navigator Fernão do Pó sighted the island in 1472, and in 1494 it was renamed Fernando Pó in his honour. The Portuguese planted sugarcane, and in 1642 the Dutch East India Company used the island to centralise its slave trade in the Gulf of Guinea. Bubi clans withdrew from the coast to the safer interior and began to build a new kingdom under chiefs such as Molambo. Under the Treaty of El Pardo of 1778, Portugal ceded Fernando Po to Spain.

After the British abolished their Atlantic slave trade, they leased bases at Port Clarence, now Malabo, and San Carlos from 1827 to 1843 for the Preventive Squadron. Under William Fitzwilliam Owen their forces detained 20 ships and freed 2,500 enslaved people. Spain raised its flag at Port Clarence in March 1843 and revoked the British lease in 1855. Late in the 19th century Krio planters turned from palm oil to cocoa; dependent on migrant labour, they failed to pay contracts, producing de facto slavery. A League of Nations investigation between 1923 and 1930 into the shipment of contract labour from Liberia found that the abuses arose from conditions on the island.

Bioko is part of Equatorial Guinea, and Malabo, on its north coast, is its largest city. The 2015 census counted 335,048 inhabitants. The Bubi, the historic indigenous people, make up 58 per cent. Spanish, official since 1844, is the language of education and administration; Bube is spoken by about 50,000 people, and the creole Pichi also developed on the island. Two protected areas, Pico Basilé National Park and the Luba Crater Scientific Reserve, cover about 40 per cent of Bioko.
birendra-of-nepal: Birendra was born on 29 December 1945 at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace in Kathmandu, the son of Crown Prince Mahendra and Crown Princess Indra. An earlier son of Mahendra, Rabindra Shah, was born to an unmarried Gurung woman and counted as illegitimate, so Birendra became heir apparent. He studied at St Joseph's School, a Jesuit school in Darjeeling, then at Eton College from 1959 to 1964, and later at the University of Tokyo and Harvard University. On 27 February 1970 he married Aishwarya Rajya Lakshmi Devi, his second cousin.

Birendra came to the throne on 31 January 1972 after Mahendra's death, and was crowned on 24 February 1975 after a mourning year and a year astrologers judged inauspicious. He inherited a country where political parties were banned and rule ran through panchayat councils, so that he was effectively an absolute monarch. Growing pro-democracy demands led him to call a referendum between a party-less and a multi-party system in May 1980. The party-less system won by 55 per cent to 45, a result that democracy campaigners later claimed was rigged.

In 1990 strikes and pro-democracy riots led him to lift the ban on parties and agree to become a constitutional monarch. He promulgated a new constitution on 9 November 1990, making Nepal a constitutional monarchy with multiparty democracy. A civil war between Maoist rebels and government forces began in 1996 and lasted until 2006. His government set up national parks, among them Chitwan and Sagarmatha, and he promoted Nepal as a zone of peace at the United Nations, a proposal 116 countries supported.

On 1 June 2001 Birendra and his immediate family were shot dead at dinner at the Narayanhiti Palace by his son, Crown Prince Dipendra. Dipendra shot himself and, in a coma, was proclaimed king, but died a few days later. Birendra's younger brother Gyanendra then became king. Monuments named for Birendra were renamed after the political changes of 2006 and the end of the monarchy in 2008.
birger-jarl: Birger Magnusson belonged to the House of Bjälbo and grew up at Bjälbo in Östergötland. His father was Magnus Minnesköld, and his mother Ingrid Ylva was, according to Olaus Petri, a daughter of Sune Sik and granddaughter of King Sverker I of Sweden. In the mid-1230s, after competition with other suitors, he married Ingeborg Eriksdotter, the sister of King Erik Eriksson, as Erik's Chronicle tells. The marriage gave him his base of power, and he was probably among the most influential men in the kingdom for years before King Erik formally gave him the title of jarl in 1248.

According to Erik's Chronicle, Birger led the Second Swedish Crusade across the Baltic to Finland, where he defeated the pagan Tavastians and forced them to convert. The expedition is traditionally dated to 1249–1250, though many scholars now place it in 1238–1239, before he was jarl. It extended Swedish rule inland, and the Swedes began building a castle in Tavastia.

Russian sources also name Birger as the leader of a campaign in Ingria in 1240 that ended in defeat by Alexander Nevsky at the Battle of the Neva. Swedish sources do not mention the battle, and the first sources linking Birger to it date from the mid-15th century.

Around 1248 the papal diplomat William of Modena urged the Swedish kings to follow the rules of the Church, and Birger took the Church's side against other members of his family. In 1249 Birger ended decades of hostility with Norway by the Treaty of Lödöse, marrying his eleven-year-old daughter Rikissa to Haakon Haakonsson the Young. When King Erik died in 1250, Birger's son Valdemar was elected king, and Birger ruled as regent. In 1252 two letters of his gave the first mention of Stockholm, which tradition treats as its foundation, though what stood there earlier is debated.

He died on 21 October 1266 at Jälbolung in Västergötland and was buried at Varnhem Abbey, where his grave was forgotten after a fire in the 16th century and rediscovered in the 1920s. He was the last Swedish jarl, since the title was replaced by duke after his death. The historian Thomas Lindkvist ranks him and Birger Brosa as the most powerful men of their eras in Sweden. His sons Valdemar and Magnus Ladulås both became kings. A statue of him by Bengt Erland Fogelberg, raised in 1854, stands in Birger Jarls Torg next to Riddarholm Church in Stockholm.
birgi: Birgi lies in the district of Ödemiş in İzmir Province. Its present name derives from its medieval Greek name, Pyrgion, which means Little Tower. In antiquity the town was called Dios Hieron, the Sanctuary of Zeus, one of two cities of that name, and it passed to the Roman Republic and the Roman province of Asia with the annexation of the Kingdom of Pergamon. It was renamed Christoupolis in the 7th century and was known as Pyrgion from the 12th century.

The Roman city had a Christian bishopric, attested as an episcopal see from at least 451 and subordinate to Ephesus until the late 12th century, when it became a metropolis of its own. Four of its early bishops are known: Stephen took part in the Council of Ephesus of 431, Zoetus attended the Council of Constantinople of 680 and the Council in Trullo of 692, and a later Stephen of Pyrgion attended the councils of 869–870 and 879–880 that dealt with Patriarch Photios I. Dioshieron survives as a titular see of the Roman Catholic Church that has never been assigned.

Pyrgion fell to the Turks in 1307 and became the capital of the beylik of Aydin. Ibn Battuta visited the town and attended a lecture by the professor Muhyi al-Din. Birgi was incorporated into the Ottoman Empire in 1390, and the future Sultan Mehmed II was educated at its Fortress Madrasa.

Since the reorganisation of 2013 Birgi has been a neighbourhood of the municipality of Ödemiş; it had 1,832 inhabitants in 2022. Besides the mosque of Mehmet Bey and the Çakırağa Mansion, built in the 18th century by the wealthy Çakırağa family, it keeps the 14th-century Aydınoğlu Baths, the 16th-century tomb and madrasa of Birgivi Mehmet Efendi, the Sultanşah Mausoleum, the 19th-century Sandıkoğlu Mansion and its city walls. ÇEKÜL has listed it for its Seljuk and Ottoman architecture since 1994, and archaeologists unearthed a Byzantine fort there in 2021.
birgu: Birgu, also called Vittoriosa or Città Vittoriosa, "Victorious City", is an old fortified city on the south side of the Grand Harbour in the Port Region of Malta. It occupies a promontory with Fort Saint Angelo at its head and the city of Cospicua at its base. It is ideally situated for safe anchorage and has a long history of maritime, mercantile and military activity. Before Valletta was founded, any military power that wanted to rule the Maltese islands had to take Birgu in order to control the Grand Harbour.

Birgu was settled in medieval times, and Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Normans, the Aragonese and the Order of Saint John all contributed to its development. After the Order of Saint John was driven out of Rhodes by the Ottoman Empire, it received Malta. In 1526 a commission of eight knights described Birgu as a small defenceless town with old houses in poor condition. When the Order arrived in 1530 it made Birgu the capital, since Mdina lay inland and did not suit its naval needs.

The city was fortified in the 1530s and strengthened in the 1550s, and the Castle of St Angelo was built, joined to the city by a drawbridge. In the Great Siege of 1565 the Knights defended it for four months, and in August the Ottoman army almost captured it, but the Knights under Grand Master Jean Parisot de Valette recaptured it. Reinforcements from Sicily arrived a month later and the Ottomans abandoned the siege. A new capital, Valletta, was then built on Mount Sceberras, and in 1571 the Knights moved their convent and seat there. Birgu lost some importance but was given the title Città Vittoriosa.

After Napoleon took Malta in 1798, French forces were garrisoned in Birgu, and the Maltese rebelled soon after. The French capitulated in September 1800 and Malta became a British protectorate. The Royal Navy's Mediterranean Fleet had its base in Birgu, and British forces remained until 1979, an event commemorated by the Freedom Monument. In 1806 the gunpowder magazine exploded, killing over 200 people, and in the Second World War heavy bombing destroyed historic buildings.

Birgu has five Auberges of the Knights, and the Malta Maritime Museum stands on the waterfront. St Lawrence's Church was once the conventual church of the Order, and Fort St Angelo still stands at the centre of the Grand Harbour.
birinus: Birinus was a Frank and a Benedictine monk. He was consecrated bishop by Asterius in Genoa, and Pope Honorius I gave him his commission to convert the West Saxons. He came to Wessex in 634, landing at the port of Hamwic, in what is now the St Mary's area of Southampton, where St Mary's Church was founded during his short stay. His commission was to preach in parts of Britain no missionary had yet reached, and may have included the Mercians, but he remained in Wessex.

In 635 he persuaded King Cynegils to let him preach. Cynegils was seeking an alliance against the Mercians with Oswald of Northumbria, a Christian who would not ally himself with a pagan, and the king's conversion removed the obstacle. Birinus went on to baptise Cynegils's son Cwichelm in 636 and his grandson Cuthred in 639. Churches ascribed to him include St Mary's in Reading, St Peter and St Paul at Checkendon and the first church at Ipsden.

Birinus died at Dorchester on 3 December 649 or 650 and became known as the Apostle to the West Saxons. His relics were later translated to Winchester. He is venerated as a saint in the Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Anglican churches. His feast is 3 December, though some churches keep it on 5 December, and in the Church of England it is a commemoration on 4 September. It was added to the Roman Martyrology in the late 16th century.

Church of England parishes dedicated to him include those at Berinsfield in Oxfordshire and Redlynch in Wiltshire, and the Catholic church at Dorchester, one of the first built after Pope Pius IX restored the hierarchy, also bears his name. A stained glass window by Thomas Denny showing the baptism of Cynegils was unveiled at St Michael's, Easthampstead, Bracknell, in 2013.
birka: Birka stood on the island of Björkö in Lake Mälaren, 30 kilometres west of present-day Stockholm. It was founded around 750 by a king or by merchants seeking to control trade, and is one of the earliest urban settlements in Scandinavia. It was the Baltic link in the Dnieper trade route through Ladoga and Novgorod to the Byzantine Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate. It most likely offered furs, iron goods and craft products for materials from Europe and Western Asia. Furs came from the Sami, the Finns and north-western Russia, and combs of reindeer antler were important. The population has been estimated at 500 to 1,000.

Rimbert's Life of Ansgar says Ansgar travelled to Birka in 829 on a mission from Emperor Louis the Pious and founded the first known Christian congregation in Sweden in 831. Its attempt to convert people from the Norse religion was unsuccessful. Adam of Bremen says Archbishop Unni died at Birka in 936. Birka was abandoned in the latter half of the 10th century, around the time Sigtuna was founded and became the main trading centre of the Mälaren area. The reasons are disputed: Gotland was better placed for Rus' and Byzantine trade, and Neil Kent has speculated that an enemy assault may have destroyed it.

No texts survive from Birka itself, and no Norse source names it. The settlement's location was lost for centuries, and the Chronicle of Sweden first claimed in 1450 that Björkö was Birka. Johan Hadorph attempted excavations in the late 17th century. Hjalmar Stolpe came in the late 19th century to study insects in amber, found so much that he suspected a trading post, and excavated between 1871 and 1895.

The remains cover about 7 hectares and include a hill fort called Borgen and more than 3,000 graves, both cremations and burials in coffins or chamber graves. Goods in the graves include glass, Rhineland pottery, Chinese silk and Byzantine embroidery with fine gold thread. Most coins found are silver dirhams from the Middle East. Ten small silver crosses and 27 pendants of Thor's hammer show that both Christianity and traditional beliefs were present. Birka and Hovgården on the neighbouring island of Adelsö have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.
birkebeiner: The Birkebeiner arose during the Norwegian civil wars of about 1130 to 1240, conflicts fed by unclear succession laws, social conditions and the struggle between Church and king, in which each party set up a royal son as its figurehead. The party formed in 1174 around the pretender Eystein Meyla, to depose King Magnus Erlingsson and his father Erling Skakke, Earl of Vestlandet. Scholars have linked it to the rapid growth of landless markamenn, border men who settled along the Swedish frontier and lived by plundering the old settlements.

Its leaders came from Trøndelag, where social tensions were milder. Their aim was to stop power passing to Viken and Vestlandet, where Erling Skakke had taken control in the early 1160s and made his young son king. They sought no social revolution, only to bring the centre of power back to Trøndelag.

Sverre, who claimed to be an illegitimate son of King Sigurd Munn, took over the party with Swedish help from Earl Birger Brosa, purged its most criminal elements and relied more and more on mercenaries from Sweden and England. Proclaimed king by his followers in 1177, he ruled little beyond Trøndelag until decisive battles in 1179 and 1184, by which time Earl Erling and King Magnus were dead. When Sverre died in 1202 he held most of Norway, but the Bagler remained strong in Østerdalen.

His son Haakon Sverresson died two years later. In 1206 two Birkebeiner, Torstein Skevla and Skjervald Skrukka, skied with Haakon's one-year-old posthumous son Haakon Haakonsson through mountains and forests to safety in Trondheim. A settlement of 1209 recognised Inge Baardsson, backed by the Birkebeiner, as king and the Bagler pretender Philip Simonsson as ruler of Østlandet without the royal title. Both died in 1217, and the boy came to the throne as Haakon IV under the regency of Duke Skule Baardsson.

The rescue of 1206 is honoured each year by the Birkebeinerrennet ski race, the Birkebeinerrittet mountain bike race and the Birkebeinerløpet run, all ending in Lillehammer. Skiers and riders carry a pack of 3.5 kg in memory of the child. Lillehammer's arms show a skiing Birkebeiner, and the mascots of the 1994 Winter Olympics were drawn as Birkebeiner children.
birkenfeld: Birkenfeld lies in the Nahe area, north of the Nahe river, on the edge of the Saar-Hunsrück nature park, about 13 kilometres south-west of Idar-Oberstein. The name comes from Old Frankish and means something like "at the field with the birches". Finds show heavy settlement in the Iron Age, as early as the 8th century BCE, and Roman legions overran the area in the 1st century BCE. The town stands on a Roman road that linked two military roads, one from Metz to Mainz and the other from Trier through Bingen to Mainz.

The name is first recorded as Bikenuelt, about 700, and a document of Archbishop Egbert of Trier of 981 shows that Saint Leudwinus, archbishop from 695 to 713, had given the churches at Birkenfeld and Brombach to St. Paulinus' Abbey in Trier. In the 13th century the Counts of Sponheim held it. When their county was divided in 1223, Birkenfeld passed to the Rear County. The castle is first mentioned in 1293, and Emperor Louis the Bavarian granted town rights in 1332. During the Thirty Years' War the town became a theatre of war in 1635, and the plague that year killed 416 people.

In 1776 Birkenfeld became the seat of the Baden Oberamt, and an economic and cultural upswing followed, with the first higher school founded in 1779. In 1798 the left bank of the Rhine was ceded to France, and Birkenfeld belonged to the Department of Sarre. After the Congress of Vienna the Principality of Birkenfeld was awarded to the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg as an exclave, for the part played by Peter I, regent of Oldenburg, against Napoleon.

A new palace, now the district administration's seat, was built in 1821 under Oldenburg, with other Classicist buildings that still mark the town. On 1 April 1937 the region was transferred to the Prussian Rhine Province, and after the Second World War it lay in the French Occupation Zone. Since 1946 it has been a district seat in Rhineland-Palatinate.

Birkenfeld is the seat of the Birkenfeld district and of the Verbandsgemeinde of Birkenfeld, a collective municipality of 31 municipalities. The town itself has about 7,000 inhabitants. The district, of which it has been the seat since 1946, lies in the south-west of the state, and about half of its inhabitants were Evangelical and 31 per cent Catholic in 2008.
birla-family: The Birlas trace their origins to the Maheshwari community of Bania Vaishya traders; they are called Marwari because merchants from Rajasthan are conventionally so termed. They come from Pilani in the Shekhawati region, where they keep their ancestral residence, Birla Haweli. Seth Shiv Narayan Birla (1840–1909) was the first to venture outside Pilani. He traded cotton through Ahmedabad and, with his adopted son Baldeo Das Birla, made a fortune trading opium with China, chartering cargo ships with other Marwari merchants to bypass British middlemen. He moved to Bombay in 1863.

Baldeo Das set up the trading house Shivnarayan Baldeodas in Bombay and in 1887 moved to Calcutta, where he founded Baldeodas Jugalkishor. He was succeeded by four sons, Jugal Kishore, Rameshwar Das, Ghanshyam Das and Braj Mohan, and was made Raja in 1925.

Ghanshyamdas Birla founded the jute trading firm GM Birla Company in 1911. The First World War raised demand for gunny bags, and the family's worth is estimated to have risen from ₹2 million to ₹8 million during the war. In 1919 he became one of the first Indian owners of a jute mill, Birla Jute, and he went on to acquire cotton mills and start sugar mills. He co-founded the Hindustan Times in 1924 and acquired it fully in 1933; Hindustan Motors followed in 1942, and after independence Grasim in 1948 and Hindalco in 1958.

Indian merchants such as the Birlas entered industries once dominated by Scots, part of Mahatma Gandhi's Swadeshi movement. Jugal Kishore Birla built the Laxminarayan Temple in Delhi, which Gandhi inaugurated and which welcomed Hindus of every caste. The family stayed close to leaders such as Sardar Patel after 1947, and the industrialists' Bombay Plan of 1944, also called the Tata-Birla plan, is said to have served as a blueprint for India's first five-year plan.

Birla philanthropy began in the 1880s with gifts for goshalas in Kolkata. In 1918 the family opened the first high school in Pilani, from which grew the Birla Institute of Technology and Science, and it went on to found schools, colleges, planetariums, hospitals and the Birla Mandir temples in many Indian cities. For decades the words Tata-Birla stood together for great wealth in India. The branches of the family are now financially independent of one another.
birnin-kebbi: Birnin Kebbi stands on the Sokoto River in north-western Nigeria and is connected by road to Argungu, about 45 kilometres to the northeast, Jega, about 35 kilometres to the southeast, and Bunza, about 45 kilometres to the southwest. Its people are mostly Hausa and Fulani, and Islam is the main religion. The town is also the seat of a local government area.

Birnin Kebbi was formerly the capital of the Kebbi Emirate. It remained the capital until 1805, when it was burned in the Fulani jihad. After it was incorporated into the Fulani Emirate of Gwandu, it was eclipsed in political importance by the town of Gwandu, 48 kilometres to the east, and as a caravan and riverside market by Jega, 32 kilometres to the southeast, which lay at the head of navigation on the Zamfara River, a tributary of the Sokoto. Argungu became the traditional seat of the king of Kebbi, and the Kebbi emirate moved there.
Birnin Kebbi nevertheless served as the headquarters of the Gwandu emirate after Emir Haliru was inaugurated there in 1906. In 1991 it became the capital of the newly created Nigerian state of Kebbi.

The town has declined as a river port because of silting and political conditions. It serves as a collecting point for peanuts and rice and as a local market for millet, sorghum, rice, fish, goats and cattle. It has a state polytechnic college and a government rice-research station, and is served by Sir Ahmadu Bello International Airport. Its oldest hospital is the Sir Yahaya Memorial Hospital. An estimate of 2007 gave the city a population of 125,594.
birsay: Birsay, in Old Norse Birgisherað, lies in the north-west corner of the Mainland of Orkney. Almost all the land of the parish is farmed, chiefly as grassland for beef cattle. Its two best-known monuments, the prehistoric and Norse settlements on the tidal island of the Brough of Birsay and the ruined Earl's Palace on the Mainland opposite, at the northern end of the village, are maintained by Historic Scotland.

Architectural fragments and excavation of the foundations of St Magnus Church suggest that it stands on the site of Christchurch, the first cathedral of Orkney in the 11th and 12th centuries, founded by Earl Thorfinn the Mighty, who died around 1065, after his return from a pilgrimage to Rome. The seat of the diocese moved to St Magnus Cathedral in Kirkwall in the later 12th century, but the Bishops of Orkney kept a residence at Birsay, known as Mons Bellus, into late medieval times.

The Earl's Palace was built in the late 16th century by Robert Stewart, 1st Earl of Orkney, and the date 1574 was once carved above its south-facing entrance. It had four ranges round an open courtyard with small corner towers, a form unusual in Scotland at that date and unprecedented in the north, and it was set among walled gardens, an archery range and a bowling green. With the Earl's Palace in Kirkwall and Scalloway Castle in Shetland it was one of the main residences of the Stewart Earls of Orkney, and it has stood uninhabited since the late 17th century.

St Magnus Church now serves the Church of Scotland parish of Birsay and Harray, and the bridge nearby may also be medieval in origin. Samuel Trail, minister of the parish from 1844 to 1868, became Moderator of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland in 1874.
biscay: Biscay lies on the south shore of the Bay of Biscay and is bordered by Cantabria and the province of Burgos to the west, Gipuzkoa to the east and Álava to the south. The southern ranges of the Basque Mountains form a continuous barrier, with passes no lower than 600 metres, and the water divide between the Atlantic and Mediterranean basins. The middle section is occupied by the valleys of the Nervión, the Ibaizabal and the Kadagua. The coast is usually high, with cliffs and small inlets, and its main features are the estuary of Bilbao and the estuary of Gernika. The climate is oceanic, with high precipitation all year.

Biscay has been inhabited since the Middle Paleolithic, and its caves hold cave paintings, those of Santimamiñe showing bison, horses, goats and deer. Roman geographers placed two tribes there, the Caristii and the Autrigones, who are thought to have spoken Basque. The Roman presence had little impact, and the Basque language and traditions survived. The name Biscay first appears in the Chronicle of Alfonso III in the late 9th century, and the territory was then controlled by the Kingdom of Navarre.

The house of Haro, leaders of the pro-Castilian lords, was granted the rule of the newly created Biscay, and tradition names Iñigo López as its first Lord in 1043. The lordship later passed by inheritance to John I of Castile and became one of the titles of the king of Castile. Each lord had to swear to defend the fuero, the Biscayan laws derived from Navarrese and Basque customary rights, which held that sovereignty lay with the Biscayans. Lords and later kings swore the statutes to the oak of Gernika, where the assembly of the lordship sits.

In 1511 the kings granted the port of Bilbao privileges for trade with the ports of the Spanish Empire, and it was already the main Castilian harbour, shipping wool to Flanders. The Carlist Wars of the 19th century grew in part from the desire to keep foral rights, and the victory of the anti-Carlists brought successive cuts to Biscay's autonomy. Iron ore discovered in the 1850s brought foreign investment and rapid industrialization. In 1937 German aircraft under Franco's control destroyed the town of Gernika, and Bilbao fell some months later. The 1979 Statute of Guernica created the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country.

Biscay is a province of the Basque Autonomous Community with its capital and largest city at Bilbao. Its name is Bizkaia in Basque and Vizcaya in Spanish, and its institutions are the Juntas Generales and the Foral Diputation. Its population is 1,167,233.
bishapur: Bishapur lies beside the Chowgan Valley and the Shapur River, 15 kilometres west of Kazerun in south-western Iran, near a river crossing. Its name combines a Middle Persian word meaning great or lord with the name of its founder. The city was laid out on a rectangular plan about 2 kilometres long and 1 kilometre wide, with two main streets, one running north-south and one east-west, meeting at the centre and ending at four gates. Its plan follows the Greek system of Hippodamus, which makes it unusual among the ancient cities of Iran. It had a royal citadel and a common citadel, the latter with houses, a bathhouse, a caravanserai and a market.

According to an inscription, Shapur I founded the city in 266 CE. He had defeated the Romans three times, killing Gordian III, capturing the emperor Valerian and forcing Philip the Arab to surrender. Archaeologists have found Parthian and Elamite remains on the site. Roman prisoners are said to have built the city, and its architect, according to the inscription on one of two commemorative columns, was Apasa of Harran. Valerian lived in a palace built for him there. Two Sasanian kings, Hormizd I and Bahram I, were born in Bishapur, and before the Arab conquest it had between 50,000 and 80,000 inhabitants.

The Arabs took it in 638 CE, and the people of the province rose against them several times, in 643, 646 and 687. In the 8th and 9th centuries its prosperity passed to Kazerun as residents moved there. The Buyid rulers, above all Adud al-Dawla, revived it for a time. In 495 AH Abu Sa'id Shabankara set fire to the city and razed it, and an earthquake then completed its ruin.

Bishapur was entered on Iran's national heritage list in 1931 and on the World Heritage List in 2018. Its monuments include the Temple of Anahita, a cube about 14 metres on a side built so that water from the Shapur River ran through it; the Ceremonial Hall of Shapur I, a cross-shaped hall of 781 square metres under a dome; the octagonal Valerian Palace; and the mosaic iwan. Georges Salles and Roman Ghirshman excavated for the Louvre between 1935 and 1940, and an Iranian team led by Ali Akbar Sarfaraz began work 28 years later. Only about three percent of the city has been uncovered.
bishkek: Bishkek stands at an altitude of about 800 metres, just off the northern fringe of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too Range, an extension of the Tian Shan whose peaks rise to 4,895 metres. North of the city a fertile, gently undulating steppe stretches far into Kazakhstan, and the river Chüy drains most of the area. The central city is laid out on a rectangular grid, with wide boulevards, marble-faced public buildings and many Soviet-style apartment blocks, and narrow irrigation channels line most streets to water the shade trees.

The site began as a caravan rest stop on a branch of the Silk Road through the Tian Shan, possibly founded by the Sogdians. In 1825 the khan of Kokand fortified it with a mud fort, Pishpek, to control the caravan routes and collect tribute from the Kyrgyz. Russian forces under Colonel Apollon Zimmermann later took and razed the fort, and a Russian settlement with the original name Pishpek was established on the site in 1868, within the General Governorship of Russian Turkestan.

In 1925 the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast was created and Pishpek became its capital. In 1926 the city was renamed Frunze after Mikhail Frunze, a Bolshevik military leader and associate of Lenin who was born there. It became capital of the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic in 1936. Until the mid-1990s Russians and other people of European descent were the majority of the population; in the 1970 census the Kyrgyz were only 12.3 per cent. The city was renamed Bishkek on 5 February 1991, and Kyrgyzstan became independent later that year. One tradition derives the name Bishkek from the paddle used to churn fermenting milk.

Bishkek is the capital and largest city of Kyrgyzstan and of the Chüy Region, with about 1.2 million people, near the border with Kazakhstan. It is the country's financial centre and its most important cultural city, with the National Library, the Kyrgyz State Historical Museum on Ala-Too Square and the Frunze House Museum. Most residents are ethnic Kyrgyz, with a sizeable Russian minority. The Dordoy Bazaar on the north-eastern edge is a major wholesale and retail market.
bishop: The English word bishop comes through Latin episcopus and Old English biscop from the Greek epískopos, meaning overseer or supervisor. The term did not originate in Christianity: it had been used in Greek for several centuries before. According to most scholars, the earliest organisation of the church in Jerusalem resembled that of Jewish synagogues, with a council of ordained presbyters, or elders, chaired, in the account of Acts, by James the Just, according to tradition the first bishop of the city. In the New Testament the word presbyter was not yet distinguished from overseer.

Around the end of the 1st century the church's organisation became clearer. In the works of the Apostolic Fathers, Ignatius of Antioch in particular, the role of the episkopos grew more important or more clearly defined, though other writers still equated bishops with presbyters. By the second century bishops were defined as the only clergy entrusted with ordaining priests and deacons. The First Council of Nicaea in the fourth century decreed that a bishop should be ordained by at least three others.

The organisation of the Roman Empire became the template for that of the church in the fourth century, particularly after Constantine's Edict of Milan. Bishops also held political office: after the 9th century they were archchancellors of the Holy Roman Empire and generally served as chancellors to medieval monarchs, and the Lord Chancellor of England was almost always a bishop until the dismissal of Cardinal Thomas Wolsey by Henry VIII. During the English Civil War the bishops' political power became a matter of heated controversy.

Traditionally a bishop is the pastor of a diocese, also called a see, bishopric or eparchy, and is understood to possess the full priesthood, so that he may ordain other clergy, including bishops. Bishops claim apostolic succession, a direct lineage back to the Twelve Apostles. They lead the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, the Anglican Communion and some Lutheran churches, while other denominations have given up the office, seeing it as a symbol of power. A bishop's usual insignia are the mitre and the crosier, and in many cathedrals a special chair, the cathedra, is set aside for his sole use.
bishopric-of-osel-wiek: The Bishopric of Ösel–Wiek was a Roman Catholic diocese and a semi-independent prince-bishopric, part of Terra Mariana, or Old Livonia, in the Holy Roman Empire. It covered what are now Saare, Hiiu and Lääne counties and the western part of Pärnu county in Estonia. It was created on 1 October 1228 as a Latin rite diocese by the papal legate William of Modena and at the same time as a state of the Empire, which made it a prince-bishopric, by Henry, King of the Romans. Its first bishop was Gottfried of the Cistercian Order, approved in August 1228.

The seat of the bishops moved repeatedly, so the see was known in turn as the bishopric of Leal (Lihula) from 1234, of Perona (Vana-Pärnu) from 1251 and of Hapsal (Haapsalu) Castle from 1279. Later the seat alone moved to the castle of Arensburg (Kuressaare) on the island of Ösel, while the cathedral and its chapter of canons stayed in Hapsal. From 1253 it was a suffragan diocese in the ecclesiastical province of the Archbishopric of Riga. After the first bishop's election there was a vacancy from 1229 to 1234, during which the Bishop of Riga and the Livonian Swordbrothers ruled it.

It was one of the five members of the Livonian Confederation and was divided administratively into two bailiwicks. The bishop was also the lord of the Teutonic Order over its fiefs on the bishopric's territory. From 1241 until 1343 the island of Ösel was an autonomous part of the bishopric, with its autonomy renewed on 27 August 1255.

The principality ended in 1560, when its last prince-bishop, Johannes V von Münchhausen, sold it to Denmark, which placed executive power in royally appointed governors. King Frederick II of Denmark's brother Magnus of Livonia, Duke of Holstein, obtained it as an appanage on 15 April 1560 and was elected bishop on 13 May 1560. The Danish dynasty was Lutheran, so Magnus abolished the diocese and on 20 March 1567 took the secular feudal style Lord of Ösel. Denmark later ceded Wiek (Lääne County) to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in exchange for parts of Ösel that belonged to the Livonian Order, and Ösel later became a Danish possession.
bishops-wars: The Church of Scotland, the Kirk, was Presbyterian in structure and Calvinist in doctrine. James VI and I regarded a unified church in Scotland and England as the first step towards a centralised state, a policy his son Charles I adopted, although many in both kingdoms thought his reforms of the Church of England essentially Catholic.

In 1636 a new Book of Canons excommunicated anyone who denied the king's supremacy in church matters, and in 1637 William Laud's Scottish Book of Common Prayer caused anger and rioting, said to have been set off by Jenny Geddes throwing a stool in St Giles Cathedral. In February 1638 delegates agreed a National Covenant, and the General Assembly meeting at Glasgow in December expelled the bishops. The Marquis of Hamilton then advised Charles that war was the only course.

Charles's plan, to avoid recalling Parliament, of an English army from the south, a landing under Hamilton and an Irish force under the Earl of Antrim fell apart when the Covenanters occupied Edinburgh Castle on 21 March 1639 and Dumbarton Castle, and Hamilton found the Forth strongly defended. The only significant fighting was in the north-east, where Montrose took Aberdeen and defeated Viscount Aboyne at the Brig of Dee on 19 June. An English army of about 15,000, mostly untrained militia, met a Scottish force of 16,500 under Alexander Leslie near Berwick-upon-Tweed. They negotiated and signed the Pacification of Berwick on 19 June.

Both sides saw it as a truce. The Scottish Parliament and the General Assembly confirmed the earlier decisions. Charles recalled the English Parliament in 1640, but the Short Parliament under John Pym demanded redress of grievances such as ship money and was dissolved after three weeks. In August 1640 Leslie's army of about 21,000 crossed the Tweed and won the Battle of Newburn on 28 August. Lord Conway withdrew to Durham and the Scots took Newcastle-upon-Tyne.

Under the truce of October 1640 the Scots were paid £850 a day and kept Northumberland and County Durham. Charles had to call the Long Parliament, which met in November 1640 and executed the Earl of Strafford in May 1641. The Treaty of London in August 1641 ended the wars and the Scots left northern England. Political differences between the king and Parliament, sharpened by the Irish Rebellion of 1641, led to the First English Civil War in August 1642. The Bishops' Wars were the first of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
biskra: Biskra is the main city of the Ziban region and the capital of Biskra Province in north-eastern Algeria, about 399 km from Algiers. It stands at the start of the Sahara, at an altitude of 87 metres, and is nicknamed the Queen of the Zibans and the Door of the Desert. Because of its position and its farming, especially its date oases, it has always been a crossroads between the cities of the north and the south.

In Roman times the city was known as Vescera. The Arab commander Uqba ibn Nafi al-Fihri was killed on his return from Morocco in an ambush by the Berber prince Koceila at Tahouda, a small village about 5 km from the oasis now called Sidi Okba, and was buried in the mosque of the town that bears his name. In the early 10th century Biskra and the Ziban area were conquered by the Beni Hammad. A book of the late 12th century describes a large city surrounded by fortresses and thriving villages, with a vast forest of palms and olives, and a centre of jurisprudence and learning.

In the 14th century Biskra became an important hub for the Hafsids of Tunisia, and in 1541 the Ottoman Turks began to conquer it. The French conquered it in 1844 and fortified it as a garrison, and it saw fighting during rebellions in 1849 and 1871. The local chief Bou Zian rallied people against the palm tax and seized the fortification of Zaatcha, 20 km away; a French force of 7,000 took it after fifty-three days of attack, and Bou Zian was killed.

Biskra had a recorded population of 307,987 in 2007. In the late 19th century it became a popular winter resort and gateway to the Sahara and a centre for artists and photographers. André Gide set key sections of The Immoralist there, Henri Matisse painted Blue Nude (Souvenir de Biskra) in 1907, and Béla Bartók collected traditional music in the town in 1913.
bismarck-archipelago: The Bismarck Archipelago lies just off the north-eastern coast of New Guinea in the western Pacific and is part of the Islands Region of Papua New Guinea. Its islands are mostly volcanic and have a total land area of about 49,700 square kilometres, around the Bismarck Sea.

They are grouped by province: Manus Province has the Admiralty Islands, a group of 18 islands including Manus, Los Negros and Lou, and the Western Islands; New Ireland Province has New Ireland, New Hanover, the St Matthias Islands and the Tabar, Lihir, Tanga and Feni groups; East and West New Britain provinces share New Britain and the Duke of York Islands; and others lie off Morobe, Madang and East Sepik provinces, among them Umboi, Ritter, Karkar and the Schouten Islands. The passage between New Britain and New Ireland is St George's Channel.

The first inhabitants arrived around 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. They may have come from New Guinea by boat across the Bismarck Sea or over a temporary land bridge created by an uplift of the crust.
