Later arrivals included the Lapita people, the direct ancestors of the Austronesian peoples of Polynesia, eastern Micronesia and Island Melanesia.

The first European to visit was the Dutch explorer Jacob le Maire in 1616, and the islands remained unsettled by western Europeans until they were annexed in 1884 as part of the German protectorate of German New Guinea. They were named in honour of Chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

On 13 March 1888 a volcano on Ritter Island erupted and caused a megatsunami; almost the whole volcano fell into the sea, leaving a small rim on the east side of the original island. After the outbreak of the First World War the Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force seized the islands in 1914, and Australia later received a League of Nations mandate for them. They stayed under Australian administration, interrupted only by Japanese occupation in World War II, until Papua New Guinea became independent in September 1975.
bismarck-battleship: Bismarck was the first of two Bismarck-class battleships built for the German Kriegsmarine, the second being Tirpitz. They were designed in the mid-1930s as a counter to the two Richelieu-class battleships that France began in 1935. Ordered as Ersatz Hannover, she was laid down at the Blohm & Voss yard in Hamburg on 1 July 1936, launched on 14 February 1939 with Adolf Hitler making the christening speech, and commissioned on 24 August 1940. She was nominally within the 35,000-ton limit of the Washington Naval Treaty but secretly exceeded it by a wide margin. Her main battery was eight 38 cm guns, and she reached just over 30 knots on trials.

Her only offensive operation, Rheinübung, lasted eight days in May 1941. Bismarck and the heavy cruiser Prinz Eugen were to break into the Atlantic and raid Allied shipping. In the Battle of the Denmark Strait the battlecruiser HMS Hood was destroyed by their combined fire, and HMS Prince of Wales was damaged and forced to retire; three hits from Prince of Wales damaged Bismarck enough to end the raid.

The loss of Hood set off a pursuit by dozens of Royal Navy ships. Heading for occupied France for repairs, Bismarck was attacked by fifteen Fairey Swordfish torpedo bombers from the carrier HMS Ark Royal, and one hit left her steering gear inoperable. In the final battle two British battleships and two heavy cruisers crippled her with heavy loss of life. She was scuttled to prevent boarding, although most experts agree that her damage would have sunk her in the end.

Robert Ballard, who had found the wreck of the Titanic, located Bismarck on 8 June 1989, upright on her keel at about 4,791 metres, some 650 km west of Brest. She had slid down the side of an extinct underwater volcano. Ballard's survey found no penetration of the armoured citadel. The 2002 expedition filmed by James Cameron concluded that the most extensive damage, including long gashes in the hull, came from her impact with the seabed.
bissau: Bissau lies on the estuary of the Geba River, off the Atlantic Ocean. The land around the city is extremely low-lying, and the river is accessible to ocean-going vessels for about 80 kilometres beyond it despite its modest discharge. The climate is tropical savanna, with almost no rain from November to May. The name may come from the name of a clan, N'nssassun, in its plural form Bôssassun.

From well before the arrival of Europeans until the early 20th century the island of Bissau was a kingdom of the Papel people. By oral tradition Mecau, a son of the king of Quinara, founded it and moved to the area with his pregnant sister, six wives and subjects of his father's kingdom. The kingdom had seven clans and was highly stratified, and the throne passed to the Bossassun clan, descended from the sister. When the Portuguese began to trade there in the 16th century the king of Bissau was among the most supportive monarchs of the region.

The city was founded in 1687 as a Portuguese trading post. The French were also active, and although King Bacompolco refused them leave to build a fort he granted them a trading factory, from which they shipped thousands of slaves. By 1696 the town had a fort, a church and a hospital. When the Portuguese tried to enforce a monopoly against the Papel policy of free trade, King Incinhate surrounded the unfinished fort, and they soon abandoned it. The Grão Pará and Maranhão Company rebuilt it in 1775 to store more slaves for shipment to Brazil, though real control stayed with the Papel kings.

Around the turn of the 20th century the Papels fiercely resisted Portuguese pacification campaigns. In 1915, after 30 years of war, the Portuguese under Teixeira Pinto and the warlord Abdul Injai defeated the Kingdom of Bissau and incorporated it into Portuguese Guinea. In 1941 the capital was moved from Bolama to Bissau. A dockworkers' strike was bloodily repressed in 1959 and pushed the nationalists towards armed resistance. After the military coup in Lisbon on 25 April, Bissau became the capital of the newly independent state.

Bissau is the capital and largest city of Guinea-Bissau, its main port and its administrative and military centre. Its attractions include the Fortaleza de São José da Amura, built by the Portuguese in the 18th century and containing the mausoleum of Amílcar Cabral, and the Pidjiguiti Memorial to the dockers killed in the strike of 3 August 1959.
bithynia: Bithynia occupied northwestern Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey, adjoining the Sea of Marmara, the Bosporus and the Black Sea. It bordered Mysia to the southwest, Paphlagonia to the northeast and Phrygia to the southeast. Ancient writers placed its eastern limit differently: Strabo at the river Sangarius, others at the Billaeus. Mountains and forests filled much of the land, above all the Bithynian Olympus, about 2,400 m high, above Prusa (modern Bursa), but the valleys and coasts were very fertile. Major cities stood on the shores of the Sea of Marmara: Nicomedia, Chalcedon, Cius and Apamea. Nicaea, the birthplace of the Nicene Creed, also lay in Bithynia.

The region is named for the Thracian tribe of the Bithyni, mentioned by Herodotus beside the Thyni. They probably migrated from the Balkans after the Bronze Age collapse or in the early Iron Age. King Croesus brought the Bithynians into the Lydian monarchy, which Persia conquered in 546 BCE. The Bithynians then asserted their independence under native princes, and Zipoites took the title of king in 297 BCE. His son Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia, which soon grew prosperous. The last king, Nicomedes IV, could not hold his throne against Mithridates VI of Pontus, and after the Roman Senate restored him he bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman Republic in 74 BCE.

As a Roman province Bithynia was usually joined with Pontus; Pliny the Younger governed the two together under Emperor Trajan, and his letters give historians valuable information on provincial administration. Under the Byzantine Empire the region was again divided at the Sangarius, and only the western part kept the name. Nicomedia and Nicaea long rivalled each other for the rank of capital. The Ottoman Turks conquered it between 1325 and 1333.
bitlis: Bitlis stands at an elevation of 1,545 metres in the steep-sided valley of the Bitlis River, a tributary of the Tigris, 15 kilometres from Lake Van. The origin of its name is not known. To Armenians it was Baghesh, one of the most important cities of the province of Aghdznik' in the Kingdom of Armenia, and the main fortress of the canton of Salnodzor. The fortress guarded the Baghesh Pass, which linked the southern edge of the Armenian plateau with northern Mesopotamia.

Under the Byzantine Empire the town was Balaleison. The Arabs conquered it at the end of the seventh century, and it became capital of the Zurārid emirs of Arzan, prospering on an important trade route. Later it passed to the Shaybanid and Kaysite emirs, and the Byzantine general John Curcuas captured it in the tenth century. Many Kurds settled there, and the Marwanid dynasty took the city. After Manzikert it came under Togan Arslan of Akhlat, after brief Dilmachoglu rule, and then Ayyubid rule, the Sultanate of Rûm and the Ilkhanate.

Bitlis was a Kurdish emirate, often subordinate to larger powers but keeping a measure of independence. In the 14th century its emirs, the Rusaki family, were vassals of the Karakoyunlu, and the emir submitted to Timur in 1394. In the 15th century the town flourished as a centre of Armenian manuscript production, the Kurdish emirs permitting monasteries to be built. An Ottoman army besieged it for three months and withdrew; the emir Sheref was killed in 1533 and his son submitted to the Ottoman Empire. The Ruzakid dynasty lasted until 1849, when an Ottoman governor evicted the last emir. Persian was the language of administration and scholarship, in the works of Idris-i Bidlisi and Sharaf Khan among others.

In 1915, during the Armenian genocide, Turks and Kurds led by Jevdet Bey massacred some 15,000 Armenians in Bitlis and its surroundings. Russian forces took the town in March 1916 and abandoned it in August.

Bitlis keeps more medieval and traditional architecture than any other town in eastern Turkey, much of it in the light-brown local stone called Ahlat stone. It has the 12th-century Ulu Mosque with a 15th-century minaret and large stone houses. Only one 19th-century Armenian church survives of the five monasteries and several churches that stood until 1915. Its population was 53,023 in 2021.
bitola: Bitola lies in the southwestern part of North Macedonia, in the southern part of the Pelagonia valley, surrounded by the Baba, Nidže and Kajmakčalan mountain ranges and 14 kilometres north of the Medžitlija-Níki border crossing with Greece. The Dragor River flows through the city, which stands at 615 metres above sea level at the foot of Baba Mountain. It stands at an important junction connecting the south of the Adriatic region with the Aegean Sea and Central Europe.

The earliest organised settlements nearby are early Neolithic tells near the village of Porodin, first inhabited around 6000 BCE. In antiquity the region was Lynkestis, part of Upper Macedonia, and Heraclea Lyncestis was founded by Philip II of Macedon by the middle of the 4th century BCE. Slavic tribes settled the area in the 6th and 7th centuries and built a fortress around their settlement. Bitola was part of the First Bulgarian Empire from the middle of the 8th to the early 11th centuries and was its last capital, in 1015 to 1018; the Bitola inscription is related to the fortress built in 1015. It then returned to the Byzantine Empire and was briefly part of the Serbian Empire in the 14th century.

The Ottomans conquered the city in the mid-1380s, and it was part of the Ottoman Empire as Monastir until 1912. It was the last capital of Ottoman Rumelia, from 1836 to 1867, and the many European consulates earned it the name City of Consuls. The region was a stronghold of the Ilinden Uprising of 1903, planned in Smilevo in May. In the First Balkan War the Battle of Monastir, from 16 to 19 November 1912, led to Serbian occupation, and the Treaty of Bucharest in 1913 ceded Monastir to Serbia, when its official name became Bitola.
In World War II the Germans took control on 9 April 1941, and on 11 March 1943 Bulgarian forces deported the vast majority of its Jewish community, 3,276 people, to Treblinka extermination camp.

Bitola is an administrative, cultural, industrial, commercial and educational centre of southwestern North Macedonia. Its population was historically diverse: about 37,500 at the end of the 19th century, including Aromanians, a Muslim population, a Jewish community of Sephardic origin and Slavic speakers divided between the Bulgarian Exarchate and the Greek Patriarchate.

The ruins of Heraclea Lyncestis lie 2 kilometres from the centre. Ottoman monuments include the covered bazaar, the Gazi Hajdar Kadi Mosque of the early 1560s, ascribed to the architect Mimar Sinan, and the Deboj Bath. The Church of Saint Demetrius was built in 1830 with contributions from local merchants and craftsmen. The St. Clement of Ohrid University of Bitola was founded in 1979.
bitterfeld: Bitterfeld was built by a colony of Flemish immigrants in 1153. Its name most likely comes from the Middle High German words bitter and Feld and means boggy land. The first documentary mention dates from 1224. The landgrave of Meissen captured the town in 1476, after which it belonged to Saxony until it was ceded to Prussia in 1815.

By 1900 Bitterfeld station was an important junction of the Berlin to Halle and the Magdeburg to Leipzig railways. The population was then 11,839, and the town manufactured drainpipes, paper roofing and machinery, and had sawmills. There were also several coal mines in the vicinity. Owing to its pleasant situation and accessibility, it had become a favoured residence of businessmen from Leipzig and Halle.

Walther Rathenau (1867 to 1922) is named as the founder of Bitterfeld's chemical industry, and the airships developed by August von Parseval were partly built in the town. In the East German era Bitterfeld gained notoriety for its chemical industry complex, which caused remarkably severe pollution, even by East German standards. On 24 April 1959 the town was the scene of the Bitterfeld Conference, known locally as the Bitterfelder Weg. The conference sought to connect the working class with the artists of the day in order to form a socialist national culture.

Bitterfeld lies in the district of Anhalt-Bitterfeld in Saxony-Anhalt, about 25 km south of Dessau and 30 km north-east of Halle (Saale). Since 1 July 2007 it has been part of the town of Bitterfeld-Wolfen. It remains an industrial town. The former brown-coal open-cast mine of Goitzsche, south-east of the town, is a source of numerous fossils in Bitterfeld amber.
bizen-ware: Bizen ware takes its name from the province where it was traditionally made, around the village of Imbe, and is also called Imbe or Inbe ware. It has ties to the older Sue pottery and appeared in the Kamakura period. The scholar Koyama Fujio counted it among the Six Ancient Kilns. Its peak came in the Momoyama period of the 16th century, and its rustic quality made it popular in the tea ceremony; early pieces are called old Bizen style, Ko-Bizen-ha.

In the Edo period the Ikeda lords of the Okayama domain supported the kilns and gave privileges to the families who ran them, among them the Kimura, Mori, Kaneshige, Oae, Tongu and Terami. After modernisation began in the Meiji era the craft almost disappeared, until the potter Kaneshige Toyo (1896–1967) revived the Momoyama style in the 1930s and was named a Living National Treasure. The government designated Bizen ware a traditional Japanese craft in 1982.

The clay of Imbe is sticky and fine, rich in iron and organic matter. It shrinks so much that an applied glaze would peel off in the kiln, and it cannot bear rapid changes of temperature, but its plasticity and strength let pieces keep their form and stay tough without glaze. Most vessels are thrown on a wheel, and their surfaces depend on yohen, the effects of the kiln.

Firings take place once or twice a year in climbing kilns, noborigama, or tunnel kilns, anagama, and last 10–14 days. Red pine is burned for its resin, and the potter adds wood every 20 minutes, day and night, raising the heat gradually towards about 1200 Celsius. Melted ash gives the yellow speckles called goma; wrapping a piece in rice-straw rope soaked in salt water produces the scarlet lines of hidasuki; burying part of a vessel in sand gives the dark sangiri.

At the beginning of the 21st century Bizen ware was made in around 300 kilns, and a Bizen ware festival is held every year around Imbe Station. The Bizen Ware Traditional Industry Hall there shows contemporary work and old pieces, and the Okayama Prefectural Bizen Ceramics Museum holds more than 500.
black-army-of-hungary: The ancestor and core of the army appeared in the early 1440s, in the era of John Hunyadi, the father of Matthias Corvinus. Matthias is said to have taken the idea of a professional standing mercenary army from boyhood reading about Julius Caesar. In his first years the army still rested on noble banners and the militia portalis, under which a noble raised one archer for every twenty serf-lots.

In 1458 Matthias borrowed 500 heavy cavalry from King George of Poděbrady of Bohemia, remnants of the Hussites whose tactics the Black Army later adapted. Under the Peace Treaty of Wiener Neustadt of 1463 John Jiskra, who led deserters plundering the north, was promised a royal pardon and two castles. The first mass hiring of mercenaries came during the Bohemian Wars of 1468–1478.

The soldiers were mainly Czechs, Germans, Serbs and Poles and, from 1480, Hungarians. The core began at 6,000–8,000 men, reached 15,000–20,000 in the 1480s, and a military parade at Vienna in 1485 showed 28,000, of whom 20,000 were horsemen. That was far larger than the army of Louis XI of France, the only other permanent professional army of the era. Every fourth soldier carried an arquebus, an unusual ratio, and the infantry sheltered behind large pavises.

Matthias paid for it by raising the serfs' taxes and basing them on households instead of portae. His annual income reached 650,000 florins by one count, though historians have speculated that it could reach about 800,000 in a good year. He also kept a river fleet, which numbered 360 vessels in 1479.

Pay was irregular, and unpaid troops sometimes left or revolted. In 1481 a group of 300 horsemen joined the opposing Holy Roman forces. The army conquered large parts of Austria, including Vienna in 1485, and more than half of the Crown of Bohemia, and it won the Battle of Breadfield against the Ottomans in 1479.

Matthias died on 6 April 1490. His son John Corvinus commanded the Black Army, but the barons invited other claimants and chose Vladislaus II of Bohemia, and the army's core was then stuck in Silesia and Styria. The captains Blaise Magyar and Paul Kinizsi joined rival claimants. The nobility in parliament cut taxes by 70 to 80 percent, so Vladislaus could not pay for the army, and its end followed Matthias's death. Left unpaid, soldiers pillaged Hungarian and later Austrian villages.

Several theories explain the name, one tracing it to a captain nicknamed Black John Haugwitz. After the dissolution the magnates also dismantled the administration, garrisons went unpaid and fortresses fell into disrepair.
black-brunswickers: In 1806 Duke Charles William Ferdinand of Brunswick-Lüneburg was fatally wounded at the Battle of Jena–Auerstedt, and Napoleon, refusing the succession to his heir, put the duchy in 1807 into the Kingdom of Westphalia ruled by his brother Jérôme. When the Fifth Coalition was formed in 1809, the dispossessed Frederick William sought Austrian help, mortgaged his principality of Oels to pay for a force, and raised a free corps of about 2,300 men: two infantry battalions, a Jäger battalion, sharpshooters, and hussars and uhlans.

After the Austrian defeat at Wagram and the Armistice of Znaim, the duke refused to stop and led his Black Host into Germany, briefly taking the city of Brunswick. Pursued by superior Westphalian forces, the corps held them off at Halberstadt and Ölper and was taken off by the Royal Navy from the mouth of the Weser. In British service it became the Brunswick Oels Jäger and Hussar regiments. Cut off from German recruits, the Oels took men from prisoner-of-war camps, and the historian Charles Oman called them a motley crew much given to desertion; yet they fought at Fuentes de Oñoro, Salamanca, Vitoria and Orthez.

Returning to Brunswick in 1813, the duke rebuilt the corps, which numbered 5,376 men in 1815. At Quatre Bras on 16 June the Brunswickers came under heavy artillery fire and broke before rallying, and the duke was hit by a musket ball while re-forming them; Colonel Elias Olfermann took command. They lost 188 killed and 396 wounded. At Waterloo two days later they stood in squares against the French cavalry and filled the gap left by the fall of La Haye Sainte; British sources count 154 killed, 456 wounded and 50 missing.

Black uniforms became closely associated across Germany with the liberation movement of 1813, and the duchy's troops kept them as a privilege until a military convention with Prussia in 1892. Brunswick's infantry regiment and hussars, numbered 92 and 17 in the Prussian Army from 1866, kept the skull badge until they were disbanded in 1918. John Everett Millais's painting The Black Brunswicker, completed in 1860, showed the corps to the Victorian public.
black-death: The Black Death was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is primarily spread by flea bites, though it may also spread through contact with infected tissues or fluids and, in pneumonic cases, through respiratory droplets. Its origin is disputed, with some evidence pointing towards China, Central Asia, West Asia and Europe. Genetic work published in 2010 and 2011 on skeletons from mass graves, including the East Smithfield burial site in England, confirmed Y. pestis as the cause. European writers of the time called the disease pestilentia or mortalitas, and the name Black Death was not used in English for this pandemic until the 1750s.

The pandemic was reportedly first introduced to Europe during the siege of the Genoese trading port of Caffa in Crimea by the Golden Horde army of Jani Beg in 1347. From Crimea it was most likely carried by fleas on black rats travelling on Genoese ships. It spread through the Mediterranean and reached North Africa, West Asia and the rest of Europe via Constantinople, Sicily and the Italian Peninsula. Evidence suggests that once ashore it mainly spread from person to person as pneumonic plague, which explains its fast inland spread.

By autumn 1347 plague had reached Alexandria in Egypt, carried by sea from Constantinople by a single merchant ship carrying slaves. By late summer 1348 it reached Cairo, capital of the Mamluk Sultanate and the largest city of the Mediterranean Basin. The child sultan an-Nasir Hasan fled, and more than a third of the 600,000 residents died. Plague recurred in Cairo more than fifty times over the next one and a half centuries. Contemporary accounts noted above all buboes in the groin, neck and armpits, which oozed pus and bled when opened.

There are no exact figures for the death toll, and the rate varied widely by locality. A 2022 study of pollen samples across Europe found high mortality in areas of Scandinavia, France, western Germany, Greece and central Italy, but uninterrupted agricultural growth in central and eastern Europe, Iberia and Ireland. The population of Europe did not regain its 14th-century level until the 16th century. The labour shortage raised wages, and in some places rents collapsed, though many labourers lost real income to inflation.

Many Europeans blamed Jews, friars, foreigners, beggars, pilgrims, lepers and Romani for the crisis. About 2,000 Jews were murdered in the Strasbourg massacre of February 1349, and the Jewish communities of Mainz and Cologne were annihilated in August 1349. By 1351 sixty major and 150 smaller Jewish communities had been destroyed. Plague returned repeatedly to Europe through the 14th to 17th centuries, and some scholars have suggested that Italy's experience of the epidemic shaped the thought of the Renaissance.
black-flag-army: In 1857 Liu Yongfu, a Hakka soldier of fortune, led about 200 men within a band of highwaymen in Guangxi under Huang Sihong. He went over with his men to the band of Wu Yuanqing under a black flag of his own, holding a ceremony that recalled the rituals of the Tiandihui. The unit served under Wu Yuanqing and his son Wu Yazhong, who both claimed to be Taiping princes. Many of its soldiers were of Zhuang background or former Taiping fighters. After the fall of Nanking in 1864, Qing armies hunted down the armed bands of the south-east, and in 1865 Wu Yazhong and Liu crossed into Upper Tonkin, looting villages on the way.

The Black Flags won the favour of the Vietnamese court by helping to suppress the Hmong of the mountains between the Red and Black rivers, and Liu received an official military title. He then taxed river trade between Sơn Tây and Lào Cai at 10 percent, took over mines, ran a protection system and robbed villages. The profits drew recruits in the 1870s; most soldiers were Chinese, but some junior officers were American and European adventurers, and Liu came to command 7,000 men from Guangdong and Guangxi. The army also fought rival bands such as the White and Yellow Flags. Its name came from Liu's large black command flags.

On 21 December 1873 Liu and about 600 Black Flags approached the Hanoi Citadel, and the French lieutenant Francis Garnier, who had attacked Tonkin without orders, was speared to death while pursuing them. At the Battle of Paper Bridge on 19 May 1883 they ambushed and killed Henri Rivière. Later defeats followed: Admiral Amédée Courbet stormed Sơn Tây in December 1883, and in 1884 the French took Hưng Hóa and Tuyên Quang without losing a man.

When the Sino-French War broke out in August 1884, Tang Jingsong of the Yunnan Army enlisted Liu, and 3,000 Black Flags served at the Siege of Tuyên Quang. At the Battle of Hòa Mộc on 2 March 1885 they killed 76 French soldiers and wounded 408, France's heaviest loss in one day of the war. The peace required Liu to leave Tonkin. He crossed into China with his most loyal followers, and most of his men, unpaid and still armed, turned to banditry under cover of the Cần Vương movement; in 1887 Black Flag bandits sacked Luang Prabang.
black-forest: The Black Forest is a large forested mountain range in Baden-Württemberg, bounded by the Rhine Valley to the west and south and close to the borders with France and Switzerland. It is the source of the Danube and the Neckar. It is about 160 kilometres long and up to 50 kilometres wide, with an area of about 6,009 square kilometres, and its highest peak is the Feldberg at 1,493 metres. The gentle eastern slopes contrast with the steeply falling terrain in the west that drops into the Upper Rhine Graben. It consists of a cover of sandstone on a core of gneiss and granite, and it was covered by glaciers in the last glacial period, which left tarns such as the Mummelsee.

In ancient times the range was known as Abnoba mons, after the Celtic deity Abnoba, and in Roman times as Silva Marciana, from the Germanic marka, border; it probably marked the border area of the Marcomanni, a part of the Suebi. Apart from Roman settlements on the perimeter, such as the baths at Badenweiler, mines near Badenweiler and Sulzburg and the Roman road of the Kinzig valley, the colonization was carried out not by the Romans but by the Alemanni. They settled the valleys first and then increasingly higher areas, so that by the end of the 10th century the first settlements stood in the red sandstone region. Rötenbach, for example, was first mentioned in 819.

The ore deposits supported mining, and for several centuries logs were rafted down the Enz, Kinzig, Murg, Nagold and Rhine. This trade boomed in the 18th century and led to large-scale clearances. Most of the long, straight pine logs went to the Netherlands for shipbuilding and were called Dutchmen; used there as piles for houses, they support many historic buildings in Amsterdam. Rafting largely ended in the late 19th century with the railways and roads.

Charcoal burners, potash boilers and glassmakers also lived from the timber. Because the valleys were relatively inaccessible, industrialization arrived late. In winter many farmers made wooden cuckoo clocks, which developed in the 19th century into a precision engineering and watch industry, and the Baden state government founded a clockmaking school at Furtwangen in 1850.

The Black Forest is mainly rural, with many scattered villages and a few large towns, and the main dialect is Alemannic. It is known for its farmhouses with sweeping half-hipped roofs, the Bollenhut headdress worn in villages of the Kinzig valley, wood carving, the cuckoo clock, Black Forest ham and the Black Forest gâteau. In the 19th and early 20th centuries its rural beauty attracted artists such as Hans Thoma. Tourism is now the primary industry, and several ruined military fortifications date back to the 17th century.
black-hills: The Black Hills are an outlying subrange of the Rocky Mountain system, rising from the Great Plains in western South Dakota and eastern Wyoming. The highest summit, Black Elk Peak, rises to 2,207 metres. The range takes its name from its dark appearance from a distance, since it is covered in evergreen trees, and the Lakota call it Pahá Sápa. Its core is granite dated to 1.8 billion years, ringed by metamorphic and sedimentary rocks, and its limestone holds more than 200 caves, among them Jewel Cave and Wind Cave. Most of the hills are covered by ponderosa pine forest.

Tools show a human presence going back as far as 11,500 BCE, with the Clovis culture. The Ponca, Arikara and Mandan were among the earliest recorded inhabitants, later displaced by the Kiowa, Plains Apache and Shoshone, and then by the Cheyenne and Arapaho. After the Lakota conquered the Cheyenne in 1776 the hills became central to Lakota culture. By 1850 the Lakota were the majority, and they call the hills wamakaognaka e'cante, the heart of everything that is. The Cheyenne, Arapaho and other peoples also hold particular sites there to be sacred.

The First Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1851 recognised the Black Hills as exclusive Lakota territory. The Second Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1868 created the Great Sioux Reservation west of the Missouri and protected the hills from settlers forever. In 1874 an expedition under George Armstrong Custer found gold in French Creek, and the reporters with it announced the discovery. Thousands of miners came during the gold rush of 1875 to 1878, and the towns of Deadwood, Central City and Lead grew up in the Northern Hills.

The conflict led to the Great Sioux War of 1876. After the defeat of the Lakota and their Cheyenne and Arapaho allies, the United States occupied the hills in disregard of past treaties, relocated the Lakota to five smaller reservations and sold off 9 million acres. On 23 July 1980, in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, the Supreme Court ruled that the hills had been illegally seized and ordered payment of the original offering price plus interest. The Lakota refused the money because acceptance would end their demand for the return of the land.

The region holds Mount Rushmore National Memorial, Wind Cave National Park, Jewel Cave National Monument, Custer State Park, the Crazy Horse Memorial and, in Wyoming, Devils Tower National Monument, the first national monument of the United States. The economy has moved from mining and timber towards tourism. Rapid City is the largest city, and the former mining town of Deadwood is preserved as a historic place.
black-isle: The Black Isle, in Scottish Gaelic an t-Eilean Dubh, lies within Ross and Cromarty. On three sides it is bounded by the sea, and on the western side its limit is broadly marked by rivers: the River Conon, which divides Maryburgh from Conon Bridge, in the north-west, and in the south-west either a minor tributary of the River Beauly or the River Beauly itself, so that some count Beauly as part of the Black Isle although it lies officially in Inverness-shire.

From its northern slopes there are views of Dingwall, Ben Wyvis, Fyrish and the deepwater anchorage at Invergordon, and to the south Inverness and the Monadhliath Mountains can be seen. The land is used mainly for arable farming and forestry.

According to the Encyclopædia Britannica Eleventh Edition, the peninsula was first called Ardmeanach, from a religious house on the wooded ridge of Mulbuie, and took its usual name because snow does not lie there in winter, so that it looks black while the country around is white; this is only one of many explanations. Redcastle, near Killearnan church, dates from 1179 and is said to have been the earliest inhabited house in the north of Scotland. After the forfeiture of the earldom of Ross it became a royal castle, visited by Mary, Queen of Scots, and later passed to the Mackenzies of Gairloch; before that the Black Isle had been Munro country.

Rosehaugh, near Avoch, belonged to Sir George Mackenzie, founder of the Advocates' Library in Edinburgh, who was called Bloody for his persecution of the Covenanters. The Black Isle was one of the first parts of the northern Highlands to undergo the clearances, and many Lowland shepherds and farmers, especially from the north east, settled there. The geologist and writer Hugh Miller was born in Cromarty, and Alexander Mackenzie, who crossed Canada overland in 1793, is buried near Avoch. From 1894 until 1960 the Fortrose Branch railway ran from Muir of Ord to Fortrose.

About 12,000 people live on the Black Isle; its parishes had 12,302 inhabitants at the 2011 census. Road bridges across the Cromarty and Beauly Firths carry the A9 over the peninsula, and since the bridge replaced the Kessock Ferry it has become in part a commuter area for Inverness. Its own dialect of North Northern Scots, spoken by fisherfolk in Avoch and Cromarty, died out in October 2012 with its last native speaker, Bobby Hogg.
black-madonna-of-czestochowa: The original painting measures 122 by 82 centimetres and follows a composition well known in Orthodox icons. Mary appears as the Hodegetria, the one who shows the way, directing attention away from herself and gesturing with her right hand towards Jesus as the source of salvation. The child extends his right hand towards the viewer in blessing and holds a book of gospels in his left. Mary wears robes with fleur-de-lis. The icon is widely venerated by Roman Catholics and Eastern Orthodox Christians, above all among the Polish people, and it is kept under high-security glass.

Its origins and the date of its composition are contested. Legends trace it to Luke the Evangelist, who painted it on a cedar table top from the house of the Holy Family, and say that Empress Helena found it in Jerusalem in 326. Art historians say that the original was a Byzantine icon made around the sixth or ninth century. The oldest documents of Jasna Góra say that it travelled from Constantinople via Belz and came to Władysław Opolczyk, Duke of Opole, who, according to a well-known story, left it at Jasna Góra when his horses refused to go on past Częstochowa.

In August 1382 the hilltop church was transferred to the Paulites, a hermitic order from Hungary. The fleur-de-lis may point to the Hungarian kings of the Anjou dynasty, which suggests that Pauline monks brought the icon from Hungary.

According to the legend of the two scars on the Virgin's right cheek, Hussites stormed the monastery in 1430 and stole the icon, but their horses would not move and they threw it down. One of them struck it twice with his sword and fell writhing to death when he tried a third time. The panel was in fact broken and the image slashed by robbers in 1430, and medieval restorers erased and repainted it, which complicates dating.

During the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge, seventy monks and 180 volunteers held off 4,000 Swedes at Jasna Góra for 40 days in the winter of 1655, while the icon was moved in secret. John II Casimir Vasa then proclaimed Mary Queen of Poland at Lwów on 1 April 1656. Pope Clement XI decreed its canonical coronation on 8 September 1717, and three popes have given it golden roses. Its feast day in Poland is 26 August, and a pilgrimage has left Warsaw each 6 August since 1711.
black-obelisk-of-shalmaneser-iii: The Black Obelisk is a black limestone Neo-Assyrian sculpture with many scenes in bas-relief and inscriptions. It comes from Nimrud, ancient Kalhu, in northern Iraq, and commemorates the deeds of King Shalmaneser III, who reigned from 858 to 824 BCE. It is one of two complete Neo-Assyrian obelisks yet discovered, the other being the much earlier White Obelisk of Ashurnasirpal I.

It was erected as a public monument in 825 BCE, at a time of civil war, in the central square of Nimrud. Some features of the work suggest that it may have been commissioned by the king's commander-in-chief, Dayyan-Assur.

The obelisk carries twenty relief scenes, five on each side. They show five subdued kings bringing tribute and prostrating themselves before the Assyrian king. From top to bottom they are Sua of Gilzanu, in north-west Iran; Yaua of Bit Omri, that is Jehu of the House of Omri; an unnamed ruler of Musri, in northern Iraq; Marduk-apil-usur of Suhi, on the middle Euphrates; and Qalparunda of Patin, in the Antakya region of Turkey. Each scene occupies four panels around the monument, with a cuneiform caption above.

Long cuneiform inscriptions at the top and bottom record the annals of Shalmaneser III. They list the military campaigns that the king and his commander-in-chief led each year until the thirty-first year of the reign. The reference to Parsua is the first known reference to the Persians.

The archaeologist Sir Austen Henry Layard discovered the obelisk in 1846. It is now in the British Museum, and several other museums hold cast replicas. The second register from the top is thought to hold the earliest surviving picture of a biblical figure. Its caption reads that the king received the tribute of Iaua, son of Omri: silver, gold, a golden bowl, a golden vase with pointed bottom, golden tumblers, golden buckets, tin, a staff for a king and spears. The tribute is dated to about 841 BCE.

In 1850 Henry Rawlinson read the name as Yahua, son of Hubiri, a prince he could not place. On 21 August 1851 the Reverend Edward Hincks identified him with Jehu, king of Israel, and this identification is now the commonly held position among biblical archaeologists. Scholars including George Smith, P. Kyle McCarter and Edwin R. Thiele have questioned it, citing the fact that Jehu was not an Omride, along with problems of transliteration and chronology.
black-power-movement: The slogan Black power was first used popularly by Stokely Carmichael and Willie Ricks of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee; on 16 June 1966, during the March Against Fear in Greenwood, Mississippi, Carmichael led a chant for it that was televised nationally. After the Watts riots of 1965, SNCC cut its ties with the mainstream civil rights movement, arguing that Black Americans had to build power of their own rather than seek accommodation, and moved from nonviolence towards militancy. In late October 1966 Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale founded the Black Panther Party.

The Panthers first used open-carry gun laws to protect members and Black neighbourhoods from the police and followed police cars to record brutality. By 1969 they and their allies were the main targets of the FBI's COINTELPRO, singled out in 233 of its 295 authorised Black nationalist actions. At the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City, Tommie Smith and John Carlos each raised a black-gloved hand during the American anthem.

In 1970 former Panthers formed the Black Liberation Army to pursue violent revolution. It is believed to have bombed St. Brendan's Church in San Francisco during a police officer's funeral that year, and its members killed police officers in New York, San Francisco and Atlanta in 1971 and 1972. A split between Newton and Eldridge Cleaver in 1971 led to four killings, and by the late 1970s the party had fallen apart. In 1985 Philadelphia police bombed the house of the group MOVE, killing several adults and children.

The movement put weight on education and its own media. The fifth point of the Black Panther Party's Ten-Point Program demanded education that taught Black Americans their true history, and their newspaper, the Black Panther, was among their most effective tools. WAFR in Durham, North Carolina, launched in 1971 as the first public, community-based Black radio station. In Australia the movement influenced Aboriginal activists from the late 1960s, and the Aboriginal Legal Service in Redfern grew out of that activism. Some have compared Black Lives Matter to it.
black-sea-fleet: Peter the Great tried to expand Russia to the Black Sea and set up a naval base on the Sea of Azov during the Russo-Turkish War of 1695–96, but he had to surrender those gains after the war of 1710 to 1713. Russia's position in the south advanced slowly after the war of 1735 to 1739 and then much faster under Catherine the Great, whose Greek Project envisaged partitioning the Ottoman Empire between Russia and the Habsburg Empire. Beginning with the war of 1768–1774, Russia and the Ottoman Empire fought seven more wars up to the First World War over which would dominate the Black Sea region. Prince Potemkin founded the fleet on 13 May 1783 as part of the Imperial Russian Navy.

The Russian SFSR inherited the fleet in 1918, and with the founding of the Soviet Union in 1922 it became part of the Soviet Navy. After the defeat of the anti-Bolshevik Armed Forces of South Russia the Soviet government took control of all naval elements. The few remaining ships were scrapped in the 1920s, and a large construction programme began in the 1930s, at first defensive and based on small submarines, then from about 1935 with cruisers and destroyers. Under the Montreaux Convention of 1936 the Soviet Union secured the peacetime right for its Black Sea ships to pass the Turkish Straits.

With the fall of the Soviet Union the fleet lost its major missions and much of its funding. In the early 1990s it had 645 ships and 72,000 personnel. In 1992 the greater part of its personnel, weapons and coastal facilities came under the jurisdiction of newly independent Ukraine, which ordered its own navy to be formed from it, and several ships declared themselves Ukrainian. This led to conflicts with the many officers loyal to Russia. In 1997 the fleet was partitioned between Russia and Ukraine, and Russia received title to 82 per cent of the vessels.

The fleet has its main headquarters and facilities at the Sevastopol Naval Base in Crimea. Its use of leased bases there was sometimes controversial in the years after 1991, for example over the refusal to let Ukrainians inspect aircraft cargo and the occupation of the Sarych lighthouse from 2005.
black-seminoles: Florida had been a refuge for enslaved people seeking freedom for at least 70 years by the time of the American Revolution. In the 18th and 19th centuries Black Seminole communities grew up on the outskirts of Seminole villages, such as Bowlegs Town on the Suwannee River and Okahumpka. In the Revolution and the War of 1812 both peoples sided with the British, strengthening their ties and earning the enmity of General Andrew Jackson. Scholars liken the Seminole system to the tributary or patron-client ties of Southeastern Indigenous societies rather than to chattel slavery, and Black Seminoles could carry firearms.

In the West slave raiders still threatened them, and in 1848 the US attorney general ordered the army to disarm the community. In 1849 John Horse and about 180 Black Seminoles escaped to northern Mexico, which had abolished slavery twenty years earlier, riding with the Seminole chief Coacochee. Mexico took them on as border guards at El Nacimiento, Coahuila. In 1870 the US Army invited them back as scouts; based at Fort Clark, Texas, the Black Seminole Scouts fought in the Texas-Indian Wars, four of them winning the Medal of Honor, and their families settled around Brackettville after the unit was disbanded in 1914.

Those who stayed in Indian Territory were freed under the treaties of 1866 that the United States imposed on the tribes that had backed the Confederacy. Many live in and around Wewoka, founded by John Horse in 1849 and now the capital of the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma. In 2000 the Nation voted to limit membership to those descended from a Seminole on the Dawes Rolls, excluding about 1,200 Freedmen; in 2022 the District Court for the District of Columbia ruled that they kept membership and voting rights.

Black Seminole culture blends African, Gullah, Seminole, Mexican and other traditions. They ate coontie flour and sofkee, a corn porridge, as the Seminole did, and brought the Gullah staple of rice. Their language, Afro-Seminole Creole, was identified as distinct by the linguist Ian Hancock in 1978. Families gave day names such as Cudjoe for Monday, and their churches keep the ring shout, a counter-clockwise circle dance with singing and clapping. Descendants also live in Florida, Texas and at Red Bay on Andros Island in the Bahamas.
black-september: After the Six-Day War of 1967 Palestinian fedayeen guerrillas relocated to Jordan and stepped up attacks on Israel and the Israeli-occupied West Bank. They were headquartered at the border town of Karameh, which Israel targeted in the Battle of Karameh in 1968, bringing a surge of Arab support. The strength of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), led by Yasser Arafat, grew, and by early 1970 leftist groups within it were calling for the overthrow of Jordan's Hashemite monarchy, leading to violent clashes in June 1970.

King Hussein feared that an independent West Bank under PLO administration would threaten his kingdom, and he hesitated to expel the fighters. The Dawson's Field hijackings of 6 September 1970 ended his patience. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine seized three airliners; two jets landed at Azraq, and a third plane was brought to Zarqa on 9 September. The planes were blown up before the international press on 12 September.

The main fighting ran from 16 to 27 September 1970. On 17 September the Jordanian Army surrounded cities with a strong PLO presence, including Amman and Irbid, and attacked fedayeen posts in the refugee camps. The next day 10,000 Syrian troops bearing Palestine Liberation Army markings advanced towards Irbid, which the fedayeen had declared a liberated city. On 22 September the Syrians withdrew after heavy losses to a coordinated Jordanian air and ground offensive.

Pressure from Arab states such as Iraq led Hussein to halt his offensive, and on 13 October he signed an agreement with Arafat to regulate the fedayeen's presence. The army attacked again in January 1971 and drove the fighters from the cities. On 23 July 1971 some 2,000 surrendered after being encircled in the Ajlun offensive, which formally ended the conflict. The fedayeen were allowed to relocate to Lebanon through Syria.

Wasfi Tal's civilian government purged the bureaucracy and military of supporters of the guerrillas, and closed many newspapers. Palestinians and Jordanians fought on both sides in 1970, so the conflict did not reflect a Jordanian-Palestinian divide, but it paved the way for one. Hussein's resilience impressed the West and Israel, and Nixon ordered $10 million in aid to be delivered to Jordan.

Fatah members founded the Black September Organization in 1971. Its members assassinated Tal in Cairo on 28 November 1971, and in 1972 it carried out the Munich massacre of Israeli athletes. In Lebanon the enlarged PLO presence stirred internal unrest and helped to precipitate the Lebanese Civil War.
black-ships: The term kurofune first named Portuguese ships. Portuguese traders reached Japan in 1543 and opened a route from their headquarters in Goa, by way of Malacca, to Nagasaki. Their carracks of 1,200 to 1,600 tons, called nau do trato or nau da China, had hulls painted black with pitch, and the name came to cover all Western vessels; it was recorded in the Nippo Jisho, the first Western dictionary of Japanese, compiled in 1603. The Nanban trade brought refined sugar, optics and firearms, and the arquebus, copied in Japan, became a major weapon of the Sengoku period.

Francis Xavier began a Jesuit mission in 1549, and Christianity won some 300,000 converts. After the Shimabara Rebellion, blamed on Christian influence, was suppressed in 1637, the Portuguese were expelled in 1639, and the Tokugawa shogunate kept to the policy of Sakoku, the locked country, trading only with China, Korea, the Ryukyu Islands and the Dutch on Dejima.

The name passed to the four American warships of Commodore Matthew C. Perry's expedition, Mississippi, Plymouth, Saratoga and Susquehanna, which anchored at Uraga in July 1853. Their hulls were not black, but their coal-fired engines poured out black smoke, and ships that moved without wind deeply frightened onlookers. Perry refused requests to go to Nagasaki, the licensed port, and threatened to attack Edo and burn it if he could not land; he was allowed ashore at Kurihama, delivered his letter and left. He returned the next year with eight ships, and after about a month of talks the Convention of Kanagawa opened formal relations. Townsend Harris stayed at Shimoda as consul, and the Harris Treaty followed on 29 July 1858.

The kurofune became a symbol of the end of isolation. A kyōka of the time plays on pivot words: read one way it tells of a costly green tea, Jōkisen, four cups of which keep a drinker awake; read another it tells of four steamships, jōkisen, that break the slumber of the Pacific and leave the country sleepless. Kurofune is also the title of the first Japanese opera, by Kosaku Yamada, first performed in 1940 and based on the story of the geisha Tojin Okichi.
black-stone: The Black Stone was venerated at the Kaaba long before Islam, and aniconic stones called baetyls were known across the eastern Mediterranean. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad set it in the Kaaba's wall in 605, five years before his first revelation. In the account of ibn Ishaq, the clans of Mecca could not agree which should replace the stone after the Kaaba was rebuilt, so Muhammad laid it on a cloth and had each clan leader hold a corner as they carried it to the spot.

Muslim tradition gives it a longer past. One account holds that Adam placed it in the first Kaaba, and that the angel Gabriel showed Abraham where it lay so that his son Ishmael could build it into a new temple. Another holds that it was once an angel set to guard Adam.

The stone is set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba in a silver frame fastened with silver nails. It was once a single rock but now consists of several pieces cemented together, and its exposed face measures about 20 by 16 centimetres. It has never been analysed with modern techniques. It has been called basalt, natural glass or a stony meteorite, but geologists regard the meteoritic idea as doubtful.

Pilgrims circling the Kaaba seven times in the tawaf try to kiss the stone, touch it, or raise their hands towards it, following what tradition records of Muhammad. Because of the crowds, it is now acceptable to point towards it. Theologians stress that it has no divine significance; the caliph Umar is reported to have said that it could neither harm nor benefit anyone and that he kissed it only because he had seen Muhammad do so.

It is said to have been smashed by a catapult stone during the Umayyad siege of Mecca in 683, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr rejoined the pieces with a silver band. In January 930 the Qarmatians stole it and took it to Hajar in eastern Arabia, and held it for more than two decades before returning it. The custodians then had a silver frame made, and it has been enclosed in such a frame since.
black-war: A British penal settlement was established in Van Diemen's Land, now Tasmania, in 1803, when the Aboriginal population was between 3,000 and 7,000 people. Until the 1820s there was only sporadic violence, often caused by competition for game and by the abduction of Aboriginal women and children by settlers. On 3 May 1804 soldiers, settlers and convicts fired on a hunting party of 100 to 300 Aboriginal people at Risdon Cove, and witnesses said that between three and 50 men, women and children died. From 1824 the conflict intensified as Aboriginal warriors resisted the rapid spread of settlement over their land.

Aboriginal attacks on colonists more than doubled each year from 1825 to 1828. The warriors fought a guerrilla war, usually attacking by day in parties of 10 to 20 men. On 1 November 1828 Governor George Arthur declared martial law against the Aboriginal people of the settled districts. It lasted more than three years, the longest period in Australian history, and only one colonist was ever prosecuted for killing an Aboriginal person. In the north-west, shepherds of the Van Diemen's Land Company ambushed up to 30 Aboriginal people at the Cape Grim massacre of 10 February 1828.

In October 1830 about 2,200 men, soldiers, convict servants and civilians, formed the Black Line, a staggered front more than 300 kilometres long meant to drive four of the nine Aboriginal nations onto the Tasman Peninsula. Bad weather and rough terrain broke the cordon, and it captured two people and killed two before it was disbanded on 26 November. Between 1830 and 1831 George Augustus Robinson and his Aboriginal negotiators, among them Truganini, secured the surrender of the Aboriginal fighters. Martial law was revoked in January 1832.

Almost all the remaining Aboriginal people were removed from mainland Tasmania between 1832 and 1835. About 220 survivors were held at the Wybalenna mission on Flinders Island, where respiratory disease and a low birth rate reduced them to 46 by 1847, when it closed. The Black War is thought to have killed more than 200 colonists and between 600 and 900 Aboriginal people. Lyndall Ryan estimates 838 killed in eastern Tasmania from 1823 to 1832, and Nicholas Clements puts deaths from frontier violence at about 600, with a possible range of 400 to 1,000.

Historians disagree about the conflict's character. Keith Windschuttle called it an outbreak of criminality, a view challenged by James Boyce, Henry Reynolds and others. Robert Hughes, Boyce and others describe the near-destruction of the Aboriginal Tasmanians as genocide, while Reynolds, Richard Broome and Clements hold that the colonial authorities did not pursue a policy of destruction.
blackbeard: Little is known of his early life. It is commonly believed that he was between 35 and 40 when he died, and so born around 1680. Contemporary records give his name most often as Blackbeard, Edward Thatch or Edward Teach. People who actually met him wrote Thatch or variants of it, but Teach is the form most often used, because it appears in The Boston News-Letter, North America's only newspaper at the time. He was most likely raised in Bristol, then the second-largest city in England, and could almost certainly read and write. Charles Johnson, an 18th-century author, claimed that he sailed on privateers from Jamaica in the War of the Spanish Succession.

Probably after the Treaty of Utrecht, Teach moved from Jamaica to the island of New Providence, whose harbour too shallow for the Royal Navy's larger vessels. Possibly about 1716 he joined the crew of Captain Benjamin Hornigold, who gave him command of a captured sloop. On 28 November 1717 his ships took the French slave ship La Concorde off Saint Vincent. He renamed her Queen Anne's Revenge and equipped her with 40 guns. His nickname came from his thick black beard and menacing appearance, and he was reported to tie lit slow matches under his hat to frighten his enemies.

By May 1718 he had styled himself Commodore, and his flotilla blockaded the port of Charles Town, South Carolina. About nine vessels were stopped and ransacked. Prominent citizens aboard the Crowley were held, and he demanded medical supplies from the colonial government, threatening to kill the prisoners if none came. On 10 June 1718 Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground on a sandbar at Beaufort Inlet. Teach learned of a royal pardon open to pirates who surrendered by 5 September 1718 and accepted it from Governor Charles Eden at Bath, North Carolina, but he soon returned to the sea.

Alexander Spotswood, the governor of Virginia, feared that Teach and his men would disrupt Virginian commerce and arranged for soldiers and sailors to capture him. On 22 November 1718 (3 December in the modern calendar), after a battle at Ocracoke Inlet, Teach and several of his crew were killed by a small force of sailors led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard. His loot was sold at auction for 2,238 pounds, and Spotswood used part of it to pay for the operation.

A shrewd leader, he relied on his fearsome image more than on violence. He was romanticised after his death and became the model of the archetypal pirate in fiction. Divers found the wreck of Queen Anne's Revenge in Beaufort Inlet in November 1996.
blaise-diagne: Blaise Diagne was born on 13 October 1872 in Gorée, the son of Niokhor Diagne, a Lebu cook and sailor, and Gnagna Anthony Preira, a Manjack woman whose family came from Guinea-Bissau. As a child he was adopted by the Crespin family, Christians of mixed race from Gorée and Saint-Louis, who baptised him Blaise. He studied in France and in 1892 joined the French customs service, which posted him to Dahomey, the French Congo, Réunion, Madagascar and French Guiana. In September 1899, in Réunion, he became a freemason in a lodge of the Grand Orient de France.

Diagne was elected to the Chamber of Deputies on 10 May 1914; two mixed-race deputies had represented the Four Communes before him. Soon after his election he played a leading part in the government's response to an outbreak of plague in Dakar. Until 1917 he sat with the French Section of the Workers' International, then joined the Independents led by Georges Mandel. In 1916 he persuaded parliament to pass the Loi Blaise Diagne, granting full citizenship to the residents of Dakar, Gorée, Saint-Louis and Rufisque. In return he helped the French organise recruitment in Senegal, and thousands of black West Africans fought for France on the Western Front.

From October 1918 to January 1920 he was Commissioner General at the Ministry of the Colonies, overseeing colonial soldiers and workers from France's African possessions. He was mayor of Dakar from 1920 to 1934, represented France at the International Labour Office in 1930, and was Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies from January 1931 to February 1932. He was re-elected to the Chamber until his death.

Diagne died at Cambo-les-Bains on 11 May 1934. It is alleged that his freemasonry kept him from burial in the Muslim cemetery of Soumbedioune in Dakar. A pioneer of African electoral politics, he argued for equal rights regardless of race but also for African accommodation to French rule and culture, and by his last years most Western-educated African elites had turned to nationalism and independence. W. E. B. Du Bois faulted him for a lack of commitment to African interests, writing that "Diagne is a Frenchman who is accidentally black". A boulevard and a lycée in Dakar bear his name, as does Blaise Diagne International Airport at Ndiass. His son Raoul was the first black professional footballer in France.
blaj: Blaj is a city in Alba County in Transylvania, lying at the confluence of the Târnava Mare and Târnava Mică rivers, where they form the Târnava River. It is 39 kilometres northeast of the county seat, Alba Iulia, in a wine-growing region. It is also known by its Hungarian name Balázsfalva and its German name Blasendorf, and the city administers eight villages. Its population was 17,816 at the 2021 census, and most inhabitants are Romanians, with Hungarian and Romani minorities.

Blaj is first mentioned in 1271 as Villa Herbordi, after the deed of a Count Herbod. In 1313 the domain passed to Herbod's son Blasius Cserei and the town was mentioned as Blasii. It began as a hamlet for the twenty families of servants at the noble's court and was awarded town status on 19 May 1737. Mănărade, one of its villages, belonged in the Middle Ages to the Cistercian Igriș Abbey, and in 1910 nearly 60 per cent of its villagers were Transylvanian Saxons.

The first public school in Romanian was established in Blaj in 1754, and Blaj was the first place to have Romanian written in the Latin alphabet instead of the traditional Cyrillic. It was also a centre of the Romanian Age of Enlightenment and the founding site of the Transylvanian School, which promoted the Roman cultural heritage of the Romanians. For this reason Romania's national poet Mihai Eminescu called it the Little Rome. In 1848 more than 40,000 Romanians met on the Câmpia Libertății, the Field of Liberty, to protest against Transylvania becoming part of Hungary, holding that their lands would be stolen from them.

Blaj was the principal religious and cultural centre of the Romanian Greek-Catholic Church in Transylvania. Its sights include the Metropolitan Palace, the Holy Trinity Cathedral, the Buna Vestire Monastery, the Greeks' Church, the Liberty Field and Avram Iancu's oak. The castle of the Bethlen dynasty is a popular site near the city.

Its schools include the Inochentie Micu Clain National College and the Sfântul Vasile cel Mare Greek-Catholic Theological High School. The Greek-Catholic bishops Samuil Vulcan and Ioan Suciu were born there, as was the priest and politician Ioan Simu.
blanche-i-of-navarre: Blanche was born on 6 July 1387, the second eldest daughter of King Charles III of Navarre and the infanta Eleanor of Castile. She became heiress to the throne of Navarre in 1413, when her elder sister Joan died. Before that she had married Martin the Younger, King of Sicily and Prince of Aragon, by proxy on 21 May 1402 in Catania, and in person on 26 December 1402. The bride was about 15 years old and the groom 28.

Martin needed legitimate heirs, having survived his previous wife, Queen Maria of Sicily, and their only son. Blanche and Martin had one child, Infante Martin of Aragon and Sicily, who lived from 1406 to 1407.

Blanche served as regent of Sicily from October 1404 to August 1405, while her husband was in Aragon, and again from August 1408 to July 1409, while he was in Sardinia. Martin died on 25 July 1409 and was succeeded by his father, Martin I of Aragon, who let her continue as regent, as she did after his death during the succession struggle in Aragon. She was a popular regent, seen as a symbol of Sicilian independence against Aragon, and there were plans to marry her to Nicolás Peralta, a descendant of the Sicilian royal house.

After Ferdinand I won in Aragon, Blanche lost her power, Sicily was annexed to Aragon in November 1415, and she went to Navarre. There she was sworn in as heir at Olite on 28 October 1415. In 1419 she married John, duke of Peñafiel, second son of Ferdinand I of Aragon, by proxy, and they married in person at Pamplona on 10 July 1420.

Charles III died on 8 September 1425 and Blanche succeeded him as queen regnant of Navarre, with John becoming king in her right as John II. They were crowned together at Pamplona on 15 May 1429. In 1433 she made a pilgrimage to Santa María del Pilar, where she founded a brotherhood inspired by chivalric traditions, whose members wore blue sashes with a gold pillar and the motto A ti me arrimo, and pledged regular fasting, prayer and almsgiving.

Blanche died in 1441 at Santa María la Real de Nieva. Her husband kept the government of Navarre in his own hands rather than yielding it to their son Charles of Viana, the rightful heir. They also had a daughter, Blanche, who married Henry IV of Castile; the marriage was never consummated, and after 13 years he sought and obtained a divorce.
blankenburg-harz: Blankenburg (Harz) is a town and health resort in the district of Harz in Saxony-Anhalt, at the northern foot of the Harz Mountains at a height of about 234 metres. It lies west of Quedlinburg, south of Halberstadt and east of Wernigerode. Above the town, on the hill of Blankenstein, stands Blankenburg Castle, and the Teufelsmauer, or Devil's Wall, a sandstone rock formation, offers views across the plain. The town was largely rebuilt after a fire in 1836.

The first traces of settlement date to the Old Stone Age, and the first recorded mention of Blankenburg goes back to 1123, when Lothair of Supplinburg, Duke of Saxony, installed Poppo, a nephew of Bishop Reinhard of Halberstadt, as count at the castle. In 1180–82 Frederick Barbarossa had Blankenburg devastated because it had pledged sole allegiance to Henry the Lion. After the last count of Regenstein died, the county went in 1599 back to the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.

In the 17th century the dukes made it a secondary residence, and it flourished under Duke Louis Rudolf, who was given Blankenburg in 1707 as a paragium. The county was raised to an imperial principality that was ruled independently until 1731, when Louis Rudolf became a duke and it was reunited with Brunswick. The present Little Castle with its terraced and Baroque gardens dates from that time. From 1815 to 1918 the town belonged to the Duchy of Brunswick.

In September 1933 the Brunswick SS commander Jeckeln herded together 140 communists and social democrats in the town, and they were severely beaten, some dying as a result. During the Second World War a subcamp of Buchenwald, later subordinated to Mittelbau-Dora, held some 500 prisoners at forced labour in the factories of Blankenburg-Oesig, and a further subcamp was occupied in February 1945 by inmates of an Auschwitz subcamp. Memorials in the town commemorate them. In 1945 the district was moved from the British to the Soviet zone and later became part of East Germany.

The town's economy rests on tourism and spa and health facilities, and the Little Castle holds the town museum. The physicist Polykarp Kusch, a co-recipient of the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1955, the archaeologist Robert Koldewey and the philosopher Oswald Spengler were born there.
blantyre: Blantyre lies in the Shire Highlands, at the geographical centre of Malawi's Southern Region, and covers an area of 228 km2. The city stands in hilly country at elevations from about 780 to 1,612 metres. Mount Soche, Ndirande mountain, Chiradzulu mountain and Michiru Mountain surround it, and rivers and streams rise in these hills and radiate from the city. The rainy season runs from November to April, and the dry season from May to October.

The mission was founded in 1876 by the Church of Scotland. The site was chosen by the British missionary Henry Henderson, who was joined there on 23 October 1876 by Dr T. T. Macklin and others. Macklin took over the leadership and began building. The first ordained minister, Rev. Duff MacDonald, arrived in 1878. The first missionaries faced local opposition, and three of them were recalled. From 1881 to 1898 the mission was run by David Clement Scott, who built the Church of St Michael and All Angels between 1888 and 1891 with a team of local workmen who had no knowledge of European building techniques. Scott also compiled an Encyclopaedic Dictionary of the Mang'anja Language, later edited by his successor Alexander Hetherwick.

A trading company grew up beside the mission. The Livingstonia Central Africa Trading Company, founded in Glasgow in 1877 and renamed the African Lakes Corporation in 1878, moved in 1881 to Mandala, across the River Mudi. Its Mandala House survives as a National Monument and is the oldest building in Malawi. Blantyre became a British consular station in 1883 and a municipality by 1895, Malawi's oldest. Its commerce began with the colonial trade in ivory, and by the First World War its people included Africans from neighbouring districts and South Asian traders.

Until 1905 the town's growth was confined to three areas within 2 km of each other: the mission, Mandala, and the government and commercial triangle. Limbe began to develop in 1906, after the Shire Highlands Railways Company set up its headquarters and workshops there and the Imperial Tobacco Group built a packaging and grading factory nearby. Indian wholesale and retail shops multiplied, and by 1910 Limbe had surpassed Blantyre. The two towns were merged into one city in 1956.

Blantyre is Malawi's centre of finance and commerce and its second largest city, with 800,264 people at the 2018 census. It is the capital of the Southern Region and of Blantyre District. The Malawi Stock Exchange, opened in November 1996, stands on Victoria Avenue. The city holds eight National Monuments, mostly historic buildings, and the Michiru Mountain Conservation Area lies among its hills.
blas-de-lezo: Blas de Lezo y Olavarrieta was born on 3 February 1689 in Pasajes de San Pedro, then a district of San Sebastián, the third of eight children of Pedro de Lezo y Urrecho and Agustina de Olavarrieta y Arnao, both of the minor nobility with a maritime tradition. He went to school in France and began his naval career in 1701 as a midshipman in the Franco-Spanish fleets of the War of the Spanish Succession. In 1704, at the Battle of Vélez-Málaga, a cannon shot struck his left leg, which was amputated below the knee.

He lost his left eye in the defence of Toulon in 1707, became a captain in 1713 and lost the use of his right arm at the Siege of Barcelona in 1714. Modern writers call him Patapalo, Pegleg, and Mediohombre, Half-man, but there is no contemporary proof that these names were used in his lifetime. He served in the Pacific from 1720 to 1728 and married in Peru in 1725. In 1732 he and José Carrillo de Albornoz led the expedition of more than 300 ships and around 28,000 troops that recaptured Oran and Mers-el-Kébir, and he then blockaded the Algerian coast.

Promoted Lieutenant General of the Navy in 1734, he took command of the Spanish fleet at Cartagena de Indias in 1737. The British attack lasted from 13 March to 20 May 1741, with 196 ships, 10,000 soldiers, 12,600 sailors, 1,000 Jamaican slaves employed as pioneers and 4,000 recruits from Virginia, against between 3,000 and 6,000 defenders and six Spanish ships of the line. An assault on the fortress of San Felipe on the night of 19 April failed, and the British withdrew to Jamaica with heavy losses from combat and disease.

A contemporary source gives epidemic typhus as the cause of his death on 7 September 1741, and his grave is unknown. The defeat contributed to the fall of Robert Walpole's government. A square and an avenue in Cartagena bear his name, a modern statue stands before the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, and a 35,000-kilo statue was erected in Madrid's Plaza Colón in 2014. Several Spanish warships have carried his name, most recently the frigate Blas de Lezo, commissioned in 2004.
blasco-nunez-vela: Núñez Vela was a native of Ávila, from an ancient noble family, the lords of Tabadillo, recorded there from at least 1403. He was a knight of the Order of Santiago and corregidor of Málaga and Cuenca; one brother was lord of the bedchamber to the king and another archbishop of Burgos. He was described as honest, loyal and courageous, but also very hot-headed.

In 1543 he was named viceroy, governor and captain general of Peru, president of the Audiencia and captain general of Chile, with a salary of 5,000 ducats. He sailed from Sanlúcar on 3 November 1543 with orders from the king to show himself a severe punisher of infractions. The New Laws, issued under the influence of reformers such as Bartolomé de las Casas, were meant to enforce the safeguards of the Laws of Burgos of 1512; the conquistadors resented them for ending what was effectively Indian slavery and sending encomienda rights to the king.

News of his measures on the voyage preceded him, and he was met in Lima on 17 May 1544 with hostility from officials and clergy. He joined the landowners in petitioning the emperor to suspend the laws but would not suspend them himself. He imprisoned his predecessor, Cristóbal Vaca de Castro, and sent him to Spain, and on 13 September 1544, in a heated late-night interview, killed Juan Suárez de Carbajal with a dagger after accusing him of treason.

The Audiencia broke with him and deposed him on 18 September 1544, counting on the support of Gonzalo Pizarro. The oidor Álvarez, who was to take him to Panama, set him free at sea, and he landed at Tumbes and raised an army, while Pizarro entered Lima with 1,200 soldiers and was sworn in as interim governor. Both sides claimed to defend the king. Retreating north, Núñez executed three officers he suspected of treachery. At Añaquito he was killed and beheaded, and his head was paraded on a pike. Fearing the loss of the colonies, the Crown watered down the New Laws and restored the encomiendas, while Charles V honoured the viceroy's memory and made two of his sons knights.
bleda: Bleda was a Hunnic ruler and the elder brother of Attila. As nephews of Rugila, Bleda and Attila succeeded him to the throne, and Bleda reigned until his death. Little is known about him. One of the few details concerns the dwarf Zerco, a Moor, whom Bleda acquired after the great Hun campaign of 441. Bleda was greatly amused by Zerco and had a suit of armour made for him so that the dwarf could accompany him on campaign.

The name is recorded in Greek sources as Bledas and Blidas, and in Latin as Bleda. Otto Maenchen-Helfen considered it Germanic or Germanized, a short form of names such as Bladardus. Denis Sinor argued that a name starting with a consonant cluster cannot be Altaic, while Omeljan Pritsak derived it from an Old Turkic word, bilgä, meaning wise or sovereign.

It is not known exactly how Bleda died. Jordanes speculated that Attila murdered him on a hunting trip. Medieval Hungarian chronicles tell of his death differently. In the Chronicon Pictum of Mark of Kalt, Attila went to Sicambria in Pannonia and killed his brother Buda, throwing the corpse into the Danube, because Buda had named the city Buda's Castle after himself. Attila forbade the name and called it Attila's Capital, the Germans called it Eccylburg, and the Hungarians ignored the ban and called it Óbuda.

Hungarian literature knows Bleda as Buda. According to medieval sources, the name of Buda, the historic capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, comes from him, and so does that of Budapest. He has been portrayed by Ettore Manni in a 1954 film with Anthony Quinn, by Leo Gordon in Sign of the Pagan of the same year, and by Tommy Flanagan in a 2001 mini-series.
bleddyn-ap-cynfyn: Bleddyn's father, Cynfyn ap Gwerystan, was a poorly documented nobleman of Powys known only from late pedigrees. After the death in 1023 of King Llywelyn ap Seisyll, whom he probably supported, Cynfyn married the widowed queen Angharad, daughter of King Maredudd ab Owain. Their sons Bleddyn and Rhiwallon, probably born in the late 1020s, were thus half-brothers of Gruffydd ap Llywelyn, who rebuilt his father's realm. Bleddyn may have lived in Powys, where he married Haer ferch Cillyn.

Gruffydd's alliance with Earl Ælfgar of Mercia made him a threat to Harold Godwinson. After Ælfgar's death in 1062 Harold and his brother Tostig invaded, and in 1063 Gruffydd was killed by traitors among his own men. The south was restored to the Houses of Dinefwr and Morgan, while Powys and Gwynedd went to Bleddyn and Rhiwallon, who swore themselves vassals of Edward the Confessor.

At the time of the Norman Conquest Bleddyn was the most powerful king in Wales. In 1067 the brothers joined Eadric the Wild against William the Conqueror, attacking the Normans at Hereford, and in 1068 they joined Earls Edwin of Mercia and Morcar of Northumbria. In 1070 Gruffydd's sons Idwal and Maredudd challenged them; Rhiwallon, Idwal and Maredudd all died at the Battle of Mechain, leaving Bleddyn sole king. In 1073 Robert of Rhuddlan narrowly failed to ambush and capture him.

Betrayed by the lords of Ystrad Tywi, Bleddyn was killed in 1075 by King Rhys ab Owain of Deheubarth. When Rhys was defeated at the Battle of Goodwick in 1078 by Trahaearn ap Caradog and killed soon after, it was hailed as vengeance for Bleddyn's blood. Gwynedd passed to Trahaearn and later to Gruffudd ap Cynan, but in Powys Bleddyn founded the House of Mathrafal, which ruled until the end of the 13th century. The Chronicle of the Princes remembered him as the most merciful of kings, terrible in war but beloved in peace, and his revision of Welsh law, which varied the size of a homestead by the owner's status, stayed in force in Powys.
bleiburg-repatriations: The Independent State of Croatia was a fascist puppet state established in German-occupied Yugoslavia, and it carried out genocidal campaigns against its minority populations. By the end of 1944 the Partisans, with the help of the Red Army, had established control in Serbia, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Dalmatia, and the collapse of the Syrmian front in April 1945 hastened the German withdrawal from the Balkans.

On 3 May 1945 the government of the Independent State of Croatia decided to flee to Austria, and the Croatian Armed Forces were ordered to move there to surrender to British forces. The Slovene National Council issued similar orders the same day. The soldiers were accompanied by civilians.

The Slovene-led columns fought their way to the Austrian border near Klagenfurt on 14 May. The British accepted their surrender and interned them in the nearby Viktring camp. On 15 May the head of the main Croatian column, some 25,000 to 30,000 people, reached the field at Bleiburg. Negotiations were held in Bleiburg Castle, the British negotiator being Brigadier Thomas Scott. The British refused to accept the surrender and directed the Croatian forces to surrender to the Partisans, which their leadership did.

Other prisoners in British captivity were repatriated in the following weeks, from camps such as Viktring and Krumpendorf, from 18 May. The British cancelled the repatriations on 31 May after reports of massacres. The Yugoslav authorities moved the prisoners on forced marches to internment and labour camps, and those who lagged behind were shot. The largest mass executions took place at Tezno, estimated at 15,000 Croatian prisoners of war, and at Kočevski Rog, Huda Jama and Macelj.

Under communist rule in Yugoslavia the killings were a taboo subject, and information about them was suppressed. Mass graves were concealed or destroyed in accordance with an order of 18 May 1945. Investigation of the graves began only in the 1990s, when 1,163 bodies were excavated from 23 mass graves at Macelj in 1992.

Historians have been unable to establish the number of victims. Estimates given in the literature range from 50,000 to 200-250,000, while others cite 20,000 to 40,000, noting that pro-Ustaše writers inflate the figures. Most victims were members of Croatian, Slovene, Montenegrin and Serb collaborationist forces, and civilians were also among the dead. Since the breakup of Yugoslavia an annual commemoration has been held at Bleiburg, and it has drawn controversy because of Ustaše symbols displayed there.
blekinge: Blekinge is one of the traditional Swedish provinces, on the coast of the Baltic Sea in Götaland, bordering Småland and Scania. It is the second-smallest province by area, after Öland, and the smallest on the mainland. Its name comes from a dialect adjective, bleke, which corresponds to the nautical term for dead calm. The relief is an uneven valley terrain with a scenic archipelago, the bedrock is mostly granite and gneiss, and oak forests characterise its nature. It has warm summers and mild winters by Swedish standards and is sometimes called Sweden's garden.

Evidence of human habitation in western Blekinge dates to about 9700 BCE in the Vesan area, then a small island surrounded by open grassland.
