A settlement at nearby Ljungaviken, dated to 6500 BCE, contains the remains of at least 50 wooden houses and a buried dog. A survey in 2021 of a pile barrier in the bay of Lyckeby showed that its wood was felled in 1113-14.

Blekinge belonged to Sweden until the early 13th century, when it became part of Denmark; the Danish Census Book is the first secure written evidence of Danish control. With Skåne and Halland it formed Skåneland, the eastern part of the Danish kingdom, where Scanian Law prevailed. As a border province it was often raided and looted by Swedish troops during the Danish-Swedish wars. Sölvesborg was the seat of administration in the west and Kristianopel in the east, and Ronneby (1387), Sölvesborg (1445), Elleholm and Kristianopel had city privileges.

In 1658 Blekinge was ceded to Sweden by the Treaty of Roskilde and has remained Swedish since. Two new towns were built, Karlshamn, chartered in 1664, and Karlskrona, in 1680, to which the populations of Ronneby and Kristianopel were forcibly relocated. Karlskrona has been the principal naval base of Sweden for more than 300 years. The province was granted its arms in 1660, based on a 15th-century seal, with the three crowns of Sweden placed on an oak trunk to mark the change in its status.
bletchley-park: Bletchley Park lies in Bletchley, Milton Keynes. The estate took its name after the architect Samuel Lipscomb Seckham bought it in 1877 and built a house there. In 1938 a builder bought the mansion for a housing estate, but in May of that year Admiral Sir Hugh Sinclair, head of the Secret Intelligence Service, bought it with 58 acres for use in a war, using £6,000 of his own money because the government said it had no budget. The site was close to Bletchley railway station, where the line between Oxford and Cambridge met the main west coast line, and to good telephone and telegraph links.

The first staff of the Government Code and Cypher School moved to the Park on 15 August 1939. Five weeks before the war began, Warsaw's Cipher Bureau had revealed its success against Enigma to British and French personnel, and the British used the Poles' techniques. Wooden huts were built from late 1939, and a neighbouring school was taken over.

The recruits included linguists, chess players and papyrologists, and in 1941 The Daily Telegraph was asked to run a crossword competition so that promising solvers could be approached discreetly. The staff were about 75 per cent women. All signed the Official Secrets Act, and the intelligence was kept as the Ultra secret.

The bombe, designed by Alan Turing with an important contribution from Gordon Welchman and built by Harold Keen of the British Tabulating Machine Company, found daily Enigma settings. Hut 3 turned decrypts into intelligence reports, and the more complex Lorenz cipher, called Tunny, was attacked with machinery that led to Colossus. At its peak about 4,000 messages a day were being read.

In October 1941 Turing, Welchman, Hugh Alexander and Stuart Milner-Barry wrote to Winston Churchill about staff shortages, and he ordered action that day. After the United States joined the war American cryptographers were posted to Hut 3, and the BRUSA Agreement of 1943 foreshadowed the Five Eyes partnership.

The Government Code and Cypher School became GCHQ, which moved to Eastcote in 1946 and Cheltenham in 1951. Because of the thirty year rule there was no official mention of the work until the mid-1970s, and F. W. Winterbotham's The Ultra Secret appeared in 1974. The Bletchley Park Trust was set up in 1991, and the site opened to visitors in 1993. It houses the Bletchley Park museum and, in Block H, the independent National Museum of Computing, which has a working reconstruction of a bombe and a rebuilt Colossus.
blida: Blida lies 190 metres above sea level at the base of the Tell Atlas, on the southern edge of the fertile Mitidja Plain and the right bank of the Oued el Kebir, which flows out of the Chiffa gorge. The stream's abundant water powered large corn mills and several factories and fed the town's fountains and irrigated gardens. Orchards and gardens surround the town, which is known as the city of roses. Its name is a diminutive of the Arabic belda, city. Chréa National Park, one of the largest in the country, lies within Blida, and the nearby Chiffa gorge is one of the few habitats of the endangered Barbary macaque.

No ancient centre preceded the city. It was identified with a medieval town of Mitidja, which was ruined during the campaigns of the Beni Ghania. The present town was founded by Moors, principally Sidi Ahmed El-Kebir, in the 16th century. A mosque was built by order of Khair-ed-din Barbarossa, and under the Turks the town was of some importance. Its gates no longer exist, but their names, such as Bab Er-Rahba and Bab Es-Sebt, are still used as reference points for streets and businesses.

After an earthquake in March 1825 the town was rebuilt on a grid plan, on a site about a mile from the ruins. In 1839 French troops occupied the city and built a military base, an airbase, a communications centre and a military hospital. Life was racially segregated: Muslims were confined to a crowded ghetto, and boarding schools kept separate dormitories. The occupation lasted until Algeria won independence in the Algerian War. Another earthquake damaged the town in 1867.

Blida is the capital of Blida Province, about 45 km south-west of Algiers. The Berbers of the province, the Djebailia, speak Taqbaylit, a Berber language close to the Kabyle varieties spoken east of Algiers. The Stade Mustapha Tchaker, opened in 2002, is the home ground of the Algeria national football team.
bloemfontein: Bloemfontein lies in central South Africa, on the southern edge of the Highveld at an elevation of about 1,400 metres, bordering the semi-arid region of the Karoo. The area is generally flat, with occasional hills, called koppies in Afrikaans, and the vegetation is Highveld grassland. Summers are hot and rainfall comes mainly as short afternoon thunderstorms, while winters are cool and dry with frosty nights. The city is also known as Mangaung in Sesotho, meaning place of cheetahs, and as the city of roses, for its abundance of the flowers and an annual rose festival.

Bloemfontein was historically a settlement of the Orana and the Barolong, and then of Boers. It was officially founded in 1846 as a fort by the British Army major Henry Douglas Warden, as a British outpost in the Transoranje region. That region was occupied by various groups, among them the Orana, Cape Colony Trekboers, the Griqua and the Barolong. The Orange River Sovereignty was proclaimed in 1848 with a British Resident at Bloemfontein, and the Orange Free State, an independent Boer republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers, existed from 1854 to 1902.

On 31 May 1910, exactly eight years after the Boers signed the Peace Treaty of Vereeniging that ended the Anglo-Boer War, South Africa became a Union. Disagreement over where the capital should be ended in a compromise that allowed Bloemfontein to host the Appellate Division and become the Union's judicial capital, and it was also given financial compensation.

Residential segregation in the town began in the 19th century. Ordinance 1 of 1860 decreed that no non-white person, without written permission from the landlord, which was the British government, had the right to occupy urban land in towns that had no municipality. On 3 June 1861 the council marked out separate locations for the black population and for Coloured people, whose inhabitants had to pay a hut tax and a grazing rights tax. This laid the foundation for the residential segregation later planned by the architects of apartheid, which the National Party began to implement after winning the 1948 election.

Bloemfontein is the capital and largest city of the Free State province, with 256,185 residents at the 2011 census within the Mangaung municipality of 747,431. It remains the seat of the Supreme Court of Appeal, formerly the Appellate Division, and the Constitutional Court has been in Johannesburg since 1994. The city has the Anglo-Boer War Museum, the National Women's Monument, the National Museum and the Oliewenhuis Art Museum, as well as Boyden Observatory.
blohm-voss: Blohm & Voss was founded on 5 April 1877 by Hermann Blohm and Ernst Voss as a general partnership to build steel-hulled ships. Its shipyard stood on the island of Kuhwerder, near Hamburg, and covered 15,000 square metres with three building berths. Shipbuilding was then dominated by the British, and even German customers preferred to buy from them.

The firm began with repairs, built and sold the three-masted barque National, and then won its first new-build order, for the small paddle-steamer Burg. By 1882 it had a reputation for quality and punctuality. It built steel-hulled sailing ships for long voyages, because steamships had a short range, and its first steamship came in 1900, although it kept building sailing ships until the late 1930s. The name was written with an ampersand until 1955.

After Hermann Blohm's death his sons Rudolf and Walther took over, and Voss left soon afterwards. The company was in financial crisis in 1933, and the brothers founded the aircraft maker Hamburger Flugzeugbau that summer, which was renamed a department of the shipyard in September 1937. With Germany's rearmament under the Nazi government the yard built civilian ships and warships, including the battleship Bismarck, and then U-boats in quantity. Most of the aircraft it built were other firms' designs, tens of thousands of them, but it also developed its own flying boats, among them the BV 138 and the very large BV 222 and BV 238.

From July 1944 to April 1945 a subcamp of Neuengamme concentration camp supplied forced labour to the yard, and a report of August 1944 mentions about 500 foreign female prisoners. A memorial stands on the camp's site, and the company continues to pay into the Fund for Compensation of Forced Laborers. The yard was badly damaged in the bombing of Hamburg, and shipbuilding was forbidden at the end of the war.

The British continued to demolish the shipyards at Steinwerder. Ship repair restarted in 1952, and the first new ship, Wappen von Hamburg, was built in 1955. The company became a publicly quoted company half owned by Phoenix-Rheinrohr, soon part of the Thyssen Group, and it built oil rigs and offshore equipment. It became a subsidiary of ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems in 1999.

Blohm+Voss built the first of the German Navy's K130 frigates, Braunschweig, launched in April 2006. The civil division was sold to STAR Capital Partners in 2011, and in 2016 regulators approved the purchase by Lürssen. The military shipbuilding arm, NVL, was sold to Rheinmetall in September 2025. The yard has built ships and large machinery almost continuously for 149 years, and its yachts have included Eclipse, 162 metres long.
blood-transfusion: Recorded research into blood transfusion began in the 17th century, after William Harvey's experiments on the circulation of the blood, with successful experiments in transfusion between animals. Working at the Royal Society in the 1660s, the physician Richard Lower devised methods of cross-circulation in animals, using closed arteriovenous connections to prevent clotting. In his own account, towards the end of February 1665 he drew blood from a medium-sized dog until its strength was nearly gone, then introduced blood from a larger mastiff fastened alongside it. The animal recovered with no sign of discomfort. Attempts to transfuse animal blood into humans gave variable and often fatal results.

Blood transfusion is the intravenous transfer of blood products into a human or other animal. Except in major trauma, whole blood is rarely used in modern practice, and instead components such as red blood cells, plasma and platelets are transfused. Donated blood is separated by centrifugation into red cells, plasma and platelets, and plasma can be processed further into albumin, clotting factor concentrates and immunoglobulins. Red cells are typically stored at 1 to 6 °C, platelets at 20 to 24 °C with continuous agitation, and plasma frozen at −18 °C or lower.

Only in 1901, when the Austrian Karl Landsteiner discovered three human blood groups, O, A and B, did transfusion gain a scientific basis and become safer. He found that mixing incompatible blood provokes an immune response in which the red cells clump. He won the Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine in 1930. George Washington Crile is credited with the first surgery using a direct transfusion, in 1906 at St. Alexis Hospital in Cleveland.

Before a transfusion the recipient's blood is typed for its ABO and Rh status and screened for antibodies. Most acute haemolytic reactions come from clerical errors or mistaken typing. Blood type O negative is compatible with anyone and is kept for emergencies.
blowin-in-the-wind: Shortly after the first performance Dylan added the middle verse. Some published versions reverse the second and third verses, apparently because he appended the middle verse to his original manuscript. The song was published in May 1962 in Broadside, a magazine of topical songs, and in June 1962 in Sing Out!, with Dylan's comment that the answer was in the wind, not in any book or discussion group. He recorded it on 9 July 1962 for The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, released in May 1963.

Pete Seeger identified the melody as an adaptation of the spiritual No More Auction Block, and in 1978 Dylan told an interviewer that the song had always been a spiritual and that he took it from that one. The critic Michael Gray found in the lyric an echo of the Book of Ezekiel, in the lines about eyes that see not and ears that hear not.

The song has been described as a protest song. It poses a series of rhetorical questions about peace, war and freedom, and its refrain, that the answer is blowing in the wind, has been called impenetrably ambiguous: the answer is either so obvious it is in plain view or as intangible as the wind. The critic Andy Gill saw in it a leap in Dylan's songwriting, from the particular, as in his earlier topical songs, to the general, so that it could be applied to almost any freedom issue.

The Chad Mitchell Trio were first to cover it, but their record company delayed the album because the song contained the word death. Peter, Paul and Mary, managed like Dylan by Albert Grossman, released it in June 1963; it sold 300,000 copies in its first week, reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and won two Grammy awards. Stevie Wonder's version of 1966 was a top ten hit.

The song has been called an anthem of the civil rights movement. Mavis Staples said she could not understand how a young white man had captured the frustration and aspirations of black people so powerfully, and Sam Cooke was inspired by it to write A Change Is Gonna Come. Many churches adopted it, and in 1997 Pope John Paul II told young Catholics that the answer was in the wind of the spirit. A report in Newsweek in November 1963 that a student, Lorre Wyatt, had written it was later shown to be false.
blue-division: Francisco Franco took power in the Spanish Civil War, which killed more than 300,000 people, with help from Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. Spain stayed formally neutral in World War II but did not hide its sympathy for the Axis. Franco met Adolf Hitler at Hendaye on 23-24 October 1940, but could not win promises of colonial territory in North Africa.

After the German invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, Foreign Minister Ramón Serrano Suñer proposed a Spanish contribution to what Spanish officials called an anti-communist crusade, and Franco agreed. Germany accepted on 24 June. Recruitment began on 27 June and 18,373 men had volunteered by 2 July. Half the officers and sergeants were professional soldiers, and General Agustín Muñoz Grandes took command.

The volunteers trained at Grafenwöhr in Bavaria and, after taking the Hitler Oath on 31 July 1941, were incorporated in the Wehrmacht as the 250th Division. Marching towards Smolensk, they were rerouted in September to Army Group North and first held a 50-kilometre section of the Volkhov River front near Novgorod. In August 1942 they moved to the southeastern flank of the siege of Leningrad, near Pushkin, Kolpino and Krasny Bor.

In February 1943, at the Battle of Krasny Bor, the division held its ground at heavy cost against a Soviet force seven times larger. Allied pressure then grew on Franco. He ordered withdrawal on 10 October 1943, and on 3 November the government ordered all troops home. Close to 3,000 refused and formed the Blue Legion, which was ordered home in March 1944; the rest joined German units.

As many as 45,000 Spaniards served on the Eastern Front by rotation. The Blue Division and its successors lost 4,954 men killed and 8,700 wounded, and 372 were taken prisoner by the Red Army. Spain and the Soviet Union had no diplomatic relations, so 286 prisoners stayed in captivity until 2 April 1954, when the ship Semiramis brought them to Spain.

Hitler had a medal struck for the division in January 1944, the only German Army component to receive one of its own. A war cemetery in Veliky Novgorod holds 1,900 of its soldiers. A Russian interpreter, Vladimir Kovalevskii, left an account of low discipline and crimes by the volunteers, and Novgorod's churches were damaged and their iconostases burned or taken to Germany.
blue-jacket: Little is known of Blue Jacket's early life. He first appears in written records in 1773, already a grown man and a war chief, when a British missionary visiting the Shawnee villages on the Scioto River noted the site of Blue Jacket's Town on Deer Creek, in present-day Ross County, Ohio. He took part in Lord Dunmore's War and fought on the British side in the American Revolutionary War, always seeking to keep Shawnee land rights. The British defeat cost the Shawnee valuable help in defending the Ohio Country.

As white settlement in Ohio grew, Blue Jacket became a leading figure of the resistance in the Northwest Indian War, in which a confederacy of many nations fought the young United States. He was present during the Harmar campaign of 1790. On 3 November 1791 the confederate army under Blue Jacket and the Miami chief Little Turtle defeated the expedition of Arthur St. Clair, governor of the Northwest Territory, at the Battle of the Wabash, the most severe defeat Native Americans ever inflicted on the United States. Traditional accounts give Little Turtle most of the credit; the historian John Sugden attributes this mainly to Little Turtle's own later self-promotion.

The United States then raised a new professional army under General Anthony Wayne, which defeated Blue Jacket's forces at the Battle of Fallen Timbers, south of present-day Toledo, on 20 August 1794. His son-in-law, Jacques Lasselle Jr., served as interpreter at Greenville in 1795. In 1805 Blue Jacket also signed the Treaty of Fort Industry, giving up still more of Ohio, and in his last years he saw the rise of Tecumseh.

In 1877 a story was published claiming that Blue Jacket had been a white man, Marmaduke Van Swearingen, captured and adopted by the Shawnee in the 1770s. Allan W. Eckert's novels spread it, and an outdoor drama based on it ran in Xenia, Ohio, from 1981 to 2007. Historians since Helen Hornbeck Tanner in 1978 have rejected it, as Blue Jacket was older and already a chief, and a DNA study published in 2006 found that the two families did not match.
blue-mosque-of-tabriz: The Blue Mosque, also known as the Masjed-e Mozaffariya, was part of the Mozaffariya complex, established through the endowment of Khatun Jan Begom (died 1469), wife of Jahanshah, ruler of the Qara Qoyunlu (1439–1467). The complex also had a Sufi convent, an underground canal, gardens, a madrasa, bathhouses and a mausoleum, of which only the mosque and part of the mausoleum remain. The mosque was completed in October 1465.

Three years later Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu overthrew Jahanshah and took Tabriz while construction was still going on. After the deaths of Jahanshah and Khatun Jan Begom their daughter Saleha Khatun oversaw the work, and under Uzun Hasan the mausoleum's cupola and main structure were finished between 1478 and 1490.

The mosque is the last remaining example of Turkmen architecture and decoration in Tabriz, and is one of the few completely covered mosques of Iran, built in the Timurid style. Its tilework combines geometric and floral patterns, calligraphy and mosaic panels, using seven colours. The wall facing the qibla is clad in dark-blue hexagonal tiles with stencilled gilding. The Kufic and Thuluth inscriptions were made by the calligrapher Nematollah-ben-Mohammad-ol-Bavab, and artisans from Herat are said to have worked with local Tabrizi craftsmen.

Its plan has a large prayer dome with a smaller domed chamber for burial. Scholars generally agree that, despite resemblances to Ottoman mosques of the Bursa type, its vaulting and structure belong to the Iranian tradition. The building stands on a raised stone platform, which protected it from floods of the nearby Mehranrud River.

When the Safavids made Tabriz their capital the mosque served them during the first half of the 16th century. In 1514, after the Safavid defeat at the Battle of Chaldiran, the Ottomans occupied and looted Tabriz, including the mosque, and at least eight carpets were taken to Istanbul. Earthquakes damaged the building between the 16th and 18th centuries, and the earthquake of 1780 left only the entrance iwan standing. In the 19th century people of Tabriz looted the ruins.

In 1928 the French architect André Godard reported that little remained apart from a few columns and parts of the outer wall and façade. The mosque was added to the Iran National Heritage List in 1932. Reconstruction began in 1973 under Reza Memaran Benam, supervised by the Iranian Ministry of Culture, and surviving panels of tilework were preserved. New bricks were made to match the old, and the rebuilt parts were deliberately made slightly distinguishable from the original.
blue-nile: The Blue Nile rises at Gish Abay in Ethiopia, where it is called the Abay, and flows through Lake Tana and out into a canyon about 400 kilometres long. The canyon, cut in the Ethiopian Highlands to a depth of some 1,500 metres, is a tremendous obstacle to travel between northern and southern Ethiopia. The Blue Nile Falls, called Tis Abay, meaning great smoke, lie at its start. The river then runs about 650 kilometres through Sudan and joins the White Nile at Khartoum. It supplies 80 to 86 percent of the Nile's water in the rainy season, and its floods contributed to the fertility of the Nile Valley and so to the rise of ancient Egypt.

The Egyptian fear that Ethiopia might block the river shaped the long relationship between the two countries. Ethiopia depended on the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria for its metropolitan, and from the 11th century the threat to block the river helped secure the appointment of Egyptian metropolitans, though neither diversion nor large-scale use of the water was ever attempted. Emperor Amda Seyon I first occupied the basin and began spreading Christianity there. Later Solomonic emperors, among them Dawit II, Yeshaq I and Zara Yaqob, used their control of the river as a diplomatic tool and identified it with the biblical Gihon.

The Spanish Jesuit Pedro Páez reached the source on 21 April 1618, and the Scottish explorer James Bruce reached the source of the Nile in 1770. The canyon defeated outsiders' attempts to follow the river, from Frédéric Cailliaud in 1821 to W. W. Macmillan in 1902. In 1968 a team of 60 British and Ethiopian servicemen and scientists, led by John Blashford-Snell at the request of Haile Selassie, made the first full descent from Lake Tana to a point near the Sudanese border.

The Blue Nile is vital to Egypt, which receives over 85 percent of its Nile streamflow from it. Its floods in lower Egypt ended with the completion of the Aswan Dam in 1970. In Sudan the Roseires and Sennar dams supply hydroelectric power and irrigate the Gezira Scheme, noted for its cotton. The river's summer floods carry a great amount of silt, which turns its water dark brown or almost black.
blue-riband: The Blue Riband is an unofficial accolade given to the passenger liner in regular service crossing the Atlantic with the highest average speed. The term was borrowed from horse racing and was not widely used until after 1910. The record rests on average speed rather than passage time because ships follow different routes, and eastbound and westbound records are reckoned separately, since the westbound crossing, against the Gulf Stream and the prevailing weather, typically gives lower averages. Of the 35 liners that held it, 25 were British, five German, three American and one each Italian and French. No formal award existed until 1935, when Harold K. Hales donated the Hales Trophy, whose rules differed from the traditional ones.

Before steam, eastbound passages of 30 to 45 days were not uncommon, and westward passages of 65 to 90 days excited no attention. The contest is traced back to 1838, when the steamships Sirius and Great Western, the first to offer regular scheduled service, raced to New York. Sirius, chartered by the British and American Steam Navigation Company, left Cork four days before Great Western left Avonmouth and had to burn spars when coal ran low. Her westbound crossing at 8.03 knots made her often considered the first record holder, though Great Western arrived faster. Cunard officially refused to recognise the title because racing did not suit its safety policy.

Cunard began service in 1840 and survived thanks to an Admiralty mail subsidy. The Collins Line, subsidised by the American government, set a record in 1850 with the Pacific, but it collapsed in 1858 after losing two steamers. Cunard's Scotia in 1862 was the last paddle steamer to set a record. Later the record passed among White Star, Inman, Guion, German lines such as Norddeutscher Lloyd and Hamburg-America, and Cunard's Lusitania and Mauretania. Mauretania's record of 26.06 knots from 1909 stood for 20 years, until Bremen took it in 1929 at 27.83 knots. Many liners were built with government subsidies and with military use in mind; Winston Churchill estimated that the two Cunard Queens shortened the Second World War by a year.

The United States set the record in 1952 at 35.59 knots eastbound and 34.51 westbound, and no passenger liner has broken it. Jet airliners entered service in 1958, ending the era of the record-breakers. In 1986 Richard Branson's Virgin Atlantic Challenger beat the speed but was not a passenger vessel, and in 1990 the Incat catamaran Hoverspeed Great Britain took the Hales Trophy.
bluefields: Bluefields lies on the central Mosquito Coast. The city stands beside the bay of the same name and consists of 17 neighborhoods, together with the port of Bluefields Bluff, which lies on a peninsula about 8 km away. Because of gradual erosion the peninsula is becoming a true island that closes the Bay of Bluefields on the east side. The climate is a trade-wind tropical rainforest one, with a drier period from February to April and extremely heavy rain for the rest of the year.

From the early seventeenth century European privateers and pirates, particularly those associated with Dutch and English interests, frequented the Mosquitian Shore and used the Bluefields River and nearby bays as harbours and meeting points. The area was already inhabited by several Indigenous nations, including the Kukra, Ulwa, Rama and Miskito. An early description appears in the Minutes of a Committee for Providence Island of 14 June 1637, in which Albertus Blauvelt, mate of the Expectation, reported a good harbour at the river's mouth. The British navy traded here and used the port for naval operations during the Anglo-Spanish War of 1779–1783.

Bluefields rose to regional prominence in 1844, when it was designated the administrative centre of the Kingdom of Mosquitia, which kept its independence and later a protectorate status under Great Britain. The Moravian Church was established in 1848 and founded the first organised schools in the region; among its first pupils was George Augustus Frederic, the future Miskito king. Between the 1860s and 1880s British and American investment made the town a commercial hub for bananas, timber and maritime trade, with a population of Creoles, Miskito, European settlers and other Indigenous communities. Growth slowed after the Nicaraguan occupation of Mosquitia in 1894, when the city became the capital of the Zelaya Department.

Bluefields is the capital of the South Caribbean Coast Autonomous Region of Nicaragua. The port was mined by the United States in 1984 during the Contra War, and the city suffered extensive damage from Hurricane Joan in 1988 before it was rebuilt. It remains a centre of Afro-Caribbean and Indigenous identity and reflects the longstanding traditions of Mosquitia. It has two universities, a campus of URACCAN and the Bluefields Indian and Caribbean University.
bob-hawke: Robert James Lee Hawke was born on 9 December 1929 in Border Town, South Australia, the second child of Arthur Clem Hawke, a Congregationalist minister, and Edith Emily Hawke, a schoolteacher. He was educated at Perth Modern School and the University of Western Australia, graduating in 1952, and then won a Rhodes Scholarship to University College, Oxford, where he wrote a thesis on wage-fixing in Australia. In 1956 he joined the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) as a research officer. He became its advocate in the national wages case, won a fifteen-shilling increase in 1959, and in 1969 was elected ACTU president although he had never held elected office in a union.

Hawke became president of the Labor Party in 1973. In 1980 he stood down from both presidencies and was elected to the House of Representatives for Wills. Three years later he was elected unopposed to replace Bill Hayden as Labor leader and, within five weeks, led it to a landslide victory at the 1983 election. He was sworn in as prime minister on 11 March 1983 and won again in 1984, 1987 and 1990, which made him the most electorally successful prime minister in Labor's history.

With the ACTU Secretary, Bill Kelty, he negotiated the Prices and Incomes Accord of 1983, under which unions limited wage demands in return for a government guarantee to minimise inflation and raise the social wage. The government floated the Australian dollar, deregulated the financial system, cut tariffs and subsidies, privatised enterprises such as Qantas, and established Medicare. In 1989 Hawke proposed a regional forum that became Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, whose first meeting was held in Canberra in November 1989.

In June 1991 Hawke faced a leadership challenge from the Treasurer, Paul Keating, and kept power; Keating challenged again six months later, won narrowly and replaced him. Hawke retired from parliament and worked in business and for charitable causes. He died on 16 May 2019 aged 89 and remains his party's longest-serving prime minister.
bob-marley: Robert Nesta Marley was born on 6 February 1945 at the farm of his maternal grandfather in Nine Mile, in Saint Ann Parish, then the Colony of Jamaica. His father, Norval Sinclair Marley, was a white Englishman who supervised a subdivision of land for war veteran housing. His mother, Cedella Malcolm, was an Afro-Jamaican aged 18 when they married. Norval gave little financial support and died when Marley was 10. Marley began to play music with Neville Livingston, later known as Bunny Wailer, at school in Nine Mile.

In 1963 Marley, Bunny Wailer, Peter Tosh and others formed a group called the Teenagers, which became the Wailing Rudeboys, the Wailing Wailers and finally the Wailers. Their single Simmer Down for Coxsone Dodd's label became a Jamaican number one in February 1964, and they recorded regularly at Studio One. By 1966 the core of the group was the trio of Marley, Wailer and Tosh.

In 1972 Chris Blackwell of Island Records offered the Wailers an advance of £4,000 to record an album, seeing in Marley the rebel image needed to reach a rock audience. They recorded Catch a Fire at Harry J's studio in Kingston, and with Burnin', both 1973, it brought them international attention. Marley then carried on as Bob Marley and the Wailers, with the I Threes, Judy Mowatt, Marcia Griffiths and his wife Rita, as backing singers. A live version of No Woman, No Cry was his first hit outside Jamaica, in 1975.

Marley survived an assassination attempt at his home in Jamaica in 1976, believed to have been politically motivated. He left Jamaica at the end of that year and spent two years in England, where he recorded Exodus. His album Survival in 1979 reflected his support for African struggles, and in April 1980 he was invited to perform at Zimbabwe's independence celebration.

In July 1977 Marley was diagnosed with acral lentiginous melanoma, a skin cancer beneath the nail of his right big toe. He declined to have the toe amputated, citing religious beliefs, and continued to tour. A longtime follower of Rastafari, he was baptised into the Ethiopian Orthodox Church on 4 November 1980 and died on 11 May 1981. He received a state funeral in Jamaica.
bobbio-abbey: The abbey was founded soon after the Lombard invasion of Italy in 568. Under the influence of Columbanus and of his wife Theodelinda, a devout Roman Catholic, King Agilulf converted to Christianity, and he granted Columbanus a ruined church and wasted lands known as Ebovium, which had belonged to the papacy before the Lombards seized them. Columbanus wanted the secluded place because he preferred solitude for his monks. A monastery was built beside the little church of Saint Peter and at first followed the Rule of St Columbanus, based on the practices of Celtic Christianity.

Columbanus was buried on 23 November 615. His successors Attala and Bertulf steered the house through the threats of Arianism under King Rotharis, and in 628 Bertulf persuaded Pope Honorius I to make the abbey subject directly to the Holy See. Under Abbot Bobolen the Rule of St. Benedict was introduced; it gradually replaced the stricter Columban rule. Bobbio became a centre of resistance to Arianism and a base for the conversion of the Lombards.

In 774 Charlemagne made generous grants to the abbey, and late in the 9th century Abbot Agilulph moved the monastery farther downstream on the left bank of the Trebbia, where the medieval village grew up around it. In 1014 Emperor Henry II obtained from Pope Benedict VIII the creation of a bishopric of Bobbio, whose first bishop, Peter Aldus, had been abbot since 999. The French occupying forces suppressed the abbey in 1803.

A late 9th-century catalogue lists more than 600 volumes in the library, covering every branch of knowledge. Gerbert of Aurillac, later Pope Sylvester II, became abbot in 982 and used its ancient treatises for his work on geometry. The books were later dispersed: in 1616 Cardinal Federico Borromeo took eighty-six volumes for the Ambrosian Library of Milan, among them the Antiphonary of Bangor, twenty-six went to Pope Paul V in 1618, and others to Turin, where many burned in the fire of 26 January 1904.

The present Basilica of San Colombano was built in 1456–1530 in a Renaissance style; its crypt holds the sarcophagus of Columbanus by Giovanni dei Patriarchi (1480) and a 12th-century mosaic pavement. The abbey's museum keeps the Bobbio collection of Monza ampullae, pilgrimage flasks of the 6th century.
bobo-dioulasso: Bobo-Dioulasso lies in the south-west of Burkina Faso, in Houet Province, some 350 km from Ouagadougou. Its name means home of the Bobo-Dioula, and the local Bobo-speaking people, who are related to the Mande, call the city simply Sia. In the late 19th century Sia consisted of two large villages, Tunuma and Sia proper, bounded by ravines cut by the We river and its tributary the Sanyo.

According to local tradition Sia was founded in the 15th century. It became an important market, particularly for the export of horses southwards, and a link in trade routes joining Djenne and the Inner Niger Delta to Kong, Begho and the Gold Coast. Seku Watara founded the Kong Empire in 1710, and members of his family conquered Sia in the late 1730s; after his death the descendants of his brother Famagan ruled the region, known as Gwiriko, with near-autonomy from Kong.

The French occupied Sia on 25 September 1897 after a brief but bloody confrontation, having been asked for help by the local Watara leader Pintyeba, and set up a military post that became the seat of a district of the same name. In 1927 they razed Tunuma and moved its people, and between 1926 and 1929 they laid out a European grid of avenues that formed the framework of the modern centre. The Abidjan railway reached the city in 1934, and after the Second World War it grew again as a commercial and early industrial centre.

Bobo-Dioulasso is the second-largest city of Burkina Faso after Ouagadougou and a major centre of culture and music. Jula is the lingua franca of the region, with French the official language. Its Grand Mosque, possibly the largest example of Sudano-Sahelian architecture in the country, was built in 1880 according to some and 1893 according to others. The city also has colonial buildings in the neo-Sudanic style, such as the museum and the railway station.
bobo-people: The Bobo, sometimes called Bobo Fing, are a Mande people who live mainly in Burkina Faso, with some in Mali. They number approximately 110,000. The main Bobo community in the south is in Bobo-Dioulasso, the second-largest city of Burkina Faso and the old French colonial capital. Further north are large towns including Fô and Kouka, with Boura in the extreme north in Mali. In writings on African art the group around Bobo-Dioulasso is called Bobo-Fing, meaning black Bobo. The Bambara use the same name for another people, the Bobo-Oule or Bwa, who are a Gur people and not Mande.

The Bobo are descended from an ancient aggregation that assembled around a number of core clans, none of which preserves oral traditions of migration into the area. Their language and culture are closer to those of their Mande neighbours, the Bamana and the Minianka, than to those of the Gurunsi and Mossi, and they are best seen as a southern extension of the Mande rather than a recent intrusion. Although over 41 per cent of Bobo lineages claim a foreign origin, they also say they are autochthonous.

Farming is central to Bobo life. The main food crops are red sorghum, pearl millet, yams and maize, and cotton and peanuts are the chief cash crops. The cotton is sold to textile mills in Koudougou. Colonial rule and the building of these mills broke down the local co-operative labour systems that had bound Bobo society together.

The lineage is the basic unit. Each village is organised by the relations among patrilines, and a lineage unites the descendants of a common ancestor, called the wakoma. Political power in the hands of one person is foreign to the Bobo, who are ruled by groups of elders deciding together. Each clan has a totem, and a Bobo introduces himself with a given name, a clan name and the totem he respects. Polygyny is common, and levirate and sororate marriages are practised.

In Bobo belief the creator god Wuro formed the earth from a ball of clay and ordered creation into opposing pairs, such as male and female, village and bush, culture and nature. Wuro gave the first mask to the first man, a blacksmith, and the Bobo still make masks in his honour. Blacksmiths traditionally worship Wuro's son Dwo. The masks have wooden structures rising above the main body and are painted red, black and silver or white, repainted at the start of each season. They honour Wuro and are held to erase evil and balance the sun, earth and rain. Some Bobo have converted to Christianity or Islam.
boboli-gardens: The gardens lie directly behind the Pitti Palace, the main seat of the Medici grand dukes of Tuscany, and are among the first formal Italian gardens of the sixteenth century. They were laid out for Eleonora di Toledo, wife of Cosimo I de' Medici. Niccolò Tribolo had scarcely begun the first stage when he died in 1550, and Bartolomeo Ammanati continued the work, with Giorgio Vasari contributing to the planning and Bernardo Buontalenti making sculptures and the grotto in the courtyard between palace and gardens. An aqueduct funded by Cosimo in the late 1550s brought spring water, and a second followed in 1565.

The main axis rises from a deep amphitheatre behind the palace, shaped like half a classical hippodrome, with an Egyptian obelisk from the Villa Medici in Rome at its centre, and ends in a fountain of Neptune made by Stoldo Lorenzi between 1565 and 1568. Giulio Parigi laid out the cross axis, the Viottolone or Cyprus Road, which leads to the Isolotto, an oval island in a pond made around 1618. The Large Grotto, begun by Vasari and finished by Ammanati and Buontalenti between 1583 and 1593, is a defining example of Mannerist sculpture and architecture; it once held Michelangelo's Prisoners, now replaced by copies, and Giambologna's Bathing Venus.

The style developed here used long axes, wide gravel avenues, a large element of stone, lavish statuary and fountains, and classical features such as grottoes and garden temples. Its open views over the city were unconventional for the time, though no one outside the immediate Medici family was admitted. The gardens were enlarged in the seventeenth century to their present extent of 45,000 square metres. They form an outdoor museum of garden sculpture, with Roman antiquities and works of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and influenced aristocratic gardens across Europe.
bobovac: Bobovac stands near the village of Borovica and close to the royal court at Sutjeska, today the village of Kraljeva Sutjeska. Within its main walls the royal town held a large residential area, a group of places of worship with the burial chapel of the Bosnian kings and the Grand Church, and the royal court, set apart from the rest of the town by inner walls and forecourts and built with decorative elements in the Gothic style.

The court was fitted into five karst ridges on three levels sloping from north to south. It had two gates, two keeps, two forecourts and three palaces. The Grand Palace was a building of at least four storeys, about 25 by 10 metres, whose north wall was formed by a stone cliff; its gate bore the coat of arms of King Tvrtko II. The second forecourt held a granary, a large water cistern, a smithy and a lime-pit. A room of the Upper Palace was probably the chapel of Tvrtko II's wife, Dorothy Garai, and its annex housed the workshops of the court's master craftsman.

The town was built in the reign of Stephen II, Ban of Bosnia, and is first mentioned in a document of 1349. It shared the role of royal seat with the court at Sutjeska, but was much better fortified. The crown jewels of Bosnia were kept there. During his war with the Ottoman Empire, King Stephen Tomašević moved the royal seat to Jajce, and the fall of Bobovac in 1463 hastened the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia.

Nine skeletons have been found in the five tombs of the royal mausoleum. Those identified belong to Kings Dabiša, Ostoja, Ostojić, Tvrtko II and Thomas. One of the others is thought to be that of the last king, Tomašević, beheaded at Jajce on the order of Mehmed the Conqueror, and the only female skeleton, beside that of Tvrtko II, is thought to be Queen Dorothy's.

Bobovac is protected as a National Monument of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Commemorations of Statehood Day, 25 November, are held at the site, and on 22 October members of the country's armed and police forces make a pilgrimage there on the Prayer Day for the Homeland.
bobr: The Bóbr, called Bober in German, takes its Polish name from the word for beaver. It is a left tributary of the Oder. It rises on a slope of the Rýchory mountains in the south-east of the Krkonoše range, near the village of Bobr in the Czech Hradec Králové Region, and has a basin of 5,874 square kilometres, almost all of it in Poland. It runs north-westwards through the Jelenia Góra valley of the Western Sudetes to the dam of Pilchowice and then down into the plains of Lower Silesia, passing Jelenia Góra, Bolesławiec, Szprotawa and Żagań, where the Kwisa joins it, and reaches the Oder near Krosno.

Since the Middle Ages the lower Bóbr, north of Żagań and the confluence with the Kwisa, marked the border between the historic regions of Silesia in the east and Lower Lusatia in the west. When Margrave Gero died in 965, the river became the eastern border of the new March of Lusatia in the Holy Roman Empire. Emperor Otto III acknowledged Polish sovereignty under Duke Bolesław I Chrobry at the Congress of Gniezno in 1000. Bolesław claimed the lands west of the Bóbr and held them for a time under the Treaty of Bautzen of 1018, but Emperor Conrad II had reconquered the territory by 1031.

The river became an internal border when King John of Bohemia brought the Piast dukes of Silesia under his rule, a process confirmed by the Treaty of Trentschin in 1335, after which Lusatia and Silesia both became lands of the Bohemian Crown. At the Potsdam Conference in 1945 the Western Allies briefly advocated a Polish-German border along the Oder, Bóbr and Kwisa, but Joseph Stalin rejected it, having already committed himself to the Oder-Neisse line.

The Pilchowice Dam, built between 1904 and 1912 near Jelenia Góra and then the largest in Europe, created a reservoir about four kilometres long. Its masonry stands on a gneiss base built on the Intze principle, and its hydroelectric plant has a rating of 7,585 kilowatts. Parts of the valley are protected, among them the Rudawy Landscape Park, the Bóbr Valley Landscape Park and the Przemków Landscape Park, and the source lies within the Krkonoše National Park.
bocas-del-toro-province: Bocas del Toro, meaning Mouths of the Bull, has an area of 4,643.9 square kilometres, comprising the mainland and nine main islands. The province consists of the Bocas del Toro Archipelago, Almirante Bay, Chiriquí Lagoon and the adjacent mainland. It borders the Caribbean Sea to the north, Limón Province of Costa Rica and the Naso Tjër Di Comarca to the west, Chiriquí Province to the south and the Ngöbe-Buglé Comarca to the east, and the Río Sixaola forms part of the border with Costa Rica. The capital is the city of Bocas del Toro, or Bocas Town, on Colón Island.

Christopher Columbus explored the area in 1502 while searching for a passage to the Pacific Ocean. His original name for the island was Isla del Drago. In colonial times the area was part of Veraguas. It was originally part of Costa Rica until, in one of many territorial disputes, Colombia took control of it with armed forces, and in 1834 the government made a reservation called Bocas del Toro. In 1850 it became a part of Chiriquí and was then separated from it to become part of Colón. On 16 November 1903 Bocas del Toro was separated from Colón and became its own province.

In 1941 the province was divided into two districts, Bocas del Toro and Crimamola, and four years later it returned to its earlier division. In 1970 the district of Bocas del Toro became Changuinola, the district of Bastimentos was eliminated and three new districts were added. The districts' areas changed in 1997, when the Ngöbe-Buglé Comarca was created, and again in 2020, when the Naso Tjër Di Comarca was established. The province is the home of the Bocas del Toro Creole of English.

The province has two national parks: Isla Bastimentos National Marine Park, and La Amistad International Park, which spans the Costa Rica-Panama border and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The population was 159,228 in 2023. It is divided into four districts and 40 corregimientos, and its other main towns are Almirante and Changuinola. The Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute runs a research station on Colón Island, and banana plantations in the province are often called the oro verde, or green gold, of Central America.
bocchus-i: Very little is known about Bocchus I or his Mauretanian kingdom. He was probably the son or grandson of King Baga of Mauretania, a contemporary of King Massinissa of neighbouring Numidia. His kingdom was bordered by the Atlantic Ocean and the Moulouya River, in Latin the Mulucha. A. Pellegrin suggests that Bocchus is the Latin form of a Berber name, possibly Wekkus.

The Roman historian Sallust, in his account of the Jugurthine War, wrote that all the Moors were ruled by King Bocchus, who knew nothing of the Roman people save their name and was in turn unknown to the Romans before that time, either in peace or in war. According to Sallust, Bocchus had many wives, as was the custom, and four known children: a daughter, whose name is unknown, who married Jugurtha; his heir Sosus, also called Mastanesosus; and two other sons, Bogud and Volux.

Around 108 BCE, as the conflict between Rome and Numidia took shape, Bocchus remained noncommittal. After Jugurtha promised him a third of his kingdom, he allied with him. Their combined forces were defeated by Gaius Marius at the Second Battle of Cirta in 106 BCE.

As Jugurtha kept evading the Romans and the war dragged on, Bocchus began to reconsider the alliance and sought a consultation with an ambitious quaestor named Sulla. Mauretanian ambassadors went to Rome, where the Senate was cautiously encouraging but asked for a demonstration of commitment.

Bocchus consulted Sulla again and asked for a meeting with Jugurtha, who walked into the trap, and Bocchus handed him over to Sulla in 105 BCE. Jugurtha was imprisoned in Rome. By treaty Bocchus and the Romans divided the kingdom of Numidia between them. Marius received a triumph for the victory, but Sulla always wore a gold ring that Bocchus had made for him, showing Bocchus handing Jugurtha over to Sulla. Bocchus also supplied Rome with African animals, including panthers and lions, for its spectacles.

Bocchus was succeeded by his son Mastanesosus, who left the kingdom to his sons Bocchus II and Bogud. Each ruled half of Mauretania, but the two took opposite sides in Rome's civil war, and Bocchus II seized Bogud's half. When Bocchus II died in 33 BCE, Mauretania became a client kingdom of Rome.
bocchus-ii: Bocchus II was the son of Mastanesosus, king of Mauretania, who died in 49 BCE. His parentage is known from the Latin legends of his coins, which read Rex Bocchus Sosi f, King Bocchus son of Sosus. By 49 BCE Mauretania appears to have been shared between Bocchus and Bogud. Bocchus held the eastern part with its capital at Iol, Bogud the western part with Volubilis.

Only three events of his reign are known: his dealings with Sittius, his part in the war against Juba I and the Pompeians, and his annexation of western Mauretania. It is not known exactly when he began to rule, but he had been hostile to Juba before the Caesarean Senate recognised him as king in 49 BCE, and he and Bogud took Caesar's side against the Pompeians and their ally Juba I, king of Numidia.

During the Roman civil war of 49–45 BCE Bocchus and Sittius invaded Numidia, overthrew Massinissa II and within a few days took Cirta, Juba's capital, so that Juba had to give up his plan of joining Metellus Scipio against Caesar. Bocchus went no further, but Sittius fought on. At the end of the war Caesar gave Bocchus part of Massinissa II's lands, which extended Mauretania to the Ampsaga; Massinissa's son Arabio recovered them after Caesar's murder.

After Caesar's death Bocchus sided with Octavian and Bogud with Antony. While Bogud was away in Spain, Bocchus seized the whole of Mauretania and was confirmed as sole ruler by Octavian, uniting a larger Mauretanian kingdom than Bocchus I or Sosus had ruled.

Bocchus died without an heir in 33 BCE and left his kingdom to Augustus. After a period of direct Roman administration from 33 to 25 BCE, Augustus gave Mauretania to Juba II, the son of Juba I. Enlarged by western Numidia, it remained a Roman client kingdom under Juba II and his son Ptolemy of Mauretania until it was annexed to the Roman Empire in the reign of Claudius.
bochnia: Bochnia is one of the oldest towns of Lesser Poland, on the river Raba. The first known source is a letter of 1198 in which Aymar the Monk, Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, confirmed a donation by the local magnate Mikora Gryfit to the monastery of the Order of the Holy Sepulchre in Miechów. The discovery of rock salt at the site of the present mine in 1248 led Bolesław V the Chaste to grant city privileges under Magdeburg law on 27 February 1253. Many residents were German-speaking settlers from Lower Silesia. Under Casimir the Great in the 14th century a town hall, a defensive wall and a hospital for miners were built, and work began on St Nicholas Basilica.

A fire in 1561 burned the town down, and its salt deposits were depleted, which began a decline. Bochnia was captured by the Swedes in 1655, the Transylvanians in 1657 and the Cossacks in 1662, and by the 1660s only 54 houses stood. The Great Northern War destroyed it in 1702. In 1772 it was annexed by the Habsburg monarchy in the First Partition of Poland and remained in Galicia until 1918. The Austrians tore down the town hall and wall, but the creation of Bochnia County in 1867 and the Galician Railway began a slow recovery.

Germans shot 52 Poles in Bochnia in 1939 in one of the first mass executions in occupied Poland. About 3,500 Jews lived in the town at the outbreak of the war, around a fifth of the population, and the Germans made it the site of a ghetto. The Jewish community was murdered in the Holocaust apart from about 200 forced labourers, and about 90 Jews from Bochnia survived the war.

The Bochnia Salt Mine, established between the 12th and 13th centuries, is regarded as the oldest in Poland and Europe and is a World Heritage Site. It is 4.5 kilometres long and 468 metres deep, with 16 levels, and its deserted chambers form an underground town open to visitors.
bodawpaya: Born Maung Shwe Waing and later known as Badon Min, he was the fourth son of Alaungpaya, founder of the Konbaung dynasty. He became king by deposing his nephew Phaungkaza Maung Maung, son of his eldest brother Naungdawgyi, at Ava, and in 1782 moved the royal capital back to Amarapura. His title was Hsinbyumyashin, Lord of the White Elephants, but posterity knows him as Bodawpaya, the Grandsire, in relation to his grandson and successor Bagyidaw. He fathered 70 sons and 67 daughters by about 54 consorts.

In 1784 his son, the Heir Apparent Thado Minsaw, led the royal armies across the Western Yoma into Arakan and took its capital Mrauk U on the last day of the year. Besides the Mahamuni image and Khmer bronze statues, 20,000 captives were carried off as slaves to pagodas and temples. The Arakanese revolted in 1794, and the Governor of India Sir John Shore sent Captain Michael Symes on an embassy to Ava. A revolt by the governor of Tavoy in 1791, backed by Siam, ended in 1793 with the Tenasserim coast in Burmese hands. A second invasion of Siam in 1809 was repelled, and with it Burma lost Lan Na after some 200 years of rule.

In 1816 the Ahom governor of Guwahati, Badan Chandra Borphukan, asked for help against his rival Purnananda Burhagohain, and a Burmese force of 16,000 entered Assam in January 1817 and won the battle of Ghiladhari. The Ahom princess Hemo Aideo was given to Bodawpaya in marriage. When Borphukan was assassinated and King Chandrakanta Singha deposed, a second Burmese invasion in February 1819 restored him.

Bodawpaya proclaimed himself the coming Buddha, Maitreya, a claim the Sangha firmly rejected. He set up a chapter of senior monks to guard the order's discipline and unified the monks under the Thudhamma order, and Burmese ordination was carried to Sri Lanka, where it founded the Amarapura Nikaya. In 1790 he began the Mantalagyi stupa at Mingun, meant to stand 150 metres high but left unfinished, and the 90-ton Mingun Bell was cast for it between 1808 and 1810. He ordered an economic survey of the kingdom in 1784. He died in 1819 and was succeeded by Bagyidaw, his son the Heir Apparent having died in 1808.
bodh-gaya: Bodh Gaya is a place of pilgrimage in the Gaya district of the Indian state of Bihar, about 110 km from Patna. It is associated with the Mahabodhi Temple complex, which contains the Vajrasana or diamond throne and the Bodhi tree. In the time of the Buddha it was known as Uruvela, on the bank of the Lilājan River, and the name Bodh Gaya itself came into use in the 18th century. For Buddhists it is the most important of the four main pilgrimage sites of the Buddha's life, the others being Kushinagar, Lumbini and Sarnath.

Tradition holds that the Buddha practised self-mortification for six years at Uruvela, gave it up because it did not bring liberation, and reached enlightenment after finding the Middle Way. His five former companions abandoned him, then became his first disciples at Sarnath. Archaeological finds show that Buddhists have used the site since the Maurya period. The first temple is credited to the Maurya emperor Ashoka, who visited in about 250 BCE to establish a monastery and shrine. Early representations of it appear at Sanchi and Bhārhut. Kittisirimegha of Sri Lanka, a contemporary of Samudragupta, built a monastery nearby for Sri Lankan pilgrims, and the Chinese pilgrims Faxian in the 5th century and Xuanzang in the 7th left accounts of the site.

For centuries the area lay at the heart of a Buddhist civilisation, until Turkic armies conquered it. From the 11th to 13th centuries local chieftains known as the Pithipatis of Magadha controlled it. Muslim Turk armies led by Qutb al-Din Aibak and Bakhtiyar Khilji of the Delhi Sultanate invaded and destroyed Bodh Gaya and nearby regions.

The Mahabodhi Temple became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002. The present Bodhi tree was originally a sapling of the Sri Maha Bodhi tree in Sri Lanka, itself said to grow from a sapling of the original tree. Buddhists from many countries, among them Tibet, Japan, Thailand, Myanmar and China, have built temples and monasteries around the complex in their own styles. An 80-foot statue of the Buddha was consecrated on 18 November 1989.
bodhisattva: Bodhisattva combines the Sanskrit words bodhi, awakening or enlightenment, and sattva, being. The etymology of the Indic terms is not fully understood, but many modern scholars read the compound as a being seeking or destined for awakening. In the early Buddhist discourses the Buddha regularly speaks of himself as an unawakened bodhisatta, and the term refers to Gautama Buddha in his previous lives and as a young man working towards liberation.

By the time the tradition had divided into competing schools, the idea of a bodhisattva vehicle as a distinct path, separate from that of the arhat and the solitary buddha, was widespread among the Theravāda, Sarvāstivāda and Mahāsāṃghika schools. It appears in sources of the 2nd century CE such as the Avadānaśataka and the Divyāvadāna. The Theravāda Buddhavaṃsa, from the 1st or 2nd century BCE, tells how Gautama received from the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara a prediction of his future Buddhahood.

In the early schools and in modern Theravāda Buddhism a bodhisattva is someone who has resolved to become a Buddha and has been confirmed in this by a living Buddha, and such people are seen as rare. In Mahāyāna Buddhism the term refers to anyone who has generated bodhicitta, the compassionate wish to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. The path is open to everyone, and Mahāyāna Buddhists encourage all to follow it.

The bodhisattva practises the perfections (pāramitās), including the perfection of wisdom and skilful means, and the four divine abodes of loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy and equanimity. The Mahāyāna sutras generally depict the path as lasting many lifetimes across many aeons. Some texts say a bodhisattva must postpone final nirvana until all beings are liberated, and the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra gives the vow: I shall not enter into final nirvana before all beings have been liberated. Mahāyāna writers held this path to be higher than that of the arhat.

Mahāyāna Buddhists venerate advanced bodhisattvas, among them Avalokiteshvara, Maitreya and Manjushri. Guanyin, a female form of Avalokiteshvara, is the most widely revered bodhisattva in East Asian Buddhism, and Tara is the most important female bodhisattva in Tibetan Buddhism. Followers of Tibetan Buddhism consider the Dalai Lamas and the Karmapas to be emanations of Chenrezig, and several Japanese schools regard their founders, such as Kukai and Nichiren, as bodhisattvas.

Four mountains in Chinese Buddhism are held to be places of awakening for bodhisattvas: Mount Putuo for Guanyin, Mount Emei for Samantabhadra, Mount Wutai for Mañjuśrī and Mount Jiuhua for Kṣitigarbha. Bodhisattvas are also venerated in Theravāda lands, and the recounting of the Jataka tales of Gautama's past lives remains popular there.
bodleian-library: The first purpose-built library known at Oxford was founded in the 14th century under the will of Thomas Cobham, Bishop of Worcester (d. 1327): a small collection of chained books kept above the north side of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin. When Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, gave a great collection of manuscripts between 1435 and 1437 a larger room was needed, and one was built above the Divinity School and completed in 1488; it is still known as Duke Humfrey's Library.

In the later 16th century the library declined. Its furniture was sold, and only three of Duke Humphrey's original books remained. In 1598 Thomas Bodley, a former fellow of Merton College, wrote to the Vice Chancellor offering to restore it at his own cost. The room was refitted, Bodley gave some of his own books, and the library was formally reopened on 8 November 1602 with around 2,000 books.

In 1610 Bodley made an agreement with the Stationers' Company, suggested by the first librarian, Thomas James, that a copy of every book registered with the company would be placed in the library. The collection grew so fast that the building was extended between 1610 and 1612, and the Schools Quadrangle was built between 1613 and 1619. By 1620 there were 16,000 items. John Selden left his books and manuscripts to the library in 1654. Until the establishment of the British Museum in 1753 the Bodleian was effectively the national library of England.

The library took over the neighbouring Radcliffe Camera in 1860, and the Copyright Act of 1911 continued the Stationers' agreement by making it a library of legal deposit. Its holdings passed one million books in 1914. The New Bodleian, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, was completed in 1940; rebuilt behind its original façade, it reopened as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.

The Bodleian works principally as a reference library, and documents may not be taken from the reading rooms. New readers must agree to a formal declaration not to remove, mark or damage anything in the library, nor to bring fire or flame into it. Its head is known as Bodley's Librarian; 25 people have held the office. Since 2000 it has been the largest member of a group of Oxford libraries, called the Bodleian Libraries since 2010. With over 13 million printed items it is the second-largest library in Britain after the British Library, and its principal store is at South Marston.
bodo-kachari-peoples: Community traditions and scholars agree that the ancestors of the Bodo–Kachari peoples came into the Brahmaputra Valley from the north or the east, and phylogenetic studies suggest that the Boro–Garo languages descend from Proto-Tibeto-Burman spoken in northern China near the Yellow River. Linguists place the first arrival 3,000 years ago or earlier and think the newcomers were fewer than the people already there, who spoke Austroasiatic and probably other languages. Many rivers of the valley still carry names of Kachari origin, such as the Dibang, Dihing and Doiyang, in which Di or Doi means water.

The grammar of the Boro–Garo languages is heavily creolised. Linguists have proposed that this happened when Boro–Garo became the lingua franca of the Tibeto-Burman and Austroasiatic populations of the Kamarupa kingdom and the polities before and after it, so that the change in the valley was more a replacement of language than of people. Genetic studies have found among the Garo a haplogroup associated with Austroasiatic populations.

The peoples are not culturally uniform. The Bodo, Deori, Tripuri and Reang follow patrilineal descent, the Garo, Rabha and Koch matrilineal descent, the Dimasa bilateral and the Tiwa ambilineal descent. The Hill Tiwa speak Tiwa and are matrilineal, while the more numerous Plains Tiwa speak Assamese and are patrilineal. Some groups, such as the Moran and Saraniya, regard themselves as Hindus of the Ekasarana Dharma. The Kacharis were the first to rear silkworms and produce silk, and were associated with ashu rice in Assam before transplanted sali rice came from the Gangetic plains.

Kachari is the older name. A 16th-century Assamese Bhagavata uses it as a synonym of Kirata, and the Buranjis and colonial documents call the Boro–Garo speakers of the plains Kacharis. In time the name was kept only by groups fully integrated into Assamese society, such as the Sarania and Sonowal Kacharis, while others took names such as Boro or Dimasa. Bodo first appears in a book by Hodgson in 1847 and became an umbrella term in anthropology and linguistics, though smaller groups such as the Dimasa resist it.

Several of these peoples founded states in the late medieval period, among them the Chutia and Dimasa kingdoms, the Koch dynasty and the Twipra Kingdom, and came under varying degrees of Sanskritisation. Among the Chutias the Burok clan held administrative and military roles, and the Manikya dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Tripura. Today the Boros, Tripuris and Garos have a strong political and ethnic identity and are developing their languages and literature.
boduognatus: Boduognatus was a Belgic aristocrat of the Nervii, who occupied a stretch of what is now central Belgium. All that is known of him comes from Book II of Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico. His name joins two elements, boduos, crow, and gnatos, son, so that it can be read literally as son of the crow and perhaps figuratively as son of war or warrior.

The Nervii belonged to the Belgae, a large tribal confederation living between the Rhine, the Seine and the English Channel. Julius Caesar began his conquest of Gaul in 58 BCE, and in 57 BCE he invaded the Belgae, claiming they were plotting against the Romans.

After the Battle of the Axona and the surrender of the Suessiones, the Bellovaci and the Ambiani, Caesar turned on the Nervii, who had persuaded the Atrebates, the Viromandui and the Atuatuci to fight on. Boduognatus commanded this alliance at the river Sabis, now thought to be the Selle, near the modern town of Saulzoir. Legio X Equestris and Legio IX drove the Atrebates back across the river, and Legio XI and Legio VIII halted the Viromandui, but these moves opened a gap through which Boduognatus led a column of the Nervii into the Roman camp.

The Romans were saved when Titus Labienus seized the Belgic camp across the river and attacked the Nervii from behind, while Legions XIII and XIV, guarding the baggage, joined the battle. The Nervii reportedly fought almost to the last man, standing on the bodies of their dead.

Boduognatus is presumed to have been killed in the battle, though Caesar never says so. He remained an obscure figure until the 19th century, when Romantic nationalism and Belgian independence in 1830 made him, with Ambiorix, a symbol of national resistance. Joseph Ducaju made a statue of him in 1861 that stood in Antwerp until the city council removed it in 1954; its head is kept at the Middelheim Open Air Sculpture Museum. The asteroid 3458 Boduognat, found in 1985, was named after him by Henri Debehogne.
boeotia: Boeotia lies north of the eastern part of the Gulf of Corinth and has a short coastline on the Gulf of Euboea. It bordered Megaris in the south, Attica in the southeast, Euboea in the northeast, Opuntian Locris in the north and Phocis in the west. Mount Parnassus, Mount Helicon and Cithaeron form its main ranges, and the Cephissus is its longest river. Lake Copais, once a large lake at the centre, was drained in the 19th century. Boeotia gained political weight from its position and the strength of its frontiers, but it lacked good harbours, which hindered its development at sea.

The earliest inhabitants, linked with Orchomenus, were called Minyans. The Boeotians themselves are traditionally said to have come from Thessaly, from which they were expelled soon after the Trojan War, and Thessalian cults and place-names in Boeotia lead most scholars to accept this. They spoke Aeolic Greek. Thebes sought to absorb the other cities into one state, as Athens had annexed the Attic communities, but Orchomenus, Plataea and Thespiae resisted and allowed only a loose federation, at first merely religious. Boeotia hardly figures in history before the late 6th century BCE, when Athens defeated its levy in about 519 BCE and again in 507 BCE.

Thebes assisted the Persian invasion of 480 BCE and lost the presidency of the Boeotian League for a time. Athens ruled the country for ten years until the victory at Coronea in 447 BCE, and the Boeotians fought Athens in the Peloponnesian War, winning at Delium in 424 BCE. In 395 BCE the league comprised eleven groups of cities, each electing a Boeotarch and sending sixty delegates to a federal council at Thebes. Boeotian contingents fought with Epaminondas at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Alexander the Great destroyed Thebes in 335 BCE, and Rome dissolved the league in 171 BCE; it was revived under Augustus.

Boeotia is a regional unit in Central Greece. Its capital is Livadeia and its largest city is Thebes. Hesiod, Pindar, Epaminondas, Pelopidas and Plutarch came from the region. At Orchomenus, Heinrich Schliemann's excavations of 1880-86 revealed a Mycenaean tholos tomb that he called the Tomb of Minyas.
boers: The Boers descend from the proto-Afrikaans-speaking free burghers of the eastern Cape frontier. The Dutch East India Company sent an expedition under Jan van Riebeek in 1652, which built a fort and gardens at Table Bay. Company workers could ask to be discharged and become free burghers, and in 1657 van Riebeek set aside land near the Liesbeek River for the first nine. In 1688 and 1689 nearly two hundred French Huguenot refugees arrived and had assimilated by the middle of the 18th century. The word boer means farmer in Dutch and Afrikaans.

The United Kingdom incorporated the Cape into its empire in 1806, and many farmers disliked British rule. An ordinance of 1812 let magistrates bind Khoikhoi children as apprentices on terms little different from slavery, English became the language of the courts in 1827, Khoikhoi gained equal rights with whites in 1828, and the enslaved were emancipated in 1834. Farmers who thought the compensation inadequate resented it. From 1835 some 12,000 to 14,000 Boers left in the Great Trek, to the plains beyond the Orange River, Natal and the northern Transvaal. A Welsh clergyman who lived in the Transvaal reported that the Boers resisted abolition.

Out of the trek came the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. After the British annexed the Transvaal in 1877, Paul Kruger helped lead a resistance that expelled them. The Boers then fought the Second Boer War to keep the republics independent, but capitulated in 1902. A diaspora followed from 1903 to Patagonia in Argentina, to Brazil, to Kenya, and to Mexico and the south-western United States.

Trekgees, the desire to wander, was a notable trait of the Boers, seen in the Trekboers of the late 17th century and in the Great Trek. Frontier Boers were known for independence and self-sufficiency, and their political notions, which verged on anarchy, had begun to be influenced by republicanism. Most belonged to a Reformed church, and the Orange Free State was named for the House of Orange. Afrikaans developed from the Dutch of South Holland during the 18th century and was long called Cape Dutch.
boethius: Boethius was born in Rome to the Anicii, a wealthy and influential family that included the emperors Petronius Maximus and Olybrius, though it had lost much of its influence in the years before his birth. His grandfather of the same name died in 454 during the palace plot against Flavius Aetius, and his father, Manlius Boethius, consul in 487, died while he was still young. The patrician Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus adopted and raised him, introduced him to philosophy and literature, and later became his father-in-law.

Taking inspiration from Plato's Republic, Boethius left his scholarly pursuits to enter the service of Theodoric the Great, whom he had first met in 500 when the king stayed in Rome for six months. He became a senator by the age of 25 and a consul in 510. His earliest documented tasks were to investigate a charge that the paymaster of Theodoric's bodyguards had debased the coins of their pay, to produce a water clock as a gift for King Gundobad of the Burgundians and to recruit a lyre player for Clovis, King of the Franks.

Boethius set out to translate all the works of Aristotle and Plato from Greek into Latin and to reconcile their teaching with Christian theology. His completed translations of Aristotle's works on logic were the only significant portions of Aristotle available in Latin Christendom from the sixth century until the 12th. He also wrote commentaries, treatises on logic, handbooks on arithmetic and music, and theological treatises, among them one against Eutyches and Nestorius.

In 523 Boethius fell from power. At a meeting of the Royal Council in Verona the referendarius Cyprianus accused the former consul Caecina Decius Faustus Albinus of treasonous correspondence with Justin I, and Boethius defended him, declaring that if Albinus was guilty then so was the whole senate. Imprisoned at Pavia, he was executed in 524. In prison he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue with Philosophy personified as a woman, which King Alfred translated into Old English and Chaucer later into English.

Boethius was regarded as a Christian martyr by later generations; his feast day is 23 October, and his cult at Pavia was confirmed in 1883. Edward Kennard Rand called him the last of the Roman philosophers and the first of the scholastic theologians.
bogd-khan: The future Bogd Khan was born in 1869 in the area of Lhasa, in the family of a Tibetan official. His name at birth was Agvaan Luvsan Choijinnyam Danzan Vanchüg. He was recognised as the new incarnation of the Bogd Gegen at the Potala in the presence of the 13th Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama. He arrived in Urga, the capital of Outer Mongolia, in 1874 and afterwards lived only in Mongolia. As the 8th Jebtsundamba Khutuktu he stood third in the Tibetan Buddhist hierarchy, below the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama, and was also known as the Bogdo Lama.

From his youth the Bogd Gegen was the object of intrigues by Qing officials in Urga. By the spring of 1911 prominent Mongol nobles, among them Prince Tögs-Ochiryn Namnansüren, persuaded him to call a meeting of nobles and clergy to discuss independence, using a religious festival as a pretext. The meeting of 10 July was deadlocked, and eighteen nobles then met in secret in the hills outside Urga and resolved on independence. They persuaded the Khutuktu to send a delegation of a noble, a cleric and a lay official to Russia to ask for help.

On 1 December 1911 the Provisional Government of Khalkha proclaimed a theocracy under the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, and on 29 December he was installed as the Bogd Khan of the new Mongolian state. As a monk he had limited means of imposing power, though some enemies were executed for blasphemy. He lost his power when Chinese governance was restored in 1919. After Baron Ungern-Sternberg's failed attack on Urga in 1920 he was placed under house arrest, and he became Ungern's puppet shortly before the baron took Urga in 1921. After the revolution of 1921, led by Damdin Sükhbaatar, he stayed on the throne as a limited monarch until his death on 20 May 1924.

After his death the Mongolian Revolutionary government, led by followers of the Soviet Communists, declared that no more reincarnations were to be found, and the Mongolian People's Republic was established. Resolutions of 1926 and 1928 forbade any search. A boy born in Lhasa in 1932 was nevertheless recognised as the 9th Jebtsundamba Khutughtu, but this was announced only after the end of the Soviet Union; he was enthroned in Dharamsala by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1991 and in Ulaanbaatar in 1999. The Bogd's Green Palace in Urga is preserved as a tourist attraction in Ulaanbaatar.
bogdan-iii-the-one-eyed: Bogdan was born in Huși on 18 March 1479, the son of Stephen the Great and his wife Maria Voichița, and the only legitimate son of his father to survive. He became voivode on 2 July 1504. He was blind in one eye, most likely from a wound received in battle. The rules of succession barred a man so marked, but they seem to have applied only to those impaired before they sought the throne or from birth.

On his accession Bogdan sought to marry Elisabeth, sister of King Alexander the Jagiellonian of Poland. Twice refused despite generous gifts, territorial concessions among them, he raided southern Poland, and in 1506 Alexander agreed, on condition that Bogdan treat the Roman Catholic Church in Moldavia more leniently. After Alexander's death Sigismund the Old broke the agreement and raids followed on both sides. Bogdan was heavily defeated on the Dniester in October 1509, and in the peace of 17 January 1510 he gave up his claims.

In July 1506 the pretender Roman Pribeagu raided south-western Moldavia with Wallachian support, and Bogdan answered with raids into Wallachia until a peace of 28 November. Fighting resumed in March 1512, when the Moldavians sacked the trading town of Brăila, and on 27 February 1514 Bogdan defeated a Wallachian and Transylvanian army and beheaded the pretender. Two Tatar invasions struck Moldavia in 1510, which are said to have carried off 74,000 people as slaves, and in 1511 the Tatars occupied most of the country; Polish troops helped Bogdan recover it after a victory in May 1512.

To guard against the Tatars, Bogdan sent his chancellor Tăutu in 1514 to negotiate Moldavia's submission to Selim I. The Porte asked a yearly sum, first set at 4,000 gold coins, a gift of 40 horses and 40 falcons, other payments and service in war, the prince leading 4,000 men under the Sultan's orders, and in return left Moldavia a high degree of autonomy.

Bogdan married three times, to Stana, Nastasia and finally Ruxandra, daughter of Mihnea cel Rău of Wallachia, but left no legitimate children. He died on 20 April 1517 and was buried beside his father in Putna Monastery.
bogislaw-iv-duke-of-pomerania: Bogislaw was the eldest son of Duke Barnim I of Pomerania by his second wife, Margaretha, who is sometimes said to have been a daughter of King Eric X of Sweden. He was co-ruler with his father from 1276 and already an adult when Barnim I died in 1278.
