His half-brothers Barnim II and Otto I were then still very young, so Bogislaw ruled Pomerania alone during their minority.

In the early 1280s Bogislaw was drawn into the war in the neighbouring margraviate of Brandenburg. His first wife was Mechtild, a daughter of Margrave John I of Brandenburg and sister of the reigning Margrave Otto IV, whom he married before 14 December 1278. All his known children, however, came from his second marriage, to Margarethe, daughter of Wizlaw II, Prince of Rügen, which took place before 1290 and possibly in 1283–4.

The partition with Otto I followed the death of Barnim II in 1295. In the early 14th century Bogislaw was allied with Władysław the Short, who sought the crown of Poland, and he took part without success in the opening stages of the decade-long Brandenburg War.

Bogislaw died on 19 or 24 February 1309 and was buried in the Marienkirche in Stettin. His share of Pomerania passed to his only son, Wartislaw IV, who later ruled in Western Pomerania and inherited Rügen. Of his daughters, Euphemia married Christopher II of Denmark, Elisabeth married Duke Eric I of Saxe-Lauenburg around 1318, and Margaret married first Nicholas I, Lord of Rostock, and then John Piast. Another daughter was named Jutta, and a further Euphemia, wife of Adolph V, Count of Holstein-Segeberg, may also have been his daughter.
bogislaw-x: Bogislaw was born on 3 June 1454 in Rügenwalde, now Darłowo in Poland, the son of Eric II, Duke of Pomerania-Wolgast, and Sophia of Pomerania, both of the House of Pomerania. For a long time the duchy had been split into splinter duchies ruled by relatives of the Griffin house. When Otto III of Pomerania-Stettin died without an heir in 1464, Bogislaw's father and his uncle Wartislaw X won the dispute over the inheritance against the Margraviate of Brandenburg.

Bogislaw succeeded his father in 1474, and on his uncle's death in 1478 inherited Pomerania-Barth as well, becoming the first sole ruler of the whole duchy in about 200 years. His father had left him in tense conflicts with Brandenburg and Mecklenburg, which he resolved by diplomacy and war. He married his sisters Sophia and Margarete to the Mecklenburg dukes Magnus II and Balthasar, and himself married Margaret, daughter of the Brandenburg elector Frederick II. In 1478 he regained Gartz and other towns and castles north of the Uckermark, but in 1479 he confirmed the Peace of Prenzlau of 1472, leaving Strasburg to Brandenburg and holding his lands as a Brandenburg fief.

After his marriage to Anna, daughter of the Polish king Casimir IV Jagiellon, on 2 February 1491, all of Pomerania's neighbours were tied to his house by marriage. He used this in 1493, when the Treaty of Pyritz declared Pomerania a fief of the Holy Roman Emperor rather than of Brandenburg.

From 1496 to 1498 Bogislaw made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. He died in Stettin on 5 October 1523 and was succeeded by his sons George I and Barnim. Anna bore him eight children; their daughter Sophie married Frederick I of Denmark in 1525 and became queen of Denmark, and another daughter, Elisabeth, was abbess of Krummin Nunnery. His first wife had died in 1479 without children.
bogislaw-xiv: Bogislaw was born in Barth on 31 March 1580, the third son of Duke Bogislaw XIII by his first wife, Clara of Brunswick-Lüneburg. When his father died in 1606 he and his younger brother George II became joint dukes of Rügenwalde, now Darłowo, and after George died in 1617 Bogislaw ruled it alone. He was also the Lutheran administrator of the Prince-Bishopric of Cammin.

In 1620 Rügenwalde was joined to the Duchy of Stettin, which Bogislaw inherited on the death of his elder brother Francis. Early in 1625 the last Duke of Wolgast, Philipp Julius, died, and Bogislaw became ruler of all West Pomerania. On 19 February of that year he married Elisabeth, a daughter of John II, Duke of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg.

He tried to keep out of the Thirty Years' War, but in 1627, by the Capitulation of Franzburg, he was forced to let imperial troops under Albrecht von Wallenstein use his lands as a base, and the duchy suffered all the consequences of the war. In the early 1630s many of the local nobles worked to reduce his power, and the struggle brought on a stroke that left him partly paralysed. In 1634 he abdicated without a clear successor, which led to a constitutional contest between his relatives and the governing council.

Bogislaw died on 10 March 1637 with the constitutional questions unresolved, no recognised male heir, and nearly all Pomerania occupied by Swedish and imperial troops. The succession was disputed between George William, Elector of Brandenburg, heir under a pact between the two families of 1464, and King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, whose forces had occupied much of Pomerania after Sweden entered the war. Bogislaw's will left his lands to Sweden, not Brandenburg, if his house had no successor.

At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 Pomerania was divided between the two powers and ceased to be an autonomous political entity. The quarrels over the succession were so grave that his burial was put off for almost 20 years: only after his widow's death was his body laid to rest in Stettin, on 25 May 1654.
bogomilism: Bogomilism arose in the First Bulgarian Empire in the time of Tsar Peter I, who reigned from 927 to 969, most probably in the region of Macedonia. The name Bogomil means dear to God in free translation, and it is hard to say whether it came from the priest Bogomil or whether he took it from the sect. Social discontent fed the movement: services were first held in Greek, which only the elite knew, and taxes rose under Peter I.

Older dualist currents in the Bulgarian lands, Manichaeism and Paulicianism, also influenced it. The Paulicians had been driven out of Armenia, and in 970 the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes settled 200,000 of them near Philippopolis. Samuil of Bulgaria, who reigned from 976 to 1014, probably relied on popular support of the movement in his revolt against Byzantium, and no persecution is recorded in his reign.

The sources are imperfect and often hostile, and the Bogomils may have been Gnostics, adoptionists or dualists. Their dualism was at first moderate: God created and ruled the spiritual world and Satan the material one, with Satan inferior to God. Later they came to hold that God and Satan were eternal opponents. In one account God had two sons, Satanail, who rebelled and made the earth, and Michael, who was sent in human form and identified with Jesus Christ.

They rejected the church hierarchy, monasticism, the veneration of images, the cross, saints and relics, and held that the bread and wine of the eucharist were not physically changed. Communities chose their own teachers and each had twelve apostles, and women could become members of the elect. The priest Cosmas, writing against them, said they taught followers to scorn the rich and the tsars.

The Bogomils spread through the Balkans. At the end of the 12th century the Serbian grand prince Stefan Nemanja deemed it a heresy and expelled them, and many took refuge in Bosnia and Dalmatia. Hungarian rulers used the sheltering of heretics as a pretext for crusades against Bosnia. The Bosnian Church broke with Rome in 1254, but the original documents of its Krstjani show no trace of Bogomilism, and the dualist sect later reported by inquisitors was probably a different body. Bogomilism was eradicated in Bulgaria, Rascia and Byzantium in the 13th century, and survived in a few places in Bosnia and Hum until the Ottoman Empire gained control in 1463.

In the 12th and 13th centuries the Bogomils were known in the West as Cathars or Bulgari. Scholars debate whether the Cathars were an offshoot of the Bogomils or whether inquisitors conflated them, and several groups sometimes linked with them were unrelated or not dualist.
bogor: Bogor is a landlocked city in West Java. It spreads over a basin near the volcanoes of Salak and Mount Gede, at an average elevation of 265 metres. The soils are volcanic and the area is highly seismic. It has a tropical rainforest climate, more humid and rainy than much of West Java, which gives it the nickname Rain City. Temperatures are lower than on the coast, which made it a resting place for Dutch officials during the colonial period.

The first mention of a settlement at the site dates to the 5th century, when the area belonged to Tarumanagara. After defeats by Srivijaya it became the Sunda Kingdom, and in 669 its capital was built between the parallel rivers Ciliwung and Cisadane. It was named Pakuan Pajajaran and became one of the largest cities of medieval Indonesia, with a population reaching 48,000. Its chronicles were written in Sanskrit in Pallava script on rock steles called prasasti.

In the second half of the 17th century Pakuan was abandoned, and West Java, while formally under the Sultanate of Banten, passed under the Dutch East India Company, a transfer made formal on 17 April 1684. The company sent the Sundanese lieutenant Tanoejiwa in 1687 to develop the area. The eruption of Mount Salak on 4 and 5 January 1699 damaged the settlement but the fires cleared land for rice and coffee plantations, and in 1701 the villages were combined into a district headed by Tanoejiwa.

In the Dutch period the city was called Buitenzorg, meaning without worries in Dutch, and was the summer residence of the Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies. Its botanical garden, founded in 1817, drew naturalists from abroad. Japanese forces occupied it from 6 March 1942 and gave it the name Bogor to promote anti-Dutch feeling.

The Bogor Botanical Garden, one of the oldest and largest in the world, covers 87 hectares and holds more than 6,000 species of tropical plants. The former residence of the governor-general is now a palace of the President of Indonesia. The city is a scientific and educational centre, largely because of institutions founded in the Dutch period to improve colonial agriculture, and is home to IPB University. It had 1,043,070 people at the 2020 census.
bogu-qaghan: Bögü was the younger son of Bayanchur Khan, and his personal name was Yaoluoge Yidijian. During his father's reign he held the title Ulu Bilge Töles Shad and served as viceroy of the eastern part of the Uyghur Khaganate. On succeeding in 759 he took a series of regnal names, the last Tengrida Qut Bolmish El Tutmish Alp Külüg Bilge Qaghan; the Tang invested him as Yingyi Qaghan, and the Manichaeans called him Zahag-i Mani, Emanation of Mani. He is also known for founding the Por-Bazhyn Palace.

The rebel Shi Chaoyi urged Bögü to march on the Tang with him, and the qaghan led 100,000 Uyghur soldiers to the border, believing the dynasty had fallen. Emperor Daizong sent an embassy in 762 recalling his friendship with Bögü's father and asking for an alliance. Li Kuo, the supreme commander of the Tang forces, met Bögü on 12 November 762, and in a dispute over protocol several of the prince's staff were arrested and killed, which left Li Kuo with a lifelong hatred of the Uyghurs. Bögü and his father-in-law Pugu Huai'en crushed Shi Chaoyi near Luoyang, and Bögü returned to the steppe on 8 April 763.

The war greatly raised Uyghur influence: Uyghur officials received the tax income of 20,000 households, and Uyghur soldiers were reported seizing civilians in the markets of Chang'an to sell as slaves. Uyghur contingents fought beside the Tang against invading Tibetan forces from 765 to 768, yet raids on Chinese territory continued, and on 22 February 778 the Uyghurs invaded Taiyuan, killing or wounding almost 10,000 Tang soldiers.

In Luoyang Bögü met four Manichaean priests, among them Ruixi, took them to Ordu-Baliq and made their faith the religion of the state. He posed as the protector of the Manichaeans, and in 768 asked Daizong to reopen their temples, which the emperor reluctantly allowed in 771. When his Manichaean followers urged him to invade China after Daizong's death in 779, the chief minister Tun Baga Tarkhan, a Tengriist opposed to a new war, led a coup, and Bögü was murdered with 2,000 to 3,000 supporters and relatives. According to Larry Clark, later Manichaean tradition revered him as the first ruler to adopt the faith as personal and state religion.
bohdan-khmelnytsky: Zynoviy Bohdan Mykhailovych Khmelnytsky was a Ruthenian nobleman of the Abdank coat of arms. His date of birth is not firmly known. He was baptised Theodore, in Ukrainian Bohdan, and used Zynoviy on religious occasions but signed as Bohdan in daily life. After his studies he entered Cossack service in 1617. His father was killed at the Battle of Cecora on 17 September 1620, and Khmelnytsky was captured by the Turks and spent two years in captivity in Constantinople. In 1637, as military scribe of the Zaporozhian Host, he signed the rebels' capitulation at Borowica after a Cossack revolt.

In the Czapliński Affair the Chyhyryn starosta Daniel Czapliński was authorised to seize Khmelnytsky's Subotiv estate. This is generally regarded as the immediate cause of the uprising, though it was chiefly a catalyst for wider discontent among Orthodox Ruthenians over religion, ethnicity and economics. At the end of January 1648 a Cossack Rada unanimously elected him hetman, and he sought an alliance with the Khan of Crimea, İslâm III Giray. In 1648–1649 the Cossacks under his leadership massacred tens of thousands of Poles and Jews, and others were handed over as slaves to the Tatars.

The Treaty of Zboriv of 18 August 1649 was unfavourable to the Cossacks. At Berestechko on 18 June 1651 the Tatars betrayed him and held him captive, and the Cossacks suffered about 30,000 casualties. On 18 January 1654 the Cossack Rada concluded the Treaty of Pereiaslav, accepting the overlordship of Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich. Historians disagree whether he intended a military union, a suzerainty or full incorporation into Russia.

Khmelnytsky died on 6 August 1657. His rising permanently changed the balance of power in Europe, since Austria, Saxony, Prussia and Russia exploited the weakening of Poland–Lithuania. Opinions of him differ sharply. In Ukraine he is generally regarded as a national hero, and a city and a region bear his name. Poles called him the Scourge of God and blamed him for the decline of the Commonwealth. Jewish historiography judges him overwhelmingly negatively, since the uprising killed an estimated 18,000 to 100,000 Jews. Russian imperial and Soviet historiography presented him as the unifier of Ukraine with Russia.
bohemia: Bohemia is the westernmost and largest historical region of the Czech Republic, with an area of 52,065 square kilometres. The name derives from the Boii, a Celtic people; Roman authors refer to their former land as Boiohaemum, the earliest mention being in Tacitus. After the Boii left, Suebic peoples, among them the Marcomanni under their king Marobodus, became dominant there. Slavic tribes arrived from about the sixth century, and the Czech name Čechy comes from the Czechs who settled the area. Its borders were mostly marked by mountain ranges such as the Bohemian Forest, the Ore Mountains and the Giant Mountains.

In the 9th century Bohemia was part of Great Moravia under Svatopluk I, and when that state collapsed the Přemyslid dynasty ruled, entering semivassalage to the Frankish rulers. After the victory at Lechfeld in 955 Boleslaus I of Bohemia was granted Moravia by Otto the Great. The title of king became hereditary under Ottokar I in 1198, and Ottokar II conquered a short-lived empire containing modern Austria and Slovenia. Substantial German immigration began in the mid-13th century. The House of Luxembourg took the throne with John I in 1310, and his son Charles IV, king from 1346, founded Charles University in Prague two years later and was the first king of Bohemia elected Holy Roman Emperor.

Jan Hus was executed on 6 July 1415, despite a promise of protection from Emperor Sigismund, and the Hussite Wars followed, led first by Jan Žižka and then by Prokop the Great. The Utraquists defeated the Taborites at Lipany in 1434. After Louis II died at Mohács in 1526, Ferdinand I of Austria became king and Bohemia joined the Habsburg monarchy. The Bohemian Revolt of 1618 began the Thirty Years' War; after the defeat at White Mountain in 1620, 27 leaders of the estates and the rector Jan Jesenius were executed on 21 June 1621. A Czech National Revival began at the end of the 18th century.

After the First World War all of Bohemia became the core of Czechoslovakia. The Munich Agreement of 1938 gave the Sudetenland to Nazi Germany, and in 1939 the rest was occupied as the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia. After 1945 the vast majority of the Bohemian Germans were expelled. In 1949 the country was divided into administrative regions that did not follow the historical borders, and since the breakup of Czechoslovakia in 1993 Bohemia has lain in the Czech Republic. It has about 6.9 million of the republic's 10.9 million inhabitants, and the historical land names survive in municipal and geographical names.
bohemond-i-of-antioch: Bohemond was baptised Marc and nicknamed after a giant of legend. His parents, Robert Guiscard and Alberada of Buonalbergo, were related within the degrees forbidden by canon law, and Guiscard repudiated Alberada for Sikelgaita, sister of the Lombard prince of Salerno, which made Bohemond a bastard. His mother arranged a knightly education for him, and he was multilingual, speaking Norman and Greek. He commanded the advance guard of his father's invasion of the Byzantine Empire in 1081, took Valona, and fought on the left flank at the victory over Alexios I Komnenos at Dyrrhachium on 18 October 1081.

After Guiscard died on 17 July 1085, Bohemond contested the succession of his half-brother Roger Borsa, and under a compromise received Taranto, Oria, Otranto, Brindisi and Gallipoli, though the war was renewed in 1087. In 1097 crusaders passing through Italy drew him east. He brought a Norman army of about 500 knights and some thousands of infantry, took the oath of homage to Alexios at Constantinople in April 1097, and served as a go-between with the other leaders. At the siege of Antioch he was regarded as its actual leader. A commander of the wall, Firouz, let his troops in during May 1098, and he is credited with the plan that defeated Kerbogha's relief army.

Bohemond kept the city, arguing that Alexios had failed to come to the crusaders' aid, and Raymond of Toulouse gave up his claim in January 1099. In August 1100 he was ambushed by Turks near Melitene and held at Neo-Caesarea until 1103, when a ransom of 130,000 dinars was paid to Gazi Gümüshtigin. After a defeat at Harran he went to Europe in late 1104 to raise troops, married Constance, daughter of Philip I of France, and gathered an army of 34,000 men. With it he besieged Dyrrhachium in 1107–1108, but Alexios blockaded his camp.

Bohemond had to submit in 1108 to the Treaty of Deabolis, becoming Alexios's vassal with the title sebastos, promising to cede disputed territory and to admit a Greek patriarch to Antioch. He never returned to Antioch, which stayed in Norman hands under his nephew Tancred, and died in March 1111, being buried at Canosa in Apulia. His son by Constance was Bohemond II of Antioch. The anonymous Gesta Francorum was written by one of his followers, and the Byzantine princess Anna Komnene's Alexiad is a main source for his life; she wrote that the sight of him inspired admiration and the mention of his name terror.
bohemond-vi-of-antioch: Bohemond VI was the son of Bohemond V of Antioch and Lucienne of Segni, a great-niece of Pope Innocent III. When his father died he was fifteen, and he succeeded under the regency of his mother. Lucienne never left Tripoli and handed the government of the principality to her relatives, which made her unpopular. King Louis IX of France, then on crusade, helped the young prince to obtain permission from Pope Innocent IV to inherit a few months early.

Louis knighted him at Acre, and he took power in Antioch. At Louis's suggestion, in 1254 Bohemond married Sibylla, daughter of King Hetoum I of Armenia, which ended a power struggle between the two states that had begun under his grandfather Bohemond IV.

As overlord of the Genoese Embriaco family, Bohemond was drawn into the War of Saint Sabas between the Genoese and the Venetians, which began in 1256. The Embriaco lords of Gibelet rebelled against him in 1258, and the dispute became a civil war. Hetoum persuaded him to submit to the Mongols, and in 1260 Antioch became a tributary of the Mongol Empire. Both rulers took part with their own forces in the Mongol conquests of Aleppo and Damascus that year.

The Mongols rewarded Bohemond with towns that had been lost to the Muslims, among them Lattakieh and Jabala, on condition that he install a Greek patriarch, Euthymius, at Antioch in place of the Latin one. This earned him the enmity of the Latins at Acre, and the Patriarch of Jerusalem, Jacques Pantaléon, excommunicated him. After Pantaléon became Pope Urban IV he suspended the sentence. The Mamluks defeated the Mongols at the Battle of Ain Jalut in September 1260, and their leader Baibars began to threaten Antioch.

In 1266 the Mamluk army defeated the army of Cilician Armenia at the Battle of Mari. In 1268 Baibars besieged Antioch and took it while Bohemond was away in Tripoli; all of northern Syria was soon lost, leaving him with no estates except Tripoli. In 1271 Baibars besieged Tripoli and sent Bohemond a letter taunting him for his alliance with the Mongols, but in May offered a truce, as the Mamluks had heard of a new crusade under the prince who would later be Edward I of England.

Bohemond died in 1275, leaving a son and three daughters. The son, Bohemond VII, was nominal prince of Antioch, though Antioch had ceased to exist, and count of Tripoli. Lucia later became titular countess of Tripoli. Mamluk rancour at his alliance with the Mongols lasted until the fall of Tripoli in 1289.
bohol: Bohol lies in the Central Visayas, with Cebu to the west across the Cebu Strait, Leyte to the northeast and Mindanao to the south across the Bohol Sea. The province consists of the main island and about 70 smaller ones, of which Panglao Island is the largest. The main island has a land area of 4,821 km2. The terrain is rolling and hilly, about half the island is covered in limestone, and the interior is a large plateau. The name is derived from the local word bo-ol, a kind of tree that flourished on the island. Boholanos share a language with the Cebuano but keep a conscious distinction from them.

Southeastern Bohol, especially Cogtong Bay in Candijay and the Anda Peninsula, is called the cradle of civilisation of Bohol because of petroglyphs and burials in boat-shaped wooden coffins, estimated to be 6,000 years old. Miguel López de Legazpi arrived on 16 March 1565 seeking spices and gold. After convincing the datus that his men were not Portuguese, he made a peace pact with Datu Sikatuna, sealed with a sandugo, a blood compact. It is marked each year at the Sandugo Festival and appears on the provincial flag and seal.

American troops took over peacefully in March 1899, but in September 1900 Colonel Pedro Samson led 2,000 men in rebellion against their harsh treatment. American forces answered with a scorched-earth policy and burned 20 of Bohol's 35 towns. Japanese troops landed at Tagbilaran on 17 May 1942, and local guerrillas resisted until Filipino and American troops landed on 11 April 1945. Carlos P. Garcia, born in Talibon, became president of the Philippines in 1957, and Tagbilaran received its city charter on 18 June 1966.

Tagbilaran is the capital and largest city of the province, which has one component city, 47 municipalities and 1,109 barangays. Its population was 1,412,726 at the 2024 census. Most people speak Bohol Cebuano, and the Eskayans of the southeastern interior have an artificial language of their own, with its own alphabet. The Chocolate Hills, mounds of limestone, are the best-known attraction, and the Philippine tarsier, one of the world's smallest primates, is native to the island. Bohol became a UNESCO Global Geopark in 2023.
bohuslan: Bohuslän is a Swedish province in Götaland on the northernmost part of the country's west coast. It is bordered by Dalsland to the northeast, Västergötland to the southeast, the Skagerrak to the west and the Norwegian county of Østfold to the north. Its rocky coast fronts an archipelago of about 3,000 islands and 5,000 islets, which form the northern part of the Gothenburg archipelago, and its reefs and sunken rocks once caused many shipwrecks. Most of the coast is Bohus granite. The province takes its name from the medieval Norwegian castle of Bohus, or Båhus.

Rock carvings made in the Nordic Bronze Age, which lasted from about 1700 to 500 BCE, are found throughout the province. They show daily life, religious rituals, ships and animals, and those at Tanum are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the Viking Age the area was part of Viken. It has been claimed that King Harald Fairhair made it part of a unified Norway in about 872, but contemporary sources cast doubt on this, and the earliest attested information is from the 11th century. The fortress of Båhus was one of the kingdom's key defences.

When Norway was united with Denmark in 1537, the province declined in wealth, because Swedish forces often attacked the border zone, and its population contained a disproportionate number of soldier families. It belonged to Denmark-Norway until the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658 ceded it to Sweden. Sweden built the fortress of Carlsten at Marstrand, which for a time was a free port with free religious practice and the only synagogue in Sweden of its day.

Herring fishing increased in the 18th century, and the province flourished in the great herring period of 1747 to 1809, when small fishing communities grew up along the coast. Timber had been its largest export, but wood was increasingly used for houses, boats and the boilers that rendered herring oil, and deforestation in the 19th century helped to give the landscape its rugged, rocky look.

Swedish provinces have no administrative function. Bohuslän was long part of Gothenburg and Bohus County, which merged into Västra Götaland County in 1998. Its cities include Kungälv, Marstrand, Uddevalla and Strömstad, and the northwest of Gothenburg lies on the island of Hisingen. The dialect of Swedish spoken there keeps traces of Norwegian.
boizenburg: Boizenburg lies on the right bank of the Elbe, 53 kilometres west of Ludwigslust, 25 km north-east of Lüneburg and 50 km east of Hamburg. Its historical old town stands on the Boize, a tributary of the Elbe to which it is connected by a harbour, between the Old and New Boize and a former moat. The German name Boyceneburg was first documented in 1158, and the name of the river and town likely stems from the Slavic boj, war. Since 17 March 1939 the town has officially been called Boizenburg/Elbe, to tell it from other places with similar names.

Boizenburg suffered during the Thirty Years' War, and Swedish troops burnt its old castle in 1628. In 1709 a fire destroyed the church and 160 or more medieval dwellings. The Town Hall was rebuilt in 1712, and Prussian architects sent from Schwerin redesigned the layout of the town for efficient movement, fire resistance, better sanitation and public space. French troops were quartered there in 1807, and a battle was fought with the retreating French army nearby in 1813. From 1815 to 1918 the town belonged to the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. A highway to Hamburg and Berlin was built in 1826, and the railway between Berlin and Hamburg, with its own station at Boizenburg, in 1846.

The Lemmsche shipbuilding yard, founded in 1793, was highly industrialized by 1852 and produced many wooden and steel ships. The Boizenburg Tile Factory, established by Hans Duensing in 1903, became Europe's largest tile manufacturer by 1937. Until 30 April 1945 a subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp existed in the town. During the Cold War Boizenburg was in East Germany, only about 7 km east of the Inner German Border, and residents were kept under close scrutiny by the Stasi.

Boizenburg is a town in the Ludwigslust-Parchim district of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and part of the Hamburg Metropolitan Region. It has a well preserved old town with baroque timberframe and brick architecture, which remained largely untouched during the East German period. The tile factory, re-established in 1991, remains one of its main employers, and the Erstes Deutsches Fliesen Museum shows tile work, particularly in the Art Nouveau style. The town lies on the Berlin–Hamburg railway.
bojang-of-goguryeo: Bojang, whose given name was Jang, was the 28th monarch of Goguryeo, the northernmost of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. He was a nephew of King Yeongnyu and a son of Go Dae-Yang. In 642 the general Yŏn Kaesomun staged a coup, killed Yeongnyu and many of his supporters, and put Bojang on the throne. His reign is recounted in the final two books of the annals of Goguryeo in the Samguk sagi.

For most of his reign Bojang was a puppet who lent legitimacy to Yŏn Kaesomun's military rule; at Yŏn's prompting he supported Taoism and issued edicts repressing Buddhism, formerly the official religion. In 642 Silla sent Kim Ch'unch'u to seek a treaty, but talks broke down when Yŏn demanded the return of the Seoul region, and Silla turned to the Tang dynasty. Goguryeo fought on against Silla in alliance with Baekje and restored relations with the Wa of Japan.

In 645 Emperor Taizong of Tang led a great expedition by land and sea, which Yŏn Kaesomun and Yang Manch'un drove back, as they did later and smaller Tang attacks. After Baekje fell to Silla and Tang in 660, Yŏn repelled invasions at Pyongyang in 661 and on the Sasu River in 662. When he died in 666 his sons fought over the succession; Yŏn Namsaeng defected, and 40 castles near the border surrendered to the Tang.

After the capital fell in the ninth lunar month of 668, Emperor Gaozong of Tang made Bojang minister of public works. In 677 the Tang crowned him King of Joseon and placed him over the Liaodong Commandery, but he organised Goguryeo refugees and allied with the Malgal tribes in an attempt to revive his kingdom, and in 681 he was banished to Sichuan. As the last ruler of Goguryeo he received no temple name.

A brief attempt at restoration was led by Anseung, a son of Bojang's second wife, who in the end surrendered to Silla. Another son, Ko Tŏngmu, founded Lesser Goguryeo, and Ko Yak'gwang settled in Japan in 666, where he founded the Koma clan.
bokmal: Until about 1300 the written language of Norway, Old Norwegian, was essentially the same as the other Old Norse dialects. In 1380 Norway entered a personal union with Denmark, and by the early 16th century it had lost its separate political institutions. The Reformation, which prompted Christiern Pedersen's translation of the Bible into Danish, helped a Danish written language standardise, and it displaced the remnants of written Old Norse and Norwegian in virtually all administrative documents.

Danish was used in Norway mainly in writing, but urban elites also spoke it on formal occasions. By the time the ties with Denmark were cut in 1814, a Dano-Norwegian vernacular, often called the educated daily speech, had become the mother tongue of the elites in cities such as Bergen, Kristiania and Trondheim. It was Danish with regional Norwegian pronunciation, some Norwegian vocabulary and simplified grammar.

Bokmål, literally book-tongue, is one of the two official written standards of Norwegian, alongside Nynorsk. It is a Norwegianised variety of Danish and is adopted by around 90 percent of the population of Norway. There is no countrywide standard of pronunciation: the government does not regulate spoken Bokmål, and Urban East Norwegian is generally accepted as the de facto spoken standard in Eastern Norway.

The first Bokmål orthography was officially adopted in 1907 under the name Riksmål, after being under development since 1879; its architects were Marius Nygaard and Jacob Jonathan Aars. It adapted written Danish to the Dano-Norwegian koiné of the urban elite. The school reformer Knud Knudsen, whose work was important for the 1907 orthography and a reform in 1917, is often called the father of Bokmål.

Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson proposed the name Riksmål in 1899, and a movement under his leadership organised to resist the growing influence of Nynorsk. When Aftenposten adopted the 1907 orthography in 1923, Danish writing was practically out of use in Norway. The name Bokmål was adopted by parliament in 1929, after a proposal to call the language Dano-Norwegian lost by a single vote in the Lagting.

Official policy then aimed to merge the written standards into a common Samnorsk through spelling reforms. The 1938 reform, which made many forms mandatory, was harshly criticised by the Riksmål movement, and resistance under Arnulf Øverland culminated in the 1950s. The Norwegian Academy for Language and Literature, founded in 1953, regulates the more conservative standard still called Riksmål. After the Samnorsk policy was abandoned, Riksmål and Bokmål converged, and the Academy's online dictionary covers both.
boleslaus-i-of-bohemia: Boleslaus was the son of Duke Vratislaus I of Bohemia and Drahomíra, who was likely a Hevellian princess and was pagan. He and his elder brother Wenceslaus were taught the Roman Catholic faith and to read the Psalms by their grandmother Ludmila. The Přemyslid dynasty had ruled Bohemia since about 870, and Bořivoj I was its first duke to be baptised. After Vratislaus died, Wenceslaus succeeded him and kept his independence from the East Frankish ruler Henry I only by agreeing to pay annual tribute.

Wenceslaus was murdered at Stará Boleslav in 935, according to other sources in 929, after accepting Boleslaus's invitation to celebrate the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Historians are uncertain of Boleslaus's motives, but argue that it was likely a desire for power, the influence of his pagan mother, or an end to Wenceslaus's political plans. Wenceslaus was soon venerated as a martyr and canonised, and some historians think Boleslaus promoted the cult because it benefited his rule.

Boleslaus stopped paying tribute, which led to war with Otto I. In 935 he attacked the Thuringian allies of the Saxons and defeated two of Otto's armies. The war declined into border raids until 950, when Otto besieged a castle held by Boleslaus's son Boleslaus II and Boleslaus agreed to peace, undefeated, and promised to resume tribute. Five years later Bohemian and Frankish armies allied against the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld, and Boleslaus crushed the remainder of the Magyar army when it turned to Bohemia.

He freed the Moravian lands from Magyar raids and expanded his territory to what later became Upper Silesia and Lesser Poland. By occupying Kraków he controlled trade routes from Prague to Kiev and Lviv. Prague was a major trading centre under him, and he had strongholds built across the countryside. About 963 or 964 he married his daughter Doubravka to the pagan Piast prince Mieszko I, who accepted baptism before the marriage. The alliance is often credited with the Roman Catholic conversion of Poland.

Boleslaus was succeeded by his eldest son, Boleslaus II. Czech historians generally respect him as an energetic ruler who strengthened the Bohemian state and expanded its territory. Medieval writers, notably Cosmas of Prague, present him as a cruel figure, and the date of his death given by Cosmas is questioned by modern researchers.
boleslaus-ii-of-bohemia: Boleslaus II, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty, was born about 932. He was an elder son of Duke Boleslaus I the Cruel. His siblings who survived to adulthood were Strachkvas, Doubravka, wife of Duke Mieszko I of Poland, and the abbess Mlada. His mother may have been Biagota, a mysterious figure known only from her coins, whom some historians consider the wife of Boleslaus I. He ruled as kníže, a title that may be translated as duke or prince, after his father's death.

Like his father, Boleslaus II at first quarrelled with the Ottonian kings of Germany. In 974 he and Mieszko I supported the rebellious Duke Henry II of Bavaria against Emperor Otto II. When Henry was defeated in 976 and fled to Boleslaus's court at Prague Castle, Otto's forces campaigned in the Bohemian lands. In 978 Boleslaus pledged allegiance to the emperor at the Easter festivities in Quedlinburg.

Relations with Poland worsened from about 980. After Otto II died in 983 Boleslaus again allied with Henry of Bavaria, while Mieszko took the side of the young Otto III. Boleslaus occupied the Saxon Margravate of Meissen, thwarting Mieszko's son Bolesław, who had married a daughter of Margrave Ricdag, and had to retire from it in 987. From about 990 he began a long conflict with Poland around Silesia and Lesser Poland. In 992 he joined an unsuccessful campaign by Otto III against the Lutici.

His reign is most notable for the foundation of the Diocese of Prague in 973, which earned him the epithet The Pious from the chronicler Cosmas of Prague. The diocese came under the Archbishop of Mainz, and Otto II enforced the appointment of the Saxon monk Thietmar as its first bishop.

The struggle with the rival Slavník dynasty flared up from 981, when Prince Soběslav began to forge alliances with the Polish and Saxons. After Thietmar's death in 982, Soběslav's brother Adalbert, later Saint Adalbert of Prague, became bishop until he left in 994 for a mission to the Old Prussians. On 28 September 995 Boleslaus's forces and the allied Vršovci clan stormed Libice Castle and massacred the Slavník members found there. This brutal triumph ensured the unity of Bohemia under a single ruler.

Boleslaus died on 7 February 999. His first wife Adiva may have been a daughter of the English king Edward the Elder, though the evidence is weak, and his second was Emma of Mělník. His eldest son Boleslaus III succeeded him but was deposed in 1002 after conflict with his brothers Jaromír and Oldřich, who became dukes in 1003 and 1012. Struggles within the dynasty shook Bohemia until Oldřich stabilised it.
boleslaw-i-the-brave: Bolesław was the only known child of Mieszko I and the Bohemian princess Dobrawa, and was named after his maternal grandfather, Boleslaus I, Duke of Bohemia. His epitaph calls his father faithless and his mother true-believing, which suggests that he was born before Mieszko's baptism. Dobrawa died in 977, and Mieszko then married Oda of Haldensleben. Around that time Bolesław became ruler of Lesser Poland, though historians differ on how: one holds that his father gave it to him, another that he seized it with the support of local lords, a third that his uncle Boleslav II of Bohemia granted it.

Mieszko I died on 25 May 992. The chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg recorded that Mieszko left his kingdom to be divided among many claimants, but that Bolesław united it with fox-like cunning, expelling his stepmother and half-brothers. He supported the missionaries Adalbert of Prague and Bruno of Querfurt, and after Adalbert's martyrdom in 997 he ransomed the bishop's remains, paying their weight in gold. At the Congress of Gniezno on 11 March 1000, Emperor Otto III permitted a Polish church structure with a metropolitan see at Gniezno, independent of Magdeburg, and Bolesław repudiated the payment of tribute to the Empire.

After Otto died in 1002 Bolesław took Lusatia and parts of Meissen, and in 1003 he entered Prague, where the Bohemian lords proclaimed him duke. A long series of wars with Otto's cousin and heir, Henry II, followed. The Peace of Bautzen of 30 January 1018 let Bolesław keep Lusatia and Meissen as part of Polish territory rather than as fiefs. Later that year, at the request of his son-in-law Sviatopolk I, he defeated Yaroslav the Wise at the river Bug and entered Kiev on 14 August. According to legend he notched his sword, later the Szczerbiec, on the Golden Gate of Kiev.

Historians dispute the date of his coronation, which scholars most often place on Easter Sunday 27 March 1025, though 1000 is also thought possible. German sources say that he crowned himself king after the death of Henry II in 1024. According to Cosmas of Prague, Bolesław died shortly after, on 17 June 1025. He was buried in Poznań, and his epitaph is one of the first sources to call him Brave, Chrobry. He established the Prince's Law, sponsored churches, monasteries and forts, introduced the grzywna as the first Polish monetary unit, and minted his own coins.
boleslaw-ii-of-masovia: Bolesław was the younger son of Siemowit I of Masovia and Pereyaslava, a Rus' princess whom some historians make a daughter of Prince Daniel of Halych and others a distant relative of his. Little is known of his early years, except that he was not with his father and his elder brother Konrad II at Jazdów in 1262, when Siemowit was killed and Konrad captured by the Lithuanians. His mother and his father's ally Bolesław the Pious, Duke of Greater Poland, governed as regents until Konrad was freed in 1264.

Coming of age in 1275, Bolesław demanded his share of the inheritance and received western Masovia with Płock as its capital. Dissatisfied, he fought Konrad for a decade, calling on the Lithuanians who had killed his father; in 1279 he married Gaudemantė, daughter of Grand Duke Traidenis, baptised Sophia. The war brought neither side gain and laid waste much of Masovia.

When Leszek II the Black died childless on 30 September 1288, Bishop Paweł of Przemankowo and the Topór family backed Bolesław for Kraków. His troops took Kraków and Sandomierz in 1288, but Henryk IV Probus drove him out after the castellan Sulk the Bear opened Wawel Castle. On 26 February 1289 Bolesław's allies won the Battle of Siewierz, and he entered Kraków that summer, yet when he handed Sandomierz to Konrad the nobles of Lesser Poland rejected him, and he withdrew to Płock.

In 1291 he married Kunigunde, sister of King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia. When Konrad died without a son in 1294, Bolesław became ruler of all Masovia, broke with Bohemia and returned to Władysław I the Elbow-high. Wenceslaus attacked Masovia and destroyed Płock, but Bolesław refused to recognise him as King of Poland in 1300 and sent Kunigunde back to Prague in 1302.

In the early 1300s Bolesław founded the stronghold of Warsaw, which grew at the expense of nearby Czersk. In 1310 he gave Warsaw to his son Siemowit II and Czersk to Trojden I. He died on 20 April 1313 at Wyszogród and was buried in Płock Cathedral.
boleslaw-ii-the-bald: Bolesław, also called the Horned (Rogatka), was the eldest son of Henry II the Pious and Anna, a daughter of the Přemyslid king Ottokar I of Bohemia, and a grandson of Henry the Bearded and Hedwig of Silesia. When his father fell at the Battle of Legnica on 9 April 1241, he and his brother Mieszko were the only heirs of age, and their mother helped them through the transition. He was briefly High Duke of Poland in 1241 and Duke of Silesia at Wrocław.

He could not hold his father's position. In July 1241 his cousin Konrad I of Masovia moved on Kraków, and the nobles there, disappointed by Bolesław's inaction, turned to Bolesław V the Chaste, who took the throne in 1243. In Greater Poland Duke Przemysł I and his brother Bolesław the Pious retook Kalisz, and in 1247 they forced Bolesław to give up all his rights there. In 1247 his brother Henry III the White rose against him and briefly imprisoned him.

To win his freedom Bolesław agreed to divide Lower Silesia and chose Legnica, possibly for the gold found in the Kaczawa and Wierzbiak rivers. He soon regretted it and fought Henry III for Wrocław, selling half of Lubusz Land to Archbishop Wilbrand of Magdeburg to pay for the war. In 1251, beaten by Przemysł I and Henry III, he ceded the Duchy of Głogów to his brother Konrad. In 1257 he imprisoned Bishop Thomas I of Wrocław at Wleń Castle and was excommunicated, and in 1261 he did public penance at the gates of Wrocław Cathedral.

In 1277 Bolesław allied with King Rudolf I of Germany against Ottokar II of Bohemia and, at Rudolf's insistence, seized his nephew Duke Henry IV of Wrocław. A coalition formed against him, but at the battle of Stolec his son Henry V turned the tide; in the settlement Henry IV was freed and Bolesław received a third of the Duchy of Środa Śląska. He died between 26 and 31 December 1278 and was buried at the Dominican monastery of Legnica.

His sons Henry V the Fat, Bolko I and Bernhard inherited his lands. He married Hedwig, daughter of Count Henry I of Anhalt, in 1242, and Euphemia, daughter of Duke Sambor II of Pomerania, in 1261; Euphemia fled to Pomerania in 1275 after he took Sophia of Dyhrn as his mistress, and he married Sophia in 1277.
boleslaw-iii-the-generous: Bolesław was born on 23 September 1291, the eldest son of Henry V the Fat and Elisabeth, daughter of Bolesław the Pious of Greater Poland. He was five when his father died in 1296. His mother and his uncle Bolko I acted as regents until their deaths, and after a brief guardianship by Bishop Henry of Würben, King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia took him to Prague in 1302 and betrothed him to his youngest daughter Margareta. The king's favour made Bolesław a rival to the king's own relatives, and after the murder of Wenceslaus III in 1306 he styled himself heir of the Polish Kingdom.

His forces were too weak for the contest: he failed to hold Kalisz in 1306 and 1307, gained Opava in 1308 and gave up his claim at Olomouc on 11 June 1311 for 8,000 pieces of silver. His ambitions exhausted his money, and in 1311 he had to divide the inheritance with his brothers Henry VI and Władysław. Given first choice, he took Brzeg, the smallest share, for the compensation it brought, and a year later took Legnica from Władysław, who could not pay his part.

Allied with Władysław I the Elbow-high, he fought the dukes of Głogów in 1312 to 1317, gaining Wołów and Lubiąż, and a second war ended in the peace of Wrocław on 10 August 1323. King John of Bohemia made him governor of Bohemia in 1321 and 1322. He quarrelled with Henry VI over Wrocław and attacked it in 1324 and again while King John was away from Bohemia, failing both times. When Władysław returned in 1329 and took Legnica in King John's name, Bolesław, lacking the means to fight, declared himself John's vassal at Wrocław on 9 May 1329.

His lavish life and travels, among them the Congress of Visegrád of 1335, forced him to raise taxes and sell lands. He was excommunicated twice, in 1337 for late tithes and in 1340 for seizing Church property, yet endowed Lubiąż Abbey and founded Franciscan and Dominican houses in Brzeg. In 1342 he gave Legnica to his sons Wenceslaus I and Louis I and retired to Brzeg with his second wife, Katharina Šubić of Croatia, where he died on 21 April 1352. He was buried at Lubiąż, and Brzeg passed to his widow.
boleslaw-iii-wrymouth: Bolesław was born on 20 August 1086, the only child of Duke Władysław I Herman and his first wife, Judith of Bohemia. His parents, without a legitimate heir, had sent gifts to the Benedictine sanctuary of Saint Giles in Provence in 1085, among them a life-size golden statue of a child, asking for offspring. Władysław had in practice given the government to Count Palatine Sieciech. Bolesław and his half-brother Zbigniew, Władysław's elder son by a union the church did not recognise, joined against Sieciech, and their forces defeated his army near Żarnowiec by the river Pilica in 1099.

Władysław Herman died on 4 June 1102 and the country was divided into two virtually separate states, Zbigniew taking the northern part with Mazovia and its capital Płock, and Bolesław the southern part. Bolesław was then only 16 and inexperienced, and the local nobility, including his teacher Skarbimir of the Awdaniec family, had great influence over political affairs.

Bolesław's pursuit of Pomerania brought armed conflict with Zbigniew, who fled and sought help from King Henry V of Germany. Bolesław blinded him, which caused outrage and a political crisis, and Bolesław recovered his subjects' favour with public penance and a pilgrimage to the monastery of Saint Giles in Hungary. With Hungarian and Kievan alliances he defended Poland against invasion in 1109.

The second half of his rule was given to Pomerania. By 1113 he had strengthened the border on the Noteć, and from 1115 to 1119 he conquered Gdańsk Pomerania. At the battle of Niekładź in 1121 (or 1119) he defeated the Pomeranian dukes Wartislaw I and Swietopelk I, and he took Szczecin by a surprise assault. Bishop Otto of Bamberg led missions to Christianise Pomerania in 1124 to 1125 and in 1128. At the Congress of Merseburg on 15 August 1135 Emperor Lothair III recognised Bolesław's rights over Pomerania, for which he paid homage, though he remained fully independent in Poland itself.

Bolesław died on 28 October 1138, probably at Sochaczew. No twelfth-century source records the circumstances of his death or his burial; Jan Długosz in the 15th century places his tomb in Płock cathedral. His testament, the Statute of Succession, set up an indivisible Seniorate Province centred on Kraków under the senior duke, and further provinces for his other sons. Władysław II received Silesia and became the first senior duke. The principle was soon broken, and almost 200 years of fragmentation followed.

Historians have seen Bolesław as a symbol of Polish political aims well into the 19th century. They also record his serious error in the treatment of Zbigniew, and see in the crime and his penance both his ambition and his ability to find compromise.
boleslaw-iv-the-curly: Bolesław was the third son of Duke Bolesław III Wrymouth and his second wife Salomea of Berg. The deaths of his older brothers Leszek and Casimir by 1131 left him the eldest son of their parents. When his father died in 1138 he was 13, and under the testament he received the newly created Duchy of Masovia, made up of Masovia and eastern Kuyavia. In his first years he remained under the influence of his mother and the voivode Wszebor, who feared the ambition of his half-brother, High Duke Władysław II. Władysław tried to restore the unity of the country and deposed the junior dukes.

Open conflict began in 1141, when Salomea met her sons at Łęczyca without Władysław's consent and betrothed her daughter Agnes to Mstislav II of Kiev. Civil war broke out fully in 1145. The junior dukes gained the backing of the voivode Piotr Włostowic after Władysław had him blinded, and in 1146, after rebellions and an excommunication by the Archbishop of Gniezno, Władysław was defeated and fled to Bohemia and then Germany. Bolesław took Silesia and the Seniorate Province at Kraków, with the title of high duke. His brother Mieszko III kept Greater Poland and Henry received Sandomierz.

Władysław's wife Agnes persuaded her brother-in-law King Conrad III to intervene, but his expedition was defeated near the Oder in August 1146. In 1157 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa invaded and laid siege to Poznań. On 30 August 1157, at his camp in Krzyszkowo, Bolesław was declared a vassal of the Empire. He paid a large tribute, swore loyalty at Magdeburg on Christmas Day and gave his brother Casimir II as a hostage. Władysław was not restored and died in exile two years later.

Bolesław then proclaimed a crusade against the pagan Prussians, but efforts to conquer them were defeated in 1166, and his brother Henry of Sandomierz was killed. Bolesław added Sandomierz to the Seniorate Province against his father's testament, and in 1168 Casimir, Mieszko III and much of the Lesser Polish nobility rebelled. Bolesław kept his rule by dividing Henry's lands into three parts.

Bolesław gave many gifts to the Church, among them the Benedictine monastery at Trzemeszno, and around 1151 he founded the collegiate church at Czerwińsk. His eldest son, also Bolesław, died in 1172 aged sixteen. The same year Mieszko III rebelled again, and Barbarossa invaded Poland a second time, ending the revolt with a peace made at Magdeburg. Bolesław died on 5 January 1173. His surviving son Leszek succeeded him in Masovia and Kuyavia, while Mieszko III succeeded him as high duke. Casimir II received Sandomierz and became high duke four years later.
boleslaw-v-the-chaste: Bolesław V was born on 21 June 1226 at Stary Korczyn, the only son of Leszek I the White. His father was killed on 24 November 1227 at the Congress of Gąsawa, and many claimed custody of the child. In 1233 Konrad I of Masovia captured him and his mother Grzymisława, and they were held at Czersk and then Sieciechów until they escaped with the help of the Kraków voivode Klement of Ruszcza. Henry the Bearded then sheltered them at the fortress of Skała. In 1239 he met his bride Kinga, daughter of King Béla IV of Hungary, and began his own government that year.

In 1241 the first Mongol invasion forced him to flee to Hungary, and then to Moravia, before he returned. Konrad entered Kraków on 10 July 1241, but in 1243 the nobility appointed Bolesław as ruler, and the victory at Suchodoły on 25 May 1243 restored his government in Kraków. He then fought Konrad and Konrad's son Casimir for years. He lost the Battle of Zaryszów in 1246, retook Lelów that autumn, and Konrad died on 31 August 1247. A second Mongol invasion in November 1259 destroyed Sandomierz, Lublin and Kraków; he fled, and the Mongols left in February 1260.

He was allied with Hungary, and took part in the Battle on the Marchfeld on 26 August 1278. He sought the Christianisation of the Yotvingians, which failed, and founded a bishopric at Łuków. As his marriage was childless, he adopted Leszek the Black as heir in 1265. He favoured towns: he granted the district of Kraków Magdeburg rights on 5 June 1257, and a year later Nowy Korczyn, among others. Deposits of halite were discovered at Bochnia in 1251, and he prompted the district to mine the salt as a regular source of income. In 1253 he and the bishop of Kraków secured the canonisation of Stanislaus of Szczepanów.

Bolesław died on 7 December 1279 and was buried in the Church of St. Francis of Assisi in Kraków three days later. Jan Długosz recorded that his own people and neighbouring nations grieved him for his modesty and majesty. His nickname, Chaste, came from the vow of chastity he and Kinga took jointly, which left the marriage unconsummated. After his death Kinga entered the Poor Clare convent at Stary Sącz, and Leszek the Black inherited Kraków and Sandomierz.
bolghar: Bolghar stood on the bank of the Volga about 30 km downstream from its confluence with the Kama, some 130 km from modern Kazan, in what is now Spassky District. A small modern town west of it has been called Bolgar since 1991. The city was founded in the 10th century and was the capital of Volga Bulgaria, though Russian incursions and internal fighting forced the Volga Bulgar rulers, called khagans, to move their capital intermittently to Bilyar.

The Mongols conquered Volga Bulgaria in the 13th century. A Russian annalist recorded that in the autumn of 1236 the Tatars sacked Bolgar, killed its people and burned the city. Once Bilyar was destroyed, the Mongol policy against rebuilding capitals meant it did not recover its status. The Mongols ended the existing political structure of the Volga Bolgars, and the realm became decentralised; the new city of Kazan, known as Bolgar-al-Jadid, the new Bolgar, grew in prominence. Tax from regions such as Bolgar, Khwarizm, Crimea and Azerbaijan filled the coffers of the Golden Horde, and the Mongols replaced the rulers of Bolgar and Khwarizm with their own.

The late 14th century brought decline. Bulat-Timur sacked the city in 1361, and in the Muscovite–Volga Bulgars war of 1376 Muscovy and Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal briefly captured it and installed their own customs collector before the Tatars retook it. It was also endangered by Timur during his war with Tokhtamysh. Bolgar remained a Muslim religious centre until the middle of the 16th century, when Tsar Ivan IV conquered the Khanate of Kazan and brought it into the Russian state. Under tsarist rule Russian commoners settled the site, and Tsar Peter the Great issued a ukase to preserve the surviving ruins, the first Russian law aimed at protecting historical heritage.

The Bolgar Historical and Archaeological Complex, the ancient hill fort, was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2014. Tatars call the medieval capital Shahri Bolghar, Persian for the City of Bolghar, and see it as part of their cultural heritage, since Volga Bulgaria was the predecessor of the Khanate of Kazan. Many regard it as an ancient and religious capital alongside Kazan. In Soviet times Muslims who could not make the hajj to Mecca travelled to Bolgar instead, in what was known as the Little Hajj.
bolivia: Bolivia is a landlocked country of 1,098,581 square kilometres in central South America, the fifth largest in the continent. Its geography consists of an Andean region in the west and tropical lowlands in the east and north, and it includes the Altiplano plateau, temperate valleys, the Gran Chaco and part of the Amazon plain. Elevations range from 6,542 metres at Nevado Sajama to nearly 70 metres along the Paraguay River.

In the Andean southwest lie Lake Titicaca, the highest commercially navigable lake in the world and the largest lake in South America, and the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat in the world and an important source of lithium.

Tiwanaku, with its capital at Tiwanaku in western Bolivia, dates back as early as 1500 BCE, when it was a small agricultural village. It grew to urban proportions between 600 and 800 CE and, around 400 CE, began expanding its reach into the Yungas by creating colonies, fostering trade agreements and instituting state cults. As rainfall gradually decreased, food stores shrank and the elites lost power, and Tiwanaku disappeared around 1000 CE. Between 1438 and 1527 the Inca Empire expanded from Cusco into the region.

The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire began in 1524 and was mostly completed by 1533. The territory was known as Charcas, with local government from the Audiencia de Charcas at La Plata, modern Sucre. Potosí, founded in 1545 as a mining town, became the largest city in the New World, with a population exceeding 150,000. After an unsuccessful rebellion in Sucre on 25 May 1809, sixteen years of fighting preceded the establishment of the republic. Antonio José de Sucre chose to create a new state rather than join Peru or the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, and on 6 August 1825 named it in honour of Simón Bolívar.

The name Bolivia was approved on 3 October 1825. In the 19th and early 20th centuries the country lost peripheral territories, among them the Pacific coastal region seized by Chile in 1879. The Bolivian National Revolution of 1952 established universal suffrage and nationalised the tin mines.

La Paz is the seat of government and Sucre the constitutional capital, while Santa Cruz de la Sierra is the largest city. Bolivia is a constitutionally unitary state divided into nine departments, and since 2009 its official name has been the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Spanish is the official and predominant language, and 36 indigenous languages also have official status, of which Guaraní, Aymara and Quechua are most commonly spoken. Major archaeological ruins include Tiwanaku, El Fuerte de Samaipata, Inkallaqta and Iskanwaya.
bolivian-national-revolution: The roots of the revolution lay in the Great Depression, which weakened the mining industry and drew the state into the economy, and in Bolivia's defeat in the Chaco War, which led a generation of writers and politicians to question the existing order. In May 1949 a conflict in the Siglo XX mines of Simón Iturri Patiño ended in a massacre, and on 27 August the MNR led an uprising in four cities, the Civil War of 1949, which the army under General Ovidio Quiroga put down by 1 September.

In May 1951 Víctor Paz Estenssoro of the MNR won the presidential election with wide support among workers, drawn by his anti-imperialist stand. A Government Military Junta was formed at once to keep the party from power, and a year later came the coup.

On 9 April 1952 the police general Antonio Seleme, the Minister of the Interior, led a coup with the support of Hernán Siles Zuazo and the miners' leader Juan Lechín Oquendo. The police and carabineros seized prefectures and radio stations, and arms were handed to MNR civilians and workers. When the army was kept in barracks and the crowds grew beyond control, Seleme withdrew, and Lechín led the fighting in the streets with the slogans of agrarian reform and nationalisation of the mines.

Over the next two days miners from Milluni took the Hunting Air Group and dropped leaflets on the Miraflores barracks, and the rebels captured the Palacio Quemado. The army surrendered on 12 April, after fighting that left 490 dead. Siles Zuazo and Lechín led the government until Paz Estenssoro returned from exile in Buenos Aires a few days later.

The vote was granted on 24 June 1952 to the illiterate, indigenous people and women, raising the electorate from 205,000 in 1951 to 1,125,000 in 1956. The Bolivian Workers' Center, founded on 17 April under Lechín, became the radical wing of the revolution. The army was cut from about 20,000 to 5,000 soldiers and replaced by militias, and the Agrarian Reform Decree was signed at Ucureña on 2 August 1953. The regime's Control Político repressed its opponents, and communists and Falangists were tortured in prisons and camps such as Catavi and Uncía.
bolkiah: Bolkiah was the son of Sultan Sulaiman and came to the throne in 1485 when his father abdicated. In Bornean and Malay tradition he bears the title Nakhoda Ragam, the singing captain, though it has been argued that the title was also given to another Sultan of Brunei and to other figures of the Malay Archipelago. He was said to enjoy playing the lute and drums, and stories remember him as an adventurous navigator who often travelled to inspect his lands. He appears in the Batu Tarsilah and the Silsilah Raja-Raja Berunai, both 19th-century genealogies, and the Spanish Boxer Codex calls him Sultan Salan.

The royal genealogies remember Bolkiah as the sultan who defeated the states of Suluk and Seludang, and his rule is said to have reached present-day Sarawak and Sabah, Manila and the Sulu Archipelago, possibly with parts of Kalimantan as far as Banjarmasin. Through his marriage to Puteri Lela Menchanai, a princess of Sulu, Brunei's influence and the spread of Islam in the region grew further. He is considered the first Sultan of Brunei to have used cannons, having paid forty Javanese blacksmiths to teach metal casting.

Antonio Pigafetta, who came to Brunei in 1521 with the ships of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition under Gonzalo de Espinosa, described a rich court where envoys spoke to the ruler only through a chain of officials. He also recorded a fleet of more than a hundred boats returning from a campaign led by the prince of Luzon, which had restored Brunei's rule over Laoe, or Labai, in western Borneo. Espinosa, fearing an attack, fired on the junks and sank two before he learnt his mistake and apologised. Pigafetta's report bears out the Bruneian oral tradition about the size of the realm.

Bolkiah died on 17 July 1524 and was succeeded by his son Abdul Kahar. His sandstone mausoleum stands on a ridge at Jalan Kota Batu above the Brunei River, two tombstones on eight tiers of carved stone. The tomb itself is unmarked: two steles, probably of the late 17th century, commemorate Sultan Muhammad Ali and Sultan Abdul Mubin, and a simpler slab between them gives Bolkiah's death date, perhaps carved later to support Hugh Low's suggestion that Magellan's expedition came late in Bolkiah's reign. A campus of the Institute of Brunei Technical Education in Seria and Kampong Bolkiah in Bandar Seri Begawan are named after him.
bolko-i-of-opole: Bolko was the third son of Władysław, Duke of Opole-Racibórz, and of Euphemia, daughter of Władysław Odonic, Duke of Greater Poland. Around 1277 his father named him co-ruler despite his place in the family. On his father's death he and his brother Casimir inherited Opole together, while their brothers Mieszko I and Przemysław took Racibórz. The joint rule lasted until 1284, when Bolko kept Opole and Casimir received Bytom.

Unlike his brothers, Bolko worked closely with Henry IV Probus, Duke of Wrocław, backing him in his long conflict with Bishop Thomas II Zaremba. After Leszek II the Black died in 1288, Bolko joined Henry III of Głogów and Przemko of Ścinawa in an attack on Siewierz on 26 February 1289. The battle was extremely bloody; Przemko was killed, and Bolko was seriously wounded and captured by Władysław I the Elbow-high, who released him a year later for a large ransom.

After Henry IV died in 1290, Bolko allied with King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, agreeing at Olomouc on 17 January 1291, with Mieszko and Casimir, to fight any enemy of the Přemyslid dynasty. He attended Wenceslaus's coronation in 1297, represented him in 1298 at the meeting in Mainz that chose Albert I of Habsburg as German king, and was made Starost of Kraków after Wenceslaus became King of Poland in 1300. The extinction of the Přemyslid dynasty in 1306 broke the alliance. In 1312, during the rebellion of the wójt Albert, Bolko came to Lesser Poland but failed to take Wawel Castle, and on returning to Opole he imprisoned Albert.

Bolko was known for his generosity to the Church, supporting the Cistercian monastery at Jemielnica and building the chapel of St. Anna in the Franciscan church of Opole, and he granted Magdeburg Law to many places in his duchy. He died on 14 May 1313 and was buried in the Franciscan church. His wife Agnes, of unknown origin, bore him three sons: Bolesław the Elder, Bolko II and Albert.
bolko-i-the-strict: Bolko was the second son of Bolesław II the Bald, Duke of Legnica, by his first wife Hedwig, a daughter of Henry I, Count of Anhalt. He appears rarely in the chronicles before his father's death, probably because he was still young, and may have fought in the Battle of Stolec in 1277. After Bolesław II died on 26 December 1278, their elder brother Henry V the Fat kept Legnica, and Bolko's younger brother Bernard the Lightsome came to hold Lwówek; the two younger brothers signed a treaty of mutual inheritance around 1281.

To guard against Henry IV Probus, Duke of Wrocław, Bolko allied himself with the Margraves of Brandenburg and married Beatrice, daughter of Margrave Otto V the Tall, in Berlin on 4 October 1284. The alliance drew him into conflict with King Rudolf I of Habsburg and Henry IV. Under that treaty he inherited Lwówek when Bernard died childless in 1286, and in the later 1280s he moved closer to King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, who gave him the castle of Chełmsko Śląskie on the Bohemian frontier.

After Henry IV's death in 1290 Bolko helped his brother Henry V hold Wrocław, at the price of the towns of Świdnica, Ząbkowice, Ziębice and Strzelin. He fortified the frontier towns of Świdnica, Wleń, Strzegom and Kamienna Góra, and in 1294 Bishop Jan Romka excommunicated him and laid his lands under interdict when he occupied the bishop's castles. In the war with Wenceslaus II that began in 1295, the Bohemian army was stopped at Kamienna Góra, and Bolko placed his lands under the protection of Pope Boniface VIII. Peace followed, probably early in 1297. As regent for Henry V's sons from 1296 he repelled Henry III of Głogów and took Chojnów and Bolesławiec, and on 21 March 1299 he was recognised as a papal vassal.

Bolko died suddenly on 9 November 1301 and was buried in Krzeszów Abbey. Because his sons were minors, his brother-in-law Herman, Margrave of Brandenburg-Salzwedel, became their guardian. Bolko encouraged German settlers on his lands and was a patron of the Cistercian movement, and at his instigation an unnamed priest composed an 8,000-line Middle High German poem on Ludwig III, Count of Thuringia. His daughter Beatrice married Louis IV, later Holy Roman Emperor.
bolko-ii-of-ziebice: Bolko II was the fourth son of Bolko I the Strict and his wife Beatrix, daughter of Otto V the Long, Margrave of Brandenburg-Salzwedel. He was named after his eldest brother Bolko, who had died two days before his birth. When his father died in 1301 he was not yet two years old, and the children were placed in the care of their mother and the guardianship of their uncle Herman, Margrave of Brandenburg-Salzwedel, until 1305, when the eldest surviving brother, Bernard, took over the government.

For fear that the duchy would be split up, Bolko II was at first meant for a career in the Church. He resisted strongly, and in 1322 Bernard gave him the district of Ziębice as a duchy of his own. That year the two brothers also joined the Teutonic Knights on an expedition against Lithuania.

Short of money, Bolko II seized goods from the monasteries of Henryków and Kamieniec Ząbkowicki, and in 1329 he attacked the suite of the papal legate Pietro di Alverni. The kings of Poland and Bohemia intervened with the support of almost all the Silesian dukes; Bolko II was defeated and excommunicated by Nanker, Bishop of Wrocław, until he paid large sums to the legate and the monasteries.

In 1335 Charles of Luxembourg, Margrave of Moravia and heir to Bohemia, attacked Ziębice because Bolko II refused to pay homage; the duchy lay on the shortest route between Prague and Wrocław. Bolko II defeated a small force and captured 150 Bohemian knights, asking only a small ransom for them, though he could not prevent Charles's army from laying waste to his lands. Once King Casimir III the Great of Poland withdrew from the Silesian dukes, Bolko II's hope of resisting Bohemia was gone, and his homage of 1336 meant that the duchy would pass to the Bohemian crown when his male line died out.

His debts, made worse by his lavish spending, forced him in 1337 to pledge Ząbkowice to Charles of Luxembourg and then Strzelin and Kąty Wrocławskie, until he held only Ziębice itself; he nonetheless cared for the town's economic growth. By 1321 he had married Bonne de Savoie, also called Guta, widow of the Hungarian nobleman Matthew IV Csák, and they had a daughter, Margareta, a nun at Strzelin. He died at Ziębice on 11 June 1341 and was buried at Henryków.
bolko-ii-the-small: Bolko was the eldest son of Bernard, Duke of Świdnica, and Kunigunde, daughter of King Władysław I the Elbow-high of Poland. Like his grandfather he was small of stature, and contemporary sources already called him the Small. On his father's death in 1326 he succeeded with his younger brother Henry II as co-ruler. Both were teenagers, so their uncles Bolko II of Ziębice and Henry I of Jawor and their mother helped them govern. After Kunigunde's death in 1331 Bolko ruled alone.

When King John of Bohemia demanded his homage in 1329, as almost every other Piast ruler in Silesia gave it, Bolko refused, as did his brother-in-law Przemko II of Głogów. He sought support at the court of Charles Robert of Hungary, from his grandfather in Poland and from Emperor Louis IV. John invaded Silesia in 1331 but in the end annexed only Głogów. In 1338 Bolko married Agnes, daughter of Leopold I of the Habsburgs, rivals of the Luxembourgs, and on 1 January 1345 his mediation produced an alliance of the Wittelsbachs, Poland and Hungary.

In the war that followed, John invaded Bolko's lands; Bolko held Świdnica, lost Kamienna Góra in 1345 and retook it in 1348 with troops disguised as merchants. Peace was signed at Namysłów on 22 November 1348, and Albert II of Austria reconciled Bolko with Charles IV on 16 August 1350. In 1346 he had inherited Jawor and Lwówek from his uncle Henry I. On 27 May 1353 his niece and heir Anna married Charles IV in Buda, and she was later crowned Queen of Bohemia, German Queen and Empress.

The alliance with the Luxembourgs and the wealth of his duchy let Bolko buy land from poorer dukes: the gold mine of Złoty Stok and half of Brzeg and Oława in 1358, Siewierz for 2,300 fines, half of Głogów through his sister Constance in 1361, and in 1364, with the emperor, lands near Lusatia for 21,000 fine silver. That year he attended the Congress of Kraków and the Wierzynek Feast.

Bolko died on 28 July 1368 and was buried in Grüssau Abbey. He was the last independent Silesian duke of the Piast line begun by Władysław II the Exile. His widow held his lands until 1392, when Wenceslaus IV, son of Charles IV and Anna, joined them to the Crown of Bohemia.
bolkow-castle: The castle stands on Castle Hill at Bolków, about 30 kilometres north-west of Wałbrzych, where the Nysa Szalona river cuts the hillside into a sharp precipice with a drop of 90 metres; the gentler eastern slope is taken up by the town. An upland stronghold covering 7,600 square metres, it is among the largest castles in Silesia and one of the largest fortresses of the Duchy of Świdnica-Jawor.

The castle is first mentioned in 1277 by Prince Bolesław II of Legnica. Bolko I the Strict strengthened a number of strongholds to control the passes from Bohemia into Silesia through the Sudeten range, which helped the duchy keep its independence until the end of the 14th century, longer than any other Silesian principality. In the mid-14th century the castle was joined to the town walls, and it was enlarged under Bernard of Świdnica and Bolko II the Small; historians hold that for about a century it served as a treasury.

Bolko II, who was childless, left his lands to his niece Anna and her husband Charles IV, and in 1392 the castle passed to the Bohemian crown. The town was destroyed in the Hussite attacks, but the castle was not taken. In 1463 King George of Poděbrady imprisoned the robber knight Hans von Tschirnhaus there.

Under Emperor Ferdinand I the castle was given for life to the Bishop of Wrocław, and in 1539 and 1540 the Lombard architect Jakub Parr rebuilt it, enlarging the fortified area with courtyards, walls and bastions and bringing Renaissance elements into its defences. It later passed to Matthias von Logau and in 1596 to the Zedlitz family. Besieged in 1640, it was taken by the Swedish army in 1646.

Cistercian monks from Krzeszów bought the castle in 1703, and it has been uninhabited since. It became Prussian state property in 1810, and in 1885 part of its walls was pulled down for road repairs. In 1922 the House of Women was rebuilt as a youth hostel and regional museum.
bologna: Bologna lies on the edge of the Po Plain at the foot of the Apennine Mountains, where the valleys of the Reno and Savena rivers meet. Its two main watercourses flow directly to the sea, so the town stands outside the drainage basin of the River Po. It is the capital and largest city of the Emilia-Romagna region in northern Italy.

Traces of human habitation go back to the 3rd millennium BCE, with significant settlements from about the 9th century BCE, in the Villanovan culture. Etruscan influence reached the area in the 7th to 6th centuries BCE, and by the end of the 6th century the Etruscan city of Felsina stood on the site. By the 4th century BCE it was held by the Gaulish Boii, and in 196 BCE it became a Roman colony and municipium named Bonōnia. In the last years of the Western Roman Empire the Goths repeatedly sacked it. According to ancient chronicles, Bishop Petronius then rebuilt the ruined town and founded the basilica of Saint Stephen. He is still revered as the patron saint of Bologna.

In the Middle Ages Bologna was a free municipality and later a signoria, and was among the largest European cities by population. Papal rule lasted from 1506 to 1796, a period that historians have generally judged one of severe decline, though the 1500s brought major developments. Emperor Charles V was crowned there in 1530, the last emperor to be crowned by the pope. In 1564 the Archiginnasio, the main building of the university, was built, and the Bolognese School of painters, including Annibale Carracci, Domenichino and Guercino, arose in these years. The city then had ninety-six convents, more than any other Italian city.

Napoleon entered Bologna on 19 June 1796, and the city passed through the Cispadane Republic and the Cisalpine Republic to the Kingdom of Italy. The Congress of Vienna of 1815 restored it to the Papal States. Papal rule was contested in the uprisings of 1831, when the rebel provinces planned to unite with Bologna as their capital; Pope Gregory XVI asked for Austrian help, and Austrian forces defeated the rebellion by 26 April.

The University of Bologna, conventionally said to have been founded in 1088 by the glossators Irnerius and Pepo, is the oldest university in continuous operation. Its Studium began as a loosely organised system in which each master collected fees from students individually, and colleges were founded to support students of a particular nationality. It attracted scholars from Italy and across Europe and was an important centre of intellectual life in the Middle Ages. The city is known for its towers, churches and long porticoes, and in 2021 UNESCO recognised the porticoes as a World Heritage Site.
bolsa-familia: The forerunner was Bolsa Escola, a payment conditional only on school attendance, pioneered in Brasília by its governor Cristovam Buarque and copied by other municipalities and states. In 2001 President Fernando Henrique Cardoso made it federal. In 2003 Lula joined Bolsa Escola with Bolsa Alimentação, Cartão Alimentação and Auxílio Gás, all parts of Cardoso's Rede de Proteção Social, and created a new Ministry for Social Development and Confronting Hunger to run it. The merger cut administrative costs and simplified matters for families and officials. Mexico's Oportunidades had been the first nationwide programme of the kind.

The money went preferably to the female head of a household, through a Citizen Card working like a debit card and issued by the state savings bank Caixa Econômica Federal; the names of recipients and the sums paid were published online. Municipal governments acted as the federal government's agents, bypassing the state governors. A family that failed the school attendance rule five times in a row lost its benefit. In 2006 the cost was estimated at about 0.5 per cent of GDP, covering about 11.2 million families, and in 2011 the programme reached 26 per cent of the population. The programme is reputed to have helped Lula win the 2006 election.

On 30 December 2021 President Jair Bolsonaro signed into law Auxílio Brasil, formally ending Bolsa Família. After his re-election in 2022 Lula restored the old name, and the second version was launched in 2023 with a promise of transfers of at least 600 reais.

Opponents claimed that the programme discouraged work and bought the votes of the poor, and Lula's critics accused it of using revenues of the CPMF tax at the expense of public health. A World Bank official, Bénédicte de la Brière, found that the transfers did not reduce adult work. A UNDP study found that over 80 per cent of the benefits went to families in poverty and credited the programme with about 20 per cent of the fall in inequality since 2001, and a 2018 study linked wider coverage with lower suicide rates between 2004 and 2012.
bolsena: Bolsena is a town and comune in the province of Viterbo in northern Lazio, on the eastern shore of Lake Bolsena.
