It lies 10 kilometres north-north-west of Montefiascone and 36 kilometres north-west of Viterbo. The ancient Via Cassia, today's highway SR143, follows the lakeshore for some distance and passes through the town. Bolsena calls itself the city of the Eucharistic miracle, from which the solemnity of Corpus Domini was extended to the whole Catholic Church.

The town is fairly certainly the successor of the Roman town of Volsinii, sometimes called Volsinii Novi to tell it from the Etruscan city. Scholars are sharply divided over whether that Etruscan city, Velzna or Velsuna, sometimes called Volsinii Veteres, stood here or at Orvieto, 20 kilometres to the north-east. George Dennis pointed out that Bolsena has no Etruscan characteristics: Etruscan cities were built on defensible crags, which the hill of its castle is not. Pliny the Elder wrote of a bolt from Mars falling on Bolsena, which he called the richest town in Tuscany, and said that the city was burned up by it. Dennis took the population to have moved to a new site, probably Bolsena itself, which kept the old name.

A number of Etruscan tombs have been found near the town. Their funerary objects are now in Italy and abroad, and the British Museum has a fine collection. The United States Navy established a naval air station at Bolsena on 21 February 1918 to operate seaplanes during the First World War, and the base closed shortly after the armistice at Compiègne.

Bolsena is known for a miracle said to have occurred in the Basilica of Santa Cristina in 1263, when a Bohemian priest, in doubt about the doctrine of transubstantiation, reported bleeding from the host he had consecrated at Mass. Orvieto Cathedral was eventually built to commemorate it and to house the Corporal of Bolsena in a reliquary made by the Sienese goldsmith Ugolino di Vieri in 1337 to 1338. A fresco by Raphael and his school in the Vatican Stanze, The Mass at Bolsena, depicts the event. Other sites include the Renaissance Palazzo del Drago, designed by Raffaele da Montelupo and Simone Mosca, and a nearby rock formation known as the thrown stones.
bolsheviks: The split began with Lenin's support for a smaller party of professional revolutionaries, set out in his pamphlet What Is to Be Done?, written in 1901. At the Second Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, held in Brussels and then London in August 1903, Lenin and Julius Martov disagreed over membership rules. Lenin, supported by Georgi Plekhanov, wanted to limit membership to those who supported the party full-time and obeyed its elected leadership; Martov would admit anyone who recognised the programme and gave regular help.

The factions were first called hard and soft. Lenin's side won the votes on most important issues and so came to be called Bolsheviks, from the Russian word for majority, and Martov's side Mensheviks, from the word for minority, though Martov's supporters had won the vote on membership and the Congress was in the end evenly split.

Between 1903 and 1912 the balance between the factions shifted and members changed sides; Plekhanov had parted ways with the Bolsheviks by 1904, and Leon Trotsky joined them only in August 1917. The Bolsheviks played a relatively minor part in the 1905 Revolution, although the Moscow Soviet was dominated by them. Attempts at reunion in 1906 and 1910 failed. In January 1912 a Prague conference of the Bolsheviks alone expelled the Mensheviks and declared the faction an independent party, the RSDLP(b).

After the February Revolution of 1917 Lenin returned to Russia and issued his April Theses, calling for no support for the Provisional Government and all power to the soviets. During the summer large numbers of radicalized workers joined, and the Bolsheviks planned the October Revolution that overthrew the government. They at first governed in coalition with the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries but increasingly centralized power and suppressed opposition during the Russian Civil War, and after 1921 the party was the sole legal party.

The Bolsheviks rested on the Leninist principles of vanguardism and democratic centralism. In 1907 most members were young: 22 percent were under 20 and 37 percent between 20 and 24. By 1905 some 62 percent were industrial workers, and 78 percent were Russian and 10 percent Jewish in 1907. Membership was 8,400 in 1905 and 46,100 by 1907.

Lenin held that revolutions must be led by people who gave their whole lives to the cause, and he paid them salaries. Unlike the Mensheviks, who relied on membership dues, the Bolsheviks also raised money through robberies, among them a bank robbery in 1907 that yielded over 250,000 roubles.
bolzano: Bolzano covers 52.3 square kilometres in the basin where the Sarntal, Eisacktal and Adige valleys and their rivers, the Talfer, Eisack and Adige, meet. In the Middle Ages the two main Alpine crossings, the Via Claudia Augusta and the Brenner route over the Brenner Pass, met there, which made the city very important for trade. The centre lies 262 metres above sea level, and the valley's shelter from the main Alps makes temperatures much warmer year-round than in similar valley cities north of the range.

In ancient times the area was a marshy region inhabited by the Raetian Isarci people. The Romans built a military settlement, Pons Drusi, named after the general Nero Claudius Drusus, who conquered the area in 15 BCE. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II conferred the area on the bishops of Trent, and in the late 12th century the bishop founded a market town, which became an important trading post on the Augsburg-Venice route. Meinhard II, Count of Tyrol, conquered Bolzano in 1277. The County of Tyrol passed to the Austrian House of Habsburg in 1363, and in 1462 the bishops resigned all rights of jurisdiction over the town.

Italian control of South Tyrol was internationally recognised in 1919. In 1910 the then separate municipalities of Bolzano, Gries and Zwölfmalgreien had 26,558 inhabitants declaring German as their daily language and 1,605 Italian. Under fascism Italian speakers became the majority. During the Second World War Bolzano held a Nazi transit camp for Jews and political prisoners. The Gruber-De Gasperi Agreement of September 1946 guaranteed the German-speaking population complete equality of rights and autonomous powers.

Bolzano is the capital of South Tyrol, officially the province of Bolzano/Bozen, in the autonomous region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, and its largest city. Three languages are spoken in South Tyrol: Italian, German and Ladin. The Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, founded in 1997, teaches in German, Italian and English. The Via dei Portici has medieval arcades along its whole length, and the Gothic cathedral was begun in 1184. The South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology shows the Ötzi mummy.
bombay-state: Under the British Raj the parts of India's western coast under direct British rule formed the Bombay Presidency. At independence and partition in 1947 Bombay Province stayed in India, while Sind Province went to Pakistan. When India became a republic in 1950 the territory was restructured as Bombay State. It took in princely states of the former Deccan States Agency and the Baroda, Western India and Gujarat States Agency, among them Kolhapur in the Deccan and Baroda and the Dangs in Gujarat.

The States Reorganisation Act of 1 November 1956 redrew the state on linguistic lines. The Kannada-speaking districts of Belgaum (except Chandgad taluka), Bijapur, Dharwar and North Canara went to Mysore State, while Bombay gained the Marathi-speaking Marathwada region of Hyderabad State, the Marathi-speaking Vidarbha region of Madhya Pradesh, and the Gujarati-speaking states of Saurashtra and Kutch. Its inhabitants called it Maha Dwibhashi Rajya, the great bilingual state.

The States Reorganisation Committee, against the wishes of Jawaharlal Nehru, had recommended a bilingual state with Bombay as its capital, while in the Lok Sabha debates of 1955 the Congress party had asked for the city to become an autonomous city-state. In the 1957 elections the Samyukta Maharashtra movement opposed both plans and demanded Bombay as the capital of Maharashtra. Its protests, in which 107 people were killed by police, and the Mahagujarat Movement led to the division of the state on 1 May 1960.

The Gujarati-speaking areas became the state of Gujarat. Maharashtra, with Bombay as its capital, joined the Marathi-speaking areas of Bombay State, eight districts from the Central Provinces and Berar, five districts from Hyderabad State and the princely states lying between them. Three chief ministers led Bombay after independence: Balasaheb Gangadhar Kher, Morarji Desai from 1952 to 1956 and Yashwantrao Chavan from 1956 to 1960, and on the division the office of Governor of Bombay became that of Governor of Maharashtra.
bon: Little is known about the religion of ancient Tibet before Buddhism, and scholars disagree about its nature. The term bon seems originally to have meant a kind of priest, among them priests of the Yarlung kings, who propitiated local spirits and guided the dead through ceremonies for a good afterlife; the most elaborate rites concerned the kings, who had special tombs. This religion was marginalised as Buddhism arrived, and Buddhist polemics against it survive in manuscripts from Dunhuang.

Yungdrung Bon, the Eternal Bon, is a living tradition that developed in Tibet in the later dissemination of Buddhism. The scholar Geoffrey Samuel traces both it and the Nyingma school of Buddhism to hereditary ritual practitioners who drew on Buddhist tantra and earlier court and village rituals. A later movement, New Bon, which began in eastern Tibet with the discoveries of Tulku Loden Nyingpo (1360–1385), is closely related to both.

Bonpos, the followers of Bon, hold that the religion began in the kingdom of Zhangzhung around Mount Kailash and was brought from there to Tibet. They name its founder as the Buddha Tonpa Shenrab Miwoche, whose historicity no available source establishes. Tradition holds that he reached Buddhahood in a western land, Olmo Lungring, several hundred years before Sakyamuni Buddha. Its symbol, the yungdrung, a left-facing swastika, stands for indestructibility and eternity and holds a place like that of the vajra in Tibetan Buddhism.

Bon teachings closely resemble those of Tibetan Buddhism, especially the Nyingma school. The world is seen as a place of suffering, with karma, rebirth and six realms of existence, and liberation comes from insight into an ultimate nature called the bon body. Its teachings are arranged in the Nine Ways, and its canon has a Kanjur and a Tenjur, and a large body of termas, treasure texts held to have been hidden in a time of persecution and found from the 10th century.

Tibetan Buddhist writers tended to portray Bon in a hostile light, and early Western studies drew on their sources and treated Bon as the pre-Buddhist religion that Buddhism overcame. The scholar David Snellgrove, who worked with Bonpo masters and translated Bonpo texts, led Western scholarship from the 1960s to treat Bon as a tradition in its own right. Some scholars, such as Snellgrove, see Bon as a heterodox form of Buddhism; John Powers writes that Bon developed as a self-conscious religious system only under Buddhist influence. Bon suffered in the Cultural Revolution as Tibetan Buddhism did. Its monasteries were allowed to rebuild after 1980, and Menri Monastery was refounded at Dolanji in Himachal Pradesh, India.
bonaire: Bonaire is one of the ABC islands, with Aruba and Curaçao, about 80 kilometres off the coast of Venezuela. It is 38.6 kilometres long from north to south and 5 to 8 kilometres wide, with a land area of 288 square kilometres. Geologists believe the ABC islands were formed about 90 million years ago along the Leeward Antilles Ridge, where the Caribbean plate collided with the South American plate. The climate is warm, dry and windy, which favours cacti and other desert plants. The islet of Klein Bonaire lies 800 metres to the west, and the coast is fringed by a coral reef.

The earliest evidence of human habitation on Bonaire is at Lagun and dates to about 3400 years ago, when people lived as semi-nomadic hunter-gatherers and fishers. The Caquetío, a people from Venezuela, arrived from South America around 500 CE, and their rock paintings and petroglyphs survive in caves at Spelonk, Onima, Ceru Pungi and Ceru Crita-Cabai. Alonso de Ojeda reached the area in 1499, accompanied by Amerigo Vespucci and Juan de la Cosa. Because the islands had no known metal deposits the Spanish thought them useless, and in 1515 they enslaved the Caquetío to work in the copper mines of Hispaniola, perhaps between 500 and 2,000 people.

From 1623 ships of the Dutch West India Company called at Bonaire for meat, water and wood. The Dutch, having lost Sint Maarten to the Spanish during the Eighty Years War, attacked Curaçao, Bonaire and Aruba, and conquered Bonaire in March 1636. They built Fort Oranje in 1639. In 1868 and 1870 much government land was auctioned, mostly to wealthy merchants of Curaçao who did not live there; the soil is poor for crops, and only salt extraction proved economically attractive, with aloe, maize, charcoal and goats on some holdings. On 10 October 2010 the Netherlands Antilles was dissolved and Bonaire became a special municipality of the Netherlands, a public body under article 134 of the Dutch Constitution.

Bonaire's seat is Kralendijk, and Rincon is the oldest settlement. Dutch is the official language, but most inhabitants use Papiamentu as their main language, and about 68 percent are Roman Catholic. The island has been a nature reserve for decades: Washington Slagbaai National Park was established in 1969, and the Bonaire National Marine Park, covering the whole coastline, in 1979. Several wetlands are recognised under the Ramsar Convention, and the Pekelmeer flamingo reserve is the most important breeding site in the Southern Caribbean. Salt pans cover about 10 percent of the island, and salt is still produced there.
bonar-law: Andrew Bonar Law was born on 16 September 1858 in Kingston, now Five Rivers, New Brunswick, the son of the Reverend James Law, a minister of the Free Church of Scotland, and Eliza Kidston Law. His ancestry was Scottish and Irish, mainly Ulster Scots. He was named after Andrew Bonar, a biographer of the preacher Robert Murray McCheyne, whom his mother admired, and was always called Bonar by family and friends. He moved to Scotland in 1870, left school at sixteen to work in the iron industry, and became a partner in the iron merchant William Jacks' firm. He turned it into one of the most profitable in the Glasgow and Scottish markets and was a wealthy man by thirty.

Law won the Conservative seat of Glasgow Blackfriars and Hutchesontown in the general election of 1900, the khaki election, with a majority of 1,000, and moved to London. His first major speech, on 22 April 1902, concerned tariff reform: he argued for an imperial customs union. He lost his seat in 1906 but was returned at a by-election in Dulwich. After Joseph Chamberlain's stroke in 1906 he became the principal spokesman for tariff reform in Balfour's Shadow Cabinet. His wife died on 31 October 1909.

In 1911, after he was made a Privy Councillor, he became Conservative leader because the two front-runners, Walter Long and Austen Chamberlain, withdrew rather than risk splitting the party. He opposed the Third Home Rule Bill, and as the child of an Ulster family he believed the gap between Ulster Unionism and Irish Nationalism could never be crossed. On 30 July 1914 he agreed with H. H. Asquith to suspend the Home Rule issue for the war. He joined the Coalition Government as Secretary of State for the Colonies in May 1915, and later served as Chancellor of the Exchequer under David Lloyd George. Ill health forced his resignation as party leader in 1921.

By 1922 the coalition had become unpopular with Conservatives, who voted to end it. Law became leader again and prime minister, and won a clear majority at the 1922 general election. His brief premiership included negotiation with the United States over Britain's war loans.

Diagnosed with terminal throat cancer and unable to speak in Parliament, Law resigned on 20 May 1923, and King George V sent for Stanley Baldwin. He died in London later that year, aged 65. He was the first prime minister born outside Britain or Ireland and the shortest-serving of the 20th century, and the first to be cremated. At his funeral at Westminster Abbey, Asquith remarked that they were burying the Unknown Prime Minister next to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a phrase that gave the title of Robert Blake's biography.
bonaventure: Bonaventure was born at Civita di Bagnoregio, not far from Viterbo, then part of the Papal States. Almost nothing is known of his childhood except the names of his parents, Giovanni di Fidanza and Maria di Ritella. He reported that in his youth he was saved from an untimely death by the prayers of Francis of Assisi, which was the main reason he later wrote the life of Francis. After entering the Franciscan Order he studied at the University of Paris, possibly under Alexander of Hales and certainly under John of Rochelle. He became a friend of Thomas Aquinas.

After defending his order against the anti-mendicant party he was elected Minister General of the Franciscans. On 24 November 1265 he was chosen Archbishop of York, but he was never consecrated and resigned in October 1266. The General Chapter of Narbonne in 1260 forbade publication of any work outside the order without permission. Modern writers have judged Roger Bacon's superiors harshly because of it, but the ban was general and aimed at Gerard of Borgo San Donnino, whose Introduction to the Eternal Gospel had been judged heretical.

Bonaventure helped secure the election of Pope Gregory X, who made him Cardinal Bishop of Albano and insisted that he attend the Second Council of Lyon in 1274. There, after contributions that led to a union of the Greek and Latin churches, he died suddenly and in suspicious circumstances. The 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia has citations suggesting poison, but the 2003 New Catholic Encyclopedia does not mention it.

His major work is the Commentary on the Sentences, written at his superiors' command when he was twenty-seven. Others include The Mind's Road to God, the Breviloquium and, for fellow Franciscans, The Tree of Life and The Triple Way. His philosophy is deeply influenced by Augustine, with Aristotelian principles added. He thought of Christ as the one true master, offering knowledge that begins in faith, develops through reason and is perfected by mystical union with God. Like Aquinas he vigorously opposed the Aristotelian notion that the world is eternal.
bondoukou: Bondoukou lies in north-eastern Côte d'Ivoire, 420 kilometres north-east of Abidjan, close to the border with Ghana and just across it from the Ghanaian town of Sampa. It stands at the junction of the main A1 highway with the roads to Sorobango in the north and to Ghana in the east. It is the seat of the Zanzan District and of the Gontougo Region. The area was originally inhabited by the Gbin, Loro and Nafana clans.

The town was founded by Soninke Wangara merchants, the ancestors of the Dyula, who made it a trading centre; it became the premier settlement of the Bighu Juula after the older town of Bighu was destroyed by the Ashanti Empire. It was conquered by the Abron, an Akan people, and became the economic hub of their kingdom of Gyaaman.

On 13 November 1888 the French officer Treich-Laplène signed a protectorate treaty with the Abron king of Bondoukou. Between September 1895 and July 1897 the town fell to Samori, who did not destroy it, as he did other centres, but deposed the Abron in favour of the Muslim Dyula.

The French included it in French West Africa in 1899. By the end of the colonial period it had shrunk to a large village, eclipsed by the nearby administrative centre of Loti. In 1964 it was made the administrative centre of its region again. In 1980 it became the home of the first secondary school strikes by students opposed to the government of the PDCI-RDA, and during the Ivorian Civil War it lay on the dividing line between government and rebel zones and became the main north-eastern base of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire.

Trade has given Bondoukou a diverse population. Its walled old city, the Medina, has neighbourhoods named for groups who came along long-distance trade routes, among them the Donzoso of the Donzo-Ouattara Dyula, the Jiminiso of the Timité Dyula, who hold the most prominent Muslim schools, the Hausa quarter of Malagaso and the mostly Christian Bambaraso.

Because of influences from the north, many of its mosques are in the Sudanic style also found at Timbuktu and Djenné, and the town became a centre of religious learning. It is also the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Bondoukou. Its buildings include the house used by the French explorer Louis Gustave Binger, Samori's headquarters, and the Limamisso and Kamagaya mosques. Its festivals include a yam harvest festival and, at the end of Ramadan, the Sakaraboutou warriors' parade and the Kourouby women's parade.
bone-regency: Bone lies on the east coast of South Sulawesi, with 174 kilometres of coastline and a land area of 4,559 square kilometres, of which 88,499 hectares are rice fields. It borders Wajo to the north, Sinjai to the south, Soppeng, Maros and Barru among its neighbours to the west, and the Gulf of Bone to the east, where it has a sea border with Sulawesi Tenggara. The climate is tropical, with a wet season from April to September and a dry season from October to March, and temperatures between 26 and 34 °C.

The regency was home to the Bone Kingdom, an adat-based Bugis kingdom founded by ManurungngE Rimatajang in 1330. Bone later joined the kingdoms of Wajo and Soppeng in an alliance for mutual defence known as LaMumpatue Ri Timurung.

In 1605, during the reign of the tenth king of Bone, Latenri Tuppu Matinro Ri Sidenreng, Islam reached Bone and changed its culture, including the names of many parts of the royal system. The state enjoyed a period of prosperity in the middle of the 17th century.
In May 1950 people in Watampone demonstrated against the royal family and against Bone's membership of the State of East Indonesia. The sultan stepped down, and Bone joined Indonesia that year.

Watampone, the administrative centre, takes in three of the regency's 27 districts, and the regency had 801,775 inhabitants at the 2020 census. Most of its people are Muslim, and there are also some churches in Watampone. Most work as farmers, growers and fishermen; seaweed, rice and fish are its main products, and along the Gulf of Bone seaweed, crabs, shrimp and milkfish are the chief sources of income. Of its five harbours the largest is Bajoe. Its coat of arms shows a harrow, an anchor, a kris, rice and a cotton plant on a blue shield.
boniface-i-marquis-of-montferrat: Boniface was the third son of William V of Montferrat and Judith of Babenberg, and a younger brother of William Longsword and of Conrad I of Jerusalem. He became marquis in 1192, after the deaths of his father in 1191 and of Conrad, the newly elected king of Jerusalem. A war lasting fifteen years against the neighbouring communes of Asti and Alessandria went badly for the dynasty. In 1194 he helped lead Henry VI's expedition to Sicily. His court was one of the most prestigious centres of chivalric culture and troubadour song, with his friend Raimbaut de Vaqueiras, Peire Vidal, Gaucelm Faidit and Arnaut de Mareuil among its guests.

When Count Theobald III of Champagne, the first leader of the Fourth Crusade, died in 1201, Boniface was chosen in his place. He was an experienced soldier, and the crusade was a chance to restore his dynasty's reputation after defeat at home. At Christmas 1201 he met his cousin Philip of Swabia at Hagenau, together with Alexios IV Angelos, son of the deposed Byzantine emperor Isaac II, and they discussed using the crusading army to restore Alexios to his throne. Pope Innocent III told Boniface not to attack any Christians, including the Byzantines.

The army owed a debt to Enrico Dandolo, the doge of Venice, who had provided its fleet, and Dandolo became the crusade's true war leader, with Boniface as only a figurehead. The crusaders attacked Zara, and in 1203 the fleet sailed for Constantinople. After the conquest of 1204 Boniface was assumed to be the new emperor by western knights and Byzantine citizens alike, but the Venetians vetoed him, fearing that he already had too many connections in the empire, and chose Baldwin of Flanders. Boniface founded the Kingdom of Thessalonica. Later sources say he based his claim on a grant of Thessalonica to his brother Renier in 1180.

In 1205 Boniface married Margaret of Hungary, widow of Isaac II Angelos, and their son Demetrius became king of Thessalonica. His son William VI by his first marriage, to Elena del Bosco, succeeded him as marquis of Montferrat. Boniface was killed in an ambush by the Vlach on 4 September 1207, and his head was sent to the Bulgarian Tsar Kaloyan. Raimbaut de Vaqueiras, who had followed him east, probably died with him, since he composed no lament for his lord.
bonn: Bonn lies on both banks of the Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia, about 24 kilometres south-south-east of Cologne, in the southernmost part of the Rhine-Ruhr region. It covers 141.2 square kilometres, and almost three quarters of the city lie on the left bank. In 1969 the independent towns of Bad Godesberg and Beuel and several villages were incorporated into Bonn, producing a city more than twice as large as before. Earlier, on 1 June 1904, Poppelsdorf, Endenich, Kessenich and Dottendorf had been incorporated.

People lived in the area long before the city. Evidence includes a 14,000-year-old double burial at Oberkassel and a trench and wooden palisades on the Venusberg dating to about 4080 BCE. The Roman governor Agrippa had settled the Ubii there in 38 BCE, and in 12 BCE the first fortified Roman camp on the Rhine was built. In 1989 the city marked its 2,000th anniversary, counting from that camp. Bonn was later part of the Roman province Germania Inferior.

From 1597 to 1794 it was the capital of the Electorate of Cologne and the residence of the Archbishops and Prince-electors of Cologne. The Altes Rathaus, in Rococo style, was built in 1737 under Clemens August of Bavaria, and the Kurfürstliches Schloss, the prince-elector's residence, is now the main building of the University of Bonn.

Bonn served as the capital of West Germany from 1949 until 1990 and as the seat of government of reunified Germany until 1999, when the government moved to Berlin. Historians often call the period of West Germany's capital there the Bonn Republic. The Basic Law, Germany's constitution, was made in the city. A political compromise after reunification, the Berlin-Bonn Act, kept a significant federal presence in Bonn.

Bonn is a federal city, with the title Bundesstadt, and a population exceeding 320,000. It holds the primary seats of six federal ministries and twenty federal authorities, and the global headquarters of Deutsche Post DHL and Deutsche Telekom. Twenty United Nations institutions have their seats there, among them the secretariats of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention to Combat Desertification. Beethoven's birthplace stands in Bonngasse near the market place, and he was baptized at St Remigius.
bonnie-blue-flag: The banner of a single five-pointed white star on a blue field is considered the first lone star flag in U.S. history. The name Bonnie Blue dates only from 1861, but the flag is identical with the banner of the Republic of West Florida. On 10 December 1836 the Congress of the Republic of Texas adopted a flag later called the Burnet flag, a large golden star on an azure field, inspired by the West Florida flag. Variants with a white star, virtually identical to the Bonnie Blue, were common, and these flags, with that of the Fredonian Rebellion, are ancestral to the modern flag of Texas.

When Mississippi seceded from the Union in January 1861, a flag with a single white star on a blue field was flown from the dome of its capitol. Harry Macarthy, an Irish Ulster-Scots entertainer, wrote the song The Bonnie Blue Flag early in 1861 and helped make the flag a symbol of independence, and some seceding Southern states took the motif of a white star on blue into their new state flags.

The Bonnie Blue served as an unofficial flag in the early months of 1861 and flew above the Confederate batteries that first opened fire on Fort Sumter, beginning the American Civil War. Confederate units from Florida, the Fernandina Volunteers among them, carried regimental flags influenced by it, with a Burnet star on a blue field, into combat.

In 2006 the state of Louisiana passed a law designating the Bonnie Blue flag the official flag of the Republic of West Florida Historic Region, formally linking the name to the West Florida banner. In 2007 one of six known Bonnie Blue flags of the Civil War era, carried by the Confederate 3rd Texas Cavalry and later shown at the 1936 Texas Centennial Exposition, sold at auction for US$47,800.

In Margaret Mitchell's novel Gone with the Wind of 1936 and the film of 1939, Rhett Butler nicknames his newborn daughter Bonnie Blue after Melanie Wilkes remarks that her eyes will be as blue as the Bonnie Blue Flag. Flag and song also appear in the film Gods and Generals of 2003.
bono-people: The name Bono is derived from Abono woo, pioneer or firstborn of the land. Techiman-Bono tradition holds that the first ancestors emerged from a sacred cave called Amowi, near present-day Techiman, under Asaman, the first ruler, and founded a settlement called Yefiri. The colonial-era scholar Eva Meyerowitz argued that the Bono came from the Sahara by way of a place called Diala; Bono oral historians reject this, and the historian Kwasi Konadu finds no evidence of an intrusive northern people, pointing to iron-smelting and settlement at Amowi, Bono Manso and Begho dating back to at least 300 CE.

Bono Manso, the capital, was organised as a confederation of matrilineal clans with roles as priests, warriors or administrators. From the 12th century the state prospered on the gold of the Twi and Prabom valleys in the Tain River basin, and gold dust served as currency in trade with Djenne, Timbuktu and North Africa. The market town of Begho, which at its peak had an estimated 15,000 people, had quarters for Bono, for Mande-speaking Muslim traders and for metalworkers. Bono Manso also became involved in the early Atlantic slave trade.

In 1722/23 Asante forces under Opoku Ware I destroyed Bono Manso, and the survivors moved their capital to Techiman, which was destroyed again around 1877 after its ruler Kwabena Fofie refused to join an Asante war. Bono chiefs left the Asante Confederacy in 1952, and in 1959 the government of Ghana created the Brong-Ahafo Region, separate from the Ashanti Region, with its own House of Chiefs.

The Bono speak Bono Twi and are one of the largest matrilineal Akan groups. The queenmother nominates the king and keeps the royal line within the maternal clan, and the two act together as spiritual and administrative heads. Society is organised in seven or eight matrilineal clans, each with its own totems, taboos and origin stories. Their royal regalia include ceremonial stools, umbrellas, ivory trumpets and gold swords, and Kete, Adowa and fontomfrom music accompany festivals, funerals and royal ceremonies.
book-of-common-prayer: Before the Reformation the parish worship of England followed the Latin Roman Rite, in local forms called uses, of which the most common in southern England was that of Sarum (Salisbury). There was no single book: the services were spread through the Missal, the Breviary, the Manual and the Pontifical. After Edward VI succeeded in 1547, revision could move faster. Parliament passed the Act of Uniformity on 21 January 1549, and the new book had to be in use by Whitsunday, 9 June. Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, is credited with the overall editorship and structure, though he borrowed and adapted material from other sources.

The 1549 book was intended as a temporary expedient. The 1552 revision, from the same editorial hand, broke decisively with the past in the view of the historian Christopher Haigh: it rewrote the baptism, confirmation, communion and burial services, removed ceremonies Protestants disliked and dropped exorcism and anointing. It was used only for a few months before Mary I restored Roman Catholic worship in 1553.

The 1549 book was the first prayer book to give complete forms of service for daily and Sunday worship in English. It contains Morning and Evening Prayer, the Litany, Holy Communion and occasional services in full, including orders for baptism, confirmation, marriage, prayers for the sick and a funeral service. It sets out the collects and the epistle and gospel readings for Sunday Communion, and tabulates Old Testament and New Testament readings, the Psalms and the canticles. With a calendar and lectionary, a priest needed only a Bible and a Psalter besides it. An ordinal for ordaining bishops, priests and deacons was added in 1550.

Elizabeth I's first Parliament authorised the 1559 book, which reintroduced the 1552 text with modifications. The Act of Uniformity passed the House of Lords by only three votes, and all the bishops who could attend voted against it. James I ordered further changes after the Hampton Court Conference of 1604. After the English Civil War, when the book had been abolished, the 1662 edition was printed two years after the restoration of the monarchy; it remains the official prayer book of the Church of England.

Anglicanism spread with British colonial expansion, and versions of the book are used in over 50 countries and over 150 languages. It was first translated into Manx in 1610 and Irish in 1712, and into Māori in 1830. Lutheran, Methodist and Presbyterian prayer books have borrowed from it, and its marriage and burial rites passed into other denominations and into the English language. Like the King James Version of the Bible and the works of Shakespeare, it has given many phrases to everyday English.
book-of-deuteronomy: Deuteronomy is the fifth and final book of the Torah, called Devarim, the words of Moses, in Hebrew. Chapters 1 to 30 consist of three sermons delivered by Moses on the Plains of Moab shortly before the Israelites enter the Promised Land. The first recounts the forty years in the wilderness, the second reminds them that possession of the land depends on following Yahweh and his laws, and the third offers comfort that repentance can restore all, even if the nation loses the land. The last four chapters contain the Song of Moses, the Blessing of Moses and the death of Moses on Mount Nebo.

Chapters 12 to 26, the Deuteronomic Code, expand the Ten Commandments into laws on worship, leadership and social conduct. Its best-known verse is Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema Yisrael, quoted by Jesus in Mark 12:28 to 34.

Mosaic authorship of the Torah is an ancient Jewish tradition, codified by Maimonides as the eighth of the thirteen principles of faith. Virtually all modern secular scholars, and most Christian and Jewish scholars, reject it and date Deuteronomy between the 7th and 5th centuries BCE, attributing it probably to the Levite caste. Since W. M. L. de Wette proposed it in 1805, most scholars have placed the Deuteronomic Code in Jerusalem in the 7th century BCE.

According to 2 Kings 22 and 23, the high priest Hilkiah found the book of the law in the temple in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign, and Josiah launched a reform of worship based on it. Many scholars believe it was the Deuteronomic Code. Hosea, in the northern kingdom, refers to the Exodus and a covenant while Isaiah does not, leading scholars to conclude that the traditions behind Deuteronomy have a northern origin.

After Babylon destroyed the Kingdom of Judah in 586 BCE, the Deuteronomistic elite in exile created a history of Israel in the books of Joshua through Kings to show that the disaster was punishment for failing to follow the law. Deuteronomy became its introduction. The mainstream view holds that it was later detached and joined to the four books before it, because Moses was already its central character.
book-of-documents: According to a later tradition, Confucius compiled the Book of Documents as a selection from a much larger group of documents, but the early history of the text is obscure. Writers from Confucius onwards drew on it to illustrate general principles, though several different versions seem to have been in use. It was cited increasingly in works through the 4th century BCE, such as the Mencius, Mozi and Zuo Zhuan. Mencius and Xunzi refused to accept it as genuine in its entirety, in contrast to the reverence of the Han dynasty, when its compilation was attributed to Confucius.

The transmitted text is grouped into four sections: the semi-mythical reign of Yu the Great, and the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties. The Zhou section is over half the text. Most chapters are represented as formal speeches by kings or other important figures, such as announcements, declarations made before battle, and commands to a vassal. A speech is often introduced with the phrase Wáng ruò yuē, which scholars take to mean that the originals were prepared scripts read out by an official on the king's behalf.

The five Zhou announcements have the most archaic language and are considered by most scholars to record speeches of King Cheng of Zhou and of the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao, his uncles, in the late 11th century BCE. They set out the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven, which explains how the virtuous Xia became corrupt and were replaced by the Shang, who in turn were replaced by the Zhou. Most scholars believe the chapters on Yu, the Xia and the early Shang were composed later, some as late as the 4th or 3rd centuries BCE.

Many copies were destroyed in the Qin dynasty's burning of books. Fu Sheng reconstructed 29 chapters from hidden copies at the start of the Han dynasty, known as the Modern Script. A longer Old Script version, with some 16 additional chapters, was said to have been found in a wall of Confucius's house in the reign of Emperor Wu and interpreted by his descendant Kong Anguo, but it was lost by the end of the Han dynasty.

In 317 CE Mei Ze presented to the Eastern Jin court a version of 58 chapters as Kong Anguo's text. It was widely accepted and made the official interpretation by imperial decree in 653. Doubts began in the Song dynasty, and in the 17th century Yan Ruoqu's study convinced most scholars that the added Old Script chapters were fabricated. Bamboo slips from tombs of the state of Chu, dated to around 300 BCE, quote previously unknown passages.
book-of-exodus: The English name comes from the Greek éxodos, meaning departure, the title of the book in the Septuagint. In Hebrew it is called Shemot, Names, after its opening words. Jewish and Christian tradition ascribes the book, and the whole Torah, to Moses, but scholars abandoned that view by the end of the 19th century because of discrepancies and repetitions in the text. Modern scholars see its initial composition as a product of the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BCE, based on earlier written sources and oral traditions, with final revisions in the Persian period. In approximate round dates, the process began around 600 BCE and ended around 400 BCE with the books as unchangeable sacred texts.

The book opens some 400 years after the end of Genesis, when a Pharaoh who does not remember Joseph fears the numerous enslaved Israelites and orders the killing of newborn boys. Moses is saved, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, flees to Midian and encounters God in a burning bush. After ten plagues, the last the death of the Egyptian firstborn, Pharaoh lets the Israelites go, and the sea parts for them.

At Sinai God pronounces the Ten Commandments and the Covenant Code of ritual and civil law, in Exodus 20:22–23:33, which resembles the Laws of Hammurabi in content and structure. The later chapters give instructions for the Tabernacle and the priesthood.

The biblical scholar Carol Meyers calls Exodus arguably the most important book in the Bible, because it presents the defining features of Israel's identity: memories of hardship and escape, a binding covenant with a God who chooses Israel, and guidelines for the life of the community. Its central theme is the Sinaitic covenant, which resembles ancient Middle Eastern treaties but is made between a god and a people rather than between a ruler and a vassal.

Most mainstream scholars do not accept the account as historical, and the consensus is that the Pentateuch does not accurately describe the origins of the Israelites, who seem to have formed in the central highlands of Canaan in the late second millennium BCE. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman argue that archaeology has found no evidence for the Exodus as described. A majority of scholars nonetheless think the story has a historical core, though they disagree about what it was, and the names Moses, Aaron and Phinehas seem to be of Egyptian origin.
book-of-fixed-stars: The Arabic title, kitāb suwar al-kawākib, means the Book of the Shapes of Stars. Al-Sufi, also called Azophi, wrote it in Shiraz in Arabic, the common language of scholars across the Islamic lands, though he was himself Persian. It followed the Graeco-Arabic translation movement of the 9th century and tried to join the star catalogue of Books VII and VIII of the Almagest with the indigenous Arabic constellation traditions of the Anwā'. Star knowledge also served worship, which required finding the direction of Mecca, the times of prayer and the start of each month.

The book follows the 48 Ptolemaic constellations, one chapter each, in four parts: a description of the constellation's stars, in which al-Sufi often criticises Ptolemy for favouring the outline over the stars; the Bedouin star groups in the same part of the sky; two drawings, one of the constellation as seen in the sky and one as seen on a celestial globe; and a catalogue of its stars. Positions were taken from Ptolemy with the longitudes increased by 12° 42' for precession, so they were correct for the year 964 only.

Al-Sufi replaced Ptolemy's two classes of brightness with three, and Ihsan Hafez has counted 132 stars in the work that Ptolemy does not mention. The introduction names sources now lost, among them treatises by Ibn Kunasa, Ibn al-'Arabi and Abu Hanifa al-Dinawari on pre-Islamic Bedouin traditions. Al-Sufi is said to have drawn the globe views by laying thin paper over a globe and copying its engravings.

The book became the standard text on astronomy across the Islamic lands and survives in many manuscripts and translations. The Bodleian copy MS. Marsh 144, once dated 1009, has been re-dated to the end of the 12th century, and a manuscript of 1125 in the Doha Museum is now thought the oldest. Many surviving celestial globes of the 13th and 14th centuries cite it as a source. It describes the Andromeda Galaxy as a little cloud before the mouth of the Arabic constellation of the Big Fish, which al-Sufi credits to astronomers of Isfahan. Hans Schjellerup translated it into French in 1874.
book-of-genesis: The name Genesis comes from the Greek for origin, the title of the book in the Septuagint; in Hebrew it is called Bereshit, In the beginning, after its first word. Genesis was written anonymously. Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the whole Pentateuch to Moses, but modern scholars believe it was the work of many authors and editors writing much later. Internal contradictions suggest this, among them two creation narratives.

By the end of the 19th century most scholars held the documentary hypothesis, in which four sources, the Yahwist, the Elohist, the Deuteronomist and the Priestly source, were combined by editors. Since the 1980s revisions have been proposed. Most scholars now agree that Genesis reached its final form after the Babylonian exile. The original manuscripts are lost, and surviving copies vary across the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Genesis falls into the primeval history of chapters 1 to 11 and the ancestral history of chapters 12 to 50. The first includes two creation stories, Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, Cain and Abel, the Flood and the Tower of Babel. God sends the Flood because human sin has corrupted the world, sparing the righteous Noah and his family in an ark, and then makes a covenant with Noah marked by the rainbow.

The second part follows Abraham, who at God's command travels from Ur of the Chaldees to Canaan, then his son Isaac and his grandson Jacob, whose name is changed to Israel. Through Jacob's son Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers and later made second in command in Egypt, the family goes down to Egypt, where the book ends. Scholars generally see a divine promise of offspring, blessing and land as the theme of the patriarchal stories.

Jewish and Christian chronologers added up the spans in its genealogies to calculate the age of the world, and this reckoning underlies the Hebrew and Byzantine calendars. From the 16th to the 19th century scholars in Europe treated Genesis as factual and tried to fit new findings in geology to its account; Johann Jakob Scheuchzer took fossils to be creatures killed in the Flood. This reading lost favour as evidence mounted that the Earth was far older. Its statement that humanity is created in the image of God became a foundational theme within Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
book-of-han: The work developed from a continuation of Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, begun by Ban Biao at the start of the Later Han dynasty and usually called Later Traditions. Other scholars of the time, including Liu Xin and Yang Xiong, also wrote continuations. After Ban Biao's death his eldest son Ban Gu was dissatisfied with what his father had completed and began a new history starting with the beginning of the Han dynasty, unlike Sima Qian's, which began with China's earliest rulers of tradition. In this way he initiated the jizhuanti format for dynastic histories that remained the model for the official histories until modern times.

Ban Gu died in prison in 92, and his younger sister Ban Zhao finished the book in 111, 19 years later. She is thought to have written volumes 13 to 20, eight chronological tables, and volume 26, the treatise on astronomy, the latter with the help of Ma Xu.

The finished work has 100 fascicles. It contains annals in 12 volumes, which are emperors' biographies in strict annal form, 8 volumes of chronological tables of important people, 10 volumes of treatises, each on an area of effort of the state, and 70 volumes of biographies. The biographies confine themselves to events that show the exemplary character of the person, and treat two or more people together when they belong to the same class. The last articles describe China's relations with peoples at and beyond the frontiers, including Nanyue, Minyue and Ba.

Where the two histories overlapped, Ban Gu adopted much of Sima Qian's material nearly verbatim, sometimes expanding it. Fascicle 21 describes the Triple Concordance Calendar System developed by Liu Xin.

The Book of Han is the best source, and sometimes the only one, for many topics such as the literature of the period. It is also called the Book of the Former Han to distinguish it from the Book of the Later Han, composed in the fifth century by Fan Ye. It is counted among the Four Histories of the Twenty-Four Histories canon, together with the Records of the Grand Historian, the Records of the Three Kingdoms and the History of the Later Han.

Its treatise on geography, in volume 28, gives the first unambiguous appearance of the people of Japan in written history: "The people of Wo are located across the ocean from Lelang Commandery, are divided into more than one hundred tribes, and come to offer tribute from time to time." The annals and the chapters on Wang Mang were translated into English by Homer H. Dubs.
book-of-jeremiah: The Book of Jeremiah is the second of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. Its opening verses name it as the words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, a priest from the town of Anatot, to whom the word of God came in the days of King Josiah. His career covered the last years of the kingdom of Judah: Josiah's reforms, Babylon's destruction of Assyria, a brief period in which Egypt made Judah a vassal, and Babylon's defeat of Egypt in 605 BCE, which left Judah a Babylonian vassal. Judah revolted twice more, and the second revolt ended with the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the kingdom.

The book falls roughly into six parts: the core of Jeremiah's message in chapters 1 to 25, biography and encounters with other prophets in 26 to 29, promises of restoration in 30 to 33, the fall of Jerusalem in 34 to 45, oracles against the nations in 46 to 51, and an appendix retelling the Second Book of Kings. Its poetic oracles speak of Israel's unfaithfulness and call for repentance. Jeremiah presents the covenant between God and Israel as conditional, and chapter 31 looks to a new covenant that will not be broken. The book also records sign-acts, such as wearing an ox yoke and buying a field at Anathoth, and shows the prophet taunted, jailed and thrown into a pit.

The book survives in two related versions, the Masoretic Hebrew text and the Greek of the Septuagint, which is about one eighth shorter. Both forms were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and most scholars hold that the Hebrew behind the Greek is older. Authentic oracles are probably in the poetic sections of chapters 1 to 25, while the whole has been heavily edited by followers, perhaps including the scribe Baruch, and by later Deuteronomists. Second Temple Judaism attributed to Jeremiah the Book of Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter of Jeremiah. Early Christians based their understanding of Jesus as the bearer of a new covenant on chapter 31.
book-of-joshua: The book is anonymous. The Babylonian Talmud attributed it to Joshua himself, but John Calvin rejected that view, and by the time of Thomas Hobbes it was recognised that the book was written much later than the period it depicts. Scholars now agree that it was composed as part of the Deuteronomistic history, which runs from Deuteronomy to the Books of Kings, first at the court of King Josiah in the late 7th century BCE and extensively revised in the 6th. The earliest parts are probably chapters 2 to 11, the conquest story. The book was not completed until after the fall of Jerusalem to the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 586 BCE.
Fragments of Joshua from the Hasmonean period were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran, and the earliest complete Hebrew copy is in the Aleppo Codex of the 10th century CE.

The book tells of Israelite campaigns in central, southern and northern Canaan and the division of the land among the Twelve Tribes. It opens after the death of Moses, with God's commission to Joshua, and ends with Joshua's farewell address and the covenant at Shechem. The conquest runs from the reconnaissance of Jericho and the crossing of the Jordan to the fall of Jericho, Ai, and campaigns in the south and north. The land is the central subject, and obedience to the Law and to the command of herem, the ban on treaties, mercy and intermarriage with the enemy, is a constant theme.

The prevailing scholarly view is that Joshua is not a factual account. Archaeology indicates a gradual, indigenous emergence of Israel from Canaanite society. The 13th-century BCE setting coincides with the Bronze Age Collapse, but with few exceptions, Hazor and Lachish among them, the cities destroyed are not those the Bible associates with Joshua, and Jericho and Ai show little sign of occupation in the Late Bronze Age, though recent excavations at Jericho have questioned this. In the 1930s Martin Noth criticised the book's usefulness for history.

Many scholars read the book as describing what would now be called genocide, and the archaeologist William G. Dever uses that word. Others hold that the label is anachronistic. They explain the killings by cultural norms, since Israel was not the only Iron Age state to practise herem, and by theology, and some take the violent language as hyperbole, comparable to extrabiblical military reports.
book-of-kells: The Book of Kells is one of the latest and finest of the Insular manuscripts made from the late 6th to the early 9th centuries in monasteries of Britain and Ireland, among them the Lindisfarne Gospels and the Book of Armagh. It was created in a Columban monastery in Ireland or Scotland and may have had contributions from several Columban houses. Its fully developed ornament places it in the late 8th or early 9th century. The woad and lichen used for its blue and purple pigments are taken as strong evidence of an origin in modern Scotland.

The Annals of Ulster record that in 1007 the great Gospel of Columkille was stolen from the sacristy of the stone church at Cenannas on account of its wrought shrine. It was recovered months later under a sod, without its gold and jewelled cover.

The manuscript contains the four Gospels in Latin, with prefaces, summaries and canon tables. It now has 340 leaves of calf vellum, or 680 pages. Its text is largely from the Vulgate, with passages from earlier Vetus Latina versions, and is in Insular majuscule by at least three scribes. Its decoration surpasses that of other Insular Gospel books: ten full-page illustrations and pages full of initials, interlace and human and animal forms in purple, red, green and yellow, with no gold or silver leaf. It seems to have stood on the high altar and been used at Mass, with appearance preferred to practicality, and errors were left uncorrected.

The book stayed at Kells until 1654, when Cromwell's cavalry was quartered in the church and the governor sent it to Dublin. Henry Jones, Bishop of Clogher, presented it to Trinity College in 1661. In the 19th century its link with Columba was used to argue Ireland's cultural primacy, and its designs influenced the Celtic Revival and were copied in metalwork, embroidery and pottery. It was rebound in four volumes in 1953, and UNESCO added it to its Memory of the World International Register in 2011.
book-of-mormon: The book was first published in 1830 by Joseph Smith under the title The Book of Mormon: An Account Written by the Hand of Mormon upon Plates Taken from the Plates of Nephi. According to Smith's account and the book's own narrative, it was engraved in otherwise unknown characters on golden plates by ancient prophets. The last of them, Moroni, buried the plates in what is now Manchester, New York.

Smith said that Moroni appeared to him as an angel in 1823, when he was seventeen, and told him of the buried plates, and that in 1827 he was shown their location and instructed to translate them into English. A different view holds that Smith himself composed the book from the material and ideas of his nineteenth-century surroundings, and in the twenty-first century the leading naturalistic explanations take this view.

The Book of Mormon is a compilation of smaller books, most of them named after a main narrator or a prominent figure, running from the First Book of Nephi to the Book of Moroni. Its English imitates the style of the King James Version of the Bible. The narrative begins in Jerusalem around 600 BCE with Lehi and his family, who are led by God from the city shortly before its fall to the Babylonians. They cross the Arabian peninsula and then sail to a promised land, presumably in the Americas. Their community grows and splits into two warring groups, the Nephites and the Lamanites, and this conflict runs through the rest of the narrative.

The pivotal event is the appearance of Jesus Christ in the Americas shortly after his resurrection. The title page gives the book's purpose as the convincing of Jew and Gentile that Jesus is the Christ. Prophets in the book see and preach him long before his birth.

Early followers read the book as confirming and supplementing the Bible, and they drew on its picture of the church in drawing up their own articles. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints counts it among its four standard works and holds it to be the word of God, and it regards the book as both literal history and the keystone of its faith.

Independent archaeological, historical and scientific communities have found little evidence for the civilisations it describes, and they point to a nineteenth-century origin in its language and content. Academics and organisations connected to the movement argue that it is an authentic account of the pre-Columbian Americas. The book has been translated fully or partly into at least 112 languages.
book-of-optics: Before Ibn al-Haytham wrote, two theories of vision competed. In the extramission theory of Euclid and Ptolemy, rays went out from the eyes to the object and let the viewer perceive its colour, shape and size. An early form of the intromission theory, held by followers of Aristotle and Galen, had agents transmitted to the eyes from the object or its surroundings. Against extramission, Ibn al-Haytham pointed out that bright lights such as the sun can damage the eyes, and that the eye could hardly fill the whole of space the moment the eyelids open on the night sky.

In his own theory every point on an object's surface sends rays of light in all directions, some of which enter the eye. He distinguished primary light, from self-luminous bodies, from secondary or accidental light, which other objects receive and emit again; both travel in straight lines, are refracted by partly transparent bodies and are reflected by smooth ones such as mirrors. From his experiments he concluded that colour behaves much like light and cannot exist without air.

To explain why the eye does not see a blur, he argued that of all the rays from a point only the one striking the eye perpendicularly takes part in vision, the others being refracted and weakened. The crystalline humour receives the rays as a visual cone with the object as its base and passes the image to the brain through an optic nerve. The first three books treat light, colour, visual perception and its errors, Books IV to VI reflection, and Book VII refraction.

An unknown scholar translated the work into Latin, where it was known as De Aspectibus or Perspectiva. Friedrich Risner printed it in 1572 in his collection Opticae thesaurus, together with a book on twilight falsely attributed to Alhazen and a work on optics by Vitello. In modern times A. I. Sabra edited the Arabic text of Books I to V and translated the first three into English, and A. Mark Smith published critical editions of the medieval Latin version with English translations of all seven books between 2001 and 2010.
book-of-psalms: The Book of Psalms is an anthology of Hebrew religious hymns, the first book of the Ketuvim, or Writings, in the Tanakh. The composition of the psalms spans at least five centuries, from Psalm 29 in the 10th century BCE to psalms clearly from the post-Exilic period, not earlier than the 5th century BCE. Most originated in the kingdom of Judah and were associated with the Temple in Jerusalem, where they probably served as librettos for worship.

Of the 150 psalms, 116 have superscriptions. The most common names are 'of David' (73 psalms), Asaph (12) and the sons of Korah (11). Modern scholars do not accept Davidic authorship as historical fact and see the attributions as a way of linking writings to well-known figures. Many scholars think the psalms were gathered into one collection in the Second Temple period, and the Dead Sea Scrolls suggest that the content and order of Psalms 90 to 150 were not fixed in the mid-1st century CE.

The book is divided into five sections, each ending with a doxology: Psalms 1 to 41, 42 to 72, 73 to 89, 90 to 106 and 107 to 150. The division was probably made by the final editors to echo the five books of the Torah. Hermann Gunkel's form-critical study sorted the psalms into five main types: hymns, communal laments, royal psalms, individual laments, the most common type, and individual thanksgivings. There are also wisdom psalms, pilgrimage psalms and others.

The poetry rests chiefly on parallelism, in which a second line restates, opposes or amplifies the first. Some psalms echo earlier regional texts, including Ugaritic poetry and the Babylonian Enūma Eliš. The numbering differs, mostly by one, between the Hebrew and the Greek manuscripts. The Septuagint adds a Psalm 151, and some Syriac versions add Psalms 152 to 155.

The psalms were written as songs. More than a third are addressed to a music director, and some headings name instruments or melodies. According to the medieval scholar Saadia Gaon, the Levites originally sang them in the Temple precincts. In later Jewish and Christian tradition they became prayers, for individuals and for congregations alike.

The earliest Christians used them in worship, and the Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and other churches have recited them in cycles over one or more weeks. In the early centuries a candidate for bishop was expected to know the whole Psalter by heart. Muslims believe that David received the Psalms, the Zabur, as a scripture. Composers from Orlando di Lasso and Heinrich Schütz to George Frideric Handel and Felix Mendelssohn have set them to music.
book-of-rites: The Book of Rites is a diverse compilation of texts of uncertain origin and date. Unlike the Rites of Zhou and the Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial, it has no consistent overall structure. Some sections define ritual terms, and others deal with the life and teachings of Confucius. Parts have been traced to earlier works such as the Xunzi and the Lüshi Chunqiu, while other sections are believed to date from the Former Han period. In China the Doubting antiquity movement questioned whether it contains genuine Warring States documents. In 1993 a copy of the Black Robes chapter was found in Tomb 1 of the Guodian tombs in Jingmen, Hubei, sealed around 300 BCE, which reopened the debate over the dating of other chapters.

Many Confucian texts were destroyed in the Burning of the Books in 213 BCE under Qin Shi Huang, but scholars who had memorised or hidden the classics helped to rebuild them in the early Han dynasty. The Book of Rites was said to have been fully recovered, though the Classic of Music could not be recompiled and survives only in fragments, mainly in the Record of Music chapter of this book. According to the Book of Sui, Dai De cut a collection of 214 books to 85 in the 1st century BCE, and his nephew Dai Sheng abridged it to 46. Ma Rong added three more. Later scholarship doubts that account.

Zheng Xuan, a student of Ma Rong, produced an annotated edition of 49 books that became the authoritative version and is still the standard one. It formed the basis of the Right Meaning of the Ritual Records, the imperially sanctioned text and commentary established in 653 CE.

Chapters of the book provided the foundation for the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean. In the Song dynasty Zhu Xi edited these two texts and, with the Analects and Mencius, they became the Four Books. After the Yuan dynasty adopted the Five Classics and the Four Books as orthodox, and the Ming and Qing upheld the choice, they became the standard curriculum for the civil service examinations. From 1313 to 1905 mastery of them was essential for anyone seeking official posts.
book-of-the-later-han: The Hou Hanshu is one of the Twenty-Four Histories. It was compiled by Fan Ye and others in the 5th century, during the Liu Song dynasty, from a number of earlier histories and documents. It covers the Later or Eastern Han, which is separated from the Early or Western Han by the fall of Wang Mang, overthrown in 23 CE by a peasants' revolt known as the Red Eyebrows.

As an orthodox history it is unusual in being completed over two hundred years after the fall of the dynasty it describes. Fan Ye's primary source was the Dongguan Hanji, the Han Records of the Eastern Lodge, which was written during the Han dynasty itself. He also drew on accounts by Sima Qian and Ban Gu and on many other works, among them the Annals of the Later Han by Yuan Hong of the 4th century. Most of these sources did not survive intact. Fan Ye's text was later annotated at least twice, first by the Liang dynasty scholar Liu Zhao and then by a team led by Crown Prince Zhanghuai of the Tang dynasty.

The book belongs with the Records of the Grand Historian, the Book of Han and the Records of the Three Kingdoms among the four early historiographies of the Twenty-Four Histories canon. Its Treatise on the Western Regions rests on a report composed by Ban Yong, presented to Emperor An of Han around 125, which presumably includes notes from his father Ban Chao. Fan Ye says plainly that the new information in this section comes from that report. It forms the 88th chapter, or the 118th in some editions.

The treatise is a key source for the culture and economy of the Western Regions, including the earliest accounts of Daqin, the Roman Empire, and some of the most detailed early reports on India and Central Asia. It records an eclipse followed by a circular halo during the reign of Emperor Guangwu, who took it as a sign that the affairs of Heaven and mankind were upended and proclaimed that he would pardon the sins of the population himself. It also contains references to events after the death of Emperor An, including a brief account of the first official envoys from Rome in 166.
book-of-wei: The Book of Wei was compiled by Wei Shou between 551 and 554 and describes the Northern Wei and Eastern Wei dynasties from 386 to 550. It is one of the Twenty-Four Histories. The Northern Wei was founded in 386 by the Tuoba clan, and its chief accomplishment was the unification of northern China in 439. An internal struggle split it into the Eastern and Western Wei.

The Eastern Wei, established in 534, was short-lived, and in 550 it was taken over by Gao Yang, who founded the Northern Qi. In compiling the work, Wei Shou withstood pressure from powerful elites who wanted him to glorify their disputed ancestral origins, with the help of the Northern Qi emperor.

The work originally contained 114 chapters and follows the format of earlier standard histories, with annals of the emperors, biographies and treatises. The biographies end with Chapter 104, Wei Shou's own preface. In it he harmonises the Xianbei cultural heritage with the Han Chinese one, arguing that the rise of the Northern Wei was mandated by Heaven and that the Xianbei were descended from the Yellow Emperor. Chapters 95 through 103 include descriptions of figures from the Korean kingdoms of Goguryeo and Baekje, and from the Khitan.

Chapters 105 through 114 are treatises. Chapter 114, the Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism, and Chapter 69, in which the court official Pei Yanjun describes a knowledge of both Buddhism and Confucianism as beneficial to social administration, show the book's positive treatment of the dialogue between Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism.

Detractors called the book Hui Shu, meaning Book of Filth, a pun on its name. Like other Twenty-Four Histories it praised its subject dynasty, and it probably overstated the power of the predecessor state of Dai, a vassal of the Western Jin, Later Zhao, Former Yan and Former Qin. It applied the sinicised surnames introduced by Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei in 496 to events long before, which makes the original names of people hard to know. Wei Shou was also criticised for including the sole Eastern Wei emperor, Xiaojing, while omitting the three emperors of the rival Western Wei. He was credited, however, with harmonising confused and fragmented accounts from the state of Dai to the early Northern Wei.

By the Song dynasty some chapters were already missing, and later editors reconstructed them from the History of the Northern Dynasties, dated to the 7th century. Dien has translated part of volume 59, on the dispute between the Northern Wei and Liu Song at Pengcheng, and Lee part of volume 111, on the case of Liu Hui, who committed adultery while married to Princess Lanling.
booker-t-washington: Booker was born to Jane, an enslaved woman, on the plantation of James Burroughs near Hale's Ford in Franklin County, Virginia. He never knew his exact birth date, although evidence that emerged after his death indicates 5 April 1856, and he never knew his father, said to be a white man from a neighbouring plantation. He worked in salt furnaces and coal mines in West Virginia, and at 16 made his way east, mostly on foot, to the Hampton Institute, where his entrance exam was to clean a room and where he worked as a janitor to pay his way.

In 1881 Samuel C. Armstrong, the president of Hampton, recommended Washington, then 25, as first leader of the Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute in Alabama, a teachers' college. It opened on 4 July 1881, and the next year Washington bought a former plantation as its site, where students built their own school and learned trades as well as academic subjects. By his death Tuskegee had more than 100 buildings, about 1,500 students and 200 faculty. He directed millions of dollars from white philanthropists such as Andrew Carnegie and Julius Rosenwald to small rural schools across the South, and founded the National Negro Business League in 1900.

His Atlanta Exhibition address of 1895 was seen as a revolutionary moment, but W. E. B. Du Bois, who had supported him, later called it the Atlanta Compromise, criticising Washington as too accommodating to white interests. Washington urged progress through education and entrepreneurship rather than direct challenges to Jim Crow segregation, though he also secretly supported court challenges to it. His autobiography Up from Slavery, published in 1901, remained the best-selling autobiography by an African American for more than sixty years. In October 1901 he dined at the White House with President Theodore Roosevelt, which drew racist attacks from Southern Democratic politicians.

Washington collapsed in New York in 1915 and asked to die at Tuskegee, where he arrived on 14 November 1915 and died a few hours later, aged 59. After his death he was heavily criticised for accommodating white supremacy, while since the late twentieth century historians have taken a more balanced view. The years from 1880 to 1915 have been called the Age of Booker T. Washington.
books-of-chilam-balam: The books are handwritten miscellanies, chiefly of the 17th and 18th centuries, in which indigenous Maya and early Spanish traditions have merged. Each is named after the small Yucatec town where it was first kept, and all are attributed to an author of tradition, Chilam Balam: a chilam was a priest who gave prophecies, and balam a common surname meaning jaguar. He is credited with predicting the coming of the Spaniards to Yucatán. Nine books are known. Their language and content show that parts go back to the Spanish conquest of the Yucatec kingdoms (1527–1546), and some terse passages seem to render hieroglyphic texts of the pre-conquest period.

The historical texts include migration legends, narratives about lords of the native kingdoms and chronicles up to the Spanish conquest, all set in the framework of the Maya calendar, partly adapted to the European one, which makes Postclassic history hard to reconstruct from them. Beside them stand prognostications for the haabs, tuns and kʼatuns, prophecies ascribed to oracular priests of the early 16th century, and the riddles of the language of Zuyua, used to confirm local lords in office.

Myths tell of the destruction and re-creation of the world at the start of kʼatun 11 Ahau, and ritual texts of the creation of the twenty named days and the birth of maize. Practical sections give classifications by the named days, agricultural almanacs, Ptolemaic astrology with the European zodiac, the Catholic liturgical calendar and herbal remedies of Greek and Arab descent, alongside saints' days, prayers and the Spanish romance of the Maiden Theodor.

Many texts recur in several books, so a concordance is basic to their study. The archaic idiom and the allusive language make translation hard, and translations vary greatly in quality. The Spanish synoptic translation of Barrera Vásquez and Rendón (1948) is still used, and there are English translations of the books of Chumayel (Roys 1933), Maní, Tizimín (Edmonson 1982), Na and Kaua.
bophuthatswana: The area of former native reserves was set up as the only homeland for Tswana-speaking people in 1961 and administered by the Tswana Territorial Authority. It received nominal self-rule in 1971, and elections followed the next year. After the 1977 elections Chief Lucas Mangope became the first president when his Bophuthatswana Democratic Party won a majority. The territory became nominally independent on 6 December 1977. The United Nations General Assembly denounced the declaration as totally invalid, and Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim said he strongly deplored another so-called independent tribal homeland. Mangope argued that independence would let the population negotiate with Pretoria from a stronger position.

Only South Africa and Transkei recognised the state, and later Ciskei and Venda, the other members of the TBVC system. Even so, the government set up a trade mission in Tel Aviv and kept an unofficial embassy in Israel during the 1980s. Botswana agreed to informal arrangements to ease cross-border travel. On 10 February 1988 Rocky Malebane-Metsing of the People's Progressive Party took power in a military coup and held it for one day; the South African Defence Force invaded and reinstated Mangope. A second coup attempt in 1990 involved large protests against his handling of the economy, in which seven people were reported killed.

Bophuthatswana covered about 40,000 square kilometres and consisted of seven enclaves scattered across the former Cape Province, Transvaal and Orange Free State, which led outsiders to call it Jigsawland. Mafeking was incorporated in 1980 after a local referendum. Townships such as Ga-Rankuwa and Mabopane, near Pretoria, continued to serve as dormitory townships supplying labour. In 1990 its population was estimated at 2,352,296. Tswana, English and Afrikaans were official languages.

It was the richest of the TBVC states. Its platinum mines accounted for two-thirds of the platinum produced in the Western world, and it also had asbestos, granite, vanadium, chromium and manganese. The Sun City casino drew visitors from Johannesburg and Pretoria, where gambling was illegal. The rand remained the official currency, though two coins were minted as a proof set. Its defence force had about 4,000 troops and its police 6,002 officers.

In early 1994 Mangope resisted the coming elections and opposed reincorporation into South Africa. Unrest grew, and he invited General Constand Viljoen of the Afrikaner Volksfront to help. Members of the Afrikaner Weerstandsbeweging also entered, shot at civilians and were driven out; three of them were executed after surrender, which ended white right-wing military opposition to the reforms. On 12 March 1994 the South African government and the Transitional Executive Council deposed Mangope. Bophuthatswana ceased to exist on 27 April 1994. Most of it joined North West province, Thaba 'Nchu went to the Free State and the Mathanjana exclave to Mpumalanga.
bor-serbia: The name of the town comes from the Serbo-Croatian word bor, meaning pine. In 1835 Miloš Obrenović invited August Herder, the son of J. G. Herder, to the region to carry out geological investigations. Later Đorđe Vajfert invested in exploration and sought foreign capital to begin industrial exploitation. He signed a contract with Mirabaud, and the Compagnie française des mines de Bor was established in Paris on 30 September 1903.

Nazi Germany invaded Yugoslavia on 27 March 1941. Führer Directive No. 25 held that possession of the Bor copper mines was very important, since they could supply 50 per cent of Germany's wartime copper requirements. Ownership was seized from the French company and taken over by the Prussian National Bank. Prison camps were quickly established, most of them named after German cities. The largest, called Berlin, stood in Bor itself and housed the headquarters of the Hungarian battalion, with satellite camps within 50 kilometres. In May 1943 there were about 23,000 forced labourers from Serbia among the inmates, not counting the Kapos.

Gerhard Fränk, vice president of Organisation Todt, devised the use of Hungarian Jews to work the mines. His reasoning was that Serbian Jews had already been killed and that Serbians could not be trusted. The plan began in February 1943 and progressed only after the resignation of Vilmos Nagy, Hungary's Minister of Defense, on 8 June 1943. The Hungarian government and Organisation Todt then agreed to send 6,000 labour servicemen to Bor in exchange for a monthly shipment of 100 tons of copper ore, and in June 1944 another 3,250 followed. Most were Jews, with some Jehovah's Witnesses and Seventh-Day Adventists.

As the Axis forces withdrew from Yugoslavia, the labour servicemen were evacuated on death marches to Germany in September and October 1944, guarded by Hungarian soldiers. Many were shot along the way, including 700 to 1,000 killed in a pit at a brickyard in Crvenka on the night of 7 to 8 October. The Jewish Hungarian poet Miklós Radnóti, one of those marched out of Bor, was shot at Abda between 6 and 10 November 1944, and his last poems were found in his raincoat when his body was exhumed from a mass grave.

Bor received urban status in 1947, when its population was 11,000, and became a city in June 2018. It is the administrative centre of the Bor District in eastern Serbia and had 40,845 inhabitants at the 2022 census. It lies by the Kriveljska River, near a reservoir called Bor Lake.
bora-bora: The main island is the remnant of an extinct volcano that was active in the Upper Pliocene, between 3.45 and 3.10 million years ago, and was later partly depressed and strongly eroded. It measures only 8 km from north to south and 5 km from east to west. Mount Otemanu, at 727 metres, is its highest point, and Mount Pahia rises to 661 metres. The bay of Tuuraapuo was the volcano's main crater, and its collapsed south-western edge survives as the islets Toopua and Toopua-iti.

A lagoon surrounds the island and is separated from the sea by a barrier reef with a single opening, the Teavanui Passage, west of the main island. To the east and north the reef carries islets of coral debris and sand, called motu. The main settlement, Vaitape, lies on the western side.

The island's old name in Tahitian, Porapora mai te pora, means created by the gods, often shortened to Porapora, first born. The Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen sighted it in 1722, and he and his crew adopted the form Bora Bora, which has stood on Western maps since.
