Polynesian settlers had arrived around the 3rd century CE. James Cook sighted the island on 29 July 1769 with the help of the Tahitian navigator Tupaia. The London Missionary Society arrived in 1820, and a Protestant church was founded in 1890. Bora Bora was an independent kingdom until 1888, when France annexed it as a colony and forced its last queen, Teriimaevarua III, to abdicate.

In the Second World War the United States chose Bora Bora as a supply base for the South Pacific. Under Operation Bobcat, nine ships brought 18,000 tonnes of equipment and nearly 7,000 soldiers, who built an oil depot, an airstrip, a seaplane base and defences, including at least eight 7-inch guns served by the 13th Coast Artillery Regiment. The island saw no combat and the American presence went uncontested throughout the war. The base closed officially on 2 June 1946. The airstrip, on Motu Mute, was never enlarged for large aircraft but was French Polynesia's only international airport until Faa'a International Airport opened next to Papeete in 1960.

Bora Bora forms part of the commune of Bora-Bora, which also includes the atoll of Tupai, in the Leeward Islands of the Society Islands of French Polynesia. Its land area is 30.55 km2, and Tahitian and French are the main languages. The economy rests almost wholly on tourism. Hotel Bora Bora opened in 1961, and the first over-water bungalows were built nine years later. The eight American guns remain in the area.
borama: Borama lies in a mountainous and hilly area near the border with Ethiopia. Its name comes from the Somali word booraan, a deep hole or geological depression such as a basin or valley, so that Borama means place of valleys. It has green meadows and fields, unusually fertile in a largely arid countryside, and these have drawn gazelles, birds and camels. Its climate is hot semi-arid, with June the hottest month at an average of 24.1 °C and January the coolest at 17.1. The Awdal region around it is inhabited mainly by the Gadabuursi clan, a subclan of the Dir.

Archaeological finds in the Borama area, as around nearby Amud, include the remains of tombs, houses and mosques and sherds of Oriental wares, particularly Chinese porcelain. They range from the 12th to the 18th centuries, with most from the 15th and 16th, a time of great commercial activity associated with the medieval Adal Sultanate, which ruled the area. Excavations at more than fourteen sites near the town in the late 1800s and early 1900s unearthed coins from the time of Kait Bey, the eighteenth Burji Mamluk sultan of Egypt, and most finds were sent to the British Museum.

In the first half of the 20th century Borama formed part of the British Somaliland protectorate. The modern town was founded in 1921 by Ughaz Elmi Warfa, ughaz of the Gadabuursi, at the direction of the British, and it became a district in 1925. In 1933 Sheikh Abdurahman Sheikh Nuur, a Qur'anic teacher and son of the town's qadi, devised a new orthography for writing Somali.

The Borama or Gadabuursi script was used mainly by Nuur, his circle and some Zeila and Borama merchants. After independence Borama was administered as part of the Awdal region of Somalia, and in the Ogaden War of the late 1970s Ethiopian forces aligned with the Somali National Movement bombed it from the air along with several other northern cities.

Borama is the largest city of the Awdal region of Somaliland and its commercial seat. A 2023 estimate gave the city about 300,000 people. It was the first area in Somaliland to adopt a self-help scheme after the civil war. It has an airport named for Aden Isaq Ahmed, Somalia's first Minister of Education, and 52 primary and secondary schools. Notable people from the city include Hassan Sheikh Mumin, a poet, playwright and composer.
boran: Boran, also spelled Buran, was the daughter of Khosrow II and the Byzantine princess Maria. Her father was overthrown and executed in 628 by his son Kavad II, who had all Boran's brothers and half-brothers killed, including the heir Mardanshah. According to one chronicle, Boran was also Kavad II's wife, an instance of the Zoroastrian practice of close-kin marriage. Kavad II died some months later in an epidemic known as the Plague of Sheroe, and his young son became Ardashir III. The Sasanian civil war of 628 to 632 followed, in which powerful nobles took autonomy, and the Persian (Parsig) and Parthian (Pahlav) noble families renewed their hostility.

The Pahlav leader Farrukh Hormizd began to support Boran, who minted coins in Pahlav areas. On 27 April 630 Shahrbaraz killed Ardashir III and was himself murdered about forty days later by Farrukh Hormizd, who helped Boran take the throne in late June 630. She was the first queen to rule the empire, and her accession probably owed much to her being, with her sister Azarmidokht, the only legitimate heir able to rule. She made Farrukh Hormizd chief minister and worked for stability through just laws, repair of infrastructure, lower taxes and coinage. Her coins were minted in Pars, Khuzestan, Media and Abarshahr, and no objection to her sex is recorded.

She was soon deposed in favour of Shapur-i Shahrvaraz and then Azarmidokht, who had Farrukh Hormizd killed. His son Rostam Farrokhzad took Ctesiphon, had Azarmidokht blinded and killed, and restored Boran in June 631. She gave Rostam overall power, and sent an embassy led by the catholicos Ishoyahb II to Emperor Heraclius, which was well received.

A revolt broke out in Ctesiphon the following year, led by Parsig who disliked Rostam's regency, and Boran was killed, presumably strangled by Piruz Khosrow. Rostam and Piruz Khosrow then agreed to place her nephew Yazdegerd III on the throne, ending the civil war. According to al-Tabari, she reigned sixteen months in all. She was the penultimate Sasanian ruler.

Her coins are the only Sasanian coins with a queen's portrait. They return to her father's design and bear the legend Boran, restorer of the race of Gods, a claim to divine descent not used since Shapur II in the 4th century. She also issued bronze coins, and one gold issue is known.
borba-newspaper: The first issue of Borba, a word meaning fight or combat, appeared in Zagreb on 19 February 1922, edited by Đuro Cvijić and Kamil Horvatin. The communist party had been banned since December 1920 but went on working in secret in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and the paper spread information among its members, activists and sympathisers. Vladimir Ćopić, its editor from 1924, was soon arrested for his articles against the government. On 13 January 1929, a week after King Alexander proclaimed the 6 January Dictatorship, Borba was banned.

During World War II the paper was published in the Republic of Užice, and after the liberation it moved to Belgrade. It was the official gazette of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia until 1954 and then of the Socialist Alliance of Working People of Yugoslavia. From 1948 to 1987 it also appeared in Zagreb, and for a long time it alternated pages in Serbian Cyrillic and Gaj's Latin alphabet in the same edition.

Stanislav Staša Marinković, editor-in-chief from July 1986, made it one of the most liberal dailies in Yugoslavia, and under Manojlo Vukotić its journalists opposed the war policies of Slobodan Milošević in 1992 and 1993. In 1994 the government took the paper over overnight; 120 employees left, and under the new editor Dragutin Brčin it supported Milošević and lost almost its entire readership.

Former Borba journalists founded Naša borba soon after the takeover, and most of them established Danas in 1997. Vukotić started Blic in 1996, and Slavko Ćuruvija, his successor as editor, started Dnevni telegraf, which appeared until Ćuruvija's assassination in March 1999. Borba itself was bought in 2002 by the businessman Stanko Subotić and printed a few hundred copies a day. A redesigned paper appeared on 15 January 2009 but sold fewer than 3,000 copies a day and closed in October 2009. A monthly magazine under the name began in 2020, which former Borba journalists criticised.
borgu: According to the Kisra legend, known all over Borgu, its petty kingdoms were founded by Kisra, a hero who in oral tradition came from Birnin Kisra in Arabia, though descent from Kanem-Bornu is also claimed; his sons are said to have founded Bussa, Illo and Nikki. Before him, local societies were organised by lineage. The legend probably commemorates an invasion by horse-mounted warriors in the 15th century, whose descendants, the Wasangari, used it to support their claim to power and the mutual defence of the Borgu confederacy.

The Songhai emperor Sunni Ali won a crushing victory at Gwangwarake in the 1490s, and Askia Mohammed I returned in 1505, suffering serious defeats but briefly occupying Bussa; Askia Daoud devastated the region in 1558 and 1563. After the fall of Songhai in 1591, Oyo, once Borgu's ally against the Nupe, reduced much of it to vassalage until Borgu defeated Oyo at Gberegburu in 1783. In 1837 Siru Kpera, king of Nikki, joined Alaafin Oluewu against the Fulani jihadists; both were killed, and Borgu's princes grew divided.

Britain and France both made treaties at Nikki during the Race for Nikki in 1894, and the Anglo-French Convention of 1898 split the country: the British half joined the Northern Nigeria Protectorate and the French half French Dahomey.

Borgu was a confederation of kingdoms led by the Wasangari. Bussa was the spiritual centre and held the status of older brother, Nikki the centre of political power and Illo the commercial emporium; Parakou, Kaiama, Kandi and others were also Borgu states. The shared Kisra legend and the Gaani harvest festival held them together. Farming of yam and sorghum was the base of the economy, and from the 16th century kola routes from Gonja and the Ashanti Empire to Hausaland crossed Borgu, their trade dominated by the Muslim Wangara. The Wasangari kept to their own religion: the Emir of Bussa was the first prince to convert to Islam, in 1920.
borgund-stave-church: Borgund Stave Church was the village church of Borgund and belonged to Lærdal parish, in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. It is classified as a triple-nave stave church of the Sogn type. Its walls are vertical boards, or staves, tongued and grooved to interlock, with four corner posts joined by ground sills on a stone foundation. The plan is basilican with reduced side aisles, and a chancel and apse were added in the 14th century. Structurally it has been described as a cube within a cube, with twelve free-standing columns carrying the raised central nave, and Saint Andrew's crosses joining them above the arcade.

The church has tiered, overhanging roofs with a shingled steeple, and a stylised dragon's head on each of its four gables, which resemble the carved dragon heads on Norse ship prows. The present heads may be 18th-century replacements. Their function is uncertain and disputed, and they may have been meant to ward off evil spirits. The west portal is carved with dragons biting each other, and the three entrances are narrow, supposedly to keep evil spirits out along with the churchgoers. They were originally painted green, red, black and white.

The interior is dark. Most internal fittings have been removed, leaving a soapstone font, a medieval stone altar, an altarpiece of 1654 and a pulpit from 1550–1570. Runic inscriptions survive, among them the common Ave Maria and a note by Þórir blaming the pagan Norns for his troubles. A local story says that deer antlers on the pillars are all that remains of a reindeer shot when it tried to enter during Mass. To the south stands Norway's only surviving free-standing stave-built bell tower, probably built in the mid-13th century.

In 1868 a new Borgund Church was built nearby and the old one was turned into a museum, which saved it from the demolition common among stave churches then. The Society for the Preservation of Ancient Norwegian Monuments bought it in 1877, after a restoration in the early 1870s led by Christian Christie, who aimed to return it to its pre-Reformation condition. The first English guidebook appeared in 1898.

It served as the example for the reconstruction of Fantoft Stave Church in Bergen in 1883 and its rebuilding in 1997, and the Gustav Adolf Stave Church at Hahnenklee in Germany, built in 1908, is modelled on it. Four replicas exist in the United States.
boril-of-bulgaria: Boril was the son of a sister of Peter II, Ivan Asen I and Kaloyan, the three rulers who had restored the independent Bulgarian state. The origin of his name is uncertain: it may come from the Slavic verb boriti, to fight, or from the Turkic böri, wolf. Kaloyan died suddenly in October 1207 while besieging Thessaloniki. Rumours held that the city's patron saint, Demetrius, had killed him. The Latin Emperor Henry wrote that Boril had imposed his will by violence and usurped the imperial insignia, and one historian, Alexandru Madgearu, concludes that Boril had his uncle murdered, most likely with Kaloyan's wife. John V. A. Fine stresses that there is no evidence against him.

Boril married Kaloyan's widow, a Cuman princess, either to strengthen his claim or to secure Cuman support, but many nobles, some of them kinsmen, regarded him as a usurper. The young Ivan Asen fled, first to the Cumans and then to the lands of the Russians. His brother Strez took refuge in Serbia, where Stefan Nemanjić gave him the fortress of Prosek, and Alexius Slav took the Rhodope Mountains around his castle at Tsepina.

In May 1208 Boril marched into Thrace against a Greek rebellion backed by the Latin Empire. Henry defeated him near Philippopolis on 8 July, and Alexius Slav paid homage to Henry. Meanwhile Stefan Nemanjić occupied the land between the Struma and Vardar rivers. Boril later allied with Theodore I Laskaris of Nicaea and Michael I Komnenos Doukas of Epirus against the Latins, but his campaigns, including an assault on Thessaloniki in October 1211, failed. He presided over a church synod at Tarnovo in early 1211, which condemned the Bogomils as heretics and ordered their persecution, and he had its decisions published in Bulgarian on 11 February.

An uprising in Vidin between 1211 and 1214 forced Boril to ask Andrew II of Hungary for help, and Count Joachim of Hermannstadt captured Vidin and returned it to him. He made peace with the Latin Empire in late 1213 or early 1214, and Henry married his stepdaughter. After Henry died in July 1216 and Andrew left for a crusade in 1217, Boril's cousin Ivan Asen invaded Bulgaria, beat him in battle and besieged him in Tarnovo. The town fell in 1218, and Boril was captured and blinded. No more is recorded of him.
borinage: The name comes from bores, the word for mineshafts in the local dialect, and the inhabitants are called Borains in French. The provincial capital, Mons, lies in the east of the Borinage, but there was a great social difference between the people of Mons and the Borains of the surrounding villages. The district is often considered the western end of the Sillon industriel, the former industrial backbone of Wallonia.

From the 18th century to 1850 the economy of thirty municipalities of the Borinage rested on coal. Between 1822 and 1829 the region's output more than doubled, from 602,000 to 1,260,000 tons, exported mostly to France and Flanders. In 1878 complete skeletons of iguanodons were found in one of its mines. In 1957 23,000 of the 64,800 people in employment worked in the coal industry, and after the collieries closed in the 1960s the writers Ladrière, Meynaud and Perin judged that the Borinage had died in the ideological and economic sense.

The district was emblematic of the Belgian general strikes, which often broke out there; according to Marcel Liebman the general strike of 1893 was begun by the Borains. The painter Henry Luyten, who lived there in 1886–1887, witnessed a great strike and its bloody suppression and painted the triptych The Strike in response. The years Vincent van Gogh spent among the miners indirectly inspired The Potato Eaters (1885), though it was painted elsewhere.

After a great strike in 1932 met a harsh response from employers and police, Henri Storck and Joris Ivens filmed the miners' poverty in Misère au Borinage (1933), shot with little money while hiding from the police. It shows evictions, children crowded into slum houses and miners gathering low-grade coal on the slag heaps at dawn, and is counted among the most important references of the documentary genre.

Four of the Major Mining Sites of Wallonia were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012. One of them, Grand-Hornu, also houses a museum of contemporary art, and the former coal mine of the Crachet-Picquery company is now the SparkOH! science park.
boris-and-gleb: Boris and Gleb, whose Christian names were Roman and David, were the first saints canonised in Kievan Rus' after it became Christian. According to the two 11th-century Lives of Boris and Gleb, ascribed to Nestor the Hagiographer and Jacob the Monk, they were younger children of Vladimir the Great, who favoured them over his other children. Boris married and ruled the town of Rostov and was probably regarded as heir apparent to the Kievan throne. Gleb, still a minor, ruled the easternmost town of Murom.

Both brothers were murdered during the Kievan succession crisis of 1015–1019. The Primary Chronicle blames Sviatopolk the Accursed. It tells that Boris learned of his father's death on returning with the army, and when urged to replace Sviatopolk replied that he would not raise his hand against his elder brother. Sviatopolk sent Putsha and the boyars of Vyshegorod, and Boris and his Hungarian manservant George were stabbed in a tent while asleep. Found still breathing in a bodybag, Boris was finished off by Varangians with a sword. Gleb rushed to what he thought was his father's deathbed. His brother Yaroslav urged him not to meet Sviatopolk, but he was killed by his own cook, Torchin, who cut his throat with a kitchen knife.

The factual circumstances of their lives and deaths cannot be extrapolated from the hagiography. Foreign sources mention that Boris succeeded his father in Kiev and was not waiting in Rostov, as the Primary Chronicle seems to imply. The Norse Eymund's saga tells of Varangians hired by Yaroslav I the Wise to kill his brother Burizleif; some historians trust it more than sources from Rus' and hold Yaroslav, not Sviatopolk, guilty, while others read Burizleif as a misreading of Bolesław, the Polish ruler allied to Sviatopolk.

The brothers became known as Strastoterptsy, Passion-Bearers, because they did not resist evil with violence. The Orthodox church in Rus' canonised them in 1071 and buried them in the Vyshhorod Cathedral, reconsecrated in their name. In 1095 parts of their relics were moved to Sázava Monastery in the Duchy of Bohemia and placed in an altar. The Catholic Church canonised them in 1724, during the papacy of Benedict XIII. Their feast is observed on 24 July, with the main commemoration of Boris on 15 July and of Gleb on 5 September. Many churches in Russia were named for them, and a monument was erected at Vyshhorod, Ukraine, in 2011.
boris-godunov: Boris Godunov was the son of Feodor Ivanovich Godunov, called Krivoy, the one-eyed, and his wife Stepanida Ivanovna. His career began at the court of Ivan the Terrible. He took part in the Serpeisk campaign of 1570 as an archer of the guard, became an oprichnik the next year, and strengthened his position by marrying Maria Grigorievna Skuratova-Belskaya, daughter of Malyuta Skuratov-Belskiy, head of the oprichniki. In 1580 Ivan chose Boris's sister Irina to marry his son Feodor, and Boris was promoted to boyar.

Ivan IV on his deathbed named a council, including Godunov, to guide his feeble son Feodor I. Boris held the second place in the regency until the death in 1586 of the tsar's uncle Nikita Romanovich, and then had no serious rival. Ivan's young son Dmitry, moved to Uglich, died there in 1591 in suspicious circumstances. A commission headed by Vasili Shuiski reported that the boy had cut his own throat in an epileptic seizure; his mother claimed that Godunov's agents had murdered him, and Godunov's guilt was never established.

As regent he founded towns including Samara, Saratov, Voronezh and Tobolsk, and saw the Russian Orthodox Church receive its patriarchate. A decree of 1597 forbade peasants to move from one landowner to another and led to serfdom in its harshest form.

When Feodor died childless on 7 January 1598, Patriarch Job proposed Boris, who accepted the throne only from a Zemsky Sobor; it elected him unanimously on 21 February, and he was crowned on 1 September. He was the first tsar to bring in foreign teachers on a large scale and to send young Russians abroad to study. In November 1600 he moved against the Romanov clan, tonsuring and exiling Feodor Nikitich Romanov. A famine in 1601–1603 killed hundreds of thousands, and peasants and slaves fled to the southern frontier and the Cossacks.

In the autumn of 1604 a pretender claiming to be the dead Dmitry crossed into Russia from Poland–Lithuania with about 2,000 Polish nobles and some thousands of Cossacks, and the southern towns rose for him. Godunov's government said he was Grigory Otrepyev, an escaped monk. Boris died on 23 April 1605, probably of a stroke, after taking monastic orders under the name Bogolep. His sixteen-year-old son Feodor II was crowned, but the army at Kromy went over to the pretender, and Feodor and his mother were killed on 10 June 1605. Many people took Boris's death as divine punishment. Pushkin's play of 1831 and Mussorgsky's opera dramatise his story.
boris-i-of-bulgaria: Boris was the son and successor of Presian I of Bulgaria. In 852 he sent emissaries to Eastern Francia to confirm the peace of 845. In 854 the Moravian prince Rastislav persuaded him to help against Louis the German, and the campaign was a disaster: Louis invaded Bulgaria, and the Croats also attacked. Peace was restored in 855, but meanwhile a conflict with the Byzantines, begun in 855 or 856, cost him Philippopolis (Plovdiv), the region of Zagora and the ports of the Gulf of Burgas. An invasion of Serbia in 853 or 854, led by his son Vladimir-Rasate, was beaten by Mutimir's army, and Boris then made peace with the Serbs.

Late in 863 the Byzantine emperor Michael III declared war on Bulgaria during a famine and natural disasters. Boris made peace, promising to accept Christianity by the eastern rite in return for territorial concessions in Thrace, and at the start of 864 he was secretly baptised at Pliska with Michael III as godfather, taking the name Michael. Historians give several reasons: diplomacy, the influence of a sister baptised in Constantinople, and the wish to unite the Bulgar warrior aristocracy and the Slavs, who had different beliefs. In the summer of 865 a group of boyars rose in revolt, and Boris suppressed it and executed 52 boyars with their families.

Boris sought an autocephalous church, and in August 866 sent 106 questions to Pope Nicholas I. When Rome refused to name Formosus archbishop, Bulgaria turned back to Constantinople, and at the Fourth Council of Constantinople in 870 its church was made an autocephalous archbishopric. In 886 his governor of Belgrade received the exiled disciples of Cyril and Methodius, and Boris welcomed Clement of Ohrid and Naum of Preslav. They set up centres of teaching and trained Slavonic-speaking priests to replace the Greek clergy, and in 893 the Cyrillic script and Old Bulgarian were declared official.

In 889 Boris abdicated and became a monk. His son Vladimir tried to restore paganism, which brought Boris out of retirement in 893. He defeated Vladimir, had him blinded, and at the Council of Preslav placed his third son Simeon I on the throne. About 895 he emerged again to help Simeon against the Magyars. He died on 2 May 907, and where he was buried is uncertain; it may be near Preslav, near Pliska or at a monastery near Varna. The Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint, the baptiser of Bulgaria and Equal-to-the-Apostles, with a feast on 2 May.
boris-ii-of-bulgaria: Boris II was the eldest surviving son of Emperor Peter I of Bulgaria and Maria, renamed Eirene, Lekapena, a granddaughter of the Byzantine emperor Romanos I Lekapenos. He had been born by 931, when he visited Constantinople with his mother. Nothing else is known of his life until 968, when he went to Constantinople to negotiate a peace with Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, apparently as an honorary hostage. The arrangement was meant to end the conflict between Bulgaria and Byzantium, which would now join forces against Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev, whom the Byzantine emperor had set against the Bulgarians.

In 969 a new Kievan invasion defeated the Bulgarians again and Peter I abdicated to become a monk. In circumstances that are not entirely clear, Boris was allowed to return and take his father's throne. He could not stem the advance of Sviatoslav and had to accept Sviatoslav as ally and puppet-master against the Byzantines. After a campaign of Sviatoslav's into Thrace was defeated at Arkadioupolis in 970, the new Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes advanced north and took the capital Preslav by setting its wooden structures on fire.

Boris became John's captive, treated with respect while John besieged Sviatoslav at Drăstăr. In 971 John returned to Constantinople with Boris, his family and the Bulgarian treasury. In a public ceremony Boris was stripped of his imperial insignia and given the court title of magistros. The Bulgarian lands in Thrace and lower Moesia became Byzantine.

The western provinces stayed under their own governors, above all the four Kometopouloi brothers, David, Moses, Aron and Samuel, who seem to have seen themselves as a regency for the captive Boris. In 977 the Byzantines let Boris and his brother Roman escape, hoping to divide the Kometopouloi from other Bulgarian leaders. As they entered the territory under Bulgarian control, Boris dismounted and went ahead of his brother. Mistaken for a Byzantine notable because of his clothing, he was shot in the chest by a deaf and mute border guard. Roman identified himself to the other guards and was accepted as emperor.
boris-iii-of-bulgaria: Boris was born in Sofia on 30 January 1894, the eldest son of Ferdinand I, Prince of Bulgaria, and Princess Marie Louise of Bourbon-Parma. In 1896 his father had the infant converted from Catholicism to Eastern Orthodoxy to reconcile Bulgaria and Russia, which brought Ferdinand excommunication by Pope Leo XIII. In September 1918 Bulgaria was defeated in the Vardar Offensive, and Ferdinand abdicated in his favour; Boris became tsar on 3 October 1918.

The Treaty of Neuilly of 1919 made Bulgaria cede territory, pay heavy reparations and cut its army. The prime minister Aleksandar Stamboliyski was overthrown in a military coup on 9 June 1923. In April 1925 a bomb at the Saint Nedelya Church in Sofia killed 213 members of the political and military elite, and military reprisals then killed several thousand communists and agrarians. In 1934 the Zveno movement seized power and banned political parties; in 1935 Boris overthrew it and from then ruled as a de facto absolute monarch.

In September 1940, with German support, Bulgaria received Southern Dobrudja from Romania. In January 1941 Boris approved the antisemitic Law for Protection of the Nation, which denied citizenship to Bulgarian Jews. In March 1941 Bulgaria joined the Axis and let German troops use its territory to invade Yugoslavia and Greece, receiving most of Yugoslav Macedonia and Greek Thrace; Boris was called the Unifier. Bulgaria took no part in the invasion of the Soviet Union. In March 1943 Bulgarian authorities deported 11,343 Jews from the occupied territories to Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka.

When Germany pressed for the deportation of Bulgaria's own Jews, a public outcry followed, led by the deputy speaker of parliament, Dimitar Peshev, and Archbishop Stefan. Boris then refused to allow the deportation of Bulgaria's nearly 50,000 Jews, though almost 20,000 were expelled to the countryside.

Boris died of apparent heart failure on 28 August 1943, shortly after returning from a meeting with Hitler. Rumours of assassination spread at once, but there is no evidence that Hitler planned it. His six-year-old son Simeon succeeded him as Simeon II.
boris-pasternak: Boris Leonidovich Pasternak was born in Moscow on 10 February 1890 (29 January in the old style), into a wealthy, assimilated Jewish family. His father, Leonid Pasternak, was a post-Impressionist painter who taught at the Moscow School of Painting, Sculpture, and Architecture; his mother, Rosa Kaufman, was a concert pianist. The family home was visited by Sergei Rachmaninoff, Rainer Maria Rilke and Leo Tolstoy.

Pasternak first studied music at the Moscow Conservatory and composed, and he later went to Germany to study philosophy. In 1912 he met Ida Wissotzkaya in Marburg. Her family, troubled by his poor prospects, persuaded her to refuse his proposal, and he told of the rejection in the poem Marburg, written in 1917.

Pasternak's first book of poems, My Sister, Life, was composed in 1917 and published in Berlin in 1922, and it soon became an important collection in the Russian language. He also became a literary translator, rendering plays by Goethe, Schiller, Pedro Calderón de la Barca and Shakespeare. His translation of the first part of Faust drew an attack in Novy Mir in August 1950, which accused him of distorting Goethe's meanings.

In 1934 Osip Mandelstam recited his epigram on Stalin to him; Mandelstam was arrested that May, and Pasternak appealed to Nikolai Bukharin on his behalf. In 1937 he refused to sign a writers' statement supporting death sentences in the trial of Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky and others. During the Second World War he served as a fire warden in Moscow and in 1943 visited soldiers at the front.

Doctor Zhivago, which contains passages from the 1910s and 1920s, was completed in 1955. Novy Mir refused it in 1956 for its rejection of socialist realism, and censors objected to its criticism of Stalinism, collectivisation, the Great Purge and the Gulag. It was first published in Italy in 1957. Pasternak was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958 and was forced to decline it.

Pasternak died of lung cancer at his dacha in Peredelkino on 30 May 1960. Despite a small notice in the Literary Gazette, handwritten notices of the funeral were posted through the Moscow subway, and thousands of admirers attended despite surveillance. His companion Olga Ivinskaya and her daughter were arrested after his death and accused of dealing with Western publishers; she served four years of an eight-year sentence.

The Soviet state kept criticising him until the 1980s. His son Yevgeny accepted the Nobel Prize on his behalf in 1989, and the house-museum in Peredelkino was founded in 1986. Doctor Zhivago has been part of the main Russian school curriculum since 2003, and David Lean's film of 1965 was unavailable in Russia until perestroika.
boris-piotrovsky: Boris Borisovich Piotrovsky was born in Saint Petersburg on 14 February 1908. He specialised in the history and archaeology of the Caucasus, and in the 1930s he began to study the Urartian civilisation of the southern Caucasus. He was married to Hripsime Djanpoladjian, an archaeologist and epigrapher.

The finds made at Karmir Blur, the Red Hill, became key to understanding Urartu. Piotrovsky went on to lead excavations at other ancient settlements in Armenia, among them Tsovinar, Redkig-lager, Kirovakan (now Vanadzor) and Aygevan, until 1971. He also worked elsewhere in the Caucasus, especially on the Scythian culture, and in 1961 he was put at the head of an expedition of the Academy of Sciences of the Soviet Union to study the Nubian monuments of Egypt. He supervised the Armenian archaeologist Gregory Areshian.

He published more than 200 works on archaeology, history and art. The History of Urartu and its Culture, published in 1944, received the Stalin Prize in 1946; later books included Urartu: The Kingdom of Van and Its Art (1967), The Ancient Civilization of Urartu (1969) and The Hermitage: Its History and Collections (1982).

Piotrovsky directed the Hermitage for 26 years, and the museum was afterwards run by his son Mikhail. He died of a cerebral haemorrhage in Leningrad on 15 October 1990, at the age of 82. He was made a Hero of Socialist Labour in 1983 and received three Orders of Lenin, the Order of the October Revolution and the medal For the Defence of Leningrad, and France made him a Commander of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres. The Hermitage holds an annual conference in his honour.
boris-skossyreff: Boris Mikhailovich Skossyreff was born on 12 June 1896 in Vilnius, then part of the Russian Empire, to Belarusian parents of probably lower nobility. He later carried a Dutch passport that gave his title as Monsieur le Baron Boris de Skossyreff, which was likely false. He said he had attended the Lycée Louis-le-Grand and Magdalen College, Oxford, and had been a childhood friend of Edward VIII, but both institutions confirm that he was not a student.

After the revolution of 1917 he sought asylum in England and enlisted for about two years in the British Army. Newspapers later mentioned him for cheque fraud, and Dutch security records of 1924 list him as an international swindler.

In the early 1930s Skossyreff lived near Sant Julià de Lòria in Andorra. On 17 May 1934 he presented advisers to the General Council of the Valleys with a document justifying his rule, and the councillors ridiculed it. He then settled in La Seu d'Urgell, a few kilometres from the border, where he gave interviews to The Times and The Daily Herald and acted as a monarch in exile. He printed ten thousand copies of a constitution that promised freedoms, modernisation, foreign investment and a tax haven. One copy reached the Bishop of Urgell, Justí Guitart i Vilardebó, who reaffirmed that the only co-princes of Andorra were himself and the President of the French Republic.

In return for his proposals he asked the General Council to proclaim him king, and it is said to have backed him, with one adviser against twenty-three. Contemporary reports say he proclaimed himself King of Andorra on 11 July 1934. He declared war on the Bishop of Urgell, but when he tried to re-enter Andorra he was stopped at La Seu d'Urgell. On 20 July the Spanish Civil Guard arrested him there, at the Bishop's command. The next day he was taken to a judge in Barcelona, and on 23 July he was sent by train to the Modelo prison in Madrid.

Skossyreff spent the next years in and out of custody in Portugal, Spain and France. In October 1942 the occupying Germans released him from a French prison, and he then served in the German military on the Eastern Front. After 1945 he settled at Boppard in West Germany, was arrested by the Soviets in Eisenach in 1948 and sentenced to a Siberian camp. Freed in 1956, he returned to Boppard, and he died on 27 February 1989. A novel about him, Boris I, Rei d'Andorra, appeared in 1984.
boris-yeltsin: Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin was born on 1 February 1931 in Butka, a village in the Ural Oblast of the Russian SFSR. His family were ethnic Russians who had lived in the Urals since at least the eighteenth century. In September 1949 he entered the Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk, where he studied industrial and civil engineering, played volleyball and kept out of political organisations, and he then worked in construction. He became a full member of the Communist Party in March 1961, and by December 1965 he was director of the Sverdlovsk House-Building Combine.

In October 1976 Yeltsin became First Secretary of the party committee of Sverdlovsk Oblast, one of the youngest provincial first secretaries in the Russian SFSR. In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev brought him to Moscow. He supported perestroika at first, but later criticised it as too moderate and called for a multi-party democracy. On 10 September 1987 he wrote a letter of resignation from the Politburo, the first person in Soviet history to resign voluntarily from its ranks.

On 29 May 1990 he was elected chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the Russian SFSR, and on 12 July 1990 he resigned from the Communist Party. On 12 June 1991 he won 57 per cent of the vote in the republic's presidential election, becoming the first popularly elected head of state in Russian history. He was instrumental in the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991, after which the RSFSR became the Russian Federation. Days later he began radical economic reform, through shock therapy, privatisation and the lifting of price controls.

In 1993 he ordered the dissolution of the Russian parliament, which impeached him. The crisis ended when troops loyal to him stormed the parliament building, and he then introduced a new constitution that expanded the powers of the president. The First Chechen War began in 1994, and he was re-elected in 1996.

Yeltsin resigned by the end of 1999 and was succeeded by Vladimir Putin, whom he had appointed prime minister a few months earlier. He died on 23 April 2007 and was given a state funeral. He has been praised for his part in dismantling the Soviet Union and introducing new freedoms, and criticised for economic mismanagement and abuse of presidential power.
borivoj-i-duke-of-bohemia: Bořivoj I is the first historically documented Duke of Bohemia and the progenitor of the Přemyslid dynasty. According to the Chronica Boëmorum of Cosmas, written in the early 12th century, he was a son of the Bohemian prince Hostivít and so a descendant of Queen Libuše and her husband Přemysl the Ploughman, but historians have not established his ancestry conclusively. Given his dependence on Great Moravia, he may have been related by blood to the Mojmir dynasty. He first resided at Levý Hradec, northwest of present-day Prague. The Frankish Annales Fuldenses mention in 872 a West Slavic prince called Goriwei, who may be Bořivoj.

Bořivoj declared himself kníže, in Latin dux, a sovereign prince, around 867, and was recognised as such about 872 by his overlord King Svatopluk I of Moravia, who sent Bishop Methodius of Thessalonica to begin the Christianization of Bohemia. In 872 he supported Svatopluk against the East Frankish king Louis the German, and they defeated the Frankish troops in south Bohemia. About 874 he married Ludmila, later canonised as St. Ludmila of Bohemia. Their two known sons, Spytihněv and Vratislaus, both succeeded him as dukes.

Bořivoj and Ludmila were baptised by Methodius, probably in 883, and he became an enthusiastic evangelist, although the religion failed to take root among his subjects. In 883 or 884 a revolt in support of his Přemyslid kinsman Strojmír deposed him, and he was restored in 885 only with Svatopluk's support. The move of the residence to the Hradčany hill and the first foundations of Prague Castle are attributed to him or, more probably, to Spytihněv.

Bořivoj died about 889 with his sons still minors, and Svatopluk made an agreement with the East Frankish ruler Arnulf of Carinthia and took over the rule of the duchy himself. Like most early Bohemian rulers he remains a shadowy figure: exact dates for his reign and vital statistics cannot be established, although several major fortifications and religious foundations are said to date from his time. DNA testing on the remains of his son Spytihněv suggests the family's Y-haplogroup was R1b.
borjigin: The Borjigin, or Borjigids, trace their descent to Bodonchar Munkhag, who is dated to the early 10th century. According to the Secret History of the Mongols, the first Mongol was born from the union of a blue-grey wolf and a fallow doe, and their 11th-generation descendant Alan Gua conceived five sons after being impregnated by a ray of light; the youngest was Bodonchar. Rashid al-Din Hamadani wrote that many older Mongol tribes, among them the Barlas, Manghud and Kiyat, were founded by members of the clan.

Bodonchar's descendant Khabul Khan founded the Khamag Mongol confederation around 1131. His great-grandson Temüjin ruled it, united the other Mongol tribes and was declared Genghis Khan in 1206, establishing the Mongol Empire. His descendants are the Chinggisids.

Many dynasties that followed the Mongol Empire's disintegration were of Chinggisid ancestry, among them the Yuan dynasty, the Ilkhanate, the Jochids of the Golden Horde, the Shaybanids and the Jalayirid Sultanate. Chinggisid descent shaped politics: Mamai had to rule through puppet khans because he lacked it, and Babur and Humayun claimed it through their maternal line. In 1368 the Yuan were expelled from China, and the last emperor, Toghon Temür, withdrew north of the Great Wall, where the court continued as the Northern Yuan.

Dayan Khan (1480–1517) brought a Borjigid revival, and his descendants held most of Mongolia in four Khalkha khanates, which remained independent until the Qing annexation of 1691. Borjigin nobles went on ruling their subjects under the Qing and proclaimed Mongolia's independence in 1911. In Crimea and Kazan the Khiyad Borjigids ruled until the Russian Empire annexed them in the late 18th century.

The communist regime banned clan names in the 1920s, and Stalin's associates executed some 30,000 Mongols, including Borjigin nobles. The last ruling Borjigin prince, Navaanneren Setsen Khan, was executed in 1937. When the ban was lifted in 1997, some families had lost knowledge of their clan. Around 700,000 people are registered under the surname Borjigin in Mongolia. In Inner Mongolia the names Borjigid and Kiyad became the basis of surnames such as Bao and Qi, and a genetic study has proposed that as many as 16 million men, from the Hazaras to the Hezhe, may have Borjigid-Kiyad ancestry.
born-in-the-purple: The colour behind the phrase is Tyrian or imperial purple, a luxury dye obtained from sea snails. Its cost made it a status symbol among the Ancient Romans, as in the purple stripe on the togas of magistrates and the all-purple toga picta worn in triumphs. By the Byzantine period it was associated with the emperors, and sumptuary laws kept it for the imperial household. Porphyry, a purple stone, was likewise rare and at times reserved for imperial use.

The princess Anna Komnene, herself born in the purple in the 12th century, described the birth chamber as a room long set apart for empresses' confinements, standing where the stone oxen and lions stood, in the Boukoleon Palace. It was a perfect square ending in a pyramid, its walls, floor and ceiling veneered with porphyry, purple throughout with white spots like sprinkled sand. Both explanations of the title were already current in the 10th century.

Constantine VII described the ceremonies held at the birth of a porphyrogennetos boy in his De Ceremoniis, and the term remained in use into the Palaiologan period; the late 13th-century Palace of the Porphyrogenitus in Constantinople is named after Constantine Palaiologos, a younger son of Emperor Michael VIII. In diplomacy a purple-born bride was sometimes sent to seal a bargain. In 968 Liutprand of Cremona came to Constantinople for Otto I to obtain such a bride for the future Otto II, but failed; Theophanu, who was not purple-born, was secured in 971.

The classic definition covered only legitimate children born to a reigning monarch after accession, or, read most strictly, after coronation. In modern usage being born in the purple is often seen as a limitation to escape rather than a blessing, since the parents' rank fixes the child's role. One writer held that the German Emperor Wilhelm I, had he not been born in the purple, could only have been a soldier. An obituary of the composer Hubert Parry used the phrase of his natural talent, which pushed him into teaching and administration at the expense of composing.
borneo: Borneo is the third-largest island in the world, with an area of 748,168 square kilometres. It lies at the geographic centre of Maritime Southeast Asia, north of Java, west of Sulawesi and east of Sumatra, and the equator divides it roughly in half. It was part of Sundaland, joined to mainland Asia, until sea level rose at the end of the Last Glacial Period. Its rainforest, estimated at around 140 million years old, is among the oldest in the world and shelters many endemic species, including the Bornean orangutan. In Indonesia the island is also called Kalimantan, a name that comes from Pulu K'lemantang, as its people called the island when the Portuguese explorer Jorge de Menezes met them in the sixteenth century.

Archaeological evidence shows that people lived on Borneo for tens of thousands of years. A cave at Lahad Datu in Sabah suggests settlement about 46,000 years ago, and the Trader Cave at Niah in Sarawak has yielded tools and human remains dated between 55,000 and 65,000 years ago. The island is home to hundreds of Indigenous communities, many grouped under the broad term Dayak. Trading settlements were connected to regional maritime networks by the first millennium CE, and Chinese records use the term Bo-ni for Borneo in 977. The Javanese poem Nagarakretagama, written in 1365 at the court of Majapahit, mentions the island as Nusa Tanjungnagara, the island of the Tanjungpura Kingdom.

Empires, kingdoms and sultanates emerged around the coasts. The Sultanate of Brunei held influence over much of coastal Borneo and parts of the southern Philippines at its peak in the 15th century, and the Sultanate of Sulu became a maritime power in north-eastern Borneo. The interior remained politically diverse and was governed largely by local Indigenous systems of authority rather than by a single state. After Malacca fell in 1511, Portuguese merchants traded with Borneo, and from 1530 especially with Brunei, but never tried to conquer it. The British began trading with Sambas in 1609 and the Dutch with Banjar and Martapura in 1644.

Japanese forces occupied most of Borneo from 1941 to 1945. Many coastal people fled to the interior, and many Indigenous and Chinese people were executed after resistance movements such as the Jesselton Revolt.

Borneo is divided among three states. About 73 per cent of the island belongs to Indonesia, as the provinces of Kalimantan, about 26 per cent forms the Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak, and the sultanate of Brunei occupies a small area on the north-west coast. The name Borneo is closely tied to Brunei, since early European travellers recorded variants such as Burnei for the sultanate before the name was applied to the whole island.
bornholm: Bornholm lies in the Baltic Sea east of the rest of Denmark, south of Sweden, north-east of Germany and north of Poland. It is known as the sunshine island for its weather and the rock island for its geology, which is granite except along the southern coast. In Old Norse the island was Borgundarholmr, a name related to words for height and rock, because it rises high from the sea. Its early names include Burgendaland in the 9th century, and some scholars believe the Burgundians took their name from it.

Strategically placed, Bornholm has been fought over for centuries. It has usually been ruled by Denmark but also by Sweden and by Lübeck, to which Frederick I of Denmark pawned it for fifty years from 1525, in payment for its support in his winning the Danish throne. Swedish forces conquered it during the Torstenson War in 1645, but it was returned to Denmark. In 1658 Denmark ceded it to Sweden under the Treaty of Roskilde, along with the rest of Skåneland, Bohuslän and Trøndelag. A revolt broke out the same year and culminated on 8 December 1658, when Villum Clausen shot the Swedish commander Johan Printzensköld. The islanders then handed the island back to the Danish kings.

German forces occupied Denmark on 9 April 1940. On 22 August 1942 a V-1 flying bomb crashed on the island during a test, one of the first signs to British Intelligence of German flying-bomb development. Soviet aircraft bombed the main towns on 7 and 8 May 1945, and Soviet troops landed on 9 May, when the German garrison of about 12,000 surrendered after a short fight. The Soviet forces left on 5 April 1946. Sweden afterwards gave aid to rebuild Rønne and Nexø.

Bornholm is a Danish island, and Rønne is its largest town and seat. With Ertholmene it is the last remaining Danish territory in Skåneland east of Øresund. The ruin of Hammershus at the north-western tip is the largest medieval fortress in northern Europe. The island has 15 medieval churches, four of them round churches, and at Rispebjerg are remains of Neolithic sun temples and Iron Age earthworks. In the early 20th century it drew artists who formed the Bornholm school of painters.
borno-state: Borno borders Yobe to the west, Gombe to the southwest and Adamawa to the south, and its eastern and northern borders form parts of the national frontiers with Cameroon, Niger and Chad. It is the only Nigerian state to border three countries and the second largest by area. Semi-desert Sahelian savanna covers the north, West Sudanian savanna the centre and south, and part of the Mandara Plateau lies in the southeast. The far northeast holds the Nigerian portion of Lake Chad. Kanuri and Shuwa Arabs live throughout the north and centre, and many other groups live elsewhere. About 85 per cent of the people are Muslim.

From the 700s the area lay within the Kanem Empire. In the late 1300s Kanem, after unsuccessful wars, moved west and became the Bornu Empire, which ruled the wider area for about 500 years. The Fulani jihad of the early 1800s weakened Bornu, and much of the south was taken into the Adamawa Emirate under the Sokoto Caliphate. About eighty years later the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr conquered the empire, and he ruled until French forces killed him at the Battle of Kousséri in 1900. The British, French and Germans then divided the lands, and in 1902 the British incorporated Borno into the Northern Nigeria Protectorate and in 1907 set up a new capital at Maiduguri.

Nigeria became independent in 1960. Borno was part of the Northern Region until 1967, when the area became part of the North-Eastern State. Borno State was formed on 3 February 1976, with ten other states, from the breakup of that state. Local government reform in 1976 reduced the power of the emirs, and by 1979 their jurisdiction covered only cultural and traditional affairs. In 1991 a group of local government areas in the west formed the new Yobe State.

Maiduguri is the capital and a major regional centre of trade and services. The state has 27 local government areas and emirate councils, among them Borno, Bama, Dikwa and Biu, which advise on cultural and traditional matters. Its economy has relied on livestock and crops, and it holds deposits of kaolin, clay, trona and iron ore. Higher institutions include the University of Maiduguri. Since 2009 it has been the centre of the Boko Haram insurgency.
borobudur: Borobudur stands in Magelang Regency in Central Java, about 40 kilometres northwest of Yogyakarta, between the twin volcanoes Sindoro-Sumbing and Merbabu-Merapi and the Progo and Elo rivers. Scholars following de Casparis conclude that the Sanjaya and Sailendra dynasties shared power in central Java for a century and a half, with alternating succession traced from 732 until 882, and that many Hindu and Buddhist monuments rose around the Kedu Plain in that period. Evidence suggests that Borobudur was built in the 8th century and later abandoned.

Its abandonment remains a mystery, and it is not known when pilgrimage ceased. Some sources name the period between 928 and 1006, when King Mpu Sindok moved the capital of the Mataram kingdom to East Java after volcanic eruptions. A poet of the Majapahit era mentions the vihara in Budur in the Nagarakretagama, written around 1365.

Borobudur is built as a single large stupa and, seen from above, takes the form of a giant tantric Buddhist mandala representing Buddhist cosmology. Its square foundation measures about 118 metres on each side, and it has nine platforms, the lower six square and the upper three circular, topped by a central dome. About 55,000 cubic metres of andesite were laid without mortar and joined by knobs, indentations and dovetails, and the reliefs were carved in place after the building was complete.

Pilgrims climb through stairways and corridors lined with 1,460 narrative relief panels. Reliefs on the hidden base illustrate the law of karma, others tell the life of Prince Siddhartha from the Lalitavistara, the Jataka stories of the Buddha's earlier lives, and Sudhana's search for truth. The temple holds 432 Buddha statues in niches on the square platforms, and 72 more sit inside perforated stupas on the circular platforms.

Under British administration from 1811 to 1816, Stamford Raffles was told in 1814 of a big monument deep in the jungle near the village of Bumisegoro. He sent the Dutch engineer Hermann Cornelius, who with 200 men cut down trees, burned vegetation and dug away the earth, though he could not uncover all the galleries. Raffles did not visit the site himself but is credited with bringing it to the world's attention. In 1885 Jan Willem IJzerman found that the base enclosed a hidden foot, and a commission formed in 1900 proposed protection. A major renovation funded by UNESCO took place in 1973.
borommakot: Prince Phon was a son of Sanphet VIII. When his elder brother Prince Phet came to the throne as Sanphet IX, known as Thai Sa, in 1708, Phon was made the Front Palace. Thai Sa, however, chose his second son, Prince Aphai, as heir, since his eldest son had become a monk. On Thai Sa's death in 1732 Phon led his armies against his nephews Aphai and Paramet, in a war described as bigger than any fought in Siam before. Victorious, he executed his nephews and their allies among the officials and took the throne.

Because the Samuha Kalahom had supported Aphai, Borommakot stripped that office of its authority over southern Siam and gave it to the Kromma Tha. His succession was troubled: in 1735 his eldest son and heir was accused of an affair with one of the king's queens, and both died. In 1741 he made his son Thammathibet, a poet, the Grand Vizier, but Thammathibet was caught in 1746 with two of the king's concubines and died under the lash. Borommakot then passed over his second son, Ekkathat, as unsuitable and appointed his third son, Duea, later Uthumphon.

In 1753 he sent two Siamese monks to restore Theravada Buddhism in Sri Lanka, at the request of a Sangha mission from Kandy. The Royal Chronicles of Siam describe him as a king who refrained from taking life and gave alms to monks, Brahmins, beggars and animals, and who enjoyed outings to Bang Pa-In, boating and festivals.

Borommakot rebuilt much of the city, and much of what survives in Ayutthaya today dates from his renovations, among them the Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit, the Royal Palace and Wat Phu Khao Thong. His reign was the last flowering of the kingdom, which fell nine years after his death, during the reign of Ekkathat. The later Bangkok aristocracy revered him, and King Rama I modelled his religious customs on Borommakot's reign and postponed his own coronation until it could follow Borommakot's.
borommarachathirat-i: The name Ngua traditionally refers to the fifth-born child in archaic Thai numbering, so it is hypothesised that he was the fifth son of his family. As the elder brother of the consort of Ramathibodi I, he was formally addressed by that king as an elder brother. When Ramathibodi I established the Ayutthaya Kingdom in 1350, he gave Khun Luang Pha Ngua the title Somdet Phra Borommarachathirat and sent him to rule the city of Suphan Buri.

In 1353 he marched to Angkor Thom to support Ramesuan, whom Ramathibodi I had sent against the Khmer king after his defection. The Khmer forces had routed the Ayutthayan vanguard, and the king summoned his brother-in-law from Suphan Buri to help. The campaign lasted about a year and ended in an Ayutthayan victory and the forced relocation of a large number of Khmer captives to Ayutthaya.

In 1370 he marched his army from Suphan Buri to Ayutthaya. Ramesuan came out to welcome his maternal uncle, then abdicated and returned to govern Lopburi. Traditional chronicles describe a peaceful abdication, but historians widely interpret the arrival of an armed force as what pressed Ramesuan to step down, and see the change as a shift of power from the Lopburi faction of the Uthong dynasty to the Suphan Buri faction.

From 1374 he campaigned against northern city-states, among them Chakangrao, Phitsanulok, Chiang Mai and Lampang, until the end of his reign. He led four expeditions against Chakangrao, modern Kamphaeng Phet, a frontier city of the Sukhothai Kingdom: in 1376 its ruler Phraya Sai Kaeo was killed, and in 1378 Thao Pha Khong fled and many nobles and commanders were captured. Maha Thammaracha II of Sukhothai later surrendered and was allowed to rule as a vassal. An invasion of Chiang Mai was repulsed at the Battle of Sen Sanuk.

In 1375, after consulting the monk Phra Maha Thera Thammakanyan, he commissioned Phra Si Rattana Mahathat in the eastern quarter of the city, the present Wat Mahathat, whose central prang stood 19 wa, about 38 metres, high. After his death in 1388 his son Thong Lan reigned for only a week before Ramesuan returned from Lavo, overthrew him and began a second reign. The dominance of the Suphannaphum dynasty over Ayutthaya that he began lasted for several decades.
borommarachathirat-ii: Sam Phraya was a son of King Intharacha, who had secured the throne of Ayutthaya for the Suphannaphum dynasty, and was appointed by his father governor of Chainat. He had two elder brothers, Prince Ai Phraya and Prince Yi Phraya. When Intharacha died in 1424, both brothers marched from their cities to Ayutthaya to claim the throne and fought each other in single combat on elephants. Both were killed, and the throne passed to Sam Phraya.

His campaign against the post-Angkor Khmer kingdom ended in the plundering of Angkor Thom. He ordered the Nakhonin to rule in Cambodia and, after the Nakhonin's death, appointed another son, the Prince of Phrak, who was assassinated by Ponhea Yat. Ponhea Yat became king and moved the capital to Chaktomuk, to escape the influence of Siam and bring the centre closer to the sea for maritime trade. Ayutthaya did not occupy Angkor permanently, but its court reportedly brought many Khmer officials, Brahmins, artisans and administrators to the capital.

In 1442, during the succession turmoil after the death of King Sam Fang Kaen, he led a major expedition against Lan Na. His forces laid siege to Chiang Mai but could not take the city or defeat the newly enthroned King Tilokaraj, and the campaign ended in retreat after the king reportedly fell ill. He also married a daughter of Maha Tammaraja IV, the vassal ruler of Sukhothai, and their son Prince Ramesuan later inherited that kingdom.

He died in 1448 and was succeeded by Prince Ramesuan as King Borommatrailokkanat. His reign is considered a watershed in the history of Ayutthaya, marking the transition from a loose mandala polity to a more centralised kingdom, and the influx of Khmer elite culture led to the adoption of the Devaraja, or god-king, concept at the Siamese court.

In 1424 he commissioned Wat Ratchaburana on the site where his two brothers had died fighting for the throne. Its prang, which blends Khmer and Sukhothai influences, is considered a masterpiece of early Ayutthaya architecture, and its crypt, discovered in the 20th century, held a large hoard of gold artefacts and votive tablets.
borommatrailokkanat: Born Prince Ramesuan in 1431, he was a son of King Borommarachathirat II of Ayutthaya. Some authors claim his mother was a princess of Sukhothai, a daughter of Sai Lue Thai, but the historian Michael Vickery holds that this cannot be verified in the sources. Sukhothai had been under Ayutthaya's suzerainty since 1412, and when King Maha Thammaracha IV died in 1438 Borommaracha II annexed it and made his seven-year-old son viceroy (uparaja) of Sukhothai. At 15 the prince was sent to Phitsanulok to rule the northern cities, and at his father's death in 1448 he was crowned, joining Sukhothai and Ayutthaya in a personal union.

He separated civil and military officials, gave nobles titular and feudal ranks, and ended the practice of appointing royal princes to govern cities, which had led to clashes at each succession. He promulgated Ayutthayan Law in 1458, introduced the Kalahom and the Mahatthai, and in 1454 had noble titles first codified in the sakdina hierarchy, measured in rai of land. In 1468 he ranked the cities under him in a mandala tributary system, with Phitsanulok and Nakhon Sri Thamarat among the eight first-rank cities. He also sent envoys to the Malacca Sultanate in 1455.

The war with Lan Na began when his childhood friend Yutthitthira, denied the promised title of uparaja, claimed the throne of Sukhothai and in 1456 brought the armies of Tilokkarat south. Borommatrailokkanat made Phitsanulok his base and in 1461 was ordained there as a Buddhist monk at Wat Chulamani with more than 2000 followers, the first Thai king to be ordained; one account dates it to 1465. His son Prince Intharacha was killed fighting Lan Na in 1463. In 1474 he drove Lan Na out of his territories, and the next year Tilokkarat sought peace.

In 1485 he made his son Prince Chaiyachettha, later Ramathibodi II, uparaja and King of Sukhothai, which became a title of the Ayutthayan crown prince. At his death in 1488 two sons inherited the two kingdoms, ending the union for a time. The system of administration he built lasted well into the 20th century.
borre-mound-cemetery: The Norwegian name of the cemetery, Borrehaugene, comes from the Old Norse words borró and haugr, meaning mound. The cemetery lies within Borre National Park in Horten Municipality, which covers 18 hectares (45 acres). Seven large mounds and one cairn can still be seen, and there are many smaller cairns. Some of the monuments are over 45 metres across and up to 6 metres high. At least two mounds and one cairn have been destroyed in modern times, and the cemetery may once have been larger.

Excavations in the 1980s showed that the oldest mounds date to about 600, before the Viking Age. The cemetery is taken as evidence of a local centre of power that lasted from the Merovingian period into the Viking Age. The first investigations came in 1851 and 1852, after local road-builders used one of the mounds as a gravel pit and destroyed large parts of a richly furnished grave in a Viking ship. The antiquarian Nicolay Nicolaysen examined what was left.

The grave held weapons and riding equipment and an unusually good collection of craft work, much of it now shown at the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo. Its animal and knot ornaments, often used to decorate harnesses, gave the Borre style its name. Some of the smaller cairns were opened in 1925 and proved to be simple cremation graves. The archaeologist Bjørn Myhre excavated in and around the park from 1989 to 1991.

Ground-penetrating radar has since added to the picture. A survey of October 2007 by the Swedish Central National Heritage Board, for the Vestfold County Administration, found the buried remains of two prehistoric hall buildings, the first substantial buildings found near Borre. A larger survey in March 2013 by the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Archaeological Prospection and Virtual Archaeology, with the county and the Norwegian Institute for Cultural Heritage Research, found another large hall. In 2015 Erich Draganits and colleagues argued from the landscape that a prehistoric harbour probably lay at Borre, and in March 2019 archaeologists found what is believed to be a buried Viking-era ship.

The cemetery forms part of Borre National Park. The Midgard Viking Center at Borre, formerly the Midgard Historical Center, opened in 2000; part of the Vestfold Museum, it was founded to spread knowledge of the Viking Age. It holds exhibitions and offers guided tours of the national park and its mounds.
borrell-ii-of-barcelona: Borrell was the son of Count Sunyer II of Barcelona and is first seen acting as count beside his father at the consecration of the nunnery church of Sant Pere de les Puelles in Barcelona. When Sunyer retired to monastic life he left his lands jointly to Borrell and his brother Miro I, and in 948 Borrell inherited Urgell from his uncle Sunifred II. Sunyer died in 950 and Miro in 966, leaving Borrell sole ruler of more than half of Old Catalonia. Outsiders called him dux Gothiae, Duke of Gothia, but his own documents almost always style him comes et marchio, count and marquis.

In 967 he married Letgarda, perhaps a daughter of a count of Toulouse or Rouergue, with whom he had two sons, Ramon Borrell and Ermengol, and two daughters, Ermengarda and Richilda; after her death around 986 he married Eimeruda, perhaps of Auvergne. He is recorded in only two battles and seems to have lost both, but he was a skilled diplomat, keeping cordial relations with Córdoba apart from a raid by Caliph al-Hakam II after 961, and in 970 travelling to Rome to meet Pope John XIII and Emperor Otto I.

He was also a patron of learning. Visiting the monastery of Aurillac in 967, he was asked by its abbot to take the young Gerbert of Aurillac, the future Pope Sylvester II, to study mathematics in Spain; Gerbert studied under Bishop Atto of Vic and went with Borrell to Rome in 970, where the pope persuaded Otto to employ him as tutor to the future Otto II.

After Almanzor defeated Borrell and sacked Barcelona in 985, taking many citizens prisoner, appeals to King Lothar III and to Hugh Capet brought no army, and no reply from Borrell to Hugh's letter is known. Catalan nationalist historians date Catalonia's sovereignty from this break and marked its millennium in 1987 with conferences and publications, though other Catalan counties kept their Frankish links a little longer. From 988 Ramon Borrell ruled Barcelona, Girona and Osona and Ermengol Urgell, while Borrell still toured his lands until he fell ill at Castellciutat near la Seu d'Urgell and died soon after.
borsippa: Borsippa is an archaeological site in Babylon Governorate, Iraq, built on both sides of a lake on the east bank of the Euphrates, southwest of Babylon and about 15 kilometres from the ancient site of Dilbat. Its ruined ziggurat is among the most clearly identifiable in the region. Later Arabic tradition identified it with the Tower of Babel, because Nebuchadnezzar called it the Tower of Borsippa, or tongue tower, in a stele found on the site in the 19th century. Modern scholarship concludes that its Babylonian builders raised it as a religious edifice in honour of the local god Nabu, called the son of Babylon's Marduk, as befitted Babylon's lesser sister city.

The tutelary god of Borsippa in the Ur III period was Tutu, whom the prologue of the Code of Hammurabi names as the god of the city. A later inscription of Hammurabi dedicates the Ezida temple to Marduk, showing Tutu being absorbed by him, and Ezida later became the home of Nabu. Ibbi-Sin's governor Puzur-Tutu is known from the closing years of Ur III. Year names of the Babylonian rulers Sumu-la-El and Apil-Sin record that one entered Borsippa and the other built its city wall. The Kassite ruler Marduk-apla-iddina I rebuilt Ezida, and Marduk-shapik-zeri restored it.

Borsippa depended on Babylon and was never the seat of a regional power. From the ninth century BCE it lay on the borderland south of which were the tribal houses of Chaldea. It had a large scribal class in the first millennium BCE. The temple of Nabu was destroyed in 484 BCE during the suppression of a revolt against the Achaemenid emperor Xerxes I. Nebuchadnezzar II's inscription tells how he restored the temple of Nabu with bricks of noble lapis lazuli.

Henry Creswicke Rawlinson directed work at Borsippa in 1854, and Hormuzd Rassam excavated Ezida for the British Museum from 1879 to 1881. In the 1890s looters took about 2,000 cuneiform tablets, mostly from Ezida. An Austrian team from Innsbruck dug for sixteen seasons between 1980 and 2003 and found that the ziggurat had a core of unbaked bricks 60 by 60 metres, with a baked-brick mantle taking it to 78 by 78 metres, and that Nebuchadnezzar's tower encased a smaller tower of the second millennium BCE. Rising in seven terraces, it reached 70 metres, and even in ruin it stands 52 metres above the plain.
borso-deste: Borso d'Este was born in 1413, an illegitimate son of Niccolò III d'Este, Marquess of Ferrara, Modena and Reggio, by his mistress Stella de' Tolomei. He was a member of the House of Este and, unlike his brother Leonello, a man of little education. He never married and left no heirs.

Borso succeeded his brother Leonello d'Este as marquess on 1 October 1450. On 18 May 1452 Emperor Frederick III confirmed him in his fiefs as Duke of Modena and Reggio, and on 12 April 1471, in St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Paul II appointed him Duke of Ferrara. He is therefore counted as the first Duke of Ferrara and Modena.

Borso followed an expansionist policy for his state and sought to raise the standing of his family. He was generally allied with the Republic of Venice and was an enemy of Francesco I Sforza and of the Medici family, and these rivalries led to the indecisive Battle of Molinella. His subjects generally appreciated him. One cause of grievance was his project in 1471 to build a mountain from scratch, a folly that he was later forced to abandon. His successor was his half-brother Ercole I d'Este.

Borso's court was the centre of the Ferrarese school of painting, whose members included Francesco del Cossa, Ercole dei Roberti and Cosimo Tura. Their most important commissions under him were the frescoes in the Palazzo Schifanoia, in which he liked to be shown as an ideal ruler, and the Bible of Borso d'Este.

He took a pragmatic view of the arts as a means of projecting an image of personal magnificence in support of his political ambitions. His reputation as a magnanimous patron, later proclaimed in Ludovico Ariosto's poem Orlando Furioso, is an idealised picture. While he spent extravagantly on culture and spectacle, he was far from generous to the artists, whom he did not think deserving of special consideration, and his miserly treatment of Cossa led Cossa to leave Ferrara for Bologna. His personal Bible, commissioned in 1455, is one of the finest illuminated manuscripts of Renaissance Italy and was enormously costly. Its principal illuminator, Taddeo Crivelli, appears to have pawned parts of other manuscripts he was working on to ease his own financial difficulties.
borte: Few facts are known about Börte's early life, and what is known comes largely from the Secret History of the Mongols, the oldest surviving literary work in the Mongolian language. She was born around 1161 into the Olkhonud of the Khongirad, a people friendly to the Borjigin, the tribe of Temüjin. Her parents were Dei-Sechen and Chotan.

When Temüjin was nine, his father Yesügei met Dei-Sechen on a journey to find a bride. Dei-Sechen described a dream that he took as a good omen, and Yesügei accepted Börte, then ten, as Temüjin's future wife, with Temüjin to stay with her family. On the way home Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars and died, and Temüjin returned to his family. In 1178, after seven years apart, he went back to Börte and married her.

Soon after the marriage the Three Merkit attacked the camp on the Burgi Escarpment. Temüjin's family escaped on horses, but Börte was left behind and was captured. The raid was said to be revenge for the earlier abduction of Temüjin's mother, Hö'elün, from the Merkit. Temüjin sought help from Ong Qan, who had received Börte's dowry, a black sable coat, and after about eight months they attacked the Merkit and recovered her. The Secret History tells how she recognised his voice and ran to him.

Börte brought independent wealth from her dowry and shared the management of the camp's people, animals and economy with Hö'elün. Her nine children, four sons and five daughters, were central to Temüjin's rule: the daughters married allies, and the sons took part in his conquests. She advised him to break with the military leader Jamuqa, and she was named Grand Empress after he became Genghis Khan. While he campaigned she stayed behind and helped his brother Temüge govern the homeland, holding her own court and much of the Kherlen River.

Doubts about the true father of her eldest son Jochi, who was born after her captivity, led to quarrels between Jochi and his brother Chagatai. Genghis Khan denied them and claimed Jochi as his son, but he chose neither of them as his successor. Ögedei was selected instead, and Jochi's descendants founded the Golden Horde.
Börte died in 1230, after her husband. She was revered by the Mongols as a mother figure, a standing helped by the orphans she adopted and raised as her own, including Qutqu Noyan and Buda Noyan.
boshin-war: After two centuries of isolation, the Perry Expedition of 1854 opened Japan to world trade. The unequal treaties brought dissent against the Tokugawa shogunate, which became the radical sonnō jōi movement, meaning revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians. The shogun sought French help for training and weapons from 1865. Chōshū defeated the shogunate in the summer of 1866 and had formed a secret alliance with Satsuma. In late 1866 the shogun Tokugawa Iemochi and Emperor Kōmei died, and Tokugawa Yoshinobu and Emperor Meiji succeeded them. Yoshinobu resigned his authority to the emperor in 1867, on a proposal from the daimyō of Tosa, which ended the shogunate.

On 27 January 1868 shogunate forces attacked Chōshū and Satsuma at the Battle of Toba–Fushimi, near Kyoto. The imperial side was outnumbered three to one but fully modernized. An imperial banner was given to them on the second day, and daimyō who had been faithful to the shogun began to defect. Saigō Takamori led the imperial forces east and surrounded Edo in May, and Katsu Kaishū negotiated its surrender. A northern coalition of domains, including Sendai and Aizu, kept fighting until Aizuwakamatsu was attacked in October.

Enomoto Takeaki fled to Hokkaido with the remnants of the navy and founded the Republic of Ezo, Japan's only republic. It won no international recognition, and the Battle of Hakodate ended the last holdout.

About 8,200 men were killed. The emperor's residence moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo, at the end of 1868, the domains became prefectures in 1871, and the samurai class was abolished, which brought some into new careers and left many in poverty. Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa held most key government posts for decades. Tokugawa loyalists were shown clemency through Saigō Takamori's persistence. The victors gave up expelling foreigners in favour of modernization. The war has been called a bloodless revolution, but conflict between western samurai and modernizers led to the Satsuma Rebellion nine years later.
bosniaks: Slavs settled the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the sixth century, during the Migration Period, as small tribal units of the Slavic group the Byzantines called the Sclaveni. The first mention of a Bosnian entity, in the De Administrando Imperio of about 960, calls Bosnia a small land belonging to Byzantium, a geographical rather than a national entity. By the 12th century Bosnia had become independent of Hungarian overlordship under Kulin Ban, who ruled from 1180 to 1204.

Bosnia lay between Catholic and Orthodox areas, with rugged terrain and poor communications, and it developed its own church, the Bosnian Church, which both Rome and Constantinople condemned as heretical. Hungary invaded Bosnia between 1235 and 1241 but withdrew. Scholars disagree on whether the Bosnian Church was dualist; John Fine stresses evidence that it kept basic Catholic theology.

After the Ottoman conquest of the Kingdom of Bosnia in 1463 a distinct community of Bosnian Muslims began to form as the local Slavic population embraced Islam. Mass conversion came in the 1480s in central Bosnia and later elsewhere, at its fullest in the 16th century. At its height Muslims were up to three-fourths of the population, but wars and plagues later reduced them, since they lived in densely populated towns and had to serve in Ottoman campaigns. In the late 17th and early 18th centuries around 130,000 Muslim refugees arrived from Ottoman lands lost in Hungary, Slavonia, Croatia and Dalmatia.

Under Ottoman rule life was structured along religious lines, and the term Bosniak was mainly a territorial designation. Austria-Hungary promoted a non-confessional unitary Bosniak identity, but only a small circle of Muslim notables favoured it, among them Mehmed Kapetanović. In the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes Bosnian Muslims were not acknowledged as a distinct ethnic group. In the Bosnian War they were subjected to ethnic cleansing and genocide, and hundreds of thousands fled. The Dayton Agreement recognises Bosniaks as one of the three constituent nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Most Bosniaks speak the Bosnian language, a variety of Serbo-Croatian mutually intelligible with Croatian and Serbian, with more loanwords from Ottoman Turkish, Arabic and Persian. They are traditionally and predominantly Sunni Muslim, and Sufi orders such as the Naqshbandiyya and Qadiriyya have played a significant role. Traditional culture includes the melancholic folk songs called sevdalinka. Their traditional symbol is a coat of arms with six golden lilies, derived from that of the medieval Kingdom of Bosnia.
bosnian-church: Christian missions from Rome and Constantinople were sent into the Balkans in the 9th century, Christianizing the South Slavs. Bosnia lay between Catholic Croatia and Orthodox Serbia, nominally under Rome, but Catholicism never became firmly established there because of weak church organisation and poor communications. Dualist heresy is first reported under Ban Kulin, who in 1199 was accused of sheltering heretics, and the Bilino Polje council of 1203 had Bosnian monks renounce schism and recognise Roman supremacy.

Historians have long connected the church with the Bogomils, but most scholars now reject this. Dragojlović argued that it grew from older, unreformed hermitic monasticism, and Minczew saw some Bogomil influence. Croatian historian L. Špoljarić proposed that it arose when the Catholic bishopric of Bosnia renounced its allegiance in the first half of the 13th century.

In 1233 the papal legate Jacobus Pecorari removed the Bosnian bishop, who was accused of protecting a heretical brother, and in 1234 Pope Gregory IX began the Bosnian Crusade under Coloman of Galicia. Coloman received the administration of Bosnia by August 1235, and a letter of 26 April 1238 reported heresy eradicated. In 1247 the Catholic bishop's seat moved to Đakovo, which ended the attempt, as local power backed the church.

Pope Nicholas's bull Prae Cunctis of 1291 imposed a Franciscan-led Inquisition. The later crusades against heresy, in the 14th and 15th centuries, were largely political. In 1459 King Thomas of Bosnia, under Ottoman pressure and seeking papal support, persecuted the Krstjani and forcibly converted 12,000 people. Forty dignitaries were banished, and three leaders were deported to abjure at Rome on 14 May 1461, after which the church was formally dismantled. Bosnia fell to the Ottoman Empire in the spring of 1463.
