Its members called themselves Krstjani, meaning Christians, or Dobri Bošnjani, the Good Bosnians. The church used Slavic in its liturgy and was headed by a bishop called the djed, with a council of twelve men called strojnici. It was mainly composed of monks, some living in small houses called hiže and others wandering as gosti, and it had no territorial organisation.

King Stephen Ostoja, himself a member, kept a djed as an adviser between 1403 and 1405. Writings of the Krstjani profess belief in one God and the Trinity, which opposes dualist teaching. Little is known, as the church left almost no records of its own and is known mainly from Catholic writings. Its manuscripts include Hval's Codex of 1404 and Batalo's Gospel, made in 1394 for a nobleman. Stećak tombstones are sometimes identified with it.
bosnian-war: The war arose from the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The League of Communists of Yugoslavia had lost its ideological force at the end of the Cold War, and ethnic nationalism had revived in the 1980s after violence in Kosovo. After Slovenia and Croatia seceded in 1991, the multi-ethnic Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, inhabited mainly by Muslim Bosniaks (44%), Orthodox Serbs (32.5%) and Catholic Croats (17%), held a referendum on independence on 29 February 1992. Bosnian Serb representatives boycotted it and rejected the result, having already proclaimed their own Serb republic on 9 January 1992.

The war is commonly dated from 6 April 1992, when the new republic was internationally recognised. Bosnian Serb forces led by Radovan Karadžić, supported by the government of Slobodan Milošević in Serbia and supplied by the Yugoslav People's Army, seized about 70% of the country in a campaign marked by widespread ethnic cleansing. Serb forces began shelling Sarajevo on 6 April. Croat forces formed the Croatian Defence Council on 8 April, and tensions between Croats and Bosniaks led to the Croat-Bosniak War in early 1993.

In 1994 the Washington Agreement created the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and allied Bosniaks and Croats against the Republika Srpska. After the Srebrenica and Markale massacres, NATO's Operation Deliberate Force in 1995 targeted the Serb army and proved key in ending the war. The Dayton Accords were initialled on 21 November 1995.

Estimates of the dead range widely, from 25,000 to 329,000, depending on who is counted. A database published in Sarajevo in 2007 names at least 97,207 people killed or missing, and over 2.2 million people were displaced. An estimated 12,000 to 50,000 women were raped, mostly Bosniak women and mainly by Serb forces. The killing of over 8,000 Bosniak males at Srebrenica in July 1995 by Serb forces is the only incident in Europe since the Second World War recognised as a genocide. In 2007 the International Court of Justice found that Serbia had failed to prevent it.
boso-of-provence: Boso was the son of Bivin of Gorze, count of Lotharingia, and Richildis, a daughter of Boso the Elder. His maternal aunt Teutberga was the wife of King Lothair II of Lotharingia. He succeeded to the lay abbacy of St. Maurice's Abbey in 869. In 870 King Charles the Bald of West Francia married Boso's sister Richilde, which opened Boso's career in the king's service. That year he was made count of Lyon and Vienne, and in 872 chamberlain to Charles's heir Louis the Stammerer, for whom he administered Aquitaine, and count of Bourges.

At the diet of Pavia in February 876 he became arch-minister and missus dominicus for Italy and a duke. He was governor and count of Provence from 877 and married Ermengarde, only daughter of Emperor Louis II. In September 878 he accompanied Pope John VIII to Troyes, and the pope adopted him as his son.

Louis the Stammerer died in April 879, leaving two adult sons, Louis III and Carloman II, and both were elected kings. Boso renounced allegiance in July and claimed independence with the title Dei gratia id quod sum, by the grace of God, that which I am. He also claimed that his father-in-law had named him heir. On 15 October 879 the bishops and nobles of the Rhône and Saône region assembled at the Synod of Mantaille and elected him king, the first non-Carolingian king in Western Europe in more than a century. The election was the first free election among the Franks, made without regard to royal descent.

His realm, usually called the Kingdom of Provence, covered the ecclesiastical provinces of Arles, Aix, Vienne and Lyon and probably Besançon. After Louis and Carloman divided their father's realm at Amiens in March 880, they marched against Boso and took Mâcon and the northern part of his realm. With Charles the Fat, they unsuccessfully besieged Vienne from August to November. In August 882 his brother Richard the Justiciar besieged Vienne again and took the city in September. Boso never regained much of his realm and was confined to the county of Vienne.

Boso died in 887 and was succeeded by his son Louis the Blind. Historians style him King of Burgundy or King of Provence. His kingship failed to win wider recognition and was accepted only in Lower Burgundy and Provence.
bosphorus: The Bosporus is a strait in Turkey, straddled by the city of Istanbul, which connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and forms one of the continental boundaries between Asia and Europe. Between its limits it is 31 km long, with a minimum width of 700 m between Kandilli Point and Aşiyan, and its depth in midstream varies from 13 to 110 m. Together with the Dardanelles it forms the Turkish Straits, and it is the world's narrowest strait used for international navigation. The name comes from the Greek Bosporos, folk-etymologised as cattle passage, after the myth of Io, who was turned into a cow and wandered until she crossed it.

As part of the only passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, the Bosporus has always been of commercial and military importance. In the 5th century BCE Athens depended on grain from the Black Sea ports and kept alliances with cities that controlled the straits, such as Byzantium. The Persian king Darius I crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of connected boats while marching against the Scythian horsemen.

In preparation for the conquest of Constantinople the Ottomans built the Anadoluhisarı in 1393 and the Rumelihisarı in 1451 on either side of the strait. The final 53-day campaign ended on 29 May 1453 and transferred control of the Bosporus to the Ottomans, who made Constantinople their capital. Control of the straits was an objective in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78 and in the Allied attack at Gallipoli in 1915. The Montreux Convention of 20 July 1936 treats the strait as an international shipping lane while allowing Turkey to restrict the naval traffic of states without a Black Sea coast.

Most of the shores are heavily settled, as Istanbul extends inland from both banks. They were once lined with small fishing villages, whose names often keep the suffix köy, village, as in Ortaköy and Arnavutköy. The strait has 620 waterfront houses, yalı, from the Ottoman period, and Ottoman palaces such as Dolmabahçe and Beylerbeyi stand on or near it. Three bridges, a highway tunnel and a railway tunnel link the two banks.
boston: Boston stands on the Shawmut Peninsula, beside Boston Harbor, an arm of Massachusetts Bay. Its highest point is Bellevue Hill, at 330 feet above sea level. Since independence the city has expanded well beyond the original peninsula by filling in land and annexing neighbouring towns. Boston Common, near Beacon Hill, is part of the Emerald Necklace, a string of parks designed by Frederick Law Olmsted.

Before European colonisation the surrounding region was inhabited by the Massachusett people, who built small seasonal communities there. When settlers led by John Winthrop arrived in 1630 they found the Shawmut Peninsula nearly empty of Native people, most of whom had died of diseases brought by earlier settlers and traders.

The first European to live there was William Blaxton, an Anglican cleric educated at the University of Cambridge. He invited Isaac Johnson, a leader of the Puritans, to cross from the failing colony of Charlestown and share the peninsula, and in September 1630 the Puritans made the crossing. Johnson, in one of his last acts before his death on 30 September 1630, named the settlement after his hometown of Boston, Lincolnshire. Puritan ethics and their focus on education shaped the early city, and Boston Latin School, the first public school in America, was founded in 1635.

Boston was home to several seminal events of the American Revolution: the Boston Massacre of 1770, the Boston Tea Party of 1773, the Battle of Bunker Hill in 1775 and the Siege of Boston from 1775 to 1776. After independence it became an important port and manufacturing centre as well as a centre of education and culture, and it has been called the Athens of America for its literary culture. Its firsts include Boston Common in 1634, the oldest public park in the United States, and the Tremont Street subway of 1897, the first subway system.

Boston is the capital and most populous city of Massachusetts and a cultural and financial centre of New England. The Boston Red Sox play at Fenway Park, built in 1912, which is the oldest stadium in active use among the four major American professional sports leagues.
boston-tea-party: The protest arose from two problems facing the British Empire: the financial difficulties of the East India Company and a dispute over how far Parliament's authority extended over colonies that elected no members to it. The Townshend Revenue Act of 1767 laid new taxes, which colonists met with protests and boycotts. Meanwhile the company, burdened by taxes, by smuggled Dutch tea that undersold it and by the Bengal famine of 1769 to 1773, amassed a large unsold surplus. Parliament passed the Tea Act on 10 May 1773 to help it.

The Act in fact lowered the price of legally imported tea, but Samuel Adams considered the British tea monopoly equal to a tax, and others saw a threat to colonial rights. In every colony except Massachusetts, protesters forced the consignees to resign or the tea to go back to England.

In Boston, Governor Thomas Hutchinson held his ground and persuaded the consignees, two of them his sons, not to give way. When the Dartmouth arrived in late November, thousands met on 29 November 1773 at the Old South Meeting House. British law gave the ship twenty days to unload and pay the duties before the cargo could be confiscated. Hutchinson refused to let it leave, and two more ships, the Eleanor and the Beaver, arrived.

On 16 December, the last day of the deadline, some 5,000 to 7,000 people gathered at Old South. After a report that Hutchinson had again refused, Samuel Adams announced that the meeting could do nothing further to save the country. That evening a large group, some dressed as Mohawk warriors and armed with axes, boarded the three vessels at Griffin's Wharf and over three hours emptied all the chests into the harbour, destroying 92,616 pounds of tea, which the East India Company valued at £9,659.

Britain regarded the act as treason. In 1774 Parliament passed the Intolerable Acts, which, among other measures, ended local self-government in Massachusetts and closed Boston's port. The other colonies answered by convening the First Continental Congress in Philadelphia, which coordinated resistance in the Continental Association of October 1774. The Battles of Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775 began the Revolutionary War. The name Boston Tea Party gained currency only in the early 19th century; the event had been called the Destruction of the Tea.
boten-vientiane-railway: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, and under French rule only the 7-kilometre Don Det–Don Khon railway was built there. Talks on a railway linking Laos and China began in 2001, and the Lao politician Somsavat Lengsavad was reportedly the driving force on the Laotian side. Plans for a standard-gauge line to Xishuangbanna in Yunnan were announced in October 2010, but the project stalled after the 2011 corruption scandal involving China's minister of railways, Liu Zhijun. In 2015 the two countries agreed to finance and operate it jointly under a build-operate-transfer arrangement.

Construction began at Luang Prabang on 25 December 2016, and unexploded bombs dropped during the Vietnam War were removed along the route. Track-laying was completed on 12 October 2021, and the line opened on 3 December 2021, a day after the 46th anniversary of the Lao PDR. About 47% of it runs through 75 tunnels and 15% over viaducts on 167 bridges. It is a single electrified track with passing loops, built to China's Class I trunk standards for passenger trains at 160 km/h and freight at 120 km/h. Its northern end joins the Yuxi–Mohan railway at Mohan, and the largest station, in Vientiane, has four platforms.

The cost was estimated at US$5.965 billion. Sixty per cent was financed by loans from the Export–Import Bank of China, and the remaining 40% by a joint venture of the two countries in which China holds a 70% stake. Of the Laotian share, the government paid $250 million from its national budget and borrowed a further $480 million from the same bank, and Western publications later claimed that Laos could default on its debts.

The line was expected to bring tourists, with passengers making up most of its traffic, and to cut the cost of Thai fruit exports to China. A branch to the Thanaleng Dry Port and Vientiane South, completed in July 2022, allowed cargo to pass between the Thai metre-gauge and the Chinese standard-gauge lines, and a bridge over the Mekong is planned to link the line with the Bangkok–Nong Khai high-speed railway. Radio Free Asia reported in October 2021 that some villagers displaced by the construction had not been compensated; by August 2023 it reported that about 85% of affected families had had their claims resolved.
botswana: Botswana has a total area of 581,730 square kilometres and is topographically flat, with approximately 70% of its territory part of the Kalahari Desert. It borders South Africa, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The terrain consists of sandy soils, rocky hill ranges and grasslands, and the climate is generally semi-arid, with highly seasonal rainfall. The north and east receive more rain than the dry southwest, and much of the population lives in the southeast.

In the northwest the Okavango River spreads across the Kalahari in a vast inland delta of channels, lagoons, islands and seasonal wetlands, rather than flowing to the sea. The Chobe River in the north forms part of the border with Namibia.

Stone tools in present-day Botswana date back two million years, and the ancestors of the Khoe and the San lived in the region 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Rock art dates back approximately 30,000 years. Around 2,000 years ago people introduced cattle, sheep, pottery and agriculture. Bantu-speaking peoples migrated into the region between 2,000 and 1,500 years ago: the Kalanga arrived around 200 CE and the ancestors of the Tswana around 400 CE, bringing iron and copper tools and establishing permanent settlements. Trade expanded from the seventh century, and the Toutswe people, the Kingdom of Mapungubwe and later Great Zimbabwe became important regional powers, with cattle and gold playing major economic roles.

From the fifteenth to the eighteenth century Tswana and Kalanga peoples formed new political communities. Tswana society was organised into merafe, governed by chiefs called dikgosi. The Difaqane of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century caused widespread warfare and migration, and by the 1840s many states had been re-established and were governed through the kgotla, a traditional community council. Missionaries arrived in 1816, followed by British traders and explorers, and David Livingstone established a mission in 1845. The discovery of the Tati Goldfields in 1868 led to a gold rush and the growth of Francistown. In 1885 the British declared the protectorate of Bechuanaland, which became independent on 30 September 1966.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city. Botswana is a parliamentary republic, and its government draws on both the Westminster system and the tribal governments of the Tswana. English is the official language and Setswana is widely spoken. The Tswana make up about 79% of the population, the Kalanga about 11% and the San about 3%. Botswana is a member of the Southern African Development Community, the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations.
botswana-democratic-party: The party was the third founded in the British protectorate of Bechuanaland, where political life developed slowly and peacefully. It was set up at Lobatse by members of the African Consultative Council under Seretse Khama, former head of the BaNgwato, with Ketumile Quett Masire as general secretary, and held its first constitutive congress on 28 February 1962. Masire began the party newspaper Therisanyo in 1963. On 30 September 1966, the day Bechuanaland became the Republic of Botswana, the party took its present name, with Khama as president and Masire as vice-president.

Khama did not seek a one-party state and kept a responsible opposition in Parliament; his government also kept foreign expatriates in the civil service until local replacements were qualified. The party's dominance in the following decades owed much to an opposition divided by tribal interests or by African socialism, and to its own hold on the Central District, the Ngwato homeland. Khama held the presidency until his death in 1980.

Between 1989 and 1993 growth of more than 13% gave way to the first recession since independence, and urbanisation and land scandals eroded support: in 1994 the party won only 26 of 39 seats. Under Ian Khama, president from 1 April 2008, factional quarrels led to the Botswana Movement for Democracy splitting off in 2010, though the party took 45 of 57 seats in 2009. After Mokgweetsi Masisi succeeded in 2018, the Khama family left and the Botswana Patriotic Front took much of the Central District, while urban gains kept the party's majority in 2019.

In the 2024 general election the party won about 30% of the vote but, its support spread thinly under first-past-the-post voting, kept only four of 61 seats. Masisi conceded two days later, and in a peaceful transfer of power Boko of the opposition UDC was sworn in as president, forming the first government since independence without the party. At its 41st National Congress in Maun the party elected Mpho Balopi as leader.

Analysts describe the party's ideology as broad, conservative and centre-right, with national unity, economic development and political democracy as its official core values, beside the ideas of kagisano, togetherness, and botho, humanity. Its early governments pursued free-market policies and low taxes to attract mining investment, spending the revenue on infrastructure, health and education.
bou-inania-madrasa-fez: The madrasa is named for its founder, the Marinid sultan Faris ibn Ali Abu Inan al-Mutawakkil, who rebelled against his father Abu al-Hasan, declared himself sultan in 1348 and was assassinated by his vizier on 10 January 1358, aged 31. It was first called the Madrasa al-Muttawakkiliya. The Marinids built many madrasas, which trained scholars in Islamic law and staffed the state's bureaucracy, and used the patronage to win the loyalty of Fez's religious elites and to present themselves as protectors of orthodox Sunni Islam. The Bou Inania was the largest and most important of them, and the only one to become a congregational mosque, where the Friday sermon was delivered.

The foundation inscription in the prayer hall gives the start of construction as 28 December 1350 (28 Ramadan 751 AH) and its end as 1355 (756 AH), and lists the endowments that funded it. One story says Abu Inan, guilty over overthrowing his father, was advised to turn a rubbish dump in the upper city into a place of learning; such tales are regarded as apocryphal.

The main building is an irregular rectangle of 34.65 by 38.95 metres between Tala'a Kebira and Tala'a Seghira streets. A marble-paved courtyard with a fountain is surrounded by galleries, with student rooms on two floors, and flanked on east and west by two square chambers of 5 metres a side that served as classrooms. The prayer hall is divided by a row of arches on marble and onyx columns and has a richly stuccoed mihrab. The brick minaret, square-shafted with a small secondary tower, marks its status as a Friday mosque.

The lower walls are covered in zellij tilework, with a band of calligraphic tiles above, then carved stucco with arabesques, muqarnas and inscriptions, and carved cedar and a wooden canopy at the top. Across the street stand an ablutions house and the Dar al-Magana, whose facade holds a hydraulic clock whose mechanism is no longer understood.

The building is widely regarded as a high point of Marinid and of Moroccan architecture. Despite the sultan's investment, it does not seem to have rivalled the older and larger Qarawiyyin as a centre of learning, and higher education in Fez was probably centralised there after a couple of centuries. The madrasa was restored many times, notably in the seventeenth century after a damaging earthquake and under Sultan Mulay Sliman, who reigned from 1792 to 1822, when whole wall sections were rebuilt. Its original minbar of 1350 to 1355, among the best Marinid examples, is kept in the Dar Batha Museum.
boudica: Boudica was the consort of Prasutagus, king of the Iceni, a tribe living in what is now Norfolk and parts of neighbouring counties. The Iceni had revolted against the Romans in 47 and afterwards kept their independence. Prasutagus ruled as a nominally independent ally of Rome and had two daughters with Boudica. In his will he made both the daughters and the emperor Nero his heirs. The name may be an honorific title, and the name she bore for most of her life is unknown.

Accounts of the revolt come from Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio. Dio wrote the longest, about 140 years after her death, and his text survives only in an epitome by the 11th-century monk John Xiphilinus. His details are often fictitious, and the speeches both Tacitus and Dio give her were never recorded.

When Prasutagus died, the Romans ignored his will and absorbed the kingdom into the province of Britannia. Tacitus tells of pillaging and of the flogging of Boudica and rape of her daughters. Dio mentions none of this and gives other causes, among them the recall of loans by Seneca. The Iceni and the Trinovantes raised an army reported at 120,000 men and attacked Camulodunum, a colony for retired soldiers. The Legio IX Hispana tried to relieve the town and was overwhelmed.

The governor Gaius Suetonius Paulinus reached Londinium before the rebels but, outnumbered, abandoned it, and they burned it. They also sacked Verulamium. Modern estimates put the dead at 70,000 to 80,000 Romans and Britons.

Suetonius gathered nearly 10,000 men and took a stand in a narrow pass with a wood behind. His javelins, wedge formation and cavalry crushed the larger British army. Tacitus says that Boudica poisoned herself, while Dio says she fell ill and died and was given a lavish burial. The crisis made Nero consider withdrawing from Britain, but the victory confirmed Roman control of the province. Interest in Boudica revived in the English Renaissance and brought her fame in the Victorian era.
boudican-revolt: Rome invaded south-eastern Britain in 43 CE and conquered it gradually, leaving some kingdoms nominally independent as allies. The Iceni king Prasutagus tried to secure his kingdom by leaving it jointly to his daughters and the emperor, but on his death his will was ignored. Tacitus describes the Romans seizing land and enslaving Iceni; Boudica was publicly flogged and her daughters raped. According to Cassius Dio, Roman financiers such as Seneca the Younger also called in their loans. The only surviving accounts of the revolt are those of Tacitus and Dio.

While the governor Gaius Suetonius Paulinus was campaigning against the island of Mona, a stronghold of the druids, the Iceni rose with the Trinovantes and others. They first attacked Camulodunum, a colonia of Roman veterans with a costly temple to Claudius, routed the Legio IX Hispana under Quintus Petillius Cerialis, and after a two-day siege of the temple destroyed the city. Suetonius reached Londinium but judged his troops too few and abandoned it, taking with him those who would leave; the rebels burned it and killed those who stayed, and then destroyed Verulamium. Archaeologists find a layer of burnt debris, the Boudican Destruction Horizon, in all three towns.

Suetonius gathered almost 10,000 men, including the Legio XIV Gemina, and took a stand in a narrow passage with a wood behind him, at a place that has never been identified. Ancient writers put the Britons at 230,000 to 300,000, figures modern historians treat with scepticism. The legionaries advanced in a wedge, the flight of the Britons was blocked by their own wagons, and the Romans spared neither women nor animals. Tacitus says Boudica then poisoned herself; Dio says she fell ill and died.

Suetonius Tranquillus writes that the crisis almost persuaded Nero to abandon Britain. Poenius Postumus, whose Legio II Augusta had not answered the summons, fell on his sword. Suetonius carried out widespread punitive operations, and after criticism from the new procurator Gaius Julius Alpinus Classicianus and an inquiry by the freedman Polyclitus, Nero replaced him with the more conciliatory Publius Petronius Turpilianus. The defeat ended resistance to Roman rule in most of southern Britain, though the north remained unsettled.
bougainville-island: Bougainville is the main island of the Autonomous Region of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, with a land area of 9,384 square kilometres. Its highest point is Mount Balbi, at 2,715 metres. Buka Island lies to the north across a narrow strait, and the Shortland Islands of the independent Solomon Islands lie less than 9 kilometres to the south. The island has several volcanoes, of which Bagana in the north-central part is conspicuously active, and is largely covered by rainforest. Most people are Christian, and Tok Pisin and English are the languages of government, alongside many local languages from Austronesian and North and South Bougainville families.

During the last ice age Bougainville was part of a single landmass, Greater Bougainville. The earliest evidence of settlement is at Kilu Cave on Buka, from between 26,700 and 18,100 BCE, left by Melanesian people likely related to modern Papuans and Indigenous Australians. Austronesian settlers arrived in the 2nd millennium BCE with pigs, chickens, dogs and obsidian tools. The French navigator Louis Antoine de Bougainville reached the island in 1768 and named it after himself. Whaling ships called for provisions from 1822 to 1881. Germany annexed it into German New Guinea in 1899, and missionaries arrived in 1902. Australia occupied it in the First World War and held it under a League of Nations mandate from 1920.

Japan invaded in 1942, and Allied forces began the Bougainville campaign in 1943. On 18 April 1943 the Japanese admiral Isoroku Yamamoto died there when his plane was shot down. Japanese garrisons held out until 1945, and Australia resumed control. When Papua New Guinea became independent in September 1975, Bougainville declared itself the Republic of the North Solomons, but it was absorbed into the new state.

Copper on the island had been under development since 1972, and the Panguna deposit is estimated at a billion tonnes of ore and 12 million ounces of gold. The mine, run by a Rio Tinto-owned operation, caused heavy environmental damage and was shut down in a revolt against it. The Bougainville Civil War of 1988 to 1998 claimed over 15,000 lives, and a blockade by Papua New Guinea left the islanders without medical supplies and caused many deaths. Peace talks brokered by New Zealand began in 1997, and a peace agreement of 2001 promised a referendum on independence.

In the referendum of November and December 2019, 98.31 per cent of voters chose independence from Papua New Guinea, on a turnout of 87.38 per cent. The result was not contested, but the referendum was not binding on the national government, and talks between the two governments followed. Bougainville is the largest island of the Solomon Islands chain although it belongs politically to Papua New Guinea.
boulogne-sur-mer: Boulogne-sur-Mer stands on the English Channel at the mouth of the river Liane, in the department of Pas-de-Calais, on the Côte d'Opale. The French name derives from the Latin Bononia, also the Roman name of Bologna in Italy. Both are thought to come from native Celtic place-names, with bona possibly meaning foundation, citadel or granary. The epithet sur-Mer, on sea, distinguishes the city from Boulogne-Billancourt near Paris.

The foundation of Gesoriacum is credited to the Celtic Boii. A tall lighthouse, the Tour d'Ordre, was built there around 39 CE on the order of Caligula, possibly in preparation for an invasion of Britain, and fell into the sea through coastal erosion in 1644. From Claudius's invasion in 43 the town was the major port linking the empire with Britain and the chief base of the Roman navy's British fleet until its admiral Carausius rebelled in 286. The junior emperor Constantius Chlorus besieged it by land and sea in 293, and its name changed to Bononia by 310.

In the Middle Ages Boulogne was capital of an eponymous county founded in the mid-9th century. Count Eustace II helped William the Conqueror conquer England, and his wife founded the church that became Notre-Dame cathedral, a pilgrimage site from the 12th century. The English occupied the town several times during the Hundred Years War, and again from 1544 to 1550, when France bought it back for 400,000 crowns. In 1805 Napoleon gathered the Grande Armée there for a planned invasion of Britain. The railway to Paris, completed in 1848, made it a bathing resort for wealthy Parisians.

Boulogne was one of the three base ports most used by Commonwealth armies on the Western Front in the First World War. Allied bombing on 15 June 1944 completely destroyed the harbour and surrounding area, and Canadian troops liberated the town in September 1944. It is France's largest fishing port, specialising in herring, and its 12th-century belfry is a World Heritage Site.
boun-oum: Boun Oum was born in Don Talad in 1911, the eldest son of Prince Ratsadanay of Champassak by his fourth wife, Princess Sudhi Saramuni, and was educated at the Wat Liep Monastery school and the law school in Vientiane. In 1943 he married Mom Bouaphanh Soumpholphakdy of Kengkok, with whom he had six sons and three daughters. On his father's death in June 1946 he became head of the princely house of Champassak, and on 27 August 1946 he gave up his rights so that a unified Kingdom of Laos could be established.

Sympathetic to the French in Laos, he commanded a force of 15,000 that fought Japanese troops and the Lao Issara in the south of the country. He became President of the Royal Council in 1947 and Inspector-General of the Kingdom in 1949. As titular leader of the royalist faction he was one of the Three Princes of the Kingdom of Laos. In December 1960 the National Assembly made him prime minister by unanimous vote, and his second government, which lasted until June 1962, was described as right-wing.

After leaving politics he turned to business from his base in Pakse and Champassak, but he remained a major power broker until 1975, when the communist Pathet Lao came to power. That year he went to France for medical treatment and never returned to Laos. He died at Boulogne-Billancourt on 17 March 1980, and his ashes lie in the Cimetiere de Trivaux at Meudon beside those of his wife. Among his honours were the Order of the Million Elephants and the White Parasol and the French Legion of Honour.
bourbon-reforms: At the end of the 17th century Spain faced falling revenues and a loss of military power under Charles II, who left no heir. On his deathbed he willed the crown to Philip, Duke of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV of France, and the War of the Spanish Succession followed from 1702 to 1713. The Peace of Utrecht of 1713 secured Philip V's throne but cost Spain the Habsburg Netherlands and other European lands, Gibraltar and Menorca, and gave Britain the Asiento de Negros, the contract to sell African slaves in Spanish America, which opened channels for British contraband. When Charles II died the army was almost nonexistent and the treasury bankrupt, and Philip V and his ministers took measures to reverse the decline.

The Bourbons kept close ties with France and employed many French advisers, and French goods, ideas and books spread the Enlightenment through the Spanish world. José del Campillo y Cosío's New System of Economic Government for America of 1743 urged Spain to manage its colonies more like France and Britain did. The Viceroyalty of New Granada was carved out of Peru in 1717, suppressed six years later and permanently established in 1739.

After Spain's defeat by Great Britain in the Seven Years' War, Charles III's counsellors launched a new wave of reform: more exploitation of colonial resources, higher taxes, new ports allowed to trade only with Spain, and state monopolies over crops such as sugar, indigo, cochineal, tobacco and cacao. José de Gálvez's general inspection of New Spain from 1765 to 1771 reorganised tax collection and steered the economy towards mining; the Viceroyalty of Rio de la Plata followed in 1776. Censuses and detailed maps of mines, forts and terrain served taxation, while mining ordinances and the Tribunal de Minería date from 1787. Militias under creole control grew until New Spain had 23,000 militiamen to 6,000 Spanish soldiers.

The reforms raised revenue and increased silver production, and they have been called a revolution in government. But local industries suffered from measures meant to favour Spanish goods, wealth flowed towards the creole and bureaucratic elites, and the reforms aimed to put office holders from the Iberian peninsula above local elites. Where wealth was very unequally shared, especially in smaller towns and rural areas, unrest grew into complaints and eventually riots and revolts. No clean, straight line runs from the reforms to the movements for independence, but the period of unrest that came in their wake helped create the conditions for them.
bourges: Bourges stands in central France where the Auron flows into the Yèvre, in the region of Centre-Val de Loire. Its name derives either from the Bituriges, its original inhabitants, or from a Germanic word burg, meaning a hill or village. The Celts called it Avaricon and Latin speakers Avaricum. In the fourth century BCE, and still in Caesar's time, the area around it was the centre of a Gallic confederacy.

In 52 BCE the Gauls adopted a scorched-earth policy to deny Caesar's forces supplies, but the inhabitants of Avaricum persuaded the council not to burn their town. Its marshes, a river that nearly encircled it and a strong southern wall spared it for a time. Caesar's forces nevertheless captured and destroyed it, killing all but 800 of its inhabitants. Rome rebuilt it with a monumental gate, aqueducts, baths and an amphitheatre, and the Roman town grew larger than the medieval one. Saint Ursinus, of the third century, is considered its first bishop.

In the 8th century Bourges lay on the northern edge of the Duchy of Aquitaine and was the first town to face Frankish attacks across the Loire. Charles Martel captured it in 731, and Duke Odo the Great retook it. Pepin the Short destroyed much of it in a siege in 762. It was capital of the Viscounty of Bourges until 1101 and of the Duchy of Berry from 1360. Charles VII sought refuge there in the 1420s, and his son Louis XI was born there in 1423. In 1438 Charles issued the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges. A fire in 1487 destroyed a third of the town, and its economic decline began.

Bourges is the capital of the department of Cher and was capital of the former province of Berry. Its Gothic cathedral, built from 1195 to 1255 and one of the earliest examples of High Gothic, was added to the World Heritage list in 1992. The 15th-century Palais Jacques Cœur and a sixty-five-hectare district of half-timbered houses also survive. From the 1860s the town became an important centre of artillery production, after Napoleon III moved the École de pyrotechnie militaire there from Metz.
bowdoin-college: The Massachusetts State Legislature chartered the college in 1794, and it later came under the jurisdiction of the Maine Legislature. It was named for the former Massachusetts governor James Bowdoin, whose son James Bowdoin III was an early benefactor. The college began to grow in the 1820s, after Maine became a state of its own under the Missouri Compromise. It drew the sons of the political elite, and in the first half of the 19th century required of its students a certificate of good moral character and a knowledge of Latin, Ancient Greek, geography, algebra and the works of Cicero, Xenophon, Virgil and Homer.

Before the Civil War the college's Phi Beta Kappa Society hosted anti-slavery speakers, and Harriet Beecher Stowe began Uncle Tom's Cabin in Brunswick while her husband taught there. Joshua Chamberlain, alumnus and professor, commanded the 20th Maine at Little Round Top at Gettysburg, was present at the surrender at Appomattox Court House in 1865 and later became governor of Maine and president of the college. Oliver Otis Howard, class of 1850, led the Freedmen's Bureau and founded Howard University. The college also gave Jefferson Davis an honorary degree; an award in his name, founded in 1972, was ended in 2015 as honouring a man whose mission was to preserve slavery.

The Arctic explorers Robert E. Peary and Donald B. MacMillan were graduates, and in 1913 the polar bear was chosen as the college mascot in Peary's honour. The college's Medical School of Maine closed in 1921. In 1970 Bowdoin made the SAT optional for admission, and in 1971, after nearly 180 years as a men's college, it admitted its first women. In 1997 the trustees decided to phase out fraternities in favour of college-owned social houses, and in 2008 the college replaced loans with grants for all students on financial aid.

The main campus in Brunswick covers 215 acres with 120 buildings, the oldest being Massachusetts Hall, and holds the Bowdoin College Museum of Art and the Peary-MacMillan Arctic Museum. The college also owns a coastal studies centre on Orr's Island and a scientific station on Kent Island in the Bay of Fundy. The Bowdoin Orient is the oldest continuously published college weekly in the United States.
bowring-treaty: The Burney Treaty of 1826 with the British East India Company had ended the monopoly of the Royal Warehouse over Western trade, but British merchants still paid measurement duties on their ships and remained under Siamese law. Neither side was satisfied, and in the 1840s Siam brought monopolies back through tax farming. After the First Opium War Lord Palmerston sent Sir James Brooke in 1850 to seek a new treaty; the Siamese rejected his proposals, and the British considered sending warships. The accession in 1851 of King Mongkut, well disposed towards Westerners, changed Siamese policy. In 1854 Lord Clarendon appointed Bowring plenipotentiary, and he reached Bangkok with his assistant Harry Parkes in March 1855.

The treaty was signed at the mansion of Somdet Chaophraya Prayurawong in Thonburi. Mongkut's five plenipotentiaries included Chaophraya Si Suriyawong, who favoured Bowring's proposals. British subjects came under the jurisdiction of a British consul in Bangkok, the first grant of extraterritoriality to aliens in Siam. They could trade in all seaports, live permanently in Bangkok, and buy or rent property more than four miles from the city walls but within twenty-four hours' journey by boat. Measurement duties gave way to the import duty, with opium and bullion exempt, opium to be sold only through the government's tax farmers. Siam kept the right to ban exports of salt, rice and fish in times of scarcity.

Ratifications were exchanged on 5 April 1856, and an agreement concluded by Parkes in May 1856 clarified consular jurisdiction. The treaty became the model for others, among them the American–Siamese Harris Treaty of May 1856 and the Franco–Siamese Montigny Treaty of August 1856, and led to a Siamese mission to London in 1857. Britain replaced Qing China as Siam's main trading partner, and the economy turned from subsistence to export, though at a heavy cost in state revenue. Its provisions were whittled away by the Chiengmai Treaty of 1883 and the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909, and the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1925 ended it altogether, abolishing the tariff.
boxer-rebellion: After the First Sino-Japanese War, villagers in North China feared the growth of foreign spheres of influence and resented Christian missionaries, who ignored local customs and used their power to protect their followers in court. Shandong, where the Righteous and Harmonious Fists arose, had long been troubled by social unrest, religious sects and martial societies. In 1897 and 1898 drought and floods forced farmers into the cities, and the movement blamed these disasters on foreign and Christian influence. American missionaries probably first called its members Boxers, because of the martial arts they practised. Their main rite was a spiritual possession with whirling swords and incantations, and they claimed invulnerability to cannon, rifle shot and blade.

From 1899 the movement spread across Shandong and the North China Plain, destroying foreign property such as railways and attacking or murdering Chinese Christians and missionaries. In January 1900 Empress Dowager Cixi, with a majority of conservatives at court, issued edicts in its defence. In the spring it moved north towards Beijing, burning churches and intimidating officials. Diplomats, missionaries, soldiers and some Chinese Christians took refuge in the Legation Quarter, which the Boxers besieged.

On 17 June 1900 the Eight-Nation Alliance, of American, Austro-Hungarian, British, French, German, Italian, Japanese and Russian troops, stormed the Dagu Forts at Tianjin. On 21 June Cixi issued a decree that was in effect a declaration of war on the powers. Officials were divided, and those in the southern provinces ignored the order to fight. The Alliance defeated the Imperial Army at Tianjin and reached Beijing on 14 August, ending the 55-day siege of the Legations.

Looting of the capital and countryside followed, together with summary executions of suspected Boxers. The Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901 required the execution of officials who had supported the movement, allowed foreign troops to be stationed in Beijing and imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver, more than the government's annual tax revenue, to be paid over 39 years to the eight nations. The Qing dynasty's handling of the rebellion further weakened its credibility and its control over China. It led to the Late Qing reforms and, to a greater extent, to the Xinhai Revolution.
boyaca-department: Boyacá lies almost entirely within the mountains of the Eastern Cordillera, although its western end reaches the Magdalena River at Puerto Boyacá. It covers 23,189 square kilometres and borders Santander and Norte de Santander to the north, Arauca and Casanare to the east, Cundinamarca to the south and Antioquia to the west. The Cordillera rises to 5,380 metres in the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy, and the department also holds high plateaux, a small part of the Middle Magdalena valley and a part of the eastern Llanos. The Altiplano Cundiboyacense, shared with Cundinamarca, is densely populated. The name comes from the Chibcha word Bojacá, which means near the cacique or region of the royal mantle.

Before the Spanish arrival the territory belonged to the Muisca. Under the chiefdom of the zaque of Hunza they lived mainly by agriculture and by mining gold and emeralds. The Spaniard Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada conquered the northern Muisca, whose last zaque was Aquiminzaque, shared out the land in encomiendas and made the indigenous people work for him. In 1539 the conquistador Gonzalo Suárez Rendón founded Tunja on sites where the indigenous people had earlier had villages, and Tunja became one of the main political and economic centres of the Viceroyalty of New Granada.

In the war of independence the region was a battleground between royalist armies and patriot armies led by Simón Bolívar. The Battle of the Vargas Swamp was fought on 25 July 1819, and the decisive Battle of Boyacá at the Puente de Boyacá on 7 August 1819; the patriots won both. Gran Colombia created a Boyacá Department in 1824. After the Granadine Confederation was formed in 1858 the territory became the Sovereign State of Boyacá, one of the original nine states of the United States of Colombia. Civil wars, among them the war of 1860–1862 and the Thousand Days War, and changing constitutions, including that of 1886, then reshaped it until it took its present form as a department.

Boyacá is one of the thirty-two departments of Colombia, with Tunja as its capital. It is divided into 13 provinces and two special districts, with 123 municipalities. Many rivers rise there, the most important being the Chicamocha and the Arauca, and it has several lakes, among them Lake Tota, Lake Sochagota and Lake Fúquene. El Cocuy and Pisba National Parks lie in the north-east. The department is known as the Land of Freedom because of the battles of 1819, and it has three universities, among them the Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia.
boyana-church: The church was built in three stages: in the late 10th or early 11th century, in the mid-13th century and in the mid-19th century. The oldest part, the eastern church, is a small one-apse cross-vaulted church with built-in cruciform supports. The second section adjoins it and was commissioned by Sebastocrator Kaloyan and his wife Desislava. It is a two-floor tomb-church, with a ground-floor family sepulchre under a semi-cylindrical vault, with two arcosolia on the north and south walls, and an upper-floor family chapel identical in design to the eastern church. The western section was built with donations from the local community.

A patron's inscription in Middle Bulgarian, dated to indiction 7 of the year 6767 (1259), records that the temple of Saint Nicholas and the martyr Panteleimon was raised with Kaloyan's funds and care. It calls him cousin of the Tsar and grandson of Stephen, King of Serbia, and says the church was decorated under the Bulgarian Tsar Constantine Asen.

Fragments of an earlier layer of frescoes, from the 11th and 12th centuries, survive on the lower apse, the north wall, the upper west wall and the south vault. The second layer was painted over it by a team of unknown artists, who decorated both floors of Kaloyan's building. In all, 89 scenes with 240 human images cover the walls.

In the oldest section, Christ Pantocrator fills the dome, angels the drum below it and the four Evangelists the pendentives. The narthex holds eighteen scenes from the life of Saint Nicholas, which include details of contemporary life: in the Miracle at Sea, the ship and the sailors' hats recall the Venetian fleet.

The frescoes were restored and cleaned in 1912–1915 by an Austrian and a Bulgarian specialist, and again in 1934 and 1944. The church was closed to the public in 1954 for conservation and partly reopened in 2006. Under the National Historical Museum it fully reopened on 2 October 2008.

The name Boyana Master stands for the unknown team, trained in the Turnovo School of Painting, and many experts hold that the frescoes mattered for the development of medieval Bulgarian and European painting. During restoration in 2006–2008 an inscription reading 'I, Vasiliy inscribed' was found under plaster. The museum's director took it for the painter's name, while other historians think an assistant could equally have left it.
boyar: The title boila was held by Bulgar aristocrats, mostly regional governors and noble warriors, in the First Bulgarian Empire (681-1018). Byzantine documents render its plural as boilades; in the 10th-century protocol of Emperor Constantine VII the Bulgarian nobles are called boliades. According to Max Vasmer, the older Slavic form bolyarin was borrowed into Old Church Slavonic from the Danubian Bulgar language, which was Turkic. In the Second Bulgarian Empire the title was bolyar, a hereditary rank divided into great and minor boyars.

In Kievan Rus' from the 9th to the 13th century boyars wielded power through their military support of the princes, though their standing came to depend on service to the state and on a family history of service. In Novgorod and Pskov they formed a kind of republic that limited the princes' power until Moscow conquered both. After the Mongol invasion the boyars of modern Belarus and Ukraine were absorbed into the Lithuanian and Polish nobility; in Galicia they were given the rights of the szlachta from 1430.

Until the 16th century a boyar in Moscow did not have to be Russian or Orthodox, and some came from Lithuania or the Nogais. Ivan IV became grand prince in 1533 at the age of three, and boyar factions competed for the regency. In 1565 he divided the realm in two and in his private part began the oprichnina terror, which crushed boyar opposition. After the Rurik dynasty ended with the death of Fedor, the boyar Boris Godunov tried to proclaim himself tsar, but several boyar factions refused to recognise him.

In Moldavia and Wallachia the boyar class emerged from the chiefs of rural communities, who made their judicial and administrative functions hereditary. The social order ran from boyar to mazil, then the răzeș or yeoman, and finally the rumân or serf. Being a boyar meant owning land, having serfs and holding a military or administrative office, a boierie, which only the prince could grant. Land was hereditary, and the prince could take it away only for grave reasons such as treason. Boyars ranked in three states, and only those of the first state could grow a beard.
boyoma-falls: The falls consist of seven cataracts, each no more than 5 metres high, that extend over more than 100 kilometres along a curve of the Lualaba River between the river port towns of Ubundu and Kisangani, also known as Boyoma, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Together they have a total drop of 61 metres. The two major cataracts are the first below Ubundu, which forms a narrow and crooked stream that is hardly accessible, and the last, which can be seen and visited from Kisangani. At the bottom of the rapids the Lualaba is known as the Congo River. A portage railway of 1 metre gauge bypasses the rapids and connects Kisangani with Ubundu.

The last of the seven cataracts is also known as the Wagenia Falls, after the local Wagenya fishermen, who developed a special technique for fishing in the river. They build systems of wooden tripods across the rapids, fixed in holes carved in the rock by the current. These tripods anchor large baskets that are lowered into the rapids to trap fish. The method is very selective, since the baskets are big and only large fish are caught.

The falls were formerly named after Henry Morton Stanley, who explored the region and noted the technique of the Wagenya. He described how the people, taking advantage of the rocks, fixed upright heavy poles, 6 inches in diameter, to which they attached enormous fish-baskets by means of rattan-cane cable. He counted probably sixty or seventy baskets laid in the river on each side every day, and noted that out of half a dozen baskets twenty-eight large fish were collected.
bp: In May 1908 British geologists found a large amount of oil at Masjed Soleyman in Khuzestan Province in south-western Persia, the first commercially significant oil find in the Middle East. William Knox D'Arcy had obtained, by contract with Ali-Qoli Khan Bakhtiari, permission to explore for oil there. On 14 April 1909 the Anglo-Persian Oil Company was incorporated as a subsidiary of the Burmah Oil Company, and some of its shares were sold to the public. Lord Strathcona became its first chairman and a minority shareholder. The discovery led to the growth of a petrochemical industry and of industries that depended on oil.

In 1954 the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company became the British Petroleum Company. After the 1953 Iranian coup d'état, Iranian Oil Participants Ltd was founded in London in October 1954 to bring Iranian oil back to the international market, and British Petroleum was a founding member with a 40 per cent stake. The consortium agreed to share profits with Iran equally, but not to open its books to Iranian auditors or to admit Iranians to its board. Since 1951 the company has published a Statistical Review of World Energy each year.

The British government sold 80 million shares in 1979 as part of the privatisations of the Thatcher years, reducing its holding to 46 per cent. On 19 October 1987 Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher authorised the sale of its remaining 31 per cent for £7.5 billion. Under the chief executive John Browne the company grew by acquisition: it merged with Amoco in December 1998 to become BP Amoco, and bought Atlantic Richfield and Burmah Castrol in 2000. In 2001 it adopted the name BP and replaced its Green Shield logo with the Helios sunflower symbol, with the slogan Beyond Petroleum.

BP is a vertically integrated company, active in exploration and production, refining, marketing and trading, with its headquarters in London. Its accidents have shaped its public record. In December 1965 Sea Gem, Britain's first oil rig, capsized and 13 crew members were killed. A refinery explosion at Texas City in 2005 killed 15 workers.

The worst was the Deepwater Horizon disaster in the Gulf of Mexico. The rig exploded on 20 April 2010, killing 11 people, and the well was capped on 15 July 2010 after about 4.9 million barrels of oil had leaked, the largest accidental release of oil into marine waters. The company's costs came to more than 65 billion dollars. In 1997 BP had left the Global Climate Coalition, and in 2002 Browne declared that global warming was real; critics have argued that its actions did not match its stated aims.
brabant-revolution: The Austrian Netherlands, with its capital at Brussels, had passed from Spain to Austria under the Treaty of Rastatt in 1714; its population was staunchly Catholic and its clergy powerful. From 1784 Joseph II launched wide-ranging reforms of economics, politics and religion aimed at institutions he judged outdated. Most of the population, influenced by the Church, saw them as a threat to their traditions, and opposition centred on the provincial Estates of Hainaut, Brabant and Flanders and their law courts.

The Estate of Brabant engaged the lawyer Henri Van der Noot, who argued that the reforms violated the Joyous Entry of 1356, regarded as the region's traditional bill of rights. After the riots of 1787, the Small Revolution, Van der Noot went into exile in the Dutch Republic, and at Breda, near the border, thousands of dissidents gathered into a small patriot army.

On 24 October 1789 the émigré army of 2,800 men under Van der Mersch crossed into the Kempen. At Hoogstraten a Manifesto of the People of Brabant, modelled on the Dutch States-General's declaration of 1581 against Philip II, declared Joseph II's rule illegitimate. On 27 October the rebels defeated a much larger Austrian force at Turnhout. Ghent fell on 16 November and Mons on 21 November; by December the Austrians had withdrawn to the fortress of Luxembourg.

The new state soon split between the Vonckists of Jan Frans Vonck, a liberal party strongest among the middle classes and in Flanders, and the conservative Statists of Van der Noot, backed by the clergy, nobility and lower classes, who drove the Vonckists into exile. No foreign power recognised the state; Prussia sent some troops but withdrew them under Austrian and British pressure.

Once Austria had ended its war with the Ottoman Empire, Emperor Leopold II offered an amnesty, and after the Statist army was beaten at the Battle of Falmagne imperial forces overran the territory. A convention at The Hague on 10 December 1790, with the Emperor and the Triple Alliance of the Dutch, British and Prussians, cancelled most of Joseph II's reforms. The restoration was short-lived: the French overran the territory in the French Revolutionary Wars.

The red, yellow and black of 1789 were taken up in the Belgian Revolution of 1830 and form the national flag of Belgium. Henri Pirenne called the revolution defensive or conservative beside those of France and Liège, and some historians see the Vonckists and Statists as forerunners of the Liberals and Catholics of independent Belgium.
brac: Brač has an area of 396 square kilometres and is the third largest island in the Adriatic. It is almost 40 km wide from east to west and about 14 km from north to south, and the Brač Channel, 5 to 13 km wide, separates it from the mainland. Vidova gora, at 780 m, is the highest point of the Adriatic islands. The island is mostly limestone, formed in the Cretaceous about 100 million years ago; it became an island only within the last 12,000 years. Its Greek name was Elaphousa, apparently from the word for stag, and the Latin name was Brattia.

The Kopačina cave near Donji Humac holds finds dated to the 12th millennium BCE, among the oldest traces of human habitation in Dalmatia. In the 2nd millennium BCE the Illyrians arrived and replaced the earlier population. Brač came under Roman rule with the provinces of Illyricum and Dalmatia in 32-27 BCE. The writer Vladimir Nazor called it an island without history, for neither Illyrians, Greeks nor Romans founded a large settlement on it. In the ninth century the Narentines, a South Slavic people, held the island, which with neighbouring islands was called Maronia.

In 1000 the Venetian doge Pietro II Orseolo set out to pacify the Narentines, and Venice conquered Brač that year. Hungarian kings held the island in the 1180s and again after the Treaty of Zadar of 1358. On 1 April 1278 Venice agreed to a plea from Brač and Hvar for protection from pirates. Venice reconquered the island in August 1420 and ruled until 1797, when the Habsburg monarchy annexed most of its territory. The Black Death struck in 1425-1427 and 1434-1436, reducing the population from 6,000 to 2,000.

The island is part of Split-Dalmatia County, with a city, Supetar, and seven municipalities. Its population fell from about 40,000 early in the 20th century to about 13,000 at its end, mainly through emigration to Latin America, New Zealand and Australia. The white limestone, quarried for millennia, was used in Diocletian's Palace in Split, and the island's olive oil has a protected designation of origin.
bracara-augusta: The site lies in the heart of Minho, in a transitional region between east and west, between mountains, forests, valleys and plains. Human occupation there dates back thousands of years, with vestiges of monumental structures from the Megalithic era. During the Iron Age the Castro culture extended into the northwest, and the Bracari occupied high ground in fortified settlements called castrum. The region became the domain of the Callaici Bracarii, a Celtic tribe who occupied what is now northern Portugal, Galicia and Asturias.

The Romans began their conquest of the region around 136 BCE and finished it, by conquering the northern regions, in the reign of Augustus. The civitas was founded in 16 BCE and, in the administrative reorganization of the new acquisitions, Bracara was rededicated to the emperor and took the name Bracara Augusta. The city developed greatly during the 1st century and reached its maximum extent around the 2nd. Towards the end of the 3rd century Diocletian promoted it to a capital within the newly founded Roman province of Gallaecia. The poet Ausonius described it as prosperous in the 4th century.

Between 402 and 470 the Suebi conquered the area. In 410 they established a kingdom in the northwest of Iberia, founded by Hermeric and lasting over 150 years, with Bracara as its capital. The old Roman amphitheatre was converted into a fortress. In 455 the Visigothic king Theodoric II sacked the city, destroying many historical and archaeological records, while the Suebi king Rechiar escaped, wounded, to Porto. A list of dioceses and parishes of Braga made in 570 still exists, and by about 584 the Visigoths took permanent control of Gallaecia.

The site is the city of Braga in northwestern Portugal, capital of the district of Braga and of the historical Minho Province. It hosts the oldest Portuguese archdiocese, the Archdiocese of Braga, and is the seat of the Primacy of the Spains. In the Middle Ages it was a main centre of Christianity in Iberia. Archbishop Paio Mendes was a contributor to the recognition of Portugal as an independent kingdom under Afonso I Henriques in 1179, and the city was later handed to the Church's direct control, giving it the nickname Paiz Bracarense. The medieval castle in the city centre was destroyed in 1905.
braccio-da-montone: Born Andrea Fortebraccio on 1 July 1368, the son of the nobleman Oddo Fortebraccio and Giacoma Montemelini, Braccio began as a page in the company of Guido d'Asciano. When his family was exiled from Perugia and lost the castle of Montone, he joined Alberico da Barbiano's Company of St. George, where he became a friend of Muzio Attendolo Sforza. He was slightly crippled at the siege of Fossombrone in 1391 and served Florence, the Pope and Barbiano in turn, until companions accused him of plotting to kill Alberico and he had to flee.

From 1406 he led a company formed largely of exiles from Perugia, and in May 1407 Rocca Contrada gave him the lordship of the town. He served King Ladislaus of Naples, then turned against him, taking Jesi, and in 1410 he defeated the retreating Neapolitan troops at Sora. The speed of his troops became proverbial, and a school of the condottiere's art, the Braccesca, was named after him. The antipope John XXIII gave him Montone and the governorship of Bologna, which he used to extort large sums from the cities of Romagna.

After Ladislaus died in 1414 Braccio gave up Bologna for 180,000 gold ducats and conquered most of Umbria. He defeated Carlo Malatesta's forces at Sant'Egidio on 12 July 1416, a battle later painted by Paolo Uccello, and entered Perugia; Todi, Narni, Orvieto and Terni also took him as lord. Pope Martin V sent two armies against him, which he defeated at Spoleto, and on 14 March 1419 the pope named him papal vicar in return for driving Antongaleazzo Bentivoglio out of Bologna.

When the pope excommunicated Queen Joanna II of Naples, she named Alfonso of Aragon her heir and hired Braccio, who faced Sforza again in Abruzzo and began a thirteen-month siege of L'Aquila. On 3 February 1424 he was made Gran Conestabile of the kingdom. When Joanna went over to the Angevins he stayed loyal to Alfonso. On 2 June he was wounded in the neck below the walls of L'Aquila and taken prisoner, and he died three days later. Having died excommunicated, he was buried in unconsecrated ground until his nephew Niccolò Fortebraccio moved his body to San Francesco al Prato in Perugia in 1432.
braclaw-voivodeship: The voivodeship lay in Ukrainian Podolia, between the Dniestr and the Boh rivers, and with the Podolian Voivodeship it formed the region of Podolia within the Lesser Poland Province. A royal commission of 1570 set its borders: the Murachwa river in the west, the Dniestr against Wallachia in the south-east, and the Black Tatar Trail in the north. In 1584 King Stefan Batory fixed the line with the Kijów Voivodeship along the Hirskyi Tykicz river.

It was divided into the counties of Bracław and Vinnytsia, with Zvenyhorodka a district of Bracław County or, by some accounts, a county of its own. Vinnytsia County was smaller but more populous. The voivodeship had two senators, the voivode and the castellan of Bracław, and six deputies to the Sejm.

In the late 16th century most of the voivodeship was a depopulated wild field, with settled life only in the farmland around the royal castles of Bracław, Vinnytsia and Zwinogrod. After the Union of Lublin it acquired Polish-style offices, starostas, sejmiks and courts. Its first voivode, in 1569, was Prince Roman Sanguszko. In 1589 the Sejm ordered that its official documents be written in Old East Slavic, and its border judges worked with officials of the Ottoman Porte and the Crimean Khanate to settle disputes between subjects of the two states.

In 1598 the courts and sejmiks were moved to Vinnytsia, where the voivodes also lived, though Bracław remained the official capital. Settlement spread south into the Pobereze: the census of 1625 counted 285 villages, and by the early 1790s there were about 1,500. Castles multiplied, most of them private, the strongest at Uman, and in the 18th century magnates built residences such as the Potocki family's Zofiowka near Uman. In 1791 the Great Sejm created a Boh County, which the Polish–Russian War of 1792 kept from being set up.

After 1793 the Russian authorities formed a Bracław Governorate, which lasted until 1796 and was then divided among the Podolia, Volhynian and Kiev governorates. The former territory of the voivodeship lies in Ukraine and in northern Transnistria in Moldova.
brahma: The origins of the term brahmā are uncertain, partly because several related words occur in Vedic literature, such as Brahman for the Ultimate Reality and Brāhmaṇa for priest. Brahman is a genderless, abstract metaphysical concept, while Brahmā is a masculine god, and some scholars suggest the god may have emerged as a visible icon of the impersonal principle. A distinct god named Brahma is evidenced in late Vedic texts, and he is frequently identified with Prajapati. One of the earliest mentions of Brahma with Vishnu and Shiva is in the Maitrayaniya Upanishad, probably composed around the late 1st millennium BCE, which links Brahma to the quality called rajas.

In the Puranas Brahma is a secondary creator who creates all forms in the universe but not the primordial universe itself, and his activity depends on a higher god or goddess. Vishnu-focused Puranas say he was born from a lotus emerging from Vishnu's navel. In the Brahmanda Purana there was only an eternal ocean, from which a golden egg called Hiranyagarbha emerged, and Brahma came into being within it. He creates but neither preserves nor destroys, and like all deities he is mortal. His wife is the goddess Sarasvati.

Brahma is traditionally depicted with four faces, each facing a cardinal direction and credited with creating one of the four Vedas, and four arms holding symbols of knowledge and creation. He often has a white beard and sits on a lotus with a swan, the hamsa, as his mount.

In the post-Vedic period Brahma was a prominent god, and a sect of him existed from the 2nd to the 6th century CE. By the 7th century he had lost importance. Historians point to the rise of Shaivism and Vaishnavism and attacks by Buddhists, Jains and followers of Shiva and Vishnu. Today he does not enjoy popular worship, and few temples are dedicated to him in India, the most prominent being the Brahma Temple at Pushkar. His shrines are also found outside India: at Angkor Wat, at Prambanan in Java, and at the Erawan Shrine in Bangkok. The name Burma derives from Brahma.
brahmanas: The Brahmanas are Vedic works attached to the Samhitas, the hymns and mantras, of the Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva Vedas. Each Veda has one or more Brahmanas of its own, and each is generally associated with a particular shakha, or Vedic school. The word is loosely translated as explanations of sacred knowledge or doctrine, and according to Sayana a Brahmana has two parts: vidhi, directions for rites, and arthavada, explanatory remarks. The oldest is dated to about 900 BCE and the most recent to around 700 BCE, though the dating is controversial, since the texts were probably recorded only after several centuries of oral transmission.

The Brahmanas are noted for their instructions on the proper performance of rituals and for explaining the symbolism of sacred words and ritual actions. They insist on exact pronunciation, metre and pitch, with coordinated movement of the hands and fingers. The Shatapatha Brahmana, for example, states that verbal perfection made a mantra infallible, while one mistake made it powerless. Scholars suggest that this care preserved the Vedas in an age without writing, when students memorised them and passed them on by recitation.

The texts also record legends and discuss scientific matters of the Vedic period, including observational astronomy and, in relation to altar construction, geometry. The Rigveda has the Aitareya and Kausitaki Brahmanas, the Samaveda the Panchavimsha, or Tandya, Brahmana, which includes the Vratyastoma, a ceremony by which people of non-Aryan stock could be admitted into the Aryan family. The Shatapatha belongs to the White Yajurveda, the Taittiriya to the Black Yajurveda, and the Gopatha to the Atharvaveda. Some Brahmanas also contain mystical and philosophical material that forms the Aranyakas and Upanishads.

Fewer than twenty Brahmanas survive. Most are lost, and the grammarian Panini and Patanjali's Mahabhasya imply that each Veda once had a much larger number. Panini also distinguishes old Brahmanas, taught before Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa set out the Vedic recensions, from new ones expounded by his disciples. The grammarian Yaska's Nirukta, a work on the etymology and interpretation of the Vedas, refers to several of them.

In the 14th century, King Bukka asked his preceptor and minister Madhavacharya to write a commentary on the Vedas so that common people could understand the mantras. Madhavacharya entrusted the task to his younger brother Sayana, who wrote commentaries on the Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads.
brahmaputra: The Brahmaputra is a trans-boundary river that flows through south-western China, north-eastern India and Bangladesh. It is known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibetan, the Brahmaputra in Assam, the Siang or Dihang in the Mishmi language and the Jamuna in Bangladesh. It rises on the Angsi Glacier near Mount Kailash. For nearly 1,100 km it runs east between the main range of the Himalayas and the Kailas Range, then breaks through the Himalayas in great gorges and enters Arunachal Pradesh near the village of Gelling.

It flows south-west through the Assam Valley and then south through Bangladesh, merges with the Ganges in the delta, and as the Meghna reaches the Bay of Bengal. It is a classic braided river, prone to channel migration, and one of the few rivers in the world with a tidal bore. It floods catastrophically in spring when Himalayan snow melts, and it is navigable for most of its length.

The upper course of the river was long unknown, and its identity with the Yarlung Tsangpo was established only by exploration in 1884–1886. Brahmaputra means son of Brahma in Sanskrit, a rare male name among the rivers of the Indian subcontinent, and the lower reaches are sacred to Hindus. The early Greek accounts of Curtius and Strabo give its name as Dyardanes and Oidanes.

Its lower course in Bangladesh once ran through the Jamalpur and Mymensingh districts, and some water still flows through that channel, now called the Old Brahmaputra. When and why the main flow moved to the Jamuna channel is debated: one account ties it to an earthquake and the uplift of the Madhupur tract, another to the heavy flooding of the Tista.

The river's delta is home to 130 million people, who depend on the annual flood to bring moisture and fresh sediment to the soils. Two of the three seasonal rice varieties, aus and aman, cannot survive without the floodwater, and fish caught on the floodplain are a main source of protein for many rural people. The Sadiya to Dhubri stretch of 891 km in Assam is National Waterway 2.
brahmeswara-temple: The temple was raised in the 18th regnal year of the Somavamshi king Udyota Keshari by his mother, Kolavati Devi. According to the inscription that records its foundation, it was built with four Natyasalas at a place known as Siddhatirtha in Ekamra Kshetra, the old name of the sacred area of modern Bhubaneswar. One of the lost inscriptions stated that Queen Kolavati presented many beautiful women to the temple, and it has been suggested that this is evidence of the Devadasi tradition, which later became important in Odia temple life.

The Brahmeswara is a panchayatana temple, with the main shrine and four subsidiary shrines at the corners around it. Its vimana is 18.96 metres tall. Like other Odia temples it joins a smaller assembly hall, the Jagmohana, to the towering sanctuary, the Shikhara. The builders applied the methods of wood carving to stone: each building was raised as a solid pyramid and then carved inside and out. Iron beams were used here for the first time in the history of temple architecture.

The temple shows a close affinity with the earlier Mukteswar Temple, in the carved interior of its Jagmohana and in the lion head motif, which first appeared at the Mukteswar and is used here in profusion. New are the many musicians and dancers on the outer walls, some holding lutes. The door frame carries flower designs and flying figures, and, as at the Rajarani Temple, the eight guardian deities of the directions appear. Tantric images include Chamunda on the western facade, holding a trident and a human head and standing on a corpse, and Shiva and other gods are shown in their fearsome aspects.

The inscriptions that were originally on the temple are now lost, but records of them preserve their contents. The foundation inscription was carried from Bhubaneswar to Kolkata, and because it is no longer in place historians have considered whether it might refer to another temple; the location and features it describes have led them to assign it to the Brahmeswara. The historian Panigrahi has argued that the four corner temples are Angashalas, associate shrines, rather than the dance halls the inscription names.
brahmi-script: Early theories derived Brahmi from Egyptian hieroglyphs on a pictographic model, but these have lost credence as purely imaginative and speculative. Many scholars link it to Semitic scripts, particularly Aramaic, which was the bureaucratic language of the Achaemenid empire and lay close to the Indian subcontinent. Georg Bühler connected it to Phoenician and proposed an early 8th century BCE borrowing. A difficulty is that Aramaic is also the accepted source of the Kharoṣṭhī script, which looks very different, and why two such scripts arose from it is unexplained.

Other scholars, among them John Marshall and G. R. Hunter, saw similarities with the undeciphered Indus script. Kenneth Norman proposed that Brahmi was devised over a longer period before Ashoka, citing sherds from Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka dated to perhaps two centuries earlier, though those finds are controversial.

Brahmi is an abugida: vowels are attached to consonant signs by diacritical marks. It changed relatively little from the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE to the early Gupta period in the 4th century CE. Sometime afterwards the ability to read it was lost. Its name is a feminine Sanskrit word meaning of Brahma. The Lalitavistara Sūtra lists 64 scripts with Brahmi first. The earliest full inscriptions are in Prakrit, from the 3rd to 1st centuries BCE, and the earliest in Sanskrit date from the 1st century BCE.

The Edicts of Ashoka were written in Brahmi and, in the northwest, sometimes in Kharoshthi. Both scripts had died out by about the 4th century CE, so the edicts could not be read when scholars began to study them in the 19th century. James Prinsep, secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, deciphered Brahmi in a series of articles in the Society's journal in the 1830s, building on the work of Christian Lassen, Edwin Norris, H. H. Wilson and Alexander Cunningham.
From the 6th century CE the script diversified into local variants, the Brahmic family. One survey found 198 scripts that ultimately derive from it, used across South and Southeast Asia.
brahmo-samaj: The name Brahmo Samaj means the community of those who have knowledge of Brahman, the ultimate reality. The Brahmo Sabha held its first assembly on 20 August 1828 at the house of Firingi Kamal Bose in north Calcutta, open to people of every religion, caste, creed and gender. Ram Mohan Roy defined the worship: two Brahmins read the Vedas, Utsavananda Bidyabagish explained Vedanta and the Upanishads in Bengali, and songs composed by Roy or his friends followed.

In January 1830 a trust deed was executed, and on 23 January the first house of prayer, now the Adi Brahmo Samaj, on Chitpore Road was publicly inaugurated, with about 500 Brahmins and one Englishman present. Roy left for England in November 1830 and died near Bristol in 1833.

After Roy's death attendance dwindled. Dwarkanath Tagore paid for the upkeep of the Samaj, and Ram Chandra Vidyabagish kept the weekly service going. On 6 October 1839 Debendranath Tagore, Dwarkanath's son, founded the Tattwabodhini Sabha, which had over 500 members within two years and counted Akshay Kumar Datta and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar among its first members. In 1843 Debendranath and twenty others took the First Covenant and joined the Trust of the Brahmo Sabha. In 1861 the first branch was founded at Lahore by Nobin Roy, and others followed in the Punjab.

Disagreement between Debendranath Tagore and Keshub Chandra Sen came to a head between August 1865 and November 1866, and Keshub's followers formed the Brahmo Samaj of India. A second split followed Keshub's handling of the Coochbehar marriage and his autocratic management, and on 15 May 1878 a meeting at the Town Hall of Calcutta founded the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj, with Anandamohan Bose as president. The movements based in Calcutta declined after 1920.

Members held that no scripture had ultimate authority above human reason and conscience, had no faith in avatars and rejected polytheism, idol-worship and the caste system. They took no fixed position on karma and rebirth. In social reform the Samaj condemned sati, discouraged child marriage and polygamy, campaigned for widow remarriage, and attacked casteism and untouchability. It also condemned the prejudice against crossing the sea.

After controversy over the underage marriage of Keshub Chandra Sen's daughter, the Special Marriages Act of 1872 set a minimum age of 14 for girls; Brahmo marriages were then solemnised under it, though many resented its declaration of not being a Hindu, Muslim or Christian. Roy's movement began the Bengal Renaissance and is described as one of the most influential religious movements in India. In the census of 2001 only 177 people declared themselves Brahmo.
braila: Before the 14th century a small village stood on the site, probably of fishermen and small merchants. It fell to the Mongols in the invasion of 1241. The origin of the name is unknown and thought to be a personal name.
