The first certain mention is a privilege from Vladislav I of Wallachia exempting German merchants of Brașov from customs duties on the road to the Danube through Braylan. After the fall of Vicina, Brăila became the main harbour of Wallachia and gained town status around 1400. Foreign merchants had to unload their goods there.

In 1462 the fleet of Mehmed the Conqueror, 25 triremes and 150 other ships, burned it to the ground, and the Moldavians under Stephen the Great destroyed it in a campaign against the Wallachian prince Radu the Fair. Bogdan III of Moldavia burned it again in 1512, yet it recovered each time as the gateway for Levantine goods into Wallachia. Around 1538 to 1540 it passed to the Ottoman Empire, which built a stone stronghold there. Michael the Brave of Wallachia held it briefly in 1595 and 1596.

A Wallachian-Russian army conquered it in 1711 during the Pruth River Campaign, and the siege of 1828 preceded its award to Wallachia by the Treaty of Adrianople in 1829. In the 19th century it was one of the three most important Danube ports of Wallachia, and its prosperity peaked at the end of that century and the start of the next.

Brăila is the capital of Brăila County in Muntenia, eastern Romania, and a port on the Danube accessible to small and medium-sized oceangoing ships, with large grain-handling and warehousing facilities. Streets radiating from the port are crossed by concentric streets that follow the geometry of the old Ottoman fortifications. Landmarks include the Greek Church of 1863 to 1872 and the Church of the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel, a former mosque and the oldest church in the city.
braille: Braille was based on a tactile code now known as night writing, developed by Charles Barbier, in which sets of 12 embossed dots encoded 36 sounds. Louis Braille found three defects in it: the symbols stood for sounds, not letters, so the code could not render spelling; the 12-dot symbols did not fit beneath the pad of the reading finger; and there were no symbols for numerals or punctuation.

His solution was a cell of six dots with a specific pattern for each letter of the alphabet, with numerals and punctuation added. He developed it in 1824 and published it in 1829, later with musical notation. The second revision, published in 1837, was the first binary form of writing developed in the modern era.

A braille cell has six raised dots in two columns of three, numbered one to six. There are 64 possible combinations, including no dots at all for a space. In the original French system the patterns followed the order of the French alphabet of the time, and the first ten letters, a to j, use the upper four dot positions and also stand for the digits 1 to 9 and 0. Braille is an independent writing system for blind readers, and the mappings vary from language to language. English braille has an uncontracted level and a contracted level that uses abbreviations to save space. Extended to eight dots, the cell can encode every printable ASCII character.

Braille can be written by hand with a slate and stylus, each dot made from the back of the page in mirror image, or on a braille typewriter. The first typewriter to gain general acceptance was invented by Frank Haven Hall of the Illinois School for the Blind and presented in 1892. Henry Stainsby developed his Brailler in 1903, and in 1951 David Abraham of the Perkins School for the Blind produced the Perkins Brailler. Braille is read on embossed paper and on refreshable displays whose pins rise and fall to form the symbols. World Braille Day is observed on 4 January, to commemorate Louis Braille's birth, and the United Nations has recognised it since 2019.
branco-river: The Branco River, in Portuguese Rio Branco, meaning White River, is the principal tributary of the Rio Negro from the north. It drains the Guayanan Highlands moist forests ecoregion and is fed by streams from the Tepui highlands, which separate Venezuela and Guyana from Brazil. Its two main upper tributaries are the Uraricoera and the Takutu. The Branco flows nearly south and reaches the Negro through several channels and a chain of lagoons. It is 560 kilometres long up to its confluence with the Uraricoera, has numerous islands, and is broken by a bad series of rapids 378 kilometres above its mouth.

The river is named for its whitish water, which can look almost milky because of the inorganic sediments it carries. It is traditionally considered a whitewater river, although large seasonal changes in its chemistry make classification difficult and some consider it clearwater. It contrasts visibly with the dark, acidic water of the Rio Negro at their confluence. Alfred Russel Wallace described its milky appearance in a paper of 1853, and Alexander von Humboldt attributed the colour to silicates, mainly mica and talc.

Until about 20,000 years ago the headwaters of the Branco did not flow into the Amazon but, by way of the Takutu Graben in the Rupununi area of Guyana, towards the Caribbean. In the rainy season much of the Rupununi now floods, draining both to the Amazon through the Branco and to the Essequibo, and the headwaters of the two systems are connected, allowing fish and other aquatic fauna to pass between them.
brandenburg: Brandenburg lies in northeastern Germany and surrounds Berlin. It borders Poland and the states of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Saxony, and the Oder forms part of its eastern border. Its main rivers are the Spree and the Havel. The name comes from the town of Brandenburg an der Havel, and its origin is unclear: it is thought to derive from the Slavic branyi, marshy, or the Germanic branda, fire. In the extinct local language Polabian the town was called Branibor.

By the 7th century Slavic peoples are believed to have settled the area, the two principal groups being the Hevelli in the west and the Sprevane in the east. From the early 10th century Henry the Fowler and his successors conquered territory up to the Oder, and in 948 Emperor Otto I established margraves over the pagan Slavs there. A great uprising of the Wends drove the imperial forces out in 983. In 1134 Emperor Lothar III granted the Northern March to Albert the Bear, who inherited the town of Brandenburg and the lands of the Hevelli from Pribislav in 1150 and proclaimed himself ruler of the new Margraviate of Brandenburg.

The Ascanian line ended in 1320, and from 1323 to 1415 Brandenburg was under the Wittelsbachs of Bavaria, under whom its margrave gained the status of prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1415 Emperor Sigismund granted the Electorate to the House of Hohenzollern, which ruled until the end of the First World War and made Berlin its capital. Brandenburg converted to Protestantism in 1539, and the Hohenzollerns acquired the Duchy of Prussia in 1618, forming Brandenburg-Prussia.

The Great Elector, Frederick William, rebuilt and consolidated the state after the Thirty Years' War, and in 1701 his son took the title King in Prussia as Frederick I. Brandenburg remained the core of the Kingdom of Prussia and, from 1815 to 1947, was a province of Prussia. After the Second World War the lands east of the Oder–Neisse line were ceded to Poland. East Germany dissolved the state in 1952, and it was re-established in the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.

Brandenburg is a landlocked state of Germany with Potsdam as its capital and about 2.5 million residents. Other major towns are Cottbus, Brandenburg an der Havel and Frankfurt (Oder). In the southeast, part of the historical Lower Lusatia has two official languages, German and Lower Sorbian. A proposal to unify Berlin and Brandenburg was rejected in a referendum in 1996, and the two states still cooperate on many matters.
brandenburg-an-der-havel: Brandenburg an der Havel lies on the banks of the River Havel, which is navigable here as a European Waterway. The name combines two Slavic words, braniti, to protect or defend, and bor, forest or wood. The town gave its name to the medieval Bishopric of Brandenburg, the Margraviate of Brandenburg and the present German state, and it was the original nucleus of the realms of Brandenburg and Prussia. It was capital of the Margraviate until Berlin replaced it in 1417.

Brenna was a Slavic fort, conquered in 929 after the Battle of Lenzen by King Henry the Fowler of Saxony, and first mentioned in documents then as Brennaburg. At the Magdeburg Assembly of Princes in 948 the bishoprics of Brandenburg and Havelburg were established under the control of Otto I. A major Slavic uprising in 983 returned the area east of the Elbe to Slavic chiefs of the Hevelli until the middle of the 12th century. The last of them, Pribislav, died in 1150.

His widow Petrissa enabled Albert I of Brandenburg to take over Brenna. Jaksa of Kopanica drove him out, and he returned in 1157 after a long siege, by agreement and with a joint German and Slav garrison, and styled himself Margrave of Brandenburg. By 1160 nobles, burghers and peasants from the Harz, the Netherlands, the Rhineland and Westphalia were settling the Elbe, Havel and Spree basin. The foundation stone of a cathedral was laid on the cathedral island in 1165, and it was consecrated five years later. In 1314–1315 the Old and New Towns joined the Hanseatic League. Plundering and destruction in the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) led the court to leave. The two towns merged in 1715.

In the late 19th century the town became an industrial centre, making steel, toys and bicycles under brands such as Brennabor. In 1933–1934 one of the first Nazi concentration camps stood here. The Brandenburg-Görden Prison later became a euthanasia centre where the Nazis murdered people with psychiatric disorders, including children, in Action T4, and it was one of the first places where they experimented with killing by gas. Heavy bombing, partly because of the Arado aircraft factory, destroyed 70 percent of the city by 1945.

The Dominsel, the cathedral island, is its historic heart, with the Cathedral of St Peter and Paul, begun in the Romanesque style in 1165 and completed as a Gothic cathedral in the 14th century; the Wagner organ of 1725 is one of the best-known Baroque organs in Germany. Other sights are the brick Gothic Katharinenkirche of 1401, the Old Town Hall with its statue of the knight Roland of 1474, and parts of the medieval wall with four watchtowers.
brandenburg-concertos: The Brandenburg Concertos are catalogued as BWV 1046 to 1051. Bach compiled them in 1721, writing the collection almost entirely in his own hand instead of leaving it to a copyist, and presented it to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, with a dedication in French dated 24 March. Its title was Six Concerts avec plusieurs instruments, meaning six concertos for several instruments.

In the dedication Bach recalled that he had been heard by the margrave some years earlier, probably during a trip to Berlin in 1719 to pay for a new harpsichord by Michael Mietke, and that the margrave had asked him to send some compositions. It is uncertain when most of the music was written. The first movement of the first concerto was based on an introduction to the cantata Was mir behagt of 1713, and the fifth concerto was probably the last composed.

Each concerto sets a different group of instruments. The first, in F major, is the only one with four movements and uses two horns, three oboes, bassoon and a violino piccolo. The second, also in F, sets a natural trumpet, recorder, oboe and violin against the strings; the trumpet part is still counted among the hardest in the repertoire. The third, in G major, is for three violins, three violas and three cellos, and its second movement is a single measure of two chords.

The fourth sets a violin and two recorders, described in the score as flauti d'echo. The fifth, in D major, has a prominent harpsichord part and is seen as the first concerto with a solo keyboard. The sixth, in B flat, omits violins and uses violas da braccio and violas da gamba. Christoph Wolff called the title an understatement, since every concerto set a precedent in its scoring.

It is often claimed that the margrave could not perform the concertos and left them unused until his death in 1734, but the musicologist Boyd doubts this. The manuscript passed to Bach's pupil Johann Kirnberger, then to Princess Anna Amalia, and reached the Royal Library of Berlin in 1914. After Bach's death only the fifth concerto won much attention.

Siegfried Dehn found the set in Princess Amalia's library in 1849 and had it published the following year, the centenary of Bach's death. The first recording of the complete set, directed by Adolf Busch, was made in 1936. A recording of the second concerto by Karl Richter was sent into space in 1977 on the Voyager Golden Record.
brandenburg-prussia: The Margraviate of Brandenburg had been the seat of the main branch of the Hohenzollerns, prince-electors in the Holy Roman Empire, since 1415. In 1525 the Treaty of Krakow created the Duchy of Prussia through partial secularization of the State of the Teutonic Order, a vassal of the Kingdom of Poland governed by Duke Albert of Prussia, of a cadet branch of the Hohenzollerns. In 1563 the Brandenburg branch was granted the right of succession by the Polish crown, and it secured the duchy when the Prussian line died out in the male line in 1618. Intermarriage had also brought the lower Rhenish principalities of Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg after the Treaty of Xanten in 1614.

The Thirty Years' War was especially devastating. The elector George William, who ruled from 1619 to 1640, was forced by Wallenstein's army to join the Catholic-Imperial camp in 1627, and later by Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden to grant Sweden transit rights. Protestant and Catholic armies swept the land back and forth. In Brandenburg the war destroyed 60 towns, 48 castles and about 5,000 villages, and an average of 50 per cent of the population died. By the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 Brandenburg gained Minden and Halberstadt and the succession in Farther Pomerania.

Frederick William, known as the Great Elector, ruled from 1640 to 1688. Convinced by the war that the state needed a standing army financed independently of the estates, he won the consent of the estates in a landtag decree of 26 July 1653. During the Second Northern War the Treaty of Labiau in November 1656 conceded him full sovereignty in Ducal Prussia, confirmed by the Treaty of Bromberg in 1657. He won the Battle of Fehrbellin in 1675 and welcomed settlers from across Europe: the Edict of Potsdam attracted more than 15,000 Huguenots. He also founded a navy and, through Benjamin Raule, a colony called Großfriedrichsburg on the Guinea coast and one at Arguin.

In 1701 Frederick III, Elector of Brandenburg, succeeded in raising himself to King in Prussia. This was possible because the Duchy of Prussia lay outside the Holy Roman Empire, and the Habsburgs and other European royals approved as they formed alliances for the War of the Spanish Succession and the Great Northern War. From then on the Hohenzollern domains were called the Kingdom of Prussia. Legally the personal union of Brandenburg and Prussia lasted until the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, but after 1701 Brandenburg was in practice treated as part of the kingdom. Frederick and his successors went on to centralize and expand the state.
branford-connecticut: Branford lies on Long Island Sound, about 6 miles (10 km) east of downtown New Haven. It borders East Haven to the west, Guilford to the east and North Branford to the north. The town covers 28.0 square miles (73 km2), of which 22.0 square miles (57 km2) are land. It has two harbours, Branford Harbor near the centre and Stony Creek Harbor at the east end. Lake Saltonstall, a reservoir, and Saltonstall Mountain mark much of the western border. The mountain belongs to the Metacomet Ridge, a trap rock ridge that runs from Long Island Sound to nearly the Vermont border and ends at Beacon Hill in Branford.

The area called Totoket, which became Branford, was part of the land bought from the Mattabesech Indians in 1638 by the first English settlers of New Haven. Before that, Dutch traders from the New Netherland settlements had set up a trading post at the mouth of the Branford River, which gave the names Dutch Wharf and Dutch House Quarter. Archaeological excavations in the 1990s hinted at the Dutch fort that Ezra Stiles described. The name is said to come from Brentford in England; early maps call the town Brentford. Branford was established in 1644.

The first shoreline community, Stony Creek, was settled in the late 18th century. Indian Neck and Pine Orchard were also settled, but neither was permanent until the mid-19th century. In 1852 the railroad brought new business, among them Branford Lockworks, the Malleable Iron Fittings Company and the Atlantic Wire Company, and railroad construction raised the Stony Creek granite quarries to prominence. In the mid-19th century Branford became a resort, with about twenty hotels. In the mid-20th century it shed that image and developed many of the traits of a northeastern suburb.

The population was 28,273 at the 2020 census. Seven historic districts are listed on the National Register of Historic Places, among them Branford Center and Stony Creek-Thimble Islands, as are more than twenty other properties. One is the Harrison House, built in 1724, which is now a museum. Boat cruises of the Thimble Islands leave from the Stony Creek dock, and the Shore Line Trolley Museum stands partly in Short Beach. Interstate 95 passes through the town, which has a station on the Shore Line East commuter rail line. The Branford Festival takes place each year on Father's Day weekend.
braniewo: Braniewo lies on the Pasłęka River about 5 km from the Vistula Lagoon, some 35 km north-east of Elbląg and 55 km south-west of Kaliningrad. The Polish border with the Kaliningrad Oblast is 6 km to the north. The German geographer Johann Friedrich Goldbeck derived the older name Brunsberg from Bruno von Schauenburg, bishop of Olomouc, who accompanied King Ottokar II of Bohemia on the crusade of the Teutonic Knights against the Old Prussians in 1254 and 1267. Another suggestion, Brusebergue, camp of the Prussians, is not documented.

In 1243 the Teutonic Order gave the settlement and the surrounding region of Warmia to the newly created Bishopric of Warmia, and the bishop built his cathedral there. The town received privileges on the model of Lübeck in 1254, was destroyed and depopulated in 1261 during the second Prussian Uprising, and was rebuilt in a new place in 1273 with colonists from Lübeck. Bishop Heinrich Fleming (1278–1300) moved the chapter to Frauenburg, now Frombork. A Franciscan abbey followed in 1296 and a new town in 1342. As a member of the Hanseatic League until 1608 the town traded with England, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands and Livonia.

In 1440 it was a founding member of the Prussian Confederation against Teutonic rule, and in 1454 King Casimir IV Jagiellon incorporated the territory into Poland. The Teutonic Knights renounced their claims in the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. After 1525 many residents turned Lutheran, but in 1526 the town was returned to Prince-Bishop Mauritius Ferber and Warmia stayed predominantly Catholic. Prince-Bishop Stanislaus Hosius brought in the Jesuits and founded the Collegium Hosianum, and a priestly seminary was added in 1564. Among its students were Andrew Bobola and the Latin poet Maciej Kazimierz Sarbiewski. The Swedes looted its library, which held works of Nicolaus Copernicus, in 1626.

Prussia annexed Braunsberg in 1772 in the First Partition of Poland and made it part of East Prussia. The Jesuit college became the State Academy of Braunsberg in 1912, and before the Second World War the town had more than 21,000 inhabitants. Soviet troops captured it on 20 March 1945; about 80 percent of the town was destroyed, and it was handed to Polish authorities on 7 July. Polish settlers, many from eastern Poland annexed by the Soviet Union, repopulated it.

Braniewo is the capital of Braniewo County in the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship, with 16,907 inhabitants in 2021, and the second largest town in Warmia after Olsztyn. The Gothic St Catherine Church, built in 1346 and destroyed in 1945, was rebuilt after 1979 and declared a Basilica Minor in 2001. Local brewing dates back to the 16th century.
branimir-of-croatia: According to John the Deacon's Chronicon Venetum et Gradense of the early 11th century, a certain Slav named Branimir led a rebellion in 879 in which the weak Duke Zdeslav, a supporter of the Byzantine Empire, was killed near Knin. Five letters of Pope John VIII sent between 879 and 882 survive. The pope decided on his blessing of the duke and the whole Croatian people on 21 May 879, during a service in St. Peter's church in Rome, and confirmed it in a letter of 7 June.

After 880 Branimir refused to recognise the sovereignty of the Carolingian Emperor Charles the Fat, even when the emperor allied with the Republic of Venice against Croatia. In his time the Venetians paid taxes to Croatia and to the Narentines for the right to sail along the eastern Adriatic coast, and the Dalmatian cities under Byzantine protection paid the Croatian ruler 710 ducats of tribute. He was succeeded by Muncimir, the third son of Trpimir I.

In 880–882 Branimir wrote to the pope through Theodosius, bishop of Nona, affirming his loyalty to Rome and the supreme authority of its bishop. Theodosius was later made archbishop of Split and confirmed with a pallium in 887–888. Branimir possibly also accepted the parallel use of Latin and Slavic in the liturgy after Methodius passed through Croatia in 882. He made a pilgrimage to Cividale, where the Evangelistary of Cividale records him with his wife Mariosa. Some historians suggest he belonged to the House of Domagojević, but this is uncertain.

Six or eight inscriptions, mostly altar beams from old Croatian churches at places such as Muć, Nin, Šopot and Lepuri, bear his name. The one from Muć has the earliest carved year, 888, of any Croatian medieval inscription, and the one from Šopot the earliest carved form of the ethnonym Hrvat. In 1891 Lujo Marun found rich burials in the ruined basilica of St. Mary at Crkvine near Biskupija, usually associated with Branimir or possibly Trpimir and Mariosa; the main sarcophagus is in the Split Archaeological Museum. Croatia's Order of Duke Branimir is named after him, and 21 May is marked as Croatian Diplomacy Day.
brasidas: Brasidas was the son of Tellis and Argileonis. He won his first laurels by leading the relief of Methone, besieged by the Athenians in 431 BCE. The following year he seems to have been eponymous ephor, and in 429 BCE he was sent as one of three commissioners to advise the admiral Cnemus. As a trierarch he distinguished himself in the assault on the Athenian position at Pylos, where he was severely wounded.

In 424 BCE, while he was mustering a force at Corinth for a campaign in Thrace, Brasidas frustrated an Athenian attack on Megara. He then marched through Thessaly with 1,700 hoplites, 700 helots and 1,000 Peloponnesian mercenaries, and joined Perdiccas II of Macedon. He refused to be made a tool of Perdiccas's ambitions against the Lyncestians and negotiated with their leader Arrhabaeus instead.

Through rapid and bold movements, personal charm and moderate demands he won over Acanthus, Amphipolis, Stagirus, Toroni and many smaller towns during that winter, together with most of the Chalcidic peninsulas. In spring 423 BCE a truce between Athens and Sparta was imperilled when Scione came over to Brasidas two days after it began. He refused to return it and encouraged the revolt of Mende, and the Scionians gave him a golden crown and called him the liberator of Hellas.

In 422 BCE, after the truce expired, Cleon was sent to Thrace and prepared to attack Amphipolis. When Cleon brought part of his army forward, Brasidas saw a chance to defeat it in detail. He led the Spartans in a sudden charge from Amphipolis against the Athenian left, and his allies, mostly Edonians, attacked from the north gate and broke the right.

The Athenians lost 600 men, including Cleon, while only seven fatalities are reported on the Spartan side, one of them Brasidas, who was mortally wounded at the head of his Spartans. He was buried within the city of Amphipolis, an extraordinary honour among the Greeks, and was regarded as its founder and honoured with yearly games and sacrifices. At Sparta a cenotaph was set up near the tombs of Pausanias and Leonidas, and an annual festival, the Brasideia, included speeches and contests open only to Spartiates.

Thucydides's portrayal suggests that Brasidas joined Spartan courage to qualities that Spartans typically lacked, and his speech to the Acanthians is of higher quality than other Spartan speeches in Thucydides. These un-Spartan virtues apparently aroused jealousy and suspicion at Sparta.
brasilia: Brasília sits at an elevation of 1,000 metres on the Brazilian Highlands in the Central-West region of Brazil. Paranoá Lake, a large artificial lake, was built to increase the available water and to maintain the region's humidity. The name comes from the Latin translation of Brazil, suggested for the country's capital in 1821 by José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva.

Brazil's first capital was Salvador, and in 1763 Rio de Janeiro became the capital and remained so until 1960. Resources tended to be concentrated in the southeast, and most of the population lived near the Atlantic coast. A geographically central capital would be more regionally neutral. The idea of moving the capital was conceived in 1827 by José Bonifácio, an adviser to Emperor Pedro I, who presented a plan to the General Assembly for a new city called Brasília, to the west of the heavily populated southeastern corridor. It was to stand upstream on the São Francisco River rather than in the region of Goiás chosen later. The bill was not enacted because Pedro I dissolved the Assembly.

According to a legend, the Italian saint Don Bosco dreamed in 1883 of a futuristic city that roughly fitted Brasília's location, and many references to him, including a church parish, are found in the city today. After the Proclamation of the Republic, the third article of the 1891 Constitution stated that the Union would own, in the central plateau, an area of 14,400 square kilometres, to be demarcated to establish the future federal capital.

The city was developed in 1956 by Lúcio Costa, Oscar Niemeyer and Joaquim Cardozo, in a scheme to move the capital from Rio de Janeiro to a more central location chosen through a committee, with Roberto Burle Marx as landscape architect. President Juscelino Kubitschek founded it on 21 April 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Brasília is the capital of Brazil and of the Federal District, and all three branches of the federal government sit there. It is laid out in the shape of an airplane: the fuselage is the Monumental Axis, a pair of wide avenues flanking a large park, and the cockpit is the Praça dos Três Poderes. Its white modern architecture is by Oscar Niemeyer. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1987 for its modernist architecture and urban planning. It is an administrative region rather than a municipality, and the Federal District is divided into 35 administrative regions.
braslav-duke-of-lower-pannonia: Braslav was a Slavic prince who ruled a province between the Drava and the Sava, the modern Slavonia, lying mostly in present-day Croatia. He took part in the Frankish–Moravian War, the bloody conflict of 882–884 between Arnulf of Carinthia and Svatopluk I of Moravia, and in the peace treaty the two rulers reached at Tulln in 884. The Frankish annals, which call him duke of Lower Pannonia, present him as a firm Frankish loyalist.

In 891, according to the Annals of Fulda, Arnulf sent an embassy under Margrave Arbo to renew the peace with Moravia. Svatopluk broke his pledges, and Arnulf decided to invade. He first met Braslav, the Slavic duke on the Sava, then raised an army of Franconians, Bavarians and Alamanni and also recruited Hungarians, for which Ottonian writers later blamed him for unleashing the Hungarians on Europe. Braslav took part in the campaign of 892.

After Svatopluk's death in 894 the Hungarians, now Arnulf's enemies, ravaged Pannonia and occupied the basin between the Tisza and the Danube. To strengthen his south-eastern frontier, Arnulf entrusted Pannonia and Mosapurc, the modern Zalavár in Hungary, to Braslav. The two could not hold back the Hungarians, who overran Pannonia and later broke into Italy for the first time with a great army, crossing the Slavic lands on the way.

Braslav also made a pilgrimage to Cividale, where his name and that of his wife, Ventescela, are written in the Evangelistary of Cividale. It has been suggested that Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia, recorded in 907 as Brezalauspurc, was named after him. Modern Croatian historiography refers to him as a Croatian duke.
bratislava: Bratislava lies in southwestern Slovakia at the foot of the Little Carpathians, on both banks of the Danube and the left bank of the Morava. It is on the border of Slovakia, Austria and Hungary, the only national capital with land borders with two other sovereign states, and only 60 kilometres from Vienna. The Danube, along which the city developed, was for centuries the chief transportation route.

The first known permanent settlement began with the Linear Pottery Culture around 5000 BCE. About 200 BCE the Celtic Boii tribe founded the first significant settlement, a fortified town known as the Bratislava oppidum, and established a mint that produced gold and silver coins known as biatecs. From the 1st to the 4th century CE the area fell under Roman influence as part of the Danubian Limes, a border defence system. The Romans introduced grape growing.

The Slavs arrived from the east between the 5th and 6th centuries. In response to attacks by the Avars, local Slavic tribes rebelled and established Samo's Empire (623-658), the first known Slavic political entity. In the 9th century the castles at Bratislava (Brezalauspurk) and Devín (Dowina) were important centres of the Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia. The medieval settlement Brezalauspurc, meaning Braslav's castle, was first mentioned in 907, but its actual location is under scholarly debate. The name Pozsony first appears in 1002.

From 1536 to 1783 the city was the coronation site, legislative centre and capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, and eleven Hungarian kings and eight queens were crowned in St Martin's Cathedral. Most Hungarian parliament assemblies were held there from the 17th century until the Hungarian Reform Era. The Diet used the University Library building, erected in 1756, from 1802 to 1848, and much significant legislation of the Reform Era, such as the abolition of serfdom and the foundation of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, was enacted there.

Bratislava is the capital and largest city of Slovakia and the seat of the president, parliament and government. The Old Town holds most historical buildings, among them the Town Hall, built in the 14th and 15th centuries, and Michael's Gate, the only gate preserved from the medieval fortifications. The Grassalkovich Palace, built around 1760, is the president's residence. Its history was shaped by Austrians, Bulgarians, Croats, Czechs, Germans, Hungarians, Jews and Slovaks.
braulio-carrillo: Braulio Evaristo Carrillo Colina was born on 20 March 1800 and studied law in León, Nicaragua. At 28 he was elected to the legislature of Costa Rica for two years and briefly presided over it. He was acting president of the Supreme Court from October 1833 to January 1834, and later that year represented Costa Rica at the Central American Congress in El Salvador.

When the head of state José Rafael Gallegos resigned in 1835, Carrillo was indirectly elected to complete his term. In August the assembly repealed the Ambulance Act, which had rotated the capital among San José, Alajuela, Heredia and Cartago, and in mid-September the other three cities took up arms; they were defeated in a civil war that lasted a fortnight. Carrillo lost the election of 1837 to Manuel Aguilar, who was overthrown in 1838 by a cuartelazo, and Carrillo returned with absolute powers.

He convened a constituent assembly which in November 1838 declared the state separated from the federation, and on 14 November he proclaimed Costa Rica a sovereign and independent state. In 1841 he issued the Guarantee Law, making himself head of state for life, and enacted the General Code of the State of Costa Rica. He reorganised the public administration and the courts, reduced the number of public holidays, planned the growth of agriculture and passed measures against vagrancy, vice and crime. Work on a road from the Central Valley to Matina on the Caribbean coast was well advanced when Francisco Morazán's government stopped it.

In 1842 Francisco Morazán, the former federal president of Central America, invaded Costa Rica and seized power. Carrillo went into exile in El Salvador, where he was killed on 15 May 1845. He is often called the Architect of the Costa Rican State for the institutions his governments built. The Braulio Carrillo National Park, between the provinces of Limón and San José, and a highway from San José to Guápiles bear his name.
braunfels: Braunfels lies in the Lahn-Dill-Kreis in Hesse, on the German Timber-Frame Road. The climatic spa stands about 100 metres above the Lahn valley, 9 km south-west of Wetzlar and 28 km north-east of Limburg an der Lahn. Besides the main town, the municipality includes the villages of Altenkirchen, Bonbaden, Neukirchen, Philippstein and Tiefenbach, which joined it in 1972. Bonbaden was first documented in 772, making it one of the oldest inhabited places in the district.

The town and the seat of the district were first mentioned in 1246, and Braunfels has had town rights since 1607. The castle grew from one built in the 13th century by the Counts of Nassau, and from about 1260 it served as the residence of the noble family of Solms-Braunfels. After the Rhenish League of Towns destroyed Solms Castle in 1384, Braunfels Castle became the seat of the Counts of Solms.

The castle was altered many times in its history of more than 750 years. A fire in 1679 destroyed much of both town and castle. The castle was rebuilt as a Baroque residence, and the town was given a regular marketplace, which still lies in front of the town wall. Beginning in 1880 the castle was remodelled in neo-Gothic style to plans by the builder Edwin Oppler, which gave it its present appearance.

Braunfels Castle holds works by Dutch masters, including van Eyck, and by the Hessian Tischbein family of painters, as well as parts of the Altenberg Altar and Saint Elizabeth's ring. The town has a Princely Family Museum, a local history museum in a former mill and the ruins of Burg Philippstein. Among its people are Amalia of Solms-Braunfels, wife of Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, and Karl of Solms-Braunfels, founder of New Braunfels, Texas, with which the town is partnered.
brazil: Brazil covers 8,515,767 square kilometres, nearly half of the land area of South America (47.7%), and borders every South American country except Ecuador and Chile. Its Atlantic coastline is 7,491 kilometres long. The country contains most of the Amazon basin, with the world's largest river system and most extensive tropical forest, together with wetlands, savannas, plateaus and low mountains. It is the only country that both the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn cross, and it spans four time zones. Most of its territory is tropical, with equatorial rainforest in the north, semiarid land in the northeast and temperate forest in the south.

Human remains found at Pedro Leopoldo, in Minas Gerais, show habitation going back at least 11,000 years, and the earliest pottery found in the Western Hemisphere, near Santarém, was dated to over 8,000 years ago. The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajó from 400 to 1400 CE. When the Portuguese arrived, the territory had an estimated Indigenous population of 7 million people, mostly semi-nomadic, among them the Tupis, Guaranis and Gês.

The land was claimed for Portugal on 22 April 1500 by the fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral, after the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494. São Vicente was founded in 1532, and in 1534 King John III of Portugal divided the territory into fifteen private captaincies. The system failed, and in 1549 the king created the Governorate General of Brazil at Salvador. In the first two centuries Indigenous and European groups lived in constant war, forming opportunistic alliances.

Brazil became a united kingdom with Portugal in 1815, after the Portuguese court moved to Rio de Janeiro. Prince Pedro of Braganza declared independence in 1822 and founded the Empire of Brazil after a war with Portugal. The constitution of 1824 set up a bicameral legislature, and slavery was gradually abolished until its final abolition in 1888. A military coup in 1889 made the country a presidential republic. A revolution in 1930 brought Getúlio Vargas to power, and his self-coup of 1937 began the authoritarian Estado Novo. Democracy returned after 1945, a military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985, and the present constitution dates from 1988.

Brazil is a federation of 26 states and a Federal District, which holds the capital, Brasília; São Paulo is the most populous city. The 2022 census counted 203 million people, and 45.3% described themselves as Pardo, 43.5% as White, 10.2% as Black and 0.6% as Indigenous. Its culture derives mainly from Portuguese culture, shaped also by African, Indigenous and other European traditions and by Italians, Germans, Japanese, Jewish and Arab immigrants in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
brazilian-democratic-movement: Under military rule from 1965 to 1979 Brazil had a legally enforced two-party system. Supporters of the regime gathered in the National Renewal Alliance (ARENA), and the official opposition was the MDB, which comprised nearly all of the Brazilian Labour Party and the main body of the Social Democratic Party. ARENA held large majorities in the legislatures, and since Congress elected the president indirectly, its candidate, in practice chosen by the military high command, could not be defeated. The MDB put forward no candidates in 1966 and 1969 and was soundly defeated when it ran presidential candidates in 1974 and 1978.

The MDB united nearly all opponents of the dictatorship, from liberal conservatives and Christian democrats to former socialists and communists, with no programme but democratisation. In 1979 the military government disbanded the two parties. Many MDB members founded new parties, among them the Democratic Labour Party and the Workers' Party, and the government demanded that new parties carry the word Party in their names, to weaken the MDB's successor, which reorganised as the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party, the PMDB.

In 1985 its leader Tancredo Neves won the presidential election but died before taking office, and his running mate José Sarney became president and served until 1990. In 1988 Christian democrats, social liberals and social democrats left to form the Brazilian Social Democracy Party. On 29 March 2016 the PMDB left the coalition with the Workers' Party, and Michel Temer became president when the Senate removed Dilma Rousseff on 31 August 2016. On 19 December 2017 the party took back the name Brazilian Democratic Movement.
brazilian-empire: Portugal claimed the territory of Brazil on 22 April 1500, when Pedro Álvares Cabral landed on its coast. In 1808 Napoleon's army invaded Portugal and forced the royal House of Braganza into exile. The Prince regent, later King John VI, established his government in Rio de Janeiro, which became the seat of the Portuguese Empire. When John VI returned to Portugal he left his eldest son Pedro to rule the Kingdom of Brazil as regent. On 7 September 1822 Pedro declared Brazil independent and, after a war against his father's kingdom, was acclaimed Emperor Pedro I on 12 October.

Pedro I clashed with a sizeable parliamentary faction over the role of the monarch. The unsuccessful Cisplatine War ended in 1828 with the secession of Cisplatina, later Uruguay. He also became king of Portugal in 1826, and, unable to handle both countries, abdicated the Brazilian throne on 7 April 1831 and left for Europe. His five-year-old son Pedro II succeeded under a weak regency, and the lack of a ruling monarch to arbitrate led to regional civil wars. By 1846 Pedro II had matured and taken control, and he called the conservatives to form a government in 1848.

From the 1850s Brazil enjoyed stability and prosperity, with railways, the electric telegraph and steamship lines. The Brazilian victories in the Platine War, the Uruguayan War and the Paraguayan War, which ended in 1870, marked a golden age. Slavery was restricted by successive laws and abolished by the Golden Law, signed by Princess Isabel on 13 May 1888. Its end ended the belief of the ultraconservatives, backed by powerful coffee farmers, in the crown's neutrality, and they shifted to republicanism. Historians attribute the main responsibility for the fall of the monarchy to Pedro II, who grew indifferent to its fate. After a 58-year reign he was overthrown in a military coup on 15 November 1889.

The Constitution of 1824 created legislative, moderating, executive and judicial branches. The emperor headed the moderating and executive branches but had few ways of imposing his will on the General Assembly, apart from dissolving it. Catholicism was the state religion, and the emperor controlled church affairs. Slaves made up 29 per cent of the population in 1823 and fewer than 5 per cent by 1887. By 1889 Brazil had 9,200 km of railway track. Noble titles were not hereditary, except for the imperial family.
brazilian-integralist-action: In its outward forms Integralism resembled European fascism: a green-shirted paramilitary organisation with uniformed ranks, regimented street demonstrations and rhetoric against Marxism and liberalism. Its ideology differed. Plínio Salgado read history as a struggle between materialism and spiritualism, the belief in God and the immortality of the soul, and wanted nationalism to be a shared spiritual identity, its Christian virtues enforced by a state that would require political activity under an acknowledged leader. Members were urged to an Internal Revolution, giving up selfish thinking to join a great Integralist family. The movement drew support from military officers, especially in the Brazilian Navy.

Gustavo Barroso, the party's chief ideologist after Salgado, held militant antisemitic views and was the author of the first Portuguese translation of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion. His views led to serious ruptures in 1935 and 1936, when Salgado almost gave up the leadership.

In the early 1930s President Getúlio Vargas, having crushed the left, turned to the Integralists as a mobilised base of right-wing support. By 1935 the movement claimed a rapidly growing membership, especially among German-Brazilians and Italian-Brazilians. From 1934 Integralists fought street battles with the Communist movement of Luiz Carlos Prestes, and the Communists launched an uprising in 1935. When Vargas took full dictatorial powers in 1937 he turned against the movement, as Salgado's presidential ambitions threatened his hold on power. In 1938 Integralists attacked the Guanabara Palace by night; police and army troops arrived at the last minute, and the gunfight left around twenty casualties. The attempt became known as the Pajama Putsch.

The party disintegrated after 1938. In 1945 Salgado founded the Party of Popular Representation, which kept the ideology without the uniforms and salutes. Former Integralists went different ways: some took part in the 1964 coup against President João Goulart, while Goulart's foreign minister Santiago Dantas and Bishop Hélder Câmara moved to the left. Under the military regime Salgado joined the pro-military ARENA, the former Integralists Augusto Rademaker and Márcio Melo sat on the junta that briefly ruled Brazil in 1969, and Hélder Câmara was the regime's best-known opponent.
brazilian-national-anthem: From the proclamation of independence in 1822 until the abdication of Pedro I in 1831, the national anthem was one composed by Pedro I himself, which remains an official patriotic song as the Independence Anthem. After the abdication its popularity fell, and Francisco Manuel da Silva presented his own composition. The date on which he wrote the music is disputed: some historians place it in 1822, others in early 1823, and others hold that it was written in 1831. The music is a patriotic march reminiscent of Gioachino Rossini. The date of its first public performance, 13 April 1831, is now the Day of the Brazilian National Anthem.

The music was first given words by the appeals judge Ovídio Saraiva de Carvalho e Silva, as a hymn commemorating Pedro I's abdication, known as the April 7 Hymn. Those words were thought poor and offensive to the Portuguese and fell out of use, but by 1837 the melody was played without words at all public ceremonies. A new text of 1841 was also abandoned, and Pedro II ordered that the music be played without lyrics whenever he appeared in public.

After the Proclamation of the Republic in 1889 a contest chose a new anthem by Leopoldo Miguez, but after protests Deodoro da Fonseca confirmed Francisco Manuel da Silva's music as the national anthem by a decree of 20 January 1890.

For three decades of the republic the anthem had no official words, and several texts were adopted in different states. The lyrics of Joaquim Osório Duque Estrada, first proposed in 1909, were adapted and made official by a decree of President Epitácio Pessoa on 6 September 1922, during the centennial of independence. The government bought the rights to the text. The lyrics have been described as Parnassian in style and Romantic in content.
brazzaville: Brazzaville lies on the north bank of the Congo River just below Pool Malebo, about 506 km inland from the Atlantic Ocean and at an altitude of 317 m. Directly across the river stands Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and this is the only place in the world where two national capitals developed on opposite banks of a river within sight of each other. Downriver the Congo has numerous rapids, called Livingstone Falls, which prevent navigation from the Atlantic to the city. The name honours the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, born in Italy, who became a French citizen in 1874.

Before colonial rule the site held two trading centres, Mfwa and Mpila, which belonged to the Tio Kingdom. Brazza officially founded the settlement on 10 September 1880, on the existing Bateke settlement of Ncuna. The Tio king Iloo I signed a treaty of protection that placed his lands under French authority, and from October 1880 until May 1882 a small force led by Sergeant Malamine Camara occupied the site to keep it out of Belgian hands. The Berlin Conference of 1884 confirmed French control. The city became the capital of the French Congo in 1904 and remained capital when French Equatorial Africa was formed in 1910 as a federation that included Gabon, the Central African Republic and Chad.

The Congo-Ocean Railway, opened in 1934, linked Brazzaville with the Atlantic port of Pointe-Noire and bypassed the rapids; its construction cost the lives of more than 17,000 Africans. During World War II the city served as the capital of Free France. In 1944 it hosted a meeting of French resistance leaders and representatives of France's African colonies, whose Brazzaville Declaration tried to redefine the relationship between France and its colonies.

Brazzaville is the capital and largest city of the Republic of the Congo, with a population of about 2.15 million at the 2023 census. It is both a department and a commune, divided into nine arrondissements. Its port receives raw materials such as rubber, wood and agricultural products, which are sent on to Pointe-Noire for export, and the World Health Organization has its regional office for Africa there. The Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza Mausoleum and the Poto-Poto School of Painting are among its landmarks, and UNESCO named it a City of Music in 2013.
brazzaville-conference: After the Fall of France the colonies were at first controlled by the Vichy regime, but one by one they went over to Free France, and after the Tunisia campaign the whole empire except French Indochina was aligned with the Allies. The war brought hardship, nationalist aspirations and communal tensions, above all in Algeria and Tunisia; the United States, on whose aid the French depended, opposed colonialism; and the British occupation of Madagascar had weakened French authority. René Pleven, Commissioner for the Colonies in the French Committee of National Liberation, organised the conference to keep the empire's future out of international arbitration.

The meeting was held from 30 January to 8 February 1944 in Brazzaville, capital of French Equatorial Africa. Invitations went to 21 governors, nine members of the Provisional Consultative Assembly and six observers from Algeria, Tunisia and Morocco. De Gaulle opened it by speaking of new foundations for France after the years of Philippe Pétain's regime. The administrator Félix Éboué figured prominently and brought in the Cercle des Évolués of Brazzaville, a group largely of elite Congolese men, whose essays were presented as African opinions.

The Brazzaville Declaration held that the empire would remain united, with semi-autonomous assemblies in each colony, equal rights for colonial citizens, a vote for the French National Assembly, public service posts for the native population and economic reforms to lessen exploitation. De Gaulle stated that the aims of France's civilising mission precluded any thought of autonomy, and that self-government must be rejected even in the more distant future.

Many historians see the conference as a first, precarious step towards decolonisation. Others disagree: Xavier Yacono held that it considered decolonisation unthinkable, and Martin Shipway has argued that it was staged largely as a propaganda event to show the empire's generosity and efficiency.
bread-and-roses: Helen Todd wrote that the phrase came from a young hired girl in whose family's house she stayed during the Illinois campaign, who said she had liked best the talk of women voting so that everybody would have bread and flowers too. In her speeches Todd explained it: life's Bread was home, shelter and security, and the Roses of life were music, education, nature and books. During the Chicago garment workers' strike of 1910 a sign was later reported to read We want bread and roses, too, and in the successful California suffrage campaign of 1911 banners carried the slogan Bread for all, and Roses, too.

The source of Todd's inspiration is unknown, but the sentiment closely parallels a saying attributed to the Roman physician Galen of Pergamon, that a man with two loaves should sell one and buy flowers, as bread is food for the body and flowers food for the mind. Mary MacArthur of the British Women's Trade Union League quoted it on a visit to Chicago in April 1907.

James Oppenheim's poem took Todd's phrase as its title and appeared in The American Magazine in December 1911, credited to a slogan of the women in the West. Its four stanzas imagine women marching and singing, and declare that hearts starve as well as bodies and that the rising of the women means the rising of the race. When Upton Sinclair printed it in his anthology The Cry for Justice in 1915, he tied it to girls carrying a banner in a parade of strikers at Lawrence, Massachusetts. A number of historians consider that account ahistorical.

In June 1912 Rose Schneiderman of the Women's Trade Union League of New York told an audience in Cleveland that the worker must have bread, but she must have roses, too, and her repeated use of the words tied her name to them. Caroline Kohlsaat set the poem to music in 1917; by the 1930s women sang it on picket lines, and since 1932 graduating seniors at Mount Holyoke College have sung it at the Laurel Parade.

Mimi Fariña set the poem again in 1974, a version recorded by Judy Collins, Pete Seeger and Ani DiFranco among others. The logo of the Democratic Socialists of America, formed in 1982, was inspired by the slogan, and the film Pride of 2014 shows a Welsh mining community singing the song during the miners' strike of 1984–1985.
brechin: Brechin is a market town and former royal burgh on the A90 between Dundee and Aberdeen, a little closer to Dundee, with Kinnaird Castle nearby. It has traditionally been described as a city because of its cathedral and its place as the seat of a pre-Reformation diocese, which continues as a see of the Scottish Episcopal Church, although that status has not been officially recognised in modern times. The cathedral's round tower stood free at first and is now built into the church, which still keeps work of the 13th and 14th centuries, notably its western tower and processional door.

Besides the cathedral and tower, part of the chapel of the town's medieval Maison Dieu, or hospital, survives. William de Brechin founded it before 1267, perhaps about 1256, since the charter was witnessed by Albin, Bishop of Brechin from 1247 to 1269. Merchants and traders formed the Guildry Incorporation of Brechin in 1629, which won recognition of its rights from the Convention of Burghs in 1666.

After the Glorious Revolution the town's Episcopalians were driven out of the cathedral in 1695, which stayed with the Church of Scotland. They met in a house in the High Street and built a chapel in 1743, whose seats and books government forces destroyed after the Jacobite rising of 1745. St Andrews Church followed in 1809, replaced by a new building in 1888. The infirmary, designed by William Fettis and opened in 1869 by Fox Maule-Ramsay, 11th Earl of Dalhousie, closed in 2015. Brechin railway station, once the terminus of several lines, closed to passengers in 1952.

Brechin is the fourth largest settlement of Angus, with a population of 7,186 in 2022. The Maison Dieu chapel is in the care of Historic Environment Scotland, and the old station is part of the Caledonian Railway heritage line. The radar pioneer Robert Watson-Watt was born in the town.
brecknockshire: The county was bounded by Radnorshire to the north, Herefordshire and Monmouthshire to the east, Monmouthshire and Glamorgan to the south, and Carmarthenshire and Cardiganshire to the west. The Black Mountains rise in the south-east, the Brecon Beacons in the centre, Fforest Fawr in the south-west and Mynydd Epynt in the north; the highest point is Pen y Fan, at 886 metres. The River Wye follows nearly all of the northern boundary, and the Usk flows east through the central valley.

The origins of Brycheiniog are obscure. Legend derives its name from Brychan, a 5th-century ruler for whom there is no early evidence, and the commemorative stones of the period show an elite but no single dominant leader. A kingdom clearly emerged only in the 9th century and was later absorbed by Deheubarth. The Norman lord Bernard de Neufmarché conquered it and founded the Lordship of Brecknock, while the cantref of Buellt, long ruled by its own dynasty, was taken by Philip de Braose around 1095 and overrun by Edward I in November 1282.

When Edward Stafford, 3rd Duke of Buckingham, was executed for treason, his lordship of Brecknock passed to the crown, and Henry VIII joined it with Buellt. The Laws in Wales Act 1535 made the combined lordships, towns and commotes into a county with Brecon as its county town, and in 1542 it was divided into six hundreds: Builth, Crickhowell, Devynnock, Merthyr, Penkelly and Talgarth. The borough and the county each returned one member of parliament.

An elected county council was created in 1889 and met at the Shire Hall in Brecon. The magistrates held that Brecknock was the county's correct name, while the council chose Breconshire by 21 votes to 16, and the two bodies never agreed.

Under the Local Government Act 1972 the bulk of the county passed in 1974 to Powys as the Brecknock District, while Penderyn, Vaynor, Brynmawr and Llanelly went to neighbouring districts. The Brecknockshire Agricultural Society, founded in 1755, is the oldest continuous society of its kind in Great Britain, and Hay-on-Wye, with its bookshops and literary festival, is known as the Town of Books.
brecon-cathedral: The round shape of its churchyard has led to the view that the cathedral stands on the site of an earlier Celtic church, of which no trace remains. The Norman knight Bernard de Neufmarché, who conquered the kingdom of Brycheiniog in 1093, ordered a new church dedicated to St John and gave it to Roger, a monk of Battle Abbey, who founded a priory there as a daughter house of Battle. Its first prior was Walter, another monk from Battle. Bernard endowed the priory with lands, rights and tithes, and after his death it passed to the Earls of Hereford, which brought it greater prosperity.

The church was rebuilt and extended in the Gothic style in about 1215, during the reign of King John, and the smoke-blackened roof of its hall was built between 1237 and 1267. In the Middle Ages it was known as the church of Holy Rood or Holy Cross, after a great golden rood that drew pilgrims until it was destroyed in the Dissolution of the Monasteries. In 1538 the prior was pensioned off and the priory church became the parish church. Some of the surrounding buildings were adapted for secular use, while others, among them the cloisters, were left to decay and later demolished.

By the 19th century the church was in poor repair and only the nave was in use. Some restoration took place in 1836, but major renovation began only in the 1860s, and the tower was strengthened in 1914. After the disestablishment of the Church in Wales in 1920 and the creation of the Diocese of Swansea and Brecon in 1923, the church became its cathedral. Until 1939 the bishop was also dean ex officio; Edward Roberts, Vicar of Brecon, was the first separate dean, from 1939 to 1949.

The cathedral, in Welsh Eglwys Gadeiriol Aberhonddu, is the seat of the Bishop of Swansea and Brecon and a Grade I listed building. Buildings of the cathedral close house a diocesan centre, a heritage centre and exhibition, a shop and a restaurant. The tower holds ten bells rung in the traditional full-circle manner, the tenor weighing 16 cwt. Charles Lumley (1824–1858), awarded the Victoria Cross in the Crimean War, is buried in the churchyard.
breda: Breda lies in the southern Netherlands, equidistant from Rotterdam and Antwerp. The name derives from brede Aa, the wide Aa, and refers to the confluence of the rivers Mark and Aa. As a fortified city it was of strategic military and political significance. Although a direct fiefdom of the Holy Roman Emperor, the city obtained a municipal charter, and its acquisition through marriage by the House of Nassau placed it at the centre of political and social life in the Low Countries.

In the 11th century Breda was a direct fief of the Holy Roman Emperor, and its earliest known lord was Henry of Brunesheim, who held it from 1080 to 1125. The first mention of Breda in the historical record dates from 1125, when Engelbertus van Breda witnessed a document. The city obtained a municipal charter in 1252, which gave it the right to build fortifications, and it built brick walls and Roman-style gates.

Its acquisition by the House of Orange-Nassau made it a residence city, and the presence of the family attracted other nobles, who built palaces in the old quarters. The most impressive, built by the Italian architect Thomas Vincidor de Bologna for the first Dutch prince, was the first Renaissance-style palace north of the Alps. In the 15th century a great church in Brabantine Gothic style was built, with a tower 97 metres high, called the Grote Kerk or the Church of Our Lady. In 1534 Henry III of Nassau-Breda rebuilt the modest medieval fortifications in impressive style.

During the Cromwellian Commonwealth and Protectorate the exiled Charles II of England stayed in Breda for a little over a month, thanks to the nearness of his sister Mary, Princess Royal and Princess of Orange. His Declaration of Breda of 1660 announced his conditions for accepting the crown of England. The Treaty of Breda, signed on 31 July 1667, ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War. Between 1746 and 1748 Breda hosted the Congress of Breda, talks between Britain and France that led to the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

Breda is a city and municipality in the province of North Brabant, the tenth largest in the Netherlands. Historically its economy was mainly industrial and it was a centre of the food and drink industry, with companies such as Hero, Van Melle, De Faam and Kwatta. It also housed the largest brewery in the Netherlands, Oranjeboom. Since 1970 it has become a city of education and students.
breech-loading-rifle: Breech-loading firearms were developed as far back as the early 14th century in Burgundy and other parts of Europe, but they became successful only with advances in precision engineering and machining in the 19th century. Before the mid-19th century most guns were muzzleloaders. Henry VIII owned a breech-loading gun, which he apparently used to shoot birds, and in China a form of breech-loading musket, the Che Dian Chong, was made for the Ming dynasty's arsenals in the second half of the 16th century. Like all early breech-loaders, they suffered from gas leaking at the breech, which was both a limitation and a danger.

Patrick Ferguson, a British Army officer, developed the Ferguson rifle in 1772, a breech-loading flintlock; about two hundred were used at the Battle of Brandywine in the American Revolutionary War before being replaced by the Brown Bess musket. The United States Army adopted the Hall rifle of 1819 in large numbers as its first standard breech-loading rifle.

A breechloader is loaded at the rear of the barrel rather than the muzzle. Its chief advantage is a shorter reload time, since powder and projectile are inserted into the chamber instead of being pushed down the whole barrel. The weapon need not be moved about as much, rifled or fouled barrels do not hinder loading, and a bullet can be made to fit the bore tightly, which adds power, range and accuracy. The main difficulty was sealing the breech. For small arms it was solved by the self-contained metallic cartridge in the mid-19th century, and for larger guns by the interrupted screw.

Jean Samuel Pauly made the first fully self-contained cartridges in Paris in 1808, and in 1842 the Norwegian armed forces adopted the breech-loading Kammerlader as their main infantry firearm. The Dreyse needle gun, adopted by Prussia in the late 1840s, had serious gas leaks but was used with great success in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, and that war and the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871 aroused wide interest in breech-loaders. In New Zealand, Gustavus von Tempsky's Forest Rangers used the Calisher and Terry carbine, which could be loaded while lying down.

At least nineteen types of breech-loader were fielded in the American Civil War, among them the Sharps, the Spencer and the Henry. The improvement of breech-loaders spelled the end of muzzleloaders. France adopted the Chassepot in 1866, with far fewer gas leaks than the Dreyse, and Britain adopted the Martini-Henry in 1871. Single-shot breech-loaders were used through the later 19th century and were slowly replaced by repeating rifles and then self-loading rifles.
breedon-on-the-hill: Breedon on the Hill lies about 5 miles (8 km) north of Ashby-de-la-Zouch, where the parish adjoins the Derbyshire county boundary, and about 2 miles (3 km) south of the Derbyshire town of Melbourne. The parish includes the hamlets of Tonge and Wilson. The village stands by a Carboniferous limestone hill that rises 122 metres (400 ft) above sea level in a generally low-lying landscape, with distant views across several counties. A large part of the hill has been cut away by a quarry, now worked by the Breedon Group for limestone and gravel.

The name is first recorded in Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People of 731, as Briudun and Breadun. It was first the name of the hill: its first element comes from the Brittonic *breɣ, hill, to which Old English speakers, who presumably did not understand the word, added dūn, also meaning hill. The words on the Hill, first attested in 1610, were added later, so that the name says hill three times over.

Excavation of The Bulwarks, the Iron Age hillfort on the summit, in 1946 found occupation from about the 1st century BCE to about the 1st century CE, and a later survey found considerable evidence of occupation in the southern part of the enclosure. Before the monastery the site was a hermitage. Medieval hagiographies record four saints buried at Breedon: Friduricus, donor of the Mercian royal monastery, King Eardwulf of Northumbria, and the little-known Beonna and Cotta. Early in the 12th century the house was refounded as an Augustinian priory.

Breedon Hall was the ancestral home of the Curzon family. The village keeps a circular stone lock-up of the 18th century with an adjoining animal pound, used for detaining local drunks and straying livestock; together they are a Grade II listed building. In 1874 a branch of the Midland Railway was built through the east of the parish, with Tonge and Breedon station at Tonge, and British Rail closed the line in 1980.

The Priory Church of St Mary and St Hardulph still stands inside the hillfort. Besides its Anglo-Saxon sculptures it keeps an ornate family box pew and Renaissance church monuments. The trackbed of the old railway through the parish is now part of National Cycle Route 6, and the parish had 1,029 inhabitants in 450 households at the census of 2011.
bregenz: Bregenz lies on the east and southeast shores of Lake Constance, the third-largest freshwater lake in Central Europe, between Switzerland to the west and Germany to the northwest, with the large forests of the Bregenzerwald to the east. It stands on a plateau falling in a series of terraces to the lake at the foot of the Pfänder mountain. It is a junction of the arterial roads from the Rhine valley to the German Alpine foothills, and cruise ships run on the lake. Vorarlberg, of which it is the capital, is the westernmost state of Austria.

The first settlements date from about 1500 BCE. Strabo mentions the Brigantii as a Celtic sub-tribe of this region of the Alps, and in the 5th century BCE the Celts settled at Brigantion, one of their most heavily fortified places. After a series of battles in 15 BCE the Romans conquered it and it became a Roman camp, and around 50 CE it was made a municipality, Brigantium. It was the seat of the Roman admiralty for Lake Constance and had a theatre. The Alemanni destroyed it in 259/60 and settled the area around 450. Saint Columbanus and Saint Gall worked there as missionaries from 610 to 612.

From 917 the castle was the residence of the Udalrichinger, the ruling dynasty of Vorarlberg, who called themselves Counts of Bregenz; the house died out around 1150. Around 1170 Hugo of Tübingen, called Montfort, founded a town settlement, first documented in 1249. The city was sold to the Habsburgs in 1451 and again in 1523 and stayed under Austrian rule, apart from a brief occupation by Swedish forces under Carl Gustaf Wrangel in the 30 Years' War, until the 19th century. The Swedes destroyed the fortress of Hohenbregenz on the Gebhardsberg in 1647. Bregenz was under Bavarian rule from 1805 to 1814, and since 1726 it has been the main seat of Austrian administration in Vorarlberg.

The harbour on Lake Constance was built from 1842 to 1850, Austrian ship service began in 1884, and railway services have existed since 1872. The Allies bombed the town in 1945, destroying 72 houses, and French troops set up the military government in April and May of that year. The Bregenz Festival, with the Vienna Symphony Orchestra, began in 1946 and is held every summer, with a stage floating on the lake. The upper town keeps remains of its walls, the old town hall of 1662 and Martin's Tower, originally built by the Romans, whose Baroque steeple is the largest bulb-shaped one in Central Europe. The Kunsthaus Bregenz, a modern art museum, was built from 1991 to 1997.
breisgau: The Breisgau is an area in south-west Germany that extends along the Rhine and takes in parts of the Black Forest. It forms part of the state of Baden-Württemberg and centres on the city of Freiburg im Breisgau. It includes the flat country around the Rhine, the foothills of the Black Forest, the western slopes of the southern Black Forest and the Kaiserstuhl hills. In the south it borders the Markgräflerland, in the west the Sundgau in Alsace, in the east the Black Forest and in the north the Ortenau.
The climate is warm, with an average annual temperature of 11 degrees Celsius and average rainfall of 900 mm. The region is known for wine and is used for fruit orchards and grain.

The earliest attested inhabitants were Celts. In Roman times the area belonged to the province of Germania Superior, and after the limes was breached in 260 it was settled by the Alemanni. The name goes back to Carolingian times, when the area was the Breisachgau, the Gau around the town of Breisach. In the mid-9th century it was a march-like territory guarding the frontier with southern Lotharingia and Alsace, and in 859 it was bestowed on Charles the Fat, son of King Louis I.

In the 10th century the Breisgau lay within the Duchy of Swabia and was ruled by the Zähringen family, who founded Freiburg there. When the ducal Zähringen line died out in 1218, the region passed to the House of Baden. From the 13th or 14th century it formed part of Further Austria, the lands in south-west Germany ruled by the Austrian Habsburgs. In 1797 it was ceded to Ercole III d'Este, Duke of Modena and Reggio, as compensation for his losses to the French, and in 1803 it passed to his heir Ferdinand Karl of Austria-Este. By the Treaty of Pressburg of 1805 it was ceded to the Electorate of Baden, which became a grand duchy in 1806.

Freiburg is by far the biggest city of the Breisgau. Other notable towns include Bad Krozingen, Breisach, Emmendingen, Endingen, Kenzingen, Neuenburg, Staufen and Waldkirch. A prominent mountain is the Schauinsland, at 1,284 m. The district of Breisgau-Hochschwarzwald is named after the region and partly consists of it.
bremen: Bremen is the largest city on the River Weser, about 60 kilometres upstream from its mouth into the North Sea at Bremerhaven, and is completely surrounded by the state of Lower Saxony. The oldest part of the Altstadt, the Old Town, is an oval bounded by the Weser and by the Wallgraben, the former moats of the medieval city walls. It begins at the Marktplatz and ends at the Schnoor quarter.

The city traces its origins to a settlement of the early Middle Ages and became the seat of a bishopric in 787. In the High Middle Ages it grew into a trading centre and joined the Hanseatic League in the 13th century. For most of its 1,200-year history Bremen was an independent city within the Holy Roman Empire, governed by merchants and guilds.

To confirm its independence it had to contend, until the Reformation, with the temporal power of the Church, and after the Thirty Years' War with Sweden, which ruled the surrounding Duchy of Bremen-Verden. George I Louis, Elector of Hannover and from 1714 King of Great Britain and Ireland, acquired Bremen-Verden in 1715 and recognised Bremen as a free city in 1720. The city was captured in 1806, annexed by France in 1810 and regained independence in 1815.

In the late 19th century Prussia drew Bremen into the German Empire. With its new anchorage and wharves at Bremerhaven it became the principal port of embarkation for German and central European emigrants to the Americas. The Norddeutscher Lloyd, founded there in 1857, became one of the world's leading shipping companies. After the First World War Bremen was briefly a Soviet republic, and it lost its autonomy under the Hitler regime. Almost two thirds of the city's fabric was destroyed in the Second World War. Its autonomy was restored, and it became one of the founding states of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Bremen is the capital and most populous city of the state of the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen, which consists of the city and Bremerhaven, with about 586,000 inhabitants. Its Town Hall, built between 1405 and 1410 in Gothic style with a Renaissance façade of 1609–12, and the Bremen Roland, a statue of 1404, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in July 2004. St Peter's Cathedral dates from the 13th century and the Liebfrauenkirche, the oldest church in the town, from the 11th. The city is also known for the Brothers Grimm fairy tale of the Town Musicians of Bremen.
bremen-roland: The Bremen Roland was erected in 1404 in the market square of Bremen, facing the cathedral. It was commissioned by the city fathers to replace a wooden statue burnt in 1366 by Prince-Archbishop Albert II. Statues of Roland, the paladin of Charlemagne and hero of the Battle of Roncevaux Pass, stand in numerous cities of the former Holy Roman Empire as emblems of city liberties. The Bremen statue is the oldest surviving example, and from Bremen the symbol of civic freedom spread to other cities. It confronts the church as a representation of city rights opposed to the territorial claims of the prince-archbishop.

Roland is shown as protector of the city, with his sword, known in chivalric legend as Durendal, unsheathed and a shield bearing the two-headed imperial eagle. The figure is 5.47 m tall and stands on a rostrum 60 cm high; a supporting column crowned by a baldachin brings the combined height to 10.21 m. It was carved in limestone from the Elm.

The inscription on the shield reads, in the original, vryheit do ik yu openbar, de karl und mennich vorst vorwar, desser stede ghegheven hat, des dankt gode is min radt. In English: Freedom I do manifest to you, which Karl and many noblemen indeed have given to this place; for this thank God, that is my advice.

According to legend, Bremen will remain free and independent as long as Roland keeps watch over the city. For this reason it is alleged that a second statue is kept hidden in the vaults of the town hall, ready to be installed should the original fall. The statue has been protected by the Monument Protection Act since 1973. In July 2004 it was added, together with the town hall, to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites, in recognition of its outstanding architecture and its symbolism of an important historical figure.

A smaller Roland, the Kleiner Roland, was erected in 1737 in Neustadt by the first Neustädter Bürgerkompanie, after the citizens of Neustadt had had very limited citizenship rights since 1642. It is based on the larger statue of 1404.
bremen-verden: The territory covered a rough triangle between the mouths of the Elbe and the Weser, the Elbe-Weser Triangle, taking in most of the present districts of Cuxhaven, Osterholz, Rotenburg upon Wümme, Stade and Verden and the city of Bremerhaven; the city of Bremen did not belong to it. In the Thirty Years' War Christian IV of Denmark, defeated at the Battle of Lutter am Barenberge on 27 August 1626, retreated into the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen and made Stade his headquarters. The Peace of Westphalia then turned the two prince-bishoprics into the Duchy of Bremen and the Principality of Verden, each still an imperial estate with its own seat in the Diet.

The two never formed a real union: Bremen belonged to the Lower Saxon Circle and Verden to the Lower Rhenish-Westphalian Circle, and they even quarrelled over taxes along their common border. The Swedes set up a General Government at Stade and turned two elective monarchies into a hereditary double monarchy run by a governor bound by Swedish instructions, and curtailed the co-rule of the Estates. Queen Christina, Duchess of Bremen and Verden from 1648, resided in the former Zeven Convent, abolished witch-burning there and tried to annex the Free Imperial City of Bremen.

Denmark-Norway sold the occupied duchies in 1715 to George I, King of Great Britain and Elector of Hanover, in return for his help against Sweden, and the Treaty of Stockholm of 1719 compensated Sweden with 1 million rixdollars. George II added the Land of Hadeln to their administration in 1731 and was enfeoffed with the duchies in 1733, swearing to respect the privileges of the Estates. French troops occupied Stade in June 1803, when the Duchy of Bremen had 180,000 inhabitants; Verden had 20,000 in 1806.

Restored to Hanover in 1813, the duchies were not merged into the Hanoverian state at once, although their status as imperial fiefs had lapsed with the end of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Only in 1823 did a reform of local government unite Bremen-Verden and Hadeln as the High-Bailiwick of Stade, run on uniform modern lines. Its first High-Bailiff was Engelbert Johann von Marschalck, whom the Estates had elected president of the provisional government after the French withdrawal.
bremer-vulkan: Bremer Vulkan AG was formed in 1893 by a group of investors and Bremen merchants, who took over the Johann Lange Shipyard, founded in 1805, which had built the first German steamship, Die Weser, in 1816. Two years later the company bought the Bremer Schiffbaugesellschaft, the former H. F. Ulrichs Shipyard, with its modern facilities. Its first director was the engineer Victor Nawatzki. By 1908 the yard covered about 32 hectares with six slips able to build the largest ships of the day, and it became the leading civilian shipbuilder of the German Empire. Its workforce grew from about 60 to about 3,300 in 1912.

Apart from the two world wars, the company built only civilian ships until the 1980s; in all it built about 1,100. In World War I it built eleven minesweepers and, with the Germaniawerft in Kiel, six submarines for the Imperial German Navy. Between the wars it turned to diesel propulsion, making engines under licence from MAN, and in 1928 launched the tanker C.O. Stillman, then the largest in the world.

In World War II it built 74 Type VII U-boats for the Kriegsmarine. A bombing raid by the US Air Force in March 1943 killed 116 people, yet U-boat production resumed within weeks. Downstream, between Rekum and Farge, the submarine bunker Valentin was built under the company's management; it was never finished, and forced labourers from nearby concentration camps worked and died there. Robert Kabelac, director from 1935 to 1960, kept the yard from being dismantled after the war, and shipbuilding resumed in 1949.

By the end of the 1970s Bremer Vulkan was a world leader in container ship design, and from 1982 it built Bremen-class frigates for the German Navy. Mergers in the 1980s made the Bremer Vulkan Verbund the largest shipbuilding group in Germany, and after reunification it took over the east German yards at Wismar and Stralsund, with about 22,000 workers in all.
