After the bankruptcy the Lloyd Werft in Bremerhaven and the eastern yards survived, and the Lürssen group took over part of the naval division.
bremerhaven: Bremerhaven lies on the east bank of the Weser estuary in northern Germany, and the River Geeste flows through it before reaching the Weser. Neighbouring villages such as Lehe existed by the 12th century, and Geestendorf is mentioned in documents of the ninth century, on small islands in a swampy estuary. In 1381 Bremen established de facto rule over the lower Weser, including Lehe, later called Bremerlehe. Swedish troops of Bremen-Verden captured it in 1653, and Bremen ceded it in the peace of November 1654 that followed the First Bremian War. In 1672 colonists tried unsuccessfully to build a castle there, Carlsburg, to control shipping bound for Bremen.

In 1827 Bremen, under Bürgermeister Johann Smidt, bought the territory at the Weser's mouth from the Kingdom of Hanover. Bremen sought it to keep its share of overseas trade, which silting of the river threatened. Bremerhaven was founded as a second harbour 50 km downstream, and trade with North America and emigration made it grow quickly. In 1848 it became the home port of the German Confederation's navy under Karl Rudolf Brommy. Hanover founded a rival town, Geestemünde, in 1845. In 1924 Geestemünde and Lehe united as Wesermünde, and in 1939 Bremerhaven, apart from its overseas port, was joined to it.

As a North Sea base of the Kriegsmarine, the city lost 79% of its buildings in Allied bombing, and the raid of 18 September 1944 left the inner city largely destroyed. Key parts of the port were deliberately spared. After the war Wesermünde was an enclave run by the United States within the British zone. In 1947 it became part of the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen and took the name Bremerhaven.

Bremerhaven is a city in its own right and also part of the two-city state of Bremen. It remains one of the busiest ports in Germany, with a large container terminal and Europe's largest car transshipment centre. Its centre was largely rebuilt after the war. The German Emigration Center and the German Maritime Museum, designed by Hans Scharoun, record its seafaring past, and the Alfred Wegener Institute, a national research institute for maritime and climate science, is based there.
bremervorde: Bremervörde lies on the Oste river in the north of the district of Rotenburg in Lower Saxony. It stands near the centre of the triangle formed by the Weser and the Elbe, roughly equidistant from Hamburg, Bremen and Cuxhaven. By 1111 the Saxon Duke Lothair of Supplinburg, later king of the Holy Roman Empire, had built the castle called Vörde at a ford of the Oste. The ford was important for the Oxen Way, an ancient trackway connecting Jutland with Westphalia.

Its position between the Elbe and the Weser made the place a matter of conflict for centuries. It came under Henry the Lion and then, in 1219, under the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen, for which it served as capital, with the archbishop's residence and seat of government. The Bremian Estates usually met elsewhere, and the cathedral chapter sat in the city of Bremen. Maurice of Oldenburg ruled the archbishopric from Vörde as administrator from 1345, and in 1362 he gave up after the castle was besieged by troops of Archbishop Albert II's brothers.

Later archbishops and administrators founded a hospital, extended the castle and built a chancery in 1608, which has housed a museum since 1960. The capital role gave the town the name Bremervörde from the mid-17th century. In 1648 the archbishopric became the Duchy of Bremen under the Swedish Crown, which moved the capital to Stade. The Danish-Norwegian king Frederick III bombed his former residence in 1657, and in 1682 the damaged castle and its church, a burial place of many archbishops, were demolished. The duchy passed to the House of Hanover after the Great Northern War and was abolished in 1823.

Bremervörde is a town in Lower Saxony. The Bachmann Museum, housed in the old chancery, covers regional archaeology, geology and history. The town is the end point of the Deutsche Fährstraße, a route connecting places between Bremervörde and Kiel that are linked with the history of ferries and river crossings.
bren-light-machine-gun: At the close of the First World War in 1918 the British Army had two main automatic weapons, the Vickers medium machine gun and the Lewis light machine gun. The Vickers was heavy and needed a supply of water to keep it firing, which tended to confine it to static defence and indirect fire support. The Lewis was lighter but prone to frequent stoppages, and its barrel could not be changed in the field, so sustained firing overheated it until it stopped altogether.

The Bren was a licensed version of the Czechoslovak ZGB 33, itself a modified version of the ZB vz. 26 that British Army officials tested in a firearms competition in the 1930s. Its designer was Václav Holek. The later Bren featured a distinctive top-mounted curved box magazine, a conical flash hider and a quick-change barrel. The first Bren guns were built at the Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield in September 1937.

In the British and Commonwealth armies the Bren was generally issued on a scale of one per rifle section. Each Universal Carrier of an infantry battalion's carrier platoon carried one, and the 66-man Assault Troop of the British Commandos had four on its nominal establishment. Seeking more firepower at section level, the army aimed at one Bren to every four private soldiers. Later it served in the Korean War, the Malayan Emergency, the Mau Mau Uprising and the Indonesia–Malaysia confrontation, where it was preferred to the heavier belt-fed L7 general-purpose machine gun.

Although the gun was well liked, each cost £40, and only 2,300 of the 30,000 Bren guns issued to the British Expeditionary Force came back to the United Kingdom after the defeat of France. The Mark II, approved in September 1940, simplified the sights, bipod and butt and cut the cost by 20 to 25 per cent. The Mark III, standardised in July 1944 and weighing 8.8 kg, was lightened for jungle warfare.

Enfield produced 220,000 Mark I guns. John Inglis and Company of Canada began production in 1940 and by the end of the war had made 186,000 of all variants, among them 43,000 in 7.92×57mm Mauser for the Chinese National Revolutionary Army. In the 1950s many Brens were re-barrelled for the 7.62×51mm NATO cartridge and fielded from 1955 as the L4, which stayed in British service into the 1990s.

The belt-fed L7 replaced the Bren as the section weapon, and in the 1980s the L86 Light Support Weapon supplemented it, leaving the Bren only as a pintle mount on some vehicles. Its last operational deployment with the British Army, on a limited scale, was in the Gulf War of 1991. Indian Ordnance Factories made a version until 2012.
brendan-of-birr: Brendan of Birr is known as Saint Brendan the Elder, to distinguish him from his contemporary and friend Brendan the Navigator of Clonfert. He is said to have come of a noble Munster family. He grew up in an Ireland where the druid tradition was giving way to the new faith and where the study of Latin learning and Christian theology flourished in the monasteries.

Brendan was a pupil at the monastic school of Clonard Abbey, where some of the most important figures of early Irish Christianity studied in the 6th century; the average number of scholars there is said to have been 3,000. The twelve pupils of Finian of Clonard who became known as the Twelve Apostles of Ireland included Brendan, and at Clonard he became the friend and companion of Ciarán of Saigir and Brendan of Clonfert. Finian's penitential, a Latin handbook of penances for sins, set fasts on bread and water and prayer as a means of reform rather than punishment; Brendan left no penitential of his own.

Brendan founded the monastery of Birr in central Ireland in about 540 and served as its abbot. Early Irish writings present him as a man of generous hospitality, known for his holiness and as a sharp judge of character, and he was counted among the chief prophets of Ireland, with the title Prophet of Ireland.

He attended the synod of Meltown, at which Columba was tried for his part in the Battle of Cúl Dreimhne in 561. Brendan spoke on Columba's behalf, and the assembled clerics sentenced Columba to exile rather than excommunication. This friendship led to close ties between Birr and the foundations of Columba.

An adviser of Columba related that Columba saw in a vision the soul of Brendan carried away by angels after his death, and ordered a mass to be said in his honour. The monastery of Birr later produced the MacRegol Gospels, now in the Bodleian Library in Oxford. Brendan is traditionally held to be a saint, with a feast day on 29 November, although he is not listed in the 2004 Martyrologium Romanum, the latest official martyrology of the Catholic Church.
brendan-the-navigator: Brendan was born in Tralee, in County Kerry, among the Altraige, a clan centred on Tralee Bay, to parents called Finnlug and Cara. Tradition places his birth on the north side of the bay. He was baptised at Tubrid, near Ardfert, by Erc of Slane. For five years he was educated and fostered by Saint Íte of Killeedy, called the Brigid of Munster, and at six he was sent to Jarlath's monastery school at Tuam.

He is counted among the Twelve Apostles of Ireland, said to have been taught by Finnian of Clonard. At 26 he was ordained a priest by Erc. His feast day is 16 May for Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox Christians.

Brendan founded a number of monasteries. His first voyage took him to the Aran Islands, where he founded one, and to Hinba in Argyll, where he is said to have met Columcille. The same voyage is said to have taken him on to Wales and Brittany. Between 512 and 530 he built monastic cells at Ardfert and at Shanakeel, at the foot of Mount Brandon.

Later he travelled to Wales and Iona. Returning to Ireland, he founded a monastery at Annaghdown, where he spent the rest of his life, and a convent there for his sister Briga. He also established the bishopric of Ardfert and founded a monastery at Inis-da-druim, now Coney Island, around 550.

Brendan is known chiefly for the Navigatio Sancti Brendani Abbatis, a Latin narrative of the ninth century whose earliest surviving version dates from about 900. In it Brendan hears of the Promised Land of the Saints from Saint Barinthus and sets out in a hide-covered boat with a company of monks. They travel for seven years among islands, including a giant fish, Jasconius, which they mistake for an island, before they are admitted to the Promised Land and return to Ireland.

The Navigatio belongs to the Irish genre of the immram, a tale of seafaring adventures, and shares features with the Voyage of Máel Dúin. More than 100 manuscripts survive across Europe. An Anglo-Norman version, probably made around 1121 by a cleric called Benedeit, is the earliest surviving narrative text of Anglo-Norman literature. There is no reliable evidence that Brendan reached Greenland or the Americas, but medieval maps showed a Saint Brendan's Island in the Atlantic.
brenner-pass: The Brenner Pass, in German Brennerpass and in Italian Passo del Brennero, is a mountain pass that forms the border between Italy and Austria. It is one of the major passes of the Eastern Alps and has the lowest altitude among the Alpine passes of the area. A railway and a motorway cross it, linking Bolzano to the south with Innsbruck to the north. The name appears first in 1328, as ob dem Prenner, meaning above the Prenner, after a nearby farm. Older theories linking it to the Breuni or to the Gaulish chieftain Brennus are now considered unlikely.

The pass was in frequent use in prehistoric times, and the Romans regularised it. It was not the first Roman road across the Alps: the Via Claudia Augusta, completed in 46 to 47, linked Verona with Augusta Vindelicorum, now Augsburg, by way of the Reschen Pass. A Roman road over the Brenner itself did not exist until the 2nd century. The Alamanni crossed the pass southward in 268 and were stopped that November at the Battle of Lake Benacus. The Romans held it until the end of their empire in the 5th century.

In the High Middle Ages the pass lay on the Via Imperii, the imperial road linking the Kingdom of Germany with the Italian March of Verona. From the 12th century the Counts of Tyrol controlled it within the Holy Roman Empire, and Emperor Frederick Barbarossa often used it on his expeditions into Italy. A carriage road was laid out in 1777 at the behest of Empress Maria Theresa. The Brenner Railway, completed in stages from 1853 to 1867, was the first trans-Alpine railway without a major tunnel; Austria lost Lombardy and Venetia to Italy in 1859 and 1866.

After the First World War the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 1919 gave Italy the Trentino and South Tyrol, and the border was set at the pass. Hitler and Mussolini met there on 18 March 1940 to celebrate their Pact of Steel. In 1943 Nazi Germany annexed the pass, and in 1945 the US Army occupied the area before it returned to Italy. Border checks were removed in 1995 and 1997.

The Brenner Autobahn, the European route E45, runs from Innsbruck through the pass and Bolzano and Verona to Modena. The Europabrücke, completed in 1963, carries it over the Sill valley at a height of 180 metres. The Brenner is the only major pass in the area, and a Brenner Base Tunnel is being built to ease road traffic.
brescia: Brescia lies in the northwestern part of the Po Valley, at the foot of the Brescian Prealps and between the rivers Mella and Naviglio, with Lake Iseo to the west and Lake Garda to the east. The centre stands 149 metres above sea level, and the highest point of the municipality is Monte Maddalena at 874 metres. The medieval castle crowns Colle Cidneo, and the old town in the northeast keeps a rectangular plan of streets crossing at right angles, a layout handed down from Roman times.

Several myths tell of the city's founding. One assigns it to Hercules, another to a fugitive from the siege of Troy who called it Altilia, and a third to Cidnus, king of the Ligures, after whom Colle Cidneo is named. Excavations have uncovered a settlement dating to 1,200 BCE, which scholars presume was inhabited by Ligures, while others attribute the foundation to the Etruscans.

In 568 (or 569) the Lombards took Brescia from the Byzantines and made it the capital of one of their semi-independent duchies. Later dukes included Rothari and Rodoald, both future kings, and Alachis II, a fervent anti-Catholic killed in battle at Cornate d'Adda in 688. Desiderius, the last Lombard king, also held the title of Duke of Brescia. From 1490 to 1640 the city was home to a school of makers and players of stringed instruments, and the word violin appears in its documents from 1530. After the Napoleonic era it was annexed in 1815 to the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia.

Brescia is a city of Lombardy and the capital of the Province of Brescia, with a population of about 200,000. In 2011 UNESCO inscribed its monumental area of the Roman forum and the monastic complex of San Salvatore-Santa Giulia on the World Heritage List, as part of Longobards in Italy: Places of Power. Its landmarks include the Renaissance Piazza della Loggia. Metallurgy, machine tools and firearms are central to its economy, and the Mille Miglia car race starts and ends in the city.
bresse: Bresse is a former French province in eastern France, in the regions of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and Bourgogne-Franche-Comté. The name has two senses: the Bresse bourguignonne, in the east of the department of Saône-et-Loire, and the Bresse of the Ain department. The plain runs about 100 kilometres from the Dombes in the south to the Doubs in the north, and about 30 kilometres from the Saône eastwards to the Jura Mountains.

It lies 180 to 240 metres above sea level with few rises, and heaths and coppice alternate with pasture and arable land. Pools and marshes are numerous, especially in the north. Its chief rivers, the Veyle, the Reyssouze and the Seille, are tributaries of the Saône. The soil is a gravelly clay, moderately fertile, and cattle are raised widely. Its inhabitants are called Bressans.

The name comes from the Gallo-Roman name Bricius. In the Middle Ages Bresse belonged to the lords of Bâgé, from whom it passed to the House of Savoy in 1272. Only in the first half of the fifteenth century was it founded as a province with Bourg as its capital. Bâgé had been the principal city, but its position near the French border favoured the rise of Bourg-en-Bresse.

The French king coveted the province, which was flat and hard to defend. The Treaty of Lyon of 1601 ceded it to France, the sovereigns of Savoy giving up Bresse and Bugey in exchange for Château-Dauphin in Piedmont. Together with Bugey it then formed a separate government, later part of the government of Burgundy.

Bourg-en-Bresse and Louhans are the main towns. The region is known for table poultry: about 1,200,000 Bresse chickens a year are reared mainly outdoors by 330 breeders, and they were the first animals to receive an Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée. Bleu de Bresse cheese comes from here. Traditional festival costumes, with a wide plate-shaped hat topped by a black cone for women, are kept by historical societies, and the conscripts' festival for twenty-year-olds, which goes back to the conscription law of 1798, is still held between January and March. Bressan, a Franco-Provençal dialect, was the main spoken language of the countryside until the 1950s. The church of Brou is a tourist site.
brest-belarus: Brest lies at the border with Poland, opposite the Polish town of Terespol, where the Bug and Mukhavets rivers meet. It is one of the oldest cities in Belarus. Its traditional name Berestiy appears in the Primary Chronicle; the name may come from the Slavic root berest, elm, or from the Lithuanian brasta, ford. It was called Brest-Litovsk from the 1600s to 1923 and Brest-on-the-Bug from 1923 to 1939. Its Yiddish name is Brisk, from which comes the term Brisker for followers of the Soloveitchik family of rabbis.

The town was first mentioned in the Primary Chronicle in 1019, when Kievan Rus took the stronghold from the Poles. It was hotly contested between Polish rulers and the princes of Rus, recaptured by Poland in 1020 and unsuccessfully besieged by Yaroslav the Wise in 1022. In 1319 it became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and in 1390 it became the second city of the Grand Duchy after Vilnius, and the first in the lands of present-day Belarus, to receive Magdeburg rights. In 1440 a Sejm held there chose Casimir IV Jagiellon as Grand Duke of Lithuania, and in 1563 the Brest Bible, the second complete Bible translation into Polish, was published in the city.

In 1594 and 1596 councils of Catholic and Orthodox bishops met there, and the 1596 council established the Uniate Church. On 13 January 1660 Russian forces took Brest Castle in a surprise attack and massacred the 1,700 defenders and their families, according to an Austrian observer. Brest was annexed by Russia with the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, and the Brest Fortress was built in the 19th century, for which the Russians demolished the Royal Castle and most of the Old Town. In March 1918 the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was signed in the fortress.

Brest was a Polish city between the wars, and Jews formed 41.3 percent of its population in 1936. After the German attack of 22 June 1941 the fortress held out for six days, and nearly all its Soviet defenders died. The Germans established the Brześć Ghetto in December 1941, and its remaining Jews, about 20,000, were murdered in October 1942; only seven survived. The Red Army retook the city on 28 July 1944, and it was annexed from Poland the following year. Brest is now the administrative centre of Brest Region, and the fortress was recognized by the Soviet Union as a Hero Fortress for its defence in June 1941.
bretislaus-i-duke-of-bohemia: Bretislav was the son of Duke Oldřich and his low-born concubine Božena. As an illegitimate son who could not obtain a desirable wife by conventional means, he kidnapped Judith of Schweinfurt, daughter of Henry of Schweinfurt, Margrave of Nordgau, from a monastery at Schweinfurt, and later married her. He was never punished for it. During his father's reign he took Moravia back from Poland, and about 1030 he invaded Hungary to check its expansion under King Stephen. The partition of Bohemia between Oldřich and his brother Jaromír in 1034 probably drove him across the border, and he returned to take the throne after Jaromír abdicated.

In 1035 Bretislav helped Emperor Conrad II against the Lusatians. In 1039 he invaded Lesser and Greater Poland, captured Poznań, sacked Gniezno and carried off the relics of St. Adalbert, Radim Gaudentius and the Five Brothers. At Hnězden he issued the legal regulations known as Břetislav's Decree, and on the way home he regained part of Silesia, including Wrocław. His aim was an archbishopric in Prague and a large state subject only to the Holy Roman Empire. The destruction of Gniezno led later Polish rulers to move their capital to Kraków.

In 1040 Henry III invaded Bohemia but retreated after losing the battle at Brůdek. The next year he returned and besieged Bretislav in Prague. After a mutiny among his nobles and the betrayal of Bishop Šebíř of Prague, Bretislav gave up all his conquests except Moravia and recognised Henry as his sovereign. In 1042 Henry granted him Silesia as a lien, and in 1047 he arranged a peace with the Poles, who swore not to attack Bohemia again in return for an annual subsidy to Gniezno. Bretislav also issued decrees on the rules of Christianization, banning polygamy and trade on holidays.

In 1054 Bretislav set rules for the succession and introduced agnatic seniority: younger members of the dynasty were to govern fiefs, technically parts of Moravia, only at the duke's discretion. This kept the Czech lands relatively undivided but led to bitter conflicts within the dynasty, until the rise of Bohemia to a kingdom under Ottokar I brought primogeniture. His eldest son Spytihněv succeeded him, while Moravia was divided among Vratislaus, Conrad and Otto, and his youngest son Jaromír became Bishop of Prague. Bretislav died at Chrudim in 1055 while preparing another invasion of Hungary. He was buried in the old St. Vitus Church in Prague, and his tomb now lies in the Chapel of St. Wenceslaus in St. Vitus Cathedral.
bretons: The name Bretons first designated groups of Brittonic speakers who emigrated from south-western Great Britain, particularly Cornwall and Devon, to the west of Armorica, mostly during the Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain. That western part of Armorica was named after them, and it is generally accepted that they also gave the region the Breton language, a sister language to Welsh and Cornish.

In the late fourth century large numbers of British auxiliary troops in the Roman army may have been stationed in Armorica, and the ninth-century Historia Brittonum says the emperor Magnus Maximus settled his troops there. Nennius and Gildas mention a second wave of Britons in the following century, fleeing the Anglo-Saxons and the Scoti, and modern archaeology supports a two-wave migration. Celtic Christian missionaries came with the second wave, among them the seven founder saints of Brittany.

In the Early Middle Ages Brittany was divided into three kingdoms, Domnonée, Cornouaille and Bro Waroc'h, which were eventually incorporated into the Duchy of Brittany. The first two seem to take their names from the homelands of the migrants, Dumnonia (Devon) and Cornwall, and Bro Waroc'h from one of the first known Breton rulers, who dominated the region of Vannes. Rulers of Domnonée such as Conomor claimed overlordship over all Bretons, though there was constant tension between local lords.

Bretons were the most prominent of the non-Norman forces in the Norman conquest of England. Alan Rufus, a cousin and knight in the retinue of William the Conqueror, received large estates in Yorkshire after Hastings and at his death was by far the richest noble in England. The Scottish Clan Stewart and the royal House of Stuart have Breton origins.

Bretons are predominantly Catholic, and religious tradition gives weight to the seven founder saints, whose graves are linked by the pilgrimage called the Tro Breizh. Breton has four main dialects. From 1880 to the mid-twentieth century it was banned from French schools, and the Deixonne Law of 1951 allowed it to be taught a few hours a week. The traditional festival of dance, the fest-noz, dates in its present form from the 1950s.
bretton-woods-system: The planners at Bretton Woods hoped to avoid the economic tension that followed the Treaty of Versailles. Creditors' intransigence over Allied war debts and reparations, together with isolationism, had broken down the international financial system and led to a worldwide depression. The architects of the new order took as their principles no more beggar thy neighbour and control of speculative capital flows.

Delegates from 44 Allied countries met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, from 1 to 22 July 1944 and signed the agreement on the last day. John Maynard Keynes proposed that surplus countries be forced to import from or donate to debtor states, but the United States opposed this. The United States, which controlled two-thirds of the world's gold, insisted that the system rest on both gold and the dollar. Soviet representatives attended but declined to ratify the agreements.

The rules provided for fixed exchange rates and committed members to convertibility and free trade. The institutions became operational in 1945. Western European currencies returned to convertibility at the end of 1958 and the yen in 1964. The Eurodollar market grew from nothing before 1957 to $80 billion in 1972, and capital flows came to dwarf efforts to regulate them. By the mid-1960s Europe and Japan had become economic powers in their own right, and the dollar, burdened by the cost of the Vietnam War, was increasingly overvalued. The London Gold Pool collapsed in March 1968.

On 15 August 1971 the United States ended the convertibility of the dollar to gold. In December 1971 the Group of Ten signed the Smithsonian Agreement, which set the dollar at $38 an ounce, but it did not restore the system. Many fixed currencies, such as the pound sterling, soon floated, and the end of Bretton Woods was formally ratified by the Jamaica Accords in 1976.

The IMF and the World Bank, created by the conference, outlasted the system. Critics argue that reliance on the dollar let the United States run deficits with fewer constraints than other nations and that fixed rates limited the policy of Europe and Japan. Barry Eichengreen attributes its success to low international capital mobility, tight financial regulation and the dominant position of the United States and the dollar.
brexit: The United Kingdom joined the European Communities on 1 January 1973. Its earlier applications of 1963 and 1967 were vetoed by the president of France, Charles de Gaulle, who feared it would be a Trojan Horse for US influence. In the 1975 referendum on continued membership, held under the Labour prime minister Harold Wilson, 67.2 per cent voted to stay, although Euroscepticism existed on both the left and right of British politics throughout membership. Margaret Thatcher warned in her Bruges speech of 1988 against a European super-state exercising a new dominance from Brussels.

By the mid-2010s the growing popularity of the UK Independence Party and pressure from within his own party led the Conservative prime minister David Cameron to promise a referendum, which he did in his Bloomberg speech of 23 January 2013. The Conservative Party manifesto for the general election of 7 May 2015 included it, and the election produced a small and unexpected Conservative majority.

The referendum was held on 23 June 2016. Of those voting, 51.89 per cent chose to leave and 48.11 per cent to remain. All regions of England and Wales except Greater London voted to leave, while Scotland, Northern Ireland and Gibraltar voted to remain. Cameron resigned on 13 July 2016 and Theresa May became prime minister. On 29 March 2017 her government notified the EU under Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union, which starts a two-year negotiation period.

The negotiations were politically challenging and deeply divisive, and led to two snap general elections, in 2017 and 2019. The UK officially left the European Union on 31 January 2020 after Parliament passed a withdrawal deal. An eleven-month transition period followed, during which it continued to take part in many EU institutions, including the single market and customs union. The EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement was signed on 30 December 2020 and applied provisionally from 1 January 2021.

The United Kingdom is the only member state to have withdrawn from the European Union, although four overseas territories of member states had earlier ceased to exercise membership. After Brexit, EU law and the Court of Justice of the European Union no longer have primacy over British law. The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 retains relevant EU law as domestic law, which the UK can amend or repeal. The UK remains bound by treaties with other countries, including many with EU member states and with the EU itself.
brian-boru: Brian Boru was one of the twelve sons of Cennétig mac Lorcáin, king of Dál gCais and of Tuadmumu (Thomond), in what is now County Clare. He was born at Kincora, his father's residence at Killaloe, and as the youngest of twelve he was highly unlikely to inherit. He was sent to study Latin and Irish history at the monastery on the island of Innisfallen, under the monk Maelsuthain Ua Cearbhaill, and was brought home at ten when his father was killed in battle with the Vikings of Limerick. The name Bóruma was given to him after his death; it may refer to a fort north of Killaloe, or to the cattle tribute of a powerful overlord.

In 964 his older brother Mathgamain captured the Rock of Cashel and claimed the kingship of Munster, which the weakened Eóganachta had held. The brothers routed the Norse king Ivar of Limerick at the Battle of Sulcoit in 968. After Mathgamain's death Brian succeeded him as king of Thomond, killed Ivar in 977, and attacked the Vikings who had taken refuge on Scattery Island, slaughtering them and desecrating the church. In 978 he defeated the Eóganacht claimant Máel Muad at the Battle of Belach Lechta, and the kingship of Munster passed to the Dál gCais.

Brian then turned to Leinster and Connacht and came into conflict with the High King, Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill. In the year 1000 he led a combined Munster, Leinster and Dublin army into Meath. After the defeat at Glenmama in 999, Sigtrygg Silkbeard of Dublin had submitted to him. Máel Sechnaill acknowledged Brian as High King at Athlone in 1002.

In his sixties Brian spent about a decade accepting the submission of the lesser kingdoms, including two full circuits of the island in 1005 and 1006. Ulster, the one province that did not recognise him, took ten years of campaigning to subdue. In 1012 Máel Mórda mac Murchada of Leinster rebelled, and in 1013 Flaithbertach Ua Néill raided the Midlands.

In 1014 Brian's army met the forces of Leinster and Dublin at the Battle of Clontarf. Accounts of his death differ: some say he died in single combat, others that he was too old to fight. According to the Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh he was killed by fleeing Viking mercenaries while kneeling on a cushion away from the fighting. Historians debate whether Clontarf ended a war between the Irish and the Vikings or was an Irish civil war with Vikings on both sides. His descendants were the Uí Briain, or O'Briens.
brics: The idea of a multipolar group of this kind goes back to the Russian foreign minister Yevgeny Primakov, who put it forward in 1998 and repeated it in New Delhi. Two forums that predated the grouping, RIC (Russia, India, China) and IBSA (India, Brazil, South Africa), played an important part in its creation. The term BRIC itself was coined by the British economist Jim O'Neill and taken up by his employer Goldman Sachs in 2001 to designate a group of emerging markets. The first summit in 2009 brought together Brazil, Russia, India and China, who formed an informal diplomatic group that would meet each year at formal summits and coordinate multilateral policies.

South Africa began efforts to join in 2010. It became a member on 24 December 2010 after being formally invited by China, and the group was renamed BRICS. South Africa's president Jacob Zuma took part as a full member at the third summit, at Sanya in China in 2011. In June 2012 the member states pledged 75 billion dollars to boost the lending power of the International Monetary Fund, on condition of voting reforms. At the fifth summit in Durban in March 2013 they agreed to create a financial institution to work beside the IMF and the World Bank, which were dominated by the West.

Later enlargement brought in Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia, the first Southeast Asian member. Leaders meet once a year in a rotating presidency, and the group has neither a permanent seat nor a secretariat.

The financial structure rests on the New Development Bank and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement, signed into a treaty in 2014 and active in 2015. The bank, operated by the five original members and also called the BRICS Development Bank, lends mainly for infrastructure and had a starting capital of 50 billion dollars, to which Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa each contributed 10 billion. The Contingent Reserve Arrangement is a framework for protecting members against global pressures on liquidity and on their currencies. Since 2011 the statistical offices of the member countries have produced an annual joint statistical publication.
bridei-son-of-beli: Bridei was a son of Beli, king of the British kingdom of Altclut, whose death the Annales Cambriae place in 627, so Bridei was born no later than 628; a verse attributed to Adomnán calls him son of the king of Dumbarton. Nennius' Historia Brittonum makes him a maternal first cousin of King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, which suggests his mother was a daughter of King Edwin of Deira. His grandfather Neithon son of Guipno may have been the Pictish king recorded as Nechtan grandson of Uerb.

He was probably brought up at the Northumbrian court, possibly taken there as a hostage by King Oswiu after his half-brother Eugein of Alt Clut killed the Dál Riatan king Domnall Brecc in 643. From 653 the Picts were under Northumbrian overlordship. In 671 Drest son of Donuel, who had led a rising against it, was expelled, and Bridei's accession was probably engineered by Ecgfrith together with Pictish supporters.

Early in his reign Bridei intervened in Dál Riata: he may have been involved in the killing of its king Domangart mac Domnaill in 673, and the Annals of Ulster record that many Picts drowned in Loch Awe in 676. After Ecgfrith's defeat by Æthelred of Mercia at the Battle of the Trent in 679 he built a confederation of Pictish territories that owed him allegiance and tribute, closely modelled on Northumbrian overlordship, through campaigns that reached Dunbeath in Caithness and Dunadd in mid Argyll.

According to Bede, Ecgfrith invaded because Bridei stopped paying tribute. On Saturday 20 May 685 the Northumbrians, lured into what Bede called the narrow passes of inaccessible mountains, were destroyed at Dun Nechtain. The site has generally been placed at Dunnichen in Angus, though since 2006 Dunachton in Badenoch has been proposed. Angles in Pictish lands fled or were killed or enslaved, and Trumwine, the Northumbrian bishop of the Picts at Abercorn, withdrew to Whitby.

Bridei was buried on Iona, and a lament for him is attributed to Adomnán, abbot of Iona. He is the first king called rex Fortrenn, king of Fortriu, in contemporary sources, and his reign opened what historians call the Verturian hegemony, in which Fortriu grew into the overkingdom of the Picts. After his victory the Picts appear in documents as a single gens rather than plural gentes. The later kings Bridei and Naiton, sons of Der-Ilei, were probably his grandsons.
bridei-son-of-maelchon: Bridei's name appears in several forms, among them Brude son of Melcho and, in Irish sources, Bruide son of Maelchú. Little is known of his origins and the sources about him are vague or contradictory. The writer John Morris, in The Age of Arthur, made him a son of Maelgwn Gwynedd, king of north Wales, but historians regard that book as unreliable. An entry in the Annals of Ulster reporting his death under the year 505 is presumed to be an error.

He first appears in the Irish annals between 558 and 560, when the Annals of Ulster report a migration before King Bruide son of Máelchú. The Ulster annalist does not say who fled, but the later Annals of Tigernach speak of the flight of the Scots before him in 558, and one version of the Annals of Ulster links this with the death of Gabrán mac Domangairt. The Annals of Ulster also report expeditions to Orkney in 580 and 581, and Adomnán mentions an under-king of Orkney at Bridei's court.

Bridei was not the only king of the Picts of his day: the Annals of Ulster record the death of Galam Cennalath, king of the Picts, in 580. Adomnán's Life of Saint Columba treats him as one of the chief kings in Scotland but does not say whether he was already a Christian or whether Columba converted him. Finds at Portmahomack, showing a monastic community there from around 550, lend some support to the view that he was Christian at least in name.

Craig Phadrig, west of Inverness above the Beauly Firth, has been suggested as the steep rock on which, in Adomnán's account, his court stood, but its ramparts were in poor repair in Bridei's time, so it is unlikely to have been a royal fortress then. His kingdom may have corresponded to the later Fortriu.

Bridei died in the 580s, perhaps in battle against Pictish rivals in Circinn, an area thought to correspond to the Mearns. The king lists of the Pictish Chronicle agree that he was followed by Gartnait son of Domelch. Juliet Marillier's trilogy The Bridei Chronicles mixes history, fiction and informed guesswork in telling his rise and rule.
bridgetown: Bridgetown lies at the head of Carlisle Bay on the south-west coast of Barbados, in the parish of Saint Michael. At its centre is the Careenage, a shallow inlet, also called the Constitution River, that divides the city in two and serves as a harbour for small craft. Its centre was originally a swamp, which was drained and filled for building. The main street is Broad Street, which runs past the Parliament Buildings and is the centre of the shopping area.

The island was uninhabited when the English arrived. The settlers found a primitive bridge over the swamp of the Careenage, thought to have been built by the Tainos, and called the place Indian Bridge. The present site was settled on 5 July 1628 by Charles Wolverstone with 64 settlers, sent by a group of London merchants who held a lease of 10,000 acres from James Hay, Earl of Carlisle. After a new bridge was built over the Careenage in 1654 the area was known as the Town of Saint Michael, and later as Bridgetown, after Sir Tobias Bridge.

Between 1627 and 1807 an estimated 387,000 enslaved Africans were sent to Barbados. In 1824 Barbados became the seat of the Anglican Diocese of Barbados and the Leeward Islands, and St Michael's Parish Church became a cathedral; royal letters patent of 1842 then named the place the City of Bridgetown. From 1800 until 1885 it was the seat of government of the Windward Islands, when the resident governor of Barbados was also colonial head of that group. The seat then moved to St. George's on Grenada. A Local Government Act of 1958 gave the city its own mayor, aldermen and councillors, but the councils were dissolved in April 1967 and the city has since been administered through the national parliament.

Bridgetown is the capital and largest city of Barbados, with a metropolitan population of roughly 110,000. Its deep-water harbour handles cargo and cruise ships and acts as a transhipment hub for the eastern Caribbean. The Parliament Buildings house what is described as the third oldest continuous parliament in the Commonwealth. The Garrison area includes George Washington House, where Washington stayed on his only journey outside what is now the United States. Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO on 25 June 2011.
bridgewater-canal: Francis Egerton, 3rd Duke of Bridgewater, sent his coal by the Mersey and Irwell Navigation and by packhorse, both slow and costly, and his mines at Worsley flooded because the seam lay beneath permeable sandstone. Having seen the Canal du Midi in France and the building of the Sankey Canal, he planned an underground canal at Worsley joined to a surface canal to Salford, which would drain the mines and feed the surface canal with water. One horse could pull a boat of 30 long tons, more than ten times a cart's load. The duke and his estate manager John Gilbert drew the plan, and an act of Parliament followed in 1759.

The canal required an aqueduct over the River Irwell and a tunnel at Worsley. Inside the mines, 46 miles of underground canal on four levels, linked by inclined planes, were dug, reached from Worsley Delph by narrow boats called starvationers.

Brindley surveyed an extension from Longford Bridge to the Mersey at Runcorn, approved on 24 March 1762 despite objections from the Mersey and Irwell Navigation Company. A flight of ten locks lowered the canal almost 90 feet to the river, which it reached on 1 January 1773. In 1795 a fifth act allowed a branch from Worsley to Leigh, later linked to the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, and in 1804 the canal was joined to the Rochdale Canal at Castlefield.

In 1791 the Worsley mines produced 100,282 long tons of coal, of which 60,461 were sold down the canal, and passengers brought in £3,781. Horses towed the barges until the middle of the 19th century, when steam boats replaced them after an epidemic among the horses. Regular commercial freight ended in 1975.

The canal is described as the first great achievement of the canal age, although the Sankey Canal opened earlier, and its success helped set off the Canal Mania. After the duke's death on 8 March 1803 trustees ran it. Railway interests bought it in 1872 for £1,120,000, and in 1885 the Manchester Ship Canal Company paid £1,710,000, replacing Barton Aqueduct with the Barton Swing Aqueduct. One of the few canals in Britain never nationalised, it remains privately owned and has carried pleasure craft since 1952.
bridgnorth: Bridgnorth is named after a bridge over the River Severn, built further north than an earlier bridge at Quatford. The town lies in the Severn Valley and is divided into High Town on the west bank, standing on a promontory called Castle Hill, and Low Town on the east bank. High Town lies at 65 to 68 metres above sea level and Low Town at about 32 metres.

The earliest reference is in 895, when the Danes made a camp at Cwatbridge. In 912 Æthelflæd built a mound on the west bank of the Severn, or possibly on the site of the later castle, as part of an offensive against the Danes. In 1101 Robert of Bellême, 3rd Earl of Shrewsbury, moved from Quatford and built a castle and a church on the site of the present town, to defend against attacks from Wales. The town became a royal borough on his attainder in 1102. Its timber walls of 1216 to 1223 were later rebuilt in stone, and the town was burnt by Roger Mortimer in 1322.

King John freed the burgesses from toll throughout England except London in 1215. The burgesses sent two members to parliament from 1295 until 1867. In the Civil War Bridgnorth was one of the main Royalist strongholds of the Midlands, and in 1646 Cromwell took it after a three-week siege and ordered the castle demolished. In 1808 the Hazledine ironworks in Low Town built Richard Trevithick's locomotive Catch Me Who Can.

Bridgnorth is a market town and civil parish in Shropshire, with 12,079 people at the 2011 census. The castle ruins lean at an angle of 15 degrees because of damage in the Civil War. Of the five town gates one survives, the Northgate, which houses the museum. The Cliff Railway, opened on 7 July 1892, links High Town and Low Town and is the only functional inland funicular railway in England. Bishop Percy's House, built in 1580, survived the great fire of 1646 and was the birthplace of Thomas Percy, author of Reliques of Ancient English Poetry.
brielle: Brielle, called Den Briel in Dutch and Brill in English, is a town and historic seaport in the western Netherlands, in the province of South Holland. It lies on the north side of the island of Voorne-Putten, at the mouth of the New Maas. Its name is derived from the Celtic word brogilo, meaning closed area or hunting grounds. The oldest writings indicate that the present town is the new Brielle, and that Den ouden Briel, or Old Brill, must have stood somewhere else on the island.

Brielle is a very old fortified town, which grew into a town of prestige in the 14th century. In 1330 Gerard van Voorne, independent Lord of Voorne and Viscount of Zeeland, granted it town rights. These gave it governmental and jurisdictional powers and trading rights, such as the right to trade fish and collect port taxes. It was for a long time the seat of the Lords of Voorne, until the fiefdom was added to the County of Holland in 1371. The town had its own harbour and traded with the countries around the Baltic Sea, and even had a trading colony in Sweden.

In the Eighty Years' War the Capture of Brielle on 1 April 1572 by the Protestant Watergeuzen marked a turning point. Many towns in Holland then began to support William of Orange against the Duke of Alba, who had been sent to pacify the Netherlands. The event is still marked each 1 April and on the night before, known as Chalk Night. After the capture the rebels tortured and murdered the Catholic Martyrs of Gorkum, and Brielle has since been a place of pilgrimage.

In August 1585 Brielle was one of three Dutch towns that became English possessions under the Treaty of Nonsuch, when Queen Elizabeth I received them as security for payment for 5,000 soldiers led by the Earl of Leicester. Its first English governor was Thomas Cecil, 1st Earl of Exeter, and in 1617 the towns returned to the Netherlands.

The former municipality covered 31.14 square kilometres and had 17,439 inhabitants in 2021. On 1 January 2023 it merged with Hellevoetsluis and Westvoorne into the new municipality of Voorne aan Zee. Brielle, New Jersey was named after the town by the Dutch colonists of New Netherland. Maarten Tromp, the Dutch admiral, was born there in 1598.
brig-switzerland: Brig, called Brigue in French and Briga in Italian, lies in the canton of Valais. Its name comes from the Celtic briga, meaning a hill fortress or height, and later a castle. The town is a crossroads of the Alpine routes: the Simplon line runs through it from Lausanne and Sion towards Domodossola and Milan, the Lötschberg line brings trains from Berne and Spiez, and the Glacier Express and the Matterhorn-Gotthard Bahn link it with Zermatt, Andermatt and Saint-Moritz. Main road 9 crosses the Simplon Pass to Italy, and cars can be loaded on trains through the Simplon tunnel.

Brig is first mentioned in 1215 but was not recognised as a town until the 17th century. Its growth then owed much to Kaspar Jodok von Stockalper (1609–1691), a merchant nicknamed the King of Simplon, whose castle still stands in the town. The thermal springs were already known in the Middle Ages; buried by a landslide in the 15th century, they were cleared in 1471 and joined to the public baths. The Jesuit Collège du Saint-Esprit, built between 1673 and 1688, is an example of Baroque architecture, and the Gamsen town wall dates from the 14th century.

On 25 January 1913 Juan Bielovucic took off from Brig on a 28-minute monoplane flight across the Alps to Domodossola, and a monument to the aviation pioneer Jorge Chávez Dartnell stands on the Place Saint-Sebastien. On 24 September 1993 the town was partly devastated by a flood when the Saltina River overflowed. The general Pierre Emmanuel Jacques de Rivaz, who served in the armies of the French Republic, and the film-maker Henri Colpi were born in Brig.

Brig is now part of the municipality of Brig-Glis. The community grew from 468 inhabitants in 1798 and 2,182 in 1900 to 11,590 in 2000, the later figures including Glis and Brigerbad. It lies close to the resorts of Belalp, Saas-Fee, Zermatt and Fiesch, and the thermal baths at Brigerbad draw many visitors.
brigham-young: Brigham Young was born on 1 June 1801 in Whitingham, Vermont, the ninth child of John Young, a farmer, and Abigail Howe. The family moved to Chenango County in upstate New York when he was three. He had little formal education, though his mother taught him to read and write. In 1830 his brother Phineas gave him a copy of the Book of Mormon, and in 1831 missionaries of the Latter Day Saint movement came to preach in Mendon, where he was drawn by their practice of spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues. On 14 February 1835 he was ordained a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.

Young moved to Missouri in 1838, the year Governor Lilburn Boggs signed the Mormon Extermination Order, and organised the migration of the Latter Day Saints to Illinois. In 1844, while he was travelling to gain support for Joseph Smith's presidential campaign, Smith was killed by a mob, which began a succession crisis. After negotiating a ceasefire, Young was unanimously elected the church's second president in 1847. He led his followers west from Nauvoo and arrived in the Salt Lake Valley on 24 July 1847, a date now observed in Utah as Pioneer Day.

He founded Salt Lake City, and President Millard Fillmore appointed him the first governor of Utah Territory and superintendent of Indian affairs. He directed settlements across a wide area of the West, issued a selective extermination order against male Timpanogos, and later made peace with Native Americans. As governor he allowed polygamy and supported slavery and its expansion into Utah, and he formalised the prohibition of black men from the priesthood.

After President James Buchanan appointed a new governor, Young declared martial law and reactivated the Nauvoo Legion, which began the Utah War. During it the Utah Territorial Militia carried out attacks that killed at least 120 members of the Baker-Fancher wagon train, the Mountain Meadows Massacre. The war ended in 1858 when Young surrendered, agreeing to resign as governor and let federal troops enter the territory in return for a pardon.

Young died in Salt Lake City on 29 August 1877, probably of peritonitis from a ruptured appendix. He had at least fifty-six wives and fifty-seven children. His teachings fill the nineteen volumes of the Journal of Discourses, and Rodman W. Paul credited him with directing the founding of 350 towns between 1847 and 1877.
brihadaranyaka-upanishad: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad is one of the Principal Upanishads, associated with the Shukla Yajurveda. It is estimated to have been composed about the 7th to 6th century BCE, though its chronology, like that of other Upanishads, is uncertain and contested. Patrick Olivelle remarks that any dating of the early Upanishads closer than a few centuries is as stable as a house of cards. The text is an anthology of material that must have existed independently before it was compiled.

Its name means great wilderness or forest, and suggests a link to the Aranyaka texts. It is credited to the sage Yajnavalkya but was likely refined by many Vedic scholars. It forms the fourteenth kanda of the Shatapatha Brahmana and survives in two recensions, the Madhyandina and the Kanva, in medieval palm-leaf manuscripts, the oldest dating to the 12th century CE.

The text has six chapters in three sections. It opens with a Vedic theory of creation in which Prajapati makes the universe from nothingness as a sacrifice to himself. The second chapter begins as a conversation between Ajatashatru and Balaki Gargya about dreams and presents the Self as beyond description, neti, neti, not this, not this. The third chapter is a dialogue among ten sages at the court of King Janaka in Mithila, with Yajnavalkya in the leading role; Paul Deussen compared his presentation to that of Socrates in Plato's dialogues.

The fourth chapter is a dialogue between Janaka and Yajnavalkya on the Self. The last two chapters are a supplement that Deussen thought was written later. The text includes one of the earliest formulations of karma, holding that a person becomes good by good action and bad by bad action, and it describes the self leaving one body for another as a caterpillar moves onto a new blade of grass. It recommends three virtues: self-restraint, charity and compassion for all life.

The Upanishad has been an important work in Vedanta and has drawn commentaries from Adi Shankara and Madhvacharya, among others. Sub-schools of Vedanta, including Advaita, Dvaita and Vishistadvaita, have read its passages differently. Shankara read neti, neti as a negation of all empirical attributes, while Ramanuja read it as an acknowledgment of the limits of human language in describing Brahman. The prayer from untruth to truth, from darkness to light, from death to immortality, comes from its verse 1.3.28.
brihadratha-maurya: Brihadratha Maurya was the ninth and last emperor of the Mauryan Empire. According to the Puranas he succeeded his father Shatadhanvan. His territories were centred on the capital Pataliputra and had shrunk considerably since the time of Ashoka.

Before his death the northwest was invaded. Between 190 and 186 BCE the Greco-Bactrian king Demetrius, also called Dharmamita, entered the region, which covers parts of modern Afghanistan and Pakistan, and occupied it. The Mauryans had diplomatic alliances with the Greeks, and the Greco-Bactrians may have regarded them as allies. The Sri Lankan Paramparapustaka chronicle states that Brihadratha married Demetrius' daughter Berenice, called Suvarnnaksi in Pali. Demetrius established his rule in the Kabul Valley and parts of the Punjab, but soon had to return to Bactria to fight a fierce battle, probably against Eucratides I.

A further Greek invasion reaching Pataliputra is hypothesised from the Yuga Purana, which describes the Yavanas, the Indo-Greeks, approaching Saketa and Mathura and reaching the city, where its mud walls are cast down and all the realms fall into disorder.

Brihadratha was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga, who took the throne and founded the Shunga Empire. The Harshacharita of Bāṇabhaṭṭa says that Pushyamitra paraded the entire Mauryan army before the emperor on the pretext of showing him its strength, and then killed his master in front of the assembled troops. His death ended the Maurya dynasty.
brihatkatha: The date of the work is uncertain. Gunadhya may have flourished under a Satavahana king of Pratishthana, the modern Paithan in Maharashtra; according to D. C. Sircar he probably lived between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE. Another account, in the Nepala Mahatmya of the Skanda Purana, makes him a native of Mathura and court poet of King Madana of Ujjain, a tradition Sircar calls less authentic. Paishachi, the language he used, is a little-known Prakrit, described as the speech of the common people of the border regions of northwest India.

The earliest surviving reference seems to be that of Subandhu in his Vasavadatta, and Banabhatta refers to the work in the Harshacharita and the Kadambari. Dandin, in the Kavyadarsha, calls it marvellous and says it was composed in the vernacular of the bhutas, though his information appears to be second-hand. A Cambodian inscription of about 875 names Gunadhya, and the Kannada Kavirajamarga of about 850 mentions a Sanskrit version, now lost, by Durvinita. A romantic work by Gunadhya can safely be assumed to have existed before 600 CE.

The adaptations differ too much for the original to be reconstructed whole, but what they share allows strong inferences. The life of Udayana of Kaushambi served as a prelude: his upbringing in a hermitage after a monstrous bird carried off his pregnant mother, his captivity under Pradyota, king of Ujjayini, his elopement with Pradyota's daughter Vasavadatta, and his second marriage to Padmavati, arranged by ministers who made him believe Vasavadatta dead. The central story was that of their son Naravahanadatta, born as a boon of Kubera and fated to become emperor of the Vidyadharas. Kshemendra's version is in eighteen books called lambakas, as the original is thought to have been.

Besides the two Kashmiri versions, the story is known from the Sanskrit Brihatkathashlokasamgraha of Budhasvamin, of which the complete text has not been found, and from the Perunkatai and the Vasudevahimdi in vernacular languages. Dandin states that the original was in prose, not in the verse of the Kashmiri recensions. Scholars compare Gunadhya with Vyasa and Valmiki, and the disappearance of his text is counted a very great loss to Indian literature.
brimstone-hill-fortress: The fortifications stand on Brimstone Hill, a very steeply sloping hill close to the sea on the western, Caribbean coast of St Kitts. They were designed by British military engineers and built and maintained by enslaved Africans. Cannon were first mounted on the hill in 1689, during the Nine Years' War, when Jean-Baptiste du Casse used them to capture the English Fort Charles. A year later the English under Sir Christopher Codrington used the same tactic to recapture it. From then on the English used the hill as a fortress, mounting 24-pound cannon and taking advantage of its height of 972 feet.

Lightning destroyed the gunpowder magazine in 1711 and again in 1731, and by 1736 the fort had 49 guns. From 1795, 40 members of the St Christopher Corps of Embodied Slaves served at the fort, armed with pikes and cutlasses. By 1780 it was considered impregnable. On 11 January 1782 the French under Admiral Comte François Joseph Paul de Grasse and François Claude Amour, marquis de Bouillé, laid siege to it. During the siege the neighbouring island of Nevis surrendered, and guns from Fort Charles and other small forts there were brought to St Kitts for use against the hill. British Admiral Hood could not dislodge de Grasse, and after a month the heavily outnumbered and cut-off garrison surrendered.

The Treaty of Paris of 1783 restored St Kitts, Brimstone Hill and Nevis to British rule. The British then strengthened the fortifications, and the hill never again fell to an enemy. The French navy failed to recapture it in 1806, though Admiral Édouard Thomas Burgues de Missiessy had blown up the powder magazine in a raid in 1805.

Local militias throughout the Caribbean were disbanded in 1838 after the Napoleonic Wars. The British abandoned the fort in 1853 and disbanded its militia in 1854, and the structures gradually decayed through vandalism and natural processes. Stabilisation and restoration began in the early 1900s. In 1973 Prince Charles reopened the first fully restored area, the Prince of Wales Bastion. Queen Elizabeth II unveiled a plaque naming it a national park in 1985, legislation made it one in 1987, and UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1999. Visitors can see the Fort George Citadel and its museum, the Western and Eastern Place of Arms and the Magazine Bastion that the French breached in 1782.
brindisi: Brindisi lies on a natural harbour that penetrates deeply into the Adriatic coast of Apulia. The name comes from the Latin Brundisium, which came through the Greek Brentesion from the Messapic Brention, meaning head of a stag, probably a reference to the shape of the harbour, which resembles a head or antlers. Within the arms of the outer harbour lie the Pedagne islands, a tiny archipelago. The surrounding municipality belongs to the Brindisi Plain, a flat and heavily farmed country of limestone and marine sand, and the climate is Mediterranean, with hot dry summers and mild winters.

Several traditions concern the city's founders. One claims that the hero Diomedes founded it, and the geographer Strabo says it was colonized from Knossos in Crete. It became a Roman colony in 244 BCE and expanded greatly; according to Pliny the Elder it was one of the most important Italian cities. The Ostrogoths conquered it and the Byzantine Empire reconquered it in the 6th century, by which time Procopius describes a small city without defensive walls. In 674 the Lombards under Romuald I of Benevento destroyed it, though so fine a harbour meant that it was soon rebuilt, and pirates stormed a Saracen settlement near the city in 836.

The port was abandoned for several centuries and the town shrank to a smaller area around the temple of San Leucio. Revival came under Byzantine domination in the 11th century and above all under the Normans and the Swabians in the 12th and 13th centuries, when Brindisi became a prime port for the Crusades. Emperor Frederick II built the Castello Svevo, to which the Crown of Aragon later added four towers. Joachim Murat turned the castle into a prison in 1813. The reopening of the Pigott channel in 1775 and the opening of the Suez Canal at the end of the 19th century renewed traffic with the East. From September 1943 to February 1944 Brindisi was the provisional government seat of the Kingdom of Italy.

Brindisi is the capital of its province and remains a major port for trade with the Balkan Peninsula, Greece and the Middle East, as well as a ferry port. Its industries include chemical works, aerospace, agriculture and the generation of electricity. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Brindisi-Ostuni; the diocese was erected in the 4th century and its first bishop was St. Leucio of Alexandria. In the 20th century many people emigrated, first to the Americas around the First World War and then to northern Europe and northern Italy after the Second.
brisbane: Brisbane lies in the south-east corner of Queensland, centred on the Brisbane River, whose mouth is about 15 km from the central business district at Moreton Bay. The city spreads across the hilly floodplain of the river valley between the Pacific Ocean and the Taylor and D'Aguilar ranges. It takes its name from the river, which was named for Sir Thomas Brisbane, governor of New South Wales from 1821 to 1825. The climate is humid subtropical, with hot, wet summers and mild, drier winters. Most central streets are named after members of the House of Hanover, and Queen Street, named for Queen Victoria, is the traditional main street.

The Brisbane region has been inhabited for more than 22,000 years by the Yagara (Yuggera), Turrbal and Quandamooka peoples. The river, known as Maiwar, formed the heart of cultural, economic and ceremonial life, and the central city peninsula was traditionally known as Meeanjin. Matthew Flinders charted parts of Moreton Bay in 1799, and John Oxley found the river in 1823 with the help of castaways and recommended the area for a penal settlement. The penal station, first set up at Redcliffe, moved to North Quay in May 1825. Under Captain Patrick Logan it gained a reputation as one of the harshest in New South Wales, and it saw recurrent conflict with neighbouring Indigenous peoples. It was closed in 1842, opening the district to free colonisation.

German Lutherans founded the first free settlement, Zion Hill at Nundah, in 1838, and in 1859 Brisbane was chosen as capital when Queensland separated from New South Wales. In the early 20th century it saw labour unrest, including the 1912 Brisbane general strike. The creation of the City of Brisbane in 1925, by merging twenty smaller local government areas, formed Australia's largest municipal authority. During the Second World War the Allied command in the South West Pacific was based in the city, together with the headquarters of General Douglas MacArthur.

Brisbane is the capital of Queensland and the third most populous city in Australia, with about 2.8 million people in the metropolitan area. Its surviving early buildings include the Commissariat Store on William Street, built by convict labour in 1828, and the Old Windmill in Wickham Park, the oldest surviving building in the city. City Hall opened in 1930 and the Story Bridge in 1940. The city hosted the 1982 Commonwealth Games and World Expo 88, and has been chosen to host the 2032 Summer Olympics. Its surrounding region includes Moreton Bay and the Gondwana Rainforests, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
bristol: Bristol lies on the River Avon, which cuts through a limestone area running from the Mendip Hills to the Cotswolds and gives the city its hilly landscape. To the west the Avon passes through the Avon Gorge, formed largely by glacial meltwater after the last ice age. The name comes from the Old English Brycgstow, meaning the assembly place by the bridge or the site of the bridge, presumably a crossing of the Avon. The final L is a later addition that first appears in the 12th century.

A Roman port, Portus Abonae, existed at what is now Sea Mills. Bristol was founded by 1000, and by about 1020 it was a trading centre with a mint producing silver pennies bearing its name. By 1067 it was a well-fortified burh, and that year the townsmen beat back a raiding party from Ireland led by three sons of Harold Godwinson. Its Norman castle was one of the strongest in southern England. The town received a royal charter in 1155 and became a county corporate in 1373, having until then been divided between Gloucestershire and Somerset.

In the 15th century Bristol was the second most important port in the country, trading with Ireland, Iceland and Gascony. John Cabot made landfall in North America in 1497, and a voyage of 1499 led by the Bristol merchant William Weston was the first expedition commanded by an Englishman to North America. Between 1700 and 1807 more than 2,000 slave ships carried an estimated 500,000 people from Africa to slavery in the Americas. In the 19th century Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed the Great Western Railway to London, the SS Great Britain and the Clifton Suspension Bridge. Competition from Liverpool, war with France from 1793 and the abolition of the slave trade in 1807 contributed to Bristol's failure to keep pace with northern manufacturing centres.

Bristol is a city and ceremonial county in South West England and the most populous city in its region. The Port of Bristol has moved from the harbour in the city centre downstream, and the old docks have been redeveloped as cultural and heritage centres. The city has two universities, the University of Bristol and the University of the West of England, and 51 Grade I listed buildings, among them the Church of St James, which dates to the 12th century. A dialect known as Bristolian is spoken by longtime residents.
britannia-inferior: Under Commodus the defences of Britain's northern border fell into neglect, and in the unrest after his death the legions in Britain were drawn into the struggles on the continent. Septimius Severus, emperor from 193, took a special interest in refortifying the frontier and in 208 moved to Eboracum to oversee campaigns against the northern tribes. Clodius Albinus, governor in Londinium, had recently made a bid for the throne, and removing the legions on Hadrian's Wall from the governors in Londinium was meant to reduce their power, as Severus had done in Syria.

No inscription records the division before Severus's death in 211, so it was probably formalised by Caracalla, perhaps around 214. Caracalla also moved the province's southern border northwards, giving northern Wales and the country around Chester to Britannia Superior. Lower Britain, as its name means, took in most of northern England and the Midlands and was governed by a praetorian legate commanding the single legion VI Victrix at Eboracum. Because of its many auxiliaries it nonetheless had more soldiers than the south, with its two legions.

Hadrian's Wall was extensively rebuilt under Severus, and small units called exploratores were sent beyond the frontier to watch the native peoples and see that the terms of Roman treaties were kept. After Severus's campaign the northern border stayed largely peaceful. From 260 to 273 the province belonged to the breakaway Gallic Empire, and its later years coincided with poor economic conditions across Roman Britain. Lead sealings show that its symbol was a bull.

In 296 Diocletian reorganised the empire, and the new Diocese of Britannia was divided into four provinces. Britannia Inferior became Britannia Secunda, with its capital at Eboracum, and Flavia Caesariensis, with its capital at Lindum.
britannia-prima: Roman Britain was at first governed as a single province from Camulodunum (Colchester) and then Londinium (London). After the revolt of its governor Clodius Albinus, the Severan reforms divided it into Britannia Superior and Britannia Inferior, with capitals at Londinium and Eboracum (York). During the first phases of Diocletian's reforms Britain was held by Allectus as part of the Carausian Revolt. Britannia Prima was probably created after Constantius Chlorus defeated Allectus in 296, and it is named in the Verona List of the Roman provinces of about 312.

The province belonged to the Diocese of the Britains, whose vicar sat at Londinium, within the Prefecture of Gaul. The Britains were divided among three, four or five provinces, which seem to have been named Prima, Secunda, Maxima Caesariensis and possibly Flavia Caesariensis and Valentia. The late 4th-century List of Offices gives the governor of Prima equestrian rank, as praeses, which makes it unlikely that the province was based at Londinium. Most scholars place it in Wales, Cornwall and the lands that connect them.

An inscription found at Corinium of the Dobunni names a rector of Britannia Prima, Lucius Septimius, and on that basis Corinium is generally taken as its capital. Some emendations of the corrupt list of bishops at the Council of Arles would put a provincial capital at Isca (Caerleon) or Deva (Chester) instead, both legionary bases, where the Second Augustan and Twentieth Valerian legions may still have been stationed. Ammianus records that in 369 Count Theodosius the Elder established or refounded the province of Valentia; some scholars place it in north-western Wales, with its capital at Deva.

Where the province lay has long been argued over. Gerald of Wales, describing the metropolitan sees of the early British church, placed Britannia Prima in Wales and western Britain and explained its name by the first settlements of Brutus of British legend, a gloss modern scholars disregard. William Camden placed it in the south, closest to Rome, and this was generally accepted after Charles Bertram's forgery of the 1740s, The Description of Britain, gave Prima borders south of the Thames and the Bristol Channel. Bertram's work was exposed over the mid-19th century.
britannia-secunda: After the Roman conquest Britain was governed as a single province, first from Camulodunum (Colchester) and then from Londinium. Following the revolt of the governor Clodius Albinus, the Severan reforms divided it into Britannia Superior and Britannia Inferior, with capitals at Londinium and Eboracum. When Diocletian began his reforms, Britain was held by the usurper Allectus as part of the Carausian Revolt.

Britannia Secunda was probably created after Constantius Chlorus defeated Allectus in 296, and it appears in the Verona List of the Roman provinces of about 312. The new Diocese of the Britains belonged to the Prefecture of Gaul and was divided among provinces that seem to have been named Prima, Secunda, Maxima Caesariensis and possibly Flavia Caesariensis and Valentia. According to Ammianus, in 369 Count Theodosius established or refounded Valentia on lands recaptured from the enemy; some scholars place it around Luguvalium (Carlisle) on Hadrian's Wall, which would mean it was cut from territory formerly governed from Eboracum.

The northern placing rests on indirect evidence. The Notitia Dignitatum lists the governor (praeses) of Britannia II as holding equestrian rank, which makes it unlikely that he sat in Londinium, and the list of bishops at the Council of Arles in 314, which is assumed to follow the Roman administration, includes one from Eboracum. The province probably lay further from Rome than Britannia Prima.

Older views were different. William Camden placed Secunda in Wales, and Charles Bertram's forgery On the State of Britain gave it borders on the Dee and the Severn, a view generally accepted from the mid-18th to the mid-19th century before the work was exposed. It was set aside after inscriptions showed that western England belonged to Prima, whose capital may have been Corinium.
britannia-superior: The province came out of the civil war that followed the murder of Emperor Commodus on 31 December 192. Clodius Albinus, who commanded in Britain, contested the empire with Septimius Severus and was defeated at the Battle of Lugdunum (Lyon) on 19 February 197, after which he took his own life. Albinus had shown how large an army a single governor of Britain could raise, and the division of the island was meant to keep so strong a power base out of one man's hands.

Herodian credits Severus with the split soon after Lugdunum, but A.J. Graham argued that the evidence for a date of 197 is weak and that the division took place under Caracalla, between 211 and 220. An inscription of Lucius Julius Julianus, of between 198 and 209, places his legions at Caerleon, which suggests that Britain was still undivided in 209. Two legions garrisoned Upper Britain and only one Lower Britain, so the governor of Superior is assumed to have held consular rank and his northern colleague praetorian rank.

Inscriptions show the governor of Superior with men of his staff on duty in the Lower province, and the most current theory gives civil jurisdiction in the north to the legionary commander at York, while the consular governor of the south took command of the whole country when needed. Among the known governors is Titus Desticius Juba (253–255), who rebuilt the Caerleon barracks of Legio II Augusta. A lead seal found at Burgh Castle in Norfolk in 1993 names the Province of Upper Britain and shows a stag beneath a tree.

London declined in these years, but it received a new wall, dated by a coin of Commodus to no earlier than 190 CE and perhaps as late as 220, built on the order of either Albinus or Severus. Villas were enlarged, among them Witcombe and Frocester Court on the outer ridge of the Cotswolds between 270 and 275.

From 260 Britain adhered, with Germania, Gaul and Hispania, to the Gallic Empire. In 287 Carausius, a senior Roman officer suspected of collusion with pirates in the Channel, rebelled and took over Britain; he was murdered in 293 by his own finance minister, who held the island until Constantius invaded in September 296 and defeated him near modern Silchester. Constantius then reorganised Britain, and by the time of the Verona List Upper and Lower Britain had given way to four provinces: Britannia Prima, Britannia Secunda, Maxima Caesariensis and Flavia Caesariensis.
british-columbia: British Columbia lies between the Pacific Ocean and the Rocky Mountains and has a varied geography of rocky coasts, forests, lakes, mountains, inland deserts and grassy plains. It borders Alberta to the east, Yukon and the Northwest Territories to the north, the US states of Washington, Idaho and Montana to the south, and Alaska to the northwest. Its southern border was established by the Oregon Treaty of 1846. The coastline runs for more than 27,000 km and includes deep fjords and about 6,000 islands.

The first known people settled in the area at least 10,000 years ago, among them the Coast Salish, Tsilhqotʼin and Haida peoples. There are more than 200 First Nations in the province. Smallpox killed at least 30 per cent of the First Nations of the Pacific Northwest in the 1770s, and the epidemic of 1862 killed about half to two thirds of the native population of what became British Columbia.

Fort Victoria, founded in 1843, was one of the earliest British settlements, and it gave rise to the city of Victoria, capital of the Colony of Vancouver Island. The name British Columbia was chosen by Queen Victoria in 1858 and refers to the Columbia District, the British term for the region drained by the Columbia River, which the Hudson's Bay Company had administered; British was added to distinguish it from the American territory to the south. In 1858 an influx of Americans during the Fraser Canyon Gold Rush led the Colonial Office to designate the mainland as the Colony of British Columbia. Richard Clement Moody founded the colony and chose New Westminster as its capital.

Further gold rushes followed, the largest being the Cariboo Gold Rush of 1862, which pushed the colonial government deeper into debt. The Vancouver Island colony had financial crises of its own, and the two colonies were merged in 1866, with Victoria as capital. Once the Canadian government agreed to extend the Canadian Pacific Railway to the province and assume the colony's debt, British Columbia became the sixth province to join Confederation on 20 July 1871.

British Columbia is the westernmost province of Canada. Its capital is Victoria and its largest city is Vancouver, whose port is the largest in Canada. Forestry, mining and tourism are among the main sectors of its economy. English is the common language of the province, and the Franco-Columbian community is an officially recognised linguistic minority.
british-empire: The empire began with the overseas possessions and trading posts that England established in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, and with Scottish colonisation attempts in the 17th century. Motivated by the wealth of the Portuguese and Spanish empires, England, France and the Netherlands founded colonies and trade networks in the Americas and Asia. The first permanent English settlement in the Americas was Jamestown, founded in 1607, and the English East India Company, chartered in 1600, challenged the Portuguese monopoly of trade with Asia.

Wars of the 17th and 18th centuries with the Netherlands and France left Britain the dominant colonial power in North America, and the East India Company's conquest of Mughal Bengal at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 made it a major power in India. Britain lost the Thirteen Colonies after the American Revolution, and independence was acknowledged at the Peace of Paris in 1783. Colonial expansion then turned to Asia, Africa and the Pacific. The first convicts arrived in Australia in 1788, and colonisation brought disease, violence and dispossession to Indigenous Australians.

Parliament abolished the slave trade in the empire in 1807, and the Slavery Abolition Act ended slavery there from 1 August 1834, with an apprenticeship system that lasted until 1838 and compensation paid to slave-owners.
