After the defeat of Napoleon in 1815 Britain had no serious rival at sea, and between 1815 and 1914 around 26 million km2 and roughly 400 million people were added. The Maratha Empire was defeated in 1818, rivalry with Russia in Central Asia became the Great Game, and the Scramble for Africa followed.

The white settler colonies gained self-government step by step, from Canada's confederation in 1867 to the Australian federation in 1901, and the term dominion status was introduced in 1907. The empire reached its largest extent after the First World War, covering 24 per cent of the Earth's land in 1920. India gained independence on 15 August 1947 with the partition that cost hundreds of thousands of lives. Harold Macmillan spoke of the wind of change in Cape Town in 1960, and nearly thirty colonies became independent in that decade.

Most former colonies joined the Commonwealth of Nations, a voluntary association of equal members. Hong Kong was handed to China on 1 July 1997, an event that symbolised the end of the empire for many. Britain keeps sovereignty over fourteen overseas territories. Historians' approaches to the empire are diverse and still changing, and post-colonial studies have led to a critical re-evaluation of the history of imperialism.
british-india: In 1608 the Mughal emperor Jahangir issued a firman to the English East India Company to establish a small trading settlement at Surat, which became its first headquarters. The company, incorporated on 31 December 1600, rented a small outpost at Madras in 1639. Bombay, ceded to the British Crown by Portugal as part of the wedding dowry of Catherine of Braganza in 1661, was granted to the company to be held in trust for the Crown. In eastern India, Job Charnock became tenant of three small villages, later renamed Calcutta, in 1686.

By the mid-18th century the three principal settlements had become the Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies, each administered by a governor. This was not yet territorial expansion: India was not colonised in this period.

After Robert Clive's victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and the defeat of the Nawab of Oudh at the Battle of Buxar in 1764, the company obtained the Diwani of Bengal, the right to administer and collect land revenue. By 1773 it had obtained the Nizamat, and with it full practical sovereignty in the expanded Bengal Presidency. Portions of Mysore were annexed to the Madras Presidency after 1792, and more after the defeat of Tipu Sultan in 1799. By the mid-19th century, after the three Anglo-Maratha Wars and the four Anglo-Mysore Wars, the company had become the paramount power in South Asia. The Punjab Province was established in 1849 from territories captured in the Anglo-Sikh Wars.

After the rebellion of 1857 the Government of India Act 1858 ended company rule, and India was directly ruled as a colonial possession of the United Kingdom, officially known as the Indian Empire after 1876. British India consisted of the regions directly administered by the British, beside the princely states, whose rulers kept a measure of internal autonomy in exchange for recognising British suzerainty. In 1910 British India covered about 54 per cent of the area and included over 77 per cent of the population.

Burma was part of British India from 1824 to 1937, when it became a separate colony. Bengal was partitioned in 1905 and reunited in 1912, the year Delhi became the capital. At independence in 1947 there were 17 provinces and officially 565 princely states. Eleven provinces joined India and three joined Pakistan, while Punjab, Bengal and Assam were partitioned between them.

The provinces in India were replaced by redrawn states and union territories in 1950. East Bengal, a province of Pakistan, was renamed East Pakistan in 1956 and became the independent nation of Bangladesh in 1971.
british-isles: The British Isles are an archipelago in the North Atlantic off north-western Europe. They comprise Great Britain, Ireland, the Isle of Man, the Inner and Outer Hebrides, the Northern Isles of Orkney and Shetland, and over six thousand smaller islands, with a total area of 315,159 square kilometres. About 136 are permanently inhabited. Great Britain, to the east, covers 217,000 square kilometres and Ireland, to the west, 84,400. The Channel Islands are normally counted among them although they are not part of the archipelago geographically. The oldest rocks, 2.7 billion years old, are in Ireland, Wales and north-west Scotland. The North Atlantic Drift keeps the climate mild and moist. Ben Nevis, the highest mountain, rises to 1,345 metres.

The region was resettled after the last glaciation by 12,000 BCE, when Great Britain was still part of a peninsula of the continent. Ireland was not inhabited until after 8000 BCE, and Great Britain became an island by 7000 BCE with the flooding of Doggerland. At the start of the 1st millennium BCE the Gaels in Ireland, the Picts in the north of Great Britain and the Britons in the south all spoke Insular Celtic languages. Rome conquered much of Britain from 43 CE. The first Anglo-Saxons arrived as Roman power waned in the 5th century and eventually dominated much of what is now England. Viking invasions were followed by settlements and political change, particularly in England.

The Norman conquest of England in 1066 and the Angevin partial conquest of Ireland from 1169 brought a new Norman ruling elite. By the Late Middle Ages Great Britain was divided between the kingdoms of England and Scotland, while control in Ireland shifted between Gaelic kingdoms, Hiberno-Norman lords and the English-dominated Lordship of Ireland. The Union of the Crowns in 1603 and the Acts of Union of 1707 and 1800 aimed to join Great Britain and Ireland in a single United Kingdom, with the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands remaining Crown Dependencies.

The earliest references to the islands as a group come from seafarers of the Greek colony of Massalia, and Polybius used the name the Brettanic Islands, which Rivet and Smith take to mean Britain with Ireland. British Isles is a geographical name, not a political unit, but there are objections to it in relation to Ireland. The Government of Ireland does not recognise the term, and joint documents such as the Good Friday Agreement say these islands. Britain and Ireland is a common alternative.
british-kaffraria: The name Kaffraria derives from the derogatory word Kaffir, used for the Black African inhabitants of southern Africa, itself from the Arabic kafir, usually translated as disbeliever. The term came to mean the Xhosa lands of what is now the Eastern Cape: the western part under British rule was called British Kaffraria, and the still independent Xhosa territory to the east, in the Transkei, Kaffraria proper.

The area's first inhabitants were Khoisan hunter-gatherers and herders, displaced by the Bantu expansion when it crossed the Kei River. The land then came under the Ngqika chiefs, of the Rarabe branch of the Xhosa, ruled by Ngqika ka Mlawu from 1797 and by his son Sandile kaNgqika from 13 November 1829.

Britain first seized the area after the 6th Frontier War, when Governor Sir Benjamin d'Urban annexed it to the Cape Colony on 10 May 1835 as Queen Adelaide Province, named after the wife of King William IV, with its seat at the new King William's Town. The Xhosa were driven across the Kei River and magistrates were placed at the chiefs' Great Places. London condemned the annexation as uneconomical and unjust, and in December 1836 it was undone and the Cape's border returned to the Keiskamma River.

After the 7th Frontier War, Governor Sir Harry Smith annexed the territory again on 17 December 1847, re-occupied the abandoned forts and moved imperial troops in. A military officer as chief commissioner governed it, with assistant commissioners acting as magistrates. Xhosa chiefs had to acknowledge Queen Victoria and kept only limited authority, their decisions open to reversal. During the Mlanjeni War of 1850–1853, Smith tried to unseat Sandile, paramount chief of the Rharhabe tribes.

German emigrants arrived in 1858–1859. On 7 March 1860, in the wake of the Xhosa cattle-killing and the famine that followed it, the territory became a separate crown colony under Lieutenant Governor Colonel John Maclean, but economic problems threatened to bankrupt it, and it was re-incorporated into the Cape Colony on 17 April 1866.

From 1853 to 1866 the territory used the stamps of the Cape of Good Hope. Its lands correspond to the districts of Qonce, formerly King William's Town, and East London, and part of the former colony was later reconstituted by the apartheid regime as the semi-independent homeland of Ciskei.
british-museum: The British Museum was founded as a universal museum on the will of Sir Hans Sloane (1660–1753), an Anglo-Irish physician and naturalist who lived in London. He gathered a large collection of curiosities and, not wishing it to be broken up, bequeathed it to King George II for the nation, with Parliament to pay his heirs £20,000, far less than its estimated value. On 7 June 1753 the king gave royal assent to the act establishing the museum, which added the Cottonian and Harleian libraries to the Sloane collection. The Old Royal Library joined them in 1757. The trustees bought Montagu House, and the museum opened to the public in 1759.

From 1778 objects from the South Seas, brought back from the voyages of Captain James Cook, drew visitors. After the French defeat at the Battle of the Nile in 1801 the museum acquired more Egyptian sculpture, and in 1802 King George III presented the Rosetta Stone. Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin, ambassador to the Ottoman Empire from 1799 to 1803, removed marble sculptures from the Parthenon, and they were acquired under an act of 1816. Assyrian and Babylonian antiquities bought from Mary Mackintosh Rich in 1825 began the Ancient Near Eastern collection.

Sir Robert Smirke's neoclassical building replaced Montagu House from 1823, and Sydney Smirke's Round Reading Room opened in 1857. The natural history collections were removed to South Kensington by 1887. The library department was separated in 1973 under the British Library Act 1972, and once the British Library left in 1998 the Queen Elizabeth II Great Court, the largest covered square in Europe, opened in 2000.

The original 1753 collection has grown to over 13 million objects at the museum. Its Middle Eastern collection of some 330,000 works is the largest collection of Mesopotamian antiquities outside Iraq, with rooms panelled in alabaster Assyrian palace reliefs from Nimrud, Nineveh and Khorsabad. Some of its best-known acquisitions, among them the Elgin Marbles and the Rosetta Stone, are subject to long-term disputes and repatriation claims. Like all national museums in the United Kingdom, it charges no admission fee except for loan exhibitions.
british-north-borneo-company: The German businessman Baron von Overbeck and the brothers Alfred Dent and Edward Dent, heads of a British trading firm in Shanghai and London, met Sultan Abdul Momin of Brunei on 29 December 1877, and he granted a concession for 15,000 Spanish dollars. Because Brunei had already ceded some areas to Sulu, Sultan Jamal ul-Azam of Sulu also signed a concession on 22 January 1878, for 5,000 Spanish dollars, with the help of the Scottish adventurer William Clark Cowie. Overbeck withdrew in 1879, and Alfred Dent formed a provisional association before the company's charter was sealed on 1 November 1881.

The first settlement, on Gaya Island, was burnt in a raid led by Mat Salleh and never rebuilt, and the company met continued resistance to its tax policies. The first governor, William Hood Treacher, worked to end slavery, but his land laws ignored the inhabitants' traditional rights; he also added the Klias Peninsula, Padas and other districts. A boundary with the Dutch along 4°10' north, dividing the island of Sebatik, was agreed on 20 January 1891. After Cowie joined the board in 1894, the territory was run largely from London for the shareholders, and Dent resigned.

The Second World War left the company unable to pay for reconstruction. It gave up its charter, and on 26 June 1946 it was dissolved by an agreement that included an immediate payment of £860,000; North Borneo became a Crown colony from 15 July 1946. In March 1949 the arbitrator Lord Uthwatt awarded £1,400,000 more, and the share price fell from 17 shillings to 9 shillings and 6d.

The territory was divided into residencies, at first West Coast and East Coast and later five, each split into provinces under district officers, with the residents of Sandakan and West Coast sitting on the Legislative Council. The company recruited Sikh policemen from northern India, set up courts and built a railway from Jesselton. The Village Ordinance of 1891 recognised only chiefs it appointed, and the disregard for traditional leaders fed the resistance of Mat Salleh and Ontoros Antanum.
british-overseas-territories: The British Overseas Territories are the remnants of the former British Empire that stayed under British sovereignty after decolonisation, with varying constitutional statuses. Early English colonies were generally called plantations, and the first, unofficial, colony was Newfoundland, where English fishermen set up seasonal camps in the 16th century. Gibraltar was captured from Spain in 1704 by a force under Admiral Sir George Rooke, acting for the Grand Alliance, and was ceded to Great Britain by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713. The Colonial Office once oversaw all British colonies. Today the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office does so, except for the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia in Cyprus, which come under the Ministry of Defence.

The fourteen territories lie outside the British Islands and are not part of the United Kingdom itself. They recognise the British monarch as head of state, and in territories with a permanent population a governor is appointed on the advice of the British government. Each has its own legal system, generally based on English common law, and the highest court for all of them is the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London. The United Kingdom keeps authority over defence, foreign relations and internal security. Three territories, the British Antarctic Territory, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands and the British Indian Ocean Territory, have no permanent civilian population.

From 1949 to 1983 residents of the territories shared the status of Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies with residents of the United Kingdom. In 1983 the British Nationality Act 1981 replaced their status with British Dependent Territories citizenship. Falkland Islanders were automatically granted full British citizenship because of the Falklands War. Of the eleven territories with permanent populations, all except the Sovereign Base Areas are on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories. Many of the territories are used as military bases.
british-raj: The name comes from the Hindustani rāj, meaning reign, rule or government. The system was instituted on 28 June 1858, when, after the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the rule of the East India Company passed to the Crown in the person of Queen Victoria, who was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. The Rebellion had shaken the British enterprise without derailing it, but the British became more circumspect and drew lessons about communication between British and Indians. The Raj extended over almost all of present-day India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, except small holdings such as Goa, held by Portugal, and Pondicherry, held by France.

Two kinds of territory made up the Raj. British India was governed directly through the Governor-General and the provinces, while the princely states, 565 of them in 1947, were ruled by indigenous princes under British paramountcy. In the princely states, external affairs, defence and most communications were under British control. The Government of India Act 1858 changed governance in London, in the central government in Calcutta and in the provinces.

Railways, roads, canals, bridges and telegraph links were built rapidly, tying the economies of India and Britain together. By 1890 some 60,000 Indians had matriculated at the universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, producing an educated professional bureaucracy, though almost all of the top civil service posts were held by Britons. The population reached 255 million in the first census of 1881. India also saw major famines. Estimates of deaths in the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 run from 6.1 million to 10.39 million, and historians continue to debate whether British rule accelerated or distorted the country's economic development.

A new middle class grew after 1880, and Indians took encouragement from Queen Victoria's proclamation of 1858. Lord Curzon's partition of Bengal in 1905 drew a largely Hindu protest, and in 1906 Muslim leaders asked the new viceroy, Lord Minto, for separate electorates, which led to the founding of the All-India Muslim League in Dacca. About 1.4 million Indian and British soldiers of the British Indian Army served in the First World War. On 13 April 1919 troops commanded by Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired on an unarmed gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar; the government reported 379 dead and 1,100 wounded, and the Indian National Congress estimated three times as many dead.

In 1939 the viceroy, Lord Linlithgow, declared war on India's behalf without consulting Indian leaders, and the Congress provincial ministries resigned in protest, while the Muslim League supported the war effort and grew rapidly. In 1946 mutinies in the armed services, notably in the Royal Indian Navy, prompted the Labour government to send the Cabinet Mission. In 1947 the Raj was partitioned into two dominions, the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan.
british-south-africa-company: The company was chartered in 1889 after the amalgamation of Cecil Rhodes's Central Search Association and the London-based Exploring Company, which had competed to profit from the expected mineral wealth of Mashonaland but united out of common economic interests and to secure British government backing. Its Royal Charter, which took effect on 20 December 1889, was modelled on that of the British East India Company and was granted for 25 years, later extended by ten. The first directors included the 2nd Duke of Abercorn, Rhodes and the financier Alfred Beit. The charter empowered it to form banks, to distribute land and to raise a police force, in return for developing the territory and respecting existing African laws and religions.

Lobengula, the Ndebele king, had granted mining concessions, including the Rudd Concession, but consistently refused to delegate general powers of government. The company nevertheless persuaded the Colonial Office to proclaim a protectorate over Mashonaland by an Order-in-Council of 9 May 1891. Its paramilitary force, created in 1889 and later the British South Africa Police, defeated the Ndebele kingdom and overcame Shona resistance in the First Matabele War and Second Matabele War. It was the first British use of the Maxim gun in combat, causing five thousand Ndebele casualties. The company named its territory Zambezia and later Rhodesia.

The gold of Mashonaland did not materialise, and the company never paid a dividend before 1924, as its administrative costs outweighed its income. It built the Rhodesian railway system and owned the railways until 1947. Rhodes retained control until his death in 1902, and after the Jameson Raid the company's relations with the Colonial Office were difficult. The company introduced freehold land ownership and acquired large tracts for settlers, and it ended the powers of traditional rulers through war or eroded them by encouraging its own officials to take them over.

The company administered Southern Rhodesia until 1923 and Northern Rhodesia until 1924, and an agreement of 29 September 1923 ended its administration. British courts had held that unalienated land belonged to the Crown, not to the company, and its land claims in Southern Rhodesia were nullified in 1918. Its mineral rights in Southern Rhodesia were bought out in 1933, and in 1964 it handed its mineral rights in Northern Rhodesia to the government of Zambia. In 1965 its business was merged into Charter Consolidated Ltd.
britons-celtic-people: There is no consensus on when Celtic languages reached Britain. The traditional view derived Celtic culture from the Hallstatt culture of central Europe, while John Koch and Barry Cunliffe proposed that Celtic developed as a language of trade in the Atlantic Bronze Age zone, and Patrick Sims-Williams that it arose in Gaul. A study of 2021 found a migration into southern Britain from 1300 to 800 BCE, genetically close to ancient people of Gaul, which the authors called a plausible vector for early Celtic languages. The earliest mention of the inhabitants is by Pytheas, around 320 BCE, who calls them Pretanoi and says that they were Celts.

Ancient Britain consisted of many tribes and kingdoms associated with hillforts, and the Britons followed a Celtic religion overseen by druids. Some southern polities had strong links with Gaul and minted their own coins. The Romans invaded in 43 and by 84 had decisively conquered southern Britain. Hadrian's Wall was fortified in 122, and the Antonine Wall was built from 142 but abandoned after about twenty years. The Britons south of the wall mostly kept their land under Roman governors. Roman rule ended about 410.

Some fifty years later Anglo-Saxons began settling the south-eastern coast. Many Brittonic kingdoms disappeared over the following centuries: Ceint, the kingdom of Kent, fell in 456 and Elmet in 627. Britons colonised Brittany and the Channel Islands, and founded Britonia in Gallaecia in north-western Spain. In the north Gaelic speakers from Ireland settled in the west. Some northern kingdoms resisted: Rheged survived into the 8th century and Gododdin until about 775, and Ystrad Clud, Strathclyde, endured until the 1090s, when it was divided between England and Scotland. How far this change involved wholesale population replacement is still debated.

Wales remained free of Anglo-Saxon, Gaelic and Viking control and was divided among Brittonic kingdoms, among them Gwynedd, Powys, Deheubarth, Gwent and Morgannwg. Cornwall was effectively annexed by the English from the mid 11th century. By the 11th century Brittonic speakers had split into the Welsh, Cornish, Bretons and Cumbrians, and Common Brittonic had become Welsh, Cornish, Breton and Cumbric. Brittany was united with France in 1532, and Wales with England by the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 to 1542.

Welsh and Breton survive, Cornish became extinct by the 19th century but has been revived since the 20th, and Cumbric and Pictish died out in the 12th century. Most place names in Wales, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and Brittany are Brittonic. The relationship of the Britons to the Picts is unclear, but most scholars accept that the Pictish language was related to Common Brittonic.
briviesca: Briviesca is the capital of the comarca of La Bureba, in the north-east of the province of Burgos, in Castile and León. It lies halfway between Burgos and Miranda de Ebro, in the valley of the river Oca between the mountains of San José and of Los Pinos, at 718 metres above sea level. The valley opens onto the extensive plain of La Bureba, which is often called the granary of Castile because of its cereal production. The origin of the name is not known exactly. It seems to be of proto-Indo-European origin and to mean the head or regional capital, from the root uiro- and the suffix -uesca.

Prehistoric finds in the zone show human presence from the Paleolithic, and Iron Age remains turn up at Briviesca and nearby places. From the 3rd century BCE the Autrigones occupied a large area of the upper Ebro valley, and the first settlements at Briviesca date from the 1st century BCE, when they established their capital there. The first document to refer to it is the Natural History of Pliny the Elder, who cites Virovesca as the capital of the Autrigones. Under the Romans it was an important population centre at the crossroads of two Roman roads.

This location, and the medieval boom of the Camino de Santiago, made the town grow gradually until its maximum splendour in the Renaissance. A Jewish community was documented from 1240 and lasted until the expulsion of 1492. The town was not always where it is now: it stood in the nearby mountains, where defence mattered most, until the fourteenth century, when Blanca of Portugal, granddaughter of Alfonso the Wise, bought it and moved it to its present site because the new location gave better access and trade.

Briviesca is a municipality of five settlements: Briviesca itself, Cameno, Quintanillabón, Revillagodos and Valdazo. It had 6,948 inhabitants in 2016 and is the head of the judicial district of Briviesca. Its monumental complex includes the Collegiate Church of Santa María la Mayor, the Monastery of Santa Clara with its Gothic cloister, the cloister of the Hospitalillo, the typically Castilian Plaza Mayor and the Church of San Martín. The sanctuary of Santa Casilda lies close by. Its arms show two Moors and a Christian, which are explained as a sign of coexistence between cultures.
brixen: Brixen, in Italian Bressanone, lies about 40 kilometres north of Bolzano at the confluence of the Eisack and Rienz rivers, 45 kilometres south of the Brenner Pass. To the east rises the Plose mountain massif, and to the west the Sarntal Alps. The town is more than 70 percent German-speaking and officially bilingual in German and Italian. Finds at Stufels suggest a Rhaetian culture here before the Romans.

The area has been settled since the Stone Age, and in 15 BCE the Romans conquered it, with their main settlement at nearby Säben (Sabiona). They held it until about 590, when Bavarians occupied it. The first mention of Brixen, as Prihsna, is in a document of 901 by King Louis III the Child, which gave a farm to Bishop Zacharias of Säben. The bishops moved here from Säben in 992, after the cathedral was finished.

In 1048 Poppo, Bishop of Brixen, was made pope by the emperor Henry III as Damasus II and died after 23 days. On 15 June 1080 the synod of Brixen condemned Pope Gregory VII in the Investiture Controversy. A first ring of walls was finished in 1115, and fires devastated the town in 1174, 1234 and 1445. After the German mediatisation, Brixen was awarded to Austria in 1802, ceded to Bavaria in 1805 after Austerlitz and returned to Austria by the Congress of Vienna in 1814.

Under the Treaty of London of 1915 Italy was promised South Tyrol, and in 1919 the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye awarded Brixen to Italy. After the Second World War Austria considered the settlement unsatisfactory, raising the South Tyrolean Question, and in 1972 South Tyrol was granted autonomy within Trentino-Alto Adige.

Brixen is the third-largest city and the oldest town in South Tyrol. The cathedral, dedicated to the Assumption of Mary, dates from the 10th century, was rebuilt in the 13th century and again in 1745–54 in Baroque style, and has a ceiling fresco by Paul Troger. The Hofburg, a Renaissance bishop's palace begun in the 13th century, houses the Diocesan Museum. The White Tower of 1591 holds a carillon of 43 bells.
brno: Brno lies at the confluence of the Svitava and Svratka rivers, between the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands and the Dyje–Svratka Valley in the south-east of the Czech Republic. It stands at the crossroads of ancient trade routes linking northern and southern Europe and has always been closely tied to Vienna, 110 km to the south. The etymology of the name is disputed: it may derive from Old Czech brnie, muddy or swampy, from the Slavic verb brniti, to armour or fortify, or from a Celtic word related to Welsh bryn, hill. It was known in German as Brünn and in Latin as Bruna.

The city's direct precursor was Staré Zámky, a fortified hillfort of Great Moravia near Brno-Líšeň, inhabited from the Neolithic until the early 11th century. In the early 11th century Brno became the seat of a non-ruling Přemyslid prince and one of the centres of Moravia, along with Olomouc and Znojmo. It is first mentioned in Cosmas's Chronica Boemorum in 1091, when King Vratislaus II besieged his brother Conrad in Brno castle. From the late 12th century until the middle of the 17th, political power in the Margraviate of Moravia was divided between Brno and Olomouc, which was the larger and the seat of the only bishopric in Moravia until 1777.

In 1641 Emperor Ferdinand III, as margrave of Moravia, moved the Moravian Diet, Land Court and Land Tables from Olomouc to Brno, since Swedish armies had made Olomouc their primary target in the Thirty Years' War. Brno, under Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches, resisted the siege of 1645 by Field Marshal Lennart Torstensson, the only Moravian city to defend itself against the Swedes, and it then served as the sole capital of Moravia. After the Battle of Austerlitz in December 1805 the French occupied it, and in 1809 Napoleon ordered the fortifications of Špilberk Castle dismantled.

At the start of the 20th century about two thirds of Brno's residents spoke German, though the suburbs were mostly Czech-speaking, and everyday life was bilingual. During the German occupation of 1939 to 1945 the Nazis closed the Czech universities and used the Kounic Residence Hall as a political prison, where about 800 civilians were executed or died. After the communist coup of 1948 the regime abolished the traditional regional governance, ending Brno's role as the capital of Moravia.

Brno is the second-largest city of the Czech Republic and the political and cultural hub of the South Moravian Region. Its traditional symbols are Špilberk Castle and the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul on Petrov hill. The Villa Tugendhat, a functionalist building, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2001. Gregor Mendel lived and died in the city.
broad-front-uruguay: The Frente Amplio was founded in 1971 as a coalition of more than a dozen fractured leftist parties and movements. Its first president, and its first candidate for the presidency of the country, was General Líber Seregni. It was declared illegal during the military coup of 1973 and re-emerged when democracy was restored. In 1994 several minor factions joined it to form Encuentro Progresista, and with Nuevo Espacio linked to the front the alliance contested elections under a joint name. In 2005 the member organisations of Progressive Encounter and New Majority merged into the front, which took the name of the larger force.
Splits occurred in 1989, when the Party for the Government of the People and the Christian Democratic Party left to form a centrist coalition, in 1993 and in April 2006.

The Broad Front became the country's third major political force at the 1994 election. Its candidate Tabaré Vázquez won the most votes of any individual candidate, but under the Ley de lemas, which gave the presidency to the leading candidate of the party with most votes, he was denied it because the Colorados and Blancos finished ahead. After the system was replaced by two rounds, Vázquez led the first round in 1999 but lost the run-off to the Colorado Jorge Batlle, and the front became the largest party in the legislature.

Vázquez won in 2004, the first time a left-leaning party took a majority in Uruguay, on more moderate policies and support for a stronger welfare state. José Mujica, a former guerrilla, became president after the 2009 election. Under him abortion was decriminalised in the first 12 weeks, same-sex marriage was passed in April 2013 and the legalisation of marijuana was signed in December 2013, although the general population did not support the last. Vázquez was re-elected in 2014 with 56.5 per cent in the second round.

In 2019 Daniel Martínez came first in the first round but lost the run-off to Luis Lacalle Pou of the National Party, ending fifteen years in government, and the front lost its majorities in both chambers while remaining the largest party. In the 2024 election Yamandú Orsi won the internal primary over Carolina Cosse with 42.22 per cent of valid votes and she became his running mate. The ticket took 43.86 per cent in the first round and won a majority in the Senate but fell two seats short in the Chamber of Representatives. In the second round Orsi beat the National Party's Álvaro Delgado by 3.9 per cent, and he took office on 1 March 2025.
broceliande: The forest was earlier known as Brécheliant and Brécilien, and the etymology is uncertain. The oldest form, Brecheliant, may join the Celtic Brec'h, hill, to a man's name; the later Brocéliande, first found in the work of Chrétien de Troyes, may come from bro, country in Breton, Cornish and Welsh. A reference to Briscelim sinus Armoricus occurs in the Cosmographia of Bernardus Silvestris, read to Pope Eugene III in 1147–48.

In his Roman de Rou of about 1160, Wace counted among the Bretons those of Brecheliant, about whom many legends were told. He described the fountain of Barenton, where hunters wet a stone with its water to summon rain, and reported rumours of fairies. Wace went to Brittany in search of these wonders and came back disappointed, writing that he had sought marvels and found none.

In Chrétien's Le Chevalier au lion of the 1170s, Yvain pours water from a spring onto a stone in Brocéliande and raises a storm that summons the knight Esclados le Ros. Robert de Boron first tied Merlin to the forest in his poem Merlin, and the prose Vulgate Cycle set there episodes of Merlin and Viviane and the Val sans retour, where Morgan le Fay trapped unfaithful knights until Lancelot freed them. The forest's unusual weather is noted by Giraldus Cambrensis, Alexandre Neckham and William the Breton.

Modern writers returned to it, among them Alfred, Lord Tennyson in Idylls of the King, Jean Lorrain in his play Brocéliande of 1898, where Viviane shuts Merlin inside an oak, and Robert Holdstock in Merlin's Wood. The name inspired J.R.R. Tolkien's Beleriand, called Broseliand in early sketches of The Silmarillion.

Early sources give unclear or conflicting locations. Since the 15th century, following Jean Cabaret d'Orville, some have linked Brocéliande to the forest of Lorge near Quintin. Some scholars think it never existed. Jean Markale regarded it as a remnant of the forest that covered central Brittany until the High Middle Ages, and William A. Young has argued for equating it with the forest of Celython, the Great Wood of Caledon, from tales of the Brythonic kingdoms beyond Hadrian's Wall.
broch: A broch is an Iron Age drystone hollow-walled structure found in Scotland. Brochs belong to the class that Scottish archaeologists in the 1980s called complex Atlantic roundhouses. The word comes from Lowland Scots brough, meaning fort. In the mid-nineteenth century antiquaries called them burgs, after Old Norse borg, and in the west they are often called dùns. Antiquarians began to use the spelling broch in the 1870s. The Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Scotland lists 571 candidate sites, though Euan MacKie, using a stricter definition, proposed only 104.

Mid-twentieth-century archaeologists mostly believed that brochs were built by chieftains displaced from the south of the British Isles. There is now little doubt that the hollow-walled tower first developed in what is now Scotland. Radiocarbon dates suggest that most were built in the first centuries BCE and CE, with a few perhaps earlier, notably Old Scatness in Shetland, where a sheep bone dated between 390 and 200 BCE has been reported. The end of broch building seems to have come around 100 to 200 CE. Most brochs are unexcavated, but those that have been examined show use over many centuries and many phases of habitation and abandonment.

Brochs have a single entrance with bar-holes, door-checks and lintels, a guard cell beside the passage, mural cells and a scarcement, or ledge, perhaps for a timber floor. A spiral staircase winds between the inner and outer wall, and the galleried walls have two skins tied together with stone slabs. The internal diameter is five to fifteen metres and the walls about three metres thick. The Broch of Mousa in Shetland is the best preserved, at 13 metres. About twenty Orcadian sites, such as Gurness and Midhowe, have small settlements round the tower. They are densest in Caithness, Sutherland and the Northern Isles.

Their purpose is debated. Nineteenth-century antiquaries saw refuges, and from the 1930s to the 1960s archaeologists such as V. Gordon Childe regarded them as castles. In the 1980s archaeologists proposed that they were the stately homes of important families, though proof is lacking. Some think they served several purposes, defensive and symbolic.
brocken: The Brocken, also called the Blocksberg, stands near Schierke between the rivers Weser and Elbe and is the highest peak in northern Germany and the easternmost mountain there. It consists mainly of granite, which emerged about 300 million years ago towards the end of the Harz mountain-building phase. Its summit lies above the natural tree line, and the mountain has a microclimate resembling that of mountains nearly 1,000 metres higher. Mists and fogs shroud it up to 300 days a year, and its mean annual temperature is only 2.9 °C. The Brocken spectre, a climber's shadow cast upon fog, is a common phenomenon.

The first documented ascent was made in 1572 by the physician and botanist Johannes Thal. In 1736 Count Christian Ernst of Stolberg-Wernigerode had the Wolkenhäuschen, a small refuge still preserved, built on the summit, and the first inn followed around 1800. Between 1821 and 1825 Carl Friedrich Gauss used the line of sight to the Großer Inselsberg for triangulation in the geodesic survey of the Kingdom of Hanover.

The Brocken Garden, Germany's first alpine garden, was laid out in 1890, and the narrow-gauge Brocken Railway opened on 27 March 1899. In 1935 the Deutsche Reichspost made the first television broadcast from the mountain, and in the following year the first television tower in the world was built there, carrying the first live television broadcast of the Summer Olympics in Berlin.

On 17 April 1945 American bombing destroyed the Brocken Hotel and the weather station. American troops held the mountain until April 1947, when it passed to the Soviet occupation zone. From August 1961 it lay in East Germany's border zone and became a military exclusion zone, with extensive installations on the summit. Two large listening stations, one of the Soviet GRU and one of the East German Ministry for State Security, could capture radio traffic across almost all of Western Europe. The mountain was opened to the public again on 3 December 1989 during a demonstration walk, and the last Russian soldier left on 30 March 1994.

The Brocken lies within Harz National Park, declared in 1990, and its summit is a popular destination for visitors. Steam trains of the Brocken Railway climb to a station at 1,125 metres, and the Brockenhaus at the summit holds a museum on the mountain's history. Folklore has long linked the mountain with witches and devils, and Goethe took up the legends in his tragedy Faust. The Goethe Way, a well-known trail to the summit, is named after him because he more or less followed the route in 1777.
bronze: Bronze made it possible to produce metal objects harder and more durable than the stone and copper tools that came before. The earliest tin-copper artifact has been dated to about 4650 BCE, at a Vinča culture site in Pločnik, Serbia. Other early examples date to the late 4th millennium BCE in Egypt, Susa, Luristan, Tepe Sialk, Mundigak and Mesopotamia. Copper-arsenic alloys, known as arsenical bronze, appear at Tal-i-Iblis on the Iranian plateau in 3800–3400 BCE. Tin became the major alloying ingredient in the late 3rd millennium BCE, because tin bronze was easier to control, stronger, easier to cast and less toxic than arsenical copper.

Bronze is an alloy consisting primarily of copper, commonly with about 12 to 12.5 per cent tin. Historical bronzes vary widely in composition, since metalworkers probably used whatever scrap was on hand. Because old documents sometimes confused bronze, alloyed with tin, with brass, alloyed with zinc, modern museum descriptions of older artworks increasingly use the general term copper alloy. In the Bronze Age, classic bronze with about 10 per cent tin was cast, and mild bronze with about 6 per cent tin was hammered into sheets for helmets and armour.

Copper ores and tin, which is much rarer, are seldom found together, so serious bronze work has always involved trade between regions; British tin from Cornwall reached Phoenicia. Large hoards of bronze objects, many unworn, suggest that bronze was also a store of value and a sign of status, and Chinese ritual bronzes were made in enormous quantities for elite burials and offerings.

The Bronze Age gave way to the Iron Age after a serious disruption of the tin trade: the population migrations of about 1200–1100 BCE reduced shipments of tin around the Mediterranean and from Britain, raising prices, while iron-working improved and iron grew cheaper. Bronze remained in use for coins, mirrors, bells and cannon. The Assyrian king Sennacherib claims to have been the first to cast monumental bronze statues, and bronze statues were regarded as the highest form of sculpture in Ancient Greek art.
bronze-age: The Bronze Age is an archaeological term for a phase in the development of material culture among ancient societies in Asia, the Near East and Europe. A culture belongs to it if it produced bronze by smelting its own copper and alloying it with tin, arsenic or other metals, or traded for bronze from producing areas elsewhere. It is the middle period of the three-age system, after the Stone Age and before the Iron Age, with a Chalcolithic transition from the Neolithic. It began at different times in different places, but had begun in much of the Old World by 3000 BCE.

In a region the arrival of the Iron Age or of writing, whichever came first, is usually taken to mark the end of the Bronze Age. The Americas use a five-period system without one, though the Moche of South America developed bronze smelting independently. In much of sub-Saharan Africa iron and copper smelting appeared at about the same time.

West Asia and the Near East entered the Bronze Age first, with the rise of Sumer in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Cultures there practised intensive agriculture, developed writing, invented the potter's wheel, and created centralised governments, written law codes, city-states and empires. Cuneiform in Mesopotamia and hieroglyphs in Egypt are the earliest practical writing systems. Egypt's Bronze Age began around 3150 BCE, and the Indus Valley Civilisation about 3300 BCE. The Near Eastern late period, from about 1550 to 1200 BCE, ended in the Late Bronze Age collapse; the Hittite kingdom disintegrated after 1180 BCE amid turmoil conjecturally linked to the Sea Peoples.

Bronze was harder and more durable than other metals then available. Iron needs about 1,250 °C to smelt and stayed out of common use until the end of the 2nd millennium BCE, while copper and tin melt at lower temperatures that Neolithic pottery kilns could reach. Yet in many areas bronze remained rare and expensive, chiefly because tin occurs in few places. Some societies used it only for weapons or elite art, such as Chinese ritual bronzes, while ordinary farmers still used stone tools. The Aegean network imported tin to Cyprus, where copper was mined and alloyed.
brora: Brora, Brùra in Scottish Gaelic, takes its name from Old Norse words meaning river with a bridge. The village stands where the A9 road and the Far North Line cross the River Brora, and it has its own railway station. The white sandstone of the nearby Clynelish quarry belongs to the Brora Formation of the Middle to Late Jurassic, and stone from the quarry was used to build London Bridge, Liverpool Cathedral and Dunrobin Castle.

Brora grew into a small industrial village. At various times it had a coal pit, the most northerly coal mine in the UK, as well as boat building, salt pans, fish curing, a lemonade factory, a wool mill, brickworks and a stone quarry, and two distilleries, the new Clynelish Distillery and the old Clynelish distillery, now called the Brora distillery. Thanks to its wool industry it was the first place in the north of Scotland to have electricity, which earned it the local nickname Electric City.

Members of the Clyne Heritage Society, recording structures eroding from the dunes of the Back Beach in 2005, found a map of 1812 marking Old Salt Pans at the spot and records showing that the pans had been built in 1598 and abandoned within a few years. Like many smaller fishing ports, Brora lost much of its fishing in the years before the First World War: in 1906 the Fishery Board reported that it was becoming more popular as a summer resort and declining as a fishing port, its fishermen working ashore as labourers for much of the year. From 1940 to 1986 the Brora Y Station, south-east of the village, served as a government listening station.

A baronial-style clock tower in the village serves as a war memorial. Brora Primary School occupies the building of the former Brora High School, whose secondary department closed in 1985, and older children attend Golspie High School. Brora Rangers F.C., founded in 1879, have played in the Highland Football League since 1962, and the village has an 18-hole links golf course laid out by James Braid in 1923.
brotherhood-of-blackheads: According to legend, the brotherhood began with foreign merchants who helped defend Tallinn during the Saint George's Night Uprising of 1343–1345. Its first documented mention is an agreement of 28 March 1400 with the Dominican monastery of Tallinn, confirming the Blackheads' ownership of the church vessels they had deposited in St. Catherine's Church and their duty to decorate and light the altar of St. Mary they had commissioned there. The Tallinn City Council ratified its statutes, the Great Rights, on 12 September 1407; those of the Riga brotherhood date from 1416.

Under the Great Rights the Blackheads undertook to defend the city and provided a cavalry detachment that patrolled the wall; six riders made rounds inside it every evening after the gates were locked at sunset. In 1526 the brotherhood gave the Tallinn council 8 rock-hurling machines, 20 cannon-carriages and 66 small-calibre guns. In the Livonian War its members helped defend Tallinn against the Russian sieges of 1570–1571 and 1577. After the Great Northern War, when Livonia passed to the Russian Empire, the brotherhood became mainly a social body, though the Tallinn cavalry kept its uniform until 1887.

In the 18th and 19th centuries the houses in Tallinn and Riga were cultural and social centres for the elite, with parties, concerts and collections of fine art. The Tallinn house at 24-26 Pikk Street, rented from 1406 and bought in 1531, was rebuilt in the Renaissance style and is the only Blackhead House to survive intact. The Riga house was destroyed on 28 June 1941 and rebuilt between 1995 and 2000. When the Soviet authorities dissolved the brotherhoods in 1940, most members fled to Germany.

Members were mostly merchants not yet eligible for the Great Guild, among them unmarried local merchants, those with no established business in Tallinn and foreigners, joined by goldsmiths, chemists, scholars and teachers. Two elected Superiors governed the Tallinn brotherhood, and by custom a Blackhead joined the Great Guild once he married. Twice a year, at Christmas and New Year and from Easter to the start of navigation, it held festivals of feasting and dancing, when new members were admitted. The brotherhood set up a tree in its Tallinn house in 1441, 1442 and 1514, the first documented Christmas trees in Estonia, and fined quarrelling brothers, often in wax.
brothers-grimm: Jacob Ludwig Carl Grimm was born on 4 January 1785 and Wilhelm Carl Grimm on 24 February 1786 in Hanau, in the Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel, into an educated Reformed Protestant family. Their father, Philipp Wilhelm Grimm, a lawyer, became district magistrate at Steinau in 1791. At the University of Marburg, a small university, the brothers met discrimination because of their social standing, and they needed a dispensation to study law. Their law professor Friedrich von Savigny, and his circle of romantics around Clemens Brentano and Ludwig Achim von Arnim, turned them towards medieval German literature and the ideas of Johann Gottfried Herder.

In 1808 Jacob became court librarian to the King of Westphalia, and Wilhelm later joined him as a librarian in Kassel. The work paid little but left time for research. At Brentano's request they had begun gathering folk tales in 1807, and by 1810 they had a manuscript of several dozen tales, written down from storytellers invited to their home. The first volume of Children's and Household Tales appeared in 1812 with 86 tales, and a second volume of 70 followed in 1814.

In 1830 both were passed over for the post of chief librarian and moved to the University of Göttingen, where Jacob published German Mythology in 1835. In 1840 Frederick William IV of Prussia offered them posts at the University of Berlin and the Academy of Sciences gave them stipends. There they worked on the German Dictionary, begun in 1838, which was unfinished at their deaths; its 32 volumes appeared between 1852 and 1960. After the revolutions of 1848 both were elected to a civil parliament, but their political activity was short-lived.

Between 1812 and 1864 the tales were published 17 times, and the seventh and last Large edition of 1857 held 211 tales. From 1815 Wilhelm alone edited and rewrote them, adding dialogue, removing anything that might detract from a rustic tone and, in later editions, eliminating sexual elements. Most of the stories were not intended for children, though the shorter Small editions of 50 tales were. The tales were not an immediate bestseller, but by the 1870s they had entered the school curriculum in Prussia. They were used to foster nationalism under the Third Reich, and the book was banned for a period in occupied Germany. The brothers' methods for recording oral tradition became a model for the study of folklore across Europe.
brough-east-riding-of-yorkshire: In Roman times the place was known as Petuaria. It marked the southern end of the Roman road now called Cade's Road, which ran roughly north for a hundred miles to Pons Aelius, modern Newcastle upon Tyne. The present name comes from the Old English burh, a fortification, a word related to borough and burgh.

In 1239 the Archbishop of York made Brough a town with the same liberties as Beverley, but there is no record that these liberties were ever used, and for centuries the settlement remained a village. The highwayman Dick Turpin lodged at the Ferry Inn at Brough from about June 1737 under the alias John Palmer, or Parmen, and lived in and travelled to and from Brough until he was captured and executed for horse theft in 1739.

Brough has a long association with aircraft making. BAE Systems, formerly British Aerospace, built the Hawk Advanced Jet Trainer at Brough Aerodrome, and new aircraft flew from its runway to Warton near Preston for final testing and painting. The company announced 450 job losses at Brough on 3 April 2008 and, on 1 March 2012, the end of manufacturing there with 845 redundancies. Manufacturing at the plant ceased on Christmas Eve 2020, by which time building had begun on the runway as part of the Brough South housing development.

Brough, pronounced Bruf locally, lies on the edge of the Yorkshire Wolds, and the Yorkshire Wolds Way National Trail passes its eastern end. With the neighbouring village of Elloughton it forms the civil parish of Elloughton-cum-Brough, and at the 2021 census the town had 13,331 inhabitants. Better rail links and new housing have changed its social make-up and raised local incomes.

The town lies about a mile south of the A63 road from Hull to the M62. Brough railway station, on the line from Hull to Selby and Doncaster, has direct trains to London, and the former air traffic control building of the aerodrome is now the Brough Business Centre. The town's primary schools are Brough Primary and Hunsley Primary, and the nearest secondary school is South Hunsley School in Melton.
brown-v-board-of-education: For much of the 60 years before Brown, race relations in the United States were dominated by segregation, which the Supreme Court had endorsed in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) on condition that separate facilities were equal. Segregation in schools varied widely: 17 states required it and 16 prohibited it. From the 1930s scholars at Howard University and activists of the NAACP pursued a legal strategy that began with graduate schools. It succeeded in Sweatt v. Painter and McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents, both of 1950, which suggested that segregation was inherently unequal, at least in some settings.

In 1951 thirteen Topeka parents, recruited by the local NAACP, sued the Board of Education on behalf of their 20 children after each was refused enrolment at the nearest school and redirected to a segregated one. Topeka's separate elementary schools rested on an 1879 Kansas law that permitted, but did not require, them. A three-judge district court, in an opinion by Judge Walter Huxman, ruled for the board, citing Plessy, although one of its findings of fact held that segregation had a detrimental effect on black children.

The Supreme Court combined five cases: Brown from Kansas, Briggs v. Elliott from South Carolina, Davis v. County School Board of Prince Edward County from Virginia, Gebhart v. Belton from Delaware and Bolling v. Sharpe from Washington, D.C. All were sponsored by the NAACP.

The Court heard the cases in spring 1953 but could not decide and asked for rehearing in the autumn, with attention to whether the Fourteenth Amendment prohibited separate public schools. On 17 May 1954 it gave a unanimous 9–0 decision in a single opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren. It found the historical sources on the Amendment of 1868 inconclusive.

Many white Southerners called the day a Black Monday, and the Deep South made no move to comply. Senator Harry F. Byrd's plan of massive resistance and, in September 1957, the blocking of the Little Rock Nine by Arkansas governor Orval Faubus led President Dwight D. Eisenhower to send the 101st Airborne Division. The Court reaffirmed Brown in Cooper v. Aaron. In Mississippi, fear of violence kept anyone from bringing a desegregation suit for nine years, and Medgar Evers, who sued in 1963, was murdered.
Black teachers and principals were fired or laid off in large numbers, and private segregation academies took at least half a million white students from public schools between 1964 and 1975.
bruchsal: Bruchsal lies at the western edge of the Kraichgau, about 20 kilometres north-east of Karlsruhe, on the Saalbach, a small tributary of the Rhine. Excavations show a Neolithic settlement on the Michelsberg in Untergrombach as early as 4000 BCE, and the oldest settlement found in the centre dates to about 640 CE. The town is first mentioned in documents in 976, and in October 980 Otto II and his court stayed for several days at the king's palace there.

In 1056 Henry III gave Bruchsal to Konrad I, bishop of Speyer, and it remained part of the diocese until the German Mediatisation. It was first called a city in 1248. The first Bundschuh peasant revolt, led by Joß Fritz of Untergrombach, chose it as its target in 1502; the authorities seized the leaders, and ten were beheaded in the palace courtyard. In 1689 the French general Duras bombarded the town and destroyed it, leaving only 130 residents.

Cardinal Damian Hugo von Schönborn became bishop in 1719 and from 1722 had a new baroque palace built, the work in part of Balthasar Neumann, whose central staircase is regarded as one of the most successful designs for a baroque staircase. After the Mediatisation the bishopric's property passed to the House of Baden.

In 1938 the Nazis destroyed the synagogue built in 1881, and the Jewish population was deported. On 1 March 1945 Allied bombers struck the town, killing about 1,000 people and destroying the entire inner city and the palace. American forces took Bruchsal without resistance on 2 April 1945.

The palace was rebuilt as a museum, with the central block reconstructed into the 1970s, though the church wing was given a modern design. The staircase largely survived. It houses a branch of the State Museum of Baden, including the German Music Box Museum. Bruchsal became a Große Kreisstadt in 1956 and since 1973 has belonged to the district of Karlsruhe, in which it is the largest city.
bruges: Bruges is the capital and largest city of the province of West Flanders, in the northwest of Belgium. The earliest mention of the name is as Brugis in an inventory of Saint Bavo's Abbey compiled between 851 and 864, and the name is more likely derived from a Scandinavian word for a quay or jetty than from the word for a bridge. The first fortifications were built after Julius Caesar's conquest of the Menapii, and Count Baldwin I of Flanders reinforced the Roman works during the raids of the ninth century.

Bruges became the capital of the County of Flanders in 1089 and received its city charter on 27 July 1128. The tidal inlet called the Zwin was crucial to its commerce. Merchants of Bruges developed new forms of merchant capitalism, including bills of exchange and letters of credit. The first Genoese merchant fleet arrived in 1277, and the Bourse opened in 1309, probably the first stock exchange in the world. The population reached at least 46,000 around 1350.

In 1297 Bruges surrendered to the French king. On 18 May 1302, in the Bruges Matins, the local militia massacred the French garrison, and the Flemish towns won the Battle of the Golden Spurs near Kortrijk on 11 July. In the fifteenth century Jan van Eyck and Hans Memling lived and worked there, and William Caxton published the first book printed in English in the city. From about 1500 the Zwin began silting up, and the secession of the Spanish Netherlands in 1584 led to the city's final decline, as Antwerp overtook it.

The historic centre, about 430 hectares, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000. The Belfry, a thirteenth-century tower with a carillon of 47 bells, belongs to the listing of the Belfries of Belgium and France. The Church of Our Lady has a brick spire 115.6 metres high, and the Basilica of the Holy Blood houses a relic said to have been brought after the Second Crusade. The city's port is Zeebrugge.
brugg: Brugg is a town in the canton of Aargau and the seat of its district, about 16 km from Aarau, 28 km from Zürich and 45 km from Basel. The name is the Swiss German word for bridge. The Habsburgs founded the medieval town at the narrowest point of the Aare on the Swiss Plateau, and the river runs through its old town, dividing the municipality into the Swiss Plateau on the southern bank and the beginnings of the Jura on the north.

In 58 BCE or shortly after, the Helvetii founded or refounded Vindonissa in what is now neighbouring Windisch. The name Bruggo is first documented in 1064, though the date is contentious, since the source was first drawn up in 1160. The Black Tower, the oldest standing structure in the old town, was built at the end of the 12th century. Before the Habsburgs moved to Austria, Brugg was the centre of their territory.

In 1415 Frederick IV fell into disfavour at the Council of Constance after helping Pope John XXIII to flee, and Emperor Sigismund asked the Swiss to take Aargau. The people of Brugg let Bern's troops in without resistance, so Bern left the town alone. It remained a subject territory of Bern until Napoleon's invasion in 1798, as a municipal town with more autonomy than comparable towns. An electric plant opened in 1892 and industry grew. Altenburg was merged into Brugg on 1 January 1901, although its town meeting had voted 42 to 2 against.

Brugg has 12,738 inhabitants. It is home to the Swiss Farmers' Union and a campus of the University of Applied Sciences and Arts Northwestern Switzerland. The Vindonissa museum, the Black Tower, the Schlössli Altenburg and the Reformed City Church are heritage sites of national significance. The educational reformer Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi died there in 1827.
bruneck: Bruneck, in Italian Brunico, is the largest city of the Puster Valley in the Italian province of South Tyrol. It stands in a wide valley at the confluence of the Ahr and the Rienz, about 35 km east of Brixen and 70 km from the regional capital Bolzano. To the south rises the Kronplatz massif, part of the Dolomites, with a popular ski area. According to the 2024 census, 78.71 percent of the population speak German as their first language, 19.31 percent Italian and 1.98 percent Ladin.

The Puster Valley was the main road connecting northern Italy with the Danube area. In 1091 the countship of Pustrissa passed from Henry IV to Bishop Altvino of Brixen. The town was probably named after its founder, the prince-bishop Bruno von Kirchberg, and appears as Bruneke in a deed of 23 February 1256, when it consisted of two rows of houses forming a narrow lane. In the turbulent interregnum after the death of Emperor Frederick II in 1250 the prince-bishop had a fortress built above the town, first mentioned in 1276. Prince-Bishop Albert von Enn enlarged it and completed the town walls and moat by 1336.

In the 14th and 15th centuries brisk trade between Augsburg and Venice passed through the valley, and goods were often stored in Bruneck, bringing prosperity. The Puster Valley painting school was founded then, and the masters Michael and Friedrich Pacher studied there. In 1500 the valley was reunited with Tyrol through a contract between the house of Habsburg and the counts of Görz, but the town remained an episcopal possession. On 11 April 1723 the worst fire in its history destroyed most of the town. After the First World War Bruneck became part of Italy.

After the Second World War industrial zones and department stores brought growth, and in the 1960s tourism led to many new hotels. The town depends on manufacturing and services, and the Kronplatz ski resort is its main attraction.
brunhilda-of-austrasia: Brunhilda was possibly born about 543 in Toledo, the Visigothic capital, the younger of two daughters of Athanagild and Goiswintha, and was brought up there as an Arian Christian. In 567 she married Sigebert I of Austrasia, a grandson of Clovis I, who had sent an embassy to Toledo with gifts, and she converted to Catholicism.

Her sister Galswintha then married Sigebert's brother Chilperic I of Neustria, who soon tired of her. In 568 Galswintha was strangled in her bed, and Chilperic married his mistress Fredegund. Fredegund is said to have had her murdered. The hatred between the two queens led to war, and the two queens persuaded their husbands to fight. Sigebert was besieging Tournai when Fredegund hired assassins who killed Sigebert with poisoned daggers. Brunhilda was captured and imprisoned at Rouen, where she briefly married Merovech, Chilperic's son, a marriage that was against canon law since she was his aunt.

Brunhilda won the regency of Austrasia for her son Childebert II against fierce resistance from the nobles and ruled until he came of age in 583. She repaired Roman roads, built churches and abbeys, reorganised the royal finances and restructured the army, which antagonised nobles whose authority she curbed. After Childebert's death in 596 she governed Austrasia and Burgundy for her grandsons Theudebert II and Theuderic II. In 599 Theudebert exiled her, and she took refuge with Theuderic, who fell under her influence and went to war with his brother.

In her later years she displayed ruthlessness. Desiderius, Bishop of Vienne, accused her publicly of incest and cruelty, and in 612 she hired three assassins to murder him. She exiled Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil, to Italy, where he founded Bobbio.

When Theuderic died, Brunhilda became regent for his young son Sigebert II. The mayors Warnachar and Rado abandoned her and joined Chlothar II, and on the Aisne several dukes deserted. She and Sigebert fled to Orbe but were caught near Lake Neuchâtel, and the boy was killed. Chlothar II accused her of the deaths of ten Frankish kings. According to the Liber Historiae Francorum she was led through the army on a camel and torn apart by wild horses. She had founded the abbey of St Martin at Autun in 602 and was buried there. Her name survives in the Chaussée Brunehaut, roads in northern France and south-western Belgium.
bruno-the-great: Bruno was born in May 925, the youngest son of King Henry the Fowler and Matilda of Ringelheim. While he was still a child it was decided that he should follow a clerical career, and in the early 940s he was educated at Trier by the leading scholar Israel the Grammarian. In 951 his brother Otto I appointed him archchaplain.

In 953 the archbishopric of Cologne fell vacant just when Conrad the Red, Otto's son-in-law and Duke of Lotharingia, had joined a rebellion against Otto. By appointing Bruno, Otto gained a powerful ally against Conrad, since much of Lotharingia fell under the archdiocese of Cologne. The rebellion had collapsed by the following year, and Otto deposed Conrad and made Bruno duke of Lotharingia in his place. Bruno was almost the last duke of the whole of Lotharingia, for in 959 two local nobles, Godfrey and Frederick, were appointed margraves of Lower and Upper Lotharingia, and both were recognised as dukes after his death.

As archbishop and duke, a combination that his biographer Ruotger called archduke, Bruno was the most powerful man after Otto. After the deaths of Louis IV of France in 954 and of Hugh the Great in 956, he acted as regent of West Francia, being brother-in-law to both and maternal uncle to their heirs, King Lothair and Hugh Capet. From 962 he was also Otto's regent in Germany while Otto was in Italy. Otto gave Bruno and his successors in Cologne royal privileges: the right to build fortifications, hold markets, strike coins and collect taxes and tolls.

Bruno died in Reims in 965 and was buried in St Pantaleon, the Benedictine monastery he had founded just outside Cologne. His court was the main intellectual and artistic centre of Germany in his time. Ratherius and Liutprand of Cremona spent time there, and many of the next generation of German ecclesiastical leaders were educated there. In the city he built a palace, extended the cathedral, brought the area between the old Roman walls and the Rhine within the fortifications and founded churches.

He was venerated at St Pantaleon throughout the Middle Ages. He was beatified in 1870 and canonised in 1895. The historian Jonathan Wright places the promotion of his cult against the background of the Kulturkampf, as an effort to preserve the Catholic identity of Cologne into the German Empire, in which Protestant states dominated.
brusilov-offensive: Under the Chantilly Agreement of December 1915, Russia, France, Britain and Italy committed to simultaneous attacks on the Central Powers in the summer of 1916. In March the Russians had launched the disastrous Lake Naroch offensive at French request, in which the Germans suffered only one fifth as many casualties as the Russians. Meanwhile the Austro-Hungarians were preparing to knock Italy out of the war and had moved experienced divisions from the Eastern Front to the Alps, replacing them with largely inexperienced recruits.

At a war council in April 1916, General Aleksei Brusilov proposed a large offensive by his Southwestern Front against the Austro-Hungarian forces in Galicia. General Alexei Evert, commander of the Western Army Group, favoured a defensive strategy, but Tsar Nicholas II approved the plan, though supporting offensives by the neighbouring fronts were denied. On 26 May, answering Italian pleas, the Tsar ordered the offensive accelerated.

Brusilov brought up reserves to the front line, dug trenches to within 100 metres of the Austro-Hungarian positions and tunnelled beneath his own barbed wire. Instead of massed formations, each army attacked along a sector about 15 km wide, in waves led by two reinforced infantry corps. The attack opened on 4 June with heavy artillery fire that opened breaches in the Austro-Hungarian defences, coordinated in advance with the infantry. Within four days the Austro-Hungarian 4th Army fell from 117,800 men to about 35,000, Lutsk was taken, and by 14 June Austro-Hungarian losses amounted to 205,000, of which 150,000 were prisoners.

The Russians captured Czernowitz on 17 June and Kolomea on 18 June. Erich von Falkenhayn organised German divisions for a counterattack near Kovel, and after Evert's belated offensive in July failed, the Russians turned to Kovel again. Brusilov halted the attempt on 9 August. Attacks continued until the autumn rains, which turned the roads to mud, but added mostly to the casualty lists.

The offensive forced Germany to halt its attack on Verdun and move considerable forces east, and it persuaded Romania to enter the war on the side of the Entente. Afterwards the Austro-Hungarian army had increasingly to rely on German support. John Keegan wrote that, by the scale used in the trench fighting of the First World War, it was the largest victory on any front since the trench lines were dug on the Aisne two years earlier.

The Russian army never again launched an offensive of the same scale, and many historians hold that its casualties contributed significantly to its collapse the following year. Russian casualties are put between 500,000 and 1,000,000. Brusilov used smaller specialised units to attack weak points, a departure from the human wave attacks that had dominated until then. The Germans used similar infiltration tactics to great effect in the Spring Offensive of 1918.
brussels: Brussels lies in the north-central part of Belgium, on the Brabantian Plateau, about 45 km south of Antwerp and 50 km north of Charleroi. The river Senne, now almost completely covered, cuts the city from east to west, and the Sonian Forest rises on its southeastern side. The most common theory derives the name from the Old Dutch Bruocsella, meaning a settlement in the marsh. Saint Vindicianus, Bishop of Cambrai, made the first recorded reference to the place, as Brosella, in 695, when it was still a hamlet.

Lambert I, Count of Louvain, gained the County of Brussels around 1000 by marriage. The town stood on the Senne on an important trade route between Bruges, Ghent and Cologne, and became a commercial centre specialised in the textile trade. It grew to about 30,000 people, and the marshes were drained. In 1183 the Counts of Leuven became Dukes of Brabant, whose duchy was part of the Holy Roman Empire. After Charles the Bold of Burgundy died in 1477, his daughter Mary of Burgundy, born in Brussels, married Maximilian I, bringing the Low Countries under Habsburg rule, and Brussels flourished as the capital of the Burgundian Netherlands.

The Belgian Revolution began in Brussels in 1830 after a performance of Auber's opera La Muette de Portici at the Royal Theatre of La Monnaie. The city became the capital of the new nation, and Leopold I, the first King of the Belgians, took the throne on 21 July 1831. From 1871 many Paris Communards found asylum there, and Victor Hugo and Karl Marx were among earlier exiles. French gradually replaced Dutch as the main language. Brussels hosted world's fairs in 1910, 1935 and 1958.

The Brussels-Capital Region, formed on 18 June 1989 after a constitutional reform, is one of Belgium's three federated regions and an officially bilingual enclave within Flanders, with a population of over 1.2 million. The Belgian Constitution names the City of Brussels as the capital. Brussels is the de facto capital of the European Union and hosts NATO's headquarters. Its landmarks include the Grand-Place, Manneken Pis and the Atomium.
brussels-agreement-2013: After the Kosovo War and the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia in 1999, Kosovo, then part of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was placed under United Nations administration by Security Council Resolution 1244. Kosovo declared independence unilaterally in 2008, but Serbia held that it remained part of its territory. Dialogue between the two, mediated by the European Union, began in March 2011, and Serbia was not obliged to recognise Kosovo during the process. Normalising relations with neighbours is a key condition for states seeking to join the European Union.

Ten rounds of talks were held at the office of the European External Action Service in Brussels, chaired for two years by the EU High Representative Catherine Ashton and then by Federica Mogherini. The negotiations for the agreement were led by the prime ministers Ivica Dačić of Serbia and Hashim Thaçi of Kosovo. United States diplomats supported the dialogue. The agreement, formally the First Agreement of Principles Governing the Normalisation of Relations, was signed on 19 April 2013.

The two-page text has 15 paragraphs. The first six concern the establishment, scope and functions of a planned Community of Serb Municipalities. Paragraphs 7 to 9 provide for a single police force for all of Kosovo, including the north, the Kosovo Police, whose regional commander for the Serb-majority areas was to be a Kosovo Serb chosen from a list put forward by those municipalities. All judicial matters were to come under Kosovo law, with Kosovo Serbs forming the majority of certain panels and a panel of the Mitrovica District Court sitting in North Mitrovica. Municipal elections were to be held throughout Kosovo under Kosovo law, and in paragraph 14 each side undertook not to block the other's progress towards the European Union.

The agreement brought Serbia close to EU accession talks and Kosovo to a Stabilisation and Association Agreement, signed in October 2015. Further accords followed on the judiciary in February 2015, on energy and telecommunications, and on 25 August 2015 on an Association of Serbian Communities; Kosovo received the dialling code +383, in use from December 2016.

In Belgrade protesters denounced the agreement as an endorsement of Kosovo's independence, and the scholars Smilja Avramov and Elena Guskova argued that it violated the Constitution of Serbia and the United Nations Charter. The Assembly of Kosovo ratified it as an international agreement; the National Assembly of Serbia did not, and in December 2014 Serbia's constitutional court called the question political, not legal. On 24 March 2022 Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić declared that the agreement no longer existed.
bryan-chamorro-treaty: The Liberal president José Santos Zelaya López had angered the United States by negotiating with France, Germany and Japan to revive the proposed Nicaragua Canal, a possible rival to the newly built Panama Canal. The United States then backed a Conservative insurgency led by Emiliano Chamorro and Juan José Estrada with arms, funds, troops and warships, forcing Zelaya and then Jose Madriz to flee. Conservative governments followed under Estrada and then Adolfo Díaz.

When General Luis Mena persuaded the National Assembly to name him Díaz's successor, the United States invaded and occupied Nicaragua, remaining from 1912 to 1933. It wrote a new constitution and supported a series of Conservative governments, while Mena's rebellion was carried on by other leaders for decades.

The treaty was signed on 5 August 1914. The United States acquired in perpetuity the rights to any canal built through Nicaragua, a renewable 99-year option to establish a naval base in the Gulf of Fonseca, and a renewable 99-year lease on the Great and Little Corn Islands in the Caribbean, in return for $3 million. Most of that sum was paid back to American creditors by the United States officials who ran Nicaragua's finances. The Wilson administration added a provision close in wording to the Platt Amendment, which would have authorised military intervention, but the Senate opposed it and it was dropped before ratification on 19 June 1916.

El Salvador and Costa Rica contested the naval base provision, and the Central American Court of Justice found in their favour. The United States ignored the ruling, which contributed significantly to the court's collapse in 1918. In time the United States accepted that a canal through Nicaragua parallel to the Panama Canal was unlikely, and in 1970, at Nicaragua's request, the governments of Richard Nixon and Anastasio Somoza Debayle held a convention that abolished the treaty and all its provisions. By then it had served to keep Nicaragua, and any European power, from building a canal to compete with the one in Panama.
bryggen: Bryggen, meaning the dock, is also known as Tyskebryggen, the German dock. It is a series of Hanseatic commercial buildings on the eastern side of the Vågen harbour in Bergen. In the Middle Ages the area took in all the buildings between the sea and the road called Øvregaten, from Holmen in the north to Vågsbunnen in the south, and according to the sagas the city of Bergen was founded within it. One of the earliest pier constructions has been dated to around 1100.

In the 14th century a Kontor of the Hanseatic League was established at Bryggen. As Bergen developed into an important trading centre the wharfs were improved and the merchants of the Hanseatic League gradually took over the buildings. The warehouses stored goods, particularly stockfish from northern Norway and cereal from Europe. The Kontor's operations ended in 1754, when all the properties passed to Norwegian citizens.

Since most of Bergen's houses were wooden, the city suffered many fires. After one in 1702 damaged the Hanseatic buildings they were rebuilt, and about a quarter of what stands today dates from after that fire. Parts of Bryggen burned again in 1955. A thirteen-year archaeological excavation followed and revealed the everyday runic inscriptions known as the Bryggen inscriptions. The Bryggen museum was built in 1976 on part of the cleared site.

UNESCO listed Bryggen as a World Heritage Site in 1979 under criterion (iii), as a quarter of Hanseatic merchants that illustrates the use of space and dates back to the 14th century. Its notable houses include Bellgården, Svensgården, Enhjørningsgården, Bredsgården, Bugården and Engelgården, and the oldest and tallest building in the area is St Mary's Church. Bryggens Museum and the Hanseatic Museum are among those found there.
brzeg: Brzeg lies in Silesia, in the Opole Voivodeship of Poland, on the left bank of the Oder, between Opole to the east and Wrocław to the north-west. It stands on the Brzeg Plain, part of the Silesian Lowlands, whose fertile soil allowed early agriculture. The Latin name was Alta Ripa and the German Brieg; the name is derived from the Polish word brzeg, meaning shore, and older documents call it the city on the high banks of the Oder. Settlement in the area goes back to the Mesolithic, with the earliest signs between 8000 and 4200 BCE.
