In the years of gold mining it belonged to the Territory of New Guinea. The town is served by Bulolo Airport, whose strip was built in June 1930 and was first 1,150 yards long and 120 yards wide.

Dredging for gold began on 21 March 1932. The whole of No 1 dredge, weighing 1,100 tons, was carried to the field in pieces by air from the port of Lae; its largest single part, the main tumbler shaft, was 12 feet long and weighed 6,870 pounds. Work on No 2 dredge began before No 1 was finished, and in all eight dredges were built and worked, the last starting in 1939.

The war halted dredging in 1941, and it did not resume for six years. On 5 February 1942, at 11 in the morning, Bulolo was bombed by five twin-engine bombers. After the war production recovered: in 1952 the field yielded 122,035 ounces of gold, valued at £1,311,241, which was 77 per cent of the gold produced in New Guinea that year. As the gold ran out the dredges were abandoned, and they still lie along the bed of the river.

Bulolo became the headquarters of a company formed to exploit the pine forests of the valley, and the milling of timber went together with a wide scheme of replanting to keep up supplies. Since the 1950s a road along the Bulolo and Markham valleys has linked the town with Lae. Forestry, led by PNG Forest Products Limited, is its main industry, and an Insect Farming and Trading Agency promotes insect farming and conservation. In 2010 the town had an estimated 20,000 inhabitants.
buluggin-ibn-ziri: Buluggin was born in the region of Titteri, in present-day Algeria. While his father was emir of the central Maghreb, Buluggin founded the city of Algiers in 960 on the site of the Roman town of Icosium, and also Médéa and Miliana; he rebuilt villages destroyed in earlier revolts. Bologhine, a suburb of Algiers, is named after him. Little is known of his private life, though chroniclers say that before he ruled the Maghreb he had 400 concubines and seventeen children.

After Ziri ibn Manad was killed in 971 fighting Kharidjite Berber tribes, the caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah named Buluggin emir of the Maghreb on 2 October 972, adding the Zab and M'Sila to his father's lands. These honours provoked the jealousy of the Kutama. The Fatimids took their treasury and fleet with them to Egypt, so Buluggin's first task was to secure his own power, and the loss of the fleet ended effective control over the Kalbids in Sicily. He remained a tributary vassal of the Fatimids, surrounded by advisers who both supported and watched him.

Buluggin fought the Zenata and their allies, defeating the Maghrawa, the Hawwara, the Nefzawa and the Mazata, and resettled many prisoners at Ashir. The Maghrawa turned to the Umayyads of Córdoba for help. He took Fez, Sijilmasa and most of Morocco as far as the Atlantic, but turned back before Ceuta, which he judged impregnable as Zenata reinforcements arrived by sea from al-Andalus; Córdoba kept Ceuta and Tangier. In 977 the caliph al-Aziz Billah added Tripoli, Ajdabiya and Sirte to his charge, and he received the titles Abu al-Futuh, Father of Victories, and Sayf ad-Dawla, Sword of Empire.

In 979 Buluggin campaigned against the Barghawata, whose ruler had been proclaimed a prophet, and brought back so many captives as slaves that the people of Ifriqiya, who had never seen such numbers, were shocked when they were paraded through the streets. He died on 25 May 984 and was succeeded by his son al-Mansur, and the Zirid dynasty he founded went on ruling the region after him.
bumin-qaghan: Bumin Qaghan, whose personal name was Ashina Tumen, was the eldest son of the Göktürk chieftain Ashina Tuwu. Chinese sources call him Tumen, and Old Turkic inscriptions call him Bumin; the two names do not match phonetically, but they are taken to refer to the same person. Before founding the First Turkic Khaganate he led the Göktürks as a subordinate of the Rouran Khaganate, and he is also mentioned as a tumen, a commander of ten thousand, in Rouran service. Scholars have proposed several origins for the name, among them Iranian and Sogdian roots meaning earth or land, and the Sanskrit bhuman.

According to the History of the Northern Dynasties and the Zizhi Tongjian, Tumen's tribe began to rise in 545 and frequently raided the western frontier of Wei. Yuwen Tai, chancellor of Western Wei, sent the Sogdian An Nuopanto from Bukhara to seek a commercial relationship, and in 546 Tumen paid tribute to Western Wei. He later put down a revolt of the Tiele tribes against their Rouran overlords and accepted the surrender of over 50,000 households. The date is disputed: the Zizhi Tongjian places it in 551, but the historian Cen Zhongmian argued that it was earlier.

Tumen then asked the Rouran for a princess in marriage. The Rouran khagan, Yujiulü Anagui, refused and replied: You are my blacksmith slave. How dare you utter these words? Bumin killed the emissary and broke with the Rouran. In 551 Yuwen Tai sent Princess Changle of Western Wei to him. Diplomatic relations with China strengthened his authority, and he united the local Turkic tribes. In February or March 552 his army defeated Anagui's forces north of Huaihuang, and Anagui killed himself. Bumin proclaimed himself Illig Qaghan and made his wife qaghatun. Inscriptions of Bilge Qaghan and Kul Tigin say that Bumin and Istemi ruled the people by Turkic laws.

Bumin died within several months of proclaiming himself qaghan. Xue Zongzheng believes the cause was injuries from the war with the Rouran. His younger brother Istämi ruled the western parts of the khaganate. His sons Issik Qaghan, who reigned 552 to 553, and Muqan Qaghan, who reigned 553 to 572, followed him. The Ongin Inscription of the Second Khaganate mentions a Yamï Qağan whom some scholars, including Wilhelm Radloff, Josef Marquart and Takashi Ōsawa, identify with Bumin, though others, such as Gerard Clauson and Talat Tekin, have challenged this.
bunce-island: Bunce Island, also spelled Bence, Bense or Bance at different times, lies in the estuary of the Rokel River and Port Loko Creek, about 32 kilometres upriver from Freetown. It measures about 1,650 by 350 feet. Its value lay in its position at the limit of navigation for ocean-going ships in Africa's largest natural harbour, which made it a convenient base for European slave traders.

English traders first fortified the island around 1670, and the Royal African Company and the Gambia Adventurers operated the castle in its early years. In 1728 the Luso-African trader José Lopez da Moura, grandson of a Mane king, led a raid that destroyed it, and the island stood empty until the mid-1740s. Grant, Oswald and Company, founded by the Scottish merchants Richard Oswald and Alexander Grant, took over in 1748, and in 1785 the island passed to John and Alexander Anderson. French naval forces attacked the castle in 1695, 1704, 1779 and 1794, and the pirate Bartholomew Roberts in 1719 and 1720; it was rebuilt each time.

Afro-Portuguese and later Afro-English traders of families such as the Caulkers, Tuckers and Clevelands sold captives there, and ships came from London, Liverpool, Bristol, Newport, New London, Salem, New York, France and Denmark. Many captives were rice farmers taken to Charleston and Savannah, where planters prized their skills. Henry Laurens, later President of the Continental Congress, was the island's agent in Charleston, and after the war he was one of the American commissioners for the Treaty of Paris, across the table from Oswald, his friend of thirty years and the British chief negotiator. After Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807, the island served as a cotton plantation, trading post and sawmill, and was abandoned around 1840.

In 1948 Bunce Island became Sierra Leone's first protected historic site, and the physician and historian M.C.F. Easmon led an expedition that cleared, mapped and photographed the ruins. They include the remains of Bance Island House, the slave yard, two watchtowers, a gun emplacement for eight cannons, a powder magazine and the tombstones of slave traders. The anthropologist Joseph Opala's research linked the island to the Gullah people of the American Low Country.
bundela: According to the historian Jaswant Lal Mehta, the name Bundela comes from a goddess, Bind-bhasini Devi, believed to dwell on the Bindhachal, the northernmost part of the Vindhya ranges. The region the clan came to rule, Bundelkhand, was known in ancient times as the Chedi Kingdom.

Bundela legends tell how Sohanpal, the younger son of Arjunpal, ruler of Mahoni, won a kingdom of his own. His elder brother Birpal succeeded their father, and Sohanpal sought help from Naga, also called Hurmat Singh, the Khangar ruler of Kurar (Kundar), who demanded a marriage alliance in return. Sohanpal refused and escaped when Naga tried to detain him. Turned away by the Chauhans, the Salingars and the Kachwahas, he was finally helped by a Panwar chief, Panpal, and their joint army defeated Naga in 1288. Sohanpal killed the Khangar men of the fort, sparing the infants on condition that the Khangars serve the Bundelas, and became king of Kurar.

Over several generations cadet lines of the clan founded states across the region from the 16th century. Rudra Pratap Singh, who reigned from 1501 to 1531 and is said to have descended from Sohanpal, moved his capital from Garh Kundar to Orchha in 1531, and Orchha remained the parent Bundela kingdom. Datia separated from it in 1626, and Panna also broke away. After the death of Panna's founder Chhatrasal in 1731, the states of Ajaigarh, Bijawar and Charkhari separated from Panna. The rulers of Chhatarpur called their clan Panwar Bundela in their official records. The Bundela chiefs often fought one another, and the Mughals often took advantage of it.
bundelkhand: Bundelkhand is a geographical and cultural region in central and northern India, and also the name of a mountain range. It lies in the Vindhya Range and is bounded by rivers such as the Chambal and the Yamuna. It corresponds to the post-Vedic Chedi kingdom. The hilly region is now divided between the states of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, with the larger part in Madhya Pradesh. It stands on a plateau and is mainly dry, with a persistent shortage of water, but it is rich in minerals, grows wheat and pulses, and has forests of teak, bamboo and tendu. Its main rivers include the Betwa, Ken, Sindh and Dhasan.

The region was earlier known as Jejabhukti or Jejakabhukti, Jeja's province. According to the inscriptions of the Chandela dynasty, the name came from Jeja, the nickname of their ruler Jayashakti. The Chandelas ruled much of central India from the 9th to the 12th century and are best known for the temples of Khajuraho, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Their power declined, and they fell in 1182. The Khangar community then ruled parts of the region from the late 12th century to the mid-14th, from the fort at Garh Kundar. By the 14th century the Bundela dynasty had replaced them, and the region came to be called Bundelkhand after them.

Rajput clans became the raja rulers of the region, later submitted to the Mughal Empire and went on expanding east into the 19th century. Lesser Rajput branches, the thakurs, were the main landlords over farming castes such as Kurmis, Lodhis, Ahirs and Gujars. After the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 the Bundelas renounced Mughal authority. Before British rule the region held princely states such as Orchha, Datia and Samthar, and Damoh and Ramgarh were ruled by Lodhi Rajputs. Chhatrasal Bundela fought the Mughal Empire and established his own kingdom in Bundelkhand.

Bundelkhand is a destination for visitors to Orchha, Khajuraho, Jhansi, Datia, Chanderi, Panna and Kalinjar, to the pilgrimage centre of Chitrakoot, and to Panna National Park. A movement for a separate Bundelkhand state, or for the region's development, has existed since the early 1960s. In 2011 the Uttar Pradesh Council of Ministers proposed splitting the state into four parts, one of them Bundelkhand. Jules Verne's novel Around the World in Eighty Days sets the rescue of Princess Aouda in Bundelcund.
bundesrat-german-empire: The Bundesrat of the North German Confederation passed into the newly united Germany with little change. Emperor Wilhelm I wished to rename it the Reichsrat, but his chancellor, Otto von Bismarck, persuaded him that the federal character of the empire should go on being emphasised, and the name stayed. Because the constitution provided for no constitutional court, Bismarck also gave the chamber quasi-judicial tasks, among them settling disputes between the states and constitutional disputes within them.

Its members were appointed by the state governments, and each state cast its votes as a block; a simple majority of the votes cast carried a motion, with the chancellor's presidential vote deciding a tie. The chamber shared legislation with the Reichstag on an equal footing, issued ordinances and administrative regulations, joined in declarations of war and decided with the emperor on dissolving the Reichstag. No member could sit in the Reichstag.

Prussia's 17 votes never changed, though its share fell from 40% in the North German Confederation to just under 28% in 1911, when Alsace–Lorraine received three votes and the total reached 61. Since fourteen votes against were enough to block a constitutional amendment, Prussia alone could do so. The chancellor, almost always also minister president of Prussia, controlled those votes and in practice often introduced proposals. Bavaria chaired the Foreign Affairs Committee and Prussia the others. The chamber met in private, and the public showed little interest in it.

On 4 August 1914 the Reichstag unanimously passed the War Enabling Act, which transferred part of its legislative rights to the Bundesrat for economic measures. The act was a breach of the constitution, but the Bundesrat used it with moderation and submitted its emergency decrees to the Reichstag, which seldom objected.

In the revolution of 1918–1919 the Council of the People's Deputies under Friedrich Ebert saw no place for the Bundesrat as a combined executive and legislative body, but did not wish to anger the state governments by abolishing it. A decree of 14 November 1918 left it only its administrative powers. The Reichsrat of the Weimar Republic first met on 14 August 1919.
bundesrat-germany: The Bundesrat's predecessor was the Federal Convention, or diet, of the German Confederation of 1815 to 1866, which consisted of representatives of the member states and was chaired by the Austrian representative. The term Bundesrath appeared in a proposed reform act of 1863. When the North German Confederation was founded on 1 July 1867, its Bundesrath, expressly modelled on the old diet, served as one legislative body beside the elected Reichstag. It kept its name when the Confederation became the German Empire in 1871.

The imperial Bundesrat could initiate legislation, and every bill of the Reichstag, the budget included, needed its consent. With the Emperor's agreement it could dissolve the Reichstag, which made it in theory the more powerful body. Its delegates were usually high-ranking civil servants, and the chancellor chaired it without being a member.

In the revolution of 1918 the Council of People's Representatives limited the Bundesrat to administrative functions. Under the Weimar Constitution of 11 August 1919 it was replaced by the Reichsrat, which could no longer initiate legislation and could only veto bills, a veto the Reichstag could overrule only by a two-thirds majority. A law of 14 February 1934 abolished the Reichsrat.

After the Second World War the chamber was re-established under the Basic Law as the Bundesrat, and it held its first session on 7 September 1949. In power it stands between the strong imperial Bundesrat and the weak Reichsrat. It has the right of legislative initiative and an absolute veto over bills that directly affect the states; other vetoes the Bundestag can overrule. It met in the Bundeshaus in Bonn, in a wing built for it, and moved to the former Prussian House of Lords in Berlin in 2000, a year after the Bundestag, keeping Bonn as a second seat.

The Bundesrat is not elected and is not a parliamentary chamber. It is an assembly of delegations from the sixteen state governments, usually the minister-president and cabinet ministers, bound to act according to their government's agreements. Each state casts its votes together, and none has fewer than three or more than six, in a degressive proportion to population, so that smaller states have more votes than strict proportion would give them. The presidency rotates annually among the minister-presidents.

It cannot amend a bill. An approval bill, which directly affects the states, needs a majority of all possible votes, while an objection bill becomes law unless the Bundesrat objects within 14 days. A mediation committee of equal numbers from both chambers negotiates when the two disagree. The Bundesrat also elects half the judges of the Federal Constitutional Court with the Bundestag and holds powers in a legislative emergency.
bungo-province: Bungo Province was a province of Japan in the area of eastern Kyūshū, corresponding to most of modern Ōita Prefecture, except what are now the cities of Nakatsu and Usa. It bordered Hyūga to the south, Higo and Chikugo to the west, and Chikuzen and Buzen to the north. In the Gokishichidō system it belonged to the Saikaidō circuit, and under the Engishiki classification it was ranked a superior country in importance and a far country in distance from the capital.

During the Kofun period the area had three main power centres, on the Kunisaki Peninsula and around what are now Ōita District and Hita District, each ruled by a kuni no miyatsuko. By the Asuka period it had been consolidated into a single Toyo Province, which was divided into Bungo and Buzen after the Taika Reforms and the establishment of the Ritsuryō system in 701. The Bungo no Kuni Fudoki, compiled in the first half of the 8th century, is one of only five fudoki in Japan that survive in almost complete form.

In 1185, after the Heike clan was destroyed in the Genpei War, Minamoto no Yoritomo established the Ōtomo clan as shugo over Bungo to suppress pro-Taira samurai in Kyushu. The Ōtomo ruled the area from the Kamakura period into the Muromachi period and expanded their control into neighbouring provinces. In the Sengoku period Portuguese traders brought firearms and Christianity, and the Funai area became a centre of Jesuit activity. Ōtomo Sōrin met Francis Xavier in 1551 and later converted. The Jesuit records call him the King of Bungo. He sent embassies to Goa in the 1550s and the Tenshō embassy to Rome in 1582, and he forced his subjects to convert and ordered the destruction of Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines.

In 1578 Sōrin came into conflict with the Shimazu clan to the south and, after a series of defeats, turned to Toyotomi Hideyoshi for help. After Hideyoshi's conquest of Kyūshū in 1587, Sōrin's son Ōtomo Yoshimune was restored to control of Bungo. Following Hideyoshi's expulsion of missionaries he recanted his baptism and began a campaign to exterminate Christianity in the province. He was later accused of cowardice during the Japanese invasions of Korea and was dispossessed, and Bungo was divided into small holdings.

In the Edo period Bungo was not dominated by a single daimyō. It was divided between territory governed directly by the Tokugawa shogunate and a number of small feudal domains. After the Meiji Restoration each domain briefly became a prefecture, and on 25 December 1871 they were merged to form Ōita Prefecture. A government assessment of the early Meiji period counted 1,812 villages in the province, with a total kokudaka of 466,611 koku.
burakumin: The name burakumin means hamlet people, from buraku, which originally meant hamlet or village. Its roots lie in the status distinctions of pre-modern Japan. The Ritsuryō codes of the late 7th and early 8th centuries divided the population into ryōmin, good people, and senmin, base people, a class that included imperial tomb guards and slaves. This made slavery hereditary and tied baseness to the polluting nature of death. In the Heian period, ideas of ritual pollution (kegare) from Shinto and Buddhist belief grew stronger, and the Engishiki code of 927 set periods of impurity after contact with death, birth and blood. Popular theories that the outcastes had Korean ancestry are generally after-the-fact rationalisations: the outcastes as a whole are ethnically Japanese.

In the Middle Ages the groups were eta, associated with butchery and leatherwork, hinin, beggars and the sick, and sanjo, such as garden sweepers and performers. In the Sengoku period warlords organised leather workers to secure supplies for armour.

The Meiji government issued the Senmin Abolition Edict, known as the Liberation Edict, on 28 August 1871. It abolished the titles eta and hinin and declared these people commoners. Many commoners reacted with hostility, and riots included the eta hunts. In June 1873 the Takeyari Ikki in Fukuoka Prefecture involved up to 300,000 people and destroyed over 2,000 houses belonging to burakumin. The family registry, the koseki, marked former outcastes as new commoners and let their ancestry be traced.

Movements arose to fight discrimination, notably the National Levellers Association (Suiheisha) in the 1920s. After 1945 the Buraku Liberation National Committee was formed, and the 1946 constitution guaranteed equality in Article 14. Living conditions stayed dire, and after the All Romance Incident of 1951 activists pressed for government action. The Special Measures Law expired in March 2002, ending the era of government-led Dōwa projects.

A 1993 government survey counted a Dōwa-related population of 892,751 in 4,442 designated communities, most in western Japan, and found that one third of those surveyed had experienced discrimination, chiefly in marriage or employment. Wider estimates of the total population range from 1.5 to 3 million. Because burakumin are not physically distinguishable, discrimination rests on ancestry and place of residence, and some people do not know their descent. Some scholars, including Timothy D. Amos, argue that the modern burakumin identity is a recent, constructed category. The Buraku Liberation League favours open challenge, while the Jiyū Dōwa Kai, founded in 1986, argues for silence.
burana-tower: The Burana Tower is a large minaret in the Chüy Valley of northern Kyrgyzstan, about 80 km east of Bishkek and near the town of Tokmok. Together with grave markers, some earthworks and the remnants of a castle and three mausoleums, it is all that remains of the ancient city of Balasagun. The Karakhanids established the city at the end of the 9th century. The tower itself was built in the 11th century and served as a template for other minarets. An external staircase and a steep winding stair inside allow visitors to climb to the top, and it is counted among the oldest architectural constructions in Central Asia.

Over the centuries a number of earthquakes damaged the tower. The last major one, in the 15th century, destroyed the top half and left it at its present height of 25 m. A restoration project in the 1970s repaired its foundation and the west-facing side, which was in danger of collapse. The whole site, including the mausoleums, the castle foundations and the grave markers, now functions as a museum, and a small building holds historical information and artefacts found at the site and in the surrounding regions.

A legend is told about the tower. A khan whose daughter had just been born invited fortune tellers and wise men to foretell her future, and one old man said that she would die of a spider bite on her sixteenth birthday. To protect her the khan built a tall tower, where she lived alone, and servants brought her food in a basket up a ladder after thorough inspection so that no spider could enter. On her sixteenth birthday the khan brought her a basket of fruit, but a poisonous spider had hidden in it, and it bit and killed her when she reached for a fruit. The khan wept so loudly, the story says, that part of the tower collapsed.
burao: The Somali word burco describes open, elevated land with soft, rich soil, and the Burao area is considered fertile. The city began in the late 18th century as a well, called Ceel-Gooni, used by nomads of the surrounding area. A town grew around it, and because of the water along the dry valley it became a small inland market linking the port of Berbera with the interior and offering trading facilities to the region's nomadic population.

For much of the 19th century Burao was the capital of the Habr Yunis Sultanate, ruled at different times by Sultan Nur Ahmed Aman, Sultan Awad Deria and Sultan Madar Hersi. The explorer Frank Linsly James, a guest of Sultan Awad Deria in 1884, described a display by Habr Yunis horsemen in the bed of the Togdheer River. British forces burned the settlement to the ground in 1900, and the modern town was re-established in 1910. The Dervish movement was founded at Burao in 1899, when Mohammed Abdullah Hassan and his followers assembled there with other clans and declared open hostility to the British.

In 1922 the people of Burao rose against a heavy tax. In the disturbances Captain Allan Gibb, the district commissioner, was shot dead, and aircraft of the Royal Air Force, requested from Aden, bombed the town with incendiaries and burned the settlement to the ground; the British afterwards abandoned the tax policy. In July 1945 the religious leader Sheikh Bashir led a rebellion of Habr Je'lo tribesmen that began with an attack on Burao's prison; he was killed in the mountains of Bur Dhab, and a secondary school in Burao bears his name. In the 1950s the expanding livestock trade, with animals exported to Saudi Arabia, made Burao the second largest city of the protectorate.

In May 1988 the Somali National Movement captured Burao in about two hours, and the Somali army replied with heavy artillery, tanks and aerial bombardment. Reports describe killings of civilians, and the city was razed and most of its inhabitants fled to Ethiopia. In May 1991 a Central Committee of the movement met at Burao and agreed to revoke the union with the Somali Democratic Republic, forming the Republic of Somaliland, with Abdirahman Ahmed Ali Tuur elected to govern for two years.

Burao is the capital of the Togdheer region and the second largest city of Somaliland. Its main residents are the Habr Je'lo, Habr Yonis, Isamusa and Arap, all subdivisions of the Isaaq clan-family. The city is divided into four wards: Mohamed Ali, Farah Omar, Lihle and Sheikh Bashir.
burchard-ii-duke-of-swabia: Burchard was a son of Burchard I of Swabia, of the Hunfriding family, and was also Count of Raetia. His family came from Franconia, and he founded the convent of St Margarethen at Waldkirch to extend its influence into the Rhineland. When his father was arrested and executed for high treason in 911, Burchard and his wife Regelinda, daughter of Count Eberhard I of Zürich, went to Italy, either banished by Count Erchanger or in voluntary exile among relatives beyond the Alps.

Around 913 he returned and took control of his father's property. In 915 he fought alongside Erchanger and Arnulf, Duke of Bavaria, at Wahlwies, after which Erchanger was proclaimed duke. Following Erchanger's execution on 21 January 917, Burchard seized all his lands and was recognised as duke. When King Rudolph II of Upper Burgundy took the county of Zürich in 919 and invaded the region of Konstanz, then the practical capital of the duchy, Burchard defeated him at Winterthur and imposed his own territorial claims.

In the same year he recognised the newly elected king of Germany, Henry the Fowler, duke of Saxony, who granted him the rights of taxation and of investing bishops and abbots in his duchy. In 922 Burchard married his daughter Bertha to Rudolph, confirming their peace, and went with him to Italy, where opponents of Emperor Berengar had elected Rudolph king.

After Berengar's death in 924, Hugh of Arles was elected by his partisans against Rudolph. Burchard attacked Novara, held by the troops of Lambert, Archbishop of Milan, and was killed there, probably on 29 April 926. His widow Regelinda married his successor, Herman I. Of their five children, Burchard III later became duke of Swabia, Gisela was abbess of Waldkirch and Adalric a monk at Einsiedeln. It has also been suggested that Burchard was the father of Theodoric of Wettin, and so the ancestor of the house of Wettin.
burchard-ii-of-halberstadt: Burchard of Veltheim came from the Veltheim noble family, possibly of Swabian origin, and was a nephew through his mother of the archbishops Anno II of Cologne and Werner of Magdeburg. In 1057 he became provost of the Collegiate Church of St. Simon and St. Jude at the Imperial Palace of Goslar, and two years later, through Anno's intervention, he succeeded Bishop Burchard I at Halberstadt.

In October 1062 a German-Italian synod at Augsburg sent him, then high in the favour of the Empress dowager Agnes of Poitou, to Rome to settle the disputed election between Pope Alexander II and the Antipope Honorius II. Although the German crown stood by Honorius, Burchard sided with Hildebrand and Alexander, who rewarded him with the pallium. He founded the Benedictine abbey of Huysburg in 1070 and consecrated the rebuilt cathedral of Halberstadt at Pentecost 1071, with King Henry IV present.

When the Saxon Rebellion broke out, Burchard joined the rebels. He witnessed the Treaty of Gerstungen in 1074, but on 13 July 1075 he was captured at Homburg an der Unstrut and handed over to Bishop Rupert of Bamberg. Banished to Hungary in 1076, he escaped and returned home. In the Investiture Controversy he supported every opponent of Henry IV, including the anti-kings Rudolf of Rheinfelden and Herman of Salm. Henry invaded the Halberstadt territory after 1085 and had him deposed at the synod of Mainz, but only briefly; on 5 June 1087 Burchard consecrated the church of Ilsenburg Abbey.

Burchard's last quarrel was with the Brunonid margrave Egbert II of Meissen, who sought to succeed Herman of Salm as anti-king. According to the Annalista Saxo, Egbert's troops ravaged the Halberstadt lands and the bishop turned to the Saxon nobles at Goslar for help. He was mortally wounded on 6 April 1088 and died the next day at the Ilsenburg monastery. Legend made him a friend of children, and as late as the early twentieth century children around Halberstadt sang a Low German rhyme asking Buko of Halberstadt to bring something to the child.
burchard-of-worms: Burchard came from a wealthy, well-connected family of northern Hesse; his older brother Franco was bishop of Worms before him, and his sister Mathilda became an abbess near Worms. As a boy he entered the monastic school of St. Florin or St. Kastor at Koblenz. Under Archbishop Willigis of Mainz he rose through the clerical grades and became provost of St. Victor in Mainz, where he founded a monastery with a cloister of canons that Willigis funded. When Franco died in 999, Emperor Otto III appointed Burchard to Worms in 1000, after the men he had first intended for it died.

His biographer describes Worms as in disrepair, troubled by robbers and wolves. Burchard rebuilt the city walls, founded monasteries and churches, and in a violent quarrel with Otto I, Duke of Carinthia, whom he accused of sheltering criminals, won the aid of Emperor Henry II; the duke's castle was dismantled and rebuilt as a monastery of Paul of Tarsus. He took in a child of the duke's family who became Emperor Conrad II. In 1016 he rebuilt the Cathedral of St. Peter, and he taught in its school. He died on 20 August 1025, leaving his sister a hair shirt and an iron chain.

Burchard compiled the Decretum with Bishop Walter of Speyer, Alpert of Metz and other clergy, drawing on the Old Testament, Augustine of Hippo, Gregory the Great, Isidore of Seville, Hrabanus Maurus and Julian of Toledo. Over 77 complete manuscripts survive, the earliest made at Worms under his supervision. Book 19, the Corrector, is a confessor's guide that is probably a 10th-century work he added. The Decretum was later supplanted by the Panormia of Ivo of Chartres and the Decretum of Gratian. From 1023 to 1025 he issued the Lex Familiae, 31 chapters of customary law for the free and unfree workers of the episcopal estate, on marriage, abduction, murder, theft and perjury.
burchard-of-wurzburg: Burchard, in German Burkard or Burkhard, was a Benedictine monk, possibly of noble birth, who was educated at Malmesbury Abbey. After the death of his parents he left England and, some time after 732, joined Boniface, who may have been a relative, in his missionary work. He lived for a while at the Abbey of St. Peter in Fritzlar, founded by Boniface, and later went as a missionary to Thuringia.

When Boniface organised the bishoprics of Middle Germany he placed Burchard over that of Würzburg. As was usual at the time, the appointment was approved by Carloman, mayor of the palace, who granted the diocese a number of endowments. Burchard officiated as a bishop at the consecration of Willibald of Eichstädt, and Pope Zachary confirmed the new see in 743.

Burchard took part in the first German council in 742 and in the general Council of the Franks in 747. The following year, as Boniface's envoy, he presented the council's results to Pope Zachary in Rome. In 750, with Fulrad of Saint-Denis, he brought Zachary the question of Pepin, whose answer was taken to justify the assumption of royal power by the Carolingians.

In 751 Burchard resigned his see in favour of Megingoz, a Benedictine monk of St. Peter's Abbey in Fritzlar, and withdrew to a life of solitude. In 752 he dedicated the Abbey of St. Andrew in Würzburg, later renamed St. Burchard's Abbey, and on 8 July 752 he brought the relics of Saint Kilian and his companions Saint Totnan and Saint Colman to Würzburg Cathedral, which was then dedicated to Kilian. He died in 753. His own relics were moved to the Abbey of St. Andrew in 986, and his feast day is 14 October.
burdur: Burdur stands on the shore of Lake Burdur in south-western Turkey. Habitation in the surrounding province goes back to 6500 BCE, and the earliest sign of settlement in the city itself dates to the Early Bronze Age. In antiquity the area belonged to the region of Pisidia. The city may have changed its location several times: the ancient town of Limnombria lay closer to the lake, and in the Byzantine period the city existed as Polydorion, from which the present name derives.

The urban history of Burdur is generally held to begin with the Turkish settlement that followed the Seljuq victory at Manzikert in 1071. Turks became the majority of the population after 1211, and the first settlement was moved uphill away from the lake because of malaria. Kilij Arslan II, the Seljuq sultan of Rum, imposed his rule in 1177, and the town was captured by the Mongol Empire in 1260. Trade through Antalya made it a commercial stop for tragacanth, wine, wax, wood and tar.

In 1300 the Hamidids under Dündar Bey took Burdur and built its Grand Mosque, around which the town developed. The Ilkhanate captured it in 1324, and Dündar Bey's son recovered it in 1328. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1330 and described a town of orchards and farms with a castle near the mosque and a guild of ahis controlling commerce and production. The Ottoman sultan Bayezid I took Burdur in 1391, and in 1478 it had four quarters, three Muslim and one Christian.

A small Greek population lived in the city until the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey, and an abandoned Greek church there has been turned into a museum with a large dinosaur fossil. Burdur has about 95 thousand inhabitants and is home to Mehmet Akif Ersoy University.
burebista: The area between the Danube, Tisza and Dniester rivers, roughly modern Romania, became home to Thracian peoples including the Getae and the Dacians around the 7th and 6th centuries BCE. The Getae lived in the lower Danube basin and traded with the Greek cities of the Black Sea coast, while the Dacians lived along the southern Carpathian Mountains, whose isolation helped them survive. From the 4th century to the middle of the 2nd century BCE La Tène Celts influenced them, introducing the potter's wheel, better metalworking and probably coinage. Before Burebista, Dacia had a succession of kings, among them Dromichaetes, Oroles and Rubobostes. Only a few ancient sources on Burebista survive, including Strabo, Jordanes and inscriptions from Balchik and Nesebar.

The date of his accession is debated among scholars. Burebista was the first king to unify the Dacian tribes, with the support of the religious establishment, and his realm was probably a weakly centralised state with a military organisation like that of the Hellenistic kingdoms; archaeologists disagree about how centralised it was. In the Orăștie Mountains he built stone hill forts at Costești, Blidaru, Piatra Roșie and Bănița, which show Greek military architecture.

He destroyed the Boii and Taurisci in the middle Danube early in his campaigns, then the Bastarnae, and probably conquered the Scordisci, and he raided Thrace, Roman Macedonia and Illyria. From about 55 BCE he took the Greek cities of the Black Sea coast, among them Olbia, Tyras, Histria, Tomis, Callatis, Odessos, Messembria, Apollonia and Dionysopolis.

An inscription of 48 BCE calls Akornion of Dionysopolis his friend and says he was sent to Pompey to seek the title king of kings for Burebista. In the Roman civil war Burebista backed Pompey, which made him an enemy of Julius Caesar, who planned a campaign against him. His force may have numbered up to 200,000 men, though it is disputed whether this was an army or all able-bodied men.

Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE, and Burebista was killed at about the same time in a plot by the Dacian aristocracy, who saw a centralised state as a threat to their privileges. His kingdom broke up. It was divided into four parts under the religious elite, and by the time of Augustus into five. Dacia was united again by Decebalus and ended as an independent kingdom after Trajan's conquest in 106 CE.

In the 1960s statues of Burebista and Decebalus were put up in Romania, and in 1980 the government marked the 2,050th anniversary of his state, a commemoration that the Ceaușescu regime used to legitimise its own rule. Historians have described the nationalist claim that Burebista's descendants are the true ancestors of the Romanians as an imaginary history.
burgan-field: The name can also mean Greater Burgan, a group of three closely spaced fields covering about 1,000 square kilometres: Burgan itself, about 500, Magwa, 180, and Ahmadi, 140, the last two on smaller domes to the north. Greater Burgan is the world's largest sandstone oil field. Burgan's structure is an elliptical dome cut by many radial faults, which with the Burgan Graben divide the reservoir into compartments and hold the oil in place.

The oil lies in four main horizons of Cretaceous age: the Wara sandstone, the Mauddud limestone and the Burgan Third and Fourth Sands, with most production historically from the middle unit of the Third Sand. Deeper reservoirs, the Ratawi and Minagish limestones and the Jurassic Marrat Formation, also hold oil.

A natural oil seep above the field was known in Neolithic times: bitumen on a reed boat found at As-Sabiyah in northern Kuwait, dated to 5000 BCE, has been traced to it. The subsurface reservoirs were discovered in February 1938, and the US and UK-owned Kuwait Oil Company began commercial production in 1946. In 1951 oil was also found in the deeper Minagish Oolite at Burgan and in Jurassic carbonates at Magwa. Output reached 2,400,000 barrels a day in 1972; by 1992 water had swept parts of the main sands.

In 1991, during the Gulf War, retreating Iraqi soldiers set the field on fire as a scorched-earth tactic. The smoke plume was about 50 kilometres wide and, seen from satellites, ran like a black snake through the desert parallel to the Persian Gulf. Red Adair's company put out 117 well fires and the Canadian firm Safety Boss 180. Declassified CIA documents of 1991 claimed that the reserves and production capacity were not significantly reduced, though three gathering stations were damaged beyond repair. Nearby, the 1st Marine Division destroyed 60 Iraqi tanks.

Estimates of the field's recoverable oil range from 66 to 75 billion barrels, though its reserve and production figures are uncertain and disputed. In 2010 the chief executive of the Kuwait Oil Company said that Burgan produced half of Kuwait's oil.
burgenland: From the fourth century BCE the area was dominated by Celts, and in the first century CE it became part of the Roman Empire, in the province of Pannonia. The Ostrogoths settled there in 380, and later it belonged in turn to the Huns, the Lombards, the Avars and the Frankish Empire. It remained the western frontier of the medieval Kingdom of Hungary until the sixteenth century. Most of its people were German-speaking, apart from Hungarian border guards, and in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries German Protestant refugees came, fleeing the suppression of the Reformation in Austrian lands.

According to the census of 1910, 74 per cent of the inhabitants spoke German, 15 per cent Croatian and 9 per cent Hungarian. The treaties of Saint Germain and Trianon assigned German West Hungary to Austria, and the Federal Constitutional Act of 25 January 1921 gave it the name Burgenland. When Austrian officials arrived on 28 August 1921, Hungarian irregulars under Pál Prónay prevented them. The Venice Protocol, mediated by Italy, ended the crisis: Hungary disarmed the irregulars in return for a plebiscite held in December in Sopron and eight villages, whose voters chose Hungary. The rest went to Austria, and its parliament chose Eisenstadt as capital in 1925.

Burgenland is the easternmost and least populous state of Austria, 166 km long from north to south and as little as 5 km wide at Sieggraben. Lake Neusiedl, Austria's largest lake, lies in the north, shared with Hungary. After the Anschluss in 1938 the state was dissolved; it was re-established on 1 October 1945 in the Soviet occupation zone, which ended in 1955. On 27 July 1989 the foreign ministers of Austria and Hungary cut the Iron Curtain at Klingenbach.
burghead: Burghead lies in Moray, about 13 kilometres north-west of Elgin, mostly on a peninsula that projects north-westward into the Moray Firth, so that water surrounds it on three sides. Locals call it The Broch, a nickname also given to Fraserburgh, and its people are known as Brochers. The fort on the headland was once believed to be Ptolemy's Castra Alata and the Torffness of the Orkneyinga Saga; General Roy's map of the 18th century shows its defences, which he wrongly attributed to the Romans.

The fort encloses 3 hectares, three times as large as any other fort of its period in Scotland, and was defended on the landward side by three banks and ditches. Six carved slabs of the 7th century, the Burghead Bulls, were found there; four are kept in the Burghead Visitor Centre and Elgin Museum, one in the Royal Museum in Edinburgh and one in the British Museum. The present settlement was built between 1805 and 1809, destroying more than half of the fort.

The chambered well, found in 1809 when an elderly fisherman recalled a tradition of a well nearby, has stone steps leading down to a spring-fed tank; first called a Roman bath, it is almost certainly of Dark Age origin and had some ceremonial purpose.

Alexander Stephen founded the shipbuilding firm Alexander Stephen and Sons at Burghead in 1750, and herring fishing long supported the town. In 1689 the church courts rebuked its young men for burning a clavie and blessing the boats after the old heathen custom.

Every 11 January, the old New Year's Eve before Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1752, the Clavie crew carry a burning tar barrel round the old streets and set it on a stone altar on Doorie Hill, the last surviving piece of the fort's southern ramparts. The well is a scheduled monument. Digs at nearby Clarkly Hill have found Iron Age round houses, Pictish foundations, Roman coins and evidence of iron smelting on a large scale.
burgos: Burgos lies in the north of the Iberian Peninsula, near the confluence of the Arlanzón and the Vena rivers and at the edge of the central plateau, at an elevation of 865 metres. Early humans occupied sites around Burgos as early as 800,000 years ago, and the nearby site of Atapuerca, 20 kilometres to the east, has yielded fossils and stone tools of the earliest known hominids in western Europe. When the Romans took possession the site had been a Celtic city. The name Burgos probably reflects the Visigothic word for walled villages, from the Gothic baurgs.

After the Visigoths drove back the Suebi in the 5th century and the Berbers briefly held Castile in the 8th, Alfonso III of Asturias conquered the area about the middle of the 9th century and built castles, from which Castile took its name, the land of castles. Diego Rodríguez Porcelos gathered the inhabitants of the surrounding country into one fortified village in 884, and the city began to be called Caput Castellae, Head of Castile. In the 11th century it became an archdiocesan see and capital of the Kingdom of Castile. It was a major stop for pilgrims on the French Way to Santiago de Compostela and a centre of trade, attracting a large foreign merchant population that joined the city oligarchy.

In the 13th and 14th centuries Burgos was a favourite seat of the kings of León and Castile and a favoured burial site. Royal charters of 1255 and 1266 relieved from taxes those citizens who owned horses and could arm themselves. In 1285 Sancho IV added a body called the jurado to the town council, and on 9 June 1345 Alfonso XI established direct royal rule through the Regimiento of sixteen appointed men. In 1574 Pope Gregory XIII made the bishopric a metropolitan archbishopric at the request of Philip II. During the Peninsular War Wellington withdrew from the siege of Burgos, and the castle was destroyed by the French in 1813.

Burgos is the capital of its province in Castile and León and its second most populated city. Construction of its Gothic cathedral began in 1221 and spanned mainly the 13th to 15th centuries; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and holds the remains of El Cid and his wife Doña Jimena. The city also has the monastery of Las Huelgas, founded in 1180 by Alfonso VIII, and the Carthusian monastery of Miraflores, with the tombs of Juan II and Queen Isabella of Portugal. The Museum of Human Evolution, opened in 2010, draws on the Atapuerca site. The University of Burgos was established in 1994.
burgraviate-of-nuremberg: Nuremberg was probably founded around the turn of the 11th century. It is first mentioned in a document of 1050, as the site of an Imperial castle between eastern Franconia and the Bavarian March of the Nordgau, and it grew in importance through its place on key trade routes. King Conrad III established the burgraviate, with the first administration and courts over the Imperial territories around the town.

The first burgraves came from the Austrian House of Raabs. When their male line died out around 1190, the office passed to the last count's son-in-law. Frederick I, originally Frederick III, Count of Zollern, had married Sophia, daughter of Burgrave Conrad II, and became burgrave through this union, bringing the burgraviate to the House of Hohenzollern.

From the late 12th century to the Interregnum (1254–1273) the power of the burgraves declined. The Staufen emperors gave most non-military powers to a castellan, and from 1173/74 the city's administration and municipal courts went to an Imperial mayor, the Reichsschultheiß. The castellan administered the Imperial lands around Nuremberg, levied taxes, judged the highest cases of poaching and forestry, and protected churches and monasteries, even those of the Bishopric of Bamberg. Relations between the burgraves and the castellan turned into open enmity.

In 1219 Emperor Frederick II granted the city the Great Letter of Freedom (Großen Freiheitsbrief), with town rights, Imperial immediacy, the right to mint coins and its own customs policy, which almost wholly removed Nuremberg from the burgraves' control. The castellan's privileges passed to the city in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. Nuremberg became, with Augsburg, one of the two great trading centres on the route from Italy to Northern Europe, and Imperial Diets and courts met at its castle.

The Hohenzollern burgraves held the title for more than two centuries, among them Frederick III der Erber (1262–1297), John II der Erwerber (1332–1357) and Frederick V (1357–1397). Frederick V's sons divided the inheritance: John III was also Margrave of Brandenburg-Kulmbach from 1398, and Frederick VI, as Frederick I, became Elector of Brandenburg in 1415 and Margrave of Brandenburg in 1417. The burgraviate was eventually partitioned to form Brandenburg-Ansbach and Brandenburg-Bayreuth.
burgred-of-mercia: Burgred, whose name is also written Burhred or Burghred (Old English Burhræd), became king of Mercia in 852 and may have been related to his predecessor, Beorhtwulf. After Easter in 853 he married Æthelswith, daughter of Æthelwulf, king of the West Saxons; the wedding took place at the royal villa of Chippenham in Wessex. The marriage made Æthelwulf's sons, the later King Æthelred of Wessex and Alfred, his brothers-in-law.

In 853 the Welsh, who lived between Mercia and the western sea, rebelled against his rule. Burgred sent messengers to Æthelwulf asking for help in subduing them, and Æthelwulf at once marched with him against the Welsh and put the rebellion down. Twelve years after this success, in 865, the Great Heathen Army arrived. After its campaigns against East Anglia and Northumbria it advanced through Mercia and reached Nottingham in 867.

Burgred appealed to his brothers-in-law Æthelred and Alfred for help, but the armies of Wessex and Mercia did no serious fighting, as Burgred paid the invaders off. In 874 the Vikings marched from Lindsey to Repton and drove him from his kingdom.

After his departure the Vikings set up a Mercian, Ceolwulf, in his place and demanded oaths of loyalty to themselves. Burgred went to Rome and died there. According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle he was buried in the church of Sancta Maria in the school of the English nation, now Santo Spirito in Sassia. Single coins of his reign continue to be found, though hoards with his coins are less common; one was found near Banbury Castle by the Birmingham University Field Archaeology Unit in 1998.
burgtheater: The original Burgtheater was set up in a tennis court, called a ball house at the time, which Ferdinand I had built in 1540 in the lower pleasure garden of the Hofburg after the older ball house burned down in 1525. The theatre opened on 14 March 1741 at the wish of Empress Maria Theresa, who wanted a theatre beside her palace. Its first building adjoined the Hofburg at Michaelerplatz, opposite St Michael's Church. Before 1776 the theatre was leased from the state, and after the bankruptcy of its curator the state under Joseph II took over its operation in 1776. Joseph II called it the German National Theatre that year.

Three of Mozart's operas had their premieres there: Die Entführung aus dem Serail in 1782, Le nozze di Figaro in 1786 and Così fan tutte in 1790. So did his Piano Concerto No. 24 in 1786 and Beethoven's First Symphony on 2 April 1800.

The old house gave exceptional acoustics but was too small for its audience. A description of 1884 said the auditorium could hardly hold half of those who wished to enter. The last performance there, in October 1888, was Goethe's Iphigenie auf Tauris. The theatre moved on 14 October 1888 to a new building on the Ringstraße designed by Gottfried Semper and Karl Freiherr von Hasenauer, whose interiors were decorated with frescoes by Gustav Klimt, Ernst Klimt and Franz von Matsch showing theatrical history. A bombing raid on 12 March 1945 largely destroyed it, and a fire of unknown origin damaged it further a month later. It was rebuilt between 1953 and 1955.

Until 1918 it was known as the K.K. Hofburgtheater, and the Viennese call it die Burg. Its company created a traditional style of speech and performance, and the Burgtheater German was groundbreaking for German-language theatre. The house kept a strongly traditional stage until the late 1960s. From the early 1970s it became a venue for some of Europe's most important directors and designers, and under Claus Peymann it staged the first performances of plays by Thomas Bernhard, Elfriede Jelinek, Peter Handke, Peter Turrini and George Tabori. Its ensemble has about 120 members.
burgundian-wars: Over about a hundred years the Valois dukes of Burgundy had built a strong state between the Holy Roman Empire and France, holding besides the Duchy of Burgundy and Franche-Comté the wealthy regions of Flanders, Brabant and Luxembourg. They pursued expansion in Alsace and Lorraine to join their northern and southern lands, and Charles the Bold's advances along the Rhine brought him into conflict with Emperor Frederick III. In 1469 Duke Sigismund of Habsburg pawned his Alsace possessions to Charles for 50,000 florins. Charles's embargo against Basel, Strasbourg and Mulhouse, enforced by his reeve Peter von Hagenbach, led those cities to appeal to Bern.

Charles's attack on the Archbishopric of Cologne failed at the Siege of Neuss in 1474–75. Von Hagenbach was captured and beheaded, and the Swiss, with the Alsace cities and Sigismund, won the Battle of Héricourt in November 1474. Louis XI of France joined the coalition in December. In 1475 Bernese forces conquered and ravaged Vaud, which belonged to Savoy, Charles's ally.

In 1476 Charles had the capitulated garrison of Grandson hanged or drowned, and was then defeated there by the Confederates, losing his artillery. He suffered a devastating blow at the Battle of Morat, and René II, Duke of Lorraine, rebelled against him. Charles fell at the Battle of Nancy in 1477. A Swiss saying held that he lost his goods at Grandson, his bravery at Morat and his blood at Nancy. Swiss infantry with long spears in the Gewalthaufen formation beat a larger Burgundian army, tipping the balance towards infantry over cavalry.

With Charles's death the Valois dukes of Burgundy died out and revolts engulfed the duchy. The duchy proper reverted to the French crown, while Charles's daughter Mary of Burgundy married Maximilian of Austria and the northern territories passed to the Habsburgs. The Peace of Zürich of 24 January 1478 returned Franche-Comté to Maximilian for 150,000 guilders. The Swiss gained a reputation for being nearly invincible and their mercenaries rose on Europe's battlefields, but they kept only Grandson, Morat and Echallens of their conquests. Disputes between city and country cantons over the spoils were settled by the Stanser Verkommnis of 1481.
burgundians: The Burgundians are one of the disappearing and reappearing tribes listed by the historian Peter Heather, which appear in Roman records in one place and reappear much later in another. The earliest named by Greco-Roman writers lived near the Vistula in present-day Poland between the first and third centuries; Pliny the Elder lists the Burgodiones among the Vandili. Roman panegyrics report that in the late third century they suffered devastating defeats by the Gepids and Goths, which may have driven some of them west. They later appear near the Main, and in the fourth century they became Roman allies against the Alemanni. Early in the fifth century, in a period of wider crisis, the Gibichung-led Burgundians crossed the Rhine and settled within the empire.

The Rhine kingdom, probably near Worms, was destroyed in 436 when the Romans and their Hun allies killed many Burgundians together with their king Gundahar. His death became a central theme in medieval Germanic heroic legend, including the Nibelungenlied, where he is Günther. The Gallic Chronicle of 452 records that in 443 Sapaudia was given to the remainder of the Burgundians, to be divided with the native inhabitants; the territory included Geneva, and later Lyon became the capital. Ian N. Wood believes that a true Burgundian kingdom emerged only between 474 and 494.

After about 480 Gundobad became principal king, sharing power with his brothers. Civil war broke out in 500 when Godegisel allied with Clovis I of the Franks and defeated Gundobad; with Visigothic support Gundobad regained control in 501. Gundobad died in 516 and left the throne to his Catholic son Sigismund. The Frankish empire incorporated the kingdom in 534.

The Burgundians left several legal codes, which are among the fullest evidence for how the early successor states legislated. Gundobad published edicts concerning relations between Burgundians and Roman citizens, and a Roman law, the Lex Romana Burgundionum. Little is known of their language beyond some names and a few words in legal texts, but it was Germanic. The court at Geneva and Lyon had an Arian faction, which held sway over some kings, including Gundobad, but several women of the royal family were Catholics, and Clovis is said to have been converted by his Burgundian wife.
burgundy: Burgundy is named for the Burgundians, an East Germanic people who moved west beyond the Rhine in the late Roman period. Gallic Celts, above all the Aedui, were the first recorded inhabitants, and the Roman Empire absorbed them after the Battle of Alesia. In the 4th century the Burgundians settled in the western Alps and founded a kingdom, which the Franks conquered in 532. In 843 the Treaty of Verdun divided the old Burgundian lands, and the north-western part went to the West Frankish Kingdom. From the early 10th century it was organised as the Duchy of Burgundy, and from 1004 the House of Burgundy, a cadet branch of the French royal House of Capet, ruled it.

Burgundy was home to some of the most important churches and monasteries of the medieval West. Cluny, founded in 910, influenced Europe for centuries, and the first Cistercian abbey was founded at Cîteaux in 1098. Bernard of Clairvaux's influence helped spread hundreds of Cistercian abbeys across Europe in the following century. During the Hundred Years' War King John II of France gave the duchy to his youngest son, Philip the Bold, and it became a rival to the crown. Philip the Good acquired Namur, Hainaut, Brabant and Holland.

The Valois-Burgundian State held fiefs from the western Alps to the North Sea, and its dukes were among the wealthiest princes in Europe, sometimes called Grand Dukes of the West. At the Battle of Nancy in 1477 the last duke, Charles the Bold, was killed. The French crown annexed the duchy, which became a province in 1482, while the Low Countries possessions passed to his daughter Mary and her Habsburg descendants. The division of the Burgundian inheritance marked the beginning of a long French-Habsburg rivalry.

The province of Burgundy lasted until 1790, when the departments replaced it. Burgundy now means the area of the departments of Côte-d'Or, Saône-et-Loire, Yonne and Nièvre, with Dijon as its capital. It was an administrative region from 1982 to 2015 and merged with Franche-Comté in 2016. The abbeys of Fontenay and Vézelay are World Heritage Sites, and Vézelay is still a starting point for pilgrimages to Santiago de Compostela. Cluny was almost entirely destroyed during the French Revolution. The region is also known for Burgundy wine.
burhanpur: Burhanpur lies on the north bank of the Tapti River. It was a town of some importance under the Rashtrakuta dynasty, from 753 to 982, but came to prominence in the medieval period. Malik Nasir Khan, the Faruqi sultan of Khandesh, founded the city at the urging of Shaikh Zainuddin and named it after the Sufi saint Burhan-ud-Din. It became the capital of the Khandesh sultanate. Miran Adil Khan II, who reigned from 1457 to 1501, built a citadel and palaces and made it a major centre of trade and textile production.

In 1601 Akbar annexed the sultanate, and Burhanpur became the capital of Khandesh subah, one of the new top-level provinces of the Mughal Empire. Its governor Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan built a new water supply and several gardens. In 1609 Jahangir appointed his second son Parviz governor of the Deccan provinces, and the prince made Burhanpur his headquarters.

Shah Jahan spent considerable time in Burhanpur and added to the Shahi Qila, and many surviving monuments date from his rule. Tradition says his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in the palace's royal bath while giving birth to her fourteenth child and was buried there for six months before her body was moved to the Taj Mahal.

The Maratha Peshwa Bajirao took the town in the 1720s, and in 1818 the Marathas handed it to the British. Burhanpur remains known for textiles and is the largest centre of the power-loom industry in Madhya Pradesh. The Shahi Qila is mostly in ruins. The Jama Masjid was begun under the Faruqi dynasty and completed under Akbar.
burhanuddin-rabbani: Burhanuddin Rabbani was born on 20 September 1940 in the village of Yaftal, in the Fayzabad District of Badakhshan, the son of Muhammed Yousuf. He was a Tajik. He studied Islamic Law and Theology at Kabul University, graduating in 1963, and was hired there as a professor. In 1966 he went to Al-Azhar University in Cairo, where he formed close ties with the leadership of the Muslim Brotherhood. He was one of the first Afghans to translate the works of Sayyid Qutb into Persian, and he spoke six languages.

In 1972 a council of fifteen chose Rabbani as head of Jamiat-e Islami, a party composed mainly of Tajiks. In the spring of 1974 police came to Kabul University to arrest him; his students prevented it and he escaped to Pakistan, where he established the party. When the Soviets intervened in 1979, he helped lead Jamiat-e Islami in resistance to the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan regime.

His forces were the first mujahideen elements to enter Kabul in 1992, when that regime fell, and he took over as president under the Peshawar Accords. His rule was limited, because the country was fractured by civil war. He fled after the Taliban took Kabul in 1996, and his government in exile remained the internationally recognised one while controlling about a tenth of the country. He served briefly as president again from 13 November to 22 December 2001, when Hamid Karzai was chosen as interim leader at Bonn.

Rabbani later headed the High Peace Council, formed in 2010 to start talks with the Taliban. He was killed on 20 September 2011, his 71st birthday, by a suicide bomber who came to his home in Kabul posing as a Taliban envoy. The Afghan parliament suggested the title Martyr of Peace for him.
burj-khalifa: The tower was designed as the centrepiece of Downtown Dubai, a large mixed-use development of 30,000 homes, nine hotels, the Dubai Mall and an artificial lake. The decision to build it was reportedly based on the government's wish to diversify from an oil-based economy to one based on services and tourism.

Skidmore, Owings and Merrill of Chicago did the architecture and engineering, with Adrian Smith as chief architect and Bill Baker as chief structural engineer. The primary contractor was Samsung C&T of South Korea. Excavation began in January 2004, and the exterior was completed on 1 October 2009. The developer, Emaar Properties, had financial problems during the Great Recession, and the president of the United Arab Emirates, Khalifa bin Zayed, organised federal support. Mohammed bin Rashid, Ruler of Dubai, changed the name from Burj Dubai to Burj Khalifa at the inauguration.

The roof height, excluding the antenna but including a 242.6 metre spire, is 828 metres. The primary structure is reinforced concrete, and some of the structural steel was salvaged from the demolished Palace of the Republic in East Berlin. The design draws on the Islamic architecture of the region, such as the Great Mosque of Samarra, and its Y-shaped floor plan was designed to optimise residential and hotel space. It uses the bundled tube design of the Willis Tower, invented by Fazlur Rahman Khan, so that proportionally only half the steel of the Empire State Building was needed. It has 57 elevators and 8 escalators.

During construction the tower passed one record after another. In July 2007 it surpassed Taipei 101 as the tallest building, and in September 2007 it passed the CN Tower as the tallest freestanding structure. In April 2008, at 629 metres, it passed the KVLY-TV mast to become the tallest human-made structure. It opened on 4 January 2010, though much of the interior was unfinished, and the last major planned facility opened on 23 January 2011. Its records include the most floors, 163, and the world's longest elevator travel distance, 504 metres. Above the 80th floor, residents wait two extra minutes to break their Ramadan fast, since the sun stays visible longer at height.
burji-mamluks: The Burji Mamluks, also called the Circassian Mamluks, followed the Bahri Mamluks, who had ruled Egypt from 1250. Like the Bahri, the ruling class were bought as slaves, freed and trained, and the most powerful took the role of sultan in Cairo. They were generally Circassians, drawn from the Christian population of the northern Caucasus.

The name Burji, meaning of the tower, refers to their residence in the barracks of the Citadel of Cairo. During Burji rule the state was often called the State of the Circassians, to distinguish it from the earlier State of the Turks. A revolt in Syria in 1377 spread to Egypt, and the Circassians Barakah and Barquq took over the government; Barquq was proclaimed sultan in 1382, ending the Bahri dynasty.

Barquq was expelled in 1389 but recaptured Cairo in 1390. He joined Bayezid I and Toktamish against Timur and executed Timur's envoys. Timur invaded Syria in 1401 and sacked Aleppo and Damascus, and Barquq's son Faraj regained Syria after Timur died in 1405 but was forced to abdicate in 1412. Sultans usually named their sons as successors, but the sons rarely lasted more than a few years before a powerful commander, often a mamluk of an earlier sultan, usurped them.

Under Sultan Barsbay the sultanate reached its widest extent. In 1426 he invaded Cyprus and made its kings vassals, but his state monopoly on the spice trade damaged the economy in the long term. An attempt to take Rhodes from the Knights of St. John was repelled in 1444.

Relations with the Ottomans worsened after Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, as both vied for the spice trade. Qaitbay fought Bayezid II in a long war that ended in 1491, and left debts of several hundred thousand ducats to Venetian trading families when he died in 1496. Qansuh al-Ghuri, who came to power in 1501, introduced the first regiment with gunpowder weapons but could not fix the economy.

Selim I, having defeated the Safavid Persians at Chaldiran in 1514, invaded Syria in 1516. Al-Ghuri died at the Battle of Marj Dabiq and his army was routed, and the Ottomans took Cairo on 22 January 1517. Power moved from Cairo to Constantinople, yet the mamluks remained a political and military class in Ottoman Egypt, holding high positions, until Muhammad Ali Pasha destroyed them in the early nineteenth century. The Circassian mamluks usually learned Kipchak Turkish, wrote mainly in Classical Arabic and spoke colloquial Arabic with the general population.
burkhard-christoph-von-munnich: Burkhard Christoph von Münnich was born on 19 May 1683 at Neuenhuntorf in the County of Oldenburg, into a military family; his father Anton Günther was of East Frisian nobility. Besides his native Low German he learned Latin and French. Like his father he became an engineer and a specialist in hydrotechnology. He entered French service at 17 and moved on to the armies of Hesse-Darmstadt and Saxony, where he reached the rank of colonel and later major general.

In 1721 the Russian ambassador in Warsaw, Alexey Grigoryevich Dolgorukov, invited him to engineering projects in the newly acquired northern territories. He presented Peter I with plans to fortify Kronstadt and the Annenkrone fortification in Vyborg, and was promoted to lieutenant general in 1722. He completed the costly Ladoga Canal, which had been under construction for over a decade, and in 1726 Catherine I made him general-in-chief.

He governed Saint Petersburg from 1727 and from 1728 to 1734 was governor-general of Ingria, Karelia and Finland, receiving the title of count. After Anna's coronation in 1730 he became general field marshal and in 1732 president of the War Collegiate, charged with reorganising the army. He founded the Izmaylovsky Regiment of the Imperial Guard and the Shlyakhetskiy Cadet Corps, created the first hussar regiments and sapper regiments, set up an engineer school for officers and had some fifty fortresses built. In 1734 he was sent to take Danzig, a siege for which he was heavily reproached.

As commander in the Turkish campaigns he stormed the Or Qapı fortress, entered the Crimean Peninsula and destroyed the Tatar cities of Kezlev, Aqmescit and Bakhchisaray, but poor logistics and the exhaustion of his troops forced him out. On 2 July 1737 he took Özi (Ochakov) with the help of the artillery. In 1739 he won the Battle of Stavuchany on 28 August, took Khotyn on 30 August and entered Iași on 14 September, forcing the Moldavian boyars to accept annexation. The Treaty of Niš of 3 October returned almost all the conquests, and he received the Order of St Andrew.

His rivalry with Biron, Duke of Courland, whom he had arrested, led to his own arrest under Elizabeth. He was condemned to death, withdrawn from the scaffold and sent to Pelym in Siberia, where he stayed twenty years until Peter III released him in 1762. Catherine II made him director-general of the Baltic ports. He died in Tartu on 27 October 1767 and was buried on his estate near it. Frederick the Great called him the Prince Eugene of the Muscovites, and his aide-de-camp Christoph Hermann von Manstein described a man of both generosity and greed.
burkina-faso: Burkina Faso covers 274,223 square kilometres. Most of the country is a peneplain, a gently undulating landscape with a few isolated hills that are the last vestiges of a Precambrian massif. The southwest is a sandstone massif, bordered by cliffs up to 150 metres high, where the highest peak, Ténakourou, rises to 749 metres. The country owed its former name, Upper Volta, to three rivers, the Black Volta (Mouhoun), the White Volta (Nakambé) and the Red Volta (Nazinon). Only the Black Volta and the Komoé flow year-round, and water shortages are often a problem in the north.

The northwest was populated by hunter-gatherers from about 14,000 BCE to 5,000 BCE, and agricultural settlements were established between 3600 and 2600 BCE. The oldest evidence of iron smelting in Burkina Faso dates from 800 to 700 BCE and forms part of the Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy World Heritage Site. The Bura culture existed in the southeast from the 3rd to the 13th century CE.

From medieval times until the end of the 19th century the central region was ruled by the Mossi, descendants of Dagomba warriors from present-day Ghana who mixed with Mandé and other local peoples in the 11th century. They established separate kingdoms, among them Tenkodogo, Yatenga, Zandoma and Ouagadougou, and defended their territory, beliefs and social structure against attempts at conquest and conversion from Muslims to the northwest.

The Tarikh al-Sudan reports that a Mossi ruler took control of Timbuktu between 1328 and 1338, during the reign of Mansa Musa, and the Tarikh al-fattash describes conflicts between the 15th-century Mossi king Komdao and the Songhay ruler Sonni Ali. The Mossi were defeated at the Battle of Kobi in 1483. The French colonised the area in 1896 as part of French West Africa, and it became fully independent in 1960 as the Republic of Upper Volta. On 4 August 1984 President Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso.

Ouagadougou is the capital and largest city. The name joins Burkina, from Mooré, meaning upright, with Faso, from Dyula, meaning fatherland. The country is a semi-presidential republic and a member of the United Nations. About half the population is Mossi, whose kingdom is led by the Mogho Naba, whose court is in Ouagadougou. There are more than 60 indigenous languages, and Mooré is spoken by more than half the population. Most people are Muslim, with Christian and animist minorities. Literature rests on oral tradition, and Ouagadougou hosts the International Art and Craft Fair, one of the most important African handicraft fairs.
burlington-new-jersey: Burlington stands on the banks of the Delaware River in Burlington County, New Jersey, and is a suburb of Philadelphia within the Philadelphia metropolitan area. The Burlington-Bristol Bridge crosses the river to Bristol in Pennsylvania. The city takes its name, as does the county, from the town of Bridlington in England, of which Burlington was a district. It was first incorporated on 24 October 1693 and reincorporated by royal charter on 7 May 1733. After independence the State of New Jersey incorporated it on 21 December 1784.

The council of West Jersey Proprietors purchased roughly 30 miles of riverfront land from the Lenape in 1676. English settlers, primarily Quakers, founded Burlington on part of that land in 1677. In 1702 West Jersey and East Jersey were combined into a single Crown Colony. The Quakers formally established their congregation in 1678 and met in private homes until Francis Collings built a hexagonal brick meeting house between 1683 and 1687. The Lenape chief King Ockanickon, a loyal friend of the English settlers, was buried in the cemetery in 1681. The present meeting house on High Street dates from 1783.

The Anglican congregation, founded in 1702 by George Keith and John Talbot, built Old St Mary's, the oldest church in Burlington and New Jersey. In 1837 Bishop George Washington Doane founded St Mary's Hall, the first Episcopal boarding school offering a classical education for girls and the first such school in New Jersey. About 1845 the druggist and Quaker abolitionist William Allinson converted the building at 301 High Street into a pharmacy and a centre of anti-slavery activity; local tradition holds that fugitive slaves hid in tunnels beneath it on the Underground Railroad. In 1796 the county seat moved to Mount Holly Township, a more central location.

The city has 9,743 inhabitants at the 2020 census. Its waterfront park was developed through urban renewal and flood control projects in the late 1960s and 1970s. Burlington has two historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the Burlington Historic District and the adjacent High Street Historic District, and New St Mary's Church, designed by Richard Upjohn and begun in 1846, is a National Historic Landmark.
burma-independence-army: Burmese nationalism grew under British rule, which began in 1824, and the Hsaya Rebellion of 1930–1932 was followed by organised anti-colonial politics. Aung San, a student leader who joined the Dohbama Asiayone, the Thakins, in 1938, went to China in 1940 to seek support, and at Amoy he was detained by Colonel Keiji Suzuki, who had drawn up a plan for clandestine operations in Burma. In February 1941 Japan formed the Minami Kikan to support Burmese resistance and close the Burma Road to China. Aung San and 29 others, the Thirty Comrades, left Burma in April 1941 and trained on Hainan Island.

At the founding ceremony in Bangkok on 28 December 1941 the Thirty Comrades and Suzuki drank liquor mixed with their own blood, the thway thauk, pledging loyalty to the cause of independence. The army began with 227 Burmese and 74 Japanese, with Suzuki as commander-in-chief and Aung San as senior staff officer, and entered Burma with 2,300 men in the invasion of January 1942. Volunteers swelled it to 10,000–12,000 by the time the Japanese reached Rangoon on 8 March, and eventually to between 18,000 and 23,000, armed largely with abandoned or captured British weapons.

Its men attacked minority populations, above all the Karens, and preyed on Indian refugees; in the Irrawaddy Delta elements of the army destroyed 400 Karen villages, with a death toll reaching 1,800. At Shwedaung on 29 March 1942 its forces under Bo Yan Naing fought beside a Japanese battalion and ambushed a retreating British force, losing 60 killed, 300 wounded, 60 captured and 350 missing. Its attempts to set up local governments led the Japanese to recall Suzuki and disband it on 24 July, forming the Burma Defence Army of 3,000 men under Aung San.

In 1943 its successor became the Burma National Army of the State of Burma under Ba Maw, with Bo Ne Win as commander-in-chief. Through the Anti-Fascist Organisation its leaders made contact with the British Force 136, and on 27 March 1945 they rose against the Japanese; the day is now Armed Forces Day in Myanmar. After talks at Kandy in September 1945 only a small number of its men entered the new Burma Army, and many veterans joined Aung San's People's Volunteer Organisation. Aung San and many of the Thirty Comrades are honoured in Burma as national heroes.
burma-socialist-programme-party: The party, also called the Lanzin Party, meaning Programme Party, was established on 4 July 1962. Its founders were the Union Revolutionary Council, which had taken power in the coup of 2 March 1962 and on 30 April had declared the Burmese Way to Socialism. Ne Win said this programme combined elements of Buddhism, humanism and Marxism, and some scholars described it as anti-Western and isolationist.

A booklet of January 1963 set the party apart from social democrats, who hoped to reach socialism through parliament, and from the Burmese communists, whom it called vulgar materialists. A book of the same year, The System of Correlation between Man and His Environment, joined Buddhist and Marxist rhetoric. Its most remembered line, one can only afford to be moral on a full stomach, struck a chord as the nationalisation of all businesses brought hardship.

A decree of 23 March 1964, the Law Protecting National Unity, abolished every other party and seized its assets, and Article 11 of the 1974 Constitution named the BSPP the single party that would lead the state. From the early 1970s government servants of every sector had to undergo three months of political indoctrination and military training at the Hpaunggyi Central People's Services Training School, while the Military Intelligence Service and its informers hunted out dissent. Opened to mass membership in 1971, the party remained dominated by the military: in 1972 more than half of its 73,369 full members were army or police personnel. All students had to join its youth wing, the Programme Youth Organisation.

Ne Win was re-elected chairman at every regular congress from 1971 to 1985, and a purge in November 1977 removed thousands, among them leftists and communist sympathisers. At an Extraordinary Congress in July 1988, after soldiers had shot students and civilians in mostly peaceful protests in March and June, Ne Win resigned and proposed a referendum on a multi-party system.
