The congress refused it and chose Sein Lwin, known as the Butcher of Rangoon, as chairman.

The army shot hundreds, perhaps thousands, of demonstrators between 8 and 12 August 1988. Sein Lwin resigned, Maung Maung succeeded him, and on 10 September the party agreed to multi-party elections, but on 18 September the State Law and Order Restoration Council under General Saw Maung seized power. On 24 September 1988 the party renamed itself the National Unity Party, which was defeated in the 1990 general election.
burra-south-australia: Burra lies east of the Clare Valley in the Bald Hills range, part of the northern Mount Lofty Ranges, on Burra Creek and a few kilometres inside Goyder's Line, at the edge of land fit for farming. The ore body, up to 70 metres wide, lay between two faults in broken dolomite and consisted mainly of green malachite and blue azurite. The original inhabitants were the Ngadjuri people, whose first Western contact came in 1839; European diseases depleted them severely, and rock art and burial sites remain.

On 9 June 1845 the shepherd William Streair brought ore samples to Henry Ayers, secretary of the South Australian Mining Association. The 20,000-acre survey was split by lot: wealthy capitalists, the nobs, took the southern half and opened the unsuccessful Princess Royal Mine, while the shopkeepers and merchants of the association, the snobs, opened the Burra Burra Mine in the north. Mining began on 29 September 1845, and until 1860 it was the largest metals mine in Australia, producing about 50,000 tonnes of copper by 1877 and paying under 100 shareholders £826,586 in dividends.

Kooringa, laid out by George Strickland Kingston in 1846, was the first company township in Australia; the association granted no freehold there, so other townships grew up, among them government-owned Redruth and Llwchwr, built for a smelting works brought from Swansea. In 1851 more than a third of the people lived in dugouts in the creek banks. Ayers held wages down, and the miners' strike of 1848 was the first industrial strike in South Australia. Employment peaked at 1,208 in 1859, and after the closure the town became the colony's main sheep trading centre.

Burra is a centre for the surrounding farms and one of the best-preserved towns of the Victorian era in Australia, declared a State Heritage Town in 1994. Its townships were joined as one town in July 1940. Survivals include the water-filled open cut, mine chimneys, the Redruth Gaol and miners' dugouts and cottages. The Burra Charter on heritage management takes its name from a conference held here in 1979.
burundian-civil-war: German and then Belgian colonial rulers governed Burundi through its Tutsi monarchy, keeping the Tutsi minority above the Hutu majority. After independence in 1962, Michel Micombero's coup of 1966 began 25 years of Tutsi military regimes. In 1972 Hutu militants attacked Tutsi with the declared aim of annihilating them, and the army answered with mass reprisals against Hutu; the dead together are estimated at over 100,000. Pierre Buyoya, who seized power in 1987, attempted reforms, but Hutu revolts in the north and the army's response left between 5,000 and 50,000 dead, and Hutu rebel groups such as PALIPEHUTU-FNL and FROLINA took up arms.

In the free elections of June and July 1993 the Front for Democracy in Burundi (FRODEBU) defeated Buyoya's UPRONA. On 21 October Tutsi extremist officers murdered President Ndadaye, and 50,000 to 100,000 people, about as many Hutu as Tutsi, died within a year as militias and gangs on both sides killed. The coup regime collapsed, but in 1994 the minister Léonard Nyangoma led a FRODEBU faction into rebellion as the CNDD-FDD. Ndadaye's successor Cyprien Ntaryamira died in the plane crash of 6 April 1994 with the Rwandan president Juvénal Habyarimana, and the state lost control to the army and to ethnic militias.

Zaire and Tanzania let Hutu rebels keep bases on their soil, while from 1995 Rwanda's government aided Burundi's and its troops attacked refugee camps that sheltered rebels. In 1996 Buyoya took power again in a coup. He brought the Tutsi militias under control and sought talks, but neighbouring states imposed an embargo and the rebels grew stronger, killing about 300 Tutsi in one attack on 20 July 1996.

The army raised armed and mostly Hutu militias, the Guardians of the Peace, which numbered 3,000 fighters by late 1997, and both sides used child soldiers widely. Talks opened at Arusha on 15 June 1998 under Julius Nyerere and, after his death in 1999, Nelson Mandela.

A transitional government took office in October 2001, with Domitien Ndayizeye succeeding Buyoya as president on 30 April 2003. Two wings of the CNDD-FDD joined the agreement in December 2002, and an African Union mission arrived. The FNL fought on, killing 160 Congolese Tutsi refugees at Gatumba in August 2004. A referendum approved the constitution in 2005, and Pierre Nkurunziza of the FDD was sworn in as president in August that year. The FNL later signed a ceasefire, though its dissidents fought on into 2008. A Truth and Reconciliation Commission was set up in 2014.
burushaski: Burushaski is a language isolate spoken by the Burusho people, native to northern Gilgit-Baltistan in Pakistan, and its name in the language means our language. About 120,000 speakers live in Pakistan, in the Hunza, Nagar and northern Gilgit districts, the Yasin Valley and the Ishkoman Valley, and a few hundred in Srinagar in India. Because the two regions where it is spoken are separated by Hunza Valley areas where the Indo-Aryan language Shina is spoken, it is generally believed to have been spoken over a much wider area in the past.

The Hunza and Nagar varieties differ only slightly, but the Yasin variety, also called Werchikwar, is much more divergent, and is sometimes considered a distinct language. Its speakers are bilingual in Khowar. The variety spoken in India has been influenced by Kashmiri, Hindi and Urdu.

Burushaski is an ergative language with a generally subject-object-verb word order. Nouns fall into four classes: male human beings, gods and spirits; female human beings and spirits; animals and countable things; and abstract concepts, fluids and uncountable things. Some words belong to two classes with different meanings, so that báalt means apple when countable and apple tree when uncountable. Words for parts of the body and kinship terms always carry a pronominal prefix, so that one cannot say mother or arm, only my arm or your mother.

The number system is vigesimal, based on twenty, so that 40 is twice twenty and 60 is three times twenty. The verb is very rich in forms: it has three basic stems, and a finite verb can take up to four prefixes and six suffixes in a system of eleven possible positions. Prefixes can mark whether an action was willing or unwilling, as in the difference between he dived and he sank.

Attempts to link Burushaski with other language families have not been accepted by a majority of linguists. Proposals include the North Caucasian, Kartvelian and Yeniseian languages, a wide Dené-Caucasian grouping, and a relationship with Indo-European. Roger Blench noted in 2008 that the supposed evidence rests on vocabulary that may be better explained by language contact, and that almost all Burushaski farming vocabulary appears to be borrowed from Dardic, Tibeto-Burman and North Caucasian languages.

Burushaski has been predominantly a spoken language. Allamah Nasiruddin Nasir Hunzai wrote poetry in it in the 1940s and devised an alphabet derived from Urdu, adding letters for sounds Urdu lacks, and Ghulamuddin Ghulam Hunzai wrote in a modified Arabic script. Hermann Berger created a Latin-based orthography favoured by researchers. A three-volume Burushaski-Urdu Dictionary was compiled in 2006, 2009 and 2013 at the University of Karachi. Tibetan sources record a Bru zha language of the Gilgit valley that appears to have been Burushaski, but no manuscripts in it are known to survive.
bury-st-edmunds: Bury St Edmunds lies in the middle of an undulating part of East Anglia known as the East Anglian Heights, with land to east and west rising above 100 metres, though parts of the town are as low as 30 metres where the Rivers Lark and Linnet pass through it. Excavation on its outskirts in the 2010s found evidence of Bronze Age activity and Roman coins of the first and second centuries. Its name is connected with the word borough, and the second part honours Edmund, King of the East Angles, called Edmund the Martyr, who was killed by the Vikings in 869. In the Anglo-Saxon period the town was called Bedricesweord or Bedericesworth.

The town was originally called Beodericsworth and was laid out on a grid pattern by Abbot Baldwin around 1080. Its Christian heritage dates from the founding of the abbey in 1020, and Edmund's shrine made it an important place of pilgrimage. Henry I granted the borough a charter, now lost, and the abbey controlled the borough until its dissolution in 1539. The townspeople sacked the abbey in the 14th century, and it was largely destroyed in the 16th century at the Dissolution of the Monasteries. James I issued a new charter in 1606 confirming the borough's ancient rights. The town stayed prosperous through the 17th and 18th centuries and declined relatively with the Industrial Revolution.

Its population had reached 12,538 by 1841. A permanent military presence began with the Militia Barracks of 1857 and Gibraltar Barracks of 1878. Zeppelin bombs fell on the town in 1915 and 1916, and in the second raid seven civilians were killed. The British Sugar factory, the town's largest landmark, was built in 1925, and the Theatre Royal, designed by William Wilkins, dates from 1819 and is the only surviving Regency theatre in the country.

Bury St Edmunds is a market town and civil parish in the West Suffolk district, with a built-up area of 41,280 people at the 2021 census. It is the seat of the Diocese of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich, with its cathedral at St Edmundsbury Cathedral, and the remains of the abbey stand in gardens in the centre. Brewing and sugar processing are industries, and the town is the cultural and retail centre for West Suffolk.
burzenland: Țara Bârsei lies within the ranges of the Southern Carpathians, bounded roughly by Apața in the north, Bran in the southwest and Prejmer in the east. It corresponds largely to the Bârsa Depression, the western part of the Giurgeu-Brașov Depression, with the mountains around it, among them the Bârsa Mountains. It takes its name from the Bârsa stream, recorded as Borza in 1231, which flows into the Olt; the origin of the Romanian word bârsă is uncertain.

Archaeological evidence suggests German settlement began in the middle of the 12th century under King Géza II of Hungary, and in 1192 terra Bozza is recorded as settled by Germans. Andrew II kept the right to mint coin and to any gold or silver found, but gave the Teutonic Knights markets, justice and freedom from taxes and tolls; they built five castles, Marienburg, Schwarzenburg, Rosenau, Kreuzburg and Kronstadt, and Saxon settlers founded farms and villages. The order disregarded the rights of the local bishopric and angered the Hungarian nobility, led by the heir Béla, and Pope Honorius III protested its expulsion in vain.

The kings also settled Szeklers and Pechenegs in the region, and archaeology points to a strong Romanian population in the villages later known as Șcheii Brașovului, Satulung, Baciu, Cernatu and Turcheș. In 1429 Sigismund proposed that the Teutonic Knights defend the region during the Ottoman wars in Europe, and a detachment from Prussia under Claus von Redewitz served there until half of it was killed in 1432. In 1495 the First Romanian School was built beside the Saint Nicholas Church, where the deacon Coresi printed some of the first books in Romanian in the 16th century.

The Romanian communities of the region and the Orthodox merchants of Brașov opposed the union of the local Romanian Orthodox Church with Rome under Atanasie Anghel in 1701, and in 1724 its parishes were placed under the Eastern Orthodox Bishopric of Râmnic. On 1 November 1918 a meeting at the Saint Nicholas Church founded the Romanian National Council of Țara Bârsei, led by Vasile Saftu, which supported Transylvania's union with Romania on 1 December that year.

The region lies in Brașov County, and its chief city is Brașov. Its population mixes Romanians, Germans and Hungarians, although most of the Transylvanian Saxons emigrated to West Germany from 1976 onwards. The smoked bighead carp of Țara Bârsei carries a Protected Geographical Indication, and a regional magazine named after the land first appeared in Brașov in 1929.
bushati-family: The family descended from the medieval Bushati tribe, a pastoralist fis of northern Albania and Montenegro whose name, from mbë fshat, above the village, recalls herders who were not permanently settled. The Bushati settled between the 15th and the late 16th century, among other places in the village of Bushat in the Zadrima plain near Shkodër, the family's home. Another part was absorbed into the Piperi tribe, and the defter of 1497 lists a katun Bushat in Piperi with 35 households.

The family traced its line to the Begaj brotherhood of Bushati, which had converted to Islam possibly in the early 17th century. Its leaders put forward differing origins to serve their aims. The traveller Evliya Çelebi recorded a descent from one Jusuf Bey Plaku of the era of Mehmed II. Kara Mahmud, seeking to expand north into the medieval lands of Ivan Crnojević, claimed descent from Ivan's Muslim son Skenderbeg Crnojević, and the writer Sami Frashëri held them to be descendants of the Dukagjini family.

The Bushatis built their dominance of the Shkodër region through a network of alliances with the highland tribes. Süleyman Bushati, sanjak-bey of Scutari, was noted for his wars against the Montenegrins, and Kara Mahmud Bushati, chief of a tribe based in Shkodër, was named governor of Shkodër by the Ottoman authorities. Other prominent members of the period included Ibrahim Bushati and Mustafa Pasha Bushati.

The family kept an important role in Albanian society after the fall of the pashalik in 1831. In the 19th century Shkodër was known as a cultural centre, and in the 1840s the Bushati library was built there. Xhelal Pasha, an Ottoman official, was related to Sultan Abdul Hamid II through marriage, and later members of the family served as diplomats and politicians, among them Maliq Bushati, a prime minister, and Xhemal Bushati, a member of the Assembly of Albania and an anti-Zogist activist.
bushehr: Bushehr is a port city on the Persian Gulf and the capital of Bushehr province. It lies about 300 km from Shiraz and 600 km from Basra. The origin of the name is uncertain. The popular derivation from Abū Šahr, father of the city, is unlikely, and the name may be an abbreviation of Bokht-Ardashir, meaning Ardashir has given, though this lacks conclusive evidence. Several supposed early mentions, including the first by an Arab geographer in 1225, have been disputed as possibly referring to Reishahr, a harbour 10 km to the south where archaeology points to a much older settlement.

In 1734 Nader Shah made Bushehr the headquarters of the Persian Gulf fleet he wished to create, and for a massive warship had heavy timber brought from the forests of Mazandaran, 1,000 km away. Its shell drew the notice of European travellers for the next 50 years. Nader's naval plans ended when he was murdered in 1747, but Bushehr continued as a prominent port for at least 150 years. The Dutch East India Company kept a trading post there from 1737 to 1753, and in 1763 its Arab ruler, Sheikh Nasr Al-Madhkur, allowed the British East India Company to build a base and residency there, with a monopoly on importing woollen goods.

Bushehr replaced Bandar Abbas as Iran's most important commercial port when the political and economic centre moved to Shiraz under the Zand ruler Karim Khan Zand, who reigned from 1751 to 1779. In the 19th century the site offered few advantages: it was exposed to pirates, European ships had to anchor about four kilometres offshore because the water was shallow, the well water was salty, and the summer heat and humidity were unbearable. British forces occupied the town in the Anglo-Persian War, and it surrendered in December 1856.

The 2016 census counted 223,504 people in the city. It is hot and semi-arid. A nuclear power plant stands about twelve kilometres away; work by a Bonn firm began under a contract of 1975 and stopped in 1979, and the plant was later completed in cooperation with Russia and began supplying electricity in September 2011.
bushenyi-district: Like many other Ugandan districts, Bushenyi District takes its name from its chief town, Bushenyi, where the district headquarters stand, though its largest town is Ishaka, 75 kilometres by road north-west of Mbarara, the largest city of the sub-region. It borders Rubirizi District to the north-west, Buhweju to the north-east, Sheema to the east, Mitooma to the south and Rukungiri to the west. It belongs to the Ankole sub-region, a group of nine districts that in 2002 was home to an estimated 2.2 million Banyankole.

Before 2010 Bushenyi was one of the westernmost districts of Uganda and covered about 4,292.5 square kilometres, of which 8.6 per cent was open water, 2.2 per cent wetland and 18.3 per cent protected national forest reserve. On 1 July 2010 an Act of Parliament divided the old district into five smaller ones: Buhweju, Mitooma, Rubirizi, Sheema and a new, smaller Bushenyi District.

The national census of 1991 put the district's population at about 161,000, and that of 2002 at about 205,700, a growth rate calculated at 2 per cent. The population in 2012 was estimated at about 251,400.

Agriculture is the mainstay of the district's economy and directly employs 86.7 per cent of its people, most of them in subsistence farming, while coffee, tea, sweet bananas and matooke are also grown for sale. Beef ranching and dairy farming are widespread on both small and commercial scales, with hybrid cattle favoured over the local breeds for their higher yields of milk and beef. The difficulties farmers face include soil degradation, weak marketing and processing, and outbreaks of crop and livestock disease.
bushido: Bushido is a samurai moral code concerning attitudes, behaviour and lifestyle. Its origins date to the Kamakura period (1185 to 1333), but the code was formalised in the Edo period (1603 to 1868). The word is rarely attested in pre-modern literature and first appears in the Kōyō Gunkan of about 1616, a military chronicle of the Takeda clan. The ideas it formalised appeared as unwritten customs in the 12th century under the shogun Minamoto Yoritomo, and a Way of the Bow and the Horse existed from that century. During the Muromachi period (1336 to 1573) the way of the warrior was refined by adding Zen meditation, painting, the tea ceremony and poetry, including the death poem written before battle.

Bushido was never a single code that every samurai had to follow. Interpretations varied by clan, by individual and by era. Sengoku bushido put honour, warfare, weapon mastery and valour first. Samurai were as practical on the battlefield as other warriors, sometimes retreated from unwinnable battles, and did not seek an honourable death, which was honourable only in the service of a daimyo and while furthering his cause.

Japan then enjoyed two and a half centuries of relative peace under the Tokugawa Shogunate, and bushido was refined from a focus on valour in battle to one on moral integrity. Miyamoto Musashi (1584 to 1645) and Yamamoto Tsunetomo (1659 to 1719) wrote at length about their interpretations. Influences included Zen Buddhism, Shinto and Confucianism.

The Meiji restoration abolished the samurai class in the 1870s. Bushido of the Meiji era stressed loyalty to the emperor and self-sacrifice more than many Tokugawa interpretations did. Nitobe Inazō's book Bushido: The Soul of Japan made it known abroad, though scholars regard the morals he described as romanticised. In Shōwa Japan before and during the Second World War bushido was used for militarism, to present war as purifying and death as a duty. In the Taishō period it was advocated as the way of the merchant, and it is still invoked in business and martial arts.
busseto: Busseto is a comune in the province of Parma, in Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy, about 8 kilometres south of Cremona in Lombardy. It has about 6,763 inhabitants. Its name appears as Buxetum in the first written sources of the early twelfth century, and may derive either from buxus, the box shrub, or from a word for a fenced pen for oxen.

The history of Busseto is well documented back to the 10th century. For almost five hundred years it was the capital of the Stato Pallavicino, which eventually became part of the Duchy of Parma. La Rocca, the fortress at the centre of the town, stands on the site of a stronghold founded in the eleventh century by Adalberto Pallavicini, a member of the family.

In the first half of the thirteenth century the fortress was laid out afresh with a moat and a drawbridge facing the square. Later damage destroyed the drawbridge and parts of the walls, and in 1857 the architect Pier Luigi Montecchini rebuilt most of it in neo-Gothic style. It keeps its thirteenth-century keep and main tower.

La Rocca is now the municipal palace and contains the Teatro Verdi, a small theatre of 300 seats built by the municipality without the composer's prior approval, although Giuseppe Verdi gave money towards its completion. The National Giuseppe Verdi Museum is housed in the Renaissance Villa Pallavicino and was opened on 10 October 2009.

Verdi was born in the nearby village of Le Roncole in 1813 and moved to Busseto in 1824. The town preserves Casa Barezzi, the home of his patron and later father-in-law Antonio Barezzi, where Verdi gave his first public performance in 1830. He bought Palazzo Orlandi in 1845 and lived there with Giuseppina Strepponi from 1849 to 1851, composing Luisa Miller, Stiffelio and Rigoletto. His villa at Sant'Agata nearby became his main home after 1851.
bussing: Heinrich Büssing (1843–1929), the son of a blacksmith family at Nordsteimke, studied engineering at the Collegium Carolinum in Braunschweig, held about 250 patents and had founded bicycle, engineering and railway signal works with varying success. At the age of 60 he and his two sons set up a works for motor lorries and buses. His first truck carried 2 tons, had a 2-cylinder petrol engine and worm drive, and was built under licence in Germany, Austria, Hungary and by Straker-Squire in England. A year later his 20 HP bus carried up to twelve passengers between Braunschweig and Wendeburg, and Büssing buses were soon running in Berlin, Vienna, Prague and London.

Before the First World War the firm built heavy trucks, and in 1914 it developed the A5P armoured car for the Oberste Heeresleitung. It became the joint-stock company Büssing AG in 1922, and its rigid three-axle chassis of 1923 gave it the lead in the German commercial-vehicle market. In 1934 it took over the Neue Automobil Gesellschaft and traded as Büssing-NAG until 1950. From 1944 to March 1945 Büssing-NAG used inmates of several concentration camps in Braunschweig, subcamps of Neuengamme, as slave labour.

After World War II it resumed civilian production with 5-ton and 7-ton trucks. As Büssing Nutzkraftwagen GmbH from 1950 it concentrated on trucks with horizontal underfloor engines, a layout it had pioneered in 1936, and it built about 71 trolleybuses between 1933 and 1966. In 1962 it took over the Borgward plant at Osterholz-Scharmbeck for military 4x4 lorries.

Büssing formed close ties with MAN AG from 1969, and after the takeover MAN used the lion emblem on trucks named MAN-Büssing. The underfloor-engined range stayed in production under MAN until the late 1980s. At least four Büssing trolleybuses survive in museums, among them the Frankfurt Transport Museum and the Historama in Ferlach, Austria.
buto: Buto lay in the north-western Nile Delta, about 15 km east of the Rosetta branch of the Nile and 30 km south of today's coastline. The Egyptians called it Per-Wadjet, House of Wadjet, and its present name Tell el-Fara'in means Hill of the Pharaohs. The site is a mound of about one square kilometre, with two settlement mounds up to 20 m high, Kom A in the north and Kom C in the south, and the low-lying temple area, Kom B. Wadjet, the cobra goddess, was the patron deity of Lower Egypt and was paired with Nekhbet of Upper Egypt as the Two Ladies.

The earliest settlement dates from the middle to late fourth millennium BCE and belongs to the Buto-Ma'adi culture, the most important Lower Egyptian prehistoric culture of the period. Its houses were of wattle and daub, and its pottery and small amounts of imported copper show influence from the Levant.

Upper Egypt's Naqada culture then replaced it, perhaps after a conquest, although Thomas von der Way reads the change as cultural assimilation around 3300 to 3200 BCE. From the start of the 1st Dynasty simple rooms grew into walled complexes at least 50 m wide. Ulrich Hartung interprets a maze-like building of the late 1st Dynasty as an Early Dynastic palace, which a fire devastated around the middle of the 2nd Dynasty.

No settlement remains have been found for about 1,500 years after the early Old Kingdom. Flooding or a shift in a branch of the Nile may explain this, and the temple of Wadjet seems to have stayed in use. Buto reappears in texts of the 18th Dynasty and was resettled from the late 8th century BCE, with high activity under the Saite kings of the 26th Dynasty. In Ptolemaic times it was the capital of the Phthenotes nome. Greek writers praised its temple and the oracle of Wadjet. Habitation most likely ended around the 6th or 7th century CE.

In 1886 W. M. Flinders Petrie suggested that the two mounds were the twin cities Pe and Dep. The Egypt Exploration Society dug at Buto from 1964 to 1969, and the German Archaeological Institute in Cairo has worked there since the early 1980s. Since 2018 Kafrelsheikh University has used satellite radar and electrical resistivity tomography to locate buried remains, and in 2021 its excavations on Kom C recovered terracotta figurines and amulets of deities, among them Wadjet and the Horus child.
buton-island: Buton, also written Butung, Boeton or Button, covers roughly 4,727 square kilometres, about the size of Madura. Its largest town is Baubau, where the Wolio and Cia-Cia languages are spoken. Major nearby islands include Wawonii to the north, Muna and Kabaena to the west and Siumpu to the south-west, while the Tukangbesi Islands lie just to the east and Batuatas Island to the south. The Bouton Passage, as it was known before independence, was an important point for navigation in the northern Flores Sea. The island is largely covered by rainforest and is one of only two habitats of the anoa, a type of buffalo.

In the precolonial era the island, then usually known as Butung, lay within the sphere of influence of Ternate. Especially in the sixteenth century Buton served as an important secondary regional centre within the Ternaten empire, controlling regional trade and collecting tribute to be sent to Ternate. The Sultanate of Buton ruled over the island until the 20th century. Sultan Murhum, the first Islamic monarch on the island, is remembered in the name of Murhum Harbor in Baubau.

The languages spoken on Buton include Wolio, Cia-Cia, several dialects of Muna, Tukang Besi, Kumbewaha, Lasalimu, Kamaru, Pancana, Busoa, Taloki, Kulisusu and Kioko, and Indonesian is widely used and taught in schools. In 2009 the Cia-Cia in Baubau began to use the Korean Hangul alphabet for their language, with textbooks made by a linguistic society in Seoul, and it continues to be taught in schools in that script.

The island has a massive reserve of natural asphalt and several other minerals. Administratively it is divided among five second-level units: Baubau City, Buton Regency, part of South Buton Regency, North Buton Regency and part of Muna Regency.
butrus-al-bustani: Butrus al-Bustani was born in January 1819 into a Maronite Christian family in the village of Dibbiye in the Chouf region of Mount Lebanon. His teacher, Father Mikhail al-Bustani, noticed his intelligence and recommended him to Abdullah al-Bustani, Bishop of Sidon and Beiteddine, who sent him at eleven to the school at 'Ayn Warqa in Ghosta. He spent ten years there, learning Syriac and Latin and several foreign languages including French, Italian and English.

In 1840 he moved to Beirut and worked first as a dragoman for the British forces helping to evict Ibrahim Pasha from Syria. Later that year American Protestant missionaries hired him as a teacher, and he worked with the mission for most of his life and converted to their Protestant faith. He married Rahil Ata, called the mother of the Nahda, and they had nine children. In the late 1840s he became dragoman of the American Consulate in Beirut, a post he passed to his son Salim in 1862.

With Nasif al-Yaziji he worked under the missionary Eli Smith on the Arabic translation of the Bible later completed by Cornelius Van Allen Van Dyck, learning Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek in the process. In 1847 he helped found the Syrian Association, and in a lecture of February 1859 on the literature of the Arabs he called for a revival of Arabic letters. That year he left mission work. After the Maronite and Druze civil war of 1860 in Mount Lebanon he published the irregular paper Nafir Suriyya, voicing the ideal of a Syrian fatherland, and for this he is considered the first Syrian nationalist.

In 1863 he founded the National School in Beirut, which taught Arabic, French, English, Turkish, Latin, Greek and modern sciences, took students of all religions and hired staff for competence rather than faith. It was closed in 1878 as religious solidarity rose in Syria. He helped found the Syrian Scientific Society in 1868, founded Al-Jinan in 1870, the first important Arabic literary and scientific periodical, and compiled an Arabic dictionary and, with his sons, eleven volumes of an encyclopedia. His works include Muhit al-Muhit and Da'irat al-Ma'arif, begun in 1876.

Al-Bustani died on 1 May 1883. He is known as the Master and Father of the Arabic Renaissance. He argued for one educational system for all the children of the nation, drew on the scientific heritage of the Abbasid age, and favoured Ottomanism within the Tanzimat reforms as a way for citizens of any religion to take part in the state. His output is credited with helping create modern Arabic expository prose. His writings are kept in the Yafeth Library at the American University of Beirut.
buyid-dynasty: The Buyids descended from Panah-Khusrow, a Zoroastrian from Daylam. His son Buya, a fisherman from Lahijan, converted to Islam, and Buya's three sons, Ali, Hasan and Ahmad, founded the dynasty. The Buyids claimed royal descent from the Sasanian king Bahram V. Ali ibn Buya served the Daylamite warlord Makan ibn Kaki and then Mardavij, founder of the Ziyarid dynasty, who granted him Karaj in 932. When Mardavij planned to have him killed, the brothers fled with 400 Daylamite followers to Fars, won Arrajan and defeated the Abbasid general Yaqut for control of the province. Ali then took its capital, Shiraz.

Mardavij's assassination in 935 threw the Ziyarid lands into chaos. Ali and Ahmad conquered Khuzistan, while Hasan took Isfahan and in 943 Ray, so gaining all of Jibal. In 945 Ahmad entered Iraq and seized Baghdad. The Abbasid court submitted to him as the real ruler, and the Buyids built a palace just north of the caliph's, while the caliph, left with no vizier, became a figurehead. The brothers took the honorific titles Imad al-Dawla, Rukn al-Dawla and Mu'izz al-Dawla. Kerman fell in 967, Oman in 967, the Jazira in 979, Tabaristan in 980 and Gorgan in 981.

Fanna Khusraw, Adud al-Dawla, who ruled from 949 to 983, took the dynasty to its height. After his death his sons fought each other, local dynasties became independent in parts of the realm and the confederation slowly broke up. In 1029 Mahmud of Ghazna deposed the Buyid ruler at Ray, who had asked for help against his own Daylami troops. In 1055 the Seljuk leader Tughril occupied Baghdad and ousted the last Buyid ruler there, and the dynasty's rule ended in 1062.

The Buyids formed a confederation of three principalities, in Fars, Jibal and Iraq, in which land was divided among the sons and each amir enjoyed a high degree of autonomy. The senior amir had formal precedence but little control outside his own lands. Their army began with Daylamite foot soldiers and added Turks to the cavalry, and the two groups often quarrelled. Soldiers were paid by iqtas, rights to a share of a province's tax revenue. The Buyids revived Sasanian titles and carved inscriptions at Persepolis, but used Arabic as the language of their realm and patronised Arabic poets and historians, among them al-Mutanabbi at Adud al-Dawla's court in Shiraz.

Initially Zaydi Shi'a, they became Twelver Shi'a, patronised Twelver scholars and built at the shrines of Kadhimiya, but they kept the Sunni Abbasid caliphs as figureheads and were known as tolerant of the Sunni majority. Their realm included many Zoroastrians and Christians. They restored the Baduriya dam, and Adud al-Dawla built the Band-e Amir dam near Shiraz, a hospital in Baghdad and a mausoleum at the burial place of Ali.
buyuk-menderes-river: The Büyük Menderes, meaning Great Meander, rises in a spring near Dinar, in west central Turkey, and flows through the Büyük Menderes graben to Lake Işıklı. It passes the Adıgüzel and Cindere dams and the towns of Nazilli, Aydın and Söke before it drains into the Aegean Sea close to the ancient Ionian city of Miletus. Its sinuous course gave its name to the common term meander, for the characteristic bends of rivers.

In antiquity the Maeander, from the Greek Maíandros, was a well-known river of Caria in Asia Minor. It appears first in the Catalog of Trojans in Homer's Iliad, together with Miletus and Mycale. Its sources were placed near Celaenae in Phrygia, now Dinar, where it gushed forth in a park of Cyrus. Ancient writers differed over whether it shared its sources with the river Marsyas, which Xenophon says rose in a royal palace, and some said it flowed from a lake on Mount Aulocrene. William Martin Leake reconciled the accounts by suggesting that both rivers have their origin in the lake above Celaenae but issue from different parts of the mountain.

The river was so well known for its windings that its classical name became proverbial. Its whole course runs south-west on the south of the range of Mount Messogis. South of Tripolis it receives the Lycus and becomes a river of some importance. Near Carura it passes from Phrygia into Caria and winds through the Maeandrian plain, to reach the Gulf of Icaros between the Greek cities of Priene and Myus, opposite Miletus and only 10 stadia from it. Its tributaries include the Orgyas, Marsyas, Cludrus, Lethaeus and Gaeson in the north and the Obrimas, Lycus and Harpasus in the south.

The Maeander is deep but not broad, so that in many places its depth equals its breadth and only small craft can navigate it. It often overflows its banks, and the mud deposited at its mouth pushed the coast 20 or 30 stadia, about 4 to 6 kilometres, further into the sea and joined several small islands to the mainland. Its river god, also called Meander, was one of the sons of Oceanus and Tethys, and a legend told of an underground link between the Maeander and the Alpheus River in Elis.
buzen-province: Buzen bordered Bungo to the south and Chikuzen to the north and west. Its short name, Hōshū, it shared with Bungo, and it was also called Nihō. Under the Gokishichidō system it was one of the provinces of the Saikaidō circuit, and the Engishiki classed it as one of the superior countries in importance and the far countries in distance from the capital. The provincial capital, the kokufu, stood at Toyotsu, now part of Miyako in Fukuoka Prefecture, where its ruins have been found and made a National Historic Site; the provincial temple, the Buzen Kokubun-ji, was in the same area.

In the Kofun period the area had two centres of power, Toyouni in the northwest and Usa-kuni in the southeast around present-day Usa, each ruled by a kuni no miyatsuko. By the Asuka period they had been joined as Toyo Province, also called Toyokuni no Michi no Shiri, and after the Taika Reforms and the Ritsuryō system of 701 it was divided into Buzen and Bungo. In the Edo period most of the province belonged to Kokura Domain, ruled by the Ogasawara clan under the Tokugawa shogunate, and a smaller part to Nakatsu Domain.

During the Boshin War forces of Chōshū Domain occupied Kokura Castle, and the domain moved its seat to Kawara, renamed Toyotsu Domain in 1870. When the han were abolished in August 1871 the former domains became the prefectures of Toyotsu, Senzoku, Nakatsu and Izuhara, which were merged at the end of that year as Kokura Prefecture. In April 1876 Kokura Prefecture was joined to Fukuoka Prefecture, and in August the two southernmost districts, Usa and Shimoge, passed to Ōita Prefecture.

The name Buzen remained in use for some purposes, and it is named in the treaties of 1894 with the United States and the United Kingdom. An early Meiji survey of the nation's resources counted 776 villages in the province, with a total assessed yield of 363,940 koku. Usa Jingū, commonly called Usa Hachimangū, is still the ichinomiya, the chief shrine of the former province.
byblos: Byblos lies on the coast of Lebanon about 42 kilometres north of Beirut. It is believed to have been first settled between 8800 and 7000 BCE and continuously inhabited since 5000 BCE. Urbanisation is thought to have begun in the third millennium BCE, making it one of the oldest cities in the world. The name appears as kbnj in Egyptian records going back to the pharaoh Sneferu and as Gebal in Phoenician inscriptions, and it seems to mean Well of the God. Because the city imported papyrus from Egypt, byblos came to mean papyrus in Greek, and the English word Bible ultimately derives from it.

In the Early Bronze Age Byblos developed from a fishermen's village around a shrine at a natural spring into a town with a temple compound. It was a wealthy ally of Egypt for many centuries. About 1350 BCE the Amarna letters include 60 letters from Rib-Hadda and his successor Ili-Rapih, rulers of Byblos, mostly Rib-Hadda's pleas to Akhenaten for military help. When the New Kingdom collapsed in the 11th century BCE, Byblos became the foremost city of Phoenicia. Five royal inscriptions of about 1150–950 BCE, among them the Ahiram sarcophagus, show a Phoenician alphabet of twenty-two characters.

Sibittibaal of Byblos became tributary to Tiglath-Pileser III in 738 BCE, and under the Achaemenid Empire Byblos was one of four Phoenician vassal kingdoms. Alexander the Great brought Hellenistic rule in 332 BCE. In the Greco-Roman period it was a centre of the cult of Adonis, and a theatre was built in the 3rd century. Prosperity returned with the First Crusade in 1098.

As Gibelet the city belonged to the Crusader County of Tripoli, and the Genoese Embriaco family held it as a hereditary lordship. Saladin took the town in 1187 and Baibars conquered it in 1266, but the Embriacos kept it until around 1300. The Ottoman Empire ruled it from 1516 until 1918, and it was under the French Mandate from 1920 until 1943.

Byblos is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its archaeological site includes the L-shaped temple of about 2700 BCE, the Temple of the Obelisks, the royal necropolis with the tomb of King Ahiram, the Roman theatre and the Crusader castle of the 12th century. A medieval wall surrounds the old town.
byelorussian-ssr: Before the First World War the lands of modern Belarus belonged to the Russian Empire, which had gained them in the Partitions of Poland. After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of March 1918 the Belarusian Democratic Republic was proclaimed under German occupation. As German troops left, the Bolsheviks advanced west, took Minsk on 10 December 1918, and set up the Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia. It was merged with the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, a union that ceased to exist in the Polish–Soviet War.

The Red Army broke the Polish front in 1920 and retook Minsk on 11 July, and the republic was re-founded on 31 July 1920. The Treaty of Riga of February 1921 divided the country: almost half, Western Belarus, went to Poland, and the rest was the Soviet republic, with 52,400 square kilometres and 1.544 million people. It became one of the four founding members of the Soviet Union in December 1922.

The 1930s marked the peak of Soviet repressions in Belarus. By incomplete calculations about 600,000 people fell victim to them between 1917 and 1953, and over 250,000 Belarusians were deported as kulaks or their families. In September 1939, after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union incorporated the territories known as West Belarus into the republic.

Nazi Germany occupied Belarus in the summer of 1941. It deported some 380,000 people for forced labour and killed hundreds of thousands of civilians. About 800,000 Belarusian Jews, about 90 percent of the Jewish population, were killed in the Holocaust, and more than 600 villages such as Khatyn were totally annihilated. Over 2,000,000 people, almost a quarter of the population, died during the three years of occupation.

After the war the republic became a founding member of the United Nations, with its own seat beside the Soviet Union and the Ukrainian SSR. Its Supreme Soviet declared sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and independence on 25 August 1991, and on 19 September the republic was renamed the Republic of Belarus.

Until 1990 the republic was a one-party state governed by the Communist Party of Byelorussia, a branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Minsk was its capital and largest city, and the official languages were Belarusian and Russian. Most of its 10 million people in 1989 were Belarusians, with significant minorities of Russians, Poles, Ukrainians and Jews. It was one of the more developed Soviet republics, with advanced manufacturing and agriculture.
byrsa: Byrsa was a walled citadel above the Phoenician harbour of Carthage and the name of the hill it stood on. The citadel dominated the city below and was its principal military installation, and its name appeared on Carthaginian coins in the form bʾrʿt. In the founding story told by Virgil, the local Berber chieftain offered Dido and her party, encamped at Byrsa, as much land as a single oxhide could cover.

Scipio Aemilianus Africanus besieged the citadel in the Third Punic War. Under Roman rule it became the seat of the proconsul of Africa. Geiseric took Carthage in 439 CE, and the Vandal–Alan kings ruled North Africa from the Byrsa until the Byzantine emperor Justinian reconquered the province in 533. The poet Sidonius Apollinaris, alluding to the supposed origin of the Vandals and Alans in the Caucasus and to their naval raids, complained that parched Byrsa now launched against him the frenzy of the Caucasus.

In 1994 the remains of a Carthaginian were excavated from a Punic tomb on the hill. Known as the Young Man of Byrsa, he dates from the late 6th century BCE, and in 2016 he was found to belong to the rare U5b2c1 maternal haplogroup, a lineage believed to represent early gene flow from Iberia to the Maghreb.

Byrsa Hill is part of the archaeological site of Carthage. St Louis Cathedral, begun in 1884 on top of an ancient temple, now serves as a cultural centre, and the Carthage National Museum also stands on the hill.
bytom: Bytom lies in Upper Silesia, 7 km northwest of Katowice. Its bedrock holds coal and iron ore from the Carboniferous period, and in the Bytom basin triassic rocks carry ore, zinc and lead reserves. The city's coat of arms shows a miner mining coal on one half and a yellow eagle on a blue field, the symbol of Upper Silesia, on the other.

The town is first recorded as Bitom in 1136, when it was part of the medieval Kingdom of Poland. Excavations show a fortified settlement, probably founded by Bolesław I the Brave in the early 11th century. It profited from its place on trade routes linking Kraków with Silesia and Hungary with Moravia and Greater Poland. The first church of the Virgin Mary was built in 1231, and the Mongols raided the town in 1259. The duchy lay under the overlordship of the Kingdom of Bohemia from 1289 and lasted until 1498, when it was reunited with the Duchy of Opole.

The town came under the Habsburg monarchy in 1526, and in 1742 it became part of the Kingdom of Prussia during the Silesian Wars. In 1683 King John III Sobieski visited on his way to the Battle of Vienna. After 1871, in the German Empire, the city grew and industrialised rapidly. According to the Prussian census of 1905 it had 60,273 inhabitants, of whom 59% spoke German, 38% Polish and 3% both.

Bytom was a main centre of Polish organisation in Upper Silesia. The newspaper Dziennik Górnośląski appeared from 1848, and Polish societies were harassed by the Prussian authorities. In the plebiscite of 1921, 74.7% of the votes in the city were for Germany and 25.3% for Poland. The synagogue was burned on 9 and 10 November 1938, and the Red Army captured the city in January 1945.

Bytom is a city in the Silesian Voivodeship of southern Poland. It is the home of the Silesian Opera and the Upper Silesian Museum, and it holds part of the Tarnowskie Góry Lead-Silver-Zinc Mine and its Underground Water Management System, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
byzantine-bulgarian-war-of-894-896: Under Boris I (r. 852–889) Bulgaria converted to Eastern Orthodox Christianity, and at the Council of Preslav in 893 Old Bulgarian replaced Greek as the language of the church, the Byzantine clergy were expelled and Boris's third son Simeon was made prince. These decisions ended Byzantine hopes of influence over the newly Christian country.

In 894 Stylianos Zaoutzes, the leading minister of Leo VI the Wise, persuaded the emperor to move the Bulgarian market. Under the Treaty of 716 and later agreements, Bulgarian merchants had lived in their own colony in Constantinople and paid favourable taxes; in Thessalonica they paid higher tariffs and had to buy eastern goods through middlemen close to Zaoutzes. Byzantine chroniclers held that Simeon sought a pretext to seize the Byzantine throne, but historians such as Vasil Zlatarski and John Fine regard his attack as a defence of Bulgarian trade.

In the autumn of 894 Simeon invaded Byzantine Thrace and defeated an army under Prokopios Krenites and Kourtikios, probably near Adrianople; he had the noses of captured Khazar guardsmen cut off and sent them to Constantinople. Leo VI then sent Nicetas Scleros to the Magyar leaders Árpád and Kurszán. In 895 the Byzantine navy under Eustathios Argyros broke an iron chain across the Danube and ferried the Magyars south. Led by Árpád's son Liüntika, they defeated Simeon, who took refuge in Drastar, and pillaged as far as Preslav.

Simeon proposed a truce and kept the envoy Leo Choirosphaktes waiting with letters and new demands while he allied with the Pechenegs. Early in 896 the Bulgarians crushed the Magyars on the Southern Bug, reportedly losing 20,000 riders themselves, and the Pechenegs prevented the Magyars from returning to their homeland, so that they moved west into the Pannonian Basin. In the summer Simeon invaded Thrace again and routed the Byzantine army under Leo Katakalon at Boulgarophygon, where the protovestiarios Theodosius fell.

The peace restored Bulgaria's status as most favoured nation, lifted the commercial restrictions and ceded the area between the Black Sea and Strandzha; the Bulgarians released the Byzantine soldiers and civilians they held, allegedly 120,000. The treaty lasted formally until Leo VI's death in 912, though Simeon broke it after the Sack of Thessalonica in 904 to gain land in Macedonia. He began a building programme in Preslav to rival Constantinople and imposed his authority on the Principality of Serbia by recognising Petar Gojniković as its ruler.
byzantine-bulgarian-war-of-913-927: After the Byzantine–Bulgarian war of 894–896 Simeon I had imposed an annual tribute on the Byzantine Empire, and he built up his new capital, Preslav, to rival Constantinople. In 904, after Arabs sacked Thessalonica and took 22,000 captives, negotiations moved the border to only 20 kilometres north of the city. When Leo VI the Wise died in 912, his brother Alexander dismissed Simeon's envoys and broke off the tribute. The historian John Fine argues that Simeon had planned an invasion anyway, judging the new leadership weak. Alexander died on 6 June 913, leaving the child Constantine VII under the regency of the patriarch Nicholas Mystikos.

An agreement of August 913 did not last. In February 914 Constantine's mother, Zoe Karbonopsina, overthrew the regency and revoked its concessions. The Bulgarians invaded Thrace and Macedonia that summer and took Adrianople in September, though the Byzantines soon bought it back with a huge ransom. Byzantium made peace with the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir in June 917 and courted the Serbs, Magyars and Pechenegs, but after the defeats of 917 Simeon had the Serbian prince Petar Gojniković seized and replaced, and led a campaign in Hellas as far as the Isthmus of Corinth.

In 919 the admiral Romanos Lekapenos took power and in December was crowned senior emperor; Simeon regarded him as a usurper and refused to negotiate while he ruled. Further Bulgarian victories followed at Pegae in 921 and Constantinople in 922. Needing a fleet, Simeon sought an alliance with the Fatimid caliph Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah, but the returning envoys were captured off Calabria and Romanos outbid him. In 923 or 924 Simeon camped at the walls of Constantinople, burned the Church of St. Mary of the Spring and met Romanos at Kosmidion. Simeon died in May 927.

Simeon's second son, Peter I, guided by his uncle George Sursuvul, raided Byzantine Thrace and then proposed peace from strength. Talks began at Mesembria and ended in Constantinople, where the treaty was signed in the Palace of Blachernae. Byzantium recognised Peter as emperor and the Bulgarian Orthodox Church as an independent patriarchate, agreed to pay an annual tribute, and Peter married Maria Lekapene, granddaughter of Romanos I, who was renamed Irene, meaning peace.

About 40 years of peace followed. Freed in the west, the Byzantines under the general John Kourkouas turned against the Abbasid Caliphate. When Nikephoros Phokas refused the tribute in 965, a Rus' invasion of Bulgaria in 968–971 began a war that ended with the Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria in 1018.
byzantine-commonwealth: The term was coined by the 20th-century historian Dimitri Obolensky, whose study The Byzantine Commonwealth is the most important treatment of the idea; in his book Six Byzantine Portraits he examined the lives and works of six people who appear in it. Obolensky described the commonwealth as the international community within the sphere of authority of the Byzantine emperor, bound by the same profession of Orthodox Christianity and accepting the principles of Romano-Byzantine law.

The area it describes is that where Byzantine liturgical and cultural tradition was spread in the Middle Ages by the empire and its missionaries. It covers approximately the present-day countries of Greece, Cyprus, North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro, Romania, Moldova, Ukraine, Belarus, south-western Russia and Georgia, a region also called the Orthodox Civilization or the region of Eastern Orthodoxy in Europe.

Other scholars dispute the idea of Byzantine cultural and ideological supremacy behind the model. They argue that documented cultural exchange was complex and many-sided, and did not fit a picture in which Constantinople was the superior core while the peoples of the periphery accepted a marginal place and merely imitated it. Anthony Kaldellis holds that the Byzantines in general had no ecumenical outlook and did not think of a pan-Orthodox commonwealth, an attitude he describes as Roman chauvinism.

The historian Christian Raffensperger proposed recasting the commonwealth as the Byzantine ideal, a conception of imperial hierarchy that rulers kept even in the empire's later period, when its reach and sway had diminished. The Bulgarian tsars, though often powerful rivals of the Byzantine Empire, framed their authority in Orthodox Roman ideology and artistic style, calling themselves emperors of the Romans as well as tsars of the Bulgarians. The same applied to the Serbian Empire and even to the Ottoman Empire, whose sultan Mehmed II styled himself Qayser-i Rûm.
byzantine-conquest-of-bulgaria: Under Emperor Peter I of Bulgaria (927–969) the Magyars raided Bulgaria from 934 and several times crossed it to loot Byzantine Thrace. In 965 Peter agreed to give them free passage to the Byzantine Empire, and the Byzantines answered by refusing the annual tribute they paid to Bulgaria. Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas then paid the Kievan prince Sviatoslav to attack. The Rus' invaded Dobruja in the spring of 968 and seized more than 80 fortresses, but Sviatoslav's own ambitions soon turned towards Constantinople.

Emperor John I Tzimiskes defeated the Rus' and their Bulgarian allies at Arcadiopolis in 970 and took Preslav on 5 April 971, capturing Tsar Boris II and his family. Boris was made to abdicate in Constantinople and surrender the golden crown and red boots of his office, and his brother Roman was castrated so that the dynasty would die out. The lands west of the Iskar river, with most of Macedonia and Albania, remained Bulgarian under the four Cometopuli brothers, David, Moses, Aron and Samuel, who went on the offensive in 976.

Samuel, soon sole ruler, routed Basil II at the Gates of Trajan in 986, expanded into Thessaly and Epirus and was proclaimed emperor in 997. The tide turned when Nikephoros Ouranos defeated him at the Spercheios river, and from 1001 Basil took back Preslav and Pliska and besieged Vidin for eight months. At Kleidion on 29 July 1014 the Bulgarian army was crushed; some medieval historians say about 15,000 prisoners were blinded, a number historians doubt, since Bulgaria fought on for four more years. Samuel died in October, his son Gavril Radomir was killed by his cousin Ivan Vladislav, and after Ivan Vladislav fell at Dyrrachion in February 1018 the commander Krakras and the other Bulgarian leaders surrendered.

The conquest restored Byzantine control over the whole Balkan Peninsula for the first time since the Slavic invasions of the 7th century, and Bulgaria stayed subject to Byzantium until 1185. Basil accepted taxes in kind rather than coin, and many of the Bulgarian elite were given military or civil posts and assimilated into Byzantine society. Greek clergy took over the see of Ohrid and tried to replace the Bulgarian Slavic liturgy with the Greek one.
byzantine-iconoclasm: By the sixth century Christian worship included a belief in the intercession of saints and the use of relics and holy images. Iconoclasm drew on the biblical commandment against graven images, which iconoclasts read as forbidding the making and veneration of icons. Traditional explanations point to Islamic prohibitions of images, but newer studies find that the spread of iconoclasm did not depend on distance from the Arab frontier. A large submarine volcanic eruption in the Aegean in the summer of 726 was probably a precursor, and many, probably including Emperor Leo III the Isaurian, took it as divine judgment on the use of images.

The classic account says that between 726 and 730 Leo III ordered an image of Christ over the Chalke Gate of the Great Palace removed and replaced with a cross, and that some of those assigned to the task were killed by iconodules. He apparently forbade the veneration of images in an edict of 730, which did not apply to the emperor's image or the cross. Germanos I, the iconophile Patriarch of Constantinople, resigned or was deposed.

Leo's son Constantine V, who ruled from 741 to 775, was personally committed to the ban and in 754 summoned the Council of Hieria, where 338 bishops declared the painting of holy figures blasphemous. Neither Orthodox nor Catholic tradition now accepts its claim to be the Seventh Ecumenical Council, since no patriarch or representative of one was present. Leo V the Armenian began a second period in 815, after Byzantine defeats by the Bulgarian khan Krum, and a synod in Hagia Sophia in 815 made iconoclasm official again.

John of Damascus, who lived in Muslim territory, and Theodore the Studite, abbot of the Stoudios monastery, were the chief opponents of iconoclasm. John held that he worshipped the creator of matter, not matter, and the iconophiles argued that the incarnation allowed Christ to be depicted. The period greatly reduced the Byzantine art that survives from before it.

The Papacy supported images throughout. Pope Gregory III excommunicated iconoclasts, and in 754 the emperor seized papal properties in Sicily, Calabria and Illyria, while Pope Stephen II made an alliance with the Frankish Kingdom. The controversy ended the so-called Byzantine Papacy and widened the gap between Byzantine and Carolingian traditions.
byzantine-ottoman-wars: After the Nicaean Empire retook Constantinople from the Latin Empire in 1261, the Byzantine Empire remained insecure in Europe, with rival powers in Epirus, Serbia and Bulgaria. To hold Thrace, Michael VIII Palaiologos withdrew troops from Anatolia, where the decline of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum let warriors known as ghazis set up fiefdoms at Byzantine expense.

His heavy taxation of the Anatolian peasantry led some to support the Turks, whose system initially demanded less. Among the beys, Osman I held the territory that threatened Constantinople most. Within 90 years of his founding the Ottoman beylik the Byzantines lost all of Anatolia, and by 1400 Byzantine Thrace was lost too.

A Byzantine relief army was defeated at Pelekanos on 10 June 1329, and Nicaea surrendered in 1331. Nicomedia fell in 1337, and in 1338 Orhan took Skoutarion, within sight of Constantinople. A civil war from 1341, won by John Cantacuzenus in February 1347, left Macedonia in ruins and much of it in the hands of the new Serbian Empire. The Ottomans took Gallipoli in 1354 and thereby reached the European mainland.

By 1371 Byzantium was reduced to a few places besides Constantinople and recognised itself as a vassal of the sultan, which it remained until 1394. The Ottomans took Sofia in 1385 and Niš the next year, and the Serbs became vassals after the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. Philadelphia, the last Byzantine hold in Anatolia, fell in 1390.

Bayezid besieged Constantinople in 1394 after Manuel II refused him tribute, and a crusade under Sigismund was routed at Nicopolis in 1396. Timur's defeat of Bayezid at Ankara in 1402 brought a respite, and the Byzantines regained Thessalonika and much of the Peloponnese. Mehmed II closed the Bosporus with fortifications and began the assault on Constantinople on 6 April 1453, and the city fell with almost no help from the West beyond a few soldiers from Venice and Genoa.

The conflicts formally ended with the loss of Constantinople in 1453, though several Byzantine holdouts lasted until 1479. The fall shocked the papacy, which called a crusade; only Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, responded, on conditions, and when Pope Pius II set out to lead one himself, his death in 1464 ended it at Ancona. Historians give several reasons for the Ottoman success.

The Byzantines were held back by Latin threats and by civil strife during the years 1341–1371, while the Ottomans treated conquered rulers as vassals and exacted tribute in money and children, and their raiding and later settlement won Anatolian peasants over. Martin Luther at first saw the Turks as God's punishment, then in 1529 urged that they be fought by secular rulers. The arrival of Greek scholars in Europe is regarded as one factor in the Renaissance.
byzantine-sasanian-war-of-602-628: The previous war ended in 591, when Emperor Maurice helped the exiled Sasanian prince Khosrow, the future Khosrow II, regain his throne from the usurper Bahram Chobin. In return the Sasanians ceded parts of northeastern Mesopotamia, much of Persian Armenia and Caucasian Iberia, and the Byzantines no longer had to pay tribute. In 602 Maurice was murdered by his rival Phocas. Narses, governor of Mesopotamia, rebelled and seized Edessa, then asked Khosrow for help. Khosrow, who called Maurice his friend and father-in-law, used the murder as an excuse to attack.

A Byzantine army was defeated near Dara, and the fortress fell in 605. In 608 Heraclius the Elder, Exarch of Africa, revolted against Phocas. The Persians took Edessa in 610, and Damascus, Apamea and Emesa in 613. They and their Jewish allies took Jerusalem after a three-week siege in 614, where ancient sources claim 57,000 or 66,500 people were killed and 35,000 deported to Persia, among them the Patriarch Zacharias.

In 618 Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt, mostly untouched by war for three centuries. Alexandria fell after a year-long siege, and the free grain ration in Constantinople was abolished that year. Persian forces also took Chalcedon and Ancyra and, by 622 or 623, Rhodes and other Aegean islands.

Heraclius, the rebel's son and now emperor, reorganised the empire and debased its coinage. In 624 he marched through Armenia into the Persian heartland and destroyed the Zoroastrian fire temple at Takht-i-Suleiman. In 626 the Persians at Chalcedon and the Avars attacked Constantinople together, but Byzantine control of the Bosporus kept them apart and the attack failed. Allied with the Western Turkic Khaganate, Heraclius invaded Iran in September 627. After the Battle of Nineveh no Persian army remained to oppose him.

Heraclius entered Constantinople in triumph, and the True Cross was raised in the Hagia Sophia on 14 September 629. Persia fell into dynastic turmoil: Kavadh II died within months of taking the throne, and Ardashir III, Shahrbaraz and Khosrow's daughters Purandokht and Azarmidokht followed within months of each other. Only when Yazdgerd III came to the throne in 632 was there stability, too late to save the Sasanian kingdom. Both empires were left crippled by the war and by a century of almost continuous conflict, and both were vulnerable when the Rashidun Caliphate emerged in the 630s.
byzantine-seljuk-wars: After the death of Basil II imperial authority weakened. The military aristocracy, enriched by earlier wars, sought to absorb the free peasantry, and officials curbed it by dismissing generals and cutting the thematic levies, leaving the empire dependent on unreliable mercenaries. John Skylitzes, Kekaumenos and Michael Attaleiates blamed Constantine IX for dismissing 50,000 standing troops in Armenia just as the Seljuk raids began. Rebellions such as those of George Maniakes, Leo Tornikios and Isaac Komnenos drew the armies away from the frontiers. The Seljuks, who had overthrown the Ghaznavids in Persia and taken Baghdad in 1055, first met the Byzantines at the Battle of Kapetron on 18 September 1048.

Under Alp Arslan the Turks sacked Ani, Caesarea, Iconium and other cities, and defeated Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert on 26 August 1071. The victory brought few gains at first, but the civil wars that followed let the Seljuks, the Danishmendids and other Turkomans spread across Asia Minor, often invited in as mercenaries by rival claimants. Alexios I Komnenos, emperor from 1081, lost Antioch and Smyrna by 1084, but in 1091 defeated a Seljuk and Pecheneg siege of Constantinople, and in 1094 asked Pope Urban II for help, which led to the Council of Clermont in 1095.

The crusaders took Nicaea, which surrendered to the Byzantines on 19 June 1097, and John Doukas recovered Smyrna, Ephesus, Sardis and much of western Anatolia, but the crusaders kept Antioch, and Iconium became the capital of the Sultanate of Rum. John II Komnenos retook the southern coast and Kastamonu, but not Iconium. Manuel I Komnenos made the sultan Kilij Arslan II a client, until a dispute over Sebastea led to the ambush of his army of about 30,000 at Myriokephalon.

The battle itself was tactically indecisive, and John Vatatzes later beat a Turkish army in the Meander valley, but no further Byzantine reconquest followed, and after Manuel's death in 1180 the Turks pressed further west. The Seljuk Empire collapsed in 1194, leaving only Rum, which the Mongols broke into the Anatolian beyliks by the 1260s. As the Turks gained ground, much of Anatolia's population converted to Islam through Sufi activity. From the vacuum left by Rum rose Osman I, whose Ottomans would take Constantinople on 29 May 1453.
byzantion: The origin of the name is unknown. It has been suggested to be Thracian, perhaps from the personal name Byzas, which means he-goat. Greek legend names Byzas as the leader of the Megarian colonists and founder of the city. The city was mainly a trading city because it stood at the only entrance to the Black Sea, and it later conquered Chalcedon across the Bosphorus. Its position, surrounded by water on almost all sides, made it highly defensible.

Tradition says Byzas of Megara founded the city after sailing northeast across the Aegean. The date is usually given as 667 BCE on the authority of Herodotus. Constantine the Great favoured that dating and marked the city's 1,000th anniversary between 333 and 334. The Persian Empire took the city at the time of Darius I's Scythian campaign in 513 BCE. In the Peloponnesian War Sparta took it in 411 BCE to cut off grain supplies to Athens, and the Athenians retook it in 408 BCE.

After the city sided with Pescennius Niger against Septimius Severus, Roman forces besieged it and badly damaged it in 196 CE. Severus rebuilt it, and it soon regained its prosperity. In 330 CE Constantine I refounded it as an imperial residence modelled on Rome, known as Nova Roma and later as Constantinople. For centuries it was the capital of the Byzantine Empire. The Ottoman Turks conquered it on 29 May 1453.

The name Byzantium was used for the Eastern Roman Empire as a whole only from 1555, when the historian Hieronymus Wolf introduced it. Its inhabitants continued to call their state the empire of the Romans. From the 9th century the names Byzantius and Byzantinus were applied to the empire's gold coinage, which gave the English words besant, byzant and bezant.
byzas: Byzas is the traditional founder of Byzantium, the city later known as New Rome and Constantinople. Later Byzantine authors recorded several versions of the founding myth, and the fullest survives in the Patria of Constantinople by the 6th-century writer Hesychius of Miletus. His preferred account derives the city's name from Io, daughter of the Argive king Inachus, who was loved by Zeus and turned into a cow, and who gave birth in Thrace to Ceroessa, the mother of Byzas by Poseidon.

The Patria also records other traditions. One holds that the Argives founded the city after an oracle at Delphi concerning the Golden Horn. Another says that the founders were Megarians led by Byzas, and a third makes Byzas the son of a local nymph, Semystra.

In the 7th century BCE the Greek city-states were founding colonies, and the Dorian city of Megara was seeking a site for one. After consulting the oracle at Delphi, the Megarian king Nisos sent his son Byzas to find the land opposite the city of the blind. At the point where the Sea of Marmara meets the Bosporus, Byzas saw that a colony, Chalcedon, had already been founded on the Asian shore. He concluded that Chalcedon was the city of the blind, since it had not taken the better site on the European shore.

He chose the European shore at the southern end of the Bosporus and named the settlement Byzantion. He later married Phidalea, daughter of King Barbizos or Babisios of Thrace. The inhabitants of ancient Byzantion considered Byzas their founder, and according to ancient sources raised a statue of Byzas and Phidalea in a prominent place in the city.

The ancients understood the advantages that Byzantion had over Chalcedon, since it commanded the entrance to two seas, the Black Sea through the Bosporus and the Aegean through the Sea of Marmara, called the Propontis in antiquity. The story of the oracle is told by the geographer Strabo and the historian Tacitus. Herodotus gives another version of the saying about blind people: when the Persian general Megabazus arrived at Byzantium, he called the people of Chalcedon blind because, though they had a choice of sites, they chose the worst one.
